The Hard Situation of the Jewish Bakers in Zagłębie

Apart from all sorts of regulations and ordinances which the guild law lays down for all artisans, there hovers before the eyes of every baker yet another, special spectre, namely: the mechanisation of the bakeries.
For ten years now various ordinances and "okólniki" [circulars] have been appearing about the fitting-out of bakeries, shops with baked goods, and the manufacture of flour products. With his last efforts the Jewish baker always strove to adapt himself to all the harsh regulations, and almost incessantly paid large fines because of the incorrect interpretation, by the local police organs, of the ministerial ordinances, which contained a series of unclear regulations or outright contradictions, and which by all accounts were not suited to the economic conditions in the country.
On 29 October 1929 there came out the latest and hardest ordinance of the Minister of the Interior, in agreement with the Minister of Trade (Dz. Ust. 78, poz. 582), on supervision over the manufacture of flour and flour products. This ordinance has in fact been binding since 24 November 1929. After 31 December 1930 the competent authority will proceed officially to carry out all the regulations provided for in the said law.
So: first, no bakeries will be permitted to be located in cellar rooms. Bakeries located in places where there is a water-supply system and sewerage installation may be opened only in such premises as are connected with the water supply and the sewerage. In places where electric power is available, the bakeries must possess appropriate machinery for sifting the flour and for mixing and kneading the dough. It is thus clear that new bakeries will arise in the said places only on condition that they are mechanised. As for the bakeries that existed on 24 November 1929, the mechanisation deadline will be set for them in each separate case by the voivodeship, depending on the local sanitary and economic conditions. At the latest, however, this must happen by 31 December 1933.
The Zagłębie municipal offices [magistrates] got in ahead and, as long as 2 weeks ago, sent all the local bakers letters of reminder that on 31 December 1930 (i.e. last Wednesday) the deadline for mechanising the bakeries expires, in connection with the above-mentioned ordinance of 29 October 1929... The delegation of Jewish bakers from Zagłębie was told at the Kielce voivodeship office that the deadline of 31 December 1930 will not be prolonged (although under the said ordinance the voivode has the right to extend the deadline in particular cases by a further 3 years). When the long-term credits for artisans were distributed by the Powiatowa Kasa Komunalna [District Communal Savings Bank], the bakers received no credits, as an element that supposedly operates with ready cash. Nor do they benefit from any other state credits or investment loans; meanwhile the tax burden on the bakers has been screwed up enormously, earnings are minimal, and for building and mechanising bakeries very large funds indeed are needed. The question arises: where is the impoverished baker to take it from? And even if the voivode, Mr. Paciorkowski, complies with the just wishes of our bakers, i.e. extends the deadline by the 3 years — is there really any prospect that the majority of bakers will be in a position to rebuild their bakeries?!
Thousands of bakers will lose their workshops, tens of thousands of bakery workers will swell the ranks of the unemployed — does that lie in the interest of the state?
We therefore hold that a mighty appeal must be raised throughout the country by the bakers' guilds and the trade unions of bakery workers to the authoritative factors in the government, that the ordinance of 29 October 1929 be properly amended and corrected. We have nothing against the very matter of mechanising the bakery workshops; we hold, however, that this is a matter requiring decades of preparation, and that the hard economic conditions now prevailing in the country, and especially the hard situation of the average baker or confectioner, in no way make possible a literal compliance with even only a part of the ministerial regulations.
What needs to be done right now is:
1) The ordinance on closing the non-mechanised bakeries must be withdrawn, and instead a commission of the "Wojewódzki Urząd Zdrowia" [Voivodeship Health Office] must inspect all the bakeries and only then issue deadlines for making good the various defects.
2) All bakeries that meet all the hygienic-sanitary regulations should be allowed to exist without mechanisation.
3) Every baker individually must at once submit a properly reasoned petition to the voivodeship, through the mediation of the starostwo [district office], that the deadline be extended for him until 31 December 1933.
A. Gancwajch.

Visit of Minister Składkowski.
This week the Minister of the Interior, Składkowski, stayed in Upper Silesia.
The minister, accompanied by the voivode and the starostas, visited several places where excesses took place before the Sejm elections, which found an echo in the German government's note to the League of Nations.
Important German documents lost.
The German Consul General in Katowice reported to the police in Königshütte [Królewska Huta] that, while travelling a few days ago by car from the Polish-German border through Königshütte, a briefcase was lost which contained documents of the German consulate.
Brawl between Hitlerites and Socialists.
In Racibórz [Ratibor] a meeting of Socialists took place. In the middle of the meeting a group of Hitlerites came in and a brawl began.
Only when revolver shots from the Socialists' side were heard in the hall did the Hitlerites withdraw.

The rare creature has been handed over to the agricultural [“Wirtschafts”] school.

Demonstration of the unemployed.
On Monday a rally of the unemployed took place in the “Tivoli”[?] hall in Katowice.
At the rally a delegation to the voivode was elected. Because the voivode refused to receive the delegation, in the course of Tuesday a larger number of unemployed gathered in the streets.
In front of the voivodeship office a large crowd assembled, which was soon dispersed by the police. The crowd shouted as it went: “For [list] Number One you told us to vote”.
Reinforced police patrols marched through the streets and did not allow any street demonstrations.
Later the delegation was received by the voivode, who accepted a memorandum.

From Katowice we have received a letter in which we read:
Moshe Apelbaum, the great artist, is lying in hospital in a most terrible state of suffering. The man is simply broken down; nothing is left of him but skin and bones.

An open letter to the rabbinate and to the kehilla representatives in Będzin

[Będzin — community; open letter.] Esteemed Editors!
We, the undersigned, ask you to give space to the following letter:
It is quite true that the Zagłębie region has been reckoned from time immemorial a smuggling region — that is, of raisins, almonds, oranges and old clothes — but not for smuggling ritual slaughterers; for we have learned that some dozors [kehilla board members], with the rabbinate at their head, actually want to smuggle in a little shochet 23 years old — on the pretext that a poultry slaughterer is needed. In the first place a question arises: why do the gmina [kehilla] and the rabbinate not take on as shochet R' Yechezkel'i[?] Wajcman, to whom the local shechita is due by inheritance, since his father R' Mordechai of blessed memory and his grandfather R' Itshe Meir of blessed memory were expert and renowned slaughterers here; moreover he holds certificates [kabbalot] from the greatest geonim of Poland and also from the local rabbinate; he has a letter signed by several hundred respected and honoured householders, who turn to the rabbinate asking that he be taken on as shochet, on account of his right of inheritance and also because he is in a critical situation. The Rabbi of Zduńska Wola[?], shlita, has also turned to the local Rabbi, shlita, on the same matter, making clear that R' Yechezkel Wajcman has the right of the firstborn and the right of precedence to the local shechita. The rabbinate, however, seeks various illegal means and stratagems to frighten the butchers, and to say such words as the local Rabbi, shlita, [said]: "Dear children, since you will not give in to me by fair means, you will have to give in to me by foul." The tactic of the existing regime[?] is no good, and [we ask] at the soonest[?] whether it befits Będzin [to have] a smuggled-in 23-year-old shochet who has no idea and is only going to learn [the trade]. We also know that a deputation of Aleksander Hasidim turned to the local Rabbi, shlita, [asking] why R' Mordechai the shochet's son should be robbed of his inheritance of the shechita — and he answered them that this time he must oblige the Ger Hasidim. We ask: is the town of Będzin really a free-for-all [hefker-petrushka]? We appeal energetically to our kehilla representatives, headed by the president R' Yekl Gutman [Jakub Gutman], that a general meeting be called together with the rabbinate; we too want to be present, and[?] we too shall see where the truth lies. In no case will we allow a smuggled-in shochet. Should it turn out that Będzin needs a 5th shochet, R' Mordechai the shochet's son must be considered first of all. — It is not at all fitting for a kehilla like Będzin, a mother-city in Israel, to receive such a lesson from a rabbinate. We pay heavy thousands of złoty in salaries every year, and we declare publicly that in no case will it be allowed to smuggle in a little shochet for a bribe [łapówka][?]; rather, the claim of R' Yechezkel, may his light shine, son of R' Mordechai the shochet-and-examiner of blessed memory, must be properly supported, for he has the right of precedence[?] and is without a livelihood, may it not befall us.
We hope that the entire Jewish population will react to this as it should, and will not by its deeds cause, God forbid, the breaking of a Jewish home, and will not tear the bread away from the little children. Remember! It is a matter of saving lives!
A group of non-party
Hasidim and householders.

The Power of Useful Institutions

[Article — tenants' associations; Będzin.] (What is happening with our "tenants' associations" [lokatorn-fareynen]? — Do they have a right to exist? — Ought we to foster them?)
Only a few weeks ago, when the question of raising rents began to be stirred up, we pointed out in this place the necessity of the existing tenants' associations in Poland, and we came to the conclusion that although many citizens think this institution is not needed, it is nevertheless one of the most necessary, one of the most urgent. Just as one must[?] be armed so as to have something to defend oneself with in case of a catastrophe, in exactly the same way we need the existence of the tenants' associations at the time when there is a danger that the tenants' rights are about to be curtailed.
And indeed we saw that as soon as a hail of protests began to pour in from every corner of the country, those "in the high windows" evidently took fright, and the question was at once removed from the agenda. True, we are sure that this was done only for the time being, so that it should not look too drastic, and that in reality what was planned will be carried out; yet we see nevertheless that it counts for a great deal that the people stand on guard, and that with the help of the proper institutions the interests of the people, the interests of the citizens, the interests of the broad strata of the population are protected.
And who does not know how much we must be on guard that dwellings and business premises should not be made dearer in the present critical time in Poland! And one must not forget that the greatest number of citizens live in cramped, noisy[?] holes not only because enlarging one's dwelling must cost a tidy sum, but because it also comes into consideration that the rent [tsinzh, czynsz][?] will amount to more every month; this is reckoned with very, very much in the present bitter time in Poland. That, then, is the best proof of how great a role the crisis plays in the country: that although there is a shortage of dwellings, they are nevertheless not snapped up, and many of the relatively average citizens conduct both their businesses and their private dwellings in conditions almost impossible for twentieth-century Europe.
It would seem that this is a sufficient motive not to raise the rent; nevertheless none of this is seen among us — and who knows, perhaps people do not want to see it, for otherwise one cannot imagine it: that, taking no account of the grave critical situation, they still insist, steel and iron, that dwellings must be made dearer, and that from the increase a capital of such-and-such will be saved up, which will be earmarked to help build new houses — so that it will turn out that with the help of poor men's pennies new buildings are to be put up, which will supposedly solve the grave housing shortage.
We have always known that as long as there are not enough vacant houses as before the war, and things do not reach the stage where one could free oneself from tenant protection, so long we must not dissolve these institutions; and not only must we not dissolve them, we must guard them like the eye in one's head. That is as plain as two times two is four. We have, after all, had occasion[?] to see it now, when amendments were put forward that are calculated to make the tenants' affairs harder. If the tenants' associations no longer existed today, who would have come forward with the protests from all sides of Poland? It goes without saying that individuals — it is not they who go and protest, not they who would have protested, and nobody would have taken account of individuals, of single persons, whoever and whatever they might be and whatever they might express in their protests. It is, after all, an old rule that private persons are never reckoned with, whereas the collective is looked upon with different eyes, and willy-nilly one has to reckon with the public.
But how backward we still are here, how far we are still from being mature, may be shown by the fact that we read in our newspaper on Friday a week ago that the Będzin Tenants' Association intends to carry out a poll [ankete] which is to pronounce on whether the association should exist or be liquidated. Well, is that comprehensible? Can the human mind grasp it? Does it not look like the Thousand and One Nights? Can the liquidation of a tenants' association not be compared to doing away with a well-prospering business? Would that not look abnormal[?], incomprehensible, inconceivable? Do such incomprehensible things occur among citizens with a well-run economy? Would such absurdities happen among nations whose economy is well ordered — absurdities that could in a single moment bring to nothing what only just now was a first-class necessity? Can one really come today and pose the question whether the institution, which stands in the midst of its current everyday work, should actually be on the point of being liquidated? If people here were well educated in the social sense, such questions would of course not have floated up into the light of day, just as we cannot imagine liquidating a business that is going well. And if, on the other hand, people come and say that the Będzin Tenants' Association is not active as it should be, that it is barely alive, that it stands on chicken legs — all that is no sign whatever that it has to be cleared out of the way, that it is a hindrance to anybody, that it is a kind of stumbling-block. Since the institution is needed, since the public, the broad masses of the population, have need of it, one must then breathe into it a fresh spirit of life, a kind of ruach-chayim [breath of life], and see to it that it takes its proper place in our economic life.
But to clear away an institution only because people take no interest in it means not understanding the interests of the people, not understanding the social necessities to which the people ought to be bound and knotted together. To treat economic and social questions so superficially and so much by rote means not being versed in them and not knowing what role they must play in our everyday economic life — something one must not forgive oneself, seeing that they have been brought to this sad state.
———
The fault is this: that notwithstanding the fact that the people are still so little mature in the social sphere, they nevertheless have too many institutions, and in the flood of all these associations they cannot find their bearings and know how to distinguish what we need to have and which institutions we have no need of.
The social institutions, whether economic or of another type, must be properly grasped and understood by the people, and for those which the people need, all means and possibilities must be applied — not merely to keep them going on artificial foundations, which at the same time undermines their true existence, but really to see to it that a firm basis is created for them, a secure, sound and healthy foundation.
As long as the housing question in Poland is not solved, as long as one may fear evictions [eksmisje], so long the tenants' associations here must not be dissolved[?]. Energy must be applied in order to put the said institutions on a proper footing; the tenants' associations must, without any excuse, be strengthened and fostered, and they must have as many members as possible, so that they may have the power to speak in the name of the whole community, in the name of all existing tenants.
R. Les.
My Sylvester Delight

By Y. Oberzhanek.
Jews, do you perhaps know of anyone who needs a flat? A fine flat, a flat with „wygody“ [conveniences], with every virtue: high, bright and dry, and on top of that one more great virtue: a landlord who is no „davar-acher“ [swine].
You think, perhaps, that I want to change my dwelling on account of the rent? That I have, God forbid, an „eksmisja“ [eviction order]? Wrong again. My landlord, you should know, is not a pre-war „gospodarz“ [landlord], and is no „członek“ [member] of the House-Owners' Association... He does not even have a „rządca“ [house manager] who would want to show that he is a good „thrower“ [thrower-out of tenants]...
Well then, why do I want to exchange my „wygodne“ [comfortable] dwelling? For a small flat, on the third, even on the fourth floor?
It is indeed a hard question, but believe me, gentlemen, that I, Harsh Machel, am perfectly in the right. I can no longer stay in my big flat, I must get out, and right away; I must change my dwelling — on account of Sylvester.
What has the flat to do with Sylvester? What sort of „semichut ha-parshiyot“ [link between the passages], you ask, is there between my fleeing the flat and Sylvester? Oh, there is a connection, a very strong connection indeed!
I have a wife, Brandl Leah is her name. From the name „Brandl Leah“ you can already understand that this is a woman who does not think much of „and he shall rule over her“. Brandl Leah is a woman who hates talking; she speaks more with her eyes than with her mouth. One look with an eye, and that is enough for the blood to freeze[?] in me.
But that is not the main thing. As you say: „the ‚pik‘[?] gets used to the hammer-blow“, and I too have already got used to the blow [„shlak“]. Ah, listen, have I got a „shlak“ [a blow; also: a plague of a wife]! You have a wife too, after all, and presumably she too is a „shlak“, but how does your „shlak“ compare with my „shlak“. If a „shlak“-prize is ever instituted, my Brandl Leah will certainly get it.
Well, the whole year round one manages somehow, not to speak of summertime, when Brandl Leah „smaży się“ [fries herself] in the sun; then I know that I am a „mężczyzna“ [a man]...
But when winter arrives, when the „holy“ Sylvester approaches, my skin trembles on me when I remember that every Saturday night I shall have to drag myself around, with my arthritic feet and my rheumatic knees, whole nights long from one tavern to another, that I shall have to stand like a lackey and kiss the women's hands, that every Sunday I shall have to lie whole days dead tired like a slaughtered beast. Is that a business — dragging myself around the halls with my broken bones and having dealings with „maseczki“ [little masks]? That is a business for a gang of young folk, lads with girls, and for wives with faces like a horrible death, who behind the „firanka“ [curtain, i.e. veil/mask] also pass for goods.. But I — how do I come to this swindle?
But when a wife wants, and especially a wife who goes by the kosher name of Brandl Leah — do arguments help at all? When Brandl Leah says: Harsh Mordechai, throw yourself into the black tailcoat, you shlimazl of mine, put on the stiff „noodle-board“ [starched shirt-front] with the tight patent-leather shoes — no excuses whatsoever help. Do I have a choice, having been blessed with a wife called Brandl Leah?
So it went year in, year out; every winter I lived through hard times. The carnival made me grey and old; after every carnival I felt broken and crippled, and if I now suffer from rheumatism and arthritis, if perhaps I have caught something on the left lung, I owe all that to my Brandl Leah's carnivals.
This year, as Sylvester drew near, I went about like a dead man. First, my sick rheumatic knees — I am barely alive as it is! That is one thing; and secondly: it is after all somehow „lav maot bras“[?] [no money], this year is after all not what it once was. Where is one to get the bit of „drobne“ [small change] for my Brandl Leah? And on top of all the troubles she is after all a woman with a broad sweep; she is not „drobnostkowa“ [petty], she does not belong to the „mężatki“ [married women] who „nabierają“ [take in, fleece] men; on the contrary: the men fleece her. Why should she begrudge them [„żałować“]? After all she has a husband, may he live to a hundred...
When the few days before Sylvester came, Brandl Leah speaks up: Machele. And when my Brandl Leah calls me by the tender name „Machele“, I go cold and hot; I understand that something more is coming here.
— Machele, do you know what has occurred to me?
— Wh...a...t, wh...a..at — my teeth chattered one against the other — what is it that has occurred to you, Brandl Leah, long may you live?
— I mean, she went on, regarding this year's Sylvester.
When I heard „Sylvester“ I began to shudder as in a heavy fever. Before my eyes I saw the black tailcoat with the stiff noodle-board, with the pointed wing collar, and everything began to swim before my eyes.
— I know, after all, she went on, there is a crisis nowadays, you torment yourself over money, it is a pity to throw money away on the masked balls, one must live with reckoning.
— Health upon your head! — I fell upon her — Bradeshi[?] [Brandl dear], my clever one, you are an angel, you have put a new soul into me! I felt that a heavy load had dropped from my head. A trifle?! To sleep at home for a winter, a whole winter without looking at the noodle-board before my eyes — a delight!
— But do you know what must be done? I shall make a „swojskie kółko“ [a homely circle of our own]. Why give money away for tickets? We have a „wygodne“ flat, so we shall „zapraszać“ [invite] a few „swojskie“ people [our own sort]; I shall invite my „przyjaciółki“ [lady friends], our Saltshele and Baltshele will invite their „kolegas“ [pals], and we shall „bawić się“ [amuse ourselves] the while; everyone will bring something along — one a little bottle, another „zakąski“ [snacks] — we shall set up the gramophone, get hold of a few new hits, and enough.
The „skromna propozycja“ [modest proposal] did not even please me at first — a masquerade in the house; but later I thought it over: anything is better than in the „sale“ [halls]. First of all, I shall after all have the option of not putting on the tailcoat with the tight „lakierki“ [patent-leather shoes].
Last Wednesday I come home for dinner — who can get in? A commotion, a tumult, cooking and frying. The rooms emptied out, my Brandl Leah stands rubbing[?] the „podłoga“ [floor] with stearin candles so that it should be smooth for dancing; bustle, hullabaloo, they are preparing for the great Sylvester celebration...
In the evening a whole „chaliastre“ [gang] began to pour in: old wives and young „panienki“ [misses], „faceci“ [fellows] in tailcoats with their white shirts on show; the scents of the perfumes choked me in the throat, the smell of the lipstick turned in my nose; my Brandl Leah was the chief hostess, and fussed around the women and the tailcoated, white-shirted fellows.
And the night? Oh, that night I shall remember as long as I live. The patephone jangled, the gang slid about[?] on the floor, shouts and screams — and in the midst of it all I get a piece of „sufit“ [ceiling] on the head, and soon afterwards pieces of ceiling began to rain down. What is this? What has happened? The neighbour who lives on the second floor also has a wife who thinks about „tachlis“ [practical purpose]. She too had arranged a „swojska“ [homely] Sylvester „bibka“ [party], and from above the pieces of ceiling are falling on me.
Jews, do you perhaps know of a room with a kitchen? I must flee from my „wygodne“ [comfortable] flat.
The German Economy in the Year 1930

If the signs reported by the economic policy-makers are correct, the past year, 1930, will be recorded in economic history as the worst in the course of the last fifty years.
Statistical figures are a thermometer of the rise or the decline of a nation: if the nation can export its products, it is a sign that the country is healthy and will develop. If the country lags behind in its production and cannot compete on the world market, it is a sign that the nation still stands low in its products.
This process of development or decline shows itself most conspicuously in the crisis years, when the world market in general can absorb little and buys the little it needs only from the most highly developed countries.
In the hardest crisis year, 1930, it turned out that Germany has the best and most developed industry in the whole world. Despite the severe crisis that Germany had to go through this year inside the country itself, the export of most products held at the old level and in part even increased.
The statistical figures that have just come out show that in the wide world sales are beginning to pick up a little, and it was precisely the last months, with their stronger turnover, that brought about an improvement in Germany's economy. Certainly the years 1928 and 1929 were better than the last year; but if one compares the normal year 1927 with the year 1930, the last year shows a larger turnover.
The International Labour Office in Geneva declared at its last session that, owing to the simplification of working methods in all branches of industry throughout the world, German trade has grown from the year 1925 until now by 45 percent. In all countries a shortage has been felt of machines, apparatus, electrical materials, building materials and the like, and it appears that Germany is precisely the one most capable of supplying all the machines and materials mentioned.
Of all technical articles Germany exported in the hard crisis year 1930 exactly as much as a year before. Of machines Germany exported more in the last year than in the year 1927. After America, Germany is now the largest exporter of machines in the whole world. Germany supplies many, many more machines than England, and has raised its export of machines by 92 percent.
Germany manufactures machines worth about five milliard marks a year; of these, machines worth one and a half million marks [sic] are exported to the four corners of the world.
It is interesting that all the industries which regularly exhibit at the Leipzig Fair did well with their exports in the last year too; the severe economic crisis in the whole world was not capable even of weakening business at the Leipzig Fair. The German electrical industry, for example, which always comes to the Leipzig fair, covered in the last year more than a third of the entire electro-technical demand of the whole world. America and England stand far below Germany. In the year 1929 Germany covered only 25 percent of the world's electrical demand. In the year 1930 Germany exported about nine million marks [sic] more of electrical materials than in the previous years. The research office in Germany stated expressly that the electrical industry owes its good business in the last year solely to the Leipzig Fair.
Apparatus, instruments, typewriters and precision mechanics, which always exhibit at the Leipzig fair, were exported in the last year only five percent less than in 1929. The large countries, such as America, France, Italy and Holland, obtained thirty percent more of these articles from Germany this year than a year ago. Only smaller countries bought almost nothing this year.
The German automobile industry fell back sharply in the last year. The industry had its greatest export in 1928, when it had a large exhibition of its products at the fair in Leipzig.
The porcelain industry suffered most this year. In 1930 it was able to export only 65 percent of what it exported in 1929. The chemical industry too fell back by 19 percent. Of course one must not forget that in Germany there are bankruptcies almost every hour. In the year 1929 Germany lost three quarters of a milliard marks to bankrupts, and in the year 1930 the sum will be greater still. — In the last year about 50 thousand people emigrated from Germany, forty thousand of them to America.
The textile branch too had a severe crisis; of artificial silk, on which great hopes had been placed, about 195 million kilos less were manufactured in the last year than a year before.
The figures of the German import trade are also worth a glance. Here too we see a sharp decrease compared with last year.
In the year 1930 about 600,000 tons less iron ore were brought into Germany than in the year 1929. Raw wool, too, came in during the last year by about 46 thousand tons less than a year before.
The building industry received a heavy blow this year. Of paving stones only 12 percent of last year's amount were manufactured this year. In the last month 275 thousand tons less cement were sold than a year before in the same period; in the whole world 40 percent less sheet metal is now being manufactured than a year ago.
This decrease in building materials is explained by the fact that today one builds quite differently than before. Iron and steel now play the greatest role in building, and whoever casts a glance at the great Technical Fair and Building Fair, which will be held in Leipzig from 1 to 11 March 1931 (the General Fair only from 1 to 7 March 1931), can see how the whole system of production has changed in all fields of our daily life.
Z. Haber.
Happy Holiday, Happy New Year!

[Feuilleton.] By “Argus”.
Happy holiday, happy New Year!
Yesterday we all grew a year older. The day before yesterday[?] in the evening[?] — still a year younger, and half a night later — already a year older.

One need not envy the girls who yesterday were still 17 years old and have suddenly become eighteen-year-old grown-ups, ready-made marriageable girls. The girls — well, girls; but their fathers are certainly not to be envied — only now will their heads begin to split, and not in jest.

— Well, what do you say, Mendl? Our Hanka is already 18, may she be healthy. So what is to be? Have you given it any thought yet?

Of course he has thought! He had even reckoned on writing a special letter to his brother in America. But there is a trouble with the stock-exchange crash, for it is, after all, a case of either way: if the brother had shares, then he has become a poor man; if he had no shares, then he was a poor man; one way or another, the American brother is now a weak prop.

And Mendl, first thing in the morning, let out the first groan of the new year...

*

Our institutions have it good. Once the balance sheet is closed, one can begin to “sin” on the new account[?]. It goes without saying that the balance sheets show deficits. Where have you ever seen an institution without a deficit? Why, it is simply a disgrace!

For what does one create an institution for? First of all, to make use of the manpower, the creative energy that seethes in every person and especially in the gabbaim of societies.

*

Our newspaper, too, has grown a year older today. Last Friday it still said “twentieth year” [“tsvantsigster yorgang”], and today it already says “twenty-first year”.
But a newspaper is not a girl; it does not grow old.

And precisely in its twentieth year it has only just begun to romp about with a fresh, youthful fire! With whom has it not quarrelled this year? Whom has it not provoked? On the contrary, just cast a glance: is there a single party, a single institution, a single social stratum with which it has not tussled? Nothing pleases it; it wants to begin everything from Genesis, and precisely with its own mud[?] [“koyt”]...
No, a newspaper does not grow older, just like... a people..

*

Here we are, the Jews, the oldest people in the world and — the youngest. Of all the peoples that exist in the world, we are the first who, back in Joshua’s times, took a little corner under the sky in order to have a home for ourselves. And now, already after the World War, when even Lithuania and Latvia sit in their nests, we must still jingle the white-and-blue collection box in order to buy a dunam of land.

And we knock[?]... And we are younger than the youngest. No people has pioneers [halutzim], and we do. And our halutzim are, after all, already old men; we also have a “Shomer”, and because it is already too old, we also have a “Shomer Hatzair” [“Young Guard”].

Oh, we are young, very young; we have even only just begun to learn to speak... truly little children..
A people does not grow old.
Argus.
Napoleon's Last Years of His Life

[Serialized historical narrative.] By M. Osherowitch [M. Aszerowicz]. 3.
Then Napoleon set to work on the second plan with more energy, and he carried it through successfully. On the 11th of March, in the year 1810 (a few months after he had divorced Joséphine), he married Princess Marie Louise, the daughter of the Austrian king Franz the First.
Marie Louise was twenty-two years younger than he. He was then 41 years old and she — nineteen. In addition she was to his taste — a blonde, and for Napoleon that was very important.
Within the year she bore him a son, and because of this he was the happiest man in the whole world. He distanced himself from all his mistresses, and even Countess Maria Walewska he no longer wanted to see, although even then he still loved her very much.
His happiness, however, did not last long. Circumstances entangled him in wars once again, and after the great victory he had in Russia in the year 1812, capturing Moscow, toward which he had long been straining, things began to go very badly for him. The vastness[?] of Russia, the Russian frosts and the Russian steppes were worse for him than the great Russian armies; he had to retreat, a beaten man, from a great victory, and later he began to suffer one defeat greater than the other.
Had he once and for all made up his mind that he was a crowned emperor just like others, his end might perhaps not have been such a sad one; but he held that, because he was not a “born monarch”, he must never remain standing in one place and must always climb higher and higher. “Only they — he used to say — can afford such a thing as losing a war; but I, myself a son of fate, not one anointed by God, cannot afford such a thing; I must always win my wars.”
But he could no longer win any wars, because if earlier, as General Napoleon Bonaparte, he had conquered countries as the liberator of peoples, as the commander of the revolutionary armies, as a son of the revolution that had put an end to the rule of tyrants, now he himself was a tyrant, whose rule the other peoples did not want to take upon themselves.
Even in France he was already regarded as a tyrant, and when the united rulers of Europe, among whom was also Napoleon's father-in-law, the Austrian king Franz, set out their armies against him, people in France looked upon them as “liberators”.
The fact that his wife's father, too, had joined his enemies and set out an army against him pained him greatly and made still stronger his enmity, his hatred of the “born monarchs”. He said then: among those who were born to sit on a throne there is not a single one who has a human heart. King Franz will not yield a hair's breadth for the sake of the interests of his daughter and his grandson. All the born monarchs have no blood in their veins, only frozen politics.
On the 6th of April, in the year 1814, the united powers, after the great victory they had won over the French army, forced Napoleon to renounce the throne, and then they banished him to the Italian island of Elba, which lies in the Mediterranean Sea.
They were certain that they were now entirely rid of him, and they placed on the throne one of the deposed Bourbon dynasty — Ludwig [Louis] the 18th. But Napoleon could not sit quietly on the island of Elba and reconcile himself to his career being over. Moreover he was greatly disturbed by what he had heard: that his wife Marie-Louise, who was now in Austria with his child, had struck up a love affair with a certain Count Neipperg and was living with him openly and freely; and that his child, his only legitimate child, dearer to him than anything in the world, was being brought up as an Austrian prince. All of this together agitated him so much that he could no longer sit still on the island of Elba, and on the 26th of February, 1815, he escaped from there. On the way, in a remarkably ingenious and successful manner, he gathered an army of several thousand men, and on the 20th of March he entered Paris and again took over power as Emperor of France. Louis the 18th fled in fear even before Napoleon had come back into Paris...
Fear fell once more upon the born monarchs, and under the pretext that they must settle accounts with Napoleon because he was the greatest obstacle to peace in Europe, they again waged a war against him. The war lasted several months, and after Napoleon lost his last battle at Waterloo, he was forced to renounce the throne again, and afterwards he was banished to the English island of “Saint Helena”.
On the 17th of October, 1815, he was locked away on the island; torn from the whole world and deceived by his second wife, toward whom he had earlier behaved so well and so nobly, he ended his last years lonely and forlorn. On the 5th of May, 1821, he died on the forsaken island at the age of 52.

Security in the Land of Israel

By V. Jabotinsky.

1. "Protected Jews" [Schutzjuden].

The greatest mistake was committed by the Zionists in allowing the dissolution of the Jewish battalions in the Land of Israel. In the years 1918–19 there were already 5000 Jewish soldiers stationed there. In the spring of 1920 — only 400 soldiers. At the beginning of 1921 they too were demobilized, and thus the Zionists fell back into the role of the "Schutzjuden" (protected Jews) of old Germany.

The position of the "Schutzjuden" looked like this: a prince or a count would permit a certain number of Jews to settle in his residence, taking upon himself the obligation to protect them from attacks on the part of the mob. Through this, however, his Jews lost the last trace of human rights. And this was understandable, because every attempt on the part of the mob to get rid of the Jews forced the prince to mobilize his Landsknechte, among whom there were often casualties as well, in dead and wounded. It goes without saying that with a certain right he could demand everything of his Jews and forbid them everything, with the simple excuse that if they did not fulfil his demands it might come to an uprising on the part of the mob. If the prince was, in addition, a cunning diplomat, he would himself invent the danger of popular unrest; often it was enough for some priest or other to stage a bit of tumult as a portent of popular revolt, in order to give the prince the opportunity to extort from his "protégés" whatever his heart desired.

That is, in a much stronger form still, the exact picture of our situation in Eretz Israel. We are colonizing the country against the will of the native population, whose number is six times greater than ours; therefore our colonization can develop only under the protection of an armed force, just as every colonization has developed from time immemorial. The difference is that in other colonizing enterprises the armed force is raised by the colonizing people, whereas in the Land of Israel the protection lies not in our hands but in the hands of the English military, which consists of soldiers and officers of foreign nations. At the slightest sign of a "popular will" directed against the Jews (danger of a pogrom), the duty falls on these soldiers to intervene actively; if victims fall here among the English soldiers, casualty lists will be published in England with names like "Peter Robinson" and "John Smith," and so on. Should these soldiers one day be compelled to fire on the mob — a task which for an intelligent soldier is more unpleasant than risking his life — then this unpleasant duty, too, will have to be carried out by a "Robinson" and a "Smith." And it is precisely in this circumstance that the root of our tragedy lies. The author of these lines has no intention of defending Sir H. Samuel or the Zionist Organization — had the actions of the two factors just mentioned always been purposeful and strong, then certainly many impermissible things would not have occurred in the Land of Israel; but at best it would have gone no further than the removal of a certain lawlessness, because it is impossible to create such favourable conditions as would serve as the prerequisite for a larger colonization so long as we play in the Land of Israel the role of the "protected," whose protection has been taken over by English, Irish and Indian soldiers. Soon after the pogrom in Jaffa — May 1921 — Sir H. Samuel received many inquiries from the Yishuv and from friends in England. All posed the question: how is one to explain the unexpected compliance toward the Arabs? On the basis of precise knowledge of the material I can state that in all the replies Sir H. Samuel gave to the inquiries and protests the conclusion was: "A firm policy would be possible only if, in case of need, we could be prepared to make full use of the British garrison; that would certainly not have been popular in England, quite apart from the question of whether such tactics would be desirable." The same argument — but in the form of a threat — runs like a red thread through all the interventions of the Arab delegation that were made in London at that time. In their rendering this argument is expressed roughly thus: "If you (the English) do not want to remove the Jews, we shall be forced to carry it out by our own means, and then you will have to deploy your military against us, which will certainly involve casualties for us and for you; therefore consider whether.." These arguments come out even more plainly in the English newspapers that belong to the said tendency. And yet in November 1917 the whole English press greeted the Balfour Declaration with sincere enthusiasm. The gradual transition of the more important press organs to anti-Zionism is a very instructive process. Looking through the newspaper clippings of that time, one can recognize the essence of the matter from the headlines alone: "Zionism can be bought only at the price of the blood of British soldiers." "Because of the Jews we must maintain an enormously large garrison in Eretz Israel," "Let the Jews themselves, with money and with men, pay for Zionism."

Under these headlines the same argumentation is always hidden: "England is exhausted by the war and no longer wants to send her sons to their death, nor even to send them to kill other people; were it not for the quarrel with the Arabs over Zionism everything would be quiet, and one could then manage in Palestine with a very small garrison. If one wants to reduce the garrison, one must remove all the things that irritate the Arab, because if the great uprising with which the Arab delegations constantly threaten should really break out and, as a result, English victims should fall, it will arouse in England a general wrath against the government that allowed such a crisis to come about." The saddest thing about it is that this argumentation is not an invented one; it is something natural and unavoidable. Therefore its results are unavoidable too. This expressed itself first of all in a Land-of-Israel garrison reduced to the point of impotence. In the year 1921 there were 15,000 British soldiers stationed in Eretz Israel; in 1925, together with the Irish gendarmerie, there were no longer even 3000. The question truly arises whether such a force would have been able to maintain order in the country if the Arabs should one day feel the urge to stage a larger action...

That is why the administration, out of its desire to secure quiet, indeed adopted the most convenient path: to remove everything that provokes the native population. Jewish immigration, which is so disagreeable to the Arab, must be reduced by direct and indirect means. There may even occur from time to time an immigration boom ("hausse"), but it need last only until the first "successful" demonstration of force on the part of the Arabs. In this respect all illusions are pointless. This is an iron law of every colonization. A people that wants to be protected by the soldiers of a foreign nation cannot even dream of true colonization. The limits of how far immigration may go are then dictated by the natives. Any threat on the part of the native population will always suffice for the order-keeping administration to close "the gates" of immigration.
Beware of Girlfriends! (From the Local Tales)

[Feuilleton — from the local tales.]
Who is base, false and deceitful[?]? — The men.
Who is subtle, fine, noble and modest? — The women.
Try saying otherwise, and you are the worst person in the world.
But all the facts, all the events of life, are exactly the reverse. They tell that the dearer and closer two women are to each other, the falser they are to one another; the more mutual kisses — the more each would like to trip the other up. Not to mention when a matter arises with a "he", when a male friend mixes in between two girlfriends — ah, then beware the cat-like little claws of such a one; envy, hatred and intrigue eat them up altogether[?], and there is nothing such a girlfriend is not ready to do to her "best friend".
The women themselves know this very well, and when a girl is clever, the first thing she does when she wants to be sure of her "sympathy" [sweetheart] is to distance herself from her girlfriends — the farther away, the healthier. There are, however, women who show off their beloveds, fiancés or husbands and make a point of having their girlfriends know him, so that it should... gall them. Such a one sometimes comes off very badly...
It is still worse when a woman really is noble and fine, loves her fiancé or husband, and also faithfully trusts her friend. Such a one finds out later that she has been nastily deceived.
Such a victim is also Mrs. A., who came yesterday on a confidential visit to the editorial office and asked for advice.
Twelve years ago she became engaged, took a young man, a very decent one, and married; the couple love each other very much, they have two children, and a livelihood too. In a word, she could have lived in peace with her husband and children — but she had a... girlfriend, from her earliest youth, from Hasidic circles. That one also took a bridegroom and married. The two girlfriends did not break off their friendship, which has now lasted over 15 years. Lately, however, she found out that for about 6 years already her girlfriend has been coming up to the house not so much to her as to her husband. Under various pretexts her husband used to disappear for whole evenings and spend them with her friend. The wife is certain that her husband is in fact the less guilty one here.
Guilty here is only her girlfriend, the little wife, who does not stop pressing[?] herself upon her husband and exploits all sorts of opportunities to be alone with him, eye to eye, and to tear him away from his wife and children. The husband of this fine little wife knows about it, but he is a milksop and is afraid to say a word to her, lest she scratch his eyes out.
The wife made no scenes for her husband, but tried with kindness and love to convince him that his step was a wrong one. The husband sensed that his wife already knew everything, and he confessed to her, literally begging to be freed [as printed: "her"] from that snake; but the little wife drew him ever more to herself, and now he has left his wife and children.
———
The woman thus poured out her heart, described what painful suffering that girlfriend is causing her whole household, and asked for advice on how to act.
We advised her to stop playing hide-and-seek and to talk it out openly[?] in the presence of all three. The milksop husband of the fine Hasidic little wife need not necessarily be there; one can manage without such a one. We are sure that such a frank talk will, in a good way, put an end to the quiet family tragedy of refined people. At the same time, however, we decided to describe the story, so that other naive women should know when one must keep one's distance even from the best girlfriend.

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Vayechi

[The "Oneg Shabbat" column — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Parshat Vayechi.]
a) אל נא תקברני במצרים ["Pray do not bury me in Egypt"] (47:29)
According to the Midrash, the reason Jacob did not want to be buried anywhere but in the Land of Israel was gilgul mechilot [the rolling of the dead through underground tunnels], so that after death he would not have to roll his way to the Land of Israel.
An old Jew came to the Kotzker Rebbe to take his leave, because he was travelling to the Land of Israel. The Rebbe, R' Mendele, asks him: what are you going to the Land of Israel for? He answers: why, our father Jacob wanted to be buried in the Land of Israel on account of gilgul mechilot.
The old Kotzker fixes a pair of eyes on him:
— You love the body so dearly that you worry it might, God forbid, have to exert itself even after death?..
—o—
b) ויברכם ביום ההוא ["And he blessed them that day"] (48:20)
ויברכם — he blessed them — ביום ההוא ["that day"]: that they should live with the present day, that they should not worry about the day of tomorrow... (Kol Simcha.)
—o—
c) באחרית הימים ["In the end of days"] (49:1)
Of the times of the Messiah the Gemara (Sotah) says: „פני הדור כפני הכלב“ ["the face of the generation is like the face of a dog"]. What is the sense of the expression?
Of the times of the Messiah it is said that poverty will reign (תכלה פרוטה מן הכיס — "the last penny will be gone from the purse") and insolence („חוצפה יסגי“ — "insolence will increase"). A dog, too, is the most insolent animal („הכלבים עזי נפש“ — "the dogs are greedy") and the poorest („לית עניא מכלבא“ — "none is poorer than a dog")... (Rav Yaakov Emden.)
פני הדור כפני הכלב.
Of the times of the Messiah it is said: „הגפן תתן פריה והיין ביוקר“ — the vine will give its fruit, and wine will be dear. Where, then, will the wine go?
„בעקבותא דמשיחא חוצפא יסגי“ ["on the heels of the Messiah insolence will increase"], and if insolence — there will be many who hold themselves to be rabbis and rebbes, of whom it is said: „הרוצה לנסך יין על גבי מזבח ימלא גרונם יין“ ["he who wishes to pour a wine libation on the altar, let him fill their throats with wine"] — that it is a mitzvah to treat them to wine. Well, with as many "Torah scholars" as there will be then, and at their "tishn" [rebbes' tables], so much wine will be consumed that wine will be dear... (The[?] Rav, R' Yeshayele Prager [of Praga].)
—o—
d) בכורי אתה ["You are my firstborn"] (49:3)
One who is a firstborn of his mother and not of his father the Gemara (Bava Batra 126) calls בכור שוטה, a "fool firstborn" — because such a firstborn must give the kohen the five sela'im, but he takes no double inheritance; and since he gives and does not take, he is a fool... (Glosses of Yaavetz.)
—o—
e) כי באפם הרגו איש ["For in their anger they slew a man"] (49:6)
„באפם“ — "with their nose": with one turn of the nose one sometimes kills a person... (Folk saying.)
—o—
f) ארור אפם כי עז ועברתם כי קשתה ["Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel"] (49:7)
What does it mean to curse anger?
A rich man, a mighty one, if he is angry about something, can permit himself to carry out his wrath. The poor man, on the other hand, must choke his anger down inside himself, because he has not the power to bring it from potential into act.
That is what a curse upon anger means: that it should be stifled in the subconscious[?]... for it was said of them that they would be „עניים וסופרים בישראל“ ["paupers and scribes in Israel"], and so they will in any case choke on their anger... (Ohel Yaakov.)
—o—
g) אחלקם ביעקב ואפיצם בישראל ["I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel"] (ibid.)
I will distribute the anger among all of them, and each will come out with a small share... „אחלקם“ — I will divide the anger up... (Peh Kadosh.)
—o—
h) וירא מנוחה כי טוב ויט שכמו לסבול ["He saw that rest was good... and bowed his shoulder to bear"] (49:15)
If „ויט שכמו לסבול“, if one bears everything as it is — one has rest, peace. (Rabbi S. B. [Simcha Bunim] of Pshischa.)
* * *
If you want it as it is — then it is as you want it; if you do not want it as it is — then it is not as you want it... (R' Aharon Karliner.)
—o—
i) דן ידין עמו כאחד שבטי ישראל ["Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel"] (49:16)
„דן“ ["judges"] — the Jew who constantly examines himself and makes a reckoning of his soul — for him עמו ["his people"], even the humblest Jew, even one of the common folk („עמך“), is as important as the head of a tribe... (Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin.)
The Two-Faced Ally

[Article — British policy and the colonies; background to the "White Paper".]
(On the development of the English colonies).
On the small island in the north of Europe, in the thick fog of the North Sea, there developed through a long historical process a people whose destiny was to become the strongest and greatest people on earth and to create the leading state in Europe. England — through her "splendid isolation" — stood throughout all of history far from all the evolutionary and revolutionary upheavals that Europe lived through. Through her own development and an external policy of conquest[?], which gave her a whole chain of colonies with which she girdled the world, she consistently forged her hegemony.
Today's British Empire comprises, apart from the European part — the metropolis — a whole series of fragments (colonies), which are bound to it by various constitutions, customs and so on. England thus does not possess one single constitution that would uniformly regulate the connection with the metropolis; all the same, it is hard to define the legal situation of the English Empire.
There was a time when the colonies — which constitute states in themselves, since they fulfil the three conditions for founding a state (territory, inhabitants[?], sovereign power) — were entirely subject to England and dependent on her in every field. With time, however, came national consciousness, and the urge for freedom grew ever stronger, and this was bound to yield political results. The first thing the colonies demanded and won was that the trade conventions which England concludes with various states concerning her colonies must have their consent. From there it is only one step to the stage at which the colonies may, without the participation of the metropolis, themselves conclude conventions and contracts. And now, by the force of evolution, comes the further development: the colony, as a legally equal contracting party, sends out its own delegates to international conferences, who (unlike the first delegations) no longer form any part of the English representation. All the concessions the colonies had conquered entitled them to ever bolder demands. But when they began to demand for themselves a deciding voice in political questions — England saw that the foundations on which her regime rests were becoming unsure and falling apart. And if England could not agree to that, because it would have meant the loss of the colonies, the World War came to the rescue, in which they saw what worth they had. And indeed the Covenant of the "League of Nations" admitted as members also colonies that govern themselves. In this way six colonies obtained representation in the League of Nations.
England's conduct is characteristic. On the one hand she wanted to maintain[?] the dependence of the colonies, and on the other to bring them into the League of Nations with a deciding vote, in order to dispose of a greater number of votes. Did the refined English diplomacy not foresee that the colonies would, in that "parliament of states" — as indeed happened — come out against England?
In the whole period of the consistent emancipation of the fragments, the conference of the year 1926 had a revolutionary significance. It broke with the supremacy, the hegemony of England, and recognized the equality between England and the colonies; with their governments the English government must reckon. And although the second conference, in the year 1930, apart from economic problems did not touch the political ones, it is clear that they will surface with greater force, and then some colonies will be able to free themselves entirely. All the same, England must in her foreign policy reckon[?] strongly with the situation in the colonies. And so the issuing of the "White Paper" was dictated by the necessity of the English interest. The national uprising in India, the threatened[?] situation, have forced England to seek allies in other colonies; for we must remember that the English people's sense of justice is one thing, and the cold, logical state interests of the English Empire are something else. The latest declaration of the English government thus springs from the temporary, changeable[?] political conjuncture.
From the historical road on which the colonies wage their struggle for emancipation and freedom we see that the future of the English realm is heavily clouded, and the time must come when the government will have need of other declarations, of "coloured books".
Eliahu Gertner.
On the Question of Our Children's Education

[Article — Hebrew education; the "Tarbut" network and preparations for a school in Będzin.]
In the day-to-day tumult of the hard struggle in which the Jewish community in Poland — both the individual and the collective — wrestles for its minimal needs in life; in the vale of tears of want and poverty, into which the broadest strata of the Jewish masses are sinking ever deeper; in the terrible spiritual desert in which broad strata of our youth wander about — there stands, like an oasis in a desert, the Hebrew school system, and it wages a heroic struggle for the rescue of the Jewish soul, of our coming generation, for the education of the new Jewish generation, both in the national and in the secular sense; hard, very hard is the road of the entire Jewish renaissance, which finds its true expression in the revival of the Hebrew language and culture in general and of the Hebrew school in particular, which has enormous obstacles to combat.
Hard, very hard, as has been said, is the road of the Hebrew "Tarbut" school, which must maintain itself from its own funds, which are taken in through tuition fees, subventions from the local "Tarbut" organizations and through the subsidies of the kehillot and town councils. Yes, the struggle is hard, but it is waged day in, day out with success; instinctively the Jewish masses feel that the Hebrew elementary school fulfils both the national needs and the secular needs, and they help the "Tarbut" organization in its hard struggle.
At the present day the number of "Tarbut" elementary schools already reaches 180, gymnasia — 14, Froebel schools [kindergartens] — 78, altogether 272 school institutions with 35,000 boy and girl pupils, who are educated by a camp of over 1000 teachers; besides this, a quite long series of Hebrew evening courses for adults with 12 thousand listeners. At the centre of the widely ramified school system of "Tarbut" stand the central institutions, which direct the entire pedagogical work, 5 seminaries, which train the proper teacher and kindergarten teachers.
It is worth noting that, despite the severe want and poverty in which the Jewish community in Poland as a whole lives, the schools are nevertheless maintained with tremendous self-sacrifice by the activists of "Tarbut" and with readiness for sacrifice on the part of the teaching body, which must often go hungry; and yet they stand firm, and with courage and energy it continues the sacred work in the school and even moves[?] society to still greater exertions, in order to secure the existence of the school. 32 schools already possess their own buildings today; this shows how deeply the "Tarbut" school has struck roots in Jewish life and how viable the "Tarbut" school is.
The fate of the entire Hebrew school network, however, depends chiefly on the seminaries, which constitute the nerve[?] of the Hebrew school system; for only thanks to the trained teacher from the "Tarbut" seminary with a five-year course has it proved possible to set the "Tarbut" school on the proper level, both in the national sense, and in the secular sense, and in the programmatic[?] sense, and in the methodological sense.
Thanks to the seminaries the "Tarbut" school does not ossify in the accepted pedagogical routine, and the teacher is occupied day in, day out with the problems put forward — how to improve the pedagogical work, so that the school may truly give the radical answer to the life-questions of our child as a Jew and as a human being. Therefore Jewish society does indeed respond to the call of "Tarbut" to rescue these very seminaries from the catastrophic situation that has been created owing to the ceasing support of the "Joint", which is altogether discontinuing its entire relief work in Poland. The warm[?] attitude of Jewish society, and first of all of the Zionist camp, awakens courage and energy to broaden the Hebrew school network in Zagłębie as well. The broad[?] "Tarbut" school in Zagłębie has already opened in Zawiercie, and now the necessary preparations must be made for a "Tarbut" school in Będzin, where there are all the prospects for the needed development of such a Jewish school institution. It is to be hoped that Będzin's Jewish society will help the Central Committee of "Tarbut" to lay in Będzin a sound foundation for a "Tarbut" school, which guarantees the future of our children as Jews and as human beings and the pride and joy of our parents, and at the same time serves as an honour and pride of our people.
A. Einstein.
(Inspector of the Hebrew school system "Tarbut" in Poland).
The Machine

(Heard from an unemployed man and given over word for word)
By Pini Baal-Loshn.
I am standing on Piłsudski Street [Będzin] watching a big machine that stands by the tunnel[?], humming and droning with thick steel voices, and every little while it stretches out a long, clumsy steel paw, digs itself deep into the soft yellow earth, crawls back out full, lifts the crumbled earth and throws it into lorries that stand ready to cart the earth away.
Hundreds of people stand and contemplate the wonder of the giant machine, how it alone does the work of hundreds of shovels.
People marvel and admire: the wisdom of man, who thinks up such machines time and again!
I too stand and contemplate the progress of our times. That is how the machine digs out the earth, the machine lays the foundation, the machine does everything, and man merely directs it!
Suddenly there springs up beside me a character — tall, gaunt, gloomy, just as if all the troubles of the world lay upon his face — and he calls out to the crowd around him:
— Oh yes, you stand there and beam with delight at the wonders of science, eh?... You greatly enjoy the business of living in such a clever world, eh?... No small thing — a world with machines!
Cattle is what you are, horses in the shape of human beings is what you are; you don't even begin to know what is being done to you.
Your Angel of Death is standing before your eyes and you do not see him; he is sharpening his sword for you and you know nothing!
If all of you here had the same sense that I have, all of us, just as we stand here, ought to gather our strength and courage and hurl ourselves at this machine and smash it and break it into little bits, so that not one whole limb of it should remain.
And after that really set off from factory to factory and everywhere break the big and small machines without mercy, until no remnant or survivor, not a scrap of a trace of a machine should be left!..
— Why are you looking at me like that? Why are you goggling your eyes so? You probably think I am mad, eh?
Though it really is a wonder. For a father of six small children, with the seventh too about to arrive in the world any day now, when one has been going about idle [shling un shlang] for nearly a year without a bit of work, and has already pawned everything from the house[?] and already sold off down to the last shirt on one's back, and the wife is ill and at home it is cold and damp and dark and there is nothing to get through the day with — one can indeed go out of one's mind, of course one can; but as if for spite I still have all my wits about me and understand perhaps even more than is needed, and I have had some schooling too — and what I am saying now I mean with my whole heart...
Do you think that only this machine here is a digging-machine [grob-mashin]? All machines are "digging-machines" [a pun: grobn — to dig, bagrobn — to bury], and they will bury our poor workers so deep that we shall no longer rise even at the Resurrection of the Dead!...
And I tell you that it would be well for the world if one fine morning people got together and made a revolution against the machine with all its wonders.
And it will have to come to that — the millions of empty stomachs and the millions of idle hands will bring it about.
For these machines have torn the last morsel out of the mouth; they have put the whole world-machine out of order.
There, where people once worked and earned, the machine came and tore his work out of his hands and threw the man himself out into the street, made an idle labourer of him...
This machine-golem goes about and lays a world waste, and there is no one to stop it.
And so it is with all machines, from the oldest to the newest machine. The sewing-machine drove out the tailors, the shoemaking-machine drove out the shoemakers, the ploughing-machine pushed out[?] the workers of the land, and so on and so forth — is it even possible to count it all up?
Thousands of steel golems have been created, and they take every bit of work away from man, and they tear the last piece of bread out of man's mouth.
And what can the end of this be? What indeed will people do? Where will they turn?
Do we not now see, all over the world, more and more unemployed all the time? Millions of people go about in every country and have nothing by which to earn a piece of bread, and even in rich America the unemployed are already counted in the big millions. The steel muscles compete with the muscles of flesh — and steel is the victor!
Why, it is a horror, a dread — just imagine a humanity that will go about idle, empty and loafing, with nothing to do!
If at least it had already come to the point where foodstuffs too could be drawn by machines from the earth or from the air, it would not be so terrible. But for the time being one still has to buy food in the shops for hard cash, and where is one to get it from?
Do you know what hunger means? Do you know what it means to sit for weeks on end without a piece of bread? Do you know what it means to find at home a famished mother with six famished children?
And here people stand and beam with delight at the machine!
They admire the "wisdom" of man, who keeps thinking up other machines; the world is becoming cleverer, more enlightened!
What use is this cleverness, if all it does is dig a pit for humanity? If it invents such demons for us?
Do you think it can go on like this, that the world can go on existing like this? — Not a chance!
Would to God, do you hear[?], that I be proved a liar; but look, you see this very machine — it is the symbol of the Angel of Death with the thousands of eyes and the sharp swords, who runs about over the whole world from end to end and slaughters people like this, little by little — a steel Angel of Death!...
———
The crowd forgot about the machine. They surrounded the speaking character and listened to his words.
The circle around him grew bigger and bigger, until the passage in the street was blocked.
A policeman came up, dispersed the crowd and drove away the speaking character, so that he should not disturb the order.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin. Tenants in Favour of the Continued Existence of the Tenants' Association.

[Będzin — housing/associations.] [Date line at the head of the page: Friday, 13 Tevet 5691 — Piątek, 2 stycznia 1931. Section banner: “What's New in Zagłębie?”; sub-heading: Będzin.]
On Sunday a general meeting of the Tenants' Association took place in its own premises.
The meeting is opened by Mr. S.(?) Lewin, who hands the chair over to Mr. S.(?) Landau.
Reports on the activity up to now and on the continued existence are delivered by Messrs. Lewin, Landau and the jurist(?) [“Rechtsmann”] Kozłowski. It turns out that the deficit of 1300 zł. still stems from the time when the collector Goliński went away, taking with him almost the same sum.
The main(?) discussion was whether the association should be liquidated or continue to exist. The majority, however, declared that the association must exist, especially at the present time, when a new danger is hovering over the tenants.
A committee of 5 persons was elected, who are to strengthen the existence of the association.
Będzin Gets a “Share” of the Olkusz County.

[Będzin — administration.] In connection with the new plan to reduce the number of starostwos (county offices) in the country, the abolition of the Olkusz starostwo is also on the agenda.
The county (powiat) is to be divided among the Będzin, Zawiercie and Miechów counties.
Former City President Michel Against the Building Plans.

[Będzin — municipality.] As we have already written, a session took place in the local magistrate (city hall) at which a series of building plans was approved, to be carried out in the course of 5 years.
Against the plans the former president Michel(?) has come out with an article in the “K. Z.” [probably Kurier Zachodni], pointing out with figures that, because of the financial situation, the plans cannot be carried out.
Propaganda Campaign of “Maccabi Week”.

[Będzin — sport/Zionism.] (W—ski) “Maccabi Week”, which has been proclaimed by the “Maccabi” World Union, begins on Sunday, 4 January. In connection with it, committees are being set up in every town, headed by Jewish communal activists who until now have had only a very slight connection with sport.
In Będzin “Maccabi Week” will begin on Sunday at 10 in the morning with a march of the “Hakoach” orchestra through the town.
At 11 in the morning a festive “Maccabi” academy (ceremonial assembly) will take place in the “Corso”(?), at which the general secretary of the “Maccabi” World Union, Mr. Ring(?), will appear with a lecture. A lecture will also be given by Dr. Rechtschaft(?) under the title “The Significance of Physical Education among Jews”.
In conclusion there will be gymnastic exercises and a concert performed by the “Hakoach” orchestra.
Don't Give Small Children Toys.

[Będzin — incident.] In the family W.(?) a small child, one year old, was playing with a toy made of tin. While the child was holding the instrument in its mouth, an iron pin fell out, which the child swallowed.
The child was given laxatives and little dumplings (kluski) to eat. This worked, and the pin came out of the bowels.
Lecture on Tuberculosis.
[Będzin — health.] On Sunday in the daytime Dr. Weinzieher gave a lecture in the “Kapitol”(?) under the title “Tuberculosis as a Plague for Society”.
General Meeting of the Charity Association.

[Będzin — community/charity.] Next Sunday, the 4th of this month, at 8 in the evening, the annual general meeting of the Jewish Charity Association (“Dobroczynność”(?)) will take place in the premises of the Jewish community (kehilla). There are important items on the agenda; among them we shall also hear a report from the committee for building the orphanage.
The invited members ought to come and thereby show their interest in so important an institution.
2,000 zł for the benefit of the unemployed.

The local police have donated a sum of 2,000 zł for the benefit of the unemployed in Zagłębie.
The sum will(?) be deducted from the salaries — minimal as they already are — that the police receive.
The starosta is said to be getting a higher post.

As we are informed, the Będzin starosta (county head), Mr. Boksa(?), is to receive the post of voivode (provincial governor) in Białystok.
Mr. Boksa(?) has meanwhile left on a 5-week leave.
Tragic consequences of a wild chase.

On the road from Siewierz to Będzin a fast 'jazda' (ride, i.e. a race)(?) took place between two cyclists and the driver of a lorry. The devil's game(?), however, ended tragically. The lorry struck the cyclists; one fell dead on the spot and the other was severely injured.
The driver of the vehicle, who disappeared after the catastrophe, was arrested in Myszków and handed over to the custody of the investigation office.
From 'Hitachdut'.

In connection with the arrival in Zagłębie of Mr. [—], a member of the Central Committee, an urgent meeting is taking place this evening in the party's own premises.
Lectures will be given by Messrs. Dr. Rechtman(?) and Kohn of Sosnowiec.
Under the wheels of a car.
In Zagórze a car ran over the 13(?)-year-old Ka[—]czyk(?). The boy's right arm was broken.
Over 100 Jewish bakers' families threatened with ruin. Delegation to Kielce and Warsaw.

In connection with the harsh decree on bakers, a Jewish(?) delegation of the Zagłębie Craftsmen's Supreme Council is travelling this coming Sunday to Warsaw and Kielce to intervene, so that the hard and sad situation of more than 100 Jewish bakers in Zagłębie, who are threatened with complete ruin, may be alleviated to some degree.
It is to be hoped that it will succeed in convincing the authoritative circles that the bakers' law, which is not at all suited to our way of life, should be properly amended.
Suicide of engineer Łuczków. After his death he received a post.

On Tuesday morning the news spread through the town that the engineer Łuczków had committed suicide in Mysłowice by throwing himself under a train.
Eng. Łuczków was born in Lemberg (Lwów) and specialised in questions of water supply and sewerage. When the sewerage system was being built by the firm 'Ulen', the local magistrate (city administration) engaged him as an inspector to supervise the work.
When the 'Ulen' work was completed the magistrate dismissed him from the post, and from then on he remained without a position.
Last Monday at 5 in the afternoon Eng. Łuczków left his flat and travelled to Mysłowice, where he bought a platform ticket and went out onto the station. At 6 in the evening the express ('courier') train from Katowice arrived; at the moment the train approached the station Eng. Łuczków threw himself under the train and was killed on the spot.
In his flat a letter was found in which he asks his friends and the magistrate to take an interest in his surviving little daughter, and that she be given the possibility of travelling to Lemberg.
The suicide took his life in the town where his wife lies buried; she died 2 years ago in Mysłowice.
When Eng. Łuczków was no longer alive, a notice arrived from the voivodeship office in Katowice that he was being engaged in the waterworks installations.
Łuczków was 52 years old.

Mr. Klarman opens the meeting, dwelling on the task of the Revisionists at the 17th Congress. Mr. Bielebrow(?) delivers a lengthy speech on the present situation in Zionism. Afterwards the following reports are given: activity of the board — the secretary, Dancer(?); school campaign — Mr. Abramowicz; KKL (Jewish National Fund) — Mr. Fajgrajch(?); press — Mr. Warysławski(?); "Keren Tel Hai" — Mr. Jungster. Mysterious murder in Zagórze

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
On Wednesday the 31-year-old Kania(?) shot dead the 21-year-old Misiar(?). After carrying out the murder, the murderess went to the police station (komisariat), where she stated that she had shot Misiar because he had wanted to commit an act of violence.
