"Commercium"

[Sosnowiec — commerce.]
Under this name several bookkeepers and experts in Sosnowiec have opened an office for bookkeeping and correspondence in all languages.
An office of this kind, which has set itself the task of relieving the merchants who are obliged to keep commercial books, or simply of easing things for them with regard to the tax tangle(?) — is very much wanted(?), and it is no wonder that the "Commercium" office receives several interested parties day after day.
Further details about the office — in the advertisement on page 8.
Dąbrowa: Meeting of the Zionist organisation / A Jewish film / From "Poalei Zion"

[Dąbrowa Górnicza — Zionism, cinema, Poalei Zion.]
Meeting of the Zionist organisation.
On Thursday a general meeting of the Zionist organisation took place with the participation of Mr. Białobrow(?) of Warsaw.
Mr. Tenenbaum opens the meeting, and Mr. Fishl Lenczner is elected chairman.
Around the report — delivered by Mr. Tenenbaum — a discussion develops in which most of the members take part. Among other things, the proposal of Mr. Chaim Pietrkowicz(?) was adopted, to protest against "Moment" [the Warsaw Yiddish daily] for its disgraceful attacks on the person of Deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum.
The following board was elected: Eliezer Tenenbaum, David Kożuch, M. Gotlib, Yechiel Rama(?), Motl Rozenblum, Yitzhak Gajer and Chaim Grajcer.
Audit commission: K. L. Gurfinkiel, Motl ben-Yeshaya(?) Rozenblum and Rozencwajg.
A Jewish film.
At the local cinema "Miraż"(?) a Jewish film entitled "The Latest Events in Eretz Israel" has been showing since Wednesday.
The picture contains moving scenes; especially tragic is the scene of the woman pioneer (chalutza) who fights with utter self-sacrifice against a band(?) of Arabs run wild.
At the end "The Ceremonial Opening of the 'Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin'" is shown.
From "Poalei Zion".
Last Saturday the annual general meeting took place, opened by Mr. Frajlich. Messrs. Treper and Kożuch are elected to the presidium.
The reports on the activity are given by Frajlich and Zygrajch.
After the discussions they proceed to elect a new committee, which Messrs. Treper, Gutman, Frajlich, Zygrajch, Nusbaum, Szywek(?) and Tenenbaum enter.
Up to 30 members took part in the meeting.
Myszków: A "Bikur Cholim" society legalised

[Local/Myszków — institutions and society.]
Last week, in the home of Mr. Chaim Bams(?), under the chairmanship of Dr. Melcer, a meeting was held of the "Bikur Cholim" (Visiting the Sick) society, which has been active for only a few months and has now been legalised by the authorities.
In such a short time the society has already managed to accomplish a great deal, e.g. it bought a "karawan" (wagon), opened a pharmacy of its own and also bought a large number of medical instruments. The balance sheet shows that the expenditure for poor sick people came, in so small a community as Myszków, to 1,494.61 zł. And if the society has been able to accomplish so much in so short a time, the first thanks are due to Dr. S. Melcer together with the feldsher Mr. Ch. Bams(?), who visit the sick and give help without any remuneration. Great merit also belongs to the chairman, Mr. Snopkowski, and the deputy, Shloymele Gajer.
At the meeting a board with an audit commission was elected, which is beginning fresh activity.
A letter to the editor

[Letter to the editor — Będzin, community affairs.]
In the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" no. 52 Messrs. Prawer and Rinski(?) declare that it is proof that I was in favour of engaging a secretary, because I did not vote against his salary. To this I declare the following: if at an earlier session the gentlemen who today have a majority in the kehilla board decided to engage a secretary, I could not at a later session vote against the salary for him. I can be an opponent of taking on new officials in the present times, but I cannot be an opponent of paying a salary to the officials who have been engaged.
It is also not true that I agreed to engaging a shochet (ritual slaughterer). At that consultation I declared explicitly that I am against the gmina (community) now engaging a fifth shochet, even without pay, because there is no need.
Let the public convince itself who is telling the truth.
Respectfully,
H. L. Goldsztajn

Weekly Notes

In Germany bloody clashes broke out between striking coal miners and the police; there are dead and wounded on both sides.
—o—
In Vienna there were scandals and clashes with the Nazis over the screening of Remarque's film “All Quiet on the Western Front”.
—o—
In the town of Horodenka (Galicia) an explosion took place in a mikveh; 14 Jewish women were killed, and the town is in mourning.
—o—
This month the Polish government is receiving a loan of one billion francs from French capitalists.
—o—
Marshal Joffre, who played a great role during the last World War, has died in Paris at the age of 78.
—o—
In England a disaster occurred with an express train; many passengers were killed.
A mother's revenge on her “stubborn and rebellious son”...

In the village of Kszykawce[?] a peasant woman set fire to the little house[?] of her son, who had married a widow from the same village without her consent. The house, and all its contents too, went up in smoke.
The “devoted” mother has been arrested.
A dangerous bandit caught.

The police in Sławków have arrested the well-known bandit Gamszyk[?]; he had been sentenced to 3 years in prison for murdering a policeman in Białystok.
After a year and a half he was released because of his poor state of health. Immediately after his release Giemszyk[?] went back to his “trade”, carrying out a series of robberies, among them one on Parecki's[?] pharmacy in Galange[?].
The job didn't pay off..
Several persons got into the post-office building in Skała. When they broke open the safe, they found[?] no more than 20 zł. 75 groszy.
When you make up in the dark...

In one of the Sosnowiec cinemas the following piquant incident took place the other day:
A smart young man came to the last showing with a young lady; they took seats in a box and were full of joy that they had not missed the showing.
Soon, however, the young lady remembered that in her great haste she had forgotten to paint her eyebrows and lips at home, so she decided to do it at the beginning of the showing, when the hall would go dark.
In the dark, however, the young lady made a fatal mistake: she mixed up the colours, so that she painted her eyebrows red and her lips black...
When the lights came up, the cinema-goers contemplated the strange decoration.. and could not take their eyes off the young lady.
Only a good while later did the young lady look into a mirror and, to her great surprise, notice her fatal mistake. Ashamed, she immediately fled the cinema.
Interestingly, the smart young man who sat with the young lady did not draw her attention to her mistake.
Visit of the “Brit Trumpeldor” commander Mr. Propes.

The Sosnowiec “Brit Trumpeldor” has recently set about conducting intensive work in its ken (branch). For this purpose the chief commander (mefaked rashi) in Poland, Mr. Aharon Propes, visited the Sosnowiec ken on Saturday.
On Saturday night a lecture devoted to the youth question in Zionism took place at the “Hotel Polski”. After Mr. Propes had been welcomed by Mr. Klarman and[?] commander Glidman, he lectured on the Betar ideology, at the same time analysing the ideologies of the other youth organisations in the Zionist movement, which do not serve the pure Zionist ideal.
After the lecture a closed consultation was held on the further work.
Dąbrowa — General meeting of “Maccabi”.

On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of Dr. Rechtman, the annual and also the reorganisation meeting of the local sports club “Maccabi” took place in the premises of the “Craftsmen's Association”.
Dr. Rechtman lectured on the general importance of Jewish sport and its development, and also on the “Maccabi Week”.
For various reasons no reports on the activity of the former[?] board were given, and the meeting proceeded to the most important point: further activity, at which[?] the organisations “Hashomer Hatzair”, “Gordonia” and others spoke. The said parties declared themselves ready to help the important institution, and a resolution was adopted to invite all the organisations of Dąbrowa to cooperate. It was also resolved, on the proposal of Dr. Rechtman, to hold an academy (festive evening) on Saturday the 17th of this month.
Then the following provisional committee was elected: S. Triger, Yechezkel Grosman, Moshe Falnowicer[?], Pruszpranski[?] and S. Rozencwajg[?].
R. Leybish Szpigelman of blessed memory

[Dąbrowa — obituary.] The Jews of Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] were shaken on Friday morning by the sudden death of R. Leybish Szpigelman, may he rest in Eden, who was torn away at the age of 52.
A very large crowd from all strata of the Jewish population took part in the funeral, as well as many non-Jews, who did not stop recounting the praises of the deceased.
Because of the poor state of health of the local rabbi, may he live long, the eulogy for the deceased was delivered by the rabbi's son-in-law.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
—o—
When "in-laws" come back from a wedding.
At the Krupiński family, on Legionów Street [?], a wedding "malbeysh" [?; unclear word] was held. After emptying [?] several bottles, the guests Kiszewski and Szywtek [?] went home. On the way they met a Christian acquaintance, with whom the drunkards began to exchange words; from words they passed to deeds, and the guests "served" their opponent a knife in the side.
—o—
A brawl among "one's own".
Our town is seething over a brawl that took place at a local Jewish rich man's with his children. The brawl broke out over "family quarrels", but they did not hit each other in jest — rather like bloody enemies.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — news.] Silesian autonomy is to be abolished.
The "Noyeste Liyurekht" [?; newspaper name unclear], which appears in Katowice, reports that government circles are planning to abolish the Silesian Voivodeship. The autonomous Silesian Sejm will be turned into a provincial sejmik and with that the autonomy of Silesia will also be annulled.
The report, however, is not credible, because Silesian autonomy is guaranteed by the constitution and by an obligation of Poland towards foreign countries.
—o—
Serious railway disaster.
In Gleiwitz [Gliwice] on Tuesday afternoon the express train Berlin—Beuthen [Bytom] collided with the passenger train Beuthen—Katowice. 15 persons were seriously injured. The stoker was killed. The collision was so strong that the locomotive of the express fell off the railway embankment and was smashed.
—o—
Further dismissals.
The management of the industry in Glushavits [?; perhaps Giszowiec] has notified all officials that from 31 March of this year they will be dismissed from their posts.
Such "glad tidings" were also received by the officials of the general management of Count Henckel von Donnersmarck. Those who get their work back will have to sign an agreement with bad working conditions. But a large number will be dismissed altogether.

Telephone calls abroad.
The Post and Telegraph Directorate in Katowice announces that from yesterday, the 8th, telephone calls are permitted with the United States, Cuba, Canada, Mexico and Australia.

On the Katowice market square a crowd of more than 2 000 unemployed gathered, who wanted to hold an open-air meeting. A detachment of mounted police dispersed the crowd; 14 men were arrested.

The magistrate in Königshütte [Królewska Huta, Chorzów] announces that until the 15th of this month the lists of young men born in 1910 are displayed at the magistrate.

The Katowice magistrate this week opened a second people's kitchen for the poor. In the kitchen one gets a lunch for 10 groszy.

A Sejm session.
Today, Friday, a plenary session of the Upper Silesian Sejm takes place in Katowice. On the agenda there are very important questions to be dealt with.

In today's issue our readers will find the new timetable of the trams running on the line Szopienice—Hajduki.
According to the new timetable a tram runs every 10 minutes from Szopienice to Hajduki and back.

While the champagne was flowing...
On New Year's Eve, when all the "tables" in the cabarets and restaurants were taken, the 24-year-old unemployed Gachlik [?] of Königshütte went off into the nearby forest, where he committed suicide in the following tragic manner:
Gachlik filled his mouth with dynamite, then lit a fuse; when the explosion came, Gachlik's body was completely shattered.

Dear Mr. Editor!
I ask you to give space in your esteemed newspaper to the following letter:
Mr. Frayget [?] Abramski!
Although it is painful for me to touch again on the matter of your expulsion from the party, I, as chairman of the Sosnowiec organisation and as a member of the district committee of "Poale Zion" (united with the Z.S.), consider it necessary to reply to your last letter in the same newspaper under the heading "For Your Attention".

10 Years of the Sick-Fund

(What do the sick-funds in Zagłębie look like? What do we know about them and what is their aim?)
[—] Sick-fund! Well, we know that not long ago in Sosnowiec they celebrated the tenth-year jubilee since the sick-fund was founded.
What more do we know about the institution? We know that it exists and that everyone who employs people pays such-and-such for them, so that in case a person falls ill he should have someone by whom to be cured.
And that is an important thing, certainly it is a great thing, which must absolutely be welcomed. A people's institution, which is intended to heal working people and has existed for 10 years, must without doubt be recognised as a useful and efficient institution.
All that would have been fine, if we knew about it; unfortunately we know about the institution only as much as the street knows, i.e. we know that it is maintained from the people's and the workers' money.
We also know this: that quite often people come into the editorial office to complain about prevailing irregularities, about the negligence of doctors, which ought not to be tolerated. From time to time we describe various wrongs, we ask: how can this be? But apparently the printed Jewish word does not reach those who need to hear about the wrongs, and no explanation is received.
We have also heard many times already that many of the sick-fund's doctors, as soon as they come in to a patient, shout and rage, so [much] that the household with the patient tremble and flutter and apologise to the doctor for having troubled him, and then it makes the impression as if he treats the patient for nothing.
Certainly a people's institution ought not to give such treatment to the working element, which is downcast as it is and at best cannot allow itself to be ill; and when the doctor comes at such a moment and shouts at him, the house certainly remains, certainly, downcast and saddened.
Of course, with such treatment the institution cannot be what it ought to be, what it could have been, what the people would have had the right to demand that it be.
And why then should the institution not adapt itself to the needs of the people? Why should it not be at their disposal and satisfy its members? After all, the people without means do not go there for pleasure's sake or to exploit anyone; they are, after all, partly the maintainers of this useful institution, which was created for the broad strata of the population. And as such it ought, after all, to have reckoned with their demands and necessities.
Unfortunately, however, it is not so; unfortunately the people's institution is far from the people, and we do not notice that it takes an interest in its pained [insured persons'] interests, the way sisters of mercy take an interest in their patients. And that is a wrong, that is not right.
The sick-funds should be merciful homes for their sick members, and it should not look as if the doctor does a favour when he does not shout at his patient. Many of the members quite often refrain from coming there, so afraid are they of this or that doctor.
Nor do we ever see any report from the institution; we do not know what the activity there looks like and what the finances look like. One must, after all, also reckon with the Jewish members, who occupy a quite respectable place in the Będzin district (powiat) — so why should we be stepchildren there? A 10-year jubilee took place in Sosnowiec — why should the Jewish world of Zagłębie not know about it, just like its Christian fellow-members? Why should we be kept at a distance? Are we not obliged to pay the same tariff as the Christian fellow-members? Do they not sell off the Jew's belongings for not paying punctually?
And if we are no better and no worse than all the other members, why should we be reckoned with so little, as if we had taken no part there at all? Why should the Jewish member not know what the institutions look like? How they prosper? What income and expenditure they have? Since this is a people's institution, intended for the working element, surely both the employers and the employees may know about it.
10 years of popular work has great significance, all the more so when it concerns a social institution intended to heal the poorest strata of the suffering population.
And therefore, as long as this institution does not reckon with its Jewish members the same as with the non-Jewish ones, for so long we cannot recognise it as a people's institution in the true sense of the word.
By no means whatsoever can we understand that a sick-fund institution should distinguish one nationality from the other. True, there are doctors there both Jewish and Christian, and yet it is noticeable that we are reckoned with very little — if only because the Jewish member never sees before his eyes any balance sheet, any report of accounts; he does not even know what rights he has with respect to the sick-fund and what rights the sick-fund has towards its members. We know only this: that one must register everyone with the sick-fund, and that one must pay such-and-such for him, and if one does not pay, they come and sell off the belongings.
That is what we know about the institution; that is all we can imagine about the sick-fund. And if until now we were told nothing, then at least at a tenth-year jubilee they could have come to the Jew and told him in Yiddish what this sick-fund actually is, what it has accomplished during the 10 years, what its endeavour is and what it aims at, what it has done until now and what it intends to do in the "near past" [sic; read: near future].
It would not have mattered — in honour of the 10 years the management could have allowed itself such a luxury.
Surely the Jewish member may know what the sick-fund actually is, which costs him enough money.
Selekt.
Little Feuilleton. Two Groszy.

[Satirical feuilleton — the price of matches and the tax.]
A packet of matches used to cost 8 gr. [groszy], and now it will cost 10 groszy. What difference does it make?
And for the state it means a fresh 18 million for the budget.
I was truly glad. Perhaps now they will spare us the raising of the "dire-gelt" [the apartment tax]!
Nevertheless, on second thought: two groszy don't walk on foot either; in a taxi[?] they certainly don't ride, but on foot they don't go either.
Look — when I had two groszy change left over from a packet of matches, I used to give them away to a poor man. Now there will be nothing left for the poor man.
And when the wife used to buy a whole ten of matches, she would have twenty groszy left from a gulden [złoty], and she would buy a newspaper and read the serial novel.
Now she won't buy a newspaper and won't read a novel — so what will she do in the evening? She'll go to the cinema and drag me along too. That will already cost 2 gulden!
Well, never mind, that still wouldn't matter: a gulden for a talking[?] picture is after all a bargain, especially since the "Nowości" [cinema] even gives 2 pictures for a gulden...
Worse will be if my so-and-so [my wife] sits down to play poker, and that can already run into the big gulden!
On the other hand, what will the government gain from it? I am afraid it will even lose on the deal.
The peasant in the village will stop using matches altogether; he will go back to the old way of striking fire from stones — quite likely, since even now, with matches cheap, many peasants do so.
And the Jew in the shtetl — he will surely, surely find a way. He will do what every miser does: take the matches and split them in two lengthwise. He will have two matches —
instead of 50 matches for 8 groszy he will have 100 matches for ten groszy — a wild[?] bargain indeed.
And if the factory gets clever and makes thin matches, it won't help it;
if the Jew with his sharp brain has learned to split hairs, won't he be able to split a sliver of wood, however thin it may be!
With a Jew there is nothing to be done at all. They raise the excise on a patent [trading licence] — he takes no patent. Ah, without a patent one may not trade — so he doesn't trade. Ah, if one doesn't trade, there is nothing to eat — so he doesn't eat, and calls[?] it "knaknetl"[?]!
With a Jew they will accomplish nothing.
And I fear that nothing will come of the whole business with the 2 groszy.
Argus.
Campaign against trade in foreign lottery tickets.

[Poland — trade; lotteries.]
As we have heard, a strict order will be issued to the police concerning the fight against the trade in foreign lottery tickets.
As is known, there is a state monopoly on the Polish lottery, and for that reason it is forbidden to distribute any foreign lotteries. Nevertheless there are agents of the foreign "kolektury" [lottery agencies] who deal in those tickets on a broad scale.
The fight against the foreign tickets is dictated not only by the standpoint of protecting the monopoly, but also because there have been cases in which the buyers of foreign tickets were swindled.
After the "Khoges".

[Feuilleton — trade, bills of exchange and bankruptcies.] (Snatched conversations from shopkeeper to shopkeeper)

It is after the "khoges" [mocking term for the Christian holidays — Christmas and the civil New Year], and what[?] khoges: after "the second festival day of the Diaspora", when the shops were shut for 8[?] days altogether. Again the merchants stand in front of their shops and, out of great boredom, talk to one another across the empty streets. One polishes the pane of his "vitrine"[?] [shop window], another peers into a newspaper and meanwhile every so often throws a glance to see whether a customer is turning up at his competitor's, as it says there in the verse: "Ach lo poh"[?] — when the other merchant takes in no money, "yimzeh"[?] — it is as good as if I had taken in money..

Meanwhile a little group of talkers forms out of several shopkeepers, and incidentally they talk of politics and of public affairs in general[?] and in particular, with a fair portion of gossip and tittle-tattle. But as soon as the conversation moves on to protests[?] [of bills], auctions [pszetargn — przetargi][?], bills of exchange and bankruptcies, all faces turn serious. — It has almost become forbidden[?] [—] a "poczontek" [Polish początek — the first sale of the day] — sighs one, raising[?] his shoulders in great resignation: — and on top of all these troubles I have[?] today a [—] from "Bank Polski", and in the drawer it is empty for now..

— And perhaps — he catches himself at once — one of you has to pay at the "Zarebkovy"[?] [a bank; perhaps Bank Zarobkowy]; I have a 50 [złoty bill] to prolong on the third day, and meanwhile I could help myself out with the couple of złotys?

— Let it be ge[—]! — the neighbour answered him — even if I had it, I would not give it either. I heard what my brother-in-law[?] got out of such a favour: recently he went to the bank on the first day to pay a hundred; on the way he meets Fishel, the one from the haberdashery, who shows him a summons [wezwanie][?] from the notary [rejent]. "Give me the hundred — Fishel tells him — and I'll redeem your[?] bill by the day after tomorrow, and you'll charge me a couple of gulden [złoty] interest costs."

He probably insisted on it, and gave him the money, my [—] ["kchiel"[?]]. That same day an agitated[?] Moshe [—] drops in on him and begs for a hundred as an interest-free loan (gmiles-khesed), because they want to send back [—] a freight consignment and he must have today some thirty-odd gulden of railway charges. He tells him that his own bill has gone to the notary and that he himself has barely borrowed a hundred for 2 days. "Fishel — Moshe implores him — I'll give you back the interest costs, keep me alive and lend me the gulden until the day after tomorrow; I'll return it to you to the minute and to the second."

This way and that — they are Jews after all — he gave him the borrowed hundred, and Moshe went home contented, where there waited for him impatiently... the "carter" [ba'al agole]...

"Are you paying, sir, or not paying?!" [Polish: Płaci pan albo nie płaci?!] — that was the welcome he gave him, and, getting no answer, he lit a candle and began warming the stick of sealing wax to put on the seals.

In short, why go on at length? The "carter" got the hundred, both bills went to protest, and the freight went back where it had come from...

— I'll tell you a nicer story from today's trade — another speaks up. — You surely remember Yisroel R. S.'s last bankruptcy, for all of 150[?] thousand. Well, that was already no news then, and he really meant to get rid of his creditors with a [—] ["shipush"[?]], with some 20—30 per cent, and go on trading until the next "trick"[?]. But among the creditors there were some "fine" Jews, the cream of the [—] ["shpaysl"[?]]; "good" Jews intervened, letters[?] went back and forth, until they came to terms at 60 per cent and customers' bills of the well-known Moshe Ramtal[?].

Not many weeks pass, and Reb Moshe says: Stop! I too am a human being[?]; so he suspends [payments] for two whole [—], [—].

A gathering of manufacturers, merchants and plain arbitrators[?] assembles at his place. They try to talk him round kindly, and when they saw that it did not help they begin talking to him in fairness; one merchant speaks to him with tears in his eyes: "Have pity, I am a father of children, and now nothing is left for me but to throw myself out of the window."

— If so — says Reb Moshe cold-bloodedly — I can spare you the "trouble"[?], and then and there he opens the window on the 3rd floor wide.

In short, they have already settled[?], agreed on 25 per cent. But don't think, God forbid, in cash — that he keeps for more important purposes; especially for the "fertil-mertil"[?] — only in "customers'" bills of Hashke[?] Krakower...

The latter, it seems, was also in no great hurry to redeem the bills on their due date, and at New Year three [—] merchants came down to him — his own[?], Reb Moshe's and Yisroel's — on the matter of a "regulation" [debt settlement]. He received them very nicely, even had a little Psalter spread open on the table, and when they asked how much, for instance, he intends to settle for, he answered pleasantly, stroking his little yellow beard:

— What fools, pardon me, you are[?]! If I had wanted to settle, why would I have needed to "go bankrupt"?..

— — — — — — — —

The shopkeepers would have stood like that for a long time yet, but just then a customer appeared in the lane, and they hurriedly took up position, each in front of his own shop, to catch a "poczontek".

Ploni.
The Jewish Artist Moshe Apelbaum Has Died.

[Mourning — art; Katowice and Będzin.]
On Saturday afternoon Jewish Upper Silesia and Zagłębie were shaken by the terrible news that the painter-artist Moshe Apelbaum, so popular among us, had died at the age of 43 after a grave illness in the Bogucice hospital.
The prematurely deceased artist was well known to the Jewish public of Zagłębie; his landscapes and portraits adorn the walls of a great number of homes in Upper Silesia and Zagłębie. Apelbaum distinguished himself especially in the field of decorative art, and in that field he was one of the pioneers.
Moshe Apelbaum devoted himself a great deal to old Jewish folk painting; he united the folk-Jewish element with modernist creation.
When the Będzin kehilla administration decided to paint the synagogue, the work was entrusted to Apelbaum. Thanks to this, the Będzin synagogue is, in the painterly sense, one of the most interesting in Poland.
In 1927 Moshe Apelbaum organized the first exhibition of paintings in Katowice. The exhibition had the greatest success, and this gave the Jewish artist courage for his further activity.
With the death of Moshe Apelbaum the Jewish artistic family has lost one of its best and finest artists.
Honour to his memory!
S. Rotenberg. — Moshe Apelbaum.

[Eulogy — art; the painter's biography.]
My hand will not rise to write; it somehow seems to me that I am about to write down a dreadful lie: "Moshe Apelbaum dead" — what a terrible absurdity, what an improbable paradox. The ever life-loving, energetic and optimistic Apelbaum, the one who even in his last days, when death had already crept into his organism, still believed that he would recover, and even unfolded before me his plans for the future — this very Apelbaum a dead man? No! It is not possible; some terrible mistake has happened here; surely someone has made up a lie that Apelbaum is no longer among us. So I would wish it to be, but the dull echoes of the heavy shovelfuls of earth that covered his grave remind me, alas, of the cruel reality and do not let my fantasies be.
Born in Amshinov [Mszczonów] to Hasidic parents, Apelbaum goes through all the transformations of a small-town boy. Until 12 in the heder; then he studies in Kalisz — by day pattern drawing and by night Talmud in the shtibl. Later he returns to his native town and becomes a house painter and sign painter. The signs little Moshe paints throw the whole town into raptures. Here hangs a new sign on a grocery shop in the market — you could swear you need only put a hand into the barrel and pull out a herring, or, for example, the cheese: just a pinch with the fingers and there is a piece of fresh white cheese. And the officer on the military tailor's sign — a real, living "panye" with a pair of moustaches that strike terror into the town's Jews.
But what comes of it? The whole of Amshinov needs, all told, a couple of signs a year, and Apelbaum's master is a Jew burdened with a family and needs a livelihood?! The master hits upon a brilliant plan: "Moshe," he says, "we must live after all, so you will go at night and tear down the signs; then there will again be something to paint, and if not — it's bitter."
Thus the young, talented Apelbaum begins his hard road of suffering, which takes him at 19 abroad, where he studies painting in Amsterdam and Vienna, and later completes a school of arts and crafts in Liverpool. He receives a scholarship and perfects himself at the London art academy. In London art circles they immediately recognised in Apelbaum an above-average talent, and they organised for him, under the patronage of Max Nordau, an exhibition that had a tremendous success. The whole Jewish and English press was full of songs of praise for the young artist. It seemed that fortune had smiled on Apelbaum, but the World War put an end to Apelbaum's brilliant artistic career. Being a convinced pacifist, he would not go and murder innocent people, and only the fact that he had officially belonged to a pacifist society long before the war saved him from death, and he got off with imprisonment.
In 1920 the artist comes to Warsaw, where he delights everyone with the stage sets he paints for the Yiddish theatre.
A few years later Apelbaum is entrusted with the initiative of painting the Będzin town synagogue, which he transforms, together with the artists Ziegler and Hanft, into a true temple of art.
One should have seen Apelbaum at work. He was a fount of inexhaustible energy; painting was for him the content, the whole meaning of his life. Always in an elevated mood, even in the hardest material conditions, which were chronic with him, he did not lose heart. Although he received a ridiculous wage for the masterpiece he created in the Będzin synagogue, he was nevertheless content. "It is indeed little," he used to say, "but for that, 'my mizrach wall' will be the most beautiful tombstone I could have afforded, and it will remain a very long time, when of my earthly existence there will be no trace."
The unfortunate man, alas, had no presentiment that the paints on the "mizrach wall" would not yet be properly dry and he would already be resting in his eternal sleep.
May the earth rest lightly on him!
The Tragedy of a Jewish Artist (At the Grave of Moshe Apelboim).

[Katowice — eulogy; art.] It is an old story — but unfortunately it still remains new, new...
After death — say "holy"...
A Jewish artist lived and created. Apart from those who pretend to be the patented leaders of Jewish society, [no one] showed the slightest interest in this artist's life: how does the famous and everywhere-beloved Jewish artist live in the capital of Silesia?
Moshe Apelboim has died.
And the Jewish population was shaken in Silesia, in Zagłębie, in Warsaw, in Paris, in London — and everywhere the gifted and great Jewish artist lived and worked.
Moshe Apelboim has died — and all his closest friends and acquaintances sighed deeply: nebekh, a pity, such a decent and fine and interesting man he was, gone from the world before his time... what a loss...
Yes, now people come to Katowice to wipe away a tear, to wring their hands, to praise and laud, to lament and glorify, to mourn and admire our dear, good-hearted, modest and life-loving Moshe Apelboim. If he was still little known to the "better" Jewish public — he has now been widely advertised.
The old-new story: after death — say "holy"...
This, unfortunately, is the tragedy of Jewish artists, Jewish artists of the word and of the brush.
A sad symptom of our national anomaly and perhaps — of our extraterritorial condition...
His life was a chain of hard trials and struggles, his untimely death — a tragic loss.
A. Ganzweich.
The Death and Funeral of Moshe Apelboim.

[Katowice — death and funeral.] The artist had felt very unwell for a long time, and only 4 weeks ago was he literally torn away by force from his tireless work and taken to the Bogucice hospital, where measures were immediately begun to keep the beloved artist alive.
To the flu, however, was added pneumonia, then a paralysis, and later still — according to the finding of the chief physician — cancer of the lungs, so that all help was futile, and after very great suffering he breathed out his soul on Saturday at 6 in the morning.
The Katowice Jewish community took charge of conducting the funeral, and accompanied by hundreds of admirers and friends from Zagłębie, Warsaw and Kraków, the great artist was brought to burial the next day, Sunday, at the Katowice Jewish cemetery.
In a long, substantive speech Rabbi Dr. Vogelmann [?] eulogised the deceased, pointing to Moshe Apelbaum's great merits for the development of art in general and Jewish art in particular. Finally the rabbi pointed out that it is a sacred duty of his friends and admirers to concern themselves with the fate of the widow and daughter left behind by the great deceased.
The second eulogy was by Dr. A[—] Schneier (Vienna); as an artist and personal friend of the deceased he took leave of him in short but warm words, which made a great impression on all present.
Further speakers were Mr. Goldberg, as delegate of the Warsaw Artists' Association; Mr. Y. Klarman (in Hebrew) on behalf of the Zionists in Zagłębie; Mr. Gutman — as representative of the Right Poale Zion; and finally Rabbi Dr. Chameides delivered a splendid and moving eulogy — and the grave was filled in amid the sobbing and weeping of all who had ever come into contact with the beloved, life-loving artist — Moshe Apelbaum.
———
Immediately after the funeral, a meeting of Apelbaum's closest friends and admirers took place in the hall of the B'nai B'rith lodge in Katowice, at which a "Moshe Apelbaum Committee" was founded, whose task is first of all to care for the fate of the widow and daughter of the deceased; to gather all the remaining works of art and, with the help of the Warsaw Artists' Association, to organise large art exhibitions in Warsaw and Katowice, and to organise various other actions for the benefit of the Apelbaum Fund.
The committee includes Messrs. Dr. Kipman [?], Grinszpan [?], Arch. [?] Guiman (president of the Christian Artists' Association) and Miss Guiman; Dr. A. Schneier (Vienna), Dr. Tirk (Gliwice [?]), Editor Szpigelman, A. Pesachzon [?] and Rotenberg (Będzin) and M. Buksbaum (Sosnowiec).
Apart from this, special Apelbaum committees are being founded throughout Zagłębie and Silesia, which intend [?] to carry out the planned actions.
Moshe Apelboim. The Art of the Renaissance.

[Art — essay; from Moshe Apelboim's papers.] [Editorial note:] The article by the just-deceased artist Moshe Apelboim was found in our editorial portfolio. The Editors.
The free artist as we [know? see?] and understand him today emerged in the Renaissance epoch; the artist who regards the world, nature and people individually, subjectively, was crowned as sole ruler of his creation in that remarkable epoch.
The artist of the Renaissance epoch also served religion with his art: he painted holy pictures, he built churches, and he hewed out of stone and kneaded out of clay figures sanctified by religion; but he conceived religion and its saints quite individually and rendered [?] them independently of tradition and of the canonized, sanctified pattern.
•
Never in the history of mankind has painting reached such omnipotence, such a wondrous, divine creative exaltation [?] as it reached in the age of the Renaissance.
Nuances of colour grew up; all are colour-sorcerers, all stem [?] from worlds of colours, all superhuman beings and all with superhuman attainments. The play of colours was the most divine play in that great age. All the secrets of the play of colours were discovered, and the brushes in the artists' hands painted a veritable play of Creation.
The painter of the Renaissance epoch was a great man, a man with a great head, with a great temperament, a man with the sharpest eye and a man with the greatest conceptions.
In one picture the painter gave a great, complicated world, full of secrets, full of marvels of beauty, and into everything — into the smallest and the largest picture — he put the greatest creative energy.
If he painted a man, the man was re-created according to the artist's great individual conceptions; if he painted a tree, it was to him [?] marvels of creation.
And through their pictures they re-created everything: they re-created Christianity, they re-created human thinking and even human feeling —
a work of Creation.
On the walls of churches they created a new religion; on the walls and on the ceilings of palaces they retold the greatest legends in the great language of colours, in a grand manner.
They elevated everything through their language of colours, they deepened everything and gave it a great breath. And the great achievement was that within the loftiness there was clear, exact humanity.
The painters were the masters of life: they set the tone, they dictated taste, they gave every new idea a wondrous body.
It was the time when for the first time questions of art were discussed with the greatest seriousness, with depth, sharpness and dazzling clarity; art problems were approached with scientific methods, consciousness was brought into art, art theories possessed clarity, perspective and certainty.
Knowledge and talent went hand in hand, and knowledge was many-sided, universal, and talent too was many-sided and universal. Talent enlivened [?], illuminated and breathed spirit into knowledge, and knowledge deepened, broadened, nourished and cradled [?] talent.
In all the cities of Italy there were art schools, art workshops led by great and learned artists.
In Florence sculpture was born; there worked the greatest master Donatello, the father of Renaissance sculpture, and beside him the wonderful narrator [?] and sculptor Ghiberti [?] — these were the great teachers of the genius Michelangelo. The third master is Luca della Robbia, world-famous for his majolica sculptures. The early Renaissance epoch is closed by the genius in all fields of art — Verrocchio [?], with whom the wonder-man of the Renaissance, Leonardo da Vinci, studied.
Whole camps of genius artists there were in all the cities of Italy, and a creative fire seized everyone; all created wonders.
But the highest and clearest point of the Renaissance are its three greatest pillars: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael,
Security in Eretz Israel

V. Jabotinsky [Vladimir (Ze'ev) Jabotinsky].

2.
Foreign protection.

Foreign protection is not only politically dangerous[?]: it is simply bad protection. The British soldier is an excellent, loyal soldier; you can send him anywhere, even to his death, and he will always fulfil his duty correctly. But the first rule taught to every officer in the British army says: "You must try with all your might never to use your unit for work which you know for certain is organically distasteful to it. By doing so you[?] undermine discipline, you destroy the morale of the army, even when your order is 'carried out precisely'."

For the British soldier, the role assigned[?] to him in Eretz Israel during the suppression of anti-Zionist riots is organically distasteful. The English soldier will, when necessary, attack India, Egypt or Ireland by force, because there it is clear to him that he is directly defending England's interests. In that case the question whether the rebels[?] are right or wrong does not arise for him at all. Eretz Israel, however, is not a British province; Palestine is the property of the League of Nations. Formally, England is carrying out a mandate there which has no direct connection with English sovereignty. This formal standpoint is known to every English soldier. He therefore knows that in "Eretz Israel he is not defending England, but only the Jews — a people whose interests and ideals are not his. Besides, every English newspaper tells him that Zionism has quite unjustified pretensions, that England's policy in this question "is an unheard-of oppression of the Arabs, that the whole Palestine undertaking is a mistake for England, that England was dragged by the Jews into an impossible undertaking; were there no Zionism, England could leave Palestine, or even stay there, and the Arabs would gladly recognise her there as the masters of the country"...

This he reads daily in the small press, which is after all the most widespread in the barracks, and which occupies itself most intensively with anti-Zionist propaganda. Even if our standpoint does reach him once in a while [the word "once" is printed twice] — which I strongly doubt — it is surely ridiculous to demand that "John" or "Tommy" should sort out a question so tangled for him, and should moreover be able to take on the role of a judge. At best "John" will remain neutral; he will say to himself: neither the Jews nor the Arabs are any concern of mine — and to meddle in their quarrel is repugnant to him.

In reality, however, we have always experienced the worse case. In 1922 the Zionist Executive sent one of its secretaries to Eretz Israel to inform himself about the political situation in the country. This secretary was an English Jew of very "moderate" convictions, a convinced supporter of Sir Herbert Samuel, an opponent of the idea of a Jewish state, an opponent of a Jewish Legion, etc. He toured the country and submitted a report to the Executive, in which we read the sentence: "The army in Eretz Israel, from drummer to general, is against Zionism." It could not have been otherwise. This does not mean, however, that Zionism appears unethical in the eyes of neutral people; on the contrary, in the eyes of everyone capable of judging, Zionism has won the moral dispute over rights. But the soldier is no judge, nor can he be one. The colonisation of North America was also a just cause. Yet if "Jewish" soldiers had had to protect the English pioneers against the natives, this work[?] would have been just as unpopular among us Jews, and one could not have relied on our protection. Exactly the same applies to the protection of our colonisation by English soldiers. And precisely for that reason the English military — as Sir Herbert Samuel boastfully stressed in an official telegram — did not fire a single shot during the pogrom in Jaffa. And precisely for that reason the soldiers went out against the ten-thousand-strong Arab demonstration in Rehovot armed with sticks and not with rifles, in order to protect the Jews from the demonstration. Every army has its psychology and the officers reckon with it, especially when they themselves are dominated by the same spirit. This psychology is naturally known to the Arab as well. Because of the daily contact between the English soldier and the Arab, from whom "Tommy" buys oranges and vegetables, with whom he chats and jokes, there arises among the Arabs, as among all Orientals, the belief in whatever they feel like believing. And in their easily aroused imagination the suspicion turns, as they pass reports to one another by word of mouth, into a real fact — and that is a very dangerous moment: "Tommy" told me that the whole business is distasteful to him. Shafiq[?] tells it on to Shevket[?]: "Tommy said he has no 'desire' at all to defend the Jews in case of riots." Shevket[?] already passes it on to Mehmet[?] in another form: "Tommy said they have a secret order not to defend the Jews." In this way the Arab masses form the firm opinion that the government, and above all the army, is with them and against the Jews. And therefore in April 1920 and in May 1921 the Arabs were not afraid to make pogroms in Jerusalem and Jaffa, regardless of the large number of English troops then present in the country.

Let us now recall an opposite case: at the beginning of 1919 serious riots broke out in Egypt; the military stationed there was too small to be able to suppress the riots, which bore the character of an uprising, and therefore almost all the English battalions were transferred from Eretz Israel to Cairo. In Eretz Israel there was then, apart from the five thousand Jewish legionaries, no European military at all. The situation was very dangerous; every day secret reports arrived about "Arab intentions[?]", and although these reports were utterly baseless, the Arab masses accepted them as genuine coin. All over Eretz Israel agitators were running about trying to provoke an uprising of the fellahin against the Jewish colonies. Despite this, perfect order reigned in the country; not the slightest clash occurred; even in the most isolated and remote colonies complete calm prevailed — and only because the Arabs knew that there were several thousand Jewish soldiers in the country, whose disposition[?] and attitude could arouse no doubts in Achmed or[?] Shevket[?]. I know very well that the strength of any garrison lies not in itself but in the power of the state that stands behind[?] it. That is why I have never been a supporter of a "national" army, even if such an army were politically possible. All we need is the re-establishment of our battalions in the form in which they existed from 1917 to 1921. These battalions were part of the British army and wore British uniforms, but the human material inside those uniforms was purely Jewish — and there lies the core of the matter. When we were still gymnasium pupils, every teacher was a representative of the same state authority. He could expel any pupil at will; nevertheless there were some whom we obeyed, and others on whose heads we climbed. It is not the power vested in the teacher, the official, the soldier that is the main thing: decisive are his own outlook, his own attitude, his own will to impress the class, the crowd, and the way in which he impresses it. The conclusion is clear: first, a garrison in Eretz Israel can give real protection to Jewish colonisation only if it consists for the greater part of Jewish soldiers; second, only on [this] condition is an administrative reform in Eretz Israel possible — a reform that would open for us the way to the actual realisation of the Mandate; above all the way to organising immigration on a large scale. Just as we cannot demand of England that she protect Zionism with money, neither can we demand the blood of her sons. If a garrison should ever have to make sacrifices, then the lists of the dead and wounded must not contain names like "John" and "Peter", but names like "Moshe" and "Yehuda". The question whether militarism and soldiering are pleasant to us is beside the point. We face an iron logical necessity[?]: we are colonising Eretz Israel against the will of the natives. This opposition cannot be removed. Therefore our colonisation is possible only on the precondition of active armed protection. This[?] protection England cannot, or will not, give us. Therefore the garrison must consist of Jews — or else Zionism is not feasible.
About the Będzin and Sosnowiec “Mizrachi” Schools / (A Conversation with the Director, Dr. Zvi Chajnsztok)

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — education: the “Mizrachi” schools; interview.]
Lately the “Mizrachi” has been carrying on a lively activity in the field of national-religious education, and in a whole series of towns schools have been opened under the name “Yavneh”; the Będzin “Mizrachi” has likewise set about introducing various improvements in the already existing Mizrachist schools. For this purpose the director of the “Yavneh” schools, Dr. Zvi Chajnsztok [?], came to Zagłębie.
We used the opportunity to inform ourselves about the content and the situation of the schools, and here is what he explained to us:
— For many years now the Jews in exile have been unable to find a solution for the education of the young. The old “cheder” can without any doubt not satisfy the Jew, because he cannot be isolated from the surrounding world; the secular schools, on the other hand, cannot satisfy the religious national Jew. Therefore one must find the synthesis of the 2 types of school. And this task the “Mizrachi” has taken upon itself: in the elementary (folk) schools the full curriculum of the “powszechne” [state elementary] [?] schools has been introduced, and alongside it all the Hebrew subjects are taught, including Gemara, so that a pupil of the school remains [?] a religious-national Jew while at the same time also possessing the secular subjects.
— The “Mizrachi” has 140 such elementary schools and 5 secondary schools; in 2 schools the language of instruction is Hebrew. Besides that the “Mizrachi” has under its control several seminaries for teachers and Froebel kindergarten teachers, and a rabbinical school, “Tachkemoni.” Of course they come up against difficulties in setting up the schools, and first and foremost — the money question. But we are carrying various plans with us: after we have raised the sufficient financial means, we will think about the future of the pupil who finishes our school. We will found trade (artisan) and commercial schools, and as the first place it is indeed Zagłębie that comes into consideration. This can be realised only after we have introduced the various improvements in the Będzin and Sosnowiec “Mizrachi” schools. I have already given these schools a clear programme and instructions for further work, and I believe that the schools will be a model for all of Poland.
—n.

A Few Words at the Fresh Grave of the Late Feldsher Hartman

[Będzin — obituary.]
Who did not know him? He lived out his years — decades of years — in Będzin; small and great knew him, rich and poor; he brought help to the sick, to the poor more than to the rich, by day and by night, brought comfort to suffering humanity at the critical moment... and of all this he left behind neither plots nor houses; and yet the Jewish population of Będzin honoured [?] him with the former deputy of 3 terms [?], the highly esteemed Dr. Weinzieher, who took leave of him with warm words at the open grave, acknowledging him as his helper; for to be a popular feldsher in a poor quarter, especially in the present bad [?] times, was not so easy: running up to the 4th–5th floor; to the end of town, often into the cellars; putting together cheap medicines; explaining to the mother something about cleanliness, about diet, how to guard against further suffering and pain — all this demands being almost a “minister” [?] of a man...
Honour his memory!
Ch. Szer.
You cry "Ach!" — here, have some more.

[Poland — taxes and the economy; followed by: Będzin — sport, "Hakoah".]
As is known, the government is now drafting a new tax law, and the draft has already been discussed in the chambers of commerce; these sent the draft on to the economic organizations so that they could give their opinion of it.
On acquainting themselves with the draft, the economic organizations raised a "va-yitz'aku" [a great outcry; biblical phrase]. The government did indeed promise to halt the draft and not to issue it, as had been planned, as a decree, but to bring it before the Sejm; this, however, does not change the situation, because the majority in the Sejm is now, as is known, such that it will presumably not come out against the government's draft... It is therefore hard to believe that the draft will be radically changed by the Sejm, or that its very sharpest points will be softened; and such points are, unfortunately, present in abundance in the draft, so that it is really worth getting acquainted with them.
First, the new draft abolishes the assessment commissions, in which, as is known, representatives of the taxpayers have taken part until now. Under the draft the officials alone are to determine the size of the tax; it goes without saying that for the taxpayer this will be a meagre favour. True, abroad (in Germany, for example) the officials also set the tax by themselves, but there tax courts exist, to which the taxpayer can appeal against an official for imposing too high a tax on him; there the official must prove before the court on what basis he assessed the person at such a tax and not a smaller one; if the official cannot rationally prove before the court why he assessed the taxpayer at so high a tax, he faces a penalty. Under such conditions one can indeed entrust the official alone with setting the amount of the tax; here, however, there are no such courts for the time being. True, the payer has the right to demand explanations from the tax office as to the basis on which so high a tax was imposed on him, but the official can answer with the usual excuse: "I had confidential information that So-and-so had such-and-such a turnover"... and with that he is in the clear.
Thus this change in the law itself — the abolition of the assessment commissions — is, under our conditions, a great blow to the taxpayers; but let us pick a few more "little flowers" from the "tax reform".
The appeals commission is to be enlarged: it will consist of 36 representatives of the payers by trade branch and of 18 officials. That seems fine — but there is a second point, which says that the commission is divided into branch commissions of 9 persons each — of them 4 taxpayers, 4 officials, and the chairman is the tax inspector. How the decisions of such commissions will turn out here is, of course, not hard to predict. In any case, on the basis of past practice, the taxpayers can expect very little from it.
And if all this is still too little, there is one more novelty: the officials may seize the goods of the taxpayer not only for past [taxes], but even for a whole 2 years' taxes in advance; and taking into account as well that the official has the right to review the taxes for 5 years back and to raise them, it turns out that the draft places the taxpayer in a dangerous position: any day an official may come to the merchant and put seals on his entire shop for taxes of which the taxpayer had no idea. Quite simply because they are additions[?] [reading uncertain] arising from the re-assessed and raised taxes of earlier years, which he has long since paid.
About all the "concessions" of the new tax reform the economic organizations are informed, but the broad masses of taxpayers still know nothing of them.
The organizations therefore have a duty to make their members aware of the danger threatening them from the new tax reform; the necessary steps must indeed be taken in good time to "shout down" this draft, which may oppress still further the already exhausted taxpayer.
Sh—n.
—o—
Sport propaganda by Będzin "Hakoah". An academy in honour of the "Maccabi" Week.
As is known, the world union "Maccabi" has proclaimed a "Maccabi Week" throughout Poland. The purpose of the "Week" is to strengthen the Jewish sports clubs that already exist and to found such clubs in places where there are none yet.
In connection with this, Będzin "Hakoah" organized on Sunday a sports festival devoted to sports propaganda.
On Sunday morning the Hakoah members (not all of them) assembled in their own premises, from which the march through the town was formed.
At 11 o'clock the sounds of the "Hakoah" orchestra "cheered up" the inhabitants[?], a large part of whom accompanied the procession to the "Korso" [Corso?] hall, where an academy took place.
The hall is packed with young people, among whom one also sees a few individuals of the older generation.
The curtain opens; at the presidium table: Doctors Weinzieher and Rechtschaffen[?], Dr. Rechtman, delegates, the press, board members of "Hakoah" with the banner, "Hashomer" and "Betar" with their banners.
Dr. Rechtman opens the academy. The Polish and the Jewish anthems are played, and the first word goes to the chairman of the academy, Dr. Weinzieher.
Dr. Weinzieher gives an overview of the Jewish people. The "People of the Book" occupied itself only with cultivating the soul, and not at all[?] with the body. But it is — a gladdening phenomenon that the present generation already understands the benefit of sport — [uncertain word] for the physical development of the Jewish people.
Dr. Rechtschaffen[?] compares sports propaganda with the campaign against tuberculosis now under way in Poland. In the countries — says the speaker — where sport is developed in all strata of the population, the number of consumptives is very small, whereas there, where sport is regarded as nonsense, the number of people sick with tuberculosis is very large.
Dr. Rechtschaffen[?] dwells on the local conditions of our club "Hakoah" and calls for active deeds.
Dr. Rechtman (in Yiddish) speaks about the significance of the "Maccabi Week" and the aim of the world union "Maccabi", and points out the broad path along which "Hakoah" goes and at which it aims. "In the field of sport we have — says Dr. Rechtman — done very much, but even more remains to be done, when the forces of 'Hakoah' grow and Jewish society understands the great importance of sport among Jews."
Dr. Rechtman announces that on account of the "Maccabi Week" the board of "Hakoah" has exempted new members from the registration fee, and the monthly dues have been reduced to 50 groszy.
———
In the second part of the academy the first ladies' group performed a sports number (with bars), which won great applause.
Then the "Hakoah" orchestra under the direction of A. Isshe[?] played brilliantly[?] "Shulamis" and other musical numbers.
It is worth remarking that the participants are too "bold": they strive only to produce loud notes, even when they are not ready...
On the whole the band[?] did very well. We are of the opinion that the greatest propaganda for physical development would be if "Hakoah" were to arrange[?] such sports performances[?] from time to time, especially for school youth.
An important clarification concerning Sunday trading.

[Law — Sunday trading; Supreme Court ruling.] It is a fact that merely keeping a business open on Sunday, but without selling and without trading — only putting the shop in order — cannot be qualified as an offence from the standpoint of the law on Sunday rest.
Recently the Supreme Court handed down a unanimous ruling concerning trading on Sunday. This ruling may be of great importance for the authorities' attitude from now on to cases of drawing up reports [protocols] for violating the obligation of Sunday rest.
In this ruling [—] we read: receiving[?] a [—] in a shop on Sunday, packing [—] of previously sold goods, and showing fresh goods — [the court] regarded these as activities[?] that bear a clear[?] character of trade. It makes no difference whether the goods were shown in the business or in a neighbouring flat. Nor does it make any difference whether a notice was hung on the shop door saying that the shop is closed.
We learn that the Minister of the Interior has issued a special ordinance on this matter.
“The Cooking Spoon” — in honour of the New Year — by Ben Amoz. New times, new songs.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl” (The Cooking Spoon) column; poem.] “The Cooking Spoon” — in honour of the New Year — by Ben Amoz.
New times, new songs.

The winter has been transformed
into colds, other and new[?];
besides the snow and frost behind it[?]
one suffers from hunger and from
the need of the podatki [taxes][?].

Once people trembled from the cold —
the tenants [lokatorzy] had no coal;
now[?] people tremble — there is no money,
tomorrow the sequestrators [bailiffs]
set out.

My wife trembles when I come home late,
and my household trembles too;
they are afraid that I am already ready
to take[?] for myself — death..

Though for[?] help nobody dies,
I fall ill from troubles;
a shudder goes through my bones
when I look at my sequestered cupboard.

Wife and children think the [—],
the [—]-elite will hide/keep[?];
they have heard that rich men in the
big cities
are already putting their beds[?] out on the pavement.
Prophecies for the New Year.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl” column; New Year prophecies, Będzin.] (If only I turn out a liar)
The head of the kehilla will be called to the last session on the budget[?] for 1931. After that he will already rest[?] in eternal rest...
———
The “pomnik” [monument] on the New Market will be finished together with the Będzin mikveh...
———
The turnover tax will be increased. The merchants will protest, and the bailiffs [executors] will carry the goods off on the “cart”.
———
Jewish institutions will conduct a vigorous[?] activity in the field of money collections, badge sales, etc.
———
There will be fewer bankruptcies this year, because there is nobody left to go bankrupt...
———
The number of Jewish banks will grow and the number of members — shrink.
———
Yitzhak Grünbaum will sit in the Sejm and the Mizrachists will be angry...
—o—
A new ordinance on signing bills of exchange.
As we learn, in the coming days of the year 1931 new ordinances will be issued on signing and issuing bills of exchange. The new ordinance provides:
1) Bills of exchange will have to be signed with the right hand (Left Poalei-Zionists and plain leftists may do it with the left hand).
2) The endorser [giro] must be a human being (i.e. war-profiteers and communal activists will not be allowed to endorse any bill).
3) Next to the signature of the drawer there must be the added inscription: “Righteousness shall go before him” [Psalms 85:14].
4) In every bank a member of the Chevra Kadisha [burial society] must be on duty.
Once and today.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl” column.] Once people said: strike up, klezmers, a freylekhs for the poor aunt — not invited, she came by herself.
Today: not to any uncle, not to any aunt — to the Sylvester [New Year's Eve] ball they come by themselves.
Once: honour to the aunt, take her into the circle, honour her with the mitzvah-dance.
Today: at the Sylvester ball at Frank's[?], Yudl dances a mitzvah-dance with his circle.
Once: the gentile is drunk, the Jew is sober —
we are the guilty ones, they are the judges.
Today: they spit in the little Jews' faces; where he is driven out from — there he crawls...
Socrates.
—o—
Biographies of tailors.
(Overheard at the artisans' examinations in the tailors' guild.)
1) My name is Gotlib and my wife's is Yente Pese.
2) I have three machines: two pieces at the disposal of the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office] and one machine is “kept” at the Magistrate [town hall].
3) I am a made-to-order[?] tailor, and my Yente Pese calls me: confectioner[?]..
4) I am a członek [member] of the Artisans' [union] and pray with the Chevra Tehilim [Psalms society].
5) I came to a tailor as an apprentice at 12. I carried water and scrubbed the master's house until 19.
6) At 20 I had already sewn my first “lapkhl” [patch?].
7) At 21 I went to serve the Kaiser, and at 25 I married my first wife; now I am already at my fourth wife.
Chronicle.

[Będzin — “Chronicle”, short items in a humorous tone (apparently part of the humour column).] A joint action.
At the last session of the Będzin kehilla board it was resolved that, together with the cheap kitchen, a coal action for the winter should be undertaken by the gmina [municipality].
—o—
From the shoemakers' guild
We are asked to announce that thanks to the Sylvester evening at the “Korso”[?], organised by “Hakoach”, the shoemakers' guild has greatly revived.
—o—
The “sport” movement.
In connection with the “Savings Week” in Poland, the kehilla board in Będzin staged a boxing match, which had the following results: Zionists and artisans — a draw [remis]; the [—] Hasidim were laid on their “shoulder blades” [łopatki, i.e. pinned]; the president's [prezes] chair took a beating[?] from the Orthodox...
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: General Meeting of the Jewish Charity Society

[Head of the local section; Będzin — charity and welfare.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 20 Tevet 5691 — Piątek 9 stycznia 1931 [Friday, 9 January 1931].)
Będzin
General Meeting of the Jewish Charity Society.
In the hall of the Jewish kehilla the annual general meeting of the Charity Society („Dobroczynność“) took place on Sunday.
Some 400 members were invited to the meeting; of that number no fewer than 7 came (read: seven..), so that together with the board the meeting — at which reports were given on tens[?] of thousands[?] of gulden, on the orphans' shelters, etc. — was attended by 17 persons.
Dr. Weinzieher opens the meeting and hands the chair to Mr. L. Rubinlicht.
From the report given by Dr. Weinzieher we learn that in the course of the period the society distributed 10,444 korzec of coal to 728 families. The coal campaign amounted to 8582 zł. The sum was collected from the town, and 2000 zł. from the gmina. The flour (Kimcha [de-Pischa]) campaign, which supported over 1000 families, cost 17,745 zł. One-time grants and rent money for widows the society gave in the amount of 3,222 zł. and 99 gr.
In the orphans' shelters (ochronki) 31 boys and 42 girls are maintained.
A detailed report on the building of the orphanage is given by engineer G. Weinzieher. It turns out that the walls and the roof are finished; to date the building has cost 188 thousand 902 zł. In Mr.[?] Weinzieher's opinion the same sum again will be needed to complete the interior. The sum will probably come from the subsidies of the Magistrat and the gmina, [and] —[?] from those who to this day have not yet contributed toward the important building for the dozens of orphans.
The total of the past budget amounts to 98 586 92 zł. [=98,586.92].
The new budget amounts to 87724 zł. The composition of the board was not changed.
As honorary member of the board the tireless communal worker R' Mendel Rozencwajg was elected.
„Hachnasat Kallah“ Holds a Real Wedding...

[Będzin — charity; dowering of brides.]
A few months ago a girl from Będzin, a full orphan, became acquainted with a young man, also such a „solid“[?] one.. and they signed the tna'im (engagement contract).
When the time of the wedding drew near, they turned to the relatives for help. The relatives, also[?] very poor people, are however not able to help the young couple jointly[?], and so they turned to the Hachnasat Kallah society in Będzin to help.
The matter was considered at a meeting, and the board declared that in this case Hachnasat Kallah should not discharge its duty with the kind of support that everyone receives, but that a wedding should be held just like decent folk have.
At the meeting each member of the board pledged a donation for this purpose, some with money, some with provisions, so that a feast for 100 guests is being prepared, fit for a king...
The wedding of the full orphans takes place next Sunday, [week of] Parshat Va'era [11 January 1931], in the hall of the „Talmud Torah“. The local „notables“ are expected to come to the wedding, which is being arranged by the board of Hachnasat Kallah.
The Financial Situation of the Magistrat Is Improving

[Będzin — municipality and taxes.]
As the Magistrat inspector informs us, the financial situation of the Magistrat has improved. This is thanks to the fact — says the inspector — that the arrears of taxes (zaległe) are being collected in a strict manner, especially from the well-to-do class, from whom the taxes had not been collected.
A large share in the improvement of finances also belongs to the „Bank Kupiecki“ (Merchants' Bank), which is always ready, and at every call the bank supplies the Magistrat with the sums requested.
Boycott or Neglect?

[Będzin — kehilla.]
This Tuesday [6 January 1931] the new kehilla president R' Avraham Liwer called the board to a meeting. But of all the invited dozors (board members) not a single one came..
There Is Coal, but the „Ha-Motzi Cutters“ Are Missing...

[Będzin — charity; coal for the poor.]
As we are informed, this year too a considerable sum of money for coal was collected through Mr. Rozencwajg. In order to distribute the coal a meeting was called on Tuesday, but of the 20 invited „distributors“ no more than two came.
Because of this the poor lie cold in the meantime..
A Railway Disaster Averted.

[Zagłębie — transport; railway accident.]
On Sunday evening a serious railway disaster was averted between Golonóg and Ząbkowice.
From a freight train travelling in the direction of Ząbkowice some 30 wagons broke loose on the way and rolled back toward Dąbrowa.
At the same time a passenger train was coming from that side. Thanks to the engine driver, who checked the momentum of the train, it came only to a small collision, in which one wagon was smashed.
They Went at It with Force...

[Będzin — crime.]
In the local prison 2 persons got acquainted and concluded an agreement between themselves that when they got out of prison they would go into a business partnership — not in the line of thefts, but by opening a bureau "for collecting debts".
The men opened a bureau; after all, there is no shortage of debtors nowadays[?]. Day by day the "bureau" got more clients — from among the children of Israel, of course — and the business prospered splendidly.
And it came to pass one day that a debtor turned up, a stubborn one, who would not pay a very old debt. So the bureau men took revenge on him and bombarded the debtor's flat with stones.
The police took an interest in this "work", and the "heroes" are once again behind lock and key.
A Ball for the Benefit of the Academics

[Będzin — students, society.]
The Association of Jewish Students in Będzin is holding tomorrow, Saturday, its yearly traditional academic ball in the halls of the Góra Zamkowa. The academics' events have already earned a name thanks to the fact that they are always the most successful. This year too the organising committee is preparing a series of attractions, and as can be seen from the preparations, the entertainment will turn out quite impressive, and Jewish society will have the opportunity to spend the evening well and pleasantly in a cosy mood.
Sosnowiec — A Dentist with “Qualifications” Arrested

[Sosnowiec — sick fund, crime.]
A few weeks ago the local sick fund (Kasa Chorych) published a competition for a dentist at the outpatient clinic in Dąbrowa.
A certain Tadeusz Szwarc was engaged for the post; he submitted documents showing that he had practised as a dentist in Wilno, Poznań, Lwów, Warsaw and lately in Kielce.
Before Szwarc came to the post at the local sick fund he had lived in Kielce, where he had opened a dental clinic. And figuring there as a doctor-dentist, he obtained credit from the local merchants, from whom he took various goods and clothes on bills of exchange.
Coming to Dąbrowa to his new post, he "healed" the sick fund's patients and pulled the teeth of the sick fund's members.
Meanwhile the police received information that the "dentist" Szwarc was at the same time a capable swindler. On the strength of this information Szwarc was arrested in Dąbrowa on Saturday at 2 o'clock at night.
When the police came in to him at night, Szwarc had only just arrived from Kraków, where he had spent New Year's Eve (Sylwester). At first he wanted to make the police understand[?] that [—] they were probably making a mistake, but at the investigation office he admitted that all the documents — even those from the ministry concerning engaging in dental practice — were forged and that he had never been a dentist.
In Szwarc's flat they found all the goods and clothes he had taken from the Kielce merchants; they also found a revolver on him.
“Maccabi” for Sport Propaganda

[Sosnowiec — sport, Zionism.]
In connection with the "Maccabi Week" proclaimed by the Maccabi World Union, the board of the local "Maccabi" undertook to carry out a series of events to propagate the idea of sport.
On Tuesday morning an "academy" (festive assembly) took place in the "Pałac". On the presidium: Dr. Melodysta[?], Dr. Troppauer[?], Markus Hamburger, Adolf Berowicz[?], Ze'ev Manes, Sh. Feldman, M. Lancman and others. Above them the flags of Betar, "Maccabi" and "Hashomer Hatzair".
The meeting is opened by Mr. Hamburger; the orchestra of the Będzin "Hakoach" plays the Polish anthem, and the first word goes to Dr. Melodysta[?], who delivers a Yiddish speech in which he points out the importance of sports development among the Jewish people. But — the speaker exclaims — we must not content ourselves with small bands of Maccabi members in closed associations[?]; the entire Jewish people must develop physically in order to be able to answer the various "White Papers" and decrees against the upbuilding[?] of the Jewish people, of the Jewish land.
Then the floor goes to Dr. K. Troppauer[?], who reads a lecture on sports culture in general and among Jews in particular.
A short but "fiery" speech is delivered by Mr. Feldman, who calls for enrolling en masse in the ranks of "Maccabi".
The orchestra plays "Hatikvah" and the meeting is closed.
Later a procession formed, in which all the national organisations took part with their flags at the head.
While marching through the streets the procession was disturbed by the police.
A Terrible Accident at the Railway Station

[Sosnowiec — accident.]
On Saturday night, late in the evening, a terrible accident happened at the local railway station, of which the 34-year-old railway worker Józan[?] fell victim.
Józan was working on the line. At that moment a manoeuvring locomotive passed through and cut off both of the worker's legs.
The Vanished Trunk Has Been Found..

[Dąbrowa / Sosnowiec — crime.]
In the month of Listopad (November) a trunk with clothes was dispatched from the railway station in Dąbrowa to Stryj. The trunk, however, was stolen on the way[?], at the station in Strzemieszyce[?].
On the order of the local investigation office the police carried out searches, and part of the stolen things were found.
The thieves and the buyers have been arrested.
The 500 [złoty note] betrayed him... "The deeds of the sons the fathers inherited."

Dr. Feichel [?] in "Zheryk" [?] employed as a servant an 18-year-old Christian, the son of a shoemaker from "Dambeinen" [?]. The servant found favour with the doctor, and the latter entrusted him with everything, even the cash box with money.
Once, when the doctor had gone out of the house [?], the "faithful" servant lad took the cash box, from which he took out 2,000 zł. When the theft was reported to the police, the servant denied it flatly ("denied stone and bone"). The father became [furious?] ("vaiger" [?]) and [railed?] at the doctor, who had performed the "good deed" of suspecting his son of having stolen 2,000 zł.
The police, having no clear proof, had treated the matter as closed; but the thief himself revealed the theft by changing a 500-zł banknote. Soon afterwards the police found at the shoemaker's, in a stocking [?], a second 500-zł banknote.
This week the "honest" family stood before the local District Court, which sentenced the servant to one year in prison, his father to 6 months and a second [?] brother to 3 months in prison.
—o—
Exhibition against tuberculosis.
This week an exhibition against tuberculosis was opened here. The opening took place in the presence of representatives of the authorities, doctors, etc.
The exhibition will be open for 10 days. Admission only 20 gr.
—o—
Only 4 days a week.
At the "Klimontów" coal mine, working time has been reduced as of the 1st of this month; work is now done only 4 days a week.
—o—
A Zionist student association founded
On Sunday the founding meeting of the Zionist student association "HaShachar" took place in the premises of the Zionist Organization.
The meeting was opened by the student Wolf Shmitshag [?], and the floor was given to stud. Pomerantz [?] (Kraków), who described the sad situation of Jewish students in various countries and called on all Zionist academics to organize and to help strengthen the national idea, and also to take part in the work for Eretz Israel.
After the lecture there was a short discussion; a board was elected consisting of the following persons: stud. Yosef Langman [?] (president), B. Fentser [?] (vice-pres.), Buksbaum (treasurer), Miss Proskurowska [?] (secr.), A. Psherghi [?] and A. Safer.
Audit committee: Ch. Shmitshag [?], Miss Lubelska, Miss Hamburger.
—o—
From the board of the Jewish "Artisans' Association" in Sosnowiec
We have been asked to announce:
In connection with the rumours that some persons have spread in Sosnowiec about our president Mr. A. Apetowski [?], we state that all such rumours are false and groundless and were intended only to compromise Mr. A. Apetowski [?], who works tirelessly for the good of our association.
At the same time we declare that the association's leadership, at its meeting of the 6th of this month, fully expressed its solidarity with the tactics of President Apetowski [?], who, as always, acted in the interests of the association; and those guilty of provoking incidents have been duly punished by the association's court of honour.
