From the Chamber of Commerce.
We are asked to inform the firms concerned that, in connection with applications for permits to import prohibited goods in the year 1931, they must send the Chamber of Commerce, together with the application, a copy of the [trade] licence (patent) for 1931 certified by a notary or by the Chamber of Commerce. The fee for this is a stamp of 50 gr.
At the same time the Chamber of Commerce remarks that when requesting certificates for foreign visas[?] one must enclose a copy of the trade licence.
—o—
Changes in court posts.
The vice-president of the local district court, Mr. Klank[?], is leaving his post and is being appointed to the same post in Warsaw. The presidency of the criminal division will be taken over by Judge Kladnicki[?].
Appointed as judges at the local district court will be: Mr. Grochowicz[?], hitherto deputy prosecutor; Henryk Jańczewski, chairman of the labour court; and Rylski[?], judge of the town of Sosnowiec.
As chairman of the labour court, Mr. Ostrowski, hitherto judge in Dąbrowa, will be appointed.
—o—
Investigation into a scandal at the gmina.
As we have already written, several taxpayers[?] made a scandal at the gmina [Jewish community office] because their tax debts[?] had been handed over to the magistrate [municipality].
The kehilla board handed the scandal-makers over to the court.
The court passed the matter on to the public prosecutor's office.
In this connection the office clerks, Messrs. Lewenhof[?], Kirszenbaum and Skrobek[?], were questioned by the police.
—o—
Today — the "Voice of Water"... [pun on "kol mevaser", 'a herald's voice']
This evening the water commission will hold a meeting at which the price of water for consumers will be fixed.

General meeting of the Craftsmen's Association.
Next Sunday the annual general meeting of the members of the Craftsmen's Association will take place in its own premises.
Very important points of great interest to craftsmen will be discussed
Councillor Gutman (Kielce) and Councillor Bach[?] (Częstochowa) will take part in the meeting.
It is worth noting that for the first time the annual meeting is taking place at the proper date.

The number of unemployed grows.
Another 790 workers laid off.
At the H. Dietel factory in Sosnowiec all the workers, 790 men in number, were dismissed on Saturday.
The reduction is connected with the economic crisis prevailing in the country.

Tragic suicide.
Threw himself 280 metres deep
In the bookkeeping office of Count Renard the 55-year-old Nalewicz[?] had worked for a number of years.
Several weeks ago Nalewicz[?] was dismissed from his post, but after many requests he was taken on as night watchman of the works
Last Saturday at 12 midnight Nalewicz[?], intending to commit suicide, jumped into the "Jan" coal-mine shaft to a depth of 280 metres.
Nalewicz's[?] body was smashed to pieces.

Presidium of the "Gemilut Chesed" fund.
On Sunday the new board of the local "Gemilut Chesed" [interest-free loan] fund held a meeting at which the presidium was constituted.
Re-elected as president was Mr. L. Segal[?]; vice-president — Mr. Reuven Czapnik[?]; and treasurer — Mr. Yisrael Michal Berkowicz.
—o—
"Bank Kupiecki" answers the "White Paper".
The board of the local "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank], in answer to the "White Paper" [the 1930 Passfield White Paper], has inscribed the bank in the Golden Book [of the Jewish National Fund].
—o—
As in the "good" times...
This week[?] one could see long "ogonki" [queues] of unemployed people receiving food products and other relief.
The "ogonek" stretched from Dęblińska Street to the middle of 3 Maja Street.
—o—
A kitchen opened for the poor.
The local magistrate, together with the Christian "Dobroczynność" [charity society], has opened a kitchen for the unemployed.
Up to 100 lunches a day will be served from the kitchen.

The number of [trade] licences bought
in Zagłębie[?] reaches up to 80 per cent. The industrialists and merchants bought their licences almost[?] on time; only market-stall keepers, pedlars, held back, as they are unable to buy the required licences.
—o—
A first-class restaurant.
This week, with the consent of the railway directorate in Warsaw, a first-class restaurant was opened at the local railway station.
Such a restaurant existed until the outbreak of the war.
—o—
Office hours at the magistrate extended[?].
The commissioner of the magistrate, Mr. Kuśniak, has ordered that all magistrate departments be closed at 1 p.m. and after that time not receive any applicants whatsoever.
A Railway Watchman Attacked

[Zagłębie — crime.] At the Gołonóg station persons attacked the railway watchman and took a fur coat from him.
One of the attackers has been arrested.

Meeting of the Gemilut Hasadim Fund in Kozłów
[Kozłów — welfare and free-loan institutions.] Last week the annual general meeting took place of the members of the local Gemilut Hasadim [interest-free loan] fund and rescue committee “Tovat Ahim”, which has existed for 5 years now as the only Jewish credit and aid institution.
Secretary Mr. Goliw gives a report on the activity for the year 1930, from which it can be seen that despite the terrible crisis that prevails today the fund conducts a very widely branched activity. During the year over 300 interest-free loans were issued for a sum of 64,487 zł. Relief grants were also distributed to the needy; the fund literally saved many families from complete ruin.
How devoted the board is to the work of the fund can be seen from the fact that during the year under report a sum of 4 113 88 zł. [presumably 4,113.88] was raised from local collections, membership dues and a subsidy from the Jewish community (gmina). After deducting the administrative expenses and donations, 2,344 73 zł. [presumably 2,344.73] remained as basic capital.
After several resolutions were adopted, elections of a new board took place, and the following board was elected unanimously: Mansa[?], Goliw, Dafner, Rapaport, Goldfrajns[?], Zonenberg[?] and Berlinski. Audit committee: S. Slobocki and S.[?] Drambiorz[?].
After thanks were expressed to the old board as well as to the “Joint” [JDC] representative in Warsaw, Mr. Gitterman, for his support of the fund, the meeting was closed.
Pinchas ze Eli.

Będzin kehilla council resolves to remove the shoḥet brought in by the „Agudah“

Interpellation by the [council] president Mr Gutman concerning the articles in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“.
After a break of almost a year the Będzin kehilla council was called to a meeting on Wednesday evening. At this urgent meeting, God forbid, the urgency of creating relief actions, of opening cheap kitchens to ease the bitter want the broad Jewish masses are now living through, was not discussed — no, for such questions it is not worth „riding on the ice“[?]; instead, for 4 hours it was „deliberated“[?] how to remove from the slaughterhouse the young shoḥet whom the rabbi and 2 Agudah „dozors“ [kehilla board members] had „smuggled“ into the slaughterhouse against the will of the majority of the kehilla administration.
The „mood“ at the meeting was a k.s.sh.[?]. Especially when the interested party, the butchers, spoke[?] plain „language“ — thanks to which it became clear how kehilla representatives barter away kehilla interests...
At 9 o'clock the president of the council, Mr Gutman, opens the meeting. After the reading of the agenda he turns to the president of the administration, R' Abraham Lichter, asking him to give explanations regarding the accusation in the articles in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ against the kehilla administration concerning the young shoḥet.
R' Abraham Lichter explains that to the interpellation put by the administration member Mr Reinski[?]. The latter, instead of the requested answer, tells the „story“ of how the shoḥet question became topical: that the first who demanded a shoḥet as long as 2 years ago was the dozor Mr Goldsztajn, and now — he says — when the [—][?] did it, so that a quarrel flared up around the matter, it was permitted, in order „to calm tempers“, that the [—] shoḥet should learn „practice“ in the Będzin slaughterhouse...
The dozor Mr Buchheitz[?] relates that when people in town began to murmur that the Agudah had engaged a stranger as shoḥet, he went with several respectable householders to the rabbi and proposed to him that in taking on a shoḥet priority should go to the son of the late R' Mordechai the shoḥet. To this the rabbi replied that „the shoḥet question is not topical at all“. But — says Mr Buchheitz — when a shoḥet from „that crowd“ had to be installed... then the shoḥet affair is topical after all...
The „finest deeds“ done in the kehilla were recounted by the dozors Lichter and[?] Goldsztajn. Through them the whole ratting-about that had gone on around the shoḥet question was exposed.
With statistical figures Mr Lichter showed that the shechita revenue had dropped by 50 percent, the [local?] treasury is empty, pensions are not being paid — and yet the ringleaders of the kehilla had no more urgent matter than to provide the town with a stranger as shoḥet.
Tempers flare, the air smells of gunpowder, butchers threaten, and it looks as if any moment now the meeting will be broken up.
At last it becomes calmer; on the question speak P.G.S.[?] M. Henpel[?] and the dozor Bżykowski[?], and they proceed to the vote on the motions submitted.
By a majority of votes the proposal of P.G.S.[?] Icchak Aron Landau is adopted, that because of the opposition of council members the shoḥet question be dealt with at another meeting, and in the meantime the „nominated“[?] shoḥet be removed from the slaughterhouse.
After the vote Mr Reinski was angry with his „co-religionists“ [faction colleagues] for voting for Landau's proposal.
At half past midnight, in an „elevated mood“, the meeting is closed.

For Three Days Thousands of Workers Besieged the Zawiercie Factory.

[Zawiercie — labour and the crisis.] In the "Zawiercie" factory 7000 workers were employed until not long ago; now 2000 workers work there. Recently a reduction was started again; the want there is very great, the workers feed on potato peelings. Because the factory management decided to dismiss another 600 workers, the workers held a meeting and resolved to agree to a reduction in working days, provided no one was dismissed. The factory management did not agree to this. The workers therefore resolved not to leave the factory and also not to start work. For three days and three nights the workers sat in the factory by the machines and did not leave the yard; several of the workers fainted from hunger, and terrible scenes took place.
Only after the three days of hunger, after the intervention of the government, was the strike liquidated.
A Symbol of the Present Times... A Ruined Merchant Asks to Be Rescued

[Żarki — distress and an appeal.] From Żarki we have received from a former big merchant of that town the following heart-rending letter for publication in our paper.
The content of the letter is:
Honoured Mr Editor! At the last moment, when I and my wife with 2 small children are about to perish from want, I turn to you with a great request that you help us out of our bitter situation.
Mr Editor! We ask of you to be so kind as to raise the alarm in the paper that a family which is going under is in great need of help, and whoever can help should be so kind as to hand in his donation at the editorial office.
I ask you not to publish my name, because only a short while ago I was a big merchant, but the crisis has so drained [?] me. With a few hundred złoty I can still be rescued."
So let the cry for help not remain "a voice crying in the wilderness", but let everyone who has the means contribute for the benefit of the family.

A Man Tried to Poison His Wife and Child. For This He Will Sit 15 Years in Prison

[Sosnowiec — the court.] The family tragedy began back in 1926 in the village of "Giepielka" [?] beyond "Głogów" [?]. In that village lived a young Christian couple. Some months after the wedding the husband supposedly became nervous and every day "delighted" his wife with a "nervous concert".
One day the husband informed his wife that, since he had no means of living, she should go to her parents and stay there until he found work.
The wife, without the slightest suspicion that her faithful husband had a mistress [kochanka], followed the advice and went home to her parents in the Kresy.
While at her parents' the wife constantly wrote letters to her husband, to whom she gave the good tidings that a child would soon be born to them. In reply to her love letters, after several weeks of waiting, she received a letter from her husband, who informed her of the whole "good" [?]...
Meanwhile the woman gave birth to a child, and some weeks later she decided to travel with the child to her home. When she came to her husband he received her not too badly, but his "kha-" [?; probably his mistress] was working out plans how to get rid of [?] her together with the child.
Once, in the middle of a meal, the woman was suddenly seized by strong pains, and the doctor whom neighbours brought established that the husband had poured arsenic into her plate [?].
This week the murderer stood before the Sosnowiec court, which sentenced him to 15 years of hard prison.

Theatre Notes

Last Monday a literary evening took place at the 'Corso' with the participation of Löwenstein, Nochimow and Wygodzki.
The first to appear was Löwenstein, in a fragment of Andreyev's 'The Seven Who Were Hanged', in the role of Mishka Tsiganok.
Löwenstein is no new face on the Yiddish stage; he already has a significant[?] stage past behind him. In the above role Löwenstein was excellent, sufficiently forceful, with good diction, and showed that he can take an important place in the Yiddish theatre family.
Also very successful were A. Blok's 'The Twelve' and Halpern's 'The Street Drummer'[?], which Löwenstein interpreted well, giving them at the same time a fine artistic colouring.
Nochimow was very successful in the fragments of 'At Night in the Old Market-Place'. His acting shows training and a fine artistic culture; his dynamics were not exaggerated and his diction good.
Besides this Nochimow recited with understanding a fragment of Greenberg's 'Mefisto' and 'Nacht-sfotim'[?] by I. Manger.
St. Wygodzki read his already well-known poem 'Potemkin'.
This poem stands on a very high artistic level and has aroused great attention in Polish literary circles. Wygodzki has thereby confirmed that his poetic talent is a fact that can no longer be contested.
Wygodzki also read the poems 'Dactyloscope' and 'Lynching'[?], which are imbued with a revolutionary spirit and were printed in their time in 'Miesięcznik Literacki', the organ of the Polish proletarian trend, of which Wygodzki is a respected contributor.
Finally Löwenstein and Nochimow masterfully performed the 'Ekster[?] Ballad' by I. Manger.
The evening was very impressive and the artists were rewarded with strong applause.
Sh. R.

The Interest-Free Loan Funds

(Why are people indifferent to the rescue institutions? What must be done to revive them?)
Among us people groan without pause that the times are bitter and that a livelihood is a very, very scarce article, almost a rarity — and yet, yet nobody thinks at all of doing something substantial, something practical that would be able to improve the economic situation.
We know that the pessimists will come and assert with proofs — not only will they say that things are not good, but they will convince us that the situation is so uncomfortable, so joyless, that there is no remedy for it, and that therefore one must dwell on this unpleasant[?] situation, on the grey reality.
First of all we must not lose heart; we must not remain dejected, helpless, because that does great, great harm; it paralyses the mind — and to fold one's hands and say that we have already fallen, that we are doomed[?] to suffer and to perish[?] — that is the greatest failing, and we must not allow it, as long as we are a people, as long as we want to live in the world on an equal footing with others.
We are, after all, the true stiff-necked people, and we hold that for a people this is a great virtue, because with tenacity, with obstinacy, with stubbornness one can achieve a great deal as a national body. When a people stands up for its national interests, when it is a matter of improving its situation, it must be stubborn, it must be tenacious; in that way it can achieve much for itself.
To let one's hands drop and say 'I am already lost, I am already done for[?]' certainly has no purpose, because that only helps peoples[?] to ruin what is already in a catastrophic state, in a dangerous condition.
If you talk to ordinary people you learn that the American crisis has found a great echo here in Poland as well, because hundreds of thousands of Jewish families here lived on the American dollars that were regularly sent here; and now, since things are very bad over there, these monies have been reduced, and every month fewer dollars arrive in Poland.
Of course this weighs heavily on our own already bad times, and we must, willy-nilly[?], reckon with the facts that have occurred, which destroy the life of many strata of the population that lived exclusively from their American relatives.
But despite all that one cannot say that we have lost[?] all the worlds, that there is no remedy left at all, and that we must live out our few years in want and misery; and therefore we say: only do not lose courage, only do not remain helpless, only do not lose one's balance.
Nowadays one can say the situation has become normal, to some extent balanced, because the thrifty[?] grosz plays a great role — and that is undoubtedly good, it is a great advantage. Today every citizen in Poland can calculate exactly how much expenditure and income he must have, because the złoty has great value, and credit is very hard to come by — credit that not long ago people used to throw around like peas. People who possess minimal capital in cash get by somehow[?]; the trouble is only that they cannot obtain loans and therefore cannot climb to a higher level.
It seems that at such a time a great role is played by the system of gemilut chesed (interest-free lending), which among us Jews has been since ancient times one of the finest traditions, one of the finest virtues. It is no trifle, the role that gemilut chesed has played among Jews in its various epochs. How much praise we find in our old holy books for those who engage in gemilut chesed; and even now our American brethren have had so much sense and understanding to address this problem. It is no secret to anyone that the 'gemilut chasadim' funds were not only founded[?] by American Jews, but their entire upkeep was theirs; they breathed their spirit into them, and therefore they have no small merit towards their Polish brethren. With these institutions they erected the finest monuments to themselves. With the gemilut chasadim funds they immortalised and glorified their good deeds.
And if [money] has become such a dear article, then the gemilut chasadim funds ought to play one of the most important roles; but unfortunately we must say that the interest in them is weak, indifferent. Here we see, e.g.[?], that in Sosnowiec a general meeting of the institution took place — a handful of people came, so few that if you counted them on your fingers you would have fingers left over. The question arises: what is this? What is the reason that, although the gemilut chasadim funds are so badly needed nowadays, people remain indifferent to them? Can there be two opinions that we must maintain these useful institutions, so topical at the present moment? We see, after all, how people make a living from the minimal sums they take[?] from the gemilut chasadim funds; so there is no doubt whatsoever that we need these institutions as never before, and therefore the reason must be found: since[?] we must have the rescue institutions, why should the people not take an interest in them? Hundreds and thousands of ordinary people are helped by the lent, interest-free[?] loans.
It follows, then, that all the gemilut chasadim funds in the Zagłębie towns must be strengthened. One must see to it that the institutions become the real factors in our hard life, and to that end proper supervision must also be carried out everywhere. Thus one must remove those who bring no benefit, and those who stand[?] around them only so that the seat is occupied... From those who stand[?] around the institutions one must get benefit, and if they do not give it, let them give up their place to others. In any case, around the institutions must gather clean people, with clean hands and an idealistic conscience. And just as we must have devoted, capable people, so must we see to it that the institutions are represented by respected and well-liked representatives, because after all one operates here with money, where so much decency and caution is required.
We know, after all, that in many towns the institutions began to sink only because the system of favouritism ('protekcja') played a significant role. Whoever had protekcja received money, even in the names of dead people, and did not need to repay; whereas without protekcja one got a 'vogs'[?]...
Relying on such slippery paths, the institution became a little shop for individuals, with the stamp in a private pocket, and that person decided the fate of the institution and of the member just as it pleased him.
The gemilut chasadim institutions must be regarded in the full sense[?], in their importance and value; around them must gather the most capable communal workers, who have the ability to bring these useful institutions to a proper state — and then the working capital can be increased too, because in the end our patrons will come and will in any case support such useful rescue institutions, for which the people[?] — the lower strata of the population — are waiting.
We also possess a number of well-off cooperative (communal) banks, which will also be able to help out at the given moment. And then America will not stand aloof either; our American brethren too will not abandon us as soon as they see that we stand at the work of relief.
So one must breathe a living spirit into the institutions; they must be the expression of the people and have one single aim: in an honest, non-partisan way, not to let fall anyone who needs a loan with which he can earn his living.

What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec — weekly feuilleton.] Rendered by Ben Amotz.

A story with 30 dollars..
— Heard the story of the 30 dollars yet?
— No — I answer innocently.
— There is — my informant tells me — in Będzin an old Jewish woman who saved every grosz and gathered herself thirty dollars. And this sum she, the little old woman, kept for a "purpose" — after all, one does not live forever; when the hour comes she should not have to depend on other people's charity or on the Jewish kehilla: with her own money, with her own gathered groszy, she should be buried after a hundred and twenty years.
And since a sinful mortal does not know [printed "heyst", for "veyst"] when "the time will come", she, the little old woman that is, resolved to hand over the "capital" in good time to one of the Chevra Kadisha [burial society] and be done with the matter...
No sooner said than done: a communal activist presented himself to her who, with eyes glazed toward heaven, took the "apotiki" [deposit] from the old woman and wished her that "she should yet live to go out to meet the Messiah"; only if, God forbid, not — he would bury her [see her off] to the other world "with all the best"...
The gabbai, by the way a "qualified" Będzin communal activist, "buried" the banknotes in his pocket and quietly prayed that his "client" should finish the business as quickly as possible...
But women have nine measures of talk; when it came to a chat, the "candidate for the other world" told her acquaintances that she had already closed the transaction with the Chevra Kadisha and got a burden off her head...
As the devil would have it, the news reached the Chevra Kadisha gabbaim, R' Mendel Ferens and R' Meir Beri, who investigated the matter and after "nine kabs" [great trouble] finally got the thirty dollars out of the Będzin communal activist...

A "geste" by a communal activist
A similar story — we are told — happened in Dąbrowa. The difference is this: the Będzin communal activist dealt in "old goods", and the communal activist of Dąbrowa dealt in young goods...
There is in Dąbrowa a rich Jew, one who busies himself with communal needs, travels to the congresses of the "Council of Torah Sages", a whole "somebody" in the "Agudah", fights for the strengthening of religion with as much "fire" as [he fights] the Jewish shopkeepers in his bazaar — in a word, the "olive oil" [the cream] of Dąbrowa.
Yes, I forgot the main thing. The Dąbrowa representative of the "Council of Torah Sages" also spread his wings over the poor children who are raised there, poor things, in the local "Talmud Torah".
And here, at the "Talmud Torah" itself, almost the same thing happened as is told in "Chad Gadya": ve-ata — the communal activist came to the magistrate's office [town hall] to pay his "podatki" [taxes], and he settled them, the taxes that is, with the subsidy for the Talmud Torah; and to the Talmud Torah he, the communal activist that is, issued promissory notes that are to fall due only at harvest time...
— Say what you will, such a "geste" for Talmud Torah children nowadays deserves to be made public...

The new "epidemic"
After the influenza epidemic, a new "epidemic" has flared up in our little town, in Będzin itself — a theatre epidemic.
When you go out into the street in the morning you are met by huge, screaming posters, announcing the glad tidings that for the first time in Będzin there will be performed, under the direction of Moshe Kvitsh...
The "artistes" are styled with foreign names; the poster notes that "after the third bell the doors will be closed" — as if, so that the simple public should think, artistes from America had come down to Będzin...
Well, one cannot make great complaints against the "artistes", since [printed "vorut"] it is a well-known matter, a familiar thing, that Yiddish theatre is "hefker petrushka" [a free-for-all]: whoever can just shout loudly and weep as if at the graves of the forefathers — he plays theatre.
To blame, though, are our representatives of the institutions, who seek income from such theatre performances — "umshteyns-gezogt"[?] [unclear expression, probably "pardon the expression"], they, our communal activists, must understand that kehilla money is not ownerless; if one arranges some "impreza" [event] in order to raise income, one must first of all give oneself an account of whom one "goes to the table" with, and what the ticket-buyers will get for their hard-earned guldens [złoty]...
— Gentlemen communal activists! This lawlessness must stop at last!...

Consistency..
"...What we are, we are, but Jews we are" — the same verse can be said about the Będzin "Tseirei Emunei [Yisrael]": what they are — they are, but "consistent" they are.
A Ger Hasid told us this story. In the ranks of the "Tseirei Emunei" there is a young man who is learning to write. Well, what's to be done about it? But the trouble is that the young man is learning not with a male teacher but, of all things, with... one of the fair sex, simply a woman teacher...
When the "Tseirei Emunei" found out about it, they warned their comrade to break off the lessons with the woman teacher, and if not — out of the camp!
The "father's son" and the father himself began to bang their fists: How can it be? Where is respect — to rebel against [printed "begn", for "kegn"] the son of such a father, a dozór [kehilla board member] to boot! — and began threatening with the rabbi and with the rebbe too, with the whole array of war tactics[?].
But the "heroic" youngsters are not frightened in the least, and they do not change their decision. We — they say — have our own opinion, and no fear of... and the proof: our rebellion in the last Sejm elections is the best answer..
How[?] the "cultural" struggle will end is hard to say, but one thing is clear: the Będzin "Tseirei Emunei" will not let anyone blow into their porridge [won't be pushed around]..

A topic that does not grow old..
How many times has this matter been touched upon already? How much pain and suffering has it already caused us. And yet, and yet we are still only at "aleph", have absolutely not moved from the spot; it is as it was, [—] our shmendriks do not change their opinion regarding the education of their daughters. "One can — they say — be right with God and with people, and send the daughters to non-Jewish schools"...
There is in Sosnowiec a Jewish girls' gymnasium which, by the way, stands at the first rank in the pedagogical sense, and it also gives what Jewish mothers long for [printed "khibshn zikh"[?]]:
— a matura with rights [state-recognised matriculation]..
Nevertheless it is much more "convenient" for Jewish fathers and mothers to send their daughters to..
One of the gymnasium's activists complains to us: things are [printed "s'in"] — he says — "the waters have come up to the soul"; the fate of the school interests none of the Jewish parents. The financial situation — a bad one, enemies within and without; the "Agudah" parents complain that the school is a nationalist one, and the "nationalist" "parents" are angry in turn — why does the school teach too much Hebrew..
— A topic that never grows old..
"Salvations and Consolations" for the Jews — (From the Sejm rostrum the world learns how well off we are in Poland.)

[Politics — the Sejm, Polish Jewry, the middle class, Zagłębie.] (From the Sejm rostrum the world learns how well off we are in Poland.)
It was interesting last week to read a report of a Sejm session at which the PPS man [member of the Polish Socialist Party] Piotrowski, among other things, also touched on the merchants' question and came to the conclusion that the tax screw is unbearable and that the biggest and finest firms have gone off the stage.
I read and do not believe my eyes — what am I reading? From whom are such words heard? From a PPS man? From a socialist, who never cares about the bourgeois element? Is it possible that they too already see how far [printed "וויים" for "ווייט"] the middle class is oppressed? How hard the tax screw presses on it? Can the mind grasp this?
But if the mind cannot grasp this, then the further debate is altogether incomprehensible, in which hostile interjections are hurled at him by none other than "our" deputy Wacław Wiślicki — who knows of nothing, who, poor man, is innocent as a lamb ["owes God his soul"], who looks upon all this as upon a riddle, as upon a wonder.
And the socialist goes on, with figures in hand, and proves in black and white that in the year 1928, 228 bankruptcies were declared, in the year 1929 — 516, and in the first 3 quarters of the year 1930 a whole 627 bankruptcies.
But "our" deputy apparently does not believe any of this, and the socialist has to tell him: "Why, you cannot even show your face to your voters on Nalewki [the Jewish street of Warsaw], because there businesses are closing en masse all the time. In the last 3 months bills of exchange for 114 million zl. were protested, and at the same time the privileged taxpayers owe millions of zl. in taxes, etc."
Well, go on, say it yourselves: is it not astonishing? Is this not the days of the Messiah, that a socialist, who is altogether against the bourgeoisie, should defend the middle class, while "our" deputy should there [?] deny it by stone and bone?
Of course, for the government this is the best proof that the handful of oppressed Jews in Poland are doing fine and dandy. A proof — that Wiślicki did not let a bad word be uttered. Besides, one must not forget — the government will say — that Wiślicki is not just anybody, and if the situation were not good he would know it very well, for he is after all the president of the Central Union of Jewish Merchants, where Jewish groans and pains would find an echo, if only there were any; and since your deputy Wiślicki — the government will surely say — says not a word and does not let anyone else speak either, that is surely the best sign that with you Jews everything is in the best of order...
And who knows, perhaps in their place we would not have been better either, for after all the government does not want to take on the task of going to check who is not well off; besides, it also has the right rather to believe its own brother, the president of an authoritative institution, than some socialist or other who is far from Jewish life, far from Jewish sufferings, far from Jewish interests.
Well, say, could one not have been well amused by such a comedy, if only it were not so tragic? Could one not have had a splendid time, if only it did not touch our sufferings and pains? Would we not have imagined it as the tales of the Thousand and One Nights, if we had not watched all this with our own eyes? If we had not heard it with our own ears and if we had not felt it on our own shoulders?
Yes, and we thought that at least all Jews in Poland know how threatening our situation is, how dangerous and catastrophic the position of the middle class and the lower strata of the population is in the present critical time — and here it turns out that even "our" Sejm representative knows nothing of all this. Apparently the cup of our bitter drops is still not enough for the "Jewish" deputy Wacław Wiślicki. It seems that Nalewki and the other Jewish quarters in Warsaw do not interest him in the least, and these "dzielnice" [Polish: districts] he does not want to look at with his own eyes.
But here in Zagłębie too the call of his hasidim [followers] was heard, who promised us mountains and hills as soon as we sent him into the Sejm — and where are they now, those who trampled on our feelings so forcefully? Why do they not come to us now? Why do they not show us now how the Jewish situation in Poland has suddenly become so good? By what, and since when, has it improved so much? Which taxes have been remitted and reduced for those who to this very day are under the hard pressure of the tax screw? And what, in general, does the happiness in Poland consist of for us Jews after the Sejm elections? Perhaps the happiness consists in the fact that here in Zagłębie there are more and more bankruptcies, and ever more shops are emptying, so that in the central streets of the big towns there are more and more closed businesses, and manufacturing keeps stopping, and the workshops cease to operate — is this to be called happiness? And when the craftsmen wander about without a scrap of work, and the poor worker and small trader and pedlar all starve together — is this hunger-unity perhaps to be called happiness?
And if all this is too little, if there is nothing with which to get through the day; if present-day Jewish life in Poland is as hard as the parting of the Red Sea — he must, on top of it all, rack his brains how he may somehow manage that the bailiff [tax/debt executor] should not come to take away the bench on which he still sits today.
Is it really possible that neither the Warsaw nor the Zagłębie Wiślickis should see all this? Very well, in Warsaw the Wiślickis have the choice not to see what is happening among their impoverished brethren: out of pity, out of great compassion, out of fear lest their tender hearts be broken, they run away from their brethren, they do not want to find themselves within their four cubits. On the other hand, this surely cannot be said of Wiślicki's devoted comrades in Zagłębie, who willy-nilly do come close to their brethren; however far they may wish to be from them, they are nevertheless near. True, they do not want to come and look at the poverty in their cellars and attic rooms, but they nevertheless see their pains every day and every week; they must, after all, encounter this poverty every day. Tell us [printed "זאגן מיר"], does a man of Będzin or of Sosnowiec, of Dąbrowa or of Zawiercie not see day by day the poverty and the oppression of his suffering brothers and sisters? Do we not already see today impoverished people who only yesterday were merchants and traders and craftsmen, who played the role of well-to-do people? Does this round-dance [korowód] not pass before our eyes every day, in an ever darker state?
Is it then possible that people should have eyes and not see all this? Can one understand that people who hear should not hear the sounds of this terrible dance of death? And if they do not hear it, if their ears are deafened to the mournful sounds, how then do they see the happiness? How do they [printed "מאס"] explain the present "salvations and consolations" for the Jews in Poland? Go on, let them tell us: how is it that we are suddenly so well off?
R. Let.
I'll Become a Shochet... (Topical Satire)

[Satirical poem — kehilla, ritual slaughter.] (Topical satire.)
Don't you disturb me
from becoming a shochet [ritual slaughterer],
it's a wonderful [?] affair,
a possession for ever.

A pension, a fine one,
and [be?] a "Moreinu" [honorific title] to me,
everywhere I'll enjoy [?]
the fattest morsel.

Who kehilla, what kehilla:
little people give [?] money [?],
a hole in the till?
Half is mine and half is yours.

And a fact took place —
they were nabbed.
Hush, hush, let there be quiet,
nobody, after all, wants to talk.

But late, after all, [in the] week [?]
it came out onto the surface [?]:
"This mustn't be let off [?],
he'll remember it [?]".

— Just look at the uproar,
they're shouting up to the sky,
you'll drive me out?
A shochet I'll stay, that's that!
Yama.
Hersh Mekhl Prepares for the Exam

[Feuilleton — humoresque; artisans.] By Y. Oberżanek.
What am I? Oy, alas and woe is me — a ladies' tailor, that's what I am.
A ladies' tailor! Do you know what a ladies' tailor is? Hardly you, or[?] thousands of other men, know what such a thing is — a ladies' tailor.
In the world there are seventy nations, and the worst nation is women; there are dozens of trades in the world, and the worst trade is a tailor, and the worst of all tailors is — a ladies' tailor.
Can you picture it: a man[?], a real[?] "khorazzane[?] mężczyzna" (man), spends whole days turning around women; and women, you should know, are all different, of different "masses" and calibres: tall and narrow, short and fat. Women with figures and women without figures, women — dolls (lalki), and women — monstrosities[?]. Women with straight shoulders, and women — may it not grow on anyone — with a bit of a hump. Elegant women and women like logs. Women with waists and women "jednakowe" (all the same), i.e. "behind and above it's the same faith"...
It goes without saying that all of them — the tall and the short, with figures and without figures, straight shoulders and crooked shoulders, logs and hunchbacks — all, all want to be "Graces", all want to be "queens"[?] (królowe). Every one wants to be a "maske"[?] and a "serpentine"[?] — just take them and recast them in a mould.. Every one you must pay compliments, every one you must praise to the seventh heaven, to every one you must chant the very same hymn: oh, how chic (szykowna) you are in this outfit, it sits on you as on a plaster figure. [—][?] from you. Just take a look in the mirror, you look "pyszna" (splendid); other 18-year-old young ladies (panienki) can go and hide before you. You look "rozkoszna" (delightful) — a real[?] princess..
And this you must say to each one separately — this "formula". She may look in the new outfit like a demon, like a "black year" — you must shower her with compliments; to each one separately you must chant a separate Song of Songs.
And the fitting? Do you know what it means to fit a woman? For hours on end you must dance on your knees and smooth — a smooth upward and a tug downward; and meanwhile, as long as you are on your knees and smoothing, all that time you must pay attention and keep answering. She stands stiff as if she had swallowed a stick. She looks in the mirror, keeps turning, and as she turns, you must turn with her. And on top of all these troubles, she keeps talking. You get swollen knees. And she — talks. From the first fitting to the last, what do you think — how her husband fell (zakochał) head over heels in love with her. How long she's been married. How many children she has, how the "mężczyźni" (men) gape their eyes out at her, what troubles she had last summer in Krynica. And how her girlfriends (koleżanki) talk about her out of jealousy (zazdrosne), how they gossip about her things that aren't in the cards. Why she avoids "ladies' company" (damskie towarzystwo)[?]. That she would rather deal with ten "men" than with one "kobieta" (woman), what a rare "gospodyni" (housewife) she is, what troubles she has with the maids — not one decent one among them, and on top of that they soon get quite cosy[?] with the master of the house.
She talks and you [crawl?] on your knees, she talks and you smooth, and at the same time you must listen to her, answer and mumble along[?]: yes, no, so what[?], how so, quite right — your head spins, your legs tremble, your bones ache as after a bad flu, your temples pound — and she talks. She stands at the mirror and [—], and when[?] at last you have luckily finished, she wrinkles her little nose and purses her lips. What is it? She doesn't look "zgrabna" (shapely).
And so it is day in, day out, every day other women, with other figures. From dawn till evening crawling on your knees and smoothing without end, whole days listening to stories about the women's husbands and about their "pakha-dzegitses"[?], and about the maids who make eyes [—] — good for nothing but kapores.
That is a ladies' tailor.
All this would not have been so terrible. I would have accepted all the troubles and calamities with love. As you say: when the worm[?] gets into the horseradish… Probably it was written for me from the six days of Creation that I, Hersh Mekhl, should darken away my years among the women's "spódnice" (skirts)[?]; probably such a bitter decree went out against me.
I would have accepted all of it with love, if not for the latest decree — the exam decree.
Have you ever heard of a tailor at an exam?! Exams were for doctors, lawyers, engineers and other good-for-nothings — they needed exams; but that a tailor should have to pass an exam — who ever heard of such a thing, woe!
But we have a world with new "wynalazki" (inventions), a world with radios and other plagues; so they, today's fashionable contrivers[?], suddenly[?] took up a "wynalazek" (invention) — a "Chamber", a Chamber of Crafts, with idle loafers sitting like batlonim and dreaming up all kinds of "wisdoms"; and since our "Chamber" — may it not happen to you — suffers from "empty pockets", they make exams.
Now I am really preparing for the exam. You hear: I, Hersh Mekhl, am to have an exam. I don't eat, I don't sleep, I don't know what world I'm in. A trifle — an exam!.. For I don't know what else the "wise men" of the guild (cech) will ask me. Had I known what they would ask, I would somehow have managed; but[?] go and know what the fool has in mind...
Had they asked how a Jew like me gets, nowadays, enough for Shabbat or a living; with what [—][?] submissiveness[?] one must [approach?] the guilds[?], the "starsi" (guild elders), the deputy elders, all the "shmakhnes"[?] — I would have known what to answer. But the trouble is that about these things they don't ask; they have other "sakhmenish"[?] questions, for instance: in what year did the first "powstanie" (uprising) break out, what was the name of Berek Joselewicz's great-grandfather, who was the author of the guild law, and other such "wisdoms".
I ask you: is this a business for a Jew burdened with little "worms"[?] (small children), to start now torturing himself[?] "studying" "history" with "uprisings" and with Berek Joselewicz's great-grandfather, when my head is swollen from chasing[?] to raise a quarter's rent money? What good to me is the whole "Chamber" with its exams, what for[?]
In the world there are seventy nations and the worst nation is women. There are dozens of trades in the world and the worst trade is tailoring, and the worst of all tailors is — a ladies' tailor..
The Wonder and the Flag

(For Nahum Sokolow's 70th birthday.)
Today, Friday, 5 Shevat, Nahum Sokolow — as he liked to call himself by his initials, "N.S.", the Wonder or the Flag — turns 70.
Yes, nes — a wonder, a great wonder. A modest young man from Wyszogród, immersed[?] in an inward, extra-souled[?], but ultimately narrow ghetto world — and a steady climb, step by step, as a writer and statesman, almost as if on a dizzying staircase, through broad and great Europe, to the very top, until he became the man who "standeth before princes and kings"; [the man whom] ministers, ministers of ruling countries and peoples, [have] open their assemblies and write prefaces to their books, books on Jews and Jewish questions. Without governesses and without teachers, without a school and without a university, without any help, without any order and without any warmth — a Jewish prodigy (iluy), whose fate was to torment himself whole nights by a tallow candle in an attic room over a hard Gemara passage, until at last the ultimate ideal of father and mother would be fulfilled: "at eighteen to the wedding canopy", and later "a millstone around the neck", and after three years of kest [board at the father-in-law's] to attain, God willing, a rabbinical seat somewhere beyond Płock. And here — a real leap into the world: precise[?] knowledge of languages with their deep, deep souls and all their subtle folds, strolling through history and literatures like a master of the house, proud friendship with free spirits, penetration into the secrets of world politics. And if you like, social questions too, and economic and technical ones as well. So anti-Wyszogródian, so different, so foreign to that place, [so] distant[?].
And a second nes, a second wonder. Without hatred for Wyszogród and for Sokat[?] and for Płock, although[?] there he was nearly stifled as a prodigy, there he was nearly lost. No, the world must be received with a loving smile, the grandfather together with the grandchild, all generations, with or without the golden chain — a singular liberalism that comes from deep wisdom, an optimism as the result of a sceptical-rational view of everything and everyone. Judaism and worldliness, East and West, two worlds living in peace, two souls in one breast — and no[?] struggle.
And a third nes, a third wonder. With all that — not the [?] of a sceptic, not the irony and the life-motto of "it's all the same" — [but] enthusiasm, youthful enthusiasm, the enthusiasm of "the eagle's youth", of a writer of poems, enthusiasm body and soul, a contagious enthusiasm for a new cause, for a new, singular revolution, with hidden[?] hearts precisely in Wyszogród and in Sokat[?] and in Płock — enthusiasm for the Jewish ideal of revival, for Zionism.
And here the nes became also a flag. Not only of "Izraelita" and not even only of "Ha-Tsefira", [but] the leader of a mighty movement, a movement across the whole globe, in whose land the sun never sets[?]; a movement — a singular International, from which and for which the whole world has troubles, whose "hand is against every man and every man's hand against him"; a movement with a hundred thousand human lives and faiths, truly a giant in the world, a great giant — the Zionist World Organization. Nahum Sokolow takes the flag from the hands, from Herzl, from the spirit[?] of "perfecting the world under the kingdom of the Almighty" — repairing the world through a Jewish state.
What remains for us to wish? Long may Nahum Sokolow live for us, the wonder and the flag together. Long may he live for us — it is not only his own affair. In our life, in our Jewish life so hard in its fate, with its monstrous trials[?], [—] we need, more than all, more than any people in the world, miracles, wonders and flags. On our climbing[?] and [—] road, uphill, one must have something and someone to look up to.
Lewi Gutgeld.
How Shall We Be Heard?

One fears[?] that precisely in the present terrible crisis, when we must suffer threefold — from the general world crisis, from the Polish crisis, and specially as Jews — our heart-rending cry will be heard less.
For our present cry looks like the grief of mourners over a dead man ("bar-minan") on the day of Tisha b'Av, when everything around is wrapped in mourning. Who can then hear the sharp[?] cry of pain of the individual?
It used to be said that Jews are special creatures. To cry out their pain[?]. And there was a grain of truth in it. Even over a dead person we express our grief unusually loudly. And there is a belief among us that we can scream death away ("opshrayen a mes").
In the days of bloody pogroms, when Jews were like sheep before the armed[?] robbers and murderers, the only remedy was the outcry, which saved Jewish lives, goods and chattels.
Have we already become hoarse[?] from crying out today? It is just that nobody hears us, because everyone cries out, everyone groans. It is a general Tisha b'Av.
And yet our pain is sharper and more specific. It is a crisis within a crisis. The calamity is so horrible that even Jews, who are already used to troubles and disasters, cannot bear [it].
Our only demand now is: let us suffer equally with you!
In the Republic things are sad. The treasury (fiscus) has fallen, the working class is vegetating. So the government takes care: dozens of departments sit and rack their brains over how to raise the well-being of the population. Diplomatic negotiations are conducted, treaties are concluded with various states, transactions are made, loans are granted — everything is connected with the one great problem of the crisis. If the officials fall to daydreaming, there is a press that wakes them with all the bells. If they stray from the straight path, there is a parliament, workers' parties, which demand and shake and warn..
This whole complicated machine turns past us, does not notice us and does absolutely nothing for us, Jews. If it does remember us, it is only to do us harm, to make our situation still worse.
We are not peasants, not workers, not officials. We are merchants and artisans. As for crafts, such laws have already been made as will take them away from the coming Jewish generation. And meanwhile the Jew chokes at his workshop and is worn down[?].
But trade is, after all, like a thorn in the eye of the reformers. It is, after all, the scapegoat for all troubles and sufferings.
The Jew is not meant, God forbid; they merely want to bring the consumer closer to the producer, and if through this rapprochement the Jew gets squeezed in the middle — well, that is merely a law of nature.
That[?] is the calamity: that in the midst of the terrible crisis we, Jews, stand with our historic [—] and modern justice, equalization[?]. Otherwise we shall perish altogether.
Everyone suffers, everyone runs to save himself and, running, they trample over our heads and stifle us. We cry: stop, let us run and save ourselves together with you! But who hears us in the general outcry?
The present government has promised us something. Perhaps it really has good intentions. But it does not see people. It sees rules, theories; perhaps it does not know that the general remedy may be a deadly poison for us. How can we let it know? How shall the mourner be noticed in this all-surrounding[?] Tisha b'Av?
S. K.
I Can't Live With Her

[Society — marriage and divorce; article.] It has hardly ever happened that a woman should come to the editorial office to complain about her husband and tell of her bitter life — how she suffers, how she is tormented, how she is sick of life. On the other hand it happens all too often [?] that men who, because of various deeds, have to come to the editorial office to justify themselves for their deeds, open up their hearts and want to prove with dozens of examples how unhappy they are, how impossible it is for them to live with such a wife.

And you understand yourselves that this is why the women keep silent and the men talk: it is because the women are such shrews [?], they truly torment the men, and the men are delicacy and subtlety itself..

When it is "I can't live with him" — the world knows nothing about it. It goes with the woman to her grave. But when it is "I can't live with her" — all the consequences follow.

This very week, too, we had such an "unhappy" young man. A young fellow who was good for nothing, at most to be an assistant teacher [belfer] in an elementary heder — they gave him a dowry, board [kest] and a Jewish girl. Thirteen years later the young man already had 2 children, and the young wife had acquired, from 13 years of hard life, the "appropriate" complexion; no paint, rouge or the like covers the face — the young wife wilts in a narrow, dirty little room beside her 2 children, never eats her fill, while the husband roams [?] the street, meets women and comes to the conclusion that if he did not have a wife now he could take a dowry and pick himself a fresh face.

He comes home and feels that "he can't live with her". And if it happens that the young man — who as a bachelor thanked God that the girl was willing to exchange a word with him — has become something of a respectable person and begins to move among people, then his own home grows too narrow for him and his wife a burden. He is simply ashamed of her: she is not "presentable" [?] and "not interesting", although all those years she [—?] in many things — besides the fact that his wife has been locked in right by the cradle: pregnant, worn out [?], nursing, not sleeping whole nights and not seeing the world before her eyes.

These men who have "become respectable" and "become clever" make no long delays — no rabbi is needed, no official rabbi [rabiner] either. One laughs at family and acquaintances. For 1 złoty one finds a little scribe who writes out a get [bill of divorce], and one throws it at the feet of the unhappy woman. And if one wishes — it is fine without a get too. One can set up a wedding canopy without a get, and there is already some "spekdekl" [?] to be found who performs [?] all 7 blessings...

A mistress [kochanka] — God forbid. It has to be according to the law.. Mistresses are known [?] among the gentiles, but "with us Jews" it is done decently..

And there are Jewish young ladies who are ready to go under such a "canopy", to share a "living husband" over a sister [i.e. another woman], and to entrust their own life to such a man..

Is the time we live in so bad, or so demoralizing?

A Shvartser ["a Black one"].
Oneg Shabbat

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Bo.
—o—
a) "And let them ask every man of his neighbour" (Ex. 11:2).
What did they need to borrow for? The "spoil of the sea" — what was taken at the sea from the drowned Egyptians — was big enough.
The whole reason the Egyptians chased the Jews is that the Jews had borrowed many precious valuables from them; had it not been for that, they might not have wanted to chase the Jews and so would not have drowned in the sea. Because of their lent-out money they chased the Jews and were drowned.
Me'or va-Shemesh.
—o—
b) "About midnight" (11:4).
Before midnight, says the Gemara, a west wind blows. This is an allusion to the Torah scholars — the darkened and extinguished ones (west — sunset); and after midnight a north wind blows — an allusion to the rich ("gold cometh out of the north"). These two part from each other. "About midnight" — the two winds do not blow together.. wealth and wisdom seldom meet.. That is why the interval between the two winds is called hatzot: division.
Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonne.
* * *
"Rabbi honoured the rich."
Rabbi [Judah the Prince] was, as is known, both the greatest in Israel and a very rich man. Therefore, by his own example — that one can be rich and also wise — he honoured the rich, removing from them the stain of shame that a rich man must be a boor.
Sihat Hulin.
* * *
Why do today's wealthy men honour Torah scholars so little?
Because the Gemara says: "He who honours scholars will have sons who are scholars" (Shabbat 24 [?]) — whoever honours rabbis has sons who are rabbis; so they are afraid to honour Torah scholars, lest, God forbid, their children too should someday become Torah scholars..
Minhat [?] Levi.
—o—
c) "And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you" (12:26).
As is known, this is the wicked son's question, and the plural is used for it, while for the wise and the simple son it says "when thy son asketh thee" — the singular. It seems that the wicked are indeed the majority, and clever [?] wise men are indeed rare exceptions...
R. Moshe Avigdor Amiel.
* * *
Someone once asked the Rabbi of Płock: why does the Torah give the wicked son's question a calm answer, while the author of the Haggadah tells us to knock his teeth out ("blunt his teeth")? The rabbi answered thus:
In the Torah it says "when your children shall say unto you" — that is, when there happens to be a larger number of wicked ones. Before a greater mob of the wicked one must bow one's head and answer quietly... a lost cause.. But the Haggadah speaks of one wicked son ("the wicked one, what does he say") — and a single one, you may indeed knock his teeth out...
—o—
d) "And they shall eat the flesh in that night" (12:8).
The Passover offering had to be eaten at night, and when one was already sated.
Would it not have been more fitting to eat it by day, since eating in the dark one does not get sated..
But that night was a bright, luminous one ("the night shineth as the day"), so the night meal too was full of light..
Kli Zayit [?]
—o—
e) "And they despoiled the Egyptians" (12 [?]:36).
The Gemara relates that an Egyptian summoned a Jew to judgment before Alexander of Macedon, demanding that he give back what the Jews had taken from the Egyptians in Egypt. The Jew calculated that for four hundred and thirty years they were owed wages worth exactly as much as the property they had taken out of Egypt.
The Maharsha asks: the Jews were only in Egypt two hundred and ten years, and if [?] the wages amount exactly to four hundred years, then the Egyptian was right.
The Vilna Gaon answers: as is known, four parts of the Jews died during the three days of darkness and only one fifth came out; so their [?] wages are due also for the four parts that died earlier — after all, they too had worked enough.
—o—
f) "And they despoiled the Egyptians."
During the "Fourth Aliyah" a certain rich man borrowed a lot of money, fled and went off [?] to the Land of Israel. Jews ask: how come a bankrupt should flee precisely to the Land of Israel?
A wise Jew answered: he did as the Haggadah says — "In every generation a man must see himself as if he had come out of Egypt"; when the Jews came out of Egypt they did the very same thing: borrowed gold and silver and fled to the Land of Israel.
After R. Yeshayahu Zlotnik.
—o—
g) "Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever openeth the womb" (13:2).
An ass has only signs of impurity, while a pig has at least one sign of purity. Yet "sanctify unto me" is said only of the ass, because it is harder to bring under holiness those who imagine they have signs of purity.. easier the one whose impurity is undisguised and open..
[—]
Artisans' examinations in Zagłębie next week.

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] (Artisans' conference in Sosnowiec.)
In connection with the fact that the master examinations for artisans in Zagłębie will take place in the coming days — a district conference of all Jewish artisans' associations in Zagłębie (of the Będzin, Zawiercie and Olkusz counties [powiaty]) was held in Sosnowiec this[?] Sunday, on the initiative of the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association, with the participation of Mr. J. Gutman, a board member of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
The conference was opened by chairman A. Opatowski with a short speech on the importance and aims of the conference, which is to consider chiefly the question of the forthcoming elections.
Invited to the presidium were Messrs. councillor (radny) J. Gutman (Kielce), W.[?] Percis[?] and Garyk (Zawiercie), Grosman, Klejman and Celersztajn[?] (Będzin), Fuks (Dąbrowa), Wajcman (Olkusz), Szwimer (Myszków), Stern and Warszawski (Sosnowiec), and as secretary — A. Gancwajch.
A detailed report on the activity of the Jewish councillors in the Kielce Chamber of Crafts was given in a two-hour lecture by councillor J. Gutman. The speaker points out that the conditions of our cooperation with the Kielce Chamber of Crafts were dictated by the Warsaw headquarters, according to which, of 24 councillors, the Christians were to have 15 seats and the Jews 9. However, because the Christian and Jewish councillors in Zagłębie boycotted the elections to the Chamber of Crafts, the "Izba" [chamber] consists of only 20 members: 13 Christians and 7 Jews. Besides that, according to an earlier agreement, the post of vice-president was to have fallen to the Jewish representatives. But things turned out differently, and the Jews received only two seats on the board (Messrs. Gutman of Kielce and Kac of Częstochowa). Since almost all the powers of the Izba lie in the hands of the president and the vice-president, who in fact decide (with the help of the Christian councillors) on all the most important matters — the Jewish councillors find themselves having to wage a very hard struggle in defence of the most painful interests of Jewish artisanry.
The main demands of the Jewish councillors — Mr. Gutman stresses — are equal treatment of all artisans regardless of religion; reducing the examination fee for candidates without means from 140 to 50 zł. And then — the main thing: that Jewish representatives should sit on the examination commission for Jewish craftsmen.
In conclusion the speaker declares that the Jewish councillors pursue a "sparing"[?] (conciliatory) tactic in the Izba, holding that only through peaceful and compromising work will it be possible, given the present composition of the Chamber of Crafts, to ease somewhat the hard situation of the Jewish craftsman and his struggle for a better tomorrow.
After Mr. Gutman further answers several questions from the delegates, in which he announces among other things that the examinations in Zagłębie will probably take place as early as next week — the following 3 resolutions are adopted:
1) the conference expresses full confidence in the Jewish councillors in the Kielce Chamber of Crafts for their efforts on behalf of the interests of Jewish artisanry; 2) a protest against those who in their time caused the reduction of the number of councillors in the Chamber of Crafts; 3) the conference sends greeting telegrams to the president of the Kielce [Chamber of] Crafts, to the Kielce voivode and to the starostas in Będzin, Zawiercie and Olkusz.
———
In the afternoon, in the above-mentioned premises, under the chairmanship of Mr. M. Jaskierowicz[?], the annual general meeting of the Artisans' Association in Sosnowiec took place.
The report on the activity to date was given by the secretary, Mr. A. Gancwajch. The report, divided into 10 chapters, covers the work of the board, from the largest to the smallest, over 13 months, i.e. from December 1929, when the board took over the association in a disastrous economic situation.
Mr. G. points to the intensity of the outgoing board, which during its term held 44 meetings, called 6 mass meetings, stood on guard and protected the members in every danger threatening artisans, the[?] organising of a number of Jewish guilds, intervened in tax matters at the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office] and at the Magistrat [municipality].
The board also took care to raise the cultural level of its members; to that end evening courses, members' talks and the like were opened.
The report, which lasted about 2 hours, had such an "influence" that at the item — criticism, not a peep was heard...
The treasury report was given by Mr. M. Stern. It turns out that for the first time "in the history of the local organisation" the association has a balance (saldo) of 52 zł.
The balance sheet amounts to 32,085.35 zł.
After the report of the auditing committee a discussion develops, in which Messrs. Ch.[?] B. Piekarski, J. M. Rater, J. Rozensztajn[?], Meler, Skórnicki, K. Eksztajn, Glirman[?] and others take part.
Replies were given by Messrs. Rotsztajn[?] and Gancwajch.
Because of the late hour, the item — elections was postponed to next Sunday.
Those assembled expressed thanks to the oldest member, R' Moshe Zylberbald[?] (feldsher[?]), for the good management of the premises.
Around the “Remarquiade” in Austria.

(A letter from Vienna).
A few weeks ago we had the opportunity to read everywhere about the unheard-of swastika-men's agitation in Berlin against the excellent American film work “All Quiet on the Western Front” (“Im Westen nichts Neues”), adapted from Erich Remarque's famous novel. Stink bombs, sal ammoniac and white mice were the weapons of war against the pacifist film. The German government, despite its strong resistance and protest from the cultured part of the population, banned the showing of this masterpiece. The Hitler people thus scored an enormous victory, but abroad this decision provoked great dissatisfaction.
Again a few weeks passed, and the said film arrived in Vienna. Everyone was eager to see the excellent film that had been banned in “republican” Germany; it did not even occur to anyone that in “Red Vienna” a few hundred swastika-men would succeed in bringing about the same result as in Berlin.
The Austrian Social Democracy hit upon an original move: it took over the ticket sales for all the performances in order to prevent demonstrations by the National Socialists (Hitlerites). [?] Everything was done and well organised, but reality brought the greatest sensation — the ban!
Already at the first performance a large number of swastika-men gathered at the “Apollo” cinema and provoked misunderstandings[?] and excesses, but the police quickly managed to put down the hooligan riots and arrest the ringleaders. It goes without saying that the Jews suffered too, for a large number of costly shop windows of Jewish cafés and shops were smashed. But that is not all, for the real rows which led to the ban began on the day of the film's premiere. The writer of this letter, too, was among the curious who wanted at least to see the photographs of the sensational picture displayed outside. So I took a walk along the Franz-Josefs-Kai, and how astonished I was when I noticed that the approach to the “Stern-Kino” (where the film was to be shown) was guarded en masse by mounted and foot police. The shops in the immediate vicinity were closed. I thought I was in a war position. At about 5 o'clock small groups of swastika-men began to gather. When their number reached a few hundred men they began to demonstrate; one heard shouts against the government, the police and... the Jews: “Deutschland erwache” [Germany, awake], “Juda verrecke” [Perish, Judah]. The police, however, did not let the rowdies reach the cinema, and the performances passed off in perfect order. On the following days, too, the swastika-men wanted to continue their demonstrations, even[?] with reinforcements from the provinces, yet everyone thought the government would not let itself be provoked and would not issue the demanded ban — but how astonished everyone was when, on the third day of the film's run, the Minister of the Interior, Inushiger[?] Winkler, published the ban.
The democratic press came out with a series of articles against this unheard-of decision. “What does it mean that Austria, and Vienna in particular, which is counted among the greatest cultural cities in the world, let itself be influenced by a few uncultured young fellows and issued such a compromising verdict — this is truly a scandal! The sharp words, however, did not help, and the film stopped being shown.
It is really sad that a small part of the population, consisting of low elements, could once again bring about a colossal victory of reaction, this time in Austria”...
And what will happen next?..
Sigmund Lichtenstein.
Paraná “herva” will find a good market in Poland.

Conversation with the Brazilian consul in Katowice.
In Brazil's Paraná the colonists complain of the small sales of the article “herva-mate” (yerba mate), owing to the great development of this article in Argentina.
The Argentine population consumes 100 million kilos of herva-mate; half of that amount is brought from Brazil.
For several years now Argentina has been buying very little herva-mate in Brazil; in particular, the inhabitants [there] are striving to have the government issue a ban on importing herva from Brazil.
Interesting information on this was given to us by the Brazilian consul in Katowice, Mr. Pavel[?] Gerster, who visited our editorial office and told us the following.
Poland — says the consul — will be able to be an important buyer of Brazilian herva-mate. [unclear word] for this reason[?], because herva-mate is cheap and is a considerably better drink than tea, on which Poland spends 20 million złoty a year. It is also important to note that herva-mate is produced by Polish colonists in Brazil.
When the Polish population becomes acquainted with the goodness of herva-mate, herva-mate will become a possible article of consumption even[?] for the poorest strata.
— Has anything been done about this yet? Yes, — the informant replies — after my interview with the Warsaw press I received many letters from firms asking for exact information and samples. For propaganda purposes I sent[?] 34 little boxes of mate.
— Are there prospects that Poland will import other articles from Brazil?
— Yes, — says the consul, Mr. Gerster — Poland will bring very large shipments of coffee and tobacco from Brazil, and will ship coal and cement to Brazil.
With this ended the conversation with the Brazilian consul in Katowice, who pays a great deal of attention to Polish coal and cement finding a market in Brazil.
Jewish Life in Zawiercie

[Zawiercie — economy, organisations, culture.]
Protest against raising the rent.
On Thursday a protest meeting was held in the premises of the Artisans' Association concerning[?] the plan to raise the rent ("dire-gelt", lodging money), as well as other economic questions.
The meeting is opened [—] by Mr. Hanokh Perlis[?], who hands the chair to the vice-president of the Merchants' Association, Mr. Fishl Shvarts. The latter invites representatives of institutions to the presidium, and Mr. Dovid Guterman as secretary. Speeches are made by the president of the small traders, Mr. Moyshe Khayim Vindman, and on behalf of the artisans by Mr. Bawszykowski[?]. The general[?] report on the questions is given by Mr. Berl Zyplanka[?], who calls on the institutions[?] to protest against the danger that lurks for the Jewish artisan and merchant with the raising of the rent. Then Mr. Zayfman takes the floor and proposes creating a rescue committee, which should come to the aid of all the needy small traders and artisans who, because of their difficult material situation, have to this day not managed to buy out their patents [trade licences], and who are therefore threatened with losing their livelihoods. Mr. Shvarts supplements Mr. Zayfman's proposal and introduces an amendment, that all the Jewish banks should lend 500 zł. each, and that the money be distributed through the "Gemilut Hasadim" [free-loan] fund for a term of 6 months without interest. The proposal is accepted, and the following banks declare themselves: "Bank Spółdzielczy", "Bank Kupiecki" and the "Gemilut Hasadim" fund. How badly the poor merchants needed this money is shown by the fact that the sum is still too small.
Meeting of "Hashomer Hatzair".
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Aleksander Turner[?] the annual general meeting of "Hashomer Hatzair" took place. The report on the activity of the "Ken" [the branch] was given by Shloyme Krazman, from which it can be seen that the activity of the "Ken" was quite satisfactory. Then the following board was elected: councillor Avrom Bornshteyn, councillor Yisroel Margulis, Dovid Verdinger, Aleksander Turner[?], Yisroel Frenk, Shloyme Krazman, Tsfira, Vaserman, Khave Tsukerman and Shmuel Zaks. Audit committee: Khave Neren[?], Khave Brat[?] and Ester Goldberg.
For the "Tarbut" schools.
On Saturday night the local "Tarbut" organised, in the home of Mr. Tsvi Landau, a coffee evening for the benefit of the "Tarbut" schools (kindergarten and secondary school) which exist in our town. Thanks to the Landau family, and especially Mrs. Landau, for her tireless work, the evening turned out impressive and brought in 350 zł.
S. A. Z.
—o—
Under the wheels of the train.
On Saturday evening, not far from the Gałonag[?] [Gołonóg?] station, the 28-year-old Janikowski[?] was found killed; as the investigation has established, the victim jumped off a freight train and fell under the wheels.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Echoes of the Events in the Synagogue

[Head of the local page; Będzin — court and synagogue.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 5 / 5 Tevet [sic; should be Shevat] 5691 — Piątek 23 stycznia 1931 [Friday, 23 January 1931].)
Będzin
Echoes of the events in the synagogue.
On Tuesday the trial was to have taken place in the local court against Mr. Lauren[?], who had been charged with provoking a disgraceful scandal in the local synagogue during Kabbalat Shabbat.
At the opening of the trial Mr. Lauren[?] asked that the trial be postponed, in order to summon a series of witnesses.
The judge agreed to summon 8 witnesses and postponed the trial to a second date.
The „Bank Spółdzielczy“ Receives Large Credits

[Będzin — economy and banking.]
In connection with the rumours in town that the „Bank Spółdzielczy“ [Cooperative Bank] will soon receive larger sums of money as loans, the writer of these lines turned to the president of the bank, Director S. Fürstenberg, with the question whether the rumours have any real basis.
To this Mr. Fürstenberg declared that the rumours are true, and that this is the result of the last visit of the auditor, Mr. Michelson[?], who during his official visit declared to me that, after carrying out the audit of the „Bank Spółdzielczy“ — because of the exemplary order now maintained in the bank, and thanks to the fact that after paying off the previous losses a profit of about 20,000 zł. still remained — the Central [„di tsentrale“] in Warsaw will give the bank 100 thousand zł. as a long-term loan.
For my part — says Mr. F. — I too will put in a larger sum of money, so that the bank may again[?] rise to the first rank and be able to satisfy the broadest strata of the Jewish population with long-term credits.
From the Relief Committee

[Będzin — relief.]
The newly founded relief committee, in which there are also Messrs. Dr. Weinzieher and Director Fürstenberg, is already active.
Meanwhile coal and kasha (groats) will be given out. Potatoes will also be distributed, which are due to arrive in the coming days.
The relief committee is located in the „Piast“.
The „Ezrat Menachem Avelim“ Society Already Has Premises of Its Own

[Będzin — charitable institutions.]
Several months ago a society named „Ezrat Menachem Avelim“ (Aid for Comforting Mourners) was founded in Będzin.
At the beginning of its founding almost everyone met the society with a dismissive tone[?], but hardly had the society begun to be active when sympathy for it grew ever greater and greater; people[?] realised that the society is very useful to all strata of the Jewish population, and the number of members grows from week to week.
The board of the society, however, was paralysed in its activity because of the premises question: it had no premises of its own, and for every meeting it had to turn to some minyan or „shtibl“ for permission to hold a board meeting.
But „to everything there is a season“ — the difficult premises question has now also been solved: to its aid came the house-owner Mr. Itshe Wolf Pikarski, who out of his good will assigned 4 rooms to the society „Ezrat Menachem Avelim“.
Thanks to the fine step of Mr. Pikarski, the institution will have the possibility to broaden its activity and to come to the aid of the unfortunate, who are kept alive by the institution.
Memorial Academy for the Shloshim of M. Apelbaum

[Będzin — mourning and commemoration.]
On the initiative of the „Gm"z“[?] „Mo'i“[?] a meeting took place with the participation of friends of[?] the late Moshe Apelbaum. At the meeting it was resolved to arrange on the 31st of this month [31 January 1931] a memorial academy with a rich programme.
An Unsuccessful Bandit Attack

[Sosnowiec / Rybnik — crime.]
The Polish press in Sosnowiec brings sensational news that in Rybnik a bandit attack had been planned on the local textile (manufaktur) merchant Mr. H. Unger.
The investigation office in Sosnowiec learned of the attack in good time and sent several secret agents there, who arrested the attackers.
Heavy Punishment for Communists

[Sosnowiec — trial; communists.]
On Monday the young people Shlomo Eisenman, Fela Gajberg and Bajla Lajtner stood before the Sosnowiec court, charged with belonging actively to the Communist Party.
Sentenced were: Eisenman to 4 years' prison, Miss Gajberg to 3[?] years in a reformatory, and Miss Lajtner was acquitted.
The Society for Tourism in Będzin

[Będzin — tourism & society.] The Society for Tourism in Będzin announces that today, Saturday the 24th, at 10 o'clock in the morning, an excursion will take place to the "Saturn" coal mine.
The meeting point is at the Old Market.
On the days from 31 January (styczeń) to 2 February (luty) an excursion will take place to the Beskids (Bielsko, Klimczok, Salmopol, Szczyrk). Departure from Będzin on the 31st of this month at 7.22 in the evening, return on 2 February at 9 in the evening.

The meeting point is at the old station in Będzin. Detailed information and registrations are accepted until the 28th of this month at the secretariat in Będzin, 3 Maja [Street] 4, telephone 85, from 6 to 8 in the evening.
General Meeting of the Talmud Torah

[Będzin — community & education.] The local "Talmud Torah", which has existed for decades already, will for the first time in its existence [convene?] a general meeting, at which reports on its activity will be delivered and a board will be elected. The meeting is set for 8 February (luty).

Sosnowiec Gets a Fresh Gift... — Investment Tax Approved

[Sosnowiec — municipality & taxes.] Through the efforts of the city commissioner Mr. Kuśniak[?], the voivode has approved the investment tax.

French Capitalists Buy Dietel's Factory
[Sosnowiec — industry.] The negotiations over the purchase of A. Dietel's factory by French capitalists have already been concluded. In the coming days the formalities are to be settled.
He "Photographed" His Customers...

[Zagłębie — fraud.] Some time ago a certain Kranc came to Zagłębie who, presenting himself as an agent of the portrait firm "Arcydzieło"[?] in Warsaw, swindled money out of very many people.
This same Kranc had once worked for the firm, but because of abuses he was dismissed.
In Zagłębie he worked with every trick in the book and did not-bad business.
