Meeting in the Artisans' Association

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] Next Sunday the continuation of the annual meeting of the local Artisans' Association will take place in its own premises.

[Zagłębie — accident.]
Collision between two freight trains.
20 wagons smashed.
At the railway station in Ząbkowice a catastrophe involving 2 freight trains took place. 20 wagons of coal were smashed and the locomotive was overturned. Fortunately there were no human casualties.

Result of the Zagłębie Chess Championship Tournament.

A new great danger for the Jewish merchants.
From well-informed economic circles we have received a report that the government is preparing an energetic campaign with the aim that throughout Poland special factory shops for the workers should be organised at the large factories and workshops.
The factory shops are to be organised at every larger factory where about[?] several hundred workers are employed.
In factories where fewer workers are employed, one factory[?] is to belong to several factories and to be located in the vicinity of the factories.
The factory shops will carry all kinds of goods, such as clothing, textiles (manufaktura), household goods[?], shoes, ready-made clothes (konfekcja), groceries (kolonialne) and food.
The government is to be ready to give special support, with cheap credits, to every factory that will have such a shop.
In return the shops are to sell at cost price. The goods they are to buy only at first hand, not from merchants.
The workers of each factory will be o b l i g e d to take goods from the shop for a certain part of their wages.
As we are informed, official representatives of the government are to conduct a big campaign in the factory centres to have such shops organised.
The purpose of this campaign is to cheapen the prices of goods so that[?] the workers will be able to buy more goods.
There is not the slightest doubt that with this campaign the entire Jewish trade can be ruined. If the workers can be compelled to take goods in the factory shops for part of their wages, thousands upon thousands of merchants will go under. And the ruin of the Jewish merchant will drag down the manufacturer with it, and unemployment will grow even greater. This can already be seen from practice.
In any case, the Jewish merchant must raise his v o i c e against the new danger.

Appeal of the Citizens' Committee in Będzin

On behalf of the Citizens' Committee in Będzin for aid to poor unemployed people we have been asked to print this appeal:
The economic crisis, which keeps dragging on, has taken from many people the possibility of earning a living from[?] work. In the town of Będzin several hundred families are today left without bread. The relief fund for the unemployed is exhausted, and all the support from the government and from the local self-government bodies can cover the needs of the unemployed only to a very insignificant extent. For this reason a Citizens' Committee has been formed in Będzin, which has set itself the task of relieving the severely suffering[?], who have been left without means of subsistence. The number of such[?] needy people in Będzin amounts to 800 families.
We are fully aware of the heavy task we have taken upon ourselves, but we are in hope that every citizen will fulfil his duty towards the hungry.

Over an Inheritance He Murdered His Brother-in-Law and Then Chopped Him to Pieces

The murderer has been sentenced to 10 years of hard prison.
Last summer a passer-by in the Strzemieszyce forest noticed a fresh grave among the bushes. The astonished man[?] scraped away a little earth with his stick and came upon a sack filled with flesh.
The matter was reported to the police, who found in the sack the head of a human being. A little further on, at another spot, other parts of the body were found.
Suspicion for the terrible murder fell on the murdered man's brother-in-law; sharp quarrels had taken place between them over an inheritance.
Last Saturday the murderer stood before the Sosnowiec district court, before which he declared that he had killed his brother-in-law and chopped him to pieces because the latter had first attacked him with a knife.
At the prosecutor's request the whole court went out to the barn where the murder had been committed.
On Monday the verdict was pronounced, according to which the murderer was sentenced to 10 years of hard prison and loss of rights.

The court in Królewska Huta this week heard an interesting case. In the dock sat the restaurateur Janusz of Lipiny, who was accused of having offered active resistance to the bailiff while the latter was carrying out a distraint.

Number of Passenger Trains Reduced.
From 1 February 34 passenger trains will be cancelled in Upper Silesia, and the service of another 15 trains will be reduced. The reason is the low traffic on the lines.
It has been established that traffic on the Upper Silesian railways is steadily decreasing. In 1928 more than 7 million tickets were sold at the 4 railway stations in Katowice; in 1929 — already 70 thousand fewer.
For last year there are no figures yet, but it is clearly known that traffic is small and 34 trains had to be cancelled.

Antisemitism in the Danzig Cafés

Our Danzig correspondent, Mr. Sakazski[?], writes to us:
Among the hundreds of pubs, cafés and restaurants there is an antisemitic café named "Sruhn"[?], whose entire income, unfortunately, comes from Jews alone. The owner, a well-known antisemite, has always sought various stratagems[?] to avoid the Jewish customer. But his latest act has now outraged all the Jewish customers. Last Sunday several dozen Jewish customers were in the "café house", among them Mr. Wechsler with a Christian neighbour (who looks like a Jew), listening to the music. The "Ober" (head waiter) came up to them and asked Mr. Wechsler whether he wanted[?] to order anything more. Hearing the answer "enough"[?], he asked them in the name of his boss to leave the hall, with the words: "Jews, go to Palestine, you have already polluted the Danzig air with your filth." He said these words to the Christian, Mr. Galigski[?], calling him "damned Jew". For this the Christian "honoured" him with two fiery slaps for insulting him by calling him "Jew". Then a delegation of several Jewish customers went to the boss with the question: "Is it true?" — "Yes," the boss replied, "you have already stunk up my establishment enough, I have suffered enough from you, go to Palestine!"...

Sport.

As we have already reported, the „hockey Olympiad“ for the title of world champion opens on Sunday, 1 February [luty], in Krynica. So far the following countries have entered the tournament: America, Canada, England, Austria, Czechoslovakia, France, Italy, Romania, Switzerland, Hungary, etc.
The Polish national team will consist of the following players: Stogowski, Kowalski, Kulej, Krygier, Sabiński and Sokolski[?] [Sokołowski?].
The famous film company „Fox“ has sent out several cameramen with sound equipment to film the hockey matches.
The German sports organisation has announced that for various reasons it will not take part in the tournament. It goes without saying that the main reason is the political situation that has recently arisen between Poland and Germany.
— The England — Poland match, which was to have taken place on Tuesday the 27th on the Katowice artificial ice rink, has been called off. At the same time negotiations are being conducted so that, right after the hockey matches in Krynica, a big 4-day hockey tournament will take place in Katowice with the participation of: Canada, America, England, Italy, the „Wiener Eislaufverein“ [Vienna Skating Club] and the Polish national team.
— Following the intervention of parents, the management of the „artificial ice rink“ has decided to hold on Sunday, 1 February, a big sports show on the ice for children. The children’s show will begin at 3 in the afternoon and will last until 8 in the evening.

A Debt That Must Be Paid. (For the Shloshim of Moshe Apelbaum)

Almost four weeks have already passed since his funeral, and I still cannot grasp the bitter truth. That [?] generous[?] man: he, the ever-cheerful, high-spirited, leaping and dancing Moshe, is no longer with us! His ever-searching spirit and his [?] body have been covered by a little mound of earth!
He stands alive before me, the through-and-through [?] man: often [—]. Again [?] and yet lively, hard-working, full of the joy of life and carefree. Yes, he was worried at times, when he lacked paint and canvas to paint — then he would sink[?] into sadness. But when some money came his way[?] — the first thing was: to buy paint and canvas and to live again as before. A piece of bread, a herring and a glass of tea — a meal for kings; what better does one need?!...
* * *
An artist through and through, the world around him, the whole of life and its manifold phenomena were for him one great artistic composition. And separate fragments of that great work of art he always absorbed into himself, chewed them over in an artistically individual way and enriched them with his own spirit, and gave them back, often expressed in a wonderful composition of colours and lines.
* * *
The artist’s studio, the workshop of paints and canvas, the artist’s holy of holies, so hidden and fenced off[?] from the eye of the [—] crowd[?] — how could our Moshe have had one? He did not have it, he did not need it. His studio, his workshop was — life itself, the very thick of life: a carpenter’s workshop where working people are bent over their work, a water-carrier carrying [his pails] in a Jewish alley, sooty workers on a heap of stones, whirling chimneys against the background of a grey-reddish sky, typical figures of our [?], who [?] the sounds of the [?] from the radio[?], the lonely crippled little tree on the back of a high mountain, the green waters of a mountain lake between the rocks, the shepherd with his sheep on a meadow deep in the mountains — that was his studio, his artist’s workshop. Four walls hung with carpets, with trinkets, a [?] stillness all around — the usual picture of an artist’s studio — who can imagine Apelbaum in such a box?! A seething[?] spirit in a seething[?] life — that is his portrait. And were I an artist, I would paint Apelbaum’s portrait so that from his figure one would hear the quiet idyll of the shepherd in the mountains, and the tragedy of the enslaved mine-worker, and the thousand-year exile of the Jewish klezmer...
* * *
Our Jewish life is poor in artists, and Apelbaum’s death is a heavy loss for us. And care must be taken that his spiritual legacy, the dozens of paintings, drawings and sketches he left behind, are not left lying[?] in a heap of rags somewhere in an attic.
It is the duty of Jewish society, both towards the deceased and towards itself, that Apelbaum’s artistic legacy should come to its proper place and adorn the walls of our public institutions, or even the homes of private persons who have the means for the creations of a Jewish artist.
Thereby we shall pay our debt for the decades of want and hunger of the artist, and shall save from destruction the works of one of our chosen ones[?].
Honour to his memory.
Yitzhak Pesachzon[?].
When Jewish Young People Go Sliding...

As often as I come to Katowice, or even to our own home-grown "Sar" [?], even on a completely ordinary Wednesday, I find Jewish young men and Jewish girls on the slide. You must know that the business of sliding, of riding on sleds, is very much in fashion today. Today you meet the most elegant ladies walking harnessed to a little sled and pulling a child. It is such a fashion; it is part of the almighty sport that is taking over the world today. If there, in Zakopane, in Krynica, guests may come even from far away, from abroad, in order to slide, to run down the mountains on skis, to ride in a sled "kulig" [sleigh party] and break their necks and cackle while doing it; if all this is done there in Zakopane, in Krynica, and, so they say, in St. Moritz in Switzerland it is downright white with people, and people come there from America, from Canada, to compete in running on the ice and to slide — if this is such a fashion today, then it is joined in also in Zagłębie. If one cannot do the trick oneself, if one is already too old to go sliding or sledding, then at least let the children enjoy it, and one has the pleasure of pulling the child on the sled through the town, exactly as it is done in Zakopane.
The business of sliding, of sledding, I understand, and I regard it as a useful and healthy sport; especially pulling children on a sled is certainly no wrong. It is democratic, humane and motherly; a mother should and must care for the child, must occupy herself with it. In the field of child-rearing, too, a certain change in concepts and notions has taken place among us. I still remember, some ten years ago, a Warsaw lady — not, God forbid, one of the Wawelbergs or Szereszewskis, but a quite ordinary woman — married off a daughter, also not to a Szereszewski or a Poznański but to a quite ordinary young man. When the daughter, in a lucky hour, gave birth to a child, the mother, i.e. the grandmother, came storming in at the son-in-law: "Isn't it enough for you that I gave you a wife — must my daughter also be a mother for you?!..."
Today, it seems, one will no longer hear such complaints. Today even the Warsaw lady understands that a mother has some obligation towards her husband and towards her child. That is why I like very much the custom of pulling the children on sleds through the town. But all this is said about children; what, however, are the grown-ups doing, the adult young men and girls, on an ordinary Wednesday in broad daylight on the ice — how do they come to be sledding? And I imagine: some stranger passes by and sees the crowd on the slide; he asks no questions, he knows the answer in advance: "What do they lack? They are doing well, they can afford to go sliding in the middle of the day, on a weekday!"
But I take a closer look at the young people and see that they are not sliding out of contentment. There is nothing to do; they have finished school; one is a craftsman, but there is no work, one gets no position, one cannot sit at home, one does not want to hear father's complaints, mother's groans — so one goes for a walk, goes to the "lonkes" [łąki — the meadows], where one meets more such graduated idlers, and they take each other by the hand and slide.
At a time when all the others, who have finished even an elementary school, get work, get a position, land a job in an office — Jewish children walk around with gymnasium diplomas in their pockets, Jewish workers walk around with sticks in their hands, unemployed, not receiving even the meagre support that other unemployed receive; one cannot sit at home, it is cold and dreary — so one goes and slides.
Jewish young people are sliding. Sliding is healthy, it is a good sport; sledding in particular is certainly a fine and healthy thing. Nevertheless, when I see in the middle of a bright Wednesday how Jewish young people slide and sled, I feel that it is not good, that it is not healthy — not for them, not for us and not even for the community as a whole — that young people are forced to slide instead of working; they will slip and fall and drag us all along. It is not good, not good at all.
Ch. Landau.
A Library Opened in the Name of Dr. Perelman of Blessed Memory.

Last Saturday night the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec perpetuated the name of its leader [?] and rabbi, Dr. Abraham Perelman of blessed memory, in whose name a library has been opened.
The opening took place in the organisation's own premises, in the presence of the late man's family, friends, Zionists, Mizrachi and nationalist youth.
The opening speech was given by Mr. Szymon Feldman, who related that with the opening of the library the testament of the deceased is being fulfilled: when, gravely ill, he left for Berlin, he asked on taking leave that care be taken for the cultural-national education of the young Jewish generation.
The well-rehearsed Betar choir sings the Polish and the Jewish anthem, and Mrs. Lewenhof [?], daughter of Dr. Perelman, cuts the ribbon stretched around the library bookcase.
The same choir sings "Mizmor shir hanukat [habayit]" (Psalm 30), and the guests are invited into the second room, where the women's association "WIZO" had prepared, in a modest but decent manner, "na herbatkę" [?] [a tea].
The chair is handed to Mr. J. M. Wajgryb, who delivers the first greeting in the name of the Jewish Kehilla of Sosnowiec.
On behalf of "Hashomer Hatzair" Mr. Fajdman [?] greets (in Hebrew); on behalf of "Mizrachi" — Mr. Lewi Jungster, who stresses that the library should also hold the Holy Scriptures and volumes of the Talmud.
A businesslike short greeting on behalf of "WIZO" is delivered by Mrs. Langer.
On behalf of Betar — Mr. Klarman, who in passing gives a portion of moral reproof to the older Zionists, who take no interest at all in the nationalist youth.
Written greetings were read from the C.C. (Warsaw) and from "Tze'irei Mizrachi" (Sosnowiec).
A longer speech of greeting is given at the end by the instructor of "Tarbut" in Poland, Mr. Einstein, who in a very fine Yiddish (just to spite the Yiddishists..) described the origin and the situation of the "Tarbut" schools in Poland.
From the great pathos one would have thought the speaker had drunk wine instead of tea, and as is well known, "when wine goes in, the secret comes out"...
The mood — a cosy one. The Betar choir "works deeds" [?] in the adjoining room.
At 12 o'clock the modest Jewish celebration came to an end.
A Sharp Family Quarrel Between a Young Householder and His Father-in-Law.

In town people are now telling an interesting story about a young man who, all of a few months after the wedding, got rid of the entire dowry [?] and was left with his wife and a wallet of protested bills.
The story is as follows:
A short while ago the merchant L. married off his elder daughter and gave 2 thousand dollars dowry. The bridegroom was indeed a fine, educated young man from good parents, but not a professional.
After the wedding the merchant proposed [?] to his son-in-law that he put a thousand dollars into the business and become a partner. The little householder, however, declined and preferred to show his own abilities.
He rented a shop on Sandoszewer [?] Street and already wanted to bring in goods. At the last minute, however, he was advised to let the deposit go, since all businesses are lying in the ground; the best thing is to lend money at interest, usually in safe places, and then one can be at ease. Time runs and the income grows...
The young man let himself be talked into it, and without much searching a whole row of persons turned up, several Jewish merchants, who took cash from him at 2 and at 3 and even 4 percent a month.
Later, however, misfortune struck: at the payment dates only a small percentage were redeemed, most bills went to protest; the debtors did not deny that they owed, but times are bitter and bad — where should they take it from? In short, of the 2 thousand dollars dowry the young man has now only a few hundred left; the rest, alas, have floated away like water, and the only consolation is the protested bills...
As is reported, a sharp family quarrel has now broken out between the young householder and his father-in-law, the merchant L. The latter simply does not let the son-in-law cross his threshold, because he did not listen and frittered away [machlował] such a sum of money...
The World Sighs

Pipi Baal Lashon.
A great radio expert, who is as at home in the ways of the air-waves as a Jew in "Ashrei", has recently voiced the following kind of opinion:
— The moon, he says, keeps throwing back the wireless waves that beat up towards it from the earth!...
Regrettably, we are small connoisseurs in matters of the air (notwithstanding that we are, thank God[?], a Jew, and a Jew explicitly does have a connection with air). And we cannot understand [—] the king of the air-waves as that great radio expert does. Nevertheless we are sure that he is not talking for nothing[?].
We understand the matter simply, by our poor understanding: the moon does not want to have anything to do with our earth.
And that is no wonder at all, upon my life.
Who — practically you yourselves[?] — would want to bother with the earth, when one can now[?] avoid it[?]...
Everyone, even people who are no air-experts, knows after all that the air around the earth, around our world, is filled with all kinds of sounds.
Every voice, every word, every groan and every sigh creates a wave in the air.
And these waves are carried perpetually[?] from one end of the world to the other.
Naturally, one cannot hear the voices with any ordinary ear; this is what the radio does. It picks up the wireless waves and tunes them in, and whoever sits next to a radio set hears them well.
So it is good for us humans that they sing in and speak out for us such melodies and speeches as are pleasant for us to hear and that we enjoy.
We pay for this pleasure and we are given it.
And when we get fed up with this pleasure too, we simply switch off the radio and hear nothing again.
———
But what should the quiet and calm moon do — mind you — when it has no such radio set that one can switch on and off at will, and all sorts of air-waves come up to it from its neighbour, the earth, and it simply cannot bear them!
So the moon thinks it over and hurls back all these wireless waves, as one says:
— Go, little children-waves, back into the earth, where[?] you came from!
Go off to your rest!
———
And why, really, should the moon not throw off the earth-voices?
And who would not do it, if only he could?
And what does one hear nowadays from our earth, so to speak[?]?
Voices of the tormented, of the robbed, of the tortured.
A whole world keeps groaning and sighing. From every corner of the earth a different kind of groan and a different kind of sigh arrives; every people has its own manner of sighing and its own way of lamenting.
———
Take America, for example, a land that for the last decades kept singing and rejoicing.
When it was sad on earth, America was lively; it kept dancing out of prosperity.
It knew[?] only some new[?] amusements[?] — "that was the life!"
And with its liveliness it infected the whole world too. The world began to Americanize in the matter of "living a crazy day".
And suddenly, there you have it: the little wheel turned backwards, the "money wall" — such a strong wall built of gold, gold[?] — broke, collapsed and buried the whole land beneath it!
The victims sigh, it is terrifying; impoverished millionaires sigh; millions of unemployed, business-less, bread-less people sigh!
As the saying goes: "when nothing is lacking in the mill, they quarrel in the house[?]" (so printed).
———
Take England: people thought that when the Labour government took its seat, it would bring salvation and consolation.
Not a chance [lit. "a yesterday's day"].
Now there too one hears sighs of the unemployed, and the government has had to open a "dole box" (pushke — a charity box) to keep body and soul together for them.
People shoot and fight, and there are troubles with pains..
The land sighs.
———
Of great Russia there is, after all, nothing to say.
There, a hundred and fifty million people have been sighing for almost thirteen years now, and one sees no end at all.
Well, and the smaller states are, after all, a sighing from Sigh-land.
And wherever you go, one does not hear a single cheerful minute anywhere.
———
And above them all, there is after all some Jewish people in the world, may it be healthy and strong.
We little Jews, apart from having to sigh along with every people and land, have in addition our own special Jewish sighs.
We have double sighs:
as human beings — and the sigh of sighs as Jews.
After all, nobody has ever loved us anywhere, and we have almost grown used to it; and we always strive to buy the world's love at any price — and exactly the opposite: the more we strive, the more we are hated. — Only lately the hatred of Jews has grown even more, higher and higher.
So now, thank God, even in those countries where they treated us a little better, we have a quite fine antisemitism too.
They give us a pinch on the sly, so that nobody should notice, but we feel the pinching, so that the nails stay stuck in the flesh.
———
And if we are short of foreign pinchers, we have our own as well!
If, for example, Christian firms, say, do not want to take Jews as employees — well, that we understand, and we have no other choice; it is a [—] pain.
But when there are still many Jewish firms that do not want to look at a Jewish face on their premises, that is already a pain and a vexation together.
And we sigh, oh how we sigh, until there is almost no strength left.
———
In short: the world sighs, and we sigh in a minyan with the world, and we sigh in private with ourselves.
And when such air-waves full of sighs are carried from our earth — is it any wonder that the moon throws these waves back and does not want to hear them?
Yes, Madame Moon, you are perfectly right, as surely as you see[?] me a Jew!
If only we could become your neighbours, we too would not want even to look at the earth.
So — to the devil with it[?]...
How Can the Housing Shortage Be Eased and the Rent in the New Buildings Reduced?

At the present moment the housing shortage has been considerably eased, in that the number of dwelling units has grown more or less. Meanwhile there are also vacant flats. But only well-off people can get at these flats, because the rent in the new buildings is so high that an average intellectual (white-collar) worker would have to spend a whole month's salary ("pensja") on rent. It would, however, also be a mistake to claim, as is generally assumed among the population, that the rent in the new buildings is so[?] expensive only because the builders[?] want to earn too much. That is not so. Figures on this prove definitely and indisputably[?] that the expensive rent in the new buildings is the consequence of a fundamental error committed by the bodies that conduct the state building policy. This error takes its revenge both on the owners of the new buildings and on their tenants, because the interest on building credit amounts to seven and a half percent a year.
According to the calculations made, between 1925 and 1930 360 million zł. worth was built in Poland with the help of state building credit. For every cubic metre of the buildings erected with the help of state building credit the house-owners received on average up to 70 zł. This already includes the value of the building plot, the interest during construction, the regional[?] fund, mortgage expenses, technical supervision and plans.
Since the most sought-after flats, of 2 rooms with a kitchen, bathroom etc., take up about 360 cubic metres, it turns out that the building cost of just 1 such flat comes to about 25.200 zł. And this in buildings consisting of a ground floor, cellar and 4 storeys.
It should be noted in this connection that the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" lends money for such building supposedly[?] to the amount of 75 percent (in the sense of the Law on the Expansion of Cities), whereas in reality the maximum building credit is only 60 per cent (including the building costs, mortgage etc.), or more precisely: it lends 15,120 zł., and the remainder, 10 080 zł. — this[?] sum the house-owners must put in from their own and outside capital. Besides this, the house-owner must cover all the expenses of maintaining such a flat (2 rooms with a kitchen, bathroom): pay interest to the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" (partly over 15 and partly over 25 years at 7½ per cent a year), which on 15 120 zł. comes to 1134 zł.; 10 percent on his own and borrowed capital (10 080 zł.) — 1,008 zł.; expenses such as light, [—][?] repairs to the buildings[?], administration, amortisation etc. — 315 zł.; altogether 2,457 zł. of costs.
From this whole picture of figures it can be seen that even on the most modest calculation, a tenant of a flat consisting of 2 rooms, kitchen and bathroom must pay at least 2 400 zł. rent a year. And this calculation does not include the costs of collecting the rent, nor the 12 percent a year that the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" charges for prolongation[?].
These figures speak clearly enough. They prove that applying the present principle is wrong and harmful, that life overturns the calculation. Witness to this is the large number of evictions of tenants from new buildings, since[?] they are simply[?] unable to pay such high rent. From this one can concretely conclude that the fault lies not with the house-owner, but in the fact that the paying capacity of an average citizen cannot bear such a rent.
In order to remove the present evil, the state building fund must be divided into 2 parts: one half must be designated for reducing the already fixed financing[?], which will automatically bring about a reduction of the rent in the new buildings and thus protect against a flood of evictions. Then the government itself will be able, and obliged, to fix the level of rent.
The second half of the state building fund must have the task of further expanding the cities.
And one more thing: it would be necessary that, instead of the 75 percent that the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" has given until now for building purposes, it should give credit of only 50 percent, but that the sums be given all at once and punctually, and not, as until now, dragged out[?] in instalments. It is also to be wished that the Ministry of Finance, when fixing the quota, take into account that neither the owners of new buildings nor their tenants are simply[?] able to bear so great a burden as the present interest on building credit.
The management of the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego", which is in close contact with the taxpayer[?], the owner of the new building, knows best how hard it is for him today to pay the interest due, and that the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" often has to protest their bills of exchange — this very bank must also intervene with the Ministry of Finance to have the interest reduced.
The owners of private buildings, as well as the managements[?] of the housing cooperatives, must also approach the competent bodies with memoranda — this is in their own interest and in the interest of their tenants — because the interest on building credit is too high and is nowadays the cause of the fact that housing conditions cannot be normalised[?]. And in the end this state of affairs can only lead to the "Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego" finally taking over all the new buildings itself.
And that is surely not what the state is after!
A. Steinschneider.
A Little Feuilleton — The Cigarette Lighter.

A great mitzvah upon her [to be rid of her].
Let it also have[?] a reason.
For years on end, how she torments and tortures us. Precisely when you have no match ("zapałka") in your pocket and you are outside the town, precisely then you crave "papirosy" (cigarettes), and either the flint[?] is worn out, or the benzine has evaporated[?], or simply some trouble — and by no means will the lighter ("zapalniczka") light, and you have to give up smoking a cigarette. Precisely when you are on a minister's stairs — the lighter "fasts"[?] on you.
And besides, the lighter is the greatest enemy of democracy.
The box of matches has one face, one appearance, and has the same pedigree with the manufacturer as with the worker, with Rothschild as with Menachem Mendel. The lighter, however, dresses up and adorns itself according to class rank. There is a gold lighter, a silver one, all kinds of models[?] and sorts — and how many times are you ashamed to take out of your pocket the little tin machine while you sit in the company of an acquaintance, and sometimes of a lady, who never let the luxury lighter out of their hands, toying with it like a fine piece of jewellery and emphasising through it what fine taste they have and how elegant they are. Then a longing seizes you for the plain[?] matches, which are free of all these frills and do not [—] your pocket.
In a word: the lighter ought long ago to have been driven out of our democratic society.
And at last it has indeed happened.
We have to thank our present-day democratic government, with its ultra-democratic and upright Minister of Finance, who have pronounced a death sentence on the aristocrat — the lighter.
We also owe it to the Swedish billionaire Kreuger, who has blessed us with the match loan, receiving in return the monopoly on matches in Poland until the year 1965. According to the agreement between Kreuger and the Minister of Finance, the use of lighters is forbidden in Poland.
For manufacturing a lighter one will be fined from 1000 to 5000 zł.
The present majority of the Sejm has already ratified this agreement.
Down with the lighter.
Down with pedigree.
A great mitzvah upon her.
Yankele
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Beshalach.
—o—
a) "Lest the people repent… and return to Egypt" (13:17).
The Jews actually longed to go back to Egypt; that is why God told the Jews to borrow gold and silver from the Egyptians ("and they asked of every man of his neighbour, and every woman of her neighbour, jewels of silver and jewels of gold"), because once they had borrowed such[?] a treasure of money, they would no longer have any desire to go back to their creditors...
Even Bochan[?].
* * *
To a Jew, a debtor, comes a creditor who is owed an open[?] debt and demands the debt from him. The bankrupt, however, takes a mouthful of water and answers him nothing. The creditor gets upset: How come — not to answer at all, one could burst! At least answer "Yishakeni" ("let him kiss me")...
— But you hear — answers the debtor — that answer ("Yishakeni") I don't give to everyone, only to whoever holds a bill of exchange [promissory note] on me... A merchant's witticism[?].
—o—
b) "Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians" (14:12).
The Jews knew that the Redemption cannot come unless [the generation] is either wholly righteous or wholly guilty; and since they knew well that "wholly righteous" was far, far from possible, they cried: "that we may serve Egypt" — let us serve the Egyptian idols, let us become complete gentiles, then [the generation] will be wholly guilty and we will be redeemed.. Tiferet Yehonatan.
* * *
Rabbi Dovidl of Lelów once argued with the Master of the Universe: "What are You waiting for with the Redemption? Perhaps until Jews repent? I give You my solemn handshake that Jews will no longer repent at all — and if You will not redeem Jews, You will redeem gentiles"...
—o—
c) "And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea" (14:22).
When they stood on the seashore, each of the tribal princes said that he was not worthy of being the first. A sham humility stemmed[?] from cowardice: not wanting to be the first at the front was called humility among them, a flight from honour. In truth this is more heroism than honour. Being the first, the leader, brings more duty than honour — and this Nachshon understood. That is why he merited kingship: by his heroic leap[?] he proved that he was worthy of being a leader. Only those who jump first into the sea are worthy of being leaders. Pal[?] le-Yisrael.
—o—
d) "All Pharaoh's horses" (14:23).
Where did the Egyptians get horses to pursue the Jews? All the cattle had died in the plague of pestilence and afterwards in the hail.
But it is said that the pious Egyptians, believing in Moses, had hidden the cattle from the hail ("he that feared the word of the Lord made his cattle flee"), and it was these horses that the pious Egyptians lent to pursue the Jews.
Even a pious gentile, the best of the gentiles..
Talmud (Avodah Zarah)
—o—
e) "And all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances" (15:20).
By the merit of the righteous women the Jews were redeemed (Midrash).
As is known, the Jews left Egypt before the appointed time, because the severity of the bondage — the hardness of their slavery — completed the time. During the two hundred and ten years they suffered as much as in four hundred years, and the ones who bore[?] the severity of the bondage were in fact the women... Rabbi Moshele of Lelów.
—o—
f) "Any of the diseases" (15:26)
It is not spelled out which disease; likewise in the Admonition it says "every sickness and every plague which is not written" — what kind of illness and plagues are these, that one does not write them out?
Here is an example[?]: when a poor man has to buy his daughter[?] all sorts of clothes and shoes according to the latest fashion[?]. Well, can one write about that that it is a curse? Are fine clothes a curse? But on the other[?] hand there is still no worse illness and plague than that.. That is why it is an illness "which is not written", about which one still cannot write that it is an illness.. Sichot Chulin.
—o—
g) "That I may prove them, whether they will walk in My law" (16:4).
How could one recognise who wants to learn?
In Avot it is said: "This is the way of the Torah: eat bread with salt, drink water by measure" — even when one has all these good things, if one wants to devote oneself wholly to learning Torah, one must throw it all away and eat literally dry bread.
The manna had all kinds of tastes. Whatever[?] taste a person wanted, he felt in it; and whoever truly wanted to engage in Torah wanted to feel only the taste of bread with salt. Kohelet Moshe (for[?] R' Yonatan Eybeschütz).
—o—
h) "And they said one to another: It is manna (man hu)?" (16:11[?]).
In Egypt there were presumably also rich people and poor people. The rich were presumably also of distinguished lineage, and the poor — coarse[?]. But when everyone lived on the manna, all were equal; there were no more rich aristocrats. "And they said one to another" — yesterday's poor man said to yesterday's rich man, calling him brother, "my brother" — "man hu?" [= who is he?] Who is he? Why all of a sudden a man of lineage? R. A. Teomim.
—o—
i) "And it came to pass on the seventh day that some of the people went out to gather, and they found none."
According to the commentary, Dathan and Abiram deliberately scattered manna on Sabbath night in order to make Moses out a liar — he had said that on the Sabbath no manna would be found. Meanwhile, as they drove the crowd out to gather, so as to prove Moses' lie — "they found none": they did not find what they themselves had scattered..
And where did it go?
The birds ate it.
That is why on Parashat Beshalach, Shabbat Shira, people scatter breadcrumbs[?] for the birds — that is their reward.
Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany.
—o—
j) "They could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter" (15:23)
"Water", according to the Sages, means Torah. "For they were bitter (marim hem)" — those[?] who make themselves into masters[?] of the Torah, into holders of the title "Morenu", into the bosses over the Torah — they "could not drink the water": they cannot learn... Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin.
On a Cultural Institution

[Będzin — culture; library; essay.] „Zangen“ [Ears of Grain]. Supplement for literature and cultural affairs.
(Będzin must have a well-founded Jewish library.)
A few months ago we had the opportunity to read a lament by a board member of the „Hazamir Library“ in Będzin. The board member pointed to the sad state of the institution and came to the conclusion that the „only way out“ to save the institution is for every reader to recruit new members. True, we doubt that recruiting new readers will really rescue the situation; but still, if a board member says so, he surely knows better than the writer of these lines. Nevertheless we hold that this is far from solving the question.
The „Hazamir Library“ is the only non-partisan Jewish library in town, and so the matter ought in general to have been handled in an entirely different way. We do not understand the by-the-way appeal of a board member to the public. We know that „Hazamir“ hates to ring bells and beat drums and advertise itself as is customary today, but one thing must not be forgotten: everything has its measure, everything must be done according to a certain system, in a proper direction. Just as it is not good, for example, to stand up and advertise and praise oneself to the skies, that such-and-such an institution makes mankind happy, so too an institution is out of place when it is too modest, too quiet, when it gives no signs of life about itself.
„Hazamir“ is to this day the only and oldest non-partisan library in town, which has been active almost all the years without interruption and buys the newest books with love and devotion; therefore it has the right to come forward officially, in its own name, and demand of the town that it not be allowed to fall at a time when it finds itself in a critical state. At the present moment, when „Hazamir“ is in such a position that it cannot continue its useful cultural activity for the community, the board is obliged to come with an appeal to the population and to request from it the necessary support, which ought indeed to be granted to it.
The noise and fuss about making mankind happy when one stands at the helm of some society or other is an ugly thing; on the other hand it is also very bad when one hides in a corner and wants the population to know what goes on in the closed rooms. One need not boast and praise oneself, but on the other hand one must tell what is being done and how the work proceeds; otherwise no one is a prophet to know what the activity in the library looks like, what is done and what is not, what the board is able to accomplish and what support it needs. This must surely be taken into account; a board must surely heed it — however modestly it may wish to work, it is after all dependent [?] on the goodwill of the public.
As usual, it is no longer news that here we are specialists at breaking up and splintering; at that we are mighty bullies. Nowadays, in the age of parties and associations, there are even many libraries in town; everyone „makes his own Sabbath“, every party has its own library, which is of course intended for its members, while a non-member or non-sympathiser has neither access nor trust there.
Until now, unfortunately, people have not yet come to the conviction that literature, belles-lettres and science have nothing to do with partisanship; unfortunately one does not want, or cannot, understand that everyone has the right to have the understanding to study or to read what his mind dictates to him, without being an adherent of this or that idea, of this or that direction.
And precisely from this standpoint Będzin must have a non-partisan Jewish library, to which every lover of the Jewish book shall have access and where he shall indeed find everything. „Hazamir“ is the single richest Jewish library in town, and as such every lover of the Jewish book and every intelligent reader must support this useful cultural institution.
Some 20 years ago the „Hazamirs“ were founded; in their time they were [?] modern and quickly became popular throughout Poland and Russia. But with time the lustre faded and the „Hazamirs“ began to liquidate, so that they vanished [„entkumen“] one by one, and their libraries — after they had lain tossed about [?] in attics — usually disappeared, and no one knew where their bones had ended up. So it was in various towns, and no differently in our sister-towns Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa. In Będzin the treasure was guarded like the apple of one's eye, and the guardians truly deserve to be honoured with distinctions, because now, in our day, the library has a historic value — something to which, regrettably, so little attention is paid here.
We hold that the „Hazamir Library“ must not merely be saved from ruin, but must be raised to the level of a large municipal non-partisan Jewish library, to be subsidised by the Jewish kehilla and by the municipal self-government — not just to discharge an obligation, like tossing a bone, but the subsidies should really be granted in a dignified manner, and the sums should be at the height that such a kehilla as Jewish Będzin deserves.
One ought to see to it that the library becomes a fine cultural monument of which Jewish Będzin can be proud. All who have an understanding for culture should be interested in this, regardless of their direction or party. Even individuals, lovers of books, could and should be drawn in. With good will much, much could be achieved.
Those who are interested in the library, who care how and in what way to enrich the cultural treasure, may review the proposal, see to giving it flesh and bones [„beyger“, misprint for „beyner“], and then present it to the public. We have only briefly pointed out that it is possible to enlarge the library properly and bring it to a dignified level.
Besides its needing support from local and party cultural institutions, patrons (Maecenases), book-lovers and [printed „in“, probably for „and“] the large number of readers that will be created in that case can also accomplish much.
We, Jewish Będzin, must have in town a Jewish library that will be a model for other Polish Jewish communities.
After all, it is well known that here people are not penny-pinching [?] [„ben nisht groshndik“]. Sympathetic proposals are gladly supported; one only has to know how to present them, in what way to ask, and at what time to come forward with them.
Y. Sh.

Moshe Apelboim (On the Thirtieth Day After His Death)

[Obituary — art; Katowice.] There are people in the world whose mission it is to remind, through their lives, their fellow men — who are forever sunk in materialism, absorbed in striving to satisfy only the needs of the body, bodily, physical lusts, driven by petty appetites — that the meaning of life does not lie in this alone, that “man does not live by bread alone”; to raise them to a higher level of outlook on life, from which alone the necessity becomes visible “to put spiritual pleasure in the first rank”, and to awaken these needs in those individuals in whom the everyday [?] life has lulled to sleep in their consciousness the drive that forms the partition between man and beast.
Fulfilling this holy mission, which they, the chosen ones, cannot renounce, just as the prophets [printed “vi’im”] could not renounce their thorny path, they meet with mockery and derision from the mob, whose nature has always been to look down with contempt on “idlers”, forgetting that only these very “idlers”, who do not know how to sell and to measure their productions [?] in metres and kilos, create the eternal values that form the cultural treasure of their own nation and of universal humanity. The fire that is alive [?] in them is the drive toward their creations, out of which shines back the divine spark that kindled the fire.
And that fire does not go out until the mission of the God-gifted one is fulfilled without remainder, until the artist’s soul has divided itself among all his creations, so as to radiate from them eternally and inevitably to kindle branching [?] sparks in other hearts.
But had the ideal [?] soul of Moshe Apelboim [Mojżesz Appelbaum] already been entirely used up, so that his physical existence too should have lost its artistic justification? Oh no! His creative drive had not yet lost its momentum, and his last word, for which he was still seeking the right expression, still stood in a forward direction.
All of us, a small group in this prosaic [?] corner of the world, which his muse had chosen for her residence, warmed ourselves in the poetry of his dreams of the future, and we were proud to be witnesses to creative conceptions which, through their realisation, were meant — this we felt — to enrich the wreath of honour of our old-new cultural history with further laurel leaves.
But alas! All these projects were not destined to be realised... Let us say openly that the snobbery and lack of understanding of those who did not feel the responsibility of wealth, who did not know the principle richesse oblige [“wealth obliges”], did much to bring about his premature death...
But let us also mention with direct [?] recognition the noble-minded [?] figures in Katowice, Będzin, Bielitz [Bielsko] and Kraków, who knew what their true intelligence obliged them to (not in “begon-fislen” [?]!), and who, not only with moral support and sincere self-sacrifice, made possible the artist’s creations, which will form one of the most beautiful chapters in our history of art and culture.
Let them [the others] at least have the consolation [?] that even our great Max Nordau recognised [?] very clearly [?]!
A time will come when we shall envy the Katowice kehilla, in whose domain lived and created, and in whose cemetery found his eternal rest, the artist Moshe Apelboim, who was so restless in life.
Levi Buksbaum.

The Dreyfus Tragedy

[Article — the Dreyfus affair; part 1.] By Eliahu Gertner.

(On the occasion of the Dreyfus drama now being performed in Vienna).

The Dreyfus trial is only a small episode in the great chain of trials that have been woven into the history of the Jewish people. Among all the methods used in the struggle against us, among all the forms of oppression that were meant to serve the goal of removing or exterminating the Jews, the groundless accusations were among the most frequent and most painful. Ritual murder, the use by Jews of Christian blood for matzot, the poisoning of wells, causing harm through contact with black, unearthly forces, treason — these were the motives under which dark antisemitism expressed itself. A great number of innocent people found themselves in the dock and were sentenced to death or martyrdom, went to their deaths for the sanctification of God's name. But right and justice always triumphed, and then a dead body was rehabilitated, the person's name was cleared.

———

At the end of the nineteenth century, public opinion in France and in the whole civilised world was stirred up by the great affair of treason that played out in Paris, and by the struggle that arose around the accused Jewish captain Dreyfus. In 1894 a note about military plans of France, written by an officer of the French General Staff, was found at the German embassy in Paris. This caused an uproar and, naturally, sharpened the hostile relations that had always prevailed between France and Germany. It was clear treason, and the traitor had to be uncovered quickly. — Who is the guilty one? — that was the question, repeated everywhere, uttered by every Frenchman, the question that occupied the whole population.

But for the officers of the General Staff, among whom the right-wing parties, monarchists and Catholics, known for their antisemitic stance, had a majority, the question was quite simple. Who can the traitor be, who can act against France, if only one Jew is a member of the highest French General Staff? So they thought, and Dreyfus, the Jewish captain in the French General Staff, was placed in the role of the accused only because he was a Jew.

Nevertheless, it was not the trial of one man, because in the dock — owing to the motives that guided the accusers — sat the entire Jewish people.

At the sound of the accusation the entire Jewish population was shaken, and how strongly the trial worked is shown by the inner upheaval and the change of views in so strong an individualist as Dr. T. Herzl.

What did the career of the young officer, who turned from a patriot into a traitor, look like?

Dreyfus came from a well-known and esteemed Jewish family. As a boy he showed above-average abilities and great inventiveness [?]. Very young, Dreyfus entered the army, where he advanced very quickly, received the rank of captain, and was the only Jew in the French General Staff. Later he married, and when his beloved wife Lucie bore him two children, his only pleasure, after the whole day's daily work, was to spend his time quietly in the bosom of his family. It is quite understandable how unexpectedly — like a thunderbolt from the sky — the heavy and incriminating charge fell upon him. For Dreyfus, the man of pure deeds and thoughts, for Dreyfus the officer with a keenly felt [?] sense of honour, for Dreyfus the French patriot — it was a death blow. He swore that he was innocent. But they did not believe him and convicted him.

(Conclusion follows).

The 'Malbish Arumim' society in Sosnowiec clothes 150 poor children.

The board of 'Malbish Arumim' [Clothing the Naked] in Sosnowiec 'woke up from its sleep' upon seeing that the winter months are already growing shorter and poor children are shivering from the cold. So they set to work with full fervour, and in the course of a month they managed to clothe 150 children with coats and shoes.
Having been able to accomplish such 'wonderful deeds', the board decided to arrange the clothing with great pomp [?]. Through large posters [?] the Sosnowiec public was informed that on Sunday, [week of] parashat Beshalach, a celebration in honour of the clothing of 150 children would take place in the synagogue. In order to 'draw' [the crowd] it was advertised that the speakers would be: first Rabbi Hager, then Rabbi Schwarz and Rabbi Halberstam.
A large crowd came to the festivity, which indeed took place on Sunday morning, but soon a large part of it became angry because the president of the society announced that 'since Rabbi Hager is in a hurry, he hands the first word over to Rabbi Schwarz'...
After the president's 'Chełm sermon' Rabbi Hager left the synagogue in protest.
On the significance of the clothing spoke the rabbis Schwarz and R' Dawidl Halberstam (brother-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe). After the cantor with the choir sings several chapters of Psalms, Mr. Reuven Binensztok [?] speaks, protesting about the Jewish population of Sosnowiec, which stands aloof from the institution.
At the end the cantor with the choir sings the Polish anthem, and when the choir alone (without the cantor..) begins to sing 'Hatikvah', the 'fine' Jews become badly frightened and in great haste they run out of the synagogue..

The new registration system is already being introduced in Zagłębie

On 1 January 1931 two new ordinances came into force concerning changes[?] in the new registration system. Under the new system two registration categories are introduced: residents, and those who stay in the town temporarily.

A resident, under the new system, is a person who occupies a dwelling in a given place and stands in personal or economic relations with the surroundings. The hitherto "permanent residents" are abolished. Only where proof[?] of local[?] belonging is concerned will extracts[?] from these books be issued[?].

The new type of book will constitute a register of the inhabitants. Anyone who stays in town and does not lodge in a hotel for more than 24 hours must register within the next 24 hours. If, however, he stays in a hotel, he must register already within the first 24 hours.

The registration books will be kept by the house owners or administrators, the registers — by the magistrates (municipalities). In doing so[?] the administrators will, on registration, issue printed forms, uniform throughout the country. Entered in the register will be persons who actually live in the town.

To establish the register a survey (questionnaire) has been carried out. Every [—] had [—] to fill in stamped[?] printed forms in two copies for every person living in the gmina[?] on 1 January. The forms of one dwelling will then be gathered into one collective[?] form and handed over to the magistrate to compile the register. In this, every person had to prove with documents the correctness of the particulars given in the questionnaire, such as state citizenship, birth, marriage, divorce[?], etc.

Persons who were married only according to a religious rite, as for example Jews, will have to legalise their marriage; otherwise the wife will be registered under her maiden name and the children under the mother's name, if[?] the father has acknowledged[?] the children as his. The survey must be completed by 1 June of this year. Entry into the register will be completed on 1 July.

In connection with the new ordinance the Będzin magistrate has already proceeded to a numbering of the houses and dwellings.

The survey will cover both persons living permanently in the town and foreigners. In the larger towns, as for example Będzin and Sosnowiec, the survey will be conducted even among[?] the temporary residents.

It is worth noting that only those who "live" in the town will have the right to vote for the town council.

Declarations for the Turnover Tax for the Year 1930

The final date for filing them is the 15th of this month.
Against no other provision of the law on the turnover tax are so many sins committed as against the provisions concerning the declarations [„zeznania“].
The law states that every year — by 15 February at the latest — the following enterprises are obliged to file declarations of the turnover they made in the past year:
1) All commercial enterprises belonging to the first and second commercial category.
2) Every industrial enterprise belonging to the first up to the fifth industrial-licence (patent) category.
3) Every industrial occupation [printed: "industrial enterprise"] for which a licence of the first and second „a-b“ licence category is taken out[?], that is, forwarding agents[?], brokers and the like.
4) Every liberal profession, i.e. doctors, lawyers, engineers and the like.
If a firm keeps commercial books but has not answered in the declaration the questions whether it keeps commercial books and whether it wishes to present them, and has not given a positive answer in the corresponding rubric of the declaration, it is regarded exactly as though it had kept no commercial books at all.
The Supreme Court has ruled that if there is no signature on the declaration, the declaration is nevertheless valid; in any case what matters then is the question whether that declaration is true.
The declarations — if they are sent by post — must be sent registered.
Whoever is late with the declaration loses the right of appeal (rekurs).
We must stress that all enterprises whatsoever have the right to file declarations, even though they are not obliged to and even though they hold a lower licence category, for example the third commercial category or the seventh industrial category; this can harm no one, only the contrary — help.
If[?] anyone thinks it is enough to write in a figure, he is mistaken. Every taxpayer has the right to attach to the „declaration“ an exact description of the business and to state the reasons why in the year 1930 the turnover reached such[?] an amount and not a larger one. One can, for example, point to illnesses and other misfortunes, and one can also point out — in order to avoid a double assessment — that one buys goods[?] on credit[?], that bills of exchange are paid at the same bank for the same goods, and the like; one can also state how much merchandise was left in stock and how much merchandise one had to take back, although it had been sold, because the merchant went bankrupt.
Do not keep everything for the appeal; rather, together with the declaration, hand the tax authority an exact picture of how your businesses looked in the dark year 1930.
Remember that in this way[?] you can help yourselves a great deal, and remember that 15 February is the final date for filing the „declarations“ of turnover for the year 1930.

A little more culturedness. (A letter to the editor).

[Będzin — letter to the editor.] The mourning academy [memorial assembly] for the shloshim [thirtieth day] of the deceased artist Moshe Apelbaum turned out imposing; the theatre hall was overfilled, and democratic Będzin proved in this case too, as in many other cases, that it possesses the necessary sense for the things of the spirit, for that which raises the people above the day-to-day greyness.
Unfortunately — unfortunately, we must point out that all the seriousness and heartfelt warmth which the audience at the academy showed at the beginning — during the orchestra's mourning music and during the speeches — was later, during the concert section, entirely wiped away, and one got the impression of being at a merry performance.
And in truth: was it suited to the seriousness of the moment — the clapping of "bravo", the calling out for "bis" [encore]! I have no doubt that the artists, with their playing, singing and reciting, honestly earned the honour. But did the deceased artist earn the dishonour that upon his grave people should clap "bravo" and demand "bis"!
Again I have no doubt that the audience meant no harm by it. It simply did not give itself an account that with such conduct it desecrates the memory of the departed and desecrates the seriousness of the moment. But a fact remains a fact: we revealed a large dose of unculturedness in this case.
It is therefore the sacred duty of each and every one to influence his own circle, so that on the various occasions of demonstrating spirituality people should show more... Europeanness.
Yitzhak Pesachson.
