First Craftsmen's Examinations in Zagłębie

Last week passed in Zagłębie under the sign of the master's examinations for craftsmen.
In a whole series of articles in the previous issues we have already pointed out in detail the importance of the craftsmen's examinations in connection with the binding Polish Industrial Law and the ordinances of the President of the State of 7 June and 15 December 1927, which radically changed the guild regulations prevailing until then — regulations which had remained in their fossilised state for over a hundred years (since the year 1816) as a relic of the ragged Tsarist regime, with their specific, genuinely [?] Russian restrictions with regard to the Jewish artisan.
Thanks to the tireless work of the Supreme Council [Oyber-Rat] of the Jewish craftsmen's associations in Zagłębie, and to the constant rousing of the great masses of craftsmen to present themselves for the said master's examinations, hundreds of Jewish craftsmen threw down their work and presented themselves en masse for this historic act in the life of the Jewish craftsmen.
The Kielce Chamber of Crafts, which is the only public-law institution called upon to manage all the social-economic and cultural interests of the artisan class in the Kielce voivodeship, correctly understood how to appreciate the role of the craftsmen's movement in one of the liveliest industrial regions of the Polish Republic, and delegated to Zagłębie an examination commission of the most distinguished craftsmen's activists, headed by the President, Mr. Stefan Stuga [?].
Apart from the locally nominated members of the examination commissions (Christians and Jews), there were delegated: the councillors Samuel Kac, the beloved leader of the Jewish craftsmen in Częstochowa; president Joel [?] Gutman, a meritorious Jewish craftsmen's leader in Kielce (both members of the board of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts; the director of the Chamber of Crafts, Dr. Akcentowicz, former head of the trade and industry department in the Kielce voivodeship office, and the secretary, Mrs. S. Kiżymińska [?].
A special delegation travelled to Strzemieszyce to meet the honoured guests, and at the local railway station, where all the guild elders (starsi) and representatives of the craftsmen's associations of all Zagłębie were assembled, speeches of welcome for the occasion were delivered by president A. Opatowski and by the head of the Supreme Council, Mr. A. Gancwajch, to which the numerous assembled public responded with resounding cries of "Long live President Stuga":
Immediately after the festive luncheon reception — during which the President and Director Dr. Akcentowicz, in their speeches in reply to the greetings of Messrs. president Opatowski, guild elder Moshe Hospel [?], [?] alderman (ławnik) Geldsztajn, secretary Gancwajch and others, pointed to their important mission in Zagłębie and underlined their loyal and brotherly attitude to all craftsmen, citizens of the Polish Republic — the commission proceeded to the practical work of conducting the examinations.
On the first day the examinations took place in the conference hall of the Będzin sejmik [district council]; on the last 3 days — in Sosnowiec, for all the craftsmen of Zagłębie. The commission worked tirelessly until 2—3 o'clock at night, and stood at the proper height of its tasks, especially in the sense of professional craftsmanship.
The first candidate was Mr. Abraham Opatowski, president of the Supreme Council, who, by the unanimous decision of the whole commission, was exempted from all questions and is the 4th craftsman in the Kielce voivodeship to have received a diploma of honour. The handing over of the diploma to Mr. Opatowski passed off very ceremonially, with a brilliant speech for the occasion by President Stuga, which left a deep impression on all those present.
Altogether about 300 craftsmen from the tailors', furriers', cap-makers', painters' and carpenters' guilds sat the examinations, and almost all of them passed the examination brilliantly.
Apart from the already mentioned councillors Kac and Gutman, the following Jews were represented on the commission: president A. Opatowski, guild elder J. Rotensztajn (carpenter), H. Geldsztajn and guild elder H. Cymberknopf [?] (painter).
The examinations for the remaining trades will begin on Monday the 9th of this month in Sosnowiec, and it is to be hoped that — at the general request of all the guilds — the chairmanship of the examination commissions will be taken over by the esteemed President, Mr. S. Stuga, who has won the fullest confidence and recognition of the broad craftsmen's circles in Zagłębie.
A. G.
Our Professional Associations.

(What do their members get from them, and what could they have got?)
Reports have once again appeared in the newspapers that tax arrears [zaległe podatki] are to be forgiven, and here I see with what satisfaction this[?] Jew reads through the notice[?]; his face shines with joy, and it is no wonder either, for the Jew knows perfectly well that he cannot bear the heavy burdens that press on him without cease, and he would gladly be freed of them — but he knows, after all, that he must not even dream of that; and here, suddenly, there you are[?], a piece of news[?]: taxes are being forgiven! He will be a little freer, he will be able to catch his breath — well, is it any wonder that his face lights up with joy? One really ought to dance for joy at such glad tidings.
But what comes of it? The Jew does not know that precisely these “glad” tidings are his undoing, because he relies on things now turning out well: the newspaper wrote that the tax arrears need not be paid, so he takes no further interest in the question and indeed does not pay. A few months go by, the bailiff [egzekutor] arrives, and by now there have accrued: arrears, interest, default interest [zwłoki], so that the former moderate sum has now become a quite considerable one.
If we go further, we shall come to the conviction that for the most part such taxes arise from the Jew’s not having kept precisely to the deadline, whereupon interest, default interest, fines and the like began to grow.
Well, one knows that this is no wonder at all. When there are so many tax arrears that cannot be paid by the broad strata of the population, it is no news that when a promissory note falls due one cannot scrape together the few złoty [“gilden” in the original], and that in general one is always 99 groszy short of a złoty. Nevertheless, despite all this, this Jew would keep up with his tax if only he had the possibility of doing so, because he knows very well that for not paying the tax due he pays double and redoubled; and later, when several instalments pile up, he is no longer able to pay the taxes loaded[?] on him, so that in the end he can no longer get out of the mire into which he crept so easily.
On top of this there is yet another drawback — which people actually think is an advantage — and that is the association on which he relies. When he receives a payment notice[?] (nakaz płatniczy — a payment order), he goes up to the association; there they write him an appeal [rekurs], and with that he is sure he has done his duty and need do no more than wait for an answer. Needless to say, this too is a great drawback, for that is not the way tax matters ought to be settled.
So it is hard, very hard, for the average Jewish citizen to meet his tax obligations, and on top of that — as if this were apparently too little — he has to overpay many times over. The Jewish citizen overpays his taxes many times over, both at the tax office [Urząd Skarbowy] and at the municipality [magistrat], and this only because he has no one to remind him of the deadline; yet even if he should for once hit[?] a deadline, he still cannot go and stand about in an office, where he will be stuck for ages, while in the meantime he has no one to leave in the workshop or in the little shop.
It is quite different with the big firms, which have clerks who see to it that every tax is paid on the due date and who do not want to overpay a single grosz. Naturally the smaller merchant, the petty trader or the artisan cannot compare themselves with the big firm, because they have to be everywhere themselves; so that this is where the centre of gravity lies — something which, for the rich man[?], does not come into consideration at all.
What, then, are the middle strata of the population to do — those who not only cannot afford any fine, but for whom even the taxes themselves do not come easily? What are these citizens to do? How can the payment of taxes be made easier for them, seeing that they cannot afford to keep people to attend to these matters?
Actually, as far as we remember, it was for this — but[?] chiefly for their[?] purpose — that the professional associations were created: the Merchants’ Association for its members, the Petty Traders’ Association for its members and the Artisans’ Association for its members. And one cannot say [otherwise] — they do, incidentally, also take an interest in these matters, but very little comes of it. It is, for example, still far from being in order when one sits on the income-tax [dochodowy] or turnover-tax [obrotowy] [commission], or when one writes an appeal. It is not even enough to take the tax instalment from the member in order to settle it; more important is to remind the member when he has to pay this or that tax, and to take the money from him in order to settle it.
The member, then, should not have to come to the association to remind them to take the instalment or to write the appeal. The member should come to the association in order to spend time, to enjoy himself, to occupy himself with this or that question; whereas whatever the member has to settle, the association ought not merely to remind him of it — rather everything should be settled completely through it.
If the association does this for him, he will know that he is not overpaying, that every tax is paid at the proper time; in this way he will not have everything to pay together — several taxes at once, with fines and interest.
The member gets little from his professional association, and therefore some reforms ought to be introduced here. We would even agree to a higher membership fee, provided only that they bring benefit to their members, that they safeguard their interests no less than clerks do for their bosses.
As things stand today the member gets nothing from his association; on the contrary, not only does he get nothing, he gets more than nothing, inasmuch as he relies on it — for in that case he comes to grief, and afterwards he has the after-pains...
In such hard times it is a pity to pay taxes with fines; every grosz overpaid is a sin at a time when earning a złoty [“gilden”] involves so much self-sacrifice, and therefore we hold that the time has come for the members to derive benefit from their associations.
The associations — if they want to exist at all, if they want to have members — must give them something. Every member should have in his association a separate card file in which all the tax documents that have to be settled at each time and deadline are to be found. Otherwise the member gets nothing from his professional association; otherwise he must not rely on it, only to suffer continual failures afterwards.
If the institutions do not introduce these reforms in the handling of [members’] affairs, they will go the way of decline.
Teleks.
Attack on a Jewish trader from Czeladź beyond Oświęcim

[Czeladź — robbery.] Shlomo Grosman of Czeladź, while in the village of Babice, beyond Oświęcim, was attacked by three bandits; one of them threatened him with a revolver and the others beat him until he fell to the ground.
The bandits then robbed Grosman of 133 pieces of toilet soap and also took his overcoat from him.
When G. reported the attack to the police in Oświęcim, a manhunt was organised, in the course of which one of the bandits was arrested.
The arrested bandit is a permanent resident of Sosnowiec.
Railway catastrophe with human casualties

[Sosnowiec — accident.] At the goods station in Sosnowiec a railway catastrophe occurred which caused human casualties.
A locomotive was shunting at the station and ran into a wagon in which there were workers.
From the collision the wagon overturned and three workers were injured. One of the injured was taken to hospital in a hopeless condition.
What Was Heard, What Was Seen

[Feuilleton — Będzin.] Reported by Ben Amotz.

If she knew.
Into a butter shop on Kołłątaja Street comes a Christian girl, a servant at the girls' gymnasium, where the number of Jewish daughters is not small — at that gymnasium where the slogan “the Jew is treyf, but his money is kosher” can be noticed at every step and turn...
The servant buys a few deka [decagrams] of cheese. While the shopkeeper is busy carrying out the “transaction”, the servant looks around to see whether there are any “suspicious” elements in the shop, and says:
— “Panie kupiec [Mr. shopkeeper]! If she, the pani sekretarka [lady secretary] of our school, I mean, were to know that I buy the cheese in a “żydowski” [Jewish] shop, she would throw the cheese out on the rubbish heap. Yes, our lady does not want to enjoy anything that is brought or bought from a “Żyd”; she does not want — so she says — to drink a glass of tea that I bring her from Państwo Gutman [the Gutmans]; she would rather drink the tea I bring her from the stróż [the caretaker], as long as it is not “żydowska herbata” [Jewish tea]”.
— Oh, if she were to know this...

A many-coloured akademie.
The akademie [memorial evening] in honour of the artist Apfelbaum, of blessed memory, was a very successful one. The composition of the programme — (the musical part) was the best expression of what is called: painting. A mishmash of colours, and each and every one holds the brush in his hand and paints...
A certain part of the participants apparently forgot that when appearing at a mourning akademie one has to behave differently from when one goes out to a fair, where there are all sorts of customers and every article is merchandise...
And as I listened to the many-coloured programme, I thought to myself:
— Oh, if a miracle were to happen and Apfelbaum rose in the resurrection of the dead, he would have material for a splendid picture:
— A “colourful akademie”...

5 and 2
... That compassion and fairness already belong to the past is, it seems, clear to everyone. These are no longer “articles” for the present time; today the system of “kol de'alim gvar” [whoever is stronger prevails] has come into fashion: whoever is stronger rules, whoever grabs — has. But that the matter of “compassion” has already gone so far, we would not have believed if we did not see it with our own eyes.
Two weeks ago a Jew, a former merchant, today a yored [a man come down in the world], turned to the Jewish population in Zagłębie asking them to come to his aid; he wrote, the yored, that he and his family are perishing for a piece of bread...
Responding to the appeal were all of two people, not from the “pnei” [the notables], but precisely from the element that works hard and bitterly for a living.
They came to the editorial office with donations and gave a total of 7 (read: seven) gulden [złoty].
One 5 and the other 2...

Do I have to be afraid?
An acquaintance, a Jew, comes into the editorial office and holds the following conversation with me.
For several weeks now I have been receiving every Monday or Tuesday by post the shlimazl, the “mikveh sheet” I mean. I have quarrelled several times with the letter-carrier over why he lets the warmth out [of my home] on account of that rag, although the gentile himself is, after all, not in the least to blame.
What shall I tell you, the “tsa-ting” [mocking pronunciation of “tsaytung”, newspaper] has become a kind of curse-word in my house. When the daughters quarrel, one shouts at the other: “may you have such a face in people's eyes as the “Vokhnbletl” [the little weekly]...
Last week a young fellow with a briefcase in his hand sidles into my shop and demands the monthly fee from me...
When I explained to him that I had not asked for the “sheet” to be sent to me, the young fellow with the little goatee looked me over from top to bottom and then said:
— “So that means you do not want to support”?...
Then he took out a pencil and noted something down, only God in heaven knows what; after all, they do say that those people are hand in glove with the “strong gang”...
So I really want to ask you whether I have to be afraid of those people?...

We and “they”..
Among them, among the nations of the world I mean, whenever any kind of celebration takes place, the custom is
— “he opened with a jug and ended with a barrel”...
Later, when the “celebration” intensifies — knives ring, revolvers bang, and so on...
Among us, among the “Thou hast chosen us” people, every kind of celebration begins with the remembrance of the Destruction...
Here now, the Będzin small traders' association celebrated a house-warming [chanukat ha-bayit] this week. In today's times such a celebration has great significance; as the saying goes: “if wet chips burn, what are the dry ones to do?” If the big industrialists, first-class merchants — groan and sigh, then what are the small, weak traders to do? And since the association has succeeded in having a resting-place of its own, and a very respectable one at that, joy in the highest measure ought to have reigned at the opening.
That, however, was not to be noticed. The well-known “lamenter” (I shall never forgive him for it) — Reb Avraham Lidzbarski once again stirred up [—] pages that tell of [—] oppressions that lie in wait for Jewish merchantry and for the small traders in particular. After him Messrs. Rus and Herszlewicz “accompanied”; it became gloomy, the faces clouded over, so that had it not been for the Land-of-Israel fruits, which “winked roguishly” at the crowd, the celebration would have been turned into a protest meeting against the high taxes...
Only later did the fruits cheer things up a little and strengthen the hope that “Israel is not widowed”, that the Jewish people has existed and will go on existing...

Also a “complaint”
Several young people come in and introduce themselves: we come in the name of a larger number of young people, of the dancing youth; you should “write up” the “great” troubles we endure from today's young wives.
— You are mistaken — I say to them — you probably meant to go to the rabbinate...
— No, we are not mistaken, it is “to the newspaper” that we have come to complain about today's modern young wives, the mothers of children, who go every evening to the dance halls to learn to dance.
“If they, the wives — they say — did not come to the dance lessons, we would have young partners... and the husbands, too, would gain a great deal...
— “Write up the injustice, let the wives spend the evenings at home, because we can no longer bear the “dancing troubles”...
The Renewal of the Talmud Torah (On Sunday's General Meeting)

[Będzin — Talmud Torah; article.] (The great riddle. — Why did it remain veiled? — What next?)
We have read in black and white that this coming Sunday a general meeting of the Talmud Torah in Będzin is to take place. We have read it, and somehow one cannot believe that those who fought so hard, those who went to such lengths and would not allow a general meeting, should suddenly allow such a "crime". However much one argued with the leaders that the general meeting would, Heaven forbid, do no one any harm, that it would only strengthen the institution and that it would make it possible to recruit new members, we never succeeded in winning their hearts, and they brought the institution to the most dreadful condition, until everything had drained away and there was nothing left to administer — and only then did they walk away, with a light conscience and an easy heart, from the institution that was supposedly so dear to them.
There are creatures that can do nothing by the light of day; in the darkness they are mighty bullies, and the darker it gets the better their work goes; but hardly does it begin to grow light than they slink out, even before the sun's rays appear.
If one spoke with the God-fearing ones face to face, they proved to you that they owe God their very soul and are after nothing more than to educate the children according to the Jewish religion. Yes, for appearances' sake that is what it was called, but behind the scenes darkness was at work: intrigues, schemes and all sorts of "good deeds" took the place of honour. But things went along deliciously for them in the darkness, when no one's eye reached there; hardly, however, had people come who dared to demand accounts so that they could publish them, than these "fine little Jews" slipped out as though it were not they who were meant, and then everything stopped at once: the T.T. had lost its holiness, and the children, apparently, need not be brought up in their spirit.
Now, as we hear and as we have had the opportunity to convince ourselves, other people have come in — such as not only do not tremble before the light of day but, on the contrary, endeavour to stay in contact with the town and wish to render an account to all those whom the institution and its activity interest.
We greet the people who have taken upon themselves the initiative of running the T.T., who do not tremble before the light of day, who have no fear of the strongman and are after nothing more than to make of this useful institution what it ought to be.
What ought the T.T. to be for the town? It ought to be a general cheder, a people's cheder for all those who want to give their children a religious education and are not able to send children to private cheders, where the tuition fee is quite high in today's critical times. True, there are communal cheders too, such as "Yesodei Torah" and "Mizrachi", but children who are not well-off cannot get in there. It would therefore be very good if the T.T. board arranged courses for children where the tuition fee would be a small one, a minimal one, so that he who does not want to send his children free of charge to the T.T., and is also unable to pay the minimal price in the above institutions, should have somewhere to place his child.
The general meeting would do well to dwell on this proposal; let it consider it properly, and if it could be realised, that would be a welcome necessity which would bring real benefit to the broad strata of the Jewish masses.
But the main thing must not be forgotten; one must remember the aim of the T.T. as such — that in the first place it must be the people's institution, whose gates must be opened wide for all who want to enter there and learn Torah. One must see to it that first of all the children there learn sacred studies and secular studies, that the child who leaves the T.T. should know "ivri" [how to read Hebrew], know the meaning of the words, and should also command the Polish language in writing and in speech — to the most minimal degree, of course, according to the limited possibilities.
It is understandable that such an institution, which belongs to the whole of Jewish Będzin, ought to be maintained by the Jewish kehilla board; it ought to be subsidised by the community at large. But all that would be well and good if we had the proper representation; and since the representation does not exist and the institution itself is now being completely re-formed, until now there has been no one to give to, and there is no longer anyone to demand from.
And here the question arises: in what way can the board run this large apparatus which it must have so that the lessons take place regularly and the melamdim and teachers are systematically paid their salaries? We are in fact far from knowing what the finances look like there; we only know that the institution is subsidised by the Jewish kehilla board; but understand we do, that, first, the subsidies are far from covering the expenses, and second, it is hard to imagine that out of the kehilla subsidies one could really and systematically pay the melamdim and teachers every week. And since the institution must be run systematically and soundly, it would be necessary for the town to begin taking an interest in this useful establishment, for pledges to be taken on, and for those who until now pay groszy to increase them. After all, the institution is no worse than all the other societies existing to date.
We know that the name does not shine, the firm is blocked [?], for which those are to blame who formerly stood at the helm and who surely had good reason to tremble before the light of day. But now, when order, honesty and intensive activity are introduced, the population will know how to appreciate it and will certainly help to bring the institution to its proper condition, and then, we are sure, Będzin will get a T.T. such as befits our kehilla.
R. Let.
Little Feuilleton: Next Year...

[Feuilleton.] Signed: “Argus”.
There is an old Jewish joke:
Why doesn't the Messiah come?
Because the Jews themselves keep putting him off from one time to the next.
At Passover the Jews say: Next year in Jerusalem; so the Messiah gets ready to come at Passover a year hence. But then at Yom Kippur the Jews say again: Next year in Jerusalem — postponed once more by half a year. So the Messiah reasons: since the Jews have time, why should he hurry? And he goes on sitting there under the Throne of Glory.
I think the joke can be interpreted the other way round.
Why do the Jews postpone the Messiah's coming every time by a fresh half-year?
So that... people should not stop believing in him and waiting for him
The Jews proclaimed “Next year” at the first Passover. The broad public then waited with certainty that in a year's time they would already be “in the Land of Israel” (be-ar'a de-Yisrael). And what would happen if the year went by and they were once again “here” (hakha)? Why, the people would stop believing...
Therefore it was ordained to say “Next year” once more at Yom Kippur, and if a simple person should some day wonder: why does he still not come? — he will be answered: how is he to blame, if you keep granting him new prolongations...
This too is nothing more than a joke, and it occurred to me in connection with another Messiah, who is awaited and never seems to arrive.
Not only Jews are waiting for him, but the whole world
This Messiah is the disarmament of all nations, which is supposed to secure the peace.
The other day I read a newspaper item that the Council of the League of Nations has resolved to convene the next conference on disarmament in February 1933.
A hard question bothered[?] me: why such a distant date? After all, we are only at the beginning of February 1931! And a dark thought occurred to me:
Perhaps they mean that by then the fresh war will already be over, and then it really will be possible to proceed to a true disarmament?...
No, that cannot be! For that war will first of all sweep away, like a cobweb, the League of Nations itself, and it will not be the League that will then be summoning conferences...
It can only be that the fellows in Geneva had the same intention here as the Jews with their “Next year”.
They thought to themselves:
The best means of sustaining faith is prolongation; that is, if a prolongation of half a year could sustain the Jewish faith in the Messiah for a full two thousand years, then if one postpones by two years at a stroke, people will go on believing and believing right into the sixth millennium!
People will believe that disarmament will, after all, come some day.
Let Curtius the Prussian [German foreign minister Julius Curtius] and Zaunius the Litvak [Lithuanian foreign minister Dovas Zaunius] make as much noise as their hearts desire — we shall drag and pull things out as long as it can be done, until.. until...
Either the squire will die, or the donkey will drop dead, or the leaseholder (arendar) will die...
And then the true peace will come.
Argus.
“Baby do wojska!” [Women into the Army!]

[Satirical feuilleton.] By Y. G. Shteynsapir.
“Baby do wojska” [Polish: “women into the army”] — that is the foundation of the proposal put forward by Madame Moraczewska about calling up girls for military service.
How many hundreds and thousands of anecdotes will be created as commentary on this new Torah!
Is it really a matter to make fun of? On the contrary, try to go into it a little more seriously and you will be convinced that this is a proposal liable to cause an upheaval in our life and to answer a great many painful social problems that are literally splitting our brains
I am not even a military man, I understand barely anything of such matters, but it is clear as day that a women's army is more important than a men's one:
First of all, the pleasure will cost a great deal less. A soldier in trousers has a youthful[?] appetite, a gut without a bottom — bread, meat, groats, and all at the State's expense. But a soldier in a little dress is something else — women nowadays are, after all, in the habit of fasting, so that the body should become more delicate — so they will be given a bit of powder and rouge, and that's that...
Secondly, the clothing will cost less. The male soldiers must be well dressed so that they do not catch cold, but for the female soldiers a scrap of “mundurek”[?] [a little uniform] in front and behind will suffice — they are, after all, used to going about naked...
And thirdly, and this is really the main thing — the usefulness of the female soldiers we shall only be able to appreciate properly in wartime:
With what eagerness the male soldiers go to war, we all know. But if a battalion of dress-soldiers is sent off to the front, the entire male army will run into the fire.
Only, as I see it, the men will not be needed at all. If we [follow?] [—] the same path as Balak son of Zippor, who put the daughters of Moab and the daughters of Midian into the fight, we shall overcome our enemies without bloodshed.
As for the enemy in the West, it goes without saying — he is cultured enough not to shoot at the fair sex; true, during the last war he tucked his culture up his sleeve, but in the end our “sugar-pushkes” [“sugar cannons”/“sugar boxes”] did prevail.
And even the neighbour in the East, with whom there is no difference between a pair of trousers and a dress — everything is “tovarishch” [comrade] — will nevertheless cease to be a bogeyman [straszydło] for us, if he only gets a whiff that at the front there are “dziewki w lesie”[?] [apparently Polish: “girls in the forest”]...
These are the benefits the State can have from a dress-army. And now, what benefits society can have, father and mother, and above all — we Jews!
Here we go about worried — where does one find a future for our youth? Well, with the young men it is still only half a trouble — a young man goes off, if need be, to serve, and he is provided for for a couple of years; but the “troubles of a daughter” — just try, pray, to advertise that you need a female office clerk for five gilden [złoty] a week, and hundreds of girls will come running, for they need: a shoe, a dress, in order to be found pleasing and get a bridegroom.
But if Moraczewska's [“Moratshevtshikhe's” — a folksy feminine nickname] proposal is adopted, they will all be provided for — they will run to the regiment [pułk]..
When a lad and a girl, both of them idlers, fall in love, they will not be afraid of the four poles [of the wedding canopy] on account of a flat, furniture and a livelihood, but will step under the canopy and from there straight to the P.K.U. [the district recruiting office]..
And now, what is an army worth that can not only fill mass graves and wreck the world, but can also bear children and build a new world?..
If Moraczewska's proposal is adopted, a marriageable young man who meets an older maiden will not need to investigate how many years she wants to shave off[?] her age. He will ask her plainly and simply — when did you serve in the army?
And should there be one who wriggles out of military service, she will be a precious wife after the wedding, for the husband will always hold a whip over her — remember, I'll hand you over to the draft[?] [“priziv”]...
An educated girl with higher schooling will not be praised[?] for being a woman doctor or a woman lawyer, but rather for being an officer, or at the very least a non-commissioned officer..
And now, the ladies of the local “Maakhal Kosher” [kosher-food society] will no longer, on festival evenings, leave their husbands to go hungry until late at night while they themselves “wait upon” [“ukhazhivat”] the soldiers — they will simply be afraid that the husbands might come running to “wait upon” the soldier-girls...
In short, this is a proposal — as the Warsaw folk say — “shoyn hobn aza yur” [“may we just have such a year”]..
*
A couple of thousand years ago an idol-worshipper came to Hillel the Elder and asked him to teach him the whole Torah on one foot. Hillel answered him — our Torah consists of three words: “Ve-ahavta le-re'akha kamokha”, thou shalt love thy fellow man as thyself!
But since that Torah did not catch on, there has come today — not to be compared — the lady Mrs. Moraczewska with a new Torah, which likewise consists of three words: “Baby do wojska”.
A pity she was not born a couple of thousand years ago..

The Key

By Deputy Dr. Y. Rozenblat.
The budget debates held so far in the Sejm have made one point clear, a point on which almost everyone agrees — that the country is not able to bear such burdens as the expenditures demand. The Minister of Finance finds himself in an unpleasant position and he is not to be envied, for he absolutely must find the means that are needed to cover the expenditures of the state. The situation becomes still worse when one takes into consideration that an enormous economic crisis is raging, not only here but in the whole world.
Some console themselves that in other countries, as, for example, in America, the crisis is stronger than here. But those who console themselves in this way forget that America is rich and we are poor. The population there accumulated money for 16 years, and we have gone through 2 wars and 2 inflations, which were just as ruinous as the wars.
The authoritative circles understand all this quite well and they are looking for means to bring more life into agriculture, into trade and industry.
It is a fact that a very important cause of the crisis is the disproportion between the prices of agricultural products and the prices of all other articles. When the peasant in the countryside must sell his products so cheaply that for the money he receives he is unable to buy anything at all in town, trade and industry receive a death-blow.
Seeking the means of alleviating the crisis, people have come to the conclusion that it is necessary to lower the prices of goods at all costs.
It is precisely in this conception that the whole centre of gravity lies. A lowering of prices cannot be carried out by coercive means at all; with anti-usury offices, with the control of price calculations and with all other administrative means one does not achieve the aim. Goods become cheaper when supply is greater than demand. Dearness and cheapness do not depend on man's good will. There are quite strict economic laws, which do not let themselves be violated.
It is said that there are too many merchants among us, and that is why prices are too high. Economic science and reality say exactly the opposite: the greater the competition, the lower the prices, and the more trade and industry are concentrated in a smaller number of hands, the more prices rise.
Precisely in Poland the gap between retail and wholesale prices is many times smaller than in the rest of the world; in no country does the retailer work with so small a profit as in Poland. The Jewish merchant in particular possesses a special quality — he makes prices cheaper.
Even the antisemites, when they want to buy cheaply, go to the Jew.
We do not at all deny the fact that there are too many merchants, but that is because all other sources of livelihood are closed to the Jews.
It is not the merchant who is to blame for the high prices: the state makes life dearer. It holds in its hands very important branches of the economy, and in precisely these branches prices are very high.
Railways, gas, electricity, tramways, spirits, tobacco, salt, in part also timber, post and telegraph — these are all fields over which the state and the municipal administrations rule as autocrats.
Can one then imagine a cheapening of life without competition? When the above-mentioned articles not only do not become cheaper but even become dearer; when the tax system presses and chokes, can cheapness then set in? And here the Minister of Finance comes along with a proposal to increase the tax burden still further!
According to the latest reports, rent is to be raised by 12 per cent; in other words — yet another very important article will become dearer.
The lowering of prices has today become a question of life. And the government's standpoint is correct. But one must be consistent and show an example; it is the state that must give the example and take over the initiative and itself bring down the prices of the articles which it holds in its hands.
That, however, is bound up with reducing the budget.
And here lies the key to the whole problem.
Tango and Foxtrot, but Poverty Is Above All

Want drives them out, the cold drives them in.
Things are bad, sad and bitter.
It is a terrible crisis: people faint for a złoty, it is hailing bankruptcies; solid [?], well-founded livelihoods, which for years were deeply rooted and stood firmly on their feet, have been shaken out as if by an earthquake. In a word, things are bad, it is a bitter time. But how bitter, how bad it is for those who have nothing to go bankrupt with, who no longer have any livelihood at all; how sad it is for the people who perhaps own nothing more than the shirt on their body and a couple of broken beds with a little poor bedding to cover the body?
Why does no one give a thought to these unfortunate people? What are the Jews of Zagłębie doing in such a terrible time?
It is quite possible that the Jews of Będzin persuade themselves that the "Dobroczynność" [the charity society], with its coal campaign, has quieted their conscience; they have already done their duty in that the tireless R' Mendel Rozenzaft exerts himself and toils beyond his strength to collect at least a few wagonloads of coal, which are distributed among the poor strata. It does not matter whether all those who ought to have taken part in the coal campaign did give something or gave nothing at all. The bare fact that something was given is enough. Who, how much and what? That is nobody's business. For the indifferent, for the passive [?] Jewish inhabitants of Będzin, it is enough merely that something has been tossed to the poor Jewish population — and let it not shout and make a noise.
In Sosnowiec not even such a coal campaign has been carried out. It may be that the coal committee, which was created in Sosnowiec a year ago, has come to the "conviction" that Sosnowiec is the "happiest" town in Poland, that in the town "there are no poor people" who in the present crisis are in need of real help...
But does one really discharge one's duty with that bit of coal alone? Secondly, is the coal committee, with the best will and self-sacrificing effort, capable of satisfying the hundreds of homes that are freezing?
At a time like today, when the number of unemployed keeps rising, when merchants are falling like flies, when workshops stand silent as if paralysed; at a time when the word "crisis" is too weak to describe the sad situation; at a time when poverty, cold, influenza, destitution and want are pushing in through door and window into hundreds, thousands of homes — at such a time one must not keep silent. A mere bit of coal is too little. In addition one must open cheap kitchens, tea-halls, where the hundreds of hungry may be fed with something and where hundreds of the frozen may warm their shivering bodies, quivering with cold
In towns such as Będzin and Sosnowiec several cheap kitchens and tea-halls need to be opened in various directions [parts of town]. However bad the times may be, there is no excuse for this. The want is great, people are quietly wasting away; in the street there is no work, no employment, no earnings whatever, and at home it is dark and slippery; want drives them out and the cold in the street drives them in.
What are the "fine Jews" of Będzin and Sosnowiec doing about it, the well-born, who pride themselves on their honours and honorary titles? What are the Jewish communal workers of Zagłębie accomplishing? And where, too, is the Jewish intelligentsia?
Sadder still, worse still, is that our Zagłębie towns are so [?] afflicted that there is not to be found even a small circle of people who possess within themselves enough courage and such a fiery spark as would give them a push, so that they would rouse themselves [?] with alacrity and set out from house to house, from courtyard to courtyard, and call out: Jews! The want is great, why are you doing nothing?
Perhaps one should also awaken the more pious class in the Hasidic shtiblekh, who are sensitive to good deeds; and if they do indeed do something in this field, they too must be roused and told that it is still too little. It would also do no harm to remind our youth and the so-called intelligentsia, which snatches a little dance at the "Trocadero", and to confide a "quiet" secret in their ear: in the street great want prevails, and it would not be at all amiss to break off one foxtrot, one tango, one waltz. It would do no harm at all if this dancing intelligentsia were to pause for a while from this European "Torah" and do something by which they might at least somewhat relieve the great want and cold.
Those, too, who nowadays in the long winter nights occupy themselves with a game of cards might well pause. But let those dance who love to dance, and let those go on playing who love the "Ober of Acorns" [the Eichel-Ober card] — but on one condition: that during the foxtrot and the tango, and while they are thus grappling with the aces [?], they remember the poor, the frozen, the hungry.
It is a great wrong that in towns such as Będzin [and] Sosnowiec, in such an extraordinarily bitter time, cheap kitchens, or at the very least a tea-hall, should not be set up.
B. Zweig.

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Yitro

[The "Oneg Shabbat" column — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Parshat Yitro.]
a) אנשי אמת... שרי אלפים, שרי מאות ["men of truth... rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds"] (18:21).
Because they really and truly were "men of truth", it did not bother them that Moses made some of them "rulers of thousands" and "rulers of hundreds" and "rulers of fifties", although all of them were equally talented. Among leaders who do not mean the thing truthfully, people are forever quarrelling over the rule, and each one holds that only he must be the "ruler of a thousand", and there is no one who would want to be a "ruler of fifty", let alone a plain soldier.
After Rabbi David of Kotzk [Kock]
—o—
b) וישלח משה את חתנו ["And Moses sent his father-in-law away"] (18:27).
After Jethro had advised Moses to appoint judges and his advice had been carried out, Moses was afraid that whenever a judge wronged[?] someone in some matter, people would at once run to Jethro and want to tear him to pieces: "See what a plague this Jethro has brought upon us with his plan" — therefore Moses promptly sent him off...
R' Yonatan Eybeschütz.
—o—
c) והייתם לי סגולה ["you shall be My treasured possession (segulah)"] (19:5).
A segol is three little dots (∴) which, however one may turn them, always remain a segol. "והייתם לי סגולה" — a Jew is like a segol: however he may twist himself about, he nevertheless always remains a Jew...
Rabbi David'l of Lelów.
—o—
d) ויבא משה ויקרא לזקני העם ["And Moses came and called the elders of the people"] (19:7).
Moses imagined that so heavy a Torah was only for the elders of the people... for those who have already lived out their lives; and when "all the people" [כל העם], the youth too, enthusiastically called out "נעשה ונשמע" ["we will do and we will hear"], it was a wonder to him, and he quickly ran to hand it over to God — "ויגד משה את דברי העם" ["and Moses told the words of the people"] — that the whole people wants to take the Torah upon itself.
Rabbi Chaim of Czernowitz.
—o—
e) הנה אנכי בא אליך בעב הענן ["Behold, I come to you in the thickness of the cloud"] (19:9).
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev once argued it out with God like this: When we made our match with each other, You made in us a match of pedigree — we are, after all, the children of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; You took Yourself a poor[?] girl from a family of pedigree. We, on the other hand, bought ourselves no pedigree in You, since You do not even have a father... So what then? We made a money match, for "לי הכסף ולי הזהב נאום השם" ["Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord"] — and if so, then do give us the dowry...
—o—
וכבסו שמלתם ["and let them wash their garments"] (19:10).
One of the enlightened once asks a rabbi: why are the freethinkers and the intellectuals more careful about the laws of derech eretz [good manners] than the pious?
He answers him thus: When the Torah was about to be given to the Jews, the call went out "והיו נכונים" ("be ready"). Well, the rumpled[?] ones and the idlers came running at once, and so they heard out the whole Torah; the intellectuals, on the other hand, when they began to gather at Mount Sinai — well, one is after all coming among people, so one must straighten one's hairdo, comb oneself, wash, perfume oneself; well, all that[?] takes time. By the time they managed to arrive, the whole Written and Oral Torah had already been read out. They only managed to arrive for the last and smallest Gemara — for tractate "Derech Eretz"...
"אסם גושם"[?] [source credit, reading doubtful].
—o—
g) והר סני ["And Mount Sinai"] (19:18)
The Carmel came and demanded that the Torah be given upon it, since it was upon it that the prophets of Baal had been slaughtered, so it is a symbol of religious patriotism. But it was not accepted. Then came the Tabor, the mountain on which Deborah sang her song of liberation — a symbol of national heroism; but it too was not chosen. Only the tiny Sinai, on which Isaac was brought to the Akedah — for it is greater heroism to bring oneself as a sacrifice for God than to slay even four hundred prophets of Baal... There are more people ready to kill another for an idea than to perish themselves for it..
"הגהות[?] לב" [source credit, reading doubtful].
—o—
h) וירא העם וינועו ויעמדו מרחוק ["And the people saw, and they trembled, and stood afar off"] (20:15).
"וירא" ["saw"] — one may see God; "וינועו" ["swayed"] — and even sway back and forth; but all the same — "ויעמדו מרחוק" ["and stood afar off"]: let one be far, far away...
Rabbi Mendel of Kotzk.
—o—
i) כבד את אביך ואת אמך ["Honour your father and your mother"] (20:12)
וראה בנים לבניך שלום על ישראל ["And see your children's children; peace upon Israel"] (Psalms 128)
Every child always has grievances against its parents, that they do not give it enough, and is always quarrelling with them. So when does peace come? When the child already has children of its own, who in turn — as is the way of the world — have grievances against it. "וראה בנים לבניך" — when your children, too, have children — "שלום על ישראל": you will have peace...
"עלי[?] זית[?]" (the Gaon[?], the rabbi of Ciechanów[?]).

The Będzin Small Traders' Association celebrates the housewarming of new premises.

In recent years the Small Traders' Association in Będzin had no premises of its own, but was merely a subtenant of a tenant... It goes without saying that, having no "roof over its head", its activity could not be what it should have been, and in many fields the association lagged behind.
The present board, with the president at its head, understood this, and thanks to their initiative the association has obtained a home of its own at 2 Małachowskiego Street.
The housewarming took place on Sunday evening. Of the invited merchants' and artisans' associations, delegates came from the Będzin Merchants' Association in the persons of the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, and the vice-president, Mr. Goldfeld, and from the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association Messrs. vice-president Berkower(?) and Żelanka; the association's own members, too (may it be no reproach to them), took only scant part in the celebration.
The president, Mr. G.(?) Rechnitz, declares the celebration open, and Mr. Herman Pinkus(?) is given the honour of cutting the silk ribbon of the handsomely decorated premises, where those assembled take their seats; and after Mr. Rechnitz says a few words on matters of the day, the greetings begin.
The floor is given first to Mr. A. Lidzbarski, who discusses from every side the tax problem and the factors that want to solve all economic questions at the expense of the Jewish merchant class(?), and comes to the conclusion that when the Jewish merchant is firmly organized he will be able to bear all these heavy burdens.
On behalf of the Merchants' Association Mr. Rubinlicht brings greetings; he points to the mutual relations between the two merchants' institutions in the town of Będzin and wishes further success.
On behalf of the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec Mr. Żelanka brings greetings.
About the association's activity in general and the significance of the new premises speak Messrs. vice-president Rus(?) and Herszlewicz.
Then a "lechaim" is drunk, and in honour of the Fifteenth [of Shevat] everyone is treated to fruits of the Land of Israel.
In honour of the celebration the board arranged a banquet at its own expense.
The banquet took place in Mr. Rechnitz's apartment. Apart from the toasts, Messrs. Żelanka (recitations) and Granek(?) (vocal numbers) entertained the participants.

A large number of friends and admirers gathered on Saturday night at the "Corso" to take part in the memorial evening (mourning academy) marking the shloshim [thirty days] of the painter and artist Moshe Apelbaum.

Three children overcome by fumes in Sosnowiec.

In a house on Bukowa(?) Street in Sosnowiec an incident occurred which could have caused three small children to be asphyxiated to death by fumes.
In a dwelling in that house a Christian mother left three children aged from 2 to 7 years.
While the children were playing, a piece of burning coal fell out of an iron stove, from which a fire broke out in the dwelling.
When the mother came back she found the dwelling full of smoke and all the children in an unconscious state.
The doctor who was called gave the poisoned children first aid and then sent them off to hospital.
The children are in no danger whatever.

The Dreyfus Tragedy

[Article — the Dreyfus affair; part 2.] By Eliahu Gertner.

(On the occasion of the Dreyfus drama now being performed in Vienna).

2.
The French population split into two great camps: supporters and opponents of Dreyfus. The make-up of the political factions of that time had a great influence on the struggle around Dreyfus. The parties of the right, the conservatives and nationalists, on the one side, and the radicals together with the socialists on the other side, intensified the political struggle they had been waging until then. The former wanted at any price to have Dreyfus convicted; the latter, as their political opponents, took their place in the ranks of his defenders. In the end the trial led to the creation of two great blocs, for because of it the Catholics, nationalists and conservatives drew together as a bloc of the right, and the radicals with the socialists as a bloc of the left.
Meanwhile the preparatory investigations were concluded, and after much further effort by the defenders the trial took place before the military court in Paris. The verdict was awaited with great tension. Cheerfully the accused Jewish captain rode in a small carriage to the court building.
Driving past the house where he had lived, he was certain that before long he would be continuing his quiet life there.
The charge that Dreyfus had committed his deed for material gain did not withstand any criticism whatsoever, for Dreyfus was rich. The defenders showed[?] that Dreyfus was a French patriot, that the handwriting of the note that had been found did not resemble Dreyfus's handwriting, that the investigations had been conducted subjectively and tendentiously — and in spite of this the court handed down a verdict that Dreyfus was guilty and sentenced him to deportation to Devil's Island; before the eyes of the entire army Dreyfus's epaulettes and military insignia were torn off — he was degraded.
All alone among the bare rocks Dreyfus began his life on the lonely island, a life full of pain and bitterness. He went about with a plan of suicide. But the letters from his wife gave him hope and courage to hold out. If you kill yourself — she wrote — the trial will be regarded as closed[?], and eternal shame will rest on your name and on your children.
Above him was the pure sky and the boundless sea. The only human beings were the guard of soldiers, who always kept their rifles pointed in his direction; no human voice was heard — only the blue sea whispered to him of endurance, and that there were still people who believed in his innocence and had resolved to rehabilitate him.
Meanwhile in France the well-known French writer Émile Zola came forward with an open letter ("J'accuse"), in which he spoke out very sharply against all those who had brought about the accusation and conviction of the innocent Dreyfus. For this letter Zola received a year in prison. At the same time a letter from the French lieutenant [porutshnik] Esterhazy was again found in the German embassy; the handwriting was similar to that in which the first document had been written. It was beyond doubt that Esterhazy was the traitor. After strenuous efforts by Madame Dreyfus a revision of the trial took place. The verdict was clear to everyone. To exonerate Esterhazy was impossible on account of the undeniable arguments that stood against him. And yet — contrary to all expectations — Dreyfus was convicted again. Narrow party antisemitism and the lie had triumphed once more.
But the supporters and defenders of the unfortunate Dreyfus did not cease their work, and they brought it about that the case once again came onto the docket [wokanda] of the Court of Cassation, and now the judges handed down a verdict that an error had occurred in this matter — that Dreyfus was innocent.
After six years the truth celebrated a victory; the organs of French justice washed from themselves the black stain which would otherwise have rested on them for ever, and Dreyfus passed in Jewish history into the ranks of those who suffered only because they were children of the Jewish people.

[Profiles — craftsmen.] Stefan Smuga.
[Portrait] President of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
Born in 1880 in Przyrów[?], Częstochowa county, into a Polish craftsmen's family of good lineage. After finishing the general[?] trade school (tailoring) he left for further professional studies in Berlin, which he completed in 1900. After returning to Poland he became a cutter in Łódź and in Częstochowa. In 1901 Mr Smuga opened a tailoring workshop of his own, and a year later he received a master's diploma.
The year 1905 finds Mr Smuga in the front ranks of the Polish freedom fighters, and in 1906, already a certified professor of cutting of the Paris "National Academy of Master Tailors", he settled in Vladivostok (Russia). There, together with the present-day Polish general Rudzki[?] and with the famous Polish freedom fighter Wilkoński[?], he did an enormous[?] amount for the Polish soldiers in the Russian army, founding a whole series of important institutions in the Polish colony.
In 1910 he came back to Poland and settled in Częstochowa. During the World War he threw himself with all his ardour into public work, and for 11 years in succession held the office of councillor, and in 1925—1927 — vice-chairman of the Częstochowa City Council.
In the same period he took an active part in the citizens' militia; he was chairman of the Częstochowa district committee of the Polish craftsmen's associations[?] (1920—1921), lay judge in the district[?] court (1920—1922), founder and chairman of the Częstochowa Guilds' Council (1922); chairman of the choral society "Lutnia" (1926—27); and finally, in 1929, Mr Smuga was elected a councillor of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts and then — president of that same Chamber.

The Present Grave Financial Situation of the Sosnowiec Kehilla

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] (From a press conference.)
In connection with the kehilla's grave financial situation, the board convened a press conference last Sunday, at which board member L. Jungster gave a brief outline report on the kehilla's activity.
The chairman, Mr. Y. M. Weinreb [?], opens the conference and gives the floor to Mr. L. Jungster.
On taking over the work of the kehilla board — Mr. Jungster begins — we found the work in a disorderly [?] state. For several years the budget has been almost a fictitious one, because apart from the income from shechita, the cemetery etc., almost the entire budget consists of the regular [?] contributions ("skladkes", Polish składki). And here it turns out that the present system of taxation is not a rational one, since the Jewish middle class has lately become greatly impoverished because of the present crisis and cannot pay the kehilla tax.
For this reason the board was forced in recent years to write off a sum of nearly 80 000 zł. And this has led [?] to the pensions of the kehilla officials not being paid regularly. It was simply a disgrace to see how the members of the rabbinate were paid their pensions. Despite the great shortage of money the board had to increase [?] the subsidy to the free-loan (gemilut chesed) fund, to spend a sum of 40 thousand zł. on social aid, especially during the last influenza epidemic, and also to provide [?] for evicted poor artisans. Besides the items mentioned, this year's budget also contains, for the first time, pensions for the rabbinate amounting to 16,500 zł., and 7 thousand zł. for premises for the kehilla.
The board has adopted a resolution to raise the rates of the wealthier taxpayers. The board is well aware [?] that it will meet with strong protests from the wealthier taxpayers, but it had no other choice.
To this has been added another urgent matter, namely: buying a plot for a cemetery, since there is no more room to bury [?], and building a mikveh.
One of those present questions the board about the arrest of Rabbi Englard, to which the board gives an official answer that it has no connection whatsoever with the whole affair; Rabbi Englard's files are with the court, where the matter will be decided.
In conclusion Mr. Jungster declares that no more scandals will be permitted in the synagogue.

You Must Not Accept Your Mandates (A Letter to the Editor)

[Będzin — Talmud Torah; kehilla; letter to the editor.]
Honoured Editors!
Allow me, through the medium of your newspaper, to turn to the Jewish population of Będzin with the following appeal:
The Będzin Talmud Torah, which for decades was locked behind seven locks, where no one born of woman — apart from the well-known clique with its “Yotzer Meshartim” [“creator of servants”] — had any foothold, and which they, through their incompetence and clumsiness, brought into a deplorable, shameful [?] state of neglect both from the economic and from the pedagogical side, faced [?] complete bankruptcy; and, fearing the elections, they supposedly handed over the management to Mr. Jager [?], who devoted himself to the institution heart and soul, wishing to rehabilitate and reform it in accordance with its proper purpose. As one of the means of rehabilitation he also considered it necessary to call a general meeting of those concerned and to interest public opinion in the institution.
The general meeting did indeed take place last Sunday, and there came to it — with the best intentions and good will to be of help in the work of rebuilding the institution — people from various strata of Jewish society. But here a provocative, sad act took place) the clique, fearing that an end was coming to its rule and autocracy, that the “parnassim” wanted to bring in a little light and life and above all a bit of order both in the finances and in the education of the poor unfortunate children — mobilised with lightning speed the whole black army with the rabbinate at its head (indeed the rabbinate — no offence meant — which all year long cares about the Talmud Torah, as about the education of the young generation in general, as much as about yesterday’s day [i.e. not at all]), and by all sorts of means they prevented the expression of a free thought and thereby forced the “parnassim” demonstratively to leave the meeting, so that everything should remain as of old. This is an unheard-of scandal, which must not be tolerated in any institution whatsoever, and especially in an educational institution where orphans and poor forlorn children are brought up; it is impermissible [?] that people who live with notions of two thousand years ago and who have not the slightest idea about education should be entrusted with the education of over 400 forlorn children, who are a burden on the whole of Jewish society, which bears the moral responsibility for their education. And instead of the system of “Educate a child according to his way” prevailing, so that the children are brought up as good Jews and useful citizens able to wage the struggle of life — they are brought up as parasites and spiritual cripples.
I therefore appeal to the Jewish population of Będzin, and especially to its public-minded section, to remember that it bears co-responsibility for the tragic crime being committed against over [—] 400 children, whom fate has cast upon the responsibility of the Jewish population of Będzin, and among whom there are certainly gifted children who, with proper and rational education, would become the pride and honour of the Jewish population — that it must react as is fitting and not allow the coming generation to sink into an abyss of ignorance [?] and darkness.
I especially draw the attention of the supposedly newly elected board members, Messrs. Ch. Goldsztajn, G. Rembiszewski, A. Preminger [?] and Meszulam Lichter [?], to the fact that by electing them the [crafty?] [?] “parnassim” only aimed to use public opinion as a fig leaf to cover their true face and intention. And therefore they must under no circumstances accept the mandates.
J. Wygodzki.
Can One Remain Indifferent?

(The serious critical situation. — Are we doing anything against it?)
If we say that the times are critical and bad, that will certainly be no news, because every one of us knows that the crisis hovers[?] over our heads in all of Poland; news, perhaps[?], will be if we say that many of our Sosnowiec inhabitants are hungry and freezing, have nothing with which to get through the day, and there is not a piece of coal to put into the stove — that is what is heard now in our little Jewish world.
True, not only in the little Jewish world are the times critical; Christian workers too are living through very hard times. But that is no help to us: the hunger of our sufferers will not be stilled merely because the Christian "enemy"[?] is hungry together with him. Besides, among others there is more care than among us, so that the Christian unemployed is not [—] [?]; whereas with us — if we do not concern ourselves with our hungry and unemployed, who will concern himself with them? Who will care for them, if they matter to us as little as last year's snow, if they "go into our left sidelock" [i.e. we couldn't care less]?
We know, after all, that elsewhere there are philanthropic institutions even in quite normal times, which care for those who have no employment — let alone when critical moments come, through which the healthiest trees and the highest mountains are swept away.
We are not of those who like to envy, but still we will cast a glance at our neighbouring sister Będzin and see what a gap, what a long distance lies between Będzin and Sosnowiec. We see, for example, that Będzin cares a great deal[?] [print apparently "little"] for the poor, the hungry and the needy. We know that every year free coal is distributed there to those in need. Besides that there is a "Beit Lechem", which sees to it that the oppressed, who has nothing with which to keep the Sabbath, should not have to go hungry. And we — what do we do for these sufferers, what do we do for the hungry?
Do we give help in the cold winter as well? Do we take care to improve their critical condition, their serious situation? Can one remain indifferent when one sees how people go hungry, children freeze and adults cannot fall asleep for want? Can one keep looking on so indifferently, as if nothing ever[?] happened, as if everything were in the best order? Has one ever[?] heard of such a cold attitude toward one's own sisters and brothers?
Well, we would still understand it if the times were calm and normal, if one could count the oppressed on one's fingers; but not now, when the times[?] are so bitter and every day, alas, brings us fresh victims and new poor people.
One must, after all, pause at such a period[?] over the seriousness of the situation and consider whether it is[?] good to close one's eyes to reality so as not to see it in that way. Will that help the burning[?] question, which is taking the form of despair? It is self-evident that in that way the misfortune becomes much greater and stronger and takes on a simply tragic character.
Do we not sin against ourselves and against the unfortunate people when we let them float on the water without any supervision and help? Do we gain[?] anything by freeing ourselves from this responsible yoke of ours[?]? May we "solve" questions in such a way? And what kind of solution is that? What do we achieve by it, and what do we aim at[?]?
But[?] what is the use of talk and empty words — what will come of it all for us? We must turn to urgent means of help, which must not be postponed. We may no longer let those go hungry who do not have a loaf of bread. Moreover we must remember one thing: among the hungry there are such who only[?] yesterday supported others, who were well-to-do citizens like everyone else, and now have no other choice but either to stretch out their hand for alms or else their fate is to die and simply perish of hunger; for here we are not dealing with schnorrers or professional poor, who have, as they say, taken off[?] the hat of shame and can agree to anything and get along with anyone.
Będzin has so far distributed 1800 korzec [a dry measure] of coal, and the "Beit Lechem" sends home[?] the most necessary products every Sabbath, so as to still the hunger at least on the Sabbath. Let us then look at our elder sister and set about imitating her — it does not matter: good deeds we may copy from anyone, for[?] nobody will count it as a wrong against us. The difference is only that now we must do all this in a stronger form and on a larger scale, because we know how strongly the crisis now reigns, sweeping more people along with it every day.
It is not nice, not honest and not proper[?] that Sosnowiec should stand aside at a distance with such a cold indifference. The city must therefore now set to deeds: not only must bread and coal be distributed to the hungry, but care must be taken to open tea-halls and cheap kitchens, where one can get a little warm food and a glass of tea.
It is certainly not pleasant to announce that pessimism is beginning to spread its wings in all corners of our already grey[?] life, but the prevailing conditions show it to us clearly, and therefore we must prepare for this moment and go[?] face to face against[?] the crisis, which keeps intensifying. Should fate will that the crisis disappear and better times arrive, so that there will be no one left to care for and no one to visit the cheap kitchens and tea-halls, then that will be a satisfaction for everyone. Then it will turn out that our view was more far-sighted and that we had prepared ourselves to meet the serious situation and the hard time.
But as long as the situation does not improve, as long as every day announces harder tidings to us, so long we cannot and we must not remain indifferent. Our conscience does not let us rest, and we must fulfil our human and civic duties.
Let our greatest and sincere public workers dwell on the words now spoken; let them convene a consultation at which the necessary relief committee will be created, which will undertake to create that which the broad Jewish popular masses need so badly, so urgently.
Dr. Papuri.
