What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — weekly feuilleton.] Reported by Ben Amotz.

A Holy War.
On Friday, at the welcoming of the Sabbath, the Sosnowiec "Agudah" [Agudat Yisrael] circulated the decree:
— Mobilisation!
"All shtiblekh [small Hasidic prayer rooms] are to be closed; young and old are to go on Sabbath morning to the [great] synagogue, to take part in the holy struggle"...
The decree was issued in connection with the arrest of Rabbi Englard [a Sosnowiec rabbi]. Surely the Jewish heart aches when things have come to such a desecration of God's name, to such a spiritual decline; but greater still is the pain when those who supposedly go to defend the honour of the Torah — bring about, in fact, the disgrace of the nation. With their tactics they give every little Polish paper the chance to give its readers pleasure at our expense... to mock our sacred things, how people fight during prayers...
— A holy war!

To One and to All.
The door of the editorial office flies open, and in comes an ordinary, everyday Jew, who puts to us such a blockheaded question:
— "What is the matter with you? Your paper is somehow not itself! How can it be? How is it fitting that a paper with thousands of readers should not announce that at such-and-such a time the water supply will not be working? A real scandal"...
— Calm down — we begged our questioner — the news item, or rather the announcement, could not appear in our paper, because we did not dance "at the wedding"...
— What do you mean? I don't understand.
— You surely know that in Będzin there are two "creatures", known by the name "Vayakhel-Pekudei" [two Torah portions read together — a mocking nickname for a pair]. These individuals put out a "tsasing" [a mock form of "tsaytung", newspaper] — so be it. What does the "tsasing" look like? — May all enemies of Israel have such a face... That is not at all what we are after; we only want to inform you in passing that these people, with their "tsating", no longer have a foothold in any Jewish institution in all of Zagłębie; every Jew, even the ultra-religious one, avoids them like mice; the "editors" are regarded within the camp of Israel as...
There came a time when "Moshke" [a mocking name for the Jew] [—?] [doubtful word: "beneyt"] the well-known bear dance, and it was a very marketable commodity. So the sold souls of the "tsating" rolled up their sleeves, hitched up their coat-tails and —
— straight into the round dance...
For this the squire promised to throw them from time to time — a little bone...
The promise is being kept. The squire keeps his word, and when an occasion arises, they remember that these people must be supported. That is exactly why, my dear Jew, we, the "disloyal newspaper", are passed over, and so our thousands of readers really do not know when the water mains will not be working...
Last week a mistake very nearly happened. The announcement about the water matter was, as hitherto, sent to our editorial office, but soon "on the high [?] place" they noticed the mistake and ordered the announcement to be given to the —
— bear dancers...

Not a Single One.
The main topic of everyday conversation is — the crisis. Wherever you turn, you hear sighing, groaning:
— Oh, the crisis...
And on such a "crisis day" the "Beit Lechem" [poor-relief society] called a general meeting. At a time like this, when the number of the needy grows by the moment, an institution such as "Beit Lechem" must be strengthened in every field: its income must be increased, [it must have] good leadership, etc.
To this end the Jewish population of Będzin was called to come to the Sunday general meeting.
But the call was "a voice crying in the wilderness" — not even one person came...
At the same time such a meeting took place at the "Talmud Torah". That meeting did have "powodzenie" [Polish: success]: together with the entire rabbinate came the whole "general staff" of the Ger shtibl, and they fought "with self-sacrifice" so that the "Talmud Torah", which is "so well cared for" by them, should not, God forbid, fall into the hands of the sect that wants to "convert" the 400 children who study at the T.T.
— Leaders of "Beit Lechem"! Do you want the next meeting to be well attended? Then spread a rumour in town that "the sinners want to seize the 'Beit Lechem' in order to give [printed "neben"] the poor people treyf food" — then you are assured of success...

Living Figures.
The Będzin tax office convened a conference of merchants.
At the conference they debated the critical situation, the merchants' position, turnover and the like.
A very nice [?] thing, upon my life: if it has already come to this, that the organs of power want to hear out our sighs, one really must recite the blessing:
— "Blessed be the Place, cheaply [Baruch ha-Makom be-zol]"...
But we have a very practical proposal on this matter, through which the "urząd" [office] will at last get a clear picture and not waste time on conferences.
My proposal is:
Pay a visit to the "Dobroczynność" [municipal charity] and ask the secretary for the lists of those who received free coal in the winter of 1931...
Then I am sure that the delegate of the "urząd" will be astonished, because in the list he will come across a great many people who in [printed "ir"] the year 1930 paid large sums in tax...

Holding Back the "Redemption"..
— It's unbearable any more, all the appointed ends have passed — with this preamble a group of religious Jews comes in, Sochaczew Hasidim, who keep repeating the words:
— It's unbearable any more!
— You surely mean the crisis? we ask them.
— No, this time we are specifically not talking about the crisis. The crisis is an everyday matter, a banal one. We have come to you to get it off our chests, oy, oy.
— Well, speak clearly, don't wear my soul out...
— Yes, let's come to the point. You surely know that last week the Będzin "Agudah" held a festive "siyum ha-Shas" [completion of the Talmud]. We did not check who the real completer is. The main thing is that the siyum took place with pomp, sermons were delivered, as is proper at a "zakończenie [?] [completion] of his Talmud".
Among the speakers was also R' Shlomo Yitzchak Dazar [?], who, while reciting a saying on the Gemara passage "For all commandments one recites the blessing before performing them", first remarked: [—] the saying comes from a great gaon; I know him — he says — but [—] not [call him?] by name, because there is a reason for it".
The audience truly enjoyed the sharp saying, but at the same time did not understand the "reason" why R' Shlomo Yitzchak did not mention the correct name, the "in the name of the one who said it"...
Later the "reason" came to light [?]: the saying comes from the Sosnowiec rabbi, the well-known gaon Rabbi Frommer; but because he is on the rabbinical council together with Rabbi Hager, Shlomo Yitzchak was told from "the high place" not to mention Rabbi Frommer's name...
Worth Knowing. (The Starosta's inspection of the Jewish Kehilla. — How does our management look in the eyes of others?)

[Będzin — Kehilla. Opinion.] Last week our readers had the opportunity to read in the columns of our paper a notice about an inspection (lustracja) that the Starosta [district head] carried out in the Będzin Jewish community (gmina), which dwelt, among other things, on the gifts the board had handed out, and on that occasion he censured such a way of managing.
The Starosta saw this — he who does not know, as we do, the poverty and the need, and is not aware[?] in what manner and with what difficulty we manage, at the present critical moment, to collect the budget (etat).
We understand that one must reciprocate; we know that when people or institutions earn recognition, one must give them a gift as a token of gratitude, and we have no wish at all to doubt that the recognition is deserved — but the medal has a second side too. In the case at hand the question arises whether the community is able to hand out gifts, and we hold that as long as it is not materially able, it must by no means whatsoever do so. In such a case a written thank-you suffices; for official institutions it serves as a diploma and for the most part means more than gifts of money.
We are sure the Pułkownik [Colonel] would not have accepted the watch costing 1,200 zł. had he known in what manner it was given. Likewise the police would not have accepted the armchairs (fotele). One may give gifts — on the contrary, we are not against it — but once that is said, it goes without saying that it may be done when one can, and not the reverse, when one cannot.
True, there is a saying that 'a poor kahal does not give', but that is only a saying. Why should kehilla affairs be ownerless to the right and to the left? May a public institution, whatever it may be, incur expenses it cannot afford? Would any private firm allow itself to make outlays beyond its means? And since nobody would do so in his own private business, why should he allow himself to do it when he sits on the kehilla bench? Or does it impress them to hand out gifts, does it suit them, does it embellish their prestige? On the contrary — may it do them good, let them do it in good health; but then they must not forget their own private pockets, to which they have access at any time, and heaven forbid if that should annoy anyone, since the whole town knows that the kehilla treasury cannot afford such luxuries.
We constantly complain of our dark situation; we point out that the middle class has lost the ground under its feet, and as for our small folk, who barely live even in normal times, there is surely no need to speak of them now. Besides, why should we operate with such arguments? Let us take a look at how management looks in the kehilla board, and that will already give us a sufficiently vivid picture. We know, after all, that wherever the budget can be collected the gmina makes no concessions, and among those people poverty whistles — may God guard and save us. The gmina is now truly tearing from the dead and from the living: a trifle — how much it costs to be buried in Będzin! The kehilla leaders then make an exact reckoning: if they will never again get anything from the dead man, let him pay for the plot of ground more than enough. And with all that there is such poverty, such need, that there is simply no one from whom to take a grosz.
What is astonishing is that, regardless of all this, the only thought is how to have more expenses, how to squeeze in one more and one more, who could ride on the so very weak kehilla nag (klacz).
From outside, when one sees what a broad life the kehilla board leads and what luxuries they can still afford, one becomes convinced that Jews have money, that Jews are well off, only they already have such a nature — always[?] to complain and to weep so that no one should know they have money. And to tell the truth, it is quite understandable that those who do not know inner Jewish life, Jewish livelihoods, the Jewish 'getting blackened' and the scheming how to push through the day by miracles, should think so.
Nor is it any wonder, for our neighbours cannot imagine that in such a lamentable state one could allow oneself to live in such a way, and even if they saw them swear in kittel and tallit they would not believe it, because they are not used to it; they do not understand how one can lead a broad life at a time when one cannot afford it. And one more thing we can say: we ourselves need not be surprised either, for we are convinced that those who do not know the kehilla's management will also be unable to grasp how one can allow oneself to make ever larger expenses at a time when one cannot cope with the previous ones, and, after all, allow oneself to give presents — and not just for form's sake, but for thousands of złoty.
Is this understandable, is this normal, is this fair? Can a person with a clear mind and sound sense grasp it? A trifle — the officials do not get their pensions paid, the subsidies, even the most necessary ones for orphans, are not distributed, whoever is owed money cannot collect it, and the merchants who sold the gifts wear down the doorsteps, and still there is no money; the inventory, the property, the office furniture — all of it together is put up at auctions (licytacje) by the creditors; and with all this, in this dark state, they permit themselves to lead a broad life and to give gifts in such a way that it strikes the Starosta's eye and he issues a reproach.
We are sure that those who received the gifts, had they known in what manner they were taken, would have declined them with thanks and would not have wished to accept; they would have renounced such an honour, which can impress no decent person.
Our kehilla leadership, in which the most varied strata of the population are represented and which is in fact the highest Jewish representation, has already fallen[?] low enough when people come from outside and reproach it for leading too broad a life. Had these people understood the meaning of the reproach, they would have known what a failure this is, what a humiliation for those who represent us before the whole community; this act would have taught them much and would have been a moral lesson for the future. But what comes of it? That they are far from being sensitive, far from grasping what sound common sense, logical understanding, honest integrity and awareness ought to understand; and thanks to that, thanks to the crookedness, thanks to the super-inventions and super-cleverness and false behind-the-scenes politics, they have set out on the dangerous, thorny road that leads our kehilla apparatus in an impossible, incomprehensible and inconceivable direction, which brings it to the level of immorality, of incomprehensible things.
Will such awareness really remain with our leaders in the future as it has been until now? Will the latest and all the previous failures teach them nothing?
It is worth knowing.
R. Let[?].

Messianic Times.

[Feuilleton — reflections on messianic times.] By R. Druk.

One of the most important Reform rabbis in America spoke these days about the Messiah. And he said that the Messiah who is to come will not be, so to speak, a "scientific Messiah", a great scientific genius[?] as Einstein holds[?], but precisely a superhuman Messiah, a divine Messiah, one chosen by God.

And one must try, he went on to say, to help[?] the Messiah come as quickly as possible. One must try to prepare for his coming, and that can only be if people become more moral and hold to the old Jewish practice[?] of justice and righteousness, as our Torah teaches us and as our prophets have taught us.

It seems to me that this alone is already sufficient[?] proof that messianic times have come. Until now only the traditional Jews talked about a Messiah etc.[?] — about a Messiah whom God will send to redeem the Jews and the world, and the freethinkers (apikorsim) thought nothing of it. But when a Reform rabbi has begun to speak of a divine Messiah, that is truly the best sign that something is not at all[?] right with our materialistic world, that people are already going back to seek salvation in our old Torah, that it is already the time of the Messiah.

Naturally there are now many other signs that the Messiah must soon arrive. These are the signs that our sages pointed out[?] long ago.

One sign is chutzpah (insolence). That is: when the chutzpah of the world grows great, it is a proof that the Messiah must come.

And when was there ever greater chutzpah in the world than now? Take a look at our politicians, public figures, cultural activists, thinkers, scientists, writers, poets and diplomats. Wherever you turn — chutzpah.

Every nobody[?] is a man of the world, every little worm is a genius, and everyone praises himself, and everyone boasts, and everyone puts on airs as if he were who-knows-who.

All these puffed-up "activists" issue manifestos and warnings to the world. Thinkers and philosophers who have read through[?] a few booklets about "thinking" write whole treatises in which there is not a single original thought, and yet they are acknowledged as "the greatest of all times" — not, God forbid, of their own time, that is too little — but of all times.

Scientists issue declarations, either[?] that the world is perishing, or that the world is seven hundred quadrillion years old. They can neither prove that the world is perishing nor that it is so old, and even if they were to prove it, it concerns everyone[?] as much as last year's snow.

The main aim is to be in the newspapers. Because otherwise nobody would even know that such great minds[?] exist. They talk and they say, they say and they talk, as long as reporters can relate and immortalise the names of these geniuses of the spirit, who are, naturally, "the greatest of all times".

And it goes without saying that this is nothing but chutzpah.

A writer need only write one sketch and he already proclaims himself the greatest writer of all times.

And further nobodies[?] [—], who live off publicists, will not stint you any song of praise for the spiritually brilliant writer. Why[?] should they stint? They make a living from singing hymns and praises.

Such a man is already entitled to give[?] interviews, and indeed he does not stint. He puts on great airs and pours out lofty phrases about everything in the world. For what can such a genius as he not do? Writing — writing. Art — is art. Politics — leave it to me. Science — no doubt about it. World problems — of course he is the only man for it.

Today one needs no great talent; one needs great chutzpah.

A second sign is poverty — until the last penny runs out of the pocket [word unclear]; that much is certain. A few years ago Jews were rich: they bought houses, travelled abroad and lived the good life.

Now, however, things are different — it is indeed a great misfortune — but the fact is that the penny has run out of the pocket. People are already in debt to the shop, to the butcher; they no longer buy 10-dollar silk shirts, but two for a dollar. It is very sad, but that is how it is.

And this is a sign that it is the time of the Messiah. The last penny is already beginning to vanish from the pocket.

Our sages say that the Messiah can come only when the world is either entirely righteous — all will be righteous — or all will be wicked [cf. Sanhedrin 98a: "a generation entirely innocent or entirely guilty"].

Now it is clear that today's world is far from righteousness and from justice. Judges are judged, and those who judge the judges are judged the next day. When someone begins to look for sins in another, it soon turns out[?] that the seeker himself is not altogether kosher either.

Trials and sins among us have reached such a degree that one already knows who and what. Every day new commissions of inquiry are set up with new expenses of hundreds of thousands of dollars, and they search[?] — and if they at least searched, it would be only half a misfortune! The truth is that they talk about searching.

The investigations among us already recall the Chinese war. Do you know who is fighting whom there? Just so one now knows among us who is judging whom, who is investigating whom.

Well, "entirely innocent" it can no longer be; so naturally it must be "entirely guilty", and it is nearly there: it is truly hard to find an honest man; today one can no longer trust one's own father.

As for money, there is nothing more to say[?]: people have almost lost all trust in one another. We are already approaching a time when people will hide their money in clay[?] barrels and bury them in the earth — and even that they will be afraid to do.

Even a word is now dangerous to say to someone. A favour — the smallest favour is hard to obtain; everyone keeps his distance; people have stopped giving charity; they have become hardened and wicked.

All these signs were enough to prove that it is the time of the Messiah.

But the matter[?] was settled by the rabbi's sermon.

If the [Reform] rabbis have already begun to believe in a divine Messiah — that is surely the best proof that messianic times have come.

No better proof is needed at all.

And between ourselves, it would indeed be only fair that the Messiah should come; it is already time, it is high time.
Islam in the Land of Israel

[Political essay — Zionism, the Land of Israel and Islam; part 1, conclusion to follow.]
V. Jabotinsky [Vladimir (Ze'ev) Jabotinsky].

1) The fear of "Islam"

There is a widespread legend among us Zionists: "the great political power of Islam". This legend now plays a large role in our life. The defenders of the official Zionist policy try to use the legend as cover for the English government, which supposedly "could not have acted otherwise" "because it is afraid of Islam".

Whether England is "afraid" of Islam is a psychological question on which we do not wish to dwell; but the question whether there is a serious basis for this fear — whether Islam really represents such a danger that so mighty and civilized a country should have to retreat [?] against its own interests and against its moral duty — is an objective question. It is a question of the balance of forces. This question we must make clear to ourselves.

Before we deal with this problem, it is worth reviewing [?] a little piece of history: up to the last war, in the last hundred years, Europe gradually took from Islam Greece, Transcaucasia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Morocco, Tripolitania, Algiers [printed "Alushir"], Egypt, Tunis, Sudan, Crete, Macedonia, Thrace — in short, everything up to Constantinople, Asia Minor and Afghanistan. The greater part of the annexations was carried out at a time when Islam was stronger and Europe weaker than now.

Eighty years ago Islamic fanaticism in the East constituted a much [?] firmer bond than at present. Besides, the head of Islam was Turkey, which then played the role of a great power of the first rank. Technology did not yet occupy such a place in the art of war as today: there were no aeroplanes, no poison gases, no armoured cars, no machine guns, etc. Therefore, both in the period of Serbia's liberation and in the period of the struggle over [?] Algiers, the difference between the armament of Europe and the armament of Islam was far from being as great as now. Nevertheless the annexations took place, and Islam submitted quite [?] obediently.

In the course of these 100 years not a single significant uprising took place in the Mohammedan colonies, not counting the uprising of the Sepoys, which had a Muslim character only in part. Not a single uprising, after they had fallen under European power. The Serbs and the Bulgarians rebelled against Turkey, the Italians against Austria, the Irish against England, and finally the Albanians — who are themselves half Mohammedan — rebelled precisely against this same Turkey; but, God forbid, not in Algiers after the year 1847, not in Egypt or Tunis after the year 1882, not in Sudan after the year 1899 did it come to any uprising. One cannot explain this submission by Christian meekness [?] — in the Koran there is no meekness [?].

To explain it by fatalism would mean clambering along the path of light fiction. Why did "fatalism" not prevent the Albanian Muslims from staging a series of revolts against Turkey in the years 1908, 1909 and 1910? One has only one choice: to explain it by plain common sense: Islam realized that it can do nothing against Europe.

This historical reminiscence is very necessary, because since that time great changes have taken place. First, war has become an extraordinarily refined matter of organization, which only very large and cultured states are capable of carrying out properly; second, the Koran as a political cement has met the same fate as all other religions: it has lost all, or almost all, of its political magnetism.

Some 35 years ago it was held that "in the East" religious fanaticism is not only identical with national fanaticism, but even outweighs it. This opinion prevailed not only regarding the Mohammedans but also regarding the Christians of the Balkans. Until recently [?] in Macedonia the Orthodox Bulgarians and the Orthodox Serbs began slaughtering one another — not, God forbid, over a point [?] of faith, since they have the very same faith, but over the language in which the divine service should be held. As this state of fighting went on for many years, Europe finally had to become convinced that the legend about the amalgamating force of the religious confessions had come to an end, that it no longer applies to the Christians of the East. But as regards Islam people still held to the former opinion.

It is remarkable that in this connection people did not notice a very instructive fact. For the first time in the year 1872 and later in the year 1889 [so printed; actually 1832 and 1839] the Egyptian Khedive Mehmed Ali waged war against the Turkish sultan — his suzerain, the Padishah, the Caliph of the Faithful, etc. The second time he even defeated him and penetrated as far as Syria. Only the intervention of Christian Europe then saved Islamic Turkey from Islamic Egypt dealing with her as she deserved. Meanwhile this has been forgotten. At the end of the last century and the beginning of the present one, strong rumblings [?] of revolt made themselves heard in Arabia; in Yemen there was a revolt resembling a war against Turkey. But to this too nobody in Europe paid attention. Even the three Albanian uprisings, which took place one after another, were unable to destroy the old legend that Islam is "a flock with one shepherd" — a flock which one fine morning, at the shepherd's command, will rise up as one, and then something terrible will happen.

(Conclusion follows.)
A Remedy for the Crisis...

[Humorous feuilleton — the economic crisis.] So there I sit, half frozen, in my shop, and I think — and what [?], if you please, does a person think about nowadays? Of course — about the crisis.
Well, I think and I think. Poland is a republic, it seems, with all its pishtshekes [?] [apparently: petty bigwigs], with ministers, deputies, chairmen [?], financiers and economists who carry such heads on their shoulders that bigger ones, it seems, no longer exist — so how is it that all these great people cannot, to this very day, find any [?] way out of the present crisis? If such people, who need not worry about their livelihood either, cannot give the one piece of advice — then who can? Maybe I, with my bundle of troubles that my head can barely carry, am to be the counsellor and drive out the crisis?
But do I have a choice? After all, it is I who feel the crisis, and not those over there with the biggest pensions — so I really took myself firmly in hand and set to thinking, this way and that, and so, weighing the crisis against all the "radical" means of the big-capital economists and politicians, I hit upon a brilliant idea that will surely and unconditionally [?] drive out the crisis, and we shall all be helped just [?] as we wish ourselves.
The plan is as follows:
Since in Poland there are about thirty million people, and of these surely a third are young men and maidens already fit for the wedding canopy but not yet married, the state should therefore issue a "prescription" [?] to all these fortunate not-yet-married ones that, whether they want to or not, they must all marry at once, forthwith!
And what will come of it, you ask? Something will surely come of it [?], because when a young man and a girl marry, they become a couple, and to set themselves up one needs, of course, to have... flats, furniture, crockery and glassware, all sorts of shmattes [?] needed for a household — and what about the dowry? And what about dozens of other little things without which one cannot even go to the wedding canopy? And when all this is needed, it will have to be manufactured, so the workers will automatically stop being unemployed; trade will revive, and when trade revives, the merchant, the shopkeeper, the textile dealer will earn too — and a cure will simply come to all of us as well.
In short, as you see, our "prescription" [?] is truly a complete cure for all, and I now recommend that the state issue our "prescription" [?] immediately and quickly, and that everyone be obliged to marry at once, so that we may get rid [?] of this bitter crisis as fast as possible.
Because, upon my life, if we do not soon get rid of the crisis, the crisis will get rid of us...
"Der Fayerdiker" [The Fiery One].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Mishpatim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Mishpatim
—o—
a) "Now these are the judgments which thou shalt set before them" (21:1)
God told Moses to lay laws before the Jews, to discuss and comment on them; yet these laws, commented on at such length, dealt precisely with the Hebrew slave. On the other hand, all the swindles that exist in commerce were not discussed at length — for fear that there might be people who would learn from the laws, from the swindling possibilities discussed there, how actually to swindle... R' Shlomo Kluger.
—o—
b) Mishpatim.
"If you do not keep the judgments, I shall take the Torah away from you." Midrash.
There are people who rob[?] and plunder, and all under the mask of piety. With the money they have swindled out of unfortunate and poor people they even perform so-called mitzvot and acts of charity. But "I hate[?] robbery for a burnt offering," says God. And the first thing a person is asked on arriving in the next world is: "Did you deal honestly in business?" For if he did not deal honestly, there is no need to ask "Did you study Torah?" — since the Torah of such a man has no value whatsoever. This is the meaning of the Midrash: "If you do not keep[?] the judgments — if[?] you go bankrupt and rob — I take the Torah away from you; your Torah has no value." Ktav Sofer.
—o—
c) "And if men strive together, and one smite another... and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed" (21:18).
Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschutz, the gaon who suffered so much from quarrels and intrigues, writes on this verse in his book "Tiferet Yehonatan" as follows:
"And if men strive" — if people quarrel — "and one smite another" — it is better that he should strike him than intrigue against[?] him and speak slander about him, for — "and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed" — a blow heals up; worse, however, is slander...
—o—
d) "The poor that is with thee" (22:23 — as printed).
"The poor" — what you give[?] the poor — "with thee" — that remains yours, that is your property... Nahal Kedumim.
• • •
The Dubno Maggid came to a doctor and asked for a donation. The doctor, a great miser, answered him: "But I know[?] that he who takes hates to give." So the Maggid asked him at least to answer a medical question:
— As is known, a person sick with fever is forbidden to eat fish. So what if someone dies of a fever — will he be allowed to eat of the Leviathan in the next world?..
The doctor stood dumbfounded before such a "medical question," and the Maggid answered:
— If one gives charity and leaves the world a "kadoches" [a fever; in Yiddish idiom: nothing at all], he will surely eat of the Leviathan. But he who leaves his wealth here and takes a "kadoches" [= nothing] with him — he will not be allowed to eat of the Leviathan...
—o—
e) "The poor that is with thee... neither shall ye lay upon him usury" (22:24).
He who shares[?] his wealth with the poor too works for himself and for the poor; with the usurers, by contrast, the poor work for them... If a poor man borrows hundreds[?] of gulden at interest in order to be able to earn something, he must work for himself and for the usurer. Therefore the Torah says: "The poor that is with thee" — you work for the poor as well, and not he for you... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt not be to him as a creditor" (ibid.).
A.
Sometimes, when one lends a friend some money, so that he will not borrow again you dun him[?] for the debt, although you want him not to repay it — just so that he will not borrow again... "Thou shalt not be to him as a creditor": not "a creditor" but "like a creditor" — like a dunner, a pretended dunning. Beit Yitzhak.
B.
"Thou shalt not be to him as a creditor, neither shall ye lay upon him usury" — the usurer does not need to dun; the interest itself is the "creditor," the dunner: the days that pass and increase the interest do the dunning themselves... R' Yaakov Krantz [the Dubno Maggid].
—o—
g) "Nor curse the ruler of thy people" (22:27).
Even if you have already become a rabbi, a ruler — you still may not curse, you still may not allow yourself too much...
Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha.
—o—
h) "Thou shalt not revile the judges [Elohim]" (ibid.).
R' Eizele Harif kept his son-in-law R' Yashe on "kest" [board]. Says R' Eizele to him:
— Tell me, Yashe, perhaps you know who is the Rabbi of Słonim? We both decide halakhic questions equally, we both live on the same food equally — so who is the rabbi, I or you?
— Let us go out into the street — answers R' Yashe — and we'll hear whom people curse more...
—o—
i) "And on the seventh day thou shalt rest" (23:12).
On Friday night one says in the Shemoneh Esreh "vayanuchu vah" [and they shall rest on it — feminine], on Shabbat by day "vayanuchu vo" [masculine], and at Mincha "vayanuchu vam" [plural].
So it is in our times too [—]. On Friday night the husband stays in the shop and the wife goes home to bless the candles — that is "vayanuchu vah"; on Shabbat morning the husband goes to pray and the wife stays in the shop — that is "vayanuchu vo"; only on Shabbat towards evening[?] does the shop assistant stay in the shop while husband and wife go for a walk — only then is it "vayanuchu vam": both rest...
—o—
j) "Thou shalt not bow down to their gods" (23:24).
A priest once came to persuade a rabbi to convert, and he described[?] to him his happy future: that he would become a bishop, then a cardinal and even a pope.
— And not a god? — asks the rabbi.
— Ah, that no longer.
— Why not? A Jew has already once been made[?] a god.
District conference of representatives of industry and trade in Częstochowa

[Częstochowa — economy and trade.] (From our Częstochowa correspondent)

On Monday, in the chamber hall [?] of the New Theatre in Częstochowa, a conference of representatives of industry and trade of the Częstochowa district took place, convened by the Sosnowiec Chamber of Industry and Commerce. Some 300 representatives of large, medium and small industry and of trade from Częstochowa and the surrounding area came to the conference.

The deliberations were held under the chairmanship of the president of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, Eng. Gawroński [?], and the presidium included Messrs. Dir. Dahagen [?], President Gajmler [?], Dir. Likiernik, Editor Wilkoszewski, Stiller and Weinsztok.

The first to speak was the director of the Sosnowiec Chamber, Mr. Dietrich, who spoke about the activity of the chambers of industry and commerce in Poland in general and of the Sosnowiec one in particular. The speaker touched [?] on all the painful [?] questions of trade and industry and reported that the Sosnowiec Chamber, although it is the youngest of all such chambers in Poland, has already submitted [?] a series of proposals aimed at improving the situation of industry and trade, and is making efforts with the authorities to rationalise [?] vocational schooling, social insurance and customs tariffs.

The main issue of the present moment — the speaker went on — is to create a unified economic front; to that end the Chamber has established contact with the agricultural [?] and craftsmen's chambers.

Also interesting is the Chamber's proposal that in future the 6 per cent deduction from tax for the sickness funds should be divided in such a way that 3 and a half per cent be credited [?] to medical costs and 2 and a half per cent be deposited in the P.K.O. [Post Office Savings Bank] as compulsory savings, to serve as old-age insurance for employees.

President Gajmler then gave a detailed report on the economic development of Częstochowa and its present situation. The speaker characterised Częstochowa's role in the history of Poland in the past and today, recounted the history of the founding of the first small factories that produced religious articles and toys, up to now, when Częstochowa has a varied industry, such as factories of paper, curtains [?], jute, wool, cotton, foundries etc., which are to be found in every other town in Poland.

Together with the development of industry, trade has also grown, but unfortunately — says the speaker — the present situation of the merchant is very sad; the merchant is pushed down to the level of a second-class citizen, although the main burden of the tax screw falls on him.

Mr. Gajmler gave in figures the number of trade patents [licences] bought in recent years and showed that with every year the ranks of the merchants grow thinner, and they are left without any means of livelihood.

The speaker says that in order to ease the situation of the merchant class, the government must strive for cheap credit, [doubtful word] production must be made cheaper, and at the same time wages must not be reduced, because otherwise the purchasing power of the workers etc. will again fall sharply.

The next speaker, Dir. Kaligitowicz [?]: the enormous investments carried out in recent years by Częstochowa industry, which give it the possibility to compete on the world market with the competition of other countries. Unfortunately, however, a great obstacle to the success of our industry against [?] world competition is the impossibility of granting long-term credits. In conclusion the speaker appealed to the government to establish premiums for the export of goods and to lower the customs tariff on raw materials.

The Chamber's tax rapporteur, Magister Szykański, reported on the Chamber's activity concerning the normalisation [?] of the statute on income tax, turnover tax etc.

In the further deliberations Messrs. Rozel [?], Epsztajn [?] and the head of the Częstochowa tax office, Mr. Germak [?], took part, and at 10 o'clock in the evening the conference was closed.
A.
Must Jews Study in Austria?

(A letter from Vienna).
"And what will become [?] of this question?" — thus [?] I ended my last letter, concerning the antisemitic excesses by the swastika-men during the screening of the film "All Quiet on the Western Front" in Vienna. And now I put a second question: must Jews study in Austria? Why should we pay the triple school fees and there [?] be thrown out of the lecture halls and beaten like a band of murderers [?]? Is there really no resting place for the Jewish student who, despite fatal material conditions, strives towards learning?
These are the questions that press themselves under my pen as I take stock of the new antisemitic agitation that has been going on all week at the Viennese institutions of higher learning. Where lie the causes of the brawls that occur day in, day out at the University of Vienna? With this question I turned to the president of the Jewish Students' Committee (Hochschulausschuss), Mr. Rensche [?] Weiss, in order to clarify this matter, so important to us.
The present rows go back to the decision of the Academic Senate, still under the chairmanship of the famous Jew-hater, the former rector Count Greispach [?] [Gleispach], — my informant readily replies, — at that time it was decided to found the nationalist associations of the general student body of Vienna. Special inquiries were sent out to all existing associations concerning this matter. The Jewish Students' Committee too received the questionnaire, and in our reply we demanded: actual equality of rights, posts [?] at the university, the right to wear colours, and other urgent demands which the Jewish student has had to forgo until now. Rector Gleispach did answer [?] the well-founded demands, but not officially, and the negotiations did not proceed further.
Naturally, — Mr. President Weiss informs me further, — we took a negative position on the proposal of the Academic Senate. We decided to remain with the old system and rejected [?] the demand to the rector.
The official circles, however, stuck to their decision and the new student regulations came into force. One of the main points of the new regulations is the right to elect the so-called "Student Chamber", which is to represent the opinion of the entire [—] student body in Vienna. In these elections lie the causes of the present antisemitic agitation, — with these words Mr. President Weiss concluded his opinion concerning the rows.
Now let us relate the facts: the socialist and democratic groupings, which are unfortunately in the minority, decided to boycott the elections. "We do not want to sit at one table with reactionaries", their agitators declared at the pre-election meetings. At the same time the socialists began to conduct a heated [?] campaign against the elections, pasted up election-boycott posters, distributed leaflets, etc.
This business, however, did not suit the swastika-men, and they began to make rows. As early as Monday [?] morning larger groups of Hitlerites in their brown uniforms began to gather on the ramp of the university. Around [?] 10 o'clock they began marching from one lecture hall to another, shouting the well-known slogans: "Juda verrecke" ["Perish, Judah"], "Juden hinaus" ["Jews out"]. The small number of Jewish listeners had to leave the halls, receiving heavy blows in the process. Similar scenes were played out in the Chemical Institute and at the Polytechnic, where the following interesting fact occurred: the socialist students are not allowed [?] to have their own notice board at the Technical College, so they put up a wooden kiosk at their own expense; this kiosk the swastika-men smashed, carried into the courtyard of the school and burned. The fire brigade had to be alarmed, but the firemen were not let into the courtyard. So it goes on all week. Jewish students are not permitted to do their normal work, the socialists fight, and Jews... get beaten...
...And this happens in the 20th century, under the "democratic" Ender–Schober government, in the "city of culture" Vienna, under the rule of Rector Uebersberger, a member of the Pro-Palestine Committee in Austria.
Sussman Lichtenstein.
Vienna, 6 February 1931.
The Autonomy of the Jewish Kehillot

(In connection with the kehilla elections as a whole.)
By Rabbi Shmuel HaLevi Brot (Rabbi of Tomaszów[?])
The kehilla system in Poland is one of the most important problems that Polish Jewry has acquired[?]. The first statute on the Jewish kehillot in Poland was issued by the German occupation authority in November 1917. After the emergence of Poland as an independent state the statute was modified several times by the Polish Ministry of Education and Religious Denominations. Now a uniform law is binding in all territories of the Polish Republic, with the exception of Upper Silesia.
The significance of the kehilla law lies in the fact that it abolished the former Dozór Bóżnieczny [synagogue supervisory board], in which actual leadership lay in the hands of government and municipal officials. Even the kehilla treasury was kept at the magistrate's office. It created instead a Zarząd Gminy [community board], in which the board, with the consent of the kehilla council, has full autonomy to direct and administer kehilla affairs, including the entire treasury. The authorities have only the right of supervision — to check and watch over the kehilla's activity, whether it conforms to the binding law.
Officially it is said that the Jewish kehilla has an exclusively religious character; even the kehilla's official name has been changed[?] to Zarząd Gminy Wyzn. [Wyznaniowej — Board of the Religious Community], in order to stress that the kehilla has no competence in general secular affairs. In fact, however, the kehilla embraces a much wider field of activity: under the law, the kehilla's competence covers not only religious matters; the kehilla is entitled to engage in social welfare and also in certain areas of education. The kehilla is thus able to form the central point which would actually rally around itself all strata of the Jewish population that take an interest in Jewish affairs, regardless of trends and views.
It is very questionable, however, whether in reality the kehillot in Poland fulfil the tasks and duties in all areas of Jewish life, as the statute makes possible for them. Unfortunately the answer is for the most part negative. The causes are various: more than once there stand at the head of the kehillot [—][?] persons who correctly assess[?] their duties[?]; petty ambitions have brought[?] into many kehillot persons of Lilliputian horizons, who push the level of activity down to a very low degree. No small blame lies also with the lack of [—] consciousness regarding the kehilla among the Jewish masses, who often forget that where one puts nothing in, one takes nothing out.
Lately one can notice in official circles a tendency to interfere in the internal affairs of the kehillot, in order, under the cloak of the right of supervision, to subject the kehillot to the will of certain groups and to dictate to them a definite direction. The government bodies, which by law approve the kehilla budgets so that they acquire executive force, permit themselves to strike out or reduce certain budget items on their own authority, and even to insert new items which the kehilla bodies did not mention in their budgets at all. All this is no accident; here we have before us a line[?] that strives — not quite in accordance with the law — to display[?] interference in the internal affairs of the kehilla and to narrow the autonomy rights of Jewish self-government.
It would, however, be unjust if we threw the whole blame on the shoulders of the authorities. No small share in the attacks on the Jewish autonomy rights belongs to certain Jewish groupings that are ruthless in their methods of struggle and, unable to carry out their will in the kehilla itself, where they are powerless, seek protection and help from those whom they regard as close family — in order to prevail[?] in the kehilla by the force of the authorities.
For truth's sake, however, one must admit that quite often the blame for this state of affairs lies with the majority's lack of tolerance towards the minority. People often forget that the kehilla, as the representative body of the entire Jewish public, must above all show a fair attitude to the minority and its demands too, even when the minority does not deserve it, either[?] by its conduct or [—] by its tactics.
It is a fact that permanent[?] cooperation between majority and minority in the kehillot is a rare phenomenon. The consequence is that the dissatisfied use it to provoke the intervention of outside factors, which [—] [—], harming[?] the autonomy of the Jewish kehilla in general and bringing no honour to Jewish society.
And this is indeed the main cause of the great resentment aroused in public circles by the latest executive regulations of the Ministry of Education to the law on the Jewish kehillot, according to which the electoral commission that draws up the list of Jewish voters to the kehilla bodies has no right to include in the voters' list persons who have publicly come out against the Jewish religion. In principle one may hold different opinions on this question. One thing, however, is clear: religion cannot be done any great good by such drastic means. It may perhaps benefit certain persons who are the sole initiators of this „[—]“ move. But this much is certain: the consequences of such a[?] law will be that the „pan referent“ [Mr. Official] of the starostwo [district office] will become the final arbiter on such subtle matters, and he will have to decide whether the person concerned has really come out against religion — which will certainly bring no honour to Jewry.
But if this „law“ is really put into practice, it means a danger to the very existence of the kehillot, because if logic still has any meaning in our conditions, it is impossible to imagine that citizens will be robbed of their right to vote for the kehilla bodies and at the same time be burdened with paying taxes for the benefit of institutions to which they have no rights. The consequences will thus have to be that these persons will be permitted to leave the kehilla; but then one must open the doors wide to leaving the kehilla according to the individual demands of every person — which endangers the existence of many Jewish kehillot.
It is possible that the initiators of the law had good intentions in this; in fact, however, they have done the kehilla system a bear's service[?] [a well-meant disservice], for which the kehillot in Poland will not be grateful to them.

Great desecration of God's name in the Sosnowiec synagogue

Last Saturday something took place in the local synagogue that ought to be recorded for generations to the account of the Sosnowiec Jewish community.
During the prayers, before the Torah reading, an organised crowd entered the synagogue, mostly young Hasidim, who made a tumult, ran wild and disrupted the rest of the prayers.
The "popular wrath" broke out because at midday on Friday Rabbi Yeshaya Englard was arrested together with his 2 sons and daughter.
The arrest was of course a surprise to everyone, but the Ger Hasidim used it as a means of incitement against the "Mizrachi" and against Rabbi Hager in particular, on whom one must take revenge.
The revenge was organised in this way: on Saturday morning the Hasidic shtiblekh were to be closed and the whole crowd was to gather in the synagogue for the holy war.
The demonstration in the synagogue began when the Torah scroll was taken out. Precisely at that moment a tumult and shouting arose; from words they passed to deeds, and between the two sides, i.e. the Mizrachists and the Gerer, it came to clashes.
The fight, which grew ever fiercer, took on a very serious character. The dangerous situation was saved by the detachment of mounted police, which was called out to the events in the synagogue..
The [?] street by the synagogue looked like a battlefield.. fighting sides, mutual attacks and interventions of the mounted police, which cleared the "battlefield"..
The sequel was "played out" in the afternoon in the beth midrash and later also in Modrzejowska [?] Street; in general the main topic of conversation for everyone (non-Jews too) was the arrest and the bloody brawls in the synagogue.
Rabbi Englard was released on Friday towards evening on condition that immediately after Havdalah he report to the police commissariat, where he was held until Monday afternoon. His children, on the other hand, were released from arrest on the same day.
In connection with this, Messrs. Shlomo Rapoport, his son Gimpel [?] and Rozencwajg, residents of Będzin, were also arrested; they were released after the interrogation.
On Monday afternoon, when it became clear that Rabbi Englard would be released, a large number of admirers from Sosnowiec and Modrzejów gathered in front of the commissariat building and shouted: "My chcemy naszego rabina" ["We want our rabbi"]..
When Rabbi Englard came out into the street he was accompanied by the cry "Long live Rabbi Englard" and went home escorted by the assembled crowd, where refreshments had been prepared in advance for the crowd.
———
As we are informed, it is planned to continue the holy war, which is to be waged with reinforced forces this Saturday in the synagogue.
A small factory of forged 10-złoty banknotes discovered

At the head of the forgers — a police sergeant (przodownik).
These days a small factory of 10-złoty banknotes was discovered here. The factory was located on Szalecka [?] Street in Sosnowiec.
The discovery came about under the following circumstances: a certain Alfred Wajda came to Katowice and changed [?] 10-zł. banknotes in several shops.
Wajda made such an exchange also in a dairy shop in Katowice; the owner (a woman) recognised that the banknotes were forged. She went out into the street calling for the police.
After Wajda was arrested, Wajda's brother, a police sergeant in Sosnowiec, came to Katowice and intervened to have his brother released.
The intervention aroused suspicion, and it was ordered that a search be carried out at the police sergeant's as well. The search brought sensational discoveries: at the head of the factory stood the sergeant Leon Wajda with his brothers and sister.
The "manufacturers" have been arrested, and they face a penalty of 4 to 12 years' imprisonment.

A small child saved by a miracle

Horrible suicide
On Tuesday morning the neighbours in house number 8 on Grabowska Street heard quiet groans coming from the apartment of the worker Mr. Maj[?].
They immediately reported it to the police station, from where a policeman came and broke open the door.
When the policeman together with the neighbours went inside, they found the 27-year-old woman Maj[?] lying in bed in a pool of blood.

And so[?] [—] — there came such "fine young fellows" for whom the T"T "lies in their left sidelock" [i.e. they could not care less about it], but when it comes to "saving[?] the Torah" they are ready for the work..
In the presence of a large crowd from all strata of the Jewish population, the president, R' Mendel Dabe, opens the meeting. R' B[?]om Benha"s[?] is invited to chair it; in the presidium are Messrs. Ab"hm[?] Hampel, Eliyah Kh[?] Khrzlavski[?], and Max Landoy[?] as secretary; later the rabbi and the dayanim (moreh-tzedek) R' Yehoshuale, R' Dan and R' Henekh Dovid join the presidium.

Upper Silesian merchants against compulsion to reduce prices.

Last Wednesday evening a conference took place at the Chamber of Commerce in Katowice with the participation of a large number of merchants. At the conference the question of reducing the prices of goods in Upper Silesia was discussed.
The assembled merchants declared that they are against the compulsion to sell the goods more cheaply. The price reduction would cause the merchants in Upper Silesia to be ruined. Instead, the government — the merchants said — ought to reduce the turnover tax (podatek obrotowy).
It was decided to turn to the Minister of Commerce about this with a memorandum.
Evictions because of renovation or building work.

The Supreme Court has these days issued a ruling of principle concerning the rights of tenant and landlord.
If a landlord wants to renovate his house, or wants to rebuild it, and for that purpose must vacate the tenants, he is obliged to give them other dwellings, equal ones and with the same conveniences that they have now.
On the other hand, if the landlord is compelled to rebuild his house because a catastrophe threatens in the house, then he can obtain an eviction against the tenants even without giving them any other apartments.
This ruling of the Supreme Court bears the number 309-19 of 22 January (styczeń) 1931.

General Secretary of the Chief Rabbinate in Eretz Israel Has Come to Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — rabbinate and Eretz Israel.] Staying in Zagłębie at present is the general secretary of the Chief Rabbinate in Eretz Israel, editor of the monthly journal "Kol Torah", the rabbi and gaon R' Shmuel Aharon Weber.
Rabbi Weber has come on a mission of the "Va'ad ha-Rabbanim ha-Me'uhad" (United Rabbinical Council) in Eretz Israel, of which he is one of the leaders. The aim of the council is to provide the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel with all its necessary religious needs, to support impoverished rabbis and Torah scholars, and to help the persecuted rabbis in Soviet Russia to reach Eretz Israel. In this field the "Va'ad ha-Rabbanim ha-Me'uhad" has already managed to accomplish much.
The council has decided to carry out a campaign in Poland, and for this purpose Rabbi Weber has also come to Zagłębie.
It is to be hoped that, despite the severe economic crisis, the Jews of Zagłębie will help Rabbi Weber with all means in his campaign, so as to enable the council to carry out its important task.
The Fate of Dozens of Jewish Families Depends on "Beit Lechem"

[Będzin — charity and social aid.] (A letter to the editor.)
Dear Editors,
We hereby have the honour to ask you to give space to the following letter.
The "Beit Lechem" society, which has existed for some years already and keeps alive hundreds of respectable Jewish families, now finds itself — because of the present economic crisis — in a catastrophic situation: the income is getting smaller and the expenses greater; many of those who until now were regular contributors to "Beit Lechem" are now[?] themselves — because of their great need — turning to it for bread. But unfortunately nobody takes any interest in the important institution, and the whole burden of its existence lies exclusively on me alone.
As proof of how far the disregard of the local Jewish population for "Beit Lechem" goes, the fact may serve that at the annual general meeting which we called 2 weeks ago, of the 16 members of the board unfortunately barely 4 came, and of the members — nobody at all...
As a last attempt, the second general meeting will take place next Sunday in the hall of "Ahavat Chesed", Kołłątaja 24, at 5 p.m. sharp, and in the name of the great number of needy we turn to the Jewish population of Będzin with the call: remember that hundreds of people, newly impoverished[?] formerly well-off people, are kept alive by "Beit Lechem". Come, then, all as one man to the general meeting, in order to strengthen together the activity of "Beit Lechem", so that it can fulfil its tasks towards the poor population.
But if the general meeting this time too does not succeed, we shall be forced to close "Beit Lechem". We take off ourselves the great moral responsibility towards more than hundreds of respectable Jewish families who suffer want and hunger.
Respectfully,
On behalf of the board
Chairman A. D. Balimowski[?].
The Call of the Eldest Gaon and Tzaddik of the Generation, the Author of "Chafetz Chaim", May He Live Long

[Zagłębie — yeshivas and fundraising.] What the Chafetz Chaim writes to the rabbi of Sosnowiec, the rabbi and gaon R' Menachem Hager.
The appeal of the Sosnowiec rabbi, Rabbi R' Menachem Hager
As is known, there exists in Poland one of the largest yeshivas, under the direction of the eldest gaon and tzaddik of the generation, the author of "Chafetz Chaim", may he live long; this yeshiva has produced geniuses and great men in Israel.
Nowadays the yeshiva finds itself in a very critical financial situation, because America, which in fact maintained the yeshiva, is now going through a very severe crisis and has stopped sending support.
There is a real danger that the most exalted thing that Polish Jewry possesses — will go under.
A great campaign has therefore been started throughout Poland, in which the entire Jewish population takes part. This campaign has also begun here in Zagłębie, and in connection with it the author of "Chafetz Chaim", may he live long, has sent the following letter to the Sosnowiec rabbi, the rabbi and gaon R' Menachem Hager:
[Hebrew:] "[—]t[?], to the honoured[?] great rabbi, great in Torah and wisdom etc., his honour our master R' M. Hager, may he live long, rabbi in the town of Sosnowiec.
I hereby turn [to you], and my request to your honour is on behalf of our holy[?] yeshiva and its three hundred students, great in Torah and the fear of God, who to my sorrow are now in indescribable distress and terrible straits because of the terrible crisis prevailing in the world and the collapse of the support from our brethren in America, through which we have sunk into enormous debts of many thousands of dollars, which put the whole existence of the yeshiva in danger, God forbid.
For this purpose my friends are travelling to your[?] community, the great rabbis renowned for their Torah and piety, namely the rabbi and gaon, head of the rabbinical court in the town of Nowy Dwór[?] (Lida district), his honour our master R' Eizik Kamenetzky, may he live long, son-in-law of the late gaon, the head of our yeshiva, of blessed memory, together with the honoured rabbi and gaon, our master R' Yitzchak Shlomo Gertner, may he live long, the rabbi of the town of [—].
And I hereby ask your honour to receive the aforementioned rabbis with your righteous right hand on their holy mission and to assist them with all your power, and also to rouse the generous-hearted and lovers[?] of Torah of our[?] honoured community to take up this holy matter with heart and soul, for the sake of the existence of the great house in which Torah has been spread for sixty years now, so that it does not collapse, God forbid, under the yoke[?] of the terrible distress and pressure.
And I sign with a blessing that the merit of the Torah may stand by your honour, and may you be blessed by the Holy Name, blessed be He, in body and soul[?] and all good, and may your eyes behold[?] the salvation of Israel and the raising[?] of the horn of the Torah speedily.
As is his wish and the wish of the one who honours and esteems him,
Yisrael Meir HaKohen,
author of 'Chafetz Chaim' and 'Mishnah Berurah'."
In connection with this, the Sosnowiec rabbi, the gaon R' Menachem Hager, has published the following appeal to the population of Zagłębie:
[Hebrew:] "In the name of God, life and all good, Selah! To my friends, the men of my peace, dear [?], all my brothers and companions, may they be blessed by His name!
After greetings of peace and well-being.
Although it is not my custom to come with flowery words, and especially in [this time of illness?], at the time of the terrible crisis in which every Jew[?] is sunk — may the Omnipresent have mercy — yet out of respect for that gaon and tzaddik, the author of 'Chafetz Chaim', may he live long, I have gone beyond my bounds; and so I ask you, my brothers and companions, that you too know how to value the importance of the matter, and [several words unclear] this time, and that you do not [?] lend your hands to destroying, God forbid, this shining edifice from which go forth geniuses and guides for Israel; and let each one help with all the effort of his strength, with proper donations of real substance, and the merit of the holy Torah and its students will protect you, that you be blessed from the abode of blessings, and that God fulfil all their wishes for good.
As is your fine wish and the wish of the writer, for the honour of our holy Torah and the honour of that holy elder, the author of 'Chafetz Chaim', may he live long.
The humble[?] Menachem Mendel Hager,
chairman of the Rabbinical Council of[?] Sosnowiec and the district."
It is worth noting that this is the first time that the author of "Chafetz Chaim" turns to Polish Jewry for support for the yeshiva, and this is something entirely unique.
The two great rabbis and geniuses of Poland have come especially to Zagłębie: the rabbi and gaon R' Yitzchak Eizik Kamenetzky, may he live long, head of the rabbinical court of Nowy Dwór[?], Lida district, and the rabbi and gaon R' Yitzchak Shlomo Gertner, may he live long, head of the rabbinical court of [?].
We believe that everyone will receive the two emissaries of the Torah with a friendly countenance and support the campaign as it deserves.

Important Information about the Sale of Thermometer Scales

When measuring temperature one usually uses a thermometer.
Because the object [?] is an ordinary one, various complications arise from this, because the thermometer is graduated according to different thermometer scales.
Most widespread here are the Celsius and Réaumur scales, which are not only inconvenient but are often the cause of serious consequences. For example, a doctor who comes to a patient measures his fever with a Celsius thermometer, and later the patient's temperature is measured with a Réaumur thermometer that is in the house; such [?] conditions can do much harm in the healing [?] of the patient.
The Minister of Commerce took an interest in this question and issued an ordinance on the basis of a decree, which states that from 1 September 1931 only thermometers with the Celsius scale may be sold. In order to give thermometer dealers the possibility of getting rid of their stocks of other thermometers, the Minister of Commerce's decree provides a concession: thermometers graduated in the Celsius and Réaumur scales may be sold until the end of 1931.
Are Such Things Permitted?

Esteemed Editors! In the name of a group of Jewish theatre-goers I have the honour to ask you to print the following lines:
From time to time the actors Lida Potocka [?] and Zygmunt Turkow come to us on tour. But such contempt as we witnessed this Tuesday we did not expect from such artists, who pretend to be the best we possess in our theatre world.
This Tuesday the above-mentioned actors performed a brand-"new" play entitled "For the Sins of the Fathers". How disappointed we were, however, to see that the drama had been disguised under another name: instead of giving it its correct title, "Ghosts", they "swapped" it for "The Sins of the Fathers".
And the question arises: is it permitted for such artists to lure audiences to a disguised play? Is this not an act of irresponsibility and contempt towards the Jewish theatre-goers?
A theatre-goer.
—o—
Second Spring Fair in Katowice.
As we are informed, the "Second Spring Fair" will take place in Katowice in the period from 22 May to 8 June ("czerwiec"), on the exhibition grounds by Kościuszko Park, organised by the "Society for Exhibitions and Economic Propaganda", Katowice, Stawowa [?] 14.
The fair, which will take place in Upper Silesia, will be a good opportunity for home production.
Producers and merchants should pay close attention to the fact that Upper Silesia is not merely a place where transactions in various articles can be made, but also possesses large branches of industry.
Reviving trade, providing employment for the jobless and improving the economic situation depend on the success of the spring fair in Katowice.
