We Must Guard the Honour of the People.

(Which way do the intriguers now want to go? — Jewish Sosnowiec must walk over their heads and stamp everything out[?].)

The arrest of Rabbi Englard [rabbi of Sosnowiec] and his household aroused an understandable agitation in the town, if only because it was unexpected for the town's inhabitants, so much so that even the Polish press had something to occupy itself with..
But if one wants to dwell more deeply on the matter itself, if one wants to consider the question — the matter of the rabbinate — seriously, sincerely, honestly and with restraint, one must surely come to the conviction that there is no reason at all to wonder at any extraordinary event or sensation, for everything could have been expected, and[?] nothing should arouse astonishment or wonder, because the fruits develop according to the deeds[?]. People let themselves go down the most slippery paths, which one can hardly[?] imagine in their nuances[?]; they stopped at nothing in order to reach the goal; they forgot [—] the [—], that there must be a border between humanity and personal ambitions, between decency and coarseness. One blushes with shame on hearing along which paths people have galloped off[?] and which means they have used; that all illegal deeds became kosher in order to reach the goal goes without saying.
And therefore we are not particularly surprised when we see that it has come to arrests, that one man wants to have the other deported[?], one side wants to bury the other, so that they may know[?]... And with all that we still do not know whether all this excessive sharpness has already reached its culminating point; who knows, it is possible that the affair will become sharper still and that we will yet have from this business enough disgrace and humiliation, enough shame and pain.
It has, after all, become a fashion[?] to set upon[?] rabbis like this, not to ask after anyone or anything, only to do as "Berl the bigwig" wants; all one needs is to dig in one's heels — this is how I want it and this is how it must be — and then[?] nothing exists any longer but one thing: ambition. And for that bit of ambition people and towns will be ruined, fires will be kindled, people will depart this world; humanity and the name "Jew" have been forgotten, the honour of the nation has been pushed aside; fires will flare up between children and parents — as long as the ambition is carried out the way this or that strongman, this or that opinion-giver, wants it.
Well then, is it any wonder when we look at the events these deeds[?] have brought about? Could one then have counted on something better and finer, on something more important and more useful? Is it then not self-evident that from harmful deeds nothing useful can arise?
And the interesting thing is this: as soon as anything happens, whatever it may be, people go and vent all the badness, all the bitterness, on the synagogue. When Rabbi Englard was arrested, people first of all went to storm the synagogue; one would think — what does one want of these ordinary, everyday Jews, who stand far from intrigues and combinations and cannot even imagine how one can let oneself go down such slippery paths, through which one loses human awareness in general and decency in particular.
Why, in such a case, does one go and exploit the synagogue? What does one want of people who stand so far from quarrels and informing[?]? Why does one go and drag[?] it in there? And then we are made proud[?] of the fact that people come there to desecrate the holiness, and to quiet it down one must call out the mounted police! Is that really an honour for us, are we raised up in people's eyes in this way? Has such a thing been heard of among any people whatsoever, that in order to incite the population one should come into the houses of study? In holy temples among the nations of the world one cannot imagine anything similar. At such moments we look in people's eyes like non-humans, like wild creatures, of whom one speaks with irony and contempt. Do we not understand on what a low level we find ourselves then? Does it really bother none of us? Do we not feel stricken, and do we not bow our heads in shame? Do we not see how deeply we sink then in the eyes of the people who live together with us in the 20th century?
Yes, when it is a matter of ambition one loses every limit of decency and humanity; one is out for nothing but carrying out what one has resolved, let it cost any price, let it involve danger to life — one does not stop on that account; one becomes bewitched and enchanted and sees[?] only that one is right and in order, and that by law one may shout down everything[?] in the world; on the contrary, one even talks oneself into believing that the most unworthy and the basest must be applied with all one's strength for the sake of a mitzvah. If only we were as steadfast and patient[?] in healthy and normal deeds as one exploits it on our crooked and twisted paths — we could boast of it and be calm and proud of it.
Now people have set about, with all their strength, taking revenge on one another, and surely they will stop at nothing and take no one into account, as long as they carry out the most terrible thing they have resolved upon. It has thus taken the turn of "Let me die with the Philistines" (tamut nafshi im Plishtim): not for me, not for you — "neither mine nor thine shall it be". One understands, then, that in such a case a wild round-dance ("korohod") and a dance of demons will begin, chasing after the most terrible and most cruel; and when one considers all this calmly and with full awareness, one's hair must stand on end from fright at the shame this can lead to in our camp, pessimistic enough as it is.
And it is worth asking the question: does the community, the broad Jewish community, which as usual always remains indifferent to such matters, discharge its duty when it keeps aloof[?] at a distance and, as if nothing were happening, looks on with silent apathy as hatred and revenge rage — which will lead to still more desecration of God's name and to boundless defilement of Jewish national interests and of Jewish honour? May we all allow so much irresponsibility and lawlessness to reign? Surely we must give ourselves an exact account of where these fine deeds may lead and what may come of it all.
The question must be dealt with clearly and openly, with all sharpness and awareness, and a resolution[?] must be brought out: what next? What will happen later, when evil winds are allowed to rage beyond all the bounds of our hard existence?
It would be justice — and not only justice but an urgent necessity — for Jewish citizens of Sosnowiec, for whom the honour of the people stands higher than intrigues and party politics, to deal with the question honestly and sincerely; they should speak out and adopt a decisive position on the question.
There ought to be created a kind of commission of serious, sincere and honest people of various tendencies, who should somehow regulate the question so that at least from now on no more filth and disgust is poured upon Jewish Sosnowiec. These people ought to go over the heads of those who have set themselves the goal of defiling and degrading with their shameful deeds the Jewish community, Jewish honour.
Such a commission must be created, and it can do very much for the good of Sosnowiec Jewry. It can crystallise and regulate the question in such a way that at least no more bitter drops are brought in there, which bring Jewish honour and pride to so much shame and pain. Especially concerning the rabbinate affair itself so much has already been done — that can now wait for the decision of the high tribunal.
Our task now, therefore, is not to allow Jewish honour to be soiled, not to defile our holiness with our own hands, and not to let any more filth be poured over Jewish heads.
— That is what our task must be at the present moment; that is what we must guard with special caution and reverence.
R. Let.
For belonging to the Left P.P.S. one will be punished in the harshest manner.

[Kielce province — state and politics; the Left PPS.] The Kielce voivode [provincial governor] has published the following proclamation:
Dated[?]: Kielce, 11 February [luty]
To the general population.
The Left PPS [Polish Socialist Party–Left], in existence since 1906 and led by the communist organisation, has throughout its activity spread communist slogans and aimed at tearing away a part of the Polish Republic.
The criminal work of the party became clear in the trials before the district courts in Sosnowiec and Lublin, and also before the court of appeal in Warsaw, which sentenced its leaders to prison terms.
The verdict of the Sosnowiec district court, issued on 26 February [luty] 1930, confirmed that the Left PPS is an anti-state organisation.
On account of the above, the Minister of the Interior, whose task is to protect the integrity and security of the state, has recognised the Left P.P.S. as an illegal organisation.
I therefore warn the population not to belong to this party and to the bodies of which it is a part.
I declare that anyone who, after this warning, belongs to the Left P.P.S. will be brought to judicial responsibility with the full severity of the law.
Voivode: Paciorkowski.
What One Hears, What One Sees.

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — weekly feuilleton; kehilla, Agudah, livelihoods.] Conveyed by Ben Amotz.

A new item on the programme..
I, dear readers, — ask you not to hold it against me for the compliment I pay the "Agudah" [Agudath Israel]; it has earned it honestly, and wherever there is even a crumb of truth, there — as you well know — we are the chief in-laws...
Before us lies an invitation from "Poalei Agudath Israel" in Będzin, which celebrated its 7th-year jubilee.
Until the year 1931 we thought that jubilees were celebrated at 5 years, at 10 years; really distinguished institutions celebrated 25-year jubilees — then came the "Poalim" and made — a "revolution" in this field and introduced a reform
— a 7-year jubilee, an allusion to "shiv'ah yemei shabbta" [the seven days of the week]..
But that is not what we are after; "important" to us is another novelty that was planned and carried out in the programme of the celebration.
Among other items, the following items of the programme were also carried out: 1) the members prayed, and after that there were — humoresques...
For that — I think — a great yishar-koach is due to the "Agudah", that its "children", the workers, are introducing reforms into our life...
— New programme items...
One thing, though, I fear: that, God willing, at the celebration of the second jubilee the "Poalim" will no longer put into the programme that "there will be praying".
— If only I turn out a liar...

New "livelihoods" among Jews
Gentlemen, I am becoming[?] an optimist, I laugh at what is called — the crisis. You will surely prove to me that a large part of the merchants have come down in the world, that livelihoods are being torn out of Jewish hands, that the taxes are ruining the community; nevertheless I can show you that there are still livelihoods which are (for the time being) exclusively in Jewish hands...
Just take a stroll in the evening hours, even after midnight — through the streets of Będzin and Sosnowiec, and you will meet a brand-new generation of traders.
— Bagel sellers,
They buzz like flies; wherever you turn, they leap up at you:
— Fresh bagels, fresh bagels...
Nobody bothers them, free trading hours, and the main thing:
— free of "obrotowe" [turnover tax]...
One shortcoming they have: the bagel sellers love to talk a lot...
And while they hand you the fresh goods, they tell you that "they used to work at the railway station, earned a few groszy taking out luggage, carrying off a parcel.
— Well? Why not go on like that?
— I ask.
— But we are Jews... They don't even let us up onto the platform [peron]... Not a single Jew may be there...
— Fresh bagels, fresh bagels...

What we demand.
The telephone directorate in Sosnowiec, on account of the difficult situation, has reduced the price of a telephone installation.
Instead of 150 — only 100 gulden [= złoty].
A very fair thing; as it were[?], the new telephone subscribers will gain — 50 gulden.
In a time of trouble — a respectable coin.
But when the above-mentioned directorate thought it over and came to the decision that discount prices must be made for subscribers, they, the directorate people, should first have taken care of the hundreds of old subscribers.
They, the old subscribers, do not demand discount prices, only that in the present hard time, when everyone's expenses must be cut down, the subscribers should not have to use medicines to strengthen their nerves...
That the "conveniences" be arranged so that, when the subscriber asks for a telephone number, his nerves are not shattered because of the flirting — that the telephone girls carry on...
— That is our demand...

They are striking off.
— You must not keep silent about this — a member of the budget [etat] commission tells me.
And he relates:
"In this year's budget the 'Agudah', that is to say those who stand at the helm of the kehilla in Będzin, is striking off the budget list dozens of people from the not well-to-do part; above all they are from the category that is far from 'Agudah' politics"...
— Who knows — says the informant — what plans the "Agudah" is already hatching for the coming kehilla elections; perhaps the "Agudah" wants to prevail upon the authorities that, apart from the "galebradnikes" [gaberdine-wearers, i.e. Hasidim], the artisans, small traders and all those who do not pray in the Ger shtibl should have no right to vote either...
— A question about a story...

One of their own speaks..
The "secret" informant from the "general staff" of the Będzin "Agudah" came to us, as is his way, with tremendous complaints: how can it be? We keep silent about such wrongs being committed in our kehilla?
— They have brought here — he says — a young man from Warsaw, to whom, outwardly, they handed the secretariat of the Będzin rabbinate, but here they are after[?] something else. The secretary is in fact a candidate for the post of the fourth moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor].. only, because they are afraid of "lamah yomru" [what will people say].. he has for the time being become the secretary, and later there will jump out of the secretary's chair
— a moreh hora'ah..
Such experiments on the part of the Agudah politicians are no news to us Będziners, and we believe that the new experiment too will succeed, especially[?] when one of their own speaks.
The Passover Campaign in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — relief; the Passover campaign; editorial.]
(The prevailing hard situation. — The question must be seriously discussed. — It must not be put off.)
When times are hard; when the crisis rules with such enormous force in every corner of our life; when the heart is heavy and the soul is sad — our hands drop, we somehow stop thinking with all our 248 limbs, we then lose our balance and are beside ourselves.
It is exactly the opposite of how it should be: one must be steadier in a time of trouble, one must keep within bounds when things are bad, one must stand on guard when the people is living through a crisis, and that is when the people's interests must be protected in a far stronger form than in the ordinary, normal period.
It is true that when the heart is heavy one has no head for anything; one loses oneself and remains helpless. But that does not mean it is good this way and that it must go on this way. When one falls, when one sinks, one must see to raising up the fallen and not letting the sinking one [printed "זינדיגן"] be hurled[?] down into the deep abyss.
Hard times have come, bitter times, and the worst of it is that the prospects for the future are not at all brilliant, and with the best will in the world nothing but[?] pessimism appears on the horizon. That is the worst of it, and that is precisely why one must indeed be steadfast and keep within the bounds of awareness and steadfastness.
Jewish Zagłębie should[?] have given timely thought to the hard situation. One must not forget, then, that after the long grey winter Passover appears, a holiday which even in normal times is not easy to bring into the Jewish home — let alone now, when it takes miracles to earn a piece of dry bread. But all year long one lives as best one can: earn a grosz today and you have something to get through tomorrow with. Not so at Passover, when one has to lay in provisions for eight whole days — and that nowadays is no small matter. Such a thing looks like a fantasy, like a tale from the Thousand and One Nights; one can have no idea how one can even think about such things [printed "עגליכעס"]. To lay in provisions nowadays, and Passover ones at that, for an eight-day holiday is no small matter for an average family — to say nothing of the destitute, of those who only yesterday were among the givers and now, poor things, figure among the receivers. Do we understand what a hard trial these people will go through in the hard Passover days if they are not given enough attention, if no proper interest is taken in them? And so it is: when things are bad, a relief campaign must be considerably bigger, because there are more needy, more hungry, more fallen and oppressed and suffering people, who in such a critical situation absolutely must be reckoned with and even kept in view. Our conscience demands this of us; our responsibility and our brotherliness demand this of us.
One must set about the great and responsible work in good time. One must not forget that this year a Passover campaign cannot be carried out just to discharge a duty, merely so that one can say a Passover campaign was carried out here or there. Now nothing may be done for the sake of publicity; it is too risky to allow oneself such a luxury in so serious a time. Now a Passover campaign is so necessary to carry out on a broad scale that the whole order would have to be changed: as usual [printed "געוועגליך"], the custom among us since time immemorial is that all the attention is given to the professional beggars and incidentally also to the professional "respectable ones", who are well versed in such matters and know how to manage quite well in their town — so that it is not to them that all the attention should be directed. On the other hand, one should take an interest in them to the extent of seeing to it that the young and healthy can earn something for Passover: for example, they should go to the matzah baking and to cleaning the houses, where they will earn quite well at the work, since one cannot get as many Christians as the towns in Zagłębie need; and those who will not want to take up the work although they are able to do it should not be provided with the necessary provisions for Passover, for there will be nicer and more deserving claimants for them.
The relief campaign must above all take care of the fallen merchants and artisans, who have no employment and who have unfortunately lost the ground from under their feet. These people languish in their rooms and nobody knows their sufferings, their downfall, their unbearable situation — for outwardly they are, so to say, people like everyone else, and many of us think that they are givers, since only a short while ago they still belonged to that rank.
Therefore it will not be easy for the people who will stand at the helm to seek out these homes, which will have to be provided with the necessary provisions.
Founding Passover relief campaigns for the towns of Zagłębie is necessary right now; it must not be put off, because this year the campaign will be exceptionally hard to carry out. Certain changes would have to be introduced; for example, a radical "sanacja" [clean-up] would be needed, because the times are hard and one cannot give to everyone, simply because one cannot exploit too much the citizens who are still standing on their feet — one does not know whether he who will give so-and-so much can give more. Therefore one will have to content oneself with the support received, and precisely for this reason a certain classification of the recipients would have to be carried out. As for the support itself, it would have to be considered whether it should consist of provisions or perhaps "in kind"[?] [printed "אין גאטור"], i.e. one should give the needy money and they should buy the provisions with it themselves. These are all technical questions that must be carefully considered from the outset. One must also consider, for example, how and in what way the funds will come in. In a word, there is a great deal of work, and the campaigns must be organised with deliberation and awareness, because this must not be done standing on one foot, as an incidental activity from which, as usual, a fiasco then results. That would mean taking too great a risk, too much and responsibly onto the conscience of thousands of human souls who will hardly be able to wait for the moment when they will have the chance to get something into their mouths for themselves and their starving households.
Sosnowiec and Będzin, Dąbrowa and Zawiercie — all must already now set about considering how and in what way to carry out this hard campaign, which must not be frittered into bits. Let no miniature expenditure be made of it merely so that one can boast: "We had a Passover campaign", while in truth few will benefit from it. Such a fiction must not be made in the present hard time; it is too risky, too fraught with responsibility. Precisely for this reason it would be absolutely necessary that in every town the Passover campaigns be created already now; first of all the committees should be formed, in which honest, logically thinking people should take an intensive part, people who of course know the town, so that the system of favouritism ("protekcja") can be entirely eliminated; one should give only to those who have no other way out, those whom it will keep alive.
At the present moment there is no need to stand and preach how necessary the establishment of these Passover relief campaigns is; one need do no more than know in what way to run them, and that their creation should indeed now be realised.
Y. Sh.
Dostoyevsky (On His 50th Yahrzeit)

[Literature — essay on the 50th anniversary of Dostoyevsky's death.]
By Szymon Rotenberg.
(On his 50th yahrzeit)
After Shakespeare, deeper and more universal than Tolstoy, Dostoyevsky portrays for us the mystical soul of the Russian people. If Tolstoy shows us the human soul in its healthy, normal condition, Dostoyevsky presents to us the sick soul in its abnormal, morbid state. Like a skilled surgeon he cuts open the human skull and shows us with great precision the finest vibrations of the human soul. Nothing escapes[?] him, nothing is hidden from his piercing eye. Just as Dante looked into Hell, Dostoyevsky gazed into the abyss of our deepest depths, and like a well-practised seismograph he records everything he saw there.
The painful ecstasy that Dostoyevsky makes us undergo almost always comes in place of a narcotic. At times we suffer so terribly that we would throw ourselves upon the man who dares to [—] in our inner depths. Often it seems that he torments us without any sense, needlessly, that he is not after our good, but that his burning thirst for knowledge drives him to it, and he uses us like laboratory animals on which one performs the most varied experiments. But every time we are already inclined[?] to condemn his writing as criminal, we come to the conclusion that the operation was necessary and was for our good, and we thank the surgeon.
Dostoyevsky's world-view is a mystical, not a realistic one. His heroes are mostly not normal types; they are sick, pathological types who are unable to think like simple, healthy people, but who constantly philosophise about the problems: God, man and the world.
Dostoyevsky's religious-mystical conception of the world prevents him from seeing the real causes of the antagonisms in social life, which lie in class difference. He holds that man himself is bad and that no social reforms whatsoever will be able to make him better. He therefore does not believe in socialism, but he hates the [—] and takes the side of the poor, the insulted and the oppressed, defending them against the attacks of the rich. He even hopes that salvation will come from the powerful, through their becoming better and changing their attitude to the poor.
Can one commit a crime and remain unpunished by one's own conscience? Is the murder[?] of a harmful, parasitic and inferior creature, at a moment when great material means are to be found [with it], permitted, when the murderer believes that with these means he will be able to make the world happy? May not non-average people break the law which is valid for ordinary flesh and blood, in order to create new values? These are the main ideas of "Crime and Punishment", perhaps the strongest work in world literature, which treats the eternal problems in the light of psychoanalysis.
Before Raskolnikov murders the old woman moneylender, he makes peace with morality and logic. Everything speaks for killing the old woman, for what use does she bring? She merely gets in the way, while Raskolnikov could bring benefit to society. He regards the social order as one big piece of injustice, where the stronger rules, where all means are kosher and everything is bought up with the price[?]; why should he not be permitted to kill such a useless, parasitic creature as the old moneylender?
Raskolnikov makes peace with morality and logic and murders the old woman. But conscience, the prosecutor who dwells in each of us, did not consent to this peace, and like a [—] [—] creature it tears itself out of the abysses of the subconscious and drives its sharp claws into the soft[?] heart[?] of the criminal, not letting go of him until the end of his life. Never does logic succeed in fully narcotising the conscience to such an extent that it would remain entirely indifferent to a crime committed.
If man cannot free himself from the punishment of conscience, Dostoyevsky nevertheless holds that the punishing of a criminal by a man is itself a great crime, because the judge would have committed the same crime had he found himself in the same circumstances in which the criminal found himself.
Dostoyevsky portrays for us with dramatic force the struggle between the divine and the devilish in man — the two mighty forces that are found in each of us and that stand in eternal struggle. We all wander about in life without realising that a great deal within us is sick. It is the sickness of imperfection that torments us. We want to attain harmony in life, but the beast that dwells in us stands in the way; it is the voice of the blood, which reminds us of our animal origin, and we sink almost always powerless towards the abyss.
Can man be blamed for his powerlessness? It is hard to answer, for after all man is no more than the arena on which the struggle between the divine and the devilish takes place; he is, after all, no more than an object of experiment, which is very often destroyed in this struggle, in which reason, logic and morality often play a meagre role.
In "Karamazov" Dostoyevsky portrays this struggle for us with incomparable virtuosity. We shudder at the sight of the sickly penitents, devoured by suffering and doubt, who dig with sadistic pleasure in their wounds and torment themselves without any sense, merely for the sake of some[?] idea of torment known only to themselves.
And yet Dostoyevsky believed that salvation for mankind would be brought by the Russian people. "Do you know," he writes in "Demons" [The Possessed], "who is the only people on earth, the only God-bearer, which will renew and save the world in the name of a new God, and to whom alone and exclusively the keys of life and of the new word have been given? Do you know that this people is the Russian one?"
With his mighty intuition Dostoyevsky sensed that the Russian people would come to the world with a new God, with new ideas; he sensed that the gigantic colossus called the Russian people would awaken from its mystical-religious half-sleep, in which it had been sunk in the course of long generations, waiting for a miracle.
The miracle came, but not from "above", from the powerful and the rich — as Dostoyevsky had believed — but from "below", from the humiliated and insulted, from the trampled and the spat-upon, who for centuries had been exposed to the "mercy" of the world-mighty, bloody tsars, of the Ivans the Terrible, the Pauls and the Nicholases.
The "Sanacja" and the Jews

By Dr. Yaakov Wygodzki [Jakub Wygodzki].
The sold-out Jews of the interested lists, which "adapt themselves to Jewish psychology", are canvassing[?] with all their might to grab[?] the simple Jews into the sack: artisans, small traders and the like — with promises to ease their difficult situation by reducing and reforming the tax which they can no longer bear; further, they promise to cheapen credit and make it more accessible, etc. In a word — a whole series of fantastic salvations and consolations. On this hook of satisfying the "devout"[?] interests of our unfortunate masses they want to catch them too[?] — naturally, gentlemen[?]! Therefore we must once and for all sort out this matter and first of all render ourselves a clear account of the causes of the economic and financial crisis that prevails in Poland generally — in very general strokes, of course.
Poland, after its resurrection ("rising")[?], lost its market in the East, from which it drew its sustenance before the war. On the other hand, Poland — because of its too-low economic culture, chiefly because of the poor organisation of labour — is unable to compete with foreign countries on the world market. Therefore its production, protected by protective tariffs, depends[?] almost solely on internal consumption — on the innermost market. With such poverty a solid householder must live very modestly, cutting all his expenses to the bone. The expenditure budget of such a householder must be fitted to his income, which must first of all be established.
In Poland, however, exactly the opposite happens: first of all the "necessary" expenses one wishes to spend are put together, extravagant[?] out of a grand-householder's feeling[?]...
To meet these expenses the state revenues are squeezed out, chiefly by the tax-screw. So it turns out that the state lives beyond its means: it demands not what it can, but what it wants to spend[?].
In Poland the state budget barely limps along behind the far-reaching foreign policy... This is the main cause of the great poverty of the Polish population in general and of the constant financial crisis from which the state never emerges.
When the foreign expert Hilton Young said at the time that the budget must be cut to 850 million, he was told to go home; the same thing happened with the second expert, Prof. Kemmerer.
Today, therefore, there can be talk of reducing or thoroughly reforming the tax in Poland only if the budget is reduced by no less than a third!
Whoever understands anything at all of Polish politics understands that this is impossible today!
Therefore all the promises, both on the part of the lists and on the part of their partners, "to abolish the turnover tax and reduce the tax burden in general" — are nothing but an utter lie!
In this very sense of "we neither want to nor can" the government expressed itself in its first appearances after the elections.
Moreover, the government has hinted at new taxes which it thinks necessary to introduce, such as the housing tax, among others. Further there is talk of rationalising and standardising the grain trade; further it is planned to help the [?] "scissors" crisis of the village by cheapening industry. This idea is a very correct one, but carrying it out in life by a decree fixing prices — we already know from wartime that this is impossible. The cheapening of prices can be achieved either by a better organisation of production — that is a surer but long road — or by reducing the tax, chiefly the turnover tax! And that, after all, they do not want!
It is clear, therefore, that the whole trouble will land on the Jew's head. The tax he must pay — in any case no smaller than before; and the price he must take — smaller!
To this one must add that the antisemitic economic policy of the renowned[?] financier W. Grabski towards Jews, in taxes, in credit and in customs matters[?] alike, has remained almost unchanged.
After all that has been said above it must become clear even to the "Jewish economic groupings" that the economic situation of Poland in general and of the Jews in particular is influenced far more, and far more often, by political aims than by economic ones.
Therefore the struggle to improve this situation must be waged chiefly on the political and national plane, and not only on the technical plane of trade and industry..
It is further clear and explicit that the game of intercession (shtadlanut) — or[?] Agudah-politics with Jews, without a change of the entire political direction, is worth nothing and is at best served up[?] for foreign consumption when it is needed — especially when a loan is being sought abroad and it is thought that this too depends a little on the Jews...
That is why the "music" is always played to the accompaniment of the foreign band's drum!
Jews who let themselves be caught on such a hook always remain fools, though very often with good intentions...
Thus it must surely be clear to everyone that the promises made to the Jews before the elections — "many[?] economic concessions" — supposedly in the name of the "Sanacja", were made only in order to dupe the Jews. The sold-out Jewish souls who ran this voting[?] business earned well from it.. When they dare to come again to the Jewish street with their slogan "Don't vote for Jews!" — they must be received as such guests ought to be received... At least they should [—]; when they sell out the foolish[?] Jews, let them not laugh at them! The "Sanacja" can come to an understanding with elected Jewish representatives openly and honestly, without the dirty elements — especially among Jews — that have attached themselves to it.
We need no Purim-play "favours", but cultural and economic equality of rights we must have, in accordance with the Polish constitution!

At last came the winter of 1917, Turkey entered the war, the "Shepherd" pronounced his word of authority — but nothing happened. In the first weeks after Turkey entered the war, the Sultan, as the Caliph of the faithful, proclaimed the "Holy War" and called on all the Mohammedan peoples in Morocco, Algiers, Tunis, Egypt, Syria, the Caucasus and India to rise up against Christian oppression.
The text of this appeal we still remember, and here it figures as a completely blank page. Nevertheless I will allow myself to fill this blank page with a few personal impressions, simply in order to liven up the boring narrative a little.
By chance I had at that time the opportunity to visit the most important places of the North African coast. Experience had taught me, as an old newspaper correspondent, a great piece of wisdom: if you want to learn Ivan's secret moods, don't question him but his neighbour Peter. And it is even more to the point to interview his neighbour Yitzhak. Out of professional diligence I also held conversations in every town with influential Mohammedans, especially with the young ones; of course they all answered that the "Holy War" was nonsense. But I was not yet satisfied with that. I had letters of recommendation from Gibraltar to respected Jews along the whole northern coast. Besides, in every town I met Zionists; with many of them I had already been in correspondence; all[?] of them were merchants, native-born inhabitants and great-grandchildren of inhabitants. They spoke openly and hid nothing from me, and it turned out, naturally, that they had nothing to keep secret. Not only in Morocco, where the Sultan was not recognised at all, but also in Oran, Algiers, "Constantinople" [as printed; probably Constantine in Algeria], Tunis, Alexandria and Cairo I invariably received the same answer:
— Have you heard about the call to the "Holy War"?
— We have.
— Impression?
— Not the slightest!
— Can one expect uprisings?
— Not even a sign of it!
— Then what will happen now?
— Nothing, only complete order and full obedience.
And so indeed it was.

The Algerian "Goumiers", Muslims only, covered themselves in heroic glory on the fields of Flanders, and that for their "Christian oppressors", fighting against the allies[?] of the Caliph. Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Terumah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Terumah
—o—
a) "And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying" (25:1).
All the speech that God spoke to Moses was only — "saying", for the sake of the Jews, so that he should pass it on to them. The great Moses, too, was raised up so high only for the sake of the people: not the people for the sake of the leader, but the leader for the sake of the people. Tiferet Uziel.
—o—
b) "That they take for me an offering" (25:2).
"For me — for My name." Rashi.
The verse speaks only of the collectors, the gabbaim [?] ("they shall take", not "they shall give", as it really should have been written), and they are told that they must demand charity only for its own sake (lishmah), not for false purposes. The givers, on the other hand, the donors, may even intend it not for its own sake, even for glory — as long as they give. Teshuot Chen (Par [?] R' Sh. Kaminker).
• • •
In Slonim [Słonim] there was a mighty rich man, but a great miser, "a Noahide who is put to death for less than a prutah's worth"; and when he already had to give something, he gave it with anger and ill-temper. Reb Eizel Charif said of him:
— If he liked being a son of Noah so much — Noah had three sons, after all; why did he choose to be precisely Ham ("anger")!..
—o—
c) "Of every man whose heart maketh him willing ye shall take my offering."
The offering did not consist of gold and silver, for that was not the main thing, but — "whose heart maketh him willing", generosity of heart. Divrei Shaul.
—o—
d) "Every man whose heart maketh him willing ye shall take my offering."
The collectors, those who will lead [?] and gather the offering, shall be such people "whose heart maketh them willing", who will themselves give. That will be the best propaganda: when the speakers and agitators for the fund contribute themselves and do not discharge their duty with mere speeches... Yalkut HaDerush.
• • •
About a rabbi who demanded [?] donations [?] for giving a blessing, and himself did not want to spend a penny, Rabbi Meir of Przemyślany said:
"This is the generation of them that seek him (this is a bad generation — a generation of vanity), that seek thy face (who demands even the spiritual gift [?]), Jacob, Selah (empties himself like Jacob-sela [coin] — because he gives not a penny)"..
• • •
Of a kohen (a symbol of a rabbi) it is said "and he shall take his hands full" — taking, he takes with full hands; whereas of giving it is said of him "and he shall sprinkle with his finger" — giving, he gives only with a fingertip... Paren [?] the Gliner Rav [Glina].
—o—
e) "Silver" (25:3).
"Kesef" (silver) means to crave (kisufa); therefore money is called kesef, because that is what a person craves most strongly.. Ibn Ezra.
—o—
"Oil for the light," etc. (25:6).
For everything it is enumerated for what holy purpose it was used: the oil — for lighting, the spices — for the incense, etc.; but for the gold and silver it is not enumerated what it will be used for, because gold and silver are really meant only for holy things... Noam Elimelech.
—o—
g) "And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (25:8).
The Jews were the first to build a Temple, and from us [?] all the religious peoples [?] learned [?] to build temples for their idols. This recalls the parable:
In the cheder a rich boy brings an expensive, beautiful little purse. A friend sees it [?], a poor boy, envies him, scrapes together his last few groszy and runs to buy himself a purse too. Another friend says to him: what good is a beautiful purse to you when you have nothing to put into it?
The moral: what good are beautiful temples when there is nothing in them?... The Dubner Maggid [Dubno].
—o—
h) "And they shall make an ark of shittim wood" (25:10).
Usually "not everyone who does much business becomes wise": those who trade and are over their heads in life with their worries cannot learn. B-ʿ-z-ʾ-f [?] therefore they should make a partnership with Issachar, so that both together form the Ark of the Torah. B-ʿ-z-ʾ-f [?] shall support Issachar, so that he can sit and learn. "And they shall make" (plural) — both together, the supporter with the Torah scholar, make the "ark of shittim wood". Kli Yakar [?].
—o—
i) "And thou shalt make two cherubim" (25:13 [sic]).
Above the Holy Ark were the cherubim. The education of the children, of the young generation, stands before the Ark of the Torah. Yalkut Peninim.
—o—
"When Israel said 'we will do and we will hear', at once the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'that they take for me an offering'" (Tanna Devei Eliyahu).
Since the Jews took upon themselves the yoke of the Torah and cried out "we will do and we will hear", they were told "they shall take" — give money... not just piety but also with the pocket...
And those pious ones who guard their pockets invented a saying: "Honour the Lord with thy substance (mehonekha) — read not 'mehonekha' but 'migronekha' (with thy throat)": better "with thy throat" — praying and learning — than "with thy substance", than a few groszy.. And they also say: "the voice is the voice of Jacob" — a Jew need only learn; "and the hands — giving something with the hands — are the hands of Esau": let the gentiles give that... Emet Moshe [?].

Let Us Only Will It! (For the "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Będzin)

By G. Gerbowski.
(For the "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Będzin.)
In the last few years memoirs of the first pioneers, who laid the cornerstone of the grandiose building of the Land of Israel, have appeared in Eretz Israel. It is a long time since a book has made such a strong impression on me as these documents of superhuman effort and stubbornness and almost angelic[?] idealism.
People came — raised for the most part in wealth, pampered in comfort — into a land where[?] even[?] heaven and earth were not at all[?] in harmony[?]: a sky, it is true, a beautiful one with an ever-blazing[?] sun, but an earth, by contrast, muddy, swampy, disease-spreading, a veritable deadly poison for whoever settles on it.
On this earth they had no recognised right; no political declaration had sanctioned their right to till it, and no economic support of any significance whatsoever accompanied them in their hard work.
Few in number they were, these idealist-angels. A small handful among the many-millioned Jewry of the world.
And few in number too were their like-minded comrades and helpers in the Diaspora. Barely a few minyanim in a large Jewish centre.
On the long winter days, or at summer dusk, these few "Hovevim" used to gather, in silence and in secret rooms[?], and pass on to one another the greetings that arrived from "Jeshurun"[?], from the holy realiser of the dream, from the pioneer, who had been laughed at and pushed aside[?] by ninety per cent of the Jews.
And rarely were the greetings joyful; not always could one rejoice at a letter written in Eretz Israel, or beside a stable for the cattle that had been built there. For the most part tidings of Job arrived. This one had died of fever and that one had left the world before his time from malaria; builders were added in the land almost one by one[?], and at the same time graves upon graves were added in the struggle with the plague-ridden earth...
And yet —
how strong was the faith in the goal, in reaching it; how mighty was the hope in the ideal of "Shivat Zion" [the Return to Zion], in its realisation!
Like the martyrs[?] in Eretz Israel, so too the vanguard of the "Hovevim" in the Diaspora was imbued with an uncommon stubbornness, and no situation, however hard, sad, even deadly, had the power to break this stubbornness.
Like the former, so the latter too were filled[?] [—] with such extraordinary courage that no obstacle had the power to stop it.
And among those of Eretz Israel, as among those of the Diaspora, there flickered in their hearts such a fierce[?] fire of love and self-sacrifice for the ideal of building Eretz Israel, such a "ner tamid" [eternal light] that burned among them, that no wind of decrees, persecutions[?] and prohibitions could extinguish it.
And if "ten kabin" of patience, effort and self-sacrifice came down[?] to the world, our builders of Eretz Israel of old took nine measures[?] of them, that is[?], the whole nine kabin, for themselves. Of this we are convinced by the memoirs of the few pioneer-guardists[?] of the building of the Land who still remain alive.
———
That was once, some fifty, forty years ago.
And today!
Today not only is the sky in Eretz Israel purer and refreshing, but also the once swampy, disease-spreading earth has, thanks to the "Keren Hayesod", become "pleasant to the sight, a delight to the eyes", and truly revives the souls of all who merely have the privilege of setting foot on it. Now, when almost ninety per cent of the consolations of our prophets have been fulfilled thanks to the funds "HaKayemet" [Keren Kayemet] and "HaYesod"; now, when despite all sorts of obstacles we are nevertheless close to the realisation of the thousand-year-old dream of our people — now, precisely now, some become discouraged[?], apathetic, so that one may say that the jug of "nine kabin" of patience and tenacity that we possessed is beginning to run dry.
And people forget that obstacles on so hard a road as the one leading us to our land, and difficulties in so grandiose a matter as our Zionist ideal, are entirely natural, simply the way of nature, and should come as no surprise.
A disturbance down[?], a disturbance up, and also the "White Paper"[?] and perhaps another one coming along — in the end they will all be removed, and we will prosper with our stubborn[?] confidence.
———
And when I hear and see how some honest people become frightened, despairing, or how dishonest ones want to make use of the difficulties and create for themselves through them an excuse so as[?] not to fulfil the duty towards Eretz Israel — I recall the saying of the Tanna: "If the first ones were like angels, we are like human beings; and if they were like human beings, we are like donkeys"...
Our first ones, fifty-odd[?] years ago, were certainly angels. That level we have not reached in our constant fulfilment of our duty to Eretz Israel. They, they, the first ones, paved the stony road for us and made Eretz Israel into something from which ordinary human beings can draw benefit — almost into an "inhabited land". If we make a reckoning of our work for Eretz Israel and slip out with this or that [—] from further fulfilling our duty, we thereby fall into the third level.. which already brings about[?] eternal servitude, eternal exile.
If not angels, then at least something like[?] human beings let us be. And as such let us fulfil our duty in these hard days.
Our enemies[?] want to ruin[?] Eretz Israel — let the Jews of Będzin demonstrate with the strongest confidence — with their proper contributions, given with a good grace, to the "Keren Hayesod".
And if only we will, truly will, with all 248 limbs, as well as [—] with the pocket, the building of the Land — which has long since ceased to be a legend — will become a living reality.

G. P.[?]

Sosnowiec — The Coal Committee Has Already Distributed 300 Korzec of Coal. Further Help Is Needed

[Sosnowiec — relief: the coal committee.] The coal committee, which was set up last winter, has become active again. The committee undoubtedly committed a great wrong in not starting the coal campaign at the beginning of the winter. But "better late than never". The situation of the poorer part of the population is today, because of the crisis, even more critical than at the beginning of the winter.
The committee, which has only just begun its activity, has already managed to distribute about 300 korzec [a dry measure] of coal. Important Resolutions of the Heads of the Tax Offices

Because the assessment of the turnover tax is to begin very soon, conferences of the heads (naczelniks) of the tax offices of the whole region are now being held in all the voivodeships.
It is highly interesting to learn that at these conferences several naczelniks made speeches about the economic situation in their districts and the financial condition of the taxpayers. As a result it was acknowledged that the taxpayers have become greatly impoverished, and that the economic situation has therefore worsened.
The fact that the naczelniks have acknowledged that the taxpayers are impoverished will be of great significance at the next assessment of turnover.
Regarding the new assessment it was resolved that turnover is to be assessed on an individual basis: the situation of each individual taxpayer is to be taken into account and his means considered.
The conference of naczelniks resolved to exempt from turnover tax all artisans of the eighth category who produce goods independently.
Very important too is the naczelniks' resolution concerning employees of shops of the third category and workshops of the 8th category. According to the law, employees and workers younger than 17 or older than 55 are counted as two persons per one adult person. On this the naczelniks resolved that, since it is not possible for the offices (urzędy) to check the age of the employees, every employee, even an older one or a minor, will be reckoned [?] as an adult. This resolution is against the law.

The Wild Chase after Mandates in the Olkusz City Council

[Olkusz — city council elections.] (A letter from Olkusz)
As is known, the local city council has been dissolved on the basis of a decree, and new city council elections will take place on the 15th of this month. As the municipal economy so far has shown, it is worth recalling that the magistracy, which used to be one of the richest magistracies in Poland, is now a debtor of close to one and a half million zł., and this weighs heavily on the shoulders of the local population. The Jewish population was represented by 11 councillors, most of whom were [doubtful word — perhaps "random"] elements without the slightest sense for public activity; and if what people murmur is true, the councillors did so, and they still have great personal ambitions [?]..
For the present elections they, the "bundle-grabbers", have thrown themselves into a wild chase to grab back their lost "bundles" in the city council. They exert themselves with all kinds of forces, make use of far-reaching "means" to strengthen their electoral positions, so that one gets the impression that the magistracy is like a private little shop. The "Agudah", for example, which until now had 4 councillors, has torn itself into 4 parts; each councillor "makes Shabbat for himself", and 4 separate lists were submitted [?], because each of them would only want to have the first numbered [?] "mizrach" seat.
There were also several attempts to create a united bloc, but the attempt did not succeed, because the existing councillors did not want to resign [?] (except Mr. Szwarcberg), and new communal figures [?] with strong appetites for "bundles" are not lacking either [?]; in any case it was impossible to divide 8 mandates among 20 aspirants so that each would get the first place.. Above all, the bloc broke up because, on principled grounds, those [others] could not agree that the same councillors as before should run again, since that would have confirmed that they agree with the economy run so far, which may have fatal consequences in the future when the defects will have to be repaired.
The arguments did not convince, and the old councillors go on working to keep their positions.
The Zionist organization in Olkusz, poor in disciplined members but rich in [?] intrigues and baseless hatred, did not have the courage to come out openly in the elections; the slogan was even put forward to create a "national youth bloc", and the Zionist org. [was] pushed into a corner. At the demand [?] of the writer of these lines consultations were indeed held to create an independent election campaign — a clear one, a clean one and far from bundle-grabbers — but the small-town intrigues of individual members, with the help of false [?], frustrated the work of those who wanted to earn respect for the organization.
Finally, a few words to the Jews of Olkusz: according to rumours, 10 Jewish lists will appear. This makes it certain that Jewish representation will this time be minimal. Let this stain of shame be a lesson to you when it comes to the representation of a Jewish community, when it comes to defending Jewish honour. For the sake of Jewish property [?] and goods you ought to shake off the shopkeeper notions [?]. Tear [yourselves] out of the narrow four cubits. Say freely what hurts you. Exert all forces to remove the small-town "bundle-heroes" [?] who want by violent means to "represent" (more correctly: weaken [?]) Jewish honour.
S. Sz.

The Katowice budget.
The Katowice municipal council (Magistrat) has already completed the new budget. The budget[?], the ordinary together with the extraordinary, amounts to barely 18 million zł.
Of the municipal enterprises the council [earns] the most[?] from the water mains (100,000 zł. income); the theatre, on the other hand, shows a deficit of 200 000 zł.
Tired of life, he hanged himself.
On Saturday [—] [—] the local house-painter Shmuel Picher[?] hanged himself in Königshütte (Chorzów). The cause of the suicide: an incurable illness.
Inspection of the prisons.
This week the delegate of the Ministry of Justice, Inspector Skibiński, carried out an inspection (lustracja) of the prisons in Upper Silesia. The results are very good. It turns out that the prisoners are not [ill-]treated[?] and receive proper supervision.
Suicide.
On Monday the 17-year-old Lehkaniks[?] shot himself in his parents' flat. The cause of the suicide has not yet been established.
Further cuts in the coal mines.
From 1 March further cuts are to take place in the Upper Silesian coal mines. The "Ferdinand" mine has again cut 448 workers, and "Emma"[?] 320 workers.
On this matter the Demobilisation Commissioner travelled to Warsaw so that the central government should issue the appropriate instructions concerning the cuts.
A sensational verdict.
In Katowice the trial took place against "Polonia", which had reprinted from "Dziennik Bydgoski" an article about the Brześć affair.
The defence counsel of "Polonia" demanded that the Brześć prisoners be summoned to confirm the facts given in the article. The court, however, rejected the motion and sentenced the responsible editor to one month's arrest.
Triumph of chess master Rubinstein.
The results of the simultaneous exhibitions of the world-famous chess master Akiba Rubinstein in Upper Silesia are as follows:
In Königshütte: 20 games won, 4 draws, 1 lost.
In Katowice: 14 won, 3 draws, 6 lost.
In Wielkie Hajduki: 17 won, 2 draws; 4 lost.
Opening of a Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund.
On Saturday night a Gemilut Hesed fund was festively opened in Königshütte. All the local existing societies and institutions were invited to the celebration, from economic institutions[?] to[?] sports clubs.
The opening was conducted by Mr Goldwasser, and after the playing of the specially composed "Gemilut Hesed anthem" came the greetings. Greetings were given on behalf of the kehilla by President Rybner; for the small traders by Mr Rozenberg; for the artisans by President Fajman; for the founders of the G"Ch by President Brzykowski; for the "Merchants' Association" by Sztelen[?]; for the bank by Szpira; for the Zionists by Goldberg; for the KKL (Jewish National Fund) by Fridman; for "Mizrachi" by Gotlib; and for "Maccabi" by Sztern.
Then Rabbi Dr Kalberg delivered an address, saying that "by creating the fund the sins of the Jews of Königshütte will be atoned for".
The ribbon of the fund's "Golden Book" was cut by Dr Kalberg, on which occasion a sum of 600 zł. was collected from those present, including 25 zł. donated on behalf of the G"Ch by the delegates Brzykowski, Granat and Mentag[?].
After the "concert" part, performed by Mr and Miss[?] Goldwasser, a dance evening took place, at which the young people spent the time until morning.
A Letter to the Editor

[Będzin — kehilla; the election commission.]
Honoured Mr Editor!
I ask you to publish my letter in your esteemed paper.
I consider it my duty to give the public an explanation concerning the election commission.
The representatives of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] came to me with a proposal that I should vote together with them, provided that the Zionists, Mizrachists and artisans would not be represented on the election commission (I possess the "Agudah" list). It goes without saying that I could not agree to such an injustice, because a circle[?] that brings the town quite fine revenues (besides the budget) — e.g. Yaakov Gutman, Firstenberg, Gebr. Szejn, the firm Potak[?], Serbarut[?], Szpigelman, Eichhold[?] etc. — should not be represented, [—] as also the artisans and Mizrachists. The Zionists came to me proposing that we go together. I set the condition that the "Agudah" with the non-partisan Hasidim must have a majority. This was accepted at once, in such a way that the commission would consist of 16 persons: "Agudah" with the non-partisans get 9, Zionists — 2, Mizrachists — 2, artisans — 3. The "Agudah" wanted to get 4, because the non-partisans have 6 on the kehilla council and 3 on the board, whereas the "Agudah" has 4 on the council and 2 on the board. So that the non-partisans are entitled[?] to more than the "Agudah".
I proposed from the "Agudah" Rygski[?], Skapilas[?], Buhart[?] and Hershele Ehrlich. They even began to contest[?] Hershele Ehrlich, but having no choice they agreed. I proposed from the non-partisans: Prawer, Gershon Rechnic, Avraham Yissachar Rechnic, Moshe Lapa[?], Wolf Danciger. Here the fight began over[?] the last 3. Then I proposed[?] to them the gabbai of the "Talmud Torah", Mordechai Danciger, or R' Chaim Wolf Sztajnhart. Both these Jews are also not Hasidim, although Chaim Wolf could still be counted[?] among the Hasidim. The "Agudah" preferred an artisan and thereby they broke the majority, for the "Agudah" with the non-partisans received only 8 mandates.
On this good occasion I wish to ask the God's Cossacks who have monopolised loyalty to the Torah: what have you done during your term of office? How many times during the term did the rabbinate visit the slaughterhouse or the butcher shops? The shochtim with the supervisors are[?] after all supposed[?] to report to the rabbinate information concerning kashrut. How do you stand with R' Shlomo Yitzchak's mikveh — is a mikveh a necessity[?] or a luxury? You call yourselves[?] so very religious — which shtetl has no mikveh? How can you rest when in such a town as Będzin there should be no mikveh! This is altogether a case of "a crooked thing[?] that cannot be made straight" (Eccl. 1:15). On whom lies the duty to build a mikveh? For whom is this Gehenna — for those who need to build a mikveh and do not build it, or for those who do not want to involve[?] tax-paying people and rob them of their rights. Let the public express its opinion.
Respectfully,
Vice-President of the Jewish Kehilla Board in Będzin
M. Y. Prawer.
