While It Is Not Yet Too Late.

[Editorial — poverty and relief.] (The present sad situation demands a system and order in our ranks.)
It is time, high time, that we stop being ashamed of our poverty; we must begin to get used to the thought that Jewish poverty is plundering[?] in every corner of Jewish life. [Words illegible in print] — that everyone works hard and bitterly, and when, God forbid, there is not even a piece of dry bread, people keep silent. The street[?], the neighbours whisper to one another that Berl has become a poor man, that he cannot make his living, etc.; that is[?], poverty is something one is ashamed to show. We are merciful sons of the merciful, we have God in our hearts, and at once we collect alms. So that before we [illegible word], before we have even looked around, we have turned the first decent family that came along into a house of beggars, and at best a family has been crowned[?] as 'respectable poor'; and what shall I tell you — may we not be punished for what we have made of[?] the respectable poor people.
No one has ever taken the trouble to approach this matter on a sound, logical basis that would crystallize the situation and bring the proper benefit — the right organization — and so as to create what we need.
We are always ashamed to say that we are poor and hungry, and when there was once a moment when the Jewish cry of 'woe' tore itself involuntarily out of the depths of the Jewish heart, our enemies laughed at our groans; they said that we were playing[?] it that way just so that no one would envy us our wealth. Now the situation has changed completely; the Jewish condition is grave to the highest degree. We are becoming impoverished, and still[?] we do not say so; we do not even try to let more [people] know of it; we stifle the suffering and the pain within ourselves until it reaches the highest degree.
We lack the courage to explain openly to the world how we look, in what catastrophic situation we find ourselves. So that it has already reached the point of culmination: more than once we have heard, from the rostrum of the Sejm, Christians describing the gravity of the Jewish situation, and only then did we come to our senses and say to ourselves: what has happened, that others see better than we ourselves what is going on among us? Why do we not see what we feel on our own shoulders? What we suffer in the depths of our soul? Why are we ourselves ashamed to say what others say about us? Is poverty a disgrace? Are we to blame that the conditions in which we live are so hard, so unbearable, so nearly impossible to endure[?]?
And something else: what do we achieve by hiding everything deep in our hearts? On the contrary, let us not be ashamed to declare boldly and openly our whole sad situation, and let us think how to improve the situation, which surely cannot remain in this state.
It is time that we finally understand that we cannot go on behaving this way, especially when it serves no purpose and when with such methods we will not get far. What comes of our hiding everything inside ourselves, of our keeping everything as [illegible word] secrets to ourselves as if from everyone? What is the point of the whispering and of being afraid to let a breath out of our mouths? The result is that no one knows how grave our situation is, and we ourselves achieve nothing by it either.
We must show openly and honestly how we look economically, and then the necessary measures will indeed be taken so that the Jewish people does not become still poorer.
Throughout Poland things have not been good for a number of years, but it is getting worse and worse; here the crisis began about a year ago and it is making steady progress in its field, so that more poor people are added, and we are astonished when we hear which firms are going under and which people are becoming impoverished in the full sense of the word. So why are we ashamed to declare this openly and honestly, to say it openly and honestly? Why do we hide at this given moment? What do we get out of it and what do we achieve by it?
We must not go on behaving this way; we must adopt another method, another system. We must not let those who can still be rescued fall into the deep abyss, and we must not support with alms those who can obtain work. We must begin to carry on a conscious, systematic activity for the benefit of our impoverished Jews. We must classify everything; we must not give alms to those for whom work can be obtained.
How can order be introduced here? Here is a small example: soon matzah baking will begin, and quite a few Jews are employed in that work. An appeal should be issued that those who stretch out their hands for alms had better take up the work, and those who will not do so should be avoided[?] and given no 'kimcha' [kimcha de-pischa — Passover flour relief].
The same with whitewashing [before Passover]: quite a few Jews are employed in cleaning the homes, and still one cannot get enough cleaning women. So the question arises: could not the young Jewish women[?] who stretch out their hands for alms and fill the streets with their cries when it comes to 'kimcha' also take up this work?
Does the people gain anything from our raising so many idlers and loafers? Are we happy when we ourselves create beggars? Has such a tactic ever been heard of among any nation or tongue? Could a healthy people have tolerated it, put up with it? Whom does it benefit and whom — does it adorn? Do we not lose heart, do we not lose courage, when we see with what astonishment a Christian listens, on a Friday or on Rosh Chodesh, to the 'Good morning — six! Good morning — ten?' Is it any wonder that it makes a bad impression on them? And what would we ourselves say if we saw this among some other people?
For a healthy, normal people such neglect[?] is a disgrace and a pain, and a Christian says to himself: you know what — with the Jews money plays no role at all; they give, and the system of a thrifty[?] upbringing lies in their left sidelock [i.e. they do not care about it], and it does not bother them when their brothers and sisters drag themselves around like gypsies and tramps.
That is the kind of impression we make in people's eyes; that is how we look to other nations.
On the other hand, we pay no attention to those who languish and suffer hunger, who have not yet shed their sense of shame[?] and cannot bring themselves to stretch out a hand for alms.
So it turns out that the professional beggars and schemers manage [illegible word] very well — people of whom, incidentally, the Jewish public thinks nothing at all. Meanwhile the quiet, modest, decent, impoverished people languish and starve, and no one hears them, no one knows of them, and no one does anything for them.
We are growing poorer and the Jewish economic situation is catastrophic; we do nothing so that what ought to be and must be rescued is rescued. We must not allow healthy, decent citizens to go hungry, just as we must not allow healthy people to become idlers and loafers thanks to begging securing their livelihood.
It would be only fair to look around and bring order to this field while it is not yet too late.
R. Let.
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie and beyond — a satirical panorama of synagogue quarrels: Łuków, Sosnowiec, Zagórze, Old Sosnowiec, Czeladź.]
(The "Panorama" has become "lively" again. — A town where a holy war is being waged. — They hacked apart the rabbi's seat. — The complaints of the simple Jews. — A small place with famous deeds, — pulled off "the Turkish way" [?]. — Paper instead of parchment sheets. — When Adar comes in, war increases. — It began with the "dead" [?]. — Washed artisans and Agudist "heroes").
For several months now we have kept completely silent about the happenings in our little Jewish mouse-hole [„gemoyzekhts"], because we wanted — so we said — not to describe the heroic deeds of our communal workers and leaders, so that "Our Panorama" would take on a "decent" look and...
But we were mistaken, very greatly mistaken. Jewish "life" is becoming more boiling, more seething; a new era is beginning. Those romantic times are already over, when people held discussions among themselves, split hairs over ideologies and programmes; no, those are matters for idlers, loafers and maskilim — today the fist rules, the kulak; the slogan has been proclaimed:
— Annihilation.
The beginning was made by the "Yevseks" [members of the Yevsektsia, the Jewish section of the Soviet Communist Party], and the "continuation" [misprinted „fartzutsung"] is being carried out by the holy youth, the youth that has been raised on the watchword that "whoever is against [misprinted „begn"] the Agudist policy deserves what Haman demanded" — to slay, to destroy and to annihilate...
Here is what we read about the events in Łuków:
"On Saturday a bloody brawl [?] broke out in front of the synagogue in Łuków among the worshippers over the rabbi whom the 'Aguda' [Agudat Israel] wanted to bring into the synagogue by force.
During the fight one of the 'Aguda' people snatched out a revolver and shot the 20-year-old non-party Gershon Śliżak [Szlizak], who was wounded in the chest; he is in hospital in a very serious condition"...
*
After Łuków, next in line comes — Sosnowiec, the first-class town of Zagłębie, the town which, thanks to the "7-year war", the fight over the rabbinical chair, became famous in the Jewish world. But what happened last Friday night will be crowned and recorded for remembrance, so that future generations too may know what happened in the month of Adar 5691 in the Sosnowiec synagogue.
And this is what happened:
"In the middle of the night from Friday to Saturday, parashat Tetzaveh, the rabbi's seat in the Sosnowiec synagogue was destroyed with an axe"...
After the vile deed [misprinted „maase-gvale"] all is hushed; the "Aguda" at once had "information" that "this was done by the Mizrachists, in order to frame the 'Aguda'"... The non-party Hasidim regret it and sigh in silence, and only one category of Jews speaks — the "holy flock", the "simpletons" [„prostakes"], and they have the very greatest complaint: if — they say — such a thing can happen, that on a Friday night people smash windowpanes, break into the synagogue and destroy the rabbi's seat with an axe, then — they say — we too want to live to see a "young fellow" come into the synagogue on the Sabbath and light up a cigarette there...
— "if the rebbe may"...
*
No smaller desecration of the holy took place in a neighbouring place, in the holy community of Zagórze. The deeds that happened in this "dew-and-rain" [?] community must also be recorded for future generations.
And thus it came to pass:
In Zagórze two minyanim have existed for a long time already, which wage constant quarrels between them. The minyanim already have a "rich past" behind them: a year ago, in this very month, a Torah scroll was stolen from one minyan; only after the din Torah before the Dąbrowa rabbi and after the interventions of the kehilla president Mr. Mitelman was the stolen scroll taken [?].
Last week, however, something happened in the holy community of Zagórze that caused no smaller disgrace and desecration of God's name than in Sosnowiec; the only difference is that in Sosnowiec the "holy" work was carried out on the Sabbath, and in Zagórze — on an ordinary Wednesday...
Peace was concluded between the above-mentioned minyanim. At the ratification of the peace agreement the warring parties came to an exchange: quite simply, they swapped Torah scrolls — a new system of peaceful acts which has yet to become popular in Europe... But at the exchange this is what happened:
The "Saxon" [„zaksishe" — presumably named after someone called Saks, ?] minyan, before the Torah scroll was sent to the other side, took out of its scroll the sheets from parashat Vayikra to parashat Ha'azinu, and in place of the sheets wrapped the scroll with paper...
When the vile deed came to light, darkness fell on Zagórze; the rabbi even intended to decree a fast, but be that as it may — in the course of this week [misprinted „heygtiger"] the places Sosnowiec and Zagórze have become famous...
*
"When Adar comes in, joy increases." The worshippers of the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec] do the opposite: instead of with joy, they again hold to their now-famous system:
— increasing quarrels...
As soon as the first "spring sun" [printed „frilings-zange", probably for „-zonne"] shone on the horizon of Old Sosnowiec, the worshippers became "belligerently minded" and "the air in the holy place smells of gunpowder"...
As our correspondent informs us, "experts" have declared that there is no danger of war. Although the Festival of Freedom is approaching — for the start of the attacks was made over the dead... and although it is known that the dead cannot... — the gabbai renounced his honour, did not enforce his authority and gave in to the worshippers' demand that before Musaf no "El Male Rachamim" should be said in the synagogue...
*
The artisans who pray in the Czeladź "polish" [synagogue vestibule] have lost "the power of speech", walk about [?] like shadows on the wall and "dare" not utter a single word...
The "loss" happened for the following reasons [printed „folbegde", evidently „folgende"]. The "polish" in the Czeladź beit midrash is "occupied" by the artisans; there they pray and there they pour out their sorrows and joys...
Such a "joy" the worshippers also had on [last?] Sabbath [„farkhtogn" — ?]: one of their members, a shoemaker, had yahrzeit and brought to the third Sabbath meal — a challah.
The crowd looked the challah over well, passed connoisseurs' remarks on its "quality", and with saliva [?] in their mouths prayed Minchah with devotion...
But the whole joy was suddenly spoiled: before the hard-toiling artisans had washed their hands, the challah was already lying "crumbled" [?] in the Agudist mouths... and the artisans were left with clean hands...
Ben Amitz.
A Roof Over One's Head.

(The great appetites of the Zagłębie house-owners. — Where are the tenants' associations?)
The country writhes in want, the citizens struggle with bitterness and with fear for their very existence, the working masses and the broad strata of the population are starving in the true sense of the word, the critical situation and unemployment take on an ever more serious and dangerous character — and they do not care about it at all, nothing troubles them, they are well off and comfortable, and they keep on scheming and pondering how to get power back into their hands and how to rule in an unlimited form, if only to fill their pockets with more money, if only to grow still richer at the expense of the critical situation, if only to satisfy their desires and let their greed for money express itself in an ever greater dose of cunning.
Here the Zagłębie house-owners have come together for a consultation, and resolutions were passed that they should have as few expenses and as much income as possible. It is not enough for them that they now, for example, economize[?] on supplying water to the tenants; the systematic raising of [rents for] flats and shops is not enough for them; it is not enough for them that during the war they bought houses for pennies — it is all too little for them. They take no account of the fact that money turned into ash and mud while their properties grew; they take no account of the fact that they paid their creditors with devalued currency and were left with the properties from which they today draw handsome incomes. They take nothing and nobody into account, they do not want to know that the times are bitter and the crisis unbearable; they want to know one thing only: to take as much money as possible and to rule as strongly as possible.
Thus, for example, they want, among other things, no more and no less than that tenant protection be abolished as soon as possible, and that meanwhile they be given the possibility of charging in the old houses the same prices that tenants pay in the new houses.
One cannot say — they do, after all, have pity on us, apparently: they take the bad times into account and want no more than these "modest" demands. And that these are not just empty words can be seen from the fact that the resolutions are being prepared to be brought into the Sejm by a deputy of their own. That means they mean it quite seriously and with full awareness. Now we must imagine what their appetites would have been if the country were not bathing in crisis and hunger, in pain and suffering — then their appetites would surely have been boundless.
The landlords of the old houses want the same rent that the tenants of the new houses pay. By what right do they put forward such unheard-of demands? Have they rebuilt their houses anew, so that they now cost so much more? It is truly unheard of that at a time when the country languishes in want and hunger, when the workers and the popular masses are starving and have nothing to give their children to eat their fill, precisely then one should want to know of nothing but keep on scheming and contriving how to grow richer and in what way to fill one's pockets with more money.
Apparently they are on the alert, the owners of the houses, for in truth they have no need at all of the increases; they simply want to exploit the present conjuncture. They know very well that when the tenants' associations stood at a high level, when these popular institutions were fully solid, they trembled to raise their heads; they did not then dare to dictate and to rule. And now, as soon as they see that the "tenants' associations" are beginning to fall apart, they want to take their place and, quietly and unnoticed, to leap up to the same height — with the difference that they want to be the dictators, the rulers and exploiters of a commodity that everyone must have and that is not to be found in the country.
And therefore, therefore the people must stand on guard and protect its popular interests. Not only must we not let the "tenants' associations" fall apart, but we must take care that they become strengthened and popular, so that they have the possibility of undertaking counter-action in case of danger.
We have always said, and we repeat it now too, that the citizens are mistaken when they think that after the issuing of the decree on how much rent to pay, there is no more need for the "tenants' associations". Once the citizens would not let themselves be persuaded of this; now, after various complications and conceptions have arisen, one sees, we believe, the necessity of the existing "tenants' associations" — which, even if they did nothing at all, we would need already just so that they raise their voices when they need to be heard.
Many, many matters have been neglected and lost here because people were not prepared for defence, and there was no authority, no representative body, no representation that would be prepared and have the possibility to conduct [the matter] with the necessary preparation.
How much would we have lost if we had not had the "tenants' associations" from the very first minute? True, we have tenant protection, but the citizens themselves must guard that protection; they must have the representation that will deflect the bullets aimed at it. There were, after all, times when the "tenants' associations" were swamped with useful work and did not allow the slightest wrong to be done to a tenant. They always stood on the side of the tenants, whose interests they defended, and that is no wonder; they, of course, did nobody a favour by it, they merely fulfilled their tasks — but that is not the point. We only aim here to show that in order to defend, in order to stand on guard and protect the interests, there must be a representation, there must be an institution and a representative body.
The landlords of the houses in Zagłębie, seeing that the "tenants' associations" are limping, are beginning to come alive; they organize themselves and show the government that they are a power, and in this way put forward their demands. In that case the population must not sleep or look on indifferently at what harmful activity is beginning to be conducted around the citizens' popular interests; and therefore it is above all important to see that the "tenants' associations" are set up at the proper level, so that they are able to defend themselves against those who want to make life and the conditions of the average citizenry harder.
Let a slogan be carried out: to revive the "tenants' associations" that have already fallen asleep and to strengthen those that exist but lack full temperament. Let people come to the awareness that as long as there are not enough flats in the country that one could at any time rent and let without extra money, so long must we have someone to protect and defend us and someone who can stand up and speak in the name of the community, in the name of the tenants, in the name of the great number of citizens.
Let the public activists in the country in general, and here in Zagłębie in particular, stop and consider[?] this meeting that has just taken place in Sosnowiec, and let them draw a moral lesson from it. Let them think in good time about how to thwart the plans that have been devised to worsen the situation of the citizens who do not own their own houses.
Let the leaders of the "tenants' associations" take a step[?] in this very important question, which is very topical today.
Let the public activists in the country rise up and raise a mighty outcry that the citizens of the country are not so well off that one should have to think how to squeeze ever more money out of them for an article of first necessity such as a roof over one's head.
Dr. Papuri.
A Little Feuilleton — "Shehecheyanu".

Let us say "Shehecheyanu", Jews of Zagłębie! We have already reached the "second days of the holiday" — we are already facing kehilla elections.

And here, you should know, we will only now have the true joy — a purely Jewish one; not a single gentile vote will be admitted to the ballot box.

And the main thing — here Wiślicki will no longer drag us to the Sanacja; however we toss about, we will always fall among our own — Jews with beards, Jews without beards, right-wing Jews, left-wing Jews, middle-of-the-road Jews; it does not matter whether with one foot in the Land of Israel, with both feet, or with the Land of Israel altogether behind one's shoulder — but [—] we will no longer..

True, for this kind of election we have no appetite at all just now — elections are already coming out of our ears[?], for we have already overeaten on them more than enough[?]; but apparently not completely — what does a Jew do when he comes to a celebration and has already had his supper? He eats without appetite, but he eats..

The same with the kehilla elections — there really is no appetite, but once the mouths are opened the appetite will come by itself; and it stands to reason[?] that our communal activists have already opened their mouths — you need not exert yourself much now to get a word out of them: just tell a local activist that you are[?] a newspaperman, and he will already run after you — so that you take an interview from him..

And why not, after all? It costs no money, and without any extra effort one can become famous in town. Without dipping a pen, without giving a speech, without even saying one clear word, just a grunt, "hm" — and that's it, the writer has already smeared it into a whole interview.

Because with the writer — you see — it is already literally "a word worth a sela", a rendl [ruble] a word; he will already take his share — before the elections and at the elections. You have no idea what a holiday, what a joy an election campaign is for a writer. When he, the writer, prays in the Grace after Meals for "a day that is wholly good", he has nothing else in mind but that there should be electing all the time.

In short, we now have the "second days of the holiday" — let us indeed say "Shehecheyanu".

Onkelos.
A Tale of an Illness Called Papyritis.

And this tale did not happen now, in our times, God forbid, but long, long ago, in olden days; and it did not happen here among us, but far, far away, as is the way in old tales that are told to good, good, fine children.

And the tale begins like this:

Once upon a time there was somewhere a country. In that country there was too much wood and too many rags. Well, yes — plain logs, trees, forests, and plain rags, worn-out old rags, of good pedigree though — silk and velvet, but rags. They did not know what to do with them, so they sat down the sages of the land, and these thought for seven days and seven nights and came up with the idea:

Out of the wood and the rags they should make paper — people will have work and the country will become happy. So they made paper, made and made, until the country was full of paper. They did not know where to put the paper, so they sat down the sages of the land, and these resolved:

The citizens of the land shall be provided with papers. A horse has a bridle, a dog — a muzzle, but — a [?] and a citizen must have — a paper. People will have to write, there will be work, and the country will be happy. And so they did. They provided and provided for so long that on every citizen a paper hump grew. A citizen had hands and feet, a nose and a mouth, a belly (for digesting) to eat with, and papers to live by; a heart and a head — not everyone, but papers — everyone. And all was good and fine, and free, and there was order in the country.

And it came to pass one day that a citizen's — may it not befall you — paper fell ill. Well, yes, his paper fell ill. A tooth[?] can ache, a heart, a lung — so a citizen's paper can also fall ill; and with a sick paper, dear children, it was harder to live in that country than with a sick heart. May such an illness never befall you, dear readers.

So the citizen with the sick paper goes to have it cured — well, yes, to have his paper cured. What don't you understand here? — a sick paper must be healed even more than a sick heart. If you don't understand, you would have been a bad citizen of that country, and you would have had to be tried under article 222, point 994, paragraph 13, of volume 88 of the penal code..

So, that is, our citizen went off to cure his paper. He comes to Paper Office number Taf-Resh-Peh-Tet Aleph[?] seventy-seven and finds everything boiling: clerks sleeping, sitting, standing, messengers running, bells ringing, typewriters clattering, and a stream of citizens carried up and down the stairs, from here to there and from there to here, like flies[?] in a fly-glass[?]. The poor citizen with the sick paper entered the first room, took his place in the queue and stood; and officials sat, smoked, drank tea and chatted on the subject: what is more convenient to take along in [—] weather — an umbrella or a raincoat.. And when they had finished the tea and thrown away the [—] of the smoked cigarettes, the queue moved, and when at last our citizen's turn came, the citizen told of his misfortune. They told him to go to another room and buy stamps for 8 dinars (a currency like, for example, a guilder). He comes to the second room, buys the stamps and sticks them on as required. They tell him to come back in eight days[?]; they sent him to room thirty-three; he got there — go to room 44; there they tell him to come tomorrow; he came tomorrow — let the citizen with the sick paper take his petition and run with it to that other office.

The country had four hundred offices, and every office four hundred departments, rooms, and our citizen went from one room to another, from one office to another, and on and on and on..

Once, as he runs across the street from one office to another, he catches sight of a woman.. it seems — his wife.. yes, once, before the illness of his paper, he had a wife after all, a home, children.. he earned, he worked.. now.. he is ill — his paper, that is, is ill. He no longer remembers how many years he has been running around the offices; the grey books with the linen spines have put a haze[?] before his eyes, the squeaking pens — a cricket in his ears. The citizen felt unwell, he fell, fainted, died.. a peaceful paradise to him.

When they had [—] him, they recorded on paper that the citizen had died of the terrible illness "papyritis" — may it not befall you. When the dead man heard the pen squeaking across the paper, he let out a groan, dead as he was, and died a second time; the funeral will be tomorrow. Come in masses — by this merit you will be saved from the terrible paper illness..

Copied from an old book.
A. Yudels.
Islam and Eretz Israel.

[Article — Zionism and international politics: Islam, India and British rule; series, part 3.] By V. Jabotinsky [Vladimir (Ze'ev) Jabotinsky].
3) England and the Mohammedans.
When people point out to us, the "most insatiable" [?] Zionists, that we must "put ourselves" into England's position and understand that England, after all, cannot for the sake of the Jews expose itself to the danger of a conflict with the "[—]" [?] power of its Mohammedan subjects — then these claims contain two great untruths. The first untruth is that 70 million Mohammedans in India supposedly set their attitude toward England not according to their own interests, but according to echoes that reach them from Eretz Israel. The second untruth is that the Mohammedan element within the British state, or outside the state, supposedly represents such a mighty power that this state cannot cope with it, although this state has the best will to fulfil its obligations toward the Jewish people.
Let us first of all dwell on India, to which the English, and especially their Zionist defenders, often refer. According to the census of 1921 the population of India amounted to 320 million. Of these, 220 million were Brahmans [i.e. Hindus] and 68 million Mohammedans.
For a long time a strong antagonism has prevailed between the two parts of the population. It is worth noting here that while religious fanaticism has long since lost its significance as a force in its own right, as a glue to fuse different elements, it has fully retained, as a distinguishing mark, the power of being [?] a sign by which entire neighbouring peoples quarrel with great hatred — even in the West, and all the more so in the East. In India the dispute between the Brahmans and the Mohammedans has been, in the last twenty years (already beginning [?] from the [—]), the hallmark of the political situation. This dispute has often taken on forms that are, by our notions, peculiar.
Let us recall the movement concerning "slaughtering the cow", which spread about 25 years ago in Bengal and on the western coast. For the Brahmans the cow is a holy animal; for the Mohammedans, the chief supplier of roast meat. At the head of the movement stood the respected national personalities of the Hindus. Their agitation reminds us in every detail of the agitation against shechita [Jewish ritual slaughter] that we know so well. But at times the antagonism also found expression in forms that were absolutely serious, from whatever standpoint one takes.
At the beginning of the present century the English government made an attempt to create, almost, for part of the Mohammedans a kind of "National home". Many provinces of Bengal in which the Mohammedans form a majority were separated off into a special province. The Brahmans replied with terrorist acts: pogroms, boycott and so on, and the government in the end had to give in, and, disregarding the protests of the Mohammedans, it never again set up [?] the united and not two-camp [?] Bengal [so printed; the sense is apparently the 1911 reversal of the partition of Bengal].
This is not the place to describe the history of the dispute in detail. It is enough to point to one characteristic main feature: the attackers were always the Brahmans, whereas the Mohammedans only "fended off" [?] and defended themselves; in other words, the situation of the Mohammedans in India is the situation of a typical minority.
Therefore their psychology is at bottom the typical psychology of a minority. The minority always and everywhere shies away [?] from regional autonomy; it is afraid to be left alone with the majority in a tightly locked room, and therefore always has sympathies for centralist, or imperialist, tendencies — not out of inclination [?], but out of fear. Therefore the Indian Mohammedans, without exception [?], in spite of the injustices done to them (as the Bengal story shows), were the only moral [?] support at the disposal of the English until after the war. In 1919 a change took place: Gandhi apparently managed to make peace between the Brahmans and the Muslims. At the head of the anti-British agitation there now also appeared Mohammedan leaders.
All this happened for reasons on which we do not wish to dwell, especially as they proved to be without substance. The peace lasted only 3 years. In 1922 the old picture gradually returned. Again reports came of pogroms against the Mohammedans. In India, Islam again began to show attachment [?] to London and — fear of the prospects of an independent India. In this backward movement, the unexpected downfall of the Caliphate plays a great role. In India it made a great stir. From 1919, and above all with the appearance [?] of Kemal Pasha, the Indian Muslims took on the role of defenders of Turkey as the fortress of the Caliphate. They sent countless delegations to London with the argument that the subjugation of Turkey means the same as the subjugation of the Caliphate, and this Islam will not tolerate.
They demanded that the old Turkey be set up anew, so that the Caliph could again become an independent and mighty monarch. It is worth noting that in one of these petitions, in a prominent [?] place, in the name of the congress of the Indian Mohammedans, the demands were put forward that Mesopotamia and Jerusalem [?] should also be given back to Turkey, contrary to the national aspirations of the Arabs.
This is a fine illustration of the political harmony that supposedly reigns in Islam. But all this had no substance whatever compared with the fact that Turkey itself abolished the Caliphate, and thereby left its [?] Bengali advocates in a state of surprise and great confusion [?].
Mazel tov, Zelde-Zlate has passed the exam! (Monologue of a certified seamstress.)

[Humour — monologue; artisans and craft examinations.]
I thank You, dear God, Father in heaven, for having pity on Your poor Zelde-Zlate: luckily, at a good hour, I have passed the exam.
It cost me plenty of health and money. Just imagine: I, Zelde-Zlate, a "bezuratate"[?] [unclear word], who all my years never had any dealings with any noblemen, now had to answer so many questions that my forefathers never knew; the very thought had never occurred to me, and I never imagined that in my old age I would have to sit and study: what is a "cech" [guild]? A "shtekh fakh"[?]? What is "rzemiosło" [craft][?]? Who was the author of "Tsan"[?]? How many guberniyas [provinces] are there in Poland? What is the name of the President? Of the wojewoda [provincial governor][?]? Of the starosta [district head]? I ask you — what do I need to know that for? Where I get the means for the Sabbath[?] — that they don't ask me? It's no concern of theirs whether I have enough for the Sabbath or not? Only [—] ["tsi shvey vi vk"m", unclear], and what good does it do? Am I a young girl[?], then? After all it is a "skhat moygs"[?] [unclear] artisans' exam!
So I bought myself a book, and "my dear husband" Todros started studying with me. My spouse is a bit "gramotny" [literate], so he started drilling me in the "laws of the exam", and to his question "Co to jest cech?" [What is a guild?] I must answer: "Cech to jest korporacja rzemieślników jednego fachu" [A guild is a corporation of craftsmen of one trade] — and may I know no more of any evil, together with you, than I know a single word of it. There you have such a trouble, such a calamity — an exam, a plague[?] that even Pharaoh did not have! And I, Zelde Zlate, a Jewish woman close to 60 and maybe a bit[?] over, must now sit day and night over the book, swaying, and cram all the "zastanigs"[?] and "vstanovigs"[?] [apparently garbled Polish legal terms]. It's nothing to me. As if I had few troubles — now a new trouble has come, exam troubles. Don't take it amiss, forgive me and hear me out. True, they do say[?] that a Jewish woman has nine measures of troubles. I have not yet forgotten my earlier blows — the flu, the "kasa chorych" [sickness fund] — and here you are, Zelde Zlate, a fresh trouble: an exam...
In short, I don't sleep, I don't eat, I have become like a black devil, and when God helped and the day of judgement drew near, the day of the exam — that's when my heart really started pounding, and I got a fever — "podwyższona temperatura" [raised temperature] — a chill went through me, my teeth chattered: what will I do if I fail the exam? I'll have to jump into the water, they'll close my workshop, I'll be a milliner [modystka] no more. So I went off to the cemetery and knocked and cried — have pity on your Zelde-Zlate, do not rest in your graves, it is a decree from heaven, see to it and pray that I pass the exam. From the cemetery I went to the rebbe — holy rebbe, it's bad, rebbe, save me! — the rebbe took fright — what is it, Zelde-Zlate?
— You don't know, rebbe, I have to sit an exam. The rebbe calmed me down and promised me that I would pass.
And the day came — that day I shall not forget as long as I live. I went into the hall where they had taken "tsum ismal"[?] [unclear] all the artisans, me among them. They call out Zelde-Zlate: "córka Abrahama Fledercycz"[?] [daughter of Abraham F.] — "Jest!" [present] — I scream in a voice not my own. — "Pani jest krawczychą?" [Are you a seamstress?][?] — asks the examiner. — What's he babbling? — I ask my neighbour. — He's asking whether you are a seamstress — my neighbour gives me to understand. — Of course I'm a seamstress — I say — what then, a rebbetzin? If I weren't a seamstress I wouldn't find myself here, in a place of calamities[?], in a place of Gehenna. In short, the gentleman [pan] turns me this way, turns me that way, and I answer — I don't know myself how my tongue got loose. "Dobrze jest!" [Good!] cries the gentleman, and everyone wishes me mazel tov. We have a good God: with one hand He punishes and with the other He strokes. What would I have done if, God forbid, it had been the other way round? I would have been a wretched woman. On the Sabbath I made a kiddush and invited all the clergy — I had all the rabbis, cantors, ritual slaughterers, judges and preachers — a small matter: Zelde-Zlate passed the exam with a diploma! That is how I, Zelde-Zlate, became a certified seamstress. Now I pray only that the Almighty send me work, and that I may sit in peace and work.
I thank You, dear God, that You did not put me to shame and I passed the exam!
Y. Wasserstrom.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tisa)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Ki Tisa
—o—
a) "A ransom for his soul" (Ex. 30:12).
"A brother shall surely not redeem; a man shall redeem — he will not give God his ransom" [Ps. 49:8].
There are people who give gladly to general philanthropic charities, because that way they are praised[?]. But when one of their own comes, a relative, and asks for a quiet donation that nobody is to know about — that he does not give. "A brother shall not redeem": his own he does not want to help out, but "a man shall redeem" — to strangers he does give charity, because people will know about it; this is proof that "he will not give God his ransom" — that his charity is not for the sake of Heaven...
Siftei Tzaddikim (Rabbi Senderl).
—o—
b) "Half a shekel" (Ex. 30:13).
The census was carried out by half shekels and not simply by whole shekels, in order — to know that every individual on his own is nothing; only when all join the community does one become whole...
Binah le-Ittim, A. A.
* * *
In Płońsk there was a rich man, a grandson of the "Magen Avraham", but a great miser. Once R' Yechezkel Michelson, may he live long, said to him: You know that the "Magen Avraham" cannot be understood at all without the "Machatzit ha-Shekel" (a commentary on the "Magen Avraham"); when you give a "half shekel", people will know that you are the Magen Avraham's grandson...
—o—
c) "This they shall give" (Ex. 30:13).
"Moses found it difficult, until He showed him a kind of coin of fire and said to him: This they shall give." Midrash.
"Moses found it difficult" — Moses wondered how a half shekel could be a ransom for the soul. A heated coin should have such an effect? Until God showed him a "coin of fire" — how much temperament and fire the evil inclination uses so as not to let a person give the heated coin... And whoever really[?] manages it — it becomes an atonement for the soul...
Or Yesharim (Rabbi Moshe of Kobryń).
A Jew complains to Rabbi Mordechai of Nadwórna[?] about his livelihood. The rabbi gives him advice: repent, for "repentance reaches up to the Throne of Glory", and at the Throne of Glory there must be a lot of money — for how else[?] did God take fiery coins from beneath the Throne of Glory (so says the Midrash)? It must be that a lot of money lies there...
—o—
d) "The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less" (Ex. 30:15).
The rich man always likes to inflate the penny he gives and make a whole business of it, although on luxury he spends far more. "The rich shall not give more" — the wealthy man should not make more noise than he gives...
The recipients, on the other hand, like the opposite — to make everything into nothing, as it is said: "and the poor shall not give less"...
Korban he-Ani (Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany).
* * *
Other commentaries have it thus: "The rich shall not give more" — the rich they do not tax with any big tax[?]; whereas "the poor shall not give less" — the poor man, by contrast, is taxed not a little...
Sichat Chullin (Rabbi Ephraim Zalman Margaliot).
—o—
e) "Moses delayed" (Ex. 32:1).
The Gemara (Shabbat 89) wants to derive from the fact that Moses did not eat in Heaven that one may not deviate from the custom of the place one comes to. Why does the Gemara not derive it from the fact that Moses did not sleep there at night[?] — not sleeping for forty days is surely a greater feat —
But once I stayed at an inn where they gave me a place to sleep but nothing to eat, and I could not fall asleep...
Therefore Moses' sleeplessness is no proof, because, not having eaten, it may be that he simply could not sleep either...
Shut[?] ha-Yeri'ah[?] (the Maggid of Dubno[?]).
—o—
f) "Up, make us a god" (ibid.).
Why did they not choose Aaron as leader in Moses' place?
Aaron was a pursuer of peace and good-natured, and the people want a leader whom they will fear ("and one we shall fear" — Onkelos) — let him even have a calf's head...
Nifla'ot Chadashot.
—o—
g) "And he made it a molten calf" (Ex. 32:4).
Is it possible that from so much gold and jewellery that the Jews had from the spoil of Egypt, and all of it handed over for the casting, there came out merely a little calf?
— That's still good; with other honest gabbaim it would have come out... a little fly.
An old joke.
—o—
h) "Why does Your wrath burn against Your people, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt?"
What annoys You so? — Moses argued — they have only just come from Egypt; it is in exile that they learned this.
Tiferet Uziel.
—o—
i) "And he cast the tablets out of his hands" (Ex. 32:19).
Moses our teacher comes down, one single Jew with a little Torah scroll in his arms, looks around — everyone is worshipping the calf, only one Jew with a little Torah — so he threw it away.
R' Yechezkele of Kazimierz.
—o—
j) "Blot me, I pray, out of Your book" (Ex. 32:32).
Let them blot out of me
— a [—] is much weaker[?]...
Chullin[?] Yekirin.
The Eternal Struggle of the Wagon-Driver with the Railway.

[Economy — transport and taxes.] The well-known PPS[?] [Polish Socialist Party] economist Herman Diamand, who died suddenly a month ago, published a few days before his death an article entitled "Szaleństwa gospodarcze" ["Economic Follies"], in which he dwells at length on the government's decision to impose a heavy tax on bus transport. Diamand first draws a parallel between the railway and the bus, and writes:
The gas engine[?] needs no rails and can move along all roads. The railway once fought the "wagon-driver"; now the "wagon-driver", with the help of the bus, has again declared war on the railway. The bus needs no stations. The passenger does not have to come to the bus; the bus has the option of driving up to the passenger, to the shop, to the factory, and carries the luggage to its destination. The bus is not late[?] like a train and does not wait without[?] passengers. The bus needs no billions in investment like a railway; and yet the railway was born in a luckier hour.
When the railway was born, the "wagon trade" was not organised; apart from weeping and wailing it offered no resistance at all, and the railway won. The bus, however, is in a worse position: the railways constitute a large, unified and powerful organisation; in a number of countries the railway, the state administration and parliament are in one and the same hands, so it is hard to compete with the railway. But the bus is very nimble and skilful and does compete with the railway, which is tied to its place; so the railway administrations have resorted to means of force, wage[?] a fight against the competitor and also use police-like methods. Government[?] help, like all help by force, is very convenient: it keeps alive the ill-starred, anachronistic[?] economy and creates disruption in a reckless way.
In states ruled by dictatorial governments, where society's influence on the government is excluded and posts and offices are obtained not through professional competence but through crawling, it is hard to run the railways in a businesslike way, and the interest of the "mafia" naturally rules. There the staff, paid hunger wages, and[?] the bus must pay for the ill-starred railway economy, although under a reasonable economic policy the bus could excellently find its place and contribute to the development of transport, being a first-class factor in the modern social economy.
The administration of the German railways long ago began a fight against the buses; it applied various means and set up a competition with a prize of 10 thousand marks for whoever proposed the best means of combating bus competition. But in Germany there is a real parliament, elected by the population, so the deputies depend on it; therefore it is impossible in the German parliament to pass a law imposing heavy taxes on buses and thus making it impossible for buses to compete with the railways.
In Poland bus transport is still weakly developed, yet the railways have already felt the competition. Already in the previous Sejm the government introduced a bill to impose taxes on buses. This method of hindering the development of new inventions, which lower the cost of living and also provide comfort, is nothing new. The tax of 20 złoty on a "zapalniczka" [cigarette lighter], in order thereby to protect the Swedish match manufacturers, is already a well-known matter; only individual deputies, who do not depend on voters, could allow themselves to protect the match monopoly. The same happens with the tax on performances. The magistrates [municipal councils] support theatres, to which they add enormous sums, because the city administrations lack the qualifications to make the theatre accessible to the broad masses; so they take the poor tax money of those same masses and cover with it the deficits of the theatres, which are created in order to please[?] the "elegant" public. The masses satisfy their aesthetic needs in the cinemas, which increasingly meet high artistic demands; the cinemas fully take the place of the theatres and offer first-class productions by world-famous artists whom one can see only thanks to the cinema.
But so that access to the cinema should not be so easy, the magistrates, without putting any capital into the cinemas and without bearing any responsibility or risk, have become uninvited partners of the cinemas and take a tax of 50 and 60 per cent of the ticket price. To its own enterprise the magistrate adds money, and from other people's businesses the magistrate draws large profits. That is why the cities have quite good[?] opera.
The same will happen when the new tax on buses comes into force. The government bill imposes on every bus ticket a tax of 30 per cent of the gross price, i.e. the government becomes a "partner" of the bus and as such takes a third of what the entrepreneur receives — the entrepreneur who after all must invest capital, pay for petrol and grease, pay the driver and the conductor, for tyres, other taxes, and himself earn a living. True, the 30 per cent tax is to be paid by the passenger, but the buses may well meet the same fate as the railway carriages: the number of passengers may shrink and produce a deficit.
X.
From Where and From Whom?

[Poland — taxes and housing.] All our[?] eyes and ears have lately been turned to Warsaw, to our metropolis.
One wants to hear, one wants to see the news from there — what is already "decreed and cannot be reversed", and which decree may still possibly be softened.
Until now nearly all town-dwellers in the country were weighed down as if by a mountain by the rumour spread some time ago that the government plans to abolish the tenants' protection law and to raise rents.
In these present hard times that would have been a terrible blow to the population.
But a report came from Warsaw that Minister Składkowski received a delegation of the Association of Tenants and Sub-tenants and declared to it that the rumours about raising rents are premature and that there is now no talk of abolishing the tenants' protection law —
which, it seems, is already a little good.
But at the same time comes the news from the other side that the budget has been adopted with all the foreseen tax increases, such as the law on the match monopoly, which imposes on the population a tax of 18 million zł., the law on the road fund, which burdens the population with 15 million zł., and finally the 10 per cent increase of income tax.
Besides this the finance minister declared that he is preparing yet another law on a tax which is to bring the state another 20 million zł.
And the minister explicitly remarked that these huge twenty million will in no way burden the rural population. The entire sum will be taken only from the town-dwellers.
And the question arises: from where and from whom does the minister want to take the new taxes?
After all, in the merchant world things look simply as after a war — and after a lost war at that; one is dealing only with poor people. From where does the minister reckon to bring in the fresh 20 million zł.?
And are we even sure that the taxes already decided can actually be collected?
A Taxpayer's Joke

[Humour — taxes and distraint; anecdote.] A bailiff (sequestrator) came to carry out a distraint on the household goods of a certain taxpayer.
Unfortunately the executor found that everything in the home had long since been distrained for other taxes, and so he turned to the citizen with the question whether he did not have some hidden articles about him.
— I have — he answered after thinking it over for a while.
The executor was pleased, noting[?] that his words[?] were being borne out, and asked him to reveal the treasure at once.
— But allow me — the taxpayer went on — it is such an unpleasant thing, one that people do not talk about...
The executor was very pleased and immediately demanded, in the name of the law, that he disclose what he had hidden.
The taxpayer could no longer restrain himself and answered — haemorrhoids..
— What's that? — the executor asked again.
— Haemorrhoids — I said..
— Be so kind as to show them, then.
— I will not show them.
— In the name of the law I demand that you show them — the executor cried out, inflamed[?].
— No, I will not show you!
— We shall see — the sequestrator insisted, and sat down to write a report, because the man refuses to show him his property and tries to hide it from him while he must carry out his official duty.
Declaring Love... (How It Used to Be Done and How It Is Done Today)

[Feuilleton — love, courtship and marriage in modern times.] „Mother, wish me mazel tov, I got married, with good luck“.
Many mothers would consider themselves happy to hear at least that much from their sons and daughters. For it does happen that a mother learns her child got married only months later, and from strangers.
If only getting married itself had become so dreary[?] and sober[?], so calculated and practical, the rift[?] between the older and the younger generation would not yet be so great. The trouble, however, is that in our days even what little love there was has also become a heap of ruins.
Young men no longer „court“[?] girls. A modern, worldly[?] girl could expire before she hears the slightest compliment from her beloved. His „angel“, his „treasure“ and his „heavenly thing“[?] she has long, thank God, ceased to be. Yes, today's young man sides with the philosopher Voltaire, who said: „The first man who compared a woman to a rose was a poet, the second — already an idiot“.
A modern, worldly girl longs and yearns for that bit of attention and a little compliment no less than her mother and grandmother and great-grandmother longed and yearned. But she does not get it, and who, do you think, is to blame for it? In nine cases out of every ten — she herself.
She demands — if she really is a modern, worldly girl — that her beloved regard her as an equal partner. From his attitude toward her it must be clear that he considers her his equal.
A modern, worldly girl does not regard it as any disgrace, and certainly not as an insult, if the young man, even when he lives alone, invites her to his place. On the contrary, she sees it as a kind of honour; to her it is above all proof that he looks upon her as a grown-up person and is serious about the match.
Speaking to each other „on du-terms“ [familiar address] is also no longer, as it once was, a piece of impudence. It is no sign of „vulgarity“, of cultural backwardness and coarseness. It is done now in the best circles. It is no longer as it once was, when such a manner of speaking smacked of „Shoemakers' Street“.
A modern, worldly girl, unless she is forced to, will only rarely ask the young man, whether he is her beloved or merely a „friend“, to „call for her“ at home. Even mothers have long since stopped demanding that the young man „come up“. Many of them are content if they see him, the young man, the day after the wedding.
There are no more sofas on which the greater part[?] of a „romance“ between a young man and a girl used to play itself out, until with good luck they reached the wedding canopy. There are no more portières on the doors from behind which mothers and younger sisters could spy out „how far it has got“. And a girl's father, if he wants to know with whom his daughter „goes out“, must, if he is a clever father, hire a detective.
The worst blow that modern times have dealt to what little romantic love there was, was the invention of the telegraph and the telephone. Young men have almost completely stopped writing letters to their sweethearts. No more „letter-writers“ [model-letter manuals], such as only some twenty years ago, containing samples of love letters, are published. „I cannot tell you this, I will try to write it out to you in a letter“ is a dead phrase that nobody uses any more. Declarations of love are made over the telephone, intimate secrets are spoken through the telegraph.
Girls no longer run out to meet the postman. Girls no longer receive letters that must be read in secret, so that nobody in the house can see the effect the letters have on them. Girls no longer come back from an encounter with the postman with tear-stained eyes; girls no longer cry at all, and fainting is altogether out of the question.
The typewriter, it seems to me, has also taken away a fair[?] bit of romance. [—][?], pardon me, to dictate on a machine such a refrain as: „My treasure, my sunshine, my little angel“. If anyone thinks it is a pleasure to read typewritten letters from her beloved on the letterhead of the firm where he works, he is badly mistaken. But she will never protest against it — it would not become her. That would after all be so old-fashioned, so out of tune with the present time.
And what has become of romancing in the parks at night, in the light of — let it be not „Mond“ [German: moon], but simply the levone [moon]? On most summer nights in recent years one can find empty benches in a [?] park. True, if one listens closely one can still, even now, on a deserted summer evening, hear a soft cooing as of doves, and from time to time even a kiss, but no sigh or groan — that never. The time of sighs and groans by the light of the moon is „over“. A pity, a great pity.
Or take the broygez [lovers' quarrels and sulks]. Over what, for instance, did an average girl only some fifteen years ago fall out with her beloved? You have all been through it, and there is no need, I believe, to write it down here. A love without a quarrel over every single word that this one said or that one said was no love at all. Well, and further[?]: today, is it right that she, or[?] he, should simply slap [the other] in the face over — over what, do you think, I hear you ask? That a girl should do it because the young man thinks that Sinclair Lewis honestly deserved the Nobel Prize for literature! I myself know of a match that was broken off solely because the girl was of the opinion that Mengelberg is a greater conductor than Toscani[ni], while the young man, on the contrary — that Toscani[ni], mind you[?], is the greatest conductor. And both of them, I would say[?], are not even klezmer musicians.
The last citadel of what little romance there was, the picnic, has unfortunately also fallen under the cannon-fire of the new age. Gone are those picnics from which girls used to return late on a summer night pale, pensive, dreamy, and then for a long while, until deep into the night, share secrets with their elder sisters or girlfriends. Today a Sunday is spent playing tennis and all kinds of other sports, and one comes back fresh and cheerful, sunburnt and laughing; one comes back without any aches, and entirely without [permission?] a young man and a girl have, mind you, spent a whole day somewhere in the countryside — and nothing hurts him or her, and neither she nor he regrets anything. Fine times we have lived to see, nothing to be said.
L. Pozument.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Będzin — local news.]
[Friday, 17 Adar 5691 — 6 March 1931]
Będzin
Five Members of the Election Commission Struck Off by the Starosta.
Success of the „Agudah“ Protest.
As we already reported in the last issue of our paper, the „Agudah“ [Agudat Israel] lodged a protest with the starosta [district head] against the elected election commission, in which the „Agudah“ had no majority. In the protest the „Agudah“ declared that „the election commission consists of intriguers, 'augists' [?] and such as are known in the field of election machinations“.
The protest had the proper success, and on the day after the „ssirhalf“ [?] was handed in, the kehilla board received an official communication from the starosta, who announces that the members of the commission, Messrs. Mordechai Yosef Frajzer, Leybish Dimant („Mizrachi“), Yitzchak Wigodzki (Zionist), Avraham Liwer [?] (Zionist) and Avraham Yissachar Radzinic [?] (non-party) have been disqualified.
On Sunday evening the board held a meeting at which, in place of the disqualified, there were elected — only with the votes of the Agudah dozors [members of the dozór, the kehilla board], since the non-party and Zionist dozors took no part in the vote) — Messrs. Avraham Liwer [?] (Agudah), Shimon Plasner, Bożykowski [?], Berish Rapaport and Yosef Szwajcer.
———
In connection with the fact that the gmina [community] secretary Mr. Frejlech presented the catastrophic state of the kehilla to the starosta, the deputy starosta Mr. Mendyszewski [?] expressed his wish to come to the kehilla premises for a meeting with the board.
On Sunday morning a meeting of the kehilla board took place with the participation of Mr. Mendyszewski. The latter, having heard out the mutual complaints of the dozors, expressed his wish that until the new kehilla elections peace should reign within the kehilla board.
At the meeting the dozors Messrs. Rygski and Bożykowski poured out their hearts. Mr. Rygski complained before the gentleman that they, that is the „Agudah“, also have an „organ“, yet the „organ“ writes nothing about the kehilla mishmash [?], only the other paper.. — he says — writes about everyone [?]. (It would be interesting to know which organ Mr. Rygski means: the Warsaw „Tog-Blat“ or the „fenomacke [?] organ“ in Będzin?!)
The same crocodile tears were shed by Mr. Bożykowski as well: hardly — he says — do I utter a word at a meeting in the gmina [?] than it is at once written up in the press.
— It is true, we know it too, that the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ is like a bone in the throat of the kehilla „providers“...
—o—
Tenants' Plebiscite Against Raising the Rent.
As is known, the tenants' convention in Warsaw resolved to hold a plebiscite of all tenants in Poland on whether they are against the level of rent being raised.
Together with all the other towns, the plebiscite is also being conducted by the local „Tenants' Association“.
Not a single tenant should be missing with his signature on this protest.
—o—
On the Cancellation of Tax Arrears (zaległe podatki).
We are asked by the „Merchants' Association“ to announce that all those who are unable to pay old tax debts should, in their own interest, report to the secretariat of the association.
—o—
A Terrible Act of Revenge on a Young Jewish Man.
First Strangled and Then Thrown into the „Przemsza“.
On Friday morning the news spread through the town that a young Jewish man had thrown himself into the „Przemsza“ [river] with the aim of committing suicide. Later, when the young man was taken out of the river, already dead, the matter became clear: a terrible act of revenge had been committed here on the 20-year-old shoemaker [?] Moshe Aharon Erdigens [?], who, as it turned out, had first been strangled and then thrown into the water.
When the tragically perished man was taken out of the water, he was still holding stiff [?] fingers at his neck, and his face was terribly red — signs that the victim had tried with his last strength to save himself and had put up resistance to the murderers.
Erdigens [?] belonged to a left-wing party, and it is suspected that the reason for the murder was that the party suspected him of doing it harm.
The funeral took place on Sunday; on that day Erdigens [?] would have turned 20.
—o—
A Serious Accident.
On Saturday morning, while going down the stairs of his flat at Kołłątaja [?] 24, Mr. Moshe Kojfman fell and broke his left leg. Kojfman was at once taken to hospital, where he was operated on.
—o—
Będzin Pioneers Have Left for Eretz Israel.
(H) Last week three realising members [chaverim magshimim] of the Będzin „Gordonia“ left for Eretz Israel; they will join the kvutza of the Eretz-Israel „Gordonia“ in Rehovot.
The departing pioneers were seen off in Sosnowiec and in Katowice by hundreds of young Zionists, who took a warm farewell of the Będzin pioneers, the first from our town after the sad events in Eretz Israel.
This month several more pioneers are leaving [?] Zagłębie, who are emigrating with the last certificates of the 1,500 entry permits that the Palestine government gave the Jewish Agency soon after the publication of the „White Paper“.
—o—
New Notary Engages Jewish Clerks.
The new notary [rejent], whose office is on Senatorska street, has broken „the tradition“ and engaged Jewish clerks in his office. The step deserves to be welcomed, and one must hope that other similar offices will also follow the good example.
—o—
One Concert by S. Bakman in Zagłębie.
Today, Friday evening, the concert of the virtuoso Shimon Bakman takes place in the „Corso“ in Będzin.
Bakman has appeared with concerts in a series of towns in Poland, Warsaw included, and the Warsaw press has devoted warm notices to the young Jewish artist.
On the programme — musical works by the greatest musical geniuses.
Incidentally, we note that apart from Będzin, Bakman will give no more concerts in the Zagłębie towns.
—o—
The Gerer Rebbe Is Coming to Będzin.
Next Tuesday — so we are told — the Gerer Rebbe [of Góra Kalwaria] is to come here, to be present at the circumcision held by R' [?] Eli' Lewin, son of the local rabbi.
—o—
A Delegation to the Starosta.
A delegation of Messrs. Fiawer [?] and Liwer [?] was with the starosta and conferred with him about the 5 members who were disqualified from the election commission.
The starosta, having acquainted himself with the material, declared that he will treat the matter entirely objectively.
—o—
From the Union of Zionist Revisionists in Będzin.
Last Friday evening, in an overflowing hall, a collective lecture took place on the life and work of Ze'ev Jabotinsky.
As first speaker, A. Diamant [?] reads an interesting lecture on Jabotinsky's appearance in the Jewish and Zionist world. (We shall bring the exact [?] content of the lecture in one of the coming issues of our paper.)
As second speaker Mr. Klarman appears, who gives a brilliant Revisionist constitution-speech [?], which met with great applause.
—o—
An Entertainment Evening of „Hashachar“.
This Saturday night the local „Hashachar“ is holding an entertainment evening in the premises of the „Artisans' Association“.
Such an evening was also held, the previous Saturday night, by the Sosnowiec „Hashachar“. At that evening a film [„bild“] was shown that depicts how Jewish children are being brought up in Eretz Israel.
Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; local news.] Election commission elected a second time.
In our last issue we brought our readers the list of those elected to the election commission for the kehilla elections. The commission, however, was disqualified by the starosta [district head]. The point is that on behalf of the board Mr. L. Jungster had also been elected, whom the starosta had not confirmed as a board member, and because the commission was elected under the chairmanship of Mr. Weinryb[?], whose presidency is being withdrawn[?].
The deputy starosta personally communicated this decision at the gmina [municipal office] and at the same time demanded that in place of Mr. Jungster, Mr. M. Jungster should join the board, and that the presidency be handed back to Mr. L. Zandel.
Therefore on Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Zandel, a board meeting was held at which the following election commission was elected for the second time:
In the vote 2 lists figured, of the non-party group and of "Orah"[?]. By 7 votes to 3 the non-party list was adopted, on which figure:
On behalf of the board: Naftali Babmeier[?], Avraham Stiglitz, Leib Apresczyk, Hirsz Nachnzis[?] and Icchak Sachs.
On behalf of the town householders: Szlomo Kimelman, Szmuel Aron Fris[?], Lewi Jungster, Zew Chm[?] Rabinowicz, Jechiel Tobiasz[?], Jankel Cwajgenhaft, Berek Cybenski[?], L. Piekarski, Lemen[?] Buksbaum, Hirsz Erlich, Awraham Zagowski[?].
Deputies: Isze[?] Wolf Brener, Berek Grojer, Baruch Zaskowicz[?], S. Ch. Y. Sztas[?] and Nachum[?] Kan.
—o—
"On that night" the rabbi's seat was destroyed
In the night from Friday[?] to Saturday a "secret hand" got in through a window into the local Great Synagogue and there carried out a "holy piece of work": namely, the "secret hand" hacked to pieces with an axe the rabbi's seat, which today is occupied[?] by Rabbi Hager[?].
The kehilla board has decided to uncover the criminal hands. A photograph was also taken as[?] a document for the coming generation...
—o—
Direct tram connection to Upper Silesia.
From Tuesday the new tram line has been opened which connects[?] Zagłębie with Upper Silesia, so that one can travel by tram from Dąbrowa to[?] Königshütte [Chorzów].
—o—
Burglary in Kucharski's shop.
In the night from Monday to Tuesday the haberdashery shop of Mr. Kucharski was broken into. The burglars took a large quantity of goods; the damage is estimated at up to 10 thousand zł.
—o—
The verdict in the smuggling trial.
All the accused have been acquitted.
The smuggling trial, which lasted 2 weeks at the local district court, ended this Monday. In a tense[?] atmosphere and before a packed[?] hall the verdict was announced, according to which the accused are acquitted.
The prosecutor declared that he will turn with a complaint[?] to the Supreme Tribunal.
—o—
A gang of money forgers liquidated.
Several weeks ago, as our readers know, the local police discovered a factory of false 10-złoty banknotes. But with the arrest of the local money forgers the business was not yet liquidated, because some of the partners continued their activity in Poland[?].
This week the partners were arrested. With this the gang of money forgers has finally been liquidated.
—o—
To spite the husband...
The 20-year-old Tilec[?], with the aim of committing suicide, cut the veins of her left hand. The reason for the suicide attempt is that there is no domestic peace between the couple.
—o—
Meeting of the Jewish girls' gymnasium.
Next Sunday, the 8th of this month, at 7 in the evening, the general meeting of the Society for Jewish Secondary Schools in Sosnowiec will take place in the premises of the Jewish gymnasium. It is to be hoped that the members in general and the parents in particular[?] will this time show more interest in the Jewish school and will attend the meeting in large numbers.
—o—
Serious accident to a councillor of the local Chamber of Commerce
On Thursday the Częstochowa councillors, Messrs. Piotrowski, Gajaler[?] and Stiller, took part in the plenary session of the local Chamber of Commerce. After the session all the councillors went home. On arriving in Częstochowa Mr. Stiller, wishing to avoid all the railway tracks, walked along a side track so as to get home sooner. At that moment a freight train came rushing along and cut off both of Stiller's legs.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — kehilla.] An election commission elected.
On Sunday a meeting of the kehilla board took place, which elected the commission for the coming kehilla elections.
On behalf of the board the following joined: Messrs. President Mitelman, G. A. Gutman, D. Weltfreund, L. Szamszanowski[?] and G. S. Szajer[?].
On behalf of the town members: Messrs. H. Gutman, Y. Wajntraub[?], H. Szpilberg, K. Garfinkel, Jechiel Dąb, L. Bachnic[?], Jakow Pajasel[?], Ch. Klajn, Jakow Meir Klajnman, Israel Erlicht[?], D. Nusbaum.
Deputies: L. Manele[?], M. Liberman, Jakow Fridman, S. Finkelsztajn and M. A. Rozencwajg.
The commission has been confirmed by the authorities.
This evening, Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat), the chairman of the commission will be elected.
"Also" for the Third Time..

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] In today's issue our readers will find a report from the Sosnowiec kehilla board, which this Sunday[?] elected an election commission for the second time.
The commission again found no favour[?] in the eyes of the "Agudah"[?], and a delegation went where one has to go... and therefore asked that this commission too be declared "kol chamira"[?] [the formula for annulling leaven — i.e. declared void]...
This was achieved, and accordingly[?] the starosta ordered the kehilla board to have the members of the election commission checked once more.
If the same commission remains, only then will the starosta give his decision.
—o—
Costume and Masked Ball.
[Będzin — culture.] This Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a costume and masked ball will be held for the benefit of the Będzin Borochov[?] Library.
The initiators[?] are taking pains to make the ball interesting and amusing.
A series of contests with valuable prizes is also being prepared.
—o—
The General Meeting of the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association
[Sosnowiec — artisans.] Before a packed hall, the continuation of the annual members' meeting of the Sosnowiec Jewish Artisans' Association took place last Sunday.
The starszy (guild elder) Josef Rotensztajn was elected chairman. In a lengthy speech of greeting, the president of the Central Union of Jewish Artisans in Poland, G. Dls[?] a Ros-ger[?], shed light on the most important current artisans' questions of the present moment, dwelling especially on the forthcoming kehilla elections.
After a lengthy discussion, in which Messrs. M. Pisloshni[?], J. Eksztajn, M. Szpren[?], J. Fridman, A. Dawidowicz, B. Choydisław[?] and others took part, the motion of Mr. M. S. Gutmler[?] was adopted unanimously, according to which the meeting expresses its full confidence in the outgoing board headed by its president, Mr. A. Tsep-Smatski[?]. Because of this, the item "election of a new board" was no longer relevant.
—o—
Preparatory Courses for Journeyman Examinations
[Sosnowiec — artisans.] Under the direction of Messrs. Gancwajch[?] and Kaner, preparatory courses for the formal[?] journeyman (Geselle) examinations will soon be opened.
The curriculum has been drawn up in agreement with the examination regulations of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts and approved by the voivode in Kielce.
Besides the trade subjects, economic[?] and Polish geography, the Polish constitution, social and industrial taxes[?] etc. will also be taught. Registration at the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association, and in Będzin with Mr. M. Kaner.

Editor and publisher L. Szpigelman, Będzin.
(Polish:) Editor and publisher L. Szpigelman [?], Będzin. Printed in our own printing house — (Yiddish:) printed in our own printing house.

Zaglembier Cajtung / ZAGŁEMBIER CAJTUNG. No. 11. "21st year" (sic; as printed — the paper was in its third year). Price 25 groszy. Postal fee paid in full (Opłata pocztowa uiszczona ryczałtem).
Friday, Parshat Vayakhel-Pekudei [printed abbreviated: ויקופ״ק], 24 Adar 5691 / piątek 13 marca 1931. Candle-lighting 5,11.

All Olkusz Jews vote on Sunday in the city-council elections for list 13

[Olkusz — city-council elections.] 13 — this is the only Jewish national list, for which all the Jews of Olkusz vote on Sunday. Not a single vote may be cast for the lists that are out for their own benefit — so remember, Jews of Olkusz: do not let yourselves be taken in[?] by the speakers of falsehood, but all as one man, you and your wives, defend Jewish rights with honour and pride and vote only for the united list 13.
—o—
[Będzin — kehilla, election commission.] "If the election commission does not live in peace, I shall perform a Caesarean section."
So declares the vice-starosta.
As is known, in Będzin too, as in all other towns, an election commission has been elected. The commission must, however, elect from among its members a complaints commission (reklamatsye-komisye). For that purpose 2 sittings took place this week, which — because of "if you hit me, I hit you" — were blown up.
In connection with this, a delegation of Messrs. G.[?] Rechnic[?], G. Banhart and H. Goldsztajn turned yesterday before noon to the vice-starosta, whom they asked whether a quorum is required when electing a complaints commission, and at the same time informed him about the situation in the commission.
The vice-starosta declared in reply that if the commission does not live in peace and begin real work, he will be compelled to perform a Caesarean section...
—o—
[Sosnowiec — craftsmen.] From the Sosnowiec Craftsmen's Association.
The board of the Sosnowiec Craftsmen's Association (Hantverker-Fareyn) has engaged Dr. Anisfeld[?], a specialist in heart and internal diseases. Those interested should apply in this matter to the association's secretariat.
