Notes of the week

[News of the week — world.] Earthquakes occurred in Serbia and Greece. Over 1000 houses collapsed; there are thousands of dead.
—o—
The Arab king has issued a decree to seize Jewish children and convert them [forcibly, "opshmadn"].
—o—
At the age of 75 the well-known writer Menachem Mendel Dolitzki died in California.
—o—
In Czernowitz [Cernăuți] a false accusation of blood libel occurred this week. The libel ended, as always, in a fiasco for the antisemites.
—o—
At the Warsaw municipality 500 officials are being cut [dismissed] as of 1 April.
—o—
In the course of the week a snowstorm prevailed throughout Europe; in Sweden the frost reached as much as 50 degrees.
Terrible tramway accident. Yerachmiel Szwarcberg has lost his right leg.

[Dąbrowa — accident.] On Monday at 10 in the morning a tramway disaster occurred by the "Paryż" coal mine, which cost the Dąbrowa[?] butcher[?] Yerachmiel Szwarcberg his right leg.
As we are informed, the disaster occurred under the following circumstances: early in the morning a tram went off the rails on Potockiego[?] Street in Będzin; because of this the tram traffic was not normal, and at every tram stop many people were waiting.
The same was the case at the tram stop Miejski[?]—Sobieskiego in Dąbrowa. Among the passengers who were waiting for a tram was also Mr. Szwarcberg, who, having no time to wait, began to walk towards Będzin. As he came near the "Paryż", a tram caught up with him. But because of the overcrowding the tram did not stop. Mr. Szwarcberg nevertheless managed to jump on, and remained standing on the tram steps. At that moment he was caught by a tram pole and fell down under the tram wheels, which cut off Szwarcberg's right leg.
At the moment when the catastrophe happened the director was driving out of the "Paryż" coal mine, and seeing what had happened he took the victim into his car and drove him to the Będzin hospital, where the operation took place at once.
The new railway timetable will be in accord with the resolutions of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce. Express ["courier"] trains will run at 85 kilometres an hour

[Sosnowiec — railways.] On 15 May the new timetable comes into force, into which all the desiderata and proposals of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce have been introduced.
In the first place a reform is being introduced on the line Vienna—Sosnowiec—Warsaw, by increasing the speed of the courier trains to 85 kilometres per hour, also shortening the stop in Sosnowiec to 1 minute, and abolishing the stopping stations at Skierniewice, Radomsko, Zawiercie, Ząbkowice, Dąbrowa, Będzin and Tychy[?] ["Tikhau"].
The couriers will depart from Sosnowiec at 8.47 in the morning and at 1[?] at night, arriving in Warsaw at 13,50 and 9.16; departing from Warsaw at 15 55 and 20 40 and arriving in Sosnowiec at 21 09 and 1,20. On the line, in accord with the proposals of the Chamber of Commerce, the timetable of the night passenger trains on the line Katowice—Warsaw is being changed in the sense that the train, instead of at 0 21[?], will depart at 1 15 at night and arrive in Warsaw at 8.40 instead of 5 06. Sleeping cars in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd classes will also be attached to this train.
With the new timetable Kraków obtains a very good connection with Zagłębie; thus, for example, a motor train will depart from Sosnowiec for Kraków (via Katowice) at 8 33 and arrive in Kraków at 10 52; from Kraków at 6 48 and 12 45, arriving in Sosnowiec at 8 37 and 14 37.
Besides this, 2 new trains Sosnowiec—Kielce—Warsaw are being added.
The timetable to Zakopane, Krynica, Rabka and Rajcza[?] has also been improved.
A district committee created to celebrate the name-day of Marshal Piłsudski.

[Będzin — district.] Under the chairmanship of the Starosta, Mr. Boxa, a large meeting took place, at which a committee was created which is organising the celebration in honour of the name-day of Marshal Piłsudski on the 19th of this month.
A programme was fixed, which provides for various events ["imprezes"].
Representatives of the gminas[?] [rural communes], the starostwo [district office], the court, the Jewish communities [kehillas] and of various organisations and associations have entered the committee.
Rabbi R' Shlomo David, of blessed memory, has passed away.

[Strzemieszyce — death.] After a prolonged illness the moreh-tzedek [rabbinical judge, "mo"ts"] of Strzemieszyce, Rabbi R' Shlomo David Zander[?], of blessed memory, passed away in Kraków at the age of 52.
For 32 years the deceased fulfilled the rabbinical duties in Strzemieszyce and earned a good name among all strata of the community there.
Because of this it is almost a certain thing that the son of the deceased will take his place, and thereby the kehilla in Strzemieszyce will fulfil its sacred obligation towards the esteemed deceased.

Behind the Railway-Car Springs — Arrived in Rome.
Last summer an unemployed man from Katowice took a fancy to make a journey around the world.
Not having any money for this purpose, he clung on underneath, behind the springs of an international train, and thus, lying there for a full 2 days, he arrived in Rome.

The Existence of the Citizens

(How do matters stand with the turnover tax? — For the attention of the assessment commissions.)
The winter was a bad one; people took in no money, the goods were left lying and the season went by with nothing. Afterwards[?] people stocked up on winter goods and looked out for the winter — but look today, look tomorrow, it did not show itself; later, when it did after all come into the land, it was already too late for everything, and the goods go on lying on the shelves. And from this one must live, from this one must draw a livelihood, from this one must pay rent, taxes and the like.
And when one has to buy a loaf of bread and a piece of meat and has a small bill of exchange to pay, and there is no money, one does not look for any strokes of luck[?]: one takes the bit of merchandise off the shelf and sells it for whatever price[?] can be had. Is there any choice? How much one earns from that kind of “takings” — we believe everyone knows[?]. But the government wants to know nothing of it; for it, the point is that one is turning goods over[?], and for the turnover[?] [obrót] everyone must pay whatever it comes to.
Naturally, under such conditions, in such a standstill, in such a dead season, it is not easy to pay the taxes. True, as we hear, the tax office [Urząd Skarbowy] is now softer; it is accommodating, grants relief and spreads the taxes out in instalments [raty] — and that only for those who cannot pay.
Now, the assessment of the turnover tax has recently begun, and in the “Urząd Skarbowy”, as every year, the order has been given this time too to “turn over”[?] on the same scale as formerly. After all, with them we always do good business and big turnovers[?]. True, the officials already see that it is no longer as it once was, but they do not want to show it either, and they have no wish at all to assess lower — regardless of the fact that they know perfectly well that trade has died off and that earnings are very minimal.
The Jewish members of the assessment commissions in Zagłębie will therefore have to stand on guard and protect the interests of the Jewish merchants, who are in a sad enough position. The Jewish representatives, like the non-Jewish ones, bear no easy mission. We hold that their work is now considerably harder than ever, because from year to year there are fewer merchants and traders, so that those who are taxed carry a very heavy yoke — if only because, although the turnover is smaller, they are taxed with higher sums. The reason is that those who have dropped out, those who have fallen behind, the “dead” ones, cannot be counted as real payers, and so the government would like to get the revenue from the merchants who are still standing.
It thus turns out that although times are hard, although nothing is being sold and one earns considerably less, the merchants who still exist are to bear considerably greater obligations than before; and it goes without saying that this is one of the hardest circumstances, one of the most responsible tasks.
More than once we have had the opportunity to hear how frivolously the representatives treat tax matters. It has often happened, for example, that they were not represented at the sittings, which take place systematically, and in that case it goes without saying that Jewish money is squandered. Now, in today's hard times, such questions must not be taken lightly; they must be at every sitting, and not only must they be at the sittings, they must see to it that their interests are defended.
We do not hold that one must set about haggling and losing[?], as usually happens; if there are those who really do make the proposed turnover, there is no need to go through fire for them; but those who do not make the turnover put forward, and whom the sums assessed may ruin — for them one must stand up and not allow a wrong to be done to them, for they are broken enough, these helpless small traders and artisans, who everywhere are the first scapegoat, who can never hold their own and come off the losers every time.
The representatives ought to be in contact with their associations, and the associations with their members, who ought to be questioned in order to know their true situation.
A sacred duty lies both on the representatives and on the professional institutions not to allow a wrong to be done to the citizens who are still on their feet and fighting honestly for their existence.
We know that this mission is no easy one, and that honest, intensive work costs health and no little heartache; but there is no help for it — in this way sacred public duties are discharged, which the people has the right to demand of its representatives, to whom it has entrusted its economic interests, which in the present critical time are bound up with existence and ruin.
Yes, the question is now so hard, and unfortunately so complicated. For as soon as a citizen is assessed in the course of the year with obligations that are too high, it is not one of the hard things for him to slip and go down from the arena. We have had not a few such examples in the course of recent years.
One must therefore approach the turnover-tax[?] [obrotowy] assessment with the greatest caution and with due deliberation, for only in this way can benefit be brought both to the citizens and to the government; for what will the government gain if it over-assesses such-and-such a percentage of citizens, from whom it will afterwards be unable to collect the taxes, and who will thus be broken, and it may come to the point that later he [the citizen] will go under altogether. Then the citizen will have nothing, and nothing can be had from him either.
What is therefore called for now is cautious, planned work that will make it possible for the citizens to go on eking out their existence.
R. Let.
Large Protest Meeting against the Aguda Attacks on Mizrachi Rabbis

Last Saturday night a large protest meeting took place in the premises of “Mizrachi”, Warsaw, Mariańska 7, convened by the Warsaw “Tze'irei Mizrachi” in connection with the latest unheard-of attacks by young Aguda men on Mizrachi rabbis.

At the end Mr. Sirek[?] gave detailed information about the events in Łuków[?], after which the following resolution was adopted:

What Was Heard, What Was Seen

[Feuilleton — Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa.] Reported by Ben Amotz.

Downhill
On Sunday, the second rest day of the week, Jews have time; people gather for a meeting in this or that institution, and meanwhile, until the "quorum" arrives, they chat — and there is certainly no lack of things to chat about, especially about what goes on in our God-blessed Będzin. The town possesses very rich material for talk. Whatever you touch upon, there is something to talk and tell about...
The talk at the meeting was devoted to the great host of young ignoramuses supplied to us by the so-called "powszechne" [public elementary] schools, and the old question was rehearsed once again:
— Why? Why do our spiritual leaders take no interest in the matter? After all, Jewish education for Jewish children is at the very least as important as koshering an oven for baking matzos...
To this new-old question none of those present found an answer, not even the vice-president. One of the "Aguda" activists, who was also listening, did what everyone else did —
— he sighed...
The sad matter was rounded off by a well-known Będzin communal worker, who told the following:
A Jewish woman from Będzin — he relates — came to the director of the Realschule to complain: why is her son being tormented with the Jewish religion lesson?...
"To wcale nie jest potrzebne" ["That is not needed at all"] — the lady fumed — what for? Whatever for?
— "Bardzo słusznie" ["Quite right"] — the director answered her — I would exempt him from the lesson of "żydowska religia" [Jewish religion], but with one amendment -- proszę pani [if you please, madam], — one amendment: let him convert, and then he will study with the priest and not with the "żydowski nauczyciel" [Jewish teacher]; but as long as he is still a "Żyd" [Jew] he must learn the Jewish religion, — tak, proszę pani [yes, madam]...
The "pani" had not expected such an answer: the "believing" [?] director himself, of all people, a defender of the Jewish religion? That would sooner have befitted a "rebbe", not a gymnasium director. "Dziwna rzecz" ["A strange thing"]... she muttered to herself as she walked away from the director...

A town of "wonders"..
For several weeks now the honour of the Sosnowiec Jewish community has risen to the "highest" level. It has become popular throughout the Jewish world. I am quite sure that if a Nobel Prize were instituted for the most wondrous town in Poland, the prize would go to — Sosnowiec.
What is there to say — why indeed not? Just show me a second town in Poland where such "miracles" occur as in Sosnowiec! On the contrary, let another town boast of such a miracle, that on Friday night of all times the rabbi's seat in the synagogue should "vanish"! Show me another town where there are as many people "close to the authorities" as in Sosnowiec?... And above all, in what town or shtetl will it happen that a "stróż" [caretaker, watchman] becomes master of the "Talmud Torah" building?
— You don't believe it? Eh?
— A true fact: it happened last week. At the time when the whole community was immersed in the holy struggle to defend the honour of the Torah and of Judaism, at the time when our "fine Jews" are devising plans to issue pamphlets against non-Aguda rabbis, the caretaker of the "Talmud Torah" became a partner in the building...
He, the caretaker that is, did not obtain this by violent means. No — the Talmud Torah gabbaim owe him a debt of several thousand gulden [złoty], and since the gabbaim are busy with "more important" matters, the caretaker's debt went onto the mortgage register. He knows nothing of the system the melamdim have — the well-known hunger system; rather: you don't pay — then I, says he, am a partner...
Well, should not such a town be inscribed for fame and glory?... The wags of the generation say that before long the caretaker will also become first gabbai; only then will it truly be —
— "equal to them all"...

"Yiddishkeit" is growing..
It is a well-known thing that "Israel is not widowed". I say it against what one so often gets to hear about the lamentable state of Jewish affairs: that people are not as pious as they once were, that Yiddishkeit is at its lowest ebb, and so on and so forth.
But as we have already mentioned above, "Israel is not widowed": in the worst of times, when it is already dark enough, a shining star suddenly appears, which drives away the darkness from amid the camp of Israel, and it becomes light.
Such a "star" has risen in Dąbrowa, in the person of the local kehilla president.
The president was revealed, that is, at a meeting of the kehilla board. The meeting dealt with the budget, and since the budget contains the item of the salary for the mara d'atra [the local rabbi], he, the mara d'atra that is, took the trouble and came to the meeting.
But that is not what we are driving at; what matters to us is only the kehilla president's interpellation to the rabbi: why does he sit quietly and permit Yiddish theatre to be played on Friday nights...
When the rabbi answered the new defender of the Jewish religion that "he has no Cossacks" [?], the president gave him a piece of advice: that he, the rabbi, should issue a proclamation by which the minds of the Orthodox Jews of Dąbrowa would be set at rest...
No such proclamation has appeared to this very day, but Orthodoxy in Dąbrowa is already reassured by the fact that Divine Providence has blessed it with such a president, who cares more for the Jewish religion than the Orthodox leaders themselves.

A brother in distress
There is in Będzin a Jewish bank, a big bank indeed, of broad scope, arranged in the European manner, not at all in the Hasidic manner...
Only one "trifle" is not recognised in the bank: the "azov ta'azov" ["you shall surely help him"]... That is a matter — they say there — for other Jewish banks, but not for a place where collection boxes stand for the "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin"...
And merchants come to us and tell:
"In all the banks (non-Jewish ones too) in Będzin the difficult situation of the merchants is taken into consideration, and in order to ease it the bills of exchange are held back until the third day. The only exception in this respect is the 'yarmulke bank', which gives secret circulars to the notaries [rejenci] that on the second day every unpaid bill is to be — protested"...
And this — the merchants cry — is done at a time when blood runs from the merchant's eyes before he can manage to pay the bill at all.
— Write it in the newspaper — they beg — and remark that the bank people interpret "azov ta'azov" according to this gloss: "azov" [?] — "dishen" [Polish dusić, to choke] and "ta'azov" — "udishen" [udusić, to choke to death]...

Permitted and Not Permitted Deeds

(I. "The Jews Have Been Helped." — Those who ride on the horse. — Is everything really permissible?)
The other day a Jew comes into the editorial office — a merry one, a lively one, in high spirits — so that we look at him and wonder: what is the joy, Reb Jew, why does your face shine so with gladness, what salvations and consolations have suddenly come upon the handful of Jews just now, in this bitter time for the community? In answer to our astonished question the lively little Jew gives a snap with his thumb and says: What do you want of me, what am I to tell you — just pop out into the street, into the study-house, into the mikveh, and you will see that "when Adar comes in, joy is increased": Jews are in high spirits, Jews dance and hum themselves a merry tune as never before.
What "the matter is," why all of a sudden, in the middle of everything, it has become so merry in the soul and so good in the heart? "Ah, what a strange Jew you are; it seems you have no sense for Jewishness, it seems you have no God in your heart, and you do not feel the closeness and the warmth that now embrace the handful of true Jews — those who understand how to force their way, with the greatest coarseness and in the most shameless manner, into every corner of Jewish life, those who scramble for the helm and for 'power', paying no heed to the fact that people will not let them cross the threshold, that people cannot bear the sight of them within their four cubits.
What salvations and consolations have come upon the handful of Jews in Poland? It is laughable, upon my life, how you fail to distinguish between good and bad, between the merry and the sad. After all, we have a right; we can decide for ourselves who shall be our representatives, who shall be the delegates of the Jewish representative bodies in Poland. We need not depend on anyone's hand; we can make ourselves such kehillas as we wish to have — a trifle, the virtues of that; a trifle, what that means? We shall be able, of our own free will, to beat and slap one another, to raise bumps on one another and quarrel, and to inform on one another for all the world is worth. Does the whole House of Israel even know how to appreciate this greatness?
And so there is a holiday in the Jewish street; it is joy and gladness. Hardly have we been told the tidings that we may put together election commissions, and already things are lively, people rejoice for all the world is worth. People inform on each other and go through fire; they run to the lord and prove to him that these are harmful elements and those are not loyal citizens, and that the true "Moshkes" [Moshke — the stock name for the squire's house-Jew] are we and none other; and the squire — what can he do, once they come to him and beg him and draw his attention and warn him — he obliges, as the world says: so that one should have no regret over not having gone.
Hardly has a hand yet been dipped in cold water [i.e. nothing has yet been done], there has been no time yet to look around and see where we stand in the world, and see how lively it already is in the Jewish swarm [?], and how all of it is already reflected in the columns of our newspaper. Both in Sosnowiec and in Będzin people have already striven to disqualify and remove the "not loyal citizens" and the "harmful elements," and now they boast that they have free access everywhere, and we are even advised — for the sake of peace, of course — to say nothing at all, for otherwise it will be quite easy to hang a lock on our mouths...
You may say what you will, and we are sure that when outsiders watch what is going on in the Jewish street, they cannot believe that we have other cares, other worries. One cannot believe that here, where there are hungry and unfortunate people, all that should be left standing and people should say: we have more important matters, we have more serious and more painful questions. For it is known that there is nothing stronger than poverty and hunger; we have an old rule that need breaks iron — so how can people from outside believe that among us people go hungry, when there is time and spirit for one to oppress the other, for one to devour the other, for one to bury the other, and that only because Shmerl the strongman wants it so.
When the heart is heavy, when the soul is bitter, one does not want to tear the other out by the root. In a case of poverty and hunger, and when the situation is catastrophic, people unite, huddle together, and each wants to help the other with whatever is in his power, even with a sigh and with a caress and with a heartfelt smile on the lips.
People from outside can in no way whatsoever form any conception of how it can be possible that in moments of hunger and want the unfortunate should be left to languish in the most dangerous conditions, while people look for places in which to pass the time and scheme how one may crawl over the other's head, ride on his shoulders.
Here we are living now in a terribly grave moment; the crisis sinks its dangerous claws ever deeper into the already wounded body; in addition, now, as every year, the time before Passover is considerably harder than the whole year, so that no one knows how Jews will make Passover — and people have turned their backs, as though existence were quite superfluous things, and have taken, with rare intensity, to conducting loathsome "politics" in the most harmful manner.
And here the question arises: can one do this? May one do this? Need one really render no account whatsoever, neither to oneself nor to the community? Is truly no one answerable to anyone? Is there really no limit whatsoever, even when it is a matter of the most important communal affairs, of the grave questions of the people? May one remain, at the people's expense, irresponsible without any limit, without any measure? Must we really carry on our already heavy and aching body all manner of parasites, who foul the air that has been fouled enough until now? Will this body not be crushed by the heavy burden, or will it not prevail with the strength of a new Samson the Mighty and shake off all the ugly parasites that have settled on it in such a dreadful form, in such a loathsome pose?
Is it then possible for a people to find itself constantly in such a terrible situation? Can one then live at all times in internal wars, in internal dissensions and quarrels? Is that called a normal life, a calm and peaceful life, when each only watches for a way to trip the other up so that he may break his neck? And at such moments, under these conditions, can one then help the other not to go under, not to lose the ground from under his feet?
Can we then begin to lead a normal life, when the slightest trifle throws us off balance and parasites and outcasts play first fiddle?
We understand that there are differences of opinion here, parties, tendencies; but in everything there are formulas, principles, permissible and impermissible things. Everything, then, has a limit, and whatever goes beyond the limit is called indecent, and what is not decent is not admitted in social circles.
Among us too a little light must be brought into this field. Life must know how to distinguish [?] decency from hypocrisy. Honest, permissible party activity from irresponsible, lawless deeds which bring the people shame and humiliations.
Social activity in this field must be crystallised, and one must not think that everything is permissible and that lawlessness and irresponsibility can take the seat of honour in party life and party intrigues.
In no parties whatsoever is it permitted that lawless deeds be done, and if this does happen once, the leadership is changed, for it is self-evident that the consequences [?] are borne by the whole party as such.
Possibly it will reach the point of culmination, and the members of this or that party will at long last come to the conviction that they must judge their "comrades," who under the cloak of the party perpetrate unheard-of, irresponsible deeds that are permitted among no people and in no land.
Y. Sh.
A Mistake in the Calendar.

[A little feuilleton.] By “Onkelos”.
Are we really already two weeks past Purim, with the Seder to sit down to before long — or is there a mistake in the calendar?
By all the signs, something here is not quite right.
First of all, the weather.
The frost had broken, the snow had melted, the sun gave a truly[?] spring-like shine — and suddenly an upheaval: a fresh winter has set in, as if nature were teasing us — stoke up the stoves and let us start all over again from Genesis..
And secondly: if it really is already after Purim, why then do we have no Queen Esther?
True, this year there were more Purim balls than in any other year, and for the balls it was announced and advertised that a choice would be made, and indeed they did choose as well, but...
No Queen Esther could be chosen.
What then will you say — that the candidates are to blame? That they are not pretty enough to put on a crown?
Not true: the daughters of Israel are fair, and especially Zagłębie, which is famed throughout the world for its beautiful Jewish daughters; and if not one of them became Queen Esther, it is a sign that it is still before Purim.
True, by other signs one could even conclude that it is actually[?] Passover — in a great many Jewish homes there is no chametz..
But if one is to go by such signs, then by rights today is Yom Kippur, Tisha B'Av or some other kind of fast — are there few Jews fasting?
In short, it is very doubtful whether we really are now between Purim and Passover — the calendar has apparently made a mistake.
Onkelos.
Will There Be War?

[Political feuilleton.] By “Argus”.
And what do you think — will there be a war, or will there not?
At a glance it looks as though we shall no longer escape this horror. It seems that if no commander gives the order to fire, the loaded rifles will go off by themselves, just like a full udder[?]: if nobody comes to milk it, the milk drips out of its own accord.
And indeed, in truth all the objective conditions for a war are there — as they say in that comedy: A crisis in the world — is there one? — There is! A third party who will rub his hands with pleasure — is there one? — There is! His name is America. A hypocritical diplomacy that twists its spodik [fur hat] this way and that, Pinchas-Mendel fashion — is there one? — There is! So what obstacle still remains?
“This crisis” — this very crisis that is raging across the whole world — what kind of factor is it for war? Quite simple: where does the crisis come from? From overproduction. People threw themselves into work, wrought wonders[?] with all the new technical means and poured out production ten times more than the world can use. Today one can already pave the streets and highways not only with potatoes but also with radios and automobiles and aeroplanes and whatever you like. The public cannot take it all off their hands, because first, there is no money to buy with, and second, once a thing is bought and installed, it stands; once it is set going, it goes — and one does not, after all, need a new one every moment.
A war is something else entirely. When all the ploughshares are reforged into[?] swords, and all the automobiles are converted into tanks, and all the machines produce cannons, and all the aeroplanes are filled with bombs, and all the chemical laboratories make poison-gas bombs — then there will never be any overproduction, because all these good things are, after all, presented to the consumer gratis, without a penny, and they have one more quality: they are soon used up, burnt up, and more and more is needed, without end. Does not our sage already say that the grave and one other thing know no satiety..
Well then, is not a war the best remedy against the crisis?
“This hatred” — the hatred between peoples: where does it come from, and how will it lead to a war? Also[?] simple. Once upon a time the peoples hated one another too, but they had no say; the say belonged to the kings and the emperors, who as it happens were fond of one another and even used to marry into each other's families. The German court with the Russian and the English, with the smaller little courts and the back-courts, were all buttoned together, dear friends and beloved. Kolya, Willy and George [Nicholas II, Wilhelm II, George V] used to correspond on first-name terms with their pet names, used to carouse[?] together over wine and women, and between one little schnapps and the next a little treaty would meanwhile be signed — and so peace was made firm.
Today, for our many sins, we have democracy. This democracy, of which we thought that “in its shadow we shall live among the nations”, has led us badly astray. The say does indeed, supposedly, belong to the peoples, but those who have the say are the party fixers, the leaders and helmsmen[?], who are never secure in the saddle, since they were not appointed by the grace of the Most High, like the emperors, but elected by the people, and are forever afraid that they may fall out of favour; so they must keep stroking and tickling the people with chauvinist delusions and patriotic fantasies, inciting and fanning the hatred against the neighbouring peoples. Through this incitement there floated to the surface Treviranus and Brüning and Hitler, and thus in every people and every country the hatred grows ever more dogged. And international little matches and love affairs with weddings there are none; instead there has arisen a Geneva with dry sermons that have been repeating themselves for 12 years now and have become sickening to listen to. So how should a war not burst out of such hatred?
“This America” — what role will she play in the coming war? The same as in the previous one. First of all she will be rid of a million unemployed: she will ship them off to Europe and lay them down there on the battlefields, from which they will rise only at the resurrection of the dead, when the Messiah comes. After that she, [—], will become the supplier of instruments of death to all the fighting sides, who this time will no longer pay in gold, because they have none left, but will sell themselves to her as bondsmen for long years, as the Egyptians once did to Joseph. Well, she will stand aside and rub her hands with pleasure.
So, since all the conditions are there, why indeed should a war not break out?
Nevertheless I must confess that I am, after all, no great believer in war — for whom does it pay? For the press what pays is rather the eve-of-war commotion, which raises the circulation; but as soon as the first shot is fired, censorship is introduced and that is the end of all sensations. The diplomats, too, are bigwigs only until the first shot, when the whole say passes to the commander, and yesterday's deputy must, poor fellow, put on a uniform, shoulder a rifle and go to the front.
The people itself, then? Tell me, pray: what difference does it make to it whether it dies of hunger or dies of a bullet? So why should it go looking for death in distant fields and desolate forests, when it has it at home?
I am afraid that the whole commotion around the approaching war is merely a kind of trick[?], meant to divert the people's attention from the troubles that torment it. Let it know that things can be still worse, and let it praise and thank its leaders, who guard it from all evil[?].
So let us indeed praise and give thanks — but there is no need to be afraid.
Argus.
The Government's Duties towards the Jewish Minority.

By Deputy Dr. H. Rosmarin [Henryk Rosmarin].
The Polish government is going through very great difficulties over the question of the minorities in the state. An unsolved problem, which is a domestic one, but which also has an international character.
There is — it seems — not a single serious and honest Pole in the country to whom it is not clear that Jews are loyal citizens of the country, that Jews are adherents and faithful citizens of the Polish state, that Jews have never been anti-state, and that the Jews in Poland are not irredentist.
It is known, and people are aware, what the Jews demand of the government and the state. Their demands are that the conditions for living be created for Jews, and that obstacles not be put in their[?] way at every step.
The Jewish population demands for itself the necessary cultural, national and economic conditions which every people so needs in order to sustain itself.
It would therefore be entirely logical and just if the authoritative government circles, in whose hands the solution of this question lies, were earnestly to set about regulating and settling at least the most justified postulates of the Jewish population.
But what do we see?
We see the exact reverse, the opposite of what needs to be done. Instead of taking a number of our needs into consideration, instead of taking an honest and serious interest in Jewish national and cultural life and raising up and supporting the most successful[?] force of the economy, the Jews are met with a harsh practice of life, and the ruin of tens and hundreds of thousands of Jewish livelihoods, which struggle hard and honestly for their daily needs and cannot attain them — leads to their pauperization.
More than once I have put the question to myself:
“Why does it come to this?”
In a country of thirty million inhabitants there is not to be found one government with an honest and serious will to solve the so important tasks of the eleven-percent Jewish fellow-citizenry[?].
The Jews in this country — and, for that matter, throughout the world — are recognized by all as capable people, as intelligent and, moreover, state-building.
As long as men with “purely antisemitic tendencies” stood at the helm of the government, all this could still be understood.
But today?
Today, when the direction of the government lies in the hands of men who in their programme have — officially[?] — eliminated[?], peeled away and cut out antisemitism with all its tendencies — with this government it can no longer be understood.
I myself have more than once, during Sejm debates, drawn the government's attention to it — to the strong agitation and despair that prevail among the Jewish population — pointing out that, through the sharpness of the crisis, the Jewish problem has assumed so great and broad a scope that it has entirely ceased to be a Jewish problem, and the government, whether it wants to or not, must think of doing something in this so painful question and bringing it to its solution; for when the three-million-strong Jewish population in the state does not have the possibility of living and cannot exist in the country — that cannot remain without harm to the state itself.
In spite of this the state goes on keeping silent about it, and nothing is being done.
It seems to me that those Jewish politicians are also to blame for this who, through their own “ambition”, have placed themselves in the ranks of those who have always and everywhere had to[?] “clap bravo”[?] and who are eternally faithful servants of the government. Not only do they fail to point out to the government the errors which the government makes and commits, but in the eyes of the whole world, too, they count as proof that the Jewish question in Poland is being treated honestly and well — although the government has not yet done anything substantial to ease the so difficult situation of the Jews in the country.
The conditions in our state as regards the participation of Jews in non-Jewish parties cannot be compared with the conditions in the Western countries — or indeed in America, where equal rights for Jews exist in truth and in the full sense of the word and are carried out in life.
With us, however, when the whole tax system[?] is turned entirely against Jews, when tens of thousands of Jewish workers are thrown out of the state monopolies, when there can be no talk at all of admitting a Jewish official to an office, when etatism contributes to the ruin[?] of thousands of individuals in the Jewish economy, when nothing is allotted for Jewish schools out of the money of Jewish taxpayers, when the Jewish “opieka społeczna” [social welfare] enjoys no state aid whatsoever from the state funds, when a boycott of Jewish labour prevails in the state institutions, and the like — then the role of certain Jewish politicians, who sit there in the government majority and have neither the courage, nor the strength, nor the will to change all the above-mentioned faults for the benefit of the Jews and the Jewish population — is, without question, for every objective person, harmful, and not at all to be forgiven or justified...
The Jewish question awaits its solution!
On the Threshold of New Elections

So we now have, it seems, an officially fixed date for new elections to the kehilla.
I believe that Jewish Zagłębie breathed more freely at the knowledge that at last a day is coming when it may perhaps be possible to change, to improve, to make healthier and more useful the institution which ought to and can play so serious, deep, great and creative a role in our grey and helpless Jewish life.
Bad, short-sighted and fanatical [?] people have by their deeds made this sort of thing [?], a "Jewish kehilla", loathsome in the eyes of the greater part of the Jewish population. And from this stems the antipathy, the failure to appreciate the importance of this institution. Instead of its being a fortress for organised Jewish communal life in general, people want, try, strive to turn the kehilla into the fortress of one group, or even of a single kloyz [small Hasidic prayer-house], and with all that they are still so incautious that they do not act as, for example, in Frankfurt, where separate sides create separate kehillas for themselves, but want to raise revenues from everyone in order to satisfy the needs of one part, and the smaller part, of the Jewish population. We have no illusions. The present kehilla statute ["ustav", Pol. ustawa] is like a bed of Sodom for Jewish life. Jewish life is far too broad, branching [?] and colourful for the present kehilla to be able to become the base, the root, from which many-sided Jewish life could draw spiritual and material nourishment. The present kehillas must strive and fight — by these or other means — for a widening of their competence. Such a fight must end in victory, for life itself is here the best and strongest helper. The present kehillas are the crooked mirror of Jewish life; the present kehillas deny the facts of Jewish life, and one need not get very excited when the conservative part of Jewish society joins in this denial, wants to put up walls as thick as possible to divide the kehilla from the great and hard Jewish life. Such is the fate, the task and the practice of the conservative elements among all peoples, and here we are no "Thou hast chosen us". The conservative element does not reckon with life and pretends not to see [?], even when with him, under his very eyes, within his own four cubits, things happen quite differently from what he thinks, even when his own children walk in other ways. And when such a conservative suddenly catches sight of what is going on around him — it is a catastrophe for him and he then resigns himself completely. The task of the healthy, creative part of the Jewish population is to create for itself such forms of communal life that the most varied needs of the Jewish population can be satisfied in the best possible way; this element must seek to fill the kehilla with living content, and this can to a certain degree be achieved even in the present kehilla — if there sit in it people who mean to serve the Jewish collective faithfully and honestly.
In the year 1924 people here treated the kehilla elections too lightly, indeed with downright disdain. And that is why it was possible that out of 30 dozors [kehilla board members] the town should know no more than 5–6 names. The rest hardly knew themselves that they were dozors. The greater part of the dozors were, after all, communal illiterates, and a large part of them are people who cannot have an opinion of their own, who cannot even act in accord with their conscience, because they are materially dependent people and must therefore act as someone tells them to.
And these factors were a particular source of misfortune for our kehilla.
Practice has shown that mere "wild" lists must have no place in the new elections.
Programmes, and people who have shown by their past that communal work is for them a service [?] for its own sake — this must be the fundamental foundation on which the parties and sides approach the election campaign for new leading bodies of our kehilla.
May the 7 hard and great [?] years of activity [?] of the last Zagłębie kehillas not go to waste; may Jewish Zagłębie not have to suffer several more years on account of disdain or negligence on the part of the leading and very healthiest [?] Jewish circles, in whose hands there now lies the fate of the coming election struggle, of the future kehilla.
Y. N—m.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah Sayings, Remarks and Anecdotes on This Week's Portion, Collected and Styled by Y. Y. — Parshat Vayakhel-Pekudei

[Religious column / divrei Torah — Parshat Vayakhel-Pekudei.] Collected and styled by Y. Y.

a) "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel" (Exodus 35:1).
"On the morrow of Yom Kippur" — Rashi.
Only on the morning after Yom Kippur, when all Jews become pious and good for a day, did Moses succeed in gathering all the Jews together. Moses seized upon the morrow of Yom Kippur, because one day later he would no longer have managed it.

b) "And the men came upon [i.e. after] the women" (35:22).
The women came first and only afterwards did the men arrive; for only the men had been asked [to give] for the Tabernacle, and since the women had not been told to bring anything at all, they came the first... The men, on the other hand, being obliged to bring donations, were lazy about it.
— "Imrei Shefer".
—o—
They had to bring the men along, because from the women alone nothing would have been accepted — lest it had been pilfered without the husband's knowledge...
— "Tiferet Yehonatan".
—o—
Ordinarily, when a collection is made for a public cause, everyone wants to be the last: perhaps by the time it comes to him it will no longer be needed... Here, at the Tabernacle, they jostled one another, "the men upon the women", for fear that it might no longer be needed and he would have no share in the holy thing...
— "Ohel Yaakov".

c) "And every wise-hearted woman spun with her hands, and they brought" (35:25–26).
Of the first, the wise-hearted, it is said "and they brought": they spun and gave it away to the Tabernacle. But of those "whose heart lifted them up" — the grand madams — only "they spun" is mentioned, and not "they brought": they did indeed spin, but adorned only their own homes with it...
— "Maadanei Melech".
—o—
Of the wise-hearted it is enumerated that they brought blue, purple and costly valuables. But as for those "whose heart lifted them up" — those who puffed themselves up and boasted that they would bring wonders upon wonders for the Tabernacle — it all ended with "matveh izim" [spun goats' yarn]: with goat hair...
— Rav Moshe Hefetz.

d) "And they brought a free-will offering in the morning" (36:3).
What could the poor workmen who laboured on the Tabernacle bring as a donation? — "In the morning, in the morning": the overtime hours; they came to work earlier, before working hours — that was their donation.
— "Baruch Taam".

e) "Altar" (37:25).
The Gemara says that when a man divorces his first wife, the altar sheds tears over him.
On account of this Gemara a man who had divorced his wife was reproached. He answered: Rather than that I should shed tears, better let the altar do it...
— A folk saying.

f) "The Tabernacle of the Testimony" (38:21).
According to the homiletic reading: the Tabernacle is a testimony that the sin of the Calf was forgiven them. With the Calf, out of money and jewellery beyond measure there leapt a little calf, whereas with the Tabernacle everything tallied. "These are the accounts of the Tabernacle" — a sign that they had already become better, since nothing was missing from the reckoning.
— "Asam Bosem" [?].
—o—
In Brisk [Brześć] there is a custom that in the study-house an eternal lamp burns for the soul of Rabbi Meir Baal HaNes, and beside it hangs a collection-box for dropping in money to buy oil for the burning. It so happened that the shammes [beadle] was caught smearing his shoes with the eternal-lamp oil. An outcry went up: How can it be — to polish shoes with eternal-lamp oil?
— Calm yourselves — answers the shammes — the shoes are holy too: they come from eternal-lamp money (which he had likewise "lifted" from the box)...
— "Nachalei Dvash".

g) "Which was counted at the command of Moses" (38:21).
Not Moses alone drew up the account, but others, at his demand; even Moses, too, wished to have a check upon himself.
— Midrash Rabbah.

h) "And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it as the Lord had commanded" (39:43).
— Like the man who wants to look into his guest's valise to see whether he has not "lifted" something from the house, and says to him: Do look in your valise, perhaps you are missing something... Moses did likewise: he took bookkeepers to draw up an account of whether he, Moses, had handed everything over in order; but what he was really after was whether the Jews had done it in order. He ordered that he himself be audited, but his aim was a different one... "And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it as the Lord had commanded."
— The Maggid of Dubno.

i) "The people bring much more than enough for the service" (36:5).
When the people sees that its communal providers work and act, it does not begrudge any donations; so much so that it had to be proclaimed: "Do no more work."
— "Yalkut Peninim".

j) "And everyone whose spirit made him willing brought it" (35:21).
An urge to give often seizes everyone, but it does not get as far as the deed. When it comes to the giving, the urge cools. That is what the verse means: "And everyone whose spirit made him willing — brought it": he whom the urge to give had seized did in fact give as well...
— "Nachal Kedumim".
What Various Countries Want to Sell

From our special correspondent at the Leipzig Fair, Z. Haber.
At a time of economic decline that has no equal in the economic history of the entire world, it is clear that all the industries of the whole world are adopting every kind of means in order to sell whatever can possibly be sold, and in this way to create opportunities for work and opportunities for earnings for themselves and for the workers.
It is therefore no wonder that precisely the present Leipzig Fair was so strongly represented, with exhibitors from 24 countries. Moreover, most countries had their own state exhibitions, which embraced all the products the country brings forth and all the articles that are made in the country. In this way one could get an overview of everything the country possesses and wants to sell in the various countries, from which roughly two hundred thousand merchants had come here.
It was therefore quite interesting to observe what the individual countries manufacture and with what they want to conquer the world market for themselves.
We do not want to dwell on Germany, which was, of course, the strongest group, the one that dominated the Leipzig Fair. German industry and German technology are so great that no picture of them can be given in a short article. Beginning with a needle and up to the largest railway carriage in the whole world, everything was present here that the “human mind could possibly devise.
Austria had 250 exhibitors, who represented the fine Austrian art industry. Leather goods, knitwear, bronzes, porcelain and other objects were shown which are manufactured in such fine execution only in Austria, since[?] for hundreds of years the Viennese-Austrian artistic taste has been known throughout the world.
Czechoslovakia: for the most part one saw glass and porcelain and, above all, the imitation jewellery made in Gablonz [Jablonec] in Czechoslovakia, which finds favour throughout the world and has no equal anywhere. In addition one also saw the Czech “heavy machinery industry”, which, however, has to this day not been able to take up competition with Germany, England and America.
France: for the greater part the country exhibited perfumes, fashion articles and, above all, silk fabrics in such colours and fine workmanship that they were truly captivating. One did not need to know that this was a French exhibition; it was enough to glance at the fine products on display to recognise already from afar that it was France exhibiting.
The exact opposite was the English exhibition. Massive products both from England proper and from its colonies and dominions were there: fabrics, hats, linen, leather, shoes and, above all, the treasures of the earth from almost the four corners of the world, wherever England extends.
Italy brought to the market fine art objects of leather, wood, stone and metal. The works have an Italian note of their own, which shows that the country has great taste and occupies a handsome place in the world of commerce.
A tremendous development has been undergone by Japan in the last ten years. It appears that the Japanese want to conquer the entire business world by every means. Not only — as hitherto — in the wood, porcelain and glass industry are the Japanese today almost the best and cheapest producers; in leather, stone, metal, precious metal and the like, too, Japan has begun to compete strongly with world industry, and, as has now been seen at the Leipzig Fair, it will not be long before Japan dominates the whole world market and pushes out the “white race” with its technology and industry, which was built up with so much toil and effort over the last hundreds of years. Here in Leipzig one could observe clearly and distinctly that Japan is capable of becoming the greatest competitor in the whole world.
Poland: Poland put on quite a handsome exhibition. Not to speak of the products with which the country is blessed by nature and which form a strong source of income in the Polish economy — Polish industry too has recently developed so strongly that Poland is beginning to become an important competitor with which one must reckon already today. Polish glass, cement, wood, coal and sugar have long had a handsome place in the world, but now it was seen in Leipzig that Polish fabrics, metal goods, spirit and chemical products are taking on forms which will soon make it so that Poland will have to be reckoned with in the entire business world.
Switzerland and the Scandinavian countries, Norway, Denmark and Finland, were also represented in Leipzig with their products: chocolates, tinned fish, wood and enamel are important products which these countries want to export, and one may reckon that in time they will oust[?] in this field their greatest competitors: Portugal and Spain.
The present great world fair in Leipzig showed clearly with which products the various states want to conquer their positions in order to improve the lot of their countrymen.
Whether they will succeed in this will become apparent within a short time. The opinion of the leading economic statesmen who gathered at the Leipzig Fair was a more optimistic one; almost all were agreed that we have already come through the hardest period of the economic crisis.
Court of Appeal Annuls the Verdict of the Sosnowiec District Court

As is known, the former deputy Kwapiński was sentenced by the Sosnowiec District Court to one year in a fortress for a speech which he delivered at a rally in Olkusz on the first of December 1929.
The convicted man lodged an appeal with the Court of Appeal in Warsaw, where the trial took place on Friday evening. As defence counsel — the same as at the first trial in Sosnowiec.
After the reading of the indictment, Kwapiński makes the following statement:
I do not acknowledge myself guilty. For a man such as I, who has spent so many years in prison, a year of prison does not play any great role; but if I have appealed against the Sosnowiec verdict, it is because I was sentenced though innocent.
After the speeches of the defence counsel, the presiding judge reads out the verdict, according to which the verdict of the Sosnowiec District Court is annulled and the accused is acquitted entirely.

A Good Mother-in-Law… (From the Local Tales)

[Feuilleton — from the local tales.] Signed: "Yankele".

As against what you say — a bad mother-in-law, a wicked mother-in-law — one ought rather to be guarded from good mothers-in-law.

But don't take my word for it; just listen to a story that happened in a very refined and respected merchant family.

There was an only son there; he was taken into the army and sent off to Galicia to do his military service there. It was in the year 1925. A lad who was used to being looked after[?] and provided for at home did not feel any too well in the military barracks in the small Galician town, and he thought that the world was coming to an end for him, that it would go on like this for an eternity. He was therefore happy when he somehow became acquainted with an important[?] Jewish householder; in his free hours he began to drop in[?] there. On the Sabbath they would invite him to eat, and he got the illusion of a bit of home. The Galician had a practical calculation in this: his maiden daughter, still of the pre-war calendar, already had to go to the wedding canopy. And how is she to blame that Franz Yosele [Emperor Franz Joseph] killed off in the war so many menfolk[?] of his "beloved subjects"?

And they brought the rabbi with a minyan of Jews into the house and led him under a wedding canopy — after all, it is still better than doing "padni"[?], "powstan!" [the Polish drill commands padnij! powstań! — "Down! Up!"] a second time.

In short, our young man got married, with good luck, and got a Galician Jewess, a Cossack. Before long a little Cossack was born, and when Leybele got his discharge and could already travel back home as a "civilian", his missus had already deigned[?] to whisper in his ear that things already stood at the second "little Cossack".

Like someone awakened from a dream was our Leybele when the train carried him back home to Sosnowiec. So that means he is free again; again he will meet with friends and acquaintances; again the old, sweet, good life! But what has happened to him? He has somehow got married, has a wife with a child, and it even seems already with two children — how did that come about? Is it not perhaps[?] a dream? But no, it is the truth: the fat Galician Jewess warned him that for God's sake he should come back in eight days' time, otherwise she will come to him in Sosnowiec.

A mixture of sorrow and fright took hold of him; he wanted it all to be a lie, and yet it is a sad and bitter truth. At home he confided the secret only to his mother; he was afraid to tell his father. Several weeks went by; he did not write a word to his missus, did not even inquire whether she had come safely through the birth — he made himself forget. In Galicia, however, they did not forget him, and one morning, all of a sudden, the door opened and a Cossack of a Jewess appeared. One child she had left at home, and the second child she had brought with her. The young fellow ran away from home — so his mother had taught him, so his mother had told him to behave; but she herself, the mother, received her daughter-in-law with outstretched arms.

— Ah, my dear daughter-in-law! My beloved child!

The mother-in-law fussed over the daughter-in-law and [—?] her, did not let a speck of dust fall on her, gave her a separate room and cared for her as for a treasure. Only she did not let her go out into the street, enjoining her that for God's sake she should not tell anyone a word.

Several weeks went by, the "bird" did not show himself, and the daughter-in-law wrote a letter home to her father: that she has a mother-in-law — a veritable angel — but the husband is a scoundrel. The mother-in-law saw to the letter at the post. Only instead of dropping the letter into the post box, the mother-in-law let it slide into her own pocket and herself wrote an answer in the father's name. In the letter the father supposedly declared that at home they miss her badly, that they are uneasy that she is not coming back, that the father now has colossal business dealings, that he has also won 10,000 dollars on the "dolarówka" [the state dollar premium-bond lottery], and that if they are being difficult with her, she should not let anyone spit in her porridge and should come home at once.

Thus the mother-in-law carried the daughter-in-law's letters supposedly to the post and brought letters supposedly from her daughter-in-law's father. Such a radiant and refined mother-in-law aroused the greatest trust in the Galician woman. More than once the mother-in-law shed tears together with the daughter-in-law over the depraved[?] son. And once the mother-in-law brought a letter from the post; in the letter the father positively begs for mercy that the daughter should come home as quickly as possible. He writes to her again about his wealth and sends her 50 dollars for trifles; he also writes that the child she left at home longs for its mother and is all but falling ill from longing — so she should write her husband off and come home. In that letter there lay another 50 dollars and a fine[?] silk shawl as a gift.

Little by little, with her sweet little talks and sayings, with her tears and sweetness, the good mother-in-law led the daughter-in-law into the rabbinate — and there a bill of divorce was written.

The mother-in-law took a warm leave of her former daughter-in-law, saw her off to the train, wished her much happiness, kissed her heartily and assured her that, since her father had become so rich, only now would she meet her true destined match.

Coming home to Galicia, however, she found her old poor home and an old, broken father, who explained to her that it was not he who had longed for her so much, not he who had become rich, not he who had sent dollars or any gifts — he had not even written a letter. It had all been a trick of the good mother-in-law, who in this way had won her daughter-in-law's trust in order to bring her to a divorce..

——

As against what you say: bad mothers-in-law.

God protect us from good mothers-in-law; from the wicked ones we will guard ourselves.

Yankele.

On patents [trade licences] for artisans
The tax authorities throughout Poland have until now held the position that artisans must purchase patents if they employ at least two persons in their workshops, regardless of whether these are the owners themselves, members of their families or hired journeymen.
This position has been recognised by the Supreme Court as incorrect. In No. [?] 160—30 the ruling of the Supreme Court recognised that, in determining whether the artisan is obliged to purchase a patent, only hired workers or journeymen are to be taken into account, and not partners or their family members.
Thus even a larger number of persons may work without a patent, if they are partners in the workshop and employ no more than one hired worker.

International Swindler(s) Fall into the Hands of the Police.
In the first days of the month of March an unknown woman came to the flat of a certain engineer in Königshütte and asked for employment. As it happened, the engineer's wife needed a servant and hired the woman, who had a document stating that her name was Tekla[?] Pawlik.
The new[?] servant fulfilled her duties properly, and her employers were satisfied.
Last Saturday the servant went out for a walk and did not come back. Together with her various objects and clothes worth 12,000 złoty also disappeared.
The police in Königshütte energetically set about searching for the thief, and after an understanding with the investigation police in Sosnowiec a gang of thieves was arrested, among them also the servant. It turned out that with the help of false papers[?] she had committed a series of thefts in Kraków, Krynica, Zakopane and other places. In fact she comes from Yugoslavia and is known as an international swindler.
The whole company was put into the Königshütte prison.

A Fast on Account of the Desecration of a Torah Scroll.
The local rabbi, may he live long, decreed a fast for the Jewish population in Zagórze on account of the desecration of a Torah scroll which happened there. The fast took place on Wednesday, the eve of Rosh Chodesh Nisan. Those who had direct knowledge [of the deed] had to fast a whole day, and the innocent half a day.
It is interesting to note that the fast was proclaimed only thanks to the local president of the kehilla board, Mr. Mitelman, because the "Menora" had other matters to attend to.
