Where Are They Leading Us?

[Article — Jewish society and politics; fragmented lists, Olkusz, leadership.]
(Progress and going backwards. — What will come of it? — Where is the way out?)

Among the nations of the world we have been crowned [?] since ancient times as a people of unity and concord. How many times do we have the chance to hear from our neighbours that we are united and that among us peace and tranquillity reign in every field, wherever we may turn. With our unity we have been [boasting?] for hundreds of years throughout the whole world, and actually it is a riddle where such a lie came from, who invented about us something that never was, something that never found any place among us?

That quarrels and splits have at all times occupied among us a very honoured place, and perhaps the most honoured, we know from history, from ancient history, from the past and from the present. We therefore know it very well ourselves, and one need not justify it, one need not strain oneself to prove it plainly; the only question is why the world says that the Jews are a united people, a people for whom unity is the creed ("ani maamin"), the principle of principles, whereas we are exactly the opposite: not only can we not maintain unity, but quarrels always and everywhere take the upper hand.

We know this very well, and therefore we have no complaints about these undesirable deeds, about these disturbances and obstacles that are brought into our camp.

In our view, what is worse is that in this field we have not stood still in one place; rather we keep "progressing", we march forward with giant strides. Yesterday, for example, something happened that today we would by no means have believed, and tomorrow they will undertake among us to carry out an even greater fragmentation, so that we are travelling the road of the unbelievable, the road of fantastic, legendary "achievements" [?].

Now things have reached such a level that one cannot even form an idea of how any common public activity whatsoever could be carried out, any political action whatsoever that would have prospects of improving our situation.

Here we see a trifle, and perhaps even a downright foolishness, and yet how much can be learned from all these foolishnesses and trifles, if we would analyse them psychologically, if we would pause over them and consider them?

Last Sunday elections to the town council took place in a small neighbouring town called Olkusz, and it is interesting that, with a minimal number of Jewish voters and a larger number of Christian voters, the Christians came forward with 5 lists, and the Jews — the united ones, the ones of unity, of course — poor things, could not manage more than 7 lists.

The failure of such fragmentation is of course a self-evident "thing" to everyone; any political novice knows with what a "gigantic" force one goes into elections with such 7 lists, and what they can give the Jewish economy. But it is impossible to understand how such a little town could, with all efforts, produce 7 lists — it can only be that every family had its own list, its followers, its sympathisers, and every more important, larger firm presumably [?] wanted to have its own representative, its own delegate on the town council; otherwise it is not possible, it is simply impossible, that a town like Olkusz should go to the polls with 7 social-political lists. Be that as it may, it is easy to imagine the gain from such fragmentation, the gain from such crumbling and chopping into tiny little pieces [?].

In the past it did not come to such surprises; formerly there was a certain limit, a certain order, a certain arrangement and system, which served as a guide and taught in what manner one should approach responsible public activity. Now one no longer needs such "foolishnesses", now one no longer plays with such "trifles" — now, for our many sins, who is not a politician, and which boy is not versed in these matters, and who does not make himself, thanks to an implanted "consciousness", ridiculous to the point of astonishment?

And when we take a look backwards [?], when we begin to draw a parallel between the whole past and today's present, our hearts grow gloomy as we see who our representatives in this or that institution were, and what kind of persons represent them now.

When we give ourselves such an accounting, when we begin to consider and analyse it soberly, we come to the conviction that we have set off on a long road backwards, that we are going back into a disgusting swamp into which we are no longer accustomed to set our feet; we no longer even wish to wash our hands of the filth and the ignorance.

Let us, for example, compare — in whatever town it may be and whatever institution we may speak of — the representatives of 10–15 years ago with the present ones; only then will we see what kind of face we have and who our representatives are.

It is a pain and a grief when one must speak of this at length, when one must prove that the representatives do not stand at the proper height, that they stand much, much lower than the proper height. But what can one do, when one must say it, when one must prove it — and if we do not tell it to ourselves, others will tell it to us, and then, then woe and alas, and shame covers our face.

Can we then compare those representatives, who had so much understanding and intelligence and awareness for their idealistic activity, with those who have now seized the helm in such a lawless manner? By how many heads did the former stand above [?] their present-day colleagues? After all, there was then a certain line and a system, and above all responsibility for the community, responsibility for deeds, responsibility for the interests of the people; whereas now everything has been forgotten, now one wants to act and not to know [?], now one scrambles up onto the bench in the crudest manner and takes nothing and no one into account — and therefore this is how we look, and therefore, so to speak, the people stands with its representatives, with its delegates, and therefore indeed fewer and fewer go to the elections, and therefore interest is weaker, colder, more indifferent.

Grown-up people, mature and intelligent people, when they see that the great, beautiful social ideal has been exchanged for a toy, have turned away from it; they are already past the age when they could take pleasure in playing with toys.

Among us things go steadily downhill. Those who deserve trust, those who are capable of representing, wished to spare their personal dignity and stepped aside so that they should not be seen [?] — and this is so in all trends and currents, in all parties and associations — and their place has been grabbed, with the speed of cinematographic shots, by people in whom there is neither trust nor responsibility, who have no merits.

Can this go on like this? Can we keep going along this road, which gives us nothing but shame and demoralises the coming generation? Must one really give no thought to this worst social problem, which in many countries has brought mankind to the very happiest condition? Can all this not be changed among us too, for the benefit of our national and economic interests?

If we look around us, if we search and rummage and try to wipe out all our shortcomings, we will be able to attain that which we need so badly. We must not allow our beautiful, lofty ideal aspirations to be exchanged for petty games, and when we understand their true meaning, we will then know that in their place we must seat conscious people, idealistic people, who will know how to defend their and our national interests.

— This is what we must now remember, and in this direction our demands must be turned.

True, we have crawled too deep into the abyss of darkness; too conspicuously do ignorance and boundless, wild lawlessness stick out among all strata of the population; too far and too conspicuously [?] has the people been dragged into the deepest depths, to the edge of the abyss; and yet, despite all this, regardless of the fact that [at times?] one becomes so coarse that one loses the image of God, one still wants to tear oneself free of the slave spirit and, rubbing one's eyes as after a long lethargic sleep, to ask, as in a dream, a question: where are we going? Where are they leading us, where are they dragging the people?

Dr. Pafuri [?].
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — satirical round-up; Sosnowiec, Koziegłowy, Pilica, Niwka.]
(A "darkness"[?] in Sosnowiec. — "Fine Jews" speak the same language as Lenin's comrade. — A revolution in Koziegłowy. — The "Torah-loyal"[?] youth wages war against a rabbi. — A tragi-comedy[?] in Niwka[?]. — Because of a wedding ring the "domestic peace" of a young couple was destroyed)

On receiving the report from our good-hearted town of Sosnowiec, I understood for the first time the true meaning of the saying "What reason will not do, time will do" — what reason, logic, cannot do is done just the same by time.

For instance, could any of us have imagined that a time would come when our "fine Jews", those who "guard the honour of Torah and faith", would speak the same language, use the same words as the radical young fellows straight out of Lenin's cheder... those who fight for "freedom", for "light"?... — Householders from Sosnowiec and "vicinity" have come and raised a "cry of woe" over the great darkness in which the Jewish kehilla of Sosnowiec is sunk.

Here we read it in black and white: "A group of dark personages, that dark clique, has organised a bojówka [strong-arm squad] of well-known[?] dark intriguers, who with their black hands informed on the honoured Sosnowiec rabbi, may he live long. An end must come, no more riding[?] on the kehilla nag, etc...."

Ha?! What do you say to such darkness? The "Bund" will surely triumph on hearing that "fine Jews" are fighting, like itself, against darkness, against dark cliques, dark personages, and above all — an end to the kehilla nag!...

That is why we really say that what one cannot grasp with our reason, time proves. Yes, a time of "popular awakening" has come, when "respectable householders from Sosnowiec and vicinity" take up a fight against the "darkness" reigning in the Jewish street...

———

In Koziegłowy darkness reigns; the air there smells of gunpowder and, according to our correspondent's description, "the little town will have long, long to sing and tell of it..."

There too, in Koziegłowy, a rebellion has broken out against the old order, against the "empire"...

And the revolution was called forth by none other than the members of "Tse'irei Emunei [Yisrael]" against their chairman. The latter, seeing that his life was threatened, did as Wilhelm did in his day — abdicated; but quietly he held[?] secret consultations with his loyal subjects and courtiers, and it was decided to attack the revolutionary camp.

The offensive failed; the abdicated chairman very nearly fell alive into the hands of the revolutionaries, and only by a miracle did he manage to retreat with his army.

As this issue went to press we received official information that "the abdicated one is gathering fresh forces, and it is planned that in spring the cannons in Koziegłowy shall find their tongue"...

———

The "holy war" too, which has been waged for several years in Pilica, is taking on other forms, more real, more tangible. Until now the local "Aguda" was active only in breaking up the rabbi's seat in the synagogue, informing on him to the authorities, persecuting him with lawsuits and the like.

But when all these "fine deeds" do not bring the desired result — the rabbi will not leave the Pilica rabbinical throne; on the contrary, the neutral ones" are even becoming the rabbi's supporters — the local "Aguda" concluded that the methods of struggle must be intensified and victory over the rabbi must come...

To this end, under the well-known slogan "save Jewishness and the honour of the Torah" — the stronger part of the town was mobilised; taken into the gang were those who possess nine measures of insolence, those who know how to "honour" an opponent with a "gift of the hand" [a slap], and
— off they went to battle...

When the rabbi enters the beit midrash, the bimah immediately fills with Hasidic lads, and after tucking their sidelocks behind their ears they set about the "commanded war": first the rabbi is insulted with the worst insults, and then they start throwing bottles at those who cannot tolerate the lawlessness of the Agudist bojówka...

As our correspondent reports, the new battle system has worked splendidly, for the "strong hand" drove the quiet public together with the rabbi out of the beit midrash, and the "bojówka men" finally had the chance to install their moreh hora'ah [religious decisor] with the bent[?] hat — in the rabbi's position in the beit midrash...

———

What happened in Niwka will "surely [ draw tears from our readers". A trifle! In our present times "a young wife has been left without a ring and a young husband without a wife"...

Because of the great sorrow "which we share", we cannot tell this "heart-rending story"; we simply pass on our correspondent's words.

Here is what he writes:

"Three weeks ago a young man from Niwka married a girl from Kromołów. Before leaving for the wedding the groom remembered that he had forgotten to buy a wedding ring, so the groom's brother ran to the jeweller P. and took a ring from him, promising to pay after the wedding.

When several weeks had passed and the jeweller demanded payment for the ring, the young fellow[?], the former groom, took the ring from his young wife and sent it back to the jeweller.

When the Niwka public learned of it, a storm broke out in the beit midrash: 'Has such a thing ever been heard?' — protests were heard: the young man may not live with his wife 'under one roof'...

The young man immediately sent to the jeweller to give back the returned ring, but the jeweller declared that the ring had been sold only the day before to a shikse [gentile girl], who 'took it shelagbi'[?]..."

— — — — — —

In the epilogue of the tragedy it is "played out" how "the young man was left without a wife and the wife — without a ring"...

Ben-A[—]
Permitted and Forbidden Deeds.

[Będzin — kehilla and elections; editorial.] (The scholar with his logical questions. Who is responsible for the community? This way or that.)
And another Jew took the trouble to come to us at the editorial office, and he was no longer at all as cheerful and in as good a mood as the first one, who was beside himself with joy. In this Jew's features one could already see the Jewish suffering and deep grief, the tremendous disappointment and bitterness. We are dealing here with a man who is at his wits' end, who can in no way understand that lawlessness and boorishness should really have already reached the level that shows itself before his eyes. Something does not sit right with him; it seems to him that he cannot believe all that his eyes see.
The Jew, who is incidentally a Talmudic scholar, begins to speak from the heart, and he wants nothing else but that we should give him an answer to his logical questions. You know me already, it seems, for so and so long, so many and so many years — have you ever heard that I did anything bad, or, God forbid, ever spied on anyone or intrigued? On the contrary, you know me; say what you have to object to in me. And since you know of nothing — and it is around your circle that Jewish life is concentrated — then how did people dare to go to the lord [the authorities], and not just some boys from the street but people with names, who, when you look at their God-fearing little faces, you would think they owe God their souls; public figures, who love to take the top place everywhere. So how do such people dare to speak so much slander, and not before our brethren the children of Israel but at the high windows [before the authorities]; and what impression such words make when one brother speaks against another — that, it seems, one need not tell you. So by what right — we ask you — do our public activists come and dare to say that I am harmful to the community, that I am an intriguer? When have I done anything in my life? When was I harmful, and what damage have I caused, either to individuals or to the community? I have been living in Będzin for about 40 years, and all that time I have worked for one firm — so does anyone have anything to complain about me? Does anyone want to avoid me? I have lived in one house for a number of years now, and as usual there are various neighbours there — let any of them say in what way I have ever been harmful, and whether I have ever in my life spied or intrigued. Had I belonged to harmful elements, people would surely have known me as such. Well, I could still have understood — says the Jew from the heart — if they had objected that I am not a suitable public activist; but in what way am I harmful? Have I ever brought damage to the community? Do I have on my conscience public sins, improper deeds? And my heart grows heavier still when I look around at whom they have replaced me with: who is more honest and finer and more conscientious and more decent than the man standing before your eyes.
Look what naive people we still have in today's lawless and hypocritical world. How do people not understand that naivety, decency and honesty are the whole defect, and that with such people one cannot sit at one table.
A strange thing, how we use our energetic deeds precisely where we ought to have remained powerless. In the field of quarrels and squabbles we are extraordinarily energetic and purposeful; among us nobody, God forbid, will be even one hour late when it comes to tripping one another up. Had we been as capable in all other public fields, where it is a matter not of destroying but of building and creating, we could surely have prided ourselves on the fine works that could have been created with our help. Had we been capable when it comes to reorganising and renewing, as we are when it comes to arriving at the squire's with a fresh little errand — which everyone could have done without — we would then have had, instead of idlers, hard-working people, and instead of lawless lads, responsible people. Our life would then have looked quite different; we would have felt more normal and healthier, and then others would have looked at us with a quite different face, and we would have had a quite different shape before the world.
We have received the authority to create our own kehilla representations — and even before anything else, before one so much as puts a hand into cold water, everything is already upside down on table and bench; how many denunciations are already springing up, and how many times are the candidates to the election bureaus disqualified. One's face turns red with shame when one watches what ugly and disgusting paths people take.
Somehow people have lately learned that everything has become permitted, both in a private name and in the name of the party; but this must on no account be allowed. One must not make light of and tolerate what degrades the honour of the people and the honour of the Jewish citizen. More than once we have had the opportunity to hear with what bitterness members of the "Aguda" [Agudat Israel] speak, who feel offended at such a moment, when its representatives act tactlessly towards the whole Jewish community. It goes without saying that not all members of the "Aguda" agree with the harmful methods of their leading elements, who are for the most part blind tools in other people's hands. They see this quite often, and hide away at such a moment.
But that is not all; with this the question is still far from solved. We can still understand that individuals should be responsible only for themselves, for their own deeds; but associations, political parties — when they betray the people, when they do not act tactfully and with restraint towards the whole Jewish people, then the party is, if not legally, at least morally responsible for the whole community. And against this, against such degrading means, when people want to blacken our representatives in the eyes of the authorities, one must take a stand and fight, wage a struggle — a decent one, of course, a restrained one, a logically founded one; we must then prove to the authorities that the people goes a decent way, on parliamentary foundations. The government must see that the great majority [rov minyan ve-rov binyan] are not the handful of shouters and rowdies and those who can crawl like real "mashkes" [?] through back doors and are ready, for their own interests, to sell the whole of Israel for a pot of peas.
One must prove to the government that the medal also has a second side, that there are decent currents that do not lose themselves when it comes to defending the honour of the people. If, however, they will not want to listen to the words, and one will not get far with the truth, then in that case there is no need at all for the whole rattling apparatus. What is all the clatter and the ringing for, that we can create our own Jewish self-governments? In that case the whole representation with its ceremonies would be superfluous; then it will be enough if in the kehilla house one or 2 nominated persons sit down whose task will be to see to it that the budget is drawn up.
To take a stand in such a situation as we find ourselves in now is a matter of impossibility. The population is disappointed and does not know where in the world it is. Its leading elements, who want to follow the path of free and decent thought, cannot afford it for many, many reasons. So in such a state there can be no talk of carrying out any purposeful activity whatsoever. Demoralisation and lawlessness have already reached their culminating point, and there is no more talk of staying on this lawless road, where anyone can come wherever necessary and say: Moshe ben Shmuel does not please me as a representative — and he will soon be removed; and afterwards that one will taunt him and say: I told you that your foot would not enter the gmina.
Does this not look like a children's game? Is it not like the tales of the Thousand and One Nights? Can a people let itself be led like this by the nose by the first lawless person who comes along? Is one not degraded when one sets out on this lawless road?
So it is self-evident that it cannot go on like this; for everything there must be a limit and a time. There are permitted deeds and forbidden deeds, and now the measure and the system of what is permitted and what is not permitted have been lost; it has become a kind of anarchy, one does not understand the other, and lawlessness and demoralisation too have lost their limit, so that one must go this way or that. To remain standing on this disgusting, bewitched road is impossible.
L. Sh.
Today's Women

(A novella) — by Lejb Goldgraber.
When business began to go badly and the bailiff came day after day to put the house up for auction in order to collect the last accumulated[?] taxes, young, charming Mania realized that from now on she could no longer sit on the shoulders of her melancholy-stricken father, who had lately come down in the world.
The taxes had truly drowned him. His heart ached even more when he remembered that his only daughter — beautiful Mania — would have to go out and take a job.
Mania understood this well, went to the newspaper office and placed the following advertisement: "Seeking a position. Any work at all, for a very small salary. Offers at the editorial office for P.L.[?] Mania". It was not hard for her; soon many firms that knew beautiful Mania, the daughter of the honest[?], ruined[?] merchant, applied to the editorial office, and she was engaged by a large firm.
The owner of the firm treated her well, even when she did something wrong; he understood that her depression[?] was temporary, until she grew used to her new life.
Mania worked all day; apart from the lunch hour she was not seen at home. From the shop she went straight to the association [farayn], where people worked for a better tomorrow for the working class.
Mania came home late at night, when her old, careworn father was still not asleep — he could not fall asleep until his consolation came home. He sensed that his daughter was gradually being corrupted, that her soul was being poisoned with "Marxism", and that she, his bourgeois daughter, was becoming a preacher of freedom, and that hatred of the old world was being planted in her.
Of the hundreds[?] of association members who came there, Berish, the journeyman tailor, was the only one who set the tone; his hairstyle bore witness that he was one of the fighters for a better tomorrow for the working class.
As soon as Mania enrolled in the association, Berish turned his attention to her, and she sensed it well. Every evening, when she had finished her Marxist activity and got up to go home, Berish took down from the hanger his patched, mould-coloured[?] jacket, which he had been wearing for a "kalebrish"[?] year, and went to accompany Mania.
They walked in silence, not saying a word to each other, until they came through the narrow, darkened alleys to the house where Mania lived; with a "good night" they both parted.
Every time Berish returned home he walked like a man crushed and thought: why have I not yet told her, to this day, that I love her, that without her my life is no life. He decided that tomorrow he would tell her.
The next day, when Mania had finished the educational work at the association and set off home, Berish went along. They walked as every evening — silently, not saying a word to each other, but suddenly Berish broke the silence and said in a trembling voice:
— Ma-n-i-a!
— What is it?
— I-l-o-v-e you..
Mania answered nothing; Berish went on:
— Mania, I love you, I[?] cannot live without you.
— Berish! I love you too — Mania whispered in a trembling voice.
Both walked on with lowered[?] heads. At Mania's house they parted. In the quiet night the expressions of love rang out — they kissed.
Mania could not fall asleep for a long time; feelings tormented her: on one side — what will her old father say when she marries a tailor's lad; on the other side — love...
———
Soon after the wedding Berish took her out of the shop; he worked with all his strength so that she would be the equal of all other women. He worked until late at night and Mania kept house — they were happy...
Mania stopped coming to the association; she exchanged it for places of amusement, where she spent whole nights with strange men, on the hard-toiled-for grosz of her Berish. He knew all this, but his love for her did not allow him to react. Lately Mania did not come home at all; when Berish returned home after a twelve-hour working day he had no one to exchange a word with; he went[?] straight to bed [—], could not fall asleep, and decided: as soon as she comes, he would tell her everything. He knew everything: that she was spending time with strange men, and that it could not go on like this.
At dawn, when Mania came back from her habitual carousing [hulankes, from Polish hulanki], he said to her in a very depressed[?] tone:
— Mania, I know everything!
— What do you know?
— You spend your [—], lately, with strange men.
— I don't love you any more — was Mania's last answer.
As soon as Mania had uttered these last words, it struck Berish like thunder. He had sensed it himself, but from her mouth he had not expected such a thing.
That day Berish did not go to work; he paced about the house deeply depressed[?], smoking cigarettes [papirosy] one after another. He went up to the wall, took down the calendar and began to count the days: until the first of the month he still had twelve days of work.
But after twelve days of work, when he received his wages, he no longer gave them to Mania; on his way back from work he bought himself a revolver with the month's wages.
When he came into the house it was already evening; Mania was already dressed up to go out. Berish did not think long; he went into the other room and shot himself several times. When Mania, terrified by the revolver shots, came into the room, Berish was already lying half dead. Mania fell upon him with a hysterical wail:
— My dear Berish, my dear!..
But his last words were: M-m-mania, I l-lived f-for you and I d-die f-for you-u-u — — — — — —
When Mania lifted[?] her head from her dead husband, it was already dark outside. The blue, clouded[?] sky had driven[?] the beautiful moon to the window, as if it wanted to say: dangerous[?] women and[?] ... the earth[?] — loved and abandoned.
— Today's women.
Islam and Eretz Israel

By V. Jabotinsky.

4) The situation in India and with us

The present situation in India is exactly the same as before the war: those in power are compelled to orient themselves toward England simply because they are a minority. Along this line they will, in the end, have to go, and they will have neither the possibility nor the desire to inquire how England conducts itself on the shores of the Mediterranean.

So it was also in Egypt. In 1882 England crushed the uprising of Arabi Pasha and annexed Egypt. Some time later England stifled the uprising of the Mahdi with his dervishes, [—] in [—] Sudan. Meanwhile Prime Minister Gladstone, in connection with the Armenian pogroms, declared that Turkey must be driven out of Europe "bag and baggage" (bag and bagage). But precisely in those years the Indian ruling circles were particularly attached to England, because for them, thanks to the democratic conditions, it was politically useful.

Now the conditions in the country are exactly the same as then: the fear of the minority before the majority. Therefore the consequence will also be the same. From that side, being[?] entirely[?] free from the English government, England may live in peace or in conflict with the local Arabs — not only in Eretz Israel but also in Mecca — and it will not have the slightest influence on the sympathies of Indian Islam.

In truth every sensible English politician knows this; but it does not follow that he will so easily give up the [—] privilege — otherwise, for instance, thus — of threatening[?] with the "bogeyman" ("straszydło") in which he himself does not believe.. People are very reluctant to give up popular illusions[?] and excuses. Our task today, however, is not to lay down rules for how we should conduct negotiations with the English government. Our task was to clarify whether it is true that the English kingdom is "actually unable" to keep the word it gave us, because a legendary hero has supposedly blocked its way — a hero before whose fire-spitting eyes whole armies sink. The answer is: there is no such hero, there are no fire-spitting eyes, and no armies sink. From that side the road is free.

We have already spoken separately about the moral strength of Islam, but in our language the phrase "the strength of Islam" has usually acquired a different, almost concrete sense — the meaning of a physical, almost military force. We are assured, and we persuade ourselves, that every step in our favour means a danger of "provoking an uprising" that it will be impossible to tame[?]. Above all, the average Zionist today lives with the trembling notion that the microscopically small Jewish people, with its present[?] national claims, stands face to face with the colossal power of Islam, with this mighty, inspired, wrathful force armed from head to foot; and that if we do not keep entirely quiet, these legions will rise, annihilate us, and at one stroke will also demolish, together with [us], our protectors[?] — simply: physically demolish them, just as the Romans once demolished Carthage and the barbarians, for their part, Rome.

This fear grew especially strong after the Greek-Turkish war ended in defeat for the Greeks. For quite incomprehensible reasons this insignificant event made upon us the impression of a revelation: we saw in it the symbol of a military victory of Islam over "Europe". Let us therefore try to take these fairy tales apart, especially since this can be cleared up with a few brief pieces of information.

Before the said fact[?] there [—] two conflicts: the Italian campaign to Tripoli in 1911, and the French expedition against Faisal when he ruled in Damascus in 1920. What is characteristic is not that Europe won in both campaigns — that would not be worth talking about, since it could be foreseen from the start; but in just the same way one could have foreseen 30 years ago that England would undoubtedly defeat the Boer people, and nevertheless that 300-thousand-man victory cost England very dearly. What is interesting for our case: the cheap price of both victories against Arab resistance — a quite unexpected, almost unbelievably cheap price. Around the Tripolitanian war the Italian gentlemen thought it necessary to make a great noise; but if one puts the literature aside and looks through the casualty figures, one learns that this war cost Italy, if I am not mistaken, 2500 men, dead and wounded together.

The French took Damascus at a far cheaper price still. Faisal had prepared and organised his army well beforehand; in any case he very diligently spread rumours about the might of this army and about his auxiliary troops of 160 thousand Bedouin horsemen from Transjordan, who were supplied with modern armament. The rumours deserved credence, because during the war the English brought a great many weapons to the Hejaz, and the commander of these [—] troops was at that time this same Faisal, who undoubtedly took large stocks of weapons with him to Damascus. Besides, during demobilisation and during its flight in September 1918, the Turkish army left behind literally tens of thousands of weapons and millions of bullets, of which the Bedouins certainly looted half. When it became known that the French were preparing an armed expedition to Damascus, everybody reckoned "it is going to get hot". But it did not get "hot" at all. The war lasted half an hour (literally). On this stroll the French lost — so it seems to me — 12 men. Faisal fled from Damascus.

(Conclusion follows).
The Prague Fair.

[Abroad — economy; Czechoslovakia.] (From our Prague correspondent).

On the 22nd of March of this year the great fair opens in Prague, Czechoslovakia, which is the biggest fair apart from Leipzig.

Czechoslovak industry has always played a great role in all countries. There is not a single branch of manufacturing that does not have a large industry in Czechoslovakia. There are towns here in which almost everybody, young and old, works at one and the same article.

For instance Prossnitz [Prostějov], a town with some twenty thousand tailors, which is known all over the world for its garments. Brünn [Brno], the second-largest city in Czechoslovakia, has tens of thousands of weavers who weave the finest fabrics. Hundreds of wagonloads of fabric are sent year in, year out from Brünn to England, and from there the very same Brünn fabrics come back as "original English fabrics". We ourselves do not know that many English fabrics which are sold all over the world at high prices were made in Brünn, in Czechoslovakia.

We do not want to dwell on the fact that, for instance, in Zlín, a Czech small town, there is the biggest shoe factory in the whole world, that of the firm "Baťa", which turns out two hundred thousand pairs of shoes a day. But in the Pardubice district too there are thousands upon thousands of shoemakers who work there in many large shoe factories.

Reichenberg [Liberec] with its thousands upon thousands of looms for fine cloth and silk [?] fabrics has almost no equal in Europe, and Gablonz [Jablonec nad Nisou], with its enormous industry of imitation jewellery, is the only town in the whole world that supplies its work to the remotest corners of the four quarters of the globe.

Not to speak of Pilsen [Plzeň] with its world-famous beer industry — but also the big iron and machine industries in Czechoslovakia are today on a par with their German, English and American competitors.

It is of course a natural thing that the industries have created for themselves in beautiful Prague, the capital of Czechoslovakia, a centre where all the industries of the country can show themselves to buyers from the whole world with their new creations, and in this way attract new customers for the great Czech industry.

The Prague fair is mighty in its size and its variety, and apart from Leipzig it has no equal among any fair in the world.

P. Langsztajn.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayikra)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Vayikra
—o—
a) Vayikra (1:1)
"Vayikra" is written with a small alef (alef ze'ira), to show that the lesson for a person ("alef" = learning [?]) is to keep oneself small. Not to learn to be "yesh" (to be a something, a "yesh"), but to learn to be "nothing" (to learn to be a nothing in one's own eyes). — Degel Machaneh Efrayim.
• • •
"Be very, very humble of spirit" —
"Me'od" ("very") also means wealth ("with all thy me'od — with all thy money"). This is what the Mishnah says: "Very, very — even if you have a great fortune and are rich — be humble of spirit"; do not think too much of yourself... Petach Einayim (the Chida).
• • •
"In the footsteps of the Messiah, insolence will increase" —
Insolence, self-importance, is usually found among the rich: "the rich man answers roughly." In the footsteps of the Messiah, in the Messiah's times, when everyone will be paupers ("the son of David will not come until the last penny is gone from the purse"), and there will still be those who give themselves airs — that is the true insolence. Sichat Chullin [?].
• • •
The Maggid of Dubno once came to a poor small-town beit midrash, which nevertheless had great brazen-faced people, and they would not let the Maggid preach. He asked to be allowed at least a few short words. When they permitted it, he said:
An eternal struggle goes on between the rich and the poor. The poor claim that the wealthy are holding back the Redemption, because "the son of David will not come until the last penny is gone from the purse" — so let them [—] the little money and be done with it... The wealthy claim: "In the footsteps of the Messiah insolence will increase", and who has as much [of it] as [—]... [—], the poor with their insolence are holding back the Redemption.
And so — concludes the Maggid of Dubno — here I have found people who are [?] the insolent ones [?] among [?] the paupers — so the Messiah must surely come soon [?], and therefore "and a redeemer shall come to Zion"...
—o—
b) "And he shall slaughter it on the side of the altar northward" (1:11)
Money is alluded to in "north" ("gold comes out of the north"); with money the Evil Inclination often [?] slaughters the kohen, the tzaddik. "Most holy offerings are slaughtered in the north": with "north" (money) the holiest of holies are slaughtered... Ben Porat Yosef.
—o—
c) "A fire-offering of pleasing odour to the Lord" (1:15 [?])
Both for an offering of an ox and for a bird, "pleasing odour" is always said, because "one who gives much and one who gives little are alike, provided he directs his heart to Heaven." Menachot 111 [?].
If both intend it for the sake of Heaven, both are equal — the one who brings the fat offering and the one who cannot [—] more than a poor bird, for "the Merciful One desires the heart", yes [?], "provided he directs". For if neither intends it for the sake of Heaven, the poor man is much lower: the rich man at least has something to be proud of — an ox; but the pauper with his little bird — what has he got out of it [?]... No'am Megadim.
• • •
"Provided he directs [his heart]" does not refer, as it is simply interpreted, to the one who gives little — for the poor man always means it for the sake of Heaven; it refers only to the one who gives much: for a rich man it is a rarity to intend something for the sake of Heaven... Rabbi David of Kotsk [?].
—o—
d) "An offering of first-fruits... but they shall not go up on the altar for a pleasing odour" (2:12)
"No leaven and no honey shall you burn" — a person who mixes in a bit of leaven (the Evil Inclination) and honey (pleasure) is not acceptable to God. But sometimes one does burn a little pleasure and honour, a tiny drop [?] — "an offering of first-fruits." For leaders and heads it is permitted, for if it were only a matter of being honest, who would want to be a leader, to count for anything at all [?]. "They shall not go up on the altar for a pleasing odour" — it does not smell good to the Almighty... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
e) "If a soul sins unintentionally against any of the Lord's commandments" (4:2)
Yes, sometimes one sins with a mitzvah... the "mitzvah" of being vengeful and bearing a grudge ("any Torah scholar who does not avenge himself and bear a grudge like a serpent is no Torah scholar") and other similar "mitzvot". [—].
—o—
f) "When a ruler sins" (4:22)
The initials of the three words spell "ani" ("I"): our leaders sin because of their "ani", because they attach such importance to their own "I"... Rabbi Nate Chelmer [?].
—o—
g) "His offering" (4:23)
For the ruler's offering the word "et" is used, which signifies an addition: he must bring a fatter [?] offering, for rulers eat of the best, so they must also bring before God of the best... Ba'al ha-Turim.
—o—
h) "If a soul sins and commits a trespass against the Lord" (5:21)
"If [a soul] sins" refers to robbery. It appears that this is worse than trespass against the Lord, than sinning against God, since it is mentioned first. [—].
—o—
i) "When he has sinned and is guilty, he shall restore what he robbed" (5:23)
If "and is guilty" — if he knows in himself that he has robbed his fellow — "he shall restore what he robbed": such a one will still repent and give back the stolen goods. Worse is it with those who rob and plunder and in their own eyes are fine Jews — "she eats and wipes her mouth and says: I have done no wrong." "You shall do no injustice in judgment" — do no injustice (wrong) "in judgment", meaning: with the law as a mask. Siftei Tzaddikim.
—o—
j) "He shall restore what he robbed... and bring his guilt-offering to the Lord" (5:25)
Only once he has returned the stolen goods can he make peace with God. If he does not satisfy the one he robbed, his repentance toward God is worth nothing at all. The first offering must be to the one robbed [?]... Ohel Yaakov.
Poland at the World Fair.

Specially for our paper, by Z. Haber.
At the Leipzig Fair, which has just been held, the Polish exhibition was a very great success and [?] showed clearly that Poland has lately developed its industry considerably and is striving with all kinds of forces to penetrate the centres of world trade.
Your correspondent was received by the Polish Consul General in Leipzig, Dr. Igusz [?] Adamkiewicz [?], who is known as one of the greatest economic statesmen of Poland, and had a conversation with him about the economic relations between Poland and Germany and about the economic possibilities in Poland.
"I hope," said Dr. Adamkiewicz [?], "that with the ratification of the German-Polish trade agreement, which will hopefully take place soon in both states, the economic situation in both countries will improve. Poland suffers not only from the general economic situation, which has after all engulfed the whole world, but also from the fall in the prices of foodstuffs. This decline has caused a great ruin in Poland, because the main means used to pay for all imported goods were, after all [?], agricultural products and foodstuffs of all kinds, which Poland possesses in abundance and can export in large quantities.
"This is best seen in the fact that whereas Poland formerly exported to Germany more than 50 percent of its entire export, in the year 1930 Germany took only 29 percent of Poland's production. It was no better with the import of goods from Germany. In earlier years Poland imported from Germany more than 43 percent of its entire need of foreign goods; in the year 1930 Poland bought in Germany only 28 percent of its need.
"The reason is that we cannot pay for the imported goods, because our food products have, like all products in the whole world, fallen sharply.
"We have now come to the Leipzig Fair, the greatest sales place in the whole world, in order to show first of all our [—], which count among the best in the whole world; and for this [?] we also wanted our industrial products to be seen by merchants from all corners of the world, so that they should see that we are striving to create industries that can withstand the competition of all world industries.
"For the first time we exhibited spirits of the State Monopoly [?], likewise our tobaccos, our products from the various animals and livestock that live in our country, and the various handicrafts of our highlanders [?] — from simple handicrafts up to artistic precious objects.
"[—] the iron, coal and sugar industries also play a great role in our economy, and we are striving here [?] in Leipzig to show the whole world to what a high level we have brought these industries in the short time of our independent state.
"I ask you," Igusz [?] Adamkiewicz [?] concluded, "to convey through the Jewish newspapers of the whole world to the Jewish merchants that we have come to Leipzig to hear the verdict of all merchants on our work, and that we certainly want to adapt [?] and change [?] our production, if the judgement of the world's merchants demands it of us."
The Command of the Hour

(A proposal for the Passover campaign).
As can already be foreseen, the number of needy who will be forced this year before Passover to turn to the community for support will be many times greater than a year ago. We know, after all, that owing to the cruel crisis that has reigned among us for so long, one can count the [?] in the hundreds. Just as in the course of the winter people died [?] of hunger and [—] froze from cold, there are unfortunately no signs that the situation will improve even a little before Passover, so that all could prepare for the holiday in dignity.
From the community one cannot hope this year [?] for a larger sum for the Passover campaign; one [?] will therefore, as usual, want to discharge the duty with [?] (printed "shhi-p.h."), which in this case will amount to mocking the poor. To burden the community-budget payers again for this purpose with special taxes will also not be so easy to carry out.
The question of how one finds [?], then, for Passover for these hundreds of respectable former rich men [?] — among whom there are not a few who only a very short time ago were able to support others — must concern each one of us, and first of all our community representatives, who are the first on whom this duty must rest.
A proposal therefore comes to mind: that this time the Passover support be carried out not as a gift but as a loan. That is, the community should, specially for this purpose, borrow a proper sum from the Gemilut Chesed [free-loan society], and those who will receive loans from this fund [?] should undertake to repay them in small instalments over a certain period. (Of course, we mean here those who are not professional recipients of charity, but are able to repay such loans.) The loans should be guaranteed by endorsers.
At first sight this proposal may seem to some not practical enough, yet in our opinion it must be seriously considered. The benefits will be twofold — moral and material. In this way the "disgrace" [?] and "shame" suffered by those whose lot it has been to have to depend on this kind of support will be avoided. The material benefit is that the money for the Passover campaign will return, if not in full, then at any rate in part, to the community treasury.
It is true that the purpose of the Gemilut Chesed is quite a different one, and the loans should in principle not be given for such non-productive purposes. But we live in a time that often compels one to overstep the narrow programmes [?] of the various regulations, and the present situation too compels us to such an overstepping.

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 2 Nisan 5691 — Piątek 20 marca 1931 [Friday, 20 March 1931].)
Będzin
Second Session of the Commissarial Council.
At Monday's session of the commissarial council the bad financial situation of the magistrat [town hall] was again touched upon. Inspector Mr. Janczek(?) declared that the amount of debts for various things(?) incurred by the former town administration is growing ever larger, and by the 1st of kwiecień [April] of this year the debts will already amount to over one million złoty.
Then the council member Director Fürstenberg asked how matters stand with the question of employing the unemployed. To this the commissar answers that, owing to lack of money, the magistrat can employ only 80 workers.
At the session commissar Ruszczeszkowski(?) put forward a project that the magistrat should take steps to obtain a 3-year moratorium on repaying the loans, and should apply to the financial authorities with the request that the debt the magistrat owes the State Treasury [skarb] be spread(?) into instalments.
In order to improve the financial position, the council authorised the commissar to issue new(?) promissory notes [weksle] for 20 thousand zł. In addition Mr. Fürstenberg declared that he is ready, on account of his local taxes, to discount magistrat promissory notes to a sum of 20 to 30 thousand zł.
A very bad fate befell the subventions for the years 1929–30 and 1930/31: it was decided in this matter that the unpaid subventions for 1929/30 shall be struck off entirely, and the subventions for 1930/31 settled(?) in this way: subventions up to(?) one thousand zł. to be paid in full, above one thousand — 70 per cent. The subventions to institutions outside the town to be struck off entirely. From this "operation" the magistrat gained 21,380 zł.
After the "operation" it was decided, on the proposal of the head of the magistrat, to grant 180 zł. to the association of the "Strzelcy"(?) [riflemen, the Związek Strzelecki] as a "nagroda" [reward].
At the session the question of taking the municipal hospital into the town's possession was discussed at length. As is known, the Supreme Tribunal has recognised that the actual owner of the hospital is the magistrat. But the sejmik [district council], which until now was the owner of the hospital, does not want to let the hospital out of its hands; moreover, the sejmik notified the present head of the magistrat that, because of the debts unpaid by the magistrat, the hospital will not admit any patients sent by the magistrat.
The commissar Mr. Ruszczeszkowski(?) expressed the view on this question that it does not pay for the magistrat to take over the hospital, since this would make the burden heavier. Mr. Fürstenberg is against this opinion and proposes coming to an understanding with the starosta [district head], who should react against the sejmik's refusal to admit patients. Dr. Barylski also agrees with this opinion, saying that the hospital will not be a burden on the municipal economy and that the magistrat must take over the hospital.
For this purpose a commission was elected of Dr. Barylski, Dir. Fürstenberg and Salski, who together with the commissar are to negotiate with the starosta on the question of taking over the hospital.

[Będzin — synagogue and court.] On Tuesday the trial of Mr. Lewin, who had been charged by the police with disturbing the Kabbalat Shabbat prayers in the local synagogue, took place for the second time in the local court.
As our readers know, the scandal in the synagogue occurred as a consequence of the well-known Din Torah (rabbinical arbitration) held by outside rabbis concerning the local cantor.
The ruling issued by the rabbis also contained a clause that "the cantor must be in 'rapprochement' [?] with the local rabbinate".
A week later, when the cantor wanted to lead the welcoming of the Sabbath, he was disturbed by Mr. Lewin, who demanded from the cantor a permit from the rabbinate to lead the prayers.
Thanks to this a great scandal broke out in the synagogue, with a brawl with knives and revolvers, and had it not been for the police who were called in, it would have come to bloodshed in the synagogue...
The epilogue of the tragic events in our holy place was "[—]" a few weeks ago. At the request of the accused, Mr. Lewin, the trial was postponed to a second date.
Last Tuesday the trial took place for the second time. Besides the witnesses of both sides, Rabbi Frommer of Sosnowiec (the Koziegłowy rabbi) was also summoned as a witness; he had been among the heads [?] who issued the ruling concerning the cantor.
After hearing the witnesses of both sides, and after the defence by Dr. Rechtman, the court sentenced Mr. Lewin, as the principal culprit, to pay 70 zł. court costs or 10 days' arrest.

Third session of the Commissar Council in Będzin

On Wednesday evening, under the chairmanship of Commissar Ruszkowski[?], a session of the Commissar Council took place, with the agenda: old-new taxes, the collection (incassation), building plans, a surcharge on the government tax of house-owners in[?] the statutes on wood[?], coal, etc.
As we hear[?], the sessions are conducted „idyllically“: the chief speakers are those of the minority — the Jews, that is — and decisions are made according to the will of the „silent ones“, of the majority..
After hearing the report of the tax commission, the old-new „plague“[?] for the Jewish shopkeeper was taken up — that is, the industrial[?] tax, which is rising again in a „resurrection of the dead“..
There was a discussion around this item. The Jewish councillors, Messrs. Director Fürstenberg, G. Rzachnik[?], D. Gutensztajn[?] and S. Hanfel[?], showed with glaring facts that in the present hard times no new taxes should be imposed on the already so[?] tormented[?] urban population. Especially since the income from the tax is earmarked for building a school in Gzichów[?], which is not so urgently needed and could not be realised so quickly anyway. „We take[?] from the same thing — says Mr. Fürstenberg — that the previous administration did, which used revenues[?] from the ordinary budget for items of the extraordinary budget.“
The chairman, wishing to satisfy all opinions, proposed that the item be discussed again at the next session, which will take place next Tuesday. On the other hand, the surcharge[?] proposal of 25 percent on the government tax on immovable property[?] was approved. This tax, which amounts to 42 thousand zł., is paid only by house-owners.
At the end of the session, on the motion of Director Mr. Fürstenberg, 1.500 zł. were allocated for poor Jews and 1.500 zł. for Christians for the holiday.

Prof. Schorr and Vice-President Meisel Visit Kraków

(A letter from Kraków).
The heroes of last year's sad events at the Kraków university, who manifested their antisemitism with the fist and with brutality, have this year set about the fight against the Jewish academics by legal means. In this way they now wanted to attain their aim: to remove the Jews from economic and social life, from all self-help and cultural institutions. Already earlier the proposal to exclude the Jews from the academic medical students' association failed to obtain the necessary number of votes. This time[?] the same institution devised[?] a splendid way: an ex[—] is for students of the medical faculty. It is said that [—] will be received only by the Catholic students and those without religion.
This year the Endeks (printed "the the Endeks") again wanted to exclude the Jews from the „Association of Students Juri“[?], and for this purpose a special general meeting was called. On the agenda[?]: amending the statute in the sense that admission of members is decided by the board (Endeks only), which may reject the Jewish ones and is not obliged to give reasons for the refusal. But the defeat of the „reformists“ was a big one. The Jews, together with a small number of democratic students (mostly socialists), rejected the proposal by 130 votes to 70 and once again dealt[?] a death-blow[?] to the would-be hegemony of the Endecja in academic life.
• • •
We have lived through an unusual sensation. In the first year of the law faculty the examinations in Western-European law began these days. Eight students a day were supposed to be examined, but the number of candidates[?] grew ever larger, and what decided was who had first occupied a place in the examination hall... No wonder, then, that many students, among them also women, spent a whole night in the corridor of the university. The next morning the dean's office[?] of the law faculty took an interest in the matter. The examinations were stopped and an investigation is to be held concerning the „night heroes“. In any case they can say that they were the first who wanted even to sleep[?] at the university.
• • •
The bad economic situation of Polish Jewry — the crisis, which has gripped[?] all of Europe and America in its pincers and caused the greatest damage among the Jewish masses — has also reflected its consequences in the activity of 4 important Jewish relief institutions which carry on fruitful work in the social field: „ORT“, „CENTOS“, „TOZ“, „JEAS“.
„ORT“ is a society that has set itself the aim of spreading crafts and agricultural work among the Polish Jews; it has created a series of agricultural cooperatives[?], maintains many schools and eases the work of the Jewish farm-workers. For a people that lacks the constructive and creative class of peasants[?] and [—], the work of „ORT“ is of great importance.
The second institution, „CENTOS“, maintains a number of orphanages, cares for and protects the poor Jewish orphans, educates them and supports up to 10 thousand Jewish children.
In the field of hygiene and health „TOZ“ has long conducted its work, not allowing so important a part of life to be neglected. „TOZ“ has founded a number of hospitals, medical advice centres, out-patient clinics, etc.
„JEAS“ is a society that serves Jewish emigrants and settles all formalities connected with the journey. Recently „JEAS“ built a fine emigrants' hotel in Warsaw.
These four Jewish institutions have lately found themselves in a bad material situation — not only because of the Polish crisis, but because the subsidies from America, which occupied a significant position in their budget, have been stopped. In order to make their activity possible the organisations have united under the name „Rebuilding and Self-Help“ (Aufbau un Zelbsthilf) and are now conducting a fund-raising campaign throughout Poland. In Kraków an „academy“ (public meeting) was held with the participation of Prof. Schorr and Vice-President[?] Meisel from Warsaw, who in warm words called upon the Jewish population to make possible the further fruitful work of the above-mentioned institutions.
A. Gertner.
An Open Letter to the Rabbi of Będzin

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We ask you to publish the following letter, for which we thank you in advance.
"And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them." (Isaiah 3).
It is quite natural[?] even on our part to speak out against "those" who speak and do everything only in the name of the Torah; after the incident that happened these days at the wedding of R' Moshe Fridrich, it compels us to come out in public with this letter. At the above-mentioned wedding the Pri-miner[?] cantor (chazzan), while fulfilling his official religious function, was brutally insulted by a group of tse'irim [young Agudah zealots] (he was publicly reviled and cursed), so that he was forced to leave the wedding without performing his office. While doing this bit of work the "heroes" shouted that by this they were defending the honour of the local rabbi.
It would actually lead us too far if we were to point out[?] the consequences to which the ways and means of the "Agudah" lead under the cloak of "strengthening the faith", for the lawlessness and demoralisation that the Torah-loyal tse'irim have brought into our Jewish religious life, with the consent of their leaders, are already all too conspicuous.
But still we want to see how the Rav, may he live long and well, will react to the insult to a member of the klei kodesh [religious functionaries] while fulfilling his religious function. Can the Rav, as mara de-atra [local rabbinic authority], pass over in silence and tolerate such wild deeds as publicly shedding the blood of a Jew — and by pious young men at that? Is this in accordance with our Torah and ethics? How will the Rav interpret "he who shames his fellow in public"? Does he agree that such [—] deeds defend his honour?
And we ask ourselves: are these deeds not a continuation (and a beginning among us in Będzin) of the vile acts of terror against all klei kodesh who do not have the Agudah hekhsher (such as the shameful attack on the honoured and everywhere respected Sosnowiec rabbi, and other similar acts)?
Do the Agudist strongmen want to display their great feats among us too? (Like the beginning[?] of striking R' Leibish Dimant off the election commission, (with which we shall yet deal specially). We therefore find it necessary to warn publicly: remember, and do not desecrate Jewish honour, and do not gallop too far with your momentary high-handedness; and we advise you: hold back your incited[?] tse'irim, for the stick has two ends.
The boards of "Mizrachi" and "Tse'irei Mizrachi" in Będzin.

A great sensation was caused in Mysłowice by the arrest of Mr. Święty [the name means „holy“], manager (kierownik) of the Building[?] and Loan Fund in Mysłowice.

Suicide in Court.
In the Rybnik court a worker was to pay a fine of 30 zł. or go to jail for 10 days. The worker turned to the judge with a request that he accept 20 zł. from him for the time being, and the remaining 10 zł. he would pay at a second date.
When the request was rejected, the worker plunged a knife into his heart. He was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
