The Commissar's Council

(The Będzin municipal self-government. — The commissar. — The commissar's council. — What next?)
The Polish press in Zagłębie has begun to deal with the question of the Będzin municipal self-government. But that is only a manner of speaking, that it has begun to deal with the question, because in truth nothing has begun at all; they have done no more than begin to throw[?] pins at one another — each side proves that they [the others] are utterly to blame, whereas the others have made mistakes — and so one sets off on the road of an unhealthy and unrestrained tactic. What will come of such polemicizing we shall yet see.
The town looks on, the citizens read what is printed and stand dumbfounded; they do not know where the mistakes lie and where the crux is. [—] one knows of no way out here that might save[?] the very unpleasant situation, and how should one find a way out when one does not look[?] for it at all? What will the citizens get out of all this? What use will the town have from one tripping up the other?
One thing, however, we see: the town is burdened with debts, the self-government has taken on many obligations, and the times are even[?] critical and enormously hard. And one must not forget one thing: that the obligations of the local self-government rest on the shoulders of the citizens, i.e. that we are above all responsible, we must above all pay, and we must see to it that the budgets are covered.
We do not wish here to enter into polemics with this or that side, with this or that tendency, simply because we are not versed in the matters that are always played out[?] behind the scenes[?]. Public questions can be handled conscientiously and honestly only when everything is told openly to the public, without any veil, without any hidden or ulterior intention.
But now is not the time or the opportunity to touch on this; besides, nothing would come of it nowadays. One must first of all speak of what is better, of what is more topical, of what is more urgent. And the more urgent thing is this: the town has become impoverished and has nothing with which to pay the great number of taxes it must contribute to the state treasury; and if one [—], if one [—] a week and another week and a month's time, nothing comes of it — or on the contrary, a great deal comes of it: interest accrues, and the question arises: can one pay the municipal taxes with interest and penalties when one does not have enough for the taxes themselves? [—] about this, one tries to take a look around at who the debtors are and in what condition they now find themselves? It must after all be borne in mind that municipal taxes do not have the same status as government taxes; the municipal authority is after all obliged to look after the town's interests, and when it sees that the citizens, its taxpayers, are in a critical condition, it is its task to come to their aid, to relieve them, to help lead them on the straight road, along the straight line.
True, one must not forget one thing: that all this is said for when there is a municipal administration and not a commissar, as is now the case with us. True, a commissar has regulations to act by the letter of the law and not by equity: you owe so-and-so much — hand it over and pay; a commissar need have no mercy and nothing need concern him. But one must not forget one thing: that here too certain reforms have been introduced — it is no longer the commissar alone, but a commissar's council has been attached to him, consisting of nominated citizens of the town, and this council at the commissar's side ought to ease the obligations of the citizens with regard to the municipal taxes.
As said, a commissar need know nothing at all; both the town and its interests are foreign to him. He is an auditor; he must audit and collect the burdensome[?] debts; he must be hard and strict, because that is what he has been appointed for, that is what he was sent here for. And therefore, since a council has been attached to him — and not of strangers who do not know the town, but local[?] people from home; people who know the citizens and their municipal interests — these people who make up the council must concern themselves with the difficult situation and [—] must remember that at a time when the country is in such a hard state, when the citizens are unable to pay the government taxes, at such a time attention must most certainly be paid to relieving the citizens, to coming to their aid.
It is a rule that when the town is better off, when its interests are better situated, one can allow oneself to spend more money on municipal purposes; but it is quite different when the situation is hard, when the citizens writhe[?] in want and hunger and find it hard to get through the day.
It would truly be a great act of justice to consider this question with full seriousness and sincerity. This question is worth devoting time to; one must confer about it — and then we shall see the result and what turn it will take.
We believe, we hope, we want to hope, that understanding[?] will be found in human hearts and that they will consider with full attention and care[?] this hard problem, which can ease the material interests of the citizens, which are hard enough at present.
For more objections[?] and reckonings and criticizing and tripping-up there is no time now. But a time must of course come for that too, because it must be shown clearly and openly[?] who seeks the good of the town and who does not. All this must under no circumstances remain veiled and concealed. But one thing must be remembered: that first of all the situation we are already in must be improved, because it must not be forgotten that first and foremost a municipal institution must see to it that the interests of the citizens should not weigh still more on the already sufficiently oppressed citizen.
The commissar's council has thus taken on a very responsible task; the council must apply all its strength in order to ease the payment terms of the municipal taxes. Be that as it may, one must after all reckon with the hard, critical situation in the country.
And therefore: if one seeks the good of the town, one must not forget at the present moment that first of all this must be safeguarded[?]: that the town's inhabitants, who at the present critical moment are living through very hard times, should be given relief in paying the municipal taxes. The commissar's council must put this as the first item on its agenda.
Selekt.
Supplicants...

(Tragi-comedy in 1 act)
In the secretariat of the kehilla.
Present: representatives of the Orphans' Society, "Linat ha-Holim", "Tarbut", "Talmud Torah", "Moshav Zkenim", a shopkeeper, an employee, etc.
Representative of the Orphans' Soc. (to the secretary of the kehilla) — For the umpteenth time we turn to you to release the subsidy for the orphans. It is an injustice crying out to heaven. Our orphans are perishing of hunger and cold. On whom are we to rely, if not on you? Touch wood, such a kehilla with such wide competences, with a budget (etat), with a plenum, with everything, in everything, of everything...
Secretary of the kehilla (spreading his hands): — There is no money, gentlemen, nobody pays the budgeted taxes, there is no income...
Representative of "Linat ha-Holim":
And we are already running to you for the hundredth time. Poor sick people are waiting for your help. What are they guilty of, the poor things, the babies in the cradle, the little ones who do not get their drop of milk? Give at least a little promissory note (wekselek)...
Kehilla secretary: —
A little note — a little note, well, yes, you are right. But where does one get a note? And who will pay for the note?
The representatives of the "Talmud Torah" and the "Moshav Zkenim" push their way forward and both want to start speaking at once. In the middle a little Jew sneaks in, pushes through to the table and tugs the kehilla secretary by the sleeve.
Kehilla secretary — (raises his head and rubs his hands with joy): Oh, the "kotsl"[?] is coming, you have surely brought the budget money?
Shopkeeper — gets flustered, turns red, stammers, winks at the kehilla secretary, calls him aside into a corner and whispers to him quietly in his ear):
— I have come to you for... for... maos hittim [Passover charity]. Things are bad for me, it is the eve of Passover, taxes, no takings, do me a kindness...
Employee (bursts into the throng and cries out to the shopkeeper):
— Boss dear, the sequestrator [tax bailiff] has come, the wagon is waiting at the shop...
(All remain standing petrified, the kehilla secretary scratches the back of his head in embarrassment, the representatives of the institutions look at one another... the shopkeeper sobs.)
(Curtain.)
Patakh Shin.
What I Heard, What I Saw

Reported by Ben-Amotz.
The "torn-away"..
I have — my acquaintance tells me — invented a new name for the "Aguda" [Agudas Yisroel]. In our opinion one should no longer call them "Aguda"-niks, but the "torn-away". Their theoretician Carlebach already preached in his time that the separation system (Trennungs-System) must be introduced, which is becoming topical and is also gradually being put into practice.
— And what do you mean by that?
— Listen then: a few weeks ago a second notary (rejent) came here to Będzin. Why not — why should such a large commercial town not have another notary? No problem, there is enough for a third one too... the more the better, so long as there is no monopoly of "I and none other"...
So the old notary heard that his "hazaka" [established claim] was in danger... He started negotiating and offered various proposals meant to guarantee that the hitherto "golden drop" would not be diminished...
But all these proposals the new notary rejected: what has been until now — he said — no longer exists, "that thy brother may live with thee", "leben und leben lassen". He opened an office and deliberately engaged Jewish clerks, so that all at once the Jewish merchants of Będzin saw that even in a notary's office Jews too can find employment...
And as is well known, we Jews are always loyal, especially to those who show us a smile; so the Jewish banks decided, as a mutual friendly relationship, to support the Jew-friendly notary — why not? — a simple matter!
But this simplicity is not understood by the leaders of the Aguda bank: they have torn themselves away from the solidarity agreement, broken their word of honour, and put on the scales the "whoever sustains a single soul of Israel"...
"We" and "They"
With this emphasis we mean this time to take up a quite side issue, an issue that is very painful and is not cared for even by our own "sisters of mercy".
It was last week: the Będzin town cantor meets me in the street, hands me a paper and asks me to explain to him the meaning of the black letters on the white paper...
Having read it, I explain to him, to the cantor that is, that he is invited by the Jewish kehilla to come on Thursday, 19 March, to the synagogue to conduct a prayer.
— A good thing I met you — says the cantor — I know no Polish and do not know what is written on the paper. To the devil! Why don't they write to me in Yiddish? Must a Jewish kehilla write to a cantor in Polish? If my little girl is at home I ask her. If not, I have to run out into the street and ask what they want of me?...
Having taken leave of the cantor, I went by chance into the "Bank Kredytowy". There the bookkeeper meets me, who wants to give me some pleasure, and he says to me:
— Would you like to see something?
— By all means, if it is something good? — let us see.
And he shows me a rich correspondence and documents of purely Jewish banks, written in the mother tongue. Only the difference is that these banks are not in Zagłębie but
— in the Kresy [eastern borderlands]. There those Jews have different notions: there, when one writes to Jews (not even to a cantor), one writes in the language that lives among the Jewish masses...
There, with "them" — he says — it will not happen that at a parents' meeting called by an organisation with such a resounding name as "Ha-Shomer ha-Leumi" not a single Yiddish word is heard, even if "their teeth break", as long as they do not use the "servant girl", the "market language"...
— Yes — I answer him — it is a sad truth, a great spiritual abyss lies between "us" and "them"...
———
And last but not least, in the last item of this column we tell of such things as will surely please our readers.
We have heard that the tax office (Finanz-Amt) has decided to call a conference of Jewish taxpayers, who are to state how much tax they are able to pay.
In the magistrate [town hall] a meeting of government representatives and municipal householders is to take place, to fix the date of the town council elections.
In Sosnowiec a consultation took place with the participation of representatives of the local Jewish banks. At the consultation it was decided that out of all the banks a large, powerful credit society should be created, which would be able to ease the economic situation of the Jewish merchants.
For some days the representative of the "Rodef Shalom" party in Radom has been staying in Będzin; he has taken upon himself the initiative to make peace between the "Aguda" and the Zionist Organisation. Both sides show willingness, and it is to be hoped that peace will come and the poor will, as every year, receive kimcha [Passover flour]...
— — — — — — — — — —
On closing this issue we received official information that the above-mentioned conferences and peace agreements will take place only next Wednesday...
Lawlessness
By the fence pasted with posters on Małachowskiego street several Jews are standing and reading a death notice (klepsydra) that has only just been pasted up.
Every so often[?] a burst of laughter rings out from the readers, so that passers-by stop to find out what is so loudly funny.
I too am among the curious, and soon it becomes clear to me what the crowd is about.
There one reads that the decea-sed "will be carried from the dead-house to the bet hayyim [cemetery]"...
The public argues among itself. Some say that this was written by a "Yiddishist"; the more sedate part, on the other hand, points out that it is only thanks to the ignorance of certain printing-house owners. If you still have any doubt about it — says one — then read this second poster:
"Cantor Tuvia ha-Kohon will sign [sic: "zigen" for "zingen", sing] synagogue pieces"...
The policeman keeping order dispersed the "zebranie" [gathering] in the street, and at that moment the thought runs through my mind:
— "When will the time come that the police also punish those who permit themselves to defile the Hebrew and the Yiddish language?"
Lectures for Merchants

[Sosnowiec — Economy and Trade.] (The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce has organised a cycle of lectures for the merchants of Zagłębie)
The Chamber of Commerce has taken upon itself a very desirable and useful work. The lectures which it has undertaken to hold for the merchants of Zagłębie are a very, very desirable and useful development, which the merchant circles may well welcome.
More than once we have already pointed to the necessity of just such lectures, and to the fact that every merchant needs them; we said that our merchants' and small traders' associations ought to take up this question, but unfortunately they paid no attention to it, and the question has remained all along at a dead point, because it was never solved.
Now that the Chamber of Commerce has taken upon itself this very useful work, it gladdens us greatly, and it remains only to wish it success in this field.
Our merchants are clever, our traders are sharp-witted and practical — and yet how helpless they are! Does not the slightest wind destroy them? Does not the smallest trickle of water wash them off the surface? We know, after all, what Jewish wealth, so to speak [?], looks like: after marrying off one child such a Jew becomes a pauper. Of course, on the one hand everything is inflated, not genuine, not real; one shows off so that the other fellow should think that one is sound, while in truth one is broken through and through, everything is rotten and rusted; and on the other hand such a Jew thinks he must imitate the other fellow in everything — whether he can or not, he must measure himself against the great and the rich and must have the same expenses that they have.
Who is to blame for this? Of course, they themselves. So the question arises: since they are to blame for all this, why do they not mend their ways, why do they not try to adopt another mode, another turn that would improve their situation, that would ease their existence? Unfortunately these people cannot help themselves here at all; they do not know it; for the most part, poor souls, they are as innocent as can be. The trouble here is only that the whole trade is a Menachem-Mendel-like affair [after Sholem Aleichem's luckless speculator]; its prospects are always painted in bright colours. The horizon is for him always an optimistic one, and it does not occur to him that a critical moment, a time of trouble, may come. In addition — and this is the main thing — these people almost never know how to calculate, in spite of the fact that every Jewish merchant imagines he has everything in his head, and when it comes to accounts he is quite an expert.
It has been shown several times already that the calculating of our merchants is never founded on firm foundations. The merchant knows only, plainly and simply, that his article costs him, let us say, one gulden [złoty], and if he wants to earn 15 per cent he must sell it for 1 gulden and 15 gr. A perfectly simple calculation, it seems, clear as day, that on the gulden he earns 15 gr. But there are other masters of reckoning who say that this „clear“ calculation is worthless, and they prove to you in black and white that here you are losing on the goods. How is that possible? Quite simply, say these people: as soon as you add up here what the shop, the taxes, the staff, etc. cost you, it will turn out that another 10 gr. are added to that one gulden. And here it is already clear to you that you have always deceived yourself in the reckoning, and that in this way you have quite often lost, and so it has gone on steadily, year in, year out, and our merchants could not understand where the hole comes from, and to this very day they do not see the deficit.
Do we not see that people trade and set themselves the most minimal profits, and on top of that hand over the goods on bills of exchange, and then run about for months until they manage to obtain cover; and often, when such a bill is got back, it looks as though one had received the great profit — and afterwards, as it is, you know what miracles one needs for the bill to survive in peace the days and the months, and may it rest in peace. And when all this has gone through well and fine, and you do not count the heart-pounding and the grief you have been through, you will see afterwards — once you take ink and pen in hand — that on the whole business you have, if not lost, certainly not earned.
Well, where then is the calculating and the good reckoning? How have you earned, and who has fooled whom — you the reckoning, or the reckoning you? And so one trades, and so one earns, and so one man takes from another his few hard-toiled-for gulden, though he does not know that it will come to this state, because he has made himself Menachem-Mendel calculations and on paper he has earned quite nicely.
Lectures for merchants — they are as necessary as life; just as he needs his existence, so the merchant needs them. Does he understand this? Does he know this? Does he feel this? Does he want to know this? He knows only that things are not good for him, he knows only that his situation is a bad one and that the crisis is crushing him; on the other hand he does not want to believe that he needs to listen to whoever is preaching; he is already out of the pen, has taken off his children's shoes, and he has no wish at all to go like a child into the cheder to hear lectures. „What do I know,“ thinks such a Jew, „what will he tell me here that is new? What will he do for me here? Anyway — if things were good, I would have managed my own little town [?] by myself; and if not — if things are bad again, he will surely not help me at all. So why make a fool of myself, why go and hear what people keep talking about in the world?“
With just such a tone a Jew dismisses it for you — and go do something with him.
It is therefore too little to say that the lectures are necessary; one must campaign for people to attend them, and in addition it is urgently necessary to publish propaganda literature in which the merchant should have instructive material before him.
Of course, because of the immaturity in this field, the lectures must be fitted into a very easy form and must be in the most elementary style. But at the same time one must not forget one thing: unfortunately we have more than 90% Jews who do not command the Polish language freely, and for them we must have Yiddish lectures. Moreover, we must always bear in mind that since we have before us quite a large number of traders who find their way only poorly in lectures generally, they must, even in Yiddish, be worked out simply enough and well illustrated so that he can chew them; otherwise they will arouse no interest in him and will be just as foreign to him as a Polish lecture.
The Chamber of Commerce is holding the cycle of lectures in Polish; the merchants' and small traders' associations must endeavour to have the same lectures arranged in Yiddish as well, because — it must not be forgotten — the lectures must for the most part be aimed at the less developed merchant and small trader, at the one with whom one must begin from aleph, those Jewish merchants whom one must now begin to teach just like a small child.
Our professional associations must come to an understanding on this question with the Chamber of Commerce; they must supply it with lecturers (prelegenci) who will be able to come to our merchant community with popular and influential [?] lectures in Yiddish. It does not matter how this is arranged technically — whether together with our professional associations or separately. The fact is that once the Chamber of Commerce has recognised the necessity of holding lectures for merchants, it is self-evident that they must be as comprehensible as possible, as well attended as possible and as popular as possible.
It seems that if anyone, then our merchants' and small traders' associations may not now, after the Chamber of Commerce has recognised the necessity of lectures for merchants, remain indifferent to this question, which so begs to be solved, to be developed, to be popularised among the most diverse strata of the civic population.
The floor now belongs to our professional institutions. Let us see how far their activity will reach, how far they will penetrate the broad masses of the Jewish trading circles.
R. Let.
Two merchants who defaulted on Łódź merchants for a quarter of a million złoty arrested on a train

[Katowice and Łódź — crime and trade.] Two merchants arrested on a train,
who left Łódź merchants stuck for a quarter of a million złoty.
The Katowice merchants Dawid [?] Blumen and Oskar Brausch, partners, travelled some time ago to Łódź to buy goods. Their last purchase came to more than a quarter of a million złoty.
Being known as solid merchants, their short-term bills of exchange were accepted in Łódź. Within a month this Katowice firm went bankrupt and let all the bills go to protest. The partners fled abroad.
One of the affected [?] Łódź merchants personally went [?] to Katowice, but nothing could be achieved. The swindled [?] merchants then lodged a complaint with the public prosecutor. Wanted notices were sent out all over Poland.
On Wednesday a police patrol at the Kalisz railway station in Łódź noticed 2 persons sitting in a second-class carriage whose appearance recalled the fugitive merchants Blumen and Brausch. When their papers were checked it turned out that one had a birth certificate in the name of Stanisław Kirsz and the other a birth certificate in the name of Mosze Krymen [?]. Both of them wanted to travel to Danzig. They had no passports, and since one cannot travel to Danzig without a passport, the fellows became suspect. They were taken off the train. At the investigation office it was established that these were indeed the wanted Katowice “defaulters”.
They were put in prison.
The Shirt of Happiness

[Literature — travel impressions of the Land of Israel; Degania.] By Gala Galaction.
The Shirt of Happiness.
We all seek it, and few of us believe at times that they have found it. Naturally, I too asked about it on my journey through the Promised Land. I asked everywhere: in Haifa, Jaffa, Rishon LeZion, Jerusalem and in Galilee... And remarkable it is that the more I wandered about the Holy Land, the more it seemed to me at certain moments that I myself was the owner of the wonderful shirt.
And so many days passed, until one evening — along the length of the Sea of Kinneret — I reached Degania, on the banks of the Jordan. I dropped in on the kvutza, which settled here almost 20 years ago, in the broad eucalyptus avenue.
Just then the men [?] and w[omen] [?] were returning from their field to rest. The estate covers some 1500 dunams, and the number of its worker-inhabitants is less than a hundred. Their whole farm, ringed with living walls, seemed as if lifted up by its pastoralism [?] and [—] in the evening colours and their magic. Larks flew up above the cypress tops in the [—] [?] which we earth-dwellers no longer found [?], and they looked like the burning arrows of the Psalmist.
A [—] rest of the fields enveloped [?] from the sapphire [?] and majestic heights [?] and deepened the shadow — the day's wages in the colony. Before we went into the colonists' dwellings we spent time in the workshops, in the cowsheds and the chicken coops. Everything one sees bears witness to diligence, to quick [?] toil and to great love for God's creation.
The colonists' horses and oxen are round and well-groomed [?], although they have worked the whole day; the c[ows] [?] are happy and pampered like the [lapdog] [?] of the ladies in Paris.
The garden — for beauty and greenery — is well tended.., according to a strictly calculated theory [?]. A cypress [hedge] [?] grows along its whole length and the evening roses penetrate here and there through its dark [?] branches. The bananas bloom [?] splendidly in the irrigation-canal area [?]. Poplars [?], cypresses in avenues and other trees grow in a certain order, caress the eye and awaken the diligence of the inhabitants.
The [scene] [?] is so enchanting that you no longer have the boldness to ask doubtfully... [—] if the shirt of happiness exists anywhere in our world, it is surely in the wardrobe of the colonists..
In the colony, which is run according to principles that neither I nor you know, the children grow up under the supervision of a group of educators and teachers. The children's rooms are the largest halls of the little “workers' republic”.
Above the great gallery [?], in the shade of light covers spread on pillars, under the blue air and lofty horizons, are the bedrooms, the playgrounds and the school benches of the children.
The Jordan, the Sea of Kinneret, mountains and amethyst backdrops [?] encircle in the evening hour the region in which a band [?] of our generation wants to create a new, better human being..
With such thoughts and moods I walked about [?], and on the shady path [?] of green trees and benches I met a teacher in a circle of little children.. This evening picture of rest captivated [?] me. The teachers, like the children, showed fire and will for play. They tell stories, laugh, wrestle and run...
In all this vegetation [?], in the [—]..., in their whole way of life and building there lies a spirit for which I have no words to explain it and to penetrate its depth.
I watch and reflect on these people... Have they really discovered the legendary shirt? Their appearance is simple and modest... devoted to physical labour, peasant labour and [—]. They have done away with [?] high-flown [?] talk, stormy [—] and disquieting questions... They are peasants, gardeners; they are comrades to the horses and oxen.
The good sense [?], the cheerful contentment [?], the sincerity of their small collective; the decision on many matters belongs to a council elected from among them, and each one for himself builds himself a well-ordered unity..
We took leave of the [—] brothers [?], laden with manifold and important [?] impressions. Are they going on a new road which will bring a happy reality in the future — or is it only a youthful dream and champagne foam [?], fleeting [—] every land and its exile-war [?] in Europe?
In any case — a grandiose and sublime fruit.. The Zionist ideal is beyond all discussion and doubt. One thing is firmly established: the Holy Land is being settled, prophecy returns and is fulfilled. The generation [?] of the future will again be at the ploughshare [?], at the [—] and at the seeds.
But what will be the fate of the social quests? Will calmer days come, which will allow the social philosophers broad research, [?] will the fields, the farms and the whole new wonderful organisation multiply?
Meanwhile we stand in a moment of blossoming enthusiasm! We stand again at “Parashat Bereshit”. Again Adam and Eve have transgressed [?] the oppressive prohibition. And in truth, where else, if not here, in the mountains, the mountains of the Bible and of dream, can one find the great prophets, the preachers of great ideals?
Will they not perhaps [?] find the shirt of happiness sought by all mankind on all roads and in all generations — which they have already found up to the crown [?] of exaltation [?], [—] admiration.
Islam and the Land of Israel.

[Article — Zionism; Islam, the Arabs and Europe.] By V. Jabotinsky [Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky, Pol. Włodzimierz Żabotyński].
(Conclusion.)

I do not write this in order to belittle the Arabs, or to mock [?] them. Of their warlike abilities I have no doubt. And if in their place there had stood even legions [?] ... [—] [?], the result would have been the same. In our time war is a scientific-financial [?] matter. Backward peoples are not up to it. At the first clash with Europe — if Europe truly and seriously wishes to carry out its will — not only will they not be able to hinder it in this, they will not even be able to put up any significant [?] resistance. And since they understand this, they make no attempt at all to wage war in earnest.

To this rule there are no exceptions. What looks like an exception confirms, when you look more closely, only the rule. This applies, for example, to the uprisings of the Senussi in Tripolitania. That was no revolt [?] against European power where it had already established itself, but unrest in the depths of the desert, where the Italians had not yet had the time, or the desire, to penetrate.

As soon as the Italians armed themselves [?] and arrived there [?], where it was necessary, there was suddenly no unrest there at all. We see the same thing, for example, also in the French zone of Morocco. The truly [?] occupied parts have submitted, but beyond these areas there are [—] areas, where until now there has been no government authority whatsoever, [—]. And only [?] there are the French compelled to send their serious expeditions. Europe received a serious blow in one place: in the Spanish zone of Morocco. But Spain as a whole, as we have seen, thereby [?] makes understandable the incompetence of the Spanish administration, and not, God forbid, the great strength of the Moors. And indeed it is so; this is also so correct and clear that my interpretations [?] and explanations are perhaps superfluous.

Nevertheless I wish now to mention just one case where Islam was really the victor: the last Greek-Turkish war. So as not to make my article too long, I permit myself to say briefly and simply that this event is no symbolic sign, no systematic sign.

It was an unusual [?] war between two small states, which were equal both in the size of their population and in their military technique. In it the [—] side lost, as often happens, which had at its disposal [?] [—] of its own [—], and was compelled to wage an over-[—] war. This has nothing to do either with Islam or with Europe. All the talk that "little [?] Greece stood against the whole of Europe" is empty chatter. The English government sympathised with Greece, but gave it neither English soldiers nor armoured cars. On the contrary, Turkey had on its side the sympathies of Italy, and not only of Italy; their [?] armament the Turks received from the [—], and what they still [?] lacked, from the Bolsheviks. But if tomorrow it should come to a clash between those same Bolsheviks and that same Kemal, Turkey will without doubt be ground to ashes. And if the Balkan war repeats itself in a few years, Turkey will probably be smashed just as in the year 1912, and for the same reasons.

But this has nothing to do with our problem.

Turkey itself has given the best proof that "Islamism" does not concern [?] it at all, and that it wishes and is able not to meddle in the affairs of Damascus, the Jordan [—]. In the reckonings between Europe and the Arabs — insofar as they interest us — both the Turks and the Indian Muslims can simply be struck out. In just the same way one can put aside the argument about the "weakness" of Europe, which [—] is quite "not able" in a matter [?] that Europe [?] is "present" to accomplish; and in the [—] and on the Syrian coast [?] of the Mediterranean, and further on from Anatolia [?] to Basra, there are no forces whatsoever that would be able to hinder Europe's actions, or even to hold them back — naturally, if Europe is seriously resolved to act in this or that direction.

Europe is in a position where it is "able" [to do] everything it "wants". Not only Europe as a great whole — such a Europe does not exist at all — but even every single Great Power by itself — and among them England too — is "able" and in a position to do everything it wants, as long as it does not penetrate into a zone that is assigned to the jurisdiction of another European Great Power.

Therefore the only question is: does Europe "want", and what does Europe actually want?

One must admit that this question is very complicated and difficult, more complicated than the problem of the legendary [?] power of Islam; but this question can, as has been shown [?], be answered at least in the affirmative.
Hebrew Pronunciation (HaMivta HaIvri)

[Book review — the Hebrew language and its pronunciation; followed by an editorial notice.] By Ze'ev Jabotinsky, "HaSefer" publishers, Paris.

Among no nation and tongue does there prevail such an indifferent attitude to the form of the language as among us towards Hebrew. Once people were very interested in the question of "plene"—"defective" spelling; unfortunately, to this day, even at the already famous [?] "HaTsefira", this "plene-and-defective" problem has not been solved. It is no wonder: the priests on Mount Scopus among the members of the Palestinian Language Committee (Va'ad HaLashon) are full to overflowing with other lofty political [?] questions, while others apparently lack the authority to be able to decide the question.

Well, the written language is more or less a matter for the select few. But speech — especially lately, when Hebraisation has taken on broad dimensions — has become, as they say, a real problem.

Once pronunciation, the dialect, provoked a great controversy: "Ashkenazi or Sephardi". The latter prevailed, because that is how people speak in the Land of Israel, the place that must regulate and be a guide for life in the lands of the Diaspora. With that the question is still far [?] from solved, because the former Hebrew speakers, wishing to adapt themselves to the way people speak "there", have completely broken the dialect, and instead of the [—] sound of that dialect what comes out is a kind of "cacophony".

In the midst of the fire of political work, Jabotinsky has devoted himself to the question of pronunciation and has favoured us with a successful [?] handbook entitled "HaMivta HaIvri" (Hebrew Pronunciation). In this little book there are first of all discussions of the related [?] languages. He [—] with you the pronunciation of the alphabet, he teaches you a chapter in the rules of the Sephardi dialect, which is bound up with a melody [?], so that when you try to read and speak according to his instructions you must admit that "for this pronunciation we prayed".

All this is done by Jabotinsky in a very easy form, and the handbook is accessible to every Hebrew speaker.
Ben-Porat.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tzav, Shabbat HaGadol)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and stylised by Y. Y.
Parshat Tzav

a) „Command Aaron, saying” (6:2).
„Rabbi Shimon said: Scripture must urge most of all where there is a loss of money.” Rashi.
On this difficult[?] saying there are various pearls[?]:
1.
From the following verse, „This is the law of the burnt-offering”, the Talmud infers that studying the portion of the burnt-offering is as good as offering a burnt-offering. Well, such a[?] law cannot please the priests, who take a share of the sacrifices. Simply: the public will prefer to fulfil its duty by studying rather than by giving... Because of the loss of money, the financial loss to the priests that the law of „This is the law of the burnt-offering” represents for them, they must be urged — „saying” — to pass it on and not pretend to have forgotten... Imrei Shefer.
2.
Once the rabbinate used to[?] involve a loss of money. One could reach the rabbinic chair only through money... Well, in such a time no rabbi felt like preaching moral reproof; he trembled for his own skin... In such a time he must be urged: he should not look [around] but tell the public what he has to say — „saying”. Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
3.
According to the Zohar this „command” means — idolatry. On this Rabbi Shimon says that „for all generations” — i.e. today — when idolatry no longer exists, its place has been taken[?] by the loss of money, by money... And just as the prophets once stormed against idol-worship, so today one must urge concerning money-worship... Nehmad mi-Zahav.
4.
„Scripture must urge most of all where there is a loss of money” — when a Jew performs a communal[?] mitzvah not honestly, not intending[?] only the mitzvah, he spends money on a mitzvah but does it with ulterior motives, thinking[?] that the mitzvah is the money — a loss of money — and he remains bald on this side and bald on that side... and so[?] one must[?] take care that he not spend[?] money for nothing... Torat Uziel.

b) „This is the law of the burnt-offering” (ibid.).
The burnt-offering is „entirely consumed”, only for God; even the priests have no share in it. „This is the law” — the Torah too must be like a burnt-offering: only for God, not for other self-serving purposes... Be'er Mayim Hayyim.

c) „And this is the law of the peace-offering” (6:11 as printed; should be 7:11).
The Midrash Tanhuma says on this verse that the commandment of sacrifices was given to the Jews because... they had accepted the Torah.
2.[?]
— „The world stands on three things: on the Torah, on the [Temple] service and on acts of kindness.” Well, before the Jews accepted the Torah the world stood on one leg: acts of kindness — and on one leg a table can stand too. After the giving of the Torah another leg was added: Torah — and on two legs nothing can stand any more; so they already prepared[?] the third leg: the service, sacrifices. Ohel Yaakov.

d) „This is the law of the meal-offering” (6:7).
In the past, when a Jew sinned — if he was rich he brought a rich sacrifice, and a poor man — a poor meal-offering. Today, when one can fulfil one's duty merely with „And this is the law of the meal-offering”, i.e. by studying the portions on the sacrifices and then saying „May it be Your will, as if I had offered” — and if it is „May it be Your will”, if it costs no money and one fulfils the duty by saying it, one may as well be generous[?] and say „May it be Your will, as if I had offered a sin-offering”; after all it costs no more than saying „May it be Your will, as if I had offered a meal-offering”. Today we are all rich men: we offer — with our mouths — only sin-offerings and burnt-offerings, and no poor meal-offerings... No'am Megadim.

e) „He that offers the sacrifice of his peace-offerings shall bring his offering” (7:29[?]).
With other sacrifices, such as burnt-offerings[?] and sin-offerings, which come for sins, one does not wish anyone „he shall bring his offering” — better that he not sin and not bring the sacrifices; only with peace-offerings, which are a free-will gift, does one wish him that he go on bringing such. Nahal Kedumim.

f) „This is the law of the burnt-offering, of the meal-offering, and of the sin-offering, and of the guilt-offering, and of the consecration-offering” (6:37 as printed; should be 7:37).
„This is the law of the consecration [lit. fillings]” — he who becomes full of his own Torah, who gets a stuffed belly from his little bit of learning and puffs himself up — of such Torah it says: „for the sin-offering and for the guilt-offering”, only for sin... Eshel Avraham.
• • •
Every sin demands an effort from a person. [But for pride] he need do nothing at all, only lie stretched out behind the stove, [—][?] and persuade himself: I am great... and how great... Midrash Pinhas.

Shabbat HaGadol.
g) „Had Israel kept two Sabbaths, they would have been redeemed at once.”
„Whoever reports a saying in the name of its author brings redemption to the world.” Well, the rabbis in their sermons mostly deliver „borrowed” sermons, taken from other books, so they are delaying the redemption... Therefore, if one kept[?] just the two Sabbaths, Shabbat HaGadol and Shabbat Teshuvah, by not letting the rabbis speak — „they would have been redeemed at once” — the redemption would surely have come immediately... From Rabbi R' Shmelke of Nikolsburg [Mikulov].
• • •
Why does one say „And a redeemer shall come to Zion” after a sermon? — Because the sermon is presumably a „borrowed” one and it delays the redemption, so one prays: „And a redeemer shall come to Zion” — may it do no harm that the preacher delays the redemption... Helkat[?] Hershel[?].
• • •
Therefore one says „And a redeemer shall come to Zion” after a sermon — because we have been waiting for the Messiah thousands upon thousands of years and cannot wait for him patiently, so we are told to take a lesson from the rabbi's sermon: we also wait impatiently for him to finish, it lasts as long as the Jewish exile... and when we finally live to see him finish, we hope that „a redeemer shall come to Zion”, that the Messiah too will come at last... Yikhbar Tzav.

h) „Ta'am ke-ikkar” [flavour counts as the substance], or: the simpleton [tam] is the main thing..
A rabbi once preached on Shabbat HaGadol on the Talmudic topic of „ta'am ke-ikkar”. A householder, an ignoramus, comes up to him and asks him: why did he make the tam [simpleton] the main thing („ta'am ke-ikkar”) and not the wise son?..
— Indeed[?], I really made a mistake[?] — answers the rabbi — the main thing is indeed the one „who does not know how to ask”... Loyt ve-Levanah[?].
It Will Get Worse...

That is just our bitter luck. We get no grace [?] from our ministers; when they take up their posts, they give us nothing but salvations and consolations.
But soon all hopes are torn out [?], the country wrestles with the severe crisis, everywhere despair and resignation reign, little by little the minister's optimism evaporates [?] too, and coming before the Budget Committee he starts singing an elegy..
"It will get worse," the Finance Minister Matuszewski announced to us.
It is an old story.
We have already heard this refrain once before, also from a minister, in the Chjeno-Piast [?] times.
Witos at that time received a delegation of officials who had come to complain about their hard lot, and he too answered them laconically: it will get even worse...
And the population, which is being choked under the burden of all kinds of taxes and unemployment, will also receive this announcement with a bitter smile, and one will ask the other:
— What could possibly be worse?
When small children come to the public schools barefoot and naked and faint during lessons from hunger, because their mothers cannot give them a piece of bread for breakfast.
When the newspapers record every day horrifying reports about mothers who abandon their children because of hunger and want.
When long-standing, solid livelihoods are ruined, and hundreds of thousands of workers and employees are thrown out onto the pavement.
From one end of the country to the other the cry of woe carries. Bitter despair, the suicide epidemic, seize ever more well-rooted [?] circles.
And if it is about us — that is not even relevant.
We certainly have nothing left to lose.
For we have already been left naked and destitute; we have been peeled bare and left standing naked.
All the earlier etatist [?] experiments, all the social ordinances, all the "ingeses" [?] and "ovshangdns" [?] [unclear terms] have radically wiped out [?] our little bit of desire and taste [?].
And now comes the minister on whom we placed so many hopes, who has a big party behind him in the Sejm, and presents us with such a marriage contract:
"It will get worse."
No, dear Mr. Minister, you will no longer frighten us Jews, because worse it cannot get.
Y. L. Sh.
The "Black" Jews in Abyssinia / They live like the Jews of old in the time of the Temple.

A beautiful, heartwarming legend — and yet the truth. This is the story of the "black" Jews in Abyssinia, the Falashas, as they are called there.
The life of the Falashas is in many respects the same as that of all the other, half-wild tribes in Abyssinia. But one great difference sets them apart from those tribes — and that is their religion.
Isolated in a remote corner, they keep the Torah as they received it when they were driven out of the Land of Israel generations upon generations ago, surrounded by "black" Christians.
They keep all the holidays except Hanukkah and Purim. The Sabbath is holy to them and they spend the whole day in the synagogue; they prepare special dishes, which they eat in congregation between the prayers.
Passover is an especially important holiday for them. They do not eat leavened bread then, nor do they drink mead [?] or beer, which are popular drinks with them all year round. Passover lasts seven days, but three days before the holiday they already stop eating leavened bread or other leavened foods, and make do only with dried peas and broad beans. On the eve of Passover nothing is eaten; one waits until the priest sacrifices a sheep on the altar. On that day everyone gathers in the courtyard of the synagogue before sunset, and the priest sacrifices the sheep in the name of the whole community. The ceremony is performed with great splendour and with all the particulars prescribed in the Pentateuch. The meat of the sacrifice is eaten by the priest and his assistants with unleavened bread.
The Falashas prepare for Passover exactly like "our" Jews. They wash, scour and clear out the whole house. The clothes, the houses and the dishes are all cleansed.
The Falashas keep the law of circumcision, but never on the Sabbath, because it is considered work. They also "redeem" the firstborn and give money for it to the priest or to the synagogue.
The "black" Jews celebrate the festival of Shavuot twice a year. The first Shavuot falls 50 days after the last day of Passover, and the second — 50 days after Sukkot. On Shavuot everyone gathers on a mountain under the open sky, where they perform certain religious ceremonies and eat their meals together.
Besides the religious holidays they also have half-holidays every month. The tenth of each month is regarded as a day of remembrance of Yom Kippur; the twelfth of Shavuot; the fifteenth — of Passover and Sukkot; they also bless the new moon every month.
There are no special classes or privileged lineages among the "black" Jews. The priests and Torah scholars are respected for their learning and wisdom, but not because they are especially holy people. They work like everyone else in the village where they live.
Their wedding ceremony is only partly [?] religious; they know nothing of a betrothal ring or a ketubah. The bridegroom and bride come together before two or more witnesses and the parents, [and declare] that they become husband and wife.
Mostly they marry at the age of 18 to 20. Although the Pentateuch does not forbid it, polygamy is not permitted, and one may not keep concubines either. Family life is very beautiful and pure.
Divorce is permitted. In such a case one comes before a judge or the village elder and declares before the elders [?] that the couple is divorced. This is done in the presence of the couple's parents.
The Jews in Abyssinia have suffered terrible persecutions and pogroms. The missionaries, who converted the other tribes to Christianity, could not "get their teeth into" [?] the Jews. Out of great anger, and in order to win favour [?] with their followers, they incited a massacre of the Jews. Some 70 or 80 years ago it nearly came to the Jews there being exterminated altogether. The Falashas did not know that there were other Jews in the world. Their situation was desperate, and many were forced to convert. But they kept their faith in secret, like the Marranos of Spain of old.
Now the situation is better; there is no hatred of Jews there, but economically and culturally they are very poor, just as the population around them is poor.

The Rabbi's pupils insolently humiliate the cantor in public.

[Będzin — religion, community.] Last Sunday the following scandalous incident took place in our town:
At the Friedrich family a wedding was held, to which cantor M. Żupowicz [?] went to the groom to perform his office. When Mr Żupowicz came in to the groom, he saw the young men whispering with the groom. Later it turned out that the young fellows had incited the groom to have no dealings whatsoever with the cantor. The groom carried out the order of his friends and did not want to let [?] his (the cantor's) name be written into the ketubah.
The real scandal, however, took place only later, when the cantor approached the groom so that he should perform the kinyan. Then the “Torah-loyal” lads came out with [sharp] tongues and shouted: “Out of here, you insolent [—], we are pupils of the local Rabbi, whose honour we are defending”..
It is characteristic that the wedding guests, mostly Ger Hasidim, did not react to the public humiliation of the town cantor, and the cantor left mourning and with his head covered [in shame]..
Has the Rebbe, too, no longer any say?..

[Będzin — yeshivas, Hasidim.] The emissary of the Baranowicze yeshiva “Ohel Torah” came to us at the editorial office and related the following:
I am — he says — an emissary of the Baranowicze yeshiva. Travelling [?] to Zagłębie, I took with me letters from the Chofetz Chaim, from the Rabbi of Wilno R' Chaim Ozer Grodzenski and from the Rebbe of Ger, may he live long and well. Over a few days I gave sermons in the local beit midrash and in “Ahavat Chesed”, and everywhere my words had an effect, and the worshippers donated large sums for the benefit of the yeshiva.
This Sunday — he relates further — I went into the Agudah [?] bank. I thought that there, among them, upon showing a letter from the Rebbe of Ger, they would receive me with a friendly face and I would get the biggest donation for the yeshiva. But I made a big mistake: they hardly wanted to receive me there at all, and later, when I drew attention to this, I received great “honour” from the director himself, who in his own person grabbed me by the collar and threw me out of the bank”...

Will, Hope and Courage.

(At a time of rest and composure. — Let us take a thought for how we look. — Is there a way out of the serious situation?)

So, one way or another, we have brought Passover into the house; true, it did not arrive easily, and if Passover has always been the hardest holiday, all the more so today, when the crisis and hunger and poverty occupy the most honoured place in our Jewish world.
All year long one is harried and tormented, racing over stick and stone; one has no time to catch one's breath and cannot take stock of where one stands in the world; one bullet chases the next, one wheel chases after the other. It is no longer as it once was, when people lived quietly and modestly; whether one needed more or less, whether one was rich or poor, each felt differently, spent his time differently, rested differently.
Since the outbreak of the war the whole order and system of human life has changed, so that it is very hard to manage to lead a normal, quiet and modest life; something drives us, something chokes us so that we cannot catch our breath, one thing chases the next; whether one earns or not, whether one has something to do or not, either way one must rush and toil. Hard, very hard has all that become which is called life, existence, livelihood.
And therefore people have never looked forward so eagerly to a holiday as now, when one wants to throw off the whole yoke and burden, to breathe quietly, to rest and to consider future prospects. And when one begins to rest, it is exactly like a weak person after an illness who, the longer it goes, begins to feel ever weaker: when one comes to oneself, when one begins to see in what kind of world one finds oneself, only then does one see what is lacking in order to get well, in order to heal from the illness.
We find ourselves in the same situation: when a holiday comes, when one has time to reflect, one comes to the realisation that it would be right to do this and that in order to make the[?] body healthy. And therefore it is understandable when we see that various institutions in Zagłębie have moved their general meetings to Chol Hamoed, when the Jew has thrown off the heavy yoke and the weekday dust and can, with composure, consider and analyse how he looks, how his institutions and societies look; he can thus carry out a kind of audit. And then, when one comes to oneself, when one begins calmly to think, calmly to grasp, calmly to analyse, only then does one see how sick the body is, and only then can it be logically established how to heal the illness.
Our body is sick, but it can be healed. Our institutions are weak, but there are medicines for them. Our parties stand on chicken legs ["piste'kh" — probably a misprint for "fislekh"], but there is a way to fortify them, to strengthen them.
So let us not fool ourselves; let us look reality in the eye, and then we shall see that we have not one healthy vein; everything is rotten, everything is sick and weak and mouldy and aged. But there is nevertheless one consolation in all this: everything can be healed, everything can be restored[?], everything can be improved, strengthened and beautified. One need do no more than set out on the straight road and think logically, grasp logically, reason logically — then we shall find a way out of everything.
We need not be ashamed; better still, we must not be ashamed of the cure we need. We may say openly and honestly that we see order nowhere, that our social institutions are far from in order, that the economic-professional associations limp much, much [unclear word], and that the philanthropic institutions are in a state where the Master of the Universe should protect and save. We may say everything openly and honestly to ourselves, and we may appeal to conscience and to fairness and to public opinion: let everything be known, so that people understand how to help themselves, how to rescue themselves, how to bring our communal interests to a decent appearance.
At the same time we must not forget one thing: just as we lack many institutions without which we cannot manage and which every normal people has, so we also have institutions that we ought to liquidate, because they stand on sick foundations, and such a luxury we certainly cannot afford today. So let everything be audited during the days of Chol Hamoed, and let it be decided and established once and for all which institutions must be dissolved and which we need. And then we shall be consistent[?] and steadfast: whatever has to go to dissolution[?] shall be stopped[?] and dismissed from the Jewish street; and the institutions we need — those we shall help, those we shall build up[?], and into them shall be breathed fresh courage, fresh spirit, fresh strength and a fresh source of life.
We must conduct ourselves on a par with decent people, so that no one can reproach us with unheard-of defects that nobody can agree with. Granted, had we had our Jewish self-governments as we once imagined them, there would have been work for the representatives of the kehilla representation, so that if they had brought order even only in that field it would already have been worthwhile; but all of it turned into a soap bubble, so that there too an audit must be carried out, and in this case there is no other counsel but to audit ourselves, to control ourselves, to carry out an audit ourselves.
A people must never lose itself; however wretched[?] its condition, it must be strong, mighty[?] and steadfast. When one loses one's head, when one lets one's hands drop, there is no life, and where there is no life there is no initiative; these are signs of annihilation, signs of dying out, of decay[?] and chaos[?]. But to that we cannot be compared: when we had nothing left, we still had hope; when we had lost everything, we nevertheless believed in trust [in God], and that has preserved us in all times and in all generations, and therefore it is so hard for us — this stiff-necked people — to perish[?].
We truly find ourselves now in a very serious and tense situation; we feel it keenly, and therefore let us now, in the days of Chol Hamoed, consider our difficult situation with full seriousness and composure.
Trade, our most vital nerve, is shattered, so that hardly any signs of life remain; the artisan class is ruined and destroyed, and no way out is seen to rescue the fallen, gravely impoverished[?] people; the workers are helpless and hungry. Certainly this is terrible, certainly it is a frightful catastrophe that the whole world[?] must reckon with; but one must not lose heart, one must not lose courage and trust.
The most important thing, then, is that we remain steadfast, constant, firm, and maintain disciplined order.
We must only not drift[?]; we need only remain firm and go on the straight road, then we shall tread it out and find the straight way out. Let us only will it — that is the basic factor[?]; the will is strong and powerful and nothing will be stronger than it. The mightiest and greatest thing in the world is the will, and with it hope and courage, and this good[?] triad[?] can break iron, undermine, break through[—], and therefore we shall remember well[?] the will, hope and courage.
Dr. Patori[?].
For a Bit of Consolation...

[Humour — feuilleton.] (A small feuilleton).
The news that the epidemic of "thinness" has gone bankrupt [?], and that the time of "plumpness" is coming, ought to arouse true joy among us.
As for our wives, you need not wonder that it is precisely now that this caprice has arisen [?] among them. As the saying goes: "It is an old story, and yet it always stays new" [after Heine].
That is the irony of life for you.
In the "sated" years our wives tormented [?] themselves with starving and keeping fasts, so that their souls barely held out inside them.
And now, in the "hunger years", they have got their real appetite.
At the time when money was plentiful and goods were in over-abundance, when the shelves and warehouses were breaking under the overload [?], our wives clung to the cult of "nakedness".
Today, for our many sins, when money is not to be had, when factories are closing, the workers are being laid off ["reduced"], the female sex [?] has now begun to drag onto itself as many garments as possible.
But it does not matter. Thanks to this we shall now have no "tishtshkes" [?], no skeletons, but real wives, as the verse says: "And he took a wife of fullness" [mock-biblical: "vayikah eshet m'le'otav"]...
So there is no (need to worry [?]); true, we have a severe crisis, we are going through a very [?] bitter time, but a bit of consolation we have lived to see.
Our wives have repented; they are becoming again what they actually ought to be...
P. Sh. ["Pasach-Shin"].
Spring and Life.

[Essay — reflections for spring and Passover.] L. Szpigelman [the paper's editor].
(Thoughts).
Now, when the snow has long since slid down from the fields, and after the naked earth has drawn the beautiful purple mantle over itself, we are sure that the heavy, cold winter is over and that its place is beginning to be taken by the beautiful and pleasant spring with all its virtues and caprices.
Spring! — oh, what beautiful memories this single word holds within it; with how many recollections and how much dew of youth is this word, spring, bound up; how much courage and youthful spirit spring has given the world.
Spring awakens mankind, spring brings light and life and hope to all living creatures that are found across the beautiful, wide world. Spring welcomes the sun, which we receive with so much love and warmth.
Spring is dear and precious to us because b e f o r e it we bore the yoke of the heavy, long and grey winter, which has become so thoroughly tiresome to us, and mankind can hardly wait for its end, one can hardly endure it, one can hardly hurl the heavy giant down from human shoulders. Spring is also a pleasant guest to us because it ushers in the beautiful, bright summer, which so glorifies the world and calls and beckons every living being to come out of its narrow cage [klatka] and go to meet the bright sun; and as if by a magnetic force every living creature tears itself out under the great, wide heavenly canopy, where everything that lives and breathes finds its refreshing sap. And the sun — as soon as it appears, we all embrace it, and we hug it and caress it and kiss it, and then we would gladly have all our loved ones and those close to us around us; and if we have lost someone of our close fellow men, we are ready to bring them back to life, if only we had the strength for it, so that we could all share together in the treasures of glorious nature.
Spring is the vestibule, the corridor, the outpost that leads us into the summery atmosphere, which announces to us the good tidings that the beautiful, bright summer will soon arrive with all its splendours, with all its magic aromas.
And a rare thing: as soon as we feel these swallows on our shoulders, as soon as we scent their steps from afar, we are at once refreshed with young dew of life, regardless of age, period and years. As soon as the sun appears, as soon as it sends out its "glistening" [?] rays, every living being begins to think differently, to feel differently, to comprehend differently, to live differently and to observe differently the mystery-filled wonder and the riddle of the world.
Spring has the wonderful power to fuse together all living creatures and to breathe into them the dew of youth and an abundance of life-spirit. Everything that lives and breathes is drawn with a rare intuition towards life and towards the joy of life.
• • •
Spring and life — what is spring, and what is life? Can one really distinguish the one from the other? Can one, for instance, imagine what a spring looks like without life, or conversely a life without [?] spring — that the real, unartificial spring should be hidden, screened from the sight [?] of the human eye? Is that a thing within possibility? Can that be a natural phenomenon? Is not the one without the other an imitation, a pretence? Just as there can be no life without air, exactly so there can be no life without spring.
And if we nevertheless — if we live without spring, it is no life; it is an imitation, a pretence, a shadow of life. Life in this case has not been killed, not poisoned completely, but that does not yet mean that such a life is called life, is called having meaning and understanding and awareness of life. It is a life of no-choice, which is approaching its downfall, and it goes without saying that such a kind of life we cannot call life, we cannot call existence.
This very life is ugly and repugnant; hardly have harmfulness and misfortune crept in there. Such a life is like "against your will you live" [Mishnah, Avot 4:22; printed "בעל ברחך"]: one lives because one cannot die, and such a life has no meaning, no content, no spirit, no form, no shape.
Beautiful is the true, primitive life, from which there gushes, as from a spring, freshness and purity and vigour all together; and when life flows on like this, without painful disturbances, one after another, it does not know how to distinguish between old and young, between poor and rich. Life bubbles with freshness, and there is no boundary to separate. Healthy, vigorous life knows nothing of time and term; for life there are no rules, no forms; it flows and pours itself out with a crystal purity.
And this life is like spring. Just as the beautiful, bright and crystal-pure life adorns and glorifies mankind with its good deeds, exactly so does glorious spring nature refresh the living creatures that are found in every corner of the globe.
Now, when we stand on the threshold of spring, when the little birds begin to sing their song to nature, it becomes so pleasant to the soul and good at heart that it seems as if spring were one long chain leading mankind into eternal, endless distance. Spring intoxicates every living being found on earth, and they all go out to meet it, each with its song, each with its love-song, each with its praises and hymns.
— Spring is just like life: everyone can enjoy it according to his understanding, possibility and need [?],
Small Remarks on Big Matters

[Będzin — railways; labour courts.]
The Zagłębie towns and the express ("courier") trains
What doesn't one get used to[?]! People could never in their lives have imagined what all they could get used to.
Who does not remember how it looked a year ago, when it was said that the express trains would no longer stop in Będzin. Like a legend from the Thousand and One Nights it seemed, like a fantasy, like a utopia that could never be realised. The news was, after all, put before the Będzin citizen. People reckoned that the reports were tendentious, the work of newspaper reporters; nobody took it seriously, nobody dwelt on it, nobody believed any of it, and it passed. And when, after the reports had been confirmed, each of us felt that it was nevertheless impossible to believe that the express train could run past the Będzin station and not stop — then there were people who said: come, one must go to the station, one must see with one's own eyes whether it is true that the train, passing through the town, will skip the station. And when people saw it, saw it with their own eyes, it became for them a riddle once again, a riddle that cannot be solved; and then people established with certainty that it cannot stay like this, that it must not stay like this, that the express trains, which stopped in Będzin when the town was a small shtetl, would now, after the town has grown considerably, certainly, most certainly stop. And with vexation and shame it was decided: well then, lost; one must start to intervene and lobby ("khlapotshen"), and then there remained: surely everything will be good again, this defect will be forgotten. That it was not foreseen[?] that the question would become so serious that means would have to be applied[?] — that occurred to nobody; nobody could have imagined it in his thoughts.
And once people had got used to this defect, it turns out that it is good this way and fine this way and this is how it must be; people even got used to going in harness[?], and can no longer imagine that it should and could be otherwise.
Now, not long ago we reported here that under the new timetable, which comes into force on 15 May, the following stations will drop out as such: Będzin, Dąbrowa and Zawiercie. That means the decision has already been taken in agreement with the ministry, so that one will not be able to arrive at or depart from the above-mentioned[?] towns by the express trains.
We know that in the present time, in the 20th century, the slogan in circulation is to make the conditions of existence easier, faster and more comfortable; here, on the contrary, it is exactly the reverse: with us they look for ways to make it harder. True, it is explained by the trains going at a faster pace; but do we not know that one minute's stop is a mere trifle ("dikduk aniyes")? That between one station and the next the engine driver can easily make up that one minute? Is it not ridiculous to argue like this about a question so very important for every town dweller?
We hold that the Zagłębie towns must not be remiss; all possible means must nevertheless be applied to obtain[?] that the trains go on stopping at the stations where they stopped 20—30 years ago; and that in the course of this period the towns have not shrunk into villages but have constantly developed and grown into large commercial centres with tens of thousands of inhabitants, who bring the government considerable revenues.
A country must reckon with such towns; a government must reckon with such a number of citizens, and must come to the citizens' aid and give them the possibility of easing their conditions of existence — and not, on the contrary, think how to make them harder.
We must exert ourselves: the institutions and the authorities, the societies and the municipal power and the industrialists — all must be interested in removing[?] the enormous injustice done to the Zagłębie towns by not giving them the possibility of using the international express trains.
We must not grow tired; we must even apply our iron patience and make possible what the town needs, what the citizens need for their comfort and their existence.
Będzin and the labour courts
Another question interests us to deal with in this place. This matter concerns Będzin alone. It is about the labour courts. Labour courts exist both in Sosnowiec and in Dąbrowa, whereas Będzin is exempt from such a court; that is, not really that one does not make use of them, but that if a Będzin worker has to sue his Będzin employer, he must turn to the Dąbrowa court and [—] both the worker and the other party must wait in Dąbrowa until their case is heard.
The question arises: is this consistent? Is it logical, practical and understandable? Must it really be so that Będzin should have to be "blackened"[?] in Dąbrowa? Let us imagine that a journeyman has some dispute or other with a master craftsman. Is it right that the master craftsman, who is a day-labourer, should spend his day in Dąbrowa and wait until his turn comes, and meanwhile he has lost a day's livelihood? Must it be so? It thus[?] happens quite often that over trivial matters people are dragged around the labour courts several times. At home it would be only half a misfortune, one manages somehow; but away from home it involves both expense and a great deal of time.
It is no difficult question at all for this matter to be settled in favour of the Będzin population, in favour of the inhabitants of Będzin. And further, the same: Będzin is surely not some outlying village that should have to belong to Dąbrowa.
Będzin can afford to have such a court in the town for itself, where all disputes could be settled. It simply does not look good before the authorities[?] when we display so much indifference and apathy. A town — once it has its own employers and employees, it must also have a court for them, and need not at all stand[?] on the mercy of its neighbours...
We are sure — though we are not very well versed in the question — that nobody from the public circles has come to demand, this time, that we too should have such a court; and in that case nobody is obliged to know that it should and could be otherwise, that it should and could be arranged otherwise for the inhabitants of Będzin.
Everyone must demand his right, and everything must be used for the benefit of those for whom the institution was created. It is surely nonsense that Będzin employers and employees should have to spend their days in Dąbrowa, while the same thing could quite easily and considerably[?] more conveniently be done in Będzin, that is, at home, in the town where one lives and earns.
So one must not remain indifferent; one must look at every phenomenon with open eyes and see to it that what the people and the population need is improved.
Będzin, which is independent in every field, must therefore absolutely demand for itself a branch of the existing labour courts.
We must do our part: we must demand, we must give reasons, we must prove that such an institution is as necessary for us as for Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec for their towns. It is, after all, a people's institution, and as such it must meet the needs of the broad strata of the population.
R. Let.
On Journeyman Examinations

(Important clarifications and remarks).
In accordance with the provisions of the Guild Law (Art. 155), every workshop worker who wishes to obtain the title of journeyman (czeladnik, "tshelodnik") must pass a special examination. Journeymen who have no diploma are recognised as unskilled ("black") labourers and never have any possibility of becoming independent masters and employing or teaching apprentices ("terminators", apprentice boys).
The special situation of the Jewish working class, which is not represented in large-scale industry and is in general not admitted to any public (state or municipal) work at all, compels[?] every qualified Jewish journeyman sooner or later to become self-employed; and it is truly a characteristically wretched[?] phenomenon that even the leftist [—] ("shbligke"[?]), who constitute the pillars of the Jewish professional class unions, the combative cadres in the eternal struggle against the class enemy — the employer — pass over the trouble[?] of the examinations in cold blood, when he [the worker] gets a "Singer" machine on instalments and a bit of credit at the small shopkeeper's[?]...
But that has nothing to do with the matter. By the way, it is well worth noting it, if only because a number of trade unions propagandise among the Jewish working youth not to prepare[?] for the journeyman examination, and thereby they cause the qualified Jewish worker one of the greatest wrongs. For sooner or later every working person, willy[?]-nilly, will have to conform to the Industry Law, and until[?] the period of grace (the "hanokhe-termin") passes for the journeymen who attended no special vocational schools and, in general, no public elementary schools.
The whole[?] journeyman examination is bound up with a series of difficulties which the Jewish worker has so far (through no fault of his own) had no opportunity to "remove" or to meet. Not to speak[?] of professional knowledge — there have in general been no courses among us that would enable the Jewish working youth to acquire all the necessary knowledge demanded of it before the examination commission, such as: correct writing and reading of Polish, elementary knowledge and arithmetic (calculation); political economy, history, economic geography and in general secular and social education, etc.
Hence, indeed, the regrettable fact that to this very day not a single Jewish worker has registered for the journeyman examination at all, and thereby the telling[?] hypothesis of interested experts is confirmed, that with the present generation of artisans craftsmanship among Jews will come to an end altogether.
Because of the provisions[?] laid down in the Guild Law in connection with the regular[?] journeyman examinations, all 17 Chambers of Crafts in Poland in their time undertook a joint action at the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, by virtue of the authorisation[?] of the said Art. 155, to the effect that candidates (apprentices, "terminators") who had not completed any vocational supplementary schools for reasons not dependent on them should also be admitted to the journeyman examination. In the Dz. Ust. [Dziennik Ustaw, Journal of Laws] No. 59 of 26 "sherpien" [sierpień, August] 1930, item 477, there appeared an ordinance of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, in agreement with the Ministry of Education, which regulates the matter according to the wishes of the Chambers of Crafts.
The said ordinance on admitting to the journeyman examination candidates who have not attended any vocational supplementary school divides the apprentices into 2 categories: 1) those who completed their term before the published ordinance came into force (i.e. before 26 August 1930), and 2) candidates who will complete their term within 3 years after the publication of the ministerial ordinance (i.e. by 26 "sherpien" [August] 1933).
Since we are interested first and foremost in the older journeymen, we shall dwell in more detail on the first category and point out the necessary facilitations.
If a worker completed his apprenticeship in a workshop where, at the time of his apprenticeship, there was no public supplementary school, or he could not attend the school because of lack of places — he must submit a properly reasoned petition to the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, which will itself apply to the School Curatorium in Kraków for an appropriate confirmation.
Besides those mentioned above there may[?] be other reasons for which the candidate had no possibility of attending any public vocational supplementary school. In that case a properly reasoned petition must be submitted in good time to the Kielce Voivode[?] concerning a confirmation establishing that, for the reasons indicated, the candidate did not attend the supplementary school.
In addition, the following must be enclosed with the petition for admission to the journeyman examination: 1) a biography written in one's own hand, 2) a certificate of the completed apprenticeship in the trade concerned (issued by the master), 3) 40 zł. examination fee, and 4) the last school certificate.
It must be specially stressed in this connection that the facilitations are valid only until 31 December 1931; whoever (of the older workers, naturally) does not present himself for the journeyman examination by the said date will have Art. 155 applied to him in all its severity, and consequently, even with the best will, nothing more can be done in this respect for the solution[?] of the Jewish journeyman question.
The young journeyman will have no possibility at all of becoming self-employed if he cannot, in accordance with the guild regulations, enclose all the proper documents and above all — his diploma.
It is therefore the duty and task of our Jewish artisans' organisations, which already have a fair[?] large number of certified masters in all trades, to develop intensive propaganda among their workers and apprentices so that they present themselves en masse for the journeyman examinations.
