This lies just as much in the interest of the journeymen as of the masters, and even more in the plain[?] interest of Jewish craftsmanship in Poland in the near future.
A. Gancwajch.
The Sick World. Its Maladies and the Charmers

Dr. A. Mukdoni.
The Sick World. Its maladies and the charmers.
Healthy and strong the world has never been. It has always suffered from a nervous complaint.
It is constantly taking cures. It constantly runs from one doctor to the next.
And there are constantly rescuers standing ready in line to save it.
A nervous, a mad world — and everyone is in love with it to the point of madness; people are ready to give their lives for its calm[?] and well-being[?].
And it, the mad world, throws itself into the arms of whoever volunteers to save it.
It has already been in the arms of dark charmers, of dreamers[?], of pure sages, of crude fools[?], of great adventurers, of unlucky schlimazels, of plain madmen and of great, shining heroes.
Our sick world keeps doctoring itself.
But never has the world been so dangerously ill as in recent years.
It survived the greatest war of its long life, and came out of the war a broken shard.
Not a single spiritual and not a single physical organ remained healthy.
And like all sick and [—] [—], the world is afraid of death; it is so afraid that it literally cannot live for its perpetual terror of death.
So it set on their feet all the cuppers, all the apothecaries, all the doctors, all the powder-grinders and potion-mixers.
— Save me, for I am wasting away[?]. Death[?] looms before my eyes; take [—] in hand, for any moment now it is all over with me.
And everyone rushed to save the world, because, as is well known, this sick affliction, the old world, has a strange luck: people are in love with it to the point of madness.
So they save the world.
And each has his methods, his remedies and his theories.
One says an operation is needed: one must cut, cut one must; proud flesh has grown, bad growths are on its body — so cut, cut out the proud flesh, the growths, and bleed all the bones[?], and in their place let healthy flesh grow[?].
A second says the world must be put on a diet; it does not live normally. The old world [—], gorges too much, drinks too much and is surfeited with pleasures.
There is [—] among the rescuers themselves; the rescuers are at daggers drawn with one another.
Darkness reigns around the great and dangerous patient.
———
And a strange thing — for thousands of years now the world is being saved, and it is still not saved. For thousands of years the sick world has been fed the same remedies, for thousands of years it has been healed with the same means, and every doctor, every rescuer[?], every [—] is sure that his remedies are brand-new, that he has only now found[?] them, that he has just discovered them.
The world has already undergone hundreds of times the most daring operations; proud flesh and bad growths have been cut out; all kinds of remedies and all means have been tried on it.
Great professors have cut it[?]. Great professors have given it various diets and prescribed it various plasters[?].
The sick world can lay out before you a whole library of prescriptions, whole pharmacies of medicines, and on its body it can show you a whole mass[?] of incisions — marks of the hundreds of operations it has undergone.
———
But the sicker the world is, the more politics spreads, and the more politics spreads, the sicker the world becomes.
The World War shook the world, shook it so hard that millions of blind people saw the senselessness of the accursed world order.
Millions threw themselves into politics; millions set out[?] to save the world from ruin and to guard it in future from such fits of madness.
Half the world was drawn into politics.
The world plays politics — the world is burning on all sides.
There is no piece of earth in the world where a person can feel [—] safe and free.
An evil, quarrelsome and wrathful world stands over us.
Nations wage war across the whole world.
Every state has its own war within its own country.
And the new politicians, who curse and damn the bloody war, have borrowed from the prince of war, the genius and [—] Mars, his teaching: that conflicts in our world can be liquidated only with a rifle, simply — either death to you or death to me.
Mars gladly lent them his merry[?] teaching — after all, it makes no difference to him how and why people slaughter one another. You want to conduct the war in comfort[?], each at home — by all means.
You want, under the veil of politics, under the cloak of world-salvation and world-redemption, to gouge out[?] one another — by all means, it is all one to me; I can go into politics, into world-saving and into world-redeeming.
That is how the world has been saved for thousands of years.
Cheap Prices

Cheap Prices.
If[?] everything cost little, if one worked little and earned a lot — it would surely be worth living in the world.
The government has therefore started an „action“: that first of all everything should become cheaper. Everything — that does not mean that freedom, rights, democracy, the honour of parliament etc. should become cheaper. That „action“ is already completed. Now it is at the stage[?] of making cheaper the prices of goods, of articles of prime necessity.
Let the economists argue whether such a reduction is possible now. I, however, agree with that philosopher who said that striving for something[?] is itself already [—], or[?], as my grandmother of blessed memory used to say: better a wanter than a can-er.
Let us at least want things to become cheap.
A shopkeeper I know assures me: if only I would come into his shop, and if[?] only for a sum[?] of one grosz — he will not let me out again. He will not even look at the price list or at the invoices, at cost or below cost — as long as I buy. He also assures me, in confidence, that this is exactly what all merchants and all shopkeepers are doing today.
No merchant is going to[?] let a customer go, as long as he comes in with a grosz in his pocket.
With our merchants and shopkeepers, then, we are in order; with them the price-reduction action will go as on butter, because it goes along with them[?]. A little difficult is the matter with someone else. Here, for example, matches[?] (zapałki) have risen terribly in price, taxes have gone up — but just take our magistrate [municipality], which says that the electric current cannot be calculated otherwise, that no tax can be reduced, that cheapness should start at the market, with the [—] on Modrzejowska[?] Street.
The well-known excuse of all those who seek to get rid of the poor man when he asks for alms.
They send him to the neighbour.
— The master of the house is not in, try the front.
— Go, if you please, round the back, the lady of the house sits there.
They send the poor man to all the neighbours, front, back, every side — anything so that he leaves you alone.
Has the magistrate not even tried to check the costing of a colonial-goods[?] merchant and of a [—] at the market?
And if[?] a whole town must say amen when its elected town council is dispersed along with its elected president and vice-president, and a commissioner is appointed over it — why should that same voivodeship authority not be capable of making cheaper the costing of the municipal enterprises?
A. Szwarcer.
With a Beard and Without a Beard.

[Kehilla — satirical feuilleton, kehilla elections.] By Y. Aberzhane[?].
(A story of two brothers, to be read by Jews with beards and by Jews without beards.)

R' Chaim Hersh and Herr Bernard[?].
By common sense you might reckon[?] that this is a Jew and a gentile — for what does a Jew, R' Chaim Hersh, have to do with a Herr Bernard? But the fact is that both are Jews, and if that is too little for you[?], they are "both brothers". R' Chaim Hersh and Bernard are full brothers, of one father and one mother. The difference between the two is that one is called R' Chaim Hersh and the other is called Herr Bernard. R' Chaim Hersh wears a satin kapote with one patch on top of the other, and Herr Bernard wears a tailcoat with patent-leather shoes and white socks. Herr Bernard swims every summer in the sea at Zoppot [Sopot], and R' Chaim Hersh swims too — every Friday in Nisan[?] Wilberberg's[?] mikveh. R' Chaim Hersh travels to the Rebbe and grabs shirayim, and Herr Bernard travels to Zakopane and climbs the mountains. R' Chaim Hersh prays with the third minyan, and Herr Bernard goes to [—] films and attends symphonic "poranki" [morning concerts]. R' Chaim Hersh has a wife, Gele Pesl, and wears a sheitl over the eyes[?], and Herr Bernard has a wife, Madame Stefania, and wears a "chłopczyca" [boyish bob]. Madame Stefania plays the piano, and Gele Pesl plays — on the [—]. Madame Stefania sings hit songs: "[—]", "Yes, very"[?], "[—] dance[?] Lamy[?]", and Gele Pesl knits socks and strips feathers. Herr Bernard has a big business and wears no beard, and R' Chaim Hersh has — poverty, and does have a beard, and a yellow beard at that — a beard according to law and custom.
So the two brothers, R' Chaim Hersh and Herr Bernard, really are two worlds; one mocks [—] the other. When they meet together[?], R' Chaim Hersh greets him with a "good morning, Herr Bernard", and Herr Bernard replies: What's new, R' Chaim Hersh, have you been to the bathhouse yet? When are you travelling[?] to him, may he live [the Rebbe]? Ah, your little beard is growing, no evil eye. When the wives meet it is the same again: they exchange mutual [—], Gele Pesl [—] the "chłopczyca", and Stefania laughs at the sheitl.
But one thing has nothing to do with the other; they really are two worlds, but brothers they are all the same. From time to time Herr Bernard pops over with Madame Stefania to R' Chaim Hersh "after the cholent"[?], and R' Chaim Hersh with Gele Pesl sometimes come to Herr Bernard for genuine Russian tea and a game of rummy[?].
[—] told[?] me the story of the beard, that [—] not that, that our R' Chaim Hersh suddenly became "political"[?] and [—] until — because of his long yellow beard.
Last week R' Chaim Hersh, with his Gele Pesl, bursts in on Herr Bernard. His face was beaming with joy; this time the beard looked much longer and yellower than ever. Gele Pesl [—], and her veil[?] had been knocked askew from sheer delight... Both of them came bursting in with cheerful faces[?], and the first word R' Chaim Hersh uttered was: Well, Herr Bernard, who is the wise one — me or you?
"What has happened?" Herr Bernard became curious.
"Here, this," R' Chaim Hersh showed Herr Bernard in the newspaper, "this is no small win[?]."
Herr Bernard reads aloud: "Jews who have no beard will, under the new kehilla law, have no voting rights and will not be able to be elected as dozors [kehilla board members] in the Jewish kehilla."
"Hm," Gele Pesl exulted, and R' Chaim Hersh and Gele Pesl burst out laughing.
Well, R' Chaim Hersh turned to Herr Bernard, who is the wise one, me or you? Me with the beard, or you without the beard?!
"Ha[?]," Gele Pesl said triumphantly: Madame Stefania, who will[?] be a "dozor's wife"[?]: Gele Pesl with the sheitl, or Madame Stefania with the "chłopczyca"?
Yes, R' Chaim Hersh goes on, he laughs who laughs last. Laugh, Gele Pesl, laugh! If the Master of the Universe has helped, so that the "bare mugs"[?] will lie deep in the earth, then let us laugh — laugh, Gele Pesl.
[—], only then did Herr Bernard think[?] about R' Chaim Hersh's greatness. Just tell me, R' Chaim Hersh, what is this greatness of yours, what?
What do you mean? R' Chaim Hersh began explaining again: only a Jew who has a beard can be elected a dozor in the kehilla — understood?
Yes, Herr Bernard answered, I understand that all those who have beards will... be allowed to be dozors.
Hush, hush, R' Chaim Hersh added.
You mean, Herr Bernard went on, that dozors may be only Orthodox men and goats.
You impudent one! R' Chaim Hersh boiled over, goats are animals, after all.
Well, yes, Herr Bernard answered, that is just what I mean...
Only then did R' Chaim Hersh jump up as if scalded: You heretic! We will show you who we bearded Jews are, and who you "bare mugs" are. Not only will you not be let into the kehilla, but even in the cemetery we will not[?] lie together. [—] a time will yet come when we, bearded Jews and Jewesses[?], will lie separately in one cemetery, and you, the "bare-mug majority"[?], and the "chłopczycas" will lie, in good health, in the earth somewhere else — enough of in-laws[?]!
What happened next? What happened next is hard to relate, because R' Chaim Hersh and Gele Pesl flew off the handle and started shouting, banging with their hands and stamping with their feet. The only thing one could make out was: impudent, insolent, treif-[—], "bare mugs", "chłopczycas", long trousers with [—] patent-[—]. R' Chaim Hersh's cap got twisted round with the peak to the back; Gele Pesl was already holding the sheitl in her hand; and who knows how it would have ended, if not for the neighbours, who, hearing the uproar, came running together; and seeing the neighbours, men and women — all of them "bare mugs" with "chłopczycas" — they took fright at the "bare-mug majority"[?] and left without a "goodbye".
Before leaving, R' Chaim Hersh repeated once more: Well, Herr Bernard, who will be able to be a dozor?
"An Orthodox man and a goat," Herr Bernard answered.
———
Two full brothers, of one father and one mother, brought up together, ate together, studied in one cheder, sat on one bench, slept in one bed and were thrashed with one belt; the only difference is that one is called R' Chaim Hersh and has a beard, and will be allowed to be a dozor in Israel, and the other is called Herr Bernard, without a beard, and will not be able to be any dozor...
The Four Sons.

[Passover — humour; satirical playlet.] A. D. Egoz.
(A play in one act, kosher for Passover and for all the days of the year.)

Characters:
Reb Zimel — — — — — a Hasidic Jew
Zelde — — — — — — his wife
Adolf, Maniek, } their children
Beniek, Staszek }
Place of action: wherever you like
Time: Passover, at the Seder.
———
The scene shows a respectable householder's home. The table is set with matzot, wine and all the Seder requisites. Around the table stand six chairs; on one chair lies a white cushion — a reclining couch. Zelde sits in holiday finery, but worried. Reb Zimel enters.
———
REB ZIMEL: A good yontev to you, my queen.
ZELDE: A good yontev, a good year, my king. Why so late? Did the cantor drag it out[?]?
REB ZIMEL: Yes, the cantor prayed [already][?] a bit drawn-out[?]. He wanted to show what he can do. Are the children here already?
ZELDE: Here already, long since here; they're already at the "Shulchan Aruch" [pun: the laid table], they eat my [?] — they pester me to give them food, they have no time; I'm holding them back as if with pincers.
REB ZIMEL: We've lived to see such years — a stroll matters more to them than the Seder. (Goes to sit down.)
ZELDE: Don't delay any longer, and let us sit down to the Seder.
REB ZIMEL: On my side there's no objection, I'm ready. (Looks around the table to see whether everything is in order.)
ZELDE: Nothing is missing!
REB ZIMEL: Nothing is missing. Call them in and we'll get down to conducting the Seder.
ZELDE: Itzik, Michl, Natl, Tsalel[?], come in!
(The sons come in, freshly shaved and powdered, with shiny perfumed forelocks [czupryny], and sit down sulkily.)
REB ZIMEL: Kadesh. The first thing — one must make Kiddush.
(Takes the cup in his right hand and with the left points at his head: "Well, eh, Kiddush." Beniek and Staszek put on their hats [kapelusze] and grumble angrily. Adolf covers his head with a handkerchief, and Maniek laughs and puts both hands on his head. Reb Zimel makes Kiddush and Zelde answers "Amen". Everyone drinks the cups.)
REB ZIMEL: U-rechatz. Now one must wash the hands.
MANIEK: We have no time, we have to go off to a lecture.
ZELDE: And if you don't go today, what will happen — a hole in the sky!
REB ZIMEL: An end, a finish. What's there to talk about? If they have more important things than a Seder, there's nothing to be done.
(Quickly washes his hands, quickly eats a bit of karpas, breaks off half a matzah for the afikoman, rushes through "Ke-ha lachma" and says to the youngest, to Staszek: "Now say it.")
STASZEK (angrily): I can't read it, I've already forgotten.
ZELDE (almost in tears): Woe to the mother, woe to the father! We paid so much tuition, kept the best melamdim, and now he can't even [read] a word of Hebrew.
REB ZIMEL: I'll say it and you repeat after me. Mah nishtanah ha-laylah ha-zeh mi-kol ha-leylot — — —
MANIEK: Father, don't be a fanatic and don't ask such things; make it quick to eat.
REB ZIMEL: Seemingly a [?] — he knows nothing of what holiday it is today, but the answer of the Wicked Son from the Haggadah he knows! Your face should have been slapped; that's what you'd have got[?], you shaygets, you!
MANIEK: A slap[?] — that's no way at all! What am I, some child? They thought[?]: slap! And where would I be?
ADOLF: Father, I'll ask you: true, the Jews were once slaves in Egypt and they were redeemed from there. Well, is that why one has to celebrate with so many ceremonies? A table with a Haggadah, with maror, with charoset, with cups, with an afikoman. What is all that for?
REB ZIMEL: I'll tell you, and you may all hear it: the ceremonial side of a celebration, of a holiday, is the most beautiful. Religious ceremonies are beautiful and sublime. The ceremonial side of the holy Sabbath — the blessing of the candles, the challot, the Kiddush, the zemirot — illuminate the day of rest. Without that, with the resting alone, the Sabbath would not have had such charm, and the day would not have been called "Shabbat Malketa" [the Sabbath Queen], and it would not have been sung about. The same goes for the Seder. There is no more glorious, no more sublime scene than the Jewish Passover Seder; but in you, woe is me, the Jewish feeling has already died; you do not feel and do not grasp in what a beautiful atmosphere you find yourselves now. Everything you see on the table, everything a Jew does at the Seder table, are symbols, sweet memories, which bind us Jews as a people, a chosen people among all peoples, and —
MANIEK: You'll tell that to Mother; we have no time to listen to your sermons.
REB ZIMEL: Avadim hayinu le-Pharaoh be-Mitzrayim — we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and here we are slaves to our own children. (Sighs, and Zelde sighs after him.)
(He rattles off the Haggadah up to "Ga'al Yisrael", and Zelde lags far behind, still only at "Dam, Tzefardea".)
ADOLF (angrily): Well, are we finally going to eat or not? Locked up as if in a prison, and there's no end to it!
ZELDE (quietly): Apostate louts[?].
(Aloud): Right away, right away, we're going to eat.
(Reb Zimel and Zelde go out. They soon come back wiping their hands with one towel. Zelde says "Ha-motzi" and goes out again, while Reb Zimel eats maror and korech. Zelde comes back with a bowl of borscht and fish and serves everyone on their plates. The sons eat and gulp in haste.)
REB ZIMEL (sarcastically): My saints are fulfilling "and ye shall eat it in haste". At least not like that — you'll choke yet, God forbid.
MANIEK (takes a look at the clock): Let's go.
(All four get up and make for the door.)
ZELDE: Why are you running, enemies of Israel, from [?] home?
MANIEK and BENIEK: Mother, we'll eat somewhere else.
(All four exit. Reb Zimel and Zelde remain as if paralysed, and tears appear in their eyes.)
ZELDE (a little later): I cooked up so many knaidlach, and now they'll have to be thrown out.
REB ZIMEL: A greater mitzvah to throw them out than to fatten the goyim.
ZELDE: Let's finish eating the food and go and rest[?].
REB ZIMEL: What's the point[?] of sitting and eating? My holidays are spoiled.
ZELDE: For me too. Is it the food that matters to me? We raised children, hoped to live to see nachas — well, so I've lived to see it. (Goes to sit down.)
REB ZIMEL: Pour the cups, Zeldeniu, and let us conduct the Seder.
ZELDE: Zimele, you've forgotten the afikoman.
REB ZIMEL: Thank God, I feel so good at heart that I could even forget that my name is Zimel.
(They eat bits of afikoman, say grace, and when Zelde reads the Yiddish translation of "Shefoch chamatcha el ha-goyim" — she bursts into tears.)
REB ZIMEL: Hush. On a holiday, Zeldeniu, one must not cry — a sin, Zeldeniu, a sin.
(He props up his head with both hands and sings to a sad melody:)
U-ve-chen va-yehi ba-chatzi ha-laylah
How good it was for me then on this night, when I and my family sat at the Seder till late at night; I was a king and my wife a queen on Passover night — and it came to pass at midnight.
The youngest asked the Four Questions on this night, the older ones dabbled[?] in the Haggadah at night, and I drew nachas by day and night. And it came to pass at midnight.
My wife would steal the afikoman every Seder night, we would make merry on this night, and act "kitzeniu-mutzeniu"[?] like young lovers in the park at night — and it came to pass at midnight.
Every little corner shone on this night, everything gleamed and sparkled like the stars of night; it was a pity to sleep through such a beautiful night — and it came to pass at midnight.
Darkened for me today is Passover, like a night at the end of the month. The sons are eating chametz somewhere on this night, and I am wretched and forsaken on this night — and it came to pass at midnight.
Dear God, "Thine is the day, Thine also the night", strengthen the hearts of Jewish children on this night, that they may serve Thee by day and night — and it came to pass at midnight.
(Reb Zimel's voice grows weaker and weaker until he dozes off. Zelde also falls asleep.)
(Curtain falls.)
His Last Seder

(From my late father's tales) — by Yitzchak Blumenkrants

It is known to all, the whole world knows, that "in Nisan they were redeemed": in Nisan the first redemption and deliverance took place. And he, of blessed memory, nearly wore himself out[?] trying to bring the Redemption in his own lifetime.
His conduct before Passover is well known and there is no need to tell it.
Every year, right after Hanukkah, he would begin searching for leaven. And what he searched out was the Evil Inclination, God save us, which is in the category of leaven.
Every night after the evening prayer two of our circle would point out to him, like a crumb, like a spark of "him" — may his name be blotted out — that was still to be found among our brethren the Children of Israel, so that he, of blessed memory, should burn it out.
Did he, of blessed memory, really need to have it pointed out?! But this I will tell you: his humility did not let[?] him show that he knew everything himself.
"I reveal," he used to say every year to his intimates, "that the Redemption will come this Nisan. And if, so to speak, He will not bring it willingly, it will be brought by force.."
And this is well known: if he, of blessed memory, said something, he knew what he was saying.
Of course every Passover at the Seder there was a great crowd, and only "pure olive oil", the very top of the press[?]. And when the time came to let people in to the Seder, he, of blessed memory, stood at the door himself — so that, God forbid, no one with a suspicion of leaven within him should enter..
And he searched with his eyes. I stood next to the Dembitzer [probably the rabbi of Dębica] — and who is greater for us than the Dembitzer! A great prodigy and a great God-fearing man, who was himself entitled to receive petition notes — and I prayed to God: may his merit stand by me, that I may get in to the Seder.
And what happens? He, of blessed memory, steps up[?] to the Dembitzer and says, in these very words: "Dembitzer Rav, you are a great pious Jew, but you cannot come in to tonight's Seder. There is a suspicion of leaven in you: this year you gave a [—] and destroyed a peaceful home."
"But Rebbe!" — the Dembitzer began to plead, and tears flowed[?] from his eyes — "the divorce had to be. For five[?] years now they had been running after me for a divorce; he is a great villain and beats her with his bare hands! And remember, Rebbe! I have been a rabbi for more than forty years, and this was my first divorce."
"The first one should not have been either," he, of blessed memory, cried out, "for great is domestic peace! And for this very reason: because you did not know about this leaven, you did not burn it out.."
And so it was. Nothing helped — not his pleading, nor that of his intimates, nor that of our circle — and the Dembitzer had to go back to his lodging.
I stand and tremble, my heart pounding[?], and I think: if someone as great as the Dembitzer has to turn back, what am I to do?!
But then I hear his voice, of blessed memory:
"Reb Itshe[?], you come in, and I will honour you with opening the door for Elijah."
At the Seder sat only such men as could each destroy worlds and rebuild them again. And when he, of blessed memory, pronounced "This year here, next year in the Land of Israel," the walls trembled! And it seemed that He, so to speak, was listening to every word of his, and that the Redemption would come this very night.
His eldest son, may he live, stands up and wishes, as is his custom every year, to ask the Four Questions. Suddenly we see him, of blessed memory, make a motion with his holy hand, a sign that he should hold back[?]; and he, of blessed memory, knocks three times with both[?] hands, good[?] knocks! — who would have believed he had such strength and might. We [—] that the knocks had shut Satan's mouth; how quiet it is now in the upper worlds, and He, so to speak, with His heavenly household, listens to every word of his, of blessed memory.
And he asked: "Dear Father, Heavenly Father: shall I ask You a question? Why are the nights different[?]. Why is the night of this present exile different from all nights? On all nights we eat other herbs — in all the exiles we ate various herbs; for a while it was bitter, we were in exile, and then a time came and it became sweet, we were redeemed. But this night, today's exile — that is[?], already nearly two thousand years — and it is still bitter!! Only One[?], Father, Father, I will not move[?] from here until You give me an answer to my question."
And he remained standing almost as if his soul had departed, not moving a single limb:
An hour passes, two hours; he, of blessed memory, is still standing. It went so far that fear fell upon his household lest, God forbid, his stubbornness harm him. And his eldest son, may he live, already wanted to rouse him, when suddenly he came to himself and cried out:
"No, sweet Father! The answer one gives only to children will not do for me. For me the answer, too, is a question."
And he, of blessed memory, began with fervour: "True, You drove us out of our land because we were slaves to the Evil Inclination, in the category of 'Pharaoh'; but now, dear God, loving Father! we are no longer its slaves, and You must redeem us."
That is how he, of blessed memory, said the whole Haggadah in the form of a question. You hear — what strength he had, of blessed memory!
During the meal he, of blessed memory, spoke[?] about the revelation of Elijah. And he, of blessed memory, said: whoever is worthy will see him, and will be worthy to see Jerusalem rebuilt.
When the door was opened I really saw Elijah, and in the very same moment I hear his voice, of blessed memory:
"Welcome, Reb Elijah!"
Holding the cup in his hand — and the cup had been filled, our circle saw it — instead of "Pour out Thy wrath" he, of blessed memory, invited Elijah into his private room. And we hoped that he, of blessed memory, would soon come back with the tidings that the Redemption was already here.
At dawn, when the first crow of the rooster was heard, someone came with tidings: that he, of blessed memory, had been summoned to the Academy on High — he had passed away.
It was told that before his passing he, of blessed memory, had said that the Redemption would come this year. But because he had pressed so stubbornly before the Almighty, wanting to bring the Redemption before its time, it was decreed there that he should not see the Redemption..
After his passing we were all sure that the Redemption would come that year, and none of our circle wanted to go home; people sat over the Torah and the divine service day and night. Almost all the signs of the Messianic age had already appeared. After Tisha b'Av tidings came from the Land of Israel that foxes had been seen running before the Western Wall.
— — — — — — —
You will ask: why, then, did the Redemption not come? When he, of blessed memory, departed, and his merit that would protect us was gone, we became slaves to the Evil Inclination again, and the answer "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt" is once again an answer — for Pharaoh, as is known, is the Evil Inclination...
What Shall Become of Me?

[“Zangen” (Ears of Grain) — literary supplement; poetry.]
Y. L. Peretz.
What Shall Become of Me?
For the 16th yortsayt (anniversary of the death) of the great poet Y. L. Peretz we bring this poem, which is among the first poems the poet [?] began to write in the mother tongue [Yiddish].
Tens [?] of years have already passed since [?] — the content remains ever new.

With hunger I lived through the world,
[the bread] torn from my mouth.
A groschen to me is already money,
I am not lazy to work.
And when I make a meagre fortune
and want to have some pleasure —
“Zhid!” they shout at me, —
“A Jew ought to be buried.”
Perhaps, I think, money from trade
is not so very honest?
With me the trade goes quickly,
I look for and buy a field.
“Prest zhidushe!” [?; a slur] — they shout at me, —
“No inheritance is destined for you!
A Jew may not buy a field,
[?] only in the earth [i.e. the grave].”
“You are not religious, Jews,
nihilists are all of you!”
Good — I keep two sets of dishes,
and bake challah for the Sabbath.
Suddenly now I hear news
— what shall remain [?] of me —
they drive my child out of school,
so that he must write on the Sabbath.
My elder son in Jewish clothes:
— That is a fault! — I hear.
The second one is no longer [?] in cheder,
— a doctor in the army.
They send him home to me now:
“Too many little Jews there.”
No more than five percent are needed —
and my son has no place.
Tell me, all of you, tell me today:
what do you intend to do with me?
Tell me, enemies, good friends,
what shall become of me?
You only keep silent — and your words
I understand quite well:
You want one thing — a trifle, —
that I should not be at all.
From the Book Table.

[Book review — Yiddish literature.]
“Stronger than Death”
by I. M. [?] Weissenberg.

Much has already been written about Weissenberg, the master of healthy prose.
Some saw in him the one and only powerful, full-blooded realist who brought into our Yiddish literature a healthy stream of fresh [?] vigour mixed with the smell of black earth. Others went still further and described him as a sculptor in Yiddish literature. But no one, I believe, has stopped to reflect on the abundance of quiet beauty that Weissenberg brought into our Yiddish literature — a stillness that often borders, in clear purity, on quiet song.
In his first larger work, entitled “Stronger than Death”, the author shows us the first pure love of the young, beautiful forest girl Sorele [Srulke], born and raised in the forest and herself a piece of the forest's quivering life — for the rich, healthy young man from the big city, Leon, who, incidentally, is himself the owner of the forest; coming from time to time to the forest, he very quickly manages to fall in love with Sorele, who has no notion at all of all the falsehoods and “tricks” that a big-city young man possesses...
And once, when Sorele's longing for Leon had grown very strong, she went to the gypsy woman [? to have her fortune told], to find out from her whether Leon still loves her...
On that morning Weissenberg shows us that:
“Behind [?] the window there already rose a lively, hidden chirping [?] of little birds. The sky in the east was suffused with purple redness. A fantastic band of cloud stretched out between heaven and earth with a golden-fiery hem on its blue back, as if it had dressed itself in a mantle of the emperor's treasures and were carrying a golden gift for the world, or as if God had made it His messenger, put a fiery stripe [lampas] on it and sent it to shake [?] the world; the field awakens with sweet bird [?] songs that pour out on an early morning in the still air... A quiet, luminous hope moves beneath the blue sky, pours itself out on every little tree, on every blade of grass, and wakes them from under the grey pre-dawn mist to come out and stand in the bright sun and gaze [?] at the sun with the hanging drops of dew, like big, comforted little children with quiet, bright little tears in their eyes. The world looks with a grateful [?] heart toward the east, as [?] the heavens smile.”
Only once does Sorele learn that Leon is coming from town by carriage; here Weissenberg shows us with what tormented longing-joy Sorele meets Leon:
“With a [—] [?] cry from the heart she threw herself into his strong arms, like [?] a tormented little fish [?] from a sandy shore into a fresh, arriving wave...”
But after the walk in the forest, when Leon tells her that he will not be able to show himself with her in town, it suddenly becomes clear to her that he, Leon, no longer loves her, and then the thought of quiet eternal sleep suddenly ripens in her. But in what a manner! Quietly she goes off into the flower garden and, picking a full apron of flowers, she goes into her quiet little room; and here we see that while picking the flowers in the garden
“her face turned [?] toward the sun with a sad, cold deathliness, and as she stood thus absorbed in her work, from below the forest came the melancholy sound of a ‘fujarka’ [shepherd's pipe], as if a little shepherd somewhere were lamenting his [?] lost lamb in the forest... The tones poured out melancholically in the still evening air, filled with a sad longing; but soon the forest started up with a light shudder; the tones of the pipe began to beat faster and angrier, and everything that was happening here poured out as if in one harmony and fell into one rhythm. The forest rustled and rustled, and Sorele picked and picked the flowers.”
Afterwards she brought all the picked flowers into her quiet little room, strewed them on the floor and, laying her bedding with the pillows there on the floor, she lay down facing the mirror, lit a pair of candles at her head and, drinking up the whole little bottle of sleeping drops, fell into an eternal sweet sleep.
The book is gripping from beginning to end.
N. Szterenberg, Warsaw.
From the Past of the Dąbrowa Basin (Zagłębie Dąbrowskie) and Its Surroundings.

That is the name of the monographic sketches which a learned society in Zagłębie has undertaken to publish under the editorship of Marian Kantor-Mirski.
Three booklets of the above publication lie before us; it is to appear twice a month.
It is something new for Zagłębie, for materialistic Zagłębie, that people should occupy themselves with historical research, that they should search and rummage in archives and in dusty books, from which we may obtain a reflection and a picture of the bygone old historical Zagłębie.
We have there quite enough interesting material on the town of Będzin, dating as far back as the 14th century. It was not easy for the author to gather this bit of material, for which he had to take pains not only in our Upper Silesia but also in German Upper Silesia, where in former generations there was more sense and understanding than among us, where history seemed a superfluous matter not worth talking about.
It is therefore a gratifying phenomenon that now people here too know how to gather the grains and make scholarly works out of them.
It is only a pity that, because of the publisher, the material is treated in booklets; in this way the interesting material gets lost. It would have been better had it appeared as a complete book; the material would then have been considerably more interesting and richer, and for anyone wishing to delve into the old Zagłębie of former times such a complete book would have been a spiritual delight and a scholarly pleasure.
We too shall yet have occasion to meet our readers in this place, once we have more material with which to treat this interesting historical problem.
In any case, a "yasher koach" (well done) is due to those who took an interest in gathering the almost-lost grains, from which a spiritual delight will arise for coming generations, for whom the Zagłębie of old would otherwise have been an unsolved riddle.
Selekt.
Heshel the Wagoner. (A Story)

Heshel was a good wagoner and a good man. Heshel had taken over the wagoner's trade as an inheritance; his father had been a wagoner, so had his grandfather, his great-grandfathers — all of them were connoisseurs of horseflesh, wagoners, and good people besides.
Heshel had heard a great deal about the kind-heartedness of his long-dead grandfathers, and old people told him even more about the good deeds of his late father.
Heshel did not break this thread of goodness[?]; he strengthened it further. When Heshel was driving on the road and noticed a tired[?] pedestrian, he would rein in[?] the running horse so that he could do him a favour.
His heart beat not only for people but also for horses. He could not bear to see wagoners torment horses, not giving the dumb creature the proper ration of food that their horse stomachs could digest...
All the townspeople knew him and respected him; more than anyone, the fair traders loved him, because he, Heshel, was the best and [most reliable?] [wagoner?] [—]: on the highway to the fair his horse tore along the road like a devil; all the other wagoners were left behind and the weak nags hung their heads, as if ashamed before their galloping comrade, before the gleaming[?] horse-devil.
Riding to the fair in Heshel's cart was no easy matter. When the day came to go to the fair, traders, women traders, horse dealers and fair merchants got up very early, quickly got ready and, helter-skelter, with a bite in their mouths, ran into the lane; everyone crowded toward Heshel's wagon. Suddenly pitiful cries were heard by the "carts". Both of them, Itzikl with the apples and Stasz with the broom, rushed over; by the carts there was[?] darkness and wailing: next to Heshel's wagon stood a thin little woman.
She was tearing the hair from her head, wailing[?] spasmodically and staring about in confusion like a madwoman.
At last the woman calmed down; with tears in her eyes she told that her purse with the money had been taken from her.
A commotion[?] arose in the crowd. When Heshel heard that the Jewish woman wanted to go to the fair and that this was why she was crying, he laughed and told her not to worry: she would ride with him without a single penny. When the little woman sat on Heshel's wagon, somewhat calmed, people wished Heshel eternal life, and when Heshel's cart was already full of travellers, blessings upon blessings poured forth; they wished him, Heshel, a happy journey there, and even Stasz the street sweeper waved his broom and called after him: "Szczęśliwa jazda, panie Heszka!" [Happy journey, Mr. Heshka!]
— — —
In the evening, when Heshel came home safely from the fair, his wife came out to meet him with a lovely, meaningful smile.
"Well, do you want to eat?" she asked. "A fine supper today..."
"Right away, right away, Chanele! I'm just going into the stable for a minute... the horse is hungry..."
When Heshel came back from the stable, the hot food was already steaming on the table. Heshel washed and sat down to eat. Chana began asking about the fair, about the earnings, about the robbed Jewish woman. But Heshel did not hear what Chana was saying; he had something else on his mind...
He remembered his dead little boy, Pinchesl, who had been his one and only son and the only child in the house...
Pinchesl had been a weak[?], thin boy; Heshel had therefore suffered much and had great heartache. He wanted the boy to grow up and become what he himself was... That is what Heshel wanted; but things happened otherwise...
Heshel remembers: once in the middle of the night Chana woke him — Pinchesl had collapsed, something was pressing under his heart, the doctor must be fetched as quickly as possible. The doctor was far away and the sick child grew worse and worse...
It was a cool autumn night. The sky was covered with black clouds, which swam quickly, quickly, as if someone were chasing them.
The horse tore through the streets like a demon. Heshel burned with fear; his teeth chattered. He saw nothing in front of him, looked at nothing, only prayed in his heart: "God, my child!.. my only child"... Meanwhile a wild storm wind rose up, tearing the signs off the houses. Heshel did not stop, did not even look around, only hurried to the doctor. Everything in his eyes began to sway like a restless sea: the houses, the streets, the pavements, the stones — everything lost its balance, rocked and shook, as on the eve of a volcanic eruption.
Heshel remembers how he could not get any doctor and had no other choice but to drive home with the same as he had left the house with...
At home he no longer found the sick child either...
Several years have passed since then, hard, gloomy years. For quite a long time Heshel was neglected, with no will to work, no courage to live; he had no mind to earn, was indifferent to the horse, spoke only of Pinchesl, and sometimes fell completely silent... Chana used to comfort him, though she suffered no less than he did... but for Heshel the blow... was stronger: all his hopes and dreams had been bound up with Pinchesl... He had wanted him, Pinchesl, to become what he himself was... and things happened otherwise...
And now, sitting at the table, Heshel remembers what happened years ago. His thoughts do not let him sit in peace, do not let him eat in peace, and it annoys him that Chana is talking, that she is disturbing him now in his thoughts.
He remembers the stories that old people used to tell him about his good-hearted, dead grandfathers, about their good deeds... And now who remains? Heshel thinks. He remembers what people used to tell him about his father... and one question torments him:
"About whom?.. About whom will people tell stories of him?"...
B. Rozencwajg.
And Whoever Tells at Length... (V. Jabotinsky)

V. Jabotinsky.

According to Jewish custom, when one tells of the Exodus from Egypt on the Seder night, one must adapt oneself to the psychology of four types of children: one — a wise one (chakham), the second — a wicked one (rasha), the third — a simple one (tam) and the fourth — one who does not know how to ask (she-eino yode'a lishol) — "one who cannot ask anything at all". And one must answer each of them in order, each according to his taste and according to his understanding.

The wise one frowns, looks on with big eyes and wants to understand: what actually happened here? Why were his forefathers at first loved in Egypt, received with open arms, and afterwards [they] began[?] to oppress and torment them, and would on no account let them go? How is one to understand that, Daddy[?] — asks the wise one.

— You see, my son, the philosophy of the Exodus is found in two portions (parshes) of the Torah. These two verses — like the Alef and the Tav of the alphabet — are the beginning[?] and the end of the prosperity[?] of his forefathers in Egypt; one may well compare them to two poles through which an axis passes, and around that axis turns the whole Jewish question in Egypt. And not only in Egypt itself. When you grow up and read many books, it will become clear to you that in all the wanderings of your people, at every step, the same Alef and the same Tav are found; and that the poles between which fate tosses your people about have not changed since ancient times and have not shifted.

"What are these two portions? — One you will find in the Book of Genesis, where it is told how Joseph presented his brothers to Pharaoh, and what he told them beforehand. A clever and cunning man was Joseph, a worthy[?] son of his father Jacob — the same one who so cleverly deceived his own father, brother and father-in-law, and whom the antisemites — you will learn about that [—] — call "the first Żyd [kike] on earth". Incidentally, that does not fit, for Jacob could both outwit and fight — with God Himself he wrestled a whole night until day broke, and he remained unvanquished; he could also love, and for fourteen years he served as a hired[?] [—]worker[?] for a beloved woman. He was a brave man, fit for everything: as a merchant, as a fighter, as a knight and as a judge, rapacious and magnanimous, cautious and bold, calculating and warm-hearted — a whole man, a broad nature, with great virtues and faults. With a soul like a seven-coloured rainbow, like a harp with all its strings. His life was and has remained the most beautiful[—], greatest[?] poem ever[?] told on earth. And you — read it as often as possible and learn from its wisdom; learn to love, learn also to be cunning, for the earth is a kingdom of wolves, where one must use all necessary means, both defence and attack[?].

"The second verse you will find in the Book of Exodus. Many years have passed already — some say 400, others — fewer, but in any case Joseph, his brothers and that whole generation have long since died out, as has the Pharaoh who knew Joseph. Now[?] a new Pharaoh reigns, and he perceived that Joseph's children had multiplied too much. Then he uttered the second phrase, which you must engrave well in your memory, for from then until this very day every [—] of your people drags this phrase along on the road of his wanderings, and as soon as this phrase rings out, he must pack anew his bit of poverty into his exile-satchel. "Come, let us deal wisely with him, lest he multiply", said the new Pharaoh.

"These two phrases, my child, contain in themselves, actually, the whole philosophy of our entire existence.

If you read later, my son, the whole history of our wanderings across the whole world, you will see that everywhere it was the same. It began with "every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians", and therefore all the disreputable professions were gladly left[?] to us.

So it was, so it is now, and so it will also be.

The second son — the "wicked one" — sits at his ease, one leg crossed over the other, bares his teeth ironically and asks: — What are these comical customs and memories of yours? It has long been time to forget the old nonsense!

Tell him that there have already been such as he — already in ancient Egypt there were such. They bared their teeth at all the hopes of their own people and preferred to go over to the foreign[?] side. Already then one of that same gang informed[?] before Pharaoh that a dangerous dreamer[?] had appeared, who was busy developing the national will of the Jewish people. In that time the world order was simpler; no public opinion existed then, and so the informer went straight to the court. In our times such a one, as befits a modern man, would probably choose other paths. He would try to blacken Moses not before the personal but before the collective Pharaoh — before educated Egyptian society. And in general, is it not a crime to tear oneself away from this rich camp, where everything is in abundance, both bread and pots of meat, onions, garlic [—]. Moses's parents are poor people, without property and without culture[?]. What are these fantasies of yours? — that man asked Moses and Aaron ironically, sitting sprawled[?], at his ease, one leg crossed over the other and baring his teeth.

"Blunt his teeth" — says the ritual of the Passover Seder about this son. But I doubt whether it is possible to blunt the teeth of such a one at all. He is too well armed, for there is nothing more invincible[?] than indifference. You will not get him with anything; once he has learned to speak of his people in the language of "with you" — he is lost. He will mock you, and material for mockery he has with you as much as you like; but in general[?] it is not hard to make jokes, all the more so[?] if the mocker is a practised[?] pen[?] and knows all the [—] and holes. There is, if you'll pardon me, something to laugh at, comparing in detail[?] our poverty with the riches of Egypt. True, fate is a stingy[?] in-law to this Egypt, but it is long known that the rich man's servant shows a stronger contempt for the master's poor relative than the rich man himself. He too will bare his teeth at you, and you will not be able to blunt them.

And there is no need at all for you to blunt the teeth of this son. Let him go his way with sharpened teeth and a poor soul; they will still be of use to him there, among the victors[?] in the camp that draws him so. Hard nuts he will have to crack there; the hardest of them — the nut of contempt. And many, many times he will still have to swallow, silently, a kick[?] as the answer to his declarations of love and a spit in the face as the reply to his flattery; and at the end of his life's road, when he sees that this whole road was full of hypocrisy and lies — then, perhaps, this runaway of yours [—] will fall in despair with his face to the ground, and he will wring[?] his hands, tear his hair and gnaw the earth — with the same teeth that till now were mockingly bared at his own sanctities. Let him take care of his teeth; they will still be of use to him both for false smiles and for gnashing afterwards in impotent rage...

The third son, a simple one, does not belong among those who brood over contradictions; the world is for him so[?] simple and without questions. He likes to believe and is inspired by the clear faith of primitive man. Such a simple and naive man was Samson the Strong. He loved to wrestle. He loved to joke, to play the wise guy, to ask riddles, to romp, to [—] well, to take a drink, and he was so trusting that after they had deceived him 3 times he fell asleep once more on Delilah's breast. A present-day tam does not have, of course, the full-blooded zest for life that Samson possessed — those times are gone — but the basic trait of this type is the same: without sophistries, good-hearted trust.

— Daddy! — he asks, staring[?] at the [—] on the table — will it get better?!

He [the father] tells him simply and quietly about everything that is happening now in the great, unhappy exile. Tells him how in thousands of places, by thousands of hands, the ruined palace of the immortal Jewish people is being rebuilt. Tells him how little by little, before our eyes, the people's will, until not long ago scattered like dust[?], is growing together; how out of single[?] limbs there is forming anew a whole people, a stubbornly proud people, equal to all healthy nations. Tells him about the Jewish youth of the European universities, how they proudly wear the Jewish colours on their breasts. Tells how everywhere, with every day, pride grows, respect for one's own root, and [—] contempt for traitors; how the poor tailor in the godforsaken Galician shtetl, who [—] in constant trembling before his lord (porets), has learned to shout proudly in the face of the whole world: I am a Jew! Tells him what a wonderful literature is being written[?] in our language, how fluently and vividly the children of the Jew of Eretz Israel speak this language, and how step by step, little stone by little stone[?], with great labour, through a series of enormous[?] obstacles — beginning with the burning rays of the sun[?] and ending with an enemy's bullet — a new creation is being set up and is growing there, a point of support for the most magnificent[?] ideas and deeds of heroism.

The fourth son cannot ask. He sits at the Seder respectfully (with derekh erets), does what he is told, and it does not occur to him to ask how and what, why and for whom. The master of the Haggadah commands not to wait until he [—] asks, but to tell him oneself and explain everything[?] to him.

This is the ordinary man, who stitches boots, sews garments, peddles eggs, buys up old clothes, writes Torah scrolls, trades[?] in a small shop, runs about on errands, draws his livelihood from the half-[—] professions from which he has not yet been pushed out; [—] squeezed[?], he fills[?] the [—], this he carries[?], [—] famous[?] [—], on his hunchback the whole burden of exile, supplying from his pure[?] human flesh both for emigration and for the pogroms. He lies dying and does not die, he goes under and is not lost, and he conducts the old Seder just as his grandfathers conducted it — almost mechanically, almost indifferently, but with that subconscious faith which in God's eyes is perhaps more precious than any ecstasy[?]. He, this great silent one of the masses, the "one who does not know how to ask" — he is the core of the eternal people and the chief bearer of its immortality.
On Jewish School Inspectorates.

Every government of every nation and tongue, along with other things, also takes care of — and considers it its duty to preserve — the cultural face of its people: to give it education and science, because "knowledge is power"; and it is held that, from the standpoint of the state, it is most necessary[?] that the people as a whole be healthy in body, and from the same standpoint it is also necessary[?] that the people have a healthy mind. To this end every ministry of education maintains subsidised[?] public schools, contributes to a number of secondary schools, subsidises evening courses, etc. Naturally[?] "the [?]" — the ministry takes upon itself the right "to have a say", and to give[?] the said[?] educational institutions a curriculum: what, when and how they are to teach. To be sure that the teachers will fulfil their "holy work" properly, there exist in every district "school inspectorates", whose task is to visit the schools of the given district from time to time, to supervise, to point out to the teachers various faults in their pedagogy and to give them instructions for the future.
True, despite all this carefulness the government school system is still far from perfect. No teacher finds it necessary (or has no possibility..) to give often, "beyond the curriculum"[?], a talk to the children about [—], morality and ethics, and to speak to them so that "words from the heart enter the heart"; and even the carrying out of the school curriculum leaves a great deal to be desired. [—] [—] disturbed when, for example, the music teacher — instead of lecturing on musical rules and mathematical comparisons and being content if the pupil mechanically masters a musical rule — would do better to see that the pupils thoroughly[?] understand musical phenomena. For that, however, the teacher would need a little good will...
But despite all this the school teachers have merits toward humanity which must be acknowledged. But how do the people who teach the specifically Jewish subjects fulfil their task?
Well, about the cheder melamdim there is really nothing to say. Never having any supervision over them, the melamed does not take the [?] trouble to explain a difficult grammatical passage in Rashi. In the Chumashim of Bereshit and Shemot you find in almost every weekly portion a great many grammatical explanations in Rashi. But the melamdim never explained it to us in detail. I remember once, learning the portion of Balak, "and he saddled his she-ass" (vayachavosh es asono), he translated[?] it "his donkey". A boy asks: Rebbe, "chamor" means a donkey! So instead of answering in a few words that chamor is the male and aton is the female of the donkey, the "rebbe" found it more necessary first to investigate where the "impudent" boy knew from that chamor means a donkey, and after all that he answered: you yourself are a donkey. The boy, naturally, after such an answer asked no more such "heretical" questions.
The late Rabbi of Będzin, R' Berish Graubart, of blessed memory, already 30 years ago took the initiative to unite all the chadarim under one "general cheder" (cheder klali), which was to be under the supervision of the kehilla. Various pious Orthodox groups began to raise an outcry that "anything new is forbidden by the Torah", and the important[?], good plan was wrecked.
In the public schools (powszechne) too, the situation regarding Jewish studies is no better. The teacher of Palestinography[?] and Jewish history ("religion" in the vernacular) goes over[?] from Schiper's textbook (which, incidentally, is not well put together and contains glaring inaccuracies) a few words[?], and there it ends. The Polish school inspector is, after all, not obliged to know Jewish history, and he is certainly not responsible for seeing that it be taught with all one's soul. Coming into the school he only checks whether the lessons are entered in the register. The teacher [—] enter the lessons that[?] the "bread-giver" demands, and adapts himself..
The Jewish public in the towns of Zagłębie, from whose bloodily earned money[?] the government pays the teachers and heads of the "szabasówki", has a right to demand that the Jewish religion be treated with more respect.
The Jewish kehillot must create special "Jewish school inspectorates", made up of experts in the full sense of the word, which from time to time would pay visits to the Jewish chadarim and the "powszechne" schools and acquaint themselves with the manner of teaching. "That we may not labour in vain, nor bring forth for trouble" (Isaiah 65:23)...
Dovid.
In Egypt

[Satirical feuilleton — for Passover.] (Feuilletonistic) By A. Szarfcyngel [“Sharp-tongue”, a pen name].

Come here, my dear readers, men and women, and I shall pass on to you greetings from Egypt. I travelled the land through its length and breadth and saw there very many interesting things.
I was also received by Pharaoh, with a great parade, as befits a Szarfcyngel; they showed me great honour and, most important of all, they asked me for advice.
But let us tell it in order.
Actually, I did not go there just for a pleasure trip. I was sent there — you must know this. Well, since I am something of an expert in — of course, apart from feuilletonism — also financial matters, and since in Egypt the finances lie deep in the soil, I was to come there and give some advice, the main thing being to obtain a loan somewhere.
— But I am a Jew, after all — I argued — and in Egypt a Jew is treyf, isn’t he.
— That makes no difference — they assured me — money is international...
So I went.
I paid my first visit to Pharaoh.
About what was done in my honour I need not tell. The newspapers will no doubt do that; I only want to report on the intimate diplomatic-financial audience.
I presented myself before Pharaoh, and the following conversation took place between us:
Pharaoh: How do you like my land?
I: I have not yet had a chance to look at it.
Pharaoh: But you have heard of my land?
I: Heard I have.
Pharaoh: What, for example?
I: That people do not live in peace with the Jews, they persecute them, they tear away their livelihoods, they turn them into poor people, into beggars; why, the whole world rattles the charity boxes for your Jews..
Pharaoh: The Jews are rich enough! The Jewish worldwide [?] kingdom has money enough. My Jews cry out for nothing and for no reason; they cry out to harm my land, to blacken my face before the world. Oh, you have no idea how rich my little Jews are! This is already the third year that I keep on taking from them, and — there is still something left to take from them... Hidden treasures lie with them.
Besides, if things are bad, why don’t they emigrate from my country? Let them go, I don’t need them here.
I: I don’t recognize you, Pharaoh! Maybe you did not let the Jews out of your land, and today you are actually driving them out?
Pharaoh: I am not driving them out, it just happens [?] that way; if they don’t like my country, my treatment — they can go.
I: Do the Jews pay taxes?
Pharaoh: Certainly! They are citizens, after all!
I: Are they treated like citizens?
Pharaoh: That belongs to the internal affairs of my country and has nothing to do with the loan that you must obtain for my country.
I: But your Jews do complain...
Here Pharaoh interrupted me:
Pharaoh: What concern are my Jews of yours? You came here to acquaint yourself with my financial situation. Why do you drag the little Jews in here?
I: Come now, [?] Pharaoh! You are no fool, so why do you play the simpleton like that?
Pharaoh: That is to say?
I: That is to say this way, that is to say that way — that is how it is: the two matters drag along together..
Pharaoh: But that is exactly why I called you — so that you should give me advice on how to separate the two.
I: Is that so?
Pharaoh: What then did you think?
I: I thought nothing at all, I just want to have a look at your land.
Pharaoh: All the gates and doors are open to you; go and look.
So I went to see.
I am riding in the street, I meet some young people, I ask them:
— Young people, where are you travelling to?
— Abroad, to study — they answer.
— And here in the country you cannot study? — I ask them.
— They don’t let us — they answer.
I wanted to walk about further, to ask, to hear and to see, but Pharaoh surrounded me with his servants, who did not let go of me and let no one else come near me.
So when I saw that I would see nothing, I had myself paid a fee for my trouble, took my leave and went away, promising to send my advice from home.
I shall go and leaf through the old Haggadah and talk the matter over with my old Pharaoh.
A Tale of an Arendar

[Poetry — a ballad.] (A ballad) By N. Melnik [?].

The tale that I shall tell here
happened in a land,
one upon the earth,
where they seized Jews and cut off beards.
Once, after a night of drunkenness [?],
they brought to a squire — his arendar [Jewish leaseholder of an inn or estate],
a Jew, a pauper with a large family,
the “success” of leaseholds, as they say!
And the squire, the oppressor, may his name be blotted out,
hurled a shout at his arendar:
“Słuchaj-no, żydek [listen here, little Jew], to what I shall tell you:
if you don’t want to go to the devil,
if you don’t want to lose your lease, your bread,
and fall with your żydki [little Jews] into hunger and need,
you shall come here towards midnight
and spend the night in the cellar with my ‘Muszka’, the bear.
After all, you have faith in your ‘Żydowski. Bóg’ [Jewish God] —
let him help you, the god of the Żydowski commune.
And if the bear lets you out whole,
tomorrow you will dance here before my guests. —
One thing only can I do for you:
here, take a bearskin, put it on;
perhaps Muszka will take you for one of his own kind,
and so you will escape death. —
In short, choose one of the two:
spend the night with the bear — or get off my folwark [manor farm]!”
What will a Jew not do for bread? —
Rather than fall with his family into need,
he said: I give myself, sir [?], into your power.
And just before midnight,
accompanied by blessings, tears and weeping,
he presented himself before the squire himself,
and amid the cheering [?] of the drunken guests
they threw him into the bear’s den. —
When the first minutes of mortal terror had passed,
he saw in the cellar, in the far corner —
a bear lying in wait for him,
twice as big as he.
“Al chet shechatati” [“For the sin that I have sinned” — confession prayer], he began to say,
and to beat his breast.
The night passed in reciting the viduy [deathbed confession],
and when day began to break
and they came close to each other,
they both recognized each other:
it was no bear at all,
but — do you know who? —
the arendar of the squire next door,
who had also crawled into a bearskin.
“Shloyme Khayims!” “Moyshe Zalmens!” — him? him of all people?!
So you are the bear? —
both cried out in one voice,
and all at once
the two Hasidim of one and the same rebbe
leapt up,
and in the cellar they broke into a rikud, a dance,
with all the Hasidic fire and radiance.
From shame [?] before the squires fate spared them,
because the “szlachtas” [noblemen] — the fine folk —
lay drunk for another day and a night
and gave no further thought to the arendars..
On the Removal of Leaven!...

By Pini Baal-Loshn.
(An Erev-Pesach feuilleton)

I always like, on the eves of festivals, to look into and contemplate the laws and customs and the historical events connected with the festival.

Not for nothing did our sages enjoin that "thirty days before the festival one expounds the laws of the festival" — thirty days before the holiday Jews must already study about the holiday.

How beautiful this custom is. We must study our festivals and know all the reasons and causes why we make such a festival and how we must make it.

With us there are no festivals just like that, as with others; we were not told simply, out of the blue: up and make a holiday, suddenly, without a why.

Our festivals are bound up either with the birth of our people itself, or with its historical events, and so on.

And more: every festival of ours has in it, besides its cause that one sees on the surface, also a moral hint, a deep secret of musar (ethics).

And that is why every festival has always been so dear to us, and why even today every Jew likes to make his festival as beautiful and as joyful as possible.

Jews prepare for their festivals, they wait for them, and they "bring them in" into the house with honour, with love.

So I sit and contemplate this festival of Pesach all around.

One of our most beautiful and best festivals — what holiday could be lovelier and dearer than that one, when from a coarse, enslaved people we became a free, noble people?

True, we were never stingy with troubles, even when we were free. "Pharaohs" we have had plenty, and still have — now too, to this very day. Likewise "Moseses". Redeemers we have had and still have now too — already even too many "Moseses". Everyone wants to lead us and everyone wants to give us his "Torah".

But a true "Pharaoh" and a true "Moses" — those we really had only once.

Now no "Pharaoh" can any longer sink us into his "forty-nine gates of impurity"; as a Jewish people we already have enough "holiness" to overcome the "impurity". There are times [printed "ציטן"] among us when impurity grows beyond measure, but that we should sink altogether — that we do not fear...

And no "Moses" either can give us a new "Torah" now. Our old Torah with its "seventy faces" we all know already, and we can already tell the difference between it and the new "false Torahs".

So I think: well, celebrating "Pesach" is certainly a great thing; the historical event of this festival is very great and beautiful. But what is the commandment of "biur chametz" (the removal of leaven) for?

Would it not have been enough to permit us actually to eat bread, and only as a remembrance we would also take bits [?] of matzah — as we do with "maror": we eat only [printed "גור", for "נור"] an olive's bulk for the sake of remembrance — and as we do with "charoset", also just a little only for the sake of "a remembrance of the mortar", and other things besides?

Why did the lot fall only on matzah, that we must eat only the poor matzah, and may not even see a crumb of "chametz"?

But, as is known, our commandments are in general not simple, common and workaday; every commandment holds in it yet another secret which we must reach.

With us, after all, every commandment has a "soul", a philosophical reason, a moral purpose, a poetic undertone — the Shekhinah always rests upon our commandments...

With us there are no simple commandments — with us it is "the secret of secrets".

Whoever has within him "the holy spirit" finds in them his own taste, just as once in the "manna".

Philosophers come — they find their own in the commandment.

Moralists come, ethicists — they find their share there.

For it is "turn it and turn it again, for everything is in it" — everything is alluded to in the Torah.

And indeed we see that our moralists do not reckon "chametz" as something so simple. They say explicitly that "chametz" means nothing other than our evil inclination, which lies within us, and we must clear it out, search it as far as possible by the candle of reason, and we must burn it so that not a crumb of it remains, "in the sense of: a person is obliged to purify himself"...

How beautiful and rich this thought is; how poetic even, if you like!

And believe me, my enlightened friends, we have no reason at all to be ashamed of our moralists; we may learn a great deal from them even today.

However much people delight in the morality of Tolstoy and all the others, whom our Jewish scholars in particular love to quote so often — may they forgive me — all of them together, with their volumes full of morality, do not even come up to one little booklet of our books of musar, which lie somewhere covered with dust in an old little beth-midrash of a small shtetl.

And I think again:

Had the nations of the world really adopted from us the commandment of "biur chametz" according to the view of the moralists, how many "chametzes" could they have burned, and how far would our civilisation stand now.

All the world's misfortunes, after all, came and still come into the world because the "evil inclination" is great; the bigger and richer the state, the bigger and stronger its "evil inclination".

And these evil inclinations lead the politicians and rulers down into the nethermost pit, and the world falls, sinks lower and lower into filth and [—] [illegible word], into lies and falsehood and despotism, and any moment now, it seems, it will sink entirely into the forty-nine gates of impurity of [—] [illegible word]!...

But why should we worry about the big world, when we have enough chametz in our own little Jewish world, which we ought to search out and burn.

Take, for example, just our own little world — oh, what a great "biur chametz" we would have to make.

No trifle, how much chametz has crept in among us — how one takes the great feather-duster and the great fire to root out this chametz.

If I had [?], for example, the real feather-duster, I would go from corner to corner and sweep out:

All those "ignoramuses", coarse lads who don't know a bit [?] of Hebrew and style themselves with the name of leaders of the Jewish people; and all those "leeches" [?], who fasten onto the Jewish body and suck its blood, while they themselves grow swollen bellies at the expense of public [?] or religious or simply kehilla institutions.

All those "donkeys" who, for the sake of their own honour, keep building [?] new synagogues and Talmud-Torahs that stand idle and empty, and thereby ruin [?] and weaken [?] old synagogues and Talmud-Torahs which have existed for a long time and could still be of use...

All those big "donors" [?] who give a hundred once a year and demand to be announced in the newspapers as giving three hundred...

Oh, oh, how much more chametz we would have to remove — only then would we look festive, beautiful and clean.

We must, we are obliged to begin to intend [?] the intentions of "al biur chametz" among ourselves, as the moralists have taught us.

For the longer it takes, the more "chametz" there is, and "crumbs [?] of chametz" fall into such [?] corners that the later it is, the harder [?] it will be to get them out...

Understood, gentlemen? — let each of you, separately [?], take up the "feather-dusters" — — —
The Incriminated "Afikoman".

[History — the Jews of Poland; for Passover.] By Moshe Feinkind.
An episode from the history of the sufferings of the Jews in Poland.

Before Passover in the year 1407, in the time of Jagiełło's reign, this scene was played out. The old Polish royal residence, Kraków, was the stage, and the priest Budek — the main hero.
An apostate had talked this superstitious priest into believing that Jews must have Christian blood for Passover, for the "afikoman"...
The priest held this fable to be the pure truth, without even knowing what such a thing as an "afikoman" is.
And not understanding, or not knowing himself, the translation and meaning of this foreign Hebrew word, the ignorant apostate explained it to the priest: "epikamen" (that is how it is written) means blood, which is put into unsalted (instead of unleavened) bread or into wine, which the Jews must have for Passover.
This matzah, the apostate persuaded the priest, lies hidden on the seder nights under the pillows, wrapped in a kosher kerchief, and on these pillows every master of the house then lies stretched out at full length and breadth. Only after the festive meals have ended is the "afikoman" taken out [?] from the bedding behind, and the whole household must eat at least a small piece of it.
This denunciation strongly affected the foolish priest, and since he wanted to free the Polish royal residence of the Jews, who had already lived there since the times of Kazimierz the Great, this great enemy of the Jews now had the right opportunity to settle accounts with the local Jews, a matter of life and death.
Indeed he soon set about spreading the foolish fable of the bloody "afikoman" in the churches, and the benighted mob of course firmly believed it — after all, it was none other than their priest himself who said so.
Just then a story arises that a Christian child has gone missing, or that it had been hidden on purpose so that revenge could be taken on the Jews, accusing them, of course, of having killed it for blood for matzot...
The Jews, frightened as always of the savage mob led by the priests with Budek at their head, shut themselves in their houses on the seder nights, nailed door and gate behind them, barred [?] and blocked the windows, not daring on the "night of watching" to stick their noses out into the street...
In such a tense and dreadful atmosphere the Jews of Kraków had to hold the seder in fear and dread in that memorable year 1407.
In the middle of the night, at midnight, Budek with the incited and inflamed mob falls upon the Jewish houses; gates and doors are broken open at once [?], the incriminated "afikoman" is searched for in the bedding, and like hungry lions and tigers they murdered and killed all the Jews who came into their hands, destroyed and plundered their property, then burned the houses with the Jews to ashes, etc., etc. (as Długosz, Hubicki and others tell us).
The epilogue, however, was played out at the green table of the Kraków bishop's court.
And being, as it were, an interested party in the matter [?], the clerical court could not, after such a terrible slaughter, act otherwise than to declare that the Jews were themselves guilty of it, because they eat "afikoman".
At the same time Jews were strictly forbidden from that day on to live in Kraków, and were permitted only to settle and to trade in the suburb of Kazimierz.
And this Kazimierz was the first official Jewish "ghetto" in Poland.

(End, from page 10).
In Kazimierz [the Jewish quarter of Kraków] there used to be a custom that every year, right after Passover, a fresh matzah was hung up in the synagogue as a memorial, in place of the old matzah, which was burned on the morning of the eve of Passover.
This matzah used to hang on the western wall, and great significance was ascribed to it.
In other old Jewish places too, such as Kalisz, Łęczyca, etc., one used to see matzot hung up in the synagogue, and in many towns this custom still exists to this very day.
In these towns it is said that the matzah is meant as a sign that the "eruv" in the town is in order, and that one may[?] therefore carry on the Sabbath.
But as a sign that the eruv is in order one could surely have fixed another mark than a matzah in the synagogue, since, as is well known, not the whole community goes to pray in the synagogue on the Sabbath...
More correct, however, is the hypothesis that, since one must leave over a piece of matzah from the "afikoman" to [—] until the following Passover, and in case somebody forgot to do so, the "synagogue matzah" is meant to discharge the community's obligation in memory of the "afikoman"...
Lately, however, it has come to my knowledge that that "synagogue matzah" in Kazimierz was indeed for nothing else than in memory of the calamity that befell the Jews in Kraków in the year 1407 because of the "afikoman". And with time the meaning of this matzah was forgotten. And on learning that in Kraków a matzah hangs in the synagogue, people began to imitate it in other towns too, without even knowing what meaning this synagogue-afikoman had...
A Little Letter.

I know in advance that after you read my letter you too will ask "Ma nishtanah" — why [?], that is, I am not coming to you for Passover as is a bridegroom's custom. But to tell you the plain truth, I deliberately refrained from travelling, so that you should not serve [?] me the "seder" — when and how the wedding is to be; especially after your father has already treated [?] me, about [?] nine — to "plagues" (see [?] the books...).
Believe me, if I were another "one who does not know how to ask", I would long ago have said to you "let him kiss me", for as is known [?] nowadays a young man like me is no "chametz" — but then again it's the same old story, since I swore love to you. For the time being, my bride [?] Malka-crown, do not ask "questions" like that "simple son" — "what does he say". As for myself, I would certainly very gladly, with all my body and soul, have wanted to be with you at the time of "whether sitting or reclining", only [—] thing, as he says, a borscht without beets [?]..
You see, however much the "bitter herb" may choke me in the throat, I nevertheless don't want to grow old [?] at your father's "with a mighty hand"; and so I am no "wicked son" to throw myself at him with "all who are hungry", because, who knows, maybe with him too the "this is the bread [of affliction]" is not so pleasant [?].
Well then, dear Esther Malka, I will now tell you short [?] and clear, as it says there: "that you may remember the day you went out of the land of Egypt" — you should know once and for all that for me you are not the last bite from under the pillow, I mean the "afikoman", but [—] the very freshest [?] of the parsley; and that the main thing — I am not after the "kneidlach" but — the Haggadah, and nothing more [?] — I do not insist that you drain the bitter "cup" to the bottom.
Well, now let us already say "dayenu" to this year's [?] Passover; next year, I hope, we will both together celebrate the "reclining bed" until after "midnight".. Meanwhile, if only I become a little "mighty in kingship", so that, God forbid [?], I need not depend on anyone — then it's "[?]" — I'll be like one newborn, and we will both "Chad Gadya" until — [—] — we grow old [?] like the [—] [?]..
