So Bad and So Bad

(Sketch) by Yitzchak Blum.
Around six o'clock in the evening, when the husband was getting ready to go to sleep — because at twelve o'clock at night he had to get up for work — he noticed how his wife was dressing up, combing her hair and, as every evening at this time, getting ready to go out.
He cast hidden, mysterious glances at her and meanwhile thought about it: she hardly ages[?]. A woman who already has three little children, and she still looks so young and pretty.
And again, smiling — he went on thinking — what does she lack? She has no worries about a livelihood, and as for having a good time, she has it in quite a lofty style. She goes out for whole evenings until late at night, and a mother, to whom she can leave the children so that she will look after them, she has too. And why should she look bad and aged?
It is — he pitied himself[?] — really not good. To have such a pretty wife, and because of his miserable night work not to be at home whole nights and to see [—] no enjoyment[?] of her. More than once he had already decided to give up the night work and take up a daytime trade.
He does not complain about the work. Working at night is not hard for him; he has been used to it for years. But the wife cries... And yet she is in fact a good woman, a capable one ("a briye"), looks after the house well[?], after the children. But when evening comes, when he gets ready to lie down to sleep, she becomes restless, something carries her off, lifts her from her place, she must go somewhere. She cannot, she says, sit at home while her husband sleeps.
And she is right, after all. He cannot even reproach her for going out — what should she do? Sit and watch him while he sleeps? And as if out of spite she still has so much life in her...
The only time she must sit at home is precisely when she is "in other circumstances" [pregnant]... Then she cannot and does not want to run around so much; she does not like to show herself to people looking like that[?]. Well, for him "the other circumstances" are truly the height of happiness, because then he is sure she will spend the evenings at home and he can sleep well and stand at his work with a calm head.
Well, he was indeed no fool and had already seen to it that she should constantly be occupied with "the other circumstances". They have now been married six years and they already have three little children...
Lately, however, a thought began to trouble[?] him, that the family is getting too big, and in this way[?] the family could grow even bigger and the burden heavier. Bearing children and raising children costs a lot of money, and he is, after all, no more than a worker — where will he get it all from?
And she, his wife, has lately become cleverer. She has apparently realised that he, her husband, is no "yold" [sucker], and she no longer wants to let herself be misled by him.
But the way it is — is no good either; he cannot bear it any more. She keeps running around until late at night; he is nearly bursting. There must be an end to it: either he gives up the night work, or she must again get "into other circumstances", she must — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —
"Mother, be so good as to put the children to bed. I have to leave soon!" he suddenly heard her say to her mother.
His heart actually gave a shudder. A shudder that he always feels whenever she goes out of the house in the evenings.
"Where... where are you going again?" he suddenly blurted out. "I mean.. Mutsh[?].. is it proper to go out every evening? You could for once spend an evening at home."
"Go, go and lie down to sleep!" — the wife jumped from her place, as though she had not expected her husband's sudden notion.
"I'm not going to sleep at all today! I'm not going to work today, you understand? I'll give up the night work," he declared as if in triumph, as though he wanted to test what impression it would make on her.
"Really? Good, stay at home!" the wife said contentedly and began to take off her coat.
"Ah, I mean... for the time being I haven't yet [—]," he became a little confused. "For the time being, that is, I'm keeping the night work until I get another one by day. You understand, dear, I must give up the night work, because working at night has lately become too hard for me!" he said with a full, aching[?] heart.
"I told you that long ago — you don't live in the world at all: in the evenings you sleep, at night you work — how long can [—] such a thing go on?" the wife said with feeling.
"Well yes, dear, I assure you, no more. Certainly[?] it is no plan[?] to live like this, neither for me nor for you. You understand, dear, I have the greatest trust in you, but not being at home through the evenings, you know[?], doesn't look nice to people; you are after all already[?] a mother of three children — what will people say."
"Oh, stop it with your 'people'. I care little what they say. You know, that the hard work falls[?] on you — that is what bothers me. You could, God forbid, still fall ill... Listen to me and throw away the night work already!"
"When will I get to see that!" he said, livened up. "But tonight I'm not going to work anyway. Somehow I feel like making a holiday today. It's been a long time since we spent an evening together as it should be... Look, do you know what, my little wife, let's go to the cinema today and afterwards we'll go to a restaurant. Somehow you look so beautiful to me today that it's frightening to look at you." — he said, and embracing her, gave her a kiss.
"Good! Excellent! We're going out today, you know!" — the wife was delighted, whether by the kiss or by the compliment.
When he stood in front of the mirror shaving, his courage little by little began to [ebb?]... Go now and start [looking for?] new work [—] with a family of 5 people — how could he exist? It is a [—]... — a doubt gnawed[?] at him.
"Here, at his [—] [—], as things are, he at least makes a living." He feels so bad, and he feels so bitter...
But he will think about that later. For the time being, however, his pretty little wife will again have to stay at home for some time... until the family grows even bigger. Well, never mind, come what may — does he have any other choice...
The Vanished Daughter

[Serial novel — chapter one.]
An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World

By Elizabeta Gorin.

Chapter One.
In the Dark Carpathian Forests

The little town of Z. lay quiet and dreamy among the dense pine trees, in the high mountains that encircled it. The town lies in the very heart of the "Tatra"; from above, the mighty Gerlsdorfer Spitze looks down from among the clouds, and below, the Dunajec flows past with a quiet murmur — the river that at the end of every winter threatens the town with the danger of drowning it, when the strong torrents, laden with the heavy melting snow and ice, burst down from the mountains.

As everywhere in the towns and townlets of the "Tatra", which lies between northern Hungary and Galicia, Z. too was inhabited by "górale", as the local peasants are called, and by Jews, mostly God-fearing Jews.

These mountain Jews kept shops and taverns, traded at fairs, did business with Pressburg, Budapest and even Vienna, and at every opportunity travelled to the Rebbe.

The town of Z. was no different from the other mountain townlets around. Once there had been large smithies there, and many rich Jewish families had lived there, but at the time our novel begins very little was left of the former abundance. Nevertheless the town, at that time — that is, in the first years of the present century — was not very impoverished, but for this it had to thank quite another sort of industry. Summer lodgers, or "dachniks" — these summer guests, who used to flock to the town in summer, were very different from one another. Some came for pleasure; they were drawn to gaiety, to dancing, singing, flirting, to passing the time as merrily and comfortably as possible. The others were sent here from the many spas, when they had been weakened by the "cure", and the doctors sent them to the Tatra mountains for an "after-cure" — to eat well, sleep and rest.

In these few months of the year the town had to earn enough money to be able to live a whole year, and that is precisely why the town looked prettier, and much cleaner and tidier, than the ordinary townlets of this sort. The lodgings had to be larger and more comfortable, in order to please the "summer pikelets", as they called the guests.

The finest house in the whole region, however, belonged to R' Shlomo Rapaport: the "Villa Róża" had a name even in Karlsbad, from where the doctors used to send their patients.

The "Villa Róża" stood a little outside the town, towards the mountain, surrounded by a wonderfully beautiful garden and overgrown with roses, on account of which the house got its name. R' Shlomo was a refined Jew of dignified, aristocratic appearance, and dressed as befitted a Jew of the old cut. His wife Zasha, however, was of quite a different type. She came from a very rich family in Lemberg; she wore her own hair, dressed fashionably like a big-city lady, played the piano and spoke Polish, German and French.

It was the beginning of May in the year 1900. The inhabitants of the town of Z. had only just begun to wake up after the long winter sleep; people had begun to clean and whitewash the walls of the little cottages inside and out, to take down the winter windows, to repair the roofs, to scrub and polish. Suddenly the whole town was shaken:

A rumour spread that Lala, the beautiful young daughter of Shlomo Rapaport, his only daughter, the apple of his eye, had vanished as if into water, together with Wojtek's Staszek, who a year ago had gone off with a circus and a couple of weeks ago had come back as suddenly as he had vanished.

The Jews of the town at once forgot all the real and imagined grievances ("krzywdy") they had always held against R' Shlomo and Zasha. The misfortune that had struck the family was so terrible that now they no longer had any other feeling towards the family. People entirely forgot that the season was already arriving and that nothing was ready yet. They stood at the doors, sat on the clay benches along the house walls, and anxiously recounted the little that was known.

"May God not punish me for these words," a tall Jewish woman with a kerchief on her head said to another, "my heart breaks for them. After all, they are our own townsfolk, in trouble..."

"True, true, Zlate. When my husband — may it not be thought of today — broke a leg three winters ago... it was indeed first God and then R' Shlomo — he drove off for a doctor... helped with money... and Lala brought warm things for him and for me, chickens, preserves and pastries; the goy [the servant] came with them three times..."

"Yes, yes, a dear child... a good and a gentle one... but not brought up the way a true Jewish daughter should be... You know, Sarah Kroyn, as they say: when one has children of one's own in the cradle... But what is there to talk about..." Zlate quickly turned towards where heavy footsteps were heard, and her eyes met the tired eyes of her husband Berish, the carter, who could barely drag his feet from weariness.

"Well, found anything? Caught them?" she asked, already reading the answer from his hopeless, sad look.

"Go catch the wind," he let himself drop wearily onto the bench. "All night we searched the roads, wore out the horses, wore ourselves out... We drove as far as Orawa... not a trace of them..."

"Has R' Shlomo come back too?" Sarah asked, looking curiously at Berish.

"No, from Orawa he telegraphed to Vienna and he himself went off to Pressburg. Somebody told him that the circus in which Staszek used to ride is now in Pressburg; perhaps he took her there... Such a misfortune... such a misfortune..." He wrung his hands.

Suddenly he tore himself from the spot and set off at a quick pace.

"Where are you going, Berish?" Zlate shouted after him.

"To the Villa Róża. I have a letter for her, for Madame Rapaport, that I forgot."

"Listen to me, Berish, better put it off for now," Zlate begged him, catching up with him and seizing him by the sleeve. "They won't let you in to her anyway; the doctor is there all the time."

"I promised him..."

"But you can send it with Moshele."

"No, I must hand it over myself... at least this much I can do," he tore himself away from her and with quick steps began striding up the mountain.

The road was narrow, but well beaten and even, which was a rarity in the mountainous region.

The higher he climbed, the fresher, cooler and more pleasant the air became, more and more saturated with the aroma of the pine trees and fresh blossom; the white peasant cottages with their thatched roofs were literally drowned in the white-pink blossom of the cherry, sour-cherry and apple trees, and the air grew ever more intoxicating with the sweet scent of white and blue lilac.

"Ha, Berish, where are you dragging yourself so early?" he suddenly heard a voice beside him, in which a light mockery could be heard.

Berish started and seized the smiling young gentile with both hands:

"Ha! So it's you, Janek?" he asked, looking into the beautiful black eyes of the young peasant with the expression of an enraged beast.

"You are just the one I wanted to see" — and he gave his hands such a twist that the other, no weak lad himself, let out a cry of pain.

"Where is your friend Staszek, and what has he done with Lala Rapaport?"

"Let go of me, you damned 'Żyd'!" Janek cried out in anger. "Since when do Jews fall upon good Christians like robbers on the highway?"

"Your shouting, Janek, won't help you at all. I know enough about you to put you away in prison for years. Where are Staszek and Lala?"

In Honour of Passover

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the Haggadah,
collected and styled by Y. Y.

a) Ha lachma anya.
Why is this said in Aramaic?
Because here one must say "Kol dikhfin yeitei ve-yeikhol" ("let all who are hungry come and eat"); well, against plain poor folk there is a remedy: lock the door.. But a pious Jew is frightened[?]: what if, at such a call, angels come in the guise of poor men, as they came to Abraham, and sit down to eat with us — against them no lock will help; so it is said in Aramaic, and "the ministering angels do not understand Aramaic"...
R. Tzvi Yechezkel Michelson.
* * *
"These are the appointed seasons of the Lord, which ye shall proclaim" —
The appointed seasons of the Lord — the true Jewish holiday that God gave is only "which ye shall proclaim [lit. call]": when you call the hungry to join you at the Seder..
No'am Megadim.
* * *
"There is no difference between a festival and the Sabbath save the preparation of food alone" —
The difference between a festival and the Sabbath is this: on a festival "food for oneself alone" is forbidden — eating alone at the table without guests; the Zohar calls the festive table of such a person "and I will spread dung" — befouled with dung..
Rabbi Zusha of Hanipol.
* * *
When the father says "Kol dikhfin yeitei ve-yeikhol", the child asks him: Ma nishtana? All year long you let no poor man across the threshold, and suddenly you invite every hungry person to the table?
The father answers: "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt"; go on, my child — just as Pharaoh decreed and did not carry out, so will I be too: I say it, but just look how the door is shut...
Emet Beshem[?].

b) Ma nishtana ha-laila ha-ze
Four questions we ask about our conduct on this night, in this dark exile:
This night it is all matza — only matzot u-merivot [a pun: matzot / quarrels], only squabbles and disputes fill our exile life.
This night it is all maror — we all chase after money, which in the end is bitterness, which embitters our life, and still we dance a demons' dance around the golden calf.
This night twice — we do not content ourselves with "other vegetables"; we need superfluities and luxury, just as Gehenna cries: "Give, give!" — everything is too little for us, we need more and more[?].
"This night we all recline" — we all sit like noblemen, as though we lacked nothing at all in exile; we feel as if "at father's in the vineyard"...
Olelot Efrayim.

c) That Pharaoh decreed only against the males.
When Pharaoh issued his decree that all the children be drowned, the verse says: "And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying" — that is, to the world it was declared that the decree was "for all his people", for the whole population, Jews and Egyptians alike; but that was only for appearance's sake — "saying", said merely with the mouth, while in fact only Jewish children were drowned.
Ma'adanei Melekh.

d) "And they set over us taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens."
A new means of tormenting Jews: taskmasters. Besides the taxes extorted from every side, they appointed tax-bailiffs specially, so that [the Jews] would be tormented still more, for to every such man[?] the Jew must[?] give a bribe to buy himself off for one day, and so — the more taskmasters, the more money..
"Imrei Shefer" by the Rabbi of Brody, R. Shlomo Kluger. In Galicia there existed exactly the same tax persecution[?] as with us today..
* * *
The taxes were not levied to enlarge the state budget, for that other sources[?] would have been possible, but only "to afflict them with their burdens" — only to torment Jews...
Binah La-Ittim.

e) These are the ten plagues
Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce liked to play a little prank while he was still a yeshiva youth. Once he saw a haughty, coarse fellow giving the bookbinder a Kinot (book of lamentations), a Haggadah and a Selichot to bind. These, after all, are the only books an ignoramus owns, so he gave them in for binding before Passover. Rabbi Naftali asked the bookbinder to bind a leaf from the Kinot and a leaf from the Selichot into the Haggadah..
On Passover night Rabbi Naftali went to the window to hear how the ignoramus would conduct his Seder..
Well, this is how the ignoramus read it: "These are the ten plagues that the Holy One, blessed be He, brought upon the Egyptians in Egypt, and these they are: we have trespassed, we have dealt treacherously, we have robbed"... (out of the Selichot).
His son pipes up: Daddy, this year there seem to be more plagues than always..
The father ponders and at once gives his son a shove: "How can you not understand, you donkey? This year is a leap year!"..
Well, soon there comes a fresh leaf from the Kinot, with the instruction written out in Yiddish: "Here one must sit down on a low bench".. The father shouts: Everyone sit on the floor, everyone down on the floor...

f) Al akhilat matza.
A village Jew took a yeshiva student as his son-in-law.
At the Passover Seder the father-in-law says only "ha-motzi" over the matza; when he hears the son-in-law also make the blessing "al akhilat matza", he resolves to correct his mistake tomorrow. Next morning he too says "al akhilat matza".. His son-in-law, however, says only "ha-motzi", as the law requires.
At the second Seder the father-in-law follows him and says only "ha-motzi" — and the son-in-law again says "al akhilat matza".
Next day, by daylight, the father-in-law wants to show himself a scholar and also says "al akhilat matza" — and the son-in-law again says only "ha-motzi"...
The father-in-law flares up: Damn it all, you always do just the opposite of me, only to spite me..

g) Adir hu, zakkai hu, chasid hu.
When the Rabbi of Chust, R. Yoel Tzvi Roth of blessed memory, was a little boy and heard his father say at the Seder "chasid hu" (He is a Hasid), the boy asked: Daddy, if God is a Hasid, then surely He must say "ve-yatzmach purkanei vi-karev meshichei" — and let the Messiah come... (In Nusach Ashkenaz this is not said.)

Motzi — they will take you out of bed at night, and
Maror — it will be very bitter...

Zecher[?] — this remains in memory[?]: in the time when the “[—]” still existed, they lived on all the bones[?], he would wrap the [—], all [—] and eat together, and all got from the Shas[?]...

(Pour the cups, and if your [—] does not accept the “Torat Freie”[?], let him ask the questions:)
Ma nishtana — this is the difference between the Radomsko and the Aleksandrów Hasidim:
On all other nights all Hasidim except the Radomsko ones, “we eat” — may be members of the electoral commission; but on this night — as soon as he prays in the Radomsko shtibl he is already “treif”...
On all other nights in Będzin and in Sosnowiec the town councils were [—]; on this night — but in Dąbrowa everything is kosher...
On all other nights, in other towns where there are calm elements, the electoral commission was elected once; on this night — but in Będzin and in Sosnowiec twice...
On all other nights, in Olkusz[?] the town-council elections have already taken place[?]; but on this night, in Zagłębie “we all recline”, the matter of elections has been postponed[?]...
(If your son[?] is a master[?] among the “election-makers”, you shall answer him the excuse quietly.)
Avadim hayinu — before we became slaves[?] we still had, after a fashion, a bit of a say[?]; but “He brought us out with a strong hand” — the municipal councils were dispersed; therefore one must tell and tell, “and whoever tells at length is praiseworthy”. He who enumerates those sins is today on horseback...
It happened with Rabbi Eliezer, when Eliezer was a “radca” (councillor)[?], “they reclined all that night”: they debated a whole night, but to find some sin; and when that did not succeed, they said: “Our masters”, my honoured gentlemen, “the time has come” — the time has come for you to resign and to get up from your little chairs...
Rabbi Elazar said — he cannot understand it at all, Rabbi Elazar; he says: “Behold, I” — I have been a “radca”[?] for so many years already, “and I did not merit”, I did not believe[?] that the exodus from the magistrate would be at night, that it would happen at night, “until [—] expounded it” and gives him to understand, “as it is said: that you may remember” — you shall [—] what [—] “all the days of your life”, as long as you live, “to include the days of the Messiah” — that such[?] a thing can only happen in the days of the Messiah.. When Rabbi Elazar hears this interpretation, he raises his hands to heaven and says:
Blessed be He — praised be the One above us, that we have left the town the “four sons”: the water supply, electrification[?], a garden in the Old Market, and the [—]...
The wise son, what does he say? He asks questions: “What are the testimonies, statutes and laws?” What laws exist today? That is the Constitution. “And tell[?] him” — tell him “one may not conclude”: he should not ask any questions. If he does, he may become a “citizen of Brest” (an allusion to the Brest trial of opposition leaders)..
The wicked son, what does he say? “What is this service to you?” — what good is it to you to become a “gam-ken” (a would-be)[?]; and because he — he is called the wicked one — wants to return to the “misl-pleter”[?], “so you shall blunt his teeth” — knock out his teeth, so that he may at least[?] be on the “pleter”[?]..
The simple son's question we will leave out this time; he is a superfluous person in society. Instead of him we will explain to
the one who does not know how to ask, and give him to understand “it is because of this”: that the Aguda merited its present power “at the time when matzah and maror lie before you” — when people toyed[?] with proposals not to run on separate lists.
How Many Good Favours.

Had we had a commissar and a council[?] — — — — dayenu.
Had the gmina (municipality) been able to liquidate its troubles and[?] the Passover relief campaign — dayenu.
Had the youth[?] org[anizations] not been sprouting like mushrooms after rain — dayenu.
Had all children of nationally-minded parents studied in Jewish schools — dayenu.
Had the commissions not raised the turnover tax — dayenu.
Had paragraph 20 of the kehilla law not come into force — dayenu.

How much more so must we sing songs and praises that we have a commissar with a council, the gmina has troubles from the Passover campaign, youth organizations grow beyond number, Jewish children are brought up in non-Jewish schools, the municipal authority fixes[?] new taxes, and the “Hasidim”[?] want to drive the “sinners” out of the kehilla — “to atone for all our sins”...
And It Is This That Has Stood...

The Mizrachi people[?] and the Zionists take the cups in their hands and say with pathos[?]: “And it is this that has stood.” Again a black camp has risen against us, but “not only one”. This is no longer news: “in every generation”, in each generation “they rise against us” — enemies within and without have lain in wait for us. But we have confidence that this time too “He saves us from their hand”..
Who Knows One?...

One we know[?]: that the Będzin[?] “Aguda” wants only that white[?] Leizer[?] should not become a “dozór” (kehilla board member)..
Who knows two? Two we all know. The “Rada Komisaryczna” (appointed council) has fixed two new taxes: road tax[?] and investment tax[?].
Who knows three? Three “unruly elements” are there in Sosnowiec: Israel Moshe Wingrib[?], Levi Jungster[?], Itche Wolf Brener[?].
Who knows four? Four I know. Four schools and hadarim receive from the magistrate[?] [—] 3,500 zł.
Who knows five? Five we know. Five Jews are on the “Rada Komisaryczna”.
Who knows six? Six we know: six Jewish banks in Sosnowiec on one street.
Who knows seven? Seven I know. For seven more weeks the present parnassim will sit on the kehilla chairs..
Who knows eight? Eight we know. The kehillot owe their officials eight months' pension.
Who knows nine? Nine we know. Nine measures of talk have women — and also the members of the “Rada Komisaryczna”..

On the Kehilla Elections in Olkusz

[Olkusz — kehilla elections; people's bank.]
(A letter from Olkusz)
Olkusz is a town without any social life. There is no communal life; hardly anyone concerns himself calmly and thoughtfully with municipal affairs, and in this matter chaos reigns. Lawlessness — and whoever wants to grabs the seat, out of ambition or also out of private interests.
The Olkusz sages always have time when it comes to municipal affairs, so they always wait for the last minute, which ends in being too late. So it was at the first kehilla elections, when nobody acquainted himself with the question and nobody took stock: what are these kehilla elections, anyway? Gmina elections? The sages woke up at the last minute, when for formal reasons it was no longer possible to submit any lists. This is always exploited by the kehilla "providers" [?], who know what the "kehilla dish" means, and they jump up onto the horse.
The political organisations are asleep too; the Zionist organisation with its "pushke-Zionists" [collection-box Zionists] shows hardly any sign of life.
People thought that after the revolutions in the organisation better times would come for Zionism in Olkusz, that the "victors" would make their voice heard, strengthen the organisations, conduct a better policy in the kehilla elections than in the town-council elections — but meanwhile nothing is heard. However, a new "era" is beginning: the "Chevra Kadisha" [burial society], sitting over a glass of liquor, "occupied themselves" with this question and decided to go to the elections with a "living" list...
• • •
The Olkusz People's Bank, which bears such a fine democratic name, is — as people have long been muttering — not so very "democratic". The public mutters, there have been protests [?], but everything always stays as it was; the leaders have firmly occupied the seats, which are by now almost regarded as their own. As if the voters no longer have a full say — the latest decision of the "bank leaders" to call the annual general meeting precisely on an ordinary Wednesday after the holiday has already driven the public somewhat out of patience. How can it be? People are already muttering louder — why are the members' interests somehow not taken into account? When the writer of these lines turned on this matter to the board member Mr. B. Heisl-Fisz for an explanation, the latter tried to wriggle out with various untrue, false excuses, which made a very bad impression and confirmed in full measure that the name "People's Bank" is a borrowed one.
It is interesting how the public will now relate to its leaders at the bank.
M. Sh.

Six More Weeks.

[Zagłębie — kehilla and elections.]
All in all, six weeks separate us from the day when the elections to the new Jewish kehillas in Zagłębie will take place. Yet it is still quiet in the Jewish street. One hears little about any preparatory work for these elections. One hears nothing about arousing[?] the attention of public opinion, about consultations or meetings.
For the "Agudah" [Agudath Israel], the opponent of the Jewish revival movement with all its undertakings, achievements and sacrifices, this suits it fine. It has its own sworn[?] holy flock, which is not obliged to think, only to be always obedient. These "holy sheep" are in any case a kind of inalienable property by the rebbe's command. Besides, the "Agudah" wants nothing at all. Only, God forbid, let there be no changes. Let everything remain as it was yesterday and the day before, let there be the same majority of its own with its stale notions, with the same view of Jewish life, which is worth a farthing and a will for a penny.
Therefore those who are dissatisfied with the present kehilla and its activity from A to Z must constantly be on the alert. Those who see a misfortune for Jewish life in the rule of the political "Agudah" — which strives, on the model of our Left, for non-Jewish forces to decide in our internal Jewish questions — must already prepare for the elections. Those who want to broaden from within the competence of the Jewish kehilla, not contenting themselves with a scope of work limited to the mikveh and the cemetery, must already prepare for the elections. Those who want to see in the kehilla an institution that brings the Jew honour and prestige must already prepare for the elections.
The present kehilla is none of this. Illustrations of it are not lacking. With all its public appearances it can serve as a model of what it must N O T be; the last few days, too, have not been poor in examples.
But all this must be made clear. All this must be demonstrated to the Jewish public. For doing so there are, all in all, six weeks here — and every day that is neglected is a pity.
It is also a pity that no effort is made so that understanding should now grow for the necessity of a common front of all those who want to see the present gmina [kehilla] with a different face. One must not forget that the common opponent ought to bring about a rapprochement of all the other groups, which, after all, have, in their view of the kehilla, much in common. Even if it should not come to a complete common front, let it at least come to an understanding on tactical questions.
This is a matter, first of all, of an exchange of opinions and also of creating the proper mood for it. In any case it is already time to think about it. All in all, six weeks separate us from the day of the elections.
General Meetings in Jewish Financial Institutions.

[Będzin — economy and banks; followed by a short item: Sławków.]
In the course of the days of Chol HaMoed, i.e. Sunday and Monday, annual general meetings of Jewish financial institutions took place in Będzin.
On Sunday a general meeting of the
Kredit-Bank [Credit Bank]
took place in the premises of the "Merchants' Association".
The meeting aroused a satisfying interest, so that the hall was packed with members.
The bank manager, Mr. M. Tenenbaum, opens the meeting with an introductory speech in which he talks about the economic crisis at the present moment, points to the difficult situation of the local Jewish banks, and proposes that the agenda should also deal with the proposal that all three Jewish banks be united and that out of them a large, sound financial institution be created which would have a right to exist.
The chair is taken by Mr. Salomon Gitman, who invites to the presidium Messrs. Sz. Dwiński, M. Lewin, and as secretary Mr. Pesachzon.
The report on the activity to date is given by the chairman, Mr. Rubinlicht. The report shows that the management was on the alert and, despite the severe crisis, the bank made a profit of over 22 thousand zł. in 1930.
On the report there was a short discussion; no criticism whatsoever was heard, and the management is granted an "absolutorium" [discharge].
After the adoption of the budget for this year a discussion develops on Mr. Tenenbaum's proposal. People speak for and against. It is resolved that the management should look more closely into whether the proposal can, and has the possibility to, be realised.
No change took place in the management, nor in the council.
— —
The next day, Monday, the annual general meeting of the
Discount Bank
took place.
At this meeting a lively mood already prevailed. Thanks to the fact that the meeting took place in the hall of the former city council, those assembled, who came in large numbers, had the possibility to "move about" freely, to conduct negotiations about the lists of candidates for the management and council, behind-the-scenes politics as to who should conduct the meeting, etc.
On behalf of the supervisory council the meeting is opened by Mr. A. Lidzbarski, who incidentally gives a survey of the origin of the bank up to the present day, points to the heavy responsibility which the management and the council bear, and expresses thanks to the chairman, Mr. A. Trapauer, who does a great deal day by day for the good of the bank, to the bank manager Mr. Jakubowski and to the whole staff, who are devoted to the bank's developing properly.
In electing a chairman, various candidates are put forward, but by a large majority the chair is given to Mr. M. Zimberknopf, who invites as assessors Messrs.: Berisz Gold, Bunem Feldbaum, Herman Pinkus, Elimelech Wrocławski, Meir Beri, H. Fride, and as secretary Icchak Granek.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting by Mrs. Reznik, the important points of the agenda are taken up.
On behalf of the management the report is given by Mr. Józef Rus, who points to the development of the bank, the management's striving to serve the interests of the small merchants and [artisans?], and that the fate of further development depends on the members.
Then reports are given: on the supervisory council — Mr. Lidzbarski; on the "revision bank" [audit committee?] — Mr. Jakubowski; and on the balance sheet — Mr. Pinkus.
The balance sheet shows the following: the bank has own capital of 92 671.00 zł., deposits of 456,589.— zł.; the bank has 435 members; net profit in the year 1930 — 10,653.66 zł.
After the reports, which a large part of those assembled hardly listened to, a discussion develops in which the activity of the management is "criticised". The "criticism" arouses a cheerful mood, especially when it begins to take on the character of private accounts — the hall becomes merrier and it buzzes like a beehive.
The "critics" receive the proper answer, and confidence is expressed in the management, especially in the chairman, Mr. Trapauer.
A storm broke out when, at the point "distribution of the profits", Mr. Herszlewicz proposed that 500 zł. be deducted from the profit for the "Keren Hayesod".
The proposal was supported by Messrs. A. Liwer[?], Silberberg, Zimberknopf, Malec, Rus and others. But because of a few individuals who spoke against it, a tumult broke out which lasted a long time; later it turned out that this had been "a storm in a glass of water", since almost all those assembled were in favour of the proposal. But the quarrel was settled after the chairman's declaration that in principle he is against the proposal, but seeing that the majority is for it, only 200 zł. should be allotted to the "Keren Hayesod".
After the approval of the budget in the sum of 64 thousand zł. (last year's budget had been preliminarily set at a sum of 74 thousand zł.) the elections are taken up.
At the elections a strong struggle took place. No fewer than 4 lists figured. The winner, however, was the list of the "Centrala"[?].
The result is this: in the management no change whatsoever took place; only to the council were the following new members elected: Messrs. Aron Feldberg and Jehoszua Klajnman.

They Were Recognised. (An interesting incident from last Passover eve)

[Sosnowiec — slice of life, Passover eve.] They came from a nearby small town, not far from Zagłębie.
There, at home in their own town, both were from respected [—]; [their families] played a big role and were regarded as the richest. Today they have lost their former lustre; business went downhill, and almost [?] the whole town knew that both families had come down in the world. Still they were held in honour, and people nevertheless believed that something of their former wealth had remained to them.
That the two formerly rich houses had sunk so low from their station that they had almost [?] nothing for bread — nobody in the town imagined that. It would [?] have been a surprise for everyone that there, in both homes, they had already suffered want and cold for a whole winter, and that for a long time they had been selling off, for bread, the few remaining silver objects — that was a secret to the whole town. When one [?] came in to them, one noticed nothing [?]: the rooms, the furniture, the whole lordly furnishing were as once in the good times. They gave alms, they still put on a laugh [?], a stiff [?], drawn [—] face; but that in the two beautifully carved cupboards the jewellery, the diamonds, the pearls and in general all the precious things acquired in the sated, rich years were gradually being emptied out — of that no one had any idea.
For a long time things had not been cosy in these two houses. Bad business and the heavy taxes [podatki] had ruined and broken them. But this was nothing new; there were many such in the town, and there was nothing to wonder at in that alone. Sad, very bad it became when winter set in, and even worse than bad and sadder than sad it became on Passover eve. By then there was nothing left to sell. Of the bit of gold and silver no trace remained — everything sold [?] and eaten up. Yes, there were still beautiful things left, but that was the rich furniture, and to decide on such a step [?] [—] as selling the household goods — that would have been the most terrible blow for them. How could one do it? [—] after all it is [—] public [?] and everyone will see. That they would not do; that was too hard a trial for two such houses that only a short while ago had been so rich and respected.
It is eight days before Passover. Everyone prepares as best he can, and in the houses of the two who had come down in the world they ponder and rack their brains over what to do — to obtain [?] matzot — where [?] will they get the money to pay? Little by little they give in; they already decide to sell the furniture bit by bit. At last they were about to dispose [?] of the [—] bit, but then a komornik [bailiff], an executor, burst in unexpectedly and listed the furniture and household goods for distraint. This last finally crushed the two fallen families, who resigned entirely from making Passover. A dreadful melancholy wandered about the decorated rooms, and the members of the household went about like lost shadows. Not only was there nothing for matzot, but not even for [—] for the eight days until Passover.
[Something] drove and pushed them out of the homes, but where does one run? From [—] [—], [—]. So they ran to Sosnowiec. On foot they fled [?] — the two formerly rich girls of the two impoverished houses — away from home without their parents' knowledge, and came to Sosnowiec to hire themselves out for the matzot. Here nobody knows them; better they should work and earn than perish from hunger and shame in the decorated rooms that already belong to others too. The two once-rich daughters had nothing more to lose. If not today then tomorrow, sooner or later they would have to run away from the town; their fathers [?] own nothing any more.
Having come to Sosnowiec, the two girls were not in rich clothes: first, so that it should not be conspicuous, and second, they no longer owned such [—]. The one did not know about the other [as printed], and each separately hired herself out to a different matzah bakery, and with tears in their eyes they swore to each other that neither would give the other away and that it would remain a secret for ever.
At early [?] dawn both girls went off to their work — rolling matzot — and on that day something happened that [—] them [—], and from Sosnowiec too.
To one of the two matzah bakeries came a Jew from that same town to sell flour. When the Jew saw how the girl, a daughter of the richest parents in his town, was rolling matzot, he felt faint and they had to pour water on him. During the commotion one matzah-roller [?] meanwhile [?] disappeared from the piekarnia [bakery].
When the Jew was revived, he no longer wanted to talk, but searched with his eyes for the spot where the vanished girl had stood before. The girl who had now run off was one of the two formerly rich daughters. She ran to the other one and in one breath told her: "If you only knew — we've been recognised. Herszel K. from our town saw me and you; we must flee, now altogether, away from home and from Sosnowiec too."
On Passover eve both girls sent their parents a little money with a short letter containing the words:
"Dear parents, here I send you kosher, festive money. I will not come home any more. I cannot and I may not. Be well and of good courage [?]."
P. Palisher [?]
The Serious Question Mark

The problem of the bank-houses must be solved. — A district conference should take this up.
We have, it seems, already been blessed with not standing in line with other people on the same level. It is not our lot, apparently, to find ourselves in the same situation as other nations. For example, not long ago there was a time when we could not imagine that Jewish financial institutions, Jewish banks, could come into being. Who could have dreamed of such things? A bank-house really looked like a kind of monopoly, a kind of kingdom, which few could ever reach. We knew only that a bank is a non-Jewish enterprise, where one must stand like a pauper at the door and not dare to utter a loud word, so as not to anger the "poretz" [the lord], because that would[?] do one's credit no great favour...
And it cannot be denied: the public kept within bounds; a bank director was treated with respect, and quite respectable merchants played before him the true "ma yofis" [sycophant] roles; and the more flattery one showed him, the more one bowed before him bent threefold, the harder credit became and the more restrictions arose, so that the Jewish merchant was left stuck: he had nowhere to discount his customers' bills, and the culmination point was reached. The Jewish middle class was formally pushed out of the bank-houses, and then the great question mark was raised: what next? How will we exist now? Where will we discount our bills? Who will give us money on them? And then, thanks to the help of our American brethren, Jewish bank-houses began to hatch.
The institutions met with sympathy everywhere and went the way of development, so that their success in the Jewish street was enormous, almost unbelievable. When we entered a Jewish bank, when we saw the benefit and the great earnings that this or that institution brings the Jewish community, we were beside ourselves with joy. Jewish society took pride and pleasure in seeing what an important branch had developed in the financial field.
But here too it reached the culmination point: as soon as one party saw that another had a bank, they envied it and also made a bank. Jews thought: why should we depend on them, when we can be the same "machers" as they are? And so it was — everyone began to "make Shabbes for himself", and today we have not only trade-branch banks but also association banks; every party has its own bank, its own little store, its own little shop, its own little bench, and every little bench — its own politics. But it did not stop even there: just as earlier the banks had begun to progress, and as they had gone the way of development, so later they began to go the way of splitting up and crumbling, and with that the prestige and the name of Jewish banking began to fall.
Now we have already gone considerably further: not every party makes itself a bank, but every few people get together[?], come together and make themselves a bank; soon there will be as many banks as shopkeepers. We already have villages that have at least 2 bank institutions, and when little banks are fruitful and multiply, just like little shops once did, they too must have customers, just like a shop — otherwise one cannot exist, otherwise one cannot run the business — and here it is self-evident what kind of fruit can grow from these trees.
The institutions can no longer stand on a firm basis; everything must be artificial, imitation — both the institutions and their clients — and so this takes on a sickly, abnormal, catastrophic form, and here one must again set up the same great question mark that was once raised when the Jewish client was driven out of the Christian banks. The difference between that question mark and the present one is only this: from the Christian banks the Jew was pushed out, and now, in the Jewish banks, he is snatched in and wanted as a customer from all sides, just as the shopkeeper wants the housewife as a customer.
We do not know which question mark is worse: the first, which concerned a danger to Jewish credit, or the second, the present one, which concerns a surplus of Jewish credit, where the Jew is grabbed from all sides and begged to take credit. Of course a Jew with a "logical" mind will say that over the first question mark there was something to debate, whereas the present question mark is nothing at all and not worth talking about, because it is better — such a Jew will argue to you — that people want to give than that they would want to take. We, on the contrary, see[?] in the latter question mark no smaller danger than in the first, for we must analyse this question: what can come of clients who want a free hand in all the banks? They will run into debt everywhere, and at that they will still have somewhere to throw themselves — out of one bank, into the next; for when people tear at him, when they want him as a client, there is no question [of restraint].
And then one must imagine the demoralization and the lawlessness that is about to arise in this field; it will take on the same character as in the old days, when the merchant could get money everywhere on bills as much as his heart desired — and then, we hold, the present question mark is, if not worse, certainly no better than the previous one.
We must render a clear account of our financial institutions in general and of the public funds in particular; we must not take them lightly, we must not abandon them to lawlessness, we must do everything with deliberation, we must calculate so that everything is done for the good of the people and for the good of its interests.
Money and banks — this is today the gravest question of existence, and therefore we must guard it like the apple of our eye. We must spare our financial institutions, we must take pains that their prestige not only should not be diminished but, on the contrary, should be raised to its former level, to its former splendour, when we took pleasure in hearing how high our banks stood. And their funds, needless to say, we must surely, surely spare, for they were taken from the people and were destined for the people and for the benefit of the broad strata of the population.
About the danger of crumbling and of bringing to nothing the prestige of these useful people's institutions we have spoken more than once already, and we have pointed out that one must beware of the danger that can come when one goes down these sickly paths.
Now one may no longer remain indifferent to this problem, which takes on an ever more serious character as time goes on. It is therefore high time to bring a little light and life into this field.
We have today in Zagłębie several well-situated Jewish banks; let them take upon themselves the initiative to solve these difficult problems. They ought therefore to convene a district conference as soon as possible, which should endeavour to bring order and responsibility into the matter of banking. Demoralization and lawlessness may no longer be tolerated, especially now, when we have the possibility of saving the institutions from a serious danger.
— The present question mark, which is no worse than the previous one, must be solved not by others but indeed by ourselves.
R. Let.
The Vanished Daughter (2)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 2.]
An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World
by Elizabeta Garin [Elżbieta Garin].
2.

"I don't know, Berish, 'jak Boga kocham' [Polish: 'as I love God'], I don't know!... He didn't confide in me, that Staszek... But I understood..."
"What did you understand? You scoundrel ['łajdak'], you!"
"That he means to go back to the circus, because the circus is soon leaving again for America and he wants very much to go there."
"Is that true?" — Berish loosened his hands on him a little.
"'Jak Boga kocham'!"
"Good, go" — Berish pushed him away with such force that the other very nearly fell from such a height that he would never have come out of there alive, had he not caught hold of a tree. "And remember," Berish shouted into his pale, frightened face, "that if I find out you told me a lie, your life isn't worth a pinch of snuff."
For a few minutes Janek looked after him, and then he turned [Polish 'skierował się'] onto a narrow, winding path ['ścieżka'] that led deeper into the forest.
"You'll see her all right," he said with a bitter smile on his lips — "like last year's snow!"
Meanwhile Berish the coachman went on to carry out his errand at the villa. He was already much calmer now; he had somewhat stilled his anger at the young rascal, and if the scoundrel had told the truth, Reb Shloyme would surely catch them in Pressburg [Bratislava]... because the circus was surely still there.
The large two-storey white villa with its rich entrance, the beautiful balconies with their white columns wreathed in white, red and yellowish roses, the trees covered in blossom, the open windows that glittered and dazzled in the sun — gave no sign at all of the terrible gloom and grief that had spread so widely inside the house; only one thing showed [?] that something unusual had happened: the doctor's little carriage stood at the entrance, and not a living soul was to be seen.
Berish went round the house and into the kitchen. There, where it had always hummed with cooks and maids, there was now no one but old Toybe. She sat at the table, her old head on both hands; the stove was cold and dark; nothing stood on the big range, as though no one had cooked on it for a long time. An inexpressible gloom was spread over everyone...
"Toybe, are you asleep?" — he touched her gently on the shoulder.
She started up from her place in fright.
"Ah, it's you, Berish?" — she calmed down a little at the sight of him. "What do you say to our misfortune?" — and she burst into tears.
"Hush, hush, one mustn't... Tell me rather, how is she?"
"She keeps fainting... In these twenty-four hours she has aged twenty-four years... my little dove... my poor child... Who could ever have expected such a misfortune?"
"Do you think I'll be able to see her? I have a letter to her from Pan Shloyme."
"I'll ask the doctor; he's the whole master here now." She got up heavily and went out, and Berish set about making a fire in the stove. He had had nothing in his mouth today [printed 'hey(g)t' for 'haynt'] and could not remember whether he had eaten anything since yesterday's breakfast... Who had such a thing on his mind at all? But now he resolved to brew himself a cup of coffee and perhaps have a bite too.
"You'll have to give me the letter, Berish, and I'll give it to the doctor... They won't let you, or even me, in to her..."
He took the letter out of the breast of his quilted jacket ['watowana kurtka'] and handed it to her, going back to the work of lighting the stove.
"Yes, Berish, I nearly forgot: when is the master coming? The doctor wants to know."
"When Reb Shloyme will come I don't know; but the young one, Pan Fritz, will probably be here tomorrow, because Reb Shloyme telegraphed him yesterday from Orawa."
"The poor boy!" — she heaved a deep sigh, and taking the coffee and a little packet of chicory out of the cupboard, she started towards the door; on the threshold she stopped for a minute.
"Meanwhile make the coffee, Berish; I'll be right back, and I'll give you something to eat."

Chapter 2.
In the Old Robbers' House.

On his way Janek stopped at a small white cottage with a fair-sized garden in front and behind, but not as clean and shining, nor as overgrown with flowers, as the others. A big dog came out to meet him, barking merrily.
"Sh-sh, Kuci, don't make a racket," he stroked the dog, "we mustn't rouse [?] the old man... let him stay [?] out there in the field..."
He went into the house and soon came out with a bundle of things and a full sack; then, still calming the dog, he slipped out through the wicket gate ['furtka'] and banged it shut behind him, because he did not want Kuci to run after him... About the errand he was now going on not even a dog needed to know...
He now took the path that led away from Z., and the road [?] — this was not the usual short road to the larger town of Orawa, and it lies through a dense, dark forest which the inhabitants of the surrounding villages and small towns used to avoid by every possible means; and yet it was the road to that town.
The further Janek went, the denser and darker the forest grew, the harder and more overgrown the paths, on which seldom anyone dared to walk, because the paths led not only to the Carpathian town of Orawa but also to the 'Robbers' House', which the people's imagination had ringed with terror and dangers. The tales one used to hear told on a cold winter night by the hundred-year-old grandmother or grandfather would send a shiver through the bodies of the younger and more civilized mountain folk.
The tales were often exaggerated; but the plain truth was also terrible enough.
The Robbers' House, to which Janek was now laboriously making his way, really had been built at the beginning of the eighteenth century, in the course of a single week, by a band of robbers who were notorious in the Carpathian mountains for their cruelty and murderousness. So terribly did they treat even the poor peasants of the surrounding villages — who were always inclined to see [printed 'veyn' for 'zeyn'] a kind of hero in a brigand, because as a rule they did not molest them — that even they regarded these robbers with dread, and swore to take revenge on them and not to hide them in time of need.

The Struggle for a National, Secular Kehilla*)

So we have now lived through the first period of the kehilla elections. What we said in advance [word uncertain] has happened — what until the last minute we did not want to believe, that the dangerous step would be taken; but the misfortune has happened. A motion was lodged with the reclamation (appeals) commission against the Zionist Mr. Liter[?] to strike him off the voters' list on the basis of paragraph 20. And on the day of 24 March the first strong page of the election calendar came to an end, and from that moment we enter the second period of the struggle, which was opened[?] by the „Agudah“ [Agudat Israel]. Now the plans of the Agudah ringleaders are coming plainly to light: they dream, by the power of the „striking-off“, of seizing all power in the Jewish kehillas with a single stroke, of rendering harmless the undesired elements, the eternal „shouters“, the eternally dissatisfied. In the fantasy of the Agudah brains the bright picture of the future kehillas is already being painted — how well and comfortably the future Agudah parnassim [kehilla leaders] will live, undisturbed by those who always have complaints, who shout, make noise and babble[?] mindlessly about some national cultural autonomy. It will be a real delight: nobody will disturb, all quiet, „and none moveth the wing, or openeth the mouth, or peepeth“.
In a number of towns in Poland the starosta [district head] simply ordered and indicated the candidates who were to be elected to the election commissions; and in Będzin too we were eyewitnesses to how the starosta disqualified certain members of the election commission who, apparently, did not find favour in his eyes.
With such sweet dreams they go about in Agudah circles. To the credit of Polish Jewry, however, it must be said that it understood in good time the great „danger“ lurking from the Agudah for the whole of Klal Israel, and promptly began the proper counter-attack. A storm of protests arose throughout the country against the usurpers of the „Agudah“, who want, with partisan means of force — which contradicts Jewish ethics and is also not in accordance with the law of the Torah — to seize the kehillas and turn them into Agudist „Yevseks“[?] [a jibe at the Yevsektsiya, the Soviet Jewish communist sections]. The Jewish „Koło“ [the Jewish club in the Sejm] also showed the proper vigilance[?] and brought various interpellations in the Sejm, pointing out the illegal actions of the starostas in various towns in Poland. And it seemed[?] that in Agudah circles they had taken a bit of a fright, that a certain sobering[?] had set in from the intoxicating opium[?] paragraphs. We believed that after the Central Committee of the „Agudah“ had published its official communiqués, in which they denied it by stone and bone [vehemently], justifying themselves that they were innocent as a lamb and had actually meant the communists — but then what was the renewed bitter struggle everywhere to obtain an overwhelming majority in the commissions? Did they have no ulterior thoughts in mind? We saw, after all, in Będzin how a dogged struggle dragged on[?] day and night over the forming of the commissions. Did they perhaps have the communists in mind in Będzin too? Still, we believed that a certain retreat had really set in in Agudah tactics, that a sense of responsibility had awakened in them too, and that they had taken account of what consequences the dangerous tactics of the [phrase uncertain: „moderne khomos u-smakhos“] could bring — that with their own hands they are destroying and laying waste the whole kehilla system, and the ones to suffer first of all will be none other than the Agudah „holy vessels“ themselves. And that was the main reason why at the last session of the reclamation commission Mr. Rinski[?] already agreed that no one should be struck off... because the lie had come out too glaringly.
And one can say boldly that, were it not for the vigilance[?] of the Zionists, who succeeded in setting up a united counter-front, who knows what face the election commissions would have had here in Będzin, and who knows what forms the „Agudah“ would then have taken on, and how far their appetites in the striking-off process would have gone. Then it would no longer have been a question of one person, as in the present case, but they would have gone on[?] further — „once licence is given to the destroyer, he does not distinguish“. And if until now there was still someone who was neutral towards the kehilla elections in general, he has now been drawn spontaneously into the election struggle. This proves the great agitation that reigns in town against the Agudah ringleaders, and nobody any longer doubts the rightness and usefulness of the Zionist election campaign, which has set itself the goal of carrying on the struggle until the national, secular, democratic kehilla that we demand is won.
Nete Landner
*) On the basis of free discussion.
Bomb Attack on a Jewish Shop in Upper Silesia

Undiscovered persons planted a powerful dynamite bomb at the shop of the Jewish merchant Yakov Chaimowicz in Wodzisław (Upper Silesia), in order to destroy the Jewish shop. Fortunately the night watchman noticed a package with a burning fuse lying on the ground by the shop. He immediately informed the police, who extinguished the fuse and took away the package, in which there was a powerful explosive.
An energetic investigation is being conducted.
