They Kept Silent

Minister Sładkowski [probably Sławoj-Składkowski] has declared that the question of the Pinsk marshes is not topical at present, because there are claimants with a prior right to the „marshes“.
The Polish peasants have little land, and enthusiasm for Jews in settling the Pinsk marshes could arouse the people's wrath.
True, the minister sweetened the bitter pill with compliments to the Jewish creative spirit, and in principle he is not against the colonising activity of the Jewish masses.
But for the time being it cannot be carried out — the poor Polish peasants come first.
And when thousands of Jewish families of small traders and artisans are perishing of hunger and shame, standing whole days, languishing, in their empty shops, waiting with a pounding heart for the sequestrator to come and take away the last listed goods[?].
And when thousands upon thousands of Jewish young people wander about the streets of the towns, searching in vain somewhere to earn a piece of bread.
When our intelligentsia wears away its best young years in hard conditions, sits for its matura, studies with self-sacrifice — and is left standing at locked doors, having nowhere to apply its knowledge and its „creative spirit“.
Nobody cares about this great desperate mass, which is drowning[?] in its own blood, in its poverty and helplessness.
None of the decisive factors gives a thought to what wrath will be aroused among the tormented masses when they are not even granted leave to crawl into the marsh...
Because — do you know why? Because the mass is a Jewish one, a mute creature, tormented, persecuted for thousands of years, and there is no one to appeal on its behalf.
Even these representatives, who listened to the minister's answer, did not find it necessary to ask the minister:
— My lord squire, and what do you intend to do with our poor masses?
They kept silent, because they know that the ruined Jewish mass, too, keeps silent and suffers..
Y. L. Sh.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shemini)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Shemini
—o—
a) "Draw near to the altar" (9:7)
"Aaron was ashamed to approach the altar, until Moses said to him: why are you ashamed? It is for this that you were chosen." — Torat Kohanim.
A.
Aaron was ashamed to approach the altar because he felt himself guilty of the sin of the Calf, in which he had had some share. So Moses said to him: on the contrary, only someone who has a sin beneath him is fit to be a leader, for such a person will not allow himself to rule too much, because he will be afraid that his sin might be thrown in his face...
"One does not appoint a leader over the community unless a basket of reptiles hangs behind him" — the best leader is only the one who has behind him a basket of reptiles, a bundle of sins... Such a one knows not to overstep the measure... But the basket of reptiles should be behind him — only in the past... Or Pnei Moshe.
B.
When Moses saw that Aaron was bashful and considered himself unworthy to serve at the altar, he said to him: it is precisely for your humility that you were raised to the priesthood; because you hold yourself so small, you were raised to be so great... Lev Aryeh.
• • •
"I have seen the men of ascent, and they are few" (Sotah 45) —
The "few", those who are small in their own eyes — they are the men of ascent, the exalted ones. — Or Yesharim.
• • •
"Him that hath a high look and a proud heart I will not suffer" —
The only cure for pride is: envy. When someone thinks too highly of himself, he is told: just look, that other one is greater still — more wealth, more honour. But whoever is a "proud heart" (a haughty man) and on top of that a "high look" (an envious man) — for him there is no help any more. If he looks ahead of himself he envies; if he looks behind himself he again thinks himself great... Havot Yair.
—o—
b) "And the glory of the Lord shall appear unto you" (9:10 [sic])
The Yalkut says on the above verse: "That evil inclination — remove it from your hearts."
Even when one reaches so high an attainment as "the glory of the Lord shall appear unto you", the revelation of the Divine Presence, one still has an evil inclination... only it is a special evil inclination, "that evil inclination" — the evil inclination of the great... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
c) "And they died before the Lord" (10:2)
Two reasons are given in the Midrash for the death of Nadab and Abihu. One: because they did not want to marry; and [the other] because they were looking forward to the death of Moses and Aaron, so as to take over their leadership.
The connection between the two reasons is:
For the sin of not marrying they could have answered: they want to study [Torah] — just as Ben Azzai did not want to take a wife because "his soul longed for the Torah". But wanting to become leaders is surely the best proof that they do not want to study... Yeriat Shlomo.
—o—
d) "Diligently sought" (darosh darash) (10:16)
The middle of the Torah by words is "darosh darash", and the middle by letters is the verse "whatsoever goeth upon the belly".
Not "goeth upon the belly", not crawling on all fours, is what we must do when we want to beg something from the government, but "darosh darash" — to demand and to claim... Osem Bosem.
—o—
e) "Because he parteth the hoof" (11:7)
The four nations among whom the Jews were in exile are likened in the Book of Daniel to four beasts. The last exile — Edom — we are with the swine... For the former beast-nations showed their beastliness openly and undisguised. But today's Edom parts the hoof: it displays the signs of purity — here, we are civilised; but in truth: "he is unclean unto you", the same vileness [paskudstvo] as the beast-nations of old... Imrei Drush.
—o—
f) Swine
Reb Eizikl Slonimer [of Słonim] once sent his little book "Merov Tevina" [?] to a rich man. The booklet is small in quantity and great in quality. The rich man asks the price. Reb Eizikl has him told: a rouble. The rich man winces: such a small booklet — a rouble?
Meeting him later, Reb Eizikl says to him: it seems you hold by "the other thing" (— the pig)... For on the verse "with all thy might" (bekhol me'odekha) there are two interpretations. One interpretation: money; and the "other thing" (— the second interpretation): measure (me'odekha — middah, "for every measure that He metes out to you"). So if you look at the size of the booklet, you hold by "the other thing"... I, on the other hand, hold by the first interpretation: money...
—o—
g) "Of their flesh shall ye not eat" (11:8)
A question came before a Vilna rabbi: an apostate who wants to repent — must he immerse himself? One rabbi writes him a responsum in which he proves that the Vilna Gaon holds that such a man must indeed immerse himself, because he gorged himself on all kinds of non-kosher food while he was an apostate.
"That is impossible for me (the Vilna rabbi writes back), for if it is because of non-kosher food, I would have to immerse all the Vilna community leaders"...
—o—
Avot — Chapter One.
h) "Let thy house be open wide, and let the poor be members of thy household" (5)
If you are a rich man and want to give charity, then appoint poor people too as distributors. For the sated distributors do not know the poor man's taste... "And let the poor be members of thy household." Yarim Moshe [?].
—o—
i) "Loving peace and pursuing peace" (12)
Peace is no great friend of mankind. When the world was about to be created, Peace would not allow it, because — so it argued — it would be a world of nothing but quarrels. In this one thing — love of mankind — one may be a "pursuer of peace": chase peace away... Petah Einayim.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: 3611 Families Received Loans from the Gemilut Chesed Fund in Będzin

[Page head:] Friday, 23 Nisan 5691 — 23 — piątek 10 kwietnia 1931 [Friday, 10 April 1931]
What's new in Zagłębie?
Będzin
3611 families received loans from the Gemilut Chesed Fund in Będzin.
On Monday morning the 5th-anniversary jubilee celebration of the Będzin G[emilut] Ch[esed] Fund took place in the Corso hall.
The city's notables had been specially invited to the celebration, but of the 200 invited only about a dozen people came — those who have understanding for the people's affairs.
Of the G. Ch. funds in Zagłębie only a delegation from the G. Ch. fund in Sławków came.
The "Joint" representative, Mr. Giterman, sent a telegraphic greeting.
In connection with the jubilee an academy [festive assembly] was held, opened by Mr. L. Bożykowski, who handed over the chair to Mr. S. Lewkowicz. Invited to the presidium were Messrs. S. Żmucki, G. Rechnitz, Ch. W. Steinhart, L. Rubinlicht, Avrahaml Liwer, Natan Goldsobel, Jakob Erlich, D. Gitler, Michał Lewin, M. Rozensaft and Moshe Hampel.
The orchestra of "Hakoach" played the Polish and the Jewish anthem.
The report on the activity over the 5 years was given by Mr. Granek. The report shows that over this period the fund granted 3,611 loans amounting to 648,000 zł. Urgent relief was given to 619 people in the amount of 6,110 zł. The fund's working capital amounts to 125 thousand zł. (This sum includes the 56 thousand zł. which the fund owes the "Joint".)
After the report Mr. Wygodzki spoke about the great merits of the fund, especially at the present moment, and he appealed for the strengthening of the fund, which plays such an important role for the Jewish masses.
Then the floor was given to the delegate from Zawiercie, Mr. Chaim Kron [?], who delivered a longer lecture on the general significance of the Gemilut Chasadim funds in Poland. With fine thoughts and quotations from the Tanakh and the Talmud the speaker demonstrated how the beaten and persecuted Jewish people is able to create grandiose things even in the most terrible moments.
The chairman thanked the participants and delegates, and the academy was closed.
In conclusion the orchestra played several musical numbers, and the audience left the hall with satisfaction.
—o—
Hanged himself with a necktie in the police station.
The local police arrested in the street the 22-year-old Maj, a well-known drunkard and brawler. The policeman locked the drunkard in the police lock-up at the local commissariat. When after some time the policeman went into the lock-up, he saw that the drunkard was hanging from the pipes of the water supply, tied with a necktie.
All medical attempts did not help; the drunkard was already dead.
The Seders for the Orphans.

As is known, the orphans who are brought up in the so-called “ochronki” [children's shelters] were always distributed among a certain part of the Jewish population of Będzin.
Two years ago this system was abolished by the board of the Charity Society, which, seeing that the children suffered very much from eating at strangers' tables, made efforts so that the children should eat in their own homes [the children's homes], in their own surroundings.
Compared with last year, this year's Passover was organised in the best way. Care was taken that the children should have every good thing.
This year, for the first time, seders were organised in the ochronka for girls, where the seder nights were celebrated with all the trimmings.
Present at the seders were the president of the Charity Society, Dr. Weinzieher, and his wife, Mrs. Ts. Szajn, R' Mendel Rozenzaft, editor Szpigelman, and Lewkowicz[?], Y. Wygodzki, B. Pelc, L. Bożykowski, A. Bolimowski[?] and others, who spent the time with satisfaction in the children's homes, rejoiced together, and over the four cups wished one another that next year the seders would be held in the new building for the orphans.
The initiators, and especially Mrs. Ts. Szajn and R' Mendel Rozenzaft, who took such pains to give the children such pleasure, deserve a hearty yasher koach.
The Contents of the Memorandum of the Będzin Merchants' Association concerning the City-Council Elections

To the Hon. Minister of the Interior, Warsaw.
On 5 November 1930 you, Hon. Minister, ordered the dissolution of the municipal administration and the city council in Będzin. The grounds for the dissolution were that the present city council had no stable majority; at the same time there were no remarks about the city's management up to now, which was good, and the population did not complain about it.
The Hon. Voivode, two weeks before the dissolution of the municipal authority, expressed his opinion that the city management in Będzin was thrifty, cautious, well-planned and the best of the separated towns [miasta wydzielone] in the Kielce voivodeship. At the exhibition in Poznań it was distinguished by the Minister of Commerce.
The appointment of the temporary commissioner has completely broken off the contact that existed until now. The population knows nothing about the city's management; the population, which was accustomed to decide on the spending of the money from the taxes collected, does not want to be merely an obedient payer, but wants also to have an influence on the management of the city's money.
This problem cannot be solved even by the appointed council, since its competences are limited to an advisory vote, and it cannot represent people who were elected and bear responsibility towards their voters.
Already in the short time that the temporary commissioner has been managing, one sees how [—] the city's interests suffer. At one of the last meetings of the commissioners' council the temporary commissioner declared that he was seeking a 3-year moratorium, and this has caused the local ones [sic; probably: the local banks] to accept only reluctantly bills of exchange issued by the Będzin magistrate; also the suppliers of the public institutions, who must accept from the magistrate bills with terms of 6–7 months, must discount them with private persons and pay high interest.
The general critical situation of the taxpayers demands the greatest relief in imposing taxes and also in making expenditures. We know that you, Hon. Minister, are an opponent of heavy taxes; nevertheless we know that the present magistrate has provisionally entered the investment tax in the new budget.
In economic and personnel policy incomprehensible things are happening: disregarding the critical situation of the city treasury, the number of officials in the magistrate has been increased by several persons. The present temporary commissioner holds office only from 12 o'clock on, since at the same time he also serves as an official (referent) at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce. As a result, the magistrate's affairs are left entirely to the rule of the officials, who also disdain[?] and badly treat the petitioners.
The examples mentioned above prove that the present temporary heads of the magistrate not only cannot represent self-government, but can even undo what has been achieved so far.
Taking into account that the 6-week term provided for in Art. 66 of the decree on self-governments has long passed, and that the further continuation of the temporary city administration is not desirable for the city, we ask the Hon. Minister to order that elections be held for the Będzin city council.
Conference for Labour Palestine.

(N—r). Last Sunday a consultation took place here on the problems of Labour Palestine (the working Land of Israel), with the participation of Mr. Neustadt (Tel Aviv), representative of the Palestinian workers, and Messrs. Lewi and Morgenstern[?], representatives of the Polish League for Labour Palestine in Poland. The conference began with a delay of two and a half hours. The chair was taken by Mr. Lewi, who devoted his speech to the significance of the chalutz, of the Jewish worker, pioneer of the Jewish future[?]. The Jewish worker went to the Land of Israel with a national urge[?], and despite the great difficulties he fulfilled his national duty. The link of the whole[?] work of construction is the chalutz, who manifests the will of the people in deed; he is the forerunner of the strong working class in the Land of Israel, the crown of the Zionist work. The chalutz — this is the result[?] of our economic, cultural and political life. We need no longer agitate, only make use of what has been done in the field of the Jewish movement; it is not only a matter of a fund-raising campaign, it is also a matter of a great moral victory. The speaker calls for an intensified campaign for the benefit of Labour Palestine and says: let this not be philanthropy, but a national duty.
Then Mr. Morgenstern takes the floor and speaks with pathos about the fruitful activity of the Palestine Workers' Fund for the Jewish worker in the country. The speakers' remarks are supplemented by Mr. Neustadt, who points to the difficulties the Jewish workers in the Land of Israel have to contend with. Every cheap, uncultured, undemanding[?] Arab worker is strong competition for the Jewish one. The educational work among the Arabs, too, meets with difficulties from the Mufti and his allies. The Yishuv also has a strong enemy in the English administration.
The Englishman can colonise an uncultured, uncivilised people — then he is a gentleman; but when he has to deal with an un[?]cultured element [sic; the sense requires “cultured”], his abilities fail him. Hence the antisemitic attitude of the Palestine administration, which again feels[?] itself [—] in London. These are the obstacles against which the Jewish worker has to fight in the work of building his land.
After the speeches a banquet took place and, in a cheerful mood, larger sums were pledged for Labour Palestine.
Sosnowiec — A Great Storm at a Session of the "Jewish Parliament".

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla.] The struggle over the kehilla budget — Mizrachist and non-party councillors leave the session — votum separatum of the chairman — eggs and benches as means of obstruction — five councillors adopted the budget

On Sunday, the second day of Chol HaMoed, the tragi-comedy entitled "The Last Budget" was "performed" with great success in the kehilla premises on Częstochowska [טשיסטא] street... As is known, the starosta [district head] demanded that the president of the kehilla council, Mr. L. Szwajcer, call a session at which the new kehilla budget should be adopted by the kehilla council.
On the basis of this demand Mr. Szwajcer called the session for Sunday at 4 in the afternoon, to be valid with any number of members present.
The invitations to the session were, of course, sent out barely a few hours before the session, so that to most councillors the matter was not clear, and they interpreted it as a sly ploy by those who wish to impose the budget as drawn up by the kehilla administration.
The unexpected session aroused a certain interest among the Jewish population of Sosnowiec, so that before the start of the session the session hall was packed with the "gallery". The crush was so great that it was not easy to make out what was going on. All one could see was a squeezed-together mass of people shouting and making a racket...
And everyone shouted, except the few councillors, who sat behind the barrier and kept silent...
— — —
The chairman Mr. Szwajcer opens the session, and after the reading of the agenda the floor is taken by councillor Dawid Zylberberg, who proposes that, since the councillors received the invitations to the session a short time before the session and for that reason the councillors had no opportunity to acquaint themselves with the main item of today's session, the budget, the session should be postponed to another date.
The same statement is supported by the dozór [board member] Mr. Brauner, who says that the artisan councillors, having no notion of the session, had gone away, and therefore the session should not take place.
When Mr. Szwajcer declares that he must carry out what the starosta ordered him and that the session is valid with any number of members, the councillors K. Langer, J. Cwajgenhaft, D. Zylberberg (later also Mr. Kalisz) leave the session, and there remain, apart from the president, the councillors Unger, Englard, Feldman, Sicemski and Danciger.
Tempers flare, the air is "stifling", the gallery begins to take part, and when the councillors present decide to continue the session an uproar breaks out and an offensive with eggs and benches begins...
The scandal reaches its culminating point; those hit by the eggs seize the telephone by force and alarm the police commissariat...
It does not take long before police arrive, who put an end to the brawl, and at the chairman's request the "gallery" is removed from the session hall.
— — —
After the "battle" the atmosphere becomes "clearer" and the 5 councillors sit down to consider the new kehilla budget.
Secretary Lewenhof reads out the report on the expenditure and income of the budget for 1930. It turns out that from that budget there are still debts amounting to 85 thousand zł.
Before proceeding to the new budget, councillor Ch. Danciger proposes that the budget be adopted at the same level as the last budget.
The majority are against the proposal, and every item that had been preliminarily set by the administration is discussed.
After examining the budget, Mr. Danciger's proposal is put forward by Mr. Sicemski and — everything stays as it was...
Throughout the session a policeman was on duty in a neighbouring room.
General meeting of the "Merchants' Bank" in Sosnowiec.

In the "Sala Angielski" hall, on Sunday afternoon, under the chairmanship of Mr B. Rozman, the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" (Merchants' Bank) in Sosnowiec took place.
After the formal points of the agenda had been dealt with, the president, Mr Natan Abramczyk, delivered the report on the activity to date.
Mr Abramczyk shows with figures the bank's operations, and owing to [lit. "thanks to"] the prevailing crisis, and because it did not "chase after big profits", the bank earned no more than 3,000 zł.
Then a short discussion took place, and after an expression of confidence in the management it was resolved to strengthen the existence of the bank.
In place of the retiring members, Messrs Luria, W. Manes and K. Fiszel were elected.

A Peretz evening in the Esperanto language
On the 16th anniversary of the death (yahrzeit) of I. L. Peretz, an evening devoted to his life and work was held by the Będzin Esperantists.
After the poet's memory was honoured by rising, a lecture was given in the Esperanto language on Peretz's work. Then Esperanto translations of Peretz were read, and afterwards Miss L. Fiszer recited several of Peretz's works.
—o—
A "Szul-Kult" branch founded in Sosnowiec
Under the chairmanship of Mr A. Ganzwejch, the founding meeting of friends of the national Jewish-secular school organisation "Szul-Kult" in Sosnowiec took place. After a detailed lecture by Mr I. Peszeni, general secretary of "Szul-Kult" in Poland, a temporary organising committee was elected, which includes Messrs A. Ganzwejch, Józef Goldberg, Pres. A. Opatowski, Dr I. Rotsztajn, B. D. Durkiewicz, Dr Tratojer [?], I. Ajbuszyc, Mrs Orbach, I. I. Piekarski, Jakub Rotsztajn, Starszy I. Rotensztajn, Miss Testelirer [?], Eng. Mangel, Miss Herszkowicz, Mrs Landau and others.

The Management.

Protest by a group of synagogue worshippers against the cantor
[Kehilla — religious life; open letter by worshippers (notice no. 423).] We express our greatest displeasure at the conduct of the cantor Mr. Żupowicz [?] (Yiddish: Zhupovitsh), who, in fulfilling his office as shliach tzibur (prayer leader), uses such means as desecrate the sanctity of the prayers. But what happened during the holiday [Passover] is already unbearable: has such a scandal ever happened, that a cantor should permit himself to attack, before the whole congregation, a member (ba'al habayit) of the synagogue who is also the leader of the morning service (ba'al shacharit) on the High Holidays, calling him an "am ha'aretz" (ignoramus)! The cantor, however, was not satisfied with that and shouted that if the member does not leave the synagogue, he will not lead the prayers. We believe that such behaviour causes demoralisation, and we turn to the kehilla administration to settle the matter as is proper.
A group of synagogue worshippers

Draft of the 1910 year-class begins on 2 May.
Those born in Będzin must report a month later
As in the whole of Poland, the draft (pobór) of those born in 1910 begins in the Będzin district, too, on 2 May.
For those who live in Będzin the draft will begin a month later, i.e. on 2 June, and will take place on 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 June.
—o—
Union of non-party Hasidim.
The initiative of the Aleksander Hasidim in Będzin to unite all non-party Hasidim for the kehilla elections against the "Aguda" is meeting with due success.
The Chęciny, Rozprza, Wolbórz, Radomsko (number 2) Hasidim and others have declared themselves in favour of the union.
This Saturday night the final unification of the bloc will take place in the Aleksander shtibl.

The Labour Inspectorate in Olkusz liquidated.
The department belongs to Sosnowiec.
On the basis of an order of the Minister of Labour, the Labour Inspectorate in Olkusz has been liquidated. Its affairs will be handled by the Sosnowiec labour inspector.

Shoot-out between a policeman and a thief
Beyond Bobrowniki the policeman on duty noticed a person who seemed suspicious to him. When the policeman approached the person, the latter opened fire. At first the policeman fired into the air, but seeing the danger from the bandit, the policeman fired at him and wounded him severely.

Echoes of the "Bank Ludowy", of blessed memory...
In the course of the past week the Investigation Office questioned a number of persons who are acquainted with the "activity" of the former Aguda bank known as "Bank Ludowy" in Sosnowiec.

Concerning income declarations.
We are asked by the Będzin "Small Traders' Union" to draw attention to the fact that the deadline for submitting declarations (zeznania) of income for the year 1930 runs only until 1 May of this year. Missing the deadline carries the threat of a penalty.

Shortage of bread and baked goods.
Recently the price of rye and wheat flour has risen sharply, but the price commission does not want to raise the price of bread and baked goods as the bakers demand. Because of this, baking is being done in very limited quantity, so that in the course of the week it was not easy to get bread or rolls.

Doings with knives.
On Tuesday a bloody fight took place on Dziewicza[?] Street between two Christian residents of that street. Both fought with knives in their hands. The result was that one of them fell victim.

Suicide of a Jewish merchant in Działoszyce.
They write to us from Działoszyce:
Last Tuesday the 54-year-old merchant Yisroel Chęciński committed suicide here by drinking a dose of iodine.
The cause is the present critical situation.

Yesterday, Thursday, Mrs Toyba Tazewicz[?], a resident of Ciasna Street, died at the age of 101.

At the "Izba Skarbowa" [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce, on the 28th and 29th of this month, the commission will consider the appeals against the turnover tax.

On Wednesday evening a number of persons were arrested in Będzin, mainly respectable housewives, who had bought various goods from a Christian woman who has long been known for her cheap goods.
As it turns out, the cheap goods that the Christian woman sells in many places[?] are — stolen.

In the coming days the leader of the Austrian Zionists, the former creator of Radical Zionism, Mr Robert Stricker, will give a lecture in Sosnowiec under the title "Why did I leave the Radicals and enter the Revisionist ranks".

A day of misfortunes in Upper Silesia.
On Wednesday an explosion occurred at the "Laura" zinc works in Siemianowice, from which six workers received severe wounds. On the way to the hospital two died.

[Theatre — Będzin, Sosnowiec, Zagłębie.] An old question that is always new.
(On today's premiere by the "Muza".)
In Poland in the hundreds of thousands, in England, Germany, America in the millions, in the whole world in the tens of millions, they stand, the masses of the unemployed, at the gates of factories and workshops, yearning for the happy, by now almost unbelievable word — work.
With eyes kindled by envy and enmity people look upon the "lucky ones", the workers smeared[?] with dirt, who hurry[?] home with their last strength so as to hand over, first thing next morning, the last bit of marrow to the capitalist golden calf.
—
At Ford, Citroën, Krupp and the like, there where the conveyor belt is the whip on the workers' backs; at those where the penalty slip is the bridle that keeps the "murderers" and "strikers" from running wild; there where "lockout" and "reduction" lurk over the heads of the half-starved workers — these are capitalist tricks.
In mine X the manager saved on gas masks[?] a round sum of 100,000 dollars and thereby caused the death of 112 people; in town V a newly built house collapsed because of bad building material and killed 4 people; and in another town a manufacturer set fire to his factory in order to collect the insurance sum, and 3 human lives perished in it.
What, then, are 112, or even 112 thousand human lives, when in their place there are tens of millions of unemployed, waiting submissively for the moment when they will be able to serve[?] the capitalist meat-grinder with life and limb.
—
On the canvas of capitalist morality, where 100 guilders are more than 100 human lives, Herman Heijermans [printed: Heyerman] gives us a piece of life which in many cases can be compared with all the larger capitalist enterprises.
In a Dutch village where everything lives from the work of fishing, the ruler is Bos, the owner of the fishing office and possessor of a large number of fishing vessels.
Bos, who conducts his business with the help of the police, forces 12 men, fathers of children, and even youths[?], to go out fishing on a rotten ship which is doomed to go down almost[?] at any storm[?]. The sinking, however, can bring in the insurance sum of 10[?] thousand guilders. While the return of the "Hope" (the name of the ship) is awaited, there are scenes of despair among the women and brides left behind, who are seized with terror of the disaster they foresee. Bos's calculation did not deceive him: the ship goes down, the insurance sum is already as good as in his pocket, and Bos's wife issues an appeal to the population to collect donations for the benefit of the widows and relatives of those who perished.
A model of typically petty-bourgeois philanthropy.
—
The step taken by the "Muza" is a daring one; is it a successful one? One has to see the performance.
Y. Tumanski[?]

"Peg o' My Heart" ["Peg, mayn harts"] by Hartley Manners [printed: Hartley Mangers[?]], performed by the artists of the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre.

Elementary Work

(The past and the future Jewish kehilla representation. — Which of them will be better?)

So it means that we shall soon be freed from our kehilla providers, from the representatives of the Jewish community, who have clamped themselves so firmly onto our body. We had thought, after all, that this autocracy would never again come to an end; now we see that this rule is drawing to a close, and the public is pleased with that if only because, on the one hand, people had simply grown sick of it. The public grumbled: why are they sitting there, what are they doing there, when their term ended long ago? And on the other hand the activity was so unsympathetic, so unworthy and coarse, that it simply began to disgust. A trifle — how much filth and shame and pain were brought in there? What did they make of the only higher Jewish representative body, of the supra-party representation, which really ought to have played the most decisive roles in our everyday life. What did they make of this institution, which had so many chances of being raised to a proper level?

The heart aches when we begin to recall what the kehilla representation was, what could have been made of it, and to what a low level it was finally brought. Who does not remember the preparations for the first elections — what did we not want to make of that institution? What beautiful dreams and fantasies were not woven in our minds back then! This was, after all, supposed to be our self-government, our — so to speak — Jewish local parliament; and if we dreamed so and thought so, it is no wonder either, for to that end we elected people of all manner of tendencies and shades, and we went then with deep consciousness and with full faith to bring in people full of temperament, who would be capable of transforming Jewish kehilla life for the good of our interests, for the good of our favourable demands.

Our parnasim, when we have complaints against them, prove to us that before they came into being we had nothing, and so there was nothing that could be lost anyway. True, we had nothing, but that does not yet mean that we lost nothing. We had poor little rooms of the dead ["mesim shtiblekh" — apparently the old kehilla rooms, concerned chiefly with burial], but innocence and cleanliness held the place of honour in them; and the parnasim took those poor little rooms of the dead and defiled them, and brought into them an unlimited dose of lawlessness and of clumsy irresponsibility, thanks to which we are humiliated in people's eyes. Can we then compare the present kehilla representations, with their large number of parnasim, to the kehilla rooms of old, where 2—3 dozors [dozorzy, the wardens of the old synagogue boards] ran things? Were that poverty and pettiness not preferable and more esteemed by us than the present gmina offices with all their clumsy clattering apparatus put together? When we draw a parallel between that little gmina room and today's kehilla representation, do we not recoil from the latter and begin instinctively to value the former?

And at just such a moment and under such conditions our kehilla representations have been dissolved, and in their place new councillors, new representatives, new parnasim are to be elected. One would think that, at a time when we had so little joy from the previous parnasim, we ought to be beside ourselves with gladness that they can be replaced; all this would be fine, however, if things were as they ought to be, if it did not look like a toy with which one wants now to play, now to tease, and now to mock. Here we have to do with a paragraph 20, and there with family relationships — which takes away from the conscious, intelligent person the appetite for public activity, for a progressive public revival.

Yes, basically one ought to be pleased that the moment has come for dissolving the present kehilla boards; but that is true only when the prospects for the future are finer and happier. The trouble, however, is that we are wedged into such a bewitched wheel that we cannot get out of it, so that the more we turn around it, the more we become entangled in it, and we see no favourable way out — how to get out of there with our bones intact, with a sound mind and with prospects that would brighten the Jewish public horizon.

Alas, alas, we now see only pessimism; and how can one approach the kehilla elections with a light conscience and a light heart under such unpleasant conditions? With such undesirable elements, who will sell you everything for a pot of lentils? How can one elect kehilla representatives when countless Jewish lists will appear on the Jewish street, and the common people will by no manner of means be able to sort them out, will not know which way is in and which is out, which ones to take seriously and which to regard as harmful. With such a mishmash of lists as is foreseen, it is quite likely that the simple Jew, who knows nothing of all sorts of combinations and falsehoods, will tomorrow choose the list that yesterday he fought with all his strength, never having imagined that he would ever take it seriously; for now they will operate with all sorts of harmful means, and will reckon with no one and with nothing. It can already be foreseen today that this will not be about ideas and problems, about fighting for permitted means and combating impermissible ones, harmful means. Quite certainly there will be personal fights here, in which people will stop at nothing in the world so long as they carry through what they please.

Things have now reached the point where Shmerl son of Berl [i.e. any Tom, Dick or Harry] will put up his own list the moment he wants to have a seat in the Jewish kehilla; and because the lists on the Jewish street will be fruitful and multiply, the turnout will be small and a mandate will not need many votes — people will find themselves some way or other, and will work wonders to bring about what they so badly want to have. That is the wind that blows in the little Jewish world, that is the slogan that circulates today.

It is therefore self-evident that honest people, conscientious people, people with names, people who would be capable of bringing benefit to the Jewish public, will not want to be put on a par with those of the lowest rank, and will have neither the courage nor the need to stand in one row with those who will at every opportunity strut with their "I" and will demand that only they be made prominent, that only they figure as the foremost of the lot [literally "the first out of the mortar"].

For honest and sensitive people this is an inadmissible phenomenon, to which they will not be able to adapt, and they will not be able to remain standing in one row with those others even if they wanted to, even if they renounced their own person; of this the future will convince us, this practice will plainly prove.

One must not remain indifferent to this harmful phenomenon, which threatens to darken still further our sad enough public situation. We must react to the extraordinary lawlessness, which has lost every limit and every measure of decency and propriety, and which leads to a banal indifference among the Jewish masses, who are beginning to lose every interest that binds society to its general interests.

If we want to ensure — and we must ensure — that the Jewish kehilla representations do not sink to the deepest abyss and that we do not look upon them with disgust and contempt, one must now see to bringing a little order and a certain system into this field. First of all care must be taken that the putting up of lists not be permitted to whoever merely feels like it, but that it be subject to a certain responsibility and a proper control.

If this elementary work is not taken up right now, with full interest and attention to our public affairs, the Jewish representation will vanish from the Jewish street and the Jewish representatives will be treated like nominated dictators.

R. Let.
What Was Heard, What Was Seen

[Feuilleton — Będzin and Sosnowiec.] Conveyed by Ben Amotz.

In Honour of Hanka...
In the little world of Jewish women a great commotion reigned this past week. The telephones were busier than ever; people talked, debated and made ready.
? ? ?
Do not, God forbid, make the mistake of thinking that the female sex of the better sort — “of the better people”, as they say — displayed, during the holiday, activity in the field of organisation, education, communal affairs. Oh no! Those are not articles in demand at the present moment, least of all in ladies’ society; their entire attention was given to
— Hanka...
She came, Mrs. Hanka [האנקא; probably the Polish singer and actress Hanka Ordonówna — a conjectural identification], to Będzin for a performance. Well, well, it hardly needs saying: when Hanka comes, should our intelligentsia not go to welcome her? And so there was a rush for tickets — no small matter! Not go and see Hanka? What is a lady of today worth if she is not at Hanka’s evening?
The non-Jews gnashed their teeth: How can it be? Our Hanka is to act and sing almost exclusively for “Żydki” [a Polish slur for Jewesses]?
But shout today, shout tomorrow — the fact is that the theatre was full of our Reginas, Stefas[?] and Adelas, and all in honour of their Hanka...

The Heavy Carriage.
The carriage that has for a good many years been hauling the kashrut baggage in Będzin has once again got stuck in the mud and cannot budge from the spot.
A year ago those who look after kashrut matters in town published a heart-rending appeal: that the Jewish population of Będzin should help rescue the Jews of Będzin from the forty-nine gates of impurity and tax itself for the benefit of the “historic” mikveh building in our town...
And we thought that the hot tears shed by the “providers of kashrut” had not been in vain, that we could now have a quiet conscience, that as far as kashrut and purity are concerned there was no longer any cause for concern; but — as it turns out — we were mistaken, greatly mistaken indeed. This was revealed to us by the new appeal, distributed over the holiday, in which it is once more announced that
— “The kashrut carriage is again sinking into the forty-nine gates of impurity”...
Absolutely nothing has changed, except that once they demanded money and today — people; quite simply, a Kashrut Council [Vaad HaKashrut] is going to be founded, which is to keep watch over the sinful souls so that they do not stumble...
A very fair thing; only one thing astonishes us: that the proclamations make no mention at all of the fact that thousands of Jewish children from the public elementary schools [szkoły powszechne] are being brought up as strangers to the Jewish people. Evidently, where there are no political motives everything may go “horodom” [?; from context: to rack and ruin], even when the fate of the coming Jewish generation is at stake...

The “Polish-Speaker”...
You know them well, the shmendrik-intellectuals; you can meet them everywhere. The greatest number of them is supplied by the female sex. When they come, these shmendrik-intellectual ladies, to the theatre for “Binke Pinke” [apparently the title of a Yiddish show], you will, God forbid, not get a single Yiddish word out of them; even during the intervals they are busy with the “laws of eating”, and the talk too is — “Polish”.
One such lady-shmendrik went on the last day of Passover “to say Yizkor”. Where should such an “intellectual” go? Presumably to the “German” [progressive] synagogue, to be among “her own”.
She arrived in the synagogue courtyard. Several young men were standing there chatting; the “lady”, prayer-book in hand, wishing to find out whether she had come in time, asked the young men:
— “Czy już mazkerowali?” [Polish with a made-up verb: “Have they ‘mazkir-ed’ yet?”]...

What Is This?...
A session of the Sosnowiec kehilla council.
At the head, the president; to the right and to the left, the “remaining ones”, those who have the say over the budget, which is being judged “for life or for death”...
Every item is examined, to the accompaniment of a quip, a joke. Sometimes also of
— a curse...
“4,000 zł. — a subsidy for illiterate [analfabetn] artisans!” the chairman reads out.
— What? For beds [“oyf betn”]?... What on earth do they need beds for in the community office? — asks one of the parnasim-judges.
— Not beds [betn] but alphabets [alfabetn] — to teach old artisans to write — a member of the “Aguda” gives him to understand.
— “To the devil with it, no need; old Fayvl won’t manage it anyway”...
The item is struck out with awe and reverence, and “the one who knows not how to ask” triumphs and mutters to himself:
“Beds, indeed! In their old age they want to turn into scribblers; let them go and work, to all the devils”...

A Cure for the Affliction...
The sages of the Będzin kehilla sat and sought some advice on how to get rid of the crisis, which has become a permanent resident of the kehilla treasury.
What is to be done? the president asks his counsellors.
For a while silence reigned; not one of them had anything to say. But it did not take long before the vice-president took the floor and declared that he had an idea how to get rid of the crisis.
— An idea? — all were curious — let us hear it, then.
— We must take care [“zorgn” — also: worry] — the giver of advice answers innocently.
— We must worry? — the president repeats the words — perhaps that really is it?
And a resolution was passed that all members of the kehilla board must
— worry...
The “advice” came into force at once, and when a rabbinical judge [moreh-hora’ah] or whatever official comes with a claim — a few zlotys! — he gets from the president the answer that redemption is drawing near, for the sages of the kehilla are very active and
— they are worrying...

A New “Party”...
In Sosnowiec a brand-new “party” has arisen for the approaching kehilla elections.
— “Old Sosnowiec” [Alt Sosnowiec] — that is the “party’s” name.
It is a modern creature: its body is non-partisan, only its innards are Agudist...
The new “party” possessed two Reuvens. And when the time had come for the party to hatch from its eggshell, the same quarrel began as between Jacob and Esau — “and the children struggled together”... Each wanted the seat by the eastern wall.
The “jostling”, however, wrecked all the secret plans, so that the non-partisan Reuven is already declaring:
— “I have no portion with them”, I don’t want to belong to that company; and the second Reuven still sits at his watchmaker’s bench and ponders:
“Shall I move, or stay standing like a broken clock”...
Nothing substantial exists as yet; one thing only is clear — that the “Aguda” has brought forth a new party.
— Old Sosnowiec is its name...
It Has Remained As It Was

(Education in the civic spirit. — What progress has Sosnowiec Jewry made?)
Say what you will, it is a rare thing; one can only marvel at how apathetic our Jewish Sosnowiec remains toward everything and everyone. Whatever we touch, wherever we turn and twist, we are rebuffed, and in a cold sweat we recoil from the idea on which, only a day earlier, we had placed so much hope and weight. More than once there arises with this or that communal worker, with this or that party, a conception that seems likely to bring so much good and relief to the broad strata of the population — and on the morrow, as soon as people have sat down at the table, the fine plans at once melt away like a soap bubble.
When, and in what, has nothing at all come of it all? Does one really need to take the trouble to prove it? Does one not see it at every step? On the contrary, let the Jewish population show us when and what has in fact been done for the benefit of its interests! When and what has in fact been done to improve local Jewish affairs?
Yes, one thing must be mentioned to its credit: that on the appeals commission [rekursn-komisye — the tax-appeals commission] in Kielce Jewish Sosnowiec is properly represented, and the activity there is intensive and conscientious — that may be said. In all other fields, by contrast, one sees no willpower whatever, no initiative, no representation, no interest, no responsibility.
We unfortunately cannot point to a single cheerful phenomenon in our sad life; none of the better-off want to concern themselves with what belongs to the community, with what belongs to the people.
It is characteristic — say what you will — that those who have provided for themselves never want to concern themselves with the community; it is always those who have enough to do with themselves, those who must hunt for a livelihood, who have to take up these matters.
It is a rule, known very well everywhere, that Zagłębie is the better-situated corner of Poland, and not a few people envy us for it — although with us too poverty whistles loudly enough, although the poor and the oppressed are not lacking at every step. But if in Zagłębie things are still, so to speak, bearable, Sosnowiec is in any case in a better position than its neighbouring towns. With us there are after all still people who "chase the ball" [yogn di koyl — an idiom; apparently: whose business still rolls along, who live comfortably], and it is precisely they who could still afford to devote time to occupying themselves with and considering the Jewish position, strained and tense enough as it is, the Jewish situation, grave and sad enough as it is.
The crisis that prevails throughout the country has already penetrated to us too, and we now feel it quite well on our shoulders; it has already settled in as a permanent guest in every nook of our existence; one feels it everywhere, it already shows everywhere — and for that very reason, before it grows thoroughly dark, before the banal monotony comes, we must act, so that Jewish society shall not be left standing forlorn and helpless, without any way out, without any counsel whatsoever.
Let us admit that we have never done anything for the people, for society. There is surely no doubt that we have had better times than now, and if we want to be sincere we must surely admit that we have had very good times — and nevertheless, what have we done for the community? What have we done for the broad Jewish public? Whom have we provided for, and what have we aimed at? In what field, for example, have we been active? Which communal affairs, for example, have prospered well? What have we to point to? What questions have been solved among us? Which matters have we settled? And what, for instance, have we to point to and say: this is ours, this is an ornament that was built for society? On the contrary — Sosnowiec is after all, thank God, quite a fine Jewish community — what is there to point to? In what field has anyone here been active? With what have we occupied ourselves?
One may say that in this and that we did not take part, that this and that is not to a town's liking [?] — but unfortunately we have nothing whatever to point to. Do we, for instance, possess fine study houses [botei-midroshim]? Have we created interesting libraries, schools, Talmud Torahs, hospitals, orphanages, old-age homes? Did we perhaps take an interest in vocational institutions? Then where are the artisans' schools, the merchants' and other organisations to which Jewish Sosnowiec could point and say: this is ours, this we built with sweat and anguish; go in there, look at it and admire it, see how strong the will is and how much can be created with the help of initiative, with the help of consciousness and the spirit of enterprise.
So we could have spoken if we had anything at all, if we were not so poor. Yes, we have a hospital built on modern lines — but, my God, what a state it is in and how hard it is to administer; every moment one trembles lest, God forbid, the locks have to be taken out and hung on the gates. One gets the impression that the people who concern themselves with the hospital are to be pitied, because such an object has been dumped on them, from which they cannot free themselves...
That is what the thing we somehow or other obtained looks like. And there is something else we have: a Talmud Torah. A Jew was generous enough to build, for the poor pale little children, an institution on modern lines, with air and gardens — and it is a heartache and a shame to speak of that institution, of the state it is in, of what has become of the large and handsome premises, and of how the little children look there...
And yet another building stands before our eyes which they have not yet managed [gedoyzhet, from Polish zdążyć] to turn into a ruin — simply because it has not yet been finished. A home for the aged, so people say, is to be there, and all that is needed is a couple of thousand gulden [gildn — the popular word for złoty] to finish it; but that is a very delicate matter for Sosnowiec's well-situated householders — they know well enough what money is and how to spare it...
And yet another building is n o t there: a Jewish school, a gymnasium for girls; that is, there are pupils, a teaching staff and everything a school needs — the government has even granted it rights [state accreditation] — but oh, how the heart must ache when one looks at the state that educational establishment is in; one can only marvel that it is possible to study there at all.
Does the town take an interest in this educational establishment? Does it lie on anyone's conscience that the institution has to eke out its existence under such embarrassing conditions?
As regards intelligence and culture, Sosnowiec holds that she is the very thing, that this belongs to her, and the Będziners she considers coarse; and here it is interesting to take a look at what understanding and love she has for the only Jewish educational institution, which ought to be flourishing — if only people showed the simplest interest, the most primitive love for the children who are being brought up there and who are to go out as independent human beings and well-brought-up daughters for the Jewish people.
Thus we unfortunately cannot point to a single trait by which Jewish Sosnowiec would care to concern itself in a civic spirit. That people should have so little interest in the community! Somehow, for these people, it is a superfluous matter with which no one need concern himself. In the course of the last 10 years people have, after all, been educated in the civic spirit; with us, by contrast, nothing whatever has changed — just as it was 20 — 30 years ago, so it has remained to this very day.
In all that time people here have wanted to learn nothing and to forget nothing.
Dr. Potpourri [pen-name].
An End to the Ban of Rabbenu Gershom!...

By Y. Oberzhanek.
(Passed on from a Jew who has lived to see revenge on the wives.)
In the Jerusalem District Court a Jewish lawyer has demonstrated that the ban [cherem] of Rabbenu Gershom was valid only until the first year of the fifth millennium (5000 by the Jewish reckoning of time). It is now already 5691 (691) in the fifth millennium, so that the ban has not been valid for 691 years, and Jews may by law marry as many women as they wish.
(From a JTA dispatch in the press.)
Do you like lawyers? I hate them, with utter hatred I hate them — people with sharpened little tongues, who twist them „na prawo“ and „na lewo“ [to the right and to the left], don't say what they mean and don't mean what they say. Each one has his own „Korban Mincha“ prayer-book (a „kodeks“ [law code] in the Gentile tongue) and „codexes“ away!...
There are all sorts of people in the world, and each one has a different wisdom: diplomats have their wisdom in the belly, today's youth has its wisdom in the feet... a „certain category“ of communal activists have their wisdom in the hands... today's „mężatki“ [married women] have their wisdom in the eyes... and lawyers have their wisdom in the tongue — as the saying goes: „Life and death are in the power of the tongue“ — with the tongue they make a dead man alive and a living man dead — that is the kind of people lawyers are!...
I really do mean that Jerusalem lawyer; a man knows of such a thing and keeps the joy in his belly! For 691 years the ban of Rabbenu Gershom has already been void, and here people torment themselves for nothing. A trifle — such a salvation, such a revival for suffering male humanity, and that fellow over there, the Jerusalem lawyer, knows about it — and nothing!...
Who was supposed to know it? To whom could it have occurred that Rabbenu Gershom issued only a „tymczasowy“ [temporary] ban?
A thousand years.
A thousand years already since Rabbenu Gershom put chains on the hands of us men. A rabbi's whim — he ups and makes a ban: you may not have more than one wife. One wife, one dowry and, above all, one mother-in-law... And if the wife doesn't please you, if it was a bad bargain [mekach-toes]: before the wedding she was a „szatynka“ [brown-haired] and after the wedding she turned out a „kanarkowa“ [canary-yellow]... before the wedding she had two long, thick plaits and after the wedding she became a „chłopczyca“ [boyish bob]... before the wedding she couldn't open her mouth and after the wedding she became „musical“ and takes the top notes... before the wedding she was as healthy as a soldier of category „A“ and right after the wedding she got „napady“ [attacks]... before the wedding she had no heart, no lung and no liver, and after the wedding she has „stones“, „wapno“ [lime, calcification] and „sand“ and other „luxury articles“... before the wedding she promised me a little plate from heaven [the moon and the stars], and after the wedding she gives me the plate on the head... The things this „gentle sex“ promises before the wedding — and after the wedding it all comes to a „boydem“ [an attic — i.e. to nothing]!...
You will perhaps say that among Jews there is a remedy — a get [divorce]? Leave me alone! I divorce my wife and marry your wife, or you divorce your wife and marry my wife — as the proverb says: „All Greeks have one face“; they are all alike, kneaded from one lump and cast in one mould. And if we men are in dire straits, if we are in exile under our wives, the only one to blame is the ban of Rabbenu Gershom. And what, I ask you, is the wonder, what? You have an only-daughter-dear in the house, a little doll, a one and only, a „jedynaczka“ [only child], something to tremble over. And if you have a „sublokator“ [lodger], you tremble even more... And if she pulls a sour little face, the life goes out of you. If, God forbid, she gets a „napad“ [attack] of the „stones“, you run with the analysis to the doctor and she runs off to „poprawiać się“ [recuperate] — to Zoppot [Sopot] or to Krynica — and you lie at home and grow black and dark with the „pokojówka“ [the chambermaid]...
And what is the wonder, what? She is, after all, a one and only, a „jedynaczka“ — why shouldn't she get „napady“, why?... Why shouldn't she „recuperate“ in Zoppot? Have you got many wives? Whom then should you „pilnować“ [guard, watch over], if not your one and only little piece of a wife? And perhaps you think you are doing her a favour by it? If you don't watch over her, your neighbour will „watch over“ her. With wives you won't be too clever...
And who is to blame for all this? All of it Rabbenu Gershom — and not so much Rabbenu Gershom as the Jerusalem lawyer. Some cleverness of a lawyer, to keep such a secret in his belly! If only we had known the secret 691 years ago, back when the term of Rabbenu Gershom's ban ran out. Oh, if we had known that 691 years ago — what a salvation it would have been for the whole of suffering male humanity.
First of all, there would have been no crisis in the world. You marry, you take a dowry, and a year or two after the wedding, when things go badly for you, you needn't grieve much, you needn't rack your brains any more: you have a match arranged with a second one, you get a second dowry — and no more racking of brains!... And when you are already close to making a „siyum“ [finishing off] on the second dowry, you have a third one matched to you with a third dowry, or you place a matrimonial advertisement in the newspaper worded like this:
[Here, in a box, comes the mock advertisement „Important for Marriageable Girls“ — see item 2.17.]
After such an advertisement in the paper they will besiege you, they will tear the coat-tails off you, the „merchandise“ will come right into the house, and you will take yourself a third wife with a third dowry. Why worries? Why cares about a livelihood? What the devil [lit. for what kapores] do you need that for? When you have a remedy: — a fresh wife with a fresh dowry, and the crisis is over!...
And a livelihood for the wives? Don't make me laugh! One is a seamstress, the second a „modystka“ [milliner], the third a manicurist, the fourth a „fryzjerka“ [hairdresser], and you go strutting about „like a king among his troops“ — like a „tchórz“[?] [polecat] among the hens — and that's the life!...
Now life itself: why, it will be quite another life. With each wife you will have several children, you will have various „colours“ and various „patterns“, yellow ones and black ones and blond ones, short ones and tall ones, singles and twins, and withal everything will cost you less, for you will of course buy everything wholesale: little shoes by the dozen, little dresses and little suits en gros, linen for little shirts by the bolt, and then: „wózki“ [prams], bibs[?], little enemas and nappies — all „hurtowe“ [wholesale]. To a midwife you will pay a „stała“ [fixed] monthly salary, the mohel too you will pay „ryczałtem“ [a lump sum], so that it works out cheaper for you — and that's the life!...
In winter-time each one will „zapraszać“ [invite] her guests „na herbatkę“ [to tea], every evening you will go to the cinema with a different one. In summer, again, each will travel in a different direction: one to Rajcza, the second to Bystra, the third to Krynica, the fourth to Olkusz. Every evening you will „odwiedzać“ [visit] a different one, and should you not be so very „punktualny“ [punctual], there will be no anger either, for she is, after all, no only daughter of yours — no „jedynaczka“, that is.
All this would have been, had the Jerusalem lawyer not kept the secret in his belly. All this would have been, had the secret been known 691 years ago. Oh, if we men had known it 691 years ago!... But go and argue with a lawyer. Do you like lawyers? I hate them with utter hatred; a man knows of such a secret — and nothing.
Yes, one thing, you see, stands in the way. One great drawback there is to abolishing the ban of Rabbenu Gershom — the mothers-in-law. What shall we do with six mothers-in-law? With six wives we shall somehow manage, but with six mothers-in-law?... Perhaps Rabbenu Gershom made the ban because of the mothers-in-law — who knows?...
Important for Marriageable Girls

A „urodzony“[?] [well-born?] „mężczyzna“ [man], aged between 30 and 60, who has two wives in all and has so far buried only two dowries, seeks a girl under 20 who should have a good trade in hand and a fat dowry in the bank; if she has no mamma, that is of course good... etc., etc.
Capitalism and the Jews

Various economists have lately been investigating the causes of the severe crisis which the Jews are going through. The well-known economist Professor Oppenheimer, who for a long time stood in the most active ranks of Zionism, has in a longer study put forward the thesis that the crisis of the Jews is closely bound up with the crisis of capitalism. And if in recent times, Oppenheimer explains, the antisemitic tendencies have grown stronger, the causes lie in the fact that the crisis of capitalism is identical[?] with the upheaval of the whole[?] of life, and in such a time, history shows, it is the Jews who suffer most.
When in Europe it came to a hard struggle between Christendom and Islam, the struggle came down first of all upon the shoulders of the Jewish people and ended with the expulsion from Spain and Portugal.
The situation of the Jews looked no better in the period when Catholicism and Protestantism waged a hard struggle for supremacy in the Germanic lands. Then too the crisis among the Jews was very severe, because the hatred of both sides was poured out upon the Jews' heads.
The Jews suffer no less severely now, when capitalism has shown itself to be a sclerosis[?]. Unable to adapt itself to the new phenomena and conditions, it is losing the influence it formerly had. It is interesting that in Germany, for example, the elections to parliament gave a tremendous majority to the opponents of capitalism, and the antisemitic expression of that opposition is Hitlerism.
When we look closely at all that is now taking place, we see that one side accuses the Jews of having ruined the world because they brought about the decline of capitalism, while the other side persecutes the Jews with hatred because they are the bearers of capitalism. But if one looks at the actual situation of the Jews, at the 16 million Jews who are sown and scattered over the whole world, one finds that the condition of the Jews is almost everywhere an immensely sad one, that for the greatest part we are "Luftmenschen" [people living on air], who have no prospects whatever of making a life for themselves economically.
In the "Golden International" we Jews play almost no role. It is interesting that among the 12 greatest dollar-millionaires in America there is only one single Jew, namely the Jewish banking house Kuhn, Loeb & Co., one of whose heirs is Felix Warburg, the representative of the non-Zionist part in the Jewish "Agency". But even this banking house stands only in 9th place on the list of the 12.
Among the 199 millionaires who live in New York we find barely 19 Jewish millionaires, which stands in no proportion whatever to the number of Jews in New York.
Among the magnates of industry the Jews play almost no role at all[.] The greatest world concerns, such as for example the match concern Kreuger[?], are free of Jewish capital and Jewish influence. Among the agrarian magnates there is not one single Jew. Thus we see that the influence of the Jews in the "Golden" International is a vanishingly small one. Therefore the opinion that we Jews are the bearers of world capitalism is certainly unfounded[.]
False too is the assertion that we brought about the collapse of capitalism. The reason why capitalism is going through the severe crisis lies in the fact that capital can live itself out only in a time of unlimited freedom and unlimited personal initiative. If obstacles are put in capital's way, if one seeks to regulate it with the help of laws and ordinances, if one wants to control it — then it withdraws, does not create and does not live itself out.
It is true that the offensive against capital has been taken up by the workers, but it is also a truth that we Jews, even in the concentrations where we live in great numbers, form a vanishing part of the working class.
From this one sees plainly that we Jews are the bearers of capitalism and not the revolutionaries against it [thus in print; from the context a negation has evidently dropped out — i.e. we are neither the bearers of capitalism nor the revolutionaries against it]. Nor do we believe that the existence of the Jews is definitively bound up with the victory of capitalism. One cannot know which way life will go, who will remain the victor in the hard struggle that is now being waged. It goes without saying that we Jews have no interest in the collapse of the foundation of the modern economy, of capitalism; on the contrary: we see the only possibility of development for the world in the ending of the restrictions and obstacles, because experience has taught that only in a time of liberalism can the world develop. It is interesting that in the year 1913, before the war, that is, in a time of a liberal form of economy, there were in the whole world one and a half million unemployed, and — today, in a time of a controlled economic order, we have 20 million unemployed.
The tendencies of world development are not yet clear, the new paths are not yet known and the wrestling is still hard. One thing, however, is certain: that the Jewish genius will adapt itself to the new development, and we shall come out of this severe crisis too as victors.
Deputy Dr. F. Rotenstreich
The Living Corpse

(A little feuilleton)
As a boy I heard talk in the cheder among the pupils and in the study-house among the young men, that a dead man — as long as he has not been laid in the grave and until the first three shovelfuls of earth have been poured on him — the dead man knows what is happening to him, hears the wailing, sees how they busy themselves at the purification [tahara], how the shrouds are sewn, how he is carried, and so on.
These tales filled my boyish heart not only with dread but also with pity for the unfortunate corpse, who must, poor thing, lie still, not say a single word, and must put up with everything that is done to him, and even listen to the false words of begging-forgiveness from those who shower praises on him only after his death.
When I grew a little older I read in the little books that when a person dies he is dead, and if the soul in the other world still carries on some sort of dealings, the body in this world is nevertheless nothing more than dust and ashes, which returns to mother earth.
That made my soul feel lighter.
Now I have become convinced that a dead man really does have the possibility of hearing and seeing what is being done and what is being prepared to be done with him — and yet is unable to utter a word.
Here we have dead kehillas [Jewish communities]; the Ministry has even already fixed the day of the funeral, and everyone knows that the „gminas“ are dead, deceased, and yet the corpse still lives; they absolutely refuse to give him his due and bring him to a Jewish burial. Here the kehilla council assembles to hold sittings, to adopt resolutions and put matters of inheritance in order and to carry out the purification.
Various parties are already beginning to tear at one another over her inheritance, and the living corpse cannot protest even when he is told to carry out things that only the living have a right to do.
And let us make a comparison.
When the Sejm died it was buried at once, and the deceased Sejm was spared seeing how another Sejm moves into the building on Wiejska Street. The same happened with the city council too.
Only with the Jewish kehilla does it go differently. Only the kehilla, poor thing, is punished by having to be present at its own funeral.
A pity, alas, on this corpse of ours.
Yankele.

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion
(Collected and styled by Y. Y.)
Parshat Tazria-Metzora

[The "Oneg Shabbat" column — Torah sayings and anecdotes for Parshat Tazria-Metzora.]
a) אשה כי תזריע וילדה ["When a woman conceives and gives birth"] (12:2)
Forty days before a child is born — says the Talmud — an angel takes it before God and asks Him: what shall it be, clever or foolish? poor or rich? — But about piety he does not ask. Whether to be a righteous man or a wicked one, that is a person's own free choice.
That is why — said the "Tiferet Shlomo" — there are pious fools. For, imagine: it was decreed for someone that he should be a fool. Later, by his own free choice, he chooses to be a tzaddik. So he remains a fool who is a tzaddik. Well, but pious he is, so he thinks he has still not discharged his duty: since it was decreed for him from heaven to be a simpleton, and pious he is, he wants zealously to fulfil God's proclamation — and so, however much [of a fool] he is, he always thinks it is still too little...
—o—
b) ושער בנגע הפך לבן ["and the hair in the affliction has turned white"] (13:3)
If a person sins once — well, for that one is flesh and blood, after all. Repentance does help. But with the one whose plagues (נגעים) — "ושער בנגע הפך לבן" — already have grey hair... when they have grown old with him — טמא הוא ["he is impure"]...
(Tiferet Yehonatan.)
* * *
Rav Hershele Levin, rabbi of Halberstadt, London and Berlin in the days of the Haskalah epoch, once said:
I have met a certain someone at three different times, and each time I found him in a different situation. The first time — despondent[?] and despairing. The second time — out of breath and in a hurry. The third time — calm, easy-going, passing his time in the taverns, merry and lively, and without a stitch of work.
Shall I introduce him to you? — It is Mr.... Evil Inclination [yetzer hara].
When I was rabbi in Halberstadt I saw him downcast; his activity was without success. A town of God-fearing and upright people. In London I saw him sweating at his work; he had work upon work. Here in Berlin he has already taken a holiday; he no longer needs to work, to agitate. People now run after him of their own accord...
—o—
c) והצרוע אשר בו הנגע בגדיו יהיו פרומים ["And the leper in whom the affliction is — his garments shall be rent"] (13:48 [as printed; correctly 13:45])
There are such unworthy ones "אשר בו הנגע" ["in whom the affliction is"], whose unworthiness is hidden deep. Only "בגדיו" ["his garments"] — his exterior, his outward appearance — "יהיו פרומים" [Hebrew "shall be rent", read as Yiddish frum, "pious"], that is — piety... His garment, in which he shows himself to the world, is piety, and "בו" ["in him"], deep within himself, he is leprous, unclean...
(Rav Moshe Kobriner [of Kobryń].)
* * *
A parable:
A mouse sends her child out to look for food. The mother warns it: beware of our mortal enemy. The little mouse creeps out into the rubbish heaps to look for food. It sees a rooster — it crows and beats its wings. The little mouse runs quickly home to tell its mummy[?] that it has met their mortal enemy. The mother replies[?]: no, it is not the crowing rooster who is anyone's enemy. He beats his wings and does nothing to anybody. A second time it sees a puffed-up turkey. But neither is the turkey, who puffs himself up so and has such a long nose, anybody's enemy. Only the quiet, pious, humble little cat — that one is our enemy, the one that creeps so quietly, beats no wings, makes no noise, does not puff itself up...
The moral:
"הזהרו מן הצבועים" ["Beware of the hypocrites" — literally "the painted ones"]...
(Eretz HaChaim.)
—o—
d) ועל שפם יעטה ["and he shall cover his upper lip"] (ibid.)
Plagues (נגעים) come for the sin of evil speech [lashon hara]. A person has two locks before his mouth: teeth and gums[?]. But it does not help, the tongue talks. So he is told to let a moustache grow; perhaps the third lock will work...
And because he spoke ill of others, his remedy is: "טמא, טמא יקרא" ["Impure, impure! he shall cry"] — he must call himself: impure...
(Imrei Shefer.)
—o—
e) זאת תהיה תורת המצורע ["This shall be the law (Torah) of the leper"] (14:1 [actually 14:2])
The Torah holds only with one who is nothing at all in his own eyes. "אין התורה מתקיימת אלא במי שמפקיר את עצמו" ["The Torah endures only in one who renounces himself"]; if you want to give yourself over to the Torah — then hold yourself to be nothing. "זאת תהיה תורת המצורע" — a leper too, whose punishment comes only because of pride, has the same remedy as with Torah: "ישפיל עצמו כאזוב" ["let him lower himself like the hyssop"], to hold himself lowly; then Torah will be able to endure with him as well.
(Mishnat deRabbi Yosi.)
—o—
f) ביום טהרתו והובא אל הכהן ["on the day of his purification he shall be brought to the priest"] (ibid.)
Is it "ביום טהרתו" ["on the day of his purification"] that he is brought to the priest? Surely he is brought only on the day of his impurity. When he is pure he does not need any priest. —
The sense of the verse is this:
The craving for evil speech is so great in a person that "ביום טהרתו והובא אל הכהן" — on the very same day on which he was declared pure, he already has to come to the priest again. In the morning he cleansed himself, and in the evening he has already gone back and sinned again...
(Uri veYish'i.)
* * *
