Facing Reality

[Article — Zionism / Labour Palestine; the Palestine Workers' Fund campaign in Zagłębie.]
(On this year's P.A.F. [Palestine Workers' Fund] campaign in Zagłębie)
The times are gone when the Land of Israel was the concern of a group of idealists and dreamers who all at once broke with their comfortable living conditions and went off to begin a new life; today the Land of Israel is the burning problem of the broad Jewish masses.
We live in a time when the great process of impoverishment of the Jewish population is taking place before our eyes. Tens of thousands of Jewish families are losing their possibility of existence because of the "numerus clausus", which is applied not only in the institutions of higher learning but in the whole of economic life. It is almost impossible for Jewish workers or the Jewish working intelligentsia to obtain any post whatsoever in the state or municipal institutions. Let these people have the best qualifications — some pretext will always be found, by which nothing more is intended than to get rid of an undesired element. This work-thirsty, helpless mass therefore seeks a place to emigrate to, and the Land of Israel is today the only country that has in recent years proved able to absorb thousands of new immigrants, who have gone over to a new life on productive foundations.
In contrast to other, economically stronger countries such as America, Canada and others, which, under pressure from the workers there, have completely shut the gates to immigration, the immigration into the Land of Israel takes place precisely at the demand of the workers there, who take absolutely no account of the possible depression of their wages and, consequently, of the lowering of their standard of living. This is an idealism without parallel, such as one meets in no other country on the whole globe.
For over two decades the P.A.F. has been carrying on its activity. These are years of hard, grey work. Under the hardest conditions the most splendid things have nonetheless been accomplished. The P.A.F., which is the main financial fund of the "Histadrut", has in the course of its existence already managed to create in the country a series of institutions in town and in village: such as the "Kupat Holim" [sick fund], the consumers' cooperative "Hamashbir", the enterprise companies "Solel Boneh" and "Yakhin", and the "workers' homes", which provide for cultural needs. The P.A.F. also took part in the creation of "Shekhunat Borochov", "Mahanayim", "Ayelet HaShahar", "Tel Hai" and others. In a word, the P.A.F. provides for all the wants and needs of the Jewish working class in the Land of Israel, both in the town and in the village, in the economic and in the cultural-educational field, thus helping to create the workers' centre in the Land of Israel.
The workers of the Land of Israel are the vanguard, which stands firm on the conquered positions and consolidates them. But the struggle of consolidation is not a question of the workers there alone; it is the question of the Jewish working class in the whole world, it is the affair of the tens of thousands of Jewish toilers ["horepashnikes"], for whom the Land of Israel is not merely a distant, unattainable ideal, a kind of "fata morgana" that will never be realised, but who believe and see in the upbuilding of the Land of Israel their future. And the Jewish future cannot be without the Land of Israel, because the transformations in Jewish economic life have in recent years proved definitively that the Jewish masses can have an existence only when they make themselves productive and settle on healthy, normal foundations — on the foundations of productive labour.
And therefore, when the call for help of the workers of the Land of Israel reaches us, when the Jewish workers' institutions, set up through hard toil and travail, demand our support, none of us may stand aside. It must be shown to the workers of the Land of Israel that together with them[?] stands the whole Jewish working class, from all over the world.
Let each of us help with all his strength to build up the workers' settlement in the Land of Israel, because supporting the workers of the Land of Israel means — first of all — creating a foundation for ourselves; it means widening our life horizons, which have shrunk greatly because of the abnormal conditions in which we have to live. The Land of Israel that is being built is the best answer to the antisemitic claims about the supposed inferiority and unproductiveness of the Jewish people. Strengthening the workers' settlement in the Land of Israel is the best tonic, which invigorates us and gives us strength and courage to believe that we shall cease to be the international[?] dust in the fabric[?] of the nations, that we too shall be among those who rebuild and renew their life on healthy, just, social foundations.
This is our one, only and last hope, without which our life would be one great absurdity — and no forces in the world will be able to make us give up this last hope.
Sh. Rotenberg
(Chairman of the League for Labour Palestine in Będzin).

The Vanished Daughter — an original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World

[Serialised novel — instalment no. 3.]
By Elisabeth Garin.
For those readers who, owing to the absence of our Passover issue, did not have the opportunity to read the beginning of this gripping novel, we give the following summary:
In the year 1900 a travelling circus came to the shtetl of Z. in Galicia. When the circus left, a rumour spread through the shtetl that the only daughter of the wealthy Reb Shlomo Rapaport, the beautiful Lala, had vanished together with the young Christian Janek, a friend of her brother Fritz.
The father and his son Fritz and all their employees went off to search for the vanished Lala. To this day there is no trace of her whatsoever, because Janek has hidden her in a robbers' house in the Tatra mountains.
Now read on:
That is precisely why the brigands built the house; and although they did it in the most terrible winter cold, and in eight days, the big house outlived not only them but a couple of dozen other robber bands, and even now, a whole century after it was built, it is strong as iron and fills everyone with fear and dread, so that people would rather add a couple of miles to their journey just so as not to have to drive past it.
It was to this old, large, gloomy building put together of logs, with its partly broken window-panes and half-collapsed chimney, that Janek was now walking, merry and in high spirits, whistling an old robbers' song:
If only I knew
where my gallows stands,
I would stud it with golden ducats...
Coming close, Janek sniffed the air: yes, Staszek is playing the master of the house, he thought; he has even made a fire in the stove; he has in him a good deal of the courage of those old inhabitants of the house — not for nothing does he say that he is descended from one of them.
As he went in, Staszek Makarna was already there to meet him with outstretched arms.
"Good that you've finally come, brother; no cheese and no bread, and even the tobacco and the brandy have run out," he said, taking the sack and the bundle from Janek.
"Ha, you've brought the boy's clothes for Lala, that's good, and white bread and coffee for the 'pani' [the lady]" — he pulled a slight grimace — "she'll just have to get used to eating what I eat... There are no Jewish delicacies and sweetmeats here..."
"How is she?" Janek asked.
"She cries and kicks and wants to go back... But never mind, with me she'll soon get better," he said quietly, putting into a pot the potatoes Janek had brought in the sack. "What's the news in the shtetl? Are the Jews raising a great outcry?"
"It will be better if they don't get you into their hands, little brother," said Janek, baring his teeth. "Berish the carter nearly threw me down the mountain; I barely got away from him alive."
"And the old man?"
"Her father has gone all the way to Pressburg. But the young one, the student, Fritzchen, is expected tomorrow, and I would advise you to clear out of here with her before he comes. He and you and I spent too much time here in our childhood, when we wanted to hide somewhere our parents wouldn't find us. The first thing he'll do is come here."
"I'm not afraid of him," Staszek said darkly. "More than once I've cracked his bones, when he and the other Jewish students stood up against us," he added with pride. But Janek, who knew him well, was not fooled by Stanisław Makarna. He saw clearly that more than anything the handsome Staszek was afraid of Lala's brother, the friend of his childhood and now his mortal enemy, Fritz Rapaport.
In the large room, blackened with age and mustiness, where there stood a big stove in which a great wood fire was now burning, there sat hunched on an upturned wooden crate the young Jewish girl Lala Rapaport, for whom the whole country was now searching. She was wrapped in a large shawl and looked ill, tired and broken... with deep rings under her eyes; yet even now she was wonderfully beautiful, with her ash-blonde hair, large black eyes, and a little face carved of alabaster. When Janek came in she sprang up from her place, ran to Janek and seized him with both hands.
"How is my dear mama, Janek? Did you see her? Is she weeping for me? Tell me, Janek, speak to me, for God's sake speak to me!"
"Don't talk nonsense, Lala!" — he freed himself from her, and his eyes met those of Staszek, who stood behind her and shook his head to signal "no".

An Open Letter to the Kehilla Board in Będzin

[Będzin — kehilla; synagogue; letter to the editor.] Esteemed Mr. Editor! Allow me to print in your esteemed newspaper the following letter to the Będzin kehilla board:
In recent weeks quarrels and market-place scenes have been taking place in the Będzin synagogue (shul), which degrade the honour of the holy place, but what happened last Sabbath goes beyond every limit of lawlessness.
This is what happened:
During the prayers I, as well as some of the worshippers, respectfully drew attention to a mistake (according to the correct interpretation of the words) that the cantor, Mr. Żupowicz [?], had made. Not to speak of the fact that the cantor gave his answer in a very unbecoming form — after the prayers, before we left the synagogue, the cantor's wife came in and attacked me with the most shameful insults of a market-woman.
Therefore I have the honour to ask you, gentlemen members of the board (dozores): 1) Has it ever been heard of that a cantor's wife should enter the synagogue and abuse worshippers? 2) Must a cantor be versed in the liturgical rite (nusach ha-tefillah)? and 3) When will the kehilla board finally put an end to the lawlessness that reigns in the synagogue to such a great degree?
With respect,
Dawid Ferens [?].

Create a Home for the “Malbish Arumim” Society!
(An appeal to the Jewish population of Będzin)

[Będzin — charity and welfare; institutions.] Forty years ago a group of young men took the initiative to found a society “Malbish Arumim” [“Clothing the Naked”]; helping to bring it about were the rabbi of that time, the great Rabbi R’ Ishele (Yeshaya) Kimelman, of blessed memory, and later the rabbi, Rabbi R’ Yissachar Berish Graubart, of blessed memory. And now that we stand after 40 years of work, it is worth recalling what “Malbish Arumim” has accomplished so far.
“Malbish Arumim” has gone through various periods. There were times when the board members carried out the annual clothing distribution with their own money, and then, for understandable reasons, monthly pledges were introduced, on which the institution subsists to this very day.
From the groszy collected with great effort among the Jewish population of Będzin, a few hundred Talmud Torah children are clothed year by year — for the most part full orphans — and many respectable adults; but all this still does not satisfy the great number who come to ask us for clothing for their families.
The most important factor, which plays a great role in the society’s activity, is that “Malbish Arumim” has no premises of its own and has nowhere to hold its meetings. The goods that are bought lie with private persons; the meetings and the secretariat, too, take place and operate in private flats.
The board understands that the monthly income must not be used to rent premises, because with the poor groszy collected the poor, helpless children must be clothed.
Therefore we have decided to turn to you, and especially to the notables (pnei ha-ir) of Będzin: take note of the situation of “Malbish Arumim”, respond, and donate premises for so important an institution as “Malbish Arumim”, so that the work can be conducted to the full.
Remember, then, that the fate of hundreds of poor Talmud Torah children lies in your hands!
Do not let the “Malbish Arumim” society, which plays such an important role at the present time, fall.
Create or donate a home for our and your clothing institution.
Respectfully,
The Board of “Malbish Arumim” in Będzin.

"10 Years and One Second".
The well-known actor Jonas Turkow with his ensemble (three persons altogether) staged in a number of towns in Zagłębie the drama in 3 acts entitled "Ten Years and One Second".
It is an old problem of a deceived family life. During a conversation between husband and wife the husband confesses that he murdered the husband of his beloved. The murder, which happened in one second, destroyed the 10 happy years and made the further life together of the couple impossible.

Existence and Decline. (I. The painful problem of our time — one must react properly to this phenomenon)

[Economy — the crisis and Jewish businessmen; article, part I.] When one looks around and begins consciously to consider our economic situation, one's heart grows heavy; when we consider calmly what a serious state we are in, we must come to the realisation that we may not remain indifferent to everything that is happening around us.
True, it is no news when we say that the situation is a bad one and that the circumstances are anything but pleasant, but it is no help that the bad is being confirmed, that it is becoming everyday and ordinary; one must after all act so that we see the bitter everyday among us only as a rare guest, and that too for a very short time.
True, we are a people of merciful ones, sons of merciful ones, and it cannot be said that we remain indifferent to the people's troubles; as soon as one learns of a „yored“ [one who has come down in the world], one wants to lift him up; for that we have interest-free loan funds, „Beys-Lekhem“ [charity kitchens] and various charitable associations, which strive that the oppressed should not, God forbid, perish from hunger. So one takes an interest in Jewish need when it has already reached the state of „the waters have come up to the soul“... Earlier one does not think of helping the fallen, only then, when he has already fallen, when he is already completely broken and has no other way out but to play the role — in the best case — of a respectable pauper. Moreover, we have no institutions at all to which the citizen hurt by the crisis could come and tell of his catastrophic situation in time, when one will not help him [sic].
It is a crisis and a bitter time, and citizens want with all their strength to save themselves so that they should not have to come down in the world. There are such as want, by every possible means, to live out their years in a respectable way; they do not want to go bankrupt, they want to pay to the last grosz, only that nobody should have cause to weep on their account; they are willing even to remain poor people, but do not want anyone to suffer because of them. They do not want to take another man's grosz; they want to save themselves by clutching at a straw, but they want to be among the saved, among the decent and noble souls, with a clear conscience.
So what are these people to do? How can they be saved, and who takes any interest at all in these citizens, in these people, who will give away their dearest to you, if only they may remain standing on their feet? Before whom can they pour out their bitter hearts? To whom can they confide their critical situation, which is for the most part only a passing phenomenon that, given proper attention, could have been saved? To whom should these people turn with their painful questions from the depth of the heart?
Had we such a revision (audit) body, many decent firms would have been saved both from bankruptcy and from total ruin.
We shall not exaggerate if we say that there are citizens who do not take in in a week as much as they need for a day; with such an abnormality it is no wonder that „healthy“ firms vanish from the arena of existence.
Granted, it is understandable that in such a case one must cut[?] every expense that is not first-class, one must at the given moment try to economise on every expense that is not very necessary, but what comes of it? That this is no help, that it is a zero compared with the expenses the firm is obliged to bear. True, one saves a złoty on the children's needs, but what comes of it, when out of the hundred złoty one would gladly save[?] it is impossible to knock off even 10 złoty.
These citizens, whose businesses have become a heap of ruins, go on paying their taxes; the turnover tax is a law that will not pass away, it does not budge; with all the other taxes things are not much better either; the government taxes must be paid according to how the citizen has been assessed; with the local taxes too it has not become easier, and if such a Jew manages to wriggle through a few months, he will afterwards have to pay double and twice double, so that everything will come on him at once, and then he will not know what to do at all; and what the end of such self-deception is, we know very well. The „cart“ [of the bailiffs] appears, which has no mercy and takes away your belongings, and then there is nothing left from which to take in money and with which to earn.
It goes without saying that it would be quite different if we had such a trustworthy revision body, whose task would be to review the catastrophic affairs of such a firm when it turns to it for help, and then, if it really turns out that the firm needs relief in order to remain standing on its feet, the body should have the possibility of putting through the most far-reaching concessions so that the existing firm may be saved from ruin.
In that case the body would need the possibility of obtaining from the government that the firm be freed from the taxes it owes until it gets back onto a normal path; the same should apply to the local taxes, and even the interest on rent („tsindz fun dire-gelt“) should be written off. No differently, of course, would it have to be with the obligations for the benefit of Jewish interests.
Of course we mean that all the concessions should be granted after it has turned out, following thorough inquiry and investigation, that the firm has no other way to remain standing on its feet, and until it gets back onto the normal line it should be subject to the control of the revision body.
In that case it would become possible to save from certain danger many existing firms that have been condemned to ruin, and it would be a great gain both for the citizens and for the government, because as long as the citizen remains on his feet and goes on buying a patent [trade licence], the government continues to have income from him, whereas as soon as he comes down in the world and gives back the patent he bought, the government gets nothing more from him, and the citizen, besides having taken people's money, is lost and has nothing from which to draw his livelihood.
One takes an interest in saving people so that they should not die of hunger; better to take an interest in them at the time when the catastrophe has not yet reached this dangerous state; better to want to help the citizen who is on the point of losing his lustre, than to stand there with a pitying face and say: let us not let him perish from hunger, he was once a merchant, or a manufacturer, or a first-class craftsman.
Once such a „yored“ was a rarity; it happened to one in a hundred thousand, and no great attention was paid to it; incidentally, because these „yordim“ were rarities, one could support them properly. Now it has unfortunately become a mass phenomenon, and the „yordim“ are no longer distinguished from beggars. So one must indeed take more care that they should not be condemned to this piece of bitter bread of shame.
Let us want to be practical and watch attentively this process, which is reflected before our eyes day by day and brings poverty and destruction among all strata of the Jewish population, sparing hardly even the best-situated people.
Besides, one must reckon with the fact that today's sound firms cannot know how they will look, let us say, in a month's time.
The situation is thus catastrophic to the highest degree, and we may not pass by such an unfortunate phenomenon with apathy and indifference; one must stop at this process — which is taking on an epidemic character — and consider it properly. One must seek means, serious and urgent means, how to extricate ourselves[?] from this witches' wheel, which is seizing the finest and best citizens of the country. To this end one must get in touch with the most authoritative personalities and demand that the government too should save the citizens from ruin.
Y. Sh.
Letters from Home.

[Zagłębie — feuilleton in letter form; kashrut, kehilla elections, the Sosnowiec rabbinate fight.]
B"H, for the portion "In righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour" [Lev. 19:15]...
My friend R' Shlomo, n"y [may his light shine].
Your grievances against me, that I have been silent so long and have not corresponded with you about our home affairs, are unfounded. You are truly an honest claimant, but if you were here together with us, only then would you understand the saying "If the earlier generations were like men, we are like angels" [so printed — an inversion of the Talmudic "If the earlier ones were like angels, we are like men"]. Can one even tell what we have lived through here since the time the sadly famous Paragraph 20 was revealed: a darkness ["khashkhes"] fell on the Jewish camp — no small matter! Every one of us imagined that under this paragraph every flesh-and-blood, naturally those who do not belong to the holy Org. [organisation?], would have to stand before a commission of experts, and the commission would measure the 248 limbs, and it would be "as clay in the hand of the potter": kosher or treyf...
But praised be He, so to speak, that the "destroying Satan" was stopped at the border of Zagłębie; otherwise it would have been very bitter — almost three parts of the "sinful creatures" would "no longer have existed". Still, the matter will not pass smoothly: although the "Agudist levy" ["pobór", Pol. — draft/conscription] will not take place here, we do not know what disqualifications [?] ["poslen"] the new kashrut committee will adopt. There is talk that an inspection is to start across the town, to see how the kashrut affairs stand with us. That is a very proper thing, but it would be even more important if that same committee began with those who "bear the yoke" of Jewishness, with those who "do the deeds of Zimri [so printed: 'zimra'] and seek the reward of Pinhas"... with those who call others to piety while they themselves despise the Torah and the Jewish people...
Yes, R' Shlomo, that is where one must inspect very thoroughly — not with a feather duster but with an iron broom; one must clean without stopping until the dull mob finally sees who our leaders in this present generation are.
Now, R' Shlomo, let us return to our subject — let us turn back to our affair, the election affair. By the mood of things it is foreseen that even in the present crisis it will be very merry in our little Jewish world: once again all the associations, societies and individuals rise from the dead [printed "tkhis"], whose only aim is to benefit the whole of Israel. To the election fair of the kehilla parties will come out with "platforms" of all sorts of qualities and colours; the parnassim will no longer be only from the outworn "black elements", but also from people known as flaming, fiery, freshly-wriggling fighters for "class consciousness"...
Believe me, R' Shlomo, this time the cunning "Aguda" [Agudat Israel] made a big mistake: she — the "Aguda", that is — should have waived the "beardless paragraph" [?] and instead worked to have the tsarist decree renewed, that "whoever pays no sum has no say"... And because the "Aguda" only wanted to be rid of the Zionists, it will get in the new kehilla such "partners" as will study a chapter of Karl Marx with them...
On the election front it is very foggy, just as in the three days of darkness; in the darkness various shapes and figures creep about, wanting to force their way into the dark burrow that people call
— the kehilla...
At "round tables" negotiations take place about concluding agreements with or against the "Aguda". A great role in this chess game is played by the "Non-Partisans", that is the well-known party on the Jewish street whose upper part of the "garment" is non-partisan, only the "patsheke" [?; perhaps podszewka — lining] is of Agudist manufacture...
The "Aguda" is very pleased with the non-partisan party; on the contrary, the "Aguda" side helps the "Non-Partisans" to run separately and carry a large number of mandates, for inside, at the gmina table, the Duvids and Itshe-Meirs walk hand in hand anyway. The situation of the "Aguda" would have been much worse had the "Aguda" been taken into the round-dance ["karahod", Pol. korowód] of the Non-Partisans: then the incendiary material addressed to the "Aguda" would have caught the "Non-Partisans" too... and then the saying would have been fulfilled: "Woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbour"...
Such is the tactic of the "Aguda": "their work is done by others" [printed "na'asin"]. They are always the "God-fearing", the neutral ones; but as soon as they need to push through any matter whatsoever, there are already such as carry out the work on their behalf perfectly. For example, when it comes to rabbinical elections they join with the Sochaczewers [Sochaczew Hasidim]; at Sejm elections — with the "squires" ["pritsim"]; at kehilla elections — with the "Non-Partisans". In the national camp they are not yet done: there one is punctilious about every jot of the programme, one does not yield a hair's breadth on party principles, and everyone makes "Shabbos" for himself...
By the same method the "Aguda" is said to be manoeuvring in Sosnowiec too. Officially the "Aguda" takes no part in the rabbinate fight; outwardly it fights for its so-called candidate, more correctly against the influence of the "Mizrachi"; but as the "jesters of the generation" tell, the "Aguda", which supposedly fights for its candidate, is actually after something quite different: when both sides are already tired, the "Aguda" is to tip the scales and install a rabbi from the occupation power [?]...
It would be worth writing about this matter at length, but this time I must cut it short, because at this moment a delegation came to me from the "Hachnasat Kallah" [dowering of brides] society, informing me that my name is being put forward on the society's list...
To tell the truth, why shouldn't the society have its own dozores [kehilla councillors]? Its sister institution, the pall-bearers' society, may have them, and "Hachnasat Kallah", as the first hand of the "burial", should be without dozores?
So have a good Shabbos, as wishes you
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! From the press I know that in your parts an international exhibition is opening in the coming days [printed "nanste"]. Let me know at once whether the exhibition also has a pavilion of "live inventory"; if so, the town of Będzin would occupy a very honourable place there... The above-mentioned.
The "Crowned" Dictators

[Sosnowiec — Talmud Torah; criticism of the trustees.]
"...The caretaker [stróż] of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah has had himself entered on the mortgage of the building for a sum of about 3000 zł. and demands that the building be put up for auction. (From the chronicle)."

In our paper's issue of a week ago many of our readers read the notice above, and no doubt there are different readers: some also [printed "אייך", read "אויך"] read through the word printed in black as if it were nothing at all, like any other ordinary piece of news; but there are also those who were disappointed and ask us in astonishment: is it possible? Can this be? Is this a real fact that happened? And are paper and print really so patient that they bear everything? That they can digest everything, just like any other logical, self-evident piece of news?
Were it not our own flesh and blood, were it not a Jewish public matter, one could choke with laughter. What does this mean: the caretaker of the Talmud Torah suddenly becomes the actual master of this educational institution, which, moreover, is intended for the children of the people, for the poorest strata of the population — is that not a farce? Does this fact not remind us of the tales of the Thousand and One Nights?
That is what is called management, that is the true understanding of public activity: one receives a fine modern building, a building specially built for a Talmud Torah, with large, fine, airy rooms and with a comfortable yard and a garden, where there is ample space, where children can develop freely and comfortably and where there are the best possibilities to educate the children on healthy foundations — one takes this building and turns it into a rubbish bin and filth; apathy and clumsy, neglected and banal activity play first fiddle. But all this is still too little; so that the set should be complete, one runs up a debt with the Christian caretaker of about three thousand gulden, and now he already knows how to settle accounts with the "Żydzi" [zhides, Polish slur for Jews]; apparently he will now stand his ground, and who knows — a question about a story — perhaps he really aims to become the actual master of the building, since he has already got onto the mortgage and demands that the building be put up for auction. It is possible that he means to buy up more such [debts?], and then, then it will turn out that he should create a board of trustees [kuratorium], and possibly he will want to be the chairman [prezes] — who will then be able to say a word to him? Once it is in his hands, there will be nothing to be done; it may even turn out that he must be praised and his dear name thanked for the kind-heartedness of the Christian master. And indeed, what will the town do then if, for instance, such a Christian says: I don't want you here at all; why should I educate żydowski children, why — he will think to himself — should I be a żydowski farmhand [parobek], when I can make myself a "maczeż" [?] here? And it is possible that one fine day he will think it over and say to himself: clear out of here with your żydowski bebechy [belongings, "guts"] — do I need you here for my headache?
True, it looks like a legend, like a utopia, like something that cannot come true, but many will understand that irony can turn into reality. Right now one just does not believe that things could be brought to that, just as a few years ago one would not have believed that it would come to the present sad state, in which the caretaker can find himself on the mortgage and be a deciding person.
Just as in Będzin, here too people trembled before public opinion; they feared the open air like a plague, God save us; they guarded against publicity as against something evil. Everything that was done at all was done behind closed doors, quietly, hush, so that nobody should find out what goes on behind the Chinese wall.
And it is interesting that at the time when every Sosnowiec householder who could not agree with the criminal behind-the-scenes politics was regarded as a dangerous element that must be weeded out and must remain outside the camp, at that very time the leaders were permitted to do anything in the world, and did not guard even against such a desecration of God's name as the caretaker being able to set the tone.
We now know of this crime thanks to the carrying out of the official formalities; but we do not know what else may happen, and that one does not know is no wonder either, because there they tremble before publicity as before mortal danger; everything there is done behind closed doors, in deepest secrecy, so that nobody should learn about the local "holy service"...
But now that things have reached the present unheard-of, abject state, it may no longer be left alone as if it were a purely private matter into which no outsider has any right to penetrate; after all, one must not forget that a Talmud Torah is a municipal institution, and that if dictators of that sort have seized it — let them grow old with it, but responsibility toward the community, toward the town, toward the members of the Jewish kehilla they must have. An accounting and a report, and the reason why they brought things to the present sad condition, they must nevertheless state and prove. Things could have gone on as until now had the situation not been brought to this terrible state, or had this been a private cheder. But it is quite different when the question is a public one, when the building belongs to the community and when the children are even taken from the people, when the broad strata of the population entrust them with their education. Those who stand at the helm must be and remain responsible to Jewish Sosnowiec, regardless of their hiding — then, when they must declare openly: we are doing this and that, we are improving the institution, we are introducing ever more order, and the children are making proper progress both in sacred and in secular studies.
It is true that the dictators take no account of the community, and it seems to them that the Talmud Torah is their private little shop which they have put into their breast pocket; and according to their "public" notions it actually follows that nobody may say a word to them, nobody need ask them anything at all, and as to what they do and how they do it, nobody may come and ask: why did you do such and such, what did you do this and that for? We know that they are not at all interested in what the newspaper writes, what public opinion says and what the population is upset about. They laugh at all this, but we must not allow such a clumsy, lawless management to go on.
Still, one must not forget that as soon as people come and ask the community: what did you do when you saw the Talmud Torah sinking, this educational institution which from the very beginning was intended for the poorest strata of the masses — what will the community answer then? Will it be able to say: we saw, saw everything and looked on at it all as if it had no connection at all with the Jewish community? Will that be an answer? A justifying answer that could satisfy society?
We understand that a true, honest public worker should not set foot there now; he should not want to crawl into the terrible swamp in which the local "crowned" trustees [gabbaim] feel so comfortable; but that does not mean that it is justified on our part to stand aside at a distance and look on indifferently at this destructive popular activity.
Those who have clean hands must not touch anything there, but one can, after all, demand of them [the trustees] not only an accounting but also that they actually prove why they brought this useful institution to such a shameful state.
True — they regard themselves as crowned dictators (by whom?) and bear no responsibility toward anyone, but even irresponsibility must have a limit, and it would have been necessary to show them that limit.
Dr. Papuri.
There Will Be Laughter...

(A short feuilleton)
The news in the papers that sequestrators will now be allowed to grope through the pockets of taxpayers is causing a complete upheaval in our fiscal system.
The official who came up with such a brilliant idea ought to be placed in one row with the greatest inventors in this field.
For he has found a cure for the crisis; he has brought laughter back to the despairing citizen.
How foolish, how outdated were the former methods of collecting taxes!
Why all the "gevalds", the weeping, the spasms, when one can take out the few groszy with a laugh.
Just imagine: when such a bailiff (executor) hugs the taxpayer, slips his hands into the lower pockets and starts to play the master there, the taxpayer will surely choke with laughter.
First, from the tickling itself; second, because his Mrs. So-and-so has already got there first, shaken out the pockets and found nothing at all. Third: an excuse for all creditors, for the state, for the companies.
In a word: the citizen will stroll freely and openly about the streets with shaken-out[?] pockets and will laugh at the world.
And if the citizen laughs, that is a sure charm for a little loan. The foreigner sees that the citizen is laughing, so he too shows a smile and becomes milder.
And if the citizen laughs, our whole life will take on entirely different forms.
The bailiffs, the officials, even the naczelniks themselves will laugh along. And even the state of health of the population will improve, because laughing is healthy; old and young will laugh, child and babe, women and men, above all the women, since the greatest number of businesses are nowadays registered in their names; they will surely laugh when the bailiffs get at their pockets.
In short, this "time reform"[?] brings cheerfulness into our gloomy life. From one end of the country to the other there will resound a true, healthy, merry laughter, because it is easier to tickle the citizen in his empty pockets than to auction off his broken chairs.
Oh, how people will laugh!...
Patach Shin.
On the Kehilla Elections

In a few weeks' time the "ice" will begin to move, the "proclamations" will crawl over one another, a danger of sermons; floods [of speeches] are unavoidable. The preparations are already being made: sleeves are already being rolled up, tongues are already being sharpened, people measure themselves against one another to the right and to the left — a small thing to say: a dispute for the sake of Heaven. They are going to hold a kind of "heavenly academy", to elect so-called "parnassim" who are to provide for our spiritual needs, take care of poor children with heders, prop up our collapsed charitable institutions and, above all, bring us to a Jewish grave...
For the gmina must, after all, according to the ruling of "the Rav" Sławoj-Składkowski, may he live long, be a — religious one; consequently the parnassim must be of pure olive oil, of genuine "pimsten"-wood[?], each more "korpirer"[?] than the other, little etrogim. How fair and how pleasant...
And as the papers have already discussed, a clique has already gathered, a kind of "black chamber", God save us, who search in holes and crevices to find who is fit and worthy to be a voter and who is not, who has the right of election (make no mistake and do not read: of the first-born, because the birthright they want for themselves) — but about that we shall still have occasion to speak.
* * *
If we were to consider this matter in the natural way, without tricks, as reason requires, as plain common sense would dictate, a picture would appear before us that looks the exact opposite of what it is in reality.
It would stand to reason that when a town has to elect a gabbai, a person to be entrusted with the affairs of a kehilla, to take upon himself the responsibility of providing a Jewish community with everything that should and must be provided, then the elders of the town, the "seven good men of the town", the heads of the community, ought to come to such a person and beg him in fear and love to take upon himself the great burden and the yoke of the public — of being the head of the kehilla; with tears in their eyes they ought to beg him to agree to take upon himself such a heavy yoke and not leave a town abandoned, and with a decree of the community compel him to take this burden upon himself.
What do we see in reality? When the time of elections comes, of electing new parnassim, there is a rush "in great abundance" of elements who would be better suited to be beadles in a shtibl than parnassim of a kehilla; like locusts they fall upon the kehilla seat to snatch it. They stop at no means, however unkosher and unfit, they rack their brains how to overcome the opposing side, i.e. those who do not want them as leaders — although this opposing side is the great majority of the kehilla; and these empty honour-chasers are not deterred even when they see with their own eyes that honour flees from them; it does not bother them in the least if they are shown an angry face, if people shout at them at the top of their voices: "Who asked this of you?" — they insist all the more with all their strength. And the end is that these strife-mongers bring bitterness, a kind of "bitter destruction", into the Jewish street, the division of hearts grows and no good comes of it...
* * *
In the electoral ordinance which the minister issued for the new kehilla elections there is a paragraph saying that a Jew may be disqualified from his right to vote for lack of religiousness. Obviously[?] a great injustice has thereby been done, and indeed also an insult to a part of the Jewish population, just as the other part of the same population would have remained deeply wronged and insulted had the minister said in his order that the right to vote may be disqualified from those Jews who cannot translate a portion of the Pentateuch with Rashi, or who do not understand the meaning of the words of the prayers...
And speaking of elections and religion, one asks: what has the sabbatical year to do with dowering a bride?... What connection, for instance, can elections to a kehilla have with a large step taken on the Sabbath?... And in general, how can one establish — what is more, with a microscope — to test religiousness, to detect a tiny flaw in the "pintele yid"? Is there then a rubric in the passport to enter it? And how can one appraise a person's soul at all? Even in the Hasidic books it is told that the thirty-six righteous men are to be found precisely among the common people, with a coarse appearance...
And as if from under the ground the "right" guardians immediately sprout up to adjudicate[?] the rights of the voters, asking nobody — and who made them a "who appointed you"?... And they will "prove" at once with signs and wonders that so-and-so is not strictly kosher...
On this point the truth must be spoken out: among no other nation or tongue can one see and hear what one sees among our brethren the children of Israel.
A. Szlezynger.
The Kehilla as a Political Factor — In Our National Struggle

[Article — kehilla elections; Jewish national politics.] By N. Telandner [?].
A scant 4 weeks separate us from the day of the kehilla elections, on which the fate and character of the Jewish kehilla must be decided — which forms and directions are to prevail in the kehilla. And when we watch the election fair that has only just begun, how the election lists are fruitful and multiply like mushrooms after rain, we must stop for a moment and reflect: what does all this mean?
Is this abundance supposed to signify great interest in the kehilla? Have the Jewish masses really already reached the level of awareness, do they understand the great importance of the kehilla in Jewish life, and is this really the driving force [printed „כח-הדוחה“] that makes everyone, from right to left, strain with all their might to gain influence in the kehilla?
Or is it rather the opposite (ipkha mistabra): that this [printed „דאגער“, probably for „דאזיגער“] election fair is nothing but the outcome of a lack of awareness, of disregard and contempt for the institution of the kehilla, of not understanding the true tasks of the kehilla — and every little circle and little prayer-house („kreyzl un kleyzl“) fits the great kehilla problem to its own shopkeeper's notions; and this is in fact the only reason why various petty people with Lilliputian notions have the nerve and the audacity to become the „madbarna d'umta“ [spokesmen of the nation], to want to speak in the name of the Jewish population? And when we become more closely [?] acquainted with the backstage election manoeuvres that have already begun, with the various machinations and combinations conducted among the various groups — thanks to our acquaintance with the „pretenders to the crown“ of the kehilla leadership — we must unfortunately come to the conclusion that the second assumption is the correct one: that the election fair is driven not by the force of awareness, but that contempt for and disregard of the kehilla is the sole cause of the sad phenomenon we see now and will yet have occasion to see.
And when we reflect for a while and with a searching glance look into the not-distant past, to the era of the Council of Four Lands in Poland, which was the prototype of Jewish autonomy; and when we further acquaint ourselves with the Jewish history of the last 50 years, with the great ideological struggles over the foundations of Jewish national politics in the lands of exile, and with the great weight that the theoreticians of that time, regardless of political orientation — beginning with Pinsker's „Auto-Emancipation“ and Herzl's later slogan of the „conquest of the communities“, down to the autonomist foundation laid by the well-known historian Simon Dubnow — attached to the structure and character of the Jewish kehillot, which were to form the core, the cell [?] of the Jewish national-cultural autonomy being fought for: the Jewish kehillot were, after all, to form the national union of all the scattered Jewish communities in the country concerned and to become part of the municipal self-governments, which were to manage all the national-cultural as well as religious affairs of the Jewish population, according to the principles of the well-known Austrian social theorist Dr. Karl Renner, founder of the theory of personal national cultural autonomy, as opposed to the hitherto accepted theory of territorial autonomy, under which we Jews, as an extra-territorial minority, could not be protected against the danger of assimilation by the dominant ruling majority. The crystallisation of this ideology found its most prominent expression at the historic Helsingfors Zionist conference in 1906, at which the basic lines of Jewish national politics in the Diaspora were worked out. That is how our dreamers and fighters conceived the kehilla problem.
These postulates were strengthened still further in 1919 by the tireless work of the „Jewish Delegation in Paris“ headed by Leo Motzkin, where the Jewish demand was sanctioned and the Jewish cultural demands, as a national minority, were confirmed under the law of nations. This historic act was also incorporated in the international agreements with the newly arisen states, among them Poland too. And who knows whether here in Poland — where the largest Jewish community in Europe is concentrated, where we form 15 per cent of the Polish population — the Jewish kehillot would not really have adopted the forms corresponding to the principles of national-cultural autonomy, on the model of the former Council of Four Lands that once existed in Poland, were it not for the circumstance that when the Polish state came into being it already found a ready-made kehilla law, left as an inheritance from the German occupation, which had been imported by the „German-loyal Torah“ [„doytsh-treye toyre“] rabbis Dr. Carlebach and Cohn, who bestowed on us, Polish Jews, a „religious community“ (Religionsgemeinschaft). And these regulations, inherited from General Beseler, have remained to this very day the foundations of our kehillot in Poland — thanks to the incessant lobbying of the „Agudah“, which saw in the restricted religious forms of the kehillot a sound basis for its various combinations: to exploit them for its own personal interests, to conduct a lively trade in the posts of religious functionaries, which goes on everywhere in Poland to this very day. This sad circumstance led to the kehillot becoming ever more restricted and confined, and clamped into the narrow frames of religion. Bit by bit the kehillot were deprived of their vital nerve, until the kehillot became what we see today — „little houses of the dead“ („meysim-shtiblekh“), and the parnasim, alas, must merely play the role of „gravediggers“. In such a state of affairs, is it any wonder that the kehilla has lost its dignified appearance? And the attitude to the kehilla is one of nothingness, of contempt; and it is no wonder either that mere nobodies, without a public sense, without understanding of the kehilla's tasks, have the audacity to crawl in with their shopkeeper mugs! But the great „Stop!“ must be said once and for all! And the Jewish voter must after all, at long last, give himself an account of whom he should elect. Let us believe that this time the Jewish voter will find the right way and will not let himself be misled by the people who want to exploit the election campaign for personal interests.
— The floor now belongs to the voter!

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Acharei–Kedoshim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Acharei–Kedoshim
—o—
a) "After the death of the two sons of Aaron" (Lev. 16:1).
The bitterest curse of the Rebuke (tokhechah) is: "Behold, I will add to chastise you wondrously" ("hineni osef leyasserkhem hapele vafele" — so printed, a free blend of the curse verses). The initials of the word "pele" (P-L-A) say: perud levavot anashim — "the division of people's hearts." Division and fragmentation among Jews is the worst national misfortune. But the guilty party is not the people, only the heads, the leaders, the sons of Aaron — "the two sons of Aaron." When the sons of Aaron, the priests, are "two," not one, but divided — this brings destruction and death; but when "the heads of the people are gathered together," when the heads live in peace — "all the tribes of Israel together" — then the people surely live in tranquillity among themselves.
Toldot Yaakov Yosef and Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
b) "When they drew near before the Lord, and died" (ibid.).
Two reasons are given in the Midrash for the tragic death of Aaron's sons: because they did not marry, and because they looked forward to the death of Moses and Aaron in order to become leaders.
They did not marry because they said: with whom shall we make a match?! What match is fit for us, the sons of Aaron?! But striving to take over the leadership of the people, any match should have suited them, for in a leader it is actually a virtue when he comes from a lowly family... "A leader is appointed over the community only if a basket of reptiles hangs behind him."
Likutei Maharal.
• • •
About today's leaders, who come from lowly families and only thanks to the luck that plays into their hands climb up onto the social chariot, R' Meir of Przemyślany said:
"This world is like a wedding feast" — the world is like a wedding; at a wedding one pays honour to the groom and the in-laws, be they the lowliest creatures — it is their time. Today the musicians play for them... So too whomever luck plays up to in the world — everyone becomes subservient to him; it is his time...
• • •
The saying "This world is like a wedding feast" was interpreted by the "Chiddushei HaRim" thus: the world is like a wedding hall ("bei hilula"). A hall that is hired out for weddings — today this one dances in it, tomorrow another, and the day after tomorrow yet another...
—o—
c) "And this shall be an everlasting statute unto you... once a year" (Lev. 16:34)
The world (printed "beltt" for "velt") cannot exist without a little sin; that is what the evil inclination is there for... But for that little sin there is a Yom Kippur, one day a year to wipe away the little sin, which is a law that must exist in the world. But for a world such as today's, "once a year" is too little to atone; for so many sins we would need at least three hundred and sixty-five Yom Kippurs a year...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
d) "That the land vomit not you out" (Lev. 18:28).
Rabbi Y. L. Fishman relates in the name of Rabbi Kook the following characteristic anecdote:
When Rabbi Kook was in America, an American magnate came to him and said that he wished to settle with his family in the Land of Israel, so that the children would be brought up there in the spirit of pure faith. Rabbi Kook encouraged him in this, and the magnate realised his ideal.
Some time later the magnate came to Rabbi Kook in Jerusalem to take his leave: he is going back. In the Land of Israel he sees only Sabbath-desecrators, free-thinking pioneers; he does not want to stay here, and he bears a grudge against the Rabbi, who persuaded him to come to a land of heretics...
Rabbi Kook then asks him about a well-known health resort in America. The magnate begins to praise the air of that town — a real wonder.
Rabbi Kook shrugs his shoulders: I have been there and saw that the air there is the worst.
— What are you saying, Rabbi?
— I saw how people there constantly spit blood; people there do nothing but cough.
— But Rabbi, on the contrary, the air there is the very best, and those who cough and spit blood come there to be cured, because the air is a healing one.
— Aha, now I understand: precisely where the air is most healing and best, people spit blood and cough, because the blood-spitting came with the people from other places, where the air is dangerous, and here they have come to be healed.
— And why — Rabbi Kook concludes his wise and apt remark — do you not understand that the Land of Israel is the same? Precisely because the air here sanctifies and purifies, one sees here the most Sabbath-desecrators and sinners, because here is the health resort to which all the sick of soul come to be healed... Precisely here more blood is spat, but that very fact proves that the air heals, that the land sanctifies and purifies..
• • •
The Rabbi of Włocławek, R' Yehuda Leib Kowalski of blessed memory, once compared the piety of the Diaspora and the non-piety of the new Yishuv in the Land of Israel in a parable:
Two sick men: in one of them a most serious disease has begun to develop; the symptoms are already there, but the patient still looks well for the time being.
A second patient — one who is getting up from a severe illness; he looks bad and is deathly pale, but he will grow stronger by the day.
To the superficial observer the second patient is the more dangerous case; he does look worse, but in truth he is getting better. The dangerous one is the first, in whom the disease is only beginning to develop and who will grow worse from day to day.
We Diaspora Jews look, outwardly, in the religious sense, quite fine, but the bacilli of a cancer of heresy are already among us and multiply from day to day. In the Land of Israel, on the other hand, the religious situation improves from day to day. It is the pale patient — whose pallor makes a worse impression than the cancer sufferer — but he is on the way to recovery...
—o—
e) "Ye shall not steal, neither shall ye deal falsely" (printed 19:18; actually Lev. 19:11)
Regarding theft the plural is used: "lo tignovu," not "lo tignov." Because people are used to granting themselves permission: that man stole from me — so I may in turn steal from someone else...
Again, people like to persuade themselves: oh, that man owes me much more, or he will in the end go bankrupt at my expense anyway — it won't hurt if I "slip" a few złoty ("zlotes") into his bill. Says the verse: "neither shall ye deal falsely" — if the customer owes you, take it openly and not by way of theft...
Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Lev. 19:16)
In the books of the disciples of the Baal Shem Tov those preachers of rebuke who see only bad in Jews are sharply censured. "My tears have been my bread" — the Baal Shem Tov interprets: for those preachers the people's tears are bread. Out of the people's faults they make a bread-business, a livelihood. He also said: "every plague which is not written in the book of the Torah" — not with Torah verses, not with sermons about the people's sins should the people be chastised, but with kindness, with love for the people. "Thou shalt not go as a talebearer among thy people" — do not be a talebearer against the people. —
—o—
Avot, Chapter Three.
g) "Men would swallow each other alive" (3:2)
A horse, when it drinks in a river, kicks with its legs. What does the horse mean by that? —
When it bends down to drink it sees another horse (it is reflected)... It is afraid that the other horse might drink up the whole river, so it kicks...
The moral:
People quarrel and fight with one another, thinking that one takes the other's livelihood away. But the river is big enough for everyone to drink...
Margenita deRabbi Meir.
—o—
h) "Anyone with whom the spirit of people is pleased" (printed 13; printed "gocha" for "nocha")
It is no proof that the people honour someone, for that is sometimes done under outward compulsion. The proof is from "the spirit of people" — what people think in their hearts...
—o—
i) "If there is no flour, there is no Torah" (printed 13)
Those who have no other livelihood but from the Torah, from the rabbinate — their Torah is worth nothing. One must live from other sources.
Midrash Shmuel.
What Benefit Will the Polish-German Valorization Agreement Bring Us?

On 16 March 1921 [sic; read 1931] the Polish-German valorization agreement came into force. This agreement was signed in Berlin by the Polish and German plenipotentiaries after 5 July 1928[?]; its ratification, however, took place only on 3 February 1931.
Since many Polish citizens have claims against German citizens dating from old times, and they themselves also owe the Germans various sums, they will surely be interested in the manner in which the mutual obligations are settled on the basis of this agreement.
We therefore wish to acquaint the readers here with the more important provisions of the agreement.
According to a general rule laid down in Article 1, citizens of a foreign state must — in the recalculation of private-law claims and in the conversion of public loans — be treated equally with the citizens of the state itself.
On the basis of this rule, Polish citizens will have the right to demand a recalculation of every claim, that is, of savings deposits, pledge bonds [?], loan bonds and the like, on the same principles as German citizens. In the valorization of personal loans secured by mortgage, the regulations of the state on whose territory the encumbered immovable property is situated decide. For other personal loans, the place of residence of the debtor at the time the legal steps are taken decides. Since under German law these claims are calculated at 25 per cent, this agreement brings our citizens very great benefit and considerable possibilities.
As regards the payment of insurance sums, there are the various kinds of insurance.
a) Sums which fall due — under the German valorization law — on claims of Polish citizens, according to the distribution plans of life-insurance contracts, must be paid out in cash before 31 December 1932. The demand for payment must be lodged through the intermediary of the Polish government with the German insurance institution within 9 months, beginning from 6 December 931 [sic; read 1931].
b) Insurances which, on the basis of the distribution plans, must be converted into premium-free insurances, or must be terminated as premium insurances — in case there is an approved distribution plan, the payment of the corresponding sum must take place within three months of the notice of termination. If, however, the distribution plan contains no suitable [?] provisions for cash payments, half a per cent is deducted from the sum for each calendar month between the day of payment and 31 December 1932.
c) Claims of Polish citizens on life-insurance contracts denominated in marks which — on the basis of German law — are not subject to recalculation, as well as claims on policies denominated in Polish marks, war notes, roubles and Austrian crowns, will be settled by the Polish government, in case the contracts were concluded before 14 February 1924. For this purpose the German government will [pay], by 1 January 1932 at the latest, a compensation in the amount of 990 thousand German marks and 426 thousand złoty, and this compensation releases the German insurance institutions from all obligations towards the insured. The distribution of these sums among those entitled will be carried out by a body which the Polish government will appoint for this purpose. The relevant ordinance will be issued after the German government has paid in these sums.
d) In the settlement of insurances concluded in German premium loans, Polish citizens will be treated equally with German citizens.
The provisions of the valorization agreement do not concern rights which were assigned by citizens of the other state after 1 January 1926.
Important is the provision according to which the limitation period of claims that have been in arrears since 1 July 1921 is suspended from the moment when the German creditor could not come forward in court with his claim — in any case from the day [?] on which the Polish law of 20 November 1919 came into force until the day on which the present treaty becomes legally binding.
Notwithstanding the fact that the treaty became legally binding very late, it can nevertheless to a certain extent make possible [the settlement of] the mutual claims not regulated until now. The agreement solves yet another very important problem and liquidates a further post-war phase between Poland and Germany.
Dr. Dor Kach [Koch?].

The Vanished Daughter

[Serialized novel — modern Jewish life in the Old and New World; installment 4.]
An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World
by Elizabeth Garin.
4.

"So you think your folks are dying of longing for you?" Janek burst out laughing. "Guests have arrived, one has to make money... For a couple of zlotys the 'Zhids' would sell their father, never mind a daughter who ran off with a goy — and with such a one at that, who was thrown out of the Vienna university for beating Zhids and became a circus rider... A fine daughter for a proud Jew," he teased her. "If he caught you with your khłopiec (lad), he'd flay the skin off you alive!"

"Ha, ha! But I knew you were telling a lie!" she cried out, and in a moment she was as if transformed: the large, bright black eyes flared up, the little face flushed, the whole graceful, slender body gained more life, suppleness and elasticity; now she was enticing, and the shkotsim [gentile lads] could not look their fill at her...

"My papa and mamenyu would have given away everything in the world for me; I acted foolishly... I should have come to them and told them that I love Staszek and cannot live without him..."

Staszek let out a quiet, suppressed laugh, but Janek, on the other hand, laughed so hard that tears rolled down his cheeks, and he jumped about, spun around and performed the strangest antics.

Lala remained standing with wide-open eyes, deeply offended and ashamed...

"Hey, I can't stand it! Hey, she's killing me!" Janek held his sides.

"Shut up, you donkey! Enough out of you! Is it her fault that she doesn't know?" Staszek finally spoke up.

He got up from the broken crate on which he had been sitting and wanted to put his arms around her.

"Don't touch me, do you hear? Don't touch me!" She stepped back from him, her eyes burning with anger.

"Let him tell me what he found to laugh at in my words. I want to know everything, everything; I'm not a child, and if there is something I don't understand, it's high time I understood it!" she shouted with tears of vexation in her eyes, stamping on the dirty earthen floor with her little French shoes.

Staszek glanced at his friend with an idle smile on his lips, stretched his shoulders and drew up his handsome, graceful, tall figure. Then he calmly, as if it were not meant for him, went over to the stove to see whether the potatoes were done yet, and to push the pot of coffee, whose delicious smell had already spread through the whole room, a little further from the fire.

"Well, I'm talking to you, after all — why don't you speak, Janek?" she began again.

"What is there to say to such a child as you, Lala?" — he suddenly became very serious.

"Do you know what your batka [dad] would have done to Staszek if you told him that you are in love with him, and all the rest...?"

"What?" Lala asked, and at his words she suddenly blushed deeply and lowered her eyes.

"All right, if you want to know... Staszek ought to have told you this, but since he hasn't had the courage to tell you, I'll do it, because I think it's time to stop playing the fool, and I don't want to see him rot in prison."

"In prison?" she cried out, frightened.

"Yes, prison — that's what he'll get for seducing a minor. Oh, believe me, the rich Shloyme Rapaport's gold ducats will win against him, the good-for-nothing, the circus rider, who was thrown out of the university for rioting and for beating Jewish students to death, such a sentence that he will never come out of there [printed 'from from'] alive..."

"But they love me so much," she began, deathly pale, in a voice soaked with tears.

"Yes, they loved you very much!" Staszek caught her up sarcastically. He stepped away from the stove and planted himself opposite her. Now he was as if transformed: his gypsy-handsome, finely chiselled face with the caressing, soft, fiery eyes was now twisted with hatred, and the eyes burned with a hellish fire; yet even now he was handsome, with a kind of demonic beauty that repelled and at the same time drew irresistibly...

"Yes, they loved you when you were their pride and their ornament. But now —" he spat contemptuously and went on talking:

"Now, when you have covered their name with shame, when everywhere in all Poland, in all Austria, wherever there is but a single Jew, people will say: 'Have you heard the terrible news? Shloyme Rapaport's daughter has run off with a shegetz!' Now they no longer love you, and when they catch us, do you know what they will do to us?"

"What?" she asked, completely frozen with fear.

"Me they will put in prison, and if the charge of seduction is not enough to keep me under lock and bolt until I croak, they will easily be able to prove that I robbed them too" — he pointed with his eyes at a sizeable chest bound with brass and a heavy leather valise.

"That's as far as I am concerned," he went on through clenched teeth, "but with you they will settle accounts quite differently... I know Jews, and your parents, too well not to know this... You they will put under the bridal veil with some fanatical, worthless little Jew, whom they will bring down from a small Galician shtetl and who, for good money, will be willing to cover up your shame... But first of all they will wipe away every trace..." He came up closer to her and whispered something in her ear... She let out a desperate scream and swayed, and had he not caught her, she would have fallen.

The election campaign for the kehilla is in full blaze.

[Będzin — kehilla and elections.] A „flood“ of lists is expected.
In the course of the week the election campaign has widened and grown stronger. The number of candidate lists is increasing; every day fresh „little shops“ (kremlekh) pop up. Especially active is the „Aguda“ [Agudat Yisrael], which is working hard[?] (lit. „deeds“) to unite the „shtiblekh“ [Hasidic prayer houses] around itself, and where the „Aguda“ has no chance it agitates for various groups to run in the elections independently, in order to weaken the opposing lists. Thus, thanks to Mr. Kaminer, the „Nos'ei“ society has decided to run separately with a candidate list; a group of Ger Hasidim has also decided to run separately. Outwardly this means that a „split“ has occurred in the „Aguda“; in general the „Aguda“ is trying to weaken the non-partisan front that was created by the Aleksander Hasidim.
An exact list of the candidate lists has not yet been fixed, but as foreseen their number will be very large.
The lists already fixed are: „Aguda“ (2), Mizrachi, Zionists, „Hitachdut“, Right Poalei Zion, Left Poalei Zion, artisans, small traders, the „Nos'ei“ society, United Hasidim, Krimilov Hasidim, the Beit HaMidrash worshippers, and the Sanacja bloc of non-partisan Jews.

Four years ago S. Grinbaum (Czeladź) took from his son-in-law in Będzin, Welgrin, a sum of 4700 dollars for the purpose of buying a house in Sosnowiec for his son-in-law.

Do Not Submit Large Numbers of Appeals

So holds the head of the tax office.
At the invitation of the „Urząd Skarb.“ [Tax Office] in Będzin a conference was held with the participation of representatives of the merchants' and petty traders' associations in Będzin.
The head (naczelnik) of the „Urząd“ addressed the representatives of the merchants' organisations with the request to explain to their members and influence them to refrain from submitting mass appeals against the assessment of turnover for 1930, because the latest assessment was reduced[?] by 40 percent in comparison with 1929.

It is already clear to everyone that criticising the “mikveh rag” (mikveh-tsetingl) is no longer worth it; on the contrary, it is downright a disgrace to mention them, so as not to defile oneself with that uncleanness...
The “editors” of that “rag” are already almost isolated from everything connected with Jewish affairs, society, etc.; not to speak of the institutions run by national elements — even the most orthodox institutions avoid these brazen-faced people; in general nobody wants to have any dealings with them any more.
But the creatures have found a “remedy” elsewhere, among non-Jews: the “source” (di kvele) opened up for them during the Sejm elections; at that time they showed themselves to be loyal “moshkes” [?], and for that they received a promise that [?] they would at last get the advertisements of the offices where for years they had not dared to show their shameless faces.
— The promise is being kept, especially by the Będzin magistrate, where last week the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” and the “Kurier Zachodni” were struck off from among the newspapers recognised until now...
— We accept the “verdict” open-heartedly, but you, Mr. Temporary Commissioner, who care for all the citizens of the town, must surely find a way by which the great Jewish mass — who, incidentally, are the taxpayers — may also know when the waterworks and the municipal power station (elektrownia) are not working...
