The Chaos on the Jewish Electoral Front. (Fragmentation from Without and Squabbles from Within. — In What Situation Does the Jewish Voter Find Himself?)

[Zagłębie — kehilla elections; opinion.] By R. Let.
So, we are already in the period of the elections to the Jewish kehillas; we have already been dragged into this uproar, people are already quarrelling and tearing at each other over what the world stands on. Every party wants to show that it is "the top of the box" and that it is entitled to become the kehilla board, that it deserves the greatest number of mandates and that everyone must give it their votes. Along comes a second one and says: what, them — the Jesuits, the sold souls, the spiteful apostates — to them you want to give your one and only vote? You will never be able to forgive yourselves for it, you will carry this stain on your conscience forever. To whomever you like, to whomever you like — so the lecturer [prelegent] ends his fiery sermon — but not a single vote may be given to them. And then a third comes to you, and a fourth, and a sixth, and each one turns the previous one into dust and mud and proves to you in black and white, with evidence and with figures, that his little shop is the best, that his party is the most responsible and most honest, and that only it will take care of your well-being in such a way that you and your household will get every good thing from them.
And when such a Jew leaves the hall, his head is muddled[?] from all the sermons and he does not know whom to listen to first. He knows that "they all take him for a fool" [?] [idiom: "have him without a teapot"]; the trust he once had in them he lost long ago. With regret and with a heavy heart the Jew tells you that the modesty, honesty and sincerity of former times are no longer in the party, and that if the cards were laid open there, one would see so much unpleasantness, so much that is bad and bitter, that God alone should have mercy on them.
That is the level party life has reached: that the simple, "everyday" Jew sees and notices what goes on there behind the scenes. To tell the truth, though, the everyday Jew knows nothing; he only feels it, he grasps instinctively that something there is no longer what it used to be.
And indeed, as soon as one begins to break into this partisan mouse-nest, as soon as one takes a sniff there[?], as soon as the curtain is raised and the figures appear — one begins to be astonished. One then comes to the conviction that only from outside, from a distance, does it seem that party life holds true holiness, pure innocence and naivety; but as soon as one draws nearer, as soon as one begins to penetrate there and sees the wheeling and dealing, one draws back at once, if one wants[?] to remain the same person with a clean conscience.
The party no longer sees to it, as it once did, that it be represented by capable people and suitable representatives, whom the town would hold in reverence and who would benefit the kehilla; instead people come along and seize the party, and with the help of intrigues and the force of power pressure is applied as to which people are to be put forward. No account at all is taken of whether the people are capable, whether they are suitable, whether they command respect; there is no control and no audit to take this responsible work upon themselves — and that is why the chaos has reached its present level.
And that is the reason why in all the parties we see disunity and fragmentation, so that the unity and discipline of former times already belong to the past; and the result of this we see [print: "are we"] in the fact that in Będzin no more than 14 — read: fourteen — lists were submitted in all, Sosnowiec could not stretch to more than 10 lists, and Dąbrowa, that "rich" Jewish kehilla, is split into no more than 2 parts. "Reden" has paid enough for "Huta Bankowa". From now on they want to be their own masters; and they are indeed going with one single list, but to speak of unity there is hardly appropriate...
We cannot form any idea of what the coming kehilla representation will look like, who will be the managers and over what they will manage. It can be foreseen, after all, that with such fragmentation, with such chaos, there will simply be no time to deal with kehilla affairs; first of all they will have to deal with themselves; first, every party, every representative, will have to settle accounts with one another — they will not forget that this is primarily what they came there for; and once they start quarrelling among themselves it is self-evident that such matters are not settled so quickly: one runs into stubborn people, then into questions of principle, on which none of them can yield an iota on behalf of his party; and we know from practice what it looks like when parties start quarrelling among themselves — let alone when so many persons, no evil eye, gather in the gmina [kehilla board]: in any case they will have no time to do anything else. It is self-evident that at a time when all the parties are so busy, they will not get round to dealing with other "side" questions.
That, roughly, is how one can now picture the "activity" of the future Jewish kehillas. We have had our fill of the previous kehilla representations; we saw no activity from them; clumsy helplessness, intrigues and lawlessness were visible with them at every step. And now? What will we have now? What will we see now? What will the new boards give us? What responsibility and accountability do they take upon themselves that they will not degrade our kehillas — never mind that they are already in such a lowly state that anyone can get in there, take the helm in hand and steer as he pleases, as it suits his nose? Who will give us the assurance that the bad will not get even worse? How do we know that the new kehillas will not be a second edition of the previous ones, with the difference that here we will have more parties, more disunity, more fragmentation?
Say what you will, but conscious people somehow cannot go to the elections with a clear conscience. They somehow cannot give themselves an account of what they aim at by dropping their vote into the ballot box. Such a voter reckons: whom shall I [the verb is missing in print]? Whom do I make my representative? And after all is said and done, what do I achieve by helping, with my vote, to bring in this or that representative? Does any of them have a platform? Does he undertake to carry one out? Does he even dream of keeping to it and carrying it out in this house of the dead, which one enters only in order to settle accounts and so that one may take revenge on the other? Do we not know all this in advance? Do we not see it now? Does it not sprout out of every candidate?
And since that is so, since one goes in only to achieve the above-mentioned, what will come of it for us, for Jewish Będzin or Sosnowiec? Does the Jewish citizen really want to send his representatives into the gmina so as to give them the opportunity to quarrel among themselves, and afterwards the starosta [district head] should have to intervene and demand by compulsion that the administration be run properly? Are we in the period of childhood, starting to play: today I'll make you, tomorrow you'll make me? Does all this not look like a real comedy? Does anyone here approach with reverence the responsible institution that costs the Jewish population so much money? Do we see [print: "are we"] today in the parnas at least the honest willpower that we saw before the war in the Jewish dozór [pre-war kehilla board], with which we were in its day so dissatisfied? Why should we deceive ourselves — if we once had 2—3 good and honest dozór members, they achieved, with minimal expenses, more in 3 months than the present kehilla representation in 3 years, the council and the administration taken together, with their large budgets.
It is therefore interesting to know what guarantee [print: "velkhevarantsye", for "velkhe garantsye"] and what promises the future kehilla representatives will give their voters. The voters have every right to put these questions to their candidates, and the future representatives must take upon themselves the responsibility of assuring their voters for what purpose they are entering the gmina.
R. Let.
A Bee's Sting.

[Land of Israel — feuilleton for Lag BaOmer.] By A. Sh. Yuris [A. Sz. Juris].
(In honour of Lag BaOmer, specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").

On Rehov Aliyah [Aliyah Street] there stands a modest house with a spacious garden. Not for nothing is this street called Rehov Aliyah. Rehov Aliyah is, for Jewish youth, the vestibule where those weary from distant journeys straighten out their bones and brighten their gaze. It is the first touchstone for toil-worn bodies and hardened souls. From this "Beit Olim" [immigrants' house] they stream out on bright mornings and no less bright evenings, when the sun sets in eastern flames [sic] over the bright streets of the first Jewish city, and with dreamy eyes and open [?] hearts they absorb into themselves the new life on the old earth.
* * *
While young lads, worn out with work at the hakhshara [training] points, and young halutzot [pioneer women], still dressed in the "last cry" of their former student berets and ladies' coats, gather for lunch, there stand in the bright kitchen, arranged according to the latest word in technology and hygiene — these are young Jewish girls who have come from all the lands of the diaspora, borne by the ideals of building and rebuilding — and they prepare fresh and healthy dishes for them. Food in our homeland is a quite special work of art; the cooking problem with us has its own history, its own light and shadow sides; more than once in young kvutzot [communal groups] girls young as fresh blood were replaced [?] — girls who in their mothers' homes had never touched any washing or cooking utensils with their delicate piano fingers, and now must cook meals for whole camps, for young farmers returning home tired from heavy field work.
So it was a good idea of one of our best pioneer women, Hanna Maisel-Shohat — and with the means of one of our noblest women's organisations, "WIZO" — to build, precisely on Rehov Aliyah, not far from the "Beit Olim", a quiet, modest house where young Jewish daughters would prepare and learn for their future mission: cooking and washing, and vegetables and "incubators", and fruit trees and flower growing, and bees...
• • •
Bees...
She leads me there, Malka Sapir, a graduate of the seminary for "household-management science" in Hamburg-Altona, but first I must pass by the laundry. Again, together with the steam from the boilers, young laughter bursts towards me from a merry [? printed "tsvingte"] band of girls. This field too lay fettered in old conservative chains. Primitive washing, too, has been raised — thanks to steam and electricity and pioneering ardour and girlish youth — to a science and an art, and thousand-year-old habits have been swept out. And so, since the laundry stands not far from the beehives, they warned us, on the basis of bitter and stinging experience, for heaven's sake not to go there...
But how not to go? When the steam from the boilers and the radiance of their beaming faces blocked my view, and I did not notice the stung faces and swollen eyes, and I rush with élan past the beehives to the fenced-off garden for the hens and geese and ducks.
At first the bees ignored us, or rather — for the sake of better strategy they pretended not to know and lured us [?] ever deeper and deeper in, and when we were already in the middle of the garden a whole camp of war-loving and vengeance-thirsty bees hurled itself upon us. One got into my eye and a second reached my ear and bit deep into it.
We barely tore ourselves away from them. But the sting in the ear was a "successful" one, and it flared up blood-red. I did not yet know the meaning of this "battle", but in the hope — supported by Büchner's [? printed "Bikhners"] "nothing gets lost" and by the good Jewish tradition of "gam zu le-tovah" [this too is for the good] — and that I would yet take my revenge on them, I continued my "voyage of discovery" through this Amazon republic...
And the truly motherly kindness of the manageress and of the "minhala" [management] made me forget my ear-ache for a while, and eye and ear were turned to her and her account. Not only is a technical, vocational [printed "melukhe-", probably for "melokhe-"] education given here. In free hours care is taken of the free spirit. Only 6 hours do the girls give to physical work; two to three hours always remain for education: a course on economics, on the women's movement; books are read together. Throughout the country, in all the kvutzot and kibbutzim, you will find the "graduates" of the institution. Over 250 in all the kitchens, and 8 women instructors are constantly travelling, teaching, supervising and giving advice. Now preparations are being made to open a fine bakery, not only for the "daily bread of labour" but also for the Sabbath-and-holiday "afro-tarts" [?].
And I keep pondering all the while: this is all fine and lovely, but what has it to do with Lag BaOmer, with the great Tanna and fighter Rabbi Akiva and with the heroic uprising of Bar Kokhba? Why has the world-wide women's organisation chosen precisely it as the mobilisation day of all Jewish mothers and daughters for the benefit of the Keren Kayemet [Jewish National Fund]?
But the doubt lasted only one second. The Eretz-Israel reality did not abandon me this time either, and brought me a bright answer. In this seemingly modest institution of modest Jewish daughters, and in the eyes of my soul, there grew up and was bewitched [printed "ibergefishuft", probably for "ibergekishuft"] in the "witches' kitchen" a revolt [printed "rehalt", probably for "revolt"] of Bar-Kokhba-like scope against thousand-year-old prejudices on the washing and cooking front, and they are burnt to ashes on the "medurah" field-fires [Lag BaOmer bonfires]. As everything in our homeland is inspired and rejuvenated, so the "kitchen" too is raised to the level of art and free creation. A thousand-year servitude is broken — of the "rolling-pin" and the "mangle" and the "cooking-pot", from which the fairer and greater half of humanity has suffered. Such modern kitchens "WIZO" wants to found throughout the country, and for that, first of all, land is needed! And land means Keren Kayemet!
Then in my mind and heart there fused together Lag BaOmer, the uprising of Bar Kokhba, the land fund and the kitchen revolution of "WIZO", into one fiery, heroic "medurah" [bonfire], in which a sooty and poisoned cooking-and-washing atmosphere is cooked over and recast into a joyful-bright, free-and-creative air — and the "witches' kitchen" becomes a "kitchen of joy". A deep world-wound is healed.
And when late at night we left the meeting, and I looked into the bright faces of the young girls, I no longer saw, in their royal countenance [printed "tsure melukhe"], flushed as on Sabbath and holiday, as at "Lekha Dodi likrat kallah", the poisonous stings of the honey-pregnant bees. --
A strange sweetness and purity shone and radiated from their eyes. That whole institution of theirs was transformed as if by magic into a kind of work-loving "beehive".
Then I understood my ear-ache, and that out of bitterness has come forth sweetness, and however much we may suffer and toil here, our sufferings, compared to the death-pangs of the diaspora, are nevertheless birth-pangs...
* * *
And in deep gratitude I blessed the day and understood the meaning of my suffering.
And it became dear to me, like the tender stroking of a little child's hand — the sting of the bee.
Existence and Decline.

II. The middle class and the working masses. — Preventing beggary, and supporting those suffering from the crisis by means of work
In the first chapter of our article last week we dealt with the question: what can be done, and what ought to be done, for those citizens who wish to sustain their existence honestly and sincerely. Now it would be worth dwelling on a second question, which is no less important and topical than the one already discussed.
In Poland people have grown used to seeing the unemployed, especially in the present critical time; it is known, and it is also understandable, that at a time when the chimneys of the factories stop smoking, the workers are dismissed and the office staff is reduced in those firms that are still holding on somehow. One thus comes to the conviction that something must be done for this mass of people, which grows larger from day to day and remains like branches torn off a healthy tree... That this unfortunate element exists among us too — that is not seen, people do not want to see it, and above all they do not want to pay any attention to it.
And interesting and characteristic is this: not only do those outside our camp fail to see our unemployed, but among ourselves too people are not used to seeing them. We have this hungry element before our eyes day in, day out, and we do not see it; we pay no attention to it, not heeding that it keeps growing larger and larger, that things are coming to the point where it penetrates the marrow of our bones. This element, which could quite often be rescued, we turn into beggars — thanks to the fact that we take pity on it and tell it to stretch out its hand; and at the same time it seems to us that we are doing it a favour by giving it the alms, whereas in truth we are poisoning it already at the moment when we tell it for the first time to stretch out its hand for alms. We must not allow this dangerous step; we must fight against this tactic, against this danger in the situation.
We have seen that in Będzin alone the Kimcha [Passover flour] campaign this year distributed support to 300 families more than last year; that means that we are beginning to treat this number of people as fresh "respectable" beggars, who in the course of time are brought to the state of professional beggars. And this we must not allow; this stain of shame, which already occupies among us quite a respectable place — in fact already too large a one — must be fought, so that it does not grow and consequently does not darken the life of honest, oppressed citizens.
We know of a large number of Jewish workers who are not registered at all, and many times we have had occasion to hear that they do not register at the magistrate [town hall] as unemployed, and therefore we do not say so; and it is not only in official circles that our working elements are looked upon with little attention — we ourselves do not see them, the workers; they themselves do not regard themselves as workers. A terrible disorder reigns in this field; nobody takes care that this branch be cultivated and that the working element should not be regarded as beggars as soon as [?] it loses its daily bread. This must on no account be allowed: such demoralisation corrupts the soul, the spirit of the hungry person who is used to living from his work, from his hard, toilsome labour.
The magistrates in Zagłębie distribute every month larger and smaller sums of money and foodstuffs as support for unemployed families. Do Jewish workers also benefit from this? Jewish unemployed? Is anyone concerned that they too should for once be allotted a quota of work? After all, we too are citizens of the country, and our unemployed too have civil rights, so that they too, as unemployed, must enjoy the same rights that their Christian fellows enjoy; and if they do not enjoy them, if they are wronged, then representatives must be found who will demand the rights due to the hungry people, at a time when they find themselves in a bitter situation and have no possibility of providing for their wives and children.
If in official and semi-official circles it is not known, or people do not want to know, that there are unemployed people among us, then one must come and prove it to them, and then one can demand and insist that these elements be supported on the same scale as their Christian fellows. We also have a large number of clerks and office people who are in a very sad state; can these categories of people be left like that, at the mercy of God, as if everything were in the best of order? Can the people remain indifferent to this mass of human beings, whose situation becomes more serious and harder from day to day? And somehow it does not look as if the question could be solved so quickly; therefore one must seek a way out which could radically solve this serious question that so poisons the air of our little home world.
It must not be allowed that the greater part of the people should be brought down to the level of beggars only because a crisis has set in in the country. We must save ourselves, and we must save those who can still be saved.
We must not forget one thing: that in Poland the middle class has almost ceased to exist, and in the best case it finds it very hard to exist, so that it keeps on falling, because it has nothing to hold on to; there is no longer, as there once was, anything to lean on. The system is such that every citizen must help bear the expenses of the state, so that whoever merely does not take, whoever merely does not stretch out his hand for alms — he must give; and the assessment is so heavy, the tax screw presses the middle class so hard, that it has no strength left to draw breath as soon as the smallest change occurs. Therefore we need not be ashamed to show the government our whole bit of poverty and abasement. One must show it the great mass of former taxpayers and established merchants, loyal citizens, who now drag themselves from door to door as common beggars; we need not be ashamed to show what Jewish fortunes look like. We must show the government our poverty in all its greatness and "splendour".
One must seek means by which the mass of people wandering about without employment may be saved from ruin; we must not let them come to the sad state of stretching out their hands for alms, because that poisons their present and their future — for as soon as workers grow used to stretching out their hands, they will, so to speak, take off the cap of shame, and lo, afterwards they [printed "zi"] will no longer want to take up work. This we must bear in mind, and this one must always remember well: we must not help to make a beggar out of a citizen — and this is what we ought to tell the government. It does no good to a country when citizens who are useful are turned into professional beggars, who are a plague for the state and a burden for the population.
Better that a fund be created which would make it possible to maintain impoverished people in a time of crisis, at a time when hands have no employment, than to make of a useful element a helpless creature that will never again rise up in a resurrection of the dead.
If it is already too late and we have not managed to save people so that they remain standing on their feet, if they have fallen out of the arena and are no longer found on the civic rolls, if they no longer have the possibility of fulfilling their civic duties — then we must nevertheless not bring them down to a further, more terrible level, the level of beggars. If it is already late and the people cannot be brought back up to their former height, if they have no possibility of getting back their professional work, then one must see to it that they get the possibility of living in a dignified way until the crisis period has passed.
The Jewish representation must show the government in what state the Jewish citizens find themselves, and that they must be protected from falling into the abyss of professional beggary.
Existence and decline — if we do not take stock now, if we do not demand that the government come to our aid in the present distress, a large number of useful, industrious elements will be turned into a camp of beggars, and on top of that into sick, helpless people with whom nobody will any longer be able to cope.
It will be quite different, however, if this impoverished mass of people, suffering from the crisis, is protected from falling into the abyss of helplessness and thus from having to lose its balance. Then, at the first moment that a better time appears, they will again become useful, industrious people, healthy citizens of the country, and each will again find his employment, his work, his existence.
Y. Sh.
Rent Money

[Poland — economy; rents; article.] Every few weeks we are blessed with the glad tidings that any moment now the rent is going to be raised.
The country has barely forgotten the uproar caused by the project of a 72-percent increase in rent, and now — a new uproar: for every pre-war hundred roubles one will pay — 45 zł.
We wish to believe that this project too will end the same way as all the projects so far, and that the rent will for the time being remain at the same level as until now; for at a moment when a state puts out the slogan "lower the prices", cuts the salaries of its officials, and the taxes flow only weakly into the state treasury because there is no money, one cannot suddenly come, in the middle of all this, and raise the rent.
Certainly the present rent is much lower than before the war, and certainly the valuation of 2.66 zł. for 1 rouble is a very low valuation. But the earnings of the population are also much lower now than before the war. It is hard and bitter for the impoverished citizen in Poland to pay even the present rent.
It therefore simply makes no sense that this project should have any foundation whatsoever.
If [?] the building fund needs money to build new houses — the government must look for other means for that. The citizen's pocket has long been full of holes, and those who think that one can still draw out of this perforated pocket the large cash reserves for the building campaign will be bitterly disappointed. There will be no money; in the present hard time of crisis, when the towns are full of artisans without a livelihood, bankrupt merchants and unemployed workers, nobody will be able to pay still more rent than is paid now. It will only bring an abundance of work for the courts, a flood of... evictions, and the need to set aside budget items for building barracks for the camps of the evicted.
That is the only thing such a project can bring with it. It is therefore impossible to believe that the government should at the present moment embark on such paths...
— Ps.
The "Agudah" in Power — A dream which, if it came true, would be woe and alas for all Jews
When Spring Awakes...

Pini Ba'al Lashon.
When spring awakes, a great pity awakes in me for our little Jewish children.
What do they know, the little Jewish children here, of spring, and of what spring brings with it?
What do they see, what do they hear, and what do they know of the feelings that spring awakens?
Their young days and years pass by workaday and dry. Their young souls feel no festiveness. Their young hearts do not flutter with exaltation.
Their young ears do not hear the footsteps of the approaching holiday, their little noses do not smell its sweet scent. Their little eyes do not see its holy beauty.
Born in a city of stone, raised between stone walls, playing away their time on stone ground, taught in a petrified environment — what notion can they have of spring?
My heart, my heart is wrung with pity for the little Jewish children!
* * *
How dear and how sweet this time once was for us in our shtetl!
The heder and the home and the street were bewitched a whole month ahead by the coming spring.
* * *
Could we have imagined "Shavuot" without its idyllic "Ruth"? "Sukkot" without its philosophical "Kohelet"? And above all "Pesach" without its spring-scented "Song of Songs"?
How strongly we felt, and how deeply we understood, its special song.
And in what symbols every song clothed itself before our childish eyes in our shtetl.
For in the shtetl everything bore the Jewish stamp; everything was Jewish through and through.
The earth, the sky, the river, the little trees, the little houses, the little shops, the stalls in the market and even the goats — all of it was truly Jewish, a hundred per cent our own!
Not to speak of the home and the heder and the synagogue — they were surely "all holy".
Every day of the week had its own particular Jewish song, its own particular Jewish flavour, its own special Jewish charm.
Not to speak of the Sabbaths and festivals — surely and surely.
The Sabbath you could actually see lying on the little roofs of the houses, on the leaves of the little trees; earth, sky, beast and cattle — all said that it was Sabbath in God's world.
The festival you could actually see floating about in every corner, at every step. You saw and felt with all your senses how the festival arrives and spreads itself out broadly, generously, regally in the shtetl.
* * *
Spring in God's world.
The thick, heavy quilt of ice that covered the river all winter has broken, melted and gone off to distant places.
The running, freed waters of the river sing wild, merry tunes, greeting the blue sky they had not looked upon for so long.
Trees blossom, birds hop, dance, twitter.
Little Jewish children run about the lanes, and with ringing little voices and beaming little faces they greet every breath of the warm little breezes.
Jews throw off their heavy winter garments, let the skirts of their green kapotes hang free, and float about like newborn angels.
Little Jewish houses fling open their sealed windows and draw in fresh air.
One feels how the "Song of Songs" floats over the shtetl and sings of itself: "The winter is past, the rain is over, the sprouts have been seen, the time of the singing bird has come and the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land; come, my friend, into the field, and let us spend our time in love"...
And one feels palpably how the holy love of man, of God and of His world fills every heart, great and small...
Spring! The festival of spring!
* * *
And when spring awakes, I am wont to this very day, out of habit, to slip out and take a look at our Jewish street here and at our little Jewish children; I look at them both and want to see whether they feel even a hundredth part of what we once felt, once in the shtetl — and my heart is wrung.
The street is not "ours" and the children are not "ours"!
Everything so petrified, so wooden, so mechanised[?]; everything so contorted in imitation, so artificial, theatrical, vaudeville-like — even when one tries to do it.
Not a trace of that naturalness, that heartiness, that was there once upon a time in our shtetl.
And how strongly the heart longs and is drawn to those times, when everything with us was our own, original, natural!
* * *
When spring awakes, a great pity awakes in me for our little Jewish children.
What do they know of all our experiences of long ago?
So let us at least refresh them with a little of our spring memories. — —
What a Beast!

(A short feuilleton)
I do not mean here, God forbid, a simple beast with a shrivelled udder — like a dried-up penkher[?] that stands all winter in the stable chewing the cud in vain and for nothing, looking at everyone with its bovine eyes, from which it shows forth: don't judge me, I am neutral!
No, not her do I mean, but the Spanish emperor Alfonso the 13th.
A true beast, I tell you! Grabbed and ran. Who chased him, who? Spent a whole life as an emperor and didn't learn a penny's worth of sense. Such, it seems, is the fate of all emperors: they remain fools to the last minute.
Actually the people did not even demand any freedom; they wanted only a republic. Well, so what? Some find, a republic! Some news in town! Is there anything here to be afraid of? On the contrary — you want a republic? Here you are!
I, you see, in his place would have acted differently. During the biggest demonstration I would have gone out onto the balcony of the imperial palace, bowed politely and spoken thus:
My dear and beloved people! Although I am the anointed emissary of God, I am no cruel man, and I will do you no harm. You want a republic? I am ready this very minute to decree elections, true five-adjective elections to parliament. Long live the republic, then! Long live republican Spain!
Ah, what joy there would have been throughout the land! They would at once have lifted me onto their hands, carried me with great enthusiasm through the streets of Madrid and shouted: King Alfonso is dead! Long live President Alfonso! For what do you think? Who would have become president if not I, if the elections had been held under my supervision?...
You think that in order to rule one must necessarily have a crown? On the contrary, the crown only gets in the way like a superfluous thing; you can't make a move, can't move your hands.
In general it is not at all modern today to rule in a crown. A present-day ruler likes his head to be free, not entangled in old bygone rags[?]. One must change laws, outdated paragraphs of the constitution, one must... who knows what one must do to be a true ruler of a true republic.
That is how I would have behaved, and everything would have been fine and dandy. But the Spanish emperor is not I but Alfonso, so he grabbed and ran, the devil take him!
He was a beast, and he remained a beast!
S. Małachow.
1 percent turnover tax for wholesale merchants who keep no commercial books

[Economy — taxes.] As we are informed by the Merchants' Association, the Ministry of Finance, thanks to the many efforts of the Centrala, on the 27th of March of this year signed a circular 2554/4/31 L. A. U. to the fiscal chambers (izby skarbowe) on granting a 1 percent turnover tax for the year 1930 to the wholesale merchants who keep no commercial books.
According to the above-mentioned circular the assessment must be made at the rate of 2 per cent. The firms concerned must, however, by the 15th of May 1931 submit individual requests to be granted 1 per cent.
The reduced rate may be applied to merchants of the 1st and 2nd category under the following conditions:
1) If the enterprise submitted a turnover declaration (zeznanie) on time (15 February — "luty").
2) If the turnover stated in the declaration is not too low in relation to the assessment of the assessment commission.
3) If [the figures] established by the assessment commission correspond to the actual circumstances.
4) If the enterprise does not trade in luxury goods or in foreign goods.
5) If the wholesale character of the enterprise is duly proven.
6) If the existence of the business would be endangered [?] were the tax to amount to 2 percent.
Oneg Shabbat

[Religion — Oneg Shabbat.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the weekly portion of this week
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Emor
a) "For his kin, that is near unto him" (21:2)
With relatives one gets on like this — well for a long time — when they live far away. Joseph said to his brothers "And ye shall dwell in the land of Goshen and ye shall be near unto me": if you live somewhere in Goshen, we will be close; but if we live together, it is rare that relatives should then truly be close...
Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany (Shem mi-Shimron [sic]).
b) "Neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard" (21:5)
"This people have I formed for Myself, they shall tell My praise" (Isaiah 43)
A rabbi once said in a moral sermon, against those who shave their beards: a man can dye in all sorts of colours, but [?] from black to white — that only God can, Who turns a man's black hair white, grey... That is God's glory. And God's glory is recognised most clearly in the beard, because everyone recognises that the man had a black beard at first and now already a grey one. And that "My praise", this glory of God — "yesapru" — they shave it right off [pun: yesapru / misparayim, scissors]...
Divrei Tokhehah.
c) "They shall not make baldness upon their head" (ibid.)
The author of "Lahmei Todah" once met a couple of hooligans (łobuzy), who bared their heads to spite him. He says to them: You do well. Ezra said "For our iniquities are increased over our head" — that means the sins are above the head. And the verse says "He that covereth his transgressions shall not prosper" — whoever covers the sins does not prosper; and sins are above the head after all, so you do not cover them...
d) "Seven complete sabbaths shall there be" (23:15)
He who accomplishes something in his life, whose days do not pass away with nothing — he possesses his accumulated days; they have weight, value. Whereas he who lives with the moment and lives it away, is like one who lends another a hundred gulden and the other repays him in gulden, one gulden a day. It means that for his debt he only receives a single gulden, because one gulden never sees the next... So too such [?] a man lives only a moment, for he lives only with the moment, and one moment does not join with the next in him... With the righteous man, however, the days are "complete" —
Ohel Yaakov.
e) "And when ye reap the harvest of your land" (23:22)
According to the sense of the verse it could have been written in the singular: "u-ve-kotsrekha".
But the verse says this: in truth it is "the harvest of your land" — the land belongs to everyone; only the rich man holds the poor man's share. Therefore do give the poor man his share, "thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger" — it is his share, after all, which by chance fell to you...
Torat Moshe.
f) "And ye shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month" (23:32)
Why does the verse express the commandment of eating on the eve of Yom Kippur in the language of fasting?
Because if the Torah simply said "on the ninth of the month ye shall eat", a commandment to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur — who knows what would have happened; would there even be a minyan for Kol Nidrei? People would drink and get drunk like nobody's business — a trifle? The Torah commands eating and drinking... Therefore the commandment of eating is expressed in the language of fasting, meaning: eat only in such a way that it may be called fasting...
R' Yaakov Kranz [the Maggid of Dubno].
Haftarah
g) "And when they go forth into the outer court" (Ezekiel 44:5 [?])
"And when they go forth into the outer court, to the people" — the leader who goes out to the people — "they shall put on other garments" — must take care not to be swept along with the current, not to fall into the abyss, while bending down to the valley of the masses...
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
Avot
h) "Who is rich? — He who rejoices in his portion" (4:1)
Ben Zoma infers that the verse "the labour of thy hands" speaks of one who rejoices in his portion. Perhaps the verse means a real rich man who actually has the coin, and is not merely content with his lot? —
Because it is said there "happy shalt thou be in this world", and who — who [?] are truly rich are seldom happy. Happy is only he who rejoices in his portion...
Yarim Moshe.
"Despise not any man" (4:3)
A characteristic literal translation of it from the book "Avodat Yisrael" by the Maggid of Kozienice:
"Despise not any man" — you shall shame no one, even ignoramuses and inferior people, even Jewish wicked men, God save us...
* * *
Rav Eizikl of Komarno writes in "Zohar Hai" [?] (portion Vayechi):
"Even about the utterly wicked, if only they are called Jews, one may not speak, and he thereby grieves the Shekhinah"...
(Yes, for the authors of Paragraph 20, Dr. Hirsch's teaching is more authoritative than R' Eizikl of Komarno's — the compiler.)
i) "There is nothing that has not its place" (4:3)
Every man has his makom, his place. So why is it so crowded among us that one pushes the other? — because everyone grabs his fellow's place.
But when we were in the Land of Israel, at home, everyone had his place. "No man said: the place is too narrow for me" — nobody needed to push his fellow —
Rabbi A. Y. of Sadhora [Sadigura] [?].

The Election Campaign.
(A sort of leading article [?])
For corns ["hen's eyes"] you get an ointment; better still is to soak them and cut them out.
For toothache it is good to apply a fig with pepper. The most radical remedy is the dentist's pliers.
"Meridn" [?] is an illness just like all other illnesses. Whoever suffers from such an ailment must turn to a doctor of philosophy.
To the reader:
Here there was actually supposed to be an election article, but as soon as I dipped my pen I remembered the number of candidate lists — so I started talking about... "meridn".
May First.

[The Kokh-lefl — satirical poem; May Day.]
May First.
The First of May is celebrated
full of love, full of fervour,
and in general the holiday's eve
was really fiery...
Imposing it was
that smoke went rising;
one drawback — that a flag
also has a stick to it...
Flags are drawn up to the sky
where the sun warms and shines,
but a stick has a nature:
it doesn't hate a shoulder at all...
—o—
Appeal for May First.
Gentlemen! Proletarians of all shtiblekh [Hasidic prayer-rooms], unite!
All our party comrades are called upon today, Friday, the 1st of May, to throw down work.
Every party member must today, until after Kabbalat Shabbat, wear a red "patshile" [?] in the lowest pocket of the quilted kapotes. At 8 o'clock in the morning every member must go to immerse in the old municipal mikveh.
Tomorrow, Shabbat, a festive Shalosh Seudos academy will be held at the premises of the "Agudah".
With proletarian greetings — the workers' party "Poalei Emunei Yisrael" in Będzin.
An 'All-Highest' Manifesto of the Newly Founded Non-Party Economic Bloc to the Whole of Sosnowiec Jewry.

[The Kokh-lefl — satire; Sosnowiec, kehilla elections.]
To all the 'etatized' [?] little Jews of Sosnowiec under the "20th paragraph", and to the subservient citizens [obywatele] of New and Old Sosnowiec.
During the election blazes for the Sejm and the Senate we kept silent. As the Scandinavian poet Dr. Oybnkroyt says (naturally in German): "When the rallies [wiece] speak, the dozory [kehilla board members] are silent."
A large part of the patented parnasim and table-sitters are "bar-mens" [?]; they cannot open their mouths.
The kehilla up to now has had the face of a "good place" [euphemism for a cemetery], where many Jewish matters were buried under the cannonade of the Passover eggs...
The true representatives, the only ones who stand on guard that Jews should do their "right", whose whole life is — to "purify" [metaher, ritually wash the dead] Jews — these people must seize the premises at Czysta Street No. 3...
Down with the old, worn-out generals!
Long live the recruits [nowobrańcy] of the Non-Party Economic Bloc for the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec.
Submitted by Honig-Fojgel.
Jewish Women and Young Ladies of the Female Sex, Unite!

[The Kokh-lefl — satire; women's vote in the kehilla.]
Esteemed lady friends [Szanowne przyjaciółki]!
An extraordinary swinishness [nadzwyczajne świństwo] has occurred in the women's street. Freely and frankly our feminine honour has been robbed; without pardon the disgusting [wstrętne] men have betrayed [zdradzili] us and taken the right to vote away from us; the "obradniashes" [?] have shut our mouths in the kehilla elections. They have plundered [zrabowali] from us the only weapon we possess —
— Enough talk!
We women must prove that we and only we are the living nerve of society, that without us there is no wedding. We must get into the gmina [community] and "clean out" the rust that has been eaten into every corner for years; the entire housekeeping must pass into our hands.
First of all we shall take care of the hospital system. The clinic that exists at the "Linas ha-Kholim" is inadequate, and a grandiose lying-in [maternity] clinic must be built, with all comforts [wygody] for women who give birth [?].
We must demand a revision of the housing decree, so that sub-tenants [sublokatorzy] receive "autonomous rights" and have a "voice" [głos] in the housekeeping.
The outdated khupe-vekidushin decree must be reformed so that the khupe and kidushin take place only after the wedding.
Women [kobiety] and young ladies! If we hold together in a "closed circle" [zamknięte kółko] we can count [liczyć] on full success [pełne powodzenie].
In the name of the General Women's Election Committee for the kehilla elections in Zagłębie.
Honig-Fojgel.
Everyone Grabs His Bundle.

[The Kokh-lefl — satire; list numbers in the kehilla elections.]
When the candidate lists were submitted, every party and non-party little shop [kreml] had a passionate craving for its little number.
In this field a clever game of chess took place, in which the participants came out vanquished and victorious.
Here, for example, the Right "Poalei Zion" yearned for its darling, had birth pangs, and hoped to get the "little six", but the Left put out a "little foot" [tripped it up] and what was born was
— a "little seven"...
Therefore the "Agudah" and the "Poalim" received the appropriate numbers. Here, for example, the "Agudah" was granted number 13, the number of the "holy" Franeitis [?] — a distant family, admittedly, but the thoughts are similar...
The "Poalim" too received the right kashering number; this number is very popular among the Jewish masses, who used to be told to kasher [their vessels] and go to the New Market number...
Should I Vote...

[The Kokh-lefl — satirical song; kehilla elections.]
(A parody [shtraikhe] of the folk song "Zol ikh zayn a rov" ["Should I Be a Rabbi"]).
Should I vote for the "Agudah"?
— I don't go to the mikveh.
Perhaps for the Zionists, then?
— I don't sing "Hatikvah".
At the meeting they meet and meet,
and the lists multiply,
and platforms take form,
— agitators feed me
with dry straw,
oy oy, oy oy.
———
Should I vote for the "Hitahdut"?
— I'm no intelligent [intellectual].
Perhaps for Poalei Zion?
— I haven't got a shlumper [slattern].
At the meeting they meet and meet,
and the lists multiply,
and platforms take form,
— agitators feed me
with dry straw,
oy oy, oy oy.

Kehilla Elections.

[The Kokh-lefl — satirical poems and notice; kehilla elections, spring.]
Kehilla Elections.
Off you go to vote, dear brother,
don't be a donkey, don't be a little horse,
put on a tallis-katan
and let yourself grow a little beard.
A voter in the kehilla must
have a dose [dawka] of Jewishness,
and a little beard he must have —
even if only a goat's [koza] little beard...
—o—
To All Comrades of the "Bund" and Left Poalei Zion
We hereby inform you [moyser modie] that today, Friday, Pesach Sheni, each of our comrades who await a redemption for mankind should — make kiddush and say "zman kheyruseynu" ["the season of our freedom"]...
(District committee of the "Bund" and Left P[oalei] Z[ion]).
[The Hebrew words are spelled here in the Yiddishist phonetic orthography.]

Spring Is Already Here
Spring is already right here,
with the fresh little breezes:
it already smells of "wiśniówka" [cherry liqueur]
with the lovely little dachas...
Spring is already right here,
it comes with grief and anger:
the old lament begins —
where should the wife travel? —
to Zakopane or to Krynica,
sea or dry land? —
and if you say a word to her,
at once there flies: "Robber! Villain!"...
(and sometimes something else flies too...)

The Vanished Daughter (5)

The Vanished Daughter. An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World. By Elżbieta Garin. (5)

— A little vodka, Janek, and pour her a cup of hot coffee; it may be black...
Some ten minutes later all three of them were already sitting at the big table, put together [printed "zizamen-", = tsuzamen-] from oak boards, around which the forest robbers of a vanished generation had celebrated their wild orgies a hundred years ago... and they ate their poor midday meal of potatoes, ham, black bread and black coffee; only Lala had white rolls, eggs and even a small bottle of sour cream (smetana), which Janek had stolen for her from his mother's larder.
Lala was still deathly pale, and her delicate little hands trembled as in a fever; outwardly, however, she was calm, with the calm of a person who sees no way out of the hopeless tangle into which he has twisted himself, and leaves it entirely to others to untangle him.
— I say the best thing for you would be to leave this place this very day and cross the border into Hungary; you have money enough... You'll be able to buy a horse and a cart, and Lala will look like a real young "góral" [Podhale highlander] in my younger brother's clothes, said Janek, peeling a hot potato and sprinkling on it the coarse salt he had brought along.
— But Lala is so weak... If she could at least rest one more day... said Staszek softly, and exchanged a stealthy glance with Janek.
— Yes, why not, then? [printed "nishtz"] the other said ironically — wait, really, a couple of days or even two... By then your friend Fritz, her brother, will arrive... Her father has telegraphed him... He certainly won't hesitate long; his [printed "zeyneb", = zeyner] first visit will be here... to this place where the three of us — he, you and I — spent so many happy hours in our childhood, knowing that none of the parents would ever poke their nose in here...
— No, Staszek, no! Lala clutched at her beloved in terror, — we must go from here now... I don't want to stay here one minute longer.
And that was the most incomprehensible thing of all: for if there was one person in the world of whose love Lala was surer than of anything, if there was one person whom she loved as only a sister can love an only brother, it was Fritz...
All the terrors with which the two young mountain men had frightened her did not exist where her brother was concerned. A student at the medical faculty in Vienna, Fritz Rapaport was due to finish as a doctor in about a year; a free-thinker like their mother and her family, he had nonetheless in recent years — thanks to the incitement, persecutions and attacks of fellows like his former friend Staszek and his kind — become nationally minded and an ardent Zionist. But she knew well that not only would he not go along with the "base acts", as she called it, but she was sure that he would protect her with all his strength, even if it were against his respected and beloved parents... And yet she feared meeting him more than all the others... Perhaps it was because the man for whose sake she had forgotten her parents and her people was Staszek Makarga, the former friend and present mortal enemy of her brother, with whom he had fought to the death when Staszek was the leader of the hooligan students and her brother of the Jews.
But who can look into the depths of a person's heart and understand what goes on there, especially when it is a woman's heart.
Even Lala herself did not understand it; all she knew was that she was ready for anything, ready to make any sacrifice, to endure any pain, only not to meet and not to have to look her ardently beloved brother in the eyes...
And from that minute she obeyed what she was told and went where Staszek wanted... She was like wax in his hands, and he himself often wondered that she did not protest.

The General Meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki"

[Będzin — economy and trade; bank.] In the premises of "Beit Yaakov", under the chairmanship of Mr S. Y. Ryński, the annual general meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki" (Merchants' Bank) took place.
Also taking part in the meeting was the auditor, Mr Szaszkes, who said in his report on the audit that the bank is run in the best of order and deserves the confidence of the members.

3 bank meetings in one day

[Sosnowiec — Jewish banks.] Last Sunday [26 April 1931] three meetings of local Jewish banks took place in Sosnowiec.
The course of the meetings was:
In the "Mutual Credit Society".
The meeting of the bank took place at Targowa 21, with 70 members present. The president of the council, Mr. S. M. Tencer, opened the meeting and handed over the chair to Mr. Marek Rajcher. In the presidium: Messrs. J. Tobiasz and H. Giterman.
The report on the activity was given by the president, Mr. L. Zendel, who gave a survey of the present critical situation and the hard conditions of the merchants, and yet — says Mr. Zendel — the management, thanks to its activity, has ensured that the bank has not [lost] even one per cent of the 40 thousand zł. of discounted bills.
After hearing the report of the audit, which was carried out by a delegate of the Ministry of Finance, the management received the absolutorium [discharge].
The profit amounting to 1,700 zł. is booked as "reserve capital".
The budget for 1931 is reduced to 32 thousand zł. (formerly 45).
After it was determined that a member may receive up to 10,000 zł. of credit, the existing management and council members were confirmed by acclamation.
In the "Kasa Dyskontowa".
In its own premises at Mańdżewska[?] 12 the annual general meeting of the bank under the name "Kasa Dyskontowa" was held at the same time.
With 60 members present the meeting was opened by the president of the council, Mr. Nachum Kahn, and Mr. Bernard Rechnic (head of the "Kasa Society" in Dąbrowa) was invited to chair it; he invited into the presidium Messrs. Naftali Besser (Katowice) and parnas[?] L. Puterka (Dąbrowa).
Reports on the founding and on the activity so far were given by the president of the management, Mr. S. N. Szalowicz, and the president of the council, Mr. N. Kahn. From the reports it can be seen that the bank has developed nicely, and thanks to the fact that Mr. Szalowicz stands at its head the bank has won[?] full[?] confidence even with the largest non-Jewish banks.
After the reports a motion was put forward that no change at all should take place in the composition of the management and council, but that the existing heads of the bank with the president Mr. Szalowicz should receive continued confidence. The motion was adopted with the small amendment: in place of Mr. Englard, Mr. N. Besser enters the council.
After acquainting itself with the good report of the government audit, the meeting confirmed the budget at a sum of 38 thousand zł.
It was also resolved to change the name of the bank: instead of "Kasa Dyskontowa" — to "Bank Dyskontowy".
"Bank for Artisans and Small Merchants".
The meeting of the bank took place in the premises of the "Kupcy" [Merchants' Association] in Kowalska Street. The president of the council, Dr. Herzman, opened the meeting and invited Mr. Ajzerowicz[?] as chairman.
Reports of the management and council were given by Messrs. Dr. Herzman and Mr. Fürstenberg.
After that Mr. Michelson, representative of the Central Co-operative Union, spoke; he declared that the bank is now on the road to recovery and is being placed on sound foundations. On the part of the Co-operative Union — says Mr. Michelson — help will also be given with the loan of 30 thousand zł. which the bank will receive in the near future.
After dealing with a number of formal points of the agenda it was resolved that every member must increase his share capital by 10 zł.
In place of those retiring from the council Messrs. Lejzerowicz, Langer and M. Stern were elected.

The jubilee tour of the "Vilna Troupe". Tonight the first performance.

[Będzin — theatre.]
The well-known "Vilna Troupe" celebrated, in the days at the end of the month of April, the 15th jubilee of its existence.
In honour of the jubilee, jubilee committees were formed in Białystok and also in other larger Jewish centres; in special appeals they turned to Jewish society to support those who 15 years ago laid the foundation for the artistic Yiddish theatre.
In the course of these 15 years the "Vilna Troupe" has written itself [sic] into the history of the Yiddish theatre, of Jewish art, of Jewish culture; therefore the jubilee of the "Vilna Troupe" is a holiday for the whole Jewish public, for the broadest Jewish popular masses, for the Jewish intelligentsia.
The "Vilna Troupe" comes to us for 3 performances; the repertoire consists of the finest European plays of our time, which [sic] also made a tremendous impression on the non-Jewish stage.
Tonight, Friday evening, "Di broyt mil" ("The Bread Mill" — "Der toyber", "The Deaf One"); Saturday night after the Sabbath "The Sacred Flame"; and Sunday evening "The Black Ghetto".
Here the performances of the "Vilna [sic, the word "Troupe" is missing]" have aroused special interest because, besides the permanent ensemble of such artistic forces as Miriam Orleska, Jakub Weislitz and Simcha Natan, the troupe has also been enriched with the well-known actors Lida Potocka, Chewel Buzgan, Jakub Szykarin [?] and others.
Director: the well-known Mr. Mazo.
An open letter to the Jewish public in Będzin.

[Będzin — education; the "Mizrachi" school; open letter.]
For years the "Mizrachi" school in Będzin was run without any public control whatever. The management was frivolous and reckless. Few took an interest in the financial situation; everything was "settled" by Mr. Buchweitz, and therefore after 11 years of existence the school was brought to ruin.
The management reached its culminating point in February [luty] '931, when the school treasury was left completely empty, while the overdue teachers' salaries reached about 8 thousand zł.; debts to the Insurance Institution [Zakł. Ubezp.] — 5 to 6 thousand zł.; "private" debts at usurious interest — 6 to 8 thousand zł.; other debts — several hundred złoty.
At the time when the school was threatened with collapse, Mr. Buchweitz travelled off to Merano and abandoned the school.
Following the advice of some of the parents, and not wishing to allow the school to be closed in the middle of the school year, the teachers formed a cooperative and within 2 months brought the treasury into order, called parents' meetings, improved the school administration, abolished the private discounting [of bills] from the school treasury, and, thanks to the removal of the intriguers, considerably raised the general level of the school.
Seeing that the teachers had put the school in order, Mr. Buchweitz and his discounters felt the urge to take over the reins again; but instead of going an honest way and paying the debts, they hit upon this invention: to stage a "pleite" [a fraudulent bankruptcy / putting assets out of creditors' reach]!
On the 17th of last month [p. ch.] Messrs. Buchweitz, Neumark, Moshe Lewin and the treasurer Moshe Openheim made a "deal", whereby one party "sold" the other the school inventory worth about 12 thousand zł. Now they are trying to repaint the signboard: instead of "Mizrachi" — "Yavneh" or something else, and... done...
But one thing Mr. P. L. Buchweitz has forgotten: that there exists a school authority [?], a court and, above all — public opinion.
Before the public we disclaim responsibility for the consequences to which the tactics of Mr. B. and others may lead.
The Teaching Staff

[Będzin — synagogue; yahrzeit society; Sosnowiec kehilla elections — appeal.]
On the initiative of a group of worshippers in the Będzin synagogue [shul], a society by the name [a. n.] of "Zecher Olam" ("Eternal Remembrance") has been founded.
The task of the society is to observe yahrzeits for childless deceased, to say Kaddish and to study Mishnayot and the like. The members of the society have also resolved to fulfil the wish of every family that wants to honour its departed parents or close relatives.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news.]
Imposing demonstration in Katowice in honour of the President of the State.
As is known, the President of the State, Mościcki [Ignacy Mościcki], stayed on Saturday in Katowice, where he took part in the 10th-anniversary jubilee of the Powstańcy [veterans of the Silesian uprisings] in Upper Silesia.
From early morning there was lively movement in all the streets; the city was splendidly decorated.
The movement grew stronger only in the afternoon hours, when thousands of people streamed in from the whole surrounding area, organisations with orchestras at their head, so that getting from one street to the next was no easy matter.
At 3 o'clock in the afternoon the President of the State arrived by special train, accompanied by the ministers Składkowski [Felicjan Sławoj Składkowski], Prystor [Aleksander Prystor], Hubicki [Stefan Hubicki], the marshals of the Sejm and other high-ranking guests, for whom a warm reception was arranged.
After the festive academy [ceremonial assembly] a march-past (defilada) took place, which lasted about 4 hours. The President of the State took the march-past for about 2 hours; afterwards he drove off to the Voivodeship [office], and Minister Składkowski represented him.
The march-past lasted until 9 in the evening. At about 11 a celebration took place on the market square, at which the President of the State and the commanders of the Powstańcy delivered speeches.
With the singing of the "Rota" the celebration was concluded.
