Small Remarks on Great Matters. / On Their Conscience.

It is already known to everyone, and we have written about it more than once, that Jewish Sosnowiec is building an old-age home — a place where a Jew in his later years can live out in peace the few years that remain to him in our sinful little world.
The building and its furnishing are almost finished; all in all, the splendid building still needs 10–15 thousand zł. One would think it would have been no great matter to raise this in a town with, kein ayin hara, so many Jews, especially from the largest part of them, who to this very day have given nothing. So at least one could have thought, so at the very least one could have understood; but quite often one deceives oneself when one thinks according to reason, when one reckons that logical understanding has the upper hand.
Unfortunately, to this day Jewish Sosnowiec still has very, very little interest in public questions; it still seems to them that social problems are either not yet ripe or altogether outlived; in any case they do not imagine that these are questions one must deal with now and that must be solved nowadays. For this reason the above-mentioned sum has not been realised, so that the managers of the institution have had to apply for a loan from a bank.
True, the loan is being taken at low interest and on good terms, but is it really fitting that, at a time when the institution is not yet even operating, one should already have to take loans? Are the Jews who can and should come to the institution's aid not ashamed? When they do not do it, thanks to whom [i.e. through whose fault] must one turn for loans to financial institutions? And if the better-situated Jews no longer want to lift a finger [lit. put their hand into cold water], if the whole matter does not interest them at all, could there not be found 2–3 Jews who would take over these few thousand gulden — on the first mortgage, let us say, and at interest for a certain time? Is it really so hard for rich Jews, who to this day stand aloof, to bring this small sacrifice for this necessary philanthropic institution? Must one really tear one's hand from one's heart in order to bring about such an important event? Should people not be ashamed to be so petty when it comes to communal matters, at a time when in private life, in grand style and gesture [?], large and significant sums play a role of the smallest importance? Why do these rich Jews not undertake to draw a parallel between their private life and, in contrast, their social apathy? Do these "philanthropists" ever [?] give themselves an account of their deeds? Do they at least understand that they sin against the Jewish collective? Against Jewish society? And if they do not, if they want to close their eyes to reality, to the living facts and phenomena, others must come and tell them so — let them at least know that they sin against the community and have thrown off every social responsibility, which ought to be borne upon their conscience.
Let Us Be Honest

The Będzin head of the Tax Office (Urząd Skarbowy) has declared that the turnover tax has been reduced this year by 40 per cent. He therefore appeals that people should not write so many appeals, because they make the course of normal work even harder; on the other hand, consideration will be given to those firms that will substantiate that they have actually been wronged — something to which the merchants' institutions will also be able to agree.
If it should really turn out to be so, it is to be welcomed. For we hold that, from the merchants' point of view, one should refrain from writing appeals as soon as one believes one has been wronged only to a minimal extent, since it is self-evident that nobody can be assessed very precisely; so that over a trifle, when one hardly feels it, it is not worth stopping and bringing the files up to the green table.
It is quite different, of course, when one has been wronged more severely and it even reaches the degree of being ruined. In that case it must not be passed over in silence; then one must defend oneself energetically and must not allow the injustice to remain an accomplished fact. It is understandable that one has to pay taxes, but under no circumstances may they be imposed on the citizen on the scale of ruination. One cannot, after all, demand that people pay an inflated tax just because by chance he was assessed too high, and those who sat at the assessment either did not know how high his turnover is, or did not listen at all to the member of the assessment commission.
It is precisely in such a case that the "Merchants' Association" must come and show and substantiate that its member was wronged in such-and-such a way, that he is not in a position to pay the tax imposed, that he did not make the assessed turnover.
But one thing we must remember: that we keep to the proper level, i.e. that in this matter we should not want to do anyone favours. The protection (patronage) system, which unfortunately has seized every field so terribly, should play no role whatsoever here. A member comes and says that he was wronged in the last tax assessment — he should be heard out, and he should prove it in black and white. If he is right, if an injustice was really done to him, he should be taken on for defence, one should fight for such a citizen, because one will have the awareness that here it is a matter of honesty and truth. In such a case a professional institution must have the power to carry its point; it must then not enter into any compromises at all, but must push its point through.
The situation presents itself quite differently, however, when the member merely wants his institution to do him a favour only because he is a member there. These are two different things: if the assessment is correct, he is obliged to pay the imposed tax, and the favour or the protection system must here be abolished entirely, because in that case the institution is disgraced and people will no longer have any trust in it; and this very trust, and the good name, and the responsibility must be guarded like the apple of one's eye.
Jewish society must guard its prestige. We must show our government that our institutions fully understand their tasks and guard honestly and conscientiously the interests of their member-citizens.
And therefore the secretariat must tell the member openly and honestly: "Reb Jew, your request is a futile one, we cannot present it, we hold that you were not wronged, and therefore go home in good health." Such a person must not be fooled and told that someone will already make efforts ("khlopotshen") on his behalf; on the contrary, one must be open with him, and prove to him and teach him that he is obliged to pay the tax, because he was correctly assessed.
All possible means must be used so that the protection system be uprooted. Those who are truly wronged must be defended, and let the government see that we want to pay taxes and that our authoritative institutions agree with this. We only do not want to be ruined, and our institutions and their representatives fight for an honest and conscientious existence.
When we guard ourselves, when we respect ourselves, and everything is done with proper calculation, we shall bring it about that in the governing circles our demands will be respected and valued.
Selekt.
What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Będzin and Strzemieszyce — satirical feuilleton, kehilla, community life.] Reported by Ben Amotz.
They Were Guarded...
A whole day they were guarded, their every step and stride followed, not an eye taken off them; people waited until the storm would pass, until the "tekufa day" [the day of the seasonal turning, held dangerous in folk belief] would go by and — — —
— "may the evil decree be annulled".
Like an evil whirlwind the news spread through the town [Będzin]; one passed it to the other "into the ear", that in the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" it had been reported that a Będzin girl, a child of a respectable householder's home, is taking a "ślub" [civil/church wedding — i.e. a mixed marriage] with...
Many fathers, and even more the indulgent mothers, took fright; their teeth chattered, and they thought to themselves:
— Maybe mine? After all, she too goes walking with Christian friends? Why have I kept silent all this time? Why did I not avoid that which I am now so afraid of? Oy, maybe it is actually mine?...
And telephone conversations — without end. They started with fashion, but every mother wanted to find out whether it was true, and "Czy pani też słyszała, że..." ["Have you also heard, madam, that..."]
— "Owszem, słyszałam, ale ja się nie boję, moja..." ["Indeed, I heard, but I am not afraid, mine..."]
— "Moja też nie, ale..." ["Mine neither, but..."]
That day the fathers forgot about their businesses, the mothers — about the household, for they had a greater task, a task — that their little daughters should not stumble...
— Oy, how they were guarded...
"Nistar" or "Nikhtar"?...
A fierce dispute has flared up among the worshippers in the Będzin synagogue. The fight is not over the dozors' [kehilla board members'] benches or other honours; it is a dispute for the sake of Heaven, a fight that must determine which editor of the mahzor is authoritative regarding the wording of the prayer.
The "outbreak" happened on the first Sabbath after Passover, at the moment when the cantor, reciting a piyyut, called out the word "nistar"; from all sides protests and an uproar were heard
— Nikhtar! Nikhtar!
The cantor, having before him the "Skarbowe mahzor", was not frightened by the uproar, but called out in a high octave:
— Nis-tar! N-i-s-t-a-r!...
After the prayers 2 sides formed, the "Nistarniks" and the "Nikhtarniks", between whom a "paper war" is being waged...
There is, however, in the synagogue also a neutral element, which complains: why does the rabbinate allow such quarrels, which bring so much disgrace upon the synagogue...
Why — argue the neutrals — should the rabbinate not declare which of the sides is to blame for the scandals that repeat themselves almost every Sabbath in the "small sanctuary"? Surely the matter of "nistar" or "nikhtar" is at least as important to the synagogue worshippers as the proclamations of "Fremd Reybekhts" [?]...
— Teyku [undecided]...
An "Important Campaign".
The three of us stood on the New Market [Nowy Rynek] and chatted.
— About what?
— About the kehilla elections; we went through the candidates who figure on the fourteen lists, recalled the activity of those who are already leaving, etc.
— "Jews, give money. I need a very necessary donation" — with this preamble we are interrupted by a young Będzin man, the owner of a shop on Sączewska [?] Street, who keeps repeating the words:
— "Give money, a great mitzvah"...
When the money-collector sees that we are still hesitating, he explains to us for what purpose he is collecting.
— There died — he says — a Jew, a very poor man; there is not even enough for shrouds.
— Well, and where is the gmina [the kehilla]? — we ask.
— Yes, the gmina; the house of the dead [the "meysim-shtibl"] always covered the burial needs at its own expense, but today the dozors no longer want to give anything.
— No subsidies, no pensions and
— no shrouds...
The crowd standing by does not refuse the "campaign". Whereupon one man, a shrewd Jew, remarks, saying:
— Give something to me too; perhaps it will already suffice to bury the old kehilla...
"Po polskiemu" ["In Polish"]...
A pity.
Truly a pity that the pillars [printed "zaln", apparently for "zayln"] of the assimilation of former days, the Dicksteins — Gostanzons [?] — did not live to see this; ah: had they been granted this in their lifetime, they would surely have died peacefully with the words:
— "This is my portion of all my toil"...
This idea came to me as I listened to the delegation from the neighbouring little town — Strzemieszyce.
And here is what they tell:
With us in Strzemieszyce an election of a rabbi is to take place on the 27th of this month. In response to the competition of the kehilla administration no fewer than 37 rabbis applied, a hint at the thirty-six righteous... But among those who are candidates for the rabbinical seat is also the son of the late local rabbi, who served the Strzemieszyce kehilla for 32 years.
The candidate. His [father's] successor is supported by almost the entire Jewish community, apart from a few who hold in their hands the "kehilla whip", which they crack in the air so that the whole cultured world should hear that Strzemieszyce must have
— a modern rabbi..
And how far "modernism" reaches among the dozors is proven by what happened these days.
The "modern" dozors in Strzemieszyce had the candidate, the rabbi's son, summoned to come to the kehilla office.
At the head sat the kehilla president, the hundred-percent Jew "of the Mosaic faith" ["wyznania mojżeszowego"], who began to examine the rabbi's son, the candidate..
— "Czy pan Zander będzie mógł spełniać funkcje rabinackie?" ["Will Mr. Zander be able to perform rabbinical functions?"]..
— Panie [Sir]... I can answer you in Polish, but...
— "Proszę mówić po polsku" ["Please speak Polish"]....
— I don't understand what is going on here — the frightened young man murmured — you all know me, you know who I am, I...
— "Zaprotokołować, że kandydat Zander nie mógł odpowiadać po polsku" ["Record in the minutes that candidate Zander could not answer in Polish"] — the president ordered the secretary.
The Jews of Strzemieszyce come to us with the complaint: we know — they say — that a rabbi had to have ordination from the great sages of Israel, but to sit an examination before a president who can speak Polish well — that is news for the Jewish world...
And we do indeed believe that "the whole cultured world" will celebrate the victory of the Strzemieszyce kehilla administration, which examines the rabbis
— "po polsku"!...
Do Have Patience...
The sun has come out of her "fur-case" [?] and she warms. The fields and trees are already covered with a green veil, and it is a delight in God's little world...
One place, however, is still "ashamed": the "square" [skwer] on Third of May Square [Plac 3 Maja] in Będzin still looks like an infertile island. Year in, year out, as soon as the first spring sun appeared, the place was planted with many colourful flowers and benches were set out on all sides, on which the tired strolling public sat down and enjoyed themselves...
This year the "Garden of Eden" was supposed to be tended only after the Third of May, but the deadline has passed and the drought on the spot continues.
— Oh well, is there a choice? We are already used to it; after all, the Minister of Commerce tells us to wait...
— So wait, do have patience; surely in the end the time will come when fruit will grow on the New Market...
What will they be left with?

(Our Talmud Torah leaders are making "economies", they are cutting... others they drive away, and they themselves do nothing.)
"A large number of parents, because of the crisis, wanted to enrol their children in the Talmud Torah, but their request was refused."
Such reports reach us from the impoverished Jewish population of Będzin, and not long ago we recorded them here in the columns of our newspaper, reckoning that the heads of the Talmud Torah would treat the matter a little more attentively and see to it that the question was resolved at least in part. But several weeks have gone by and nothing — nothing moves from its place; evidently the whole matter lies in their left sidelock [i.e. they could not care less]...
A rare thing, what luck our institutions have — institutions meant to educate the poorest children of the Jewish population, children who really ought to be torn out of the low, damp cellar and attic rooms, out of the narrow, dirty alleys, and have a fresh spirit of life breathed into them; to give them, the poor little Moishelekh and Shloimelekh, the chance to be educated and to grow up on normal foundations, so that a new generation of productive people and healthy citizens may be raised from them, who will bring benefit both to the Jewish people and to the country in which they live. Yet instead of heeding this necessity, which is so understandable and clear to every one of us, people close their eyes to the true reality, as if there were nothing here to think about, and leave everything to its fate.
And what else can one call the fact that precisely now, when the crisis has settled so firmly into the Jewish body and poor parents come to enrol their children, they are shown the door: there is no place for you, we have nowhere to put your children. Does anyone understand the heart of such a father or mother, who resolved to hand over "the apple of their eye" to the Talmud Torah, when even from there they must turn back empty-handed and have no one to teach their child Hebrew? Does anyone understand the pain, the psychology of these parents? And is it any wonder that their hearts grow faint, since they cannot afford to send their children to learn where it costs money? What is left for them to do in such a case? What can become of the children if they have to wander idle and empty-handed through the streets? Does this really not concern our Talmud Torah leaders at all? Does this painful public question not interest them in the least? Do they not know that the Talmud Torah is intended exclusively for these very children? And if a Talmud Torah will not care for them — who then will?
It would seem that educational institutions of this kind ought to belong to the whole town, they ought to be above party — and yet, what has become of these municipal houses of education? They have been turned into little shops and tiny party splinters, where one is afraid to open a window lest the bright sun appear there with its rays and the pure, innocent truth be revealed just as it is; and for this reason a way out was found: hush, quiet, just don't make any noise, close the windows, draw the curtains, so that no one may see what goes on inside; and if someone comes and asks what is going on in there, how things are, what it looks like — one must turn one's back on him and answer in an angry tone: what business is that of yours, what connection do you have with the institution, where we are the masters and which has been entrusted to us? Whereas in truth they have taken the monopoly for themselves and made of it a miniature object. The institution [printed "vinstitutsye"] has been crippled, the marrow has been drawn out of its bones, and dry bones are all that remain. So it is in Będzin, and it is no different in neighbouring Sosnowiec.
Not long ago Dr. Papuri [?] described to us here the state in which the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah finds itself: having a splendid building, it had the best chances of becoming a general Talmud Torah embracing all strata of the town's needy population; and nevertheless they managed to dismember that fine building and to make of it what we see before our eyes in such dreadful colours that, hearing it, one shudders at it all and wants to run as far as possible from the place.
Będzin has never had such a building and still does not have one to this day, but it has a plot, and more than once it also had prospects of enlarging the institution; a beginning was in fact made by our patron Mr. Fürstenberg, and in his time he promised to come to their aid substantially as soon as order would prevail and people would want to make of the institution what it ought to be — but that is exactly what frightened them. What he had given was, on the contrary, taken away. And for the future they told themselves: "neither your honey nor your sting", "don't be my uncle and don't sew me shoes". These plain words they began to fear like something evil, and then they bolted door and gate even more firmly, so that, God forbid, no one should have the chance to take a look at the mould that had grown so thick, and to touch it; and so they kept it, the mould, until... until they saw that no one was sniffing around there any more, and then, really cautiously, very cautiously, they began to open a little air-vent through which a tiny ray of sunlight might squeeze in — which was done under control; and when these "professors" saw that the Caesarean section [printed "ksezer-shnit"] had to be performed, they opened the whole window — and let the sun come in there, they said, with its life-giving rays and heal the rotted, mould-covered body; and after specialists and "surgeons" had established that the body could be saved only if nothing were hidden from those close to it, it was at long last decided to become "democrats" and to call a general meeting at which the institution would be handed over to the town.
But here a storm wind arose. The "Torah-faithful" saw that this was no joke, that someone really wanted to create a proper municipal Talmud Torah that might, God forbid, develop well and win a name for itself — and they began "tearing up graves" [i.e. raising hell]; they climbed on table and benches and, with the slogan "Jewishness must be saved", they saved it — and drove outside the camp those of whom they were so afraid: those who had the means and the will to make of the Talmud Torah what it ought to be, what a kehilla such as Będzin ought to have.
They drove out "the dangerous elements", and when they saw that they had prevailed, that they were now only among "their own", they were beside themselves with joy, felt as if in Satan's vineyard [?], and began to rule as though there were something to rule over. But revenge is a powerful morsel and does not see reality. They began to conduct a kind of autocracy, like Nicholas [the Tsar] in his day. First of all "economies" must be made: cut the melamdim's salaries ["pensyes"] and enrol as few pupils as possible, i.e. cut a challah off the "hamotzi". Whether the Talmud Torah takes on an ever worse character, whether nothing at all will remain even of the miniature, whether they stop [printed "oyfher"] paying the groszy paid until now — this concerns the "Torah-faithful saviours" little, as long as they have achieved what they wanted and have prevented the institution from being brought into proper condition.
But you do hold the power there — so see to it that you make of the institution what those you drove out, those who were so harmful and dangerous in your eyes, wanted to make of it. How is it that you may not make of the institution what those you chased away so wanted to make? Are they really hindering you from building up and running [?] the Talmud Torah? Since you had so much courage to drive those people out, you surely must have even more courage than those who wanted to create something — and follow their example.
Does your whole art really consist in being experts [?] at driving people away? First you drove away those who came to do something, afterwards you drive away the melamdim, and now it has come to the children. Once you have driven everyone away — what will you be left with? With whom will you build, and over what will you rule? Not to mention that you will turn the Talmud Torah itself into an everlasting ruin. On what road are you walking now with such confident steps and with so light a conscience.
— On the contrary, perhaps you could tell the town your perspectives, your calculation, your programme, your agenda.
R. Les.
It Has Finally Turned Warm.

[Poetry — rhymed feuilleton; Zagłębie, economic crisis.]
(Rhymes of the Day.)
It has finally turned warm,
and the sun shines as if new,
a mild breeze blows in the street,
warm spring — a sheer delight.
Yet our world has still
not been redeemed from winter:
take a rich man's heart, for instance —
frozen as in the hardest frost...
* * *
In the societies and associations
the books show in black and white
that winter has settled
there for good, firm and secure;
grass and flowers, man and beast
may rejoice in the spring —
but in all the institutions
it is constantly cold and dread!
* * *
A shopkeeper struggles with poverty,
sees not a grosz in cash —
can such a shopkeeper feel
that spring has come?
In drops a bailiff (executor),
(some small tax is owed there),
they carry his goods out —
a chill runs through his bones!
* * *
Old artisans sit
and long for the old years —
and hope for something better
has, thank God, long been lost,
and on top of that, to an examination
one must go, in old age —
and the artisan grows
colder than in the hardest frost!
* * *
Instead of love serenades
a young man sings dowry-songs —
when a father has a daughter,
he is cold in all his limbs;
* * *
A wave of redundancies
has swept over us here in Zagłębie —
whoever is left without work
is shaken by cold and fever!
* * *
The New Market is full of people,
the sun hands out warmth and light;
the crowd comes here to warm itself
not from well-being but from misery.
The air is fresh and warm by now,
the air can suffice for everyone —
but what good is that
when there is nothing to chew?!...
D-L.
This, That and the Kehilla Elections...

[Satirical feuilleton — kehilla elections; a barber's monologue.]
M. Mandelzon.
Once a week I have a tradition of bringing my overgrown jaw to the barbershop and handing it over to the barber, so he can take it into work. Yesterday I did so too, and on the way I calculated in my mind roughly how long I would have to wait with my jaw for my turn (otshered); but as it happened I found not a single customer in the shop, and the proprietor, on seeing me, received me with the politest politeness that only a barber (printed "friziyer") can manage:
— Moje uszanowanie dla pana! [My respects, sir!] Proszę bardzo! [Please!] Why are you standing on the threshold? There, you're already sitting down! You'll only have to wait a few... Przepraszam, [Excuse me,] zaraz [right away] I'll attend to you! Pan Józef siada! [Mr Józef is taking a seat!] — Maniek! Why are you standing like a golem? Quick, hand me a towel and make lather! How powoli [slowly] it moves! Just like the Magistrat paying out the Jewish subsidies... A thousand times I've taught him: when a customer comes, everything must be ready to hand, and he — jak byk [like an ox] — it's like talking to a communal functionary once he's already in his chair... Nowadays, proszę pana [if you please, sir], when a customer comes you must lather him natychmiast [immediately]; only then have you got somewhere with him, that he's yours; otherwise he may suddenly "pull a Nate-had-regrets" and run off, beard and all... Pytanie! [Of course!] When there's no "bash"[?], it comes down[?] to shaving at a loss of capital... Just recently I had a customer, and before I began lathering him he suddenly thought better of it — he would shave the day after tomorrow, at his cousin's pidyon ha-ben... Pan rozumie! [You understand, sir!] That's how goły [broke] they are today, the young men!
Zresztą [Anyway], what is there to say? When there are no groszy[?]... when the crisis... It pulls, you say? You have too delicate a skin. I have customers, proszę pana, with a hide like a pelt... such thick-skinned ones that you pull and pull and it doesn't bother them... Jak Boga kocham! [As I love God!] Those I like to rub down the mug (morda)... but nowadays with them too it's "dasik"[?]...
I had a customer, proszę pana, a young fellow who not long ago took a fat dowry; for the shave he gave me a "shmargal"[?], to jest wekselek [that is, a little promissory note], i po wszystkiem [and that was that] — and what do you think, did he pay it? Skąd? [Not a chance!] He is today goły jak święty turecki [naked as a Turkish saint]... W ogóle [In general], proszę pana, this is such a time that everyone is "goły"... You go to collect a debt — you come back goły; you want to borrow from a free-loan fund — they answer you that they are goły; your wife searches your pockets — it's agreed in advance that they're goły; what more do you need? Even in the banks it's goły today... Jak się mówi [As they say]: "Goel Yisrael" [Redeemer of Israel — pun on "goły"]... — all Jews are goły...
And worst of all, proszę pana, in our trade... it hangs by a hair... As if the crisis weren't enough, on top of our heads have been sent elections to the gmina [the kehilla]... A little scab, you say? No, proszę pana, it's a blister... a prawdziwy [real] blister... I won't touch it... Bądź pan pewny! [Rest assured, sir!] I'd have advised you the same...
You see, proszę pana, a barbershop on a summer's day? Empty as the cash-boxes of our institutions... And all because of what, do you think? All because of the gmina!... They say, niby to [supposedly], that only those who own a beard of their very own will be allowed to be dozór members [kehilla board]... na przykład [for example]: Agudah men and goats... Słowo daję! [Upon my word!] So people are growing beards, because everyone wants to be a dozór, przepraszam za wyrażenie [pardon the expression]... And it really seems to me, proszę pana, that I'll submit an offer that they take me onto the beard-commission, because such a znawca [expert] on beards doesn't exist! I'll know, proszę pana, which beard is a prawdziwa [genuine] one and which is not... Aha!
W ogóle, proszę pana, I must tell you that this business with the beards pleases me... moim zdaniem [in my opinion] they'll come in very handy in the gmina... Jak Boga kocham, only first one must... sprinkle them with eau de Cologne (kolońska)? Dobrze! [Fine!] It's not a good zapach [smell], you say?... Pan się myli! [You are mistaken, sir!] That's from the gmina... That's how it always is, proszę pana, at elections, and to the voters, proszę pana, the little candidates fawn with the sweetest little words, at every step and turn... Służę panu! [At your service, sir!] That's how masked they are! Maniek! Dobrze oczyścić pana! [Brush the gentleman down well!]... The powietrze [air] is very paskudne [foul] now in Kongresówka [Congress Poland]... I would advise you, proszę pana, to go abroad natychmiast [immediately] (printed "gatychmiast")... Niech pan mnie słucha! [Listen to me, sir!] You'll... Dziękuję panu! [Thank you, sir!] Do widzenia! [Goodbye!] Moje uszanowanie! [My respects!]
Money in Time of War and of Peace.

[Economy — Poland and the crisis; article.]
Our readers already know the opinion of the [Polish?] economist Senator Daniel Kras [so printed; further on "Gross"], who holds that Poland must and can rescue itself from the severe economic crisis through a peculiar kind of inflation, adapted to peacetime. Yesterday Senator Gross published another article on this subject, and whatever one's attitude to this question, it is in any case worth acquainting oneself with the author's very interesting conception and opinions.
We bring here the most important passages of his article: "Inflation in Time of War and Deflation in Time of Peace."
"In time of war," writes Senator Gross, "governments make use — to the greatest extent — of inflation and have no fear whatsoever of devaluation. One must ponder this problem, because now, in time of peace, out of fear of devaluation — although there is a necessary and urgent need — we nevertheless do not increase the means of circulation, but keep burdening ourselves with foreign loans. In time of war one does not look at the sum of gold and foreign currency held in the bank of issue; one prints and puts into circulation as much paper money as one needs, and with the help of paper money the government then runs its economy, buys food products and everything it can and must. Why then should one not be able now, in peacetime, to do the same; why do we not use such a means to build roads, railways, hospitals and the like? Why do we not now buy, in the same way, foodstuffs for the population, which could be employed in building up the country? After all, today we have far more products than in wartime; now the urban and rural population works and creates, whereas in wartime the population is at the front and the enemy destroys the country with its products. Why then are we afraid now to print and put into circulation such money as would be destined to create values and not to destroy them?
In wartime states can print [misprinted 'press'] money without limit. And why then should it now be limited? In Poland the state has been deprived altogether of the possibility of carrying out the most necessary public works.
To the question why in peacetime the state is not permitted to issue money for public works, the economists answer that in wartime there is no danger that people will come to exchange the banknotes — such a thing is suspended, and then the bank of issue needs no cover. After all, it does not exchange the banknotes for foreign currency. And because one cannot exchange, one observes in wartime the phenomenon that savings deposits in the banks grow at a record rate.
And what happens to our banknotes abroad? Why in wartime does the foreign money world [doubtful reading] not trade in the banknotes of a state engaged in war; why are there no speculators then? The reason is that, because private trade with foreign countries is stopped, there is no one there to sell the currency to.
It is different in peacetime: then there is private export of goods, and then speculation with money is possible. One knocks down the rate abroad, then transports the banknotes into the given country, and devaluation begins. Then one can stage orgies with the banknotes.
From all this it is clear that Poland has no choice here but to do something. Poland now finds itself in exactly the same situation as at the outbreak of a war. Poland must therefore resort to inflation and stop the exchange of banknotes within the country itself. But in order to guard against speculation abroad on the part of foreign moneyed interests and stock-exchange people, a state monopoly must be created for the exchange of goods with foreign countries; there must be an end to the private exporter, who is exploited by big industry and agricultural capitalists.
This monopoly must be handed over to a central institution representing all spheres of the population. This export-monopoly institution will have a public-law character, but it must not be a state-bureaucratic institution."
N.—
A Little Feuilleton. Floods.

[Będzin — feuilleton; satire on public life on the eve of the kehilla elections.] By Gur-Aryeh.
As long as the larger rivers were forged in thick, solid chains of ice, they lay there, the mighty giants, with clenched lips, quiet and calm. But no sooner had a warm little wind blown and the sun sent its hot rays down to the earth than these giants tore the ice-chains off themselves, stretched out their clumsy limbs and set off running helter-skelter ["hendum-pendum"], flooding as they went field and forest, village and town.
Lately the newspapers have been reporting to us about mass flooding in the Wilno and Grodno districts. The rivers there have burst their banks and drowned and swept away continually everything they found in their path. The devastation they have wrought is enormous. Hundreds of people have been left without a roof over their heads and without a piece of bread in their mouths; dozens have already drowned, etc., etc.
So I think to myself: how lucky we Będziners are! We laugh at the world. With us there is not a drop of such river water, not even for a cure. We can sleep peacefully. No water-flood threatens us.
Then I think again: perhaps it really would not have hurt for us to have such a "little Niemen" ["Niemandl"] around the town. With fish for the Sabbath we would then surely have been provided for. And a flood? No great matter. Once in a while, as a novelty ["novine"], a bit of flooding would not do any harm either.
In our public life a fairly large bundle of filth and dirt ["brud"] has piled up over the last few years. Especially now, on the eve of the kehilla elections, we have become rich in a goodly number of uninvited "benefactors" and "communal workers" of every sort; freshly baked "experts" and "connoisseurs" have settled like pesky [doubtful reading] flies on our sick social organism and are sucking out of it the last bit of blood it still possesses; new "politicians", just hatched from the egg. "Cultural workers" have set about with great relish making all kinds of experiments on our weak, dried-out body, and we must watch it all with our own eyes and keep silent.
What is needed, indeed, is a little "cleanup" ["otshiske"]. A little cleansing is as necessary to us now as life itself. It would therefore be no harm at all [printed "bein" — doubtful] if suddenly a flood came here — a flood that would wash and rinse thoroughly on all sides and free our public life from the various shady swindles that have pushed their way into it, from the nasty flies and microbes that gnaw at its body, and from the rest of the filth that has gathered in it over the course of the last years.
Such a little flood would do no harm to anyone.
Gur-Aryeh.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Behar-Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Behar-Bechukotai
—o—
a) "And thou shalt number seven sabbaths of years unto thee" (Lev. 25:8).
A beggar persuades himself that he possesses a hundred thousand, for he has begged together a hundred thousand... groszy; when he changes the sum into hundred-złoty notes, he has only ten banknotes.
So too man persuades himself that he is a full citizen of the world: he has more than twenty-five thousand days to live (seventy years)! Twenty-five thousand! But the Torah tells him: reckon the days as years, and the years as sabbatical cycles, and the sabbatical cycles as jubilees — and you will see, little man, that you do not have even one and a half jubilees to live; one and a half — not often... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
b) "Ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family."
"Ye shall return every man unto his possession" — when someone becomes rich, then "ye shall return every man unto his family": suddenly from all sides he acquires family and relatives who earlier, when he was a poor man, did not want to know him...
Similarly one interprets:
"Yet setteth He the needy on high from affliction" — if a poor man is helped out of poverty, then "and maketh him families like a flock" — suddenly he acquires families without measure... Alei Zayit.
—o—
c) "Ye shall not therefore oppress one another; but thou shalt fear thy God" (25:17).
1.
"Ye shall not wrong one another" — you shall not cheat your fellow with "thou shalt fear thy God", by pretending to be a God-fearing man... Milin Hadtin.
2.
"Ye shall not wrong one another" — even when the other is "your fellow", your colleague in fraud, a swindler like you — you may not cheat even such a one.. Bina Le'itim.
3.
A characteristic rule is laid down as halakha in "Hoshen Mishpat", siman 228, se'if 1, in the glosses of the Rema: whoever likes to fool himself may be fooled; the "ye shall not wrong" was not said about him.
—o—
d) "And if thy brother be waxen poor, then thou shalt relieve him" (25:38 [sic; should be 35]).
Two men are walking in a marshy area. They see a weak man walking nearby; he totters, and any moment now he will fall over. One says: let us go and lead the weak man out. His companion answers: but he has not fallen yet... And there he falls into the marsh. Still, they are human after all — they run up, drag him out of the marsh with great effort, carry him on their shoulders to a settlement, and there he has to be washed, cleaned and healed. Had they helped him while he was still standing on his feet, they would have saved themselves the work...
"And if thy brother be waxen poor" — when your friend begins to totter economically, "then thou shalt relieve him, that he may live with thee" — you should help him while he is still alive, when he needs only an injection, and not wait until he is already lying in the marsh. The relief work will then be much harder... Torat Moshe.
—o—
e) "Take thou no usury of him, or increase... that thy brother may live with thee" (25:36)
1.
When someone lends to his fellow at interest, the lender wants the days to advance as fast as possible, so that he may live to see the money back with the interest, and every day is to him like a year... The borrower, on the other hand, wants the days to drag on, to crawl as slowly as possible, and every month is to him like a day. "A month already, eh?"... Well, they do not live equally: to one a day is like a year, and to the other a year like a day... But if you take no interest, there will be "that thy brother may live with thee" — you will both live equally... Nahalei Dvash (before the Alshich [?]).
2.
As is well known, the Talmud says that whoever takes interest will not rise at the resurrection of the dead. Says the verse: take no interest, and there will be "that thy brother may live with thee" — you will both rise together at the resurrection of the dead... Nahal Eitan.
—o—
f) "And I will give peace in the land... neither shall the sword go through your land" (26:6)
The Mishnah says in Avot: "The sword comes into the world because of justice delayed and justice perverted." Wars come only because of the false judgments of the judges. Therefore, when "I will give peace in the land" and people will not go to law, there will be: "neither shall the sword go through your land"... Maharam Teomim.
—o—
Haftarah
g) "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron" (Jeremiah 16 [sic; should be 17]:1)
An iron, steel, durable pen is needed to write down the sins of the Jews. For an ordinary one would long ago have broken from using it too much... Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
Avot.
h) "He who says: what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours — this is the average trait. And some say: this is the trait of Sodom" (5:10)
Can it be that there should be such a difference of opinion between two Tannaim, that what to one is an average trait is to the other a trait of Sodom?
The meaning is this: "mine is mine and yours is yours" — you take care of your poor people and I will take care of my own close poor — that is an average trait. But when "some say" — when one merely says so, as a mere lame excuse — that is a trait of Sodom...
Alei Zayit.
—o—
i) "He who wants to give and wants others to give — is a pious man" (3 [?])
He who gives himself first, before "others give" — he wants to be an example — he is truly pious, beyond the letter of the law.
Yarum Moshe.
—o—
j) "The brazen-faced is for Gehenna... may it be Thy will that the Temple be rebuilt" (20)
"In the footsteps of the Messiah, insolence will increase"; says the Tanna: if there are brazen faces — well, "may it be Thy will that the Temple be rebuilt"; the Messiah may as well come already...
Benaot Barama.
Lag BaOmer in Jewish History

[History — Lag BaOmer.]
After the destruction of the Second Temple (the year 70 after Christ) by the idol-worshipping Romans, the latter were not content with the material destruction of the Jewish people; even "Yavneh and its sages" was too much for them. They strictly forbade keeping the Jewish faith or even studying the Torah of Moses, which speaks of one single God who cannot be grasped by the 5 human senses. The Jews, the motto of whose faith is "the God of these hates lewdness" [printed "shina zima"], could not get used to the thought that the dissolute, demoralised Romans should rule over them. It is enough to read the "Annals" (year-books) and the "Histories" of the greatest Roman historian, Tacitus (Cornelius Tacitus, who lived in the days of Emperor Hadrian [printed "Adrigus"], to be convinced that the orgies of debauchery which Sienkiewicz describes in his "Quo Vadis" are not exaggerated at all; there is a supposition that a large part of the Romans had simply become impotent and had to marry with Germans in order to secure the survival of the race.
When Hadrian [printed "Adrigus"] became emperor in Rome (Hadrian, who reigned from the year 117 to 138), the persecutions against the Jewish religion intensified, and the Jews decided to go out to fight against the Roman occupier. Soon great preparations were made for the uprising, and at its head stood Bar Kokhba, who in the last [?] year of the uprising (the year 135) was besieged with his armies for a whole year by the Roman legions in Betar near Jerusalem.
The great Tanna R' Akiva ben Yosef — about whom, according to a legend in Menachot 29, Moses our teacher asked the Master of the Universe: "You have such a man, and You give the Torah through me?", and who was later killed for the sanctification of the Name — this very great Jew said of Bar Kokhba that he was the Messiah (Midrash Rabbah, Lamentations ch. 2), and issued an order to his 24 thousand disciples and followers to break off the study of the Torah and go out onto the battlefield against the idol-worshippers. For 3 years (132–135) these "disciples of R' Akiva" led a true soldier's life! They slept together in barracks, ate from the same kitchens, etc. It was therefore quite easy, given the minimal knowledge of medicine of the time (when people knew nothing at all of the existence of bacteria), for one or several in the camp to fall ill with spotted typhus or typhoid fever, and for hundreds of others to be infected from it.
After a certain time of bloody battles throughout the land, when the smell of blood was felt everywhere, and especially "between Passover and Shavuot", when there are great heat waves in the Land of Israel, the specific diseases of war such as spotted typhus and others began to break out, and of the diseases thousands of the uprising's armies died. Of the disciples of R' Akiva, fortunately, not a single person died on Lag BaOmer.
Lag BaOmer is therefore a holiday for school youth, because they were the most active in the battles mentioned.
On Lag BaOmer also falls the yahrzeit of the great posek, the Rema (R' Moshe Isserles), who died at the age of 52 in Kraków in the year 5332, 1572, the same year in which the last Polish king of the Jagiellonian dynasty, Zygmunt August, died there.
On this occasion it is worthwhile, for the sake of truth, to establish the real history of an event which was later distorted by a legend. Namely, the legend runs: in Kraków a wedding once took place on a Friday at nightfall. The Rema went there and rebuked the wedding guests. When they laughed at him he cursed them, and whether by natural cause or by miracle... they afterwards sank into the ground.
In truth, not only did the Rema curse no one, but on the contrary, the Rema himself permitted a wedding canopy to be set up on Friday towards evening.
The story — as the Rema describes it in his "Responsa" — happened thus:
2 brothers were marrying off a sister, an orphan. The wedding was set for Friday. Shortly before the canopy the bridegroom had second thoughts and demanded that the dowry be paid out to him. Because of this there were claims and counter-claims, and the matter dragged on until evening. The Rema, who was present, ordered the canopy to be set up and sent word to his synagogue that they should wait with Kabbalat Shabbat. He later justified this by saying that he was afraid that over the Sabbath the bridegroom would again change his mind and the orphan girl would be put to shame. But since the "Agudah-niks" of those days began to grumble that the Rema had not acted well, the heads of the community made an ordinance that no wedding date should be fixed on a Friday, and in an exceptional case the wedding should take place outside the town.
Gdud.
To the Public!

As a sympathiser of the Mizrachi I gave, in full awareness, my consent to appear on the Mizrachi candidates' list for the kehilla elections.
Recently, however, the following happened: at the cheder "Yesodei HaTorah" a melamed, R' Shlomo Lustiger of blessed memory, died. A considerable sum was owed to him by the cheder. According to a beth-din ruling between the son of the deceased and the cheder "Yesodei HaTorah", the cheder was to pay the son of the deceased a total of 1650 zł. Despite the explicit beth-din ruling, they have until today wanted to pay off the son with mere acceptances of the cheder, which have no real value, without the endorsements (giro) of the members of the cheder's board.
In order to save the money for the widow and orphans of the deceased, it was agreed among the shtibl people of the second Radomsko shtibl that I would consent to appear on the candidates' list of the Agudah, on condition that the members of the board of the cheder "Yesodei HaTorah" give their endorsements on the above-mentioned bills of exchange. Carrying this out was undertaken by one of the finest Radomsko hasidim, to whom I gave my signature on the declaration in favour of the Agudah. The declaration was to remain with the said Radomsko hasid as a deposit until the Agudah people gave their endorsements; if not, the said Radomsko hasid was to return my signature to me that same day.
That was on Sunday of parshat Emor, 26 April, when the Mizrachi list had not yet been submitted to the gmina. And had the Agudah people kept their word, I would have made the sacrifice for the widow and orphans of the deceased and would have withdrawn my signature in favour of the [Agudah?], despite all my sympathies for the Mizrachi.
Unfortunately the said Radomsko hasid explicitly deceived me: he did not obtain any endorsements on the bills from the Agudah people, and he handed my signature on the declaration in favour of the Agudah over to them.
I therefore declare to the public: my signature on the declaration of the Agudah list stems from a moral robbery, and therefore it has no moral value.
Respectfully,
Chaim Wolf Steinhardt.

From the general meeting of the Cooperative Bank in Będzin.
On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Cooperative Bank in Będzin took place in the hall of the town council. Interest in the meeting was much smaller than in the "stormy times", but nevertheless about 160 members came, among them one woman member...
The chairman of the council, Mr Israel Regirer, opens the meeting, and the chair [printed "פאריץ", a misprint for "פארזיץ"] is handed to Mr A. Liwer.
Reports: from the management — Mr Jakub Erlich, and from the Auditing Union — the delegate Mr Michelson.
The rapporteurs describe the sad state to which the previous management had led. The management took over the bank at the moment when the losses had reached as much as 250 thousand zł. And thanks to Mr Fürstenberg, who financed the bank with his own capital, and also to the assistance of the Auditing Union and in the form of rediscount, the bank is back on the road of normal work and has regained confidence. Now — say the rapporteurs — the fate of the bank's further existence depends on the members themselves, who must pay new shares into the bank. When that happens, the Auditing Union will give a larger sum as a loan!
From the balance sheet presented by the manager, Mr S. Trojb, it appears that during the past year the bank had a turnover of over one and a half million zł. Net profit — 18 thousand zł. At the wish of those assembled, the sum is entered as reserve capital.
In the discussion, in which Messrs Jakubowicz, Hampel, Kamiński, Fajgenblat and others take part, thanks are expressed to Mr Fürstenberg, the council and management and the bank's directorate.
It is also resolved that the members shall pay in new shares.
In the composition of the council and management there is no change at all; only the deputies were changed.
Elected as deputies in the management: Moshe Szpigel and Moshe Lejb Kowalowski.
In the council: Noach Auzer, Abraham Hirsz.
The Vanished Daughter (6)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 6.]
An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World
by Elizabeta Garin [Elżbieta Garin].
6.

He found out that already a year ago, when his sister Lala had come home on vacation from the high school for girls in Budapest, where she had spent two years, her behaviour had been conspicuous. Soon afterwards Staszek arrived, also from Budapest, where he had gone right away. After the Vienna unrest, when he had been expelled from the university, it turned out that she had met him there and renewed their childhood friendship, regardless of the fact that he and her brother had fought each other to the point of bloodshed in Vienna, in opposing camps. Her father, of course, would not tolerate this and forbade him — the "hooligan", as he called him — to come to the house. Before long he disappeared altogether, and in the town it was said that since his father had taken away his means to continue studying, he had joined "Ringling's Circus" and gone off with it to America. The Rapaports breathed more easily. They had seen nothing bad in Lala's friendship with Staszek — they had in any case regarded her as merely a child — but all the same they were very pleased when he left, as it seemed, for good.

To their great distress he had come back three months earlier; he did not, however, bother them, and Lala did not take much interest in him; now they understand that she had probably been corresponding with him and seeing him too... But who could ever have imagined such a thing.

"Has anyone been to the robbers' house?" Fritz asked Berish the coachman. "Has anyone searched there?"
"God be with you!" Berish took fright. "Who is going to go there?"
"I am, Berish, and you too, if you like," Fritz answered. "I'm only afraid that we are too late..." he added with pain in his voice.

They got there that very afternoon and thoroughly searched the whole house. Now Berish no longer had any doubt that the two lovers had spent two whole days in that house and that somebody, a third person, had helped them; nor did they have any doubt who that third person was, and on the way back home Fritz and Berish stopped at the little white house of Janek's parents, and, as they had expected, he was not at home.

"Lately there's no putting up with that boy," his mother, an old peasant woman, said with annoyance. "He stays away from the house whole days, doesn't lift a finger to work, and drags everything out of the house — he even drags out food."
"And what do you think he does with it?" Fritz asked, wanting to know whether she suspected anything.
"Sells it, or gobbles it up with loafers like himself — who can know with them?"

On returning home Fritz found a telegram from his father: a man and a girl somewhat resembling the two runaways had been seen on the road to Vienna, he wrote. Fritz merely shrugged his shoulders; he knew well that if Lala and Staszek had left the robbers' house only a day earlier, nobody could yet have seen them on the road to Vienna.

Sasza Rapaport felt a little freer with her son's return home, but she did not stop weeping and blaming herself for their misfortune.
"I didn't notice, because I didn't look; I was always too busy with myself, too great an egoist, too proud even to think that precisely to me such a thing could happen — my daughter with a peasant... with a simple szlachcic [petty Polish nobleman]..." she lamented.
"And if it had been a nobleman, a little baron, a little count?" — her son looked at her with dark, shaming[?] eyes, and every tenderness vanished from his face, as if wiped away.
"How you talk..." Sasza sobbed, and hid her tear-stained, grief-stricken[?] face in both hands.
"Am I not a mother, then?"
But now Fritz already knew everything that until then he had merely suspected: that if Staszek had been a nobleman with an old name, it would not have affected his mama so badly... And lying in his beautiful room, sleepless and in despair, he once again took stock of what had happened, searching for the cause, the real cause... not taking into account his sister's love for that scoundrel ["łajdak"] Staszek... the reason why so many such tender beings as Lala go to ruin and are lost to Judaism...

— His own mother, the beautiful, accomplished, three-quarters-assimilated daughter of one of the finest Jewish families in Austria, would also have married a handsome aristocratic officer, like a younger sister of hers, had not the rich and respected Shlomo Rapaport come along at that time, fallen in love with the beautiful Sasza and taken her without a kreuzer of dowry...

Her father had once been a very rich merchant in Brod [Brody]. But he became impoverished together with the town; when he moved to Lemberg [Lwów], there was still enough to give the children a good upbringing and to live in such a way that "people shouldn't know". The eldest son became a doctor, the second got a good position in a bank and married the banker's daughter... But the two daughters...

The Celebration of the 3rd of May

[Będzin — 3 May celebrations.] The celebration of the 3rd of May [Polish Constitution Day] was impressive. The front of Mr. Szwajcer's house, where the police commissariat is located, was splendidly illuminated by hundreds of little lamps; all the houses were decorated.
In the synagogue a festive prayer service took place, after which a procession of all the school youth was formed, which marched through the town.
In Sosnowiec the synagogue was full of school youth, for whom the cantor sang the appropriate chapters of Psalms.

The Election Campaign Has Begun.
"Poalim" Withdrew Their List.

[Będzin — kehilla elections.] At Sunday's session of the election commission the remaining candidate lists were examined, in which the commission found "sirkhos" [adhesions — a koshering term, i.e. flaws]. But thanks to the interested parties having "worked" on them [i.e. cleaned them up, as one porges meat], the commission declared them kosher, except for the list of "Poalei Emunei Yisrael", which was withdrawn; thus only 13 lists now figure.
— —
List number 17 held its first election rally on Saturday in "Nowości". Messrs. Wigański, Liwer, Marek Szajn and L. Rubinlicht spoke. The speakers criticized the activity of the kehilla leaders up to now, pointed to the harmful work of the Agudah dozors [kehilla board members] and called for voting for list 17.
———
This Saturday a collective discussion on the topic "What do we expect from the kehilla?" takes place at the premises of "Hitachdut".
During the week several larger meetings were held by those who group themselves around the "Hitachdut" list no. 8.
Register Your Children in the Public Elementary Schools.

[Będzin — education.] According to a special circular of the school authority, the registration of children for the new school year begins on the 7th and will last until the 11th of this month, i.e. today, Friday, Sunday the 10th and Monday the 11th there is still time to register children born in the year 1924 and also those who are subject to the compulsory-schooling law. After this deadline registration will no longer be possible.
As we are informed, the school situation for the coming school year has in general become more difficult, so that children, especially of the younger ages, who are not registered in time will remain outside school.
The Magistrate Assigns 10 Thousand Zł. for Putting the Square around the Station in Order.

[Będzin — municipality.] For weeks the dispute lasted between the railway directorate and the local magistrate [town council] over putting in order the area surrounding the new railway station. The dispute consisted in the magistrate not wishing, owing to a lack of cash, to carry out the work to which it had at the time committed itself.
This week the magistrate assigned a sum of 10 thousand zł. for the above-mentioned purpose, and with that the dispute has been settled.
As we are told, the station is to be opened on 1 July [lipiec] of this year.
General Meeting of "Linat Ha-Cholim".

[Będzin — institutions.] The general meeting of the members of "Linat Ha-Cholim" [society for night care of the sick], which was to have taken place on 26 April, was postponed and will now take place this coming Sunday, the 10th of this month, at the society's premises.
The meeting is arousing wide interest because, for the first time since the institution has existed, a new board will be elected at the meeting.
A Bandit Attack on Szelecka Street.
[Będzin — crime.] On Sunday evening 3 bandits attacked Aron Rajcensztajn, who lives on Szelecka Street, as he was walking home. One of them held his hands and the others took 93 zł. from him.
At the "Collection Point" of the "Prams" Purses Vanish...

[Będzin — crime.] On 3rd of May Square, the only place where mothers gather with their little children, the following incidents occurred this week:
Mrs. E., while busy with her child, put her purse [sakiewka] down on the pram; in it were 29 zł. in cash and the flat keys, but in the blink of an eye the purse vanished.
On the same square Mrs. Lemkowicz's purse was stolen. There were 40 zł. in the purse.
—o—
Bank Kredytowy.
[Będzin — economy.] On Wednesday the plot of the Cukerman family was registered by the local notary in the name of the "Bank Kredytowy".
A Plot Bought
For the plot, which is located on Piłsudski Street, the bank paid 32,500 zł.
The “Malbish Arumim” society is already caring for winter clothing.

The board[?] of the “Malbish Arumim” society [“clothing the naked” — a charity providing clothes to the poor] has a “tradition”: as soon as the first spring sun appears, it already takes care that the poor children should have winter clothes. This year a campaign is being undertaken for this purpose in the form of a sale of [—?] and badges.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish public will, as every year, support the fund-raising campaign, so as to enable the board to buy larger stocks of winter goods for the great number of poor Jewish children.
A new Jewish bank.

On Sunday the founding meeting took place of a new Jewish bank called “Kasa Udziałowa” [shareholders’ loan fund]. A sufficient number of members took part in the meeting, among them also several well-known wealthy men of our town.
Mr. T. Szapira opens the meeting, and Mr. H. Zylberszac is invited to serve as chairman, Mr. H. Białka as secretary.
After the statutes had been read and approved, a series of proposals was adopted, among them that a member can receive credit of up to 10 thousand zł. and that the bank can take upon itself obligations of up to 50[?] thousand zł.
Then the following board and council were elected: M. Kramałowski (president), Tuvia Szapira (vice), Yisrael Mincz.
On the council: Hersz Unger (president), Henech Zylberszac, Y. Langfus and Henech Kahn.
A “matinee” for children and adults.

On the initiative of the Society for Police Families in Będzin, a “matinee” [poranek] will take place next Sunday at 11 a.m. at the “Nowości” [cinema]. A film called “Animals like People” will be shown, and a sound film as a supplementary programme.
Children 50 gr., adults 1 zł.
When a goy goes to a little celebration...

At a Christian family on Podzamcze Street a “bris” [i.e. a christening, said jokingly] was celebrated. When the company was already tipsy, they began to “honour” one another with knives, axes and the like. The result was that 2 guests were taken in serious condition to the local hospital.
Sosnowiec — The 1st and 3rd of May in Zagłębie

In Sosnowiec the communists organised a communist demonstration on the “hałdy” [mine spoil heaps]. Police soon arrived, and were received with anti-state cries. When the police demanded that the crowd disperse, stones were thrown from the crowd and revolver shots were also fired. Thereupon the police fired several volleys, into the air and then into the crowd, from which several people were wounded.
Then the crowd began to flee, taking the wounded with them.
In Będzin the “Left Poale Zion” demonstrated through the town; the demonstration was not disturbed.
In Dąbrowa the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] held a meeting in the courtyard of the “Miraż”. In the street larger crowds gathered, which were dispersed by the police.
On the whole, the 1st of May passed quietly.
A large fraud discovered at the office for unemployment relief — the state has suffered a loss of tens of thousands of zł.

At the local office for unemployment relief, the number of unemployed exceeded what the actual lay-offs warranted. The judicial and police authorities took an interest in the matter and carried out an inspection, and it turned out that hundreds of documents of the “laid-off” workers were forged.
The further investigation uncovered three Christians, the “manufacturers” of the lay-off certificates. The “factory”, which had “in its possession” all the factories and coal mines, issued certificates for “laid-off workers”.
The fraud caused the state a loss of several tens of thousands of zł.
The “manufacturers” were arrested on the order of the prosecutor.
Tragic result of carelessness.

On Tuesday afternoon 23-year-old Ostrowski of Modrzejów[?] wanted to board a tram that was going to Będzin. The jump, however, was unlucky: Ostrowski fell under the tram, and the wheels cut off his right leg and injured his body. Ostrowski was taken to hospital in a very dangerous condition.
The “Poalim” do not agree with the policy of the “Agudah”.

[Zagłębie — Poalei Agudat Israel and the kehilla elections.]
On Sunday a report meeting of the “Poalei Agudat Israel” took place here.
In the lecture by Mr. Hachman A. G., “Our position on the kehilla elections”, the speaker declared that the “Poalim” must not go to the elections together with the “Agudah”.
When Messrs. Sycemski and Dafner wanted to speak on the matter, a great uproar broke out, and shouts were heard: “Enough of your favours already!” etc.
In the end a resolution was adopted that the Poalim have a free hand in the kehilla elections.
From the Sosnowiec “HaShachar”.

[Sosnowiec — organisations.]
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Wiernik the semi-annual general meeting of the organisation “HaShachar” took place. Reports were given, from which it emerges that in the course of the short time the organisation has existed it has developed very nicely in the national-cultural field. A board was elected consisting of the following persons: Gedalia Cawar, Y. Szydłowski, Wiernik, Chana Rajzman, Tanenberg. Audit committee: Milsztajn and Kołatach. The meeting was closed with the singing of “HaTikvah” (printed “Tchukah”).
—o—
A father tried to strangle his own son.
[Dęblin — crime.]
The railway guard at the Dęblin station, Tomasz Brylunski, came home drunk and started to beat his wife. Then he threw himself on his 16-year-old son, who put up resistance, and wanted to strangle him with a necktie. At the mother's screams the neighbours came running and tore the already unconscious victim out of the hands of the murderous father.
Olkusz.

[Olkusz — town council.]
The Endeks dissolve the new town council.
On Monday the third, in order, session of the new town council took place. After the reading of the minutes of the previous session they proceeded to elect a president [mayor].
The hitherto president, Mr. Starkiewicz (Sanacja), was elected with 13 votes (last time only 12 votes). (9 Jewish, 3 Sanacja and 1 PPS.) The rival candidate, Mr. Majewski (Endek), received 10 votes. After the elections the Endeks held a lengthy consultation and proposed for themselves the vice-president (Mr. Zbieg) and 2 ławniks [municipal board members] (Messrs. Kipiński and Gałański). According to the agreement of the Jewish club with the Sanacja, the latter [the Jews] also wanted to obtain the post of vice-president and 2 Jewish ławniks (Mr. Talerman and Dr. Chain). Before proceeding to the vote a difference of opinion arose among the Jews. B. Zylberberg and D. Glajtman split off from the Jewish club and decided to vote for the Endek vice-president, because of which there was a threat of losing the second Jewish ławnik, since (printed “heyl”) the Jews would thereby have lost the Sanacja votes. The chairman, the newly elected president, seeing the newly created difficult situation, adjourned the session for 3 days. Soon afterwards all 11 Endek-Chadek councillors together with their substitutes resigned their mandates and thereby dissolved the town council. The starosta at once set supplementary elections for 1 June.
T. Y.
—o—
The 3rd of May celebration.
[Olkusz — national holidays.]
In the 3rd of May celebration [Polish Constitution Day] the sports club “Maccabi”, with its commandant Mr. Wolfin at its head, and “HaShomer HaLeumi” took part for the first time. The march-past of the Jewish drużynas [squads] before the defilade [review] was impressive and made the best impression.
A. B.
A Jewish boy found.

[Dąbrowa — news.] The merchant Himelfarb of "Kolonia Redeń" in Dąbrowa, while travelling near Olkusz, was handed by a peasant woman from the village a Jewish boy aged 5, whom she had — according to her words — found in the nearby forest.
Mr. Himelfarb took the child with him and brought him to Dąbrowa.
The little boy understands when spoken to in Polish, but Gypsy habits are rooted in him; according to the assumption, the boy was raised among Gypsies, who afterwards abandoned him in the forest.
—o—
The traditional Lag BaOmer excursion.
[Sosnowiec — youth movements.] The Lag BaOmer excursion of the Sosnowiec "Hashomer Hatzair" went off very impressively. At 6 o'clock in the morning more than 160 people marched off in closed ranks to the "camp" (obóz), which is located at "Wysoki Brzeg". There various sports exercises, entertainments and various assemblies took place. Great enthusiasm was aroused in the camp by the news, received from the Chief Leadership in Warsaw, that the Sosnowiec branch (ken) is this year counted among the best and strongest branches.
The return was splendid. Hundreds of people waited and greeted with loud applause the camp, which marched singing Hebrew songs all the way to the clubhouse.
For the first time Jewish Sosnowiec witnessed such a festivity.
District conference concerning the kehilla elections.

[Będzin — Zionism / kehilla elections.] Next Sunday, 10 May, a district conference devoted to the forthcoming kehilla elections will take place in Będzin, in the premises of the Zionist Organization. The following towns and townlets will take part in the conference:
Sosnowiec, Modrzejów, Dąbrowa, Czeladź, Grodziec, Ząbkowice, Niwka, Pogoń, Strzemieszyce, Myszków, Siewierz and Zawiercie, etc.

Our Reply — To the Jewish Public.

[Będzin — education: the "Mizrachi" school; statement of the board.]
In connection with the open letter of the teaching staff of the "Mizrachi" school in Będzin, in which the person of our esteemed founder and long-standing president of our school, R' Lejbisz Buchwajc, is insulted — he who in fact has carried the entire burden of the school for 11 years, and to whose devoted and tireless work the teachers indeed owe their existence — as thanks for his selfless services for the good of the school, these same people permit themselves to pelt him with dirt and disgraceful insults, at a time when no more than 6 weeks' salary was owed to them. And this, in the severe crisis, when we must accept long-term bills of exchange for tuition fees so as not to let the school go under: the teachers not only refused to agree to a reduction of salaries, but by means of strike terror they extorted a supplement and by violent means seized the school's account books, without the knowledge of the board (Kuratorium), declared themselves sole rulers, and exempted themselves from all administrative expenses such as rent, sick fund etc.; and although by this act they made themselves punishable and we ought to have handed them over to the prosecutor, we did not want to take that un-Jewish path, because it is beneath our dignity.
On top of all this, the above-mentioned people still have the impudence to meddle in a man's private life and to reproach him for his trip to Meran, which concerns his state of health, and also for the interest which we were forced to pay in order to be able to pay out the salaries, because the teachers would not accept any bill of exchange.
Now as to their threats of court: we would have plenty of interesting material, which would bring them no honour — especially that "Herr" who hides under the name "teaching staff".
In particular we ask our religious teachers, headed by the Musaf reader R' Beryl Besser: even if your claim were a just one, surely you know that there is justice in Israel (yesh din be-Yisrael)! And besides, we did propose to you teachers an arbitration court, which you rejected for fear of the truth, and you sought other ways... to the prosecutor.
As to your discovery that we want to change the name of the school: it is no secret to the teachers that at the demand of the central Mizrachi school organisation "Yavneh" we were compelled to join it and also to bear the name "Yavneh".
On the contrary — let the public judge the high ethical level of our educators.
Incidentally, we declare that we shall conduct no further discussion in this way.
On behalf of the board (Kuratorium) of the "Mizrachi" school, Będzin
J. M. Kurland
J. J. Najmark.
The Trial against the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" — Postponed.

[Będzin — court: the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".]
As we have already written, Mr. L. Szpigelman, as responsible editor of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", was administratively fined 100 zł. or 2 weeks' arrest for printing an article entitled "Barg arop" ("Downhill").
An appeal was lodged against this verdict, explaining that the content of the article is far from any tendencies that might "incite the public", and that therefore the penalty should be annulled.
Last Friday the trial took place in the Będzin court. Officials of the Starostwo (county office) appeared as accusers; the defence counsel was Dr. Rechtman.
The [sworn?] translator at the Sosnowiec district court, Mr. Lebowicz, was also summoned as an expert.
For formal reasons the trial was postponed.
Echoes of the Events in Zawiercie.

[Zagłębie — court: Zawiercie.]
At the Sosnowiec district court the trial of 14 men who had provoked the bloody events in Zawiercie in April of last year lasted two days.
After the speeches of the prosecutor and the defence counsel, the court pronounced the verdict, under which several of the guilty were sentenced to two years and the rest to 10 months.
The Rabbinate Question in Strzemieszyce.

[Strzemieszyce — community and rabbinate.]
On Sunday the kehilla board in Strzemieszyce held a meeting at which the question was considered of admitting to the competition the deputy (memale-mekoym) of the late rabbi of Strzemieszyce.
No settlement was reached; instead the question was handed over to Mr. Yechezkel Taub, who is to issue a final decision on it.

A Decree against the Jewish Market Traders
From the Small Traders' Association in Königshütte (Królewska Huta) we have received a desperate letter, crying to heaven, about the chicanery and persecution which the 80 Jewish market traders have to endure only because they are Jews. The letter says that the association has already knocked on all doors and intervened everywhere, but without any result.
The persecution has been going on for several months already; simply, no Jewish trader is allowed to come to a market with a little merchandise.
The Small Traders' Association appeals through our mediation to the relevant Jewish public institutions to take an interest in the business situation and to save some 400 souls from the new decree.
