The Chain That Is Falling Apart. (The critical situation in the country. — Is the question being taken seriously, or is it being made light of?)

The Polish citizen, the taxpayer, has already noticed several times that when the taxes with which the citizens are to be burdened are being weighed, reports then appear in the newspapers that the taxes will be reformed, that is to say, lightened, and that care will be taken that the tax-screw should not press so hard on the popular strata. In that case the citizen feels easier, he gathers strength, he strives with all his powers to pay the taxes imposed, he goes about in the consciousness that next year things will be made easier for him. The newspaper itself — he tells himself — wrote explicitly that in government circles they are beginning to see to it that the taxes be lightened; but almost every time he has been disappointed. Later it turned out that everything had remained as of old and that no effort whatever had been begun to solve the question in the sense that it should ease the citizens' cares; on the contrary, instead of alleviations we were able to read in the newspapers reports that fresh projects are being put forward, new tax proposals, with which still more pessimism will penetrate the commercial circles.
Similar reports, only this time not in the field of taxes but in the field of commerce, appeared in the newspapers last week. We read in black and white that now it will be laid down that on Sundays trading shall be permitted for a few hours, and that every day the trading hours will be extended; then the 8-hour working day is to be abolished, after that apartments are to become cheaper — in short, whole "salvations and consolations" [yeshuos unechomos].
The reports aroused general attention and a discussion on the subject began to develop. Some were of the opinion that it had come too late: now they are going to extend the trading hours, when trade is a corpse and there is nothing to do in the time in which trading is permitted. The same goes for the 8-hour working day: why does it have to be curtailed precisely now — perhaps so that there should be more unemployed?
Others said that it is not worth disputing about it, because these are idle words; nothing will come of it anyway. And still others said: what do you mean, the rent will become cheaper, at a time when the government has for some while been striving to raise the rents? How, then, is it possible that reports which so contradict one another should be confirmed? Others went further still: who knows, they said, whether out of all these "alleviations" there will not come new difficulties, new worries, new burdens? And indeed, two days later we were able to read that a part of the above-mentioned reports are not correct, and now it only remains to wait, that there should not come out of this a fresh worry, fresh burdens, which would make the critical situation in the country still heavier.
It is possible that all these reports have been sucked out of a finger, possible that in government circles nothing at all is being thought about these matters, possible that they are not occupied with them at all — that there is no wish to improve them, to ease them, nor any wish to make them harsher for the population; but that is still not enough: meanwhile people take fright and keep brooding without knowing what will come of it.
These are, after all, questions too topical, matters too painful, for them to be taken lightly by those who worry so much that their condition, which finds itself in such a threatening situation, should not become still worse, still more catastrophic — which quite often throws one out of normal equilibrium.
It was said that now, when trade has already died off and there is no longer anyone from whom, or anything for which, to take in money, they begin to concern themselves and to think about extending the trading hours. True, there is no need of that at the present day, and the reports turn out to be incorrect. But one would like to know what is in fact correct, and what they are in fact thinking about in government circles? Can the economic situation really remain standing on its present pedestal? Can one let oneself be content with nothing being done about the crisis? Does not the crisis in this way take root ever deeper and stronger?
Trade is impoverished, industry is prostrate, unemployment is growing and the productive citizens in the country are going hungry — so ought one not to give a thought to what will be next, how one is to get out of this dangerous tangle, which as time goes on becomes more and more entangled[?]? May one and can one stand at a distance, while one catastrophe after another keeps showing itself? Can one not compare the present state of affairs in the whole world to a fire which has begun to burn on all sides, so that everywhere one must stand on guard and put out the fire, lest it engulf[?] everything and everyone? Is a country helped by people saying that it is not only bad with us, that it is bitter in the whole world, that the fire has flared up not only in Europe but also in America — are we in any way helped by this answer? And can one remain helped by it? Can one in such a manner solve questions which bind existence together with ruin?
Every country finds itself in different conditions, and everywhere the question must be solved differently. One must not rely on miracles; to say that because it is bad elsewhere it may also be not good with us is no answer at all, above all when the one is not helped by the other.
With us in Poland the economic troubles could be removed, the questions would let themselves be solved, if people had not taken it into their heads that trade must be pushed out of Jewish hands; no sooner do they begin to consider the tax question in the Sejm than it takes on a character as if it were a Jewish question.
If one saw that the economic question must be solved in a unified way, one would consider that industry and taxes and small manufacture and the artisan class are links in the great chain, and that as soon as one link — no matter whether the weakest or the strongest — comes unhooked, the whole chain is in danger of falling apart. If all this were considered as it ought to be, if one took a sincere interest in the questions, one would succeed in forging together again the great chain, which keeps on falling apart and from which the whole country, without exception, must suffer, must feel it.
Now one can no longer shout it down, that all is good and well in the country and that the citizens merely put on a pitiful face, that they cannot pay the taxes; now one already sees that no smoke rises from the factory chimneys and that the machines keep on rusting, and that the workers wander about without work, and that the shopkeepers have no one from whom to take in money, because there is no cash and one cannot give on a bill of exchange. Now — we believe — they already see in government circles how grave the situation in the country is; therefore it would be high time to occupy themselves with the questions seriously and first of all to set it [the question] on a path, that there be the will to solve it, the will to consider it and to treat it with full seriousness, with full sincerity and warmth, as matters must be solved which are to avert grave dangers in the country and to lead to a state of happiness and prosperity for all citizens of country and government.
R. Let[?].
In Honour of Shavuot

[Poem — for the festival of Shavuot.]
— by — Reb Mordkhele.

Where does one get a new Mount Sinai of holiness,
where does one get a second Moses our Teacher,
that the mountain might smother our spiritual shame,
that Moses might put our cowardice to death.

Two thousand years now since the anchor was lost,
and the Jewish ship strays 'over seas',
and wherever there is a harbour — with venom and with wrath
it shuts the gate before us and seeks to damn[?]...

And here, on the way, we have lost everything,
trampled the faith, ruined[?] the East,
and dead as a desert the soul has become,
no more holiness in life, no fragrance!...

And where there are foreign doors, there we knock,
and where there are foreign gods, there we bow down,
our own seal, through the stages of the generations,
no longer to be recognised, the "I" melted away.

And where there are foreign temples, and faiths and tongues.
With customs that spray sparks and flame,
there we are plentiful, and there does not awaken
the feeling that takes pride in the Jewish stock...

But would it not be more fitting to tread
our own paths, with our own God,
and rather than kneel and beg at strangers' doors,
to hold to our historic commandment?

We may no longer sell the soul,
barter away the tiny "pintele Yid" [the Jewish spark]:
that is the faith of generations that run by,
that is the heritage of Jewish song...

And should we be deeply winged with belief
in our own powers, in our own wellspring.
Then history itself would lift us up
to cast upon mankind a golden ray.
The Vanished Daughter — an original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World

[Serialised novel — instalment no. 7.]
By Elisabeth Garin.
For those readers who have not read the beginning of this gripping novel, we give the following summary:
In the year 1900 a circus came to the shtetl of Z. in Galicia. When the circus had left that shtetl, the news suddenly spread that the beautiful Lala, the only daughter of the wealthy Reb Shlomo Rapaport, had gone off with the young Christian Wacek[?], a schoolmate of her brother Fritz.
The father and her brother set about searching for the vanished Lala, but without result, because Staszek had hidden her at his friend Janek's, in a house in the Tatra mountains. Lala begged her seducer to let her go home, but Staszek laughed at that. Lala took it very much to heart[?], but having no choice she did what the comrades Staszek and Janek told her to do.
The task of finding her was taken on in particular by Lala's brother Fritz, who could not rest at the thought that people of such a kind[?] as Lala should be lost to Jewry?...
— — —
Fritz's thoughts passed over to his own upbringing... He had had a rebbe [teacher], who studied with him when he was still a small child... on [—] in later times the rebbe came to them, Berish used to bring him, but in summer he, Fritz, used to go down the hill into the shtetl to the rebbe's house:
"Presumably 'she' did not want to put up with people seeing the 'matted-haired Jew'; it did not look nice in front of the gentile guests," he thought without bitterness.
She, his mother, had also had nothing at all against his keeping company with Staszek and Janek; on the contrary, she seemed to be very pleased with it. But when she found out that he was standing up for Jewish students and fighting on the Jewish side... and afterwards, when he told her and his father that he felt drawn to national Jewry, she told him openly that it would not lend him any extra charm as a doctor, and that she did not understand at all what "a son of hers" had to do with "those" people.
When, in fact, at that time he began[?] to say that it would be desirable for Lala to go to the girls' school of a Jewish professor, an acquaintance of his, where she would also be able to receive Jewish instruction, his mother answered him that over his upbringing his father had had the say, but over Lala's she would let no one exert any influence. She alone would have the say about that...
"And she got her way," he muttered with chagrin, "but not what she wanted: a simple peasant, and a circus rider and a hooligan into the bargain..."
The terrible news
When Fritz at last fell asleep after a painfully sleepless night, it was already daybreak. And when he woke up the sun already stood high in the sky, and his first thought was that he must get hold of Janek as quickly as possible.
He went straight in to his mother; she was still lying in bed, pale and weakened, but much calmer than he had found her on his arrival; she was already prepared for the worst that was still to come...
"With Father it will be worse!" the thought crossed his mind, and at once, without eating his breakfast, he went down the hill, ready to go once more to the little white house of Janek's parents.
But Janek barred his way; he met him on the narrow path that led from Orawa.
Janek, who had been hiding for two days in another village, hoping to avoid the meeting with his former Jewish friend, was the first to catch sight of him coming down from the hills, and threw himself into the bushes, hoping to hide, but he did not succeed. With one leap Fritz was beside him and seized him by the throat with both hands in such a rage that the sheygets turned blue as a spleen and his eyes bulged out.
"Where is my little sister, where is Lali?" Fritz asked him, trembling with anger and agitation.
"I.. I.." Janek barely managed to wheeze out, trying to free himself from Fritz's hands. The latter loosened his grip a little, but did not release his throat altogether,
"Well, why don't you speak"
"What, am I her keeper?!" the other, feeling himself freer, shouted out in a half-choked voice.
"I'll strangle you on the spot, you scoundrel, if you don't tell me where Staszek has taken her," Fritz assured him, and indeed showed that he meant it by once again tightening his grip on his throat.
"Will you talk?" But that was now impossible; all Janek could do was blink his eyes, but that language Fritz Rapaport understood too. He let go of his throat for a moment [printed: "זיי, האלז"], still holding him firmly by the hands so that he should not run away.
"Pest, they have gone off to Pest [Budapest]..."
"When?"
"Three days ago."
"By train?"
"Only from Orawa."
"Did they have money?"
"I... I don't know."
"Janek!" Fritz shouted at him.
"Over a thousand crowns, and Lala's jewellery."
"You mean my mother's, which she stole at his demand?"
To that Janek no longer replied, and if he did, Fritz did not hear it; he walked quickly, almost ran, down the hill to the telegraph station in Z...

A Tragic Shavuot in Grodno

(A page of history). By Moshe Feinkind.

The Shavuot tragedy already has its written page in the history of the Jews in Poland.

In the year 1719 [as printed] the righteous convert (ger tzedek) Potocki was publicly burned in Vilna, beside the Castle Hill (Schlossberg), on the second day of Shavuot; the same also befell the Reizes brothers in Lemberg [Lwów], who breathed out their souls on the auto-da-fé at Shavuot 1728 because of a libel that had been raised against them; and in the year 1790 (5550) quiet Grodno was once again the scene of a similar tragedy.

A Christian girl was digging sand at a hill that lay behind the town, having laid aside the kerchief in which she went about wrapped.

Suddenly, in the course of the digging, the hill caved in and the girl was buried under the upper part of the hill; just then nobody noticed it, and she met her death there.

A Grodno Jew, R' Elazar Verbilover, happening to pass by that hill, noticed a kerchief lying on the ground and, reckoning that someone had lost it here, took the kerchief with him and went on his way.

When later the servant-girl was searched for at that spot, she was found there already dead.

Witnesses soon came forward who confirmed that at the moment when the girl was digging sand at the hill, the Jew Elazar Verblozer [as printed] had been hanging about there; and the Jesuits at once spread a rumour that the Jews had killed the Christian girl for ritual purposes. A crowd of people did indeed promptly set off for the dwelling of R' Elazar Verblover, and finding in his house the "find", the fatal kerchief, they at once forged him in chains and threw him into a dark prison, accusing him of having been the girl's murderer and of having, after drawing off[?] her blood, buried her here behind the hill in the earth.

For two years the unfortunate man was kept in prison, tormented with the harshest tortures, while it was demanded of him that he confess his guilt and also give up his accomplices; but the innocent martyr steadfastly withstood the trial. He did not confess to a crime he had not committed, nor would he buy his life by converting, as his tormentors demanded of him.

The trial then took place in the Grodno tribunal, which stood, as in other towns, under the influence of the Jesuits; the tribunal sentenced R' Elazar Verblover to death by quartering his body, the hacked-up parts to be hung around the corners of the town.

But every death sentence had to have the sanction of the king, and so the execution was indeed postponed until he should sign it.

2.

In Grodno Stanisław August, the last Polish king, had his residence-castle, in which he used to stay for weeks on end and conduct the affairs of the state.

The king was well informed about the content of this trial and also convinced that R' Elazar Verblover was wholly innocent [lit. "owes God his soul" and nothing else]. In general this liberal king did not believe in ritual murder among Jews,

and when the Jesuits interceded with him to confirm the sentence upon the poor Jew, he refused them. Therefore the Jesuits grew greatly incensed at the king and resolved to carry out the death sentence without his consent, regardless of the prohibition of the law.

For Stanisław August the time was altogether unfavourable, on account of the political events that were then playing out in Poland concerning the throne, on account of his concluding the unfortunate agreement with Catherine the Second; because of this the days of his rule were already numbered, and he had no wish at all to fall out with the Jesuits and their henchmen; the courage for a fight with the Jesuits over a "Jew" was already lacking in him, although he was one of the most liberal kings in Poland.

Learning that the Jesuits were preparing to carry out the execution of the Jew R' Elazar Verbover [as printed] without his consent, the king left his castle in the town of Grodno for a certain time and thereby gave the murderers a free hand to act as they saw fit; and when the only hope the Jews had placed in the good king, that he would avert the decree, was thus also lost, the Jews sought other means to ransom the Jew's life from the Jesuits' hands for a fortune of money, but in this too they did not succeed; the masters of the land demanded their own — that the Jew should convert — to which the Jews could not agree...

And reckoning that the Jews might yet succeed in obtaining the victim's release, the Jesuits began to hurry with the execution; feverishly the scaffold was set up on the market square, and on the second day of Shavuot, when the clock on the church had struck the twelfth hour, the condemned martyr was brought, forged hand and foot, in a faint, bent threefold and broken, and in the presence of thousands of onlookers he was laid upon a broad, long table with pointed nails sticking up from it, and the hangman, swinging his broad axe, quartered and hacked up the body of R' Elazar Verblover, and the bloody pieces of flesh were then hung up with pitchforks on tall pillory-posts around the corners of the town.

3.

After the execution the Grodno kehilla interceded and expended much effort at least to bring the dead body to a Jewish grave, and with the help of a great deal of money it succeeded in ransoming the "little pieces" of the martyr R' Elazar Verblover and burying them on Isru Chag of Shavuot, with great reverence, in the old cemetery, which is said to date back to the earliest times, when the Jews received the right to live in Grodno at the end of the 14th century (1389).

A quite ordinary tombstone stands at the head of the Grodno martyr, on which is found the inscription: "Here lies... our teacher R' Atezer [as printed; read Elazar] the martyr, son of R' Shlomo Verblover of blessed memory, who was killed and whose blood was shed for the public sanctification of the Name, Friday, the eve of the holy Sabbath, Isru Chag, 8 Sivan 5550"; and at Shavuot, at the memorial prayer for the dead (Hazkarat Neshamot), he used to be commemorated in the synagogue.
A Tale of a “-kowski” within a “-kowski”

In Nowy Sącz a certain person with a triple-barrelled name has been arrested: Jerzy-Stanisław Koszczeżyna[?]-Kakowski. The police were then searching for him all around, but he could by no means be found, because for a considerable time he had been hiding in the Częstochowa monastery of the Paulines, where he was received with open arms because he introduced himself as the nephew (brother's son) of Archbishop Kakowski; but there too he did not last long. One day he vanished from there, taking with him a good many gilded "sacred vessels" and the like. After that he made guest appearances in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Zawiercie and Königshütte [Królewska Huta], with beard and moustache shaved off, and with an R instead of a K, i.e. as Rakowski. In the end it very nearly paid off for him altogether, for he wormed his way in as a friend with a wealthy squire, S., on a manor farm beyond Łask; he made the squire's 17-year-old only daughter fall in love with him, and things were on the verge of the wedding canopy. But then it so happens that he insists on being a gentleman and buying the bride a present, and there is no cash to be had; so what does he do? He goes and steals from his future father-in-law a gold watch, 3 thousand złoty and a diamond pin. As the devil would have it, the lad gets found out, and he must, poor thing, "for our many disgraces" [a pun on "for our many sins"], take to his heels — feet and hands and all — and uproot himself once again...

Running off to Nowy Sącz, however, this time turned out "bokiem" for him [Polish: it backfired], because there he was arrested.
Lived to See Revenge

By Y. Oberzhanek.
Monologue of a Będzin merchant who has been blessed with a Cossack of a wife.
Revenge is a good thing. Yes, revenge is a tasty morsel. True, it is not at all a Jewish trait for a Jew like me, who thanks God when nobody bothers him. Here is a sign for you that I am far from revenge: to this very day I have not killed my matchmaker. I do believe I have no greater enemy than the matchmaker who paired me off with my woman of valour, and if I were a man who thirsts for revenge, I ought to have shot him long ago.
This week, however, I did live to see revenge. And on whom, do you think? You think perhaps on my landlord, who keeps chasing me with „eksmisje“ [eviction orders], or on my mother-in-law? God forbid — on my wife! On my own wife I have lived to see revenge. A real revenge at last, and let her know what it means to be a husband, let her too feel the taste of worry, of head-breaking, what it means to bear the yoke of a livelihood; yes, let her know. Revenge I now have on her. All husbands who have wives, and Cossack wives at that — there, to all those husbands I wish that they may live to see such a revenge as I have lived to see.
I am telling it to you precisely so that the husbands of such „Cossacks“ may draw a moral from it, and may they live to see what I have lived to see:
As you know, I am a Jew, a merchant — a war-merchant, that is. Before the war I was in the timber line: I stood with little sticks in the street.
During the war I went over from the timber line to other trades: I dealt in saccharin, in coconut butter, in tallow, in powidła [plum jam], in... in... in — ah, you know yourselves, I needn't tell you; I was quite a capable fellow, I became quite a big shot.
When the war came to a halt, what does one take up? What all Jews took up — manufacture [textiles]; but that is not what I am out to tell you. I only want to tell you about the recent period. As long as the „going“ kept going [„הלוך האט געילכט“ — apparently: as long as money and goods circulated][?], as long as the leading role in trade was played by the thumb, as long as the only cash-box was the bill-of-exchange blank, as long as one took [goods] on twelve months' credit and for the money taken in one discounted a little bill — so long was I, to my missus, a capable fellow, an energetic merchant, a man with a head, a go-getter whose equal the world did not have.
These last months, however, since people began complaining: „Little bundle, don't budge“ [the goods lie and do not move], since creditors and „komorniks“ [court bailiffs] began pouring in, since they sealed[?] and pasted the shelves over with lacquer-sealed strings, since I „cleared out“ [as one clears out leaven] the sideboard, together with the „pomocnik“ [the bailiff's assistant], out of the house — since then I have ceased, to my wife, to be a capable fellow, ceased to be a man with a head, ceased to be „energiczny“ [energetic]. All at once I became for her a shlimazl, a beaten-out hoshana [a threshed willow-twig], a cripple by the grace of His dear Name — I'm no longer good, says she, for anything...
What was the end of it? The end was that she, my missus, took over the reins. Since she had a deed of „intercyza“ [a marriage contract separating the spouses' property], she put herself up on the signboard. Me she dismissed altogether, and she set about settling accounts with the creditors. I'll see, said she, who will get one broken grosz out of me. And perhaps you think she did not keep her word? She indeed gave nobody a penny. No sooner did a creditor open the door and she opened her „głośnik“ [loudspeaker] on him, than he thanked God to be kissing the mezuzah from the other side of the door...
Since then I really do have a bright life: I know nothing of debts, no protests [of bills] interest me, I laugh at the komorniks and the „sekwestrators“ [tax distrainers]; I sleep on time, eat on time, read a newspaper, pray every day with the congregation — a paradise, do you hear, a paradise on earth.
So it's good, eh? What could be better? A wife works, bears the whole yoke of the livelihood, and you yourself don't put a hand in cold water; what could be better, eh? — It doesn't even begin to be. Would you relish sitting whole days at home, warming little bottles and giving a pair of twins their drink? Would you fancy turning, from a merchant whom people rated at a million in „obrotowy“ [turnover], all at once into a wet-nurse? Would you like to bear the yoke of a dinner; would you like, on a plain Wednesday, to harness yourself to a „wózek“ [pram] and ride with the pram to the New Market or up the „Górka“ [„the Hill“]? Would you like to beg your wife every day for a złoty for a packet of „Awanti“ [cigarettes]? Would you relish it if your wife had complaints against you: why don't I keep an eye on the shiksa [the gentile maid], why don't I watch that the dinner shouldn't burn? Would you like to sit and stitch socks, and in the morning go with the jug for milk? To go to the butcher's stall for meat — one male among nothing but women; go on, I should like to see whether you would feel like standing at the butcher's and begging him to give you a cut without a makeweight... Go on, that I should like to see.
But it is worth it: I have lived to see revenge on my wife, a real revenge at last; listen and enjoy:
Like every summer, my missus this year too rented a summer lodging. Ay, what does she need a summer lodging for? Who is going to stay in the summer lodging? Evidently she had clean forgotten that this year she wears the trousers.
The other day, when the sun began to warm, she says to me: You know what, you'll start getting ready to go out there.
Who should get ready? Go out where? — I had forgotten the whole business of the summer lodging.
Well, says she, to the summer lodging. Look over the linen, says she, see whether buttons are sewn on the children's little trousers, whether the hammock is in order, whether the „leżak“ [deck-chair] doesn't need repairing — this year, says she, you will be the „letnik“ [summer holiday-maker]!
Here I lived to see my revenge on her. Where is it written that for ever I should be the one, a whole summer long, worn out and melted away in town, while she fattens herself like a stuffed goose on the deck-chair?! Why indeed should I not rock a little in the hammock, and my wife melt for one summer in town? Is it really a law from Sinai that on Friday towards evening I should be the one crushed and suffocated on the train and arrive at the summer lodging like a drenched cat? Whence does it follow that a whole summer I should eat in town fever with chopped sores [i.e. nothing at all], and she, my wife, should tuck into poziomki [wild strawberries] with cream — whence does that follow?
This summer I shall lie on the deck-chair, rock in the hammock I shall, I shall eat wild strawberries with cream, and my wife will get it into her head. On Friday towards evening I shall put on my Sabbath kapote and go out to meet my wife; she will be laden like a mule with parcels, with suitcases. Every Friday I shall tell her how many pounds I have put on on the scales, what a fine dacha we have, how well the children are recuperating, what dearness there is, how dear milk is; I shall have complaints against her, why she brings so little money; I shall tell her how well I „amuse“ myself [„bawię się“] with the women neighbours. Sunday at daybreak, with the first train, she will grab the emptied valises and — off, back to town.
Ay, do you hear, I have lived to see revenge; she had a fancy to stand on the signboard. May all Cossacks in skirts end up so — a precious thing, this „revenge...
Spain and Portugal (The Pyrenean [Iberian] Peninsula)

[Article — history and geography; Spain and Portugal, first in a series.] By 'Gdud'.
In connection with the latest events in Spain and in Portugal, we shall give, in a series of articles, interesting details from the history of these 2 countries, which have inscribed themselves so bloodily in our own history.
More than 3 thousand years ago, when in most of Europe — on the site of today's nicely paved streets, well-tilled fields and intensively exploited mines — there stretched enormous dense forests and swamps, there was already in southern Spain a civilised settlement (by the notions of that time, of course), created by the travelling merchants, the Semitic Phoenicians.
Later, in the Middle Ages, an important culture of the Arabs arose here; they were, as is known, the first to devise the arithmetical numerals which, incidentally, we still use today. They were also innovators in the fields of geometry, algebra and others.
For the Spanish Jews this was then the golden epoch: materially — well-to-do, politically — enjoying equal rights, and culturally — the Jews of that time reached a high level. There lived then the poet R' Yehuda Halevi (author of the beautiful lament 'Zion, wilt thou not ask after the welfare of thy captives'), R' Shlomo Ibn Gabirol (author of the splendid piyyutim that are recited between Passover and Shavuot, such as that of the first Sabbath after Passover, 'A poor captive in a foreign land... every destruction has an end, but there is no end to my breaches. How long, O Lord, wilt Thou prolong my term? When will the voice of the turtledove be heard in my land?', that of the 2nd Sabbath, 'Our years are spent in poverty and disgrace... and the end of the fourth [kingdom] is hidden from every eye', those of the 3rd and 4th Sabbath, and many other yotzrot), Ibn Ezra, and the great philosopher, the greatest authority in the field of halakha — the Rambam [Maimonides].
In modern times America was discovered thanks to Spain's assistance, which contributed to the first voyage around the globe. Thanks to Portugal the sea route to India was found. In the first half of the 16th century Spain, under Emperor Charles V Habsburg, was the greatest monarchy in the world. To it belonged, besides all of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Holland and Italy, also the newly discovered lands in North and South America. In the 2nd half of the 16th century, under Emperor Charles's son, King Philip 2 Habsburg, Spain was smaller only by Germany and Austria-Hungary, where Philip's uncle Ferdinand ruled; the remaining kingdoms, on the other hand, continued to belong to Spain and are designated in all documents as belonging to the 'Spanish Monarchy'. Later a gradual decline begins, until it arrives at the situation of today.
It will not be superfluous, on this occasion, to acquaint our readers briefly with the geographical position, climate, trade, etc. of Spain and Portugal.
The geographical position.
The Pyrenean Peninsula is surrounded by water on 3 sides, namely: to the west and north-west lies the Atlantic Ocean. To the south — the Mediterranean Sea (on whose southern shore, opposite Spain, lie Morocco and North Africa) and the Strait of Gibraltar, through which the ships plying between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea and back must pass; to the east — the Mediterranean Sea; and finally to the north — the high, barely accessible mountain chains: the Pyrenees and others.
The Pyrenees divide Spain like an iron wall from France, which lies to the north of them; their forestless limestone crags, with their gloomy appearance, resemble the Spanish Jesuits: awe-inspiring, stubborn, hard towards every human culture and technology.
The area: its size and shape.
The Pyrenean Peninsula occupies an area of just under 600 thousand square kilometres. Of this, a scant 500 thousand square kilometres belong to Spain (not counting the colonies). By size it thus occupies the third place in Europe (after Soviet Russia and France). Portugal has only 90 thousand square kilometres.
3 quarters of the land are highlands, lying — on average — 640 metres above sea level.
Climate and vegetation.
The Pyrenean Peninsula has 3 kinds of climate; the central part has a pronounced continental climate. In summer the heat reaches up to 50 degrees, while in winter there are frosts of 10 degrees. Because of this no trees grow here, and the grass too is of a special kind — not juicy, hard, just like the grass of North Africa. The north-western part has a maritime climate, without too great heat in summer and without cold in winter. Here stretch splendid beech and oak forests, especially cork oaks, and also chestnut trees. The rest of the peninsula has a Mediterranean climate: warm, rainy winters and hot, rainless summers. Here grow southern fruits such as oranges, lemons and dates (the only date palms in Europe).

The Tragedy of the Jewish Merchant

Every death is a tragedy; suicide is a double tragedy, because the form of life is torn off suddenly and because such a death is always the end of a life's tragedy, of a misfortune that torments many of the living. Many times greater, however, is the tragedy of a suicide on account of the crisis, which casts a dark dread over almost everyone.
Fallen merchants there have always been, but the decline was never as sharp as it is today. And besides, such a man always had around him a circle, a family and good friends, who were able to help him out and not let him reach a state of despair.
Today, when someone falls, he has no one to help him; even communal aid has itself gone bankrupt. So the former rich man must live through the sufferings and pain of material want, when even the most necessary things are already beginning to be lacking, when before his eyes there already gapes the black abyss of complete poverty, when soon even the plain bite of bread will be missing. Into this are woven the terrible forlornness, the loneliness, which make loathsome a life that is hard and senseless as it is — suddenly the black melancholy attacks, and it is the end.
But the first cause of all these causes is the general crisis, which crushes and shakes up settled, well-founded life and is already calling forth the sad side-phenomena, the direct causes of the tragedy.
So we must remember the commandment of our Torah, which bids us help our brother even before he falls completely. We must revive within ourselves the atrophied feelings of comradely love, we must listen with more attentiveness to a comrade's stifled sigh, and not let his expressions of pain pass by with indifference.
We must, finally, revise our attitude to social aid of every kind; not let existing institutions vegetate, but, on the contrary, strengthen and enlarge the old ones.
The main thing, however: it all leads to our great and difficult political struggle for social and economic equality. Let only the atmosphere around us be cleansed a little, let only the specific pressure be lifted from over our heads, let us only get a little more air to breathe — and the number of such horrifying tragic cases will diminish of itself.
The fallen man will then find a firmer support in his surroundings.
P. K.
Shavuot

And after all that, we want to talk ourselves into believing that we are a "wise and understanding people" [am chacham ve-navon], when in fact we are real scatterbrains[?] ["plutes"], hotheads. We grab at everything and do not even listen to what is being said to us; with us the "we will do" [na'aseh] always comes before the "we will hear" [nishma]...
You are walking, little Jews, in a wilderness; you have in your pocket an ironclad "certificate" from the Creator of the World Himself to come to the Land of Israel — so why on earth do you go crawling up mountains?...
And once we had come to the mountain, you already know what happened next: they got us in under the mountain, just as a milliner gets a lady into her shop; there they tried a "little hat" on our heads and gave a thunderclap — if you take the Torah, fellows, well and good; and if not, the "little hat" gets a tug down over your eyes and you will never again see the bright world...
In this way we no longer had any choice and clinched the deal — and that is called a "Giving of the Torah"![?]
But had we gone then in the ways of Uncle Ishmael, it would have been good for us and it would have been good for them.
We would have been spared the drudgery of becoming "podryadchiks" [contractors, purveyors] and supplying them with religions, and they would have been spared thanking us for it with crusades, pogroms and the like...
And then, what would the Bolsheviks look like with their "war against God"? The "Yevsektsiya" [the Jewish section of the Communist Party] would simply have gone mad from walking about idle...
And as for the missionaries, it goes without saying: if there had been no Torah, where would they have got verses to twist?...
And the American Reform rabbis would to this day still be sitting in the shops sewing underwear — what would they have reformed?...
And the Polish Minister of Education, the overseer of the religious communities, would have been spared sweating over the "Shulchan Aruch"...
In short: if our forefathers had not been in such a hurry, things would now be a little merrier for us — not for nothing is it our custom to eat dairy on Shavuot, just as in the Nine Days..
Shavuot is, it seems, a fine holiday, a precious holiday. My grandmother — may she have a bright Paradise there — even[?] used to say: the best holiday the Jews have, far better than Passover or Sukkot; for on Passover you may eat where you like but may not eat what you like, and on Sukkot you may eat what you like but may not eat where you like, whereas Shavuot is a sheer delight: you may eat where you like and what you like, even dairy — on the contrary, the mitzvah is all the greater, and it is healthier for the stomach and for the pocket...
And nevertheless — may I not be punished for these words — I am no great devotee of Shavuot; on the contrary, this holiday casts a black melancholy over me...
Just imagine, a few thousand years ago, at this season, that is, on the eve of Shavuot, before the Giving of the Torah — what did we lack then?
We were truly free birds, a people equal to all peoples, without worries, without troubles and without that "Thou hast chosen us" [Atah bechartanu], which sticks in our throat like a bone to this day...
No small thing — Jews without a Jewish question!
True, the Land-of-Israel problem was on the agenda then too; then too we had a "Declaration" to build a "national home" in the Holy Land, but that was no "Bluffer"[?] Declaration from England [pun: Balfour / bluffer], but a declaration from His Majesty the King of Kings Himself, who spoke plain words to our father Abraham — "the land is for you and your children forever"...
Of closing the gates there could be no talk at all — what sort of figure did closed gates cut with us in those days? You can see how impressed we were by the closed gates of Jericho — walked around and around a few times, gave a blast, and that was the end of the closed gates...
And if anti-Zionists turned up in our own ranks, who longed for the fish they had eaten in Egypt, there was a ready verdict for them: "to rot in the wilderness"...
In a word: that was an eve of Shavuot — may we all have such a year; but Shavuot itself — who asked them, our forefathers, to go crawling to Mount Sinai?...
You think that if we had not taken the Torah we would not have been given the Land of Israel? Nothing of the kind — our father Abraham had obtained the Declaration hundreds of years before the Giving of the Torah.
And perhaps you will tell me: we were young, we had no sense? One learns from one's elders: we saw — Uncle Ishmael does not want it, Brother Esau has no desire for it — so one does the same as they...
And you can indeed see that they came off better than we did — we took the Torah, and the Land of Israel has remained with them after all: Brother Esau has spread himself out there as if at home, and tickles[?] Uncle Ishmael...
Y. G. Shteinsapir.

A Spoiled Eve of Shavuot

Dedicated to the friends of my youth who live today in Będzin.
In these times, when at the market one can buy everything one needs and everything one fancies, without any toil or trouble, my recollections of my childhood years will surely be of interest — in my native shtetl of Słomniki, where nobody knew of buying ready-made matzah meal for dumplings, ready-bound willow twigs for "hoshanos", and least of all ready-cut greenery for Shavuot, which everyone, without exception, had to procure for himself straight from nature...
The burden of procuring greenery for Shavuot the toil-worn parents usually laid upon us, the children; but if for the parents it was a burden, for us it was one of the merriest and happiest of occupations, for which we children used to hope for weeks and months...
Right after Passover, when it had only just begun to turn green in the fields and on the banks of the river, curiosity had already begun to peck in our hearts too — to cast a glance and see how things stood with the "tatarakes" [tatarak — sweet flag, calamus], or, as they are called in some places, "kvitshers", which grow by the river bank and in the water-swamps. Among us children these grasses were called nothing other than "Shavuot grass", and we were certain that this was their correct botanical name...
I was the only one among all my friends who had the possibility of observing day by day the growth of the Shavuot grass, because we lived a little way off from the town, near the great meadow and the river, where there was an abundance of Shavuot grass. My parents were also good acquaintances of the porets [the squire], to whom all this belonged, and I myself was on familiar terms with his big dogs, which cast terror upon other children. About my observations I used to tell my friends every day in the cheder and in the beit midrash, and together with the growth of the Shavuot grass our hearts grew with joy and pride.
You surely remember the passages in the Gemara where the ceremonies and rejoicing are described with which, in olden times in the Land of Israel, the omer was reaped and the first fruits were brought to Jerusalem. With no less joy and pomp did we children also use to cut greenery for Shavuot and willows for "hoshanos".
But more than anywhere else the joy and merriment resounded in our house, because at my place was the assembly point of the friends before setting out for the traditional occupation, and at my place the division of the green spoils also took place.
In my young, scholarly-fantastic little head there was always painted a comparison between our house and that place below Jerusalem where, according to the Gemara, people from the surrounding little towns came together to reap the omer in company...
It goes without saying that on account of all this I played the first role in the "field campaign". I was the leader, the expert, and also the vanguard, to guard the gang against the squire, against his big dogs and against "all sorts" of wicked peasant boys who were to be found in the surrounding fields. The second, also very important role was played by our friend Chaiml, a son of the pious Sore Zisl. (About the pious Sore Zisl it would be worth writing a separate monograph.) This Chaiml distinguished himself by the strength of his hands and by great energy. He alone among us all was not afraid to lean out far from the bank and cut the finest Shavuot grasses, which grew over there, out in the water. The other friends were merely ordinary helpers in the holy work.
Only once, I remember, was the joy of the eve of Shavuot spoiled for us in a fatal manner.
It was a glorious, beautiful May day. The sun was shining, the sky deep blue, the fields green, the meadow many-coloured and the air filled with scents of lilac, with the pleasant twittering of all sorts of little birds — all this excited and bewitched our young, fluttering hearts so that it gave us no rest.
On the eve of Shavuot, first thing in the morning, against the will of my mother, I snatched from the dining room the good "motzi" knife [the knife for cutting the challah] and dashed off with the gang to the meadow to cut Shavuot grass by the river.
And do you think the cutting was such an easy thing? The sweet flags have, after all, this nature — that precisely the finest ones grow in the water, far from the bank, and every incautious bend smells of the danger of falling into the water. But for that we already had a remedy. Perhaps you still remember from the Russian chrestomathies what remedy the old peasant hit upon who could not pull out of the earth a deeply rooted turnip: he pulled the turnip, the old peasant woman pulled the peasant, the old uncle pulled the peasant woman, the old aunt pulled the old uncle, and so on, until the turnip was pulled out. The same remedy we applied so that our friend Chaiml should not slip into the water.
And it came to pass on that eve of Shavuot: Chaiml cuts with the "motzi" knife and leans over the water without any fear; I pull at a flap of his little kaftan, Ozer — at a flap of my little kaftan, Berish — at a flap of Ozer's little kaftan, and so a long string of friends stretched right into the meadow. Suddenly a rip is heard, and at once a splash in the water, and we all tumble over, heads down and feet in the air... An outcry, a scream... I was left with a [piece of?] [—] alpaca kaftan in my hand, and Chaiml, with my "motzi" knife, was drowning[?] in the water.
But a miracle happened: the wave gave him a push[?] back towards the bank, and the heroic Chaiml caught hold of a thin little tree and got himself out onto the bank...
Dejected and ashamed, we led the dunked friend Chaiml home, and I received my sentence only in the evening at the table, when it was discovered that the good "motzi" knife had, through my fault, been drowned.
That unlucky eve of Shavuot was for us a moral lesson: that a mother must be obeyed, that a "motzi" knife must not be taken along, and that instead of holding on to the flaps of thin little kaftans it is better and safer to gird oneself with belts and to hold one another by the belt...
Kielce. H. Niebelski.

Ruth.
It is already the fate of the "Book of Books", of the Tanakh, that it should be classic and exemplary in all its parts, not only for its own time — but for all generations and times.
Ruth — the green book. The breath is caught by the blessed scent of field and earth that is borne from every passage, from every word.
The eyes are struck by the fresh, green gleam of grass and tree, the golden barn of ripe grain.
Simple, modest, unaffected, and yet how enchantingly beautiful! What splendid wreaths of colour-rich flowers this heroine weaves for us with her heartfelt, devoted declaration of love to Naomi, to her people and God, her mighty and self-sacrificing words: — "Thy people — my people, and thy God — my God". One may therefore call it by the name "the book of proselytes", i.e.[?] the book of gerim.
Yet[?] Ruth has in it still other elements, which are closely bound up with the open-hearted[?] proselytism of Ruth, but which also form[?] separate chapters in themselves. One of such chapters is certainly Boaz.
Moved by Ruth's noble deed, he resolves to redeem her for himself by buying up Naomi's estates, even if he should have to pay over the price. His heart pounds within him lest the diamond be snatched by a nearer kinsman of Naomi, who has more right of redemption; and he is egoistically pleased when that one puffs himself up with empty pedigree and, on account of the "Moabitess", does not wish to redeem the brother's estates.
Is it not the same problem of "redeeming" the poor and beautiful Ruth by buying up the estates? Shall there really not be found someone, a "hero", as the book crowns Boaz, in whom conscience would "turn back" from the "fields of Moab" to the "Jewish home" of "Bethlehem in Judah", and who would say, like that Boaz: "Im yig'alekh tov yig'al, ve-im lo — u-ge'altikh" (if Tov will redeem you; if not — then I shall redeem you)?
Meanwhile, until now, the only Boaz who says it is the Jewish people in its poorer strata. The great ones, the Boazes — they are still silent.
Yosef Avrekh.

From the Ten Commandments.
a) "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt."
When Moses heard God say "I am" [Anokhi], he made the blessing: "Blessed be He who has not made me a gentile." [Midrash Peliah.
This puzzling midrash [midrash peliah] becomes intelligible through an idea of the Taz [Turei Zahav] (Orach Chaim, 46): that this is why we say in the blessing, "Praised art Thou, God, who hast not made us gentiles." Why do we not simply say: "Praised art Thou, God, who hast created us Jews"? Because — explains the Taz — to thank God for having created us Jews? Is it then so good for Jews?... Ah, "it were better not to have been created"... To be a Jew is not good either, only it is worse still to be a gentile... Therefore we give thanks only for the negative, "who has not made me a gentile," and not for "who has made me an Israelite"...
When Moses heard God stress "who brought thee out" and not "who created thee," it evidently follows that for creating us we have little to thank Him for... so he made the blessing "who has not made me a gentile" and not "who has made me an Israelite."
Imrei Tzaddikim (R. Meir A"Sh)
—o—
b) "Thou shalt not bow down to them, nor serve them."
A missionary succeeded in catching a Jewish soul for a big coin [a handsome sum]. The Jew agrees to become a gentile, and the missionary tells him: From today on you shall no longer be called Yekl; Ivan is your name — remember! And also, meat you may not eat on Friday, only fish you may — remember!
— Good.
One Friday the missionary drops in on the convert at home and finds him over a bowl of meat... He then berates him: Is that what you call a pious gentile?...
— Don't be so angry; you surely remember how you told me that I am no longer called Yekl but Ivan — so I said the same to the meat: you are no longer called meat, but fish... and fish one may eat, after all... if it is a matter of changing the name...
—o—
c) "Honour thy father and thy mother — that thy days may be long."
Why is "that thy days may be long" promised with no [other] commandment?
The meaning is: hold your parents in honour, do not push them about when they come to old age, because — "that thy days may be long": you too will one day grow old... "Unto thee also shall the cup pass"...
A popular saying [veltsvertl].
—o—
The Torah.
d) Torah and wine.
In Midrash and Talmud the Torah is likened to wine. And today too it is like today's wine. We have wine today that is wonderfully finely coloured, handsome in appearance, fragrant from afar, exceedingly sweet — only there is no wine in it... merely counterfeit...
Such Torah-Jews we have today as well: the Torah is fragrant on them from afar, finely coloured, but it is no Torah... counterfeit...
Osem Bosem.

e) The evil inclination and the Torah...
Once R. Yekele Blendover [of Błędów] runs about his room clapping his hands as though he wanted to catch someone; so he chases the unseen Adversary [baal-dovor, Satan], runs up to the bookcase and snaps his fingers: Lost!
— I was chasing about after the evil inclination — he later explained to his Hasidim — I had already almost caught him, and here I have him already, I almost had him — when he made a dash into the bookcase. To hide himself in the Torah — and here, ah, here[?], he is well hidden indeed... The best point of escape for the evil inclination is the Torah.
—o—
f) On a low mountain indeed, but not in a valley...
The Torah was given on Mount Sinai to show that one must not hold oneself great on account of the Torah, since Sinai was the lowest mountain. The question arises: if so, then why was the Torah not given in a valley, which would have been the true symbol of lowliness?
The answer is: to find oneself in a valley, to be truly a nothing — it is no feat to hold oneself low; one really is nothing... Whereas to stand on the mountain, having climbed the rungs of the spirit, and yet to be humble — that is the symbol of a Torah scholar.
Likutim Chadashim.

g) Torah and... money.
"Thy word is very pure, and Thy servant loveth it" (Psalms 140 [sic; Ps. 119:140]).
Rabbi Meirl of Premishlan [Przemyślany] interpreted the verse thus: "Thy word is tzerufah" — Thy Torah must be [print: "mit zayn"] joined, brought together — "me'od" — with money (me'od = wealth)... One cannot sit and study and fulfil the Torah when one is a poor man. Therefore: "and Thy servant loveth it" — your friend has no dislike of money...
Margenita de-R. Meir.

h) If one grows weary of the Torah...
Two merchants come to a town: one a diamond merchant, the other deals in iron. Both carry travelling-bags of samples. The valises look alike, but inside one lie diamonds and in the other — iron. Handing their valises to porters to carry, the diamond merchant notices that his porter is sweating and tiring. It is too heavy for him. — He says to him: Ah, you must have made a mistake and switched the valise, for carrying diamonds one does not sweat, they are light; this must surely be the valise of iron...
"But thou hast not called upon Me, O Jacob; for thou hast been weary of Me, O Israel" — if "thou hast been weary, Israel", if you have grown [weary — the word is missing in the print], Israel, with the Torah, it is a sign that "thou hast not called upon Me", that it was not Me you meant; one does not grow weary from Torah. Diamonds are no burden. It is a sign that you have exchanged the Torah — diamonds for iron and heavy stones...
Rabbi Yaakov Kranz [the Maggid of Dubno].

Ruth.
i) "And a man went from Bethlehem in Judah" (1:1).
Elimelech [print: "Avimelekh"] stole out of Bethlehem in Judah as "a man", as an unknown. He was afraid, typical rich man that he was, that if it became known that a rich man was emigrating, poor folk and relatives would come for parting-money [letsgelt]; so he stole away quietly, unnoticed. "Va-tavo va-tachmod" [so printed; should read "va-ta'amod", "and she came and stood", Ruth 2:7]: Ruth stood a whole day in Boaz's field. Truly a wonder — what woman can stand so long in one place?...

What's New in Zagłębie?
Thursday, 5 Sivan 5691 / czwartek 21 maja 1931
Będzin
The Będzin kehilla got a samovar for the holiday — and lost its cantor...
About two weeks ago the municipal mikveh was closed by order of the authorities. (The old one, naturally, for the new one is only just beginning to be built...) The lessee of the mikveh turned many times to those "who look after the upholding of religion", asking them to put things in order so that the mikveh would be reopened; but those who fight against the "enemies of religion" had more important matters to settle, especially before the kehilla elections, and — it goes without saying — did not see to it that the mikveh was opened.
The "situation" was saved by our kehilla president, who is a strong adherent of the old system... He advised the mikveh lessee to travel to Żarki and take from the mikveh there a "pattern" (wzór) of the samovar.
The lessee fulfilled his mission, travelled to Żarki and brought back a samovar for the Będzin kehilla...
But at the same time the Będzin kehilla was left without a synagogue cantor. Mr Zhupovitsh [Żupowicz?], who had been so harassed, has been engaged as cantor in the Kraków synagogue named "Ahavat Re'im", where he will already be leading the prayers this Shavuot.
—o—
A 12-year-old girl run over.
On Monday evening a lorry ran into the 12-year-old Orzhal [?]. The girl was injured and is in hospital.
—o—
The post-office and station buildings are to be opened next month.
This week a commission delegated by the Ministry of Railways was here; after acquainting itself with the work on the new station building, it decided that the station should already be opened on 15 June.
The Minister of Railways, Kühn, is also to take part in the opening.
In the first days of June the new post-office building on Kościuszki Street is to be opened as well.

The little denunciation did not succeed..
The fighters against the "enemies of religion" did not remain in anyone's debt, and just before "Ne'ilah" [at the last moment] sent in a little denunciation against the technical bloc of the Zionist and Mizrachi lists.
The denunciation, signed by the well-known Mr Kaminer, was considered at the special session of the election commission on Monday evening.
When Messrs Skoczylas and Rinski saw that they were in the minority, they walked out of the hall in the middle of the vote.
The chairman establishes that there is a quorum, and the denunciation is rejected.

Identity cards for the merchants who call in customers.

After the Kehilla Elections in Olkusz

(A letter from Olkusz).
Our little town, which numbers in all 560 Jewish votes, was represented at the last kehilla elections by a front of 10 lists with no fewer than 160 candidates.
7 lists suffered defeat, some because of the election ordinance, which mercilessly harmed lists that had a considerable number of votes, and because of 1 vote fell out entirely.
3 lists received a number of mandates such as they themselves had not even dreamed of.
This is, God forbid, not because of the great influence that the "victors" have over the Jews of Olkusz. For as always, now too no political or cultural idea had any say in the elections. Not even an economic one. The biggest and strongest slogan, which embraces a large number of voters, is "do nothing". Let all Jewish buildings — the synagogue, the beit midrash, the mikveh — collapse, let the Talmud Torah be a mockery and a disgrace, as long as the "dozores" [kehilla board members] take no money, grab nothing. All other slogans the Jews of Olkusz can forgo, but the slogan of "do nothing" was strongly embraced. That was the current coin at the elections.
And the saddest thing is that almost all the non-elected councillors perhaps also belong to that sort of people who have no standpoint at all, stand powerless, and do not know what to undertake in the kehilla. This has clearly confirmed their dissatisfaction with their election. What do I need it for? Why do I need this trouble?
It is characteristic that of the 160 candidates nobody even had the courage to explain to the voters what their tasks in the kehilla would be. Without enlightenment, without agitation, without struggle — quietly, hush, without commotion the elections went by. The defeat of the Zionist list must not be understood as a failure of the Zionist idea in Olkusz, because the list had nothing at all to do with Zionism nor with the Zionist programme for the kehilla. The slogan "Conquer the kehillas" is altogether foreign to the representatives of the list and its activists; the list was created in the street, without any connection to Zionism and without forethought.
But, Zionists of Olkusz! The blame falls on you when you leave such a matter to such "strong" Zionist leaders, who a short time ago, during the city council elections, had the chutzpah to serve the list of the "Agudah" publicly; or when the whole of Zionist work consists of praying in the so-called Zionist premises, and in all the time of your praying you have not found it necessary to pledge even a single grosz to the Keren Kayemet. Well, can one hope for Zionist victories from such lists?
M. Sh.

He Writes an Engagement Contract with a Girl in Sosnowiec — and Has a Wife with 4 Children in Zgierz.
In Warsaw there was a well-known house painter, Shlomo Knobel. He did not consider himself an ordinary "malarz" [painter], but an artist. He wore long hair and a broad black cravat and kept company with writers; when he painted the rooms in dark colours he then considered himself a humorist. He also decorated Dr. Gotlib's apartment, and then he considered himself a publicist, and so on.
This Shlomo Knobel went so far in his megalomania that his wife Feige, from Mazowieck, began to disgust him.
Ah, Knobel had lived with her for twelve years already, squandered the dowry and, the main thing, had 4 little children [printed "kider"] with her — that hardly bothered Shlomo the artist.
Knobel put on a pair of American spectacles, tied his cravat even wider and began to "frequent" better society. The painting work no longer suited him either, and in the middle of a bright Wednesday he became a music conductor.
"Ah, you robber," people argued with him, "you understand music like a goat at a shalom zachar!" That did not bother him either, and he went on styling himself Conductor Knobel.
Meanwhile in Knobel's home they began to go hungry; the painter's ladders stood orphaned, and the conductor's baton could by no means conjure up any bread. So Shlomo the painter-conductor thought it over, quietly sold off everything sellable from the house and vanished completely from Warsaw, leaving his wife and children. In addition he tricked her out of the copy of the "akt ślubny" [marriage certificate] she had with her.
They looked for Shlomo, but he was gone; people said he had run off to Łódź. So the wife sold the remaining bit of belongings and came to Zgierz, where she settled with her family.
Meanwhile the wife Feige from Kalibiel-Mazowieck [Kołbiel?] received an engagement card sent from Sosnowiec, where it is written black on white that the conductor Shlomo Knobel is signing, in good luck, an engagement contract with Miss Chana S.
The unhappy woman, who is literally dying of hunger, asks that Sosnowiec be informed that she has documents [of marriage] with her husband and that nobody should marry him.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — accident.] A motor accident.
In Żory a motor accident occurred on Monday. A passenger car crashed into a tree, and the result is a terrible one: the driver was killed on the spot, and 3 passengers were seriously injured.
—o—
A „znachor“ (quack healer) punished.
[Katowice — court.] Before the district court in Katowice there stood a certain Józef Bral, who had been charged with healing sick people with his own „prescriptions“.
In court the accused defended himself by saying that he had done it because he is unemployed.
The court sentenced the „znachor“ to 3 months in prison. After the verdict Bral asked that the sentence should take effect only in the winter months, since — he said — he would be warm in prison...
—o—
The „Latowice“ [sic; read Katowice] fair opened.
[Katowice — economy.] On the 22nd of this month the 2nd Katowice fair was opened in Katowice. At the opening there were present representatives of the local authorities, deputies of the Silesian Sejm, etc. — Opening speeches were delivered by the president of the Katowice Chamber of Commerce and the president (mayor) of Katowice.
The fair (targ) is very richly represented with kiosks (pavilions) of the largest Polish firms; especially outstanding are the kiosks of Kołłątaj soap and of Sommerfeld's instrument manufactures.
—o—
Shot his fiancée and then himself.
[Gleiwitz — crime.] In Gleiwitz (Gliwice) a young man shot his fiancée and then himself. The reason for the double murder is this: the groom was unemployed, and his fiancée had thrown him over because of it.

Further mass dismissals.
[Upper Silesia — labour.] The dismissals of workers in the Upper Silesian coal mines and factories continue. In the course of the week larger dismissals took place at the „Bali Szarlej“ mine, at the „Król“ steelworks (huta) and at the „Elektroliza“ works.

„Hakoach“—K.S. 07 Siemianowice 0:1.
The Silesian league team did not show what we had expected of it[?]. Had it not been for the weakened line-up of the Będzin side, the result would have been even more favourable for „Hakoach“. „Prybica“[?]—„Maccabi“ 1:0[?].

Ring (Chain Donation Drive)

[Będzin — charity, health.] For the benefit of sending sick people to a cure (kuracja).
Year in, year out, at the beginning of summer, the board of the Charity Society in Będzin occupies itself with the necessary action of supporting respectable (genteel) sick people who need a cure.
This year too the action is being renewed. In connection with this we have received the following appeal from the board of the Charity Society:
Most esteemed and honourable citizenesses and citizens!
The Jewish Charity Society in Będzin turns to you, in the name of the poorest, unfortunate respectable sick people, for help. The situation of the needy is much more serious than in previous years, because many sick people used to receive support from the Magistrate (municipality), but owing to a shortage of money the Magistrate has this year struck out the subsidy for this purpose.
We therefore ask you, honourable citizenesses and citizens, to support with a generous hand the help-ring (chain of donations), so as to enable the poor sick to enjoy fresh air or a cure, which secures them further existence.
The first donation, of 100 zł., is given by Mrs. Cesia Szejn, and she challenges the ladies: M. Szpigelman, J. Szpigelman, J. Gutman, S. Gutman, B. Gutman, J. M. Kurland, J. Hutner, A. Kramałowski, J. Ch. Merin, L. Bauszykowska[?] of Kołłątaj.
Stepchildren

[Poland — Jews in the judiciary; discrimination.] Dr. Jakub Wygodzki.
If it is so hard today for a Jewish doctor to obtain a state post in Poland, it is a great deal harder still for a Jew who has completed the faculty of law to make his way to a state post, or even just to receive a penny of salary so as to be able to "devote himself entirely to the work in the court.
It goes without saying that one cannot take into account here the exception that is made for the few "Żydki" [derogatory: "Yids"] who trade so floridly with their Jewishness. On the contrary — this underlines all the more the unfortunate situation of the young Jewish jurists in comparison, for instance, with the famous "directors" who make of their ugly betrayal an "ideological" little livelihood...
When a Pole completes the faculty of law, then, if he does not take up some other state post, he is admitted as an aplikant [judicial trainee] at the court (or at the general public prosecutor's office), where he works for three years; without this aplikantura a jurist cannot become a professional: neither a judge nor an advocate! Only the completed aplikantura opens for him the way to the judiciary or to the bar. For every Pole the way to the aplikantura is open; for Jews, however, this way is a thorny one: he must sometimes wait for years until he is admitted as an aplikant.
The courts in Poland have a considerable number of paid posts (etaty) for aplikants, in which the latter, receiving a salary, are not forced to look for other employment and can therefore devote themselves entirely to their aplikantura work.
In Congress Poland it is impossible for Jews who do not bend their Jewish nationality to obtain a salaried post; that is, here it is relatively easier to obtain the aplikantura, but obtaining a salaried post is very hard for a Jew and very rarely succeeds, while the Polish aplikants almost all receive the post.
Once, under the governments of the "reactionary Endeks" [National Democrats], a kind of "numerus clausus" was introduced for the Jewish aplikants: from five to seven Jewish aplikants used to receive the salaried post. If one of them left the post, another Jew would be appointed in his place. Now, however, the salaried posts are being cleansed of Jews more and more! One is passing from numerus clausus to numerus nullus.
Every salaried aplikant, on entering the service, signs an undertaking (declaration) to serve in the judiciary; therefore, after completing the court examination, they receive from the president of the Court of Appeal a notice in a set official formula: "Since you have passed the examination, I appoint you judge, or deputy, or assessor, etc.
So it is with Poles. How it happens with Jews we shall soon see from the following fact, for which I take full responsibility upon myself and which throws a bright light on the real state of Jewish equal rights in Poland...
At the end of 1929 two Jewish aplikants, after a year of waiting and unpaid work, received the salaried post; in doing so they had to sign an undertaking to remain in the judiciary after completing the aplikantura. One of the two lucky young Jewish jurists who were privileged to receive the post is well known as a scholarly researcher of Polish writers, especially of Mickiewicz, whose works are printed also in the serious Polish journals; he served in the Polish army during the war of 1920. The second young jurist who received the post is also a well-known young man with the best references in court circles; he served in the Polish army as a volunteer (ochotnik) in the Wilno regiment in 1919—1920 and took part in the capture of Wilno. Both young jurists are decent people without any reproach.
In January 193[—] the two aplikants passed the examination. 13 men were examined then, of them 5 Jews.
After the examination the president invited the Polish aplikants to his office and proposed to all of them that they take up posts at the court. To the two salaried Jews the president declared that they must submit their resignation — they would not get any posts! When the two Jewish aplikants, pointing to the undertaking they had signed at the time to remain at the court, refused to submit their resignation — the president of the Court of Appeal informed them two days later that they had been "released" from service!
With the non-salaried Jewish aplikants they did not want to talk at all!..
As a Polish citizen I must after all ask: where is the Polish Constitution? Where is Article 96 of this Constitution on the "equality of all citizens before the law"? This is, after all, the fundamental article of the Constitution and the cornerstone of democracy in all modern constitutions!
This legal requirement is, after all, the expression of that "minimal morality" which is necessary to make the living-together of human beings possible! What kind of "moral healing" can possibly take place when such a requirement is renounced?
Further I must ask: since when has the Polish March Constitution of 1921 acquired such an optional character: sometimes one observes it and sometimes one transgresses it? If so, there is simply no need to amend the Constitution, since it lets itself be "adapted to life" and to any changes whatsoever!...
After the election fair

[Zagłębie — kehilla elections; Agudah; Sosnowiec.] The kehilla elections in Zagłębie brought unexpected results for the national lists. The "Agudah" [Agudat Israel], which had organised lists under various "firms", came out damaged, and the number of its mandates is barely a third of the total number.
The result had a strong echo on both days of Shavuot in all the shtiblekh and minyanim, and the main conversation was devoted to the election result.
In the shtiblekh where the goal had not been reached there was agitation; people investigated and inquired who the traitors had been, and as soon as it was discovered which one was the traitor, he was sent off with "great parade"...
A big scandal also took place in the Gerer shtibl when the "co-editor" of the "Mikveh Organ" rebuked the Tseirim [Agudah youth] for being rebellious against the "Agudah".
The Tseirim did not keep silent either and said to him, to the "editor", so to speak, that "for a few guilders you would sell yourself even to the Communists"...
In Sosnowiec the "Agudah" pulled schemes [lit. "worked deeds"] to get the 14th mandate. The election commission held a special session on the matter and by 8 votes to 4 it was recognised for the porters.
The Agudah men nevertheless did not desist from their work, and on Friday at daybreak a delegation went off to Będzin to take counsel with Mr. Riński [?].
The porters, learning that the "fine" Jews had gone to Będzin to intervene at the starostwo [district office], also hurried to Będzin, and still caught the "fine" Jews on their way to the starostwo.
On Sączewska [?] Street the delegation was stopped, and thanks to that their mission was not carried out over Shavuot.
A great sensation was the election result of the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association. The association, which counts nearly 900 members, got through only 1 mandate... As rumour has it, several hundred artisans have been "infected" with the same disease as the leaders up to now...
Telephone calls Zagłębie—Paris

[Sosnowiec — post and telephone; Chamber of Commerce.] Last week, on the initiative of the Post Directorate in Kraków, a conference took place in which representatives of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce also took part.
At the conference, among other things, the proposal of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce was also discussed, that the project of telephone calls from Zagłębie to Paris be realised.
The director of the Post Directorate declared in reply that negotiations on this are under way with the postal administration in Paris, and it is to be hoped that within a month the plan will be realised.

[Sosnowiec — attack; demonstrators.] On the road from Jaworzno to Sosnowiec a crowd of demonstrators attacked with stones the car in which the director of the Radocha factory, Dr. Likiernik, was travelling with his family.
