What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton.] Conveyed by Ben Amotz.

Kosher guests.
We Jews are a people that has nothing but grievances; we are not content with the "favours" that are done for us. We constantly go looking for injustices, exactly as if we were "at father's in the vineyard."
But what did we come to talk about! Here we have in our town a "Górka," where every mortal, if he only has 15 groszy, can refresh himself with fresh air, and what is more, if he has 30 gr. he can also bring in his suckling infant.
What would we do, for example, if, God forbid, the owners of the "Górka" took it into their heads to hang such an inscription at the entrance:
— "Entrance forbidden to Jews"..
What would the great number of Jewish visitors do? Ha, you say the till would suffer? Firstly, we know that wherever we are driven out, that is exactly where we push in all the more; and secondly, where would we draw fresh air — perhaps soak in the benzine smells in the square on the New Market?
Yes, but what did we come to talk about? We mean the new "secret," which by chance was discovered this week.
The "secret" is this: a Jewish young lady, a teacher, applied to the chief proprietor of the "Górka" to issue her a season ticket, as all the non-Jewish women teachers have — and she received the answer that according to the regulations only Catholic women can receive season tickets...
Well, should we not [be] "grateful" to the "air monopolists," who allow us to breathe freely for 15 groszy? It is bad and bitter when people think it over and dig out a paragraph saying that only their own may enter the "Górka," "z naszych" [of ours] in the plain sense of the word.
— Kosher guests...

"Betzidkho" [sic] — gathering of waters.
Pity on them, on those who pray in "Shmedrish." Once again they will have to wait a full 5 years to reach their goal.
For 7 round years they have been suffering, the "Shmedrishniks": they have no water, no decent ceiling, no whole floor, and often also — no light...
Well then, what does King Solomon say? To everything there is a season — for all things the time comes; and the time indeed came when "Shmedrish" went out into the street with a fight against the old kehilla, against the house of the dead [the purification house], against the disorder of no water and no ceiling...
When Satan saw that the "Shmedrish" people too had strayed from the straight path, he — Satan, that is — declared:
— "No! Shmedrish must stay as it was"...
Then the "Sitra Achra" [the Other Side] prevailed and asked for a "flood" to "drown" the "Shmedrish list"...
And if you talk with such a "Shmedrishnik," he tells you that they were harmed because of the sins of the "Agudah."
"By their righteousness — a gathering of waters"...

Small traders with great attainments
..."Vote for our list! Our candidates will defend you in the kehilla; small traders — you will not be burdened with an 'etat' [tax quota]."
Eh, nonsense, answers the voter.
— Perhaps you need a "pożyczka" [loan]?
— No, I don't need one.
— What do you want, then? ask the canvassers.
— I need to be helped..
— A "dolarówka" premium [prize on the dollar bond]?
— Not that either...
One of the canvassers suddenly puts a question to the voter:
— And perhaps a male child?...
— You have guessed it exactly...
And when two canvassers of the Small Traders' Association "assured" him that Sarah Sheindel would be helped with a male child, the voter went off with great joy to the ballot box.

The zealous hasten...
At the giving of the Torah the "fine Jews" hastened ahead, and before they had even heard what was demanded, they cried out:
— We will do!
The zeal has remained for generations: men of Moses, pious Jews, like the Agudah people for example, do not wait for the reward of any commandment whatsoever, but are always ready and hurry to fulfil the "Ten Commandments" which were given
— in Frankfurt...
And if any of you, dear readers, saw on the first day of Shavuot early in the morning how several Jews dressed in holiday clothes were running from Sosnowiec to Będzin, do not, God forbid, suspect them of hurrying over weekday business; no, these were people who were going to fulfil the "chief commandment" of the Agudah
— "masorovatshu" [?; apparently a Polonized form of mesirah, informing to the authorities]...
But a mishap occurred. Already close to Mount Sinai — pardon, I mean already at the doors of the Starostwo [district office] — they were met by some "spies," who bear the name "Tregers" [?], and these spies said to them:
— "If you accept — if you heed our words and go back to Sosnowiec — well and good; and if not, if not — here it shall be... we will give you here 'what you deserve'...
The holy emissaries of the Sosnowiec Agudah took fright and said:
— Turn us back, "nazad" [backwards]...

Wake up..
When one starts poring over the "election papers," one must willy-nilly admit that in the field of chutzpah and lawlessness the record was broken by list number 7 in Dąbrowa.
Other lists, for example, also of those who "care only that the community of Israel should not stray from the straight path," promised in their "publications" such things as have a connection with this world; whereas the "sevens" of Dąbrowa called on their voters to help the victory, so that "in the kehilla the voice of Oraita, Kudsha Brikh Hu ve-Yisrael [the Torah, the Holy One blessed be He, and Israel] shall be heard"...
As if this were still too little for the "Torah-loyal," they permitted themselves to distribute "jednodniówki" [one-day leaflets] with the following content:
"Awake! Awake! Rise to the service of the Creator, go and sanctify the Name of Heaven in public; the time has come when you must prove that there still lives the pure Jewish soul, which clings to the holy ideals of Torah, faith and self-sacrifice for the ideal of our fathers"...
And the camp did not betray, but helped the "holy" list bring its representatives into the Dąbrowa kehilla, where [?] thanks to them the voice of "Oraita Kudsha Brikh Hu ve-Yisrael" will [?] be heard...
— Woe to you, Dąbrowa kehilla, that you possess such representatives...
The Artisan of Today and Tomorrow / The Artisan's Hard Struggle for Life. — Can His Situation Be Improved?

[Zagłębie — artisans; article.]
The difficult situation of the Jewish bakers in Zagłębie. More than 100 Jewish bakers' families are threatened with ruin. Delegations are being sent to Kielce and Warsaw.
This is what is now on the agenda among the artisans, this is what gnaws [?] at their minds nowadays and gives them no rest — and that is understandable, for it is a matter of livelihood, of having the piece of bread taken out of one's mouth. Things have thus already reached the culminating point, the waters have already come up to the neck, and therefore the groans can already be heard and one begins to see the wound...
Let us consider: what has actually happened here, what in the bakers' question has provoked such a storm and so much disappointment in artisan circles? Can one deny that the introduction of mechanical bakeries is far more convenient and hygienic than the old-type bakeries, where so much dirt and disorder prevail? There can be no two opinions about that. Every cultured person knows perfectly well that the newest technology is more hygienic, more convenient, healthier and easier than the antiquated economy, which involves so much toil and, moreover, operates in very unsanitary conditions.
We and you and every cultured person know this perfectly well, but one must not forget one more thing: is it possible to carry this out without its costing too many victims? We know that the mechanical bakeries, like every modernised trade, will push out many people; but we have not yet reached that stage, because if the mechanical bakeries were introduced right now, they would push out all the bakers, since none of them can at present attain to the colossal enterprises — not to speak of now, when the critical situation prevails over almost the whole globe. Under such difficult conditions one should therefore have waited for better times, and only then set about the work in question [?] systematically and carried it out with good sense, fairness and deliberation. Rebuilding old-fashioned bakeries on modernised foundations is, after all, not one of the easy things. We know that at present bakeries are mostly located in cellar dwellings, whereas under the new regulations they may not be in cellar dwellings, but must be in spacious modern rooms with all conveniences.
And the question arises: is it so easy for the average baker to exchange his old-fashioned cellar rooms for large, modern rooms? Has the government given him the possibility of doing so? Has it built houses and made dwellings on such terms that the broad strata of the population could rent them? Did the government consider, when issuing the new regulations, how they could finally be carried out? The government ought to come to the aid of its citizens when it drafts new ordinances for them and orders them to comply with the new decisions that have to be put into practice.
Apparently in the high windows no account at all is taken of the present hard life of the citizens; had one given any thought to it, one would have understood that when drafting new decisions one must at the same time give the citizens the possibility of putting them into practice — something the high windows have cared about least of all; otherwise one would have understood that people losing their livelihood is at the same time also a burden on the state, which certainly does not improve the situation in the country.
That is one side of the coin, but there is also a second side, at which one must also cast a glance.
The artisans have their professional unions, their organisations, their supreme councils and central bodies, their representations and representatives — so what did they do when they saw the danger in all its seriousness and gravity? Did they realise that today the bakers are on the agenda, and tomorrow it will be the tailors, then the shoemakers, who are in fact already now going through horrors, and then things are not very pleasant with the apprentices either? So what are they doing now and what did they do before? How are they fighting for a finer tomorrow and a better day after tomorrow? In what way are they warding off the bullets aimed at their hearts?
When one does set about doing something, it is only when one already sees the danger before one's eyes, when one already sees the dark colours in their full magnitude — without taking into account that one knows in advance that the time will draw near and that one will later have to adapt to the binding regulations.
It must be said openly that they have been a little too lazy; otherwise they could have achieved much more for themselves, for one must not forget that until now they were represented everywhere. They had their representation in the Sejm, in our local self-government and in the Jewish kehillot, and wherever they could reach they got in — but hardly had they got in than their pulse beat very weakly. Let them know this for the future; it must be a lesson for them for later.
We need not go far: we see here that in Zagłębie they are well represented everywhere, both in the towns and in the villages, and yet they have achieved so little for their fellows, for their members.
How many times, for instance, have we already spoken and written about creating an artisans' school for the Jewish population of Zagłębie, and yet this most necessary thing has not been created — which is also vexing. The question was even once debated in Będzin at a kehilla council meeting, and it received almost no support from the artisans' representative. It was said then: if you want, create such a school and we will take it; for in fact the artisans' representative said — you need the school so that you can teach your children trades, whereas we artisans have no need for such a thing, because we can teach our children a trade, each in his own workshop. And how out of place such an answer was! It is very embarrassing when questions that urgently need solving are treated like this. Everyone knows that the child will not learn the trade from his father in the workshop; and even if we grant that he will learn it, will he grasp it thoroughly? Will the father manage to have his child specialise and make a qualified artisan of him? We know that this is a matter of impossibility; that in order to be qualified one must complete a modern school, which must be set up on modern foundations and must have a firm basis beneath it.
And something else: can someone be a qualified artisan today who has not completed any school, does not know how to calculate costs and does not understand how to make proper use of the situation? In our century an artisan must hold the pen in his hand no less than learn the trade; he must be able to reckon and know how to calculate, and the world must be open to him as to an educated person, because he has to impress society; he must seek customers and see that he finds favour with them. And why should we fool ourselves — since all this cannot be found in the craftsman of today's workshop, who still understands so little of modern world-views and very often has no work merely because he cannot help himself: as soon as he sees that something is beginning to change outside, he becomes helpless and loses his balance.
Of course we can have no complaints against this craftsman, because he was brought up in quite different conditions, and it is quite fine of him that he has raised himself to his present level; on the other hand it cannot be said that the string can go on being drawn out like this and that we need no artisans' school, from which intelligent and well-trained skilled tradesmen would emerge.
One must dwell on the question seriously and with deliberation, so that there should not be so many worries about the future craftsman, who must be able to find his own way on his hard path through life.
R. Let.
The Vanished Daughter (8)

[Serialized novel — "Di farshvundene tokhter" (The Vanished Daughter); installment 8.]
An original novel of modern Jewish life in the Old and the New World. 8.
By Elisabeth Garin.

He sent the telegrams to a good friend of his, a Jewish officer in the Hungarian army. In a few short lines he explained to him what had happened and asked him to detain the couple — if necessary even on a charge of theft — and said that as soon as he received an answer he would leave for Budapest.

Instead of waiting for an answer, however, he wired his father to return home, and he himself left for Budapest on the next train.

But he could have spared himself the trouble, because the answer to his dispatch arrived before he reached Budapest. It was handed to Shlomo Rapaport when he left the train and got off at the railway station of the little town Z. The telegram read:

"My good Fritz! The person concerned adopted the Catholic faith in the village M. near Pest and on the spot married Stanisław M. They also soon left Hungary.
With deep sympathy, your
Ferenc"

Fritz did not stay long in Budapest. Everything had happened as his friend had written him. The couple had not even entered Pest; they had stopped in a small village near the Hungarian capital, and there the old Catholic priest had the "mitzvah" of converting the only daughter of the distinguished Shlomo Rapaport and, right there on the spot, marrying her to the circus rider, former Viennese student and leader of the swastika-men, Stanisław Makarna.

Fritz did not content himself with this. He went to the police and filed a report about the theft, even giving a description of the jewellery. But he knew it would all be in vain, and knowing that his friend had sent out a telegram and that his father must already be at home, he travelled back home, crushed and desperate.

When Berish met him at the station he was simply frightened, so badly did Fritz look.

"Don't ask, Berish, please, don't ask anything," he waved his hand hopelessly.

"Tell me rather how my poor parents are. Has my father come back yet?"

"Yes, paniczu [Polish: 'young master'], the day before yesterday already. He received the telegram on his arrival; he [?] is sitting shiva, has torn kriah..", he whispered quietly, his head bowed and tears in his eyes.

"And my mother?" Fritz asked, and his voice now sounded cold and sharp.

"The gracious lady is busy... The season has already begun, guests have come... Someone has to, after all..."

"Play the hotel-keeper, ha, isn't it so, Berish?" Fritz burst out laughing, with a laugh that cut Berish to the heart.

"Paniczu! Herr Rapaport! I beg you, for God's sake! Don't speak like that of the gracious lady. She feels it — the misfortune, I mean — no less than your father, no less than you yourself, but she can control herself better. She has pride, and I am more afraid of her than of..."

He did not finish, and urging on the pampered mountain pony of the "porets" [?], he added in a choked voice: "May the dear God have mercy on us!"

The Convert.

It was late in the autumn of the same year in which our story begins. A cold, stinging wind blew across the long narrow bridge that separates the little town of Piešťany [printed "Pestiane"] from the magnificent Hotel Thermia Palace and from the baths from which the town, with its large Jewish and Slovak population, draws its livelihood. On the bridge appeared the figure of a woman.

To judge by her clothes and her long boots, she belonged to that class of poor women who in summer, in the bathing season, haul the heavy closed chairs [?] with the sick from the baths into the town, and in winter occupy themselves with knitting, "oysnemen" [so printed; probably embroidery] and coarser work for the shops, which make their living from the few summer months when the many guests come to Piešťany in the hope of finding a cure in the healing baths.

The girl, or the woman, walked in the direction of the hotel, but the going was very hard, because the wind pushed her back. The damp sulphurous air got into her throat and into her eyes; she could barely see where she was going because of the thick fog. She trembled with cold and wrapped herself still more tightly in the long woollen shawl she wore on her head, which was the only protection for her and for the little child she carried pressed to her breast...

Jews Say Psalms.

[Article — taxes and the economic crisis.] The wave of bankruptcies that has now poured down has aroused panic among the public. Everyone thought that, since the state itself has already recognised that the crisis is a fact and one is looking for a means to get rid of it, since everything is crashing and falling, when big banks suspend payments and the public sticks out its tongue for a groschen in cash — after all that, along comes the tax office and takes from the public an assessment that amounts to double and redouble that of last year! The public stands astonished; nobody understands what is going on here. Such a thing would be understandable if we were dealing with a foreign authority — with some stray[?] „Revizor“ who came down to a town and knew that he had to take out of it so-and-so much, so much and so much, without knowing whether that is too much or too little. But we are dealing with our own people, with „heymishe“ (home-grown) people, who know what goes on in the street; with us, after all, one makes an assessment, that is, one takes into account what happens in reality and measures out the taxes accordingly. And today one assesses somebody as if this year he had sold 5 times as much merchandise as a year ago — at a time when even a child in the cradle understands that this year one has not taken in even half of what one took in in previous years.
We stand here before a riddle. With ordinary human reason this cannot be understood, and since human reason can no longer accomplish anything here, Jews turn to the old remedy: one says Psalms.
When do Jews say Psalms in public (betsibur)? With us in the shtetl, Jews used to gather in the synagogue on the Sabbath after the afternoon nap and say Psalms together; in winter one used to get up at dawn and say Psalms. But that was a voluntary Psalm-saying: everyone came by himself, nobody called him, and out of great contentment he wept a little over the Psalms.
But there were cases when the public was called into the synagogue to say Psalms. There were cases when a Jewish woman burst into the beys-medresh in the middle of the day weeping and asked for Psalms to be said — that was when a man or a child, God forbid, was dying, when the doctors had already given up his life; when an evil decree, an elemental disaster, a fire, a flood had broken out and people had already despaired of help — then one went to say Psalms.
„Jews say Psalms“ — so the newspapers report. The present public Psalm-saying belongs to the second kind of saying: among Jews it is already „after despair“. One no longer believes that anything can help, that one will be able to clear up, shed light on and regulate the tax screw; this year it already turns without any system at all. No human reason can grasp what is happening here, and if human understanding no longer comprehends, then there remains only the one remedy: saying Psalms.
Moreover, saying Psalms is almost the only thing for which one need not pay any tax. You may turn over the Book of Psalms ten times a day, recite it from cover to cover — and you still do not have to pay any turnover tax („obrotowe“, podatek obrotowy). So Jews do indeed what is permitted and do indeed say Psalms. But if the public says Psalms instead of trading and working — where will the „ososhand“[?] (the treasury?) take taxes from, and where does it take them from now?...
S. Y. Stupnicki.
A Sweet Dream

Forty "fasts" did Berl Eli, the "Agudah man" [member of Agudat Israel], fast — fasted and fasted without pause, and without pause kept saying one "prayer": that the "Agudah", God forbid, should not be put to shame at the elections to the kehilla, that it should not, God forbid, lose its last position. But the fasts and the prayers had not yet calmed him entirely, for the risk seemed to him too great to rely on miracles, especially since he, Berl Eli, knows quite well [printed "„אנץ" for "גאנץ"] that his prayer does not come from a whole heart with the proper devotion. He was also afraid that the sins of his youth might be remembered against him, when he had very nearly become an official "Mizrachi" man [religious Zionist], God save us — not because he thought anything of the Land of Israel.
God forbid! He has not yet crawled that deep into impurity. Even then he hated the Land of Israel with the utmost hatred; he wanted to become a "Mizrachi" simply because it was then a time when the lords of the land and their officials, for our many sins, had an inclination towards more modern people. And how could such a man as Berl Eli not be close to the authorities? — but the merit of his fathers stood by him then. Heaven did not let Berl Eli stumble into a Zionist stain, of which "none that go unto her return again", and once the eyes of the government were opened, they looked around through the high windows to see who is the "real" Jew, who can "speak in the name of the Jewish people". The wheel turned, and Berl Eli, the real Agudah man, is today among those "who sit first in the kingdom".
And now, for that sin, of having once stood at the "gates of Sheol", Berl Eli trembled lest it should hold back his prayer and his self-mortifications, and the thought gave him no rest by day or by night.
Only when Berl Eli had "interceded" with the "gracious ruler" [ironic for the authorities] and had been promised from "above" that they would assist in everything that he and his friends would "pull off", did Berl Eli calm down and begin to sleep at night again.
In his dream he sees: how the election commission sits after the votes have been cast, opens the envelopes, and out fall only slips, and the "Agudah" wins an extraordinary victory.
It takes all the candidates. The joy is beyond measure; the next day Hallel is said at prayers, and that very same evening a meeting of the kehilla council is fixed, a board is elected and they set about at once introducing new regulations in the community [gmina].
First of all it is resolved to close the Zionist premises and to set up in their place a hekdesh [poorhouse] with all the trimmings, as was the custom in the days of our great-grandfathers, for one may not depart from the old customs introduced by the earlier generations, who were wiser than we; the premises of the Zionists will be turned into a place where "when a man's evil inclination overpowers him, he shall put on black, go there and do as his heart desires"...
Secondly it was resolved not to pay out the subsidy of the Talmud Torah, so that the melamdim may fulfil the Mishnah in Avot "and live a life of hardship while you toil in the Torah", and secondly "poverty befits Israel", which suits the melamdim best, as in the custom of ancient years; better to use that money to take on another secretary at the rabbinate, who knows how to "go" where one must.
The orphanage too will from today on get no subsidy, for where has it been heard that children who have no parents should have a building of their own? And all this people should give? He who is the Father of Orphans should provide for His children Himself, and He does not need those born of woman to provide for His children.
The old-age home need not even be mentioned: "He who gives the old life, gives them food". We can show the old respect, rise before them — but that we should provide for them? For what good deeds?
As for the gemilut chesed [interest-free loan] fund, that is truly an unheard-of thing: our sages devised the heter iska, through which one Jew may lend another a few guilders even at 8 percent a month — and along come people and dream up interest-free loans? Then "what have the sages achieved with their enactment"? And not only that, but it even robs Jews of their livelihood: what is the well-known usurer to do, who lends a Jew 100 zl. on a pledge and earns his 8 zl. a month on it? Should he die of hunger even though he has a heter iska? No! We will not allow it! Not a single grosz for the institution that encroaches on Jews and takes the bite out of their mouths.
The greatest misfortune is with the mikveh: they took advantage of the opportunity that we were not properly represented in that kehilla board and spent tens of thousands of zl. of our money... to put the mikveh in order, since it has to be clean — and the sinners of Israel transgressed a Torah prohibition: "neither shall ye walk in their ordinances", and there is, after all, an explicit Gemara: "the gentiles [?] are particular about cleanliness".
But thanks be to His dear Name, "truth" has prevailed, we have clipped the wings of the Other Side, and we shall know how to "apply" the kehilla's grosz to "useful" purposes.
Who knows what other "important" regulations the "kosher" parnassim [community leaders] would have introduced in the Jewish community, had it not occurred to the Agudah circles that Berl Eli should already have been out in the street to settle a quick "matter" at the starostwo [district office]; they quickly sent a messenger to call Berl Eli, who was still sleeping soundly, although the time for the Shema had long passed.
Berl Eli woke with a start and, seeing the messenger, remembered reality, which is as far from his sweet dream as the east is from the west...
HaMitbonen [The Observer].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Naso)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Naso
The Portion
—o—
a) "They shall confess... and he shall make restitution for his guilt in full" (Num. 5:7)
When a person is badly off, he vents his anger on God — God owes him. And he has grievances against Him: why, he is so good and pious, and God cannot [?] take it into account... So the verse tells him: "Confess your sin" — admit your transgressions; "and he shall return his guilt upon his own head" — the guilt will be taken off God and laid upon you, and you will see that it is not God who owes you, but you yourself — your own deeds...
Divrei Shaul.
• • •
In the "Shemoneh Esreh", when we ask God: "Hear our voice, have pity and compassion on us", we add a prayer: "Please, O Lord, I have sinned". Why remind God of our sins when we are asking Him for mercy?
But we see, for our many sins, that it is precisely the wicked who fare well in the world, that precisely those who sin have it fine and good; so we say to God: "Please, O Lord, I have sinned" — I too, dear God, have sinned, so give me too all the good things...
Alei Zayit.
—o—
b) "If any man's wife goes astray" (Num. 5:12)
A divorced woman comes to Rabbi Gershon Henekh of Radzyń and asks whether she should be matched with a young man who has a "green ticket" [a temporary military deferment]. She does not want to make the match, lest they take him for military service next year. Rabbi Gershon Henekh, however, promises her that he will not be taken into the service.
When she had gone out, Rabbi Gershon Henekh says to those around him: Don't think that I said it by way of prophecy; but if she is a divorcee, her former husband presumably divorced her because she is a great shrew. Well then, I am sure the new husband will not improve in health with her during the year — let us hope he won't get worse... so he will surely be exempted..
—o—
c) "Then the man shall bring his wife to the priest" (Num. 5:15)
The section of the terumah offering and the section of the sotah stand side by side in the Torah; what is the connection?
According to the Talmud there are two ways to become rich: 1) to give tithes, 2) to honour one's wife — "Tithe so that you may become rich" and "Honour your wives so that you may become rich". Well, presumably everyone will choose the second way, and instead of tithes he will make his wife expensive clothes and buy her jewellery. So the verse tells him: if you behave like that, if you surround your wife with luxury, there will be "and she commits a trespass against him" — she will seek something more... Therefore it is better that you take the first way and give tithes..
Moshe Torat [?].
—o—
d) "Thus shall you bless the children of Israel" (Num. 6:23)
Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce, who was a very sharp-witted man, once travelled in a "boyd" [covered wagon] to Lublin, to the "Seer". As he stopped at a village, the innkeeper comes out to him with his two boys and says:
— Rebbe, bless my boys for me.
— Well, and a pidyon [the customary gift]?...
— Bless them for me "just so", without money...
— To bless "just so" only God can; He needs no money, so let Him bless them for you for free... I need money...
— Is that what the Torah says? — the innkeeper is already getting angry.
— Yes... it is said explicitly: "Thus [koh] shall you bless the children of Israel... and we [sic, = I] will bless them" — if a Jew wants "koh tevarkhu", that the children be blessed "just so" (koh = so) without money — "and I will bless them": let him send them to Me...
—o—
e) "The Lord bless you and keep you" (Num. 6:24)
"Bless you — with wealth, and keep you — from harmful spirits."
Midrash.
Such luck the rich have. The Gemara (Pesachim 111) says that even harmful spirits, demons, are afraid to pick on them... If "He blesses you with wealth", then automatically "He keeps you from harmful spirits", for even they tremble before the wealthy...
Brit Shalom.
—o—
f) "And give you peace" (Num. 6:26)
"Thus shall you bless the children of Israel" — you shall bless the Jews only when you will be able to say to them "yevarekhekha" [may He bless you, singular], i.e. [that] all will be united and you will be able to speak to all of them as to a single person, because they will have one heart; not "yevarkhem" (plural) but "yevarekhekha" (singular) — then, and only then, shall you bless them.
No'am Megadim.
The Haftarah
—o—
g) "And Manoah went after his wife" (Judges, 3 [= 13])
The Gemara says about this: "Manoah was an ignoramus, for he walked behind his wife."
Yes. If "he walked after his wife" — if he went after his own wife, it is a sign that he was a coarse boor; for had he been able to study, he would have gone after other women... for whoever can study persuades himself that a page of Gemara covers up everything.
Rabbi Mordechai of Chernobyl.
Avot
—o—
h) "Let your house be open wide" (7 [= 1], 5)
People come to a rich man to ask for a donation, and he excuses himself: "Know that I am, God spare us, a great pauper, that I cannot afford even bread. And the fine house I keep is only to fool people, so that they give me credit... but in truth even the shirt I wear is not mine"...
Ah, if you lead a life of luxury for people's sake, to fool them — why don't you give charity for people's sake too?..
"Your habitation is in the midst of deceit" — so you sit amid deceit, but [?] "through deceit they refuse to know Me" — to give charity with that very same deceit — that, no...
Nahalei Devash.
—o—
i) "And I found nothing better for the body than silence" (7 [= Avot 1:17])
A person has two ears and one mouth — to show that he should listen more and talk less!..
Shiyurei Middot [?].
Spain and Portugal. II.

[Geography — Spain and Portugal; article series.] Gdud [signature/pen-name above the headline].
Spain and Portugal as European Africa.
Both the structure (composition, build) of the territory of these countries and the dry hot climate of a large part of them (of the provinces that do not lie by the sea) are — as already mentioned — quite different from what is found in other countries of Europe. One may rightly call them "European Africa". Indeed the French proverb says: on the other side of the Pyrenees (on the southern side) Africa begins.
Naturalists put forward the hypothesis that the narrow strip of land that stretches in the extreme south of Spain at the Strait of Gibraltar, and is altogether 1 kilometre wide, stretched in prehistoric times further south as far as North Africa. Only later did the Atlantic Ocean cut through this piece of land, and today's narrow strip of sea, or strait, which we call Gibraltar, came into being. The said strip of land measures 4 and a half square kilometres and has belonged since 1713 to England.
Spain (España). Its principal provinces.
Because of the difference in climate between the provinces that stretch along the sea coasts (of the Mediterranean Sea and of the Atlantic Ocean) and the provinces that lie farther from the sea, i.e. in the interior of the peninsula, we divide Spain into coastal provinces and provinces of Central Spain.
To the coastal provinces belong — from north to south — Catalonia, on the western shore of the Mediterranean, with its capital Barcelona, which possesses Spain's largest commercial port; Valencia and Murcia with their capitals, which bear the same names as the provinces.
To the provinces on the northern shore of the Mediterranean belong: Granada with the capital Granada and the commercial port of Málaga; the rich province of Andalusia (in a deep valley between the Granada mountains) with its capital Seville and the historic city of Córdoba. On the eastern shore of the Atlantic Ocean lies Galicia (Galisien), and finally on the south-eastern shore of the Atlantic Ocean — the provinces of Asturias and the Basque province (the second to the east and south-east of the first).
To the provinces of Central Spain belong: New Castile, in which are located Spain's present-day seat of government, Madrid, and the former seat, Toledo; Old Castile, to the north of New Castile. Between New and Old Castile stretches the mountain range Sierra de Guadarrama with the famous mountain pass of Somosierra, where in the year 1808 the Polish legions fought under the command of Napoleon's commanders. Finally Aragon (to the north and east of Old Castile and to the west of Catalonia) with its capital Zaragoza.
There are 9 cities in Spain with a population of over 100[?] thousand people; of them 7 lie in the coastal provinces (Barcelona, Valencia, Murcia, Málaga, Granada, Seville and Bilbao) and 2 in Central Spain: Madrid and Zaragoza. The largest city is — Madrid.
Trade and industry.
Horticulture is very widely developed in Spain's eastern and southern provinces lying on the Mediterranean. There grow: oranges, lemons, almonds, rice, olives, sugar cane, dates and grapes. From the last, very good wines are produced (Málaga wine, so called because it is exported through the port of Málaga). By the size of its wine production Spain occupies 3rd place in Europe (after Italy and France). Cotton is also planted.
Spain possesses enormous natural treasures such as silver, iron, copper, lead and quicksilver, whose mines are counted among the richest in the world! Mostly these mines are found in the coastal provinces, e.g.: silver and lead to the south of the Andalusian mountains, copper in western Andalusia, iron ore — in the Basque provinces; only the very rich quicksilver mines are located at Almadén (in New Castile).
Had Spain had good statesmen who truly cared for the welfare of the people, she could, by importing coal, have developed one of the greatest industries in the world, and the people would not have sunk so deep into poverty and filth. Unfortunately the Spanish kings, beginning with Isabella ("Isabel the wicked" and Ferdinand), may their names be blotted out, and ending with the Bourbon dynasty, the kings always cared only that they themselves be rich, handing over all Spanish mineral treasures and the whole wholesale trade into the hands of foreign merchants such as: Englishmen, Frenchmen etc., and these see to it that Spain's raw materials are exported. Spain's annual trade balances close with deficits, while the people live naked and in want of everything.
Education.
At a time when in most of Europe compulsory education was introduced long ago, in Spain it was introduced only a mere 10 years ago. Despite this there are tens of thousands of children who do not attend any school, and in the schools too the level of education is meagre. Spain has ["osh 0" — garbled number] universities, and no one has ever yet heard of any invention or theory that a Spanish professor created. To science, which is so rich thanks to human mental efforts over hundreds of years and which has as a result yielded all the inventions and theories of the English, French, Germans, Italians, Poles and Jews, even the Dutch (Huygens) — to this blessing-bringing science Spain shamelessly contributed nothing.
The statistics of illiteracy in Spain give the dreadful figure of 687 per thousand. Portugal has even more illiterates: 786 per mille.
What's New in Zagłębie?

Friday, 13 Sivan 5691, 13 | czwartek 29 maja 1931 [Thursday, 29 May 1931].

Będzin

—o—
First session of the new kehilla council.
Next Thursday the first session of the newly elected parnassim (kehilla councillors) will take place; on the agenda is the election[?] of a presidium of the kehilla council.

—o—
The 'Ne'ila days' of the municipal budget.
This week the budget commission finished its work on the municipal budget.
The acting commissioner has travelled with the budget to Kielce, and in the first days of next week the budget will be dealt with at the plenary session of the council of commissioners.
The 'Courtiers' Are Active.

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — kehilla elections.] The outcome of the kehilla elections in Będzin and also in Sosnowiec has caused consternation among the 'Agudah' [Agudat Yisrael] leaders. In the course of the week they took action: they knocked on doors even of the Left 'Poalei Zion', with whom the 'Agudah' is willing to ally itself, if only to harm the national camp; but, as we are informed, the interventions have so far not had the slightest success, and the only hope is to get help from the 'high windows', where delegations from both towns keep coming and going...
A 'Purge' Planned in the Radomsko Shtibl.

[Będzin — kehilla elections.] We are told that this week a consultation of the group that leans towards the 'Agudah' took place at the home of one of the most respected Radomsko Hasidim. At the consultation a resolution was adopted that the agitators against No. 13 (against the Agudah list) are to be removed from the shtibl.
Greetings from the Local Y.Sh.A.
[Będzin — culture.] The board of the local Y.Sh.A. branch sent warm greetings to the orthography conference organised by the Yiddish Scientific Institute [YIVO] in Vilna.
Guest Performances by the 'Vilner'.
[Będzin — theatre.] Today and tomorrow the 'Vilner' [Vilna Troupe] will be with us again; they will stage 'It's Hard to Be a Jew' and 'The Black Ghetto'.
Next Month There Will Not Be a Single Unemployed Person in Our Town.

[Będzin — municipality and employment.] So the acting commissioner assures us.
We are informed by the magistrate [town hall] that the loan of 40,000 zł. has already been received from the insurance company. The sum is earmarked for building a central reservoir of the municipal sewerage system.
Up to a thousand workers are to be employed on the work.
A Boy Has One Sidelock Shaved Off.

[Będzin — incidents.] On the eve of Shavuot a boy aged 7 went into Mr. Bartnik's tobacconist's (trafika) in the Halls [covered market] to buy cigarettes. There, 'for a joke', one of the boy's sidelocks was shaved off...
The saleswoman defended herself by saying that the 'joke' had been carried out by a customer who 'happened' to be in the shop.
The "business" did not work out for him...

The young man Lejzer Gnisław[?] of Strzemieszyce traded according to today's "system". He also did such "business" with Mr Velvel Malach, from whom he took jams (confitures) worth 200 zł.
Mr Malach handed the matter over to the local court, where the trial took place this Tuesday. G. was sentenced to one month's arrest.
For the orphans' library

From the headmistress of Public School No. 4, Mrs Szancer-Perlmutter, the board of the Charity Society received, through the mediation of Dr Weinzieher, 400 zł for setting up a library in the orphanage.
For this fine deed the board expresses its heartfelt thanks.
Celebration in honour of "The Week for the Child"

On Tuesday the local public schools celebrated the day of the so-called "Week for the Child". The schoolchildren, led by the orchestra of Public School No. 2, marched through the town. Afterwards they received sweets and milk.
"Gordonia" on the eve of the summer colonies

The regional leadership (hanhagah ha-gelilit) of the pioneering youth organisation "Gordonia" in Zagłębie is organising in the coming weeks 2 summer colonies in the village of Nickulina[?] (5 kilometres from Rajcza), which lies in a beautiful area in the Beskid mountains.
This week a parents' conference took place at the Będzin "Gordonia", at which the tasks and the educational significance of the colonies were discussed.
A "Suna"[?] early in the morning

On Wednesday around 8 o'clock in the morning a thief got into the shop of Retman &[?] Berkowicz, where he took a motor out of the shop window.
At the "hot moment" the job was interrupted, and the thief was taken off to the police station (komisariat).
An institution the public has "rested" from for a whole 3 years

There is in Będzin a society called "Linas ha-Cholim". Once the institution played the most important role in the town and was very popular; the public did not begrudge money, and thanks to this "Linas ha-Cholim" grew into a mighty institution and was able to take the "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) under its protection, and later also opened the clinic for women in childbirth.
But ever since a "proliferation"[?] of institutions arose on the Jewish street, little societies of all kinds, "Linas ha-Cholim" began to lead a "modest life": it held no fund-raising campaigns at all, but contented itself with the subsidies from the Magistrate (town council) and with the paltry monthly pledges.
Such a "quiet life", however, did not have a favourable result: expenses nearly doubled and income decreased, so that the society has a colossal deficit.
The newly elected board has therefore decided that the hitherto system of "neutrality" must be changed and that various campaigns must be undertaken, so that the threefold cord — "Linas ha-Cholim" with its "two worlds", the maternity institution and the "Moshav Zkenim" — may be maintained and continue their meritorious activity.
In this connection, from next week on, stickers (nalepki) will be sold for the benefit of the institutions. At the same time the sticker sellers will recruit new members and also increase the pledges of the old contributors.
It is to be hoped that the campaign will be received as it should be, and that the institution, which has kept silent for 3 years, will be broadly supported.
Sosnowiec — The appeals against the budget will be considered by the new kehilla heads

Under the chairmanship of Mr Zendel a meeting of the kehilla board took place on Sunday. At the meeting Mr Zendel proposed that the appeals against the budget (etat) assessment should be considered by the present board members, arguing that this would facilitate the budget's income.
The majority was against this proposal and resolved that the appeals should be considered only by the future kehilla board.
So he lived and so he died..

The Litvak Asher Lewit was „popular“ among the local population. Where he spent the night he did not spend the day [i.e. he had no fixed abode]; he rolled about in attics and on hard bare floors, many times also on the pavement, until his strength was exhausted. And walking on the 2nd day of Shavuot along Małachowska street, Asherke collapsed in front of the building of the „Bank Polski“ and remained dead.
Asherke was sixty-four years old.
Stormy meeting at the artisans’.

On Monday a stormy meeting took place in the premises of the Artisans’ Association, at which the defeat of the artisans’ list found its echo.
The president, Mr. Opasowski, and the entire board resigned because of the betrayal by the majority of the members.
The discussion was stormy and it nearly came to blows. Finally the storm was liquidated with the resolution that the board shall consist of representatives of every guild.

Embezzled a cheque for 25,000 zł.
The culprit sentenced to 3 years in prison.

Over the course of 2 days the trial of Mr. Skielski, an official at the Mandżew [?] steelworks (huta), took place in the local district court. The official was accused of having embezzled a cheque for 25,000 zł.
After hearing 30 witnesses and after the defence, the court sentenced Skielski to 3 years in prison and to the loss of [civic] rights.
A Bolshevik agent arrested.

The local police arrested a certain Antoni Kowal, who lived here with his wife on false passports.

The fight over the Gemilut Chasadim fund in Katarzyna liquidated.

Last week a general meeting of the members of the G[emilut] Ch[asadim] fund took place here. At the meeting a board of the so-called „opposition“ was elected, so that the previous board was not represented at all.
The isolated board members informed the directorate of the „Joint“ in Warsaw about this, saying that they were casting off the full responsibility for the fund.
The upshot was that the director of the „Joint“, Mr. Giterman, turned to Mr. L. Zendel, president of the Sosnowiec G.Ch. fund, asking him to acquaint himself with the newly created situation in Katarzyna and to report whether it was necessary for the „Joint“ to use its right and nominate half the members from the previous board.
On Monday Mr. Zendel, together with Messrs. Berkowicz, Ajbeszyc and Werdiger, was in Katarzyna, where a joint meeting of the old and new board members took place.
The meeting, which was held in the beit ha-midrash, was stormy in character; had it not been for the „strong hand“ of Mr. Zendel, it would have come to fights among the agitated members.
After much effort and explanation by the Sosnowiec delegates, peace was made, and in the present board the old board is represented in equal number.

The first meeting of the Sosnowiec kehilla council. A presidium and a commission to elect an executive chosen.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Yesterday at 11 a.m. the first meeting of the newly elected kehilla council took place in the premises of the Sosnowiec kehilla.
The Zionist, Mizrachi, artisans' and porters' parnasim came to the meeting. The "neutrals" of the Koziegłowy side, of the "Aguda" and of Englard's side did not come. The latter sent a letter in which they announce that, since in their view the distribution of mandates is not correct, they are taking no part in the meeting.
Mr. Zendel[?], chairman of the executive, opens the meeting and stresses that, since there is no quorum, he cannot continue to conduct the meeting, and leaves the premises.
Then the parnas Mr. Finkler takes the floor and points out that there is in fact a quorum at the meeting, because the "Aguda" and Englard's side are against the decision of the starostwo [district authority], i.e. they thereby confirm that they exclude themselves as parnasim.
After this statement the vice-chairman of the executive, Mr. Weinryb, takes over the chair; he thanks [them] for the election and proposes to elect a chairman and a vice-chairman of the kehilla council.
With 7 votes Mr. Mendel Szapiro is elected chairman, vice-chairman — Icchak Steinfeld; Mr. Chaim Jungster receives 1 vote.
Then a commission is elected to choose a kehilla executive; the commission includes: Markus Hamburger, (chairman) M. Szapiro, Abraham Apatowski, Baruch Żepkowicz and Szalom Pilc.
Deputies: Icchak Steinfeld, Chaim Jungster, Noach Abramczyk and Mordechaj Kleinberg.

[Poland — trade and taxes.] A "ryczałt obrotowy" [lump-sum turnover tax] should be introduced.
Next week a conference of representatives of all chambers of commerce in Poland will take place in Warsaw, devoted specifically to the question of the ryczałt obrotowy.
The Sosnowiec chamber of commerce and a number of other chambers of commerce have decided to come forward at the conference with a demand that steps finally be taken to introduce the ryczałt obrotowy.
For all small merchants of the third and fourth category the turnover tax (podatek obrotowy) should not be assessed for each one separately; instead a lump sum should be assessed for the whole branch, and every shopkeeper will pay an equal amount.

Jubilee performance of the "Vilna" Troupe in Będzin
As in all the larger cities of Poland, the idea arose in Będzin too of taking part in the jubilee celebration of the "Vilna Troupe", which was the first to lay the foundation of the great work called — theatre art, for those who enriched the Yiddish word, Jewish culture.

Horrible family murder. A father murders his 6 children.

A gruesome family tragedy took place on the night from Friday to Saturday in the village of Ku-garów [?] (Rybnik county), where a local inhabitant, a worker, murdered with an axe his 6 children, girls aged 19, 18, 15, 14, 12 and 8.
Afterwards the murderer father wanted to murder himself with the same axe, but he was only wounded and is in hospital.
At the investigation the murderer told that he had been carrying this devilish plan around with him for about 6 weeks, since he was laid off from work, and so that his children should not suffer want he decided to kill them. He also wanted, he says, to kill his wife, but he did not manage it, because at that moment the woman went down to the yard.
The father killed the children while they were asleep; he went with the axe from bed to bed, and in their sleep he put an end to their lives.

Philanthropy in the Social Sense — How Does the Council of Commissioners Relate to This Question?

[Będzin — municipality and philanthropy.] How does the Council of Commissioners relate to this question?
Year after year the Będzin magistrate (municipality) used to assign to the Jewish ‘Dobroczynność’ (charity society) a certain sum, intended for treating poor sick people and sending them out to summer quarters. Now the magistrate has freed itself of this burden; the subsidy is no longer approved, on the grounds that there is a lack of money.
And it is a remarkable thing how, at the very first opportunity, one knows to pounce first of all on the helpless, on the sick and suffering. First of all one wants to save the groszy which the sick await with impatience — the sick who feel happy when they have still been granted to see the summer sunbeams that warm their worn-out, sick bones. How one knows from the very first moment to save on such money, which poor broken people need so badly, people who must have their summer cure.
Did the magistrate really have nothing else left to economise on, as on this particular expense? And is this subsidy really so useless that one could rid oneself of it with an easy conscience? And one more thing: it would be interesting to know whether the Council of Commissioners has applied this savings[?] method to all other matters as well, so that it has already come to the point that subsidies concerning the healing of poor, sick people shall not be approved?
‘It doesn’t matter,’ they surely thought. ‘If one year we do not give the subsidy, and the people cannot be healed and sent out to summer quarters, the magistrate will give them comfortable places in the local spa institutions, and they will breathe fresh air, free and easy, without paying a grosz, in the local parks, in the local promenade gardens, in the local splendid forests, which are simply life-reviving...’
Upon my life, it is a farce how little understanding there still is today for society in general and for philanthropy in particular, that at the first moment a first-class philanthropic subsidy is removed as if it were nothing at all, as if one could also manage without it. Well, of course, we will have to cope somehow; we will after all have to heal our suffering and sick, our poor and helpless. But one must not forget that, firstly, we are not able to give twice for everything in such bitter times, and secondly, we do pay to the magistrate, and we have the right to demand that the magistrate, out of its large budgets — in which we occupy such an honourable place — should also support our poor suffering people.
The magistrate must, after all, stand on guard and see to it that the interests of the suffering population are resolved on as good a scale as possible, in as good a form as possible, in as large a dose as possible. A magistrate must, after all, take up such urgent questions and not abandon them, as though nothing at all had happened. A sacred duty lies upon the magistrate to see that everything is resolved in the best possible way, and not to take away even what one used to give merely to fulfil an obligation.
It is truly unheard of that a magistrate should abandon everything, leave it to God’s care, and give the impression of ‘go bang your head on the pillow’ [i.e. nobody cares]. The sick remain in town — where are they to go? Which gardens are they to visit? Where are they to enjoy fresh air? Such tactics are simply unheard of. In town even healthy people choke from the heavy heat — not to speak of the sick and weak, who must have clean air and shade. Where does the magistrate send these helpless people? In what way can those be healed who cannot travel out at their own expense? Can one let these people torment themselves throughout the whole summer in their hard conditions, in the stifling cellar and attic rooms? Can they stay there the whole time? Will they be healed there?
True, it is self-evident that these are unbearable conditions. But did the magistrate stop to give it a thought for even one minute? Did it put the question on the green table? Did it take an interest in how to solve it, how to settle it?
Well, we know perfectly well how rich the town is in air, how we bathe in greenery — so much so that when one climbs up to the Górka [the hill/park in town] one cannot go further than the little gate unless one pays for a ticket every time one enters.
Has it not yet occurred to the magistrate that the ‘Górka’ should be opened once and for all to the general population? Is it so hard to understand, so hard to grasp, that we here in crowded Będzin cannot always stay within our four walls? That one must sometimes enjoy fresh air, and that when we go out into the street we feel no air at all — the only thing we get outdoors is being covered in dust — does not every local resident know this? One should at least have seen to it that access to the ‘Górka’ be free for everyone! Well, those who can still travel out for a month or two to a dacha still enjoy the summer somehow. But what are those to do who have no possibility at all of moving out of town the whole summer? Where are they to enjoy the air? Why should these people torment themselves in stifling closeness between four walls all summer long? One should at least have taken care of these poor elements!
After all, one cannot leave a town full of people sitting packed as in a box, as in a barrel of herring. One must take into account what may come of it, what benefit this could bring in the sanitary field. We know, after all, that heat, stuffiness and crowding cause diseases.
Must one then wait until it reaches the culminating point? Should one not think in time, so that nothing too undesirable, too dangerous, should soon occur? Is it not a disgrace when a magistrate does not approve a minimal subsidy intended to heal poor people? Should it not be the reverse — that a magistrate should take care that those people can be rescued who have no possibility of rescuing themselves? Should not the public concern itself with the broad strata of the population when they need healing? Must a public institution wait until the matter takes on a dangerous character?
It is enough that we live in Będzin in the worst hygienic and sanitary conditions; one should at least have taken care that the sick be sent out of town to fresh air and for a cure, and not let the people languish in the worst conditions. The town is, after all, burdened with the municipal budget — so the magistrate is obliged to care for those who need the support of society.
R. Les.
Which taxes must be paid in June?

This month the following taxes must be paid:
1) By 15 June — the 2nd instalment of the difference between the assessed industrial tax for the year 1930 and the statutory advance payments that were paid in that year; 2) by the 15th the industrial tax is payable on the turnover of May of this year achieved by commercial enterprises of the first and second category and by industrial ones of the first to fifth categories that keep proper books; 3) by the 15th the instalment of the property tax is payable, at the rate of 0.3 per cent of the value the property amounts to, according to the assessment of this tax, for payers of the 2nd and 3rd contingent group, from the 5th bracket upwards; 4) by 7 June the income tax is payable on officials' salaries, pensions and wages for hired labour that was deducted in May of this year.
Besides this, all overdue taxes are payable, those deferred and split into instalments whose due dates fall in June.

— Is this the editorial office?
— What is your wish?
