..."It was in the days when the Aguda together with its partners "purified" the last kehilla budget. On one of those days — it was then the Sunday of Chol ha-Moed Pesach — early in the morning the young son of a well-known local Hasidic magnate comes in to me, and he, the young son I mean, says to me:
— "Reb Chaim, today we are going to Zawiercie; there we are meeting an engineer with whom we have to conclude an agreement, and it is necessary that you be present, so that we can get an idea of how much the building ought to cost"...
Hearing such liquorice-sweet little speeches, and from the son of the well-known magnate to boot, I felt festive in my soul all over again, and gladly agreed to the travel proposal.
— When do we go, then?
— You, Reb Chaim, be at the railway station punctually at half past eleven, because before twelve the train leaves for Zawiercie; I want to be sure we don't miss the train, because the engineer will be waiting for us — there in Zawiercie — at the train...
Reb Chaim did indeed hurry, ate his breakfast in haste, and in his mind were woven plans of huge enterprises, and above all he praised the One above us, who does not forsake him and sends him, right after Pesach — well, something to earn...
The magnate's young son came at the appointed time, bought tickets for both, and off to Zawiercie.
On the way, says Reb Chaim, the magnate's son was strangely friendly to me, pampered me like a father his only son, asked me all about my situation, and from time to time expressed regret about the present situation in general, and about the Jewish artisan in particular... But who could have hit on the idea that this "true love" was connected with Aguda politics? Who could have had the thought that I was being led the way pimps transport their "living merchandise"?...
— Excuse me, Reb Yid, make it short.
— What do you mean, short? Chaim grows angry with us. "All the pages ought to be full of this story, which is like the tales of the Thousand and One Nights."
— Well then, hear me out: arriving at Zawiercie, at the station my companion vanished; but it did not take long before he comes back and says:
"Reb Chaim, we shall have to wait; as it turns out, the engineer is late; meanwhile let's stroll along the avenue; it is quite certain that we shall meet the engineer here, who has the building plans with him"...
Well, so we stroll through the streets and wait for the engineer to come with the "plans"; but it was not the engineer who came — suddenly up popped the shammes of the local rabbi, who greets me with a broad "Shalom aleichem", and at once he invites me to pay a visit to the rabbi...
Despite my explaining to the shammes that time does not permit me, that the engineer is supposed to arrive, the shammes would not let me go, and pestered me to come with him to the rabbi. How could it be? To be in Zawiercie and not pay one's respects to the rabbi, especially on a holiday? And directly my "breadwinner" helped too, giving me to understand that most probably the engineer would only come later and meanwhile I could pop in for a visit to the rabbi...
The magnate's young son "stayed" at the station, and we, i.e. I and the shammes, went off to the rabbi.
I was very pleased with this visit, for in truth, during the whole time I was a "dozór" [kehilla councillor] I was never granted such honour and grandeur as was bestowed on me in the rabbi's home — a magnificent honour of the best food and drink. I saw how the whole family was simply "self-sacrificing" just so that I should enjoy myself the more: Reb Chaim, drink; Reb Chaim, eat; such a distinguished guest; wait a while, the Rebbe will receive you soon, right now he is sleeping, but there is a time for everything; well, Reb Chaim, perhaps a little glass of wiśniak [cherry liqueur]? A good piece of fish, after all it is Chol ha-Moed...
Later I was received by the Rebbe; a series of new honours began, which I "had not seen even in a dream"; but for God's sake — I thought to myself — where has my breadwinner got to? Where is the engineer?
— Come now, don't be so gloomy, Reb Chaim, where is the joy of the festival?...
— — — — —
At about the time of the afternoon prayer the magnate's young son comes in, all sweaty and out of breath, and says to me:
— "Reb Chaim, it turns out that the engineer has fooled me; in half an hour the train leaves for Sosnowiec"...
Only on coming home did the whole business become clear to me. The "Aguda", wanting to annul the budget of the kehilla administration, had worked out strategic plans for how the "enemies" should be removed from their "front"...
The "strategic" plan succeeded for them, and I too am "satisfied": would that all the parnassim up to now could boast that at the "koniec" [the end] they had such honour as I had?...
Handed over for printing by
Ben Amotz.
The fate of poor brides depends on the success of the badge sale for the "Hachnasat Kalla" society, Będzin.
The fate of poor brides depends on the success of the badge sale for the benefit of the "Hachnasat Kalla" society, Będzin. Support the campaign!
The Little Horse Is Collapsing Under the Load

[Commerce — the economic crisis; opinion piece.]
Had any class gone under — the working class, the peasantry, a Negro tribe — what an outcry would have arisen in the world! But when a class of merchants goes under, an "unproductive" element — a lumpen-proletariat — who cares?
After all, it goes under at once [sic]. Little by little, bit by bit, they die out, these lumpen-proletarians, one by one — first the lean ones, the weaker ones; afterwards the turn will come for the fatter ones too.
And now, who cares about them? Has the government perhaps taken care of them? Perhaps set up sick funds, an unemployment fund, a pension ["emerytura"] for them? Perhaps provided them with credits, protected, strengthened, safeguarded them — these Belgian horses [heavy draught horses], which have been harnessed to a big [printed "nroysn"], heavy wagon, driven on with whips — with taxes — and ordered to haul the heavy load?
Our great, powerless, dear coachmen! Have you not noticed that the little horses are collapsing under the heavy load? Where is your loyalty, as a coachman, to a horse? Don't doze, coachmen, on the rut [koleina]: the little horse stops dead, and the whole wagon with it.
Don't take it lightly; think it over and rescue it while it is not yet too late. When the little horse has completely run out of strength, no medicines will help it either. Read a newspaper carefully — how many firms are asking for "supervision" [court supervision, i.e. receivership]; take a look at the signboards: almost shop after shop a "spółka" [partnership] — one more little horse harnessed. But it does not help; as long as you do not find a radical remedy, the merchant class will perish [printed "intergeyn"], the dear little horse will stretch out its legs.
Think it over!
Gershayim.
Don't Neglect It!

[Civil registration — a public warning.]
We consider it our duty to warn the Jewish population and draw its attention to the great danger brought about by failing to register marriages, divorces and births in time.
We point out that the matter should not be taken lightly in the belief that it will be possible afterwards to make "propushchene[?] akten" [omitted/belated registrations]. As regards marriages, this is already now entirely impossible. And if one can still now legalise a marriage that was not registered in its time, by performing the wedding once again, there is already quite precise information that this possibility too will soon be abolished. The same will also apply to children who were not registered in time.
The misfortune of those who lack proper civil-registry ["metrical"] documents is so great that it often leads to great family tragedies. Children are separated from their father, the wife from her husband; women who want to travel to their husbands abroad cannot do so, because they have no marriage certificates; the father cannot bring his children over to him, because officially they are not his, because they were not registered.
There is no counting all the troubles one has when one has no documents. Remember that by not registering your children or your marriage in time you bring eternal troubles upon yourselves, your wives and your children.
Therefore do not neglect your vital ["bloody"] interests and register everything in time. Do not put it off until tomorrow! For afterwards it will be too late.
—o—
Echoes of the Crash of the "Hansa Bank"
[Bytom — bank collapse.]
As is known, the "Hansa Bank" in Beuthen [Bytom] has suspended its payments. In this connection a meeting of merchants took place, who sharply censured the management of the director. The latter, under the impression of the reproaches, committed suicide by throwing himself under the Gleiwitz [Gliwice] — Beuthen train, and was cut to pieces.
On a Summer Night.

[Literature — humorous sketch.]
A drama in one act.
(A bench on the Górka [the "hill"]).
SHE: — Sir, where are you moving to? I did not permit you that.
HE: — My dear miss, I did not ask you for any permission.
SHE: — Kindly go away!
HE: — No.
SHE: — You are a scoundrel ["podlec"].
HE: — You guessed wrong. I am a dramatist.
SHE: — That I don't need to know.
HE: — Knowing is making [sic; probably "knowledge is power" — Wissen ist Macht].
SHE: — Make [it] with the gall! [?]
HE: — Quite a successful pun; I like you.
SHE: — Kindly go away!
HE: — I've already told you: no!
SHE: — I will call the police.
HE: — The police you may call.
SHE: — Who gave you the right to sit down next to me!
HE: — Freedom, miss, the freedom of the benches.
(She jumps up hastily and walks away; he walks after her)
SHE: — By what right are you following me?
HE: — Miss, already for the second time you ask only about my right. I am not a lawyer. If you need to know something about rights, I can recommend you one of the finest lawyers.
SHE: — I don't need any lawyers.
HE: — Don't say that, miss. You are young, pretty, full of temperament and... a good lawyer comes in handy.
SHE: — Stop following me!
HE: — Why?
SHE: — My mother does not allow such things.
HE: — Your mother? Who is following your mother, then?
SHE: — Be quiet, you are not worthy to mention her name.
HE: — Excuse me, miss. I don't know your mother's name. What is your mother called?
(She bursts out laughing; it is evident that the man is beginning to please her)
SHE: If you behave like a decent person, I will allow you to come to my home.
HE: — Home? Whose home?
SHE: — My home. If you behave like a decent person.
HE: — Like a decent person, in spring? Impossible, miss, unfortunately...
SHE: — Come, are you going?
HE: — You are in a hurry, miss, and I must tell you, that is not nice of you at all. You forget that we are not yet married; the fact is, we have not even been introduced yet.
SHE: You are actually reproaching me!
HE: — Yes, I am reproaching you; I am older than you. It is my duty to see that you behave decently...
SHE: — (impatiently) Are you going?
HE: — Yes, I'm going, I'm going home, to my own home I'm going... I'm going home to write down the scene before I forget it. A very fine scene... The ending you did spoil, but the rest came out very well for you... The ending should have taken place at my home.. a very dramatic ending...
SHE: — Do you live [printed "vint"] far from here?..
(Curtain.
"Sheker et Shlimazl Company" [i.e. "Lies & Bad Luck Co."]

[Sosnowiec — crime; Łódź.] A true story of 2 young men from Łódź.

A few days ago, on the order of the public prosecutor, 2 important international swindlers, Chaim Pożencki [?] and Lejb Kilman of Łódź, were arrested in Sosnowiec.

The "activity" of the two swindlers over the last few months is truly legendary.

Last winter the said fellows were employed by the Łódź manufactured-goods [textile] merchant Szmul Blum. In the middle of the month of March Blum sent his 2 employees off with a consignment of goods to Piotrków.

Pożencki and Kilman, who were trusted home-grown lads, decided that instead of going to Piotrków they would go and pay a little visit to Paris.

To that end they went off towards Częstochowa, to the little town of Żarki, where they sold part of the goods, the horse and the britzka [cart], and in that way they raised several tens of thousands of zlotys.

Having so considerable a sum in their pocket, they paid 15,0[?] zl. to a smuggler, who smuggled them across from Poland to Berlin.

Their visit to Berlin lasted altogether a few days and ended very tragically: the authorities believed they were dealing with traffickers in women, so they arrested both of them and sent them back across the Polish border, from where the Polish border guard dispatched them to Częstochowa.

Here, however, luck shone on them a little: the voivodeship investigation office in Łódź, to which the Częstochowa police had sent an inquiry, replied that there was no charge whatsoever against Pożencki and Kilman, and therefore both of them were released.

Still having a little money on them, they bought a luxury car, got themselves across the border and this time went off to Paris itself, but here too they did not linger long.

Playing cards, they lost in a single night the whole little bit of cash they had on them.

They therefore decided to go back to Poland as quickly as possible, while they still had enough for third-class railway tickets.

Via Berlin they came to Poland and travelled to Częstochowa, where they gave themselves up into the hands of the police, handing in an exact report of their activity in recent times.

The Częstochowa police at once got in touch with the Łódź investigation office, from where orders came to detain the young men and put them in prison.

And so it was done.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Behaalotcha)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on the portion of this week. Collected and styled by Y. Y.[?]
Parashat Behaalotcha

The Portion
—o—
a) "And this was the work of the menorah" (8:4).
"Moses found the making of the menorah difficult." Sifrei.
According to the Midrash the menorah is a symbol of the Jewish people, and therefore it had to be "miksha", wholly of one piece, because Jews too must be cast together like a single being. When Moses heard this — "he found the making of the menorah difficult" — it seemed impossible to him. That faithful leader knew how hard, how hard it is to carry out such a thing among Jews. So God pointed him to Aaron, "who loves peace and pursues peace", that he should take the mission upon himself. Imrei Shefer.
—o—
b) "Make thee two trumpets" (10:2).
Moses our Teacher chose an original means of calling the princes together: he trumpeted and they assembled... And why did he not simply have each one summoned separately?
— Because he knew the princes, the "representatives of the people", well: each one would have been offended — why was he not sent for first... Having no choice, he had to use a means that would call them all together at the same moment... Ralbag.
—o—
c) "These were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their hosts, and they set forward. And Moses said unto Hobab: We are journeying" (R' [=10], 28–29).
Moses' gesture recalls that host of a celebration who, travelling to a wedding with his relatives and friends, sent invitations many days in advance to those he really wants to come along, whereas those he does not want to come along he invites, only for politeness' sake, at the last moment of departure, when he is already on his way to the train...
Moses did not want Jethro to come along. "Proselytes are hard for Israel"; but after all he was his father-in-law, so at the last moment, when "these were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their hosts, and they set forward", when they had already begun to travel, he invited his father-in-law: "Come thou with us". But Jethro understood that a last-minute "come thou with us" means: stay at home...
R' Shlomo Kluger.
—o—
d) "And it came to pass, when the ark set forward" (10:35).
Ben-Ami, coming once into a synagogue and seeing how during the Torah reading the congregation goes outside to hold conversations, exclaimed: Now I understand the words "and it came to pass, when the ark set forward" — when the Torah is taken out, "let Thine enemies be scattered and let them that hate Thee flee": the congregation scatters and runs about as at a fair.
—o—
e) "We remember the fish which we did eat in Egypt for nought" (11:5).
1.
The Jews said thus: "We remember the fish which we did eat in Egypt — for nought": to recall the fish and the costly dishes we ate in Egypt is in vain, surely wasted words... but let us at least have the onions, the garlic and the melons — at least the onions and garlic... Ohel Yaakov.
2.
"Which we shall eat" [nokhal] — not "which we ate" [akhalnu]. They hoped that they would yet go back to Egypt and feast on the onions, garlic and "plitsern"[?]... Likutim Hadashim.
—o—
f) "Now the man Moses was very meek" (b. g. [=12:3]).
There is no commandment to be humble; the Torah only tells it as praise of Moses —
for how could there be a commandment here? A person must be nothing in his own eyes. And if there were a commandment: keep yourself low! — that would mean: although you really are something, nevertheless be lowly. But the meaning is that you should really be lowly in your own eyes, not because you are commanded to, but because you really are nothing... Merom HaRim.

Haftarah.
—o—
g) "Be silent, all flesh, before the Lord" (Zechariah 2:4 [=2:17]).
The present-day masters of the world give the impression of a gang of thieves who have got into a strange room and, thinking the master of the house is asleep, turn everything in it head down and feet up — and suddenly one of them gives a shout: The master is waking up!.. Hush!..
So too in time to come a cry will be heard among the uninvited masters: "Be silent, all flesh! for He is passed [sic; =aroused] out of His holy habitation"...
Shaar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
h) "The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan, yea, the Lord rebuke thee" (ibid. 6 [=3:2]).
Why "rebuke" twice?
According to the Zohar it turns out that Satan too has a... Satan, who persuades him to make man sin even more than Satan needs to, more than is his duty... therefore "rebuke" twice — both Satans... Tiferet Uziel.

Avot.
—o—
i) "Nor can an ignorant man be pious" (2:5).
The difference between a pious scholar and a pious ignoramus is:
the same difference as between a poor man who comes to sell a diamond and an expert diamond merchant. The poor man, having no notion whatsoever of the value of a diamond — however much he is given, even more than the true value — will always find it too little; whereas the merchant knows the true value and does not overestimate it.
So too a pious ignoramus thinks that if he recites Psalms every day he is at least Abraham our Father... only because he is humble does he hold that he is worthy at any rate of being a David or a Solomon... in the worst case — a little less... but more than that — no; whereas a pious scholar always knows his worth..
Sefat HaYeriah.
—o—
j) "A plastered [sic; =sealed] cistern that loses not a drop" (b. ch. [=2:8]).
And an ignoramus is one who loses a drop. What does that mean? When at the Seder they come to the plagues, the coarse fellow thinks that the Plague of the Firstborn is two separate plagues and pours off 2 times — so he loses a drop, a superfluous drop of wine...
Osem[?] Bosem.
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin: What did R' Leibele 'mend' in Będzin?

[Będzin — community, elections and Agudah.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 20 Sivan 5691 — piątek 5 czerwca 1931 [Friday, 5 June 1931].)
Będzin
What did R' Leibele 'mend' in Będzin?
On Saturday night the bakers were informed "from above" that R' Leibl was coming here for the purpose of intervening with the authorities so that the decree against the bakers would be annulled...
With this news the politicians of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] were out to weaken the bad impression that had been produced in the whole town by the fact that the "Agudah" had dared to take the step of bringing R' Leibl down here, so that he should obtain, as needed, that the distribution of the mandates be changed in their favour...
In the course of Monday the main talk was: "Has Leibele already come? When is he coming, what has he spoiled"? But these were only empty rumours; R' Leibele arrived only on Tuesday at half past five in the morning. His first visit he naturally paid to the Rabbi, who, as rumour has it, had a large part in engaging the "hero" R' Leibele...
Soon afterwards there began a running about and a commotion. Messengers ran back and forth; the first to come running was the dozór [kehilla board] member Mr. Rinski, then the "R' Duds"[?], the Kaminers and all those who conduct the local Agudah politics.
R' Leibele, may his light shine, held a meeting with his advisers and then went off to carry out his holy mission on behalf of Klal Yisrael — pardon — to intervene concerning the bakers...
The next day, Wednesday morning, Messrs. chairman Abraham Liwer and gmina [community] secretary Y. Frejlich were invited to the vice-starosta [deputy district head] Mr. Mandyszewski[?], who declared that the distribution of the mandates must be changed in the sense that from the Zionist list the "Hitachdut" receives 1 mandate, and at the discretion of the election commission a second mandate may also be taken from the same list, which Mr. Mordechai Dafner is to receive.
The vice-starosta also pointed out that at the first council meeting the parnas Aharon Hampel, the son of parnas Abraham Hampel, may not be present.
Then Mr. Frejlich pointed out that with regard to the change of the mandates the combined bloc of the Agudah groupings must also be taken into account. The vice-starosta agreed with this opinion and declared that the Agudah list loses 2 mandates, and these go to the Aleksander Hasidim and the Beit Hamidrash list.
Because of the changes it was ordered that a meeting of the election commission take place on the same day.
The "historic" meeting was set for 5 in the afternoon. Around the gmina premises a large crowd gathered, which awaited with curiosity the result of the planned change.
Half of the election commission, 8 persons in all, came to the meeting; the other half, also of that number, headed by the chairman Mr. Gershon Rechnic, did not come to the meeting. But the "Agudah" parnassim nevertheless dared, regardless of the fact that there was no quorum, to hold the meeting, at which the following "division" was made: from the Zionist list they took off 2 mandates and allotted 1 to "Hitachdut" and 1 to Mr. Dafner.
From the Agudah list they likewise took off 2 mandates and allotted 1 to the Aleksander Hasidim, and the 2nd to their ally R' Yekl Welgrin[?] (Beit Hamidrash).
The municipal budget is ready. Water price unchanged.

[Będzin — municipality.] On Tuesday evening the budget commission closed the ordinary and the extraordinary budget for the year 1931/32.
The ordinary budget has been reduced, compared with last year, by 70 thousand złoty. The extraordinary budget amounts to no more than 300 thousand złoty.
At the third reading the proposal that the price of water be reduced to 40 groszy was rejected. But [?] the price has remained as it was until now.
Confiscations of the Zionist election appeals annulled

[Będzin — kehilla elections.] During the election campaign an election appeal of the Zionist election committee was confiscated because the appeal stated that "we are waging a struggle against the dark force of the 'Agudah' [Agudat Israel], which wants to remove from the kehilla everything that has any connection with culture and progress."
The district court in Sosnowiec found nothing wrong in the appeal and annulled the confiscation.
Working Eretz Israel on the eve of the 17th Zionist Congress.

[Będzin — Zionism.] This week the election committee of Working Eretz Israel was constituted in Będzin; it comprises the Right Poale Zion, "Hitachdut", "HeHalutz", "Gordonia", "Frayhayt" and "HaShachar".
In the present elections to the Zionist Congress all the groupings that recognise Working Eretz Israel appear for the first time with a single unified list, which bears the number 5.
In recent days several larger meetings were held in the premises of "Hitachdut", devoted to the most topical questions of Zionism and of Eretz Israel.
Tomorrow, Saturday, there will be a rally organised by the joint election bloc of Working Eretz Israel about the forthcoming Congress in Basel.
In the halutz circles people are preparing intensively for Sunday's elections.
The Landlords' Association

[Będzin — associations.] The Landlords' Association asks us to announce that house-owners who have been punished with a fine, arrest, etc. without any grounds should apply to the House-Owners' Association in order to register.
The rabbinate proclaims treyf, and the customers shout kosher! kosher!

[Będzin — kashrut.] For quite a long time now the butcher Michał Jakub Piekarski has had to endure bans from the local rabbinate because he brings meat from Sosnowiec. Because Piekarski sells meat more cheaply, the bans have had no success at all.
Last Monday the entire rabbinate, with the Rabbi at its head, went to Mr. Piekarski's butcher shop and, before the assembled public, proclaimed a ban on the meat brought in from outside.
In answer to the ban Piekarski again reduced the price of meat. That did indeed have an effect, and the women answered the proclaimed ban: kosher, kosher...
The new station will be opened this month.

[Będzin — town.] As we have already written, the building of the new station will be opened this month.
The celebrations committee has decided that the opening should take place quite modestly, without the promised parades.
The opening is definitively to take place in the last days of June (czerwiec) of this year.
A boy saved from danger.

[Będzin — accident.] On Tuesday afternoon a car ran onto an 11[?]-year-old Jewish boy; thanks to the driver's quick presence of mind the car was stopped instantly and the boy was saved from certain danger.
Bitten by a cat
On the Old Market (Stary Rynek), house number 7, a cat — at a time when nobody was at home — bit a small child of the local house caretaker (concierge).
The conscription commission

At the magistrate we are asked to draw the attention of those liable to conscription (pobór) that when reporting they should bring along a photograph or a "dowód osobisty" [identity card]. Without these documents he will not be admitted to the conscription commission.
Sosnowiec. A little "factory" of counterfeit 10-złoty banknotes in the cemetery

In a small shop on Szelecka [Sielecka?] Street in Sosnowiec a young Christian woman was detained who wanted to pay for the groceries she had bought with a counterfeit 10-zł. banknote.
The police, searching the woman's flat, found 600 [?] such counterfeit banknotes.
Under questioning her husband declared that he is as poor as can be ("owes God his soul") and that he had found the treasure in the cemetery.
"How so?" asks the commissioner.
"I," he says, "saw a beautiful flowerpot in the cemetery, and when I took it I saw that under the flowerpot lay a packet of paper. At first I thought it was communist literature, but only later did I see my luck..."
The police went to the place he indicated and found there a well-equipped factory with printing blocks (clichés), stamps and the like.
As it turns out, the factory is still a legacy of the Widaw [?] brothers, who were arrested a few weeks ago for circulating counterfeit banknotes.
The critical situation of the Jewish carpenters. Intervention not to bring in furniture from outside

The local Jewish carpenters find themselves in a very critical situation because there are no buyers for their products.
For this reason a meeting of the carpenters' guild was held, which resolved to appeal to the local furniture dealers not to buy furniture elsewhere, in order to ease the crisis of the local carpenters.
Jews fight over a livelihood

On Targowa Street a quarrel broke out over a customer between the Jewish shoemakers Gruba and Gerszegowicz [sic; below Gerszenowicz]. Gruba's wife also came to help, and the two of them dragged Gerszenowicz into a gateway, where Gerszenowicz was stabbed.
Medical aid was given by the Jewish community (kehilla). The wounded G. now needs a longer course of treatment.
A brawl between customer "grabbers"

On Modrzejowska Street a brawl took place between the customer-grabbers (touts); during the brawl a large shop window of the firm Markowicz was smashed.
The shop window costs 8 hundred zł.
Elections to the 17th Zionist Congress

Next Sunday elections to the 17th Zionist Congress take place throughout Poland.
The local Revisionists are conducting a strong election campaign, which is being run under the slogans: "The leadership must pass into other hands, the policy of submission (hachnaah) has definitively failed, and Zionists must send new representatives to the Congress."
Meeting of the small traders.

On Sunday morning the annual general meeting of the local small traders will take place in the "Angielski" hall.
As we are informed, it can be foreseen in advance that the meeting will have a stormy character. For that reason a delegate of the Central Committee (Ts"K) in Warsaw is coming specially.
Fires from lightning.
During Sunday's storm, fires broke out in Wojkowice Kościelne from lightning strikes. The damage is considerable.
The hot days — a paradise for thieves.
In the first days of the week, when a strong heat prevailed, a series of thefts took place, which were carried out through windows being kept open.
A recruit sentenced to 1 year in prison.

At the local district court the trial took place of the 22-year-old Mazur of Dąbrowa, who, as a recruit, had made an anti-state speech at the station in Dąbrowa.
Mazur was sentenced to 1 year in prison.
—o—
Died suddenly.
Mr. Janicki, councillor of the Chamber of Commerce and member of the commissarial council, went last Sunday to Mysłowice to bathe. On the way he suffered a heart attack and death came instantly.
—o—
The municipal budget
will be dealt with at the voivodeship office in the course of next week. To defend the budget, the commissioner, Mr. Woźniak, is travelling to Kielce.
—o—
A trial over a servant.
Today, Friday, the trial takes place at the local municipal court of 2 Jewish young men, residents of Modrzejowska [?] Street.
The young men were charged by the police with fighting with each other over a Christian servant.
With a short-term visa one cannot stay in France

Lately false rumours have been spreading among emigrants that if one obtains in Poland a short-term visa to France, one can settle down there.
In this connection we point out that it is practically impossible; people who come to France on the strength of short-term visas can in no case obtain permission to work there, nor to remain in France. When the term of the visa expires, the persons holding such visas are sent out of France.
A group of young people who were misled in this way find themselves there now in a difficult situation and are asking to be sent back to Poland.

Yesterday evening the first meeting of the newly elected kehilla council took place in the premises of the Będzin kehilla.
Already an hour before the meeting a very large crowd gathered in front of the gmina [community] premises and afterwards went into the meeting hall. The crush was so great that the councillors (parnasim) could hardly get into the "parliament".
At last the chairman's bell is heard and the agenda is taken up; it is read out by the secretary, Mr. Freilich.

The Piotrków crafts school of the Society for the Spread of Crafts and Agricultural Work among Jews (licensed by the Ministry of Education) is holding a new enrolment for its departments of mechanical locksmithing and furniture joinery.

The Result of the By-Elections to the Town Council in Olkusz

(A letter from Olkusz).
On Sunday by-elections were held here in place of the 11 councillors of the "Klub Mieszczański" [Burghers' Club], who had laid down their mandates in protest.
Standing in the elections were the B. B. [Non-Party Bloc], the PPS ("Frakcja") and 3 Jewish lists. The result: B. B. 6 mandates, PPS 1 mandate and the Jewish lists 4 mandates. Together with the old councillors, the town council consists of 14 Jews, 8 B.B. and 2 PPS.
The greater part of the Jewish population did not take part in the elections, because the Jewish population did not want to exploit the fight being waged between 2 Polish parties; but 2–3 Jewish councillors, on their own responsibility, without any consultation with the Jewish population as a whole, publicly supported and campaigned for the list.
A painful impression was made by the fact that the rabbi took part in the campaigning for number 1 and sent the shammes round to all the minyanim [to announce] that according to Jewish law Jews must vote for No. 1.
And here the question must once again be put to the honoured rabbi: would it not have been better for your dignity and for the dignity of the Torah not to meddle in political affairs? Is it not the task of a rabbi to care for purely Jewish matters? Do you not know, honoured rabbi, that the synagogue and the Talmud Torah are in a sad, dreadful state?
Some of the Jewish councillors fought hard for the victory of number 1. On Saturday the mayor, accompanied by 2 policemen, made a speech to the worshippers, and when the newly elected councillor Szarf wanted to say something, the chairman of the meeting, a second "Leibele"[?], turned to the policeman in these words: "Posterunkowy, zabierz go!" ("Constable, take him away!") — and at once dissolved the meeting.
According to rumours, the old Jewish councillors are to resign in protest that the Jewish lists have now obtained mandates — and new elections are to take place...
Be that as it may, the Jews of Olkusz are "insured" a livelihood...
M. Sz.
The Jubilee Celebration of the Vilna Troupe

Last Saturday night a festive jubilee performance of the Vilna Troupe took place in Będzin.
As we already wrote in the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", the Vilna Troupe is now celebrating the 15th jubilee of its existence, and for this reason a special jubilee committee was founded in Będzin — as in other towns in Poland — which carried out the celebration.
The performance aroused great interest in the town, so that already by Friday almost all the tickets were sold out, and on Saturday evening literally hundreds of people went away from the box office without tickets.
In the name of the jubilee committee Mr. Frejlich opens the evening and greets the Vilna players in heartfelt words. He points out the thorny road that the troupe has travelled until now.
Mr. Frejlich also reads out a series of greetings from Będzin cultural institutions such as Hazamir, Muza, Kultur-Lige, the evening courses and the Brenner Library.
In the greeting of the editors of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" it was pointed out that there actually exists not one Vilna Troupe but several Vilna troupes. In this case, however, the splitting is a virtue, because each branch has grown into a beautiful tree.
A strong impression was left by the greeting of the Będzin school organisation. In this greeting the celebration in honour of the Vilna players was linked with the latest Vilna event — the closing of the teachers' seminary there — and at the words: "Let the mighty voice be heard against the assailants of the rights of the masses", the hall literally thundered with protest against the monstrous injustice that the Vilna school curatorium has committed.
After a longer reply of thanks by director Mazo, the actual performance of the Vilna players began at about 10 o'clock.
The programme consisted of a series of scenes from various plays and also of humorous songs.
The performance ended after midnight and left a very good impression.
On Monday the performance was repeated, and this time too the theatre was packed and the audience — satisfied.

The Failure of the Artisans — The artisans' organizations then and now — The reasons for the downhill slide

[Zagłębie — artisans; article.] The artisans' organizations then and now. — The reasons for the downhill slide.
Ten years ago Jewish artisanry in Poland stood at its highest level; it was then in its period of blossoming. Everywhere it was well represented, everywhere it had its representatives. In almost every town there was an artisans' organization, and in the larger centres, such as ours in Zagłębie, the organization occupied a very honourable place, so that all strata of the population had to reckon with it, whether they wanted to or not.
When, for example, city-council elections, Sejm elections or kehilla elections came round, or even when a new board had to be chosen in any institution whatsoever, people first of all looked to see what face the artisans were making, which way they were leaning, and they had to be reckoned with. Every side used every possible means to draw the artisans' sympathy to itself.
Nor was that any wonder, because with their votes they had the chance to penetrate everywhere and to hold sway everywhere.
In the course of the last few years they began to go backwards. We noticed this very well and drew their attention to the slippery paths on which they had set out, but their broad gesture, their mania of grandeur and their arrogance did not allow anyone to point out to them what was not to someone's liking — and they took offence: how could it be, who dares say anything of the kind to them? And the answer was short and simple: we ask nobody, and nobody needs to give us any opinion. Never mind — they said in a tone of assurance — we can manage our little town ourselves, we can get along without advisers and without guides.
But in spite of everything they went downhill everywhere; they lost one position after another. One of the finest, soundest and oldest financial institutions, which they possessed in Będzin — the bank, in which the public had so much trust — they destroyed themselves: they stood at the helm and broke it systematically and consciously, and rendered no account of their harmful deeds. Then the system of destruction penetrated into the organization itself and made colossal progress there...
To what extent this can be confirmed we can see from the result of the kehilla elections. It will surely be no secret to anyone any more that in the kehilla elections the artisans throughout Poland suffered the greatest defeat. This shows us how far the artisans have steadily sunk, and only because of this have they reached their present level, which proves their fall.
So the question arises: what is the cause of this? What is the reason that they have sunk so low, although in human material they are, after all, the majority? The number of craftsmen has nevertheless not diminished; they still have their huge army — so where have their members gone? For whom did they vote, and why did they not vote for their own people, their own representatives?
From this it is plain to see that they have lost confidence in their own people, in their leaders. Self-evidently this did not happen unwittingly; when people lose confidence in leaders, they must have thorough motives for it.
When the organizations began to form in Poland, the craftsman found himself on the lowest level. Then the better, the more intelligent among them came and began to raise them up, began to care for a better today and a brighter tomorrow, and this impressed the members, the onlookers and sympathizers, and all those who respect the Jewish craftsman and want to see him in a good condition. Unfortunately, however, their leaders went further: they did not occupy themselves only with what concerned them, but spread themselves freely and openly over every field, regardless of whether they were competent and whether the organization needed it. The burden was therefore too great, the undertaking an unnecessary one, and it was exactly this that took the leaders off the rails; they quite simply lost their balance, and then the downhill slide began.
The board took too much upon itself; their fellow members noticed mistakes, enormous mistakes, which those at the helm did not want to acknowledge, so that in time the activity — the true, honest activity — turned into ambitions, into tripping one another up, and then it was forgotten that whoever takes on public offices must reckon with the members. A constant struggle began, but here, God forbid, no one fought for any idea or for improving the material situation of the members. Intrigues, quarrels and squabbles began. Naturally, both the organization and the members began to suffer from this: the treasury began to empty, the member began to be held cheap, nobody looked after him any more, and so the members in turn began to "dismiss" their leaders, so that they lost confidence in them.
And so, one by one, one by one, it led to the culminating point: a competition of intrigues and splits began, which led to the saddest phenomena in the field of artisanry. One had to blush with shame when reading the Zagłębie election "literature", where one artisan — that is, one fellow member — called another a thief, an informer (moser) and other such pearls of expression. Naturally the other side did not keep silent, and curses were simply poured out.
In that case it is no wonder that the prestige of and respect for the artisans' leaders were lost, so that the defeat could have been foreseen and therefore did not come unexpectedly. But the question arises: what next? How, and in what way, will they react to this unwelcome phenomenon? Surely people must understand the meaning of the slap in the face they received throughout Poland at the kehilla elections. Surely this lesson must be a matter of the greatest importance, one with which the artisan elements must reckon.
Thanks to this failure the artisans' leaders must see that public activity, public interest, demands the recognition and sympathy of all kinds of artisan strata; and if this is neglected, if one thinks that the mass must follow its leaders blindly — they have now had the opportunity to convince themselves that they are no blind tool in someone else's hands.
If one wants to lead a mass, if one wants to be anyone's guide and chosen representative, one must earn it through honest, sincere and fruitful activity, which on no account is ever lost.
R. Les.
The Policeman Is Coming!

(A little picture with a moral.)

Every morning I make a habit of dropping in on my shopkeeper, taking two "Avanti" [Awanti cigarettes] from him on credit and meanwhile reading through the newspaper.
I am not the only one. Many come for "Avanti" and for the newspaper. It is a real reading room there.
At the invalid's [the disabled tobacco vendor] I cannot buy: he neither gives on credit nor gives a newspaper to read.
On Sunday morning I went in to the shopkeeper by the back way. I stood in the dining room, waiting for my "Avanti" and devouring the newspaper with my eyes. Behind [?] me a couple of customers were already waiting in line.
Suddenly the shopkeeper's younger girl ran in, out of breath:
"A policeman!"
And before I had managed to slip out, he was already in the house, with the black satin [?] strap of his cap let down — a sign that he is on duty.
What happened there after that I do not know. I believe they did not "hang" the shopkeeper, for had they hanged him "um khoge" [?], he could not have traded during the week. But he surely had bloodshed enough, if it did not cost him a protocol [police report]...
Only as I went out did I think: why does the policeman have to come in by the back?
In former years, too, trading on Sunday was forbidden, and the policemen used to content themselves with seeing that the doors were shut and the street looked festive. But why should a Jew be forced to keep, in his own home, the commandments and transgressions of the Christian faith?
And because Christians were not allowed to smoke and write on Sunday, should a Jew in his own home also not be allowed to smoke and write? Why? God gave each people its own Torah!
Granted, when in Konstanz they seized the goldsmith Eliezer (in the opera "Żydówka" [Halévy's La Juive]) and beat him for working in his own home, one can excuse it by saying that by knocking with his hammer he offended the religious feelings of the masses in front of the church. But selling "Avanti" in a little shop behind closed doors — whom can that bother?
I would therefore ask our government: before it goes to abolish compulsory Sunday rest — which will surely happen soon — let it meanwhile abolish the custom of a policeman coming in by the back. He has nothing to look for in the shopkeeper's home.
Unless he himself wants to buy "Avanti"...
Abi Ver.
Our Panorama

(Piccard flies up into the sky and the Jews of Porąbka appeal to the conscience [?] of the world. — A gabbai who treats people to "bitter waters." — "Yetziv Pitgam" for a barrel of beer. — The "domestic peace" between the Revisionists and the League. — "Cases" in the Dąbrowa kehilla.)

Professor Piccard took a fancy to fly "up into the sky"; he wanted to see what goes on there under the clouds, and whether there too there is such a little world with so many parties, strongmen and plagues as multiply on our world. If he, Piccard I mean, had cared to listen to me, I would have sent him with his balloon to Porąbka [near Sosnowiec], because according to the reports from Porąbka "it is high time the public knew who is leading the Jews of Porąbka by the nose"...
And truly "heartrending" is what goes on there. A group of Jews, residents of Porąbka, considered how they might enjoy this world. After lengthy deliberation it was decided to found a minyan called "Early-Risers' Prayer." Quite simply: on Shabbat they would pray early and then go out for a stroll and enjoy nature.
The reform, however, met with fierce opponents. Among them also the local beadles, who are qualified [?] in matters of "with a strong hand," and "a war of life and death flared up."
The fight, which takes place every Shabbat, has become very popular even among non-Jews, who gather to watch the "wicked wonders" and take delight in the "strong family" that will not let the "Żydki" pray [modlić się] early in the morning...
If "public opinion" does not react to this "injustice," our correspondent assures us, the Jews of Porąbka will be "blackened and darkened" the whole summer long...
— — —
The society "Nos'ei" [?] in Będzin also has a big trouble [kłopot]. The society, whose pedigree goes back to the first "Powstanie" [Polish uprising], is now occupied with a very "grave matter."
From time immemorial, as we know, say the society's members, the fourth aliyah of the portion Naso was with us an honourable "portion"; is it a trifle, the laws of the sotah? A whole tractate is devoted to the matter of the sotah!
So we honoured, as it were, the Torah reader with the aliyah; but how surprised we were when the reader actually got angry with us and, instead of a drink, said:
"Bitter waters you can get"...
There is, however, a second side in the society, which agrees with the angry reader: he is right, they say; "as you make your bed, so you sleep"; if a gabbai sells off the "Yetziv Pitgam" for a "fiftl" [a fifth — a measure of liquor], the reader ought to treat the society's members to
"bitter waters"...
— — —
Since we have come to speak of "bitter water," one must also not pass over indifferently, without touching on, the "bitterness" that reigns between the League [for Labour Palestine] and the Revisionists in Sosnowiec.
You surely know the scene that often occurs in the Hasidic shtiblekh, especially on the holidays, when little Yisroel has a glass of liquor, and when one man steps up to the lectern and begins "Va-yedaber," another shouts out "Ashrei"...
Just such a similar scene played out during the "holidays" of the elections to the coming Congress.
The Sosnowiec Revisionists arranged a meeting under the open sky, probably intending that "the waves of the 'radio' should catch the just resolutions and carry them to the British power"...
But it happened otherwise: when the speaker, a Revisionist, had barely begun to speak, suddenly "secret voices" were heard from the side against the Revisionist arguments...
Well, what do Revisionists do? They carried out a "revision" [search] in the house and found...
"Whom do you think? An Agudah man?"
"You are mistaken — they actually grabbed a 'Hitachdut-nik'"...
So the vexation is greater: "according to the cry thereof"? Can it be? A hard question!
The "question" was soon answered by a third party, the police, and the meeting was dispersed on account of the "crowing" of their own people..
— — —
In the Dąbrowa gmina "wonders" are happening. It was always accepted that the holy sheep cried:
"Meh, meh."
And today the situation has changed: today, when the "Agudah" hears a Zionist shouting: hypocrites, Black-Hundreds men,
the answer is: "Meh..."
The "symphony" has now repeated itself for the second time. The only Zionist councillor of the Dąbrowa kehilla wants to read a Zionist declaration; the other side says to him:
"Neither your honey nor your sting... We don't want you and don't want to hear your declarations."
The councillor is stubborn and reads. But right at the start the other councillors leave the premises.
The Zionist councillor gets angry: Can it be? Why, he shouts at the Agudah councillors, did you not walk out of the hall when the Bundist preached about "darkness"?
A hard question indeed, but the "Agudah" councillors answer that they suspect the Dąbrowa Zionists: if, they say, they were kosher Zionists, they would have seized with both hands the concept that would let them bring 2 members into the kehilla board...
Which side's claim is "justified" is "hard" to decide; one thing, however, is clear: in answer to "Black-Hundreds men, hypocrites," the reply is:
"Meh, meh..."
Ben Amotz.
We Demand Reconstruction.

It took five years before the Sanacja camp came to us with a clear programme for rebuilding the machinery of state. That too was a kind of piatiletka [five-year plan] — a piatiletka from the left side [i.e. in reverse]: squeezing all the juice out of the citizen in order to sustain the state. Now that it has come to the last drop, now that there is soon nothing left to squeeze out of the citizen, they have come with the reduction [austerity] plans.
For us Jews these 5 years were a period of a characteristic experience: that the bitterest persecutions of Jews are possible without formal antisemitism. Now, in the new programme, this method is being fixed and stabilised — evidently for many years.
During those 5 years we kept thinking that the Sanacja, which fights antisemitism so hard, wants to do us good but cannot. It seems that others in that camp thought so too, for instance Bartel, who after all gave us such enormous promises. They themselves had no concrete plan and interpreted things thus: as soon as political antisemitism is smoked out, a way to heal the Jewish plague will somehow be found anyway.
The error has now been cleared up. There is no cure for the Jewish plague. On the contrary, every new experiment is a fresh blow for the Jews, and the latest reform promises us only heavy blows.
And indeed, what is Prystor [the prime minister] to blame for, if over generations the Jewish economy took shape in such a way that it became one of the sick parts of the present Polish state? He is after all only the doctor who must burn out the proud flesh; he will burn out the overgrowth of officialdom and of the merchant class, regardless of whom it hurts.
What has that to do with antisemitism?
Nothing whatsoever. And we really ought to stop complaining about antisemitism. Moreover, we ought even to hold back our sufferings from the operation, for, after all, we are citizens of the Polish state and... "pray for the welfare of the government."
But the doctor's duty is not only to burn out, but also to apply a healing balm, to soothe the pains — and the balm must be applied precisely to the burnt parts.
This is our right, our duty: to demand it of the government.
The government has changed the front; we must turn our political attack to the new front. We must not weep over "who shall die" but over "who shall live"; we must complain not about what is taken from us, but about what we are not given.
In Poland the process of declassing the Jews has advanced with slow Menshevik steps; for 12 years now the discrimination of Jews has been going on, and they have still not reached the end; there are still remnants left which must be sifted through and thrown out onto the rubbish heap [śmietnik].
But there are other countries where the machine works faster, more decisively. In Spain a revolution has just been carried out, and they are already about to abolish Isabella's decree against the Jews. In Mexico they have only just discriminated against the Jewish petty traders, and already there is talk of settling the expelled on the land.
The main thing, however, is our neighbour [the Soviet Union], the classic state of breaking down and rebuilding. There the work of breaking and destroying was carried out at a quick Bolshevik tempo. Of the former Jewish bourgeoisie — the industrialist, the merchant, the petty trader, the "Luftmensch" — not a remnant is left. The state has included the Jewish element too in its reconstruction plan, and it does all it can, in its own way, according to its own notions; there they are not content with burning out the wounds, they also apply balm.
And there nobody demanded it, nobody could demand it; the state itself understood that it is a disgrace to show itself before the world with such a blemish, and that it is useful for itself as well to transform the Jewish community into a creative and constructive element.
We here, after all, have political freedom and a Jewish political representation. We can demand, and therefore we must demand. A mute child — the mother must feed it of her own accord; but one who can speak will not be given anything as long as he does not ask.
Our representation must demand from the government a clear reconstruction programme for the Jews. Instead of always repeating the familiar "Avinu Malkenu" about tearing up the evil decree, we must now move on to the new "Avinu Malkenu" — about inscribing for us salvation and consolation.
And first of all Jewish society itself must make this clear to itself. We must cut down a little on the lamentations over the ruin and seek within ourselves the strength for reconstruction, organise these forces, give expression to our mighty will to live in new forms. With this we shall push our politicians to fight in that direction. Whoever will not want to engage in this struggle must be washed off the public stage; he may not represent us.
We must say openly to the government: you have destroyed us — you must rebuild us.
P. K.
Norway and Poland.

A conversation with the economic chief of the Norwegian state.
Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", by Z. Haber.
At the last Leipzig fair the exhibition of the Norwegian government made a great impression. One could clearly see how the Norwegian state is making every effort to compete with its products on the world market.
During my journey in Norway I sought an opportunity to talk with the head of the economic industry, Ernst P. Hagen, who let me take a look at his records, which cover almost the whole world, where Norway wants by all means to sell its goods.
Hagen is very pleased that it is precisely a Jewish journalist who comes to him, because he knows what role Jews play in the world of commerce, and knows that if Norway is to sell its products in the world, the Jewish merchant will help with it to a great extent.
His statistics show interesting figures concerning Poland. In 1926 Poland exported goods to Norway for one and a half million dollars, and in 1929 Norway received goods from Poland for more than five million dollars. In the same period Norway supplied Poland with goods rising from half a million dollars in 1926 to 3 million dollars in 1929.
Mostly Poland supplies Norway with coal; no less than 4 million dollars' worth Poland supplied to Norway in 1929. Calcium nitrate, an artificial means of fertilising the fields, Poland obtained from Norway in the same year for two million dollars.
Besides this Poland supplies Norway with rye, barley, beans and bran; for a small sum also sugar, galoshes, wood and other things.
— In 1929 Poland had various ships built in Norway for four hundred thousand dollars. In Norway shipbuilders are strongly represented, and almost every larger ship has been built there.
Besides this Norway supplies Poland with a great deal of fish and fish products, such as fresh and salted herring, canned fish, fish meal, cod-liver oil for medical articles, technical skins[?], edible fats, which are made in Norway in a most successful manner.
For the Polish iron industry Norway supplies iron briquettes and sinter, sulphur, aluminium and silicon; iron and metal scrap too are a strong article sent from Norway to Poland.
Hagen thinks that Norway has hundreds more articles which would be good business for Poland and in which the Jewish merchants in particular could take an interest.
Between Poland and Norway there exists a very good trade treaty, which has granted large customs reductions between both countries, and there are certainly possibilities of exporting various Polish products to Norway and bringing Norwegian products to Poland.
Both countries have legations with good commercial representatives.
Freight conditions are also very good, since Norwegian ships constantly arrive between Norway and the Polish port of Gdynia and also Danzig, and Polish ships too come regularly to the Norwegian ports.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's sidra
Collected and styled by Y. Y.[?]
Parshat Shelach
—o—
Parsha
a) "And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Yehoshua" (13:16).
"When Moses saw his humility, he called Hoshea son of Nun: Yehoshua — may God save you." Targum Yonatan.
When Moses noticed humility and modesty in his disciple and successor, he called out to him: "Yehoshua — may God save you!" May God help you. For it is hard, hard for such modest and quiet great men to take their proper place in society, where the top seats are reserved only for those who make a noise: "We are the great men of the generation!"
"May God help you!" Pity on you, Yehoshua! Little will you gain with your quietness, your modesty. Ah, you poor thing, you need God's help... Kesef Nivchar.
—o—
b) "And surely it flows with milk and honey... nevertheless the people be strong."
1.
When someone wants to speak ill of a thing that everyone accepts as good, he first begins to praise the thing, and thereby wins trust for himself. Only then does he start smuggling in his slander...
The spies did the same: first of all they told that it is a land that drips with milk and honey and every good thing is found there. Only after so much praise does the real point begin: "Nevertheless the people be strong..." Beit Shmuel Acharon.
2.
The spies did not set out to spread libels about the Land of Israel. They merely held that it was not right to acquire the Land of Israel by natural means... But those pious ones ("frumakes") were after honour (as the Zohar says: they feared that on coming to the Land of Israel they would cease to be princes). And although they reasoned only in a pious spirit, their thirst for honour led them to rebel against God... Shelah.
—o—
c) "And all the people that we saw in it are men of great stature" (13:32).
If the whole people are men of stature, gigantic and strong, then how is it "a land that eats up its inhabitants"?
— The spies reasoned thus: in the land there are only giants. And how does it come about that there is not a single weak person in the land? — Probably it is "a land that eats up its inhabitants", a land with an unhealthy climate where only giants can live, and the slightly weaker ones pack up for the next world...
Thus one can aim an arrow out of every praise... [printed "shvah", apparently a misprint for "shevach", praise.] Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
d) "I have pardoned according to your word — but as truly as I live, all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord" (14:21).
The two verses seemingly have no connection at all. As is known, the spies also spoke slander against God ("for they are stronger than He"). But slander spoken in the presence of the person concerned is not called slander. The prohibition of slander means only when one gossips behind the other's back, when he has no chance to defend himself.
This is what God said[?]: "I have pardoned according to your word" — for the slander against Me I forgive, because "the whole earth is full of the glory of the Lord", for God's spirit is everywhere. Well, wherever they speak slander against Me, it is always in My presence, so it is no sin... Nachalat Yaakov.
—o—
e) "But it shall not prosper" (14:41).
A remarkable and quite wondrous passage on this verse we find in the book Tzidkat ha-Tzaddik (section 46) by Rabbi Tzadok ha-Kohen, one of the most brilliant Hasidic thinkers, a principal disciple of the Rebbe of Izbica —
The passage reads:
The ma'apilim, those who wanted to storm the Land of Israel against the will of Providence, held to the rule: "Whatever the master of the house tells you, do — except 'leave'". That is: when the master of the house drives you out of his home — do not obey him... But "it shall not prosper" — they did not succeed then.
Then — but there is a time when such a tactic will indeed succeed, "and that is in our present time, the footsteps of the Messiah"...
—o—
f) "And that ye go not about after... your eyes" (15:39).
"Your eyes" — these are the "eyes of the congregation", the great men of the generation. But at times it is said: "that ye go not about after your own heart and your own eyes" — one need not always blindly follow the "eyes of the congregation". The spies, too, were righteous men and great men of the generation, and Jeroboam son of Nebat, too, was considered a leader...
Sefer ha-Zechut (Rabbi Y. M. of Ger).
—o—
Haftarah.
g) "And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy."
For spies had been sent in the days of Moses and only two proved honest: Joshua and Caleb. Therefore that same Joshua considered the wrong and sent no more than two... so that the affair of Moses' time should never repeat itself.
Or Pnei Moshe.
—o—
Avot.
h) "And whither thou goest" (3:1).
Rabbi Eizikel of Komarno, in his book Netzer Chesed on Avot, relates on this mishna the following episode from the life of great rebbes of old:
"I heard from my holy father Rabbi Alexander, of blessed memory. I was then a small child, and two days passed when there was not a piece of bread in the house, and he sat and studied and his face shone and glowed. Afterwards he came in to his family and saw our distress, and he said: 'My children, after all it is no more than [the] seventy years'..."
That is how the great rebbes of old lived...
—o—
i) "Morning sleep" (14).
One of the things that "remove a person from the world" is "morning sleep" — sleeping away the years of youth; a person always regrets it afterwards.
Likkutim Chadashim.
Będzin. The investment tax has risen from the dead; Jewish council members leave the meeting.

On Tuesday's meeting of the Commissioners' Council [the appointed municipal board] of Będzin the „idyll“ burst. The Jewish nominated members, who until now would not let themselves be convinced that they have very little say, this time saw the truth, and only then did they run away.
At the beginning of the meeting Mr. G. Rechnic[?] takes the floor, reacting to the fact that the statute of the investment tax is again on the agenda. „After all, we decided together — says Mr. Rechnic — that the tax would not be levied this year; why is it on the agenda again?“
To this the Commissioner replies that at the first meeting he too was against the tax, but because the public school („powszechna szkoła“) in Gzichów must be built, he is in favour of the investment tax.
Mr. Rechnic asks for his first statement to be entered in the minutes and leaves the meeting. Messrs. Hampel, Gutensztajn and Szwajcer declare their solidarity with this step.
The new „masters of the house“ are apparently pleased with this, and the statute of the investment tax is adopted without any discussion.
The same fate befell the statute of the waterworks. The proposal of 40 gr. is rejected, and the price in force until now, 50 gr. per cubic metre, is fixed.
An amendment to this statute is adopted, that persons supported by the „Opieka Społeczna“ [municipal social welfare] be exempted from the water charge.
After a longer break (because one person was missing for a quorum) the town's „masters of the house“ sat down at the table again and began to think about „town affairs“. The question was raised of finding a suitable name for the new street being opened on the area towards the Warpie. Various names were proposed, but they did not find favour, and the „child“ remains nameless for the time being...
Characteristically, one of the councillors complained in passing about the „injustice“ that Kołłątaja Street is almost a Jewish „dzielnica“ [quarter], whereas Kołłątaj had nothing whatsoever in common with Jews...
Before adopting the budget for 32/ 193 [probably 1931/32] the Commissioner delivers an exposé in which he admits that the economic situation is critical, revenues are falling, and above all it is foreseen that the revenue from the turnover tax will not amount to more than 20 percent of the preliminary sum; and he proposes adopting the budget, which in his opinion is very realistic. At the same time the Commissioner submits a series of proposals on granting new and reducing old subsidies; the new „portion“ amounts to 15 thousand zł. This item is to be covered by raising the levy on goods brought in by rail.
The councillors agree to everything, and in haste the budget is adopted in the amount of 1,819 694 [1,819,694 zł].
—o—
Support the „Keren Hayesod“!
If you want a strong and mighty Land of Israel — support the „Keren Hayesod“!
The „birth pangs“ of the new post-office building.

The opening of the new post-office building was supposed to take place this month already, but as it turns out, the matter is again postponed by several months. The furniture that was brought from Kraków is unusable and will be exchanged for a new complete set of furniture; the work on the telegraph cable is not yet finished either.
Mr. Fürstenberg's resignation accepted.
The Kielce voivode has accepted the resignation of President Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg as a member of the Commissioners' Council in Będzin.
Hooligan act of a Christian waiter.

On Saturday evening Mr. Judel Potok[?] was playing billiards in Czerwiński's confectionery. On leaving, Potok told the waiter that tomorrow he would give him 2 zł for the „time“, to which the waiter did not agree, and an exchange of words arose between the two. The result was that the waiter struck Potok on the head with a beer glass and seriously wounded him. Potok was taken to the local hospital, where an operation was performed.
The hooligan act aroused indignation among that part of the youth who are frequent guests in the said „Jew-friendly“ confectionery.
One-day strike in the „Talmud Torah“. „Geese and cheesecakes are marketable articles“.

The situation in the Talmud Torah is getting worse from day to day. The deficit grows ever larger and the melamdim [teachers] are not receiving their tuition fees.
The consequence of the critical situation was that on Sunday the melamdim went on strike. After much effort by the administration it was achieved that the melamdim should return to their work; for this they received promises that they would get a few guilders a week...
In connection with the situation the interested party turned to the Rabbi with the request that he set right whatever he could for the Talmud Torah.
The Rabbi, having heard out the delegation, said: „To blame for all this are the Hasidic Jews, who do not help at all for the good of Judaism; had the shtiblekh gone together to the kehilla elections, there would have been other dozores [kehilla board members] and the Talmud Torah would have been saved. Yes, Będzin is a town of a great many geese and cheesecakes“...
The delegation answered him: „And what have the Agudah dozores done so far for the Talmud Torah?“...
The „street“ competes with the Magistrate...

According to the latest registration regulations every house-owner is obliged to enter the list of his tenants in a new book.
The Magistrate sold such a book for 5 zł. But in the street such a book was sold for 3 zł.
As we are told, the Magistrate has lowered the price because of the „competition“...
The Pledges for “Beit Lechem”

[Będzin — charity.] At the last board meeting of the “Beit Lechem” society in Będzin, after hearing a report on the situation of the institution, which every Sabbath distributes foodstuffs to nearly 100 families, it was resolved that the synagogue pledges (nedarim) of this Sabbath, parashat Shelach, shall go to “Beit Lechem”.
National Conference of Tenants

[Będzin — tenants.] On Sunday the 21st of this month a conference of all tenants' associations in Poland will take place in Warsaw, to protest against the project to raise rents.
At this conference the local tenants' association will be represented by its delegates. For this purpose a collection will be made among the population for the expenses [of the journey] to Warsaw.
Pupils of the Real-School Throw Stones During the Break

[Będzin — violence.] On Monday morning a group of pupils of the real-school (Realschule) “amused themselves” in the yard during the break with stones, which they threw at the people strolling in the lane by the Christian cemetery.
One stone hit a passer-by, Józef Rozenzaft. The latter turned with a complaint to the school director, who promised to punish the guilty.
“Guardians of Morality”...
[Będzin — antisemitism.] On Tuesday evening young Christian hooligans attacked a Jewish couple who were strolling on Kościuszki Street.
Mr. Kwiatek's Proposal That the Turnover Tax Be Collected from Industrialists Rejected

[Sosnowiec — chamber of commerce and taxes.] Session of the Chamber of Commerce.
In the premises of the local Commercial Bank a plenary session of the Chamber of Commerce took place.
When the item “reform of taxes” was discussed, Councillor Mr. Kwiatek proposed that the turnover tax be collected from the first source, i.e. from the industrialists, and on payment of customs duty on foreign goods.
The proposal was referred to the budget committee. On the other hand, the government's proposal was approved, which is against the turnover tax being collected as a “ryczałt” (lump sum).
It was also resolved to take a loan in the sum of 650 thousand złoty to build its own building.
General Meeting of the Small Traders' Association

[Sosnowiec — small traders.] On Sunday the annual general meeting of the small traders took place, attended by over a hundred members.
To the meeting, which was expected to take a stormy character, came the Central Committee member Mr. Liberman, who took over the chair.
The president, Mr. Aliner, opens the meeting and hands over the chair to Eng. Mr. Zusman. Assessors: Messrs. Zylberman and Rozyner, and secretary — A. Mangel.
The report on the activity is given by Mr. Aliner. He changes the system adopted until now, but he criticises the members, who treat the association with apathy.
The treasury report is given by Mr. Dwiński. It turns out that the annual budget amounts to about 12 thousand złoty.
After the reports a discussion began, in which the peddlers took part. A tremendous storm broke out which went as far as brawls, and the police dispersed the meeting.

Important Resolution of the House-Owners on the Water Mains / When the Mute Come to “Speak”... / An Assault on Ostrogórska Street / Terrible Death of 2 Workers / The Budget Is Being Considered Today / A Fire / “And Thus He Would Count”...

[Sosnowiec — house-owners and the water supply; followed by six short news items from Sosnowiec.] On Sunday a large meeting of house-owners took place here. At the meeting, among other things, the question of the water mains, which will shortly begin to operate in our town, was also discussed.
In this connection it was resolved that meters shall be installed in all dwellings, showing how much water is used.
—o—
When the Mute Come to “Speak”...
As is known, efforts are being made to have the porters' mandate invalidated.
Last Tuesday a rumour spread that the porters had lost their only mandate. The news provoked bitterness among the porters, and the upshot was that one porter, a mute, “honoured” the parnas Mr. Ciecemski [?] with a few blows...
—o—
An Assault on Ostrogórska Street
On Saturday evening 4 bandits attacked a local resident of Ostrogórska Street, Mr. Balcer. The bandits, calling themselves “secret police”, searched Balcer's pockets, where they found 8 zł.
—o—
Terrible Death of 2 Workers
In the “Mortimer” coal mine an explosion occurred, in which 2 workers were killed.

The great „historic session“ of the Będzin kehilla council

Waiting for a quorum. — A council presidium elected. — A proposal that the session be conducted in Polish. — Declarations by the left-wing groupings.
On Wednesday evening, in the premises of the Będzin kehilla, the first act came to an end. A presidium of national-religious elements was elected without the help of the „Agudah“.
The session aroused enormous interest; almost the whole of Third of May Square [plac 3 Maja] was full of people, who waited with curiosity for the result of the session.
Present this time was also the representative of the Starostwo [district authority], Mr. Mandyszewski [?]; of the parnasim [councillors] present were Wigadzki, Rubinlicht, Liwer, Buchweitz, Kurland, Rudzin, Strachlitz, Rozynker, Hampel and Rinski. The last-named sees that with him there is a quorum — and walks out. After a longer pause councillor Feiner finally comes in, and completes the „minyan“... The Agudah councillors, who were at the Bank Kupiecki [Merchants' Bank], on receiving the news that the „sinners“ have a quorum — come running, and the session opens in a very tense atmosphere.
Before proceeding to the election of the presidium, on the motion of councillor Mr. Rinski a 10-minute pause is declared. During the pause the Agudah councillors tried to give broad „concessions“ to the „Mizrachi“, provided they would not go together with the Zionists, but the attempt did not succeed; all the proposals were not taken into consideration.
Before the elections councillor Feiner makes a statement that the rumours to the effect that the Left Poalei Zion had formed a bloc with the Zionists are false.
The presidium elections gave the following result: with 9 votes Mr. Icchak Wigadzki (Zionist) was elected chairman of the council (councillor Rinski received 7 votes), and as vice-chairman Mr. Icchak Meir Kurland (Mizrachi); councillor Landau received 7 votes, and 1 vote went to Jehuda Feiner.
Chairman Wigadzki, who takes over the conduct of the session, thanks them for the honour and says: „I am aware that many stones will be laid on the road of real work in the kehilla, but nevertheless I promise to conduct the work with justice for the whole Jewish population.
Mr. Wigadzki naturally delivers this statement in Yiddish, but councillor Rinski turns to the representative of the authorities with the question: why does the chairman not conduct the session in Polish?...
After the second pause they proceed to elect an electoral commission for the kehilla administration.
The result is as follows:
The electoral commission comprises: Rubinlicht, Rudzin, Strachlitz, Ch. Fiszel, Buchweitz. Deputies: Hampel, Kurland, Feiner, Rozynker and Landau.
After the elections, statements are made by councillor Hampel on behalf of the Right Poalei Zion and by councillor Rozynker on behalf of the „Hitachdut“.
The statements say that in order not to allow the „Agudah“ to obtain power over kehilla life they voted for the „Mizrachi“ candidate.
Councillor Ehrlich (Agudah) points out (in Polish...) that in electing the electoral commission the religious group was ignored. To this Mr. Liwer remarks that Mr. Ehrlich's words are not true, since Messrs. Jechezkel Fiszel, Icchak Aron Landau, Lejbisz Buchweitz and Kurland represent religious Jewry.
Councillor Rinski wants to give an explanation regarding the statements of the left-wing groupings, but because he does not give the statement in Polish, the floor is taken from him and the chairman closes the session.
Bloody demonstration in Katowice

The mob fires at the police. — 1 person killed, 2 wounded.

On Wednesday bloody events took place in Katowice in connection with a demonstration of unemployed.
From early morning larger groups of unemployed began to gather in Zawadzka Street and on the "Gwiazda" sports ground for the meeting that was to be held there.
At 10 o'clock the crowd began to march into the town; the police intervened, fired into the air, and the crowd dispersed.
An hour later a demonstration of several hundred men formed again; they attacked the police patrol with stones, and revolver shots aimed at the police were heard. The policemen then answered with gunfire, as a result of which a certain Dawid Emil was killed and 2 persons were taken to hospital.
The Voivodeship authorities have delegated a commission to investigate the course of events.

Meeting of the artisans of List 12
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Lejbl Fuks, a general meeting was held on Wednesday evening in the "Piast" hall in Będzin, at which Mr. Klajman pointed out the terrible situation to which the present presidium of the association has led: in the previous kehilla the association had 7 representatives in the kehilla, whereas in the present Directorium the association has no more than 1 mandate. Despite all this the Directorium does not want to convene a general meeting. Messrs. Fromerman and Pluśnik also spoke, and the following resolution was adopted:
1) The general meeting protests against the temporary Directorium, which has brought about such a split in the artisans' ranks.
2) The general meeting protests against the Directorium because the auditing committee did not first check the books and afterwards submit a report, but immediately handed the books over to the prosecutor without the consent of a general meeting.
3) The general meeting expresses no confidence in the Directorium and demands that a general meeting be convened at which a board will be elected.
