Give Me the Earthquake!

By L. Kusman.
Not with all the inventions that are made in our little world am I pleased; not all of them are for the sake of progress, lighten our struggle for existence, make us happier, beautify our days, light up our nights and make us feel more comfortable.
And even the inventions that go in the name of progress, of humanity, are not all to my heart. For as soon as I come into contact with them I feel that they disturb me at every step, and I begin to regard them as an act of violence against my freedom and my peace.
Take, for example, an invention such as gunpowder and the rifle. Certainly it was a step of progress in man's struggle for his existence. When does all this hold? When man points the rifle at the beasts of the forest that surround him; but when he points the rifle at my chest, I no longer see any progress at all in such an invention.
So it is with many other inventions, even of our own times. Certainly radio is a great and useful invention, but when my neighbour [a woman] keeps the radio switched on all day long and makes me listen to the cheapest street music, or even a speech by some old animal-welfare man [a "tsar-baley-khayimnik"] about protecting dogs and cats, then I often lose my patience to the point that I would smash all the radio stations in the world together with the sets.
Yes, the inventors are not always careful enough with their inventions. Along with the conveniences they give us, they nevertheless do not guard us from the disturbances and plagues that often come in their train.
I hold, for example, that a kind of law ought to be introduced against radio too: just as one must have a special permit to carry a rifle and a revolver, so one ought to have a special permit not for keeping, but for switching on [aiming] the radio set, because the aiming of a radio at your ear is often no less deadly for you than the aiming of a bandit's revolver at your chest. The latter mostly takes from you the few dollars and the gold watch, if you have one, and goes away; when you come to yourself you feel a free and a new man.
But when your neighbour keeps the radio aimed at your ear by day and by night, when you eat and when you read, when you think or when you laugh, when you are by yourself or with guests — from such a robber you will not so quickly come back to your senses.
In short, the best and most useful inventions can often be disturbing and distressing when they are not in the right place and in the right hands.
But now an English scientist assures us that the world will soon be provided with a new and most remarkable invention, namely: it will be possible to make earthquakes whenever one wishes.
You see, this invention, I hold, will be of great use — of course, if it is in the right hands and is used in the right place and at the suitable time.
If this English invention were to fall into my hands, I would already know what to do. First of all I would shake up the ground of the English Labour government, which writes us "to-my-beloved" [le-ahuvi] little letters and bluffs us right and left, at every step, in our work of upbuilding in the Land of Israel.
I would also shake up all those caretakers of "Klal Yisrael", the leaders, who have fallen into a lethargic sleep and no longer feel and do not see the Jewish troubles here and there.
And many other earth-shakings would I make, which are very, very necessary. An earth-shaking is also needed for our Yiddish [Jewish] culture and literature, which dozes quite comfortably in the resolutions of the "bearers of culture" and on the shelves of the bookshops where the literature lies. Whether the shakings would help or not is another question, but necessary they are.
And while I was at it I would also make an earth-shaking in Soviet Russia, so that it should have such an effect that overnight the Five-Year Plan would be finished. Let us know at last, as soon as possible, where salvation lies.
Yes, the earthquake invention can be of great use, but, as I said, in my hands. In strange hands I would not want to leave such an invention, because then a shaking might come under my own feet, and that will not do.
The earthquake — give it to me!
Backwardness or Immaturity?

[Będzin — taxes; leading article.] (Why did Będzin not have its representative in Kielce at the income tax?)

Our patience and negligence, our indifference and apathy know no measure at all. We know, for example, that people have patience, or suffer, up to such-and-such a degree, up to such-and-such a strength, up to this or that height.

Yes, all that is said of our private life, of our private dealings and of every kind of way of life that has to do with our private property. By contrast, as soon as it comes to the community, as soon as it touches our public interests, every limit is lost; here there is no control whatsoever. Nobody troubles to find out whether the disturbance is a loss, and whether it is a wrong and how great the wrong is; in that nobody takes an interest; in such a way it does not occur to anyone to pose the question; people are simply not accustomed to consider properly our public affairs, our painful communal problems.

Now we know that this week the income tax imposed on the population of Będzin was considered in Kielce. Once we had no representatives sitting there, and year after year we suffered defeats, so that efforts were made that there should be a representation there, which, by the way, often accomplished a great deal for the good of the population. Well, that would seem to be good; but apparently people have already grown tired of it, and now we know that at present the Będzin commercial world has no representative in Kielce. Why this is so, and what causes have led to the former state of affairs ("tsum prirign matsev" — as printed), we of course do not know; for us, however, it is enough to establish that the Będzin merchant world is not represented in Kielce.

It would, however, be interesting to know what causes led to this. Is it possible that things are already so good with us now that it makes no difference whether a firm is over-assessed by so-and-so much? And lest this take on that incomprehensible character — what, then, is the story behind this irresponsible indifference? Is the income tax such a side matter that nothing at all can be done about it, or that it is not worth dwelling on? Have few firms been ruined in the assessment of this tax? And are taxes in general so arranged that it makes no difference whether one is over-assessed with them or not? Is it really a side matter, in which one may by chance take an interest or not? Can one remain indifferent to this question, as though nothing had happened? May one treat our tax problems with such apathy? Is it tenable that tax questions in general should be solved in such a manner? What does it mean, that by chance one should take an interest in these matters and quite by chance neglect them? Is it some kind of luxury item, some superfluous object which, if one wishes, one buys, and if one does not wish, one can do without? Does it not make roughly that impression?

It would be fitting (thus, literally) that we should not constantly find ourselves under the impress of the tax screw; does not every one of us know how hard it is nowadays to pay the taxes, even if they were rationally calculated — to say nothing of when the rates are too high. Who, then, has seen to it that the taxpayer should not be wronged — to say nothing of such a critical time, when life and the conditions of life are so hard.

Without doubt the population ought to know the reasons for this criminal indifference. How can one play with the fate of the people's economic interests? Who permitted the representatives of the professional economic institutions to play with our most painful tax problems, which weigh so heavily on the shoulders of the town's citizens? Can it be tolerated that such important questions should be solved in passing and in passing be neglected? Can it be borne that existential interests of the first order should be treated in such a way? Can a class that finds itself under the pressure of taxation afford such a luxury? Should not the representatives who represent the branch remain responsible for their actions, when these are neglected by them and thereby inevitably bring harm upon the people?

It is incumbent upon our people's delegates that their opinion be heard (literally: "to hear their opinion"), so that we may know why they so often trivialise in this way their very hard and responsible mission, which is necessarily bound up with no little self-sacrifice and enormous exertions.

We know quite well that it is no small thing to be a representative in tax matters; we know with how much responsibility and caution it is bound up, and precisely for that reason it is all the more astonishing how, knowing all this, feeling it on one's own shoulders, being thus tied up with the most important threads, one can nevertheless suddenly move aside and think to oneself: what do I care, this time let us do without ceremonies. That is with what eyes these most painful matters are regarded.

Of course, among no people would it be comprehensible that such burning questions should be settled as it were on one foot — yes, yes, no, no. Only among peoples that find themselves in abnormal conditions can this be a fact, a real, living phenomenon.
How does this look to the authorities, once they see that one time people stand like steel and iron, and the next time they let their hands drop and take no interest at all in the most topical matters.

If people cried out several years ago, when the crisis was not raging in Poland, that various categories were too heavily threatened by the tax burdens, then one must surely understand in what manner this weighs on the people's shoulders now; yet it turns out that now no representative is needed in Kielce, and there is no need at all to intervene and to shed light on how heavy the income tax is for the broad strata of the population.
Can one, then, remain so ice-cold towards our most painful questions of the day? May one treat our tax affairs with such indifference? May we make of this problem a matter that is to interest none of us at all? Does one thereby discharge one's duty to the community, to society, to Jewish existence, which struggles so hard both for today and for tomorrow?

Must we not demand from any of these responsible representatives an answer as to why they make the essential into the incidental? Can it be allowed that things should continually be conducted thus, and that no one should come and say that this is not good, that it ought to be otherwise?

What, then, is one to call this kind of "activity" — short-sightedness, immaturity or backwardness?
R. Let.
Business nowadays... (A monologue)

[Humorous feuilleton — monologue of a small shopkeeper.] As for having businesses, trade, buying-and-selling — may one not sin with one's words — one only turns green and yellow from today's "business", Heaven preserve us, and whatever one puts one's hand to always lands butter-side down... Go on, then, be so clever and show me whether there is still a trade from which a man could draw a living?
I beg you — may you stay healthy and enjoy long days "and wives" [a pun on "long days and years"] — who was it that thought up promissory notes (vekslen)? A tumult, a fire, a plague ought to have come upon the inventor of such a wretched affliction, which still has the honour of being called promissory notes. But first of all I must introduce myself to you, so that you know who is speaking to you here and pouring out his heavy and bitter heart.
"Mam zaszczyt się przedstawić" [Polish: I have the honour to introduce myself]: here I am, Tsodek the shlimazl, who once went by the name of a small retailer. In my shop poverty strolls about and whistles away like a railway locomotive before a station. My customers are: the sequestrator [tax-distraint officer], the requisitioner, the administrator and the executor [bailiff]. Cursed should have been the day when I, Tsodek, became a merchant. Everybody looks at me as at a man already lying in the ground.
The big merchants always want to see me outside the door, and look [at me] as at a pesky fly. Among the "proletarians of all countries" I am reckoned a "lump" [scoundrel], and they know no other name for me than "parasite" and "counter-revolutionary". Do you know where I am held to be an honoured guest? — in the tax office, in the Izba Skarbowa [Treasury Chamber]. There I am the big merchant, so that with every passing year I become ever more important; and nakazy, prikazy, wezwania [payment orders, commands, summonses] and papers I have so many that I could already open an Izba Skarbowa of my own...
That, my friends, is how things look today: there is no livelihood and the businesses are going under — oy, gevald, business nowadays...
V.
The Lonely Tree (For the "Yizkor" exhibition of the works of Moshe Apelbaum)

[Poem — in memory of the painter Moshe Apelbaum.] Leyzer Shikman [Lejzer Szykman].
The Lonely Tree.
(For the "Yizkor" [memorial] exhibition of the works of Moshe Apelbaum.)
Somewhere in a far-off corner
there grew a tree,
far from any path,
wrapped in a sweet creative dream.

The tree struck deep roots,
and the stout, handsome trunk
bore within itself the joy of b e i n g,
though it was always lonely.

Yet it always had a quiet longing:
that people might rest in the shade of its branches,
so as to catch, some time, a quiet sound of life —
this could be seen from its pensive silence...
Strokes with the Pencil (Złoczew and — Radom)

[Polemical feuilleton — the anti-Jewish riots in Złoczew and Radom; Jewish sport.] (Złoczew and — Radom)
There is no need to call the events in Złoczew and Radom by their old name, so well known to us; one can call them by the new, modern, Europeanised name —
— excesses!
The course of the events, the result — is one and the same: hundreds of beaten Jews and thousands of smashed window-panes in Jewish houses.
There do not fly in the air, Heaven forbid, the feathers let loose from Jewish featherbeds; there do not fly about the streets, Heaven forbid, any shattered and broken Jewish goods and chattels; — for that would then, unavoidably, have been called by the old name —
— pogrom!
And that is not fitting, nor is it necessary in this day and age and in a country where Jews enjoy all rights and are —
— equal — with all equals!
But just like that — to give a few dozen Jews a good beating, to smash a few thousand Jewish window-panes — that is quite another matter; it is not so dangerous and not so shameful either, for it is merely —
— excesses!
For us Jews, however, these [events] in Złoczew and Radom, so similar in their course and results and so different — outwardly, at any rate — in the causes from which they arose, must serve as an instructive factor in many respects.
Złoczew! A small shtetl with a small, poor Jewish population of petty traders and artisans, amid a somewhat larger, or even similar, Christian population; and when the local —
— bearers of culture!
teachers of the public elementary (powszechne) schools, take a fancy to becoming known in the wide world by reminding the local Jews that they are, after all —
— Jews!
then the old and well-tried means suffices, one from the very ancient days, all the way from —
— the Middle Ages!
A clumsy libel that Jews insulted the religious procession; who, when and where? — that makes no difference, that is how it is, and that's that; and the peasants of the surrounding villages are gathered together to settle accounts with the Jews for their shameful deed, and the game is ready —
— excesses!
Radom! A large city now, with a varied and also more intelligent population; here it is already rather difficult to play on religious ground — yet one does want to become known, and one does itch for a prank at the expense of Jewish heads and backs — and so there is at one's disposal quite a different, more modern means —
— sport!
Jewish sportsmen came to blows with Christian ones; a Jewish young man supposedly stabbed a Christian; where, who and whom — that makes no difference, that is how it is, and that's that; and the feeling of vengeance awakens, this time not among the benighted mass on account of an offended religious feeling, but precisely among the intelligent school youth, on account of —
— sporting jealousy!
And once again the game is ready —
— excesses!
And if in the case of Złoczew we bear absolutely no guilt on our side: — after all, we cannot suddenly —
cease to be Jews!
merely so that nobody should be able to invent against us a libel that we insulted a Christian religious procession, — in the case of Radom the matter is already somewhat different, and a certain guilt for the events there is borne by us ourselves as well.
We must acknowledge that with us not everything is in order with the question of sport. True, Jewish youth strives, like all others, for physical development, to which it has every right; but we have already shifted the centre of gravity of our pride too far —
— from the head to — the feet!
Too much ardour and too much ecstasy do we bring into the question of —
— goals and championship!
After all, we have come through our long road of exile to this day, and with dignity, with —
— head-intelligence!
And we do not yet know at all how far and with what dignity we shall walk the road ahead with —
— foot-intelligence!
A Jewish sports club should have before it chiefly only the task of the physical development of Jewish youth, and absolutely not the question of —
— championship!
Nothing will be subtracted from our national pride and glory if this or that Jewish sports club scores one goal fewer and belongs to —
— Class B and — not A!
Our pride and glory we have always won, and we wish the same for ourselves in future too, on worthier positions than —
— goals and — championship!
Yes — if our helplessness and sad situation among those around us are demonstrated in conspicuous form and measure by — the events in —
— Złoczew!
then our inner brokenness and lack of understanding for our tasks and aims are at the same time demonstrated by — the events in —
— Radom!
Emes [signature — pen-name, "Truth"]
At the End of the School Year

[Article — education; first in a series.]
1.
Apart from kehilla elections, apart from rabbinical questions, apart even from the questions of the sad economic situation in which the Jewish middle class, the Jewish intelligentsia, the Jewish artisan and the Jewish worker find themselves at the present time, there are questions of no lesser importance, on which the existence and the future of the Jewish people depend. And these very questions are being settled almost without any discussion, without any attention on our part. One may say that in this matter chance has more of a say than our purposeful striving.
How much time and attention do we devote to the question of the education of the coming generation? We are now living in a time of a transitional epoch. The traditional cheder, in which the earlier generations were brought up, has lost the ground beneath its feet. A new Jewish secular school is coming into being, which wants to unite Jewish and secular education. As regards the education of boys, the following situation has arisen. In his first years the boy is sent to the old cheder, or to the reformed one such as the "Cheder Mizrachi". When the father finds that his son already knows enough that he will not grow up an ignoramus, he usually sends him to a Jewish gymnasium. Sometimes he combines the old cheder with the present-day school in such a way that the son attends the elementary school and the cheder at the same time.
As regards the education of Jewish daughters we have always been more liberal; we attached little weight to the fact that, when we send our daughters to an alien school, she is not merely assimilated there, but she is also brought up in an environment. In which she learns to hate and detest everything that is Jewish. Her soul and character are crippled there; she is torn out of her own environment, but she is not taken into another. The home of her father and mother becomes alien to her; she will certainly be ashamed to show herself with her father and mother in the street — let alone when the father wears a beard and the mother a wig — lest, God forbid, her non-Jewish schoolmates see her. For shame she would not know what to do with herself at such a moment.
But another moment comes in life, when our Jewish daughter has already finished a non-Jewish secondary school and has also finished a university, and it so happens that she has finished philosophy; this time she must come into the school a second time. She comes into the school not to be educated but to educate. She is no longer a pupil, she is now a teacher; properly speaking she only now wants to devote herself to the teaching profession. She has only just finished the philosophical faculty; she must have a workshop in which to work, she must have a school in which to do her practice. Here her tragedy begins; here she suddenly becomes aware that she is a Jew.
Very close to us the following case occurred. A Jewish young lady completed the mathematical faculty. Having received her master's diploma, she begins to look for a school in which she could do two years of unpaid practice as a trainee teacher. By chance, in the very gymnasium where the young lady had studied for 11 years as a pupil, a teaching post in mathematics was vacant; well, our master of mathematics was sure that she was extraordinarily lucky. It goes without saying, after all, that no one has such good prospects of getting the post as she, who studied for 11 years as a pupil in that same school. It seemed to her that she need only take the trouble to go to the headmistress of the school — the very one who had brought her up — and at the first word she would at once receive the post as a teacher in the same school, the school she had entered while still quite a small child. What happiness that will be for her, what an honour? With such joyful feelings our master of mathematics went to her former headmistress and declared to her that she was ready to take over the post which was vacant for mathematics. But the answer she received was short: "How does a Jewish girl dare to want to educate Christian children". The young lady lost her tongue; unable to answer a single word, she left the headmistress's office.
Fate sometimes likes to play such a wicked game with a person. Our candidates for teaching posts who were brought up in alien schools hear such an answer very often. But this time fate willed that our young lady should hear these words precisely from the person by whom she had been torn out of her own Jewish environment.
As we see, the question of education is very closely bound up with economic questions. One of the reasons — also a very important one — why we must send our daughters to Jewish national schools is in order to create employment opportunities for the Jewish intelligentsia, which is being mercilessly pushed out of all branches of economic life. In those same private schools in which 80–90 per cent of the pupils are Jewish girls, there is no room for Jewish teachers. Where here and there one or two Jewish women teachers are nevertheless to be found, this is done only for the sake of business, in order to attract as many Jewish girl pupils as possible.
That is how we pay with our own money for the assimilating and crippling of our daughters' souls. But when they want to find employment in those same institutions, this is called impudence.
What has nevertheless been achieved in this field, and what still remains to be done? — in the next article.
Elen.
Wives at the “Letnisko”, or Women's Mouths

[Humorous feuilleton — Zagłębie; summer holidays.] By “Alim”.
“Help! What is a man to do, what advice can he give himself, where is he to run?” — a Jew bursts into the editorial office — “there is simply no strength left to bear it.”

“What has happened, Reb Yid?” I ask.

“Oh, them, it's all them — the wives. I've gone deaf already, I have no ears left; give me some advice, for I'm going mad.”

“But tell us what happened — what on earth have the women done to you?”

“What have they done, you ask? Very well, I'll tell you; only listen with your head, and you shall write it up in the newspapers — let the world know what women are and what women are capable of.”

“You know, of course,” the Jew begins, “that we Zagłębie people are blessed with a ‘letnisko’ [summer resort] with a forest and every good quality — I mean ‘Raytshe’ [Rajcza]. So my wife, too, took a fancy to go to a ‘letnisko’, and nowhere else but to ‘Raytshe’, because there, she says, there are big mountains, and the air there is very clean, and the main thing, she argues, is that she doesn't want to be far from her husband — from me, that is.

“Well, what shall I tell you: a whole week — ‘jak’ [as good as] a whole week. She, my wife that is, sits in ‘Raytshe’ scooping the good air into herself and running about on the ‘mountains’, while I sit in Zagłębie, run the business, and peace be upon Israel.

“For the Sabbath, come what may, one pops down (up, I mean) to ‘Raytshe’; all the husbands of the wives living there at the ‘letnisko’ gather, and we have not at all a bad time of it, especially since one of our crowd has installed a radio, which entertains the company a little.

“That is how things went on for quite a while. My wife ran about on the ‘mountains’ and I ran about looking for a little gemilut-chesed [interest-free loan], and everything would have been fine and dandy, had I not taken a fancy, in the middle of the week, to have a look at what my wife was doing there; for in truth I could not understand it at all: in all the long time my wife has been sitting in Raytshe she ought already to have scooped up all the air, and the ‘mountains’ ought already to have been ‘dug away’ and level with the rest of the earth. And without thinking long — I am already in Raytshe.

“But here my real Gehenna begins. I come up to the dwelling where my wife is staying and I see some fifteen chairs and little benches standing around; on them sit women, younger and older, deep in conversation. So I think: they are surely talking about the splendid landscape, about the fine day, pine woods and dry air, or other such things; and then I hear how among the fifteen women there passes a chain of little slanders and little ‘plotki’ [gossip], so that the smoke rises.

“My wife did not notice at all that I had come, and I stand there behind the wall and listen to the women's gossip-mongering: Master of the Universe! If I am not yet deaf, then I am stronger than iron. Here one tells how yesterday Shmerl was here and today Berl is coming; a second tries to guess what for and to whom he came; a third already knows for certain what he meant; a fourth saw how he looked up at the sky — and so they crawl into another person's heart and soul, drag out all his innards and lay them down before the eyes of the whole collection of women, who will no doubt see to it that it comes to the light of day.

“And in this hubbub of ‘plotki’ and slander I stood some fifteen minutes under the wall and listened to it all, and I thought at the time that any moment now I would fall down, any moment now I would go mad; my head was simply spinning.

“I did not even see my wife; I left the whole circle [printed ‘krenkl’] sitting at their tasty ‘feast’ and began to run. I ran like that the whole way, and straight in to you at the editorial office.

“Now, Panie Redaktor, my dear, give me some advice — what is one to do? My head is going round as if on wheels from the women's gossip; say what is to be done!”

“Yes,” say I, “you are quite right; but from women's mouths, especially when they are at the ‘dacha’, it is hard to guard oneself.”
A Jew with a Stomach...

By B. Sovner.
"...Ay-ay-ay, what doctors there are — may no good Jew ever get to know them! They know as much about doctoring as a goat knows about Tisha B'Av. Woe and misery to the man who falls into their hands! Such a one may as well take leave of life — take leave he may.
I have — may you be spared it — trouble with my stomach. Something is not quite right with it, this stomach of mine: when I don't eat, I have an appetite and my tongue is red, and when I finish off a good meal, my tongue turns white and I lose my appetite.
So I go to doctors!
One doctor says: "Don't eat; if you don't eat, your stomach will rest and it won't cause you any troubles; and if you do want to eat something after all, you should not eat, he says, any red meat, only a bit of poultry, not much, and drink tea, hot tea, weak, with a lot of lemon and little sugar."
It helped me like cupping-glasses help a corpse; I only got worse.
So off I went to another doctor. He scours my eyes thoroughly, listens to my heart, winds a black rag around my arm, looks at some kind of gadget with numbers and says to me:
— You have too high a blood pressure. A Jew like you ought to have no more than a hundred and thirty-five, and you have, no evil eye, two hundred and a scant seventy more.
— Well, that's good — say I — more is always better; when a man owns half a million dollars, that is surely better than if he owned fifty dollars.
— True — says the doctor — true, but in the laws of blood pressure it is better not to have too much.
In short, this way and that, he took 5 zł from me and told me to come again, "he will see."
So off I went to a third doctor — one might say: half a professor.
The half-professor heard me out and asked me: how old I am, and how old my father was when he died, [and] my mother, and how many children I have, and whether my uncles had consumption [printed "סוכאסקע"(?)].
Say I: Herr Professor, why are you turning my head with foolishness? What do you need to know idle things for? Just make me well!
Says he: I must know this; when I know these things, I shall know what is wrong with you [lit. what you lack].
Say I: What I lack is health; when I am healthy I won't need any doctor.
Says he: If so, go off to another doctor — you are an idiot.
So off I went to a fourth doctor.
And the fourth doctor is an even bigger beast than the first three.
"First of all I want to know what you eat, that is the main thing, because you have gas."
Say I: "I have no gas in the house."
— I don't mean that kind of gas, he says, I mean gas in the stomach, poisons! It comes from eating too much and not the right foods. You must not eat any meat, not even poultry, only greens: cabbage, carrots, radish, onions, salads, cherries and red beets.
So I saw that he hasn't the faintest idea [lit. "doesn't begin to know who veiled him"], I gave him 10 zł and off I went. Now I'm really going to obey him and sit down to eat grass! What am I, a beast?
Along comes an uncle of mine, a melamed, and says to me: "Sender (my name is Sender; I am named after my grandfather), — says he to me — Sender [printed "טענדער"], handsomer men than you are laid in the grave; why don't you go in to a doctor?"
Say I: I have already had more doctors than you have hairs in your sparse little beard; my whole fortune has stayed with them.
Says he: That is mud [nothing], money is nothing, the main thing is health, says he, come.
— Where should I go?
— Come, says he, with me to our society's doctor. He treated Boruch-Elye the watchmaker too; true, Boruch-Elye — may you be spared it — died, that is true, but a great doctor he is. Come.
So the uncle leads me in to his society doctor. A tall one, a thin one, like a dried-out lulav, and he feels me all over, sniffs me all over, and he asks me what I eat.
Say I: As it happens — sometimes I eat fish, sometimes a bit of fish [so printed; probably "meat" is meant], a bit of duck, a plate of broth with noodles, and if I have no appetite, I eat nothing at all!
Says he: Eat you must! If a person doesn't eat, he cannot live. Eating and drinking and sleeping and good air sustain a person. When all these things fall away, the person falls away too. But what then? Instead of poultry or duck you should eat calf's liver; calf's liver adds blood, and you are very poor in blood; your blood pressure is all of 99, and what you need to have is a hundred and forty! So you are short, that is, about 63 [so printed]. Low blood pressure weakens, brings on dizziness, an unsteadiness on the feet, and that you can remove with your diet, that is, by eating a lot of calf's liver, at least three times a day.
I did not think long, paid the society doctor and went home.
Then it occurred to me: I have gallstones anyway, so what on earth do I still need to go to doctors for? So I knocked all of this out of my head, and I feel, thanks to the One Above, healthy and strong. I have neither gallstones, nor blood pressure, nor anything. I eat and I drink and I laugh at the Angel of Death together with all the doctors.
"Der Kokh-lefl" — compiled by Ben Amotz: Buses, Buses...

[Humour and satire — the bus crisis.] "Der Kokh-lefl" ["The Stirring Spoon" — the paper's regular humour column]
compiled by Ben Amotz.
—o—
Buses, Buses...
(Dedicated to the bus strike that is due to break out on the 1st of July.)

Buses, buses,
the wheels went round,
Jews latched on to it —
whoever had a gulden [złoty] — everyone.

Put it into buses,
and very quickly they became
specialists in the trade
and connoisseurs of motors.

And knew every detail
and could make a bet with you
which make is the best:
Essex, Fords, Chevrolets.

Wherever a young householder
had a bit of a dowry,
he was at once invited
as a partner into autos.

Wherever a town, wherever a shtetl,
Jews chase, run, ride —
Jews bustled about
like that for some two or three years.

And rode and ran,
wore themselves out day and night,
until the money and the strength,
thank God, were got rid of.

Worn-out buses
are no longer worth a three-groszy piece,
and on top of that the government
now demands a new tax.

And for each and every bus
the reckoning is quite simple:
the tax will come to more
than the whole bus now costs.

Much Jewish money has already
been buried in this business —
to my very best friends I may
safely wish that they had as much.

Jewish fortunes burst
just like soap bubbles —
as from the Jew's good fortunes always
"a river came out" [idiom: it all came to nothing]!
D-L.
What Do the New Parnasim Say? (A mock survey by "Kokh-lefl" on the present situation in the kehilla)

[Będzin — kehilla; humour and satire.] What Do the New Parnasim Say?
(A mock survey by "Kokh-lefl" on the present situation in the kehilla.)

Dozor [kehilla board member] Comrade Gimpel.
"What will the coming kehilla look like?" we asked the dozor.
"First of all the kehilla must be democratised, beginning with the synagogue, which needs to be reorganised according to the socialist programme."
— Meaning?
— Quite simple. On the Sabbath the Torah reader shall, at the end of the weekly portion, also read out the "Arbeter Tsaytung" ["Workers' Newspaper"]; on Yom Kippur an 8-hour service must be introduced, with a one-and-a-half-hour lunch break.
The new cantor will be engaged through the mediation of the trade union, because a cantor belongs to the proletariat — he says "Hineni he-ani" ["Here am I, the poor one" — the cantor's prayer on the High Holidays].
The eastern wall must be abolished. In the place of honour will pray Comrade Preger, Zuckerkandl and Comrade Rosenblum; "shishi" [the sixth, most honoured call to the Torah] will go to Comrade Kozłowski; the hakafah "Ozer dalim" ["Helper of the poor" — one of the Simchat Torah circuits] we leave to the leaders of the "Bund".

Dozor Feinschmecker [Fajnszmeker — "the gourmet"].
We found the dozor standing at the Shemoneh Esreh not toward the eastern wall but toward the west ["ma'ariv"]. After he had bowed at "Modim" he turned around and declared:
"In the new gmina [the kehilla] I shall endeavour to take over the supervision of the bookkeeping, because I know my way around complicated matters; even in the programme of the Left P.Z. [Poalei Zion] I find my way very well.
In the gmina I intend to introduce proletarian reforms; of all the religious institutions only the mikveh will remain, which is the one place where the proletariat and the capitalists have equal rights...
Aliyot [calls to the Torah] will be sold in the premises of the 'evening courses' on Modrzejowska Street.
As a revolutionary I shall demand that 'Mah tovu' be said after the prayers, and that 'Aleinu leshabeach', at which one spits, be the opening before the prayers..."
—o—
Oh, the Sun!...
1.
You see, the earth has freed itself
from sleep — from rain and snow,
but look! my wife has "renewed" herself [got herself new things],
and it hurts me terribly.
2.
I know, there now begins
for me a new life:
to the dacha [summer place] my wife must go,
and I must give in to her in everything.
3.
I must provide her
with a dozen new dresses
and help her boil juice [preserves]
in the village room...
4.
There I shall carry little pots
in the greatest heat,
and with the big suitcase
I shall, poor me, sweat mightily.
5.
The sun shines warm and bright,
people are happy,
only in me the heart is torn
into bits and pieces...
Shlimaliatzki [a jocular pen-name, from "shlimazl"].

Oneg Shabbat — Torah Sayings, Remarks and Anecdotes around This Week's Portion (Chukat-Balak)

[Religion — Torah sayings for the weekly portion.] Regular column: Torah sayings (vertlekh), remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion, collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Chukat-Balak
—o—
The Portion.
a) "In which there is no blemish — upon which no yoke has come" (9:2) [misprint for Numbers 19:2].
"In which there is no blemish" — these are those "fine Jews" who see no faults whatsoever in themselves, for whom everything they do is kosher and upright, without any flaw, God forbid — they are the very ones "upon whom no yoke has come", who do not bear the yoke of true piety; a sign of false, self-deceiving, would-be religiosity.
[From] Avodat Yisrael.
—o—
b) "Thus says your brother Israel" (2:14) [misprint for Numbers 20:14].
The way of the world is that two brothers stay on good terms as long as both are paupers or both are rich. If one is a pauper and the other grows rich — brotherhood is over... This is what the Jews had conveyed to Edom: "your brother Israel" — even now, when we have come to power and are no longer called Jacob but Israel ("for you have striven with God and with men"), we still do not renounce brotherhood...
[From] Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
c) "And the Canaanite heard" (21:1).
An interesting passage in the Chiddushei Aggadot (Maharsha), Kiddushin 82: "The most 'kosher' of butchers is Amalek's partner" — the most pious shochet is Amalek's partner. And even if he speaks to people gently and puts on a pious face — do not believe him, for that is exactly why he is likened to his partner Amalek, of whom the Midrash says on this verse that he deliberately changed his Amalekite tongue to Canaanite so that he would not be recognised...
—o—
d) "And Balak son of Zippor saw" (22:2).
A portion should be named after a gentile, after a Balak?
He deserves it, because he was an honest goy. [A goy] who disguises himself as a friend of the Jews is not honest — not honest towards the rule "it is well known that Esau hates Jacob"... And Balak was such an antisemite that, although he knew the Jews had been warned "Do not harass Moab", and so had nothing whatever to fear for himself, he nevertheless brought Balaam down to curse the Jews — now that is pure antisemitism. And therefore, on account of his open, sincere, goyish hatred of Jews, on account of his honest goyishness, he merited that a portion be called by his name.
[From] Marganita de-Rabbi Meir.
—o—
e) "And Moab was sore afraid of the people, because it was numerous [rav]" (ibid.) [Numbers 22:3].
The evil inclination is called "Moab", and this "Moab" is afraid of the people; he has no wish to bother with the masses, "ki rav hu" — because he has a better way: to the rav [the rabbi]... Yes, a surer and better way. Once he has the rabbi, the masses are his too...
[From] Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
f) "Am I really not able to honour you?" [Numbers 22:37].
Balak's complaint calls to mind that doctor who, on coming to the patient, at once demands his fee, because, knowing that the patient may die at any minute, he wants first of all to grab his fee... And if Balaam insists on reward beforehand, it is a sign that he does not want to wait for his fee because he is not sure that he will not later be seized by the scruff of the neck...
[From] Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
g) "How shall I curse whom God has not cursed" (23:8).
The Midrash relates that Balaam stood up with this argument before the Master of the Universe: "Would You not rather be the God of seventy nations than the God of one small people?" What use are the Jews to You?
God's answer sounded like that of the doctor whom two noblemen (pritsim) invited to live on their estates: one was a sick man who needed the doctor's help every day, and the other a healthy, strong man who needed the doctor only as a luxury. Although with the second the doctor would have had nothing at all to do, he nevertheless chose the post with the first, for precisely because that one would make use of him day after day, he would be the more honoured there. Rather than be a God over the peoples who live in luxury and pleasure and have no need of a doctor, a helper, it is more fitting to be a God with the poor, tormented Jewish people, which so needs a God, a helper, a doctor for its many wounds...
[From] Sefat ha-Yeri'ah[?].
—o—
e) [sic; should be h] "And he saw Israel dwelling according to its tribes" (24:4) [should be Numbers 24:2].
"He saw that their doorways were not set opposite one another, so that no one should peer into his neighbour's tent; he said: these are worthy that the Divine Presence rest upon them." (Bava Batra, ch. 3)
The Divine Presence rests only upon one who is also wealthy (Nedarim, ch. 4) — meaning not necessarily a rich man, but one who is content with his lot, one who is always "rich" in that he is satisfied with what he has, one whom material worries do not trouble. And because Balaam saw that "no one peers into his neighbour's tent", that nobody looks into another man's pot and each is satisfied with what he has, he said: "these are worthy that the Divine Presence rest upon them."
[From] Peninim Yekarim.
—o—
The Haftarah
i) "And to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 5) [should be Micah 6:8].
1.
"'And to walk humbly' — this means dowering the bride and escorting the dead." (Makkot 24)
A puzzling saying.
In ordinary life a person cannot be recognised for what he is. In extraordinary moments, by contrast, a person's character can be recognised. In time of misfortune the wise man is recognised, who even then shows steadiness and does not lose his head. The fool, on the other hand, is best recognised at a celebration, when he is in high spirits — then "when wine goes in, the secret comes out".
He who both at the bringing-in of the bride (symbol of joy) and at the escorting of the dead (symbol of misfortune) is the same man and does not change — that is a sign that his inside is like his outside, that people were not mistaken in him...
[From] Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
—o—
2.
"To do justice, to love kindness and to walk humbly with your God" — to be modest in loving kindness and in doing justice, to give charity modestly, without commotion, without noise; then it will be measure for measure: God too will give you wealth without noise and without clamour... "With your God" — to be modest with God. If you are modest, He too will be modest with you...
[From] Tiferet Uziel.
—o—
Avot
"Types among those who give charity" (5:16).
Townspeople came to the "Chofetz Chaim", may he live long, and wanted to give him support, but he would not have it. His old mother asks him:
— Yisrael Meir, my son, we are going hungry, after all; why won't you save yourself and take what good people want to give you?
— Oh, go on, Mama dear — answers the "Chofetz Chaim" — they want to give only because they know that I do not want to take; the moment I want to take, they will not want to give...

Betrothed for the Third Time...

[Będzin — local news; humour.] On Targowa Street in Będzin the following comic episode took place this week:
A widower married a divorcee. The matchmaker (a woman), who had brought the couple together, lent the groom a ring with which to betroth the bride. Well, the groom did as the matchmaker told him and performed the betrothal with the borrowed ring.
The morning after the wedding the matchmaker told her husband, a Hasidic Jew, that she had lent the groom a ring. When the matchmaker's husband heard this he began to shout that the betrothal (kiddushin) was not in accordance with the law and that “Yekum Purkan” would have to be said a second time...
The matchmaker went off to the couple and informed them that the kiddushin was not kosher and that a second kiddushin must take place.
Well, when one must, “no doctor helps”; so the young wife took a ring out of her jewellery, handed it to her husband and said: “Here you have a ring from me, now say ‘Harei at’ once more”...
The husband carried the thing out properly, according to law and rule, but later the couple learned that the kiddushin was again not in order, because the ring belongs to the bride...
The end of it was that the groom bought a ring with his own money and said “Harei at” for the third time...

[Będzin — incidents; antisemitism.] The other day the following thing happened to the luggage porter Hillel Reich.

Sosnowiec — Peace agreement between the rabbis Englard and Hager

[Sosnowiec — local news.] Sosnowiec
Peace agreement between the rabbis Englard and Hager.
A president and vice-president of the kehilla council elected. — Satisfaction among the Jewish population.
In the night from Monday to Tuesday the angel of peace spread his wings over the town of Sosnowiec. That night there came to an end "the 7 Years' War", which had brought about so many disgraces and had cost a great deal of money.
The peace negotiations had in fact begun several days earlier; the above-mentioned sides, already weary of the struggle, at last realised that the matter must be liquidated. A contributing cause were also the parnasim [kehilla councillors] of the Koziegłowy side, which — in their own expression — held the "key" of power... and on that account dictated such conditions as were not favourable to accept, neither for Rabbi Englard and above all not for Rabbi Hager.
The upshot was that both rabbis bypassed the "key side" and held out their hands to each other — peace!
The "birth pangs" of this peace were very hard; more than once it seemed that any moment now the negotiations would be broken off and "we shall have to take up the former weapons again"... But all obstacles were removed, the power of peace prevailed, and at 5 o'clock before dawn the historic peace agreement was signed.
The news spread through the town with lightning speed; yesterday's enemies held out their hands to one another, wishing each other mazel tov; in the Hasidic shtiblekh (except in the Gerer and the Sochaczewer ones) people drank lechaim, and the chief topic of the Jewish population over the last few days was only "the peace between Mizrachi and Rabbi Englard".
The peace agreement contains a series of provisions, among them also the following: 1) officially Rabbi Englard becomes Rabbi of Sosnowiec, and Rabbi Menachem Hager head of the rabbinical court [rosh beit din]; 2) all accusations against Rabbi Englard are withdrawn; 3) the salaries, both for Rabbi Englard and for Rabbi Hager, are equal; 4) the functions in the synagogue are performed by both rabbis according to their mutual understanding; 5) all income from religious needs is divided half and half; 6) "Mizrachi" receives the "portfolio" of kehilla president and Englard's side — the president of the kehilla council, and so on.
The ratification of the "peace agreement" took place on the same day, during the session of the kehilla council. The allied parnasim passed their first examination and mutually supported one another on the candidates for president and vice-president.
The parnasim of the "Agudah" and of the Koziegłowy side too, for the sake of diplomacy, supported the candidacy for president of the council, who was put forward by Englard's side; on the other hand they could no longer bring themselves to grant "Mizrachi" its "victory", and voted against its candidate for vice-president.
At the idyllic session there was also present the representative of the starostwo [district office], the referent Mr Mandyczewski[?], who ordered that only the elected representations and representatives of the press be admitted to the session.
Kehilla president Mr L. Zendel opens the session in Polish, and they proceed to the agenda: election of a president, a vice-president and a commission for the kehilla elections.
As president of the kehilla council, Mr Mordechaj Klajnberg was elected with 14 votes, and as vice-president, with 10 votes, Mr Icchak Sztajnfeld.
Into the commission entered: Markus Hamburger, B. Sicemski, M. Szapira, A. Opatowski and M. Klajnberg.
Substitutes: Sztajnfeld, Rzepkowicz, Majtlis, Wajnsztok, Abramczyk.
On the whole the peace agreement has called forth great satisfaction among almost the entire Jewish population.

There Is Only 1 Way Out!...

Dr. T. Meladysta [?].
(Thoughts and sketches for the 3rd yahrzeit of Dr. Avraham Perlman of blessed memory.)
Sometimes it is interesting to stop and for a while to go deeply into how a person's life and outlook take shape; more interesting still is this analysis when it concerns those who rise above the average measure, who thanks to the power of their spirit are destined to become leaders, folk heroes and guides for the tormented, suffering masses of the people. In such an analysis we will see clearly how strong the inner struggle was, what mighty factors had a say in the forming of the views and in the choice of the ideal, and how the spirit wrestled, until the victory of truth came and determined the life-line and life-ideals of these chosen spirits.
With us Jews, because of our highly entangled spiritual and political life, this problem is doubly difficult, and in this perhaps lies the tragedy of the Jewish people: that so many great Jewish spirits did not understand it, or were not able to penetrate to Jewish self-awareness and with their creations to enrich Jewish culture and raise the pride of the Jewish name in the world.
———
We stand again, and already for the third time, on the day of the yahrzeit at the grave of the prematurely deceased public worker and leader Dr. Avraham Perlman of blessed memory.
In the first moment there come to mind thoughts of the splendid and noble figure, especially for those who stood close to him and who knew his path in life.
A hard path it was, a long path of inner and outer [printed „אויערליכער“] struggle — the well-known struggle of the Jewish intellectual. We see how the conscience wrestles — the Jewish soul — of Dr. Perlman, when [printed „וועט“] logical consideration, the sense of comfort and the urge for momentary achievements [contend] with the dreamy idealistic disposition that slumbers deep in the soul: internationalism and cosmopolitanism as an expression of love and respect for humanity on the one side, and on the other side devotion to his own people, which has accomplished [„געלייסטעט“] so much and has been so grievously wronged [„בעעוולהט“].
The struggle in Dr. Perlman continues; it becomes ever stronger and hotter, until it comes to a revelation [„אפּנבארירונג“], until there comes to him the certainty that the only right way is to serve those who suffer most [—] [perhaps „most miserably“]. This Dr. Perlman understood as a deep-thinking doctor; this the Jew Perlman also understood, and he came to his sick, suffering people and placed himself at its service, because he sensed the possibility of making it healthy, because he understood that this was the only way out for himself too, to find a path in life, an ideal in life.
———
The revival of the people became the ideal. To it Dr. Perlman devotes all his young strength; countless day-to-day questions interest [him] and find a solution. With him — organising, encouraging, helping, advising, defending — these are the things that occupy him, and he understands that in the solution of the problems lies the key to the building-up and revival of the people. Dr. Perlman does this with the whole fire of his inexhaustible life-force. He wants to prove to everyone that one can and must live a full life as a Jew wherever we are, as a proud and honest co-worker of humanity, but as an independent national unit.
But soon there come, as with everyone of that time, the natural conclusion and the question: can a people that is scattered and dispersed throughout the whole world form a united body? Yes! — comes his natural answer — because on the long road of exile we have not lost our culture, our language [printed „אויזער“], our tradition, our historical connection from generation to generation.
And if so, one must think historically and create anew the centre of our moral strength, which will gather again all the rays of the past and present, the bright rays of the Jewish national strength that is spread over the whole world.
There, in Eretz Israel, in the old land, a new homeland must arise for the Jewish people; there the treasures of the Jewish spirit and Jewish strength will gather. This is the only way out for us. Thus Dr. Perlman came to Zionism, thus he came to the great idea which became the content of his life.
———
Here began the intensive work, the ploughing-through [„אדורכאקערן“] of the Jewish masses for the Jewish [printed „יורישן“] land. For years Dr. Perlman worked quietly and often lonely, overcoming difficulties, inner and outer by nature, among close friends and alien opponents. The output of strength was great; the struggle for the new idea, which opponents stamped as a utopia, was hard, but the victory — great. Years of work brought, thinking historically, hundreds of years [of progress] — success. At such a tempo went the building and rebuilding. And with pride Dr. Perlman, the enlightened and dreaming idealist, looks upon the fruits of his world-view, upon the only way for the eternal people.
But this does not suffice him: he wants to see with his own eyes the work he has helped to create. A „טראדיגע“ [?] force drives him to Eretz Israel.
There the specific factors of the splendid Eretz-Israel atmosphere act upon him: of sun and air, of sea and land. The life and spirit of Eretz Israel make the mightiest impression on him, strengthen his will, give him courage to work and to endure. Refreshed and inspired he comes back. His first word, spoken in a circle of friends and comrades, is that there is no other way out than to keep on working, to keep on building until the complete redemption comes.
———
To this thought Dr. Perlman remained faithful until the last minute of his life. To the ideal of revival he dedicated his best years, his best strength; and when the terrible time came, the first signs and a serious illness, when suspicion crept into his head and soul, the sad foreboding that the splendid bond of life and creation could be torn — then too, and perhaps only then, the strong power of conviction of our unforgettable comrade and friend found expression: that only there, in the old-new Jewish land, could he find eternal rest.
His last thought was that the mother-earth of Eretz Israel, for which he had suffered so much, should receive him and give rest to his soul.
In his testament too Dr. Perlman remained faithful to the deep Zionist ideology: that there is only one single way, on which we must go until the last minute of our life, until the final victory.
Rest in peace, dear comrade, we will not abandon the way.

5 Years' Prison for Stabbing His Own Child.
In the dock in Katowice sat a young Christian from Upper Silesia who had murdered his illegitimate child, aged 11 months. After committing the terrible murder the father himself cut the child to pieces and buried it piece by piece in the ground.
The murderer was sentenced to 5 years' hard imprisonment.

During the night exercises of the „Strzelec“ (riflemen's association) outside Katowice, the porucznik (lieutenant) of the uhlan regiment, Mr. Mitas[?], wanted to set off a rocket. The rocket exploded prematurely and killed the officer.

The international[?] motorcycle race held on Sunday in Katowice drew a crowd of 100,000 people.

On Sunday morning a strike broke out among the tram employees in Upper Silesia. In the course of Sunday the police intervened because the strikers tried to obstruct the tram traffic, which was being run under police guard.

In the Vacation Days — (Which Children Are Remembered and Which Are Forgotten)

(Which children are remembered and which are forgotten)
The doors of the schools have closed and the children have received their time off. The moment has come when the little ones, the school youth, can free themselves of their studies and will in this way get the chance to rest their young, worn-out little bones and straighten their bent little backs.
All year long the children do truly hard mental and physical work, and therefore the parents too should be glad of this liberation of the children.
When one looks and thinks it over, one comes to the conviction that children now have value, that everything and everyone cares for them, that they should be brought up in hygienic conditions and that good and loyal citizens should come out of them who will bring benefit to the country and to the community.
Yes, that is how it looks, that is what people think, and so it is clear to the superficial eye, to the most outward-looking person.
But the situation appears quite different when one begins to analyse the matter from all sides, when one dwells on every detail. Take the children of the public schools, those real little Moishes, Shloimes, Sarahs and Rivkas: when they are freed from school, where do they go then? Are they not shut up then in the narrow cellar and attic rooms? Are they not then stifled in the narrow, stuffy atmosphere where the sun does not show itself and no refreshing breeze has any access?
True, we will be told, people now take an interest in these children. They are looked after, sent out to the health resorts, to the countryside and to the colonies. Yes, that is indeed true. But are all those whose grievance, whose wrong, should be taken up actually satisfied? And can one at all fulfil the requests of all those who plead that their children [printed 'kigder'] be rescued? Do we see few such children roaming about in Zagłębie, who ought by all means to be sent out of town into the country, out of the stifling air and under the green trees? Do we see few of these little children roaming the town as if orphaned?
True, we will be answered that there are not enough material means to satisfy everyone, and it is indeed understandable; the answer is a factual, balanced, logically founded one. Not to mention when one also takes into account in what critical period we are living — it is surely self-evident that one cannot help everybody, cannot send everyone away at public expense.
But here too it would have been desirable to take a deeper look, to analyse this question more seriously and more honestly, and then we would come to the conviction that here too [printed 'ikh'] not everything is in order. In this question too the system of patronage (protekcja) prevails on quite a respectable scale. Those who knock on the doors where needed, those who know how to manage, those who clamour and shout and make a racket, carry through everything they undertake; whereas those who do not know how to manage, those who choke back their tears and do not show themselves — their children are left at home, they are passed over, they are forgotten, and they really languish the whole summer in town, in the narrow cellar and attic rooms; they do not enjoy the free air, they get nothing of the summer vacation, and even their parents cannot attend to them — those parents who toil hard all year for a dry piece of bread.
Would it not be only just to take more interest in those children who cannot manage at all by themselves and whose parents have no courage to wear out the doorsteps of those whom it is necessary? Should one not pay more attention to these silent victims and modest parents, who will never want to blacken their faces? After all, one must finally reckon that one sins against [printed 'negn'] these parents, who suffer only [printed 'gur'] because they are not brazen-faced, because they are ashamed to fall on their knees [printed 'poreim'] before whom it is necessary.
Those who concern themselves with sending children away at public expense must not forget that these children must be placed at the very top of the agenda. One must remember them of one's own accord, if only because they do not make themselves heard, because they move aside so as not to be noticed, so that no one points a finger at them. They must have priority over those who make themselves heard, such as those who manage here. For the latter will manage their own affairs; they will use every opportunity, they will grab everything from you and get along with everyone. They belong to the shrewd ones, the specialists, and one need not worry about them at all, because they can always [doubtful words: 'gefiuer kumen'].
And therefore we say that first and foremost one must care for the poor who run away from you, for the poor whom we do not see and who are ashamed to look at the bright light.
True, one cannot say that nowadays no interest is taken in the fate of our schoolchildren; people want to give them as much pleasure as possible, special entertainments are organised for them, excursions, etc. Certainly, in our day no one took such an interest in us as we do for our children, but that does not yet mean that we have already risen to the proper height, that we are already doing everything for our children.
How far behind we still are in the upbringing of children can be seen from the difference between us and Upper Silesia — no small matter, how they care there for the future generation. When one takes a look [printed 'kum' for 'kuk'] across to Katowice, one is beside oneself on seeing what the children's world looks like there. First of all care is taken [printed 'gshvargt'] that the child should have somewhere to spend time, somewhere to romp, somewhere to walk, somewhere to swim, somewhere to go on excursions and somewhere to turn round and about, whereas with us the child in town has practically nothing; apart from dust and keeping out of the way of cars and trams the child has nothing.
Well, the rich and the moderately well-off manage: they send their families away to rest and recuperate; the poor who are shrewd already know from practice how to manage their affairs. But there remain only those who are helpless and do not like to push in where they are not wanted and where it seems to them that people do not want to see them. With this element one must reckon, with these people one must have a talk, and in their children one must take an interest, because forgetting them is truly a sin. Against these children and against their parents one sins, because they must not be left at a dead point; they must not be forgotten — on the contrary, those who themselves forget about themselves must be sought out and helped with whatever is at all possible.
It is precisely the modest and honest poor people whom one must remember to rescue in the course of the few summer weeks, when their children are freed from school and can have the possibility of resting their worn-out little bones and their bent little backs.
R. Les.
On Visiting the “Gordonia” Summer Colony

[Zagłębie — youth movements; “Gordonia”; summer colonies.] As is known from the local press, this year, in the months of July and August, we are organising two summer colonies in the village of Guckulina [?], which lies 5 kilometres from Rajcza. Since many inhabitants of Zagłębie are staying in that area nowadays, spending the summer and rest months in the Beskids, we would ask them very much not to burden us with any unnecessary visits, so as not to disturb our educational work at the colony.
Guests are received by us every Sunday in the afternoon hours.
It goes without saying that the parents of our children who take part in the “summer colonies” (moshavot kayitz) are requested to visit us, in order to appreciate our work.
We believe that this appeal, through the medium of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung”, will meet with understanding, and that our work will bear the proper fruit and success.
