Orangeade and Soda Water (A Tax Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — taxes; Jewish trade; reprinted from the Polish paper “Kurjer Warszawski”.]
“Szmul Cukier... a rich man... enjoyed great esteem in his county town and in the whole surrounding area; all the gentlemen knew him, and the movement in his business was a great one, from early morning until late in the evening; the boss Szmul Cukier ran everything with his 3 sons-in-law and a bookkeeper, a specialist.
This specialist had great trouble on account of the tax office; he carried the books to the office as evidence, and from the office people used to come to the business; the proprietor himself used to check all the accounts and lists in person: everything tallied, as right as gold... and here the office keeps on protesting; there must be — they claim — a double turnover! And they imposed such taxes that the proprietor very nearly had a heart attack; they took counsel with a clever lawyer, they wrote an appeal. What else, there must surely be a little justice in the world!
A senior tax official came, with a briefcase full of papers, and announced:
Your appeal has been rejected.
Szmul Cukier turned pale.
— What does rejected mean? How can the office reject it? Is there or is there not any bookkeeping? You checked the books at the office...
— Certainly; but at the office it was ruled that the accounts are not accurate; the turnover must be twice as large, or even more than twice; in the books one can write whatever one likes...
Szmul felt that he was getting unwell and his heart was seized.
— I — he defended himself — have been trading with the villages in the whole county and with other counties for three generations now; my grandfather already ran this business; everybody knows that my business is a solid one; God has helped me, I do not complain. In recent years it is going even worse, but I do not complain; I keep honest accounts; everything can be checked; Mr. naczelnik [head of the office] says that the turnover was double; give me at least one proof of it, at least one unrecorded transaction, at least a shadow of suspicion... well?
We need no proofs; either you will pay, or we will take enforcement measures.
— But I will be utterly ruined, Mr. Nachenik [sic]!
— And for travelling with your wife to Ciechocinek you have [the money]?
— What has that to do with my business? I, Mr. naczelnik, am already 65 years old and my wife 62; at such an age the organism is usually not in order; besides, God did create the mineral waters in Ciechocinek — may one not take a cure now, in free Poland?
— One may, but it arouses suspicion that one is hiding one's real income; well, I leave the demand in force; either you pay by the deadline, or...
•
— Why don’t you come to me, Panie Szmul? I have wheat, clover... there is also wool.
— May God grant you success, squire! Let the squire hold on to the prices, they are rising!
— Will you buy everything up?
— I will buy nothing, not a thing!
— What sort of jokes are these?
— I am not joking; I no longer trade! If I buy 500 metres [metr = quintal, 100 kg] from the squire and record it so, the tax office will say that I bought a thousand... I am liquidating my business; I will wait — may God just give health — perhaps better times will come.
— But, Panie Szmul, I was counting on you so; you are, after all, the only big and solid merchant in the whole county!
— What can one do? I have paid a double tax: a second time I cannot do it; my end may come soon; I will live somehow without trade...
*
A year later.
— What is this, Mr. Cukier, you have sent declarations to the tax office that you are not trading and that you have had no turnover at all!
— No, there was [sic] liquidation... I neither buy nor sell.
— Then who does buy?
— I don’t know; the tax office ought to know everything.
— Why did you liquidate your business? It was going quite well!
— Certainly, it was going not badly, but the tax office wanted it to go twice as well; a year ago I paid twice as much as was due; now I must rest a little together with the business...
— Well, well, to liquidate such a business!
— What can one do? It ran for almost a hundred years — it got tired. — Today such heat outside, such a heatwave; one simply has no strength to go after taxes!
— I can treat Mr. naczelnik to a tasty cold glass of water; it really is hot; I would advise you to drop in at the confectioner’s at the end of the street; there they have a cold orangeade with a straw.
— You are joking, Panie Szmul, or do you think that an official in Poland can afford to go to a confectioner’s for an orangeade, especially now, after the [salary] reduction?
Do you know what, Mr. naczelnik? I will tell you something; for the official to be able to afford to drink a portion of orangeade, those who pay him his salary [lit. “pension”] — the citizens, that is, who pay taxes — must at least be able to afford a little glass of plain soda water”...
•
We have reprinted this feuilleton from the Polish newspaper “Kur. Warsz.” [Kurjer Warszawski], which cannot, God forbid, be suspected of any sympathies for Jews.
Jewish trade is in a fine state indeed if an antisemitic newspaper already finds it necessary to come out in defence of the Jewish merchant against the excessive tax burdens...
Hundreds of Jewish Women Graduates Bid Farewell to Their School Principal

Together with the great host of girl pupils who have finished this school year, the principal of the Powszechna School [state elementary school] No. 4 in Będzin, Mrs. Szancer, who worked in the field of education for 42 years, also took leave of the school.
To the farewell came, like loyal soldiers, in the front row the great number of women graduates — among them many who already send their own children to school... — the school authorities and public figures who helped develop the enterprise — "Powszechna School No. 4".
The farewell ceremony, held on Sunday, began with a prayer in the town synagogue (Shtot-shul). To the sounds of the school orchestra a procession of "Landsturm-women" [militia girls] formed, but from their marching through the streets one could not believe that these were mothers of children...
In the synagogue things went as always — on the benches and under the benches, not a crumb of decorum, lawlessness on top, an ingrained demoralisation.
Cantor Lipa Pietrykowski sings "Ma Tovu" and Mi-sheberakh blessings for the President of the State, Marshal Piłsudski, and for the jubilarian. And when the shammes Kaplan announces:
— "The ceremony is over" — there is a hubbub and a wild rush out of the synagogue...
— — —
The academy [formal assembly] in the "Światowid" cinema turned out festive. It was somewhat delayed, but it was worth it. We had the satisfaction that the "bad angels", hearing [sic: "herenedig"] how Jewish children speak Polish, sing and play, had willy-nilly to nod their heads and acknowledge that we Jews cultivate Polish culture better than they themselves... We only need free hands to create in every field...
The stage was sunk in flowers and greenery. The principal of Powszechna School No. 2, Mr. Rapaport, opens the academy with a short introduction and hands the chair over to Dr. Weinziher.
After the playing of the Polish anthem the following are invited to the presidium: the jubilarian, Dr. Wasserzweig, the president of the g.[?] city council Żebrowski, the "g." [probably = former] president Ryp, and the school guardians: Rudzin, Hampel and Wajcenberg.
Then come the greetings: the first to greet is the school inspector Mr. Łuchowiec[?], who acknowledges the great merits of the jubilarian, who raised the school to a higher level; in general — the inspector stresses — the "Jewish" Powszechna schools in the Będzin district (powiat) stand higher than the non-Jewish ones.
On behalf of the teaching staff Mrs. Pawłowska gives a fine speech of greeting; on behalf of the women graduates Miss Fiszer takes a heartfelt leave. Her "beautiful" diction and manner of speaking make a very good impression.
On behalf of the male graduates Mr. Glezer greets, on behalf of the school principals — Mr. Krawczyński.
Under the impression of the greetings the chairman Dr. Weinziher "gets" the floor and tells interesting memories from the Russian regime, when as a gymnasium pupil he fought together with the jubilarian for the Polish language. The speaker also relates some [sic: "eynege"] details of how the jubilarian, at the outbreak of the war, energetically took up the development of the Powszechna school.
On behalf of the Office of Social Welfare at the Magistrate [town hall] Dr. Wasserzweig greets; he points to the field of hygiene in the above-mentioned school.
Great applause went to the pupil G. Perlsfater[?] for her greeting on behalf of all the girl pupils.
On behalf of the kehilla the president of the kehilla council, Mr. Icchak Wygodzki, greets; he wishes that the elementary schools be expanded in a Jewish spirit and satisfy the children of the popular masses who also need higher education.
Then a series of telegrams and letters is read, among them a letter from the Rabbi of Będzin, who apologises that he cannot take part because of his departure for Marienbad. Embarrassing is the fact that the letter (written, by the way, in Polish) does not mention a single word having any connection with Jewish education.
A successful greeting is delivered by the school guardian Melech Rozenberg, who turns to the jubilarian, the "mother" of thousands of Jewish children of the popular masses: may she continue her work as the "mother" of the orphans brought up by the charitable society in Będzin.
Then greetings come from the former city president Mr. Ryp, the school principal Mr. Rapaport, and the principal of Public School No. 8 Mrs. Brude[?]; the latter, as the jubilarian's sister, cannot control herself and her words are broken off...
After the jubilarian's thanks for the honour, the first part of the academy ends.
— — —
The second part, the musical one, was very successful and left a good impression: the choir under the direction of the teacher Miss Kornblum, then the very young mandolin orchestra (girl pupils) under the direction of Simcha Lustig, and above all the well-rehearsed orchestra (boy pupils) under the direction of Icze Barnblat performed splendid numbers, for which they were showered with resounding applause.
With the whole audience playing and singing the well-known "Sto lat", the festive academy is closed.
Later a grand banquet took place in the halls of the "Hotel Bristol", at which the male and female educators also displayed "strong abilities"... During the toasts Dr. Weinziher spoke about the rapprochement between Poles and Jews as an important objective in the all-round development of the country.
The school inspector and Mr. Żebrowski spoke on the question and agreed with the opinion expressed by Dr. Weinziher.
The opinion was at once "realised" by a group of women teachers, who made merry singing "zmires" [table songs] in honour of the g.[former?] president of the city council Mr. Żebrowski, who sat at the head of the table and "took pleasure"...
Towards evening the reunion of the women graduates was held at the "Piast". At the reunion Dr. Rechtman told some memories that provoked merriment.
In the evening a reception (raout) took place.
The Story of the Bone

(A short feuilleton).

You remember Krylov's fable about the two dogs who lay warming themselves in the sun and carried on a friendly conversation between them. They all but kissed each other on the muzzle out of love, until the mistress of the house threw them a bone and they tore each other apart, mauled each other till the blood ran!

One can tell the story differently.

The dogs did not lie in the sun and did not kiss each other on the muzzle, but, on the contrary, tore at each other just like real curs. Between them there was a permanent war mood. First of all they could not get along over places: wherever one lay down, the other always argued that he was taking his spot. This one must lie close to the kitchen window, that one must have free access to the inner courtyard; this one wants to be right under the fence, that one demands a free piece of sky above him, so that the rays should peck him directly on the fur.

They did not even lack food — the mistress used to throw them plenty — and yet they would constantly fight over every little bone; whatever one of them snatched, the other thought it was the best portion.

Constant brawling went on between them, and people said that with them there would never be peace, that it is simply such a doggish nature, such boiling blood, that cannot live a minute without growling and brawling and is always ready for the bloodiest wars.

And in just such a war mood they found themselves on that historic day too.

They were both standing, supposedly guarding the yard against impudent attackers, fulfilling their task and waiting for their reward. But since no strange intruders came, they kept on quarrelling among themselves. Each threw old sins in the other's face and merely suspected him of malicious intrigues for later. They stood there sulking, the hair of their coats bristling, eyes goggling [?], and growled with ferocity, and it was evident that at any moment a dogs' quarrel would break out and blood would be spilled.

The mistress saw this through the window and decided to intervene. She would throw them a bone, they would be delighted with the find, and out of great joy they would stop quarrelling.

So she did. But only then did the real quarrel begin.

Even before they touched the bone, they barked every forbidden thing at each other and scratched at each other's eyes; then they ate and growled with full cheeks. And when they had eaten their fill, they started tearing at each other all over again.

That is how one can tell the story.

You think dogs have no such nature, to quarrel just like that, without a reason?

True. But it is only a fable about people. And people do have such a nature...

Argus.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah thoughts on parashat Pinchas

[Oneg Shabbat — Torah thoughts on parashat Pinchas.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the portion of the current week. Collected and stylised by Y. Y.
Parashat Pinchas
The Portion.
a) "My covenant of peace" (25:12)
When Pinchas became a popular hero, when he displayed such valour and sacrificed himself for the community — the greatest blessing for him was: peace. Because mostly the "zealots for the Lord of Hosts" are rewarded with... strife.
Tiferet Yehonatan.
b) "Let the Lord, the God of the spirits, appoint" (27:16)
1.
Nowhere do we find that Moses called God "God of the spirits", only here, when it was a matter of choosing a leader, "a man over the congregation" —
because usually a leader is "blessed" with such blessings as: "a spirit [i.e. a demon] in his bones"... "a spirit into his father...". Therefore Moses said: only the "God of the spirits", the God over all spirits, should appoint a leader and guard him from all the various spirits that the people will later send at him...
Alei Zayit.
2.
Moses did not turn to the people to choose a leader, because a leader "of all flesh", who would please everyone equally — such a one only God Himself can choose...
Imrei Shefer.
c) "And thou shalt put some of thine honour upon him" (27:20)
"The elders of that generation said: the face of Moses was like the face of the sun, and the face of Joshua like the face of the moon — alas for such shame, alas for such disgrace", Bava Batra (75a).
The elders, the "fine Jews", always say: "Eh, today's leaders, said of stones [i.e. not to be compared] [?]. Once, once..." The Joshuas (today's leaders) are always paler in their eyes than the Moseses (the leaders of old) —
It is this bad trait that the sages lament: alas for such shame, alas for such disgrace...
Me'irat Einayim.
d) "My offering, My bread for My fire-offerings" (28:2)
"If you say that there is eating and drinking before Me — learn from Moses; see what is written of him: and he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights, he ate no bread" — Midrash.
The Gemara (Bava Metzia 86) derives that a man should not deviate from the custom of the place where he is from Moses, who was forty days in heaven and did not eat. The question arises: why is it not derived from the fact that he did not sleep in heaven for the forty days? — after all, holding back from sleep is a greater wonder (see Nedarim 15) —
To this the Maggid of Dubno told the following episode from his wanderings through Jewish towns and townlets. Once he strayed into a village. He comes into a villager's house and asks for something to eat; it is late at night, and the other tells him that he has nothing in the house. He asks for a dry piece of bread, but receives the answer: there is nothing. He asks at least for a place to sleep — they lay out a bed for him on the floor. Late at night, when the villager thought the Maggid was already asleep — he takes out of the "pikelik" [?] a pot of "warm food" and stages a feast...
With this incident the Maggid found the answer to the question mentioned: for if one says that Moses did not eat in heaven because the angels do not eat either, then it follows of itself that he did not sleep either, for if he had slept, how could he have been sure that the angels do not eat? Perhaps, while he was sleeping, they were meanwhile staging a feast, like that villager...
Siftei ha-Yeru'a [?].
e) "A new meal-offering unto the Lord in your feast of weeks" (28:26)
The initials of "Ḥ-adasha L-aShem B-shavuoteikhem" spell: ḤaLaV, milk. From this there is a hint that on Shavuot one must eat dairy foods, because the Torah is very much like milk: milk keeps best in earthenware vessels, better than in golden ones; likewise the Torah, too, loves only simple, not gilded people... there it endures (Bava Kamma, ch. 8 [?]).
Olelot Ephraim.
f) "And on the Sabbath day" (28:9)
Of the Brisk rabbi, R' Yoshe Ber, it is told that once he spent a summer in a village. On a Shabbat Mevarchim a few village Jews come to him and ask him when the molad [new moon] is. R' Yoshe Ber sees that he has landed in an ugly trap: if he does not answer such coarse fellows when the molad is, they will say the rabbi is an ignoramus by Torah law. What does one do? But a Jew, a scholar, finds a way out: he answers that by law one may not rule on and announce the molad as long as [?] there is a calendar in the place...
The villagers set about looking for a calendar and came back: "Rabbi, there is no calendar here in the village". If so, R' Yoshe Ber told them a time as it occurred to him, being sure that nobody would catch him in any mistake...
Haftarah
g) "And he sat down under a broom tree" (I Kings 19)
The broom tree is a tree of which the Yerushalmi (Pe'ah, ch. 1) says that it burns inside while outwardly it is cold — and such a tree was provided for Elijah when he wandered in the desert, to serve him as a symbol that a leader must keep his temperament and ardour hidden within himself, and outwardly be cool, calm...
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
h) "Not in the earthquake... not in the fire..." (ibid.)
What is meant is the leader. Not with noise, not with fire, but with "a still small voice", with tolerance and calm must he deal with the masses.
Akedah.
Avot.
i) "Beloved — loves the Omnipresent (ha-Makom)" (6:6)
A man must not have a separate judgement for himself and another judgement for his fellow, must not preach water to others and himself drink wine... "Beloved" — if you want to be beloved — "love ha-Makom" [lit. "the place"]: measure yourself by the same measure as the place, as the situation in which your fellow finds himself; "Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place" —
Maharei Yavetz.

Messrs. Rubinlicht and Feiner disqualified as members of the election commission.
On Tuesday the kehilla board received a communication from the Starostwo [district office], which announces that, of the members of the election commission for the kehilla board, the persons of Mr. Rubinlicht as member and Mr. Feiner as deputy in the above-mentioned commission are disqualified.

Today, Saturday, the railway station will be opened.

Tomorrow, Saturday, the new building of the local railway station will be opened. The festive opening will take place in the morning, and in the afternoon the station will already be in operation.
At the station, which thanks to its installations and construction is the first in Poland, there are two platforms: one platform for the direction of Katowice and one platform in the direction of — Warsaw.
He evicted his own brother.

The residents of Mandzhever [Modrzejowska ?] Street had the opportunity to see how a brother of one's own is evicted from his flat.
As we are informed, the eviction was carried out by Mr. Shlomo Fischer, who holds legal documents showing that the house left as an inheritance from his father belongs to him. His brother Max, however, did not want to recognise this right, and between the 2 brothers a long lawsuit was conducted, which went all the way to the highest tribunal.
The tribunal, as in all the courts, recognised that the house belongs to Shlomo Fischer.
On this basis Max Fischer was evicted from the flat that he had occupied in the house until now.
The demoralisation of today's school youth. Because of a bad report card a 14-year-old schoolgirl commits suicide.

Last Saturday afternoon, while her parents were away, 14-year-old Esther Wechslman left home and did not come back. When several hours had passed the parents grew uneasy and began to search for her. The suspicion grew even stronger later when it was seen that she had left her wristwatch and her Sabbath clothes at home.
All efforts produced no result whatsoever until Tuesday evening; only on Wednesday morning did the terrible news spread that the girl had been found drowned in the Przemsza near Małobądz. A Christian who wanted to draw water saw an apron moving on the water; at the alarm several Christians came running, and they took out the dead body of the under-age suicide.
The heart-rending scenes that took place when the drowned girl was brought home to her parents are indescribable; the mother, who had lost her eldest daughter, fainted so badly that several doctors were occupied reviving her.
As we are told, the main reason is said to be that the suicide had received a bad report card and was the only pupil who had been held back in the 6th grade (oddział) of Public School no. 4 in Będzin.
This is a glaring proof of how deeply demoralisation has already taken root among today's school youth.
The 'Urząd' [tax office] took away the baked goods meant for the customers.

On Wednesday before dawn bailiffs (tax executors), accompanied by 2 policemen, came into the bakery of Abraham Damskurski, where they took away 115 loaves of bread and all the wheat pastry that had been ready for the regular customers.
He 'treated' his competitor to a bayonet.

The Tag Sale

The tag sale in aid of the summer colony of the „Gordonia“ organization brought in 337 zł. and 72 groszy.

Guest performances of the actor Baratoff.
The Yiddish theatre-goers have received with satisfaction the news that the famous actor Paul Baratoff will give guest performances in our town.
Baratoff is a great artistic force, and with his acting he has made a name for himself in America and Europe.
Today, Friday, „Hinkemann“ is being performed.

Meeting of Esperantists.
In their own premises an extraordinary general meeting took place, at which the following board was elected: Kozłowski, Zauberman, Zweigenbaum, Frajerger[?], Sochaczewski, Herszlikowicz and Wierzba. Deputies: Tenenbaum, Fischer and L. Szpigler.
Meeting of „Beit Lechem“

In the premises of the „Merchants' Association“ a meeting of the „Beit Lechem“ society took place on Monday.
Despite the fact that the board had issued a public appeal, calling on the population to come to the meeting in order to secure the existence of the institution, which ought to be active at the present moment — no more than 2–3 persons came, the kind one sees at every meeting.
Mr. Max Landau takes the chair, and in a mood of „Eikhah“ (Lamentations) a board is „nominated“...
27th Yahrzeit of Dr. Herzl, and Third Yahrzeit of Dr. Perlman

Sosnowiec. On Sunday, 20 Tammuz, it will be 27 years since the death of the creator of political Zionism, Dr. Theodor Herzl, of blessed memory.
According to tradition, the Keren Kayemet committee is arranging an academy (commemorative evening) in the Municipal Theatre; speeches will be given by Dr. Melarista[?] and Dr. Chameides of Katowice.
At the academy the local Zionist activist Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, will also be honoured, on the occasion of his 3rd yahrzeit.
On Sunday at 10 in the morning memorial prayers (hazkarot) will be held in the synagogue; afterwards a procession to the cemetery will be formed.
Strike of Buses and Taxis

As in all of Poland, the owners of the buses and taxis in Zagłębie have also gone on strike.
In Zagłębie, because of the strike, about 100 buses and 50 taxis are not running.
Over a Ball He Killed His 17-Year-Old Friend. Deeds of Today's Children...

On Wysoka Street in Sosnowiec a group of underage Christian children were playing ball.
During the game the ball fell into the neighbouring garden. One of the players, 16-year-old Brajdak, climbed over the fence into the garden to retrieve the ball.
His friend, 17-year-old Kulak, would not allow this, and a fight broke out between the two, during which Kulak stabbed Brajdak in the heart with a knife, and Brajdak instantly fell dead on the spot.
The young murderer, after carrying out his murderous deed, disappeared.
A New Tram Line

The tramway management is starting in the coming days to lay a new tram line from Sosnowiec to Milowice.
Several hundred workers will be employed on the work.
Demonstrations of the Unemployed in Zagłębie

In the course of Tuesday the unemployed tried to demonstrate in a number of places in Zagłębie.
The demonstrators were dispersed everywhere; only in Czeladź did the crowd throw itself upon the police in order to disarm them. Because of the crowd's superior numbers the police withdrew; only when a larger police detachment arrived was the crowd dispersed. One policeman was seriously wounded by a piece of wood.
Suicide of a young man from Pilica

On Friday night, at 12 Pańska Street, 29-year-old Lipa Herzberg committed suicide by drinking a small bottle of vinegar essence.
The suicide was taken to the Jewish hospital, where he died in great agony at the close of the Sabbath (Saturday night).
Lipa Herzberg, a native of Pilica, had been without employment and was staying with his brother on Pańska Street.
His wife tormented him, so he slaughtered her

At 16 Ostrogórska Street lives the Ostrowicz couple. Quarrels often broke out between husband and wife because Ostrowicz suspected his "woman of valour" of betrayal.
On Tuesday evening the couple quarrelled again, and in the course of it the husband slaughtered his wife with a kitchen knife.
At the police station the "slaughterer" declared that he had done it because she had tormented him very much.
At dawn "Lilith" took 940 złoty off him...

A Silesian from Królewska Huta (Königshütte) came here to have a good time. Not content with visiting a series of restaurants, towards dawn he paid a visit to the "Lokarno", where he spent a very pleasant time with the dancing girls.
On leaving, the Silesian opened his eyes and saw that his wallet with 940 zł. had vanished...
A student from Warsaw arrested

On Piłsudski Street the police arrested Mr. Izaak Lipszyc, a student of Warsaw University.
A large quantity of material connected with Communist activity was found at Lipszyc's.
A Communist printing shop discovered

Recently Communist leaflets printed in a single printing shop appeared in a number of places in Zagłębie.
The police investigated energetically and finally discovered the printing shop on Rybna Street, in the private flat of 21-year-old Roman Matyla.
The owner of the Communist printing shop has been arrested.

Olkusz.
Constitution of the new kehilla board.

Fires in the villages.
The heat waves have begun here, and with them come the terrible fires.
This week a terrible fire broke out in the large village of Pradła, Olkusz county. With lightning speed the fire began to engulf the village, and one house caught fire from the next. Firemen came from Pilica, Zawiercie, Szczekociny and the surrounding villages, who finally managed to contain the fire, but “thanks to” the wind 25 houses, 10 barns and other farm stock were destroyed by the fire.
The damage amounts to 100 thousand zł.

Stormy meeting of the town council in Olkusz.
On Monday evening a meeting of the town council took place. At the meeting there was no longer a Jewish majority, because the members of the magistrate, consisting solely of Christians, had been added. On the agenda was the budget for the year 1931/32, which the committee had cut by more than half compared with last year (formerly one and a half million and now 700 thousand zł.).
Before proceeding to the budget the following scene took place: the leader of part of the Jewish councillors, Mr. Muszkatblat, submitted an urgent motion to expel from the town council, for taking bribes during a transaction of the old magistrate, the councillors Avremele Paluch and Mendel Kerzer[?]. A counter-motion was in turn submitted by the representative of the Jewish club, Mr. Flaszenberg, to expel from the opposing club the councillors David Glajtman, for slandering the present magistrate, and Wolwile Gelbard together with Hershel Gliksman for “disgraceful acts”[?]. The motions as well as the continuation of the budget will be dealt with at the next meeting. The meeting was very stormy and passionate; tempers were red-hot. The epilogue of the meeting will have an echo in court...
A. B.

The struggle with the difficult economic situation.
The Warsaw Chamber of Commerce held an important consultation these days, devoted specially to the question of how to combat the present severe crisis and what measures should be taken in order to ease the economic situation as far as possible.
The presidium of the Warsaw Chamber of Commerce will in the coming days present itself to the Ministry of Finance and put before it what immediate measures should be taken to protect merchants and manufacturers from a great upheaval.

The rescue measures will cover almost all branches of the country's economic life, and it is hoped to ease the situation until times get better.

Letter to the Editor.

[Letters to the editor — Będzin: school and education, a sports club, a school excursion; followed by: the JNF in Sosnowiec.]
1
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
In connection with the tragic death of my daughter Esther, barely 14 years old, I ask you to print the following lines in your esteemed newspaper:
During the days of shiva I had the opportunity to analyse precisely the unfortunate case of my daughter, and it is certain that those guilty of the death of my innocent child are her "certified" educators.
However bitter it may be, it is a fact!
Her educators directly brought it about that the young child put an end to her life.
Mrs. Szancer, whose 40th jubilee of educational work was celebrated here not long ago, did not show the slightest understanding of child psychology and modern education; on the contrary, she proved to be outdated and harmful.
What happened today to my child may, God forbid, happen tomorrow to another child, and let society take this well to heart.
What actually happened to my child?
This year she did not receive a good report card (cenzurka) for the 7th class; besides that, my child committed an enormous crime: from the bouquets of flowers that had been prepared for Mrs. Szancer she took for herself a few little flowers, which she particularly loved.
Unfortunately this incident played the main role in the fate of my child.
Mrs. Szancer felt personally offended by it, and because of that she insulted my child, her pupil, in the presence of her schoolmates, threw her out and did not allow her to take part together with the other children in the school ball, which took place a day before the unfortunate Sabbath. That was still not enough: on Sabbath morning Mrs. Szancer had me called and told me: my child should not eat at one table with us, I should punish her in the presence of my other children, impose house arrest, hide her clothes, not let her continue her education but hand her over to a craftsman, etc.
So I ask: is this called education? Is it really pedagogically necessary to apply so many cruelties to a child at once? Is the only task of a teacher really just to set grades (stopnie) and arrange marks? Should the educator not take an interest in the psyche of the child? And when will our educators finally understand that today one cannot apply the same educational methods as 20 years ago?
I did not carry out everything that the head of the school, Mrs. Szancer, of long practice in the field of pedagogy, told me, but even that was already enough to embitter my child's life and drive her to the desperate step.
Let the educators have the death of my innocent child on their conscience, and let society finally draw from it the proper lesson and be guarded against such a similar case.
The desperate father.
Josef Zalman Wekselman.

Theatre and Music Notes

„The Father“
A drama in 3 acts by A. Strindberg
(From Dr. Paul Baratoff's guest performances in Zagłębie).
Just like the brilliant woman-haters Schopenhauer and Weininger, Strindberg too holds that woman is the source of all evil; that between man and wife an eternal struggle of life and death is waged, and in this struggle the woman always wins, because she is cunning and unpredictable, her tactics are low, her cat-nature makes her invincible and she enslaves the man.
In „The Father“ this struggle between the sexes finds vivid expression.
Nietzsche's influence is strongly noticeable in the drama. In the Rittmeister Adolf, Strindberg wanted to create a type of Übermensch who stands alone in struggle against his surroundings, who fights the old way of life, but who must fall in this struggle because his opponents are women.
The father wants to bring up his daughter as an independent, emancipated woman. He wants to free her from the old-wives' notions [?] that her mother plants in her. And on this ground the struggle between husband and wife breaks out.
The wife, unable to overcome her husband's firm will, tries the last but most effective means: she plants in the Rittmeister a doubt about his paternity of his daughter.
The means works. It throws the Rittmeister off his mental balance and finally drives him to his death.
The paternity problem is no longer topical today, because on the basis of the „Landsteiner reaction“ [blood groups] paternity can be established with certainty, and the court issues its verdict on the basis of the said reaction.
Dr. Paul Baratoff is an actor of great artistic culture. He acts directly through his facial expression, his voice and every smallest movement; even when he is silent he is still acting, and the tragedy is felt in every stroke of his wonderful mimicry.
His Rittmeister Adolf is a creation that will long remain in the memory of the spectators. A particularly strong impression was made by the closing scene of the second act, where he throws a burning lamp at his wife.
The rest of the cast are very pale in the glow of such a „star“ as Baratoff, yet they introduced no disharmony.
„Hinkemann“
A tragedy in 6 scenes by Ernst Toller.
Toller wrote the tragedy after the World War, at the time when people tried, with the help of the most diverse „isms“, nude [?] dances and jazz, to drown out the cry of the millions of unfortunate cripples who had flooded the capitals of the whole world.
And if, despite everything, the cry of the various kinds of cripples was heard, there still remained a huge camp about which nobody spoke — neither the unfortunates themselves nor society. These are the tens of thousands who lost their sex on the battlefield.
Such an unfortunate is Hinkemann, who went off to the war at 20, healthy and full of the joy of life, leaving behind a young, beautiful wife who idolised him for his physical strength, for his manliness. And this athletic young man comes back from the war a physical cripple, a living golem, no longer capable of married life with his wife.
At first the wife even tries to comfort him; she swears to remain faithful to him — but what use are oaths, morality and modesty when sexuality demands its due, when the whole human being is flooded by an erotic deluge? The boundaries of logic and reason are then blurred, man is then ruled by [?] pan-sexualism and becomes a slave of „Eros“.
The wife, regaining her balance after betraying [?] her husband, when from the depths of her soul memories of her former ideal life together with him begin to awaken, can no longer bear such a situation and commits suicide, which drives Hinkemann to the same.
„Hinkemann“ is a mighty cry of protest against war. Let the women, the greater half of mankind, see what has been made of their children, brothers and husbands; a great deal will depend on the women no longer allowing a senseless fratricide. And when the gentlemen diplomats and war-hungry fascists crave a war, let them murder one another themselves — the world will be rid of a superfluous ballast. For the great, enormous mass, however, there is one single slogan: „War on war“.
In the role of „Hinkemann“ Dr. Baratoff embodied not only his own tragedy; he personified the tragedy of hundreds of thousands of unfortunates who cry out their protest: what compensation can any order give us, can any regime give us back our capacity? — the unfortunates ask through Hinkemann's mouth.
Baratoff's wonderful mimicry, the timbre of his voice, his sorrow-soaked eyes affect the audience so powerfully that they fall into a trance and live through the artist's tragedy together with him.
Baratoff can rightly be counted among the coryphaei not only of the Yiddish but also of the world stage.
Victor Chenkin
(From his song recital at the summer Capitol)
Chenkin possesses a baritone voice of no high range, but with a broad, warm timbre.
With Chenkin, however, it is not a question of voice but of the manner of interpreting a song, which he carries to a very high level, and which places him in the ranks of the great international artists.
Besides being a singer Chenkin is also a great actor. His singing is at the same time theatre; witness his brilliant facial expression, his splendid characterisation and his wonderful, never overdone gesticulation.
Most successful were the songs „Rataplan“, the Italian song „At the War“, in which the artist displayed a tremendous technique; the Yiddish songs „Where does a Jew come from“ and „A Song without Words“; and from the Ukrainian ones „The Blind Beggar“ and „Alone I drink, alone I make merry“.
The evening left a very pleasant impression and the artist won himself a number of new admirers.
Sh. R.
The System of Education. (The causes of suicides among schoolchildren. — Should we look on indifferently?)

L. Szpigelman.
1.
The question of education and the school problem is one of our most painful issues, and it is a fact that we treat them with little attention, with little heed, and in general with a rather scant interest.
Not long ago we were shaken here by the incident that took place in Będzin, where a 14-year-old Jewish girl committed suicide because she received a bad report card [cenzurka]. In fact we hear from time to time about similar incidents from pupils' life, and each time we are astonished at these abnormal events; but at the same time we must not forget one thing: each time it seems to us that this is a personal matter, a private affair, and as such the community need not concern itself with it — that is exactly where the failing lies, that is exactly where we ourselves are to blame.
One must therefore, in full awareness, regard this question as a first-class social problem with which the community must deal. We must finally get it out of our heads that we are dealing here with personal incidents, personal events. As soon as they take on a mass character, they thereby become a social matter, and then the community must come and study them, investigate them, analyse them, find the causes of their origin and seek a remedy and a solution for them.
Problems of education, school questions, child psychology — these are the most delicate threads; one must know how to touch them and in what manner to think about an improvement, about a change for the benefit of children's education.
When a child does not learn well, when a child receives a bad report card, those who stand at a distance think that the child does not care, that it makes no difference to him, that he treats it apathetically — whereas in truth this is far from so. The child is indeed not so developed mentally as to have the strength and understanding to express his inner sufferings, the pains pressing on his young heart; but inwardly the childish soul suffers beyond measure, and we adults do not see it, do not feel it, because its strings are too delicate, the threads too thin. Child psychology is a deep, endless field of research which, just like the sea, has no bottom. The more one delves into the research, the further and deeper one penetrates into it, the more one comes to realise that this problem belongs to the most delicate and complicated science, one that asks to be researched, to be studied, to be treated in various, various ways.
When we look attentively at children's education, when we delve into the way the child thinks, suffers, feels, comprehends, we then come to realise that it is a quite special world with original outlooks, with a train of thought of its own. How many times do we have occasion to be amazed and to marvel at childish fancies and original deeds that would never have occurred to an adult, intelligent and well-educated person.
With us, unfortunately, one is very backward in this field; in general one pays [?] very, very little attention to this young sapling, which needs so much to be tended and guarded. True, nowadays people take considerably more interest in the little world of children, but this is only superficial, and besides, it suffices at best for average children, i.e. for those who are neither too little nor too much developed. With the latter — that is, with the backward, the little-developed and the over-developed children — one must deal in a quite different way; their childish souls must be explored with a special reverence, with a special originality; here boundless awareness and delicacy are demanded, and here one must penetrate deeper into the child's inner sanctum, where the most original ideas must be sought in order to reach children's little hearts, which are in any case very sensitive. The child's little heart has strong inner sufferings; one barely touches it with plain coarseness, with simple vulgarity... True, we do not see it, and many of our simple pedagogues do not even feel it, but child psychologists, those who research and study children's souls, know it excellently; they take a deeper and more serious interest in the problem, and for them it is no news that children must be given the greatest attention so that they are well brought up.
In our little Jewish world in the 1880s there was a slogan that children must not attend schools. A father who sent a child to school was counted among the apikorsim [heretics]. Now, in the 20th century, one cannot conceive how a child could be educated without attending school; but on the other hand things have been brought to the point where all parents want their children to finish school, without reckoning with the fact that not all are capable of it. It is understandable that one must apply all possible means so that children do not remain ignoramuses [amei ha-arets], but when one sees [?] that some child is not capable of finishing a gimnazjum, or cannot advance a grade every year in a public elementary school [folks-shul], one surely should not torment him; never mind, let him repeat another year — in that case it is surely no danger to life. Why then torment children in vain and for nothing, since they are not capable of it? Just as not all people can have one and the same taste, one and the same ability, so not all children can have the same will and the same interest in school.
It is no news that in Europe studies are constantly being made easier. Thus, for example, efforts are made for children to learn in a playful, willing [?] manner, so that pupils feel no fatigue while learning at school.
We are still far from that system, but we see that it will come to it, since in government circles they are nevertheless thinking of introducing this very system. But as long as this is not an accomplished fact, one could surely lighten the children's over-strenuous work by whatever means; thus, for example, one must also comfort a child who did not manage to move up to a higher class, one must give him courage so that he does not lose heart down to the deep abyss, as unfortunately happens in our present times.
At such a moment one must consider the psychology of the unfortunate child and come to his aid in a time of trouble. And here we see that Germany stands at a very high level in the field of education. With us these children are ignored, whereas in Germany they are given precisely the greatest attention. It is characteristic, but it is an accomplished fact. The "Berliner Tageblatt", for example, wrote that in Berlin, at the end of the present school year, a banquet was held for the children — and guess for whom? Precisely for the n o t - c a p a b l e ones, for those who have fallen behind, and the banquet was intended to cheer up and comfort the children who do not have the same strong willpower as other children, to whom studies come more easily.
The "8 Uhr-Abendblatt" took upon itself the initiative to stage the "Frühmorgen" [?] as impressively as possible, so that the newspaper appeared in honour of the children with masses of illustrations. It was thus done with German chic and with love for the children who had fallen behind.
Let us learn from the Germans, let us learn from the great civilised world to give more trust and attention to the children who cannot keep pace with those of average ability.
The problem of education, the education system, is the most sensitive sanctum for our future generations.
Oneg Datshe (The Delight of the Dacha)

[Humorous feuilleton — Będzin, summer holidays.] By Y. Aberżanek[?].
Gentlemen, I can bring you good tidings: — I already am!
What am I already? Well, guess! Yes, as if you had been standing right there — a "letnik" [Polish: summer holidaymaker]! What did you think, that I had struck it lucky, that I had won the big prize? Of course I am a letnik! Which Jew is not a letnik? Whoever has just enough to pay for a "furmanka" [cart] becomes a letnik...
If all Jews are letniks, why, I ask you, should I be outside the camp — "garvos" [misprint for "farvos": why]? If all the wives go off to "freshen up" [odświeżyć], then why shouldn't my Rivke Hendl "take advantage" [skorzystać] of the "air" [powietrze], why? Where is it written, I ask you, that my missus should — may it befall the enemies of Zion — walk down the street watching how all the neighbour-women bustle around the village ladder-wagons [wozy drabiniaste], how they pack straw sacks, deck chairs [leżaki], hammocks, camp beds [łóżka polowe], empty jars [słoiki] for cherry liqueur [wiśniak], boxes and trunks — why, one could, God forbid, burst with "envy" [zazdrość]!...
Eh, am I a Jew, a pauper, a beggar "by his dear name"[?]? And those whose wives pack the straw sacks and the deck chairs, with the camp beds, with the jars for cherry liqueur — are they rich men? They are the very same paupers as I am. Eh, you will ask: since they are beggars seven times over, why don't they "khalen"[?] in Będzin? Air is indeed a fine article, but the stomach too has a bit of a say, doesn't it? Have they forgotten the "and if ye shall say, what shall we eat"? The excuse is — fashion: a fashion for dachas has come out, and it is just like silk stockings — they all go about in silk stockings, the servant girl just like madame; it is exactly the same with the dacha: "we are all wise, we are all understanding" — silk stockings, they all go about in silk stockings — it is a fashion, the dacha. The rich man rents a villa with all the comforts [wygody], and the pauper rents the tip of a barn [stodoła], a corner of a cowshed — but letniks they all are. And if everyone is a letnik, then why, I ask you, shouldn't I be a letnik. Why?
To tell the truth, this year my missus "decided" [postanowiła] not ["gisht", misprint for "nisht"] to go and "graze" on the meadow [łąka]. Does she need it? What is she lacking, God forbid — in weight[?]? Does she need to "fatten up"? And which Jewish woman travels for her own health anyway? The wives only go to the dachas because of the children... They only "sacrifice" themselves for the children's sake, but they themselves — God forbid!...
This year my missus, may she be well, gave her word — she is not going! And when "mine" says "nie pojadę" [I won't go], she keeps her word. She is, you should know, "stanowcza" [resolute], and she did indeed keep her word — she really did not go.
Eh, so how come I am a letnik again? It is not my wife's fault. That I am now a letnik is my own fault, "I do remember my faults". This I took upon myself alone to get off and push it [so printed; the line is garbled, apparently duplicated from the next column]. The chief culprit is — the hot May.
Eh, listen, this year's May got me into hot water [lit. "led me into the bathhouse"]. Eh, that May, I shall remember it for a long time, that blazing May.
As you already know, my missus had "decided" not to go to any dacha this year. I was a happy man. I would not have to hang every Friday on the railing [poręcz] of a "freight train" [pociąg towarowy] or on the roof of a bus that has a habit of jumping up "kadosh" [as at the Kedusha prayer] in the middle of the road, so that one has to get off and push it, so as not to commit "a stab into the Sabbath" [a Sabbath desecration]... And how many times does such an "invalid" simply do a "koziołek" [somersault], and you come home to your "letniczka" [holidaying wife] with one trouser leg [nogawica] — well, you know it yourselves, surely you too have travelled by bus on a Friday towards evening; have you never ["gisht"] arrived at your wife's with one trouser leg?...
When I remembered that this year I would not have to recite the "Gomel" blessing every Sabbath for the Friday-evening "rides" [jazdy] by bus, and for the "5-course" dinners, I was a happy man.
But then came a May. It began to fry and roast. A May of 40 degrees; people puffed and panted [sapać] like force-fed geese. Not to compare, people started running to the villages as if from a fire, the carts went like the army trains [obozy] in wartime, and the world grew too narrow for me. What now[?], I thought to myself. If May is such a fire, what will June be like, and who knows what Tammuz will have to say.
When I took a look at my Rivke Hendl, how she puffs and pants, poor thing, how she cannot find a place for herself, how she lays wet[?] towels on her head, how she swallows ice, how she fans herself, how she sleeps whole nights by open windows, and still cannot catch the "air" [Russian vozdukh] — when I saw my missus's "torment" [męczarnia], I lost pounds. It was bitterly pitiful to watch — cruelty to living creatures...
In the midst of all this, while mine could not find a place for herself, in comes a neighbour-woman with a proposition: "You know," she says to my missus, "what has occurred to me? Let us rent a summer flat in partnership; we'll[?] rent a room with a kitchen in partnership; for a couple of weeks we'll manage somehow. Will it be 'pleasant' [przyjemnie] for you together with me at the summer resort [letnisko]?"
Mine answered nothing at all. Mine, you should know, is "stanowcza", and when she has said no, it is no.
Then I put myself into the business, and out of it came the "spółka" [partnership].
And last Sabbath I did indeed make my first visit to my "wspólna" [shared] "dacha".
You see my red eyes with the black marks on my face? That I got from my first visit.
Where did I get the red eyes with the black marks? From two things: from not sleeping and from not eating.
Eh, listen, did I have a "Oneg Datshe" [dacha delight]!
Imagine a room like a perforated egg-crate. The ceiling [sufit] rests on your head. And since I am, no evil eye, a tall fellow, I have to walk bent in three. In this egg-crate stand my two beds and the neighbour's two beds, my two children's cots and my neighbour's two children's cots; in the kitchen sleep my shikse [gentile maid] and my neighbour's shikse. My shikse has "bridegrooms" and my neighbour's shikse has "bridegrooms". I have six imps and my neighbour has seven devils. My missus wants to cook and the neighbour-woman, the partner, wants to cook; my missus puts out the neighbour-woman's pot, and the neighbour-woman puts out my wife's pot; so it is one long putting-out — out go the pots — and the best part is that neither of them cooks.
The thirteen imps (mine and the partner's) play a "mecz" [football match] in the room with "bramki" [goals]; every day a different window pane bursts, and the uproar reaches the heart of heaven.
Well, by day — it is day; but when night comes, one puts the 13 bandits to bed, and things come alive; and where are we ourselves? After all, we too ["yoykh", misprint for "oykh"] are living souls. One couple waits for the other couple to lie down; one sits and chats and waits. One waits until the roosters ["heger", misprint for "hener"] begin to crow, then one drops like flies.
Quite something goes on in this egg-crate. 19 people (13 children, two couples, two shikses) — the flies and the other vermin have a feast; every morning one gets up bloodied[?] and battered as after a battle: at night, when the shutters are closed, the "air" [powietrze] is such that one need only put on gas masks... And if you now see the red eyes with the black stains on my face, it comes from not sleeping and from not eating.
So that was my first visit to my "wspólna" dacha.
Oy, that May — it did ["tot er", misprint for "hot er"], that hot May got me into hot water [lit. "led me into the bathhouse"]...
The Situation of the Jewish Artisans

(A reply to the article in the "Zagl. Tsayt." [Zaglembier Tsaytung] under the title "The Artisan of Today and Tomorrow".)
1.
The author of the article assessed very correctly the situation of the Jewish artisan in general, and in particular of the Jewish bakers and journeymen, who are threatened with losing their livelihoods. The artisans' representatives used all their influence for the cause; had it not been for the various interventions with the proper organs of authority, the bakeries would already have been closed 3 years ago.
Also thanks to the energy of the artisans' representatives, the Magistrat [town council] did not join the mechanical bakery in Sosnowiec as a partner, and at the same time the town was also freed from responsibility for the damage which the bakery causes.
But this is not the means that leads to the goal. It is only a means of holding off the decree for some 2–3 years, and in the end the bakeries will not be able to survive, because on the one hand the law, and on the other hand competition, will gradually push out the small bakeries. For new mechanized and competitive bakeries are now opening, set up by individuals, and there is a well-founded fear that precisely these will take the livelihood away from the small bakeries that have existed until now.
Yes, the situation of the bakers is a serious one; it cannot be put off until tomorrow; one must therefore think it over seriously, and the bakers must be prepared to be able to take on both the competition and the decrees.
— — —
At the beginning of 1931 the privileges which the law provides for older artisans came to an end.
For the artisans who already existed at the time the guild law came into force — namely: no more craft cards will be issued, and only trained artisans will be able to sit for the regular journeyman's and later master's examination, such as those who have completed a crafts school or at least the municipal continuation school (Fortbildungsschule). And how many such there are one can see from the report in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung": namely 10 (read: ten) pupils. So for Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa and Czeladź, 10 candidates for tailor-journeymen were added this year; in other towns too, for example Zawiercie and Częstochowa, things look no better.
The older artisans are glad; those who managed to pass an eased examination are glad; those who managed to obtain craft cards this very year are glad — they are glad because they think they will be the only ones on the market. New artisans, and above all Jewish ones, will surely no longer be added, for who will be able to pass the regular examination? Consequently people will have to stand in line at the old artisans...
So think those who do not know the circumstances. But in reality the matter looks quite different.
H. L. Goldsztajn.
Economic Life

The B.B. Club [the BBWR parliamentary club] has at the present moment — because of the prevailing conditions — become almost the only place where decisions of first-class political and economic importance for the state are adopted. Quite understandable, therefore, is the interest aroused in the country by the exposés of the new Premier Prystor and of the Vice-Minister of Finance, Dr. Starzyński.
The Tax Question
It is superfluous to add that the state enterprises pay no taxes whatsoever and are able to develop only thanks to the high taxes paid by the private enterprises. This year's budget foresees that the turnover tax will amount to 300 million zł. and the income tax to 250 million zł., i.e. as much as in the years of a favourable economic conjuncture. But what turns out? Life is often the best corrector and convinces one that real facts must be reckoned with, willingly or unwillingly. It is enough to look through the figures relating to state revenue and expenditure in order to be convinced that a sharpened economic crisis must have an effect in the direction of reducing both the direct and the indirect taxes, and first of all the turnover tax, customs and monopolies. In such a situation Mr. Starzyński speaks out against carrying out a thorough tax reform, which without any doubt could precisely have had an effect in weakening the economic crisis and would certainly not have reduced the state revenue.
Premier Prystor, wishing to weaken the impression of the truly catastrophic situation in the country, points out that the general index of production fell during the last year in Poland by only 11.5 per cent, whereas in the United States of America — by 17.3 per cent, in England — by 22.6 per cent and in Germany — by 23.3 per cent. The same may also be said about unemployment, which during the same time increased in the United States by 30 per cent, whereas in Germany — by 56 per cent, in England by 57.4 per cent, and in Italy by 83.6 per cent, so that altogether for every 100 inhabitants there are 7.4 per cent unemployed in Germany, 5.9 per cent in England, 4.5 per cent in Austria, 1.7 per cent in Italy, and in Poland — in all 1.2 per cent unemployed.
We are not of the opinion that conditions in weakly developed and backward countries, among which Poland unfortunately must be counted, can be compared with conditions in the rich and advanced countries.
But since Premier Prystor thought it expedient to bring comparative figures, it is a pity that he did not use them in other fields as well. It would then have turned out that while the average citizen in, for example, Czechoslovakia is able to save 100 dollars a year, the same citizen here in Poland saves barely 5 dollars a year. Still more interesting would it have been to point out that while the tax burden here amounts to 15.4 per cent in relation to the national income, the same burden in the United States amounts to barely 4.7 per cent.
M. Goldsztajn.

A Little Feuilleton (from a modern chiromantic [palm-reading] book).
2nd July. An enormous harvest of bankruptcies. A great drought ("zasukha") in the cash-boxes... Flies will drop like the... people and like the businesses...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Matot-Masei)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Matot-Masei
The Portion.
—o—
a) "He shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth" (Num. 30:3)
In their private business dealings rich men are ashamed to deal in groszy [pennies]. They are ashamed even to let the word "grosz" pass their lips; but when it comes to a vow, to charity — then their customary coin is nothing but groszy; then the grosz is to them no such paltry coin at all...
"According to all that proceedeth out of his mouth" — the very coin with which a man deals in his business — "he shall do" — let him use it for charity too...
Shir Yedidut.
• • •
When people come to ask a rich man for a donation, he begins to complain about the bad times, since he is a great pauper; he only has to keep up the household for appearances' sake, but in truth he is poor and destitute — so how can one demand a donation of him?
Of this the prophet says: "Thine habitation is in the midst of deceit; they refuse to know me" — thus you live in the midst of deceit, you fool the world into thinking you are rich, and meanwhile you lead a life of luxury; but — "they refuse to know me" — charity, large donations, you will not[?] give out so that people should think you are rich; here you are not ashamed of your poverty...
Nahalei Devash.
—o—
In the hekdesh [poorhouse] of Brisk [Brześć] a poor man died, and sewn into his clothes they found a hoard of money. This served the rich men as an excuse no longer to give any charity to the poor, pointing out that the poor possess the treasures of Korah.
So Rav Yoshe rebuked the public:
Just see how unfortunate the poor man is: although even the rich men of Brisk are in truth disguised paupers — hush, all quiet; whereas when it turned out that one poor man was a disguised rich man — such an uproar...
—o—
b) "Now the children of Reuben and the children of Gad had a very great multitude of cattle" (Num. 32:1)
"This is what Scripture says: For not from the east, nor from the west" (Ps. 75:7)
Midrash Rabbah 22.
According to the system of medieval astronomy, the natural course of the sun is from west to east, but a certain "encompassing sphere" (galgal ha-makif) pushes the sun onto a reversed route: from east to west.
The natural course of man's soul, too, is from west to east, from darkness to sunrise, to elevation; but the encompassing sphere — money, which is "a wheel that turns in the world", that very wheel which turns with the world — pushes man's soul back: from east to west; it pushes it toward its setting. But "not from the east nor from the west" — not from east to west is man's true way. One must stand up against this strange wheel and go the neutral[?] way: toward the east, toward ascent —
Olelot Efraim.
—o—
c) "We will pass over armed" (Num. 32:32; printed "Nehni" for "Nahnu")
A Masoretic note on four occurrences of "nahnu" ("we"):
"We are all one man's sons" — "and what are we" — "we will pass over armed" — "we have transgressed and have rebelled; thou hast not pardoned" —
This refers to the "sons of a man", the sons of the righteous ("man" in the Torah means a righteous man), who persuade themselves: although "what are we" — although we are idlers and good-for-nothings — still "we are all one man's sons", we are after all children of one righteous man, and that is enough... Says the Masorah further: "If we have transgressed and rebelled, thou hast not pardoned" — if you sin, the merit of the fathers will not help you a bit... Only "we will pass over armed" — work yourselves, for yourselves, by your own merit...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
d) "So shall not the inheritance remove" (Num. 36:7)
The whole law of inheritances was given through the daughters of Zelophehad, because an inheritance is, after all, taken from the dead, and the woman Eve, after all, brought death into the world...
Rabbenu Bahya.
—o—
e) "For Mahlah, Tirzah and Hoglah etc. were married" (Num. 36:11)
In parashat Pinhas the daughters of Zelophehad are listed in a different order than here in parashat Masei, so that it is impossible to find out which of them was older and which younger — for it is, after all, women's nature to conceal their years and their age...
Otzar ha-Derushim.
—o—
Haftarah.
g) [printed thus; should be f] "And all the families of the house of Israel" (Jeremiah 2:1 [as printed; = 2:4])
In Jerusalem there were separate families, castes, each family with its pedigree, with its pride towards the "inferior"; but now, when you are in exile — Jeremiah mocks them — "all the families of the house of Israel": you are all equal. There are no people of pedigree; you are all slaves... That is for your criminal pride of lineage —
Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
g) "As the thief is ashamed when he is found, so is the house of Israel ashamed" (Jer. 2:26)
The Gemara says that a robber who robs openly is less sinful than a thief who steals at night, in hiding. Jeremiah, too, complains that Jews sin in disguise, in hiding, "as the thief is ashamed" — guarding themselves before people, but not before God... If only they at least sinned openly and showed that, just as they have no fear of God, so they have no fear of people either...
Ibid.
—o—
Avot
h) "Let thy house be open wide" (Avot 1:5)
The Reitsch Maggid once comes to a rich man to ask for a donation. They show him the door. Says he: this is what is called fulfilling the Mishnah "Let thy house be open wide" — let your door be wide open — to throw people out...
• • •
The aforementioned Maggid once comes to a rich man; they will not let him across the threshold because his boots are muddy. Says the Maggid: the rich man has God's attributes.
— What do you mean?
— Of God we say in prayer: "Blessed is He who has mercy on the earth" (has pity on the ground) and then "Blessed is He who has mercy on the creatures" (has pity on people); you too have pity first on the earth — on the floor — and only afterwards on people...
Będzin — Nearly a catastrophe.

[Będzin — road accident.] On Tuesday, in the daytime, a bus with passengers was driving fast along Kościuszki Street when one wheel came off, and the bus was left with 3 wheels on the tram line; meanwhile a tram arrived, so that only by a miracle did the tram driver manage to brake the tram quickly. Thanks to that a terrible catastrophe was avoided.
“It’s not my fault, it’s the long dresses.”

[Będzin — street life.] In Będzin a fine Christian woman, dressed in a long dress, got off a tram. Below, a young man was walking, who stepped on the dress, and so the dress was torn as the passenger was getting down the tram steps.
The injured woman called a policeman. But the young man defended himself, saying that the one “to blame” for the damage is only the originator of the fashion for long dresses.”
A ceiling collapses at a poor Jewish tenant’s.

[Będzin — house accident.] In the house at Kołłątaja 41 in Będzin, on the third floor, lives the poor tenant Hendler. On Tuesday at dawn Hendler’s wife saw lumps of clay falling from the ceiling. The woman woke her husband and children, who, seeing the danger, rushed out of the flat in great haste.
At that moment the whole ceiling came down with great force, dragging the iron rails [girders] along with it.
By a miracle the family was saved from a catastrophe.

[Będzin — missing person.] Since Friday no one knows where 15-year-old Meir Berman is; he was brought up in the boys’ ochronka [children’s home] of the Jewish “Dobroczynność” [charity society] and was to be sent to the summer colony in Sławków.

Tried to drown a child.

[Będzin — crime.] On Tuesday, in the daytime, a young Christian woman was hanging about the Czarna Przemsza for quite a long time. The neighbours noticed her and began to keep an eye on her, and then they noticed that she was holding a small child; people guessed that she wanted the water to take it. They questioned her and meanwhile fetched the police, who took the “devoted mother” away to the commissariat, and so the child was saved.

Last Monday a 7-year-old girl, whose parents live on Kołłątaja Street, was playing with a 5-groszy coin, put it into her mouth and began to choke on it.

Sosnowiec — Dr. Herzl Academy

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, memorial.]
Last Saturday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon the Revisionist organisation in Sosnowiec held a mourning meeting in its own premises, dedicated to the memory of the late leader Dr. T. Herzl.
The comrades Fiszel, Grin and Dafner lectured on the life and work of Dr. Herzl, and especially on his work "Judenstaat", which brought light and encouragement into the Jewish people.
With the singing of "Hatikvah" the mourning meeting was closed.
— — —
On the same day in the evening an academy took place in the municipal theatre, organised by the "Keren Kayemet", dedicated to the 27th yahrzeit of the late Zionist leader Dr. T. Herzl and the 3rd yahrzeit of the local communal worker Dr. A. Perlman.
The hall was packed with a young audience; the stage was splendidly decorated with Dr. Herzl's portrait and an artistically set-up grave surrounded with greenery.
The academy was opened by the deputy mayor J. Fajnrajch; representatives of all Zionist factions were invited to sit on the presidium.
Longer speeches were delivered by Messrs. Kołodny (Eretz Israel), Wygodzki[?] (Będzin), Feldman and Kohn. All spoke about the great personality of the unforgettable leader Dr. Herzl and of the local communal worker Dr. Perlman. With this the official part of the academy was closed.
The second part was a musical one, in which a choir, solo singing, recitations and a little scene of pioneer (halutz) life in Eretz Israel took part. Almost all the items were performed well, and the audience rewarded them with applause.
The next day, Sunday, a memorial service was held in the municipal synagogue with the participation of the cantor and his choir.
Rabbi Hager delivered a longer speech.
After the choir sang several chapters of Psalms, the gathering was closed with the singing of "Hatikvah".
At 12 noon a large crowd of friends, comrades and acquaintances gathered at the cemetery at the grave of the late local communal worker Dr. Perlman.
The cantor recited "El Male Rachamim", and many donated trees in the "Herzl Forest" in the name of Dr. Perlman.
The Summer Colonies of "Hashomer Hatzair"

[Sosnowiec — youth movements, Zionism.]
"Hashomer Hatzair" in Sosnowiec has organised four colonies this year, in which up to a hundred people will take part. The first colony, for the youngest, already left on Sunday for Chruszczobród. The second colony goes next Sunday to Sopotnia (Beskids); the third colony will leave on the 26th of this month for Jeleśnia (Beskids). The fourth colony will be an instructors' colony in the Kielce region — and will begin next Sunday.
It is worth noting that the number of young people taking part in the Shomer summer colonies grows from year to year. Four years ago, in all, some twenty-odd young people went out; three years ago — thirty-odd shomrim; two years ago sixty-odd; a year ago — seventy-odd; and this year the number will reach 100. The broad Jewish public has not yet sufficiently appreciated the great efforts of the youth organisation "Hashomer Hatzair" in carrying out such undertakings as the summer colonies. The Jewish population of Sosnowiec, however, regards the educational significance of the Shomer colony with ever greater understanding. The proof: the number of participants in it keeps growing.

From Sporting Life.

[Sport — football; Będzin — donations.]
Vienna's Hakoah loses and wins in Katowice.

The great chain of series-victories [?] of Austrian football sport was broken by Vienna's Hakoah with its compromising appearance in Katowice. A team that belongs to the first football league may by no means lose to a team like "Naprzód" of Lipiny; but we still know quite precisely the psyche of our Jewish teams: one Jewish club plays against the other brother club with great ambition and very brutally besides, but against a Christian one they lose their ambition and their skills, both technical and tactical. This could be seen in the two matches, which ran as follows:

"Naprzód", Lipiny — "Hakoah", Vienna 1:2 (1:0)

The Viennese's first appearance in Katowice ended with a deserved victory for "Naprzód", which played with great self-sacrifice the whole time. Hakoah gave the impression that they were playing because they... have to play. In the first half the guests had more of the game, yet because of the "hyper" [?] combination play on the one side and the excellent goalkeeper of the Silesians on the other, they managed not to score a single goal. Only shortly before the break does Mausner score the leading goal. After the break the strength of the "seasoned" professional players fails, and Naprzód shoots two goals through Nastula and Karczmarczyk. The best on the field were: Wysacki [?], Naprzód's goalkeeper, Michalski and Komar; for Hakoah, Feldman, Zucker and the wings Danenfeld and Fischer played well. Referee Mr. Gritz [?] very weak. Over three thousand spectators.

"Hakoah" — "ŻKS" 2:3 (2:0)

The Viennese's second guest match also ended with a surprise. Hakoah narrowly beat ŻKS of Katowice. Already in [?] the 4th minute ŻKS leads 0.1 [sic]. The following minutes belong to the home side, and the jubilation of the public is indescribable when Katowice scores the second goal through Kac. Half-time 0:4 [sic; read 2:0] for ŻKS. After the change of ends Hakoah wants to equalize, but instead of applying its technical means it plays brutally. In the 4th minute Mausner scores the first goal for the guests. A few minutes later Grünfeld scores the equalizer despite very strong resistance from the Katowice players. Mausner sets the result of the day in the 37th minute. Of ŻKS, the goalkeeper Hochzeit, the veteran Tichauer and Gottreich in the attack distinguished themselves. Referee Mr. Lagand [?] very good. Spectators altogether a few hundred.

The representative match between the above-mentioned regions ended in a drawn result. The goals were scored by: Jaksz [?] 2 and Woźniak for Kraków, Przybyłek 2 and Żmijewski 1 for Zagłębie. Referee Mr. Koszyrucki [?] good.

Nothing to Do — So They Fight.

[Czeladź — the beit midrash; a brawl.] It is an old rule: when there is nothing to do, one goes to the beit midrash for the afternoon and evening prayers, and there God already helps and some work turns up.
And if in town one wanders about without a stitch of work, in the village it is even worse: there one wanders about idle and bored and — as the saying goes — neither here nor there.
In such a situation the poor inhabitants of Czeladź find themselves; but they are blessed with a beit midrash, where all questions are finally resolved and everyone can there „stand up for“ his own little town[?]; that, after all, is what a beit midrash is for, where everyone has full freedom to do as he pleases and as suits him.
So on Tuesday evening Jews gathered in the Czeladź beit midrash and, as usual, began to speak slander about the living as well as about those already in the World of Truth; well, there was a commotion, a storm, and they began to hit one another in a thoroughly un-Jewish manner.
The end of it was that the Gelbards together with Brzegowski[?] fell upon Binyomin Berman and beat him till he bled, so that the latter needed medical help.
The epilogue of these events will, as usual, find its echo in court.
That is what Jews have a beit midrash for.
The Husband Forges Bills — and the Wife Throws Herself under a Train.

[Sosnowiec and Królewska Huta — crime and suicide; followed by two items: Zagórze — accident; Olkusz — free-loan fund.] A great sensation was caused in Sosnowiec by the arrest of Mr Dovid Z., owner of a shoe shop in Królewska Huta, who has been accused of forging bills of exchange in his father-in-law's name in Piotrków.

No More Supplementary Tax Assessments Will Be Made / Cycling Race of the Sosnowiec „Maccabi“

[Poland — taxes; followed by a short item: Sosnowiec — sport.]
Recently the tax offices („urzędy“) have often made supplementary assessments of the taxes („podatki“) — the turnover tax and the income tax (podatek obrotowy and dochodowy).
They used to do this on the grounds that by the deadline of the assessment they did not have all the materials needed to assess the tax. Therefore a sum was assessed provisionally, and later a supplementary assessment was made.
Because of this one could never know whether the payment order („nakaz“) already contained the whole tax, or whether „something“ more would still be added.
The Ministry of Finance has in these days issued an order to all the offices that they are to stop making supplementary assessments. The assessment of every tax must be final, and all the materials must be collected beforehand, in order to know how much to assess.

Notes of the Week
