An Appeal from the Rabbi to the Jews of Będzin

With God's help, Marienbad, Tuesday of [the week of the portion] Matot-Masei, 22 Tammuz 5691.
To the honourable dear householders of the holy community of Będzin, may God preserve them.
Dear Jews, men and women!
While staying in Marienbad I have heard again that, despite all the warnings of the Rabbinate, people go on using meat from the butcher shops that have been banned, and that the remaining butchers, too, do not obey everything the Rabbinate demands of them.
I therefore come to you all with a fervent request. Is it possible? Has everything really become ownerless [hefker]? Believe me that I am to you all like a faithful father who strives only for your good — that you should walk in the ways of the holy Torah, for then it will be well with you in this world and in the world to come. Unfortunately the Evil Inclination comes through its many emissaries and persuades people that the Rabbinate has vested interests. What vested interests do we have? All we want is that kashrut be put in order, so that when one buys kosher meat at the butcher shop one can be sure that it is truly kosher — and that can only be when it is under the supervision of the Beth Din and when you obey the Rabbinate. Unfortunately there are such people who degrade the honour of the Rabbinate and stop at nothing, and bring about — may it not befall us — stumbling into nevelot and treifot [carrion and forbidden meat]. Therefore, dear Jews, believe me that I truly love you with a love of the soul.
When I was in Eretz Israel, at the holy places, I prayed first of all for all of you; I truly mean only your good. Believe me, beloved Jews, that I write this letter to you with weeping and tears. Do not let yourselves be misled by the bad elements who want to lead you away from the holy Torah; do not eat any meat that is forbidden, do not use any meat from any banned butcher shop, for when the Rabbinate forbids meat it is exactly the same as nevelot and treifot. Obey everything the Rabbinate commands, for it is for your good; you shall be sure that when you buy meat it is truly kosher, and when you obey in everything, it will be well and bright for you, and you will have joy, blessing and success.
With a soul that hopes for your good with all my heart,
Chanoch Tzvi HaKohen Lewin
Head of the rabbinical court here [Będzin], at present in Marienbad.

Highly esteemed Mr. Editor!
In the last issue of your esteemed paper there appeared a statement by the "long-standing board member" Mr. Jakub Montag about our club's activity.
Not considering it necessary to enter into any polemic whatsoever with Mr. Montag, whose frequent "slamming of the door" and quick reconciliations we are already sick of, we nevertheless ask you, highly esteemed Mr. Editor, to grant us space in your esteemed paper for a factual clarification of the situation.
First of all we wish to state categorically that nobody has forced his way into the board of "Hakoach", and there can be no talk of conducting any party politics whatsoever in "Hakoach"; and Mr. M.'s claim that "Hakoach" has been turned into a party "Kremlin" we brand as a deliberate lie.
The present board was elected at the last general meeting with the participation of 300 members and received the confidence of the overwhelming majority of the club. Throughout the whole year our activity has had in view only the organisation and development of physical education in all its branches among Jewish youth.
Last week the following case occurred: the League for Labour Palestine in Będzin approached us about arranging a sports event whose proceeds were to go to the Palestine Workers' Fund (P.A.F. — Kapai).
The board of "Hakoach", which is affiliated to the world federation "Maccabi" — which only at its last convention once again endorsed our bond with the Zionist Congress and Eretz Israel — saw in this no political or party crime whatever and met the request of the "League"; the board decided in principle to agree to their proposal and to hand over to the appropriate section the decision on the technical possibility of holding the event.
That was the reason which Mr. M. searched for with a candle, in order to be able to wriggle out of the responsibility which he bears towards the club and which he did not discharge (the tennis section).
At the same time we declare that we will no longer conduct any polemic on this matter, and Mr. Montag's outrageous conduct we shall hand over to the judgement of our club's authorities.
The Board of the Jewish Gymnastics and Sports Club "Hakoach" in Będzin.

What Must Be Done...

[Politics — economy and taxation; article by a Sejm deputy.] On the worsening of the economic crisis in the country, Deputy [Sejm deputy] Sommerstein [Emil Sommerstein] writes:
At a time when we stressed year in, year out, at every opportunity, that the state budget is too high, that it exceeds the population's capacity to pay, that it must be reduced by at least a billion złoty and that a proper reduction must be carried out of the local self-government budgets and of the other public burdens, a constant, energetic "no" was heard from the government benches. And all the Sejm groupings, regardless of their political convictions, helped the government, adopted the budgets and even put forward a series of proposals to raise individual budget items or even to insert new ones.
Only we ourselves consistently stressed that the budget's revenues come mainly from taxes and public levies, that the revenues from the monopolies and state enterprises are only proportionally small because of their poor management, and that to the extent that these revenues fall, the government strives, by tightening the tax screw, to find new cover for the enormous three-billion expenditure budget.
The decisive factors remained deaf to all our appeals and calls, which demanded changing the faulty tax system and revising the excessively high tax assessments, especially since these burdens fall exclusively on the urban population, on trade and crafts, oppressing first and foremost the Jewish population, the Jewish merchant and the Jewish artisan.
Constantly there was talk of the need to maintain the balance of the budget, and meanwhile for years three-billion budgets were set, investments were planned on a large scale and burdened exclusively on the present generation, while everywhere they are spread over a series of generations by raising long-term loans.
Today we have on one side an enormous bureaucratic apparatus, a whole series of state enterprises and, besides that, a participation of the state in 51 private enterprises, while on the other side we have before us the people, worn out and exhausted by the heavy taxes of many years, which have swallowed not only the incomes, not only the working capital needed to maintain production, but have also touched and damaged the foundation of foundations, diminishing the national wealth itself.
Only today are voices heard from everywhere demanding a so-called "compression" of the budget and demanding that the state treasury withdraw from a series of enterprises. These voices, however, have been raised at a time when such a liquidation is altogether impossible, or is bound up with great loss to the state treasury.
The compression, i.e. the restriction of the budget, is now being carried out mechanically by a reduction of officials' salaries — a method which, from both the economic and the social point of view, is far from expedient. Officials' pensions in Poland were never too high, and perhaps only in the higher categories did they provide some sort of means of existence. So what consequences can such a mechanical pension reduction have, which takes in even the lowest grades, which until now did not provide the possibility even of a subsistence minimum?
Officials and functionaries together with their families make up 40 percent of the urban population here, and they are perhaps now the only consumers of industrial products because of the impoverishment of the rural population, and the reductions will bring a further restriction of consumption and production.
What must be done is — to abolish as quickly as possible the unnecessary posts, the superfluous offices and institutions, the semi-official associations, delegations and branch offices [ekspozytury], to give up the investment experiments, to commercialise the state enterprises and the monopolies. Not to increase the number of unemployed by taking away from people their posts of professional and honest work held until now and handing them over to "privileged" organisations, as happened, for example, recently in the well-known affair of the so-called "salt concessions".
And at the same time one must not merely discuss and consider, but actually carry out and realise a tax relief, which may yet soften the further liquidation of the economic establishments [placówki] still active until now.
Jews Want to Flee Honduras

Everyone lives off bananas. — One must have a revolver. — A story of two roosters. — He chops off two of his own fingers. — 60 Jewish souls in all. — Endless bloodshed. — Where can one flee?
(From a private letter.)
Very few remember that some 25 years ago, when the late Zangwill founded the Territorialist Organization, one of the plans was to create a Jewish state in Honduras.
The plan was buried together with Territorialism, and Jews forgot the name Honduras. Now the name has surfaced again, in connection with the unrest that has taken place there.
It turns out that there are a few Jews there. After North America closed its gates, several dozen wandering emigrants made their way to that god-forsaken corner of Central America.
And here is a short excerpt from a letter written by a local Jewish immigrant, Luis Fartnay[?].
Altogether Honduras has 600 thousand souls on an area of over 50 thousand sq. kilometres — 13 souls per sq. kilometre on average. Most people there are occupied with bananas. The land is concentrated in the hands of rich men; the masses live in poverty and everything revolves around bananas, whether one works or trades.
It has been calculated that Honduras exports forty million dollars' worth of bananas every year.
A great deal of land lies entirely uncultivated. The climate is good, the soil fertile, but the Hondurans are lazy; there is no desire to work as in Europe, and in particular they do not like working the land. Besides, the rich planters have a policy in this: they cultivate only as much land as there are bananas that can be exported.
The Hondurans are not even a bad lot, but very hot-tempered; to grab a revolver and shoot is a trifle for them. Therefore every merchant has to carry a revolver, although he seldom has occasion to use it.
I myself — relates Fartnay — saw a curious scene:
In Honduras a sport of cockfighting is customary. They set up two roosters, tie two little knives to their legs and goad them. They fight until one falls dead. People bet on these cockfights, just as elsewhere on a horse race or a bullfight.
Once two Hondurans at such a scene bet 5 dollars; afterwards some quarrel broke out between them, they began to fight like the roosters, and one was left lying dead right alongside the rooster. The crowd applauded the fighter, and he walks around free...
There are Indians here who have this nature: when one gets angry at another, he grabs [a blade] and chops off two of his own fingers, and then takes bloody revenge on the one who caused his anger.
Last year the government conducted propaganda abroad for broad immigration for the purpose of colonization. But it is very hard to make a living here. The hunted and tormented Jewish wanderers should not come here; the few who are already here are looking for ways to get out — but there is nowhere to go...
There are altogether some 90 - 70 Jewish souls here; they are called "Polacos", "Rusos", "Rumanos" — that they are Jews, nobody knows. They make a living from peddling in the two cities: San Pedro Sula and Tegucigalpa (the capital).
Perhaps one would somehow have settled in by now, but there is the trouble of the constant uprisings. Two parties fight each other here, the Blues (conservatives) and the Reds (liberals); every few years one party stages an overturn and seizes power, and every revolution costs blood.
The leader of the liberals is the military general Gregorio Ferrera. Recently he had already seized several smaller towns scattered over the whole country, but at the gates of the big city of San Pedro he was repulsed.
The country is in a state of war, peddling has collapsed, the Jews feel very bad and want to flee — but where to?
Y. Grim.
Between Mountains and Valleys.

[Zagłębie — summer holidays and camps; Zionist youth movements; travel letter.] By Ben Amotz.
(Impressions of a visit to the summer colonies of "Gordonia", "Sinai" and "Hashomer Haleumi".)

The village of Rajcza, which lies in the lap of the Western Beskids, has this summer been "occupied" by the Jewish dacha-holidaymakers of Zagłębie. A few years ago this resort was as if orphaned, a place for tourists. But it was fated that this splendid region should be revealed to exhausted mankind. Our Berysz Rapaport took a fancy to going to Rajcza in summertime, and on his return he conducted, in his own way, a broad campaign in favour of Rajcza.
The campaign began to have an effect. A member of the shtibl, Mr Frajberg, opened a guest-house, and from then on Rajcza began to be counted on the list of resorts lying around the Beskids.
But that was still not much; the number of Rajcza-goers was still insignificant, because the name was not popular with that sex which is able to pave the way — or, better said, Rajcza was somehow unappealing to the fair sex. But as King Solomon says — "to everything there is a season"; the time came too when Rajcza rose to the surface and took first place in this year's dacha season. The place is especially favoured by people from Zagłębie, or more precisely by the wives and little wives of Będzin...
This time we will leave the distinguished dacha-guests in peace and take a walk through the summer colonies of the above-mentioned organizations, which have followed the "fashion" and "Judaized" the eastern, western and southern parts with their summer colonies.
A magnificent road leads us into the village of Nickaliny[?], where the summer colony of the Będzin "Gordonia" is.
— — —
The colony's camp lies amid an abundance of natural beauty. When you look around, it is almost hard to believe that such natural treasures are to be found in Poland at a distance of 4 hours' travel from the coal mines of Zagłębie...
As we approach the colony we no longer need to ask anyone where it is. The blue-and-white flag fluttering on high is the signpost to the place where 40 children live, brought up according to the "Gordonia" programme.
The camp of children, the future pioneers, are content and cheerful; every hour is occupied; strict discipline and comradely relations are woven together. It is hard to part from them, but we must say goodbye, because our guide, the sportsman (sportowiec) Mosze Gelbard, explains to us that we still have to make a hard hike over the mountain "Tampal"[?].
— — —
Not lagging behind in this field is the still very young youth organization "Sinai". This organization too has set up a colony, at "Rycerka". The colony building, by the way a very spacious one, stands right by the road, and that is a "bit of a drawback", because the older members of the colony are "close in-laws" with the passers-by...
The "Sinai" colony resembles a guest-house in miniature. The initiators and the management had other intentions, educational ones, but to a great extent they did not succeed this time. Those staying at the colony, especially the older members, lead a "life" no worse than all those who make up the "dacha exile"...
We arrived at the colony while the director Hilel Żabner was lecturing on the life of Maimonides (the Rambam). The lecture is listened to with little attention and is interrupted several times because some of the members (only from among the older ones) are meanwhile doing business: eggs, berries (jagody) and the like.
In general indiscipline reigns at the colony; the crowd feels "like a fish in water" — a Mizrachist colouring; but one may hope that next year the Sinai colonies will be put on different foundations, as the saying goes: "once you have burnt yourself on something hot, you blow on something cold"...
— — —
On a low hill in the village of Ujsoły a blue-and-white flag flutters as an announcement that here rests the Będzin "ken" (nest) of "Hashomer Haleumi".
As soon as one steps onto the colony's grounds, one gets the impression of being among shomrim in the Land of Israel. Genuine joy, gladness that comes from work, pioneering spirit reign in full measure in the Shomer camp. The management — exemplary; the discipline — pioneering; and the daily routine? — for the people and for the land... And this in spite of the fact that not a single one of Będzin's "certified" Zionists has the slightest interest in this Shomer material...
Getting to know the activity more closely and seeing with what enthusiasm they prepare for the Sabbath, I regret that among our visitors there are none of those "fine Jews" who trumpet at every opportunity with the shofar from Mount Sinai.. They would no doubt receive a lesson here from the shomrim, not about "shtibl Judaism" but about
— holiness and morals...

The System of Upbringing

L. Szpigelman.
II.
As has been said, the problem of upbringing is one of the most painful questions among all peoples and in all countries — and all the more so among us Jews, where it plays so great a role in what way we should bring up our children, both as modern citizens and as national Jews. That, however, is another chapter, a quite separate matter, about which there will no doubt be occasion to speak more than once in this place. This time, however, we would like to dwell only on the most elementary system of bringing up our children.
Let us not fool ourselves; let us be honest and open-hearted, and then we must come to the realisation that in school the children are not brought up at all. We may agree unanimously that the children are taught — well or badly, it makes no difference — in this or that elementary school, in this or that gymnasium; but in no way can we agree that time is devoted there to upbringing, which is a quite separate branch of pedagogy.
We have had the opportunity many times to hear how the teachers reproach the parents of the children for not taking an interest in their children — that they should learn their lessons properly — and lecture them for it. The parents are ashamed, the blood rushes to their heads, and they leave the teachers' room upset and downcast.
Here, however, one must stop and consider: is this the task of the teacher or the head? Must they not give thought to the children's parents? After all, one must first of all know what kind of parents the children have — are they capable, and are they in a position to take an interest in their children's homework? Among the broad strata of the population there are still such simple parents who, with the best will and the greatest attention, cannot occupy themselves with the pedagogical question: not only can they not form any notion of it, they do not have the time for it either. But let us say it concerns even better-off parents, such as do understand in what way their children ought to be brought up — one still cannot demand of them what they are not in a position to do. The father may even be a good bookkeeper or correspondent and yet, on the one hand, not be competent in the upbringing of children, and on the other hand his time does not allow him to occupy himself with his children.
We understand very well that the home, the surroundings in which the child finds itself, has a great bearing on the studies in that very school, and precisely about this one must think: one must consider how the child can become more attached to the school than to the home, which does not bring the proper benefit for bringing up the child as it must be done in the present century. We understand that the teachers ought to be in contact with the parents of children who require special attention, special examination. But one can by no means agree that the parents receive a letter from the school saying their child is not learning well, and that this is supposed to mean that the school has thereby fulfilled its duty and from then on it is up to the parents to see that the child keeps up [?] with the studies together with its classmates. Can one really demand that all parents, whoever they may be, should be able to devote so much to their children? Are pedagogy and upbringing not special fields, with which only trained people should deal? How then can parents deal with them, who are not professionals in this field — and besides, everyone has his occupation, from which he must pull the yoke of making a living on his shoulders.
True, pedagogy is not one of the easy occupations; moreover, one must admit that children are now badly demoralised and are not easy to get along with. Thus we see that, for nothing and again for nothing, parents are afraid that their children might take their own lives. The agitation and demoralisation that prevail among school youth today have never been seen before. Because of the smallest trifle serious incidents occur.
No doubt under such conditions it is hard to get along with pupils, but one must not forget one thing: that precisely for this reason they are the educators and the pedagogues, and they must have command over their children; and precisely because the children are now demoralised and agitated, one must pay more attention to them, occupy oneself more with them and take more interest in them.
Nowadays children are not brought up in the schools; at best they deal there with the dry subjects, which is decidedly too little. Children must not merely be taught subjects in the schools; they must be brought up there in the true sense of the word, and for that one must have truly modern qualifications.
(The formulas of pedagogy and the practice of real upbringing. — Will anyone give thought to this?)
For this purpose the pupils must grow into a common life with their teachers. Only then is harmony created, friendly relations form between teacher and pupil, and then comes the living together that brings so much benefit to the pupils and the teachers alike.
In the great world people have come to the conviction that studies and lessons should be made playful not only for small and less able children, but also for grown-up and able pupils. They have come to the conviction that everything done in a playful, enjoyable way gives more pleasure and more profit than straining oneself with all one's strength; the advantage being that it does not seem as if one were carrying some heavy yoke that tires and does not allow one to continue [?] the necessary work, however useful it may be.
We see that in the modernised schools the studies are so elaborately arranged ["complicated"] that one passes from one class to the next without noticing that one is learning. It always looks as if one is playing; and the relations between teachers and pupils are so distinctive, so sympathetic and close, that it gives the impression of two friends playing together.
It is therefore self-evident that with such a conception of upbringing there can be no thought of any frictions that might provoke hostile relations between teachers and pupils.
It is therefore high time that we begin to think in what way children can benefit [?] as much as possible from school, fear their teachers as little as possible and live with them as amicably as possible. All this can only come about after people seriously and honestly give thought to child psychology.
If it is our view that things cannot go on like this, that the system so far is harmful both for the present and for the future, then one must adopt the method of modernising the system of children's upbringing in the way it is done in the great civilised world.
Negroes Who Speak Yiddish and Ask for Support

The editorial office of the „Morgen Zhurnal“ [the New York Yiddish daily] has received a letter from the black Jews of Brownsville [Brooklyn], saying that they are in great need, and appealing to their white Jewish brethren to help them maintain their Talmud Torah.
„Brothers and sisters! We, the black Jews, who come from Spain, from Africa and also from Palestine, have founded a school and Talmud Torah, where our children are taught Judaism, praying, speaking Yiddish and observing all Jewish laws. Many of the children are very poor and some are orphans, whom we must help with clothing and with meals, and guard them so that they do not get lost among the black Negro Christians.
„But we ourselves are great paupers, and even with our greatest effort it is impossible for us [printed „אינו“, a misprint for „אונז“] to maintain the school and Talmud Torah on our own and to help the poor orphans. We therefore ask you, Jewish brothers and sisters, come to our aid, help us with whatever you can. Our children sacrifice themselves in order to be Jews. So help them remain among us“.
The letter is signed by Mordechai Herman and Benny Rakman.
Everything Must Die! (The Last Word of a Samovar)

Menachem Rubinsztejn.
It seems it is already a law of nature that every thing must die out; nothing lives for ever; whole cities go under, mountains sink in, seas dry up, suns go out, there is no eternity; the mightiest nations have been wiped off the globe, forests have been obliterated, thousands of animals [printed „היות“ for „חיות“] have been destroyed — everything dies; I am dying too, or I have already „died“...
Who does not know me, who does not remember me — the „distinguished“ samovar? Who does not know what an honoured place I once held in every Jewish home? At every celebration, at a wedding, at a bris, at a tnoim [betrothal contract], at a mazl-tov, at a Jewish bar mitzvah, at a „zehung“ [the matchmaking meeting], at a „vort“ [engagement], at a knas-meal, at a forshpil [the bride's party before the wedding], at zmires — everywhere I was the „fernem“ [?, the distinguished one], in first place; without me nobody could manage a single turn.
The gentleman, the madame, the boss and the boss's wife, the master of the house, the mistress of the house, the husband and the wife, the „he“ and the „she“, the squire and his lady would not stir from their beds in the morning before the maid announced: — The samovar is already on the table!
With respect they served me on the table, carefully, as with a trembling child, so that I should not get any knock; I shone like a little mirror. Under me a little brass tray, for the sake of my honour, so that I should not stand barefoot on the bare table; my ears were bound with 2 snow-white napkins, and a flowered little porcelain teapot was fitted on me. I was the beauty of the house!
When the young wife wanted to catch a glimpse of how she looked after the night, in her morning dress, she took a peek into me and saw at once what a face... she had. With me people made a fuss, with me they showed off, they flaunted me before others — just look at my samovar! — one woman used to boast to another, wishing to show off as a lady of wealth.
With a glass of tea from me people used to revive themselves, they could not stop relishing it: „I have just drunk a glass of tea from a samovar“ — so people used to talk among themselves.
At the wedding of a young couple I was the most beautiful and most expensive, also the most impressive [?] drashe-geshank [wedding gift]. What kind of face, so to speak [?, „משטיינס געזאגט“], would all the presents have had, together with the guests, with the in-laws, with the bride and groom, if my honoured [printed „בכבורע“] figure had not stood on the table?
Already on Thursday night the mistress of the house or the maid would lie on the floor in the kitchen, with sand and bathed in sweat, scouring the samovar in honour of the Sabbath, rubbing it with lime so that it should get a shine; otherwise she would have had a spoiled Sabbath... — You haven't even scoured the samovar! — the husband would reproach her.
When guests came, on a Sabbath, a holiday or a Saturday night, I at once took the place of honour at the head [„oybn-on“]. I was the first to set the tone, with my si-si-sizzling and letting off steam. The first topic of conversation was me — the samovar: — Where did you buy the samovar? How much did you pay for the samovar? Which factory does the samovar come from? Everybody examined me, looked me over, touched me, gave expert opinions, assessed my value, praised me no end [lit. „into the day“]; I boiled, seethed, sprayed sparks and melted with joy and pride.
Bride and groom loved each other, hugged and kissed; the in-laws rejoiced; good friends regaled themselves together; learned men, sons of Torah, debated in pilpul; husband and wife nestled up to each other; girl and boy romanced, swore eternal love with compliments — all in my presence [printed „בעגנווארט“], before my eyes. They were not ashamed before me; they regarded me as one of the family, as their own; they knew I was a good friend of theirs, that I would not betray them, nor abandon them in bad times either. For indeed, in a time of trouble, to whom did people run for help if not to me? At once [printed „גרייך“, probably „גלייך“] I let myself be pawned, without fuss, at a pawnshop [lombard] or with some benefactor in town... and one got a few roubles straight away.
But today I am going out like a candle, I am in my death throes, extinguished without a spark of fire, cold as ice, shoved away in the kitchen under the bench; I knock about among the old junk, dusty, covered in dust, smeared with mud, soiled with filth; green moss has already grown on my body; they throw me, fling me from one place to another, there is nowhere to put me, to set me down; to everyone I am superfluous, too big in their eyes — you might as well throw me out into the street.
— What is this old rag [„trante“] knocking about here? — the maid asks the „present-day madame“ from the kitchen.
Hearing such words of abuse, I turn even more yellow and green than I am; my brass heart bursts within me from pain and shame; every time a limb falls off me, another member cracks; now my tap falls out, now I get a crease in my belly, a crook in the grate [„reshotke“], in the crown of my head; my right hand is about to fall off, the left has long since fallen; I am already limping on one foot — in a word: I am going under, I am dying!..
Bride and groom kiss in the cinema and drink soda water; the in-laws chat in the café [„kawiarnia“] and drink black coffee; good friendship [printed „גוטע פריינט איז“] has gone under completely — they would gladly drown each other; learned sons of Torah have already died out, and what remain are only hypocrites, false people, supposedly pious... They need no tea; a glass of liquor suits them better...
Girl and boy do not romance at home today; according to the new method of science... it has to take place in hidden places, in more comfortable spots: on the river in a little boat, far from town and village — there it is more convenient... They need no tea either; they are hot even without tea... and they have a river to cool off in...
Today's husband and wife are not the same as they once were either; each finds his own corner, drinks whatever he fancies and with whoever comes along [printed „זיך.ז.“]. At home they go about puffed up like quarrelsome roosters and drink Vichy water [?, „ווישע-וואסער“]; and so I have become useless, superfluous in God's world.
Everyone washes with me: the „madame“ heats water in me to wash her feet; the daughter — the young lady — to wash herself; often [printed „אמט מאל“, probably „אפט מאל“] I am also used to heat purification water [for washing the dead] when someone is in a hurry to bury somebody as fast as possible.
That is what I have come to — oh, woe is me...
Technical Wonders.

[Science and technology — general knowledge; three parts.]
1) Where do our clothes come from?
A statistician of the Leipzig Fair has taken the trouble to find out where our clothes and the various articles we carry about with us come from. First of all it is worth noting that every person carries around with him perhaps a hundred things every day to which we pay no attention. It is a small dwelling-house that we drag around with us. Apart from our garments, which consist of shoes, stockings, underwear, suit, collar, ties, hat, one must not forget the studs of the collar and of the cuffs, pins, little chains, rings, a watch, a money purse, a wallet, a briefcase, an umbrella, a walking stick, a cigarette case, a lighter — not counting the various articles of women's fashion which ladies carry with them and which are hard even to enumerate.
It is interesting that in order to satisfy our needs and clothes, things had to be brought from the whole world. Our cutlery, for example, with which we eat, is of steel, which is made from Swedish and Spanish ore; the silver comes from Mexico; the little "takalo" [?] with which our child plays is made of camphor from the island of Formosa. The knitted little dress of the "tak" [?] is made of wool from Africa; the horsehair needed to stiffen the collar of our coat comes from Russia; our ties are of Chinese silk, which is glazed with German coal.
For modern fine furniture one has to use wood from South America and from Africa. From snakes and lizards that live in the warm places, fine ladies' shoes are made today.
It is worth knowing that the clothes every person wears today are made of materials that come from the four corners of the earth. The shoes are made of Indian goatskin (Asia), the soles of American cowhide, the underwear is of European linen, the suit of Australian wool and the stockings of Egyptian Mako cotton.
2) Where does porcelain come from?
Today there is no house without at least porcelain dishes. In most houses there are porcelain figurines and vases, which are an ornament in the home.
Where does porcelain come from? Eighteen hundred years ago Chinese potters invented porcelain, which they made from feldspar, quartz and kaolin; Portuguese seamen brought it to Europe. To this day one cannot explain how porcelain could [spread] [?] so strongly throughout the whole world. In Europe for hundreds of years they could not discover the secret of how porcelain is made. Only in the year 1709 did a potter in Meissen (Germany) succeed in discovering the secret, and a few months later at the Leipzig Fair Frenchmen, Englishmen, Italians and above all Polish and Russian Jews literally fought over the porcelain wares that Meissen exhibited; and the German government began to build porcelain factories there, which are famous to this day throughout the world. Today large factories operate almost all over the world and sell porcelain every year for billions of dollars. In Germany alone some seventy-odd thousand workers are employed in porcelain manufacture.
3) Where does aluminium come from?
From day to day the use of aluminium grows, not only in the metal industry but also in all the articles we use in life. Automobiles, airships, kitchenware and the like are now made of this light, shining, fine metal.
Aluminium was obtained for the first time in the year 1827. It was made from bauxite, which is found in America, France, Germany, Yugoslavia, Hungary, Africa and Asia, and with which for years nobody knew what to do.
Only at the beginning of the twentieth century did aluminium kitchenware appear at the Leipzig Fair, and it sold very well. In 1913, 54 thousand wagon-loads of bauxite were processed. Today 200 thousand wagon-loads are already consumed every year, from which about 20 thousand wagon-loads of aluminium are made — which has today become almost the most important metal of almost all industries in the whole world.
Z. Haber.
A Little Feuilleton — A Discontented World.

[Feuilleton — humour and satire.]
Nobody is satisfied today.
You borrow a few gulden from someone for a few days and you don't keep your word — he is not satisfied.
And you are not satisfied that he is not satisfied with your dissatisfaction.
You see that the other fellow has a nice house, a nice maid, a nice few thousand zł. in the bank, and you don't have it — you are not satisfied; and he, who has all these things, is not satisfied either; he would like to have a thousand times as much. And if he had a thousand times as much, he still would not be satisfied — he would want a million times as much...
And who knows whether he would be satisfied then?...
Your friend has a good position and makes a nice living — you are not satisfied, because you have a bad position and don't make a living; and your friend is not satisfied either, because there are better positions than his...
Your daughter has married a doctor who charges ten zł. a visit — she is not satisfied; after all she could have married a professor who charges 50 and 75 zlotys a visit.
You send your wife to Rajcza and give her a hundred zł. for two weeks — she is not satisfied, because there are richer boarding houses; and you are not satisfied, because she is not satisfied...
You buy your wife a dress and pay 25 zł. — she is not satisfied; she has seen a nicer dress for 50; had you bought the 50-zloty dress, she would not have been satisfied either, because there are dresses for two hundred and fifty zlotys.
Now I have bought my little wife a fur coat for 500 zł.: nice money, one would think — and she is not satisfied; Mrs. Kalb has a coat for 100 [sic] zł.
You surely think Mrs. Kalb is satisfied — it turns out she isn't, because Mrs. Oks has a coat for 1800 zł. You surely think Mrs. Oks is satisfied — not in the least, because Mrs. Shmelkis's coat costs three thousand zł., and Mrs. Zhebre has a coat for five thousand zł. And so it goes on and on.
Nobody is satisfied.
What more do you need: an acquaintance of mine became an orphan and received 50 zł. inheritance from his father — nice money, one would think; and he is not satisfied. Another father died and left his son 190 thousand zł. — and he is not satisfied either.
Now I have written this feuilleton. You think I am satisfied? Not a chance! The feuilleton could have come out much better, finer and wittier.
No, I am not satisfied.
B. Kovner.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on the portion of this week
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Devarim
—o—
The portion.
a) "And, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude" (1:10)
Moses our teacher said to the leaders and heads: you are like stars, for we have found that even the moon is sometimes ashamed, and the sun too is sometimes put to shame, as the prophet says: "Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed." Of stars, on the other hand, we find[?] nowhere that they are ashamed. You heads too are thereby likened to stars: you do not know what such a thing as shame means... In your "multitude", in your self-importance, you are like those heavenly beings that wink from on high and never possess even a dose of shame...
There is one piece of advice for you: "May He add unto you a thousand times so many" — let heads upon heads multiply and swarm, and then you will no longer be so self-important...
Me'or va-Shemesh.
—o—
b) "Ye are to pass [misprinted 'ov"im'] through the border of your brethren the children of Esau" (2:4)
"You are passers-by, but the children of Esau are dwellers"
Yalkut.
Jacob and Esau divided things between them: Jacob took for himself the World to Come and left poor Esau only This World. The children of Seir are dwellers, permanent citizens of the world, whereas we, the children of Jacob, are only passers-by, only wanderers passing through Esau's border. We have only a transit visa through the world, therefore: "meddle not with them" — the world is theirs, they are the masters of the house.
Imrei Shefer.
—o—
c) "And we smote him, and his sons" (2:33)
The final kaf of the word "va-nakh" is an enlarged letter, and in another verse, "and ye shall sell yourselves as bondmen" ("ve-hitmakartem la-avadim"), the kaf of "ve-hitmakartem" is also a large one; but in the latter verse the enlarged kaf is a bent kaf ( — a bent kaf, which comes at the beginning and in the middle of a word), while in the first verse the enlarged letter is a straight kaf ( — a long final kaf, which comes at the end of a word.
This is an allegorical hint: if the bent kaf is the enlarged one, that is, if towards the poor man the kaf (hand) is bent, closed, and only for oneself is it enlarged... then: "ye shall sell yourselves as bondmen" — your end will be a sad one. If, on the other hand, the enlarged kaf (hand) is a straight one, stretched out to the poor man, then: "and we smote him, and his sons" — you will win victories.
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
Haftarah: Hazon
d) "From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it" (Isaiah 1:6)
The feet still lead, supposedly, into the house of study; the head still sways, supposedly, during prayer; but from the sole of the foot even unto the head — between these two mechanical acts — "there is no soundness in it"...
Shir Yedidut.
—o—
e) "Though your sins be as scarlet" (printed: 1:16)
When a young person gallops off into some sin — well, after all he is young, when the evil inclination glows. But when "an old man commits adultery" — that is already ugly... Likewise, when a rich man gives himself airs — well, after all he is rich... But when a poor man displays impudence — that is already unbearable. When a downtrodden person goes bankrupt — well, after all he is downtrodden; but a rich man who denies [his debts] — that is murder. Therefore, says the Talmud, God hates three people: an old man who commits adultery, a rich man who denies, and a poor man who is proud...
"Though your sins be as scarlet" — if your sins accord with your years and with your circumstances, then "they shall be as white as snow" — they can still be forgiven; but if an old man commits adultery, a poor man is insolent and a rich man goes bankrupt — that can no longer be forgiven...
Tiferet Uziel.
—o—
f) "Righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers" (printed: 1:19)
"Righteousness" — when one wants some charity from someone — "lodged in it", meaning he lets it stay overnight: come tomorrow, the day after tomorrow... But "murderers" — when it comes to some act of murder — "now": it is carried out instantly, on the spot...
Misgeret ha-Sha'ar.
—o—
g) "Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water" (printed: 1:2)
"Thy silver is become dross" — the money you pay for the merchandise is no money (bills of exchange, rags), and "thy wine mixed with water" — the merchandise is no merchandise either, it too is counterfeit...
Alei Zayit.
—o—
Avot.
h) "Do not separate yourself from the community, and do not trust in yourself" (2:5)
"Do not separate yourself from the community" — by not wanting to give any charity, thinking to yourself: peace be upon my soul, I, thank God, need no charity... But: "do not trust in yourself" — it is a world in which even "the angels of God ascend and descend on it", a world-ladder on which some go up and some go down... and therefore you yourself may yet have to come to need charity...
Midrash Shmuel.
• • •
"This world is like a wedding hall."
A provincial Jew once comes to Warsaw and passes by a wedding hall where a grand wedding is being celebrated. Being a small-towner, he thought the hall belonged to a private person. The next day he passes by again and again sees a wedding in the hall. The day after — the same again. He wonders: a father who has so many children to marry off, one after the other?!... They explain to him that it is just a hall, in which today this one dances, tomorrow another, and the day after tomorrow — a third...
Just such a "wedding house", such a wedding hall, is the world. Today this one dances, tomorrow that one dances at the wedding...
Rabbi Yitzhak Meir of Ger [Góra Kalwaria].
—o—
Eikhah (Lamentations).
i) "Her adversaries are become the head" (printed: 1:4)
All our foes have one head; although they are many, they have only one leader, and therefore they succeed. We, on the other hand, are so few and have so many heads — that is our misfortune...
Nahal Eshkol.
—o—
j) "We get our bread with the peril of our lives" (5:9)
The soul and the body formed a partnership. The former was to occupy itself with spiritual matters and the latter with physical, material ones — like that coachman with the Torah scholar: the former earns and feeds the latter, who sits and studies. But what will it look like when they swap roles, when the scholar takes the reins in hand and the coachman sits down at the Gemara?...
The soul and the body have today also swapped roles: the spiritual matters are performed by the body... one believes in God mechanically, one prays and studies mechanically, and one is pious without a soul... while the soul has to earn its bread... the spirit is harnessed to the carriage of livelihood... "We get our bread with the peril of our lives"...
Ohel Ya'akov.
The Situation of the Jewish Artisans

[Artisans — article.] II.
As is known, the labour inspectors and the chambers of crafts are now drafting a bill on limiting the number of apprentices in proportion to the number of journeymen employed in the workshop. And since there are almost no Jewish journeymen — for only those who have passed a journeyman's examination are called journeymen, and such an examination our Jewish journeymen have hardly yet passed — the Jewish artisans, even the diploma-holding masters, will therefore not be allowed to employ anyone, so that the Jewish journeymen are threatened with being removed from the trade.
There now exists a widely ramified network of government craft schools, or schools supported by the government, and these schools graduate thousands of pupils every year, who receive the rights of a diploma-holding journeyman and after 3 more years will have the possibility of becoming masters.
For apprentices up to the age of 18 there is a possibility of entering the municipal continuation school (Fortbildungsschule). Whoever has the proper preparation can finish the school within one or two years and then pass a regular journeyman's examination. It is worse with the journeymen who are already over 18 — such are not readily admitted to the continuation school.
But for them too there is a way out; as far as I know, a group of young commercial employees has approached the director of the continuation school with a request to organise for them a commercial course for a minimal fee. It looks as if the request will be granted. Had artisans applied, I am convinced that he would have organised trade courses for them too.
This is for the time being the only way out that can save the thousands of journeymen and apprentices from losing their bread, and also give the masters the possibility of employing people in the future.
This is the duty of everyone who wants to earn his bread by a craft and must therefore adapt himself to the law.
Incidentally, let the Warsaw Jewish press be reminded on this occasion that it is passing over the whole matter in silence. This is incomprehensible and unforgivable.
Now about the practical side of the guild law ("ustawa przemysłowa" [industrial law]). The point of the guild law is surely not simply to impose a harsh decree on artisans. The aim of the guild law is to raise the level of the artisan and make him competitive with respect to foreign countries. It is a fact that Germany introduced the guild law already 5 [?] years ago, and the result is that the German artisan has now grown enormously.
The guild law and the continuation school and other schools created in connection with the law must be regarded as a necessity that life demands. We see that with every year work becomes more refined and more polished. We see that with every season the clothing, shoe and other shops — in Zagłębie, for example — are forced to place more and more of their orders elsewhere. The local artisan who works for shops loses his employment because he cannot adapt to the new demands; he falls further and further behind. The local artisans complain about bad times, when with almost every train and every lorry ready-made goods are brought in, produced in already modernised workshops. The local artisan serves only as a side matter; he gets work by chance — when there is a shortage just then, or when it pays because of cheapness.
Everyone who takes up a trade and wants to earn his bread by it must first of all receive practical training and even be talented enough to be able to do a good piece of work. But with this the goal is still far from attained, for he will only be a good worker when he punctually carries out the work entrusted to him. Independence, however, he will always lack.
Finally, let everyone who goes into apprenticeship with an artisan know that in no field can an artisan or industrialist be sufficiently competent if he has merely technical without theoretical training. The state, the gmina [municipality] and also various other institutions indeed found and maintain trade schools and supplementary courses. Large sums of money are spent in order to give the young generation and its path in life not only the skill it acquires through technical training and in the workshop during the apprenticeship, but also theoretical training, because in parallel with the modernisation of the trade goes the necessity to educate oneself.
Whoever does not use the opportunity to keep on educating himself, but does only what he must in order to get his work done, will at best be only a good worker. But he will never attain independence! Keeping the workshop with the same primitive equipment as until now will not succeed for long. One must not close one's eyes to the fact that a new generation is growing up, trained and prepared, ready with every fibre of its being to take up the most modern equipment of the trade.
The short-sighted man will try to argue that many such who were simple workers have after all reached a very high rank in life. But they forget one thing: these people did indeed begin as simple artisans, but their great success they owe only to their constant improvements, their constant tireless work to improve technique. Ambition led them to educate themselves more and more, in order to be able to advance continually.
A competent artisan must be able to think out how to deal with raw materials; he must think how, now or later, he is to set himself up independently.
A special exception among all other artisans is the tailor, for rarely does an artisan in his trade have so many and such varied materials to consider as the tailor. All the treasures of nature in the old classification — animals, plants, metal and stone — must supply material so that the tailor can make a garment from it.
Does he need education for this?
What today's artisan must know and be able to do — in the next article.
H. L. Goldsztajn.
Beware of the Terrible Disease That Robbed Me of My Child.

A father writes on the anniversary (yortsayt) of his son's death.
In the press we often read medical articles of enlightenment about various diseases, especially about those that are well known and widespread.
I believe, however, that it is worth writing for once also about a disease that occurs rarely, but which, owing to people's lack of awareness, claims needless victims.
I myself was struck by a terrible misfortune, and therefore, although I have no connection with medicine, I take the liberty of writing about such a disease, because it took a victim from me — a son in the bloom of life, aged 28.
It is a disease one can easily guard against if one only knows its cause, but once it seizes someone, that person is already condemned to death!
In Latin the disease is called „Actinomicosys“, in Polish „Promienica“ or „grzyb“ [fungus].
My son developed a swelling on his neck below his right ear, which a municipal surgeon opened. Within 6 weeks the wound had not healed; so my son, of blessed memory, went to Dr. Sołowiejczyk[?] in Warsaw, who immediately asked him whether he had anything to do with grain, or perhaps chewed kernels? And on hearing that he worked in the office of a mill, the doctor at once made the diagnosis of the aforementioned grave disease.
The diagnosis was confirmed by all the other doctors and professors with whom my unfortunate son was treated, as was the cause of the disease, which comes from kernels, or even from picking one's teeth with a straw, because on grain there lives a special microbe (discovered by Prof. Israel in Berlin in 1878). It penetrates the body through the mouth and causes inflammations and wounds that cannot be cured, because the microbe spreads in the body in the form of rays. It is therefore called in German „Strahlenpilz“ [ray fungus].
I will not dwell on the course of this cruel disease and the sufferings my son endured — suffice it to say that he was tormented for 3 years and 8 months, was treated in Warsaw, Lemberg [Lwów] and Berlin by the greatest professors, and could find no rescue with them.
Incidentally, the disease is not so rare — in Lemberg I saw over 30 pictures of such patients, and almost all of them died.
Now, on the first anniversary of the death of my son Max Löw, who died young, I write this note in his memory, in order to make the public aware of this terrible disease. Perhaps my few words will prevent needless victims!
A. Löw.
Tax Matters.

In connection with a ruling of the Supreme Administrative Tribunal that income tax must be assessed only according to actual income, the Finance Ministry has issued an „okólnik“ [circular] which abolishes the unlawful interpretation by the tax authorities. The said circular is of particular importance in the time of the present crisis, when every portfolio of bills of exchange is of doubtful value.
The same circular states that in assessing income tax, debts written off as a loss must be recognised when proof is submitted that the debt has lost its value, e.g.: bankruptcy (upadłość) of the debtor, a settlement (regulacja), etc.
Among Wild People.

(An expedition among African tribes who still live like animals.)

Where is the lowest kind of human being to be found? This was never known for certain; it was always thought to be the Bushman of Australia, who resembles a monkey. In his appearance he is more closely related to monkeys than anyone else, and in his way of life too he is not much higher than a wild animal. And yet it was hard to believe that the Australian was already the lowest stage of human development.

Some time ago an expedition of American scientists set out for distant Africa, because it had been learned that people living there stood at a far lower stage of development. The expedition consisted of: Mr. S. J. Cadle [?], Mr. Paul Hoefler, a famous cinema cameraman who had worked for years in famous Hollywood, and Dr. Grans Dushan [?] [probably Grant John], who was the expedition's doctor. And these 3 set off for Africa, where they searched for and found the people who are, in the scientists' opinion, the lowest stage of the human species.

The name of these human creatures is the Heikum Bushmen [Hai//om]. Judging by their behaviour they are not human at all. They have no dwellings, nor any fixed place to stay; they know nothing of cooked food or of pots. To them anything that falls into their hands is good. A worm is good, a snake that has already lain for months under the burning sun of the tropical region. The Heikum Bushmen know nothing of married life. In this respect, too, they do not differ from other wild and domestic animals. No woman has her own husband and no man his own wife. The children, while still small, keep to the mother, because they know nothing of any father. And when they grow up, they go off to look for food for themselves. The only thing these people lack is food; they have no other worry. Of faith, of higher concepts, they have no notion. It is an eternal chase after food. And when an animal is caught, they throw themselves upon it and eat it up all at once. They leave not a trace of it. And about tomorrow they do not worry. When they do go hungry, every one of the Heikums is thin and "kvar" [?] — you can count his bones.

The other inhabitants of those regions do not regard the Heikums as human. When one of them is spotted, a bullet is put straight into his head; nobody feels that he has killed a human being, and it occurs to nobody at all to punish the murderers. The Heikums are quiet and bother nobody. While the Australian Bushmen are cannibals (man-eaters), the Heikums are peaceful and approachable. This can be seen from the fact that when an animal is killed and there is something to eat, the rest of the tribe is told at once and the morsel is shared; not a single case is known of one trying to do harm to another. And even in the worst times, when they go hungry for eight days in a row, when they can no longer drag their feet — even then it never occurs to anyone to eat his fill of another's body.

And if the Heikums are nevertheless cruel, it is because of their terrible ignorance: when a woman dies and leaves a small child who cannot yet provide food for himself, the little soul is buried together with the mother in one grave, and it does not bother them that the child is alive. But it does not occur to anyone at all that this is cruel, that one must not do it — for how will the child manage without the mother? Who will look after it?

The Heikums are very good hunters. Few can hit the mark as well with bow and arrow as they can. There is nobody who can steal up so close to an animal that it does not sense the danger beside it. The Heikum shoots at the animal from his bow; it is wounded and starts to run. The Heikum runs after it, and keeps running until one of them falls — but the animal falls sooner, because it is not as quick on its feet as this wild man. Then the Heikum lets his friends know and they hold the feast.

Paris fashion has not yet reached the Heikums. There nobody wears short dresses yet, because nobody wears any clothes at all. The only thing they allow themselves is a belt around the loins, and that is enough. By day it is very hot and there is no need to cover the body. At night it is cold — well, they snuggle up to one another and get by somehow. Being ashamed of their bodies — that does not occur to them, although in general the Heikums are shy: when they happen to meet people from another tribe, they are quiet and withdrawn and do not make a sound, just like children.

The Heikums excel above all in their dancing; in this respect nobody can compete with them. There is not a single living thing that they cannot imitate with their movements. They have a snake dance in which the body has to be twisted in the strangest way.

The greatest wonder is that these Heikums do not die out, that they survive the hot, burning days and the frosty nights. The Americans had blankets with them, they were prepared for all kinds of weather, and still they had a hard time; there were nights when their teeth chattered with cold. But the Heikums lay in the open field and slept soundly. In the morning, when the sun rose, they woke up cheerful and fresh — there was no sign that anyone had caught a cold.

'Rapid' medical aid.

Last Sunday the 62-year-old Łańcucka-Wercka, Piłsudskiego 64, suddenly fell ill. As it happened, the maid was in the flat; she was busy with the sick woman and could not go out to fetch a doctor. When the maid saw that in this way she was endangering the life of the lady of the house, she turned to the police to see to getting a doctor.
And only then did it turn out that in Sosnowiec it is not so easy to get a doctor. The police alerted the doctors and could not get anyone. The doctor of the sick-fund could not come, because the patient is not a member.
Only some time later did they manage to get Dr. Branicki, who gave the necessary aid. But the end was that the doctor came too late, and the sick woman died a short time later.
That is how easy it is here to obtain medical aid.

Profitability in Trade and in Industry

All know that the economic situation in Poland is now very difficult. Yet the tax offices want to know nothing of it, and the taxes usually stay at the same level as in previous years. Sometimes they are even raised, and almost never reduced.
Now the time for assessing new taxes is approaching again. The assessment commissions must therefore know what the real situation in Poland looks like at the present moment, on the basis of factual material, i.e. regularly kept commercial books. (We quote from the weekly "Polska Gospodarcza" nos. 21 and 22 and "Przegląd Kupiecki" no. 17):
— "Huta Pokój", Silesian Smelting Works and Mines Joint-Stock Company — the total balance sum amounts to about 204 million zł. The losses amount to almost 3 million zł.
— "Glass Factory, Joint-Stock Company in Zawiercie", formerly S. Reich — shows losses amounting to 47,124 zł.
— The "Klucze" cement works — with a profit from the sale of cement in 1930 amounting to 114 thousand zł., shows a balance-sheet loss of 46,331 zł.
"Union-Textile, Joint-Stock Company in Częstochowa" — shows, with a balance sum of over 32 million, losses amounting to 1 million 721 thousand 312 zł.
"Zgierz Dye Works and Finishing Plant, J.-S. Co." — with a capital of 800 zł. [sic] had losses in 1930 amounting to 96 thousand 652 zł.
— "Electricity Company, Ltd.[?] J.-S. Co. in Warsaw" — shows losses amounting to 276,490 zł.
— "Polish Works Babcock-Zieleniewski" J.-S. Co. (formerly Fitzner et Gamper) in Sosnowiec" — show losses amounting to 86,492 zł.
— The "Perkun" engine factory in Warsaw — shows losses amounting to 54,140 zł., with a share capital of 1 million 400 thousand zł.
— "The Belgian Company of the Sochaczew Artificial Silk Factory" shows losses amounting to 77 thousand 560 zł., with a simultaneous gross profit from the sale of its production amounting to 804 thousand 990 zł.
— "Commercial Bank Wilhelm Landau J.-S. Co." — shows a loss of 551 thousand 940 zł., with its own capital of 2 million zł.
These are mere figures; comments are superfluous. We hope that the Ministry of Finance will draw the proper conclusions from the figures presented by the largest Polish enterprises and, by means of circulars, will instruct the tax offices how fundamentally the profitability of trade and industry has changed since the year 1925, when the profitability scheme was issued.

The situation in Germany must be cleared up by today, Friday.
For the time being the situation in Germany has not yet eased. With every day the mood grows more tense.
The leaders of German economic life absolutely want the situation to be cleared up by Friday, so that work in the banks can be resumed.
Meanwhile one day passes after another, and there is still no certainty that the important financial operations will succeed.
On Saturday the wages ["pensions"] of the workers in the factories must be paid throughout Germany. To achieve this, the banks must be operating, and without[?] the help of the banks it is impossible. The economic circles in Germany absolutely do not want to allow a situation in which the workers are not paid their wages, being well aware of what this could bring with it. Therefore far-reaching efforts are being made so that today, Friday, Germany's financial apparatus will be working again.
—o—
A large credit aid for the new harvest.
One of the greatest causes of the present crisis in Poland, and also in the whole world, is that the largest part of the population, the rural inhabitants, have completely lost their purchasing power.
20 million rural inhabitants in Poland are unable to buy clothing, shoes; they are unable to repair their dwellings, to renovate their houses, to buy tools. The standard of living of these 20 million inhabitants has fallen to the lowest level.
Were it not for this, the present crisis would not have been so great, so catastrophic.
The government is now taking energetic measures so that this great mass of inhabitants, the 20-million rural population, should become financially stronger again and be able to buy.
The government is now organising broad credit aid for the farmers. Every farmer will receive a large credit on his grain at very low interest, up to 4 per cent annually. The farmer will thus have money and will be able to sell the grain only when it pays better. Further financial aid for the 20-million rural population is being prepared. It is therefore hoped that this will help to a great extent so that the coming autumn brings a certain revival in the country.

The New Income Tax.

In all the tax offices throughout the country energetic preparations are now being made in connection with the forthcoming assessment of income tax for the year 1931.
In a few days the assessment will already begin.

The offices [?] are now collecting material about the "incomes"; taxpayers are being summoned to the offices [?] to give explanations; the books and turnovers of the commercial enterprises are being examined; and, most importantly, all efforts are directed toward finding that the incomes were larger.

Despite the catastrophic situation of trade and manufacturing, despite the bankruptcies, the ruin and the complete standstill in all branches that prevailed last year — nevertheless! there is no tendency in the tax offices to reduce the income-tax assessment.

On the contrary. We learn from a well-informed source that preparations are being made to increase the income tax for middling merchants, especially those who keep no commercial books. To this end the norm of average income will be raised, so that in this way a larger tax can be assessed.

In the present catastrophic situation, an increased income tax will break a large part of the merchants, who are keeping afloat by miracles as it is.

In this connection it is extremely important to do something already now; one must not wait for "after the fact" [lit. le-achar ha-ma'aseh], when nothing will help any more. Already now, before the assessment, one must turn to the leading personalities of the Ministry of Finance and point out the threatening danger facing the merchants and manufacturers if they are now saddled with too high an income tax.

"H. Ch."

Ben-Zvi Baratov.

[Theatre — Będzin and Sosnowiec.] Y. M. Neiman
(On the appearance of the great Jewish actor).
He is the greatest Jewish actor we have seen in Poland so far. I saw him in Vienna, some nine years ago. He appeared incognito in a play by Jacob Gordin. Vienna discovered him; he became the sensation of literary-artistic Vienna. A master. He was compared to the very greatest.
Only later did people learn that the man under the pseudonym Ben-Zvi is Dr. Baratov, a doctor of medicine by profession, who had played in Stanislavsky's Art Theatre. His Yiddish was then, in Vienna, still halting. But from his every movement and from his every word one felt the great Russian actor.
He played in a melodramatic story by Gordin, "Der fremder" ["The Stranger"], but in Baratov's hands it grew into a King Oedipus figure, a Sophoclean shape, a Michelangelo figure. To this day I remember the fever that ran through my body.
Now he is in Poland. Before that he played in Berlin, on the Piscator stage, and in New York with Maurice Schwartz. He has already settled in and become naturalized in Jewish cultural life, and yet: a "stranger" — he stands sky-high apart, on a pedestal. He has a good Russian schooling and European fame.
I leaf through the Baratov album. There are simply hymns there about his acting. The greatest world newspapers have praised him.
Baratov is not a naturalist but[?] a realist. Even his "Moshke Chazir" and his "Yenki Shapshovitsh" are ennobled in his hands. He is one of those actors who want to give their personality — the soul.
•
Dr. Baratov, who has already appeared in Będzin with extraordinary success, will, before his departure abroad, give another 3 performances in Zagłębie: today, Friday, at 9.30 in the evening in Będzin at the "Światowid" cinema, "Der fremder" by J. Gordin; tomorrow, Saturday, in Sosnowiec at the "Pałac" theatre, "The Father" by Strindberg; and on Sunday the 26th in Sosnowiec, "Hinkemann" by Ernst Toller.
What's Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — industry and labour; the Sejm; an accident.] Reductions at the "Laura" Works.
The "Laura" Works [Huta Laura, Siemianowice], which in 1924 employed 4,000 workers, was reduced almost by half, i.e. to 2,200 men, and now it employs in all 1,000 workers, who work from 3 to 7 shifts a week.
Now new reductions are being planned, after which only about 500 workers are to remain. In connection with this the workers held a discussion meeting, at which they spoke with bitterness about their catastrophic situation, which is bringing them and their families to a state of hunger.
They also protested against the officials, who remain in their posts regardless of the fact that they have houses and other property they could live on.
In the end they adopted resolutions of protest and came to the decision that in the event of further reductions they will be forced to protest with strikes.
From [printed "Fu."] the Upper Silesian Sejm.
The plenary session, which was to have taken place yesterday in the Upper Silesian [Silesian] Sejm, has been postponed to an indefinite date.

A Letter to the Editor.
Most esteemed Mr. Editor!
To my explanation of why I resigned from the board of "Hakoach", the latter have replied in such a way that I am forced to write further the following:
You, honoured gentlemen of the board, would in fact have done well not to polemicize at all; yet with your reply you have shown your true party face.
Although "Hakoach" has belonged to the Maccabi World Union for 6 years already, "Hakoach" kept itself — until you, party comrades, turned up there — apolitical, as can be confirmed by resolutions of the board, according to which no political direction whatsoever is to be supported. As soon as you came into "Hakoach", your first move, with the help of outside factors who now play first fiddle in "Hakoach", was to break away from the Maccabi World Union and join a workers' union. And the resolution passed at the last-but-one meeting on supporting the Palestine Workers' Fund ("Pa"m") is likewise nothing more than a political manoeuvre of your party comrades.
