The Summer-Cottage Troubles of the Zagłębie Women.

(Letter from Rajcza) — by Ben Amotz.
As I already mentioned in my previous letter, this year the summer-cottage contingent has "transmigrated" to Rajcza. Nobody can explain the reason for it, but it is quite simple: if Genia and Stefa went "do Rajczy" [to Rajcza], why should Gucia and Bronia be a "wyjątek" [an exception]? And so a chain began:
— Rajcza!
— What Rajcza? When Rajcza? — Nothing. If everyone goes, I went too...
And the crowd of travellers is indeed great. Whom don't you meet here? From the "Sączewska" [?] and from the "Zimna D...." [?], from the "Modrzejower" [ul. Modrzejowska] and from the "Czysta", from the "Kołłątaja" and from the "Czeladzka" — the whole set with whom you are in contact all year round: the made-up and the "bewigged", "intelligentsia" and people from rebbes' courts. A menagerie of all creatures and shapes.
The summer guests divide into 2 categories: 1) "pensionatniks" [boarding-house guests] and 2) "kvartirantniks" [room lodgers].
The first category can be compared to a flock of fowl that stroll about a big yard and wait until the "gospodynia" [landlady] comes out to them and scatters rye or wheat out of her broad apron...
From early morning until late at night the eating question is dealt with. Especially when the "children" sit down around the big long tables and strain their gazes toward the kitchen, from which the "angels" in human form shuffle out, carrying the "portions".
"Interesting" are the scenes of "sending back": as soon as Stefcia says:
— "Ja tego nie jem" [I don't eat that], the boarding-house owner is no longer to be envied — all declare as with one voice:
— "Ja też tego nie jem" [I don't eat that either]..
When the "waiter" in his little Galician cap runs back to the kitchen fully loaded, a little voice is heard:
"Kartofelki proszę!" [Potatoes, please!]
— "Zabrakło!" [They've run out!] — comes the "waiter's" answer...
An uproar breaks out. The head proprietor appears and with a smiling face he pleads:
— "Eat, children, calmly, please" [ruhig, bitte].
— I don't want any "jarzynowa-rycynowa" soup [vegetable / castor-oil soup?], give me a few potatoes — pleads, with tears in her eyes, a "lady" who all year long in Będzin suffers from lack of appetite...
— "You will get a bigger portion of potatoes next time, although they really ran out"...
—
Much worse, poor things, is the situation of the second category, the "kvartirantnitchkas", i.e. of those who rent half of the peasant huts and run their own households...
This category consists mostly of the modest women, who are very thrifty, and when summer comes they prove with statistical figures that it is "smarter" to rent a "mieszkanie" [flat] and keep house as at home, so that the "skorzystanie" [benefit] of the "powietrze" [air] will come out almost free...
And the "reckoning" is indeed right. The góral [highlander] gladly gives up his "mieszkanie", and the "letniki" [summer folk] settle in as at their father's in the vineyard and enjoy
— the air... for "times change". The "good time", when "the world" learned that Rajcza is an earthly paradise, that an egg costs 7 groszy — already belongs to the past. The prices of all kinds of products grow together with the number of guests coming here. As soon as the cab owners see that the train has brought new [printed "גייע"] "goście" [guests], they immediately inform the peasant women in the villages, and there is a "hausse" [price rise] in eggs, butter etc. It happens quite often that these kinds are not to be had at all, and if the baker too is afraid, because of the heat, to fire the oven, then bread and rolls are also lacking, and instead of bread, butter and milk one swallows
— air...
He [i.e. God], as it were, saw that "the outcry" was very great and sent a remedy for the affliction. The "remedy" consists in this: that a Będzin man, a certain Hershel Gelbard, brings here from Katowice, out of "pity", a few potatoes, carrots and other kinds of vegetables, which are bought with great joy by those who rent "mieszkania" here and have come here "to recuperate".
A great role in the eating question is played by the local "Kultus-shammes" [beadle of the Jewish community]. Besides other occupations he also supplies "cheap" fowl to those who find no "bargains" at the market [targ], which takes place 2 times a month.
But these are matters of no great importance; the main thing is that the guests spend their time here not at all badly in other fields. Here, for instance, there is a beach [plaża] in Rajcza, even with a stony bottom, but the pleasure is "à la Zoppot" [Sopot]...
The beach was threatened by a great "danger" from the local inhabitants, who for the sake of "morality" fought for men apart and women apart — men separately and women separately.
And they, i.e. the "morality preachers", indeed won a victory and set up at the beach an "eruv chatzerot" [boundary partition]: they put up a post with the inscription "ad kan" [up to here], i.e. here is the place for women and here for men.
The "eruv", however, existed only until the beach guests from Zagłębie came here. When the latter saw it, there was a "va-yitz'aku" [outcry]: how can there be such a scandal! A beach is, after all, no mikveh...
And a struggle began between the "moralists" and the "beachists". The latter won, the posts were removed, and a life of unity began: a beach with all the "pitchevkes" [?], and the crowd sweats, burns and "beaches" together...
— — —
Rajcza, which possesses very beautiful natural scenery and is visited by thousands of guests, is very neglected: in the evening a dense darkness reigns, darkness of Egypt, and the young part of the great number of summer guests has nowhere to spend the free hours. There is still no dancing, cinema etc.
The only "number" that entertains the guests are the Gypsy "musicians" who come here from time to time and favour us with their "concerts".
The "stage" is set up in the big yard of Hertz's well-known boarding house; the programme consists of the "newest hits", our "panienki" [young ladies] accompany with their sweet little voices, and life is lively.
Such a concert indeed took place last Saturday night (motzei Shabbat). The big yard was full of "in-laws". It looked like a wedding in a small shtetl before going to the chuppah. The Hasidic guests at first murmured that "it isn't proper, after all it's Shabbat Chazon". But when "nobody saw" they quietly shuffled up to the "stage" and through a "crack" snatched a look at the place where little Jewish girls very nicely performed the newest dances.
— : —
About Jewishness and Jewish matters — another time.
Urgent Help for Zagłębie

(Can Zagłębie remain without a pogotowie [emergency ambulance service]? — The institution must be created at any price.)
How many times has this already been written about, how many times have we illuminated the question from all sides and come to the conclusion that there is no other way, that Zagłębie must apply every possible means in order to realise that which must be, that without which it is impossible to manage — and yet, and yet the matter has remained at a dead point, as if it had never been talked about, as if it were a superfluous affair.
We mean the creation of a pogotowie for the towns of Zagłębie, the realisation of a rapid rescue service in case of an accident, in case of a mishap, in case of a catastrophe, where help can be given through immediate rescue.
Just last week we read in the chronicle a report that in Sosnowiec a woman died only because it had not been possible to obtain a doctor at once.
As a rule, in the present period we have grown accustomed to being terribly indifferent, enormously apathetic to all the events of our life; somehow life has become so cheap that nobody cares about it. Events that once threw us off balance, that drove us out of our minds when we heard of them, today make no [lit. "pll", for "klal" — no] impression at all. Somehow our sensitive fibres [?] have ceased to feel delicacy and tenderness. Apparently the war has also torn its way into our organism and wrought a whole upheaval there, a thorough revolution.
Today we have become indifferent to everything and to all; human life has no value whatsoever; however tragically it may end, it interests no one. One never tries to stop and reflect that one may be committing a great crime when human lives could have been saved and one does not do it, merely because one does not feel like, as the saying goes, dipping one's hand into cold water.
If not — if it were not so — how could one remain indifferent to these terrible phenomena, which are already taking on an almost epidemic character? How often do we hear that people depart from the world only because they do not have the possibility of obtaining immediate medical help?
When the Christian woman who died last week needed rescue and it could not be obtained, the police were applied to and they alerted the doctors, but she did not get [—], and then, when she [i.e. those around her] turned to the sick fund (Kasa Chorych), the doctor could not come, because the unfortunate woman was not a member there.
This mishap is no rare occurrence; whoever attentively reads "Life in Zagłębie" notices similar events quite often. Such victims have become almost an everyday phenomenon, and were we to compile statistics, we would obtain gruesome figures. Usually one reflects for a moment on the mishaps after they have happened, something pinches at the heart, but by the next day everyone is again busy with his everyday worries and forgets once more, as if nothing had happened.
But may one regard in such an offhand way such serious problems, which decide neither more nor less than a person's life? Is that right? Do we thereby discharge our duty towards our humanity? Does the human conscience permit us to bring so many victims in such a way?
However much we progress, whatever we attain on the path of our existence, we nevertheless remain backward when it comes to such understandable matters, such primitive questions, which can be solved quite easily; no Pithom and Raamses need be built for it in any case.
One must not forget, after all, that Zagłębie has a well-branched railway network, then there is the tramway line, which is becoming ever more branched. Besides this there is motor traffic. Because of this movement no few catastrophes occur; for this reason alone Zagłębie needs first-class rescue apparatus, so that in case of an accident quick help may be on the spot immediately and people not remain helpless and unprotected, as is the case now.
Our town councils (magistrates) have quite handsome budgets — so why should they not concern themselves with so urgent a question? Who else should concern himself with so topical a question? Who else should concern himself with improving the living conditions of the citizens in the face of danger [?]?
True, the times are now terrible. The crisis is immensely great, and perhaps one cannot afford to make new expenditures — we understand that perfectly; but one must be restrained and think consciously about this question, and there is no other counsel than to affirm with full awareness that one must not halt even at this critical situation, however terrible and frightening it may be.
We must not forget that what is at stake is neither more nor less than not letting people depart from the world, than saving people from danger when an accident befalls them.
In truth, we still stand at a very low level, when one has to start getting up to agitate and prove in black and white why Zagłębie needs urgent help. Is it not just as if one were to get up and say that a person must eat in order to be able to live, or that he must have air in order to be able to breathe? Is this not comparable to these examples for children?
We are, after all, grown-up people, so we understand perfectly why such an industrial corner as Zagłębie needs urgent help in case of a catastrophe. Why stand up and explain with signs and wonders that, for example, white paint is white and not red, when everyone sees it?
So the explanation is superfluous, and nobody needs agitation. One need not explain to anyone that 2 times two is four; everyone knows perfectly well that to be in Zagłębie without a pogotowie is just as if we said that one should turn back the wheel of history; and therefore serious measures must be adopted to realise the creation of rapid medical help for all citizens in Zagłębie.
If today we have no self-governments (elected municipal councils) in Zagłębie, the magistrates must take up the necessary work. One must not forget that the work is so necessary that every day brings harm to the inhabitants; and who else should think of the welfare of the inhabitants if not the city father?
Now the question must be raised in all its sharpness and clarity, for there is no more time for playing and coquetting; that would be a crime and would give the possibility of increasing the victims and sufferings of mankind.
Let the local public workers set about seriously and energetically realising this incomparably necessary institution, which will be a salvation for mankind in a time of trouble.
Dr. Papuri.
“Eikhah” and “Nachamu”

[Essay — Tisha B'Av and Shabbat Nachamu.]
Eliyahu Załudkowski [?].
(The "Three Weeks", "Tisha B'Av" and "Shabbat Nachamu").
The "Three Weeks", the gloomy, mood-laden days, begin with the Seventeenth of Tammuz. — From that sad day on, every nationally minded Jew lowers his head, recalling with a hot sigh [?] the happy times of long ago, long ago...
Nebuchadnezzar the wicked knew that as long as the Jewish spiritual centre remained whole, he would not be able to defeat the people. And that is precisely why he concentrated his whole military force on the city of Jerusalem, on the centre of the Jewish spirit, on the place of the Shekhinah.
A great scholar once explained the difference between Zion and Jerusalem:
Zion, he says, is the Jewish political centre. There all the politicians lived, all the ministers, all the kings. And from there the policy of the land went forth. Jerusalem, however, was the spiritual centre. There was the Chamber of Hewn Stone, the Sanhedrin and the masters of Torah and ethics. And it was much easier for the enemy to take Zion than Jerusalem. For with his strong, disciplined army he could easily fight the Jewish government in the Land of Israel. In Jerusalem, however — here he had a struggle with a stiff-necked people, which was hard to bend, unless it was broken altogether... And on the Seventeenth of Tammuz he began his struggle against the strong Jewish power — against the spirit of Israel, against the religion of Israel and against the Torah of Israel.
And the sages tell us that when Jeremiah went along with the Jews into exile and could no longer bear to watch their grief and their pain, he wished, being near the rivers of Babylon, to turn back; then the whole people raised its voice in bitter weeping, crying with choked tears: Jeremiah, our father, to whom are you leaving us? Do not go away! And Jeremiah answers them: had you wept like this only once, there in Jerusalem, you would have spared yourselves much weeping here in exile.
The same can be said the other way round, here in exile: if the Jewish people understood better the situation in which it finds itself. And did not make its heart lighter by imagining the redemption before its time. And did not dismiss with a wave of the hand all the memories and traditions of the past, did not abolish Tisha B'Av before its time — they would surely have been able to have the true joy in the Holy Land.
Our days of mourning are a part of the whole Jewish faith. They are more than national-political commemorations [?]. They are the tear in the eyes of the Shekhinah. With them and through them the consolation will begin. A complete redemption of the spirit and of the body, of morality and of politics. Both together must be raised up. A redemption of the land and a redemption of the Jew — a redemption in matter and a redemption in spirit.
On the threshold of "Eikhah" lies the "Nachamu". — That is the summary — and, if you like, the whole of Jewish history.
One page a tear, the other — a smile... shadow and sunshine, night and day, calamities and salvations.
That means that there is only one step from Eikhah to Nachamu, and whoever believes in Eikhah must necessarily also believe in Nachamu.
The Talmud tells us a story:
Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva were once walking on the road to Jerusalem, and when they came to Mount Scopus they rent their garments as a sign of the destruction, and when they approached the Temple Mount they saw a fox running out of the Holy of Holies, and they burst into tears. Rabbi Akiva, however, laughed. They ask him: Akiva, why are you laughing? He answers them: why are you weeping? They tell him: how should we not weep, when on the place of which it is written "and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death" foxes now run about. He answers them: that is exactly why I laugh, for once the prophecy about the destruction has been fulfilled, the prophecy about the consolation can surely be fulfilled as well. They called out to him: Akiva, you have comforted us. Twice they told him that he had comforted them, and in this very consolation, which we hope must necessarily be fulfilled, lies the whole Jewish philosophy. And not for nothing did the ancient sages tell us: "He who does not mourn over the destruction will not see the consolation". And that is the symbol for all Jews, for the pious as for the free-thinking. The pious, who sit with their heads bent over the kinah, must not and may not forget Nachamu. The free-thinking — in whom the bright flame of Nachamu has been kindled... may not, for their part, forget Eikhah...
Both make the people whole. Both ideas flow through our history from the first day of our existence to the present day. And both kinds of Jews must guard one thing within themselves: not to lose Jewish pride in the time of Eikhah and not to forget it in the time of Nachamu, for "pride lost, all lost"...
And the Talmud tells us the following story: when Rabbi [Judah] ha-Nasi took the kinah [?] in his hand on Tisha B'Av and began reading the kinot, and when he came to the verse "He hath cast down from heaven unto the earth the beauty of Israel", the kinah fell out of his hand. And we see in this a hint for the coming generations: you masters of Eikhah, you good and pious Jews, who shed tears over the destruction — do not despair, do not lose your pride, and you will see the consolation.. And you, free national Jews, you who "press for the End", you masters of consolation because of the bitterness of Eikhah — do not lose yourselves in the consolation, because of the heaviness of Eikhah...
And thus say our sages: "On the day the Temple was destroyed the redeemer was born" (on the day of the destruction of the Temple our redeemer was born). For in the greatest misfortune we nevertheless did not lose our pride. In the times when the people was driven into captivity with its hands bound in chains, there were found the chosen of God, who deeply felt Jewish pride. And when the wicked one ordered them to play from the songs of Zion, they bit off their own fingers so as not to play the holy melodies before the wicked one. That is heroism — not heroism of army and sword [?], but heroism of the spirit, heroism in keeping Jewish pride — and in the bitterest time of Eikhah — a consolation.
— — —
Shabbat Nachamu is a symbol of the Jewish people, a symbol without which it could not have existed. A symbol without which its existence would have had no existence — if an existence were at all possible without the luminous consolation that always shone out of the dark, gloomy days of mourning.
What content would the life of the Jewish people have had without the rich voice of the prophet, which for hundreds of generations has rung out with "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people"?
A people cannot continue its existence by means of memories of a past, especially when that past is, with a few bright exceptions, dark and sad throughout.
Under the mourning cloak that the people put on after the national destruction, the consolation was always hidden. Above the melancholy tones of "Eikhah yashvah" the heralding voice could always be heard. And thanks to the hope of consolation, which was so strong (if not stronger than the national grief..), thanks to the heralding voice of Isaiah, which grew stronger than the lamenting cry of Jeremiah, the Jewish people was able to continue its existence.
The "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" rang out at all times more strongly than the wild cries of our enemies; it silenced all the evil tongues, shut the mouths of our own [?] wailers and of foreign "friends" [printed "freygd"], who only waited for our end and pointed with their fingers, remarking that the end was approaching...
Shabbat Nachamu is the seal of the Jewish visions; in it are embodied all the dreams of the future that sad Jewish history has spun for the Jewish people; into Shabbat Nachamu the people's hope of national restoration and revival has been woven.
Instinctively the Jewish people has accepted Shabbat Nachamu as a Sabbath of encouragement. It has been received with satisfaction because it marks the end of the period of national mourning, because it comes after Tisha B'Av, because it presents the contrast to the previous Sabbath [Shabbat Chazon] with its dark visions. When the Jewish soul pined away in grief, sighed from pain, murmured melodies of mourning, swayed in kinot and weeping — the soft voice of comfort was heard, the cheerful, refreshing voice of the prophet: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people,
The Situation of the Jewish Artisans

[Artisans — trade and vocational training; series, part III: the tailor.]

In today's article we want to answer the question that has been posed: what must a modern craftsman know and be able to do? And first of all, what must the tailor know?

Tailoring already had first-class importance in ancient times. As the excavations show, primeval man, who lived thousands of years ago, already made himself various tools of stone and bone, such as needles and tailoring tools. The climate forced people to protect themselves against cold, wet, heat, etc. In time there even arose in man the desire to adorn and decorate himself by means of clothing. The materials for this man took partly from the hides of wild and domestic animals and partly from leaves. It did not take long before he learned to use various plaitings of the materials that nature had given him, all in order to make himself clothes that protected his body better than unworked materials.

It is hard to establish exactly when people began to use plaiting, knotting, weaving and the like, but already in ancient times, thousands of years ago, people in many places stood at a high level and used the finest woven fabrics, which only skilled craftsmen could have produced. From that moment tailoring began.

Out of this primitive "tailoring" fashion grew up over the course of generations.

From a capable tailor one demands first of all great skill in sewing, but in no case is that the alpha and omega [lit. the aleph and the tav] of a modern tailor.

A capable tailor must be able to reflect on fashion. Our fashions today bring nothing fundamentally new; they derive from the costumes of earlier periods, such as Renaissance, Rococo, Empire, Biedermeier, etc. One glance at the history of costume confirms it.

For the craftsman who has studied the development of costume it will be easy each time, from the character of the fashion that has arisen in each season, to recognise its idea; he will carry out with understanding what the fashion-maker has poured into it, and his work will surely be stylish.

Drawing is of great value for a tailor. A tailor who can draw looks at everything with a different eye. With the help of sketches the craftsman explains to the client the idea of the fashion. The woman of taste will not be content with the fashion magazine [journal]; she wants something of her own, she wants to see a design that will suit her individually; and if he is able to serve her in this, his standing grows in the eyes of his clients, and — the main thing — the value of his work. There are already tailors today who are able to make models themselves; they study the new fashion and from it work out new ideas themselves, which they present to the client no longer according to the journal but directly as their own elaboration.

Quite special importance for craftsmen attaches to the cultivation of t a s t e. If the craftsman possesses no taste, he has no prospects of success.

The Englishwoman Jenny Watt [?] writes about German dress: "As regards clothing, the German woman lacks taste." Certainly the reproach hits the German woman directly, but indirectly also the tailor; for if the customer had a suitable adviser, she would not have been exposed to reproaches of tastelessness. The tailor must no longer be a simple servant of his clients but a valued adviser.

Is not the work of French dressmaking regarded, from the professional standpoint, as deficient [printed "mag-glhaft", for mangelhaft]? And yet Paris is the dictator of fashion, because through hundreds of years of cultivating taste and style the Paris dress is exemplary; although our work is highly renowned, as regards taste one unfortunately often hears the opposite opinion.

A tailor must be able to combine colours that harmonise. It is his duty to match the colour of the cloth to the client's face. The tailor is obliged to advise the client which colour of shirt, tie, hat or shoes goes with his suit.

The colour of the cloth must first of all be suited to the purpose the garment is to serve: for working and walking clothes other colours are used than for evening ["society"] clothes and for those in which one will appear only in closed premises. Here the effect of natural and artificial light also plays a role.

Short or stout figures must also be treated differently, and tall or slender ones differently again. Some colours for youth and others for older persons. In matching colours one must take into account: the complexion, build, temperament, etc.

Every colour has its definite expression; thus, for example, red and white count with us as colours of the joy of life, black is the colour of seriousness and mourning, violet is supposed to signify friendliness, blue bears the stamp of modesty and reserve, etc., etc. From this one understands that the colour of the clothes must complement the colour of the skin and not be its contrast. The tailor who has mastered the theory of colour creates harmonious colour tones.

It is the task of the tailor, and above all of a ladies' tailor, through attentive observation to recognise in a person not only what is attractive but also to find out what she lacks; the art of dress must possess the ability to emphasise the beauty of a figure and to cover what is not beautiful; it must possess the means to make the natural beauty of the woman more prominent, and to fit the lines of the cut to her figure, so as to shape her form harmoniously. If the lines are well formed and the ornamental trimming, and above all the colours, are well matched, one calls it beautiful. The costume must to a certain degree have character, that is, the tailor must give something of his own; he must give the feeling for form — that is a feeling for beauty which cannot be explained in detail in words, and whoever understands feels that there is something in the dress that works well. He must put his stamp on the item of clothing; without that it is no work of art. When we see the work of the Paris fashion houses, we can establish that every dress bears the character of the house from which it comes. It goes without saying that the wearer of the dress herself has much to say here; but if the tailor fulfils his task as an artist, he will partly correct the client's faults.

H. L. Goldsztajn.
Moshe Apfelbaum — His Life and Work

[Art — books; in memory of the painter Moshe Apfelbaum.]

On behalf of the "Apfelbaum Committee", Mr H. Goldberg has sent us a "monograph" on the prematurely deceased Jewish artist Moshe Apfelbaum [Mojżesz Apfelbaum].

The booklet is small and thin, but how much warmth, devotion and love for the artist one notices at the very first moment, as soon as one takes this thin little booklet in hand — a modest tombstone for the artist from his sincere friends.

Modest is the booklet, but with how much taste it has been published. The reproductions have come out clean and successful. The biography, articles and press opinions have been put together aesthetically; the cover is splendid in relation to the modest smallness of the edition. True, many landscapes, pictures and portraits that are masterpieces of the artist are missing there, but from this booklet one can quickly form an idea of who and what Moshe Apfelbaum was for the Jewish art world.

The edition, which in any case presents itself very nicely, has appeared separately in Yiddish and separately in Polish, and thanks to its cheap price it is accessible to all strata of the population.

A pity that his friends did not have the material means to publish a comprehensive work that would broadly encompass the life of this gifted, prolific artist.

Zagłębie and Upper Silesia know what Apfelbaum was for modern art in general and for Jewish art in particular, and with what thirst he seized the brush.

He spent his last years with us and left Będzin the finest monument; so why should we not take care to perpetuate the artist's name? It would be only just for us to complete what Warsaw did not accomplish.

Dear Moshe Apfelbaum has deserved that Jewish Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, which have interest in and understanding for Jewish art, should properly perpetuate his name.

P. S. [?]
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'etchanan)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y. [?]
Parashat Va'etchanan
The Portion
—o—
a) "Ye shall not add unto the word... that followed Baal-peor."
The verse speaks of the idolatry of Peor, against which it warns that whoever serves it will be destroyed. But every foolish Hasid thinks it is not enough that he will not serve the idolatry; he must wage war on it, revile it and decry it. Says the Torah: "Ye shall not add". Do not do what you are not commanded, do not get mixed up, do not push yourself into such battles about which you were not warned, for from the battles with idolatry you will come to... serving the idolatry. "One fights the opponent so long that one learns his wicked ways"..
Kli Yakar.
—o—
b) "That hath statutes and judgments so righteous" (4:8 [printed 4:6]).
The laws of the Torah divide into mishpatim (judgments) and hukim (statutes). "Mishpatim" — understandable commandments, such as theft, robbery and the like. "Hukim" — incomprehensible laws, such as the red heifer for example, whose reason nobody knows. Secrets.
But there are even tzaddikim, rebbes [?], who are in the category of mishpatim — their ways are clear and understandable; and there are those in the category of hukim, whose deeds are secrets of secrets, about whose conduct you would have so much to ask, but — hush... it is a mystery of mysteries, like the red heifer for example... one must not ask...
Milin Yakirin (Rabbi Yitzhak of Radziwiłłów)
—o—
c) "A graven image, the similitude of any figure" (4:16).
This means those creatures that are "the similitude of any figure". When they come among Hasidim they are more pious than the Pope; when one comes among "their own" — then there is neither law nor judge. Whatever they want they can make of themselves: Hasidim, sinners, and whatever you only wish to hear and remember. Against them the verse warns, against these idolaters.
Rabbi Levi Yitzhak of Berdyczów.
—o—
d) "And all these things are come upon thee in the latter days" (4:30).
A fruit dealer sells cherries, nuts, apples and the like in his shop. But when late August comes, everything is already sold out; only two or three little apples, a few cherries and some nuts are left. So the merchant takes all the kinds together, mixes them up and sells them together.
The Holy One, blessed be He, has sold us the most varied fruits: the most varied troubles.:. Whatever kind of trouble there is, we were given a taste of it... But in the latter days, when the troubles in the heavenly treasury of calamities are about to run out, mixed troubles will pour down on us: cherries with nuts with apples... like that merchant who mixes together all the remaining produce when he hurries home... "And all these things are come upon thee". All sorts of misfortunes will tangle together and hail down on our heads, all mixed together...
Kol Yaakov.
—o—
e) "And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not" (6:11).
Wealth is not even a remedy for piety. It lies in the very nature of the thing: "And thou shalt eat and be full — lest thou forget the Lord". But if among well-established rich men piety can still sometimes go together with wealth, then among those who have "houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not", whose wealth came to them without effort, among the upstart magnates who neither toiled nor scraped: "thou plantedst not, thou hewedst not and thou filledst not" — and yet they have "houses full of all good things" — among them piety is already a rare phenomenon. They know that although one does not work, one still has... so they will probably have the World to Come too without effort...
Imrei Shefer.
—o—
f) "But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord... if thou seek Him with all thy heart."
"But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord" — you will seek God somewhere there, in the tangled dark labyrinth of "speculations" and philosophical brooding. But not there will you find Him. "Thou shalt find Him... with all thy heart" — you will find Him right in your own heart. You think, who knows how far your thoughts must stray in order to find God. But He is so near to you, so near: in your heart... and you did not know it, and you did not know it..
Kol Simcha (Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha)
—o—
Haftarah: "Comfort ye, comfort ye."
g) "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" (Isaiah 40:1).
At the time of the First Temple the Jews sinned in deed. They committed various crimes openly, in the sight of all — so they had only a fixed exile: seventy years in Babylon. At the time of the Second Temple they already sinned in thought, in secret. Groundless hatred, intrigues — all things that are done in hiding — therefore we have such a long, boundless, thousand-year exile, so says the Talmud.
Therefore: a double "Comfort ye". We must mend [?] both kinds of sin, and above all: "Speak ye to the heart of Jerusalem" — the theft of hearts, the secret intrigues...
Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
h) "That her iniquity is pardoned" (ibid., 2)
A rich man took a poor yeshiva student as a bridegroom [for his daughter]. For the wedding the boy's father had a pair of garments sewn for him with his last pennies; as bad luck would have it, they were stolen from him on the wedding day. So the rich in-law had to have new garments sewn in a hurry. The bridegroom rejoices at the theft: had he not been robbed, he would have had to wear the poor home-sewn garments that everyone would have laughed at; now he has expensive garments that his rich father-in-law had sewn for him...
"That her iniquity is pardoned" — through repentance the sins become favour. "Deliberate sins become for him as merits". Well then, the merits a tzaddik performs are like those poor home-sewn garments; but the merits that are turned out of sins through repentance, when God makes commandments out of transgressions, are rich garments sewn by the rich father-in-law... Bravo for the theft. Sinning was almost worth it.
Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
—o—
Avot.
i) "Where there is no wisdom there is no fear [of God]" (3:17).
Various Hasidic sayings mock the pious fools. Rabbi Yisraeltshe of Rużyn used to say: "If a (pious) fool gets the World to Come, I will let my right hand be cut off"... The clever Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce said: "When I am in the upper world and see a fool being led along, with thirteen [?] carriages of World-to-Come following him, I will run after him and shout: a fool remains a fool"...
Once the Ropczycer saw a foolish Hasid banging his head against the wall while praying. He smiled and said: good, good, either way: if he means it for the sake of Heaven, then it is good; if he means it only so that people should see — then let his head really hurt him...
—o—
j) "Give unto Him of His own" (ibid., 8)
"Give unto Him of His own" — give the poor man of what is his, for the money you possess belongs also to the poor man; it was only given to you to administer...
Lev Avot.
A Chairman of the Election Commission Elected

[Page 5 header band:] What's New in Zagłębie? — Friday, 10 Av 5691 — piątek 24 lipca 1931 [Friday, 24 July 1931].
Będzin
Last Wednesday a meeting of the election commission, which is to conduct the elections to the kehilla administration, took place in the gmina [municipal] premises. On the agenda were 2 items: electing a chairman and fixing a date for the elections.
Mr. Avraham Liwer (Zionist) was elected chairman of the election commission. The date of the elections has been postponed for the time being.
Będzin — Tarnowskie Góry
For 2 weeks now a bus service has been running regularly twice a day between Będzin and Tarnowskie Góry. The route goes via Wojkowice - Szarlej.
Hershl Jedwab and Sam Goldberg in Będzin

On Saturday evening we shall have in Będzin the humorist Hershl Jedwab, well known from old times, who became popular with his satirical topical humoresques, at which the audience laughed till they cried.
Jedwab is a master in his field and every word he lets out is delicious; the audience holds its sides with laughter. Jedwab will touch upon topical social questions of Będzin.
The acclaimed artist Sam Goldberg will also give a folk concert with a very rich programme of the most beautiful Jewish songs.
The evening thus promises to be interesting and will surely be well attended.
Będzin in the Future

Under this heading we read a notice in the "Polonia" that a plan has been worked out and that the town intends to have boulevards built from the railway station as far as Dąbrowa. The boulevards are to cut through the whole town, and the "Polonia" concludes that as soon as the plan is really carried out, the town will in reality acquire a European appearance.
Truly a beautiful dream — and we residents know nothing about it!
Czeladź—Siemianowice

When the Będzin starosta Baksa[?] was in Warsaw on Thursday, he discussed the question of building a new road Czeladź – Siemianowice, which, once the plan is carried out, will make it possible to shorten the distance by 2 kilometres.
A Gang of Thieves Uncovered

Last Friday a daring theft was carried out at the home of the Sosnowiec mortgage judge Rutkowski at Małachowska[?] 9.
A gang of thieves stole clothes, 19 "dolarówki" [Polish dollar-loan bonds] and many valuables to a sum of 5000 zł.
The police were notified at once and soon conducted an energetic investigation, which did not yield the desired results. Only on Tuesday did the police manage to pick up the trail of the gang, and arrests began.
Besides this, the police arrested in Będzin a well-known thief, Leokadia Jańczakowa[?], and Helena Zając[?], both from Będzin; the latter are well-known figures of the underworld in Zagłębie.
A Suicide

In the fields around the town, 21-year-old Natalia K. drank vinegar essence with the aim of taking her own life.
The suicide, who lives at Wapienna[?] 3, was taken to hospital in a dangerous condition. The reason for the suicide is not known.
Sosnowiec: The municipal water from Maczki

For a short time now the local inhabitants who use the municipal water supply, which is drawn from Maczki, have been complaining that the water has somehow acquired a different taste — it is somehow sweetish and too sharp.
Many people have turned to the magistrate (town council) for explanations, but there too nobody knows anything; only, as people say, it is supposedly connected with the destruction of a galvanic[?] mine in Bolesław, the mine being an old one whose owners are French. Nobody can say what caused the destruction.
The filters which purify the water are not yet in use[?], because, firstly, they are not all in operation yet — which will only happen when water is supplied to Upper Silesia — and, secondly, even if all the filters were in operation it would still not be possible for them to purify the water of the harmful chemical substances.
The annual meeting of the bakers' guild

Last Sunday the annual meeting of the bakers' guild (cech) took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association.
The meeting was opened by Mr L. Lupner, and Mr Moshe Hilchelm[?] was unanimously elected chairman, with Mr Dragner as secretary.
Reports were given on the activity to date and on the state of the treasury.
A lengthy discussion developed around the reports, and they proceeded to elect a new board, which consists of: L. Lupner (starszy cechmistrz — senior guild master); vice: Yudl Barenkiewicz[?] and Yaakov Szwajcer. On the board: Chaim Dawid Ważnica and Yitzchak Presajn.
On the commission: Yudl Barenkiewicz, Chaim Piekarski, Chaim Asher Hamburger and Eliasz Rubin.
As deputies: Alter Mandelbaum and Efraim Zinder.
“The Messianic movement and political Zionism”

Last Sabbath the local Revisionist organisation held, in its own premises, a collective lecture on the subject “The Messianic movement and present-day political Zionism”. Speeches were given by Messrs Prezurowicz[?], Szwajcer and Fiszel, who described the period and the movement of the messiahs David Reubeni (printed “Harbeni”), Shlomo Molcho, Shabbetai Zvi and Jacob Frank, who strove to redeem the people and the land, as well as the causes that led to the decline of messianism. Then a parallel was drawn with present-day political Zionism.
———
Tomorrow, Sabbath, at 4 in the afternoon, a collective lecture will take place on the subject “What is a normal people?”. At the end there will be discussions.
Founding meeting of the tailors' guild

On Sunday at 4 in the afternoon the founding meeting of the tailors' guild will take place at the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association.
A representative of the Będzin starostwo (district office) will take part in the meeting, as well as representatives of various artisans' associations in Zagłębie.
After the meeting there will be a banquet.
Result of the cycling race

Last Sunday the cycling section (printed “sektsir”) of the Sosnowiec “Maccabi” organised a cycling race for the championship over the course Sosnowiec–Murcki and back, i.e. 35 kilometres.
Instead of at half past 9 in the morning, the race was postponed at the request of the Katowice police to 12 noon.
At half past 11 a parade (defilade) of the cyclists through the streets took place. In front drove three cars decorated with blue-and-white flags, in which the judges and controllers sat. The procession made an aesthetic impression on the strolling inhabitants.
At exactly 12 o'clock, in the presence of several hundred people, the cycling race took place, in which 10 men took part.
Already before the half-way mark 4 persons dropped out, as did the former[?] champion (“g. meister”) Federman, who broke his bicycle while riding up the hill.
As a result of the race, first prize went to Natan Kiwkowicz, with a time of 57 minutes 10 seconds; second, Getreidehändler[?], 58 min. 2 sec.; third — Romankiewicz, 61 min. 3 sec.
The distribution of the diplomas took place at 9 in the evening over a glass of drink, to which representatives of all the sections came.
The banquet was opened in the name of the cyclists' section by Mr Szwajcer, who invited the representative of the central world union “Maccabi”, Mr Gutowski, to preside over the banquet.
In a very convivial mood the company spent several hours, during which several serious speeches were also given by Messrs Gutowski, Szwajcer, Skocylas[?] and others on the importance of physical education for the renaissance of the Jewish people in its old-new land, Eretz Israel.
With the singing of “Hatikvah” the first part of the banquet was closed. Later the young sporting crowd took to dancing, not forgetting the “hora” too.
Kiepura in Sosnowiec

On Sunday the well-known Polish singer Jan Kiepura arrived here from Vienna in his car; on Monday he drove on in his car to Olkusz and Ojców, from where he travelled via Kraków to Krynica for a 3-week cure.
From Krynica the great singer is going to Paris, where he has been engaged for a new sound film.
As is known, Kiepura is a native of Sosnowiec and in his time graduated from the Będzin Realschule (real school).

[Sport — Zagłębie.]
Hakoach — Sarmacja 0:1 (0:0)
It has already become an everyday phenomenon among us that even on their own ground the Jews do not feel safe. At this match between the above-mentioned teams, too, the hooligan supporters of Sarmacja once again allowed themselves to break onto the pitch and to prevent the referee from conducting the match. We shall come to the reasons later. The match itself was not interesting, especially in the first half, when one had the impression that a friendly match was being played. Both sides had chances to score goals, but all without success. Here one must stress the great mistake committed by the Hakoach halves ("runners"): Wekselman and Rozen, who do not keep up with the attack. The task of the halves is: to supply the attack with good balls and to help in the offensive. This, unfortunately, was not seen; Rozen 3 in particular was always by... Brama and guarded him... Only in the second half does the game become more interesting, when Rozen 1 unexpectedly shoots the only goal for Hakoach. The Sarmacja players go for the feet instead of the ball... The referee, however, is on the spot and does not permit brutal play. In the 19th minute Brama and Puszecki fall to the ground; at that moment the Sarmacja man Kenecki rushes up and gives Brama a slap. That was the signal for the Sarmacja supporters to come onto the pitch. The good referee Mr. Kojska had no choice but to whistle the match off in favour of Hakoach.
Brynica [?] — Makabi 2:3 (1:1)
We have already written many times about the enormous failure that Makabi is having in this year's championships. This time, too, Makabi should have won the match, but that unfortunately did not happen. Already in the first minute the Brynica centre-forward managed to score a goal which Szostak could have held. A few minutes later Szmidt equalises from a free kick. After half-time Brynica manages to score two more goals, and Szmidt again scores, from an "eleven" [penalty], the second goal for the blue-and-whites. Distinguished themselves: Szmidt, Jakubowicz, Klajner and Szlezynger. Referee Mr. Okularczyk good.

Another Tram Victim on Małachowskiego Street in Będzin

[Będzin — tram accident.]
Yesterday at 11 o'clock in the morning, on Małachowskiego Street in Będzin, opposite Kubiczek's house, 40-year-old Tojba Fajgenblat was killed by the tram.
The tragically deceased had come from Piłsudskiego Street and wanted to cross Małachowskiego Street. When she saw that a car was approaching from the direction of the station, Mrs. Fajgenblat started to go back towards Piłsudskiego Street, but at that moment the tram, which was going to Sosnowiec, ran over her and killed her on the spot.
Tojba Fajgenblat, a mute woman, lived in Dąbrowa; a few days ago she had come to her brother, who lives in Szuster's house and is also mute — and here she met her death.
———
The accident happened before the eyes of Messrs. Wielgus and Berger. The latter went into Wielgus's shop and began to have convulsions [?]. By chance the lawyer Radzin[?] was in the shop. When this „sentimental“ man saw what a shattering impression the tram catastrophe had made on the Jewish young people, he blurted out:
„Ładnie na was, dranie, bardzo ładnie, psiakrew“ [Polish: „Serves you right, you scoundrels, very nice, damn it“]...

The „Yesodei ha-Torah“ Cheder in Będzin Engages Non-Jewish Teachers.
From the Jewish Teachers' Association in Będzin we have received the following:
In the Sosnowiec Polish newspaper „Express Zagłębia“ of the 19th of this month an advertisement was printed by the management of the „Yesodei ha-Torah“ cheder in Będzin, that it, the management, is seeking teachers for the school year 1931/32 „without distinction of creed“. It is worth telling what this is actually about: a few weeks ago the management of the „Yesodei ha-Torah“ cheder dismissed all the Jewish teachers without any justification and in contradiction to the binding contract. Besides that, the management did not consider it necessary to pay the teachers their salary. It is therefore an unheard-of scandal, in such a situation, to engage new teachers — at a time when terrible unemployment reigns in the Jewish street, and [נויט ?] a Jewish school (at whose head surely stand „Torah-loyal“ Jews) engages teachers „without distinction of creed“. Have freethinking[?] ideas already wanted to penetrate the „Yesodei ha-Torah“ chadarim? It is only a wonder that the head of the school, a personality who is, by the way, known to us, covers with his authority such a scandalous act of the management. We therefore consider it our duty to submit the matter to the public opinion of the Jewish population of Będzin.
Association of Jewish Teachers in Będzin.

A Sensational Jewish Divorce. In the Częstochowa Prison

Izrael Iser Żołądek is a young man who hates working hard and looking for a living, especially in the present critical times, so he has found himself an easy source of income. He travels around the Polish towns, signs engagement contracts (tenoim) or marries Jewish daughters, takes their dowry and a few things from them and goes off to another town, where he again signs tenoim or sets up a wedding canopy, and so on without end.
On such a "guest tour" he also honoured our Częstochowa, where he made the acquaintance of a local Jewish daughter, Malka R., set up a wedding canopy with her, lived with her a few weeks, and then took 600 zł. and a few things and vanished.
Only then did his little wife learn that she was not his "only one" ("jedynaczka"), that from before he already had a wife in Zagłębie, besides others who have not yet come to light, and that in general he is not particular about the ban of Rabbenu Gershom.
At her request the Częstochowa rabbinate turned to the rabbi in Kosów [?], where, according to the information received, this person had gone, and asked him to take up the matter of the agunah. To this the local rabbi there replied that this person was "touring" those parts; he was engaged and was already about to go under the wedding canopy with a Jewish daughter, but at the last minute his 2 previous wives were found out, so he was arrested and put into the Ostrów prison.
Then the rabbinate turned about the matter to the Ostrów rabbi, and an answer came that the lad had already "advanced" and was already sitting for these sins in the Łomża prison; the rabbinate then sends a letter to the Łomża rabbi, and from there comes the answer: "and he journeyed from Łomża and encamped at Ostrołęka" — the lad was already living in the Ostrołęka prison.
So it went on for months, while he was constantly being transferred from one jail to another, until a few weeks ago he was brought in person, in all his glory, to Częstochowa, precisely in connection with his wife's trial.
First of all, for robbing [?] the local wife he got 10 months in prison with board.
Then Mr. Mendel Asz went to the prison on behalf of the local rabbinate and had an interview with him about his view on releasing the Częstochowa little wife by a get.
Our Żołądek at first demanded a handsome "pharmacy bill" as fee for the work, but after long negotiations they agreed on a 50 zł. honorarium.
After receiving the proper permission from the prosecutor, Malka R. was at last freed of her un-destined "Żołądek"...
?1 Jewish Families Have Lost Their Livelihood Because of the Opening of the New Railway Station in Będzin.

There came to us at the editorial office those who for 15—20 years have drawn their livelihood from carrying luggage parcels at the Będzin station, and told us that from the moment the new station building was opened they have been persecuted and are not allowed up onto the station to catch whatever earnings there may be.
The desperate porters therefore appeal to the Jewish population that the luggage or other parcels be carried out by the passengers outside the station, where they do have access, and in this way they will again be able, by their hard work, to earn a living for their wives and children.
Dąbrowa Will Have a New Post Office Building, and the Owners of the 'Budki' Will Not Suffer.

As is known, an agreement was reached between the Kraków Post Directorate and the Dąbrowa Magistrat to build a post office building in Dąbrowa.
According to the plan the building was to be put up on the Magistrat square in Sobieskiego Street, where the "budki" (stalls) are located.
The Jewish shopkeepers, who were condemned to lose their livelihoods through the removal of the wooden "budki", intervened many times at the Magistrat, but without success. The vice-president too took the position that because of the post office building the "budki" must be removed.
The only hope of averting the decree still lay with the president, Dr. Madejski, who, thanks to his conduct as town president, is very popular with the Jewish population of Dąbrowa.
And so it indeed happened: when the president, Mr. Madejski, learned that it was planned to harm [?] a certain number of Jewish merchants, he called those concerned to him, acquainted himself with their wishes, and after a personal intervention at the Kraków Post Directorate he obtained that the post office be built in Kościuszki Street, so that the "budki" remain once again in the possession of the merchants who have held them until now.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ekev)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by[?] Y. Y.
Parashat Ekev
The Portion
—o—
a) "Which He swore to your fathers" (7:12).
"Your testimonies are very sure; holiness befits Your house... for length of days" [Ps. 93:5].
A customer comes into a goods warehouse — one who is not considered reliable. Still the merchant shows him all sorts of goods and remarks to him in passing, with a roguish little smile: "I suppose you'll pay, won't you?" (meaning: in cash). The customer pretends not to understand and answers: "What do you mean? Of course I'll pay, what else?" And the customer keeps repeating his promise that he will pay, until he swears by his wife and children that he will pay. At this point the merchant rubs his forehead and thinks: the trouble is ready. He already means credit; for if he meant to pay cash, why is he swearing? I'll see him count out the money. If he swears and talks so much — he already means a promissory note...
The moral:
If God swore to us to give us all good things, it is a sign that He means it as a "promissory note", payable who knows in which years?... Had He meant to do us good right away — why, "Your testimony is very sure": God's word is credible enough today as well. Why the oath? — It must be that this is a matter "for length of days", a matter for the day after tomorrow...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
b) "You shall be blessed above all peoples; there shall be no barren male or female among you or among your cattle" (7:14).
"You shall be blessed above all peoples" — in what way can the nations bless you? — "There shall be no barren male or female among you or among your cattle": that your cattle should be fruitful... A gentile's understanding reaches no higher; for him this is the greatest blessing...
Imrei Shefer.
—o—
"And you shall consume all the peoples" (7:16).
At all the weddings of all the nations Israel dances along. Their celebrations are his celebrations — "and you shall consume all the peoples": he eats along at all their festivities, rejoices along; but at your own celebration — you are "a people that dwells alone", forlorn and lonely. Those with whom you share so much at the time of their joy — do not know you at all...
Noam Elimelech.
—o—
"And your silver and gold is multiplied" (8:3 [as printed; should be 8:13]).
Too much money is like too much blood. Too much blood is not healthy for a person, especially when something impure flows in the blood; and is there not a great dose of impurity in the way a person earns his money: robbery, theft? — What is the remedy for such an excess of blood? — "Hakazah", bloodletting: draw off a little blood and the remaining blood will be purified --
Just such a "bloodletting" is needed with an excess of money. Draw off a little, distribute a little charity... the only remedy...
One more thing: impure blood must flow out; it already seeks ways — through a haemorrhage, or the like. So it is better to draw off a little oneself. Impure money must also flow out: through taxes, or the like; so it is better to draw it off oneself through charity...
Binah le-Ittim.
—o—
e) "Then your heart be lifted up, and you forget" (8:14).
An impoverished rich man once travelled about the country calling himself "the Brody Preacher" [Brody]. He had never been a preacher and could not deliver sermons, but he had once been a very wealthy man in Brody, and so they called him "the Brody Preacher": because his lowliness — the fact of what could become of such a magnate — is the best moral sermon...
Today's magnates too, who fall from day to day, present in their own persons the best moral lesson about the worth of money... This decline of the magnates is the result of their "haughty heart", of their boasting: "Who is lord over us?"
Nahalat Yaakov.
—o—
f) "Therefore you shall lay up these my words in [lit. upon] your heart" (11:18).
Why "upon your heart" — on the heart and not in the heart?
Because — a person is not always capable of taking higher, spiritual things into his heart; many times the heart is closed to the spiritual... Therefore a person must keep the divine words ready upon the heart, so that when a higher feeling takes hold of him, when the heart opens — they may at once penetrate into the heart...
Rabbi Mendel of Kotzk [Kock].
Haftarah [printed "Haftorah"].
—o—
f) [as printed; should be g] "Why, when I came, was there no man; when I called, was there none to answer?" (Isaiah [50:2; printed "5:6"]).
In the time of Ezra most [printed "srov"] Jews did not want to go up to the Land of Israel, arguing: it is not yet the End, it is not yet the "footsteps of the Messiah". But had they emigrated to the Land of Israel then, the days of the Messiah would have come then... This is what the prophecy calls out: "Why, when I called, was there none to answer? Why have you stopped your ears from hearing Zion's call? You had an excuse: it is not yet the Messiah's time, one must not hasten the End — but: 'Is My hand shortened, that it cannot redeem?'" Had you gone up en masse to Zion, the complete redemption would have come then.
Ahavat Yehonatan.
• • •
That is why such a cruel wrath (the Expulsion from Spain) was poured out upon the Spanish Jews in 1492: because they had not wanted to go up to the Land of Israel in the days of Ezra.
Don Isaac Abarbanel.
Avot.
—o—
h) "Who is rich? — He who rejoices in his portion" (4:1).
Only he is rich who rejoices in his wealth, who rules over it. There are rich men who do not rule over their fortune at all — he is actually enslaved to it...
Petah Einayim.
—o—
i) "Every assembly... that is not for the sake of Heaven" (ibid., 14).
In the time of Rabbi Yohanan ha-Sandlar various sects, associations arose among the Jews. All of them spoke in God's name — so the Sadducees, so the Pharisees — until one no longer knew who truly spoke in God's name. The only consolation was: "but one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not endure in the end" — they will fall away by themselves.
Sforno.
—o—
An explanation of the "Baal ha-Turim" on this week's portion, Ekev (9:12).
On the verse cited (9:12) the Baal ha-Turim says: "'You brought out of Egypt' — meaning: from the city of Zoan; and wherever it says 'from the land of Egypt' — meaning: from the whole country". The quoted passage in the Baal ha-Turim is a riddle to everyone, for surely one cannot say that the sin of the Golden Calf was committed exclusively by the Jews who came out of Egypt's capital, Zoan, and not by the other Jews. Firstly: whence does the Baal ha-Turim draw such a strange assertion? And secondly, we find in the same matter of the Golden Calf, as it is written (Exodus 32:7), "whom you brought up from the land of Egypt". The passage in the Baal ha-Turim is so incomprehensible to everyone that a certain printing house of Pentateuchs — the Vilna one, it seems to me — allowed itself to throw the whole passage out of the Baal ha-Turim.
I, however, have the pleasure of explaining this enigmatic passage in a quite simple way, and I hope that many readers will be grateful to me for it.
As is known, every language has a figure of speech called pars pro toto (a part instead of the whole), i.e. when speaking of a whole thing one can express oneself as if speaking of a part of it. For example, when Lot said to the men of Sodom (Genesis 8:9 [as printed; should be 19:8]) "for therefore they came under the shadow of my roof [lit. beam]", he did not mean the beam alone, but the whole dwelling; when Isaiah the prophet says (ch. 49) "But Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me", he does not mean only the capital Zion, but the whole country. The same is true in all languages: a part identifies the whole, and the name of a capital identifies the whole country. A Pole can say today that he has been freed from the yoke of Moscow, and he means by it the yoke of all Russia. And exactly this is what the Baal ha-Turim means to say here: that in speaking of the Exodus from Egypt the Torah too often uses the figure pars pro toto, and instead of "from the land of Egypt" we find only "from Egypt", i.e. from the capital Zoan, and in any case the whole country is meant. According to this explanation the passage in the Baal ha-Turim is perfectly comprehensible, and all he means by it is that the capital Zoan was called Egypt (see Numbers 13:22), and this explains the verse (Deuteronomy 16:1) "[the Lord your God] brought you out of Egypt by night": for from the capital the Jews really went out at once, by night, and from the whole country only the next morning (see Ibn Ezra, Exodus 12:31).
Zvi Hirsch Niebielski[?], Kielce.
How Do Things Stand with the “Mizrachi” School in Będzin?

In connection with the rumours that the “Mizrachi” school in Będzin is to be liquidated, we have received from the Board of Trustees (Kuratorium), in reply to our inquiry, the following explanation:
Under the pressure of the general economic crisis the “Mizrachi” school in Będzin, too, went through a very hard struggle this year. The deficit, which kept growing because the income became ever smaller, and also because of various other reasons on the part of the teaching staff, caused the school's activity to be disrupted in its normal course.
After great efforts and hard toil the present Board of Trustees has succeeded in overcoming all the difficulties and in liquidating the conflict with the teachers, and we are already making the necessary preparations for the new school year.
Proceeding from the recognition that in such a Jewish town as Będzin a religious-national school has a right to exist and is even an urgent necessity, and being inspired by the sincere will to establish a school that shall be the smithy-workshop from which a truly Jewish religious-national generation shall go forth, and having the conviction that in Będzin the possibilities exist to realise our wish, we have undertaken a complete reorganisation and have carried out, for the new school year, a fundamental change in the technical and spiritual structure of the school.
As headmaster we have engaged Mr. Dr. A. Gottesdiener, who is a well-known personality in the Mizrachi world in Poland, a specialist in the field of pedagogy and a capable organiser. And it is to be hoped that under his direction the school will flourish and develop into a model school for the whole of Zagłębie. The present Board of Trustees gives its time and effort to the school's advancement and strives to stay in close contact with the parents, because only through a harmonious, mutual understanding between the parents, the Board of Trustees and the school management can the education of our children improve.
Unfortunately, in the past year we had to note a very cold, indifferent attitude of the parents towards the school. Parents' meetings and teachers' conferences were always very poorly attended by the parents.
We now expect from the parents a positive, warm cooperation.
A Letter from Bystra.

The train has only just left the district full of chimneys and factory smoke, the pounding of the machines and the pulsing of big-city life still ring in one's ears, — and already we have before our eyes a splendid picture of the green and gentle mountain ridge of the Western Beskids, and among them Bystra, the most popular summer resort in the Polish Beskids. Twenty minutes' journey separates [?] Bystra from Bielsko. In this short time we pass from one world into another: from the black, dusty urban district, crushed by the prevailing crisis — into the world of nature and freedom. The nearness of the towns has won Bystra a very great popularity, and thanks to this there are here every summer plenty of “letniks” (summer guests) who spend the hot summer days in the lap of pure and gentle nature. Bystra is ringed by mountains and cut through by a rushing mountain stream; on one side lies the wooded “Jawesberg” [?] (933 m), on whose summit there is a fine shelter-house for tourists. On the other side a chain of mountains is formed by “Stefanka”, “Kamitzer Platte” and “Klimczok”. The shelter on the “Kamitzer Platte” is one of the most beautiful in the Polish Beskids. From “Stefanka” a fine landscape view stretches over Bielsko, Biała and other towns. “Klimczok” (1069), the highest mountain, is the one most visited by tourists. Every Sunday whole rows of tourists, town-dwellers, stream up the gentle and wooded “Klimczok” in order to spend their only day of rest far from the city dust. Bystra also belongs among the best Polish tourist centres and represents a convenient mountain junction [?], from where the road leads to “Barania Góra”, to “Polska” [?] “Babia Góra”, — which is the highest mountain in the Beskids.
Among the bright sides of Bystra belongs in the first place the electric light which it possesses, something only a few, countable Polish health resorts can boast of. But there are also other “traces” of Europeanness: fine villas, tennis courts, plenty of guesthouses, etc. But in this area much still remains to be desired. The number of guesthouses is very large, which sharpens the competition, especially since the number of guests this year is minimal. In some guesthouses a day costs 7 zł., and at the same time there are some in which the number of guests does not exceed 5 persons. In general this year's attendance is smaller than every year. This is a result of the economic crisis prevailing in the country. The majority in Bystra is formed by the... “minorities”; Będzin and Sosnowiec are numerously represented.
Among the local buildings the splendid building of the sanatorium for the sick stands out; it is built according to the latest technical and sanitary requirements. Staying at the sanatorium for a cure is the former Marshal of the Sejm, Ignacy Daszyński.
To the address of the local climatic-resort administration it must be remarked: for the high resort tax one pays, one gets almost nothing; for a long time after a car has passed it is hard to breathe because of the dust that rises from the highway; the swimming pool is too small; there is no special promenade with music; there is no night-house (hostel) for tourists, and many other conveniences are lacking — these are the dark sides of Bystra. It is to be hoped, however, that further development will transform Bystra into a health resort in the European sense.
• • •
The yahrzeit of the unforgettable leader and creator of political Zionism, Dr. T. Herzl, also found a strong echo in Bystra. In the hall of the Frenkel guesthouse a memorial academy was held in the presence of a very great number of attendees. Messrs. Frenkel, Liwer [?] and Wigadzki of Będzin and Dr. Wdowiński [?] (Bielsko) described the great merits of the tireless fighter for the Jewish future and his Zionist ideology, which now — at a time of the struggle over the final aim of Zionism — is very topical.
Eliyahu Gertner.
The Income Tax (The Citizens' Dread of the Tax, Which Is Planned to Be Increased. — What Should We Do in This Case?)

[Editorial — taxes; the income tax.] (The citizens' dread of the tax, which is planned to be increased. — What should we do in this case?)
The newspapers have brought us the tidings that throughout the country serious preparations have begun for the income tax, and according to what the informational reports show, this tax is not merely to be no smaller than in previous years — it is to be even larger. Put plainly, it means that the citizens of the country earned more last year than in the years up to now.
It is, upon my life, a riddle that no one can get into his head: how can there be even a reason to think that in today's critical time people should have more income than until now? From what, then, can the increased incomes come now — from the fact that there are no takings at all, that a dead stillness reigns in all branches of trade, and that if one does see a customer one is afraid to sell to him against a bill of exchange (wechsel), and if one does give, there is the prospect of receiving, instead of money, a protest? Is it all this, then, that brings these dreadful incomes?
Do our "urzędy" [government offices] really still not know to this day in what a catastrophic state our citizens find themselves? Does one still not know that all citizens of the country, beginning with the very giants and ending with the smallest, have all become impoverished? Do those who must know this, those who must concern themselves with it, really not know all this?
Possibly they still hold to the old methods: as soon as one sees that a person goes about dressed like ordinary people — then pay for it. They do not stop to think for a single minute that we are not living today in the 18th century, that we all live in the centre of Europe, that moreover we are in a cultured country and have dealings [printed "sikhsukhim", "disputes"] with cultured people, so that this must be adapted both to the times and to the conditions in which we find ourselves.
Or perhaps they will fasten on the fact that sick people, unfortunate citizens, travel away to cure their sick hearts, lungs, feet, livers and other such trifles? Must they pay for that? Must sick people pay for the fact that under the worst conditions they have to seek a cure for their bit of life? Or perhaps people should have to pay for the fact that at the time when the children have their holidays (ferie) the parents want to treat their children to a few weeks of fresh air? Shall that be called leading an extravagant or lavish life, when parents want to show their children, over a few weeks, that there is also a clear blue sky without smoke, and that the earth yields, besides coal and ore, also greenery and fruit and flowers? And that instead of heat, stuffiness and fumes there is also a refreshing shade and a cooling breeze that brings freshness, courage and health into the children's little bones? Must parents really pay for wanting to raise a healthy generation, which is an ornament to a country?
It goes without saying that many, many citizens must give up these necessities because of the hard conditions of existence; whereas for those who do manage it, it does not come easily, and that is no wonder either, for what will a Jew not do for a bit of health for himself and for his children. Therefore it surely cannot be taken into account that, thanks to the fact that citizens can allow themselves such expenses, this should be taken to mean that they have the income for it.
There are all kinds of people. Some do not want to show their nose in daylight, whereas there are others who will deny themselves the most necessary things, but cure themselves they will, and the children they will send away, so that they may freely and deeply breathe in the healthful air.
Shall it then be said that because of this he has a larger income? That because of this the income tax can be increased? How is it possible that the citizens should have a larger income this year than in previous years? One must, after all, be consistent: from what have the citizens earned more — from the fact that they are afraid to trade and to let goods out [on credit] even when they do have a customer before their eyes? Then where is the great number of bankruptcies, of "nadzory" [court receiverships] and lawlessness in general that reigns in the commercial world today? As soon as one reckons income, one must surely reckon losses too.
In the course of the year many citizens have left the arena; many, many have liquidated their enterprises, so that there will be no one from whom to collect the income tax. The "urzędy" will surely not take this into account and will not want the total sum of the income tax to be smaller than last year's — on the contrary, as we hear, it is to be even larger. Well, how then can this be carried out? It follows that those who are still on their feet will have to pay for those who have fallen, and how "healthy" that is we surely know very well from practice. From previous years we know that the overload, the excessive pressure, makes him incapable; he falls into a faint [printed "agmakht"] and slips away completely.
The question therefore arises: in the present collapse, in the prevailing crisis, in the grave situation in which the whole country finds itself, can one permit oneself such experiments? Is this not too dangerous a game, one that drags heavy and serious complications along with it? Must one not, at such a serious time, render a clear account of what may come of this unsound calculation?
The assessment commissions will surely begin soon, and there, as usual, we shall also have our representatives, who must be conscious in the true sense of the word. They must fight hard enough [lit. "enough must they fight"] so that the Jewish economic situation, which is in such a sad state, should not be completely shattered.
We must have sitting there representatives who will be able to defend us and who will fight by every means so that the Jews who have still remained on their feet should not have to collapse owing to the excessive tax burdens.
That is the one and only goal our representatives must keep in view at the coming tax assessment.
R. Let.
Pictures of Jewish Need

The Happy Man.
The economic organisations are the barometers of the severe crisis. There you can find out how things stand with Jewish poverty, how the Jews suffer and fight for a piece of bread.
A Jew comes in in a cheerful mood and asks that someone write him a petition to the naczelnik [district head] about remitting the whole bit of tax arrears.
He is asked [printed "אי"]: Reb Yid, why are you so content, what is your joy? He answers — "I have great privileges [misprinted]"... What? Once he was a Jew, a merchant, trading wholesale [printed "נרויס"], leading a fine sort of life; now, however, everything has gone downhill. On top of that he was robbed, a fire broke out in his home, and from great distress his wife became paralysed and lies in the Jewish hospital. Does one need better grounds for remitting taxes?
Truly a happy man.
*
A frightened Jewish woman bursts in on the secretary of the "Merchants' Association", with tears in her eyes [printed "כרערן"] and a pack of papers.
"I never stop paying taxes, I save from my food and pay, and yet, when the sequestrator comes, he says that I owe from the year 1926...
Now, during[?] the flood of distraints, I live in mortal fear. I expect that any minute the sequestrator may come running and take away my last bit of poverty. My only request, therefore, is that you make me a little reckoning of where I stand with them in the world."
The woman scatters over a couple of tables tax orders, sequestration papers, paid receipts — until it starts to swim before your eyes.
Be a clever one [printed "ארבה א בריה", doubtful] and tell her where she stands in the world.
Zh.
The 17th Zionist Congress and the Tasks Ahead

Lecture by Sejm Deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum
A large audience of admirers from all strata of the Jewish population of Będzin gathered last Sunday in the "Kapital" [Kapitol?] cinema, where the Sejm deputy Mr. Yitzhak Grünbaum gave a lecture on the above-mentioned subject.
After the greeting by Mr. Yitzhak Wygodzki, the floor is given to the distinguished guest, who delivers a 3-hour lecture in which he characterises in bold strokes the course of the 17th Zionist Congress.
The era of Weizmannism — the speaker exclaims — was brought to an end at this Congress. But Weizmann's shadow still accompanies the new Executive, which faces great efforts of work and energy.
The lecture ends very finely with the call to continue supporting the building of the Jewish National Home in Eretz Israel.
After the lecture "Hatikvah" is sung.
Mr. Grünbaum gave the same lecture on the same day in the evening in Sosnowiec.
An Old Woman under the Tram Wheels

On Friday morning a tram accident happened on 3 Maja Street in Sosnowiec, which cost the life of an elderly woman, a Christian.
The old woman wanted to cross the tram line on 3 Maja Street. At that moment a tram approached at speed, ran over the old woman and killed her.

When the family goes to the spa, the thieves become the masters of the house
In broad daylight thieves got into the flat of engineer Krupiński in Niwka. The Krupiński family left a few weeks ago for Switzerland and left the gardener and his wife behind as guards.
The thieves, disturbed by no one [printed "נעשטערט"], played the master of the house and rummaged in every corner of the flat.
