My Dacha Torments

(Experiences of a schlimazel husband who sent his wife off to a dacha.)
If you see me running in the street, dusty[?], sweaty, in a tattered[?] jacket (marynarka) and loaded like a camel in the desert with parcels, bundles and boxes — please, I beg you, don't laugh at me. For today I am not the only one. Many, poor things, have been punished: I am one of those who sent the wife off to a dacha.
It seems these last few words already make my present situation entirely clear to you, especially since the dacha is not somewhere far away but really, as they say, under your nose — all of a couple of hours' ride there.
You think you would have acted differently from me? — A mistake, begging your pardon. Well, try being a clever one and receiving a little letter from the wife — what am I saying, a little letter: a real order, such that travelling salesmen of the biggest firms, who drift about on the road for weeks, don't send their firms any bigger orders.
Here, out of curiosity, read the latest "note" my wife sent me:
— Go into the butcher's and "take" meat for cutlets and veal schnitzel and a piece of veal liver and a chicken... For my neighbour "take" the same kinds of meat and chicken — only a double portion. May the devil take her! That dried-up "granzhe"[?] wants to become as "corpulent" as I am, so she stuffs herself with nothing but meat...
Now send me slippers [shtek-shikh], and 3 "ganshers"[?] with two jars for preserves, a napkin, a new broom — send me.
I forgot to take the sweater, send it too. Pack a few rolls for today; tomorrow you'll send me fresh ones.
Pack my slippers, pick out and put in 3 pairs of socks, whichever you like. Send me a few pounds of butter, the fine comb, sour cream and tooth powder. Don't forget to send carrots and parsley, lemon, salt and beetroots.
In the flat where I am staying mice have appeared; it would be very good if you bought poison against them at the pharmacy. But best of all would be if you came yourself and brought a cat with you...
Here, you see, my patience burst: Master of the Universe, I say to myself, what has become of me? What is my wife going to make of me? Where am I to get a cat? How does one handle such a creature? But then I think: — fool son of a fool [shoyte ben pikholts], thank God for that; what would you have done if your wife wrote you to send her a dog? Just a dog, you hear — I would already have managed: at night [printed "בייגאכט"], when everyone is asleep, I would have gone out with the dog-catcher through the streets and grabbed a dog — I would perhaps[?] have slipped the dog-catcher the "smitshik"[?]. For what doesn't one do for a wife, I ask you?...
I had, begging your pardon, to bow my head, rush to the market, to the butchers' stalls, grocery shops, haberdashery shops, and in a hurry I bought everything, paid as much as they cared to ask, because the cart is already leaving, and if I don't manage to send it off, I stay at home with the parcel, and mine, may she live, would give me such a sweat-bath that I'd have plenty to sing and tell about...
In short, with the help of a good brother (when the wife is at the dacha there's no shortage of good brothers)
I packed everything — that is, actually he packed it; my strength no longer served me, for why should my strength serve me? Since my wife left I haven't eaten a midday meal...
And here now my whole misfortune begins, for as you say: with other people's hands it is easy to rake the fire. Next day I receive a letter from my wife. What am I saying, a letter — a Tisha b'Av lament it was. Imagine, she writes me that of the whole parcel I sent her — my blood, my toil, woe is me — she, poor thing, couldn't taste a thing.
The fine comb was lying in the butter... (it didn't even harm the comb...). The sour cream spilled into the slippers and from there — onto the meat. The socks torn, patched, not a penny's worth[?] to tie into them...
It is already the second day she is starving. Have pity, she writes — buy a fresh parcel and come over.
Jews, merciful sons of the merciful, give me advice: how does one lure my wife out of the "lovely" dacha back home? I can't stand it any more, I'm going under; dragging myself about with the parcels will tear me out of the world while still young.
Jews, help [ratujcie], give me advice!
A. Geshtrafter ["the Punished"].
What Is Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: “Domestic Peace” in the Commissarial Council

What Is Happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, “Yod-Nun”[?] [misprint for 17, Yod-Zayin] / 17 Av 5691 — piątek 31 lipca 1931 [Friday, 31 July 1931].)
Będzin
“Domestic peace” (shalom bayit) in the commissarial council.
At the last session of the commissarial council [the town council appointed under the government commissar] the disharmony prevailing among the council members came out even more glaringly. Not only the Jewish councillors, who feel as though “bound”, but even the Sanacja members are now beginning to speak in a different tone and to show dissatisfaction.
For 3 hours a discussion dragged on around the question “to be or not to be”. The members Dr. Borylski[?], Rechnic[?] and Salski[?] took the position that all economic matters must also be considered by the council. Against this was the commissar, who holds that not on everything does he need to have the council's opinion.
The matter concerned the project to lay sewerage in some of the streets. The cost of this, amounting to 400 thousand zł., is to be provided by the “G.Sh.Z.”[?], which built the houses by the barracks.
After a long discussion the commissar finally agreed that a commission should be elected, which is to give its opinion on all questions concerning the sewerage works.
The commission comprises: Rechnic (he declined, and in his place Szwajcer came in), Salski, Gutensztajn and Kiszyński[?].
The Kehilla Board to Be Elected Only on Chol HaMoed Sukkot.

On Monday evening the commission for electing the kehilla board held a session, at which the date for electing a kehilla board was fixed for Chol HaMoed Sukkot [the intermediate days of Sukkot].
The reason given is that during the holiday season part of the council are at the spas, and later, during the Days of Awe, some of the members travel to the rebbes.
Because of the Crisis the Kehilla Board Declines to Buy a Painting by Moshe Apfelbaum.

At the time of the “Yizkor” [memorial] exhibition of the paintings of the artist Moshe Apfelbaum, who died young, the kehilla board assigned a sum of 300 zł. to buy a painting. For this purpose a representative was delegated on behalf of the board, who chose a painting for the assigned sum.
But to this day the painting has not been bought out, and therefore this week the committee of the painting exhibition turned to the board with a request to buy out the painting.
The kehilla president gave a written answer that because of the crisis the board is not in a position to buy out the painting.
A Terrible Murder in Grodziec.

On Sunday afternoon several Christians, residents of Grodziec, spent time over a glass of drink in one of the local restaurants. Late in the evening, when the restaurant was closed, the company went off to the flat of Józef Nowak, where the little bottles of brandy enjoyed great success...
At a certain moment a conflict broke out among the company, which then came to “activity”: first chairs, bottles, pots and other implements went flying, then they measured themselves against each other with knives, so that the “entertainment” ended tragically. One of the company was stabbed to death with a razor.
Caught at the “Hot” Minute.

In the night from Saturday to Sunday thieves got into the small shop of Icchak Klajnman, 3rd of May Square [Plac 3 Maja]. The thieves packed up the whole little bit of merchandise from the shop and began carrying it out. At that moment a tenant of the house passed through and came upon the theft. Thanks to this the theft was discovered and the thieves ran away.
The Kehilla President on Leave.

At Sunday's session of the kehilla board leave was granted to the kehilla president Mr. A. Liwer[?].
During his absence the office will be filled by Messrs. Szlomo Icchak Riński[?] and Szymon Plesner.
A Gathering among “Tse'irei Mizrachi”.

Taking part in the meeting will be the members of the World Union and of the Actions Committee, Messrs. Moshe Shapira and Elimelech Neufeld.
Shooting during an Eviction

[Będzin — politics, arrest.] On Targowa Street Yoel Eisner [Joel Ajzner] hung out a red flag. In the middle of the job he was arrested.
He Fulfilled the Mitzvah of “Returning a Lost Object”..

[Będzin — town news.] In the bakery of Mr. Szpigel a stranger hen took up quarters. Mr. Sz. received the guest properly and gave her food and drink. Several days went by, and nobody came to ask whether the hen was there. So Szpigel carried her off to the police station.
The police indeed already knew about it, and the “lost object” was handed over to its rightful mistress.
Sosnowiec — The “Dead-House” Takes Care of the Dead...

[Sosnowiec — community, cemetery.] The question of buying a plot for a cemetery is becoming ever more urgent. The negotiations conducted so far about an exchange with the “Sosnowiec Society” have not brought the desired result. And the gmina [Jewish community] representatives who are concerned with the matter have begun new negotiations with several peasants from Piaski, who want to sell 5 morgs of field at the price of 75 thousand złoty.

Hooligan Deeds against the Family of Rabbi Hager

[Sosnowiec — rabbis, hoax.] Last Friday, at midday, the telephone rings at Rabbi Hager's.
— Hello! Who is speaking? asks the rabbi.
— This is Amstov [Mstów] speaking — someone answers [?] over the telephone — come quickly, because your son Elazarl, who studies in Amstov, is very dangerously ill, his hours are numbered...
Rabbi Hager, naturally, on receiving such sad news went at once to the railway station and left for Amstov on the next train.

Only on arriving in Amstov did he see that he had suffered needless torment thanks to the hooligan prank of irresponsible, unruly youths, who allowed themselves to cause the rabbi so much grief.

Wolbrom too now boasts its "jewels"..
In Łódź Mrs. Chana Rubinsztejn of Wolbrom fainted.
When she was revived she told that a few days ago she had come to Łódź with the purpose of searching for her husband Hirsz, who had left home a few weeks ago saying that he was travelling on business matters, but it turned out that he had simply run away, and, as she was told, he lives in Łódź with a girl with whom he has been having an affair for quite a long time.
In Łódź, however, she has no relatives or acquaintances at all, and she had no money either, so she had to go hungry and spend the nights under the open sky.
She searched there for her runaway husband in vain. She did not find even a trace of her husband.
The unfortunate, desperate woman thus wandered about the city for several days and went very[?] hungry, until her strength gave out and she fainted in the street.
Only then did compassionate people take pity on her and provide her with food and a place to sleep, and the kehilla gave the woman travelling expenses to go back to her wretched home.

When will the crisis be somewhat eased?
Words of comfort from the "commercial world".
Among merchants and manufacturers great disappointment now prevails. When one talks now with a merchant about the prospects for the coming months, he does not have enough words of despair to express his disbelief that things can get better. And yet it will soon get a little better.
When the crisis will end is hard to say at the present moment; it is a world question and depends on how the international financial and economic matters will be settled. But that a certain relaxation will come soon is completely certain.
The relaxation in economic life will come about both abroad and also here, in Poland.
Those who do not now believe in an improvement did not want to believe a few months ago that the crisis would be so tremendously severe in the present months.
But the hardest time of the crisis has already been passed. The coming two or three weeks will still be hard. Around 15—20 August (sierpień) the relaxation will begin.
Already at the end of next month a slight improvement will be felt in all branches of trade. Seasonal transactions will begin, which will bring money into trade. These first cash transactions will somewhat ease the shortage of money in trade and production.
In the first weeks of the season the relaxation will come slowly, but it will be clearly felt. Merchants and manufacturers will not need to chase after the discounters so hard; they will have enough for the most necessary payments.
Only in October (październik) will the relief be felt better. Then the crisis, now so acute, will be eased to a considerable degree.
In our opinion, this year's winter season will be the beginning of the general improvement, and one must hope that it will be so.

[Będzin and Zagłębie — local news.]
When one goes to a summer cottage ("dacha") and leaves the flat under lock, it often happens that on returning the flat is open, because thieves have paid it a visit.
This week, however, the opposite happened: a young man came back from the dacha and found the flat even more firmly shut than he had left it: on the door hung a red seal of the komornik [bailiff].
It turns out that the bailiff had come to the debtor to list [distrain] his belongings over a protested bill of exchange; since he found the flat locked, he put his seal on it to be on the safe side.
Since the poor young man had no cash to redeem the bill, he had no choice but to go back to his wife at the dacha.

Are the Talmud Torah children really fair game?
[Będzin — Talmud Torah; criticism.]
This week there were terrible heat waves; yesterday in particular the heat reached as much as 35 degrees in the course of the day, and it was simply impossible to breathe. But the "guardians" (opiekunowie, so to speak) of the poorest little children who study at the Będzin Talmud Torah gave an "order" (prikaz) yesterday that the ragged, exhausted, pale children should demonstrate with their little throats at the funeral of a well-known Będzin magnate.
Well, that the rabbinate are all too frequent guests at "rich celebrations" is a well-known thing — but what do they want of the poor children? By what right are they tormenting them? Why did the children even have to march from Sielecka Street in such stifling heat and, poor things, shout:
— "Righteousness shall go before him!"
— Don't you dare, gentlemen leaders, do this again; you have no right to it — poor children are not fair game!...

About a thousand people took part in the funeral. The deceased was eulogised in front of his house by the rabbi, and at the cemetery — in the name of the kehilla — by the president of the Będzin kehilla council, Mr. Yitzchak Wigarzki [?], who portrayed the deceased as a man of keen wit, who with his abilities accomplished a great deal for the Jewish community of Będzin and in the process suffered very much grief.

We and Our American Landsleit

[Zagłębie — community institutions; ties with the landsmanshaftn in America; article.]
That the Jewish institutions of Zagłębie find themselves in a difficult situation is no novelty. Even in good times, when the general situation was good, the institutions worked with deficits; all the more so today, during the severe crisis, when every family and every individual does not have enough for his own livelihood — one can well imagine how hard it is for the institutions to procure means for their upkeep.
And here one would also like to touch upon a fact which shows that our town is once again an exception among other towns.
We mean our relationship to the Będzin and Sosnowiec people in America, and vice versa.
Notwithstanding that, as they say, there is a crisis in America, America has nevertheless remained, even to this day, the financial reservoir for most of the Jews in Europe and for their institutions.
We read the provincial press, which brings reports about the warm contact that prevails between the small towns and their landsmanshaftn in America. To this very day the landsmanshaftn there raise certain sums for the institutions in their home towns.
And now, when we consider our poverty, the grave condition of our institutions, and when we know that in America there are hundreds of thousands of landsleit from Będzin and Sosnowiec — and not poor ones — with a certain attachment to their home town and perhaps a bit of good will, the question arises: what is the reason that Zagłębie has such a meagre connection with the Zagłębie people in America?
Why does no one look for ways to establish closer relations with the Zagłębie landsleit who are in America and who surely have a warm attachment to their native town?
Perhaps such a consultation, or a meeting, or a conference of all the public institutions should be held even now, to consider the matter?
Perhaps someone will take the initiative to call this consultation?

From the Public to the Public. (A free platform for our readers.)

[Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa — letters to the editor; kehilla, charity, education.]
1.
Esteemed Editorial Board! Allow us to print the following letter.
It is well known to everyone that when a poor man dies, nobody takes any interest — neither the paid burial attendants (mesasskim) nor, especially, the honorary ones. It happens more than once that a poor man, God spare us, lies 2–3 days before he reaches a Jewish grave. But what happened last Friday goes beyond the bounds of all lawlessness.
Last Thursday, as is known, the deaf-mute woman Tova Fajgenblat was killed by the tram. The body was taken into the hospital, and there an autopsy was performed, because after all nobody bothered to see to it that the body of the poor woman should not be cut to pieces...
The scandal, however, lies in this: only on Friday, half an hour before candle-lighting, was the dead woman sent to the cemetery (the "house of life"); the one who drove the wagon was, of all people, a Christian, and when they arrived at the cemetery with the body there was nobody there to take the body down, and it remained in the wagon right until the end of the Sabbath...
And one asks: was it not the duty of the Rabbinate, may it live long, to see to it that such a desecration of the dead should not happen?...
— Where are the 30 kehilla representatives, the new and the old delegates of the community? Even in the smallest shtetl such a scandal would not happen — to disgrace a dead person like this just because the kehilla treasury receives nothing...
A group of readers.

3.
Esteemed Editorial Board!
Allow me to print the following report in your esteemed newspaper, for which I thank you in advance.
The Sosnowiec "Dobroczynność" (Charity) society, as every year, has organised a summer colony in Ujsoły (Rajcza district), where about 50 children, for the most part full orphans, enjoy the pure (printed "reyger") fresh air.
In connection with the rumours that had spread that the matter of kashrut is "limping" a little at the colony, I was delegated by the kehilla board. And here is what I saw with my own eyes:
At the colony kashrut is observed in the strictest manner, according to the law. The children have very good supervision, receive good care and feel as if in the lower Garden of Eden.
The order is exemplary; the manager of the colony, Miss Hofman, is like a devoted mother to the children.
One thing is greatly to be regretted: that a Jewish kehilla such as Sosnowiec takes so little interest in the fate of the poorest Jewish children, especially orphans, for whom no thought at all is given so that a large number of poor children could at least once a year enjoy healthy fresh air.
— A great responsibility lies upon the kehilla board, which does not find it necessary to give a decent subsidy for sending orphans to summer lodgings (printed "vagung" — probably "voynung").
It is very desirable that the notables of Sosnowiec should visit the colony of "Dobroczynność" and convince themselves of what is being done for forlorn Jewish children.
Respectfully,
Icze Zaks.
4.
To the esteemed editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
We earnestly ask you to print the following declaration in your esteemed newspaper, for which we thank you in advance.
The explanation by the Jewish Teachers' Union in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 31, that we did not lawfully justify our dismissal of the teachers in our school, is not true.
What is true, on the contrary, is that we lawfully and in good time gave notice terminating the contract with the Teachers' Union — a contract that had been made back in the school year 1929/30 and is in no way suited to today's hard economic times — on 26 April, according to point 6 of the contract.
The Teachers' Union, however, paid no heed to this and called a boycott of our cheder already in June, before they had even begun to negotiate with us about employing them further; this compelled us to place the advertisement in the "Express Zagłębia" of 11 July.
It is characteristic that in the same issue Z. G.[?] in which the advertisement about a boycott of our cheder appears, there are also the resolutions of the Teachers' Union at their 6th convention, among which is the following resolution:
"The convention of delegates declares once again that the cheders are a remnant of the Middle Ages, which maintain fanaticism in Jewish society and set back in the worst way the outlook, character and thought of the future citizens; they cause unheard-of damage to the children's health through their anti-hygienic conditions; in connection with this the convention calls for the liquidation of all cheders."
But that does not yet mean that we do not want to employ any Jewish teachers.
Further, it is not true that we did not pay the teachers their salaries (and when, God forbid, the payment was delayed by a few days, or when a few dozen złoty were missing from the full amount, which comes to about 2 thousand złoty a month — they went on strike...)
Also, one of our board members turned to the president of the Teachers' Union with a request that the Teachers' Union delegate 2 members to settle accounts with us, and if any money was due to them it would be paid out to them at once. To this request we have to this day received no answer.
As for the tactics and "respect" of the Teachers' Union toward the board, the management and the cheder in general, we do not wish to touch on that now, since we do not think it right to polemicise any further on this matter.
Respectfully,
The Committee of the Cheder "Yesodei HaTorah", Będzin.

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We have the honour to ask you to allow us to print the following in your esteemed newspaper, for which we thank you in advance:
On Sunday, the 26th of last month [26 July 1931], a report meeting of the artisans' parnassim (kehilla councillors) was held at the Artisans' Union in Dąbrowa concerning the planned campaign for a summer colony for schoolchildren.
Our parnas, Mr. Granatman, reports in detail (printed "gegnoy" = "genoy") on the planned campaign: how from the very first step he was put stones [in his way] and [they tried] not to allow the above-mentioned [colony], on the part of the Orthodox and other parnassim, on the pretext that the initiative came from a representative of the Artisans' Union — that was reason 1; and reason 2, because at a kehilla session he had declared that the kehilla is no more than, and remains, the "dead men's shtibl".
After these statements a storm of ovations broke out from the assembled artisans in favour of Mr. Granatman for his campaign, and of contempt for the obstructers of every kind.
The board of the Artisans' Union in Dąbrowa publicly declares that it agrees with the entire conduct of its parnas Mr. Granatman and with all his appearances in the kehilla, and wishes him to continue to lead the struggle in the kehilla in the same way.
Respectfully,
The Board of the Artisans' Union in Dąbrowa.

In connection with the declaration of the board of trustees (Kuratorium) of the Mizrachi school in Będzin (No. 30 of the "Z. Ts."), we consider it our duty to declare the following:

The meaning of sport as education.

(The sickly state of sport from the standpoint of children's upbringing. — This lawlessness must be reacted to.)
Now, when summer is at the very height of its blaze, when the sun and the plants and nature and everything around it calls to life, there awakens in every living creature the will to bloom and revive; and if nature and the sun and the field and the grasses and the waters call, entice and beckon to life and to the enjoyment of life, this belongs first and foremost to youth, to those before whom life ought to reveal itself in the most beautiful colours, in the richest fantasies.
Thanks to this very beauty of nature, various summer sports have arisen which give pleasure to young people. Thus, for example, the summer months are set aside for the most varied excursions, walking, swimming, football matches, etc.
It goes without saying that not all amusements suit everyone; not all can take pleasure in one and the same excursion, just as what is harmful to one is healthy for another. One must therefore be very, very careful not to take part in every sport one has a craving for. For example, not everyone can or may climb to the various heights of the mountains, just as not everyone can take part in races on bicycles or motorcycles.
The most popular sport among Jewish children, among the children of the broadest strata of the population, is football. All sorts of children, of the most varied ages and classes, have become attached to football matches, and it would therefore be worthwhile to dwell somewhat more broadly on this one branch and to treat the matter from all sides. It goes without saying that not all are suited to take part in football either — neither for reasons of health nor of physical build. In this field a terrible lawlessness reigns: there is no supervision whatsoever, nobody takes the trouble to see that everything is kept within certain bounds, and so demoralisation penetrates there, among Jews as well as among Christians.
How often do we hear of bloody brawls on the playing fields? How often do they play with their lives during the contests? How many times do the contests turn into bloody war-battles? And how often are we shaken when we hear of the most varied deeds, from which neither the parents nor the people derive any joy.
The most popular sport among Jewish children of various ages and strata is the football contest, and as such one must reckon with it. First of all a registration must be carried out, in order to check whether all are able to take an active part in the matches; then leaders of the section must be appointed who, under certain obligations, will guard and uphold various regulations that are to serve as formulas, so that the sport can be continued in such a way that it is truly sportsmanlike — and not as it has begun to take on the character of brawls and fights that turn the very nature of young people savage.
Football is truly a very simple [?] and pleasant pastime for the lovers of this branch, but it has begun to turn into such a kind of embittered fight that one no longer sees in it the sport at all, nor the pleasant amusement towards which sport strives. One must therefore consciously [?] reflect on the present situation and adopt all norms for beautifying and ennobling youthful amusement.
There is no point whatsoever in young people being without proper supervision, able to do whatever they like; in this way the demoralisation grows ever stronger and stronger, and sympathy for this pastime is lost. It would of course have been quite different if attention had been paid to the children and if they had been taught to keep within the bounds of sportsmanship. Then it would have taken on quite another character, and in this case it would not have come to the present low state of lawlessness, so that more than once the town takes fright when a match is due to take place between Jews and Christians — and quite often when it is a matter between Jews and Jews.
Let us not forget one thing: between youth and grown-up people there is a boundary of very great significance. Thus, for example, if mistakes are made in the social field by adults, it is not as dangerous as when it happens among youth, who have yet to be brought up. With children everything is bound up with upbringing, and upbringing, as we know, is very, very sensitive. So it is, for example, with sport too: if — let us say — the child understands sport otherwise than it is in reality, if vengeance and hatred on the playing field are implanted in the childish brain [?], this means that the child acquires a different notion of the beautiful, pleasant sport, and the little childish heart is poisoned with feelings of vengeance and with bloody fights in such a way that the idea of sport is not seen at all; and here one must come to the realisation that the child is being badly brought up in this field, that it is being spoiled in the true sense of the word.
With children, with school youth, everything is bound up with upbringing, and therefore one must be very careful with children. Because the matches are not properly taken care of by people who understand child psychology — because of this they have lost the true principle, and people have begun to forget that this is sport and pleasant amusement.
If we would take stock, if we would consider that children, whatever they may do, must be under proper supervision, the matches would not have taken on such a lawless character; and the results of this lawlessness we have already seen more than once.
Football is nowadays in such a sickly state that it must be radically cured. Young people do not understand at all the true meaning of this sport; it has simply taken on the character of brawls in the most dangerous manner, so that if all this is not reacted to properly, there is a chance it will be forgotten that football is a branch of sport. Soon its true form will no longer be visible.
After all, we have more than once had occasion to witness how knives flash at matches and blood — real human blood — is shed, as if it were a battlefield.
Can the leaders of the sports institutions look on calmly when they see how low the beautiful idea of sport has fallen? Is it a matter of indifference to them that on the one hand the true meaning of the idea of amusement is no longer seen, and on the other hand youth is being spoiled and acquiring a completely different view of what sport is, what football is?
The demoralisation has thus already broken the record, and it must not be allowed to go on like this: that would mean a crime against the sporting education of youth and a sin against the ideals of the sports clubs.
Let people think this over; let them dwell on the beautiful ideal, which must not be desecrated in the sense in which it finds itself today.
Dr. Papuri.

What One Heard, What One Saw.

What one heard, what one saw. Submitted by Ben Amotz.

Jewish chutzpah.
We, the “Thou hast chosen us” people, have, as everyone knows, created a great deal for the nations of the world; there is not a single field in which we do not gain the upper hand. Only one thing we ought to have learned from them, from other peoples:
— Derekh erets [manners]!
In this field we are unfortunately very backward [?], above all when it concerns Jewish matters. You will not, for example, see among any nation or tongue that, when a non-Jew is reading a newspaper in a railway carriage, another person should pull the middle part of the newspaper out of his hands without so much as a by-your-leave. The thought often occurs that if we had Jewish conductors, a large part of our brethren, the Children of Israel, would have the greatest grievances against them, against the conductors — namely: how come they are such villains as to demand tickets?...
A Jew has derekh erets only [printed “gur”] when he finds himself among gentiles; then his heart swells with joy when the non-Jew offers him his hand or says a friendly word to him; at the smallest thing the Jew is thrilled, and he will forever tell what honour he received there...
On the other hand, when “amkha” [the ordinary Jew] comes into a Jewish institution, there he feels like a “fish in water”: there he settles all his business, chatters about everything under the sun, takes a peek where one should not — why not? After all, one is among one's own...
And in connection with what did this come up?
You surely remember those times when there was a Jewish vice-president in the Będzin magistrate; the corridor was always full of our people, and every one of them had special grievances, grievances against the vice-president, because he is so bad and will not settle what somebody wants — such a scandal! A Jew a vice-president, and nothing. — “It would really have been better if a gentile sat in your place,” — this “prayer” was heard quite often...
And the “prayer” was answered: on the very same chair there now indeed sits a gentile, and
— it is hush-quiet...
Nobody dares to utter a loud word; all afflictions are accepted with love, let alone — as long as the gentile does not get angry. Surely, surely it is good and fine...
Different, however, is the situation up there, one floor higher: there, on the second floor, in the “Wydział Meldunkowy” [registration office], there also sits a Jewish (woman) clerk, and there you will hear how Jewish chutzpah gallops away... There you will hear “sermons” from our own [? “mishlanudige”], worse than the serious antisemites, addressed to the one and only Jewish clerk, because she, as an official, observes the regulations of her office.
And the Christian officials glow with delight when the “Moszek” [? Polish slur for a Jew] threatens her that he will go to the commissioner and ask him why he does not remove the “Żydówka” [the Jewess] from the magistrate.
And Kamtza does not remain in debt, but [printed “arer” = “oder”, or] his mission has no success: the commissioner, having heard out what “Moszke” wants, declares on the contrary that he wishes all officials fulfilled their functions as honestly as she, the “Żydówka”...
Kamtza leaves the commissioner's office in shame, and we see him off with the words:
— Jewish chutzpah...

Some woman...
In front of the hospital building on Third of May Square in Będzin a poor Jew sits and weeps. I become curious and ask an acquaintance:
— What happened here?
— Some woman was killed...
— Huh? How?
— Something with the tram...
Through the cold answer — and precisely from a Hasidic Jew — I am carried away by my thoughts far, far away, to that time when the human being, man, had [worth?] — once, in that time, when a slain man was found, the community brought an eglah arufah [the heifer of Deut. 21], the elders of the town went out beyond the town, measured the distance into the town, and they were happy when they could say with a quiet conscience:
— “Our hands have not shed this blood” — it is not we who are guilty of this innocently spilled blood...
Yes, that was once, in those “dark” times, but not in the twentieth century, when 10 million people were slaughtered like sheep — should a human life play any role?
Some woman was killed...
A dog plays a greater role nowadays than a human being; there are societies for the prevention of cruelty to animals, which see to it that no horse, dog or other four-footed creature should suffer any wrong, and it indeed happens quite often that a killed dog is lamented more in eulogies in the press than a human being, because the cheapest article today is — the human being, — cheaper than dog meat...
— Some woman...
We live in general in an epoch of cheapness: cheap art, cheap press, cheap literature and — cheap people.
— Some woman has been killed...

“Sport”.
The true meaning of the word we all know:
it means play, a pastime, gymnastic tricks, etc.
Life is hard, it lies like a heavy burden on one's shoulders. And from worries the body grows weak and old and bent, and in a weak body there is also a weak soul — so “sport” was invented: gymnastic exercises, bodily movement, strong muscles, and on top of it
— I am a contented Jew [idiom: “bin ikh mir a yid”]...
And as is our way, we Jews have taken over the plague of “sport” — or, to say it in the proper language, of football; it has eaten deep into our bones; sport already competes with the spirit; it is already one hundred percent “body” and not even one percent “soul”...
It is already coming to the point that football players will go out to battle armed: for scoring a “goal” in the “enemy's” camp one threatens with knives and irons — Złoczów, Radom and also the last match in Sosnowiec already say too much about what football has led to...
— Perhaps we might withdraw a little from this gamble which you call — “sport”?!...
The Situation of the Jewish Artisans

IV.
In all other fields people already know that if someone wants to create something, he must prepare himself for it; he must study in his youth and later perfect himself.
Abroad, especially in the Western countries, people long ago understood the need to educate the artisan class, and already decades ago artisans' courses and continuing-education courses came into being.
When setting up his workshop the young craftsman has illusions: everyone wants, and imagines, that he will set up his workshop as big and as modern as so-and-so's — but does he study, does he prepare himself to be [one]? There is a folk saying: "Everyone would like to be a doctor, but studying — that he doesn't feel like."
Everyone who engages in a craft must strive to be a conscious professional. The older craftsmen say: "I am already too old for that, for me all this is no longer relevant" — to which we answer with the old folk saying: "One is never too old to learn." Whoever sets himself the task of being an artist in his trade will certainly achieve it; but whoever says he cannot — he does not want to.
Have the journeymen thought about this: what must one know in order to pass a journeyman's examination, and what are the trade unions doing?
It is the task of the artisans' associations, of the guilds and of the trade unions to make their members aware that the craftsman must be raised to the level of an educated and artistic professional. It is their task to organise trade courses for older craftsmen and to see to it that their apprentices attend the continuing-education school.
We know that, owing to lack of funds, the associations cannot undertake broadly ramified work; but let them at least begin to do something. The support, and also the upkeep [?], must be taken on by the Jewish community [gmina], because the Jewish community is obliged to take on itself the initiative to found and maintain artisans' schools and continuing-education schools.
There is much talk about the restructuring of the Jewish population, about Jewry passing from trade and dealing to productive work — to the crafts; for however conditions may develop among the Jewish people, the artisan class will always be its core. Artisans will always occupy an honourable place not only among the Jewish people but among all other peoples too; the difference is that all other peoples long ago understood how to prepare the means to be able to train the artisan class.
We Jews — if we do not set about organising schools for artisans in good time and make an effort for artisans to be educated in the schools — will remain out of line, and we will have no artisans at all. To blame for this will be, first and foremost, the artisans' associations, the guilds and the professional journeymen's associations, as the directly interested parties; to blame also are the parents, who, when they apprentice a child to a craftsman, do not see to it that their child, once he has learned the craft, may be allowed to practise it.
But a very great responsibility will rest on the Jewish kehillas, which are indifferent to the question; they will not let themselves be convinced that an artisans' school is not a special artisans' affair but an affair that should concern the whole Jewish people.
Who does not remember how the artisans' representatives fought at the meetings of the kehilla council in Będzin to put into the budget a sum of 30 thousand zł. for building an artisans' school in Będzin. At that time a certain patron also promised to give the second 20 thousand zł. and undertook to collect another 30 thousand zł. from the notables of the town, if the community would take on the initiative and begin building with its 30 thousand zł. To this day absolutely nothing has been done to train the artisan class — whereas the future of the Jewish people depends to a great extent on the existence of the Jewish artisan class.
H. L. Goldsztajn.
Wonders of Technology

At the Leipzig Fair, which will be held from 30 August to 3 September, thousands of things will again be exhibited — among all sorts of little items which show, however, that the world is constantly striving to invent something new in all the needs of everyday life.
A few of the things that will be on view are worth mentioning.
An electric shaving apparatus.
There are hundreds of people who shave themselves. It is hygienic, practical, convenient and cheaper than going to the barber. But most people cut themselves while shaving, and so they constantly go about with nicked-up faces. Or they get fed up and return to the barber. The reason for cutting oneself lies in our nerves. Our hand lacks the steadiness always to guide the blade straight. Now we press a little harder, now a little weaker; now it is straight and now it is up to half a millimetre crooked — and that half millimetre already means that we cut into the flesh, or that we take off only the soap and not the hair of the beard.
— Now, for the first time, an electric shaving apparatus will be exhibited, just like the previous apparatuses, only with an electric battery which can be plugged into any lamp. The apparatus makes no crooked movements at all. It goes straight and can in no way cut; it is not nervous and presses neither harder nor weaker. With such an apparatus, which will cost very little, anyone can shave without any danger.
Hot sausages.
Today it is already possible everywhere, in gardens and in buffets, to get something to eat quickly. Automats dispense all sorts of foods, but no hot dishes. In Leipzig an automat that dispenses hot sausages will now be shown for the first time. In a kettle of boiling water sausages lie and cook; once they are done, the electric cooker can be turned off. When you throw in a coin, a paper plate drops out with a piece of bread and horseradish or mustard, and while the plate slides out, a fork lifts a couple of sausages out of[?] the boiling water and throws them onto the plate with the bread.
This automat can be set up anywhere there is an electric lamp from which the heat can be drawn to cook the sausages.
A typewriter with a thousand letters.
There are times for every person when something has to be typed on a typewriter — a necessary letter or a petition [„prosheniye“] must for various reasons be written by machine.
Sometimes one gets help from a neighbour who owns a typewriter, but the second time the neighbour already looks a little cross, and the third time he says the children have just broken it... And a typing bureau that takes in typing costs a fortune [lit. "the wealth of Korah"], and one does not always have one at hand.
The new typewriter which will now be exhibited at the Leipzig Fair will type a thousand letters — that is, about one page of paper — for only ten pfennig. You throw in the coin exactly as in any other automat, and you can type a whole page of a sheet of paper on it. If you have more to write, you must throw in another ten pfennig. These automatic typewriters will be set up at every post office, in every telegraph office, in cafés, in hotels, in associations, in banks — in short, everywhere people gather. For the ten pfennig the company will already carry out repairs if necessary, and will buy ink ribbons and everything else the machine needs.
Lampshades of wood.
Until now people knew of lampshades of glass, of cardboard or of silk. These were the only materials that could be used for the purpose, because these materials let the light through and the lamp could shine through the shade.
Glass, however, broke easily, paper tore, and silk frayed into thin threads, or at the very least became very dirty.
Now it has been discovered that very thin veneered wood lets light through, and at the Leipzig Fair lampshades of wood will now be shown for the first time, which can, of course, be washed whenever one likes; they do not break and do not tear, and a further advantage is that thanks to the veneer and the grain of the wood such a beautiful light is created that one is truly astonished when one sees it. This invention is capable of causing a great upheaval in the manufacture of lamps throughout the world.
Z. Haber
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Re'eh)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Re'eh
The Portion
—o—
a) "Behold, I" (Deut. 11:26).
"Re'eh anokhi" — see yourself, look deep into the "anokhi", into the "I", says the Zohar. For one of man's chief tasks is "le-minda yat garmeh" — to know oneself...
A Hasidic saying.
—o—
b) "If there arise in your midst... you shall not listen" (13:2, 4).
About the enticer and seducer against whom the Torah warns, "lo tishma" — do not listen to him — the Baal ha-Turim says that what is meant is... the woman, for the word "be-kirbekha" ["in your midst"] amounts [in gematria] to "zo ha-ishah" ["this is the woman"]; so the woman is the constant enticer and seducer, and against her the verse warns: lo tishma! Do not listen to her!...
—o—
c) "If he entices you" (13:7).
There once lived [?] in Russia an apostate, Yakov Brafman. He talked a shoemaker into converting for a couple of roubles. But the shoemaker kept getting poorer, because the shtetl boycotted him for his conversion; so he meets Brafman and complains to him: why, because of the conversion, has he become a pauper?
— Enough — answers Brafman — that I have earned you the World to Come; do you also want me to give you this world as well?...
• • •
Once a little Jewish girl came to Tsar Nicholas to plead for her father, against whom a blood libel had been provoked. With her tears the girl did indeed obtain an audience with the Tsar; but he shows her a crucifix and says:
— Give the bridegroom a kiss, little girl — and points out Jesus to her.
The girl stays embarrassed for a moment. But she answers at once: —
— With us Jews, however, the custom is that the bridegroom must first kiss the bride...
—o—
d) "For the poor shall never cease out of the land" (14 [sic; should be 15]:11).
God says: "The poor shall never cease out of the land" — I did not leave out the poor man from the whole world. That is: the world order is like a feast at which everyone was given equal shares, all equal portions; but some came and snatched their fellows' portions, climbed up to the top and pushed the "be-volhte" [?] [unclear word] off the table of the world order. That is what King David prays for (see Midrash Rabbah, Mishpatim): "May he sit before God for ever" — "may Your world sit in equality, the poor and the rich": let the world-table be set again with everyone equal... let the outcasts be brought back down [to the table]...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
e) "The Lord your God will surely require it of you."
"Ki darosh" — whatever you preach to another, "yidreshenu ha-Shem Elokekha me-imakh" — God will demand it from you yourself too. What you preach to another — observe it yourself as well...
Noam Megadim.
• • •
"So shall you put away the evil from your midst, and all the 'her' [sic; for 'people'] shall hear and fear"
If you remove "from your midst" — from yourself — all that is bad, then it will be: "and all the people shall hear and fear" — people will listen to you; but when the preacher himself is not in order with himself...
Rabbi Levi Yitzhak of Berdychiv.
—o—
The Haftarah
f) "Be far from oppression" (Isaiah 54).
Sins between man and his fellow are much graver than those between man and God.
Like that king who commissioned two painters to paint pictures for him: one — a landscape, and the other — his own portrait. Both pictures turned out badly, not true to life. The king ordered the first to take back the landscape, and the second — to break the picture and to arrest him. Because the first painted a landscape falsely — well, that can still be forgiven; but the latter distorted and falsified my own image, therefore I take such revenge on him.
Man is the image of God, and when he robs and murders he distorts God's image; it means then that man, who was created in the image of God, harbours base ways within him — that is, he has falsified the image of God...
Petah ha-Sha'ar.
—o—
g) "Why do you spend money for that which is not bread?" (ibid.).
In the Talmud informers are called "akhil kurtza bei malka" ["one who eats slander at the king's court"], i.e. the informer snatched a little feast at the lord's for whom he informed. Nowadays you inform, "tishkelu kesef" — you take Jewish money, and "be-lo lehem" — sometimes you do not even get a little feast at the squire's...
Beit Peretz.
—o—
Avot.
h) "Kinds of almsgivers" (5:13).
The Maggid of Dubno once comes to a rich man, a scholar. Well, the Maggid begins with words of Torah — the master of the house also tells him words of Torah. The Maggid begins to speak of charity — the scholarly rich man also speaks about the commandment of charity and adds more sharp-witted sayings. The Maggid sees that there will be no end to it — so he says:
— I will tell you a story. In a far-off country they did not know of onions, and when they saw an onion with a traveller they paid him a great deal of money for it. A second traveller hears of this and wanders there with garlic. In that country they did not know how to thank him for the precious kind he had brought them; they took counsel and paid him with the dearest thing they had: with onions...

What else one must know about the income tax

[Zagłębie — taxes; explanatory article on income tax. Followed by: Wolbrom — fire; Będzin — Hachnasat Orchim.] We consider it necessary to give a few more important explanations about the income tax, the assessment of which will soon begin.
Merchants who are now receiving notices of doubts from the urząd [tax office] asking them to submit supplementary explanations about their zeznanie [tax return] should keep these notices. This may be very useful should it become necessary to file an odwołanie [appeal].
If the office and the assessment commission take no account of the taxpayer's supplementary explanations and assess the tax higher, the office is obliged to notify the taxpayer of this before the assessment of the tax.
If this is not done, it is unlawful. So provides the judgment of the Supreme Administrative Tribunal, number 27—2592 of 20 May 1929.
— — —
It is also necessary to cite here the ministerial circular [okólnik] number 30—2460,2, in which the Ministry of Finance gives the following instructions on how to proceed in the new assessment of income tax.
The statute [ustawa] on income tax does not require the payer to keep official commercial books. To prove the true income it is enough to keep a simple book, even if the book is not kept according to the requirements of bookkeeping. The main thing must be that such bookkeeping be recognized as a sufficient document if it inspires confidence that it is kept correctly and genuinely.
Sufficient evidence of income must also be provided by submitting documents or notes, or by naming witnesses who can clarify the size of the income. The tax authority must hear the witnesses, examine the evidence and on that basis establish the size of the income. In doing so the opinion of experts must also be taken into account.
But if assessing the tax on these foundations proves impossible, only then should the income be estimated according to the average earnings on the basis of the Ministry of Finance's earnings lists for each branch. In this one must be very careful and consider separately in each particular case how far the system of average earnings can be applied.
Every merchant can rely on this circular and demand that witnesses be heard about his income, or that the documents and books he has submitted be examined, concerning his income for the year 1930.
— — —
A very important problem in assessing the income tax is the deduction from income of the various expenses provided for in Art. 10 of the statute. The assessment commission estimates the size of the income, and the office collects the income tax due on the estimated income. In doing so they forget to deduct all the sums, such as expenses for insurance, for taxes, for interest and debts, for discount, etc. The office takes the assessment as net, whereas it is actually gross, and from it the expenses for the items mentioned must be deducted.
Adv. G. Gr.

A vigorous distraint campaign for tax arrears is being prepared

On His Deathbed He Divorced His Wife for the Third Time.

[Częstochowa — a get.] Last week the Częstochowa rabbinate was alarmed about a get (bill of divorce) for a mortally ill man who was in his death throes.
The story goes like this:
At Garncarska Street 64 lived the couple Yisrael K. and his wife Teltse, both aged 27, who had married for the first time in 1920. Their life together, however, was not a happy one, and a few months after the wedding they divorced. Only a few weeks passed and they married again, but after 4 weeks of living together they divorced for the second time, and again the couple remarried a few weeks later.
Recently Yisraelke, a locksmith by trade, caught a chill at work and fell ill with a lung disease. His illness grew steadily worse, so that death was inevitable, and since they had no children Teltse would have had to undergo halitza — and Yisraelke's only brother is in America. So his wife's mother came running to the rabbinate, begging them to take pity and write a get, and as quickly as possible, so that she would not be left bound to halitza.
The attic room on Garncarska Street is crowded with people. The families of both sides have gathered, neighbours and plain curious onlookers. The sick man breathes heavily and watches the ceremony. The scribe begins to write the get, and the wife's family keeps urging the scribe to finish the get as fast as he can.
Suddenly, while they were writing the fourth line, the sick man grew weak and turned to the wall; they thought he was about to die any moment, and there was an uproar with shouts to the dayan to take pity and give the get at once.
But a "miracle" happened: the sick man felt a little better, the scribe and the witnesses finished the get, and the dying Yisraelke the locksmith divorced his wife on his deathbed for the third time.
— — —
The next day Yisraelke the locksmith breathed his last.

Killed for Singing German Songs.
On the night from Saturday to Sunday several persons sat in a night-spot in Siemianowice, getting drunk and singing German songs.
Against this the porter (woźny) of the local tax office protested; after a sharp exchange of words he went off home, where he took his revolver.
In the street he met one of those who had sung the songs, and with 4 revolver shots he laid him dead.
The murderer has been arrested.

A Terrible Rainstorm.
On Sunday evening a rainstorm accompanied by heavy thunder and lightning swept over Katowice.
A thunderbolt struck in the area of the “Eminenz” coal mine; the electric telephone wires were torn by the blow.

Under a Load of 800 kg.
At the Baildon steelworks beyond Katowice a worker fell under an iron roller weighing 800 kilos. The worker was crushed.

He Wanted to Dig Up a Few Potatoes and Found His Death.
An unemployed man from Siemianowice went out to the Czeladź fields, where in the evening hours he wanted to dig up a few potatoes for himself.
The owner of the field fired and killed the “potato thief” on the spot...

77-Year-Old Woman Dies of Hunger.
In Racibórz (Ratibor) a local resident, an old woman of 77, was found lying dead in her bed; all her life she had lived in poverty and occupied herself with begging.
In her poor bed a savings book for several thousand zł., a thousand German marks and a large sum of worthless banknotes were found.

2 Fatal Motorcycle Accidents.
On Sunday evening a terrible catastrophe occurred near Cieszyn. The Jewish resident of Katowice Mr. Silberstein set out on a motorcycle to Cieszyn and at a certain moment ran into a tree. The motorcycle was damaged and Silberstein was killed on the spot.
The same day a second tragic motorcycle catastrophe occurred, and here too the victim was a Jew, the Katowice merchant Winer.
Winer was riding through Freistadt (Frysztat) in Cieszyn Silesia. Since the railway barrier had not been closed, he drove at full speed into a passenger train and perished on the spot.

A Spy Arrested.
By order of the authorities the grocer (colonial-goods merchant) Rosner, who is accused of espionage, has been arrested in Katowice. Through a mistake of the post office a letter addressed to someone else was dropped into Rosner's letterbox. The letter contained important information which could have been of value to a neighbouring state. Rosner read the letter and worked out what to do: he went to the German consul, where the letter was duly made use of. Later he returned the letter to the post office, but there they suspected that the letter had been exploited. They therefore put Rosner to the test and “by mistake” sent him another secret letter, this time with false information. Rosner carried this letter too to the German consul, and then he was arrested.

Theatre Notes

[Zagłębie — theatre (review).]
“The Accursed One”
A drama in 3 acts by Sofia Biela
(from Samberg's guest performances in Zagłębie).
A former prostitute marries a man who is himself not pure as an angel either.
He is arrested for squandering other people's money; to free the arrested man a larger sum is needed, and the woman obtains the sum from an old, extraordinarily ugly usurer, whom people call “the Accursed One”, at the price of physical intercourse.
As the product of this relationship a child is born, whom the mother hates very much.
The “Accursed One” constantly pursues the woman, demanding that she come to him with the child. She rejects his proposals with disgust, and in revenge the usurer tells the husband everything and demands the child. At that moment the woman shoots the “Accursed One” dead.
The content of the drama is a very banal one; it is literary trash of the worst sort; there is in it no logic [“ligie”] whatsoever, no tendency whatsoever — just anything at all.
Samberg was excellent in the role of the “Accursed One”; he had a brilliant make-up mask, which recalls the brilliant Lon Chaney in “The Hunchback of Notre Dame” (“The Bell-Ringer of Notre Dame”).
Samberg possesses a wonderful diction; his words are as if hewn from granite, and he leaves an unforgettable impression on the spectators.
It is only regrettable that an actor like Samberg chose a bad drama, and moreover such an ensemble, which with its “acting” brought in a terrible dissonance.
Sh. R.
