The Educational Institutions and the Teaching Staff

[Zagłębie — education; article: educational institutions and teachers.]
(Harmful things that ought to be concealed from the public.)
For a good several weeks now the columns of our newspaper have been unable to free themselves of the "letters to the editor", statements, appeals and clarifications from teaching staffs against their schools and, conversely, from the schools against the cheders, which pour out their hearts and show how hard it is, under the prevailing conditions, to run the educational institutions.
The teachers cry out that they are owed money for many months and that they have no possibility of setting aside larger sums, which they earn by the sweat of their brow; the managements and committees cry out, conversely, that the teachers are obstinate and will hear of nothing — if they are not paid off to the minute and second, they at once threaten strikes and boycotts, so that the people in charge tremble before the teachers just like fish in water.
First and foremost, then, it is important to know clearly and plainly, without hair-splitting, without any combinations, whether the teachers have earned debts [owed to them] or not, whether their salaries ("pensions", Pol. pensje) are paid according to the agreement, or whether the managements stay in arrears. This is important to know in order to hear where the frictions stem from: whether from the fact that they [the teachers] consider themselves dictators and can do with the institutions as they please, or possibly that larger amounts are due to them and they [the institutions], even with the best will, are not in a position to keep up [?] with the institutions. This must be known once and for all; it must at long last be said plainly and clearly. Only then can one know how to react to the undesirable phenomena.
And who knows, perhaps it really is the other way round; perhaps the managements and committees think themselves so grand that, being in a position to exploit the teaching staff, they do so, without giving themselves any account of what consequences this may bring in the future. And therefore it is important here first of all to know who is fighting against whom, who wants to rule dictatorially over whom.
That, then, is what should have been established before people went out into the street with the quarrels, before they went out to the press with the statements, which bring honour to neither side.
One must after all consider the state of affairs and the circumstances in which both the institution and the educators find themselves as soon as one shows, so to speak, the dirty laundry before the public.
Cheders, schools, teachers, committees — these are after all educators, and educators as such must always reckon with the public. One must after all, at long last, not forget what shape an educational institution takes on as soon as the quarrels are carried out into the street, as soon as everyone can see what is cooking in the pot and how...
And here is where both sides are guilty: because whatever the case, carrying it out before the public should not have been allowed; both sides ought to have been ashamed to carry out into the street all these fine "little flowers", which bring so much shame on the teachers and the establishments alike. And the better parents, the more conscious ones, shake off such "intensive activity"; and what can be said about the average parents, who have a scant notion of what education is — they lose their respect for the teachers and the establishments alike after they read through these "letters to the editor" which say so much. And let us also give a thought to the fact that nowadays the children too read a newspaper — what impression do all these stories leave in the children's souls when they read such things in the press? How can children then have good manners and reverence for their educators, as soon as they see on what road those have set out who are supposed to show them that all this is harmful?
We do not know, of course, who is right here and who is not, who has greater claims against whom; but one thing must be established here: that both sides should not have allowed things to come to the present state, and even more [printed "more more"] not to the point that all this should be told frankly and freely before the street, before the public.
Could no way out really have been found, so that the quarrels and the undesirable matter — undesirable both for the public and for the institutions and teachers — would find an echo only within four walls? Would that not have been healthier in this case, and more practical, and more restrained, and also more expedient? Can one not get along better among oneselves when one sits down at the green table and deals with the painful questions calmly and in full awareness, rather than letting the most varied claims and counter-claims, with all sorts of harmful complications, out into the wind, which can bring nothing but harm? Where then is the logic, and in what does the restraint consist? Perhaps the disease will be cured by the fact that the management of "Yesodei HaTorah" has begun to drag the affair into the Polish press, to seek Christian teachers in the "Expr. Zagł." [Expres Zagłębiowski]? Is that, then, to be the remedy for the wound?
Yes, that is how it is when one lets oneself onto slippery roads, when one does not calculate in advance what will be later; otherwise one could have foreseen that the means are harmful and will bring no benefit and no good — neither to the teachers nor to the institutions.
One must after all not forget that with educational institutions one may not go out into the street frankly and freely as with "babes" [old women / market wives]. Education is, after all, a rather deeper problem, over which one ponders day and night how to reach the desired goal.
Certainly all this should not have been carried out before the public; certainly the responsibility was a great one; but undoing what has happened is a matter of impossibility. Yet even now there is no other counsel than to take the practical road, and practical means being honest and open-hearted, so that for this purpose one must sit down at the green table and deal from all sides with the just and unjust claims, so that, with good will on both sides, a settlement can be reached that will satisfy both the educational enterprises and the teaching staff.
There would be nothing wrong in it [lit. "it would make no difference"] if both sides wanted to understand the seriousness of the situation and neither of them wished to rule dictatorially over the other.
R. Let.
The "Żołądek" of Piaski also has a big appetite...

[Zagłębie — bigamy; a warning.] In No. 28 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" we reported the "fine" deeds of a certain Żołądek [Polish for "stomach"], who is in the business of setting up wedding canopies.
But as it turns out, we in Zagłębie also possess such a heroic "Żołądek", who has a past in the field of setting up wedding canopies...
Here Mrs. Fajgla Krycler of Żarki[?] reports to us the following fact:
Eleven years ago Mr. Gecel K. married a girl from Żarki. After living with her for 8 years he left and married a second one, from Szarlej. With this woman he lived 3 years, and after that [he left], taking a little cash from her.
The "jewel" went off to his father in Piaski, and now he wants a "reward" from the abandoned wives...
Mrs. Krycler warns Jewish parents to be careful with this person. His marks: a tall, blond man; he is missing three fingers of his right hand.
Two who hold on to a pipe...

[Feuilleton — humour; summer resort.] When a wife comes back from a spa resort and brings her husband a present — a pipe with her name carved on it — that seems quite nice on her part; but when she also brings her "acquaintance" exactly the same kind of pipe, that is no longer so nice, and above all — not clever.
Then again, one can find excuses for the heroine of the story. Could she have expected that the two of them would meet over one pipe?...
The husband goes for a couple of hours to a relative of his, who lives not far from the dacha [summer villa]. There they invite him, on another veranda, to be the "fourth hand" in a game of "telefon"[?] [apparently a card game]. Suddenly he sees one of the players smoking a papieros [cigarette] in "his" pipe. He reaches for his pocket — it really isn't there, and he immediately turns to the other man:
— Excuse me, that is my pipe, I have only just lost it.
— You are mistaken, sir — the other man turns pale...
In short: they start tearing the pipe from each other until they break it, and both get something extra into the bargain — mutual slaps.
The husband comes home nervous and no longer wants to tell his wife anything. But then she hands him the pipe — whole — and even smiles while she does it:
— Very nice, my husband: the present I brought you had simply rolled away under the table...
Only now did he grasp that she had brought two little pipes from the resort — and the bomb went off.
The finale: instead of smoking the pipe, he would rather "smoke out" his wife...
Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — weekly feuilleton; Siewierz, Olkusz, Gołonóg.] (When you have no luck — a "find" under the mezuzah[?]. — Like modern Hittites. — A happy little town. — A Jewish councillor with a gentile soul. — Householders[?] over aliyot — the police have worked.)

It is a well-known thing that "the bit of luck is above everything" — just success and nothing more. "Even a Torah scroll in the Ark needs luck"; and because Siewierz, poor thing, has no luck, the local kehilla treasury is "black as the earth", and the Chevra Kadisha [burial society] is tearing itself to pieces —
— because they have no luck...
And one fine morning the Chevra Kadisha in Siewierz receives "the joyful news" that there is a "little pike" [a fat catch] — or, more correctly, a "big pike".
— A rich baker-woman from Ząbkowice has died.
The mood among the society men was very elevated; no wonder — a whole round year they sit without a stroke of work, and here such a gain!... An unexpected salvation, upon my life!...
So the society gathered and held a meeting at which the price was fixed:
— Six hundred złoty; not a grosz less than six hundred złoty to be taken for the plot.
In the middle of the meeting a messenger burst in, who could barely get the words out:
— They're coming! Here they are already!
Indeed it was not long before the sons of the deceased arrived on bicycles, and the negotiations began, much like those of the children of Heth with our forefather Abraham.
At the head sat the "al gabehen" [the official in charge] at his ease, stroked his beard, and innocently explained to the orphans that for the plot their mother would receive from the children of Heth in the Siewierz cemetery, one must "give" six hundred.
— "And they answered", said the orphans from Ząbkowice: gentlemen, we will give you 200 zł.
The children of Heth replied: no, that is what it costs — not less than six hundred złoty.
— Perhaps 300, 400?
— No — nothing else.
Said the men of Ząbkowice: if so, we must go home to our father and ask him whether we should pay the sum demanded.
— Go home, we'll wait, God be with you — said the children of Heth.
The orphans indeed left and never came back; they took their dead to Kromołów and left the Siewierz people holding their "bundle"...
Now the people of Siewierz run around as if poisoned: how could it be? What have we done, letting such a kosher find slip away to Kromołów?
But shout today, shout tomorrow — when there is no luck, nothing at all helps...
— — —
If Siewierz possessed such a "public worker" as the well-known Olkusz councillor, I am sure the whole world would have envied it — the Siewierz kehilla, that is.
Here before us lies a letter from a group of Jewish children, from Będzin Jewish girl-patients, who beg us with tears in their eyes to make known "all over the world" the heroic deeds of the Olkusz public worker and councillor, comrade Hashkome-blat...
On Saturday afternoon a group of "letniki" [summer holiday-makers] were strolling in the forest, as is the custom: one laughs, one sings — why not? A whole round year Jewish children are sunk in troubles; so one goes out into the open air, jokes and pretends to be merry, to show the world that —
— we live too...
At that moment councillor Hashkome-blat was also strolling in the same forest, and when the Jewish "man of the people" saw and heard how Jewish children were enjoying the "świeże powietrze" [fresh air] and even had the nerve to sing, he could not bear it; patriotic feelings awoke in him and he opened his mouth and delivered a speech in the style of "dwa grosze" ["two groszy"], just as befits a "man of the people"...
He, the Jewish councillor, who sees to it that not one blade of grass is taken from the municipal gospodarstwo [economy], was not content with his patriotic performance and called a policeman, who "invited" several Jewish girls from Będzin into the commissariat [police station], where, on the intervention of the "pan radny miasta" [Mr. City Councillor], reports were drawn up...
— Well, are we wrong when we say how good it would have been for the Siewierz Chevra Kadisha if they had possessed such a hero as the Olkusz councillor known as Hashkome-blat?
— — —
The report from the holy community of Gołonóg simply revived me. We thought the crisis, may its name be blotted out, had caught every place in its net; but in the end it turns out there is still a happy community "whose name is Gołonóg", where the crisis has not the slightest influence and "amkho" [the common folk] busy themselves with the old affairs as before, as in the good, well-fed years, and the only worry of a Gołonóg resident is just:
— to get an aliyah [call to the Torah]...
And getting an aliyah in the Gołonóg beis midrash is not one of the easy things; it is easier there to get a few wounds in the head than an aliyah...
The "aliyah-thirsty" have even tried to organise an early-morning minyan, but that did not save the situation either, because the demand is great and there are, after all, no more than 7 aliyot...
So things there really get dark: Jews fight with irons, bottles, lamps, and —
— the police write reports.
— Happy are you, men of Gołonóg, that you have "nothing to do" with the crisis...
Ben Amotz.
The Jewish Mother Is to Blame

[Zagłębie — education; article.] The Jewish mother is to blame for the fact that one of the greatest dangers threatens us: that our young Jewish generation is being torn off the branch of the old Jewish tree and handed over to assimilation. We must begin a tireless campaign of enlightenment in order to open the eyes of our Jewish mothers and prove to them that they commit the most terrible crime against their own children when they do not raise their children in the Jewish national spirit in the Jewish school. It is truly impossible to understand how the same mother who makes the greatest sacrifices to raise [printed "איפצוציען"] a child that is healthy in the physical sense — that same Jewish mother cripples the soul of her own child. How much the Jewish mother sacrifices herself when times are at their worst, and yet the child must, for the most part, spend a few weeks in the fresh air. How many preparations are made for this, with how much trouble it sometimes comes about — and yet, for the child's health it is necessary, and it must be as the mother wishes: the child must go away for a few weeks to draw fresh strength.
That same Jewish mother is one of the most light-minded mothers in the world when it comes to bringing up her child. Here her clear, pure understanding no longer plays a role, nor the maternal instinct that ought to show her how she must educate her child, how she must shape her child's soul so that it will be strong and able to hold out in the storm of life. It is true that one must care for the child's body, but it is no less true that the child's spirit, its soul, must receive the necessary nourishment, the necessary education, so that a healthy person in the full sense of the word may grow out of it. And the child, as we know, is educated at school. Can it be a question for any mother in the world that her child must be educated in her own national school? There, where the national spirit, national pride and national dignity of the child are cultivated, its attachment to its own stock, to its own people. Can it be a question, for any mother in the world, that her child must be brought up in a warm environment of love and sympathy?
Can it be a question that at school the child must feel as at home, sometimes even better than at home; the child must be able to develop freely there; for it the school is not only a place where it learns, but chiefly a place where it meets and lives its life with schoolmates, boys and girls.
The young people at school live together in close circles of friendship, which sometimes have an effect on their whole life. This is possible only in our own national schools; only here is there mutual understanding and love between children and teachers. The children are attached to the Jewish school; for them attending school is a pleasure. Unfortunately not all Jewish schoolchildren find themselves in this happy situation. A large part of Jewish youth is sent to non-Jewish schools, where the child already in the first years of its life tastes the bitter drop merely because it is a Jew: instead of love it feels hatred, instead of sympathy it feels rejection, both from the teacher and from its own classmates; its national dignity is trampled underfoot at every step; the child is regarded as something inferior, and when it shows great abilities it is reproached with "Jewish cunning", "Jewish chutzpah". And it is in such atmospheres that a great number of Jewish girls are being educated in Zagłębie. For their future is decided mainly by the Jewish mother, while the son is mostly looked after by the father, who will not allow him to grow up an ignoramus (am ha-arets). That is the reason why in some non-Jewish schools in Zagłębie there are up to 50 per cent Jewish pupils.
It is worth the Jewish mother's while to reflect now, in the holiday season, whether she is not committing a great wrong against her own daughter. It cannot be allowed that, while we have in Zagłębie an excellent Jewish gymnasium for girls, which turns out year after year dozens of matriculants ("maturas") and educates the youth in the national-Jewish spirit, at the same time an enormous number of Jewish girls should be assimilated — with our own money — in non-Jewish schools.
The women's [girls'] gymnasium in Sosnowiec is this year setting about building its own building according to the most modern requirements of present-day pedagogy; the number of pupils grows from day to day; something truly imposing can be created. All this can happen only with joint forces. Every Jewish mother should consider it a matter of her honour, of her pride, that her daughter be educated in such a school.
Elen.
A Remedy for Jewish Troubles.

[Feuilleton; satire.] (A Chatter).
Mazel tov, Jews! I can announce good tidings to you: the Jewish question has been solved. All for nothing we tormented ourselves some two thousand years in exile, let ourselves be killed, pogromed and driven out [?], bought ourselves a world of enemies, beginning with Amalek and Haman and down to a Passfield, the Grand Mufti and Nowaczyński. How could it have happened that so clever a people could find no counsel for itself, could find no cure for its plague? Truly incomprehensible. People toiled [?] and built new theories about the "eternal hatred for the eternal people", about the causes of antisemitism. But all in vain — and how remarkably, how simply, how astonishingly easily Bernard Shaw has found the cause!
Who is Bernard Shaw? Bernard Shaw is the greatest English writer of our time. Although, to tell the truth, I have not yet read a single one of his works (I believe his fame will not be diminished by so much as a hair because of it), people say he is a great head, "one in his generation". When he says a witticism, it is carried at once over all five continents; at a paradox of his all nations lick their fingers. Bernard Shaw took a fancy to travel to Soviet Russia and take a look at what Stalin's kingdom looks like. No sooner said than done, and he is already in Russia. Incidentally, it was very, very unkind of him that while passing through Warsaw he would not even get off the railway carriage and visit our capital. But that is not what I am driving at.
But how does he come to the Jewish question? Don't be hasty, I shall tell you everything. Bernard Shaw is a great man, and as soon as one is a great man, says my aunt Tsipe, he must be a Jew. So she believes that Graf Zeppelin, Mussolini, Marconi and whatever their names are, are Jews.
Evidently our JTA [Jewish Telegraphic Agency] holds this opinion too: that as soon as it is a great man, either he himself must be a Jew, or one must hear his opinion about Jews.
So the Moscow JTA correspondent indeed did not hesitate and asked the great Bernard what his opinion is regarding us Jews. And although he does not like answering correspondents, for a Jewish correspondent he made an exception, and here is what he said, the great, the clever, the unexpected thing: that our whole trouble is that we suffer from a superiority feeling. In mother tongue that means we consider ourselves above other nations — hence our exile, hence our troubles! Well, is that not brilliant? Are not all the inquiries and philosophies concerning Jewish suffering sheer foolishness compared with this revelation? And it is so simple, so simple. Thus spoke the brilliant Bernard Shaw.
Therefore we must congratulate one another; let us think it over well [printed "גיט"] what he meant by it — and we are saved!
Jewish merchants, if, for instance, a large turnover tax is imposed on you, do not complain, do not write any appeals. Remember that you must uproot from yourselves the superiority feeling, and you will be helped. Further: Jewish unemployed, do not ask and do not demand to be taken on in government posts. Remember that your misfortune is the superiority feeling, and you will be helped. Jewish manufacturers, do not ask for credit from the government banks, because that has to do with the superiority feeling. Jewish teachers, do not ask for posts in the public elementary schools ("powszechne"), because it may awaken your superiority feeling. Jewish schools, do not demand any rights, because that is superiority; and finally, Jews, do not demand a land of your own, because that is surely superiority.
Happy are we that Bernard Shaw has shown us the way. We have been redeemed. What exile? What troubles? Bernard Shaw's name must be inscribed in golden letters in our history. He has honestly earned it...
Edgar.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. D.[?]
Parashat Shoftim
The Portion
—o—
"Judges and officers shalt thou make thee" (Deut. 16:18)
a.
Even "thee" — even for you who "make" him a rabbi, even you who seated him on the "pisse ha-rabbanut" [misprint for kisse ha-rabbanut, the rabbinic chair] — for you, too, he shall be rabbi... You, too, he is obliged to admonish, and you are obliged to obey him... Torat Moshe.
b.
Most quarrels between people come about because everyone measures his fellow with a different measure than himself. What he sees in another as wrongdoing and injustice is, when he does it himself, kosher and upright. Against this it is said: "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee" — the same judgment you apply against your fellow, apply also to "thee", also with regard to yourself... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
b) "Thou shalt not wrest judgment" (16:19)
"If you saw a Torah scholar commit a sin at night, do not suspect him by day — he has surely repented [asah teshuvah]" (if you see a Torah scholar commit a sin at night, do not brood over it, for he has surely done penance).
Do not brood over the Torah scholar who committed a sin — "he surely made a teshuvah": he has probably written a "teshuvah" [a rabbinic responsum] in which he proves with evidence from the Talmud that it is no sin at all... After all, can one not declare even a creeping thing pure with 150 reasons?... A popular saying.
—o—
c) "For a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise" (ibid.)
A rabbi of a small town, about whom people murmured that he took bribes, went deaf in his old age. People ask: according to the Torah one should go blind from bribes, but not deaf.
A clever Jew answers:
A rabbi who sees the bribe before his eyes does indeed go blind; our rabbi was only promised bribes, but he never saw what was promised before his eyes — so he only went deaf in the ears...
—o—
d) "Justice, justice shalt thou follow" (printed 17:20; actually 16:20)
Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan [Spektor], the famous Rabbi of Kovno [Kaunas], was once asked why in Kovno, where there are more pious Jews than freethinkers, the freethinkers nevertheless win every public dispute.
He answers: in every dispute the truth wins. Well, the freethinkers are free in truth and with a whole heart, whereas the pious are not truly pious... therefore the former win.
* * *
In the company of the Chiddushei ha-Rim [R. Yitzchak Meir Alter of Ger], Hasidim were discussing: why is Warsaw, which was then a city of nothing but pious Jews, known[?] all over[?] as full of real "Daytshn" ["Germans", i.e. modernised, assimilated Jews]?
To this the Chiddushei ha-Rim says: because even in every pious man there is also a "little German", that is, he too possesses a certain percentage of "Germanness". Well, measuring by "akhut" [so printed; probably meant: quantity], there are more "Germans" in Warsaw: the genuine "Germans" (in whom there is surely no "little Hasid") — and with the "Germanness" of the Hasidim there is here an outright majority of "Germans"...
—o—
e) "And that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand or to the left" (17:20)
The leader was told not to take away from the word "mitzvah" [מצוה] its right (the letter mem) and its left (the letter he), for these letters form one word: "mah" [what], which signifies humility and lowliness; without the "mah" the "mitzvah" is a mere "tzav" [צו], which means idolatry... A mitzvah done with pride is like serving idols... Or Yesharim.
* * *
"A haughty stride takes away one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight."
"A haughty stride" — a single step in arrogance makes a person blinder... Rabbi Aharon of Keidanov [Kėdainiai].
—o—
f) "Thou shalt be wholehearted with the Lord thy God" (18:13)
Some disharmony prevails between God and the Jew. When the Jew is content with himself and has every good thing, God is not content, because "Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked" — "when the oats prick him"... When God is content, when the Jew is pious, then the Jew is not content, since he is pious only when he is in great trouble...
"Thou shalt be wholehearted with the Lord" — see to it that you finally make it up with God, so that both of you are content with each other at the same time... Ohel Yaakov.
Haftarah.
—o—
g) "For his people is taken away for nought" (printed Isaiah 21; the verse is Isaiah 52:5, "my people")
God sold us as slaves for nothing, because He thought it was only for a short time: we would repent and return to the Land of Israel. Had He known it would be for thousands of years, He would at least have enslaved us for money, so that we would at least get something from our work for strangers... Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
—o—
h) "When the Lord returneth to Zion" (ibid.)
"The meaning of the days of the Messiah is: when the Jews again become a kingdom and return to the Land of Israel, and all the verses say of it that the Messiah will succeed and we Jews too. And nothing at all will change from what is now, except only that the Jews will have a kingdom."
Thus did Maimonides (in his Commentary on the Mishnah: Sanhedrin, chapter Chelek) conceive the Jewish redemption.
Avot.
—o—
i) "And live a life of hardship" (printed 6:5; in Avot it is 6:4)
His wife came to the well-known Rabbi of Mir, R. Eliyahu Baruch [Kamai], and quarrelled with him: there is such want at home, and she worries about it a whole week, while he only sits and studies and knows no worry at all.
He answers her: I will tell you the reason. People say of me that I am sharp-witted [a charif]. What is the difference between a charif and an ordinary person? What the ordinary person attains through a week of study, the charif grasps in an hour. Well, now you can understand why one hour of worry is enough for me over what you need a week for...
—o—
j) "And live a life of hardship — and toil in the Torah" (ibid.)
If you live a life of hardship, you will indeed sit and study... Chasdei Avot.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: How the Kehilla Budget Was “Cut” at the Ministry

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla, budget.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 1 / 1 Elul 5691 — piątek 14 sierpnia 1931 [Friday, 14 August 1931].)
Będzin
How was the kehilla budget “cut” at the Ministry?
On Wednesday the gmina [Jewish community] finally received back the budget, approved by the Ministry of Religious Affairs.
A series of changes was made in the budget, among them: 1) the 13th salary for all kehilla employees has been struck out, because of the economic crisis; 2) the salary for the rabbinate secretary has been struck out entirely, the reason given being that the gmina already has enough employees and there is no need to engage new employees at the present time; 3) the subsidies for “YIVO”, “Muze” [?] and a gratuity for Rebbetzin Graubart — struck out, because “the subsidies exceed the competence of the gmina”; 4) all subsidies for public and philanthropic institutions from the year 1930 have been struck out; among the struck-out subsidies is also the subsidy for the orphanage, in the amount of 16,000 zł.; 5) the subsidy for the “Gmilas Chesed” fund has been reduced from 2 to 1,000 zł. All other subsidies have also been considerably reduced.
In total the budget has been reduced by a sum of 67,500 zł.
According to the Ministry's proposal, the sum must be entered in the coming budget as a balance carried forward (“saldo konta”).
Memorandum of the “Merchants' Association” against the New Loan of the Local Commissioners' Council

[Będzin — municipality, trade.]
In connection with the fact that the commissioners' council has resolved to take a loan of 400 thousand zł. and with that sum to build the sewerage collector, the local “Merchants' Association” has turned with a memorandum to the Voivode.
The memorandum reads as follows:
To the Voivode in Kielce.
We learn from the local press that the provisional head (kierownik) of the town of Będzin intends to take a loan to build a sewerage collector, which is to serve the new buildings that have been built by the insurance company in Lwów; the loan with the interest is to be repaid over 15 years in the amount of 660,00 zł.
We therefore draw attention:
1) that taking the loan is contrary to article 66, point 5, of the decree on self-government.
2) at a time of such a crisis the town is to be burdened with a debt of 660,000 zł. solely for the benefit of the above-mentioned company.
For this reason it is requested not to approve the loan
The Synagogue Committee Rises from the Dead”...

[Będzin — the synagogue.]
Because of the approaching holidays, the plan arose to elect a synagogue committee, which is to “keep order in the synagogue” and, above all, to let out the synagogue seats.
A meeting on this matter was held of the old dozors [kehilla board members] and several synagogue worshippers, and after a discussion which lasted 2 hours it was resolved to nominate a synagogue committee.
At the very first meeting of the synagogue committee changes already arose concerning the persons [?]: old ones were disqualified and new ones nominated, so that fresh quarrels among the synagogue worshippers are to be expected.
Protest against Calendar Reform

[Będzin — Kehilla, religion.]
The president of the Warsaw kehilla, Mr. Farbstein, has turned to the local kehilla board that a protest resolution be adopted against the project to reform the calendar.
A Fight between Mother and Son

[Będzin — street life.]
The residents of Zamkowa Street witnessed a sensation on Tuesday. A son lay in wait in the street for his mother, against whom he has grievances, and treated her to... a “gift of the hand”.
The mother, however, is no “sleepyhead” either, and paid her son back with interest...
A Court Inspection at the Mikveh

[Będzin — Kehilla, courts.]
As is known, a lawsuit is being conducted by the kehilla board with Messrs. Zajberman [?] and Jakubowicz, who come forward with a claim as heirs to the plot of the mikveh building.
On the 31st of this month the court will come to the site and publicly establish whether the heirs' claim is justified or not.
The President of the State Passes Through

[Będzin — the state.]
On Tuesday at 10 o'clock in the morning the President of the State, Ignacy Mościcki, passed through on his way to Spała.
In Gzichów the proprietress of the restaurant presented the President with a bouquet of fresh flowers.
Received a 'gift' from above...
From a balcony in Steier's house on Modrzejowska Street a piece of wood fell down and wounded Mr. Akiva Arushal[?] on the head.
Everyone must file income-tax declarations

The 'Merchants' Association' (Sokhrim Fareyn) asks us to draw the attention of all income-tax payers who have received declaration forms (zeznania) that, in their own interest, they should file the declarations, so as not to lose the right to file appeals (rekursy).
At the same time it is recalled that until the 15th of this month there is time to pay the third advance instalment (zaliczka) of the turnover tax.
A third bandit attack.

On Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat) Mr. A. Rodaler (printed 'Hodaler'), his wife and 2 sons were walking from Sosnowiec. As they came near Sielce they were stopped by 4 persons who, revolvers in hand, shouted:
'Hands up!'
In mortal terror the family kept from making any movement, and then the bandits took from them everything that had any value at all. The rings were pulled off Mrs. Rodaler's fingers.
Sosnowiec — the kehilla board is to be 'born' only on Chol HaMoed.

On the 23rd of this month [August 1931] the new kehilla board was to have been elected. But because a certain number of members are not at home, the election commission held a meeting this week, at which it was decided that the board should be elected on Chol HaMoed Sukkot.
Mass meetings of Jewish artisans

Next Sunday afternoon a conference of representatives of the Jewish tailors' guilds in Zagłębie will take place in the Artisans' Association (Hantverker-Fareyn).
Representatives from Częstochowa and from all the surrounding localities are also to take part in the conference.
In the evening mass meetings of shoemakers and of painters will take place.
On the agenda: to discuss how to improve the situation of the Jewish artisans.
New prices for flour and bread.

At the magistrate (town hall) a conference was held of the price commission and representatives of the bakers, the flour merchants and a delegate of the starostwo (district office).
At the conference it was decided to reduce the price of bread flour: instead of 40[?], a kilo of bread now costs only 39 gr.
Because a continuing fall in the price of flour prevails, a second conference will take place next Thursday, at which the price of flour and bread will again be reduced.
— An ox for a grosz — but where does one get the grosz?...
The writer Yoel Mastboim in Zagłębie.

The well-known writer and 'Moment' contributor Mr. Yoel Mastboim (Joel Mastbaum) has been staying in Zagłębie for several days.
The purpose of Mr. Mastboim's visit is to investigate and become acquainted with the situation of the workers of the 'black diamonds' [coal miners], and also with Jewish and general life in Zagłębie.
Mr. Mastboim will also appear with a series of lectures in Będzin and in Sosnowiec on the topic 'Man, woman — who is right?'.
Commissarial council in Czeladź.

The Kielce voivode has appointed by decree a commissarial council numbering 6 persons.
The council also includes the hitherto councillor (Ratman) Mr. Chaim Szwajcer.
The Chamber of Commerce is building its own premises.

At the last session of the Chamber of Commerce it was decided to proceed to build its own building; for this purpose a commission was elected, which is to publish a tender shortly.
It was also decided that the construction should be entrusted to a local firm.
For the sixth time no settlement reached...

On Tuesday, for the sixth time, a conference took place at the labour inspector's between the caretakers (stróże, "dozorcy" in the vernacular) and the house owners.
Neither side is willing to retreat from its decisions, and this conference too ended in nothing.
A dead body on the railway line.
On the railway line between Sosnowiec and Będzin the dead body of a man aged about 50 was found.
Do not leave your flats unguarded.
On Friday towards evening, while the Zelinger[?] family in Strzemieszyce was away, thieves got into the flat, from which they took 563 zł in cash.
A terrible revenge.

In Wojkowice a terrible tragedy occurred on Tuesday. A certain [name missing in print], walking in the street, was doused with acid by a young woman.
In a dangerous condition he [?] was taken to hospital.
It is high time.
The local magistrate has decided to put in order Będzin Street (ul. Będzińska) up to the power station.
Olkusz. — From the town council.

[Olkusz — municipality and kehilla.]
From the town council.
On Wednesday a town-council meeting took place, at which the debate on the budget for the year 1931-32 was concluded. The budget amounts in total to 750 thousand złoty (previously 1½ million zł.). Among the items cut, the Jewish subsidies were "in the first line of fire". Thus the subsidy of 1000 zł. for the Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund, the "Postęp" library and the Orthodox library was struck out. There remained only the one and only item of 3 thousand zł. for the "Dobroczynność" (charity society).
Among other things it was also approved: to raise the water fee by 25 per cent, the income from which will be 18 thousand zł.; to lease out from 1 October the targowisko (market square) on Górnicza Street, from 950 zł. upward, by public auction, and the market stands for small traders and carters from 3000 zł. upward, on condition that the fee for poor shopkeepers be reduced (according to the proposal of the Jewish councillors).
From the kehilla administration.
On Sunday elections were held for a president in place of the resigned A. Blum. Chaim Bezalel Eibeschitz (Agudah) was elected president. The rabbi, may he live long, also took part in the elections. The rabbi's participation in the elections aroused great displeasure in the nationalist circles.
A. B.
Zawiercie. — From "Brit Trumpeldor".

[Zawiercie — Zionism, Betar.]
From "Brit Trumpeldor".
On Sunday "Brit Trumpeldor" held in the synagogue a memorial service in honour of the holy martyrs who fell in Eretz Israel during the Av events of the year 5689 [1929], to which all Zionist organizations were also invited.
In a packed synagogue Trumpeldor's mourning song "Biglal" is sung and the cantor recites an "El Male Rachamim". Then Mr. Yishaihu [Yeshayahu] Grynberg delivers a mourning speech, calling on the Jewish population to work intensively for the benefit of Eretz Israel.
Then an "academy" (commemorative gathering) took place in Betar's own premises. The commander of the branch (mefaked haken), Yosef Chmielewicki[?], opens the academy and asks those present to honour the memory of the fallen martyrs with one minute of silence. Then he gives a lecture on the subject "Betar and the Av events". Longer speeches were also delivered by Messrs. Israel Herman and Aleksander Turner, who pointed to the heroism with which the martyrs fought and perished.
To the strains of "Hatikvah" and "Beshuv H'" the academy is closed in an elevated mood.

Letters to the Editor.

[Będzin — education; letters to the editor.]
1.
Dear Mr. Editor!
We ask you to print the following letter in your esteemed newspaper, for which we thank you in advance.
In connection with the statement of the Teachers' Association (Z. Ts. [Zaglembier Tsaytung], No. 32) we have the honour to declare the following:
1) Regarding the conflict, we declare that although, after your seizure of our school by force on 1 March 1931 and your turning it into a so-called cooperative, while refusing to pay the current school expenses such as rent, light, telephone, sick fund etc. (not to mention, God forbid, any interest), we were already free of any obligations whatsoever towards the Teachers' Assoc[iation?], we nevertheless wished, at the end of the current school year, to settle amicably all kinds of money claims (justified and unjustified) of the teaching staff. The teachers of religious studies (limudei kodesh) agreed to this and we settled with them; only the teachers of secular studies (limudei chol), who shelter under the protection of their "dictatorial" "związek [union] with principles", which exists only in the Jewish street of Będzin, and to which we turned many times (as well as to the teachers personally) about settling with them, possibly through arbitration — they categorically rejected any amicable settlement whatsoever (to which, by the way, we still adhere at every moment), and instead declared a boycott of our school. As proof of the correctness [of our words] we publish the following document from the school inspector:
[In Polish:] School Inspector in Sosnowiec, 14 July 1931.
I confirm that the board (kuratorium) of the private school "Mizrachi" in Będzin wished to settle the disputed questions arising from the occupation of the school by the teaching staff of that school, and lodged with me a declaration that it would submit without reservation to an eventual arbitration award, whereas the teaching staff has so far been unwilling to submit to an arbitration court.
School Inspector
Stanisław Luchowiec.
2) As regards the causes that brought about the difficult situation of our school, we do not intend to polemicise with you, because you have no right to interfere in our internal affairs. Only in passing do we remark that the cause of it was you, with your "związek", which dictated to us "bright[?] salaries" (67 zł. per hour, when in neighbouring Sosnowiec only 42 zł. is paid), as well as your constant terrorising of us by strikes. You even had the impudence to insult our members of the board, who to this day are paying heavy thousands of zlotys out of their private money because of your blood-sucking exploitation of our school over so many years.
3) Now, concerning your ironising about the future reorganisation of our school, we declare that "we do not live by their mouths" (lo mi-pihem anu chayim), and we regard you as rather poor "experts" in the pedagogical field; your "opinion" with your "specific views" about our schools may be worth to us whatever it is worth, and therefore we pass over them as "[—]" and null. And as regards personalities, we do indeed have "something" to tell about our former "pedagogical personalities", but for the time being we hold back.
Now let Jewish society judge who wanted and still wants an amicable settlement, and who aims only at war and terror.
The Board (Kuratorium) of the "Mizrachi" School in Będzin.
2.
We ask you to give space in your esteemed newspaper to the following letter, for which we thank you in advance.
Last week we came, as to every wedding, to collect money at the wedding of Mr. Hershl Trajman; but how astonished we were when, right upon our entering, his daughter Branka "received" us with the words: "Please, out of here." When we drew the young lady's attention to the fact that we had come to collect money for philanthropic institutions, she began to shout: "Vand stand" [probably Polish "Won stąd!" — "Get out of here!"], and she indeed pushed us out of the house.
We consider it our duty to bring this scandalous fact to public notice.
With respect,
Icchak Fiszman (collector for "Malbish Arumim" [clothing the poor]),
Israel Binjamin Szyf (collector for "Talmud Torah").

A madman cuts the throat of a nurse

In the Lubliniec lunatic asylum (Upper Silesia) a horrible incident took place. The 21-year-old insane student Witnicki[?], in a moment of madness[?], attacked the nurse M'ensak[?], began beating her on the head with a piece of iron, and then grabbed a knife and cut her throat. The madman then ran away, and the wounded woman was taken to hospital in a hopeless condition.
The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce favours reductions also for owners of private cars

At the last meeting of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce the question of the amendment of the regulation concerning the levy on buses was discussed.
The Chamber of Commerce takes the position that the owners of cars for private use should also benefit from the planned reductions.
On this question a series of proposals was worked out, which the Chamber of Commerce will submit to the competent government bodies.
—o—
Summer colony of the Dąbrowa Hashomer Hatzair.
The ken of „Hashomer Hatzair“ in Dąbrowa organised a summer colony this year in Jeszczenicze[?] (near Olkusz). The colony, which was run under the direction of Yaakov Zeev Prachtzweig and Shlomo Bernsztajn, had about 50 members, boys and girls, who had a very good time and used their free time for cultural and national work.
Half of the colony's expenses were covered by the president of the patronage committee, Mr. N. A. Gutman.
„Ulen“ is giving way

For quite some time now negotiations have been taking place between the Sosnowiec municipality and the „Ulen“ company, which demands a huge sum for the „favour“ of carrying out the sewerage system.
This week the commissioner, Mr. Woźniak, received word that the „Ulen“ company is no longer setting the earlier harsh conditions, but is ready to agree to certain reductions.
Because of this Mr. Woźniak went to Warsaw to acquaint himself with the new financial conditions.
The „Mizrachi“ school in Sosnowiec is getting under way

Next Sunday lessons will already begin at the Sosnowiec „Mizrachi“ school, which has been improved for the new school year in the pedagogical field and in all areas.
A gratifying development is that the school will be run under the supervision of the local rabbi, Rabbi R' Menachem Hager.
New pupils can still be enrolled.
Bread prices have not been changed

The price commission at the Sosnowiec municipality held a meeting on Tuesday, at which new prices for flour and bread were to be set.
The result of the meeting, however, was that the price of bread remained the same as last week. On the other hand the price of rolls was reduced, from 80 gr. to 70 groszy per kilo.
This week the price of meat also unexpectedly went up: instead of 1,80 it already costs 2,40 a kilo...
—o—
„From Herzl to Jabotinsky“
On this topic Mr. S. Feldman will lecture on Saturday afternoon at the premises of the Revisionist organisation in Sosnowiec.
—o—
When the steam runs out...
Yesterday at 6 o'clock in the afternoon the tram to Dąbrowa suddenly came to a standstill on Małachowski Street in Będzin.
The reason was that during the heavy rain and thunder the electric power was cut off.
The vice-voivode against the new loan of the Będzin municipality

As we are informed, the vice-voivode has refused to approve the plan to build the main sewer collector in Będzin. The reason is that in the present crisis the town must not be burdened with any new loans.

[Notes of the Week — abroad and Poland.] In Dęblin an air disaster occurred. Two Polish airmen were killed.
—o—
The unemployed in Poland will receive produce instead of cash relief.

In China a flood disaster has taken place; the number of victims reaches into the thousands.

The committee to examine the credit questions of Germany has decided to prolong for Germany [the term of] its debts, which amount to 100 million dollars and 5 billion German marks.

The Importance of Vocational Schools

[Będzin — education.] The school year is about to begin, and parents and educators must give themselves an exact accounting of how to determine the further fate of their children. It is a rather difficult and complicated problem, for the future of the child depends on the choice of school. The school must educate the child so that in the future he can win a proper place in life. On rightly directing the child's abilities along the appropriate paths depends his fate, his happiness, as a future citizen. The task of parents and educators is to increase the number of capable, bold, life-loving people with a sense of their duties and rights, and to reduce the number of pessimists, malcontents and semi-illiterates. All this depends on a correct, sensible direction in keeping with the individual abilities of the child.
Today's social and economic conditions demand, besides school, also professional knowledge, as a weapon in the hard struggle of life. To this end serve the vocational schools ["zawodowe" schools], which besides general education also give them a trade. The importance of vocational schools is already well enough known throughout Poland; in this field we already have a whole network of such schools, which are directly connected with the economic life of the country. There are thus technical schools that turn out technicians in the fields of electrotechnics, mechanics, textiles, architecture and many others. But the vocational schools also deal with the craft and industrial trades and with commercial studies, in which we Jews, as a commercial element, are for the most part interested.
To the Polish government schools, however, we Jews have quite little access. Therefore we can make use of the opportunity and give our children the possibility of a vocational education. We can achieve this through the commercial school of Miss [Frl.] Bojarska in Będzin, which has the rights of government schools and gives the proper opportunities for it. Besides general subjects the school teaches foreign languages, such as German and French, and also commercial studies such as: bookkeeping, stenography, typewriting, commercial law, correspondence, knowledge of goods, etc. The school thus gives an all-round office and commercial education, which enables every pupil who finishes the school to take up an independent position.
Let us look at the gymnasium schools, which are heavily attended by Jewish children, and see what perspective they have for the future. After 8 years of toilsome work the child is put before the matura, which only the most capable manage to reach with great effort; and once one has the matura one must go on to further studies, and if material conditions do not allow it, one possibility remains: to take on private lessons. And after so many years of torment the child is left standing in despair, unable to find a way out of the difficult situation. For office work they are not prepared, because they have no vocational training. Let us therefore give our children the possibility to develop not in useless work over dead languages such as Latin and Greek, which bring no positive benefit whatever, but in work let us make human beings of our children, for in our hands lies their fate.
An Onlooker ["A Tsushoyer"].
Daring Bandit Raid on the Railway Cash Office in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — crime.] About 60 thousand zł. robbed.
A great sensation was caused in Zagłębie by the extraordinary bandit raid carried out on Friday morning on the cash office of the freight station in Dąbrowa.
The raid, which was carried out by skilled "professionals", took place in the following way:
In the cash-office room the cashier, ratman [?] Mr. Bernarski [?], was on duty. In a neighbouring room, the first one from the entrance, the storekeeper was on duty.
At that moment 2 elegantly dressed persons came in. One was dressed in the uniform of a senior railway official, and saying a friendly "good morning" they went very boldly in to the cashier, before whom the bandits introduced themselves as having come to inspect the books.
The cashier, without the slightest suspicion, laid the books before the "inspectors"; they showed that the cash office held in cash [printed "mowmen"] about 60 thousand zł. to pay the officials.
At that moment revolvers flashed before the cashier's eyes. Then they bound the cashier and stuffed his mouth with a handkerchief in which there was a potato.
The "inspectors" took the 60 thousand zł. and with a polite "do widzenia" to the storekeeper they went out.
Soon afterwards the storekeeper, who was in the first room, heard knocking of feet and groaning from the adjoining room. When he went in he saw the cashier lying bound and that such a daring raid had been carried out.
Until today there is no trace whatever of the bandits.
— — —
On suspicion of taking part in the daring raid several persons were arrested, among them also the owner of the beer tavern, Mr. Olszewski. After questioning Olszewski was released.

Said „Harei At“ and Remained a Bachelor. / If You Can't, Don't Undertake It...

[Częstochowa — a disputed betrothal; police and rabbinate.]
In Częstochowa the young bachelor Nachman P. cast an eye on the beautiful 18-year-old Miss Chana K. From time to time he would watch her regularly from his window opposite, study her movements, admire her fine figure, and keep dreaming of how to win her as his wife.
At the same time, however, Chanale paid no attention to her neighbour, but to another man, with whom she had indeed often been walking out lately.
Nachman suffered more and more because of this; he understood that by the straight road Chanale would not become his destined one, so he began looking for various plans how to „conquer“ her. Recently he heard that his „sweetheart“ was about to write tna'im [an engagement contract] in the coming weeks, and therefore he decided to carry out his plan as quickly as possible. He waited for her at the gateway of Warszawska 32 and, as he says, in the presence of 2 witnesses he put a ring on her finger and pronounced the „Harei at“ [„Behold, you are consecrated to me“].
Soon afterwards he did indeed turn to his „father-in-law“, asking him to give him „his“ Chanale, whom he had betrothed according to the law of Moses and Israel.
Chanale, however, contends that, true, he waited for her at the gateway, ran up to her and wanted to snatch something, but she fled in fright; she saw no ring before her eyes, no witnesses, and therefore she does not recognise him as her husband.
When Nachman went on spreading rumours that he had after all betrothed Chanale and that she may belong to no one other than him, Chanale's father turned to the police with a complaint of blackmail.
The police arrested Nachman, and during the investigation, in which the witnesses who had supposedly been present at the betrothal were also questioned, they declared that they knew nothing to tell. Nachman has meanwhile been released until the trial.
In recent days a hearing of witnesses (gvit edut) on this matter took place at the Częstochowa rabbinate. Nachman claimed that he had betrothed Chanale. Chanale, for her part, declared that there was not a word of truth in it („it neither climbed nor flew“), and that she had never even spoken with him at all.
Other persons were also questioned about the matter, and on the basis of all this the rabbinate ruled that this supposed betrothal has no validity whatsoever.
So Nachman, after his „Harei at“, has remained a bachelor.
—o—
[Humour — anecdote; a Będzin woman at Ustroń.]
If You Can't, Don't Undertake It...
My uncle, may he rest in peace, had a great longing for the amud [the prayer-leader's lectern]; he was really straining „toward the little board“, but the poor man could not do it, and every time he suffered a defeat...
My aunt, may she rest in Paradise, would every time stand up to him:
— You old fool, she would shout, what good is this to you? — and at the same time she would sing him the little song:
— „Oy, you old sh..., if you can't, don't undertake it“.
Why has this come up? Here before us lies a little letter from Ustroń. There, in Ustroń, a great miracle happened. A Będzin woman wanted to prove that she too knows the „laws of swimming“, and began to drown. A great miracle occurred: she was barely rescued.

Esteemed Editor!
In No. 33 of your newspaper, in the column „Our Panorama“, Mr. Ben Amotz writes that a letter lies before him from a group of Jewish children, who beg with tears in their eyes that you should publicise before the whole world the heroic deeds of the Olkusz town councillor „Hashkome-blat“. I declare that my name is not Hashkome-blat but Muszkatblat. The writers need not have been ashamed to write out my name. For my part it remains for me to remark that every cultured person must know how to value trees in a town, and when he does not understand it, he must be taught. The tactless comparison of me with the „black kehillot“, which lie in wait for a dead person in order to extract a few hundred złoty, is out of place here.
I thank you and remain
respectfully,
A. Muszkatblat, Olkusz.

Our Telephones (Responsibility and Irresponsibility in Telephone Communication — What Must Be Done?)

[Zagłębie — telephones; public service.] Not for the first time, and not for the second, and more than certainly not for the last time either, we find ourselves having to speak about this very question.
It concerns telephone calls in Zagłębie. Several times already we have had occasion to draw attention to the prevailing disorders and to treat the telephone question from every side. But it never brought any substantial benefit; it always ["shtets"] stays as it was — as it was before, so it remains afterwards.
Telephone communication is not today [?] as it once was, when there were only a handful of subscribers. In recent years the telephone network in Zagłębie has spread so widely that there is hardly a house which is not connected to telephone communication; and with such popularity, with such spread, it becomes a public question, and with such questions the proper authority must reckon.
So one might have thought, and so indeed it ought to have been, for we know from practice that a business — the bigger it grows, the more customers it gets, the better it prospers — offers ever better conditions and makes things ever better and more convenient for its clients.
Quite different is the case with the telephone administration: the bigger the network grows, the more subscribers it gets, the harder it becomes to get a connection and the longer one must wait until one gets the requested number. Formerly people used to complain constantly that the service was unbearable, and now it has become considerably [?] worse. Very often one holds the receiver ["tube"] for several minutes and the operator does not answer; on the other hand, as soon as she does answer, she is in such a hurry that she does not hear you out but connects you with a different number. For example, if you need, let us say, number 387, she gives you 380, because the 7 she no longer hears; and so it is with other numbers too. And should you try [?] to reproach her, she would at once want to hold you responsible. They, on the other hand, may make every kind of mistake; they may wake you from your sleep several times in the middle of the night, paying no attention to the fact that it is the middle of the night, when she could be more careful, especially when she is not then swamped with too much work — and you can do [?] nothing about it, because in such a case she will not tell you the number, and if you shout at her she will play such a trick ["kavol"] on you that you will not be able to get connected so quickly at all. That is the way they settle accounts with the subscribers. Whatever happens, they ask nobody; every time they always ["shtets"] wriggle out of their responsible work.
It often happens that a Będzin subscriber asks for Sosnowiec, or a Dąbrowa subscriber [Dąbrowa Górnicza] asks for Będzin, and you are told that the line is busy, so that you cannot get the desired town so quickly; and when you finally do get it at long last, she connects you with a different number. Of course, with such service you lose your patience and begin to "go on strike" with the telephone...
It has thus lately become unbearable, and the worst of it is that the further it goes the worse it gets: the more subscribers are added, the worse the service and consequently the harder the connection.
More than once subscribers have satisfied themselves that, having asked several times for a connection, the operator answered them that the number was busy, while this did not accord with the truth. Apparently she has no patience for the work, and yet that did not bother her.
The telephone network, both in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia [Górny Śląsk], is becoming ever more popular, so that the telephone administration ought in fact to reckon with it, and it should be the reverse [of what happens] — [not] that subscribers should be served worse merely because new subscribers are being added.
Must the subscribers really be wronged merely because the telephone company is gaining new customers? Because the business is growing — something so rarely [?] found nowadays? Is such disregard really permissible? Why, then, should the telephone company not have operators who will carry the responsibility on their shoulders? After all, every official bears responsibility for his department, so why should such lawlessness ["hefkeyres"] reign in this particular field, especially when it has to involve so much punctuality and care? For it is well known that the telephone was not created merely for amusement, but depends for the most part on quick and punctual connection; otherwise people would not use the telephone.
We often stand with the receiver in our hand and in impatience throw it back down, so agitated do we become when we see that nobody answers us. Of course, such disregard is not permissible. One must surely bear in mind that the telephone was created to ease our conditions of existence, not to make them harder to the point that we lose our patience over the slowness [?] and the disregard of the staff.
We know that individual persons, however energetic and prompt they may be, the telephone company will not reckon with them, and incidentally they will not be believed that the grievances are justified. It is quite different, however, if the matter took on a public character, and a public character it can take on only in the event that it is handed over to our public institutions.
It would therefore be absolutely necessary that the industrial and merchants' institutions should undertake to deal with the question, that all the grievances, intolerable conditions and negligences should be recorded by them, and that they should intervene in the question wherever necessary.
One must not forget that the telephone network is a public matter; therefore one must not turn the public question into a private affair. The institutions whose members are telephone subscribers can achieve a great deal in this question; it is therefore necessary not to allow the matter to be neglected, but to set about solving the question in such a way that, instead of a yoke, instead of a burden, it should become a convenience for the broad public — for which purpose the telephones were in fact created.
— A sacred duty thus lies upon our economic institutions to see to solving the telephone question in such a way that the female officials should be fully responsible for their deeds.
R. Let.
Finally got his deserved verdict... (The ugly end of the antisemitic 'apostle' Alojzy Mach in Katowice)

[Silesia — antisemitism; Katowice.] For barely 3 years now a Jew-devouring gutter rag of the worst kind has been appearing [?] in Katowice under the name "Do Czynu" ["To Action!"], which incites ceaselessly and calls on the faithful to take active steps against the "Jewish invasion of Silesia". At the head of this hate campaign stands the sadly notorious "editor" Alojzy Mach, concerning whose past, hypocrisy and plain loutish [?] deeds we have already several times drawn the attention of the local supervisory authority.
Mr. Mach (read it backwards) [i.e. "cham", Polish for "boor"] did not content himself merely with snake-venomous articles or plain insinuations in the columns of his rag against the peaceful Jewish population, but also travelled across the whole Silesian province as an "apostle" (together with the Warsaw priest Leszno-Brodzki [?], specially engaged for the purpose) and preached hatred, bloodthirsty revenge and the extermination of all Jews, the "enemies" of Poland, the allies of the devil, the leeches who suck out the marrow and drain the blood of the Silesian peasant and worker...
From time to time a disgusting hate campaign would start in "Do Czynu" against some respectable Jewish firm, and he, the faithful Jew-devourer, barked for so long until he had squeezed out his "lo yehoreg" [hush] money...
Because of his base libels, especially against the Jewish pedlars of Zagłębie and Western Galicia, an interpellation was even submitted at the time by the Jewish "Koło" [parliamentary club] at the plenary session of the Sejm. Also [sic]. But all without success. "Do Czynu", with its title illustration showing an elderly Jew with beard and sidelocks selling off Silesian industry, churches and towns, went on appearing, and Mr. Mach, with the most shameful licentiousness, poured pitch and brimstone "upon the Lord, upon His anointed and upon 'let us break'" [printed "נגתקה"; after Psalms 2:2–3]...
At last the bubble burst.
The Jewish population grew used to the barking of the "apostle" from Wierzbnik [?] (Mach comes from "Hierzbnik" [sic], Olkusz county) and paid no more attention to his blackmail tricks. The Silesian working masses too realised that the "apostle" was only out for his own pocket, and stopped believing his teachings.
What did Reb Mach do? He went and turned the shaft around [changed direction]. He [printed "שר"] threw himself, with his idealistic organ, upon a series of Christian merchants, whom he blackmailed in an ugly manner (as he had the Jewish ones before), until he finally fell into the trap; and as the latest number of "Wolne Słowo" [?] (also published in Katowice) reports — it publishes a whole series of blackmail documents against Christian merchants — the whole affair has passed to the public prosecutor. First of all he got caught in a "Chad Gadya" [chain of retribution] over the lost case of Mr. Mentschel [?], but now the well-known Katowice merchant Stefan Warczyński [?] and others come forward with a very large blackmail charge.
"Wolne Słowo" unmasks the fine "hero" and exposes the shameful action of "Do Czynu", which — whomever it may have served [?] — has certainly brought no extra honour to the Polish cause in Silesia; just as it is superfluous to stress the satisfaction of the Jewish, especially the merchant, population at being rid of such a pest.
A. Ganzweich.
