A Town without Jews — From a visit to Saybusch (Żywiec)

[Travel sketch — Żywiec.] Reported by Ben Amotz.
The Viennese writer "Bauer" [sic; i.e. Hugo Bettauer] wrote a work under the title "A Town without Jews". The book describes what the town looks like that has at last had the merit, thanks to the efforts of the enemies of the Semites, of becoming "free of Jews".
A big film company staged the book as a film, but the film was not permitted everywhere; if I am not mistaken, it was forbidden here too to show the film under the name "Miasto bez Żydów"... And it will, I believe, be a "sensation" for a great number of our readers when they learn that, travelling [?] about 3 hours by train from Zagłębie, one comes to a town where to this very day it — the town, that is — is free of Jews, in the literal sense: not one single Jew lives in the town...
To tell the truth, we too knew nothing of this "secret"; it reached us thanks to the "good communications" on the Cieszyn–Silesian railway line, where waiting at the stations lasts longer than the journey...
At Żywiec station we hear the "good tidings" that we have to wait nearly an hour and a half before departure.
— Splendid, just splendid! — a young man calls out.
— What is this great joy of yours? A pleasure for you to wait an hour and a half?
— I wish we had to wait even longer — says the young man — in a moment we'll go into the town where Jews are forbidden to live [printed "וויגען", probably a misprint]...
— What? In liberated Poland there is still such a mad and senseless town?...
— Don't be so astonished; come with me and you'll ask your questions later...
And we went, we went along a long street that is covered with clouds of dust whenever a motor-car drives past. We walk and see all the while Jewish shops, Jewish women in wigs, Jews in long kapotas, Jewish children at play on the narrow pavements — a truly Jewish place.
— What do you want? — we ask our guide — a Jewish settlement no worse than on Modrzejowska Street in Będzin...
— But this is Zabłocie, a suburb of Żywiec — we get the answer — here Jews do live; there is also a synagogue, a beit midrash, a community life with all its trimmings; but Jewishness applies only up to the bridge — see that bridge over there? It divides the Jewish ghetto from the town of Żywiec. Up to the bridge a Jew can rent a flat, a shop, but in "holy" Żywiec — no! It is an old prohibition that dates back to the Austrian "kingdom of grace", and to this very day it is upheld by the local non-Jewish population.
——
The three of us stride into the town of Żywiec. Here one already sees splendid buildings, magnificent hotels, shops in the European style, a large spacious market square, monuments, and —
— free of Jews...
At the moment when we are looking around the market square the town clock strikes, but the striking is so frightening that it seems to us at that very moment that we are in medieval times, in a town where the Marranos [anusim] lived.
— Let's speak Polish — one of us whispers [printed "אייגער"] — so that we don't provoke any annoyance among the locals. And indeed we take care not, God forbid, to utter a single Yiddish word, and in a depressed mood we leave the place where no Jewish eye may stay overnight...
——
The sun had set in the west when we returned to the Jewish ghetto; there we found the ghetto Jews going, faint [from fasting], into the synagogue to pray minchah (it was on Tisha b'Av).
Inside, the synagogue is lit with a great deal of light. Jews wrapped in tallitot are praying minchah; many have already prayed and are waiting for the rabbi, who is to come and deliver a sermon on the destruction of old and of today...
Our eyes are still turned over there, to where people laugh so freely and live so securely. We want to cast one more look at the "happy" town in Poland, but suddenly we are interrupted by the voice of the cantor:
— "Answer us on the day of our fast, for we are in great distress"...
— Zabłocie and Żywiec...
Joel Mastbaum: What Did I See in Zagłębie? (A Letter to Będzin)

Joel Mastbaum.
What did I see in Zagłębie?
(A letter to Będzin).
I have always loved you, Będzin; I have loved you more than all your little Zagłębie sisters. You have always been the Jewish town, with all your „pitshevkes“[?].
Without exaggeration, Będzin always makes on me the impression of something whole, Jewish, folksy; coquettish assimilation never came visiting here, here there was never a place where Jewish life is a kind of melted-fat garnish[?] to a big, fat dinner of Polish-Jewish girls and Polish-Jewish wives. A wonder that Katowice came along and „jazzed up“ the youth a bit and showed them a way into the paradise of dancings and night-clubs; otherwise Będzin would still be today the most colourful[?] town, full of Jewish riches, of the Jewish press and the Jewish book and a good Jewish performance. Is there little echo of it even today?
I remember, at my first acquaintance with the Jewish poetess Mrs. Roza Jakubowicz, and at the first few conversations and the few poems of the lady's that I read, I always had the impression that such a language and such poems and such a manner of writing could have been born only in a town that is Jewish from the deepest root.
Będzin is a town with long and deep Jewish roots. The grandfather and the great-grandfather still lie on the face of every young man. That is the virtue of the folksy town: its Jewishness is not artificial in the Kraków manner, it is a Jewishness born of itself.
— — —
Four, five years ago I had such a notion of the town; I was enchanted by your wholeness, and today too the town still holds on to its wholeness; there is a truly well-developed working class, perhaps the only working class in Zagłębie that reads, defines[?] and understands.
And the older generation, too, cannot be dismissed with a wave of the hand. In Będzin I met (no longer of today — very interesting older Jews); they have remained, but something is now missing for me in the town. Here, for instance, I enter the new railway station — splendour, it smells of Europe here, such fine waiting-rooms, such benches and buffets and tables. But I no longer see at the station the masses of Jews with faces full of drive, Jews who are breadwinners and men of trust; here I come upon a few sleepy faces — they are dozing soundly.
— Are you travelling somewhere? I ask the Jews.
— Travelling? one of them answers, there is nowhere at all to travel to; one just sits here like that, one dozes, there is nothing to do.
— And you have a station? I say.
— But what good is this palace to us — he points at the station — a livelihood we have not got either way, believe me, he says; we were better off once without the station. Some four, five years ago a Będzin Jew was „in the feathers“ [well off]; he could allow himself to travel and to go about and to give a handsome donation. Today, you see, everything is going under; the trade in the bit of black diamonds [coal] is slipping out of Jewish hands. And what there is does not give big profits either.
— Are you not pleased with your station?
— Give me, upon my life, a bit of livelihood.
I leave the station, I go into the little gardens; fine and decked-out are the Będzin little gardens. I remember that a few years ago, when I came to Będzin for the first time, I felt terribly a lack of good air. So I brought a protest to my friend Szpigelman:
— Tell me, why have you not got a bit of good air here in Będzin, at least some well-planted little garden?
And my friend Szpigelman gave a broad[?] smile:
„A Będzin Jew who has luck with the black diamonds forgets altogether about fresh air. That you ought to know from of old“.
And of that I indeed convinced myself later. I noticed that Będzin Jews are, no evil eye, so absorbed in their businesses that they forget altogether that there is such a thing as air.
Only not long ago I came back from such a Będzin garden. Well, nicely in bloom are your little gardens, truly little paradises, and there is air there. So that one „forgets“ about Zakopane; and young ladies — you now possess whole film actresses.
Yes, I saw myself how two such young ladies were sitting in a garden with a pack of film-picture literature, and one said to the other:
— Czy już byś sama nie umiała grać? [Polish: Wouldn't you yourself know how to act by now?]
— Idź no — says the other — moja twarz[?] i me oczy, bym się na pewno nadała do filmu. [Polish: Go on — with my face and my eyes I'd surely be fit for film.]
— A ja? [And me?]
— No, a ja? [Well, and me?]
Word by word, until both young ladies began to insult each other and to quarrel.
Not far from me a little Jew was walking about with lowered eyes and sighing bitterly:
— Why are you sighing? — I ask.
— I am not sighing — answers the little Jew — I am only catching a bit of air here; better said, I am not catching any air either; I am only sitting here in chopped-up troubles and thinking what one does with the pack of protested bills in my pocket. And going away from him I lamented: Będzin, did you really deck out fine stations and fine little gardens only so that Jews should groan and sigh there from worry about a livelihood? And so that on the benches there should sit no more young ladies with Yiddish books in hand, but just girls who are itching to become film actresses?
The Unveiling of the „Gordonia“ Flag

This week, at the summer colony of „Gordonia“ in Nickulina (near Rajcza), the unveiling took place of the blue-and-white flag which the Będzin „Gordonia“ has won for its 5th anniversary. Messrs. Yehuda Anzelewicz, Yona Goldberg and Matek Hampel appeared with speeches on topical matters.
After the hammering-in of several silver „zhetabnen“[?] [nails/plaques], a march-past (defilade) took place around the flag, which fluttered high, to the tune of the celebration, in the Beskid mountains.
With „Teḥezaknah“, Hebrew workers' songs and „hora“ dances the event came to an end.
In the coming weeks the consecration of the flag (ḥanukat ha-degel) will take place in Będzin.
Towards the Start of the New School Year

As we learn, the planned reforms in the school system will not be carried out this year, because of the difficult economic situation in the country.
The textbooks in force will be the same as in the school year 1930-31.
The school year will begin on 1 September at 9 in the morning with general religious services.
On the 4th of the coming month religious services will be held in all schools in memory of the late Minister of Education Czerwiński.
The one innovation to be introduced this year will consist in this: instead of 50 minutes, a lesson will this year last 45, and the breaks between lessons will last a quarter of an hour.
From 33 to 3 Dollars: Visas to Argentina Reduced

It is announced by the Argentine consulate in Warsaw that for a certain category of emigrants travelling to Argentina the visas have been reduced from 33 dollars to 3 dollars.
This concession applies to those called over by relatives, or — on the basis of labour contracts.
The other categories of emigrants will, as before, pay 33 dollars for a visa.
Presumably for those who go there to dance the tango...
Jews, Learn to Faint!...

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton; the economic crisis.] By Y. Oberżanek [?].

(A secret: how to make a living in times of crisis).

As against what you say: crisis. There's no livelihood, goods get cheaper and the złoty dearer. The customers are frozen and a wind blows through the till. Manufacturers turn scribes and write mezuzot, and merchants turn astronomers and gaze up at the sky. "There was not a house where there was not one dead." There's no merchant without a "nadzór" [supervision, i.e. receivership]. There's nothing to take hold of.
That's what you say? And I say otherwise: Zagłębie hasn't croaked yet; you only need to have your head screwed on the right way [lit. "on the right side"], and then one can still make a living in Zagłębie, even in the crisis years. Here, I know a Jew — a Jew without a factory, without trade licences [patents], without "podatki" [taxes], without "obligi" [promissory notes], without headaches — and he makes a pretty fine living. This Jew handed me the secret, and I will hand the secret on to you, and if you are "energiczni" [energetic], you too will be able to make a living.
Listen with your head:
This week a Jew comes to me for advice. "I know," says he, "that you are 'cfany' [streetwise, shrewd], so I have come to ask your counsel."
— What advice do you need? — I ask the Jew.
— About matters of livelihood, about my "branża" [line of business] — answers the Jew.
— What are you, a merchant?
— What's got into you? Do you take me for such a fool? Writing bills of exchange and later going into "Chad Gadya" [slang for prison] for an "odpoczynek" ["a rest"] — I don't hold with that.
— Then what are you, a craftsman? A tailor?
— A craftsman, of all things? Having dealings with the Chamber of Crafts, with examinations? For what atonement do I need that!
— Perhaps you're a matchmaker, then?
— Go on, go on, that has completely stopped being a "branża". When there is in Będzin (printed "בשדין") a "związek" [association] of the "krajoznawcy" [the touring / sightseeing society] which sends boys with girls on "wycieczki" [excursions], what does one need matchmakers for, what for?...
— So what are you, Reb Jew? And what do you live on?
Here the Jew unpinned the flap of his coat, cleared his throat and answered:
— I'll tell you a secret on one condition: that the secret stays a secret, for you know our brethren the Children of Israel — they love to compete, and I don't want any competitors, since up to now I am still the only one with my article.
— I make a living from fainting — the Jew handed me the secret.
— From fainting? What sort of article is that, fainting? It's the first time I've heard of a fainting "branża". Explain to me — I've become even more "ciekawy" [curious] — what sort of "business" [?] is this?
— Heh... heh... — the Jew burst out laughing — it's a branch of business all right. How I work the branch, you want to know? Very simple:
In the morning I go out into the street, pick myself a "wygodne" [convenient] spot and I drop down in a faint. Naturally a crowd gathers. They start to revive me, they tear pieces off me, and I "faint"... They unbutton my waistcoat, my shirt, and, "za przeproszeniem" [pardon the expression] — my trousers — and I faint... They give me ether to sniff — and I faint... They push valerian drops into my mouth — and I faint... I "faint" for as long as it takes until I feel a couple of złotys. As soon as I feel the złotys, the fainting passes...
The worst, though, is when they start pouring water over me. When they "revive" me with water, they pour one bucket after another over me, until my teeth chatter [lit. "a tooth knocks against a tooth"]. And if it weren't that I am a Jew who needs a livelihood, I'd jump up and kill the lot of them. What sort of sense is that, just pouring water? Who needs their water, when (printed "ווערן") what I need is a livelihood!...
In the morning I faint at the Old Market [Stary Rynek]; having fainted at the Old Market, I go off to faint on Kołłątaja Street. From 1 to 3 I have lunch, and in the afternoon I go off to faint in another district. So I faint three, four times a day, and "abi handl shedl" [folk saying, apparently "so long as there's trade" (?)]...
And perhaps you think I faint all by myself? My wife faints too. She is a real "artist" in the fainting trade. She faints and adds sobbing — and not just some little sob, but with a shriek thrown in. If you heard a bit of the shrieking, if you heard such a "tekiah gedolah" [the great shofar blast], you'd jump out of your skin.
So I faint in one street and my wife faints and shrieks in another street, and since [?] my wife helps me in the "livelihood", we make, thank God, a living...
So you see, the fainting branch is not a bad one at all. From fainting one makes Shabbes, with fainting one marries off daughters in great honour — I have no complaints about my fainting branch...
— Yes, may you be well, — I interrupted the Jew — you said you've married off daughters. I'm "ciekawy" [curious] to know what your sons-in-law are — what do your sons-in-law occupy themselves with, with what?
— Also with the same "branża" — answered the Jew. — I gave them no dowries; instead I taught them the "trade". They "faint" in the provinces: one faints in Zawiercie, a second son-in-law faints in Katowice, a third son-in-law faints in Sosnowiec; they all faint and make a living... With fainting they support their wives, with fainting they hold circumcision feasts — a thoroughly decent "trade", the fainting trade.
— Well, — I say — if you have such a "pewna" [sure] livelihood in hand, why have you come to consult me? If your wife helps you in the "livelihood" and you have also provided the children with a "decent existence", what more do you need?
— That's just it, — says the Jew — that's exactly what I wanted to consult you about.
— For instance?
— It really was a good trade until now. Until now I really was the only one: when I put on a faint, it was news; when my wife let out such a "tekiah gedolah", there was "for the Jews" [i.e. "light and gladness", a great stir]. Ten-groszy pieces, twenty-groszy pieces and half-złotys came pouring in. That was once upon a time. Now, since the reductions [lay-offs] began in the factories, since the artisans started swallowing spit [i.e. going hungry], I've lost my exclusivity [lit. "fallen out of pedigree"]; they make my life a misery, they do it better than me — they faint for real: in the market halls [hale] the merchants faint, at the bazaar in Sosnowiec the market-tax payers [?] faint, and as for the provinces, that goes without saying — there they faint ten times a day...
So I have come to you for advice — you really are "cfany", after all; give me some advice: what does one take up now? If the fainting branch is no good any more, then what is still any good?!...
Before leaving, the Jew once more warned me that he was handing this to me as a secret, and I must, God forbid, not drum the secret about, since he doesn't want any "competitors". I promised the Jew, and I will on no account drum out the "secret".
I am only telling you the story as against what you say: crisis, there's no business in Zagłębie — it isn't that terrible yet. Here you have a "business" without licences, without "podatki", without promissory notes, without protests [of bills].
In short: Jews, learn to faint!...
Jewish Life in Upper Silesia

Slowly but gradually Jewish life is developing in Upper Silesia. Not to speak of the larger Jewish centres such as Katowice and Königshütte (Królewska Huta) — lately a sign of revival can also be noticed in the smaller provincial towns, such as Siemianowice (Laurahütte), Mysłowice, Pszczyna (Pless), although these are only individuals. But it is to be hoped that in time the Jewish settlement will grow stronger, as in the old days; for the time being the beautiful, well-founded synagogues, which recall the good times of the past, still stand empty. Some are still opened for prayer on Sabbath and holidays, and some are completely closed, such as Woźniki, Żory (Sohrau), Stary Bieruń, Lubliniec. Incidentally, about the Lubliniec synagogue, the following interesting fact: there, in the synagogue building, lives the only Jew, Mr. Feuermann, well known to us, a son of the Będzin scribe [sofer] R' Yehuda Leib — a relic of those „good“ times when all the Jews emigrated to Germany, selling their estates for pennies; he, the cantor-ritual slaughterer of that time, remained the only Jew in the place, and so he stands to this very day like a priest before the Temple. However many times they have wanted to requisition the synagogue, he was its only defender. Meanwhile he has found himself a new livelihood: he is a sweets manufacturer, and when one of our Jews happens to come to Lubliniec on business, he finds an open door with warm hospitality. And one would like[?] to hope that old Lubliniec, where great rabbis (geonim) once lived, will flourish once again.
In general I would advise all those who want to settle in Upper Silesia not to push specifically into Katowice or Königshütte, but into the provinces. I was recently in Pszczyna; 3 years ago there was barely a minyan on the Sabbath, today they already pray there every Friday and Sabbath; they have already brought[?] a rabbi, a cantor-slaughterer from Grajewo. The local Jews complain, however, that the meat is sold in a non-Jewish butcher's shop together with pork. I think that a Jewish butcher, a professional, could do well there.
In general Pszczyna, the former Principality of Pless, is a place of livelihood with a rich farming district around it. It is desirable that a few more Jewish families should settle there. Those who have settled there do not regret it.
The same can be said of other towns and villages in Upper Silesia. The former racial antisemitism has almost ceased, and as far as I know the conditions, there is room in Upper Silesia for many hundreds of families of artisans and small traders.
By the term small traders I mean everyone, only not pedlars, of whom there is in fact a great surplus here. There is, however, room for so-called market-stallholders („mark-shteyers“), since, as is known, every day there is a weekly market in another town, to which people travel a great deal; and although some towns make difficulties, such as Nowa Wieś, Lipiny, Świętochłowice, still one manages, and above all for someone living locally no difficulties are made.
Artisans too, such as independent barbers, hat-makers, shoemakers of workers' shoes etc., can still find a livelihood.
In general it would be only fair that the respected public figures of Zagłębie should create some kind of council or commission whose task would be to seek out and investigate all livelihood opportunities for individual families.
That is the commandment of the present hard time, when emigration possibilities are completely closed and the artisan together with the small trader are toiling with a dying livelihood: an economic council must be created especially for our region, composed of the merchants', small traders' and artisans' associations. That, I believe, will bring more benefit than the constant squabbling over rabbis and seats on the dozór [kehilla board].
Finally, a small episode from Katowice life. Recently a Hasidic Jew from Piotrków, a Stryków Hasid, came here; looking for a livelihood he obtained a licence to sell Jewish newspapers in the street. And where does one find our brethren, the children of Israel, if not at the railway station? But this did not please all sorts of „Do czynu“ [„To action!“] heroes. How could it be — in Katowice, in front of the railway station, a Jew, and with such a majestic beard! They set about persecuting him with all hooligan means, so that the police had already grown tired of writing up reports. What does God do? Recently such an incident was witnessed by the great industrialist Mr. Juliusz Fajwel, the present owner of the Hotel „Monopol“; he called the Jew in and handed him a letter to his manager, that from this day on he is to receive a table in the gateway of the Hotel „Monopol“ free of charge. Just imagine — the Jew will now have a livelihood, God willing.
So let all locals and travellers indeed know: in the gateway of Dyrekcyjna 1 one gets the entire Jewish press.
Dawid Szerlich[?].
(President of the Small Traders' Association in Katowice).
Whom Are You Kidding?...

(An open letter from Yisroel Bunem the shoemaker to the American President Hoover).
Dear friend of mankind, Hoover, may you live long with your wife and children!
Firstly I have come to ask you: what did you want from me? Why have you set upon my life? I go around like a dazed man[?] („vi an aptsasn“) and. don't know what world I am in. Here yes crisis — here no crisis. Here you do give a loan — here you don't give a loan. Moratorium there — moratorium here: whom are you kidding?
I take up the „Radio“ to read, and I see in black and white that that's it! „After all“ — the crisis is over! And the main thing — one will be able to afford to eat warm pletslekh [flat rolls] with butter, just as in the „good times“... I take up the „Letste Nayes“ again, and I see the boot-tops turned exactly the other way round, — that „Reb Note[?] regrets it“, that you almost had no intention at all of lending dollars... You only put out „a pogłoska“ [a rumour] on purpose, so that the „paupers“ might rejoice; but lending money — that's a decent Jewish thing... As my mother-in-law says: „Borrowing — makes worrying“ — a true sage [„be-umones“, also: in craftsmanship]! Just like me — you want a pair of half-soles? Then it's „nóżki na stół“ [cash on the table]! To go running after the money afterwards — that's where the corn hurts him [„odcisk“]... You're right, honestly ge-rest[?], but whom are you kidding?...
Are you making a fool of me, Yisroel Bunem? One of the two: yes or no! As my mother-in-law says: you can't force anyone to lend money or to love, but leading everyone by the nose — that you really don't need to do. Ah, you'll surely want to ask me: what has this got to do with me? Whether Germany gets a moratorium or not, I remain Yisroel Bunem, the same pauper... the same „pitch-head“ [smale kop, i.e. shoemaker]... I'll explain it to you right away with a parable:
For example, here in Będzin the artisans' association has split, and I, Yisroel Bunem, don't know which one to join — should I belong to the „bourgeois“ artisans on Kołłątaja [street]? — if indeed, friend Hoover, you won't give any money and the crisis goes on, I'd rather be a journeyman with one of our own, a proletarian, and let him carry on his shoulders the „cech“ [guild] with the „sick-fund“ and the „Fundusz Bezrobocia“ [Unemployment Fund] and more and more of all those good things.
And one more thing: the wife needs to have her coat altered; winter is coming, tailors ask more for altering than one pays for a new coat; and if the crisis is over — „it bursts“, „it crashes“, everything — then it's better to wait and buy a new one.
And more: I'm waiting with marrying off my Beylke; for more than 3 years already she has been going around with the red-haired Fivish, and the lad wants to be gilded [a dowry]... and if the crisis is over, I could after all get „something decent“ for Beylke, and cheaper...
And more — and many more other things, in which you stand in my way with your yes-loan and no-loan; therefore I beg you, stop your jokes, and write to me immediately what you really mean by your moratorium...
You see, by the way, write to me soon how Moshe Henekh, formerly[?] „the Gegrivete“ [a nickname], is doing over there with you in America, since I have heard it said that he is „all right“ there, better off than a vice-president of the artisans' association here.
I beg you, write me an answer soon, because I am waiting with „impatience“. From me, your unknown shoemaker, Yisroel Bunem Dratwa [„shoemaker's thread“].
Passed on for printing by A. S. Moszkowicz.
Oneg Shabbat

[Oneg Shabbat — Torah thoughts on the weekly portion.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's sidra. Collected and styled [?] by Y. Y.
Parashat Ki Teitzei

The Portion.

a) "And thou wouldest take her to thee to wife" (21:11)
"The Torah spoke only in view of the evil inclination."
The evil inclination urges a person to do precisely what is forbidden to him. A pleasure, as long as it is not forbidden, does not stir a person's desire at all. Therefore the Torah permitted taking the captive gentile "beautiful woman" (yefat to'ar), because if there is a permission, the man will not crave to take her at all...
Kohelet Moshe.

b) "Then thou shalt bring her home to thine house" (21:12)
Wishing that the yefat to'ar should soon become repugnant to him, the Torah tells him to take her into the house. Had he kept her somewhere outside his house, she would always have remained dear to him; but being with her constantly at home, life itself will become loathsome to him... For "a continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike" — even the incessant dreary autumn rain, which seems as if it will drip like this forever, has its end — with the passing of autumn, of the rainy days. The contentious woman, however, the quarrelsome wife — "are alike": with her it is always the same, she rains curses forever, she has no fixed term... Therefore the only way to become sick even of a beautiful woman is to be with her constantly...
Alshich.

* * *

"A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike"
Rain does not torment you only while it is falling; but — if you have a rotten roof — it makes itself felt even when the sky is already clear and cloudless, for then it drips from the ceiling. A bad wife, even when you drive her out, also leaves after-pains behind — for example, a "stubborn and rebellious son". That is why the passages of the yefat to'ar and of the stubborn and rebellious son are close to each other.
Ohel Yaakov.

c) "That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days" (22:7)
On this it is expounded that only for two commandments — honouring father and mother, and sending away the mother bird — is the reward of long life stated. Honouring parents is the hardest commandment and sending away the mother bird the easiest.
This homily is sharply challenged: after all, we find the promise of long life with various other commandments, such as "that your days may be multiplied", "to the end that he may prolong his days" (regarding the appointment of a king), and more.
But the meaning is that with honouring parents and sending away the mother bird, "that it may be well with thee" is added to the promise of long life, i.e. a long and good life. That is indeed a blessing, whereas elsewhere only long life alone is stated — and long life without good is rather a curse...
Maadanei Melekh.

"And let him write her a bill of divorcement" (24:1)
The final letters of this verse are: B, H, R, T — "baheret" (a kind of leprosy), because the Gemara says: a bad wife is a leprosy for her husband; let him divorce her and he will be cured.
Rabbenu Ephraim of Worms.

* * *

Therefore a bad wife is compared to leprosy, because a leper is compared to a dead man ("four are considered as dead: the poor man, the leper, one who has no children, and the blind"), and "a bad woman is more bitter than death"...
Why, then, is it not said: a bad wife is compared to a blind man, who is also considered as dead?
Because for a husband who has such a wife it would be better to be blind and not to look at her...
Milin de-Rabbanan.

e) "A perfect and just measure shalt thou have, that thy days may be lengthened" (25:15)
In heaven the sinner is not punished until "his measure is filled", until his measure is completed. But he who measures with a false measure — "above" his measure also soon becomes full, although in truth it is not yet full. Measure for measure... But if you keep the measure honestly, your measure in heaven will also be kept honestly, and "thy days shall be lengthened" — you will breathe [?] longer, until your [?] little measure truly fills up...
Peninim Yekarim (BYLH"G).

f) "When thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God" (25:18)
"When thou wast faint and weary" — you can be worn out by fasts and mortifications and all sorts of "piety", and still "he feared not God" — not have God in your heart...
Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin.

* * *

The Baal Shem Tov had a pair of horses with which he made his journeys. Once the Baal Shem Tov made his way by "shortening of the road" (kefitzat ha-derekh). The horses, racing lightning-fast past the inns at which, on ordinary journeys, they used to stop and be fed, began to ponder: perhaps we are human beings... But they soon pass the places where, on ordinary journeys, the people rested and ate, and now — they just fly like lightning; so they began to think: we must be angels, who do not need to eat... And so it remained with them: they are angels...
When they had already arrived at the appointed place and the horses were put into the stable, they fell upon their fodder like horses..
Yes, when one fasts [?] one is not yet an angel. What counts is after the fast...
Maamarei Simcha.

Haftarah

g) "But with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee" (Isaiah 54)
God drove the Jews out of their land because they had sinned, and waiting with the redemption until they stop sinning would have taken a bit too long... But: "with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee" — the world, too, could not have existed by strict justice alone; by that same "everlasting kindness", the kindness God shows the world, He will then deal with the Jews too — only by looking away from the Jewish sins will the redemption be possible.
Binah la-Itim.

Avot.

h) "And on deeds of loving-kindness" (1:2)
When the "Noda bi-Yehuda" was received as rabbi in Prague, people "visited" him day and night; everyone wanted to be in the company of the clever gaon, and he had no time to study, until he hit upon this plan: from the wealthy visitors he asked for loans of money, and to the poor ones, in turn, he lent money.. In a short time they all left him alone.
Ruin and despair

[Opinion — the economic and cultural crisis of Polish Jewry.] ...And the wheels keep turning,
and the years keep going,
and the little wife keeps scolding,
and... one wants to live...
Branch after branch, trade after trade, Jewish life is dying away before our eyes.
Slowly but surely he strides about, the angel of death of our economic well-being, with his gleaming [?] sickle and — — — — — —
— he mows, annihilates and sows ruin.
On the one side the world crisis, the shortage of money; on the other side the etatist policy of our governments, which has torn everything away from private initiative and monopolised it; and on the third side — — — — —
— progress, the technology growing from minute to minute, which mercilessly pushes out human labour — this threefold cord has set to work and in the end has laid everyone out "on the cold", as the underworld says of a murdered man.
Everyone is lying low: the merchant, the small trader, the cab driver [dorożkarz], the musician, the artisan, the worker — all are embittered and steeped in melancholy, and in everyone's brain it gnaws [?]: what shall we eat?
There is nowhere to earn, even if you crawl out of your skin — and taxes must be paid, or else your belongings will run away [be distrained]; a groschen of credit is not to be had. We used to have banks where Jews got a groschen, cashed a bill of exchange, took out a freight consignment, pulled off some Jewish deal — as long as it would go with him "to live until evening" [?] [Polish do wieczora] — now they lie like overturned giants, on blood-stained groschen and on the ruins of their own and others' plush sofas and rooms.
And if there is no flour, there is no Torah: when one is shackled [?] by the worries of making a living, one cannot have any spirituality in mind; a wasteland reigns in the field of cultural work too, and everyone's interest in intellectual work has dried up.
Who reads a serious book today? Who needs to toil over a serious newspaper today? Whose head has room for culture — shmulture?
— It is a luxury to hold a literary reading today — says Rachel Fajgenberg, the writer of the people, who knows well the life of the majority of the Jews in Poland.
And since the public's interest in spirituality has died out, all the little channels of culture have become "useless". All culture-creating forces have been paralysed, and to the surface have floated graphomaniacs, junk-peddlers and riff-raff, who have flooded the Jewish literary market with a deluge of trash and smut; they have called up from the graves the characters of "Shapshovitsh's little house" and "Shaber's gang", long since banished from the printed word of the press, and with their help they aim, by tickling with pills of smut [?] and narcosis [?] the erotic feelings of the downtrodden public, to lull to sleep the worries of livelihood and the feeling that had developed for the beauty and purity of the printed word.
It goes dark before one's eyes when one ponders today's Jewish press.
Well, and what does it look like in the field of our political and social life?
Do we have a single healthy institution? Do we have a single institution that would inspire honour and respect, faith and trust? Do we have a single party whose foundations would not be shaken and trampled by the steps of real life?
The conclusion we draw from this is bitter and dark. Like a fish against a glass wall, so we all beat ourselves in want, in penury and in sinking obscurantism, without the faintest ray of hope that we shall yet live to see better times soon, in our days.
Fallow [?] and lamenting.
Ruin and despair.
Sz. Bazan.
He told the pure truth...

[Sosnowiec — humoresque; landlord and tenants.] A true story that happened here in our town and looks just like a humoresque...
It happened on one of the main streets of Sosnowiec. There the well-known landlord Mr. X has a large house (one of the most beautiful buildings in our town).
He is, as such, a good man, always smiling, has a kind word for everyone, sometimes even does a favour, has many friends; with the residents of his house, i.e. his tenants, he behaves, it is true, very officially (as a landlord does), but quite correctly... He has only one fault: he does not like children. That is, his own children he actually likes quite a lot — truly "my life" — but other people's children he does not care to see... Not to speak of the children of the tenants who live in his house — those he positively hates. The reason is quite a simple one: he says that the children — help, the children! — turn his whole house into a ruin-heap... They, the children, spoil his walls, the children wreck his pump, the children play football in the courtyard and knock out a couple of window panes in the process, etc.
So you understand by yourselves that when he had the opportunity to let a flat of 2 rooms and a kitchen, he looked as far as possible for a couple without children, or at worst with one child, but on condition — no more...
And it came to pass, one fine bright day, that a Jew in a hard black hat came in to the landlord; as it later turned out, he was a Litvak, one of the genuine Litvaks, and between the owner of the house and the Litvak the following kind of conversation developed:
— A good morning to you, panie landlord.
— Good morning, good year, what is your request?
— Why, I have no request of you at all. Here I have come to you to Sosnowiec, and in the street I learnt, you see, that you really have a flat to let, and so [?]... well, how else — I have come to you on that account.
— By all means — says the landlord — if we can agree on the price... But the main thing, tell me please, have you got a wife?
— Certainly I have a wife, may she live to a hundred — answers the Litvak in the hard black hat.
— One more question I wanted to ask you — and little children, have you got those too?...
— Nein... — answers the Litvak with a certain pride.
They came to terms on the price very quickly, for what is there to say — with a tenant without children... will the landlord haggle over the price? And barely 2 weeks had passed when the new tenant moved into the new flat with his whole household.
And here begins the very heart of the story. The landlord had only just come back from Karlsbad. The next morning, first thing, he goes out into the courtyard to take a look... and imagine his astonishment: right in the middle of the courtyard a whole army of children, from 2 years to 10, is running about, and the new tenant, the Litvak, stands commanding them like a general on the battlefield.
— What? What is this? — the landlord asks him in great alarm — what, have you set up a Froebel school [kindergarten] here in my house?
— God forbid — the Litvak answers calmly — these are, you see, my very own children, may they live, healthy in their little bones!
— H-e-l-p, robber, murderer, you have slaughtered me without a knife! — the landlord cried out — you told me back then, to my question whether you have children, expressly that "nein"...
— What do you mean, God be with you, panie landlord, did I, God forbid, deceive you? Here there really are little children, no evil eye — nine ["nayn"]...
Please, count them yourself, pardon me, and you will convince yourself that I told you the pure truth...
The landlord, Mr. X, fainted, and it took a long time until he was brought round...

Talmudic Literature and Its Methods

Elchanan Zider.
Our great, rich, widely branching Talmudic literature is, as is well known, a product of the creations of many generations of scholars, who are called Tannaim and Amoraim.
The Mishnah, which was edited by R' Yehuda ha-Nasi, or as he is called for short — Rabbi, was closed 130 years after the destruction of the Second Temple (200 years according to the common reckoning of time) in the Land of Israel.
The Jerusalem Talmud, which was created in the Land of Israel, is a product of the creations of five generations of Amoraim and was closed in the Land of Israel at the end of the 4th century.
The Babylonian Talmud, which was compiled in Babylonia (present-day Iraq, Mesopotamia), is a product of the creations of 7 generations of Amoraim and was closed in Babylonia in the year 500 according to the common reckoning of time.
Besides this we possess from the above-mentioned scholars a rich literature bearing the names: Tosefta (a supplement to the Mishnah), Baraita (remnants of the Baraita are cited in the Talmud, but the greater part was lost), halakhic Midrashim, such as: Mekhilta, Sifra (with a hiriq under the samekh) and Sifre (the samekh with a hiriq and the resh with a tsere; among us the reading of these has been corrupted), and aggadic Midrashim such as Midrash Tanhuma, Midrash Rabbah and many others.
This rich literature, which in itself represents great encyclopaedias of various sciences, was created thanks to the study which the Jewish people devoted to the Torah [printed "rer"] and also to the Prophets and Writings. Mostly thanks to the Pentateuch, which was called the Written Torah, and so the whole Talmudic literature is called the Oral Torah, because for many generations it was forbidden to write this literature down; it was to be studied only by heart.
In studying the Torah the Tannaim and Amoraim made use of various methods and logical rules. Thus we know that Hillel ha-Nasi, who lived in the time of King Herod the First (a hundred years before the destruction of the Second Temple), already made use of seven rules, middot, in the study of Torah, and thanks to using this method on a certain Torah problem (whether one may offer the Passover sacrifice on the Sabbath) he succeeded in occupying the high post of a president, Nasi over the Sanhedrin; and he became so esteemed among Jews that his children too inherited the high office of Nesi'im over the Sanhedrin for 15 generations, until the year 425.
(See: Pesachim folio 66, also Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim, chapter Tamid Nishchat).
Later, again, we find that Rabbi Yishmael already uses thirteen rules in the study of Torah (bi-shlosh esreh middot ha-Torah nidreshet); R' Akiva his colleague (who is known from the Bar Kokhba revolt against Hadrian the Roman emperor in the years 135 132 [sic, i.e. 132–135]) also uses thirteen middot, but in a different combination (for instead of kelal u-ferat he uses the middah of ribbui u-mi'ut) — see Shevuot 26.
The thirteen middot of R' Yishmael are also found in the prayer book. The thirteen rules were used in studying the halakha, the laws of the Torah.
In studying the aggada (the non-halakhic part of the Torah) thirty-two middot were used, which were finally formulated by Rabbi Eliezer, the son of Rabbi Yose ha-Gelili (this Rabbi Eliezer lived in the middle of the second century, in the time of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda).
And because all these middot are very important, if only because through their help the Talmudic literature was created, many works have therefore arisen which treat all these rules seriously. In recent times Dr. A. Schwarz, rector of the Rabbinical Seminary in Vienna, who died this year, distinguished himself in this field. Some of the works have also been translated into Hebrew.
And in order to interest the readers in this problem, and especially the youth, and to give them the opportunity to reflect a little on this important matter, I shall pose a few questions here:
1) Looking into the prayer book, we read: bi-shlosh esreh middot ha-Torah nidreshet, the Torah is studied by thirteen rules; but trying to count them, we see that there are sixteen rules. The question arises: how must one count here so that it comes out thirteen?
2) Hillel ha-Nasi counts seven middot (Tosefta Sanhedrin ch. 7, Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 37) and Rabbi Yishmael thirteen; the question arises: did they in Hillel's time know no more than the seven?
3) Why is the middah which the Talmud calls hekesh (analogy) not also counted among the middot?
There are many more questions to pose, but we want to see what echo the above-mentioned questions will find among the readers; [then] we shall devote several articles to the subject.

A swindler in the role of a 'tsore-klaper' (hard-luck pleader)

In a time of crisis, when human hearts "grow softer", it is the best opportunity for swindlers of every kind to arouse pity with their "heart-rending stories", and in this way they manage to swindle the public, from whom they cheat money, clothes and the like.
Just such a person has been "touring" our town for about a week: wherever he comes he tells about "tragedies" taking place in "respectable families", and that he is the emissary whose only intention is to help them, the "fallen" (impoverished), so to speak.
The person also came to Mrs. Ts. Kugelman, to whom he related that on Modrzejowska street there is a very respectable family that is perishing of hunger, the children go barefoot, so he wants Mrs. K. to give a few pairs of shoes for the fallen family.
Mrs. K. realised that the "benefactor" is a plain swindler and told him to come the next day.
The person, however, did not come again, but sent his female companion, a fellow helper, who also wanted the shoes for the "respectable family".
As has been found out, a gang of swindlers is working in this field, and one must be very careful, not too light-minded, and not give to these fellows.
It is also worth adding that our rabbinate, may it live long, should be a little more careful and not issue any "qualifications" (recommendations) to these shady people, who only seek to "fish in troubled waters"...

The Assessment of Income Tax.

How can the commission members defend the taxpayers?

The commissions for assessing income tax will soon begin their work. The representatives of the merchants on the assessment commissions will this year have to fight a hard battle, because, despite the catastrophic situation of the merchants, there is a tendency to impose a considerably larger tax than last year.
This will be felt most of all by the merchants who keep no commercial books, and by the merchants of the third and fourth trade categories. The income tax will come out [high] because the turnover is assessed as many times greater than it was in reality.
The offices [urzędy, tax offices] now have, as one sees, the task of assessing income much higher than it was last year.
They do it quite simply. The merchants are notified that last year they had a larger turnover, 3–4 times greater than in the previous year, and even three times greater than the assessment commission for the turnover tax had assessed their turnover. And on that basis a large income tax will then be assessed from the "inflated" turnover.
It will be very hard to defend the merchants who keep no commercial books, because unfortunately they have no proper factual documents with which to prove that their turnover and income were smaller than they want to assess.
Nevertheless, the members of the assessment commissions must not give up their work of defending the taxpayers.
The commission members can demand that in assessing income one should rely on the materials which the office [urząd] holds from the commissions that assessed the turnover tax, and demand [?] that income be assessed from this established turnover. This can succeed above all in 90 percent of cases with merchants of the third category, about whom there is no certain proof that the turnover was larger.
The merchants' representatives must pay special attention to cases when [?] the commissions themselves will assess income "by eye" according to the personal expenses of daily life.
The commission members have the right to demand that all assessments of merchants about whom they have no precise information be postponed to the next session, in order to gather [information]. The naczelnik [head of the tax office] or his deputy must comply with this demand.

The Robbery at the Railway Cash Office in Dąbrowa Was Staged by the Railway Cashier Himself, in Person..

[Dąbrowa — crime.]
As our readers know, a robbery was carried out at the railway cash office in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], in which 60,000 zł. were taken.
The robbery put the entire police of Zagłębie on its feet. Several persons were even arrested, who were, however, released after the investigation.
But like a thunderclap in broad daylight came the sensational news that the whole "robbery" had been carried out by the cashier himself with the help of his friends.
The news electrified everyone; nobody could believe that the railway cashier Bednarski, who has held the post for decades at the Dąbrowa railway station, who also plays a role in Polish public life, and was elected councillor on the Sanacja club [list] in Dąbrowa, should be capable of such a big affair.
How was the matter discovered?
On the very day of the robbery the tavern-keeper Olszewski, a resident of Koszelew, and a certain Kizioł [?] from Sosnowiec were arrested; the latter is a professional safe-breaker. Since both of them "proved" that at the moment of the robbery they could not have been at the Dąbrowa railway station, the investigating judge released them — but they were closely shadowed.
A secret agent was also posted at Bednarski's home, who followed his every step. The secret agent kept watch like this for several days, day and night, until "the curtain rose" and the culprit was revealed...
It was Thursday night, a terrible rainstorm accompanied by thunder and lightning, and the agent hid from the storm in the front house of Bednarski's flat.
Three o'clock at night. The agent hears Bednarski's flat being unlocked, and there he sees the "sick" Bednarski going down into a cellar, where he spent several minutes.
One goes out, the other comes in: when Bednarski came out of the cellar the agent went down, and searching with an electric torch he noticed that the earth had been dug up, and found there a tin box with 9 thousand 600 zł.
The agent immediately went off with the money to the police station, handed over all the details, and soon afterwards Bednarski was arrested.
Bednarski, already after his arrest, played the role of a poor wretch, wept, feigned illness; only when the bundle of money found in the cellar was laid before his eyes did he finally confess. Together with Bednarski, Olszewski and Kizrał [sic; above "Kizioł"] were also arrested; no money was found on them.
On the order of the investigating judge the official Milkowski, who was in a room adjoining that of the cashier Bednarski, was also arrested. After the investigation Milkowski was soon released.
What does Bednarski declare?
The main investigation is being conducted to find out where the money is. According to Bednarski's statement, there were 58 thousand zł. in the cash office. A day before the robbery he took 10 thousand zł., and the rest was taken by his accomplices.
In connection with the big affair a ministerial commission has also come to Dąbrowa, with the aim of carrying out an audit of the books. According to conjecture, great disorder has prevailed in the railway books for 2 years already, and great abuses have been committed in this area.
This Saturday, by order of the investigating judge Mr. Polak, a confrontation of 10 witnesses with the accomplices in the robbery will take place in the Będzin prison.
The confrontation is to bring out certain facts which will clarify a series of details not yet [known] until now.

Compassion Is Cruelty.

[Essay — Jewish charity and philanthropy.]
A talk about our philanthropic institutions.
Today is a time of revisions. Stalin is revising Communism — whole camps of revisionists are busy re-examining Capitalism, Germany is revising the Treaty of Versailles, Davidovich is revising the Tarbut movement.
So I will allow myself to carry out a tiny revision in our own little Jewish corner. I want to revise our philanthropy.
I do not mean revising a particular philanthropic institution, although that too would be very important. I am sure that in every single institution one would find something that would be of great interest to the public; this time I want to deal with philanthropy itself, in general.
We Jews pride ourselves greatly on our feeling of compassion; after all, we are merciful sons of the merciful, a people of feeling, different from and better than the dry, hard-hearted gentiles, who can watch a hungry man die in the street.
It is precisely this that I want to revise.
Have you not noticed a strange contradiction in the nature of every charity gabbai?
To begin with, he must surely be soft-hearted, otherwise he would not have been drawn to philanthropy; but in the philanthropic work itself he is a cold robber, a heart of stone, for whom human tears are like water from a tap... Where does this duality come from?
Of course, one can be a sceptic about all his soft-heartedness; one can say that he came to the office of gabbai with quite different intentions — seeking honour, or even a livelihood. Certainly we do not lack gabbaim of that kind. But as a rule, the feeling of compassion is the key to philanthropic activity; why, then, does this feeling become so hardened, so blunted, in the work itself?
The reason is that the feeling of compassion which leads to philanthropy is a blurred, diffuse [?] one, like all sentiments, without control and discipline; whereas philanthropic work, like all work, must be organised, disciplined, must be subject to strict order.
"Compassion is cruelty." — This saying the gabbai pronounces when someone tries to appeal to him to do something that goes beyond the frame of his programme. But earlier, when he sets about building the philanthropic institution, he knows of no such sayings; then he knows only compassion, philanthropy without measure...
Our philanthropy has turned out exactly like the economy of the world. Just as in the world today goods are manufactured without reckoning and without a plan, so we manufacture charity without any calculation. The difference is that there, in manufacturing, one must later look for buyers, and if one does not find them, one must drown the goods so that they do not spoil the price. In charity there is never any lack of "buyers"; it is givers who are lacking, and one is drowned in debts and deficits...
There, in the world economy, the chaos has shaken up peoples and states, created unemployment and hunger for tens of millions, and so one is forced to revise the matter. Here, however, in our Jewish philanthropy, we do not feel the fatal results of the chaos so strongly; we still think that by out-begging [?] and out-competing one another we will save something.
In reality it is a flood of philanthropy, in which all the institutions are drowning, and no ark at all has been built in which even one charity society could save itself...
So I want to say that it is very doubtful whether our compassion, which reaches only as far as the threshold of the charity institution, is such a great virtue. Would it not be better if this cold calculation, which the gabbaim display later in the work, governed them earlier — before they drag themselves and the whole community into an unwieldy tangle of grand undertakings [?] out of which we cannot disentangle ourselves?
Is not our compassion, on the whole, a great cruelty? Perhaps with the energy and the money that are so often wasted, like seed sown on the sandy desert, one could have achieved truly great constructive acts of help!
The revision must be deep and thorough; it must embrace all our communal work in all fields, classify it according to its usefulness, establish which of the bodies live as parasites at the expense of the other, more important ones — and close them mercilessly.
"Compassion is cruelty" — this rule must apply not only to those who are in need of charity, but also to the charity societies themselves.
A Jew of the whole year.
The Poverty of the Citizen and the Wealth of the State.

[Article — economy, state and taxes; Poland. Followed by an editorial note on an anonymous etrog letter.]
In the time of the inflation, Witos [Wincenty Witos], the then prime minister, said: you citizens want to be rich and leave the state in poverty; we want to turn it round — the state shall be rich and the citizen poor.
Witos's prophecy came true only by half: the citizen did indeed become poor, but the state did not become rich.
At first sight it seemed that the Polish citizen possessed inexhaustible possibilities to make rich, if not himself, then at least the state. And for several years that is indeed how it went. The citizen strained his last powers of combination, turned work and initiative into money; the government with its strong hand created the necessary conditions for the stability of the situation, on that basis also obtained a little foreign currency, and the state had the possibility of drawing enough abundance for its budgets.
And when the citizen groaned and moaned and argued that the pump was sucking his last strength out of him, nobody believed him, until... until the citizen's till showed its bottom [lit. "the lid"].
Private enterprises went under or were reduced. The monopolised and nationalised state enterprises too were weakened, and the state's revenue budgets began to show large holes [lit. "bubbles"].
Then one saw the falseness of Witos's theory: there can be no wealth in the state when the citizen is poor.
The misfortune would still not have been so great if the state could, just like the citizen, adapt itself to the situation and let its expenditure shrink in proportion to the shrunken revenues. But the trouble is that the state, however poor it may be, must stay with its rich ambitions. It cannot shrink, adapt itself; it must pinch the citizen's cheeks so that its colour will hold...
On top of that it is pushed by its companions, the other states, which took it into the European round dance. Those too have trouble enough and rack their brains how to crawl out of the crisis. But with them the waters have not yet "come in unto the soul" (Ps. 69:2): their citizen is not yet so impoverished and pumped out, they can still live on income tax, because the citizen has an income. With us income tax is after all a caricature; with us people who do not earn enough for bread are told to pay this tax; with us the state must live on turnover tax, on the so-called "zabin u-zabin" [buy and sell] transactions, which have long been carried on for the most part without money, only on tokens, on trust — and from that the state must fill its treasury.
It is indeed very bad. Our ministers thrash about like fish in water. Now they talk of a tax mobilisation, now they deny it, now there is talk of a "small tax" — out of pennies shall come gold coins — but evidently the penny too has already gone out of the pocket.
Now the citizen is already believed that he has nothing, that he cannot give; but with believing one can do nothing.
The only thing gained from the present situation is the lesson that the calculation about the poverty of the citizen and the wealth of the state is a false one: the citizen is the foundation of the state, and when the foundation rots, the building cannot stand firm.
This teaching, if it is taken to heart, will have to lead to new conclusions, which will set the state on firm ground and not on foundations of contrived theories.
P. K.

"Pompadour": I Snatch a Chat with the World

[Satirical feuilleton — world politics; an imaginary conversation.] By "Pompadour" (pen name).
I. — Hallo, World! How are you doing? How do you feel?
World. — (wiping off the sweat): Hot! Very hot!
I. — You, World, are hot too! But surely you can fan yourself with the best winds!...
World. — Yes... I can... but what good is fanning oneself when lime-kilns are burning on all sides, and everything burns and blazes...
I. — For example?
World. — One need not go far to look: Hoover's "salvations" set my brain on fire... the Moratorium makes my temples pound... my mouth goes dry from French stubbornness, and I am drenched in sweat from MacDonald's speeches...
I. — So, as I see, you are not very wrapped up in politics?
World. — (grimacing): No! I hate politics... since time immemorial... My motto is: leave the world in peace!
I. — Does that mean, World, that you are pessimistic, as they call it?
World. — Anything but that!... Do you understand? The whole point is that I cannot be pessimistic even when I want to!...
I. — Why?
World. — Because I am, my child, too old and too experienced, and I know that all fevers pass — world-fever as well as love-fever — and from the heat only those die who are too weak to bear even the cold... and as for despairing — there's nothing to despair about!...
I. — After summer comes winter, you mean?
World. — In that sense... I know that whatever may happen, and however much the leaders of the world may want to drive me off the rails, I shall not go under!
I. — The world remains the world, you mean?
World. — Yes, yes... that is exactly what I mean...
I. — (with a smile) And you are not even afraid of MacDonald's dark premiership?
World. — (also with a smile). I don't take him seriously, this MacDonald. He is quite a good, quiet citizen[?] of mine! And the revolutionary speeches he makes for the benefit[?] of the Right Poale Zion...
I. — And what about Trotsky's world revolution?
World. — (ironically) Trotsky? — Do you know what he looks like to me with his world revolution?... Like that Jew who will not plough and sow his field because he is waiting for the Sabbatical year... Trotsky's world revolution, my friend, is a Jewish flourish from the festival prayer-book: it sounds like "Hayom harat olam" ["Today the world was conceived"]... They do say it with great pomp, but is anyone actually frightened by "Hayom harat olam"?...
I. — And what do you think[?] of the world crisis?
World. — I am already so old, much older than I look, and I have already lived through more than one world crisis...
I. — (with a jab). But nevertheless you are wiping off the sweat a little too much?...
World. — When it's hot one sweats, and when one sweats one wipes off the sweat... a law of nature, that's all...
I. — But you are a tiny bit agitated all the same?
World. — Well, you know: heat makes one agitated, and when one is agitated a sharp word sometimes slips out... But it's nothing... Soon the weather will become milder... and soon Bernard Shaw will come back from Soviet Russia and set everything right with a joke...
I. — May I ask you, World: do you think anything of Bernard Shaw?
World. — Of course!... How could one not think highly of him? Bernard Shaw is the all-world radio announcer: he talks to fire and water... and goes out on all programmes and stations... he even speaks on the "Jewish Hour"...
I. — And what is your opinion of Coolidge?
World. — Coolidge? The cleverest man of his time: he left Hoover an inheritance — a not-bad mess of mud — and he himself goes fishing in real rivers...
I. — (with a jump). And what do you think, World, about Germany? — Will she be helped?
World. — (with a roguish little smile). Germany will conquer the world! If not with her politics — then with her film operettas... Germany is now in the best position: she is like the one and only pauper in a little town full of come-down householders... The come-down ones are ashamed to take! It doesn't suit them, they are still not real poor people! But the pauper — he takes for all he's worth ["for whatever the world stands on"]... Germany has a great future!...
I. — And what will become, dear World, of America?
World. — America? There is nothing to worry about for her! In the end she will work her way up to being the official broker of mankind. She will fly about in aeroplanes... twirl her little cane like an Odessa broker... chew a straw... arrange matches, knot deals... collect brokerage fees — sky-high ["into the father's father"]!... and drink on it — to console herself over her achievements — with a drop of brandy...
I. — As I see, World, even in such a crisis your sense of humour does not desert you?
World. — You understand, my friend, if I didn't make fun of myself, I would long ago have gone under... It's a good thing that the "end of the world" is also no more than a joke...
I. — Thank you, World, for the conversation! I have learned a lot from it!
World. — Thanks for thanks! For I too have gained a great deal from it... You see, when one gets talking, one forgets for the time being all the troubles and conferences...
Now Is the Moment of Decision. (Reflections on the Start of the School Year)

(Reflections on the start of the school year).
In a few days the streets of Zagłębie will take on a quite different appearance. The schoolchildren, and those who will have the privilege of coming to school for the first time, will await impatiently the moment when the school gates open before them; but this year there is the threatening danger that the gates of the schools will not stand open for all children. Very many, unfortunately, will remain outside. Others again will be transferred from the public (elementary) schools for Jewish children to the public schools for non-Jewish children. All this is happening because, for the sake of economy, many teachers will be cut and many classes will be closed. The critical moment will also not allow many parents to send their children to the secondary schools, where the tuition fee is rather high.
The moment now is a very serious one. The most immediate duty of the parents is to give the children a proper education and upbringing. Bringing up and educating the child cannot and must not be postponed to later, better times. One cannot leave the child in the school years even for a single day without a school, otherwise the street with its bad deeds will become its educator. Parents must always keep this before their eyes. Parents must also remember that Jewish children can be educated only in Jewish national schools; not only the son must be educated in a cheder, but the daughter too. The future mother and educator of the Jewish people must be brought up in the Jewish national spirit, in a Jewish national school.
In Zagłębie we have for Jewish girls the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec, which has been set up on a very sound basis. The most important thing for a Jewish national school is the curriculum. On the one hand the curriculum of the state schools has been adopted; on the other, it is combined with the curriculum of Jewish studies created by the Jewish National School Union in Łódź. A great obstacle to the proper implementation of the Jewish curriculum is the fact that not all pupils begin attending the school from the preparatory classes; on the other hand — however sad the phenomenon may be — the school struggles with the parents, who do not feel so strong a need for Jewish studies for their children...
No small difficulties came also from the school authorities, which at first did not want to approve the curriculum. Despite all these obstacles, the management of the gymnasium told itself that in this respect no compromises whatsoever must be made. The moment a Jewish national school makes any compromises at all regarding the Jewish curriculum in order to find favour in the eyes of the authorities and obtain the rights of government schools, at that moment it must lose the trust of the public, because the curriculum is the banner of the school, and to betray the banner is a crime.
The Jewish public in Zagłębie must know how to appreciate the pedagogical value of the Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec, which has received the rights of government schools without giving any promises. And that in the future the school will have a building of its own. With pride the national character of the school has always been emphasised.
The recognition by the authorities the school obtained thanks to the harmonious work prevailing there among the management, the teaching staff and the supervisory board, for whom there exists all the time only one aim — to devote effort for the good of the school. With slow but sure steps the school goes forward, and now the moment is not far off when, with their own resources, they will set about building a building of their own.
Now, when the parents stand before a moment of decision which may decide the future of their daughters, the parents must come to the conclusion that the only school that gives the best guarantee that their daughter will be brought up in the Jewish national spirit is the Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec. When the attendance of the school increases, it is to be hoped that the tuition fee will become smaller, and in this way it will be accessible to the less well-off parents. The school is built on democratic foundations and wants to serve the broad masses. This can happen, however, only when our so-called intelligentsia, and sometimes also "patented" (card-carrying) Zionists, will not send their daughters to non-Jewish schools. It must be absolutely impermissible that a communal activist, a Zionist, a member of the dozór (kehilla board) should be admitted to any Jewish national society whatsoever while he educates his children in a non-Jewish school.
The Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec, which develops in exemplary fashion, grows and flourishes from year to year, and only with its own resources, without bowing to anyone and without becoming dependent on anyone, because the parents carry the burdens as a sacred duty, because the school is dear to them.
This school is a living example for the pupils who have grown up together with it. The untiring work must sooner or later lead to the goal. Such an atmosphere prevails in the educational institution, and this gives all those involved in the work of education the best hope for the future.
The problem of educating the Jewish daughter is one of the most important problems. The parents must take stock before they decide which school to send their daughters to. One must also remember that just as harmful as non-Jewish schools are also those schools which want to be Jewish only in that their owner is a Jew, but which have nothing whatever to do with a Jewish national character.
The healthy sense of the Jewish parents will surely show them the right way in which they must bring up their daughter. Their ambition will be to enlarge in Zagłębie the circle of conscious parents who have set themselves the task of creating with their own resources a great work of national education.
They too will join the work and help to ensure that the 10-year jubilee, which the Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec celebrates next year, shall be celebrated already in its own building.
Elen.
Whom Can One Trust? (A Little Feuilleton)

(A little feuilleton).
An upheaval has come upon the world — one cannot trust anybody.
Once the surest authority was a state. And today — just try lending some state or other a little money. Not a few groszy, of course, but some tens or some hundreds of millions of dollars — it would be worth making a "moratorium blessing"...
About trusting a magistrate (municipality) there is no need to speak; take even our magistrate, which is still one of the creditworthy ones — how many subsidies for institutions has this same magistrate already promised to give and not given...
Now, as regards trust in our kehilla — there is no need to speak of it; in town people even say that...
In short: the whole world is in burnt-up [?] troubles and one cannot trust anybody — neither the community nor the individual.
The highest degree of honesty nowadays is [—] when one requests a "nadzór" (court supervision) over oneself...
Even your own wife you cannot trust today — the wife perhaps even less than anyone else, for they, the women, are surely not at the highest degree of honesty, and the proof: so far not a single wife has yet asked her husband to appoint a "nadzór" over her...
And nevertheless one can still trust somebody! — Him, the One and Only!
Take for example this year's summer, which distinguished itself by there being almost no rains, no thunder and no lightning, and we already thought that in heaven now it is just as on earth — a moratorium.
In the end you see how "He" pays with interest. Hardly a day goes by without "Him" giving something on account...
A world is bankrupt, nobody pays — only "He" has been and has remained creditworthy!
Onkelos.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tavo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parashat Tavo
The Portion.
—o—
a) "A wandering Aramean was my father, and he went down into Egypt" (Deut. 26:5)
It seems: all the hatred of the nations towards us stems from our separateness, from "their laws are different from those of every people", and therefore there is surely nothing to thank God for when He saves us from our enemies, since all the hatred of us is only because of Him, because of God... But the hatred of the Jew has another source, not separateness. Here: "an Aramean, (would have) destroyed my father" — Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, one of his own kin, no longer someone separate, and yet "he sought to uproot everything". And again: "and he went down into Egypt" — we ourselves went down to Egypt, sought the Egyptians' closeness, wanted to "mix in", and that did not help either — "and they afflicted us", they then actually tormented us... That does not help either.
Divrei Shaul.
• • •
Under the reign of Franz Joseph many Jews converted in order to obtain government posts, but the baptismal certificate did not always help; it could not disguise the Jewish nose...
One such convert, who was left disappointed, made his way to the Emperor himself and told him that he had accepted the Christian faith and had also persuaded many Jews to do the same, and so he asked for a reward.
The Emperor pats him on the shoulder: "You have done so much for our faith by this that I am quite unable to reward you. I must leave that to God Himself..."
—o—
b) "And the priest shall take the basket from your hand" (ibid. 4)
The law reads:
The rich had to bring first fruits in golden and silver baskets, and poor people may bring them in ordinary baskets woven from twigs. The golden baskets the priest must give back to the rich, and the ordinary baskets, the poor people's, the priest takes for himself.
That is what is meant by "after the poor man goes poverty": misfortune follows the pauper — because he is a beggar and has nothing but a simple basket, they take even that away from him...
Bava Kamma (92)
—o—
c) "And the Lord has avouched you... to keep all His commandments" (ibid. 17 [?])
Does God have to keep commandments? —
Yes, God is obliged to give us the possibility of fulfilling His commandments...
Likkutim Hadashim.
—o—
d) "Cursed be the man... who does it in secret" (27:15)
All these curses were said only against those who sin in secret, who are ashamed to sin before people, only not before God... Whereas the one who sins openly may not be cursed. On him repentance will work; lost is only the one who is outwardly pious and inwardly sinful...
Beit Shmuel Aharon.
—o—
e) "So that you shall be mad for the sight of your eyes" (28:34)
A madman is mad only in appearance, in the eyes of people, but in his own eyes he is the cleverest man in the world...
Ohel Yaakov.
• • •
An old anecdote:
Ibn Ezra had a son who lived in a faraway country. Once the son writes to his father that he sees, according to the science of the astrologers, that the grain that will grow this year in that country will drive mad the people who eat it. So he asks his father to send him grain from his own land.
The wise father answers him: Better, my son, that you eat that grain and be mad like everyone else, than that you be the one sane man among a country of madmen, for then they would actually take that exceptionally sane man for mad...
—o—
f) "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you" (28:10)
According to the Talmud's homily the verse means the tefillin. The Talmud also says that God lays tefillin and that in His tefillin it is written: "Who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth".
And therefore, if the nations learn of such an inscription in God's tefillin, they will come to fear the Jews, for they will understand that God must forgive the Jews' sins, because otherwise His tefillin would surely become unfit... And when Jews are without sin, then there is indeed reason to fear them.
Or la-Shamayim.
—o—
The Haftarah.
g) "Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as doves to their windows?" (Isaiah 60)
Two men are quarrelling over a dove, whose it is. The one who keeps it in a cage claims it is his, and the other claims it is his. Says the latter: let the dove out of the cage and we will see to whom it flies —
Over the Jews, too, people quarrel about whom they belong to... But just let them be freed from their cage, and one will soon see where they will be drawn — to their home, to Zion...
After Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
—o—
h) "Arise, shine, for your light has come" (ibid.)
Like someone who falls asleep in a dirty, bad and dark place. A friend of his comes with a lantern and wants to wake him, but the other feels like sleeping on, so the friend goes away with the lantern.
We too feel like sleeping in the dark exile; more than once God has shone upon us with an awakening light, but we have shut our eyes tight — we do not feel like waking up..
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
Avot.
i) "Whoever's deeds exceed his wisdom" (ch. 3)
He who does more than he preaches to others — his wisdom, i.e. his preaching, endures: people look to him [as an example]...
Lev Avot.
—o—
j) "And honour" (ch. 4)
"Whoever chases after honour, honour runs away from him", and whoever runs away from honour, honour chases after him.
What is the difference between the two? Either way neither of them has the honour: from the first the honour runs away, and the second runs away from honour — both are running and both have no honour —
The difference is when they stop...
Divrei Shaul.

What's new in Zagłębie?
Będzin
The holidays are no obstacle to holding the elections to the board.
