As we reported at the time, the outgoing kehilla board adopted a resolution that, because many members of the council are away at their summer residences, and also because of the holidays, the date for electing the new kehilla board must be postponed until Chol HaMoed Sukkot. At what hour must the gates be locked?

[Będzin — Municipality.]
Some time ago we raised in the columns of our paper the question of locking the gates at 0 [sic; probably 10] o'clock in the evening. We pointed out that the hour was wrong, especially in summer, when night begins at 9 o'clock and an hour later the residents are already locked in.
The Householders' Association took an interest in this matter and approached the Magistrat (town council) about it with a memorandum.
This week the association received a reply from the Magistrat that it has been decided that the gates of the houses in Będzin may be locked: 1) in the summer months, i.e. from 1 May to 1 October (październik) — at 11 in the evening; 2) in the remaining months at 10 in the evening.

Expenses for supporting the family in the income tax.
Very many merchants are now receiving demands from the urząd [tax office] questioning the correctness of the declaration (zeznanie) they submitted; therefore supplementary explanations about income are requested.
We have already explained that every taxpayer has the right to demand from the office that it show him precisely what doubts the office has about the declared income. One can answer this in writing, and the office is obliged to state why it suspects the correctness of the income declaration. Now we wish to explain a second important point about the income tax.
In the income tax the offices mostly rely on the taxpayer's standard of living. The naczelniks [heads of the offices] hold that one must earn in order to support the family, and if, according to the family's standard of living, one has spent, for example, 10 thousand zł. a year, they assume that one has earned that sum.
It is, however, a fact that many, very many merchants did not earn enough in 1930 to support the family; rather, they had a deficit because of the bad state of trade.
Taxpayers must know how to answer the office's demand.
In cases where the merchants earned little in 1930, having sold too cheaply, at cost price or below cost, they must give the reasons in their answer, and as an illustration one should state the cost price of some main articles and the selling prices, and how much goes on administrative expenses; it is also most important to state that such-and-such a sum was spent on supporting the family, and that this is a pure deficit of that year's trade.
This must be added so that, if the office does not accept it as correct and nevertheless sets a higher income tax, one can on this basis file an appeal with the Appeals Commission (Komisja Odwoławcza), and this will be the most important point of support for one's defence.
H. W.

[Sport — football.] Hakoach — Shimshon-Jutrzenka, Tarnów 0:2 (0:1)

The law on trading hours again on the agenda

It is becoming ever clearer to the government that the present regulations on trading hours are outdated and utterly useless, because life itself forces them to be broken. A few months ago a draft reform of the law on trading hours was worked out. The government, however, took fright at the uproar that arose over it in the antisemitic press. But the conviction about the harmfulness[?] of the present situation grows stronger from day to day, and the fear of the shouting from the right is losing all meaning. The government has therefore again decided to put the questions of trading hours on the table.
Inter-ministerial conferences on the question are due to begin in the coming days. Whether the government will take fright again, or whether this time it will already put an end[?] to the abnormal situation, which aggravates the crisis in commercial circles, is, of course, hard to predict.

From Week to Week. Tadeusz Hołówko.

[Politics — Poland.] At the very time when, from the tribune of the Congress of Minorities in Geneva, Deputy Milena Rudnicka spoke out sharply in the name of the Ukrainians of Poland — in Truskawiec the well-known Sanacja activist, Deputy Tadeusz Hołówko, fell dead from a secret, murderous bullet; he had set himself as the goal of his life to solve the minorities question in Poland, and especially the Ukrainian problem. Hołówko, like most of Poland's present statesmen, had been a member of the P.P.S. and had already made himself known through socialist work. Later he went over to the Sanacja and became one of the permanent activists in Piłsudski's camp, handling the minorities questions.
He set out his ideas on this matter in a brochure about the minorities in Poland. Regarding the Jews, Hołówko held the position that the government must come to an understanding not with Orthodoxy, but with the progressive and national Jewish parties. Above all, however, Hołówko was interested in the Ukrainians; he wanted to ease their situation and give them equal rights, but only on condition that they renounce their statehood, irredentist demands and become loyal citizens of the Polish state. Nevertheless, the negotiations between Hołówko and the Ukrainians produced no positive results.
Hołówko did not realise his ideas. He left the minorities question in the same state in which he had found it.
A. Gertner.
How Did Welwel Schlimazel Take Revenge on His Heroic Little Wife?

[Sosnowiec — family life.] Mrs. Hela is a young and pretty little wife; for the sake of her poor father and mother she agreed to marry the Hasidic young man Welwel G.
And as is the custom all over the world, Welwel rented a summer flat for his young wife near Rajcza; Hela felt very good there. Every Friday afternoon Welwel used to come there, bringing along various sweets and good things; he paid off Hela's debts and on Sunday set off back home to the grind in Sosnowiec.
Welwel left every Sunday around 7 in the morning; his wife Hela saw him off to the train each time, waved her white handkerchief when the train pulled away, and Welwel beamed with joy.
When the train with Welwel had vanished from sight, Hela did not go home, but waited until the train from Bielitz arrived; on that very train Hela's "heart's love", a young lawyer, came regularly every Sunday and spent the time with Hela until Monday morning.
So it went the whole summer, and last Sunday, when Welwel was travelling home in the morning, he met on the train a woman neighbour who was already going home to Sosnowiec.
— Enough, I've kept silent for 3 months, she said, I can't stand it any longer. To deceive a husband like that, and such a husband too.
She told Welwel this while sitting with him on the train. Welwel did not think twice and took the next train back to his wife.
And what is there to tell — Welwel arrived just at the moment when, in the middle of broad daylight, the window shutters of his flat were closed and inside were Hela and the lawyer.
So he got up and left the house, went in to the landlord and said to him:
— Panie gospodarzu, I still owe you a hundred zł. for the flat; I wanted to come tomorrow to pay you and go home — I tell you that I will not come and will not pay; you must therefore guard my wife, so that she does not slip away from here, because otherwise your money is lost. With the same refrain Welwel went everywhere Hela owed money.
Welwel then wrote a little letter to Hela with the following content: "You can sit here until the new potatoes", and went home to Sosnowiec.
Now all the creditors are guarding the young wife so that she does not vanish from the village, and torment her to pay the debts; Hela is ashamed to show her face and thinks to herself:
— Who would have expected that Welwel Schlimazel could pull such a trick?

[Częstochowa / Będzin — swindle.] A young man approached the president of the community council in Częstochowa and declared that he had been delegated by the Political-Social Department of the Ministry of the Interior to carry out the necessary formalities so that the Częstochowa Jewish community should receive 5000 dollars, left by the late Jewish millionaire Benjamin in America.
Mr. Goldstein took the whole matter for the truth and waited until he would be summoned to Warsaw, to the Ministry of the Interior, in order to receive the money.
In the meantime the "delegate" borrowed 50 zł. from Mr. Goldstein and also turned to the rabbi for another loan of 50 zł.
The rabbi found the matter suspicious and at once got in touch with the police, who "invited" the "bird" into the commissariat, where it turned out that the fellow possessed 10 blank forms of birth certificates (metrykas), and also many such letters from the Ministry of the Interior to a series of Jewish communities. Among them also a letter to the Będzin community council.
Thanks to this the fellow has been spared the trouble of coming to Będzin, and has remained a Częstochowa "resident"...

For a false oath — 3 persons sentenced to 4 years' prison

Thou shalt not swear falsely!
This age-old commandment was transgressed by three peasants. They once appeared as witnesses in court and swore. On the strength of their oath one party won the case. The injured party, however, did not keep silent and came forward with a complaint that the above-mentioned had sworn falsely.
These days the trial took place in the district court; 20 witnesses appeared and established that the above-mentioned had given a false oath and had received money for it.
The court heard the witnesses, the prosecutor and the defence counsel and then pronounced a verdict, according to which all 3 defendants were sentenced to 4 years' prison.

A New Chapter of World History.

In our present time, almost every month and sometimes even more often, a new and interesting chapter of world history is written. The lines are written with a very nervous[?], shaky hand, and yet — what has once been written is not erased. The following lines cannot be anything other than a continuation of the previous ones.
And so, after the thrilling and interesting chapter "Germany", we had a chapter "England", which was read with truly breathtaking interest. And now there has arrived, as if suddenly, from one side, the chapter "Russia", which is even more important and more thrilling than the previous ones.
In Moscow, Paris, Warsaw and Berlin this chapter is being written simultaneously.
And there is surely no doubt that the relations [lit. "conditions"] between the Soviet Union and the peoples that sit behind the Bolshevik barrier are much more complicated than the relations between the democratic states themselves.
All peoples and countries have various "social" accounts among themselves, but the "common denominator" between them is their attachment to the democratic regime and to the capitalist economic system, and consequently their common bitter hatred of the Soviet Union, which made "kapores" of both of these fundamental foundations of the old world.
When England demands loans, it is a question only of her creditworthiness; the same is true of Germany. At the same time it means securing and consolidating the old regime, which is so dear and precious to everyone that even Otto Bauer, the radical socialist, agitated hotly[?] for it, and MacDonald, because of it, even broke with his party...
An agreement with the Soviet Union means holding out one's hand to the bitter natural enemy who, by the way, through his "dumping" has become everyone's most dangerous competitor.
What zigzag combinations have not already been made in the relations of the nations with the Soviet Union! America does not recognise the state, does not even admit its diplomatic representative, and nevertheless conducts the liveliest business with it, and even helps it carry out the Five-Year Plan. Poland lives with it in the greatest friendship, in the most refined diplomatic relations, and nevertheless has no dealings whatsoever with it, as though a Chinese wall stood between the two countries. England plays with it like a cat with a mouse: now they are friends, now they are on bad terms, now negotiations are opened, now they are broken off. France behaves roughly like Poland, but with more nervousness[?] and wavering. Germany is the only country which, since Rapallo, has bustled around the Soviet Union with enormous intensity, which further and further strengthens the romantic[?] relations between both countries.
There is no doubt that Germany, apart from the direct commercial benefits of this infatuation, also wanted to make political capital out of it with regard to France and Poland.
The Soviet Union, however, apparently has its own aim. In former years, when Trotsky was still at the helm, Moscow strove to kindle the fire of revolution in the whole world. Stalin, however, wants only one thing: to consolidate its own existence. The rest will come by itself later... In European intrigues the Soviet Union has no interest whatsoever and does not want to lend a hand to them.
At the present moment, as it seems, a hole is being bored in the Chinese wall between the Soviet Union and the rest of the world, and this is certainly a further step on the road of consolidation among the nations. An understanding with the Soviet Union has a much greater significance than the understandings among the democratic states. A non-aggression pact between these natural enemies will ease the way to the problem of disarmament in the world. One may say that thereby the heaviest stone would have been removed.
But here one immediately encounters the European intrigues. Peace with France! Does that not mean a betrayal on the part of France towards Poland? And if not — if Poland is also in this game — is it not a conspiracy against Germany? And then the whole mouse-nest is stirred up, the Balkans and Italy and so on and so forth!
That is why Litvinov had to stop in Berlin and from there reassure the world: no intrigues whatsoever are being woven here; one simply wants to draw closer to peace.
And one must believe in Litvinov's sincerity, because his words accord with the whole Soviet policy of recent years.
It follows that the various negotiations with Russia are a further chapter in post-war world history.
P. K.
In a Few Months We Will Be Rid of the Crisis!

A few days ago a well-known German astrologer — one of the modern "prophets" — published an article in which he prophesies that during the present winter, and generally in the first half of the year 1932, the crisis will intensify, but afterwards, i.e. in the second half of the year 1932, the crisis will end completely and a true golden age will begin.
To tell the truth, we do not much believe in the "prophecies" of these "prophets", who look up at the sky when they want to know what will happen on earth...
But this time, it seems, one can treat the prophecies of this star-gazer with a little more trust. (It happens sometimes that a star-gazer hits the mark...) Because almost at the same time a famous American economist, Stuart Chase, came out with a similar article; he prophesies not on the basis of stars that he sees in the sky, but on the basis of facts and figures, and he too reassures the public — people should not be alarmed by the winter, which will be even harder than the summer. This, he says, is the death-throes of the crisis and the birth-pangs of a new golden epoch.
Chase shows with factual material that the overproduction which brought about the present crisis is already over. Thanks to the fact that many factories did not work during this time, most shops have emptied out, and soon there will be such a demand for goods that they will literally be snatched out of one's hands.
Well, where will people get the money to buy goods? That, he says, is nothing — as long as there is work, there will be money...
Of course this answer is valid only for America, where money [of this kind?] is not lacking, only work is lacking. By the way, with his prophecy he indeed has only America in mind. But what will become of us? Here, after all, both work and money are lacking; so what will we get out of work if there will be nothing to pay with — here there is, after all, a shortage of cash?
But it is out of the question that in America things will be good and here no money will be lacking — surely a remedy will be found...
It is also interesting that this same Stuart Chase was one of the few economists who foresaw the present crisis and warned the American public, while they were still sitting by the fleshpots, to prepare for an exceptionally bad time; and now too he warns that during the coming prosperity people should keep their heads on their shoulders and not throw themselves too eagerly into work, because otherwise in the year 1940 a crisis will come that will many times exceed the present one.
But who can think now about the troubles of 1940, when there are still enough troubles of 1931...
Izydor.

What I Heard, What I Saw.

[Będzin and district — feuilleton.] Reported by Ben Amotz.

At „Bij tego Żyda“ [Beat that Jew]...
I am in a public school in Będzin. It is the eve of the new school year; Jewish mothers come with entreaties that the Pan Kierownik [Mr Headmaster] should have pity and enrol their children in the school, in the „Jewish“ school...
— Bij tego Żyda! — a voice is suddenly heard, and I look around: where does this „reverent“ cry come from here? After all, we are among Jewish children only, and in a „Jewish“ school, and yet...
And yet it is so after all: it is the same Yente, only with a Jewish lining. The „Bij tego Żyda“ was uttered by a Jewish boy; he is from Dąbrowa, all his days he studied in a non-Jewish school, soaked up the lowest hatred of everything that is Jewish, of Jewish children, and when he saw in the school corridor a Jewish boy in a long kapote standing next to him, he went red with anger and called his brother, also a pupil from Dąbrowa, to beat the Jewishly dressed boy
— „Bij tego Żyda“...
The Jewish mother, who came here to enrol her „treasure“, has a face burning with shame. „I must“, she says, „tear him out of the Christian environment; he cannot look at any Jewish child, he shows more hatred towards Jewish children than towards non-Jewish children.“
— „Bij tego Żyda“!

Mah-sim[?]...
The time is approaching when more than one Jew will boast: „Oh, have I got an etrog!“, a real „hadar“, a real gem, a genuine Corfu one, truly worth saying a blessing over...
— So what then has come up to be spoken against?
Here before us lies a proclamation (kol kore) of the Chief Rabbinate for the district of Jaffa and Tel Aviv, and what do we read in this proclamation?
...In the Jewish capital Salonica the Greeks tortured our brethren; they slaughtered small children and old people, students of Torah, robbed and burned Jewish goods and property, and those who saved themselves from the fire were shot.
But our hearts bleed even more seeing how „our own“ Jewish hands support the hooligans, those whose hands are spattered with Jewish blood...
And reading the appeal, a hard question awakes in me:
If a green spot on an etrog is a blemish, how can one fulfil the commandment with etrogim that bear red bloodstains from the Salonica slaughter?...
But why ask questions? We, the „Thou hast chosen us“ people, take no revenge on those who torment us. Never mind — there will surely be found such „rabbis“ who will give „hekhsherim“ for Corfu etrogim, just as hekhsherim are given for matzah meal... Yes,
— „Thy destroyers and they that made thee waste shall go forth of thee“ [Isaiah 49:17]...

An Unpaid Debt...
In a few weeks it will be the first yahrzeit of the Jewish artist Moshe Appelbaum, who died young.
It is almost a year already, but the stir that Appelbaum's death aroused has not yet been forgotten. For weeks on end the eulogies did not stop; countless friends and admirers, each in his own way, assessed the loss of Appelbaum's death to Jewish art, to Jewish culture, and after „Kedoshim“ — „Emor“ [allusion to the order of the Torah portions „Acharei Mot — Kedoshim — Emor“]
— it became hush, quiet...
It has almost been forgotten that there once lived and created among us, among so many friends and intimates, a Jewish artist Moshe Appelbaum, and — above all — it has been completely forgotten that the deceased left a wife and a child, who have the same needs as all living people...
• • •
A small living monument has been erected. A group of Jewish artists, friends of the deceased, have published 33 works of art in which the life and work of Moshe Appelbaum are reflected.
Care was taken that the book should be accessible to everyone: the de-luxe edition costs altogether 1 gulden [złoty] and 50 groszy.
Who, who, if not we, those who lived together with the artist, we who feast our eyes on the splendid mizrach wall in the Będzin synagogue, should surely, surely take in the de-luxe editions and thereby settle at least a small part of the debt still owed by us
— an unpaid debt...
— a debt of a gulden and a half...

„Dobry sposób“ [a good method]...
In a carriage of the Katowice — Będzin train.
Two young ladies are sitting — Jewish ones. One is the daughter of a well-known, sharp-witted Gerer Hasid, and the other is already a „meyukheses“ [one of distinguished lineage, ironically]
— her sister is already there...
The latter pours out her „bitter heart“ to the Hasid's daughter.
It is, she says, „bardzo nieprzyjemnie“ [very unpleasant] for me that my sister, the „baptised one“, came to visit us; it is not pleasant, w ogóle [altogether]...
— Cóż? [So what?] — the Hasidic daughter wonders — Co takiego? [What of it?] That one converts — is that such a misfortune? That was, she says, once upon a time, in those superstitious [zabobon] days, when parents rent their garments and sat shiva when a child of theirs left Judaism; but today? Today is it a disgrace? Does anyone today condemn [potępiać] the step? Zresztą [Besides], continues the Hasidic daughter, today it is done in an easy way too. Once they made a whole ceremony of it: ran off with the Christian man into a convent, stayed hidden for months, so that no human eye should see her; but today all these ceremonies are niepotrzebne [unnecessary], one goes through a wedding act [akt ślubny] and
— one goes on being with the family..
— a very good method...
Between Life and Death. (A Conversation about a Topical Matter).

[Feuilleton — the economic crisis; suicides.] By M. Postman. (A conversation about a topical matter).
A strange crisis we have today. Once people used to say of someone: “He is very badly off”, he is dying of hunger”. For what does it mean: he is dying? How long does the process of dying last in a person? A moment. Either a person has died or he lives. Nevertheless there were still people who really did simply die of hunger. All the rest, who barely had their livelihood, were candidates for death by hunger.
Do you remember Mendele’s [Mendele Moykher Sforim’s] groats? A big bowl of water in which one groat chased the others and could not catch up with them. With it one also ate a piece of dry wholemeal [“razowy”] bread — that is how the Jewish masses lived in the shtetl; for anything better there was not enough money.
And if even those couple of groszy were not there, the groats vanished together with the piece of bread, and one simply had to go hungry.
Today’s crisis, as is well known, comes not from dearness but from cheapness; not from a shortage of bread but from too much bread.
Now some wise man has already made a proposal that the state should supply all citizens with bread just as it supplies them with water: completely free of charge, every home should have two taps — from one water would flow and from the other grain would pour; one would have to pay only for the delivery.
Do you think the crisis would then have been avoided? At first sight it seems so. For what does a person need more than bread and water to keep body and soul together —
but that is not even the beginning. Today people indeed do not die of hunger, but they die of the crisis, they die of nerves.
A Jew comes home from the shop, puts his walking stick away in the corner, hangs his hat on the hook, takes the newspaper, runs his eyes over it — until dinner is ready.
He sits down at the table with wife and child; the maid serves the fragrant dishes, a dinner as usual, of 3–4 courses. After eating, the wife goes out for a walk with the child, and he, the master of the house, stays at home to rest a little. An hour later they come back — and already: he is hanging from a towel, cold as a piece of iron.
Or:
An elderly woman paces about the house. She lacks nothing, not even bird’s milk; maids pour veritable honey into her mouth; but her nerves are shattered: she longs for her late husband. What is it? First love? No, they were merely a second couple, married already in old age, each had children of their own. It is just that she longs for the prosperity, the abundance, the security and the calm. She begins to imagine that they want to take everything away from her, that she will be put into a cage of two rooms and a kitchen, and be allotted for her living a mere hundred gulden [złoty] a month..
No, one cannot live like this. The nervous breakdown grows ever stronger and passes into madness. A special guard watches her every step, but she does not want to live, she cannot live — she throws herself from the third floor and dies.
Once the candidates for suicide were mostly among the young. Disappointment in love, wounded ambition, career difficulties were the agents and brokers in that enterprise. Today yet another “candidate” writes that a rescue committee should be founded especially for candidates. But how can one know who is the real candidate deserving the loan? So what — he holds that all are candidates. Well, we already have a free-loan (gmiles-khesed) fund, and if you like, all the banks are intended for this purpose. The trouble is that for the true candidate no remedy whatsoever helps any more.
A Jew, a shopkeeper, says to me: people are too lazy or too ashamed to grab a free loan — so they go and hang themselves! I, he says, have toiled my whole life with free loans. How many times my face burned with shame, how many times I was sick of life — but that is only talk: you grab the little loan, give the cart a push onward, and life runs as if greased...
That is no heroism, he goes on, holding me firmly by the button, but cowardice, desertion, running away from the front — from the struggle for existence. If you like, it is simply foolishness, because the worst life is still better than death.
As it says there in the verse: Behold, I have given into your hands life and death — so choose life!...
M. Postman
If You Were Reb Levi Yitskhok of Berdichev! (A Dudele).

[Satire — a “dudele” before Rosh Hashanah; Jewish distress and the Land of Israel.] By Onkelos. (A dudele).
If I were Reb Levi Yitskhok of Berdichev, if I had in me as much boldness as he, I would now, on the eve of the balance-sheet of the past year, say to “the Old One” thus:
What do You want of Your people Israel? Why have You set upon Your people Israel?
Paying taxes — Your people Israel; cutting subsidies — from Your people Israel; issuing troubles[?] — upon Your people Israel?..
Oy, Father, how much is the limit? True, You gave us a summer that was not bad, the weather was good and the cucumber season even better — cucumbers, there is nothing to earn on them, at half for nothing; but what is the bottom line? “Man and beast”!
The beast has come in from the field — so it will eat cucumbers in the stall; but the wife has come back from the dacha, and besides cucumbers she surely needs something more — a coat, a little dress, a pair of shoes.
Oy, Father, why did You not think of that?
Once, when there was no fodder in the land of Canaan, our forefathers went down to the land of Egypt; but today, when in the land of Egypt too there is no fodder any more...
Oy, Father, where shall we go?
By common sense we ought to go back to the land of Canaan, for if it is to be no fodder and lying in the ground, then surely the earth of Eretz Yisroel is preferable...
But here is the trouble, “I am in a great strait”: it is very narrow there — the Holy Land has actually become an “Eng-land” [a narrow land]..
And the English, what do they say? Their emperor is an emperor — if he signed a declaration for the people Israel, he also signed it “with wisdom”, as it is written: “Who formed man with wisdom”.
But You signed a declaration for us without tricks and without twists, that the land belongs to us, to our children and children’s children...
Oy, Father, why do You not keep Your word?..
You have scattered us to all the corners of the world: east, west, south, north.
You have strewn us to the right and to the left.
The leftists shout — you, little Jew, are too right-wing.
The rightists shout — you, little Jew, are too left-wing.
Ay, Du - du - du
Du du!
Onkelos.
“The Return”...

[Feuilleton — humour; summer resorts.] Surely you have read Remarque's latest work, “Der Tsurikker” (“The Return”; Der Weg zurück, “The Road Back”), in which are analysed the thoughts of the exhausted soldiers who wasted [“gepatert”] their best years on the battlefield, and now they come home and life is so empty, empty and monotonous...
In this very “Return” I am reminded — fittingly[?] — of acquaintances of mine who have come back from the dacha-front [the summer-cottage front].
They went off with the idea of resting. But arriving in the mountain places, the poor things had to fight like heroes on the battlefield.
They had to fight at night with sleep; being at the dancing, to fight with tiredness; clambering up the mountains; and above all, to fight with their conscience when they were “having fun” [“gebavyet”, Polish bawić się] — women with cavaliers and men with “menzhatkes” [mężatki, married women]...
Now they come back exhausted, exactly like Remarque's heroes from the battle...
Therefore, when you meet a lady acquaintance who has come back from a dacha, do not ask her how much weight she has put on, because when one fights one gets thinner, and fight they did — with everything: with conscience, modesty, tiredness and sleep; they fought, I tell you, like true heroes...
It is just a pity that Remarque did not immortalise these “heroes” in his “Return”; for them too life in town is now empty and monotonous...
I, for my part, pity them, the dacha “heroes”, on their return to town... They look now so helpless and pitiable, just as after a noisy ball night, or like exhausted in-laws after a tumultuous wedding.
I sympathise with them, and therefore I recommend that they enrol as[?] members in one of our societies — there one will be able to “nudzić się” [be bored, Polish][?] together with a whole crowd...
I would even have recommended that they join a tennis club, but somehow the Almighty does it to spite us, and every day He sends a bit of rain and the tennis court is flooded...
There occur, as you see, floods, natural catastrophes. Most likely the world really is that sinful, but it is not the “dacha heroes” who are to blame — they are, after all, the true fighters, real martyrs...
What do you say?
HaTsofe
Once There Were Selichot.

[Feuilleton — memoir; the High Holidays and Selichot.] By S. Erdberg.
Every day a new sun. Every year a new spring, and every eve of Rosh Hashanah — new Selichot.
And we humans must thank and praise His dear Name for every new sun, for every new spring and for every new Selichot.
And how is it really:
One God everywhere. The Jew is, after all, the same everywhere. If he is not, the gentiles make him the same. But Selichot are no longer the same everywhere.
Selichot in the little homely shtetls and Selichot in the big European cities — how different they are, how other.
Lucky[?] are those born today: they have not seen any other Selichot, so they have lost nothing, and to them it is quite natural.
But we, born and raised in the little homely shtetls, filled and soaked with the yearning mood of Selichot, with the fear and the thoughts of repentance of those days — for us it is hard with the Selichot here. It is missing, the Selichot air of the shtetl is missing.
Do you remember, my friends, born and raised in the homely shtetls, do you remember the first Selichot of old, at home?
Just remember! Remember!
Well now, once you have remembered — has your heart not grown warm, has yearning not filled your blood, is that Selichot time of town and shtetl not dear and precious to you?
Two kinds of Selichot we had in the shtetl: in the shul and in the shtibl.
The shtetl sleeps. A hand knocks on the window, a voice calls:
Rise for the service of the Creator!
Rise for Selichot!
Frightened, silent, people jump up, leap out of their beds, one-two — dressed. Not a word is spoken.
The service of the Creator!
One opens the door into the dark night. One falls into a thick darkness. People steal through the darkness; the dark snatches them out of the houses, swallows them up; quietly they go to the shul. No one speaks. Neighbours meet on the way and say not a word, as if they did not know each other; they are afraid to open their mouths in that solemn hour.
Big ones, little ones, men, women, children — all are drawn with heavy hearts into the shul. The shtetl goes into the shul.
In the thick darkness stands a house, bigger than all the houses, and lit. Pieces of light thrust[?] into the dark — the brightness of the lit-up shul.
I go to Selichot and with me goes the whole world. The gentiles — they are sleeping now, they have no Selichot. And we, exalted and uplifted, go to — the service of the Creator.
And good is the darkness, the gloom; dear is the fear, so sweet — the dread before the yearning heart.
You become filled with repentance. You gather up remorse, and a happy man you are, for happy is he who feels penitent and is full of remorse, for pure becomes his soul and clean — his blood.
In the shul, the pre-dawn one, one becomes still more remorseful, more penitent, more forgiving; the Selichot melodies work in the blood like the cooing of the pleading dove, soften the heart and fill it with goodness and love for one's fellow.
Great is the fear, heavy — the dread, deep — the yearning, and it becomes so easy, so light, and the heart opens to goodness, to purity and to clarity.
With relief, with hope one waits for the great, awesome days, the Days of Awe. The first relief strengthens one's courage, assures [“ferzoykhert”, sic] that one will succeed in praying for a good year, a healthy year, for oneself and for all Israel.
For one says the prayer, after all, with one's whole heart.
And together with all Israel it is also easier, dearer.
• • •
Beautiful too was the saying of Selichot in the shtibl.
People gathered in the shtibl right after Havdalah, sat down at the tables over the Gemaras and studied.
The Gemara chant carried over the dark, sleeping shtetl. Big and small sit over the Gemaras. Grandfathers, fathers and children, all together around the long tables, and three generations sing out the singing Gemara chant together.
The shtetl sleeps. The shtibl studies.
After 12 the Gemaras are closed, the gartels are tightened, and [“un un”, sic] Selichot are said. They are said with fear; the voices tear up toward heaven, the hearts become yearning, and it becomes easier, easier, pure and clean around oneself and within oneself.
That is how Selichot were in the little dear shtetl at home.
And here? Here is the same God, the same Jews, the same Selichot — I mean the prayers and melodies. And yet — different, different.
No one knocks on the window, no voice calls to the service of the Creator. One goes to hear the cantor, to say Selichot; one buys “tickets” for the Days of Awe.
When one goes to shul, the streets are bright, Jews are coming from the theatre. No one trembles, no one is afraid, there is no sign of fear in the heart.
It is not hard going to Selichot, and it does not become easier after saying them. One is not seized [“ongenumen”] by repentance, one is not filled with remorse; the heart cannot become yearning, the soul cannot become pure and clean.
One goes to Selichot, one hears the cantor. A fine prayer leader — fine, beautiful, but not Selichot-like.
When the shammes does not knock on the window, when one does not jump up frightened from one's bed [“belegger”, prob. for “geleger”], when it is bright and lively in the street — how can it feel like Selichot here?
Oh, how one yearns in the Selichot days for the old, dear, pure and clean Selichot of the beautiful, heartfelt childhood years.
Once there were Selichot.
The Hard Situation of the Jewish „Chałupniks“ [Home-Workers] — and What Is the Way Out.

[Zagłębie — crafts and economy.] 1.

In the last issue of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ there was a short note about the conference held by the Jewish master tailors in Zagłębie, at which a way was supposed to be found to ease the difficult situation of the craftsmen of the tailoring trade. After a long discussion — as the said note reported — it was resolved to carry out an inspection of the tailors' workshops, and to have the illegal ones (meaning those that do not possess a „karta rzemieślnicza“ [craftsman's card]) closed with the help of the authorities. In addition, to turn with a memorandum to the Chamber of Crafts, so that without the approval of the tailors' guilds [cechy] no one should obtain the so-called dispensations.

If the initiators of the said conference naively believe in the effectiveness of the quoted resolutions — and, what is more, that they will thereby succeed to some degree in easing the situation of the Jewish master tailor — then it was truly a pity about the work, effort and time that such a conference involves.

First of all, any discussion about closing illegal workshops is superfluous, since there exists on this matter a special decree of the President of the State (of 7 June 1927), which is slowly being put into effect; the supervisory authority surely cannot close at one stroke hundreds of existing workshops and thereby ruin the livelihoods of thousands of souls.

The memorandum to the Chamber of Crafts is also entirely superfluous, since the Kielce Chamber of Crafts has, in any case, for the second year now not issued any dispensations without the agreement of the guilds concerned. Incidentally, a very small correction: not the Chamber of Crafts but the Industry Department at the voivodeship [województwo] is empowered to issue dispensations... The „Chamber“ is thus only an intermediary body with an almost decisive voice.

And let us say, in the best case, that the adopted resolutions are indeed carried out to the letter. Well, will everything then be fine? Will the situation thereby be improved?

2.

It is truly astonishing that among the resolutions not a single word is mentioned about the appalling situation of our tailor chałupniks [home-workers working for merchants]. After all, every master tailor is dependent in hard times on this very difficult livelihood, so why should the thousands of impoverished chałupniks not raise their outcry with the direct help of their brothers in the trade? Quite apart from the fact that the chałupnik has only seasonal work [printed „se an-arbet“, apparently for „sezon-arbet“] and for most months of the year walks about idle and empty-handed, the situation has lately become simply unbearable — to such a degree that for sewing a marynarka [jacket], for instance, one is paid up to 3 zł., for a pair of trousers 1 zł., for a waistcoat 75 gr. — and that, too, from the worst materials, since this kind of ready-made clothing is intended for the poorest population. Very often the paltry wage is moreover paid with long-term bills of exchange, and, God help us, these are even protested too; one can thus already form an idea of the lamentable situation of such a craftsman. If one further takes into account the fact that the tax office forces the chałupnik to take out a patent [trade licence] and assesses him for all direct taxes, which are dunned with all the severity of the law by means of distraint — one can easily understand the desperate situation of the poor chałupnik, who, having no choice, throws himself onto the lowest rungs of dishonest and shameless competition. Everyone, after all, wants to live...

The question arises: what, then, must actually be done to ease this difficult situation of the chałupnik? And is there a real way out at all? Statistics show, after all, that precisely among chałupniks the greatest number of deaths is found, and that among their children, who help their parents in the work and work 15—16 hours a day, there is the highest percentage of tuberculosis and other diseases, from which it is not at all so easy to be cured.

It is therefore beyond the slightest dispute that steps must be taken at once to save the situation. But does such a radical remedy exist?

One thing, however, is certain: the resolutions of the Zagłębie tailors' conference will absolutely not ease the situation. Besides, we already know our conferences with our resolutions — talked out and preached out [printed „opgerershnt“, misprint for „opgedrashnt“], and — there it remains until the 2nd conference, and so on round again...

In the sense of substantial work, unfortunately absolutely nothing has yet been done in this field.

3.

Common sense requires that the turnover tax be levied only once on each object of trade. It surely cannot be that for one and the same suit both the craftsman and the warehouse-merchant [magazyner] should pay. Never mind, therefore, new ones — all the old outstanding tax debts of the chałupniks must unconditionally be annulled. The turnover tax, after all, is paid by the warehouse-merchant.

Chałupniks must be fully exempted from buying patents, since they do not produce from their own goods but from other people's goods entrusted to them. It should be stressed, incidentally, that in almost all identical cases the Supreme Administrative Tribunal has taken the side of the chałupnik against the arguments of the tax authorities.

Further: since the chałupnik is not an independent craftsman (although he owns his own tools of work), he must unconditionally enjoy social protection, such as a sickness fund, labour insurance and the like.

All this will indeed ease the situation of the chałupnik to a great degree. But it is still far from a cure for the painful livelihood question of the at least 1000 chałupniks in Zagłębie. No better, if not even worse, is the situation of the shoemaker chałupniks, who make a pair of elegant men's shoes for 4 zł. 50 groszy, which usually takes a whole day's work (and the warehouse-merchant charges for them — let it stay between us — a whole 30 zł...).

An especially important role could be played here by the trade organization of the chałupniks themselves or by the guilds concerned, namely [printed „nzemlikh“, misprint for „nemlikh“]: a price list must be clearly and sharply established, which shall unconditionally bind all the members concerned. All those who will not submit to the decisions of a managing committee must be placed under strict control. Such workshops must be fought in a merciless manner with all possible means. A self-help fund for chałupniks must be founded, which shall serve the members in the time of unemployment, and — what is the most important of all — an energetic campaign must already be undertaken, with the help of the larger warehouse-merchants, to find a sales market for our home-made ready-to-wear articles in a number of places abroad, where we are able to compete thanks to the cheapness of our labour force.

But it is worth devoting a separate article to this last point.

A. Gancwajch.
Sharp Wits — and Mathematics Corner.

[Puzzles — mathematics corner.] Compiled by G—D.

Problem No. 1.

A certain arithmetical number has the following property: adding together 2 times as much as the number + half of it + a quarter, we shall obtain the sum of 99.

What number is it?

(2 solutions: arithmetical and algebraic).

Problem No. 2

The following inscription is found on the tombstone of the Greek mathematician Diophantus:

Diophantus was a child for 1/6 part of his life; for 1/12 part he was a youth; after that he married and lived as a husband for a 1/7 part of his life plus another 5 years, until a son was born to him, who died 4 years before Diophantus and lived only half as many years as Diophantus had lived.

How many years did Diophantus live?

Problem No. 3.

2 children each have a certain number of nuts. One says to the other: if you give me 5 of your nuts, I shall have 3 times as many as you have.

— No — says the second — if you give me 2 nuts, I shall have 5 times as many nuts as you.

How many did each child have?

Problem No. 4.

In a jug there were 8 litres of wine, which one wanted to divide into 2 equal parts, i.e. 4 each. But one had only 2 measures: one of 5 litres and another of 3 litres.

How does one pour from the jug into the measures so as to have 4 litres twice?

Problem No. 5.

How many minutes is it to 4 o'clock, if three quarters of an hour ago it was twice as many minutes past 2 o'clock?

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Nitzavim-Vayelech)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Y. Y. [?]
Parashat Nitzavim-Vayelech
The Portion
—o—
a) "Your heads... every man of Israel" (29:9)
1.
"From the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water" — from wood-chopper to water-carrier, all of them: "your little ones, your wives", all, all of them want to be "your heads, your elders and your officers"; all of them want to be leaders of the people and heads... Arvei Nahal.
2.
"Your heads" — with you they are the heads and those others water-carriers; but "before the Lord your God", before God, it is sometimes quite the reverse: the water-carrier is sometimes more esteemed by God than the would-be "fine Jew"... Torat Moshe.
—o—
b) "To serve the gods of the nations" (29:17)
A priest once asked a Jew:
— If your God really is the only one, why doesn't He destroy all the other gods?
The Jew writes down a figure: 1, and shows it to the priest:
— You see? The 1 is our God. Now, if I add a zero, the one grows to ten, and if one more zero — the one turns into a hundred. So the more zeros are added to our God, the greater and more prominent His oneness becomes...
Folk saying (found in "Ohel Yaakov").
—o—
c) "Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord" (29:24)
"Wherefore did the land perish? — Because they forsook My Torah."
The Dubno Maggid was once passing through a village in his cart on a Friday afternoon. He asked the son-in-law of the local innkeeper how far it was to town. The young man was a Torah scholar and wanted the Maggid to spend the Sabbath with them so that he could pass the time with him in words of Torah, so he told him on purpose that the town was still far away and that he would not manage to get there before the Sabbath.
Some time later, when that young man had already taken over the inn and no longer had any time for Torah, the Maggid again came to the village on a Friday afternoon, and when he asked him whether he would still manage to reach town before candle-lighting, the young man answered quickly that yes — fearing that the Maggid might, God forbid, stay with him over the Sabbath...
The Maggid smiled: "Wherefore did the land perish?" — Why has a piece of land suddenly been lost? Why has the road from the village to the town become shorter over time? — "Because they forsook My Torah": because study has been put aside...
—o—
d) "The blessing and the curse which I have set before you" (30:1)
When the whole world has nothing but curse — well then, it is surely not specifically because of Jewish sins; but when blessing and curse reign together, that is, when others have blessing and "the curse which I have set before you" — with you, Jew, there is curse — oh, then you must think about repentance... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
e) "The blessing and the curse... and you shall take it to your heart" (ibid.)
Wealth, for example, is not always a blessing for a person. It depends on "and you shall take it to your heart" — on the heart. If someone has a base [?] heart, the blessing of wealth is in fact a curse... Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
f) "Choose life, that you may live" (30:19)
People nowadays live and look for something to fill their time with. It is a l i f e of searching how to k i l l time... But the Torah says: "Choose life, that you may live" — choose a life that shall be full of true, higher, overflowing life, and not a life of searching how to kill time... Drashot Al-Ami.
Haftarah
—o—
g) "Keep not silence!" (Isaiah [62:6])
"Rachel weeping for her children" — like that mother who is in a dark cellar and does not know whether her child is alive or not: she begins to weep, and if the child is alive it weeps along, for a child's way is to answer its mother's weeping with weeping; but if the child is silent, it is a sign that it is dead, and only then does the mother truly weep.
Mother Rachel weeps over our exile, and when she does not hear us respond with weeping too, only then does she begin to weep in earnest, for she sees that we are dead, that we no longer feel anything... Kol Yaakov.
—o—
h) "I will no more give your corn to be food for your enemies" (ibid.)
According to the Midrash, in exile the divine bounty cannot go directly to the Jews but must pass through the nations. But like that prison warder: if you want him to pass something on to the prisoner too, you must give him so much that it overflows from his mouth, so that he will leave something for the prisoner as well, for whom the food was actually brought — so too Providence must bestow so much upon the nations that at least something of it reaches the Jews, who are the ones chiefly intended... Misgeret ha-Sha'ar.
Avot
—o—
i) "His master called him" (6)
In the little town of Podhajce there was a doctor whom people called "Rebbe" — not because he was pious, but because a Rebbe brings people to the World to Come, and he too brought his patients to the other world... Siftei Hakhamim.
—o—
j) "Bread with salt shall you eat... and if you do so, happy are you in this world" (ibid.)
Like that merchant whose takings are so large that he has not even any time to eat — is not the not-eating a pleasure for him? So too "bread with salt" is sometimes "happy are you in this world". An outsider cannot feel its taste, just as not everyone understands the merchant who has no time for a bite because of his takings and is nevertheless overjoyed.
Sefat ha-Yeri'ah.
Kraków — the Poland of Old.

When you find yourself on the Market Square (Rynek) of Kraków, you can't believe you are in the twentieth century; rather you begin to believe that a sorcerer has carried us into a city of the Middle Ages that has remained petrified. I stand and look and I don't know where to look first: at the whole roundness and breadth all around, which is somehow so festive because the reflections of the palaces and churches, full of gold and red, fall upon it; or at the palace of Count Potocki, called "At the Rams" (Pod Baranami), which on the outside is full of gold, stone figures and tales; or should I look at the monuments that tell of Polish heroes, Polish victories and Polish poets. Here is Kościuszko and here is Mickiewicz, and here are the great paintings of the greatest Polish painter, Jan Matejko — giant canvases depicting battles of the Poles with the Russians, with the Prussians — and pictures and monuments that tell: heroes we have been...
I thought that the Place de la Concorde in Paris was the most beautiful and interesting square in the world. The Market Square in Kraków competes with it.
And when you walk away from the Market Square and stride further through Kraków, with a map or without a map, you keep having the impression that you are in the Middle Ages. Here is the famous Jagiellonian Library with an arcaded courtyard and Gothic halls, and in the middle of the courtyard stands a monument to the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, and you look at him and ask: who dragged this heretic, who cried out that the earth turns, into exile among the believers? The answer is right here, in the inscription on the monument: he studied at the Kraków university. It is not so important that he is Copernicus as it is important that he studied here. He is a part of Kraków, a part of Poland. A famous Polish antisemite says that when he meets an old rabbi in Kraków on a Saturday evening, he feels like going up to him and kissing him. He is a part of Poland, and the history of Poland can take in a Copernicus too, and a couple of rabbis too. They add charm, and they can have no influence. In the whole National Museum there are two pictures depicting Jews — Hirszenberg's "Talmudists". They are Jews who climb into heaven, little earthly, and therefore they disturb little. Jews in general disturb little in Kraków. The living Jews don't disturb much either. The pious demand little, and the non-pious are partly Germans, partly Poles, and partly they put on top hats and go to the Temple. The Jews who demand a distinctive life in their own language are still very few in number. But even less is demanded by the no-longer-living Jews of Kraków: their past here is proportionally not much smaller than the past of the Poles, and what do they have here? Nothing... A few old synagogues, one old cemetery next to the Rema's kloyz in great disorder, and that's it.
And on and on — the Middle Ages. Even the blooming Planty park is full of monuments that lend its youthful, spring-like bloom an appearance of antiquity; and here is the Franciscan church, distinguished by having paintings by the great Polish poet Wyspiański, who was also a painter.
And here is the Wawel itself, the Polish Mount Sinai and Holy Temple together. From here Polishness was given to the Poles. It is a great limestone hill looking down on the Vistula. They say that a part of the royal castle, which is made of wood, dates back to the 10th century. Under the Austrians the Wawel, which is a great piece of Polish and royal history, was neglected. Magnificent halls, masterpieces of old art, were turned into barracks; some old "trapeen" [tapestries?] were taken by the Russians. The Poles have restored everything that was possible, and the work is in full swing. What gripped me strongly at the Wawel was a great deep cave. You have to go down 104 steps until you get into it. It lies 9 metres deep, next to the Vistula, and is made of rock; you can see that over thousands of years the water has ground away [?] the rocks and worn out various figures. You see here something like a great chair with small chairs around it. Here, according to the legend, sat the dragon himself, who ate children (the dragon is a legendary creature, gigantically large, half man and half serpent). Every year they had to give him a fixed number of children — then came a man named Krakus who fooled the dragon. Instead of a lamb he gave him a lambskin full of poisonous grass and put an end to the dragon. That is why the city was given the name Kraków, after the name of the rescuer Krakus.
The royal castle consists of countless halls, each richer and more beautiful than the other. Magnificent furniture, splendid pictures. The largest Gobelins in the world, ceilings with many paintings. Tens of thousands of people had to work so that one could live in luxury [?] here. After the castle you go into the church and into its crypt, where it is damp, cold and dark, and sarcophagi of kings and patricians lie there; among the kings lie also Poland's great poets, Słowacki and Mickiewicz. They illuminate the Wawel, the hill of Genesis of Poland.
And when you pass through the middle Jewish quarter, Stradom, to the ancient Jewish quarter of Kazimierz, you again come up against the Middle Ages — but dusty, muddy, unadorned, unrestored. You find synagogues here older than 300 and 400 years, but in them there is nothing but uncleanliness, dust and legends of all kinds, beautiful and not beautiful.
There is a cemetery by the Rema's kloyz; it has graves older than 500 years, but they are in a pitiful state; around almost every grave there is a legend. There are dybbuk tales — after death they came to demand justice — and countless martyrs.
In the middle of the quarter there is a large plot fenced around with boards. They tell that once there was a wedding here on a Friday evening; they celebrated a little late, and the klezmers were still playing when the stars were already out. The Rema passed by and ordered them to stop playing; they did not obey him, so he cursed, and the house collapsed, and the plot was fenced in because people were afraid to come near.
The Poles have done everything to preserve their past in Kraków. Jews have done nothing. There are a few names there, a few graves and a few legends.
Jacob Botoshansky.

(H) For several weeks red flags and anti-state posters have been hung up in the premises of the local Zionist youth organisation "Gordonia" (Sienkiewicza Street). Talmudic Literature and Its Methods

[Culture — rabbinic literature, polemic.] Elchanan Zider.
2
Reading the remark of an "Acquaintance" [a pen-name] in the "Zagl. Tsaytung" No. 35, that to the 3 questions I formulated about the thirteen middot (hermeneutic rules) of R. Ishmael in the "Z. Ts." No. 34 one can find an answer in the "Kitzur Klalei ha-Middot" printed in the Gemara "Berakhot", I was reminded of the following joke:
To R. Eizikl Harif, the rabbi of Słonim, there came a young man with a nicely developed body and plump cheeks, in order to be examined by him and to receive ordination (semikhah) for rabbinic rulings.
In the course of the conversation the rabbi realized that the young man had always studied only from abridged books, such as "Hayyei Adam" and "Hokhmat Adam", because when he asked him about the sources from which the laws derive, from the Talmud and the Rishonim, the young man did not know.
"Of you," says the rabbi to the young man, "the verse says: 'A man's wisdom (hokhmat adam) makes his face shine' [Eccl. 8:1] — because you have always studied only the 'Hokhmat Adam' alone, which is an abridged book, you have a 'shining face'; for he who studies everything deeply and thoroughly cannot have such plump cheeks!..."
Such is the end of one who makes do with studying abridged books!
No, Mr. "Acquaintance", in so important a problem as the thirteen middot one cannot content oneself with taking a glance into a little abridged book, at a time when there exists a rich literature in this field. And when such a scholar as Prof. Dr. A. Schwarz devoted three decades of his life to the study of this very problem, and published seven thick volumes in the German language on the thirteen middot [printed "marot"] of R. Ishmael.
(See "Miesięcznik Żydowski" 1931, No. 6, the article about Dr. Schwarz by Docent Dr. Abraham Weiss.)
Now we proceed to give an answer to all the questions:
1) How must one count so that out of sixteen middot there become thirteen? (The question is that of the Rabad, R. Abraham ben David of Posquières, who lived in the twelfth century in Maimonides' time.) To this there is a short answer by the Rabad which can be interpreted in various ways, and on that basis many have formulated the thirteen middot, counting "binyan av from one verse" and "binyan av from two verses" as one rule; "a general rule requiring a particular" and "a particular requiring a general rule" as one rule; and finally "a matter learned from its context" and [and — printed twice] "a matter learned from its end" also as one rule.
R. Saadia Gaon (in the 10th century), however, counts differently, and he counts precisely "general and particular" and "particular and general" as one rule; and so too does A. H. Weiss [sic; I. H. Weiss] count in his famous work "Dor, Dor ve-Dorshav", part II.
R. Samson of Chinon, the author of the book "Keritut", counts "something that departed to bear another charge not in its category" and "something that departed to be judged in a new matter" as one rule.
R. Aaron ibn Hayyim in his book "Korban Aharon" and R. Isaiah ha-Levi Horowitz in his famous book "Shelah", gate "Torah she-be-al-peh", count the middot quite differently, in an entirely original way. (See the book "Kovetz Midrashim Ketanim", Vilna edition.)
Now, Mr. "Acquaintance", as you see, it is not quite as easy as it seems to you!
2. Hillel the Nasi counts seven middot — did people in his time not know more than these seven?
As an answer to this question many theories were created by great methodologists of the 19th century, but it was Dr. Schwarz who finally showed that R. Ishmael's middot are all already found in the 7 middot [printed "marot"] of Hillel, and that the rule [printed "marah"] "general and particular" in Hillel also encompasses another 7 middot which are enumerated by R. Ishmael and in which the words "general" (kelal) and "particular" (perat) are mentioned (see also the introduction to the book "Korban Aharon").
3. Why is the rule of "hekesh" (analogy by juxtaposition) not also counted among the middot? R. Samson of Chinon (Keritut, Bayit 2) says that "a law that is derived through a hekesh has the same force as if it had been explicitly written in the Torah." And we may add that Maimonides (in the twelfth century) writes in his famous work "Yad ha-Hazakah" (Laws of Marriage, chapter 1, halakhah 2) that acquisition by deed (in betrothing a woman by a written document), which is derived through a hekesh, has the same force as a matter of Torah law, while acquisition by money (betrothing by money), which is derived through a gezerah shavah, is called "divrei soferim". (Here the law also has a force as if from the Torah.)
Maimonides calls "divrei soferim" everything that is not explicitly written in the Torah but which the Sages innovated with the help of the thirteen middot and other expositions, and such new laws are not counted in the number of the 613 commandments. (See "Sefer ha-Middot she-ha-Torah Nidreshet ba-Hen" by Rabbi Moshe Ostrowski, and the remark by Rabbi Kook.)
And because the problem is a very interesting one, I would advise taking an interest in the matter and studying also the rich literature of this field in all European languages, lately also in Polish; and the youth should not rely merely on the short textbooks [?] such as the histories of Graetz, Dubnow, Balaban etc., because from them one cannot even form a clear idea about the historical side of the middot.
Also a remark to Mr. "Acquaintance": that the Tosafot and all other commentators are against the words of Rashi in "Sukkah" 31a, and that he has attributed to Rashi something which he does not say at all.
Będzin — Annual general meeting of the Small Traders' Association

[Będzin — trade associations.] Będzin
Annual general meeting of the Small Traders' Association.
On Sunday the annual general meeting of the local small traders took place in the association's own premises. According to an accepted "tradition", Mr M. Birka, delegate of the Central Committee (C.C.) from Warsaw, came to the meeting, but even this did not "attract" the members, and the meeting was held with 50 members present, at a time when the association counts (on paper) up to 400 members...
The meeting is opened by Mr A. Lidzbarski; he delivers his traditional exposé, speaks about the situation of the small traders, and at the request of those assembled the chair is taken over by Mr P. Jakubowski, manager of the "Discount Bank".
The report on the activity to date is given by the president, Mr G. Rechnic. The report shows that the board did what it could within its means for the benefit of the members.
The treasurer's report is given by Mr Stopnicki. In the course of the year the income, and also the expenses, reached up to 6,000 zł. To the treasurer's report Mr Stopnicki attaches the outcome of the last kehilla elections, and this causes the entire debate to revolve around the internal "political events"...
The floor is given to Mr Herszlowicz, who points to the internal frictions that arose over the small traders' association's part in the kehilla elections, and he declares that because of this he will no longer accept any mandate on the new board.
After the remaining formal items of the agenda had been dealt with, elections were held, which gave the following result:
To the board: G. Rechnic, J. Rus, H. Stopnicki, A. Zylberberg, Sz. Klajnman, D. Gitler and D. Gutensztajn. Deputies: A. J. Rechnic and A. Flak.
The next evening Mr Burka [sic, for Birka] gave a lecture on the subject "The present economic crisis and its effect on the small traders". In a fine 3-hour speech Mr Birka showed that the small trader is the scapegoat for every misfortune, may it never come, and what is even more painful is that the small traders have no understanding for organisation.
On Tuesday evening the first constituent session of the new board took place. At the session Mr Rechnic declared many times that he would not accept the office of president, but the board would not agree to this and again elected Mr G. Rechnic as president, and Mr Gutensztajn as vice-president.

Out of Craving for a Revolver Permit He Faked an Assault

[Sosnowiec — police.]
This week the local police were alerted that a bandit assault had been carried out on the railway official Smura in Klimontów.
Police went to the spot where the assault was supposed to have been carried out, and before them the victim declared that the bandits, having tied him up, had robbed him of 25 zł. and vanished.
The whole statement seemed suspicious to the police, because the circumstances were such that Smura had the possibility of calling for help.
He was therefore taken in for a grilling, and he confessed the whole truth: in order to obtain a permit to keep a revolver, he had faked being attacked by bandits...
The Stepmother Got Her Due Sentence...

[Sosnowiec — court.]
In Dańdówka lived the Christian family Kubkow. "He", that is the husband, was 59 years old, and "she" was his second wife and 3 years younger...
The woman schemed that her husband, who had always been sickly, should sign over his entire fortune to her, but her plans were not realised because her husband did not want to wrong his children by his first wife.
At a certain moment, when Mr. Kubkow fell seriously ill, the wife slipped him ink and pen and prevailed upon him to sign a certain number of promissory notes.
After the husband's death the widow, on the strength of the notes in her possession, put up the house of her late husband for auction.
The children, learning what the stepmother was up to, turned with the help of their relatives to the district court, where it was shown that their father had never been a debtor, but that this was a simple swindle by their stepmother.
The prosecutor's office took an interest in the matter and brought a case, which took place this week at the Sosnowiec district court.
After hearing a series of witnesses who unmasked the whole swindle, the court handed down a verdict according to which the "woman of valour" and her accomplices are sentenced to 18 months in prison and loss of rights.
The verdict aroused great satisfaction among the large number of those present.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
After Carrying Out the Robbery the Bandits Held a Feast...
At midday four persons entered the flat of Director Krutka in Königshütte [Królewska Huta], declaring as soon as they came in that they were conducting a population census.
Once inside, the bandits tied the maidservant to a chair and then went in to the director, whom they also tied up, gagging his mouth.
Then the bandits set to work, opened the drawers, from which they stole 70 German marks, 283 zł. and besides [printed „א הוץ“, apparently „אחוץ“ — besides] gold objects.
After the robbery the brazen bandits sat down around the table and held a feast of the drinks and food they had found, and also forced the director to take part in the „celebration“...
After the feast, which lasted about 2 hours, the bandits left.
—o—
An Accident.
On Saturday at 7 in the evening the following terrible accident occurred in Königshütte:
A motorcyclist drove at full speed onto the pavement, where he ran over 4 persons and smashed the shop window of Żylis's [?] store.
2 of the injured are in a serious condition.
—o—
An Attack on the Train.
On the Katowice–Poznań express train, not far from the Neu-Tarnowitz railway station, a robbery attack was carried out on the railway official Takacz, who was struck on the head with a blunt iron, from which Takacz fell unconscious.
A commotion arose on the train; the bandit, afraid of being detained, jumped off the train and was seriously injured.
The bandit will stand before a summary court.

A Lecture by Yitzhak Margoshes.
Next Monday, the Fast of Gedaliah, at 8 in the evening, the writer Yitzhak Margoshes will give a lecture at the B'nai B'rith lodge in Katowice on the subject „Jewish Life in Soviet Russia“.
—o—
A House Collapsed and Buried 6 People.
On the 1st of this month lightning struck the house of Mr. Borecki in the village of Frydek, starting a fire, which was put out. The police authority did order that the Borecki family leave the house, since the house could collapse at any minute.
Disregarding the order, the Borecki family went on living in the endangered house.
In the night from Saturday to Sunday, when the Borecki family was already asleep, the remaining walls collapsed.
The rescue operation lasted 7 hours. Of all 7 persons they managed to save only an 8-year-old boy; the rest were taken out already dead.
The family's breadwinner was, at the moment he lost his wife and 5 children, at work in a coal mine.
The eldest child was 16 years old and the youngest 1 year.
The Writer Yitzhak Margoshes in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — lectures; Zionism.] For a few days now the well-known writer Mr. Yitzhak Margoshes of Tel Aviv has been staying in Zagłębie.
While living in Russia, Margoshes had to endure great persecution because of his membership in the Zionist Central Committee. The G.P.U., on learning of this great „crime“, sent him off by prisoners' convoy (etap), together with other prominent Zionist activists, to Siberia. After various severe tortures over 13 months, Margoshes finally managed to get to Eretz Israel.
During these wanderings Margoshes visited the Jewish settlements in the Near East [first printed „פארער-אזיען“, then „פאדער-אזיען“ — Vorderasien], studied their way of life and customs, and later described this in a brochure entitled „A Jewish Refugee in the Near East“.
This brochure, which appeared in German, aroused wide interest. Besides this, Margoshes wrote a number of other works, among them „The Persecution of Zionists in Russia“, „The Jews in the Lands of the East“ and others.
Yitzhak Margoshes has since visited a number of Western European countries, where he lectured on Jewish life under the Bolshevik regime in Russia, as well as on the life of the Jewish communities in the Far East.
Mr. Margoshes will give the same lectures in Zagłębie on the following dates:
Sunday, at the close of Rosh Hashanah, in Sosnowiec, in the „Angielski Hall“.
Monday, 8 p.m., in Katowice, at the B'nai B'rith lodge.
Saturday, 2 p.m., in Będzin, at the „Capitol“ cinema.
The subject is: „Zionism under the Bolshevik Dictatorship“.
From „Ha-Shomer ha-Leumi“ in Będzin.

[Będzin — youth movements; Zionism.] Last Saturday night the annual general meeting took place in Będzin, in the premises of the Zionist Organization. At the opening of the meeting tribute was paid to the 2 tragically deceased members of the Warsaw ken (branch), Avraham Szuchmacher and Asher Pinkert, of blessed memory. After hearing the reports it emerged that the ken at present numbers 120 members, who are divided into 2 gedudim (troops). The ken carries on lively educational and scouting work, takes part in all Zionist activities, and the ken is especially active in the field of the K.K.L. (Jewish National Fund). This year the ken also organized a summer camp in the Beskids, which went off with the greatest success. After the reports were delivered, the outgoing leadership was granted an absolutorium (vote of discharge), and a new leadership was elected, consisting of: Moshe David Horowitz, Zishe Malach, Hanokh Malach, Rivka Sigraich and Sarah Suszek. At the end of the meeting recognition was expressed to Moshe Suszek and Gershon Freiberg for their untiring work for the good of the organization.
