The trade in bills of exchange.
By Jacob Lestschinsky.

[Small-type introduction:] The well-known economist Khelber [?] has studied the economic situation in Poland and characterised what the situation looks like in general, and that of the Jewish merchant class in particular.

In Poland one pays for everything and everyone with bills of exchange, even the doctor and the dentist, who then discount the bills in the street; eighty percent of Jewish workers are paid their wages in bills. I say "Jewish", because Gentiles, with their healthy Gentile heads, do not understand such combinations as a bill for twenty złoty with which one has to go to the exchange and sell it for 17, or even for 15 złoty.

How is such a phenomenon, which looks wild and incomprehensible in the readers' eyes, to be explained?

In Poland there is no capital for business. For a population of 30 million souls there are in all one and a half billion złoty in existence, while the state budget amounts to three billion złoty. No loans come in from abroad. The country's production is small, six times less than in Germany, while Poland's population is only twice as small. Every złoty passes through many hands, and therefore people pay such crazy interest rates here as 25 and 30 percent a year. Even big firms are often forced to discount bills on the private exchange and to pay such high interest.

The trade in bills has become so widespread that many bill "matchmakers" have also sprung up, brokering the exchange of bills.

In the small towns the "Americans" — those who receive 10–15 dollars monthly from their relatives — made a living from buying bills; small and great wrote bills. And it goes without saying that under such a system of trading the slightest little wind can shake the whole edifice. A new decree ruins a branch of the economy, and thousands of Jews go bankrupt; heavy mud in the autumn months and a small turnover in the towns call forth a larger number of protests; the slightest wobble on the foreign grain market causes ruin. In general, the slightest stir in one wall or another of the Polish economic edifice gives the whole building such a strong shaking that all the walls begin to crack and tremble, and the crisis grows and grows.

The "bill turnover" is most developed in the trades that lie almost wholly in Jewish hands and in which this kind of trade was already widespread in the pre-war years; indeed, even before the war it was a rule that no textile-goods shopkeeper dies before he has gone bankrupt a couple of times. The entire Łódź textile trade, which is 90 or more percent in Jewish hands, deals only in bills: the manufacturer gives credit to the big merchant, the latter to the middle wholesaler, the wholesaler gives credit to the shopkeeper — to the "lakhdimnik" [?]; but a few years ago the shopkeeper at least mostly sold for cash, especially to the village peasant. Lately, however, the consumer has been taught to write bills. And the mountain of bills kept on growing.

Merchants heard that there is some system that consists of selling in instalments and thus making it easier for the consumer to buy things that he cannot buy at once for cash. And a rush began to shower the consumer with goods. It is enough to be a short while in Poland to feel at once that for the small Polish state there is too much Jewish energy, too much Jewish entrepreneurial force. Once this energetic force had an outlet — through distant, broad Russia and also through emigration to America. Today it is locked up as in a cage, gathered, concentrated in a limited number of trades that lie in Jewish hands. And Jewish energy set about working the internal market, forcing it to consume as much goods as Łódź can produce, creating an artificial purchasing power among the population.

Łódź did indeed work well for a few years, but for its goods it received thick portfolios of bills bearing tens of thousands of signatures. One can pay Jewish workers for their work with bills, but not Christian ones; besides, one must also pay in cash. A crisis was bound to come, but in normal times it would not have been so terrible.

But a misfortune happened that made the crisis general all at once in all the trades in which Jews are more strongly represented. The price of grain fell so sharply that the peasant gets for his grain half of what he used to get before. Poland actually had a very good harvest this year, but the low prices of grain on the world market brought it about that the peasant can barely cover the expenses needed to keep running his farm.

If the peasant has no money, the small-town Jewish shopkeeper feels it at once. The shopkeeper at once passes it on to the middle shopkeeper through the protested bills, and as through an electric current the protested bills carry the sad tidings up to the big wholesaler and up to the manufacturer, and it bursts out [?] — the hail of protests no longer stops. Like an epidemic it infects ever wider circles. Even one who can pay does not want to give up the last bit of cash he has, and many abuse the situation and mock those who demand payment. When one or two in a town go bankrupt, it is a misfortune and a disgrace for them; but when hundreds and thousands go bankrupt, it ceases to be a disgrace and becomes only a misfortune.

A frivolous, even cynical attitude has developed towards money obligations and business. This is a result of the mountain of bills, protested bills, under which Jewish trade in Poland is being smothered, for one may safely assume that the great majority of protested bills are Jewish.

I have dwelt so long on the bill epidemic and the protest plague because in it the sickliness and abnormality of Jewish economic life in Poland are revealed most strongly, and lancing this boil will surely have a colossal effect on the fate of the Jews in Poland.
The Campaign for the Unemployed and the Tax Arrears.

[Poland — unemployment and taxes; opinion piece.] For several weeks now the government has been occupied with the campaign on behalf of the unemployed. A special committee has been formed at the Council of Ministers, which is working out various plans: how to draw the whole of society into the campaign, where the funds needed for it are to be taken from, and in what way the relief is to be distributed among the unemployed.
The government has given the committee broad powers, and it is devoting great attention to the campaign.
The reasons for this tremendous concern of the government for the unemployed are natural and understandable. The number of unemployed in the country is growing steadily. Even according to the optimists' estimate, the number of unemployed will reach as much as half a million in the winter; according to the pessimists' forecasts it will even reach 800 thousand. Poland has never before had such a great army of unemployed, and it is the government's duty to provide these people, who have been left without work through no fault of their own, with bread, a warm dwelling and winter clothing.
All this is fine, good and understandable.
What is not understandable is only where the means needed for this purpose will be taken from.
The government's plans on this question are for the time being kept secret. What has reached the public must arouse unrest and anxiety.
One of the sources of income for the campaign to help the unemployed is to be the tax arrears; that is, out of the billion złotys owed to the government in tax arrears, it will devote a part to aid for the unemployed. The government, in other words, is "donating" a few hundred million zł. of the debts that the tax bailiffs have been unable to collect.
The question arises: where will the taxpayers, who until now have been unable to pay their tax debts, now suddenly get the money for it?
Say what you will, our tax officials are certainly energetic and rigorous [?]. If the taxpayer has anything of value at all, the bailiffs have surely already distrained it and put it up for auction.
And if, in spite of all this, a billion zł. in taxes is still owed to the state treasury, it is solely because there is nothing left to seize [?] and nothing left to auction.
So where can it be taken from now? Even if we assume for a moment that the poor small trader and artisan still has a few "gulden" [złotys], or a bit of merchandise from which he barely squeezes out his meagre living — must it now be taken from him because — because the money is going to the benefit of the unemployed?
In what way is the merchant, the artisan, worse than the worker? Why should one part of the citizens be ruined to the ground in order to reassure and help another part of the citizens? The situation of the small traders and artisans is perhaps much worse than that of the worker who has been temporarily left without employment. The latter has not lost his capital — his working hands. Let the bitter time pass, and pass it must, and he will take up his job again. But if the small trader loses his poor little bit of capital and his few scraps of merchandise, he is lost for good. All that is left to him is to commit suicide.
A rescue campaign for the unemployed must unconditionally be carried out, but it must not be at the expense of another part of the citizens; one must not destroy what still exists in order to help others.
If the campaign to help the unemployed is to regard the tax arrears as one of its sources of income, the results will be anything but cheering [?].
But it will certainly ruin a few thousand more livelihoods.
Ben Moshe.
Yom Kippur... (Not a Feuilleton).

[Yom Kippur — satirical piece; communal leaders and city councillors.] "For Thou knowest that the heart of man is evil by nature, therefore Thou hast appointed a day of pardon and forgiveness. A day when sin is wiped away"...
Yom Kippur.
Only we Jews are blessed with such a day, which by itself, automatically, atones for transgressions.
Only one small thing is needed: make yourself, Jew, a bit of a soul-searching, and cry out with your whole heart "Al Het":
The great prayer that ushers in this day, "Kol Nidrei", has at all times [?] been badly misunderstood by our enemies and falsely interpreted. In Kol Nidrei the Jew tries to free his conscience from various vows, promises and obligations that he has taken upon himself.
Yom Kippur.
A fine, trusty [?] thing, this day, and even more so the Kol Nidrei night, when one can thus with one toss throw off oneself the whole little lot of vows, promises and oaths.
A fine thing above all for our gmina presidents, who have sinned with promises of financial support for fallen merchants, poor small traders, famished artisans and hungry workers — promises of 10, 20 and 40 thousand zł. All this can today so easily be annulled with a "sh'vuatana lo sh'vuot" [our oaths are no oaths].
The same applies to our "Ratmänner" [?] [city councillors], who swear by heaven and earth. They assure us that, God forbid, it is not seats they care about, not party tricks; only "the plight of our brothers and sisters" lies close to their hearts — and now, when the seats are already standing empty under their feet, it's "call me a nutcracker" [i.e., they couldn't care less], because there is a Yom Kippur and — "nidrana lo nidrei" [our vows are no vows]...
And so it goes from top to bottom. Shohatim who go into partnership with butchers; Yiddishists and Hebraists who agitate hard that O T H E R parents should not send their children to any Polish school; Zionists who reproach O T H E R S for not paying to Keren Hayesod; "Shomrei Shabbat" people who know from experience that "the small ones are hanged and the big ones are pardoned"; "TAO" [?] people who are great personages on other people's shoulders; small traders with great delusions and wholesalers with petty little ambitions — they all feel so calm and secure, because they are Jews and know from experience that Yom Kippur atones for everything.
I have deliberately left out very important bigwigs — our former deaf-and-dumb representatives on the city council, may they rest in peace; one now feels bitter pity for them, poor things. Soon the true Day of Judgement will come — elections — and who knows what the "kvitl" [ballot slip] and consequently the seat will look like; they will surely, without any preaching from me, cry out on Kol Nidrei louder and more heartfelt than all the criers and supplicants [?] —
Forgive us!
Yes, Yom Kippur is indeed able to wash the greatest sin clean, like an innocent child, like a white little angel. But there is one condition: whoever thinks to himself "I will sin and repent" or "I will repent and sin" — his repentance is not valid. — — —
For such a person even Yom Kippur does not atone.
A Shvartser [a "black one"].

[Regular column — 'Oneg Shabbat': Torah remarks for parshat Haazinu, Shabbat Shuva and Yom Kippur.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
Parshat Haazinu
The Portion
—o—
a) A God of faithfulness (32:4)
Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasów used to argue with the Master of the Universe: "Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us, according as we hope in Thee" — just as we Jews pray and hope to You, God, although we do not see You and do not comprehend You, because we have blind faith in You — so repay us measure for measure, and although You see no good deeds among us, have faith in us... believe us on our word...
(Siftei Tzaddikim).
—o—
b) A perverse and crooked generation (ibid. 2[?])
An old anecdote:
A Jew was a great debtor. He comes to a friend of his to take counsel on how one gets rid of the creditors. The friend, who had an interest in his not paying those creditors, so that the debt he himself was owed by him would be more secure... gives him this advice: when the creditors come to dun you, pretend to be mad, start dancing and whistling, and they will leave you alone. The advice worked. Afterwards that friend goes to demand his debt. As soon as he steps over the threshold the other starts dancing, jumping and whistling... He gets upset:
— You rascal [łobuz]! I gave you that advice against the other creditors — and you use it against me? Will you tell me too that you are mad?...
The moral:
Moses defended the Jews before God by saying they were a stiff-necked people; when the Jews heard this, they became a perverse generation toward Moses too. And Moses indeed got angry: I taught you that excuse myself — and you will tell me, too, a story that you are obstinate?..
(Kiflayim le-Tushiya).
• • •
With the same anecdote the Maggid of Dubno, in his wonderful book 'Ohel Yaakov', explains the verse from the same portion: "Of the Rock that begot thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee" (32).
God created[?] in man a good trait: forgetfulness. Yes, a good trait, for if a man did not possess the faculty of forgetting, then after a misfortune — after the death of someone close, for example — he could no longer do business or do anything; and in the end man uses the trait of forgetting with which God endowed him with regard to... God Himself: man indeed forgets God Himself... "and hast forgotten God that formed thee".
—o—
c) A foolish people and unwise (32:6)
"A foolish people" — a vulgar and sinful people, and besides: "and unwise" — not clever. If at least they were clever... A wicked man, if he is clever, can still be tolerated. Worst of all is a wicked man who is a fool — from him nothing good will ever come...
(Divrei Shaul).
—o—
d) For they are a very froward generation (32:20)
A froward generation. You ask a rich man why he never comes to synagogue — he answers that he has no time, he is busy with his business. You come to him again for a donation — he answers that there is no business nowadays, that one goes about idle... You ask a Jew, a rich man, why he permits himself [not] to fast on Yom Kippur — he answers: today's generations are weak. Who has the strength to fast today? You come to him again to ask a donation for a respectable poor man — he answers: is he too sick to work? Has he no strength to go and earn a living?..
(Minhat Ani).
• • •
Rabbi Bunem was once in Danzig [Gdańsk] at the home of a Jewish friend, who on Friday night sent his two servants, a Jew and a gentile, to the cellar for wine. The Jew carried the candle and the gentile the wine. The rabbi smiled: had it been the other way round — had the gentile held the candle and the Jew the wine — everything would have been fine... But it has to be exactly backwards — that is what is called a froward generation...
—o—
Haftarah: Shuva
e) Return, O Israel, unto the Lord thy God; for thou hast stumbled in thine iniquity.
"For thou hast stumbled in thine iniquity" — you have stumbled through the sins: the evil inclination fooled you and persuaded you that the sins are mitzvot...
(Karnei Re'em).
• • •
"Return, ye backsliding children" —
Repent of your so-called repentances, for mostly the repenting too is fake — fooling oneself and others...
(Rabbi Zusha of Annopol).
• • •
The Maggid of Dubno was, as is well known, for a time[?] in Berlin. Once he came into the company of maskilim, who said to him: Rabbi, let's see — bring us back to repentance.
The Maggid, as was his way, at once had a parable for it:
A European once comes to an Asian country and sees how smiths blow on glowing coals and thus make a fire in which they heat the irons. He says to them: you are making yourselves ill this way; I will bring you from Europe a blowing instrument ('bellows'), and you will not need to blow with your mouth and lungs, only work with your hands.
The tool is brought. The Asians start working with all their might and — no fire is seen. Then the European calls out: fools, if you do not put in a spark of fire, no flame will come. You may blow from today till tomorrow — the instrument can only make a fire if there is at least a spark.
The moral:
You bid me blow a spirit of repentance into you at a time when there is not a spark of Jewishness in you...
—o—
f) The just shall walk in them, but the wicked shall stumble therein.
It sometimes happens that one gets ill from eating. That is when a person's stomach is spoiled, or he suffers from some other illness.
We claim that the commandments of the Torah are not for us, that they are hard to bear; but that is because we are spoiled, because we are sick...
(Kol Yaakov).
—o—
Yom Kippur.
g) On the morrow after Yom Kippur...
On the words "And Moses gathered all the congregation of the children of Israel" Rashi says: "on the day after Yom Kippur". For on Yom Kippur all Jews are in unity and peace, but on the morrow after Yom Kippur everything is forgotten... That is why Moses strove to assemble the Jews also after Yom Kippur, so that the unity should not hold only over the day of Yom Kippur...
(Olelot Ephraim).
—o—
h) A hundred Rhenish for every drink...
In the synagogue of Sanz [Nowy Sącz] a Jew once fainted on Yom Kippur — a rich man and a great miser. Reb Berish the dayan rules that he may be given a spoonful of water to drink every minute. But the fainted rich man wants to drink without limit. Reb Berish goes to the Tzaddik of Sanz to ask what to do. The rabbi goes up to the rich man and says to him:
— You may drink as much as you like, only for every spoonful you will have to give a hundred Rhenish [gulden] to charity...
— Rabbi, Rabbi, I don't need to drink any more, I've had enough already...
Strokes.

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton; taxes.] The "series" of the "obrotowy" [podatek obrotowy — turnover tax] has not yet ended, and already a "series" of the "dochodowy" [podatek dochodowy — income tax] is beginning.
We are, after all, a bad people! They forget about us! They take no interest in us!
Gevalt, they never stop remembering us... If only those who take such an interest in us had to pay "obrotowy" themselves, things would already be very bad!...
So we are now facing a "series" of "dochodowy". It will be a hard "series". Not a single Jew is believed. Never mind that we are in the middle of the Days of Awe... they send us "wedding cards" [i.e. tax assessment notices] and write: you say that you had a "dochód" [income] of 3 000 zł.; that is impossible, because you have your shop on the main street, and you must have made an "obrót" [turnover] of at least 50.000 zł. As for earning — you surely earn at least 15 percent, so how can you say that you had no more earnings than 3,000 zł.? So be so kind and tell the whole truth right away...
Whether you answer or whether you do not answer — they are not waiting for your answer anyway. They will pass judgment on you regardless...
And what the earnings looked like, you surely do know. Ha! I am reminded of a little story:
A well-known thief served his sentence, and only a few weeks later he again committed a fresh theft and was again sentenced to 2 years' imprisonment.
After he had served the 2 years he comes home and arrives just in time for the funeral of a child of his, which his wife had borne him two weeks earlier. The man walks along in the funeral, comes home and sits shiva. Nine [?] neighbours and acquaintances come over to console him. The thief looks at them all sadly and says: Listen, my dear friends, I have already sat quite a bit in my life, but as innocently as I am sitting now I have never yet sat...
On whose earnings we are now supposed to pay "dochodowy", I do not know; but that we Jews have had no "dochód" — that, unfortunately, I do know!...
Av"hs [?].
Poems — by Yitzchak Margoshes (now staying in Zagłębie)

[Zagłębie — literature; poetry.] By Yitzchak Margoshes
(now staying in Zagłębie)
The Storm.
The sea is raging — its current branches [?]
with wild, tyrannical might,
and the Jew leaps from the turmoil into the abyss
and fights a desperate battle.

The sea roars, it booms and it seethes,
so terrible, so wild and so angry;
the desperate Jew wrestles with the abyss,
his strength drenched in sweat.

With wild force the sea rages,
strengthened by the storm wind;
the waves — they chase him to and fro
and drag him into the deep chasm.

They swallow him, but they spit him out;
the Jew's strength is already running out,
yet he fights a desperate fight with them
with his last breath, with his last convulsion.

He struggles — he wins
and he reaches his goal;
here he comes as victor,
already coming to the shore.

Oh, My Child...
Oh, my child! You are a Jew;
prepare yourself for pain and want;
you will have to fight many foes,
hunger, for a piece of dry bread.

You will have to fight for your faith,
for your Torah, for your God;
you will have to wander in foreign lands
in poverty, pain and mockery.

Wherever you go, wherever you are,
when you step across a foreign street
you will meet presumptuous [?]
evil glances — full of hatred.

You will have to wander without end,
not allowed to stay long in one place;
you will wander... and crawl away
from misery — only into pain.

And wherever you may turn [?],
you will find blood that seethes with hatred;
make ready for the fight, my child,
for you are and remain a Jew.
A Few Words to Mothers. (For the start of the school year).

[Education — for mothers; school year.] (For the start [?] of the school year).
Many mothers consider it their sacred duty to accompany the child to school and to fetch it from school. Of course, in very big cities, in the bustling streets where there is heavy traffic, this still makes sense; but if the school is near, or the town is a small one, one must never take away the child's independence.
Have you ever watched how proudly and seriously the child strides to school by itself? And have you noticed what a gloomy and sad face a child has who is led day in, day out to school and back from school?
It must be a rule: do not take the child's independence away! Train the children in good time so that they can make small excursions, such as going to school by themselves. The child must absolutely be accustomed to come home from school straight away for lunch. It must not linger anywhere or just stroll about the streets.
The importance and pride of every pupil is his satchel (tornister). We often meet children who carry a heavy satchel under their arm; apparently their mothers do not know how harmful this is: from carrying heavy satchels under the arm for long, children get tired, and the weak, not yet firmly developed spine can become crooked. It is best to carry the satchel with the books on the shoulders; besides that, one must take care that the children take in the satchel only the most necessary books and do not simply stuff in everything they have.
Children like to oversleep in the morning, and afterwards they wash in a great hurry or do not wash at all, eat standing up, chew badly and the like. This must not be allowed.
The child must be accustomed to get up on time, to clean its clothes, to wash properly, to comb, to brush its teeth, to eat calmly and chew well; the breakfast to take along should consist of bread and butter, an apple and the like.

In honour of "the Season of our Rejoicing" — a humorous section by Ben Amotz.
So-and-So. — I Do Kapparot with Money.

[Feuilleton — Yom Kippur eve.] I am in the habit of doing kapparot with money. And I do it for two reasons. First, because my wife, may she live, has been accustomed to it since time immemorial. As long as I can remember her, she does kapparot with money, and not only on Yom Kippur eve but on every day of the whole year: when she goes to the dressmakers she puts down a nice couple of dollars, heaves a sigh [?] and says:
"This is my substitute"...
And secondly, I do it because of a rebuff I once got from a rooster when I tried to swing it over my head and say "This is my atonement." He was a strong fellow; he tore himself out of my hands, jumped into my face and nearly scratched my eyes out. And on top of that he opened his beak, gained speech like Balaam's ass, and crowed at me the following sermon:
"You have the audacity, you darkness-dwelling son of man, to want to make a rooster like me into your atonement. It is impudence, it is chutzpah of the first degree! For what, after all, is the pedigree of you and your whole kind?
"True indeed, you were created to be the chosen of creatures, the elect of all creation. That is why Providence gave you reason and the power of speech. But you never raised yourself to the high rank for which you were created. My opinion is that you never were, and are not, the 'chosen of creatures.'
"You have never used your great qualities for good. Quite the opposite — you have used them for evil.
"You took your reason and made of it a tool for forging all kinds of vileness. Just tell me, pray, which of the other creatures, even the worst and lowest, has on its conscience as many terrible and cruel crimes as you? Take, for example, the beasts that tear and rend. They are cruel indeed, brutal, murderers. But how do they compare to you in the measure of brutality? First of all, they always keep within the bounds of their predatory need [?]. There are certain kinds of creatures, weaker than they, over which they have dominion, and only these creatures are their victims, no others. In any case, most of them will never murder and never devour the flesh of their own kind.
"It is different with you, sons of man. You know no bounds. Today you shoot [?] birds, tomorrow you undertake a lion hunt, and the day after tomorrow you even fall upon your own flesh and blood and murder thousands, hundreds of thousands and millions of people.
"Secondly, you indeed possess incomparably more possibilities of murder than the beasts. Each beast by itself can in its lifetime tear apart and rend only a limited number of weak creatures, because it must do this work with its own paws or teeth. For other murderous tricks they have no brains, whereas you can lay low huge camps of victims with a single hand. One man with a big head and a lot of brain takes and invents some engine of destruction that can lay waste whole cities and countries.
"That is how you, the chosen of creatures, use [?] and misuse your intellect, which is 'a divine portion from above'! You are wise to do evil, clever, sharp brains for perpetrating all sorts of deeds of Sodom.
"And in this matter you might especially learn wisdom [?] from us, for we roosters are also endowed with understanding — you yourselves admit it. You say in your prayers: 'Who gives the rooster understanding,' but we use our understanding only for the purpose for which it was given us, namely 'to distinguish between day and night.' We always stand on watch and are ever careful to announce to you, people, the great tidings that the darkness is vanishing, the night is passing and the day is about to arrive.
"And if you were willing to listen to our tidings and to prepare yourselves properly for the day, for the light, you would truly be well off. But the fact is that you do not want to listen to us; you are positively filled with murder when you hear our call; we interrupt your sleep, your laziness draws you to bed, the darkness suits you, you love the night... Why, a certain sleepyhead threw a shoe at my head because I dared to crow and remind him that it was already day, that it was already time to open his eyes and get up... He very nearly killed me.
"And many, many of my brothers have indeed been slaughtered through the generations for no other sin than that they tried to carry out their mission, to announce the coming of the day and wake people from sleep...
"Therefore I say that I am beginning not to see the 'Morenu' [the honour] of being an atonement for you, son of man, or for others of your kind. I might perhaps already have suppressed my innate inclination to live and agreed to be a martyr and let myself be sacrificed for your benefit, if — if I could acknowledge that you are indeed a greater rooster than I, a nobler aristocrat. But as things stand now, I cannot concede that you are worth more than I, that your merit is higher than mine."
— — —
Thus that rooster sermonised, and his sermon went into my bones. I sometimes have a bit of a weakness for admitting the truth; well, I had to concede that there is a great deal of truth in his words, and from then on I resolved to leave the roosters in peace and not force upon them the tragic role of being my atonement.
So I do kapparot with money. Money has the virtue that it has no living spirit; it is a cold metal and an ownerless one. You can do with it whatever your heart desires — it is none of its grandmother's worry; it has no complaints against you and makes no demands on your conscience. You can, with it and with its power, commit the greatest wickedness in the world, and it will not rebuke you or reproach you...
Therefore money is — my atonement...
A Piyyut for Shabbat Shuva.

(Especially for communal activists, seat-grabbers, former councillors and just fine Jews) By Ben Amotz.

Laws of Swinging Kapores.
Kapores are swung in different ways: artisans who held out a whole year must swing kapores with hens... Kehilla councillors who in the course of a whole year were not at a single meeting must swing kapores with a fish...

Who Needs Whom for Kapores?
The temporary commissars in Będzin and in Sosnowiec need the nominated[?] "Rada" [council] for kapores.
The "Dozór Szkolny" [municipal school board] swings kapores with the Jewish teachers.
The Hebraists swung kapores with "Ha-Tsfira".
And the Jewish subsidies in the kehilla budgets were the real kapores...

Al Chet..
The Left Poalei Zion say:
For the sin we have committed by hardening the heart.
That we made our hearts like stone and went to the Sosnowiec kehilla elections.
For the sin we have committed unknowingly.
We did not do it knowingly, and had such a fiasco.
A Sosnowiec "breger"[?] (citizen?):
For the sin we have committed by wronging a neighbour.
I sinned against my comrades, and because of one "vote" our comrade Shalom is not a dozor [kehilla board member]...
A member of the tax-assessment commission:
For the sin we have committed by speech of the mouth.
I said what one must not, and thanks to that they assessed my neighbour to death...
The Jewish press;
For the sin we have committed in an assembly of lewdness...
The examination commission:
For the sin we have committed in eating and drinking.
We held banquets in Katowice with the Kielce "big shots", lived it up at the expense of the toiling masses; in the end it all came to nothing and 83 artisans were left without diplomas.
The board of "Hakoach":
For the sin we have committed with a strong hand.
We ran our activity with a strong hand, and thanks to that the "public" has scattered and we no longer even have a minyan..
Sosnowiec "Maccabi":
For the sin we have committed by the running of the feet.
We ran about the football pitch the wrong way, and meanwhile let the opponent's goals through..
Dacha wives and "sick" wives:
For the sin we have committed under duress.
For the dacha season I had a dozen new dresses sewn, at a time when my husband cannot afford even a shroud...

A Tkhine [Supplication] for a Dozorcowa [wife of a kehilla board member]
Lord of the World, I have a request of You: do not take away my [—], which is dearer than money. For Mrs. Dozorcowa there is no one higher; honour I had — a full cup; admission cards to the kehilla council meetings I used to share out among my relatives, those who found favour with me; at the fish market the fishwives used to shout: "Come to me, Pani Prezesowa [Madam President], a little pike or a live little tench for your[?] husband the dozor"; in shul I had the seat at the eastern wall; all the women showed me great respect — a trifle! [ironic] The wife of a dozor!
Therefore I beg You, Master of the Universe, annul the names the newspaper compared my husband to, for instance horse, kosher beast and the like, and at the elections of the new board let my honour not be diminished.
Beat Harder

[Satire — a High Holiday poem.] By Anatol.

Beat stronger, beat harder,
as much as you can,
even the best of you
must beat "al chet".

No excuses will help,
my dear people,
tell of your sorrows if you like —
beat harder, "al chet"!

Hey, providers and big shots,
make your hearts ready!
Hey, bluffers and chatterers[?],
it's the time of "al chet"!

Hey, benefactors and fixers,
you wheeled and dealt so well.
Hey, liars and hagglers,
wallop now "al chet"!

Beat stronger, beat higher,
peck and punch all right,
so they hear on the rooftops
your true "al chet"!

To do a favour, to care for another —
you were always ready at once,
but always put it off till tomorrow —
so beat for that "al chet"!

And you, little young-lady girls,
don't stand at a distance,
you had a time as in paradise —
so strike loudly "al chet"!

For a porucznik [lieutenant], a soldier or
just a uniform
you lay down full length and breadth,
caroused, went on dates without a by-your-leave —
so why shouldn't I beat
"al chet"!

"Na sto dwa" [full blast] for so long
until you got divorced;
I know it pains you —
so beat on your little hearts "al chet".

"Others must beat too,
ja tobie dam [I'll show you]!"
Boom-boom-crash taraar!
But the [—] catches them [?],
it's bitter, nothing left to rhyme.
The Merchant's Unetaneh Tokef.

And He writes and seals: the tax office writes down the merchant's earnings and they get sealed.
And You remember all things forgotten: they always remember the arrears of old taxes.
And You open the book of records: the book always lies open before one's eyes.
And the angels hasten: the sequestrators [bailiffs] rush in great haste.
And fear and trembling seize them: when the merchant catches sight of them, he is seized by fright and trembling.
For they shall not be found righteous in Your eyes in judgment: with them nobody has any merit of the fathers.
And all who come into the world pass before You: every new business that comes into the world must pass through the tax office.
And You count and number: one must constantly keep on counting...
Who shall live: it is hard to survive such troubles.
Who by strangling: who is not being strangled today for a złoty?
And who by stoning: who does not carry a heavy stone on his heart today?
Who shall rest: who has a quiet hour today?
Who shall be rich: who is rich today?
And who shall be exalted: where does one see today that people are exalted?
Leib Sztybinski[?]

I Appeal to You!

[Education — the "Mizrachi" school; a teacher's open letter (paid notice, no. 499).] I appeal to my hundreds of pupils, boys and girls, whom I taught with earnestness and devotion over 15 years. I appeal to the parents of the pupils, who know that I gave my whole "self" to the education of their children. Also to the board of the "Mizrachi" school, headed by R' Leibish Buchweitz, I appeal that they should not keep silent and not hide from the public, but speak out whether I was treated rightly by the "Mizrachi" school, when after 12 years of teaching with self-sacrifice and in want they go and trick me into signing a Polish slip of paper saying that "I have no claim whatsoever against the "Mizrachi" school", and take on someone else in my place.
Who better than you knows that for 12 whole years I taught your children for a pitiful salary. How many times did I get my money for the Sabbath an hour before candle-lighting, how many times did you give me money for Passover on the eve of the festival at dusk. Who better than you knows how many weeks and months there were, many a time, when I taught your children without seeing the shape of a coin before my eyes. I stood on guard like a soldier, a faithful one, a devoted one, for your children, for the community, and now I deserve to have my dry piece of bread taken from me and to be left to starve, I and my wife and children! And do you know why? Because of the single sin that a misfortune befell me: once, going out of the classroom in a sweat, I caught a chill, God spare us, fell ill and lay in bed for 2 months. For that they talk the public into believing that for the good of the community it is not useful that I should teach in the school. For this very "sin" it follows that I and my family must go hungry!
I also turn to my fellow teachers. You who worked together with me, you surely do know with how much mortal danger and superhuman strength I worked 12 whole years for the school, for the community, and what kind of reward I have received for it — how can you keep silent and look on indifferently as they take my bread from me and give it away to another, who has not suffered, who has not sacrificed himself for the community, only because of the single "sin" that I was ill for 2 months! "Is this the Torah and is this its reward"? Speak out — a holy comradely duty lies upon you; declare publicly whether the "Mizrachi" school acted honestly towards me, and whether I, who gave my years and strength to the school, really have no right to have a claim against the "Mizrachi" school; can you, comrades, go indifferently about your everyday work, teaching children humanity, honesty, self-sacrifice for others, at a time when your honest comrade is thrown out into the street, without a why and without a wherefore, and his mouth is stopped so that he cannot even cry out!
— Let the public see and judge!
Dawid Landner.

Sick-fund bailiff wants to take away the office equipment of the Jewish Community.

The administration of the sick fund (Kasa Chorych) is claiming from the Jewish Community a debt amounting to about 8 thousand zł. Years ago the sick fund already placed a distraint on the office furnishings for this sum, but by various means the auction was postponed.
Last Friday a bailiff came to the Community with the aim of already taking away the distrained items.
Having no other recourse, they turned for help to the vice-starosta Mr. Matryszewski [?], who intervened with the head (naczelnik) of the sick fund that the removal of the items be postponed until Tuesday.
The matter was settled in the sense that the sum is to be paid in instalments, i.e. the Community must pay 20 zł every week, besides the current bills of the sick fund.

The municipal economy is "neither dairy nor meat"...
Session of the Commissars' Council.

On Tuesday evening the 19th session of the Commissars' Council took place. At the session the commissar Rzeczkowski [?] gave a report on the state of the municipal economy. —
According to the figures given, it turns out that the economic situation is neither a bad one nor a good one.
In the course of the commissar's administration the amount of debts has been reduced by a quarter of a million zł., with which the creditors were settled, who are the contractors on various works.
In his report the commissar also explained that the matter of building the sewerage collector is as good as settled. The terms are also more favourable now than before: instead of 10 per cent it will cost only 8½ per cent of the sum that the Lwów company has projected.
It is also planned that Małachowskiego Street, too, is to be connected to the sewers.
There wasn't enough steam...

The news in our paper on the eve of Rosh Hashanah that the municipal bath-house is already in operation has, as it turns out, aroused great interest. On that day 590 tickets were sold. Such attendance has not been seen since the establishment opened. Even in the last days before Passover the largest number of visitors reached up to 200 [the text breaks off here in print].
Registration of the 1913 class.

We have been asked by the Magistrate to announce once more that the young men born in the year 1913 must without fail register at the Magistrate.
The registration will last until the 30th of this month.
Plate money for "Linat ha-Holim".

The administration of the "Linat ha-Holim" society with its various institutions asks us to point out that this year on the eve of Yom Kippur the society's plate collection (ma'ot ke'arah) should be supported. At the same time thanks are expressed to the children Leslau [?] for the donated furniture such as beds, mattresses, chairs and the like.
The general meeting of "Hakoach".

As we are informed, the general meeting, which takes place on the first day of Sukkot, will have an interesting course. Because almost the entire board no longer agrees to stand as candidates, each section is holding consultations and various combinations are being made in putting together the new board; the items of the agenda are being discussed, which has a very important significance for the further development of the club.

Courses of "WIZO".

On the initiative of the Zionist women's association "WIZO", Hebrew and English courses for members are being opened in its own premises.
One can register with Mrs. S. Erlich, Sączewska [?] 9.
The association has also opened the "Gan Yeladim" (kindergarten). The interest of the Jewish parents is great. The number of places is already limited.
The magistrate's cutbacks have begun with the Jewish teachers.

In the local magistrate [municipality] the system of "economies" has begun, but the start was made with the Jewish teachers.
As we are informed, almost all the Jewish teachers have been dismissed from the vocational courses and from the evening courses, and those who did remain have had their teaching hours cut.
Fee on the demands to pay for water reduced.
Through the intervention of Mr. Repnitz[?] it has been achieved that the demands sent to the population to pay for water shall cost only 50 gr. instead of 1 zł. as until now.
"Zionism under the Bolshevik Dictatorship".

This Sabbath at 2 o'clock in the afternoon a lecture will be given in the "Kapitol" cinema by the writer Yitzhak Margoshes, entitled "Zionism under the Bolshevik Dictatorship".
Mr. Margoshes was a member of the Zionist Central Committee of Russia and, together with 500 Zionist activists, made the journey on foot from Siberia to Eretz Israel via the Caucasus, Persia, Mesopotamia and Syria.
Of the group, after 13 months of wandering, only 48 men reached Eretz Israel; of the rest, 300 men were killed by the Bolsheviks before the Persian border and 152 men perished on the road of suffering from various diseases.
At the time this story aroused a great sensation in the entire world press, and recently Mr. Margoshes published a special work about these sufferings in the German language entitled "Als jüdischer Flüchtling durch Vorderasien" (As a Jewish Refugee through the Near East).
Mr. Margoshes has published other works on the life and struggle of the Zionists in Russia. Various Jewish and non-Jewish newspapers recognise him as an authentic expert in this field.
Mr. Margoshes's lecture takes place this Sabbath in Będzin and is awaited with great interest in all strata of the population because of the precise information about the two and a half million Jews of Russia.
Systematic thefts of postage stamps.

The manager of the Discount Bank had noticed many times that postage stamps were disappearing from a certain place. He kept an "eye" on the matter and found out that the "craftsmen" behind it were the clerks Szperling and Ważnica.
Rent may be sent by post. An important ruling of the Supreme Court.

A few days ago a case was heard in the Supreme Court under no. 1645 whose verdict has general significance.
The landlord K. L. sued his tenant S. K. for eviction for not paying him the quarterly[?] rent. In the municipal court the tenant had proved that S.[?] had sent the money by post and that the landlord had refused to accept the money. The court dismissed the eviction.
The landlord lodged an appeal with the Court of Appeal, pointing out that the tenant had not sent the full amount of the rent by post.
The Court of Appeal annulled the verdict of the first instance and awarded an eviction.
The tenant appealed the verdict to the Supreme Court, which quashed the verdict on the eviction and justified its ruling by stating that sending money by post in disputes between landlord and tenant is provided for in the decree on tenant protection, and must be regarded as a payment on account (a konto) until the disputed questions are decided by the court or by the "Urząd Rozjemczy" [rent arbitration office].
Sosnowiec. While husband and wife were out visiting, the Christian maid committed a large theft.

On the evening of the first day of Rosh Hashanah, Mr. Moshe Yosef Retman and his wife went out to visit friends and left as guard the Christian maid, who had been with the Retman family for a few days.
On returning, everything was in order. But Mr. Retman, already lying in bed, had a premonition that something had happened during their absence.
Unable to calm himself, he got out of bed, went into the dining room and suddenly saw that the drawer in which there were 5 thousand zł. and other valuables was open...
Retman immediately went into the kitchen, but the maid was no longer there. Only then did it turn out that the new "good" maid had taken the money and 2 fur garments and run away.
"The shofar blasts cost him dear".

A well-known local shofar-blower has the custom that, as soon as Rosh Chodesh Elul comes, he already holds "rehearsals" with the shofar; usually the "rehearsals" are held in the beit midrash every morning after prayers. This shofar-blower, however, had to travel before Rosh Hashanah to Beuthen [Bytom]. And together with his tallit and tefillin he also took the shofar along.
When the train was already on German territory, our shofar-blower felt "at home", put on tallit and tefillin and stood up to pray; after praying he took the shofar, as is his habit, and —
— tekiah...
The shofar signals reached as far as the train driver, who, hearing such unfamiliar sounds, stopped the train.
The train stood still and the shofar-blower went on blowing until...
Here the tragedy begins: the poor shofar-blower had to pay a fine of 50 marks...

Meets her "intended" on the train.
A certain Miss M., who travelled from Warsaw these days on the express train, made the acquaintance in the carriage of an intelligently dressed young man. The acquaintance of the couple quickly turned into devotion with sympathetic signs, which led them even to questions of the future — what this chance acquaintance would become for them, through declarations of love.
The young man introduced himself to Miss M. as now travelling from abroad, where he had already completed his education with a diploma as doctor of medicine, and he intended to settle [?] in a town somewhere in Zagłębie that had a hospital, so as to be able to practise. Miss M. did not think long and suggested he come to Sosnowiec, where there are several hospitals, also a Jewish hospital, so that their present acquaintance would bring both of them a happy future. The young "doctor" was very pleased with this plan, and the couple became quite intimate with each other.
When the train arrived at the station, the beloved young doctor quickly helped the young lady down from the carriage, and right away the train indeed began to depart, so that they had no time even to take proper leave of each other. Only a few minutes later did Miss M. realise that in her haste she had left in the carriage her luggage worth several hundred złoty and a wallet with 84 złoty in cash, which in her haste she had forgotten to take down.
As it later turned out, the young lady had been dealing with none other than a common swindler.

Doubtful debts must be deducted from income.
The merchant community is greatly alarmed about the new assessment of income tax. If this year's assessment is carried out by the same methods and principles as in previous years, the merchants will suffer great damage, which in the present crisis may undermine their existence.
Among the most important causes alarming the merchants is also the question of deducting doubtful debts from income, or better said, of deducting lost debts from income.
Last year every merchant had a fair number of such debts, which were counted as lost debts of bankrupts. Some buyers [?] have gone away, others are simply insolvent, so that the debt is already considered bad.
Under Art. 34 of the Income Tax Act every merchant has the right to deduct from his income the sum of debts that are lost and that there is no longer hope of collecting.
In practice, however, the tax offices refuse to recognise the lost debts and deduct them from income. They say that it will be possible to collect them some day, and that under the law one may write off from income only if there is no longer any hope of collecting the debts.
On these matters several cases have already come before the Supreme Administrative Tribunal, which handed down judgments against the tactics of the tax offices.
The Administrative Tribunal ruled, namely, that the assessment commission must deduct from income such uncertain debts for which there is proof that claiming them in court did not bring a proper result. For example, if the debtor is bankrupt, it is clear that part must be deducted from income. If one has sued a debtor in court and has not been able to collect the debt with the help of the bailiff (komornik), it must be deducted from income.
This judgment of the Supreme Administrative Tribunal bears the number 27—3745 of 2 October 1929.

It very often happens that the provincial Jewish press, and also the Warsaw press, reprints articles and larger news items from the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" without giving the source from which they took them. We have already drawn attention to this several times: we have nothing against the matter itself, but it is not rational when this is done by a press that reacts to such matters when others do it...

Two weeks ago "Radio" and "Moment" printed, from the "Zagłębie correspondents", whole and fragmented sentences from Mr. Gangdibz's [?] articles, which were printed in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". It goes without saying that the name of the writer and also the source were not given; apparently there they do not hold with "whoever reports a thing in the name of the one who said it"...

This week "Undzer Ekspres" again reprinted word for word the story "Laytenberg [?] Kakhan". Here the editors have already galloped far ahead and even forgot to add that the story happened in Będzin...

How the Olkusz Artisans' Representatives Fulfil Their Duty.

[Olkusz — artisans.] As in all towns, so here too there exists an artisans' association, which as such sends its representatives to various institutions, such as the town council, the gmina, etc. Thus Mr. Blum was sent as ławnik [member of the municipal executive] on behalf of the artisans, in order to defend the artisans' interests, and he "defended" them like this: at the time the Olkusz magistrate [municipality] was parcelling out plots; Mr. Blum, as ławnik, began to think how one obtains loans for the magistrate, so he went up to one of his fellow artisans and told him: if you also want a plot from the parcelled-out municipal plots, come and pay in 500 zł. to the magistrate's treasury. The fellow artisan thought that the aforementioned meant to do him a favour, and paid in 500 zł. Here is what turned out: the aforementioned ławnik, who represented the artisans, aimed thereby "to shoot two hares at once". The 'poritz' [the squire — i.e. the Polish town head] was pleased with the Jewish artisan who supplied the municipal treasury with money, and his fellow artisan was pleased with his representative, who was looking after him so that he should have a plot. Only later did the role that Mr. A. Blum had played come out, because even then, when he told him to pay in the 500 zł., there were already no plots left. Two years later the magistrate still gives no thought at all to parcelling, and as for returning the money, there is certainly[?] nothing to talk about, because, as people say, the magistrate has a deficit of one and a half million zł. and is now trying to obtain long-term loans. Had Mr. Blum not resigned as ławnik, the magistrate would not have needed to look for any loans, since the aforementioned would have provided all his fellow artisans with plots...
The artisans' association could recently no longer put up with such a "representative" and reported his treachery in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", and it is high time that the Olkusz artisans, when they elect representatives, should not elect such people as come to them before the elections and are not seen all year; such people who, when they sit down at the table with the poritz to drink a glass of tea, forget through whom they were elected.
The Olkusz artisans' association has recently begun to cleanse itself a little, but with the "outcry" in the press about Mr. Blum and his treachery it is not yet clean; it must energetically continue to cleanse itself and dismiss the remaining representatives. About the activity of the remaining representatives — another time.
An Artisan.
Examinations of the Pupils of Goldstein's Cutting School in Będzin.

[Będzin — artisans / vocational training.] On Wednesday evening the festive examination ceremony of a group of pupils of Goldstein's [garment-]cutting school took place at the Będzin Artisans' Association. Present were: the director of the vocational schools in Zagłębie, Mr. Kuszyszkiewicz; the representative of the Starostwo [district office], Mr. Lehowski; the elder (starszy)[?] of the Christian tailors' guild in Sosnowiec, Mr. Rusak; the representatives of the Jewish tailors' guild in Sosnowiec, Messrs. Szajer and Czarny; from the Jewish guild in Będzin, Mr. B. Aronow; on behalf of the Będzin Artisans' Association, Mr. L. Brama; and several activists close to Jewish artisanry.
The examinations opened with a lengthy speech by Mr. Goldstein, who, after greeting those present, spoke at length about the significance of the new cutting system, which is still a novelty in Poland, and demonstrated theoretically the benefit of this system for artisanry in the future.
The representatives of the authorities examined the pupils. The examinations were a great success; the pupil Kelner in particular showed much knowledge.
Those who received diplomas are: Yehoshua Wekselman, Avraham Yehonatan Rozenek[?] (Sławków), Moshe Barensztajn, Ezel[?] Rozenes[?] (Siemianowice), Israel Yitzchak Ajzenberg, Szymon Aronowicz, Dawid Kelner and Józef Gruszenda.
Afterwards the guests spent time over a glass of tea and fruit. Instead of toasts, a series of current questions concerning the development of artisanry were discussed.

Yom Kippur in Katowice.
Already half an hour before Kol Nidre the great synagogue was packed full; at the entrance stood community (religious-service) officials and firemen, who let people in only with admission cards. Yet this could not help, and in the end they were compelled to permit entry even without admission cards.
The chief cantor Mr. Dembitzer with the choir beautifully performed the Kol Nidre prayer, and Rabbi Dr. Vogelmann delivered a sermon. In a very successful form he portrayed the significance of this day for the Jewish people.
On this Day of Atonement, says Rabbi Vogelmann, we forgive even our enemies. But we do not renounce even the most elementary rights which we, as a nation, have the right to enjoy.
On the whole, Yom Kippur in Katowice passed in an elevated, festive mood.

The Crisis and the Unemployed Jewish Intelligentsia

[Article — economy and society; unemployment.] By Dovid Wożnica [Dawid Woźnica].

One of the sharpest and most difficult socio-economic problems of the present time is, beyond doubt, the problem of unemployment.

In recent years unemployment has seized even the strongest and economically well-built states, and with its negative consequences it threatens to undermine the firm foundations on which the whole world economy has until now calmly rested.

Over this painful question the greatest statesmen and economists in every country are now racking their brains, wishing to find a solution or means to relieve the want of the great masses of physical and intellectual workers, to which the last cruel world war, with its victors and vanquished, has led.

History already shows us that in a time of economic, social or political crises we Jews are the first victims who fall in the struggle, so that others may eat the fruits which we sowed with hard toil and sweat on the fields of foreign owners. At a time when other nations, among them also the Polish people, are straining all their forces to tear themselves out of the bewitched economic wheel into which we have been pushed for various reasons, we Jews stand with hands hanging down and look on indifferently as our whole life is being ruined and is approaching with quick steps the threshold of complete downfall, both spiritual and material.

Have we really already fallen into such terrible despair that we no longer see any rescue from the situation?

Have we already entirely lost hope of a better future? And where is our feeling of self-help, which once played such an important role in our life and saved us from various greater dangers that threatened us at all times among the nations of the world?

I believe that in the depths of the souls of our Jewish intelligentsia there still smoulders a small fire, which waits only for the proper moment to flare up into a great fire that will light up the road darkened by the crisis and rouse the fallen-away elements to life and to positive deeds for society and for their people.

That the moment has come is proven by the great action of the government, with Polish society at its head, aimed at helping the unemployed in the spirit of the slogan put forward: "Hold out and wait it out" until the economic conjuncture in the country improves.

But we Jews will not benefit much from this action, although some Jewish representatives will be represented on the various civic committees — the reasons for this are known to everyone.

All the more is it our sacred duty to begin a rescue action within our own society itself, but on a smaller scale and in a different direction, because we live in quite different, specific conditions from our neighbours.

The relief action in our town must first of all be conducted in the direction of relieving the want of our unemployed intelligentsia and intellectual workers, who because of the crisis have lost their workplaces and find themselves with their families in terrible material want, which will probably grow still greater towards the approaching winter.

We must not close our eyes and look on indifferently as our unemployed intelligentsia wrestles with death and stands on the threshold of complete downfall, because "to save the intelligentsia means to save the people" — and this we must remember at the present moment!

More than once I have happened to talk with laid-off ["reduced"] Jewish intellectual workers, who complained of their fate and asked with tears in their eyes: "What is Jewish society doing? Save us. We and our families are dying of hunger!"

Let this outcry be a "memento" for those who are still working at their posts, and also for the whole of Jewish society, which at the present moment must not make light of the problem of unemployment in the Jewish street.

With the slogan "Save our unemployed intelligentsia" the relief action must begin.

Dovid Wożnica.
To the Jewish Public — Help Build the Great Edifice of Jewish Culture and Scholarship!

[Public appeal — YIVO (Yiddish Scientific Institute), Vilna.]

Help build the great edifice of Jewish culture and scholarship!

On 25 October 1929, during the first conference of the Yiddish Scientific Institute [YIVO], the cornerstone was laid of its own building for this world-wide centre of Jewish culture and scholarship. This act of construction aroused deep enthusiasm throughout the whole Jewish world, among all friends of Jewish culture. And this enthusiasm accomplished great things: despite the severe economic crisis in all the lands of Jewish settlement, there was erected in Vilna [Wilno], on YIVO's large plot at Wiwulskiego Street 18, the house of Jewish scholarship — a home of its own for the centre of Jewish culture, a fire-proof treasury for Jewish creative works of all lands and all times.

The Institute's building has been erected but is not yet entirely finished. The fire-proof storehouse for YIVO's collections has been built; the walls and [printed "in"] the roof of the building are finished outside and inside; floors have been laid in all rooms, stairs put in, central heating installed, the windows glazed. But it still remains to install water and sewerage, to finish the electrical installation, the smithing work and the interior fittings in the halls and work-rooms. Everything can be finished within a month, if the necessary means are available.

It is very cramped in the Institute's rented premises! There is no room for the precious treasures of Jewish life and creativity that stream into YIVO from all corners of the world. The library room is overcrowded, the archives are stacked away, the museums are not on display, there is nowhere to turn round in the work-rooms. The unhindered growth of all branches of YIVO is no longer possible outside its own, specially adapted building.

To finish the house of Jewish scholarship and culture is now an urgent task that must not be postponed.

The times are hard and bitter; the Jewish masses and their intelligentsia are struggling hard for their existence. But precisely in such a critical time we must strain all our forces to maintain what has been achieved.

The Yiddish Scientific Institute is a cornerstone in the cultural edifice of our people; the YIVO building is the cornerstone of the Institute; we must finish it!

We turn to all friends of the Yiddish Scientific Institute, to the Jewish popular masses all over the world:

— Lend a hand to finish the house of Jewish scholarship and culture! Buy up the stamps just issued by the Institute's building fund! We turn to every man of the people: let there also be a brick of yours in the building of the Yiddish Scientific Institute, walled into the fortress of world-wide Jewish cultural creation!

Help build!

Central Administration
of the Yiddish Scientific Institute.
