The Tragedy of a Russian Righteous Proselyte.

[History — the Jews of Russia in the 18th century; a page from the past.] By Moshe Feinkind.
(A page of history from the past.)
When the Russian tsarina Anna Ioannovna (1730—40) took over the Russian throne after Catherine I, she at first showed a certain sympathy towards Jews, in spite of the fact that her whole entourage was ill-disposed and full of prejudices against Jews.
This tsarina had a Jew — a favourite, Lipman was his name, who was the financial agent of the Courland duke Biron. She also kept at her court the Portuguese Jew (a Marrano) Jan d'Acosta as court jester, whom Peter the Great had brought from abroad to Petersburg.
Both Jews found great favour in the eyes of the Russian autocrat, and the largest leases (Pachten) she gave out to her favourite Lipman of Courland.
But all of a sudden a great reversal took place in Anna Ioannovna's attitude towards Jews. The clergy influenced her, and she showed great hatred, especially towards the Jews who lived in the former Polish territories.
In the shtetl of Zverovichi [printed „Zvierkovich“] in the Smolensk district lived the rich leaseholder (arendator) R' Baruch Leibov, who had set up a little synagogue for prayer at his home; the Holy Synod ordered the synagogue destroyed and annihilated entirely and the Torah scrolls burned, and then all the Jews were also driven out of there on the pretext that Jews were spreading the Jewish faith among the Orthodox population.
This blood-libel-like accusation did not keep itself waiting long: a trial was indeed brought against R' Baruch Leibov for having persuaded a Russian naval officer to become a Jew...
This naval officer, Captain-Lieutenant Alexander Voznitsyn, had become acquainted with R' Baruch and often used to visit him to have a chat with him.
And while constantly holding debates between them on religious topics, this captain became acquainted with the essence of Jewish religion and life and, to [his] misfortune [?], actually decided to convert to Judaism.
R' Baruch is said to have taken him to Dubrovna (Mogilev district), and there they circumcised him, Voznitsyn, and he became a true Jew.
The Russian tsarina found out about it and ordered the naval officer to be arrested at once together with R' Baruch and brought to Petersburg.
General Ushakov, who was in charge of the matter, applied all sorts of inquisitorial means and tortures against both accused, thereby forcing [?] them to confess their guilt...
Having no choice, both confessed to everything that was demanded of them.
The trial then passed to the Senate, and although the justice commission of the Senate found no grounds to convict the accused, since the confession of the crime had been squeezed out of them by violent means, the Senate nevertheless had to act according to the demand of the empress, who was strongly influenced by General Ushakov, and therefore sentenced the righteous proselyte together with R' Baruch Leibov to death by burning their bodies alive, so that „they may know and see“ [lema'an yed'u ve-yir'u], that the Jews should be afraid to make Jews of Christians...
It did not help that her Jewish favourite Lipman interceded with the empress on behalf of the condemned, that they might at least be granted their bare lives. The tsarina remained deaf to the request and naturally confirmed the Senate's terrible death sentence, and on Sukkot 1738 R' Baruch Leibov of Smolensk, together with the righteous proselyte Alexander Voznitsyn, was led out, hands and feet forged in heavy chains, to the execution ground outside Petersburg, and there, on an auto-da-fé specially set up for these holy victims, they were burned alive in the presence of a large public, which drew satisfaction and joy from this terrible inquisitorial procedure.
Anna Ioannovna, however, was not yet satisfied with these two victims; she also poured out her bloodthirsty wrath on all the other Jews in her country, ordering them all to be driven out of Little Russia [Ukraine], again out of fear that through the influx of Jews the number of Jewish proselytes among the Russian population would grow...
But in the meantime a war broke out between Russia and Turkey, and after a great deal of debate between the civil and military authorities it was not considered expedient under these circumstances to expel the Jews from that region, owing to which the expulsion was indeed postponed until after the war.
It was further feared that the Jews would take revenge on Russia for the expulsion and would support the enemy in word and deed, although the empress was not very pleased with this consideration.
But as soon as the war had ended, the clergy again pressed for the Jews, who mostly originated from Poland, to be driven out of Little Russia; but thanks to the premature death of Tsarina Anna, who had died in the meantime, the greater part of the Jews was saved from expulsion and remained in their place.
These same Jews indeed used every Sukkot to recite memorial prayers and celebrate [?] the holy memory of the two martyrs who perished for the sanctification of the Name at the hands of the Russian tsarina Anna Ioannovna.
Only recently were the trial records concerning the righteous proselyte Alexander Voznitsyn found in the archive of the Holy Synod, and part of them were published in the second volume of „Perezhitoe“.
The Circumstances of Our Life (The consequence of the lawlessness and demoralisation that took hold in the 20th century)

[Essay — society and economy; the crisis, taxes and lawlessness.]
L. Szpigelman.
(The consequence of the lawlessness and demoralisation that took hold in the 20th century.)

People here complain bitterly — and not only here, but truly in the whole world — about the crisis, which does not stop [?], but becomes ever more serious as time goes on, and ever more dangerous the later it gets. The difference, however, is this: elsewhere people pause, in full awareness, over the serious problem called crisis. They make every effort to solve the question, they look for a way out that would ease this centre of gravity. They know that when things are bad one must restrict the budget, one must live more economically, more calculatingly, save what can be saved.

Here, however, it is quite different. We do not want to save, and indeed we cannot save anything at all, however bad the situation may be, however bitter the circumstances may turn out — for, let us not fool ourselves, on what, for example, can one save, and what can one cut down on? Perhaps on fruit, which one cannot afford anyway — however healthy they may be and however much we may need them for the children, this is after all counted as luxury? Or shall we not give the children the necessary education? Or perhaps shall we restrict ourselves and reduce our dwellings, which are here in the most terrible state? On the contrary: on what can one save and in what can we restrict ourselves, since one is not at all accustomed to living in comfortable conditions, as European citizens live?

And even if one were to take the bite out of one's own mouth or the child's — how much in total can one save, compared with the expenses that an average family has to bear today? On top of this the trouble lies in the fact that the government does not teach the citizens to economise; rather, the impression is created that one must constantly live more lavishly and more lawlessly. Thus, for example, it is self-evident that at a critical moment, in hard times, taxes ought to be reduced, one ought to economise at every step. We see, however, exactly the opposite: the worse the times become, the harder life becomes and the more expenses are required to fulfil one's civic duty. Here, for example, it is no longer a secret that taxes are increased from year to year — and who pays them, if not the people? if not the citizens? On top of this one is constantly devising how to procure new tax revenues, which are likewise drawn from the people. Now they are about to raise the prices of dwellings; then it turns out that the income tax, too, is being raised. So it comes out that the more bankruptcies occur, the fewer goods one lets out of one's hands, the more cautious [?] one is — the more one earns. Is this comprehensible? Can the mind grasp it? Where is the reckoning, and where does the logic lie? So it comes out that it is not enough that taxes and our expenses should have been reduced at a time when one trades little and earns even less — we must also protect ourselves by fending off the bullets that make it harder, indeed simply impossible, to carry on our livelihood. Is it any wonder, then, that the situation becomes harder in any case, that the circumstances become ever more unbearable? How can one economise here, when expenditure and unforeseen expenses become ever heavier and more incomprehensible? Is all this logical, comprehensible and consistent? Can one progress under such conditions? Is it possible that these grave wounds of the crisis can be healed in such a way? And once one finds oneself in such a hard situation, can one shut one's eyes and say: let it go as it goes? Does not such indifference smack of the most dangerous thing that can befall a country, and of the most catastrophic situation of its citizens? Can one, in this case, find a favourable way out that would try in some way to heal the dangerous wound?

A wound can only be healed when one takes an interest in it, when one tends it and truly wants to heal it. It is quite different, however, when one wants to profit from the wound, when one wants fruits from it — fruits that are dangerous both for the country and for the citizens, because in that case the citizens become cripples. One by one, one by one they wean themselves from human duties, from civic obligations. People grow accustomed to grabbing from one another. In place of compassion and fairness, truth and honesty, lawlessness and demoralisation are planted. No one has any respect or decency towards the other. One is not ashamed to say simply and openly: I managed to get hold of goods, so I was entitled to take them. I need not pay, because I was not paid either.

True, the first time it comes hard; it is somehow unpleasant: the other one comes, he demands what is his; after all he knows that this is robbery, plunder [?]. Later on, however, it goes as if greased: one grows clever and refined in the field of grabbing, running, robbing, plundering — so that later one cannot understand why one did not do it until now, why one let such good opportunities slip by for so long... And what at the first time was called "seizure" [?], robbery — he cannot by any means understand why it should have been called by such an incorrect name, by such an unpleasant expression.

For he is as sure as two times two is four that all the goods and money and whatever he managed to obtain, in whatever manner it may be — all this was due to him, nothing more; he would have committed an injustice against himself and an act of violent robbery [lit. a "violence-grab"] against his wife and children had he not taken it at once. He cannot even imagine how there could be people who would blame anyone [?] in this case. For he is sure — just as sure as he is that the sun is shining now — that everything he does is fine and good, nothing more; that what he has and the other has not is nothing more than because he is capable, clever, energetic and in full possession of his understanding, whereas the other, his neighbour, is a schlemiel and a good-for-nothing and is not worthy of living in the world...

Who speaks today about another's labour, about another's hard-earned money and property? These are such outlived notions, antiquated themes, that no longer have any place in our modern period.

Unfortunately, unfortunately, we now live in such conditions. Perhaps we do not notice it, we do not grasp it, but when one takes stock, when one draws a parallel between former times and today, one is easily convinced of it. The good, penetrating, searching eye sees it in any case already now: that we have begun to go down the road of lawlessness and demoralisation, and that the latter occupies the top place in our present-day world.

Unfortunately, unfortunately, the forms now are such that for killing a person an excuse suffices, and for form's sake he receives a few weeks' arrest; for deliberate swindles nothing happens; for defrauding people of their property one has little to fear. One need be no more than clever and know how to manage, and one remains moreover a hero and a man of honour with the noblest conscience — which is in fact, for our many sins, a superfluous thing.

This way of life, the order and the whole system bear great blame for the unchangingness [?] and the unfitness of the world and of mankind. Lawlessness and demoralisation reign in every corner of our life, but the worst of all is that people want to persuade us that the bad and the false is now good and fine and true.
The Only Etrog

(A story.) By P"ni Baal-Loshn.

Russia was sealed off on all sides after the Bolshevik revolution, both by sea and by land — no getting in and no getting out.
Every shtetl was a separate state unto itself. And getting from one state into the next was harder than the parting of the Red Sea. One was not allowed to travel in or out, from one to the other.
Besides, the roads meant mortal danger. Robber bands lay in wait on every hill, in every valley and in every copse, and if anyone dared venture out beyond the "gate" onto the road, he never came back.
There was nothing to light the houses with — so people made oil lamps [kaganets] and sat together in whole companies. There was nothing to dress in — so they wrapped themselves in sacks and rags.
But the shtetl did not lose itself; it drove despair away. Jews would stand whole days in little circles in the market square, chatting, talking politics, telling stories and even joking and making quips at the expense of the wild world, and —
hoping, hoping for better times!...
• • •
So the summer went by and the Selichot days drew near.
And the shtetl's heart grew even gloomier — here come the Days of Awe already, and after them the cruel winter, the long, cold, wet, muddy, ingrained winter that has clung to the shtetl since time immemorial, let alone in these panic-stricken times.
And more worried than anyone went about the rabbi, Reb Shlomke.
— How can it be! Jews are so careworn, poor things, that they have quite forgotten that Sukkot is coming in God's world and one needs etrogim to say the blessing over! At least one etrog for the whole community! What can be done? Where will one get one now?
So the rabbi sent for Reb Leybele the dayan and a few elderly householders, and with a broken heart lamented before them:
— True, it is a time of trouble; one cannot, God forbid, blame the shtetl, poor, downcast thing — but... still... an etrog... what does one do?
The next day there was an uproar in the shtetl: indeed, no one could remember such a thing — that the community should be left without an etrog!
Where will one get an etrog?
And Reb Shlomke the rabbi called a meeting in the beit midrash. He actually wept tears:
— Gevalt, Jews! After such troubles, with ruin, with panic, shall the community, God forbid, be left without an etrog for Sukkot?... Gevalt, he has not known such a thing since he came of age!... And the sin falls on his old, weak shoulders! As for lulavim, he still has some from the year before last [or: from last year], but what good are lulavim alone?...
The rabbi, the dayan and the elderly householders argued noisily, the whole shtetl wrangled with one another, and it was decided that the community should club together, raise the necessary sum of money, and send a couple of emissaries to Odessa at once.
Odessa is, after all, "a city and mother in Israel" — and in Odessa stands the Frenchman with his ships!
— And the Frenchman is hand in glove with the Englishman!
— And the Englishman has only just given us Eretz Israel and even wants to make a Jewish kingdom there.
— All Englishmen are steeped in our Bible; they are among the Righteous of the Nations!
— Never mind, with God everything is possible: He will help us, never mind!
Shining faces, merry faces, hearts full of hope: Odessa! The Frenchman! The Englishman! Eretz Israel! A Jewish kingdom! An etrog! An e-t-r-o-g!
— Yes, but how does one get to Odessa? At such a time, on such deadly roads: no one goes out and no one comes in!?
Up rises Reb Shlomke the rabbi, his hat pushed up, his face aflame, the sleeves of his kapote rolled up, and he cries out in a voice not his own:
— Jews, who wants to earn the World to Come, who?... Who wants to take this great mitzvah upon himself, who? I trust in Him Who lives forever that, as it is written, emissaries on a mitzvah come to no harm!
And two wagon-drivers, strapping lads, strongmen, jump up:
— Rebbe, the two of us will go, Rebbe!
The whole crowd is left stunned. No one would have believed it of them. Two such lads, whom the whole shtetl knows as unruly good-for-nothings, desperadoes [?] — and here, self-sacrifice for a mitzvah?!
In a single moment these two fellows were raised up in the shtetl's eyes: true heroes, Jewish heroes! The finest householders, together with the rabbi, surrounded them, shook their hands and looked at them with reverence.
And at the break of dawn the two emissaries were already at the gate of the shtetl; they climbed onto a light little wagon harnessed to three eagle-swift horses that tore up the ground beneath them, and the whole shtetl together with Reb Shlomke the rabbi came to bid them farewell.
— Stay well, Rebbe, and all you Jews, and pray to God for us!
And the whole community answered:
Go to life and to peace, come back well, and God be with you!
A resounding crack of the whip cut through the air:
Giddy-up, children, gi-d-d-y-up!
And off they went like an arrow from a bow.
• • •
Day after day goes by, and the emissaries have vanished as if into water.
The shtetl whispers, speculates; people go about as if headless with grief.
No trains are running — the world is locked shut. No news at all; who knows what has become of the emissaries!
Rosh Hashanah passed — nothing seen, nothing heard. The shtetl seethes, sways; Yom Kippur has already gone by too. No voice and no answer; the shtetl is dejected, in mourning...
The wives and children of the emissaries run day after day to Reb Shlomke the rabbi, weeping and lamenting and making claims against the community. The rabbi comforts them, lets them unburden their hearts, while in his own heart it is heavy, as though heavy stones lay there.
Somewhere a village had risen in revolt, and whole nights long one heard cannons booming.
Somewhere the Ukrainian Cossacks were fighting Denikin's men, and through the nights one saw tongues of fire far, far away rising, whirling and making the skies glow all around.
The shtetl trembles. Anxiety gnaws, bores like a worm. The wives and children of the emissaries run through the shtetl crying "gevalt" and drilling into [?] people's brains:
— Their husbands, their fathers — let them be brought back!
The shtetl is desolate and dark and is already trying to console itself:
— Nobody, God forbid, forced them!
Reb Shlomke the rabbi turns green and yellow with suffering, and gives hope.
And of the two emissaries there is no sign.
• • •
It is already the eve of Sukkot, after sunset.
The beit midrash is already full of Jews, but no one can bring himself to start praying. The wives and children of the emissaries stand at the eastern wall wailing, turning worlds upside down — and who could quiet them? One can see what is going on here...
Reb Shlomke the rabbi, too, is already standing with his head in the Holy Ark, pouring out tears, the congregation watching him.
And — ...
A running, a leaping, one over the other; people run and... and shout:
— They've come!
— Here they are!
— Safe and sound, thank God!
Everyone pushed out of the beit midrash into the street; up to the door rolled the little wagon, now with only two horses, sweating, steam pouring from their nostrils [?], and the two lads jumped down with joy:
— We brought it!
— A horse burst, but we brought an etrog!
Reb Shlomke the rabbi raised both hands upward and gave praise to the Almighty for His grace; he took the "little parcel" and went to welcome the festival.
When the Current Rages

[Education and culture — assimilation; the Jewish school.]
Dr. A. Gottesdiener. (Director of the "Mizrachi" school).

Water is a dangerous element, like fire. When the torrent is already overflowing its banks and sweeping along with it everything it meets on its way, there is no longer any rescue. Against the torrent one must warn and guard before it begins to swell, and, starting from its source, one must watch over its whole course — truly guard its every step.
So it is also with spiritual and moral currents, with the currents of the times. That current too grows quietly. It slowly undermines spiritual and moral foundations which for hundreds and thousands of years stood firm, strong and secure, like rocks, like mountains — and wipes them off the face of the earth.
How, for example, did assimilation begin among Jews in various countries? It began quietly, modestly, truly for the sake of Heaven, in order to raise Jewish honour in the eyes of the nations, in order to be equal to other people; but with every step it took on a faster tempo and a more radical direction, until it turned into "Yahudim" [the assimilated German Jews], until of all Jewishness nothing remained but "Yizkor" (the memorial prayer), and of the whole Torah nothing but Abraham our Father's first commandment.
It is also a complete mistake to think that the chapter of assimilation already belongs to last week's Torah portion. Among us it is starting anew, and it strides along various paths: left and right of the true Jewish centre. Yes, it winds and bends very elastically, and its movements are as in the good old days; but it goes ever further and ever deeper into the Jewish street.
There are only few towns in Poland where assimilation has not yet conquered a respectable place in Jewish life. But here too it is in the state of being born, and quietly it makes its way to the child.
Here is Jewish Zagłębie, with its strong religious and national core, of which Jewish Zagłębie can be proud. Even here something is stirring in the Jewish camp, something that smells of the first birth pangs of assimilation.
When I stroll on a Sabbath or holiday through the streets of Będzin, it seems to me that I am somewhere in a kind of Tel Aviv; only the sound of the Hebrew language is missing. All Jewish shops are closed, and the Sabbath with all its holiness is felt in the air; the "Sabbath Queen" is celebrated like a true princess. And more than one "Jewish town" in Poland, which in the Jewish imagination goes about all week as if in a shtreimel, could take an example from Będzin in the matter of Sabbath observance.
Between the matter of religion and the national élan of the Zagłębie Jews there is undoubtedly a connection here. Religion and nationalism are here two streams that draw from one and the same source, and that is why both are so even and strong.
But something begins to stir, something begins to crumble — and again among those who stand at the very "top". And this in a matter which constitutes the foundation of Jewishness.
I mean Jewish education, religious-national education.
From the heavy, bitter crisis which Jews are living through in Poland today, no religious Jew has yet come to the conclusion that he must buy non-kosher meat for the Sabbath.
He saves from what he can and from what he cannot, and the "pintele yid" [the Jewish spark] he does not touch, God forbid. He even often gives charity beyond his means. On the other hand, people begin to legitimise things that undermine the Jewish soul of the youth — he sends his children to a school where Jewishness is not taught at all, to a school that was created from the outset for the sake of assimilation. Were it done by such parents as are really unable to keep their children in a private school, one could at least — if not justify, then at any rate understand it. But it is mostly done by those who can afford it, and quite pious Jews at that; and this is truly something that already smells of a desire for assimilation.
What is the excuse one seeks for it? Well, in the afternoon he will study with a melamed. From this one can see that the parents have learned nothing and forgotten nothing of the old mistakes. However bad a school may be in its Jewish subjects, if only they are taught there to a proper extent, the child will always benefit more there than from the best afternoon melamed.
One must go deeply into the psychology of the child. When Polish culture is presented to him by a modern person and in a nice room, while the Jewish one goes about dressed in an old bekishe with torn boots and sits in a "kebel" [a shabby little room?], then he is drawn to the former and pushed away from Jewishness. Precisely in this lies the achievement of the Jewish school system. And where the Jewish school truly fulfils its promise and its duty with regard to Jewish education, it is one of the greatest dams [?] against assimilation.
If, however, the Jewish school is not a private one but a communal one, then the complaints that people sometimes have about it, concerning its approach etc., fall away here too; for the duty to care for the flourishing and growth of the Jewish school lies first and foremost on the parents who have their children there. At least this much they may fulfil of "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children": that they take an interest in the school and help it, not only in material but also in moral matters.
The Jewish school must distinguish itself by its order and punctuality, by its rich content, by its fine form, so that it can truly serve as a fortress against assimilation, which is dressed in gloves [?] and a top hat. This fortress, however, is a general Jewish question, for nobody knows when and where the current will touch him — and the current has already begun to rage...
If Not Now, When?

[Education — Jewish education for children in the state schools; article.] The problem of the thousands of Jewish children of both sexes who attend the state elementary (people's) schools, receiving there almost no Jewish education whatsoever, or — at best — learning somewhere from a benighted "belfer" (assistant teacher) the art of mechanical praying and reciting grace after meals, without understanding a thing and without feeling any taste in it other than that of a kind of affliction one must get rid of as quickly as possible — this problem, which we have already discussed in the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", can and must be solved given good will.
One of the local cultural activists, who takes an exceptional interest in this painful matter, is trying — as is known — to solve it in this way: to prevail upon the school inspector to introduce into the local people's schools the teaching of Hebrew 2 hours weekly (besides the 2 hours of "religion" that have been taught until now), as provided for by a certain authoritative ordinance[?] of the Minister of Education, which appeared some three years ago and which has so far been used only in some regions, and even then only partially, namely 1 hour of Hebrew a week instead of 2.
To this it must be remarked first of all that the said ordinance was from the outset a stillborn child, a clumsy creature. It is absolutely out of the question that with 2 hours a week one could achieve anything substantial, especially under the conditions in which one has to work in the state people's schools for Jewish children, where 65 or more pupils in a class are no rarity. And if the child learns this subject for years and never lives to see any sign of blessing in it, he will quickly grow sick of it and will try to wriggle out of it as far as possible.
That is how things look with this ordinance, even if it were to be fully carried out — something that has not happened so far.
Secondly, it seems to us that the present moment, when the ruling circles are permeated with the slogan of reductions and savings, is altogether unsuited for coming to them with proposals to assign new funds precisely for... Jewish purposes. On the contrary, one may rather expect a reduction and partial abolition even of the teaching of "religion", which is compulsory under the constitution. The proof: we have already read, in the form of a notice in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", about the abolition of religious instruction in Będzin People's School No. 8 and in a number of other schools in Zagłębie, and about the vain intervention of the local kehilla with the Sosnowiec inspector and the Kraków Curatorium (school board). So no good fortune is to be expected from "above"...
Again and again it must be warned that we shall come to an ugly and, at the same time, a deserved end if we continue to rely on the government and entrust it with the education of our descendants in the... Jewish spirit.
Here we must recall the old, profound Jewish maxim: "If I am not for myself, who will be for me?" Who will care for our soul? Who will guard the light of Israel, so that it is not extinguished? It seems so simple and self-evident that only we ourselves, the Jewish community, are called upon to fulfil this task and to create the necessary institution, whose purpose will be to cultivate our tradition and culture among the children of the broadest Jewish popular masses.
But we must also remember the second half of the said maxim: "And if not now — when?" It is clear as day that the right hour has already struck to set about, at last, a great action whose aim shall be to equip our young generation with the necessary baggage of Jewish knowledge and Jewish feeling for its hard road of life. It must not be dragged out any longer, for the waters have already come up to the soul... Not only is the Hebrew book being orphaned and left lonely, but even the Yiddish book is already being pushed aside and is losing its buyers and readers...
The Jewish kehilla administrations should and must take this sacred duty upon themselves. It must become their chief task and the main content of their existence. And as is proper to deal with it[?] — for it is their elementary duty to make it possible for, and even to encourage, all community members to give their children a certain minimum programme of Jewish upbringing and Jewish education. The programme must be constructed so as to satisfy as far as possible the moderate demands of our various circles in this field; and to find the right synthesis of all these demands, provided they are put honestly and sincerely, is not at all as difficult as it seems.
Nor are there any special difficulties on the technical-financial side of the matter. Since we are dealing with children who attend the "powszechne" (general elementary) schools, the instruction must take place in the hours when the children are free from school, that is, mainly in the afternoon hours. At that time the premises of the "powszechne" schools are also free. And precisely these same premises with their equipment should also be used for conducting in them the instruction in Jewish subjects for the very same children who attend them in the morning. No great matter — the municipal authority, which has charge of these premises, can and should do this for our sake; after all, it concerns the spiritual education of the children for whom the premises were created. Teaching staff is also amply available, especially in the afternoon hours, so that a shortage of it, particularly in the initial period until the institution grows properly, will certainly not arise. The teachers' salaries and other smaller expenses will be covered partly from the small tuition fee the parents will pay, partly from the kehilla budget and possibly also from other sources.
For the instruction to make sense and to be conducted purposefully and expediently, and not merely as a mockery, it must be given at least 10 hours weekly, i.e. 5 times a week, 2 hours each, and that, too, not in such overcrowded classes as we observe in the "Jewish" people's schools.
Bearing in mind that in the better Jewish utraquist (bilingual) gymnasia (in Łódź, Kraków and a few other towns) so much is likewise devoted to Jewish studies, and that in the Mizrachi schools as many as 25 hours a week are sacrificed to them, and considering the rich and ramified material to be covered, we shall come to the conclusion that in no case can fewer than 10 hours a week be given to it. At the same time, however, the setting of homework must be excluded so as not to burden the child; the whole material must be worked through during the lesson itself.
But until the kehilla bodies are ripe to create such Judaic courses for school youth, the initiative should be taken up by those activists and public workers who have a proper understanding of the matter. In doing so they will have a splendid opportunity to earn the deepest gratitude of the broadest popular masses and their warmest recognition. The present "bein ha-zmanim" (between-terms break) at the beginning of the school year is the most suitable moment for carrying out a successful action in this field, to which all circles that can and should contribute substantially must be drawn in, not excluding the youth organizations.
Remember: "If I am not for myself — who will be for me, and if not now — when?"..
A. Z. Borensztajn.

“Mój mąż siedzi” [“My husband is sitting”]

[Humour — a Sukkot tale.]
By Y. Oberzhanek [?].
(A little Sukkot story, told by a Jew who was reduced to poverty because of his wife’s speaking Polish.)
Do you like Sukkot? For me Sukkot is the worst holiday of all the holidays. For all Jews Sukkot is zman simchateinu, “the season of our rejoicing”, and for me Sukkot is a time when I remember my troubles and my pain.
On the face of it, there is a question here: how come? It seems a lovely holiday, a cheerful holiday — one rejoices, makes music with Jews in the sukkah, sings a little zemer, brings into the sukkah the finest and the best; the only holiday when one is separated from the wife — and when you don’t have the wife before your eyes, what better holiday could you want, eh?..
Yes, for me too Sukkot was always the finest, the best holiday. Just as for all Jews, Sukkot was for me the season of our rejoicing, and today Sukkot is for me a time that reminds me of the troubles I have lived through. For because of Sukkot I became — may it not happen to you — destitute, and all because of what? All because of my wife’s speaking Polish.
I have always had one complaint against my missus: what do you speak Polish for? If you can’t, do as I do: you gesture with your hands or you shrug your shoulders. I don’t know any Polish; I answer only: “tak” [yes], “nie” [no], “nie rozumiem” [I don’t understand], “dzień dobry” [good day], “do widzenia” [goodbye], “psiakrew” [damn it] — and basta... The rest I leave to my hands — that is what hands are for, so that what one doesn’t finish saying with the mouth, the hands “dokończyć” [finish]...
But since she wants to show [printed: “heyzn”] that she can speak “po polsku” [Polish], she speaks only Polish — and with that very “Polish” of hers she buried me. You may hear the story, so that you know how to be “ostrożnie” [careful] with a wife who chatters “po polsku”, and above all beware at Sukkot, when you are sitting in the sukkah and your wife is alone at home.
It was last year at Sukkot. As always I sit with my sons in the sukkah. We eat, we drink, we enjoy ourselves, we say a bit of Torah from “him, may he live” [the rebbe], we chat about politics, nobody hurries — it is Sukkot after all.
My wife, may she be well, was alone in the house. In comes a young fellow with a briefcase, rummages through a mountain of papers, searches and ferrets about, until he pulls out a long sheet of paper, sits himself down comfortably at the table and asks my missus:
“Czy tu mieszka pan Icek Cybelplecel?” [Does Mr. Itzek Tsibelpletsl live here?]
“Kto to nie wie,” answers my missus, “że my tu mieszkamy?” [Who doesn’t know that we live here?]
“Gdzie mąż?” [Where is the husband?] — the fellow asks further, ferreting in the sea of papers.
“Męża [?]?” — says my missus. “Męża nie ma” [The husband isn’t here].
“A gdzie on jest?” [And where is he?] — he asks further.
“Mój mąż,” answers mine, “siedzi” [My husband is sitting — i.e. in the sukkah; but in Polish ‘siedzi’ also means ‘is in prison’].
“Siedzi?” — the fellow’s eyes pop out — “A gdzie on siedzi?” [And where does he sit?]
“Na w sukie” [in the sukkah, in broken Polish] — answers mine.
“W ciupie, pani myśli” [In the clink, you mean, madam] — he corrects her and straight away writes on the paper: “Pan Icek Cybelplecel siedzi w ciupie” [Mr. Itzek Tsibelpletsl is in the clink].
“A gdzie jest starszy syn?” [And where is the elder son?] — he asks further.
“Też siedzi” [He sits too], mine answers him.
“A młodszy syn?” [And the younger son?] — the goy grows curious.
“Też siedzi, nawet mój zięć też [?] siedzi, cała rodzina siedzi” [He sits too, even my son-in-law sits too, the whole family sits].
“Cała rodzina siedzi?” [The whole family sits?] — the fellow’s calf’s eyes pop out — “A na długo?” [And for long?]
“Nie,” she answers, “siedem dni tylko” [No, only seven days].
The fellow listens to my missus’s explanations. My missus speaks “Polish” and he, the wise guy, writes. Everything my wife says, he writes down.
“A dlaczego siedzą?” [And why are they sitting?] — the fellow with the briefcase marvels further.
“No bo to pan nie wie?” [Why, don’t you know, sir?] — she gives him to understand — “Co rok to mój mąż z całą rodziną siedzi siedem dni” [Every year my husband with the whole family sits seven days].
“Aha,” — the chap grabs his pen again [printed “feber”, probably a misprint for “feder”] — “Co rok siedzi — doskonale” [Every year he sits — excellent].
The fellow noted everything down exactly and, with a broad “Moje uszanowanie” [My respects], off he went.
When I came in from the sukkah, my missus told me the story — what he asked and what she answered.
— Probably, I say, a sequestrator [tax bailiff], or the notary’s [rejent’s] lackey — it wouldn’t have killed him to come after the holiday.
But as you say: when a misfortune is decreed, it comes straight into the house. Hear the story:
The first day after the holiday I get a little letter from the bank that I should come at once.
I come into the bank, the director explains to me: “Panie Tsibelpletsl, be so kind as to take back your bills of exchange.”
— What is the matter? I ask the director.
— With people who sit in prisons we do no business.
— Eh? What sort of language is that? Do you mean me, panie dyrektorze [Mr. Director]?
“Be so kind,” the director explains to me, agitated, “take your bundle and goodbye to you.”
That they had to douse me with cold water and rub my temples with vinegar, you can understand for yourselves — and what wonder is it, eh? I, Itzek Tsibelpletsl, who have never yet seen a prison with my own eyes — such a slander! One could, God forbid, get a stroke on the spot!
I come home more dead than alive, tell my household the story — a wailing rises in the house, and my missus and I went to the bank. She is, after all, not me. In any case [?] she can talk things over with the director in “Polish”. For “Polish” the director will surely have a bit more respect...
When the director saw the two of us in such an agitated state, he showed us where it was written that:
“Mrs. Tsibelpletsl declares that her husband Itzek Tsibelpletsl together with the whole ‘rodzina’ [family] sits w ciupie [in the clink]; they got [?] — to sit they have for 7 days. Every year they sit for 7 days, etc.”
I look at my wife and my wife looks at me. What is going on here? Is it he, or are we [?] mad? Who sat? What have we to do with prison, and what have we to do with 7 days?
So my missus let loose with her tongue, the way she can, until the whole bank came running together [?]. It took little for all the inkwells, with the desks [biurka], with the window panes, to fly into the air — and would she not have been right? A trifle, such a slander! It had really come to the point where everything was about to fly. If not for a coincidence: just as my missus was shouting and raging so, in came that very same lad with the briefcase, and when my missus saw him she fell into a faint.
How my missus later talked things out with the lad, and how the director still could not get the story into his head — that I will spare you. The main thing is what came after. From under the ground creditors sprang up; each one shouted and raised a din: my money, defaulter, “katorżnik” [convict], “aresztant” [jailbird]. To each one I had to justify myself. To each one I had to tell the whole story from A to Z — how my wife talked it out with the bank’s inspector, how she “tłumaczyła” [explained] to him in “Polish” that a sukkah in Polish is “w sukie”, and the goyish head interpreted it as “w ciupie”; that my wife meant well, only the “wise man” from the bank understood “Polish” badly. Whom could it occur to that a bank inspector should not understand a word of “Polish!”...
What use are all these stories to you. I justified myself — but woe and alas when one has to justify oneself. — I was reduced to poverty. Because of Sukkot and because of my wife’s “Polish” I am now a Jew, a pauper by law and custom.
Hear me, Jews: as long as I live I will remember last year’s Sukkot, and my wife’s speaking “Polish”...
—o—
Mother and Woman.
In today’s issue we begin to print a novel entitled [a. n. = unter’n nomen]:
“Mother and Woman.”
The novel depicts in a very gripping manner how a mother relates to her son her past as a naive small-town daughter; the consequences of her honest faith in her first lover, who later turned out to be a common charlatan; the accusation against a congregation of Jews that they murdered an illegitimate child; the heavy sufferings of an innocent Jew as the Jewish guarantor, etc.
The novel “Mother and Woman” reads very grippingly and with the greatest interest.
So don’t forget today to read the beginning of this very interesting novel.
In Honour of Sukkot — Torah Sayings and Anecdotes about Sukkot

[Torah sayings and anecdotes about Sukkot. Collected and styled by Y. Y.]

I. The First Days.

a) "The fruit of a goodly tree" (pri etz hadar).
"Hadar — that which dwells in its tree from year to year" (Sukkah 35 [printed "לת"]).
Every fruit has its own particular climate in which it can grow. There are fruits that grow only in the cold; others, again, grow only in the heat. The etrog is the only fruit that withstands all kinds of climates: frost, heat, snow and rain. All year round the etrog is on its tree, and no frost freezes it and no heat withers it.
This is the symbol of the Jew, who goes through heat, frost and all sorts of opposing climates in his exile. To everything the "Eternal Wanderer" adapts himself..
Beit Yaakov (Rabbi Yaakov of Izbica).

b) In Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev's sukkah.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev invited into his sukkah all the lowly people — ruffians ("lobuzes", Polish łobuz), porters and the like. When his wife asked him why he did so, he answered her:
— You know that in the time to come a sukkah will be made of the skin of the Leviathan, and all the righteous will sit with the Shekhinah at the head. And when I, Levi Yitzchak, will also want to slip into that sukkah, and the Garden of Eden usher ("vozhni"[?], Polish woźny) will shout at me: How do you come here, Levi Yitzchak, among the righteous?... — I will answer him: Hush! In my sukkah I too let in porters and ruffians and was not ashamed of them...
Siftei Tzaddikim.

c) "The fallen sukkah of David."
The sukkah is a symbol of Jewish life in exile. And when we study attentively the conditions under which the Talmud declares a sukkah kosher, we indeed see in them a mirror of Jewish life. Namely:
A sukkah of two walls with a third wall one handbreadth wide is also a "dwelling", and a wattle of four handbreadths is already also a "wall".
A sukkah on a moving wagon or on a sailing ship is also kosher...
A sukkah that is only ten handbreadths high, in which one cannot raise one's head, is also a sukkah...
A sukkah is sufficient if it holds only a person's head, and the feet may already be outside...
The skhakh (roof covering) must not be attached to the ground — it must be "groundless".
Of the sukkah it is said: "Make it, and not from what is already made." A Jew must always create and build anew by himself, and not enjoy what already exists. He must build new industries, create new branches of trade, but not enjoy "what is already made"...
Knesset Yisrael.

d) "Every citizen in Israel shall dwell in booths."
The "citizen" — the truly pious Jew ("Abraham Eitan ha-Ezrahi") — sits constantly in a sukkah, not only the seven days; for him the whole world is a temporary dwelling, he feels like a stranger in life.
Like that guest who came to a rabbi. He sees that at the rabbi's the room is empty and there is not even a chair to sit on. He asks him: How can a person manage without a single chair?
— And why have you no chair? the rabbi asks him back.
— Because I am not at home, I am wandering, after all.
— And I too am not at home. "I am a stranger in the land"...
Yaarot Devash.

e) At the Simchat Beit ha-Sho'evah
At the Simchat Beit ha-Sho'evah [Water-Drawing Celebration] — the Gemara relates — the Tanna Hillel said: "If I am here, all is here; and if I am not here, who is here?"
Hillel, the famous humble man, allowed himself to express himself so haughtily?
Hillel was a poor man, a respectable poor man. At a celebration, in the sukkah, in company, people befriend him, drink together, in friendship; but when everyone goes home, he is forgotten. That is what Hillel lamented: "If I am here" — now, at the Simchat Beit ha-Sho'evah, when people dance and drink together — "all is here" — everyone is with me; "and if I am not here" — when everyone goes home — "who is here?" — who remembers me?
Osem Bosem.

II. Kohelet (Ecclesiastes).

f) "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth... but know that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment."
This is precisely what King Solomon achieved: a synthesis between "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth" and "know that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment." To enjoy life, but at the same time to bear in mind that there is a God in the world.
Rabbi David of Kotzk.

g) "Sweet is the sleep of a labouring man, but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep."
"Sweet is the sleep of a labouring man" — the poor man's life would already be sweet to him "whether he eat little or much"; he would be content whether he has little to eat or more. But — "the abundance of the rich" — the fact that the rich man is sated — that "will not suffer him to sleep" — does not let the poor man sleep... It is not his own poverty that bothers him, but the other man's wealth...
Chatam Sofer.

h) "All is vanity... money answereth all things."
"All is vanity" — everything is indeed foolish, but "money answereth all things": money suppresses the "all is vanity"; money brings to naught the "all is vanity"...
Pitgamei Orayta.

i) "Riches kept by the owner thereof to his hurt."
There is a wealth that guards its owner, so that he should, God forbid, not have any benefit from it, so that he should not enjoy it...
Tiferet Uziel.

j) "Cast thy bread upon the waters."
Water — the more one draws from it, the more water flows in. Charity is likewise: the more charity one gives, the richer one becomes...
Olelot Efraim.
Mother and Woman.

[Fiction — serialised novel.]
S. Relkes.
(A gripping novel of Jewish life).

"David," said the mother, "Sorele was here again yesterday."
"Oh, bitter," David growled through his teeth, "she makes me sick."
The mother cast a sharp glance at David, saw how he ate with a wolfish appetite, how his face was young, energetic and a little vulgar, and it became clear to her that the one sitting here with her at the table was her flesh and blood, but in truth he was a stranger to her.
She hastily put down her fork and knife and said:
"What do you mean, David, she makes you sick? Sorele is a young girl, she loves you, you turned her head, exploited her trust in you, and now you throw her off and don't even want to see her."
David suddenly rose from the table; his face flushed, his eyes shot sparks, but he spoke calmly:
"Mama, I ask you not to meddle in my affairs. I am already grown up enough to look after myself."
For a minute the mother remained crushed; her large black eyes filled with sorrow. Her delicate face turned pale; she could find no words to answer her son. She felt as if something were choking her throat; a whole sea of words wanted to tear out of her heart, but at that moment the right word stayed stuck, as if strangled. She saw David heading for the door — soon he would leave, and all the bitterness would remain in her unspoken; she needed to utter only one word and the whole torrent would be released.
When David was already standing on the threshold, the mother ran up to him, grabbed him by the jacket, placed herself between him and the door and barred the way. Now she trembled in every limb, her face was already burning as in a fever, and the torrent of words burst out of her.
"What, David. I want to talk to you.."
"Oh, leave me alone," David lightly pushed his mother away, "I've had it up to here [lit. it crawls out of my gall], you preach sermons at me as if I were a child."
But the mother was already standing in the door and had dug both feet into the floor, not to budge from the spot. David suddenly saw that this time his mother was obstinate, that he would not be able to wriggle out of the conversation, that now he would not get off with an excuse, as had happened several times in the last couple of weeks. He therefore stepped back from the door and growled:
"Very well, Mama, come in..."
The mother sat down on the chair by the window and pointed David to a chair opposite. She made a majestic gesture with her hand. In that movement there was the command of a proud ruler. David sensed that a hidden strength had awakened in his mother, one that had lain in her for many years. He had always had respect for her, he certainly loved her too, but he had never felt any authority over himself. His mother had surrounded him with much love, with devotion and boundless attention, but David had had the feeling that she was a weak, submissive woman, that she had no will, that she could not speak harsh words to him; it was enough for him to pull a sour face and she would give in.
And here, suddenly, such firmness, so much strength in a single wave of the hand. David did not know where it had come to her from, but he grasped the seriousness and submitted. He sat down on the chair she had pointed to, in a pose as if the whole thing did not concern him at all. He was merely doing his mother a favour.
"David," the mother began in a firm voice, "I know that you are no longer a child, that you already have your own path in life, but this time you will have to listen to what I am going to tell you."
"Very well, Mama, I'll listen."
"Sorele was here yesterday and wept bitterly. She is a dear child, and it is a great sin to treat her like this."
David began to squirm on the chair as if he were sitting on hot coals. It was evident that for him Sorele was no problem at all; what did he care whether she was happy or unhappy?
"Mama, I have nothing to do with her."
Although David spoke quietly, there was so much brutality in his tone that his mother actually jumped up. She ran up to him, grabbed him firmly by the hand and squeezed him with all her strength.
"Do you know what you're saying, David? She's none of your concern! Then why was she your concern when you dragged yourself around with her through the nights, lay with her in her house and..."
Here the mother broke off. She still could not say everything she wanted to. Something made her ashamed to say that she knew how her own son had treated Sorele. Before her, indeed, stood a young man of about twenty-two, a grown man who had already had his experiences in life, but to her he was still a child, and the most intimate things must remain hidden. With a daughter it might have been easier to speak of such things. But with a son it is hard. Yet what she had said was enough for David to understand that there was no secret for her, that as far as Sorele was concerned she knew everything. That is why David looked at her somewhat surprised, but he did not lose his composure; on the contrary, a smile still played in his eyes.
"Mama, you are a modern woman after all..."
"And if I am a modern woman, must I keep silent when my own son commits the worst villainies? What do you call modern, David? Seducing young girls, making them unhappy, breaking their lives forever?"
"Mama, you know yourself that she is not for me. Sorele is a poor girl, she is not clever, just a pretty little face and nothing more."
"I don't know whether she is for you, but I know that you should not have started with her. One does not play with a human life."
But David was obstinate. The mother saw clearly that Sorele's misfortune did not concern him. Suddenly she recognised in him his father. Just such an egoist as he was. Only his own pleasures concern him, only his own lust, and to satisfy it he will not mind if others become unhappy. A deep abyss opened before her when she grasped this naked and evil truth.
"David," she pleaded with him, "have pity on me and don't cast her away. After all, I have done so much for you, you know it, my son — have pity on me."
But this David no longer understood at all. Why on earth must he have pity on her and marry Sorele? He could still understand that if he took Sorele for a wife he would do it out of pity — but what did that have to do with his mother? And in general, why did this foolish girl, who had given herself to him so easily and with whom he had had a good time, matter so much to her? Mama is strange. On the contrary, she ought to help him get rid of Sorele, and the devil take it [?]. No, David does not understand why his mother goes to such lengths and wants him to marry a girl he does not love and who, on top of it, is as poor as death. What kind of life will it be when he takes her and has to toil to earn a crust of bread?
And David did indeed tell her so:
"Mama, I am beginning not to understand you: why does Sorele matter so much to you?"
The mother looked at him for a long time; her eyes expressed despair; she was torn by the urge to tell him something, but she bit her lips and kept silent. A deep secret weighed on her heart: how could she tell it to her only son, for whom she had given up her whole youth, sacrificed her days and nights, toiled hard, stood up against everyone — how could she tell David the secret she had been carrying within her for twenty-two years? Will David understand her? Will he turn away from her because of it? No, David does not understand why she takes Sorele's part so, but she herself knows: for twenty-two years she suffered so that her son would grow up a decent human being, would look the world straight in the face and would not have to be ashamed before anyone. How will David understand, when he knows nothing at all?
David stood beside his mother with large questioning eyes; he saw that she was hiding something from him, and his heart grew heavy. David was in fact a solid young man, hard-working; he studied at the university, studied medicine and was preparing for a career. At the university he was well thought of, because he studied well, took his profession seriously and wanted to be conscientious [printed "gshvisnhaft", a misprint for "gevisnhaft"]. But something was hard for him with his mother. Ever since he had come of age he had felt that she was hiding something terrible from him. He felt like a tree in the middle of a desolate field; he did not have a single relative, as though his mother had uprooted him, carried him off into the desert and left him to grow alone, without a single close person.
"Why are you silent, Mama?" David asked, and in his voice one could feel a sharp reproach to her, or even a challenge.
"My David," said the mother, and her eyes filled with tears, "I am silent because... because... well, because I have nothing to say..."
But David was not satisfied with the answer. He saw clearly that she did have something to say, only she did not want to, and that annoyed him: what is it? Would he not understand? Why does she still regard him as a child? But [?] the main thing that bothered him was the deep secret surrounding himself. Who is he? All right, Mama says that their father [printed "zeyer"; perhaps for "zayner", his] died when he, David, was still a small child. That, he understands, can happen; but why does he not have any aunt, any uncle, not even a distant cousin? And again, if his father died, something must surely have remained of him: a picture, a letter, something to recall that a man had lived and brought a child into the world. And if not that, then somewhere there must be his father's grave. Yes, he would travel to the grave and take a look at it. He would like to read the tombstone: Here lies buried... But why had Mama never told him what his father's name was?
(To be continued)
The Będzin Girl in Katowice

[Feuilleton — satirical sketch; Będzin and Katowice.]
Yoel Mastbaum.

In my eyes the young ladies of Będzin split into two persons. One person is the one who works the whole day at household matters — such as standing in the shop and housework; the second person of the same young lady sojourns in Katowice. And it is remarkable, what in the course [?] of one person there are two kinds of colours, or a double paint in one person.

For example, not long ago I made the acquaintance of a very nice young lady in Będzin.

It went like this:

I was standing in a shop picking out a white collar for myself. A young lady holds out to me her [?] white little hand.

"Do you recognise me?" she asks.

"It seems to me we got acquainted at the Yiddish theatre in Warsaw."

"No," she interrupts, "more than that: we even got acquainted at the Writers' Association [Literatn-Fareyn]. I even remember who introduced us."

To make a long story short, within a quarter of an hour I found out that I was dealing with a thoroughgoing Yiddishist, with a connoisseur and expert of everything and everyone, of all that goes on in the Yiddish world.

What did the young lady look like?

A head of shiny black hair combed to both sides, like two halves of a velvet curtain; eyes of dark charm; thick [?] brows as if cast onto her smooth forehead; and her figure, her proud gaze, looked like a king's daughter. What else did the velvet girl talk about? She lamented the times, it seems — how the Yiddish school suffers from crisis, how the Yiddish book is living through hard times.

"There," I thought, "nowadays we meet very rarely the forms [?] of such Jewish young ladies; they are a rarity. Yet they exist." I even thought of dedicating to the young lady, if not an article, then at least a poem; and it was enough that she merely gave me her hand for images and golden thoughts to start tangling in my brain. Who is this young lady? Is she not the deepest echo of our woman of the Bible? Does she not speak with the language of those women?

But this picture was wiped out a few hours later.

Evening. I am sitting in a Katowice café; the electric lamps sparkle, the jazz is playing, and not far from me sit a few young men with a young lady. Who the young men were I could not know at that moment, but the young lady was familiar to me from somewhere. She wore a black-brimmed little hat and long earrings; her lips were closed and heavily painted — exactly as if a cherry lay on her mouth; her eyes moved lightly, she flirted lightly and looked like a film actress.

"And yet, who is she?" — I decided to draw closer — "Might she perhaps be a Parisienne?"

And I was even more convinced that she was a Parisienne when I stood next to her and, to the sound of the jazz, she lightly swayed her hands, just as if she were swimming in the clouds; and soon a young man invited her to dance. She threw off her coat. She wore a long black dress with velvet trimmings [?]; in the dance she became still more graceful.

"And you don't believe that the young lady is one of ours, that is, a Będzin young lady?"

"But she speaks French, it seems," I answer.

"There you are mistaken. She is only mangling the German language. Będzin and Sosnowiec young ladies who want to prove that they are not Jewish girls mangle the German tongue. You want to hear? By all means, come."

"But I hardly believe that the young lady has anything to do with Będzin," I say, "it seems to me..."

"And what a Będzin girl!" the other one jumps in. "She even makes the kugel for the Sabbath. You don't believe it? You can find her tomorrow, Friday, at work. She is certainly capable of the cholent."

"And her language?"

"[?] Just listen, you won't have to strain yourself for long."

And indeed I did not have to strain myself for long. The language was a kind of mixture [?] of Polish, German, Yiddish and English all mixed together, and this time, up close, I recognised her: the very same one who a few hours earlier had defended the Yiddish language so. When she caught sight of me she turned her head away; she was in great embarrassment, and then I saw that I was dealing with one of our "cholent-ovnas" [?], who are known to us already from Warsaw — and Będzin, naturally, sends them over to Katowice.
The Lulav — Temporary Dwellings...

[Sukkot humour page — satire, current affairs.] Shaken in honour of Sukkot by Ben Amotz.
Temporary Dwellings...
The essence of the sukkah is "for-the-time-being"-ness. Our life is the same: we live only for the time being... The disarmament conferences in Geneva are also for the time being...
The Jews in Germany enjoy equal rights with all citizens; only when they come out of synagogue on Rosh Hashanah after prayers, a "little pogrom" is staged against them — for the time being...
The government is devising measures to ease the situation of the unemployed; but because of those measures hundreds of Jewish families will lose their livelihoods — for the time being.
One thing is not for the time being: Sosnowiec, Będzin, Czeladź and Olkusz — the cashiers [„kasjery“] have nothing, for the time being...
Rebuilding Again.

[Sukkot humour page — satirical poem.]
Rebuilding again — again rebuilding.
It is coming now to the Jews' land,
And whoever has a foot, a hand
Sets up the fine sukkahs.
For everything's boiling all over Europe,
It's a hard one, this problem,
"Odbudowa" [Polish: reconstruction], "rebuilding" —
So the Jew too gets down to it.
He takes a pole, a rolling pin
And a noodle board as well,
And it counts as an "odbudowa"
Till smoke comes out of it...
Quickly little boards are knocked together
And a bit of schach is laid on top,
And a "sky-scraper" is ready —
Already with a green roof...
Poor indeed is our life,
There's no money for a flat,
But castles in the air we tower up
For the short life of the hour.
And the castles in the air and the sukkahs,
Put up one-two —
I don't know whether it pays
To exchange them for palaces.
It pays[?]; it's forbidden to exchange them,
Truly, no joking —
For who would come there, after all,
On the holiday as an ushpizin guest?...
And one more merit the sukkahs
Have in the holidays:
That they are not burdened
With taxes and mortgages...
Yankl ben Flekl.

Laws of Blessing the Etrog.
The etrog must be taken with clean hands; one who has no clean hands — for example, he meddles in kehilla institutions, is a board member of a bank, a member of the tax-assessment commission — may not take the etrog into his hand...
It is customary to make seven shakings with the lulav and the etrog. Merchants who have already "shaken" over the year are exempt from this...
Those who have already received today the new payment orders ["nakazy"] from the income tax ["dochód"] are exempt from blessing the etrog on the first day of Sukkot...
Besides the lulav and etrog there must also be myrtles and willows, corresponding to the Four Species. The Sosnowiec Commissars' Council has only three species — the lulav, the etrog and the myrtles; it is very desirable that it borrow one "willow" from the Będzin Commissars' Council and make the "shakings" with them...
The Będzin Kehilla's "Bulletin".

[Będzin — kehilla, satire.] The Będzin kehilla, as is known, publishes every year a "bulletin" of its activity. "Der Kokh-Lefl" [the "Ladle", the humour column] has therefore decided to publish a bulletin of what the kehilla ought to do and does not do.
In our opinion the kehilla ought to have come to the aid of the summer holidaymakers ["letniki"] who are still squeezed into the dachas to this day; and if the kehilla does not come with immediate help, they are threatened with wintering in the village huts.
The kehilla must see to it that orphans do not multiply. For this purpose the kehilla must organise a "straż honorowa" [guard of honour] at the "Poalei Agudas Yisroel".
The "guard" must "keep an eye" ["uważać"] on the masked balls, on the "pipe-knocking"[?] after midnight on "Góra Zamkowa" [Castle Hill], and a word to the wise. In this way no orphans will multiply and the kehilla will not need to provide for them.
The kehilla has one project (it seems the "project" is already celebrating a three-year jubilee...) to open a kosher soldiers' kitchen.
"Der Kokh-Lefl" thinks that the kehilla should at the same time open a free kitchen in the "Merchants' Association" ["Sokhrim Ferayn"].
At the same time the "wydział" [department] of the Chevra Kadisha should be transferred to the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce...
The kehilla must open a "priyut"[?] for cripples. We think the qualification commission should consist of the "Muze"[?].
Over a "Shtot" [Seat].

[Humour — court, prayer house.] The gabbai of a shtibl [small Hasidic prayer room] sued in court one of the worshippers because the latter refuses to pay for the "shtot" [fixed seat in the prayer house; in Yiddish also "town"].
We give here the court proceedings [in broken Polish in Hebrew letters]:
Judge (to the plaintiff): "What is owed to you by the defendant?"
Plaintiff: "For a town [miasto — literal rendering of 'shtot'], Your Honour."
Judge: "For a town? What does that mean — maybe a village?"
Defendant: "Not a town, not a village, only a place [plac]."
Judge: "Ah, I see — what size?"
Plaintiff: "Not big — half a metre."
Judge: "So small? For what sum?"
Plaintiff: "For 20 złoty."
Judge: "That's dirt cheap; where is this place?"
Plaintiff: "This place lies on the eastern side" (on the Mizrach seat [by the eastern wall]).
Judge: "And do you have witnesses?"
Plaintiff: "The whole little room" (the entire shtibl).
The verdict will be published next Hoshana Rabbah.

The modern Kohelet.
(New interpretations)
"Man cannot utter it": it is not good, and one may not say a word.
"For all his days are sorrows": the merchant's days are full of pain.
"Even in the night his heart takes no rest": even at night he cannot fall asleep for worries.
"All go unto one place": all the money falls into the tax office [Kasa Skarbowa].
"[Woe to] him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up": when a firm falls today, it is hard to set it up again.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin

[Będzin — local news.]
The Agudah's New "Revue Hit"
The election commission says "tak" [yes] and the starosta [district head] says "nie" [no]..
For the upcoming [?] elections to the new kehilla board the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] has once again resorted to its familiar tricks; it stops at nothing, so long as it reaches its goal of gaining influence over kehilla life in our town.
As our readers know, Mr. Yitzhak Wygodzki was elected president of the kehilla council months ago. Although a long time has passed since the elections, Mr. Wygodzki has still not been officially confirmed by the authorities; apparently the "Agudah" kept watch and worked to have the matter dragged out, so that the "Agudah's" prospects in the elections to the kehilla board would be favourable to it.
This came out best this week when the "Agudah", in order to have Wygodzki's candidacy disqualified, put up as a candidate for the board the very old man R' Eli Ber Werdiger (Wygodzki's father-in-law). With this the "Agudah" meant to shoot 2 hares at once: to have a man of its own on the board and at the same time to be "rid" of Wygodzki...
At the close of Yom Kippur a meeting of the election commission took place. At the meeting Mr. Wygodzki lodged a protest against his father-in-law's candidacy. The commission took the protest into account and struck out Mr. Werdiger's candidacy.
The "Agudah" people did not rest; the very next morning they went where one needs to go and obtained that a few hours later the gmina [local authority] received official notice that the commission has no right to annul the person of Mr. Werdiger...
On Tuesday evening the election commission again held a meeting, at which Werdiger's candidacy was struck out for the second time.
How this tragicomedy will end, the future will show...
On Wednesday, amid all this commotion [?], a great sensation was discovered. It was namely established by the magistrate [town council] that in Będzin there lives no such person at all by the name of Eli Ber Werdiger..

How the kehilla budget was „purified“?
For six whole months the kehilla administration waited for the kehilla budget, which had been sent for approval to the supervisory authority.
After long and hard sufferings the budget has at last come back, already made „kosher“, „without any doubt“...
First of all, the pension for the trustees (ne'emanim) and the pension of the 6th shochet were struck out. Apparently they know at the Ministry too that the religious functionaries are not burdened with heavy duties, and that every side expense at the kehilla's expense is superfluous.

On Wednesday evening the new Będzin kehilla council met for a session in the kehilla premises in order to hold the election of the presidium of the new kehilla board.
Of all the parnasim [council members] the only one absent was the sole parnas of „Hitachdut“, Mr M. Rozynker.
The chairman of the election commission, Mr A. Liwer, opens the session, announces the agenda and proceeds to the elections, which gave the following result:
List no. 1, „Mizrachi“, carried 2 members in the persons of Messrs Pinchas Leibish Buczajc[?] and Yaakov Neumark.
List no. 2 (United Bloc of non-party Hasidim, Zionists, artisans, small traders) received 5 members in the persons of Messrs: Elazar Rubinlicht, Avrahaml Liwer, Aharon Hampel, Chaim Dawid Rudzin and Herman Strochlitz.

The result of the elections came as a surprise to the „Agudah“, because they had been sure that they would win a sure victory thanks to the incessant lobbying and the promises of „both worlds“ [this world and the next], if only people voted for the Agudah list.
The greatest disappointment the Agudah got from parnas Mr Yitzchak Aharon Landau, who acted on his own judgment and voted for the national list.
After the elections Mr Landau was assailed by the Agudah parnasim with the most disgraceful insults, such as „sinners of Israel“, „missionary“ etc. Mr Landau did not stay in their debt either, and answered those who had besmirched him with the same vocabulary.

The First Days of Sukkot in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — the Sukkot festival, notes from the prayer houses.]
For many years now the merchants of Zagłębie have not remembered such a hard eve of Sukkot as this year. Even in the war years there did not reign such want and such a depressing mood. In trade and in the workshops the crisis was felt in an extraordinary way; on top of that a heavy rain poured down. In the evening, when Jews had to go into the sukkah, the rain stopped.
—o—
In the shtiblekh this year a „control“ of the etrogim took place. Despite all the proclamations [kol koreh] of the great sages of Israel in the Land and abroad, it still turned out that precisely „fine Jews“ [notables] had Corfu etrogim. As people relate, a certain rabbi in Sosnowiec too, who had issued a proclamation to buy Eretz Israel etrogim, bought himself a little „hadar“ from Corfu...
Such a control also took place in the Sochaczew [Hasidic] shtibl, where several Corfu etrogim fell as „sacrifices“...
—o—
In Dąbrowa the „Season of our Rejoicing“ was „more conspicuous“ than in the whole of Zagłębie.
In the „Mizrachi“ minyan a cheerful mood prevailed because one of the worshippers, who at the kehilla elections had won [printed „zufe“, read „zoche“] the seat of a president [printed „przs“], bought himself a „set“ [of the four species], but instead of myrtle branches [hadassim] he decorated the lulav with bridal-myrtle leaves [„mirtn-bleter“], as if[?] so that the public would have something to be merry about...
In the Dąbrowa town synagogue the gabbai refused to give an aliyah to someone on [printed „if“] whom there was a suspicion that he had not fasted on Yom Kippur. The situation became very „serious“ and the upshot is that the gabbai has for the time being resigned...
—o—
The greatest „simcha“ was in the Dąbrowa Ger [printed „Gersher“] shtibl. One of „our people“ [anshei shlomenu; printed „shlmnu“] had yahrzeit and led the prayers at the lectern. But in this shtibl there are 2 „sharp“ young men, who for a joke „derailed“ the unskilled prayer leader, and instead of praying [printed „davfen“] „our people“ rolled about with laughter...
A Big Fire in Dąbrowa.

[Dąbrowa — fire.] On Sunday at noon, „eyt“[?] [doubtful word, perhaps a time], the fire-brigade sections in Zagłębie were alerted to the fire that had broken out in Rogalewicz's[?] house in Dąbrowa on 3 Maja Street.
Owing to the crowding in the street a terrible panic arose among the residents and every tenant began carrying out his goods and chattels. Only thanks to the energetic rescue work of the firemen was the fire localised. Only the roof was burnt.

From the General Meeting of „Hakoach“ Będzin.

[Będzin — sport, the „Hakoach“ club.]
In the hall of the „Góra Zamkowa“ the annual general meeting of „Hakoach“ took place.
The general meeting was more „interesting“ than all the general meetings so far. The postponement of the meeting by 15 minutes in order to find a chairman, and the running away of the chairman together with the assessor after half an hour of conducting the meeting — that alone says enough. Those present showed great enough interest in the general meeting.
With 120 members present, the president Dr. Rechtman opens the meeting and proposes to elect Mr. Sabkowski as chairman. Mr. Sabkowski takes over the chair and invites as assessors Messrs. Tenenbaum and Gertner, and Nechama Landa as secretary.
Before proceeding to the agenda, the late member Mr. Yakub [Jakub] Gutman is honoured by rising.
Mr. Rozenblum gives a general report, in which among other things he sharply censures the conduct of the „opposition“, which did great damage to the club. The cash report is given by Mr. Gelbhard, from which we learn that as of today the club possesses about 200 zł. The technical report is given by Mr. A. Ehrlich; the sum total of the report is a very sad one.
After the reports of the audit committee a lengthy discussion develops, in which Messrs. Tenenbaum, Ehrlich, Sabkowski, Podliński, Oppenheim and others take part. Almost all speakers demanded an explanation of why the former board members Bażykowski, Montag and Winer deserted; an answer is given by the president Dr. Rechtman, who shows with facts and logical arguments that the club today finds itself in a financially critical situation owing to the general critical situation prevailing in the country, and that Mr. Montag did great damage to the club by his conduct, in that he tore down the prestige of the club in the columns of the press; as for the other members who ran away — the speaker explains — medicine has to this day not yet found any means that could compel members to remain on the board.
At the end thanks are expressed to the treasurer Mr. Gelbhard for his exemplary orderly keeping of the cash books, and an absolutorium [discharge] is granted to the outgoing board.
Mr. A. Ehrlich gives a lecture on future activity, but because of the late hour the lecture is listened to with little interest. For the same reason the meeting is also broken off; the continuation of the meeting takes place today in the evening in the club's own premises. On the agenda — elections.
A. Wrocławski.

Theatre Notes — From the „Ararat“ Guest Performances in Zagłębie

We saw the „Ararat“ [Moyshe Broderzon's Yiddish kleynkunst (cabaret) theatre from Łódź] here two years ago, and we can note with satisfaction that in the course of time it has developed very well artistically.
„Ararat“ has a first-class ensemble as well as a rich, artistic repertoire, and rightly deserves the name „chamber and [printed „in“] kleynkunst theatre“.
The 2 programmes, „Khay-gelebt“ [„We've Lived It Up“; „khay“ = 18, a pun] and „Afn himl a yarid“ [„A Fair in Heaven“], contain numbers that are true pearls of kleynkunst creation, such as: „Jews Sing“, „Man and Machine“, „Jewish Blacksmiths“, etc.
The whole programme, apart from a couple of weaker numbers, is a colourful mosaic that carries the audience into the most varied moods, giving them artistic enjoyment.
Throughout the whole repertoire one feels the artistic breath of Moshe Broderzon, who took pains to select texts that are not banal. The jokes are fine; they do not suffer from over-peppering and therefore do not shock the listeners.
The acting of the artists was very good. We could, of course, have singled out individual performers for first place, but we deliberately do not do so. We do not want to favour anyone, because the point is not whether someone plays a little better or weaker — that has no great significance when the differences are very small; what matters above all is that in „Ararat“ we have very good ensemble playing, and that is the most important thing. Each one finds his place and strives to give the maximum.
It is only a pity that the sets and the orchestra remained on the posters: in the theatre we unfortunately did not see them, and this somewhat disturbed the harmonious whole.
Sh. H.

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
I ask you to give me space in your esteemed newspaper for my following letter concerning the lie in „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ number 39 by the management of the so-called Esperantists' Society in Będzin, whose aim was to besmirch my name for not wanting to submit to their orders.
After my statement in „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ no. 33 about my resignation, there appeared in number 39 of „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ a statement by the management of the Będzin Esperantists' Society under the innocent title „A Letter to the Editor“, saying that my resignation came about because I was dismissed as a paid teacher.
