Sugar as a Serious Remedy

Sugar is not only a nutrient necessary for the organism; it also possesses a number of virtues: it is a remedy in heart diseases.
As early as 1903 Müller, through a series of experimental studies, demonstrated the positive influence of sugar on the course of heart defects.
The heart muscles consume the more sugar the more active they are; that is precisely why every acceleration of the heart's functioning, which is met in various cases of heart defects, is often relieved after [printed „nabn“, evidently for „nokhn“] the use of a certain amount of sugar. Not long ago Listiapis[?] and Novier[?] once again confirmed this assertion. For this purpose they selected such [printed „oyne“, evidently for „azoyne“] heart patients as had until then not responded to any other methods of treatment. These patients received for 8–10 days 50 grams of sugar each in a supersaturated solution, and after 20 minutes they would be injected with small amounts of insulin. In a number of cases the improvement in the patients' state of health became noticeable already in the first few days.
Again, Loeper, Lemer[?] and Degos, in their clinical practice with heart patients (published in Presse médic[ale] no. 81 of 1930), used to give their patients 150 grams of sugar syrup each, establishing thereby a strengthening of the reflex force of the heart, its greater moderation, the slowing of the heart's activity, the disappearance of functional disturbances and the fall of heart pressure. According to the experience of the said authors it could be seen that sugar strengthens the effect of cardiac remedies, which thanks to it can be used in smaller doses. In the opinion of these researchers, heart patients have diminished sugar reserves, and therefore their treatment must consist first of all in increasing the sugar reserve in the heart musculature through abundant intake of dissolved sugar.

On Guard Against a Catastrophe

(I. Our poverty and the "merciful people, sons of the merciful." — Helping without a system and the creation of new beggars.)
Granted, that times are bad and bitter, that the situation is unbearable and impossible to sustain — every one of us knows that, and we will achieve nothing by dwelling on it; it is superfluous to prove it in black and white — on the contrary, it would amount to rubbing salt into the wounds. We are beginning, step by step, systematically, to enter the phase of poverty, the phase in which it is ever harder to earn even the barest necessities of human need. Many of us who are still standing on our feet, after a fashion, may not notice it, but when one begins to look deeper, when one begins to investigate and analyse, one sees it quite positively. The keen, penetrating eye noticed it long ago, confirmed it long ago.
Our Jewish press in Poland, the Warsaw press above all, has made light of our economic question; it hardly dealt with it, it paid it no attention whatsoever. Rarely, very rarely, did it — the press — put its heart into it and devote an article to the question, and even that, it goes without saying, only for form's sake: since one could not always turn away a public activist, one did him a favour and gave him space in the paper for his stated opinion; the editorial boards themselves, by contrast, took absolutely no interest in these matters. To them it was, unfortunately, a superfluous thing, a side issue in which they took no interest, and they did not take the trouble to develop the column that ought to have dealt with Jewish livelihood. Only lately, thanks to the enormous defeats and catastrophes that have taken such feverish root in every aspect of our Jewish life, has the question begun to receive more attention, and we already meet in the pages of the Jewish press articles on this painful question — not merely contributed pieces, but also ones by professional writers, by members of the editorial boards.
In fact we wrestle with the thought whether these deeds are to be welcomed, or perhaps, on the contrary, whether they — the caretakers — are to be blamed for having let this most important nerve of ours go to waste. With us such a problem should never have been allowed to be neglected. But be that as it may — it is still good that the question has now been taken up. As the saying goes: better late than never.
It is indeed high time to give this problem the most serious attention. After all, we are living through such hard moments as have rarely been seen; and at the same time we live in such an abnormal period, and in such a lawless time, as we do not encounter in our history. We know that Jews went hungry because they were not admitted to various occupations and professions. We know that our great-great-grandfathers suffered because they were not able or agile enough to go along with the stream of the other citizens; we know that as Jews and as zealots they suffered a great deal — yet never did it bear such a character as now.
We know that we are living through an enormous crisis, and in truth it is not only with us in Poland, but everywhere, almost in the whole world; but what interests us at the moment is only Poland, here where we live. We know that there is an enormous number of unemployed, competition is great, there is nothing to be done, and there is nobody to whom one can give goods on credit, so that the struggle for life is a hard one. It goes without saying that when countries and peoples find themselves in such hard living conditions, people must fall from want and hardship and must stretch out their hand for alms; and if this element has arisen among the nations of the world, then among us, the "merciful people, sons of the merciful," it is certainly, most certainly present, and no wonder that among us it is incomparably, enormously larger and stronger in number: after all, to this very day we live for the most part on wind and smoke, on air and miracles. We are not admitted to the soundest and most normal occupations, and so the slightest wind breaks and ruins our existence at the first instant, so that before we can look around, before we manage[?] to get our bearings, yesterday's rich man is already a ruined man (yored).
Do we do anything in time so that this ruined man, who conducted himself as an honest citizen, should not fall into the deepest abyss? Do we do anything so that he need not step down from the arena of life? Do we take any interest in him, so that he need not wander about the country and simply stretch out his hand for alms like any professional beggar? Does his professional association do anything in this field — whether it concerns merchants, small traders or artisans? No, it does not go that far; it does not even occur to anyone. One takes an interest in a member as long as he lives and the institution has some use from him; but as soon as he becomes a yored, he is, for it, a dead man — and who has any interest in occupying himself with a dead man? What use can he still bring the association as such?
We understand very well, we give ourselves an exact account, that we are not dealing here with professional associations such as exist among other people, where the members are insured for their old age or in case of becoming impoverished, etc.
Our associations are poor, and very poor; neither do the members have any connection to them, nor the other way round, so that to this very day the one has almost nothing from the other. But still there must be a limit, and the limit must not lie at the very point when he becomes impoverished, when he ceases to exist for the institution, when the one becomes free of the other.
The association must not let its member go wandering about the country; it must take an interest in such a person, so that he does not remain fallen to the point of stretching out his hand for alms, or so that he does not languish quietly and modestly at home and go to bed hungry and broken.
It is an old rule that Jews give money for what is needed and for what is not needed. All that is lacking is a system, an arrangement, an order. Before our eyes there appears a Jew of dignified countenance; he stretches out his hand for alms, and if we have time to look at him, to observe him, it pinches the heart, and the fallen man receives a decent donation. But do we really help him with this single decent donation? Do we not then make this man into a permanent ruin (tel olam)? Does he not thus[?] penetrate into the camp of the professional beggars, into which we push him with the "decent" donation? Does he not in this way become cunning, and begin to understand the ins and outs? Does he in this way have the possibility of returning to his former station? Does it occur to him when there is a moment to think about it? And even if the idea of returning to his occupation had come to him, would he know when the right time for it is, when the opportune moment is, since he is busy with constantly going from door to door?
At the same time we must not forget one more thing: when it comes to giving a decent public donation, it does not go easily — then one stops and considers the matter; daily alms, on the other hand, have become a kind of current coin, and nobody takes account of the fact that they cost a fortune. And to whom, and what kind of benefit, do they bring? Whom do these current-coin alms help, and what does the salvation consist of, so to speak[?]? What honour does it bring the people, and what does the one who receives it get from it, given that he does not want to become a professional beggar? Do we not push him in this way into this very trade? Do we not make him, with this donation, into a fallen being[?] for ever and ever? It is possible that for the time being he is helped, since he has a piece of bread; but here one must not forget: it is not only about the single person who stretches out his hand to you — this Jew, after all, carries on his shoulders a family with worries. How, then, do we help this category of people? Do we not in this way make them into real beggars? Do we not, by such a kind of "pity," help to enlarge the beggar-family, which has been big enough until now?
We must, then, once and for all give ourselves an exact account of what we achieve by giving so many alms, and whether they bring the benefit that they should and could bring — since they already come out of our own ranks, in such hard times.
L. Szpigelman.
Vanity of Vanities.

[Poetry.] By Yitskhok Margoshes
My youth I spent in much happiness,
and yet now I am old, already very old;
my glances have gone out,
and I am sad as the forest in autumn.

The crown [of the tree] brought me much joy,
youth sang me a song,
yet now I am old, already very old,
broken, bent and tired.

Very quickly the leaves have withered,
youth — the joy has flown away,
and now I am tired, already very tired,
my back bent with age.

Now the truth has revealed itself to me:
O life! I hate you and curse you!
Vanity of vanities is everything,
a dream is life, the world.
What a Defeat I Suffered!

[Feuilleton — Sukkot.] (Told by a landlord who, poor man, suffered a fiasco on the first days of Sukkot.)
No, a thousand times no! I said once that I will not let the schnorrers, the "kabtsaniakes" [beggars], over the threshold of my sukkah, and I keep my word! What is it — did they make a contract with me that I should provide them with a sukkah every year? Do I have too few troubles from these drifters all year round? Too little that I provide them with troubles? Do they pay rent, perhaps? A fine favour they do me — if only they had not paid... Other "gospodarzes" [landlords] have luck: once a wall cracks, once a fire breaks out, and once in a while one gets to see a couple of live dollars... But here, may it not befall them, I always have the eternal paupers, always the same tenants ["lokators"] — if only one could see a spare[?] groschen before one's eyes for once!...
Isn't it enough that I provide the kabtsaniakes with troubles — must I also provide them with sukkahs? I said no once, and no it is: from this Sukkot on I won't let them over the threshold of my sukkah.
You think I hate Jews? On the contrary, I love Jews, long may they live — why should I hate them? So why did I decide not to let them into my sukkah any more? If you had suffered such a defeat as I did, if on the first day you had sat in your sukkah and watched others stuff themselves with your fish, others lick their fingers over your meat — you would not have been a saint either.
As you know, besides a house I also have my own sukkah. A fortress with massive walls, with a floor ["podloga"], with a roof with wings [flaps], high and airy — a palace ["palats"].
When one has such a "palace", why shouldn't Jews enjoy it? So indeed the neighbours have had, year after year, a "khuke" [sic, for khazoke — an established right] to eat in my sukkah. Everyone already had his fixed place; so it went Sukkot after Sukkot, and that Sukkot too I laid the table with a snow-white tablecloth, and as always my neighbours came to the ready table.
On the first day of Sukkot I come from the synagogue into the sukkah and want to sit down in my place at the head — but who can get in? The sukkah is packed, no evil eye, no room to drop a pin to the ground, everyone with his "baggage" [household], shouting and din — you might as well go and move yourself to another sukkah...
Barely, with toil and trouble, I squeezed in and sat down somehow. Lost, I think to myself — what would have happened if they had not let me in?...
I sit in my place. I wait for them to bring me down [the wine] to make kiddush; I sit ten minutes, twenty, half an hour. Nothing heard, nothing seen. I sit like a guest, my belly is rumbling, I am faint with hunger, and I watch how Yakel the shoemaker chops away with all his molars, how Yakel's shiksa [gentile maid] keeps serving dish after dish; there the shiksa brings him down the genuine bottle of wine. Yakel drinks l'chaim, one l'chaim after another; then the same shiksa serves him the head of a two-kilo carp with fresh yellow challahs; Yakel cuts "hamotsi", dips the challah in the fish broth, and the two-kilo head goes up in flames under Yakel the shoemaker's hands; and before you know it the shiksa is here again with a plate of noodles yellow as wax. The broth with its "eyes" [of fat] winks and teases me, as though saying: "Well, honourable[?] gospodarz, what do you say about your tenants? They eat yellow noodles and you eat fever [i.e., nothing]!"... I look and squirm, and before Yakel had even finished the plate of noodles, the shiksa had already handed him the real portion of meat: a whole lower quarter of goose, plus gizzards ["pupkes"] with stuffed necks, with the usual[?] carrot tsimmes, with a plate of compote as a side; the company sings zmires, Yakel works over the goose[?] with the carrot tsimmes and the apple compote, and I feel my soul flying out of me.
One thing puzzled me: how is it that Yakel the shoemaker, the pauper who dies ten times a day of hunger — where does he, the patch-sewer ["latelayger"], get such a lavish holiday? How does he come by wine with carp heads, with yellow noodles, with quarters of goose, with apple compotes?
But why should I meddle in other people's business? I have another worry now: what has happened to my "yidene" [wife]? Why doesn't she send me down [wine] for kiddush, why? I'm going out like a candle, it's a terrible disgrace for me before the tenants — what has happened here? I ponder this way, ponder that way, and meanwhile it pulls at my heart so long and so wide until... until it gripped me under the heart, black wheels began to fly before my eyes, and I fainted.
When I came to, my wife stood beside me with tear-stained eyes, wringing her hands: "What's the matter with you, Zeligshi? Surely you ate with too strong an appetite?" — and she doused me with cold water...
— Why are you pouring cold water on me, why? — I said — better give me something to put in my mouth, I'm fainting from hunger, give me something to taste.
— What's going on with you? — my wife goggled — I sent you down kiddush through the shiksa, fish with meat fit for a king. What do you mean you're fainting to eat? You've eaten up everything I sent down to you.
Only now did I begin to understand what had happened here, whence Yakel had suddenly been blessed with a shiksa, with wine, with a carp head, with yellow noodles, with a lower quarter of goose, with apple compote — only now did the whole story become clear to me.
How did the misunderstanding happen? This is how: on the eve of Sukkot my yidene took on a new shiksa. When my wife sent the shiksa down to the sukkah, she told her: "The master sits at the head." Since the sukkah was packed, Yakel the shoemaker sat down in my place at the head; a shiksa is just a shiksa — since the madam told her "the master sits at the head", she asked no questions, and what was meant to be mine went to Yakel the shoemaker...
No, no, a thousand times no! God willing, next year at Sukkot I will not let the kabtsaniakes over the threshold of my sukkah.
Y. A. S.

Torah sayings and anecdotes about Sukkot.
Collected and styled by Y. Y.
III.
The other days [of the festival].
a) "Ata hor'ata", Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev [Berdyczów] and the Evil Inclination.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak was once, as a young man[?], honoured in the synagogue with reciting "Ata hor'eita". Rabbi Levi Yitzchak goes up to the lectern, takes the tallit to wrap himself in it — and puts it back down. He takes it a second time and again puts it down. So several times. At last he waves his hand and says something to someone invisible: "If you are a scholar and a Hasid — you say Ata hor'eita."
The congregation looks around: what has happened here? To whom did he speak like that?
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak relates:
"When I went to say 'Ata hor'eita', the Evil Inclination came up to me: he wants to say 'Ata hor'eita' with me. So I ask him: what is your pedigree?"
"And what is your pedigree?" he answers me.
"I am a scholar, I have studied a great deal."
"I too am a scholar... I studied together with you."
"But I am also a Hasid, I have been at rebbes'."
"I too am a Hasid, I too have been at rebbes'..."
So I got angry: if you are a Hasid and a scholar, then say 'Ata hor'eita' yourself..."
• •
Once the Adversary would not let a man be a Hasid; today he has thought better of it. Today he says to the Hasid: you travel to the rebbe — I will travel with you... you shout while praying — I will shout along... And a time will come when the Adversary will say to a rebbe: you sit down on the chair — I will sit with you, we will sit together...
Rabbi Moshe of Kobryn [Kobryń].
b) The Ropshitzer's hakafot.
Between the "Seer" of Lublin and Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz [Ropczyce] there once took place this conversation:
The "Seer": You had good hakafot.
Rabbi Naftali: Yes, I had good fish and expensive wine...
The "Seer": No, the Shelah was at your hakafot.
Rabbi Naftali: Yes, but he was cross with me, he stood with his back turned to me...
The "Seer": ?
Rabbi Naftali: He was standing in the bookcase...
(He meant the book "Shelah"...)
c) While beating the hoshanot.
The willow, as is known, symbolises the masses, the lowest of society. These, however, sometimes like to persuade themselves that they are "the top of the shtetl"; and when the etrog with the lulav is put aside at the hoshanot and the willow is taken in hand — it surely persuades itself that it is the main thing. Therefore one beats it out and flings it to the ground, saying the while: "That all the peoples of the earth may know"...
"Osem Bosem"[?].
d) "Whoever sits in the sukkah on the Eighth Day is called a hedyot [a commoner]."
As is known, there is a great dispute among Hasidim whether one eats in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret. The "Chiddushei HaRim" was a genius, and he interpreted the sentence in the Shulchan Aruch "whoever sits in the sukkah on the Eighth Day is called a hedyot": a hedyot — smooth without knots ["senkes", Polish sęki], plain and smooth...
Another rebbe said: a hedyot I want to be, and in the sukkah I want to sit...
e) "Tarry with Me one more day."
"All seven days many bullocks and rams were offered for the seventy nations. When the Jews already want to leave, God says to them: I beg you, make a small feast just for Me" — Shemini Atzeret. Midrash.
Like those in-laws who bustle about at a wedding: they keep honouring strangers, the guests, and they themselves taste nothing at all. Only at the end of the seven days of feasting do the in-laws make a small feast for themselves.
Jews too bustle about at other people's weddings: we offer sacrifices for the nations of the world, we honour the strange guests. Only at the end do the real in-laws make a small feast for themselves...
"Kiflayim le-Tushiya".

A beaten hoshana
During the intermediate days of Sukkot poor boys went out beyond the town to the stream, tore off willow switches there, tied them together seven at a time and sold them in the shtetl as hoshanot, two groszy apiece. When buying[?] people took care that the leaves should be quite fresh, moist; and on the morning of Hoshana Rabba they are carried into the synagogue carefully, leaves upward, like a holy thing.
In the synagogue, during the prayers, when "Kol mevaser, mevaser ve-omer!" was proclaimed, people began beating the hoshanot against the benches and the lecterns with such vehemence that sweat broke out on their faces, and they beat them so long that almost all the leaves fell off.
Afterwards the hoshana was not thrown away, it was carried back home — but, oh dear, what a sight it already was! Leaves torn off, hanging down, and roots upward.
That is why of a person who once played a role and afterwards fell entirely from his glory, people say: "He is a beaten hoshana"...
Mother and Woman (2)

[Serialized novel — "a thrilling novel of Jewish life"; installment 2.]
Sh. Relkes [?].

While David stood there like that, seeking an answer to all his doubts about himself, his mother was absorbed in her own thoughts. She saw that David had understood that she was hiding something from him, and she knew that she had to tell him something, that she must say something; but in this moment of confusion she could not find the right word. So she said quietly:
— David, you haven't finished eating.
She herself sat down at the table and showed David to his place as well. The two of them sat like that, quietly, at the little table, eating and keeping silent. The summer evening descended over the town. In the homely room the twilight shadows spread. Two silent people finished a meal, and each carried within a hidden vexation and a … [unclear word: "khaymke" (?)].
When they had finished eating, David was the first to rise from the table, and he said:
— Mama, I'll go to the park.
His mother wanted to cry out: "Don't go, David, don't leave me alone now." But she said nothing at all, only looked at him in silence. She was afraid that with her outcry she would only strengthen in him even more the suspicion that she was hiding something from him, that all these years she had deceived [?] him. Better to stay alone with her own dark thoughts than doubt.
David went off. He went to the park, and in a dark avenue he sat down on the soft, fragrant grass. He thought about Sarahle, about his mother and about himself. The more he thought, the less understandable his mother's behaviour became to him. She loves; she has sacrificed so much for him — to bring him up, to support him at the gymnasium and now at the university. Surely she herself must want him to take a bride with money, so that he could settle himself. And Sarahle? So what — nowadays it is a simple phenomenon: a young man goes about with a girl, spends time with her, is intimate with her, and afterwards marries another. If he had to marry all the girls he had spent time with, he would need a small harem, like a Turkish pasha.
At the university, David thought, all the students have sweethearts, and not one of them even thinks of marrying one of them. The girls themselves know it and it doesn't bother them. And Mama does live with today's world; she is not "old-fashioned" — so why does she take the business with Sarahle so much to heart?
If he had a father now [?], David went on spinning his thoughts, everything would be quite different. But who was his father? If he could at least picture to himself what his father looked like, he would talk to him in his imagination. But Mama never once described his father to him, never mentioned a word about him, and now the figure "father" is dead for him. Even in imagination he has no one to talk to. And why did Mama always hide his father from him? Why was she careful not to let slip even one word about him?
— Oh God, a Sarahle on my head! — he cried out into the emptiness of the night, and the voice knocked against the trees and fell back at his feet like a heavy lump of lead. — Mama, Sarahle, and I — a stranger in the world.
David fell asleep in the park, and when he woke with a start it seemed to him that he had got lost somewhere in a dark forest. He did not know where he was. His head grew heavy and his heart full of fear. It took several minutes before he came to himself. He realized that his mother would worry [?], would not know where he had vanished to, and he ran home quickly with a pounding heart and with a vague feeling that something was going to break in his life. What? He himself did not know; he only felt that the break was coming.
When David came home he still found his mother sitting wrapped in a shawl in the chair by the window. A book lay open, but she was not reading. The clock [printed "veyger" (?)] struck two. David went up to his mother, kissed her on the forehead and said:
— Mama, so late — go to sleep.
— I waited for you, David. Did you spend [the time] [?] in the park?
— Yes, a cool breeze was blowing. I fell asleep on the grass.
His mother rose from the chair, embraced him and pressed him to herself:
— Dovidl, good night.
Quietly she went off to her room.
The next morning was a gloomy one, as sometimes happens in summer. The sun did not come out; the sky was covered with watery clouds. A wind blew, shook the branches of the trees, tore down leaves and carried them who knows where. On such a morning people are sad and serious, and somehow distant, forgotten times come back to them. Women are especially melancholy on such mornings. They wrap themselves in shawls as if they wanted to hide from a danger coming upon them. Their eyes grow large and the colour of the face such a dull, pale [?] and pensive one. Young David, as soon as he opened his eyes, at once heard a shadow creeping about the house. He knew it was his mother. He sensed her step, although he did not see her. He scented her mood with his youthful nose. David jumped out of bed, snatched up his dressing gown and wanted to go out of the room. But he stayed, because he felt he had to think something through. Today, this very day, everything must become clear to him. If Mama goes on carrying her secrets inside her, he will become completely estranged from her. She [printed "di"] will become a stranger to him. He will even come to hate her.
(To be continued)
What's New in Zagłębie?

[Będzin — municipality and neighbourhoods; flood.]
Friday, 21 Tishrei 5692 — 2 October 1931
Będzin
A whole Jewish quarter under water.
There is in Będzin a Jewish quarter known by the name "Bukowina". This place is flooded quite often during cloudbursts, and to this day the Magistrat [town council] does not see to carrying out the necessary work so that the residents there should not often be threatened with the danger of flooding.
Out of the annual budgets tens of thousands of złoty are used to build paved roads etc. in the most out-of-the-way lanes (naturally, where no Jews live...), while a place like the Zawadże[?] lane is neglected, and the fate of dozens of human lives depends on the smallest natural occurrence.
This year too, at Sukkot, the residents of the "Bukowina" were cut off — "none going out and none coming in". Because of the frequent cloudbursts the lane was flooded on Friday night.
The water rose from minute to minute and burst violently into the ground-floor rooms. The roar of the water woke the sleeping tenants, who by a miracle managed to rescue themselves and their small children through the windows...
Until morning those who had fled the water knocked about in the attics, until they were finally taken out on a cart into the town, where they spent the holiday days with relatives and acquaintances. Only on Tuesday did the residents return to their wet and mud-filled homes...
— Perhaps the Magistrat would at last treat the residents there with a little seriousness? Surely it is high time that the lane were put in order, thereby protecting the residents there from the frequent dangers?
Festive opening of the WIZO premises and the “Gan Yeladim” in Będzin

[Będzin — WIZO.] On Tuesday evening the Zionist Women’s Association in Będzin celebrated a double festivity: 1) the opening of its own large, splendid premises, and 2) the official opening of the Hebrew Froebel school, called “Gan Yeladim” (kindergarten), which began operating at the start of the new school year.
But the members of WIZO showed indifference and apathy toward this double festivity, and most of them stayed at home. That was why the celebration began nearly 2 hours late. Seeing, however, that the “panie” [the ladies] were not coming, they finally proceeded to the agenda.
The celebration is opened by the chairwoman of the Będzin WIZO, Mrs. Ratner, with an introduction in Hebrew, in which she points out the great importance of the occasion, and then switches to Yiddish, in which she appeals to those present, and also to all Jewish women in whom a Jewish heart beats for the national revival of the Jewish people.
Mrs. Ratner greets the delegates of the WIZO organizations in Katowice, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie and, last but not least, the chairwoman of the Central Committee (C. K.), member of the Executive, Mrs. Dr. Lewite of Warsaw, who praises the activity of the WIZO board headed by Mrs. Ratner.
Then come the greetings. Here one again sees the tendency of our intelligentsia, which considers it beneath its dignity to speak Yiddish among Jews. In this field WIZO has a great deal to do. The “panie” must be made to understand that their intellectual standing will not be diminished by a hair’s breadth when they appear in public with a few Yiddish words...
On behalf of WIZO Katowice Mrs. Halpern brings greetings; from the Sosnowiec WIZO, Mrs. Rozman (in Yiddish); on behalf of the Zawiercie WIZO — Mrs. Margolies (an olive’s-worth of Hebrew and the rest in Polish); on behalf of the Keren Hayesod committee and the Zionist Organization in Będzin — Nata Landner; from the “Hitachdut” — the parnas [?] S. Rozynker; from the Fürstenberg Gymnasium — Director Dr. Einhorn; from the school supervisory board of the same gymnasium — L. Rubinlicht; on behalf of “Gordonia” — Mordechai Waspel [?] (his dress and his ringing Hebrew make one entirely forget that one is in exile...); from the Keren Kayemet — Mr. Horowitz; from “HaShachar” — Miss Kapłowicz; from “Betar” — Kahan; from the Będzin WIZO — Mrs. Hutner; from “HaShomer HaLeumi” — Löwenstein; from “Herzliya” — Gutman; from “Tze’irei Mizrachi” — A. Zyder.
Written greetings were read from the Łódź WIZO, from the Będzin Mizrachi and from Mrs. Strachlic, and the floor for the lecture on the topic “The Tasks of the Jewish Woman” is given to Mrs. Dr. Lewite.
In an hour-long lecture the speaker describes the epoch when the Jewish people lost its independence, wandered through various countries among various races, and nevertheless preserved its national existence thanks to religion, nationalism and its own culture. The gifted speaker then sets out a series of postulates for the Jewish woman in the field of Jewish education and nationalism.
After that comes the material part, namely “a glass of tea”, at which the participants spend a very pleasant time until late at night.
During the “pause” the audience becomes acquainted with the newly opened “Gan Yeladim”. It is truly an artistic kindergarten, and it is set up according to the latest rules of pedagogy and hygiene. Parents who have [—] the means (incidentally, the tuition fee is minimal) should make an effort to have their small children spend a few hours every day in the Froebel school.
— — —
On Wednesday during the day, with the participation of Mrs. Lewite, the founding meeting of the Young WIZO took place.
A temporary committee was elected, whose task is to recruit members for the young Zionist women’s organization.
— — —
The same rich lecture that Mrs. Dr. Lewite wanted to give to the members of the Sosnowiec WIZO — only because the lecturer had to return urgently to Warsaw, the lecture will take place at another date.
The fight against unemployment in Będzin

[Będzin — unemployment relief.] On Monday evening a meeting took place of public workers and representatives of various institutions, in order to found a committee that should come to the help, in winter, of the broad masses of the unemployed in Będzin. The meeting is opened by the commissioner, Eng. Rzeczkowski [?], who describes the aims of the committee. The committee will collect money and products in kind, which will be distributed among the unemployed. A short discussion develops. The speakers call on those assembled to work hard for the humanitarian aim, which has a state character. Afterwards elections took place. Eng. Rzeczkowski was unanimously elected chairman; of the Jews, Messrs. S. Fürstenberg entered the committee as vice-chairman, and as members of the sections: Rapaport, Goldfeld, Rechnic, Patak, Serczarz [?] and others.
General meeting of the Będzin Zionist Organization

[Będzin — Zionist Organization.] On the evening after the first festival days of Sukkot, under the chairmanship of Mr. S. Lewkowicz, the annual general meeting of the Zionist Organization in Będzin took place in its own premises.
A very small number of members took part in the meeting; given such disregard on the part of the members, it is no wonder that the outgoing board is powerless [?] and is unable to ease the organization’s difficult financial situation.
The report on the activity is given by the outgoing chairman, Mr. Wygodzki. He points out under what conditions the present board took over the leadership, and for what was not done — he says — the members themselves bear the responsibility.
After the report a discussion develops, in which Messrs. G. Landner, A. Liwer [?], Suszek, Preger, Żbudzki and others take part.
The discussion revolves around the matter of how to settle [things].
After the discussion a temporary committee is elected, which, together with the board, is to settle first of all the financial matters and to begin intensive work in all fields.
The unveiling of the “Gordonia” flag

[Będzin — Gordonia.] On Monday, Isru Chag, the festive academy in honour of the unveiling of the Zionist flag will take place in the “Kapitol” theatre — the flag which the Będzin youth organization “Gordonia” has had made for the jubilee of its 5 years of existence.
The flag dedication promises to be impressive and rich in content. Taking part in the event on behalf of the Chief Leadership (Hanhagah Rashit) are Messrs. David Ofir (Eretz Israel) and Michael Rajzman (Łódź), who will lecture on the situation in Zionism.
Also taking part in the academy: the music society “Lyra”, which will perform several Hebrew pieces, as well as the “Gordonia” choir, which will sing the newest Eretz-Israel pioneer (chalutz) songs.
Sosnowiec — A New Kehilla Board Elected.

On Monday evening our town finally had the privilege of a new kehilla (Jewish community) board.
The chairman of the election commission, Mr. Markus Hamburger, opens the meeting, establishes that all the councillors are present, and proceeds to the election procedure, which gave the following result.
From list 1 (National Bloc) elected were Messrs. Yisroel Moyshe Vayertsh[?], Levi Yungster, Itshke Zaks and Itshe Volf Braner.
From list 2 (the Koziegłowy and Agudah bloc), Messrs. Hershl [printed: Ḥrshil] Erlikh, Leybish Grilak and Shmuel Pshezatshevski[?].
From list 3 (Englard's faction), Messrs. Mendl Klayber, Mendl Loyfelski and Shloyme Dlutman.
As can be seen, Englard's faction, which had gone hand in hand with the national camp, changed its tactics this time and united with the Koziegłowy Rebbe's faction.
A Warsaw Firm Files a Denunciation against a Local Merchant.

[Sosnowiec — trade.] The paper merchant Mr. Dafner frequently had inspections by officials of the customs office. When Mr. D., seeing that the inspections were based on an informer's denunciation (mesirah), began to investigate and search until this week he obtained an official document which uncovers the whole affair.
The document states that the firm "Kopernikus" in Warsaw had written a letter to the Minister of Commerce, pointing out that the merchant Yitskhok Dafner in Sosnowiec brings certain goods from abroad illegally and thereby hampers the development of domestic[?] production.
Mr. D. has decided to bring a lawsuit against the above-mentioned firm.

A Real-School Pupil Stabbed a Jewish Boy on the Tram.
On Thursday several schoolboys from Dąbrowa were travelling by tram to Będzin. On the way a quarrel broke out between the Jewish and the Christian boys, during which a Christian pupil stabbed Kleiner from Dąbrowa with a knife.
Kleiner was taken to the Będzin hospital, where he remained for treatment.
—o—
A 17-Year-Old Suicide.
In Ranaszniki[?] [perhaps Rogoźnik] the 17-year-old Duda committed suicide by throwing himself under the wheels of a train. The reason for the suicide is that Duda's parents forced him to learn a trade, whereas their son wanted to continue his education.

„Świenta“ Has Become a „Saint“...
Echoes of the abuses in the Mysłowice loan fund.
At the Katowice district court the trial took place of the former director of the Mysłowice loan fund, Mr. Świenta, who had committed a series of abuses in the fund's books.
According to the indictment about 1700 members were wronged. The former director was sentenced to 4 years' prison and to loss of rights for a period of 5 years.

Friday, 28 Tishrei 5692 — Friday 9 October 1931.
Berek Joselewicz Street in Będzin

[Będzin — municipality.] At Wednesday's session of the Council of Commissioners in Będzin the item of designating new streets in view of the population census, which is already beginning throughout Poland, was considered.
On this item councillor M. Hampel proposed that Synagogue Street (ul. Bóżnicza) be renamed Berek Joselewicz. Although the hero Joselewicz has great merits for Poland, there were nevertheless some of the Christian councillors who were against the proposal...
After the support of councillors Rszbnik[?] and Gutenstein it was decided that not Bóżnicza but Targowa (Market) Street in Będzin will be renamed Berek Joselewicz.
The names of the following streets were also changed: the new street by the post office received the name Narutowicza, and the Third of May Square — President Mościcki.
Inquiries Concerning the Rabbinical Elections in Strzemieszyce

[Strzemieszyce — community.] As is known, the party that supported the rabbi from Jaworzno during the rabbinical elections in Strzemieszyce submitted a complaint to the voivodeship against the rabbinical elections.
The complaint was signed by fifty-odd voters.
This week the voivodeship carried out an investigation into the correctness of the complaint, but of all the persons summoned only 11 men appeared; the rest apparently did not have the courage to support the complaint.

The murderer was sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment and loss of rights.

[Dąbrowa — accident.] Tragic Death of a Young Child in Dąbrowa.
In the Kożeniec[?] colony a terrible accident occurred in the family of the worker Edward[?], which cost the life of a 14-month-old little girl.
The accident happened under the following circumstances: the child was playing by the stove; at that moment a pot of boiling soup tipped over and poured onto the child. The child died of the wounds.
Suicide of the Postmaster in Skała

[Skała — suicide.] On Saturday the postmaster Wiktor Kianka[?], with the aim of committing suicide, climbed up to a height of several dozen metres and threw himself down from there.
The suicide broke his arms and legs. In a dangerous condition he was taken to a Kraków hospital.
The cause of the suicide is a nervous breakdown.

The Great Guest (On the visit of H. N. Bialik to Sosnowiec)

(On the visit of H. N. Bialik to Sosnowiec.)
Next Monday the great Jewish national poet Hayim Nahman Bialik is coming to us. He will stay with us for several days, and we shall have the privilege of seeing him and hearing his voice. Days of a true national holiday lie before us.
"What sort of holiday is this?" — more than one of our poor brethren in the Jewish [street] will ask — "there is nothing festive in our hearts. We suffer and we struggle, we are sunk in a sea of want and troubles, we have no strength to make a holiday!"
That, alas, is the truth. Unsteady[?] and sad is the whole world. Sadder than anywhere else it is with us. The horizon is covered with black clouds, through which not the faintest ray of light can break. We are politically humiliated, economically oppressed, culturally fallen, ideologically impoverished. The present is desperate, yesterday we have forgotten, and who knows — whose tomorrow will be.
And yet we must tear ourselves with all our strength out of the sad everyday and make a holiday in the Jewish street. The holidays have always saved us from national ruin; they will save us today as well.
Bialik is one of the prophets who wake us from the heavy sleep with its evil dreams and bid us rise to a new, festive life. These prophets work on us by various means: with anger and with wrath, with love and with consolation, like a stern father or like a merciful mother.
Bialik is the prophet of our generation, the great awakener. In his poetry our whole degradation is mirrored, but also our whole titanic greatness. No one has yet penetrated so deeply into the depths of the Jewish soul as he — the most faithful son of our ancient people.
Into Bialik's hands were given the keys to the great treasures of Jewish culture of the past. He has opened wide for us the gates of the Jewish Aggadah, and lately he has begun to lead us also along the paths of Talmudic Halakhah. He has awakened from their thousand-year sleep the poets of the Jewish Middle Ages; he has poured new life into the language of the prophets.
But not only the keys to the past are in his hands — he also holds the key to the future. He is the educator of the young generation, to whom he speaks in his children's language as none of our poets has yet managed to this day. Bialik's love of the people is embodied most strongly in his love for the Jewish child.
Let us forget for a few days our daily worries, our pettiness and poverty, our party splits and quarrels; let us greet with festive joy the greatest son of our people, the immortal Bialik, with the traditional "Barukh ha-ba!" (Welcome!)
Dr. Y. P.
From the Last Days of Sukkot

No less than on the first days of Sukkot and the whole of Hol ha-Mo'ed, the last days too brought an abundance of... rain. Damp[?] and cold in all districts. A little festive "mood" was still to be found in the shtiblekh and in various minyanim. As it was, people "pinched their cheeks to make them red", but it was no longer what it once had been.
— — —
In the Ger shtibl of Będzin this year the hitherto customary claims (hazakot) to the honours of the "hatanim" [Hatan Torah / Hatan Bereshit] were abolished. The gabbaim issued a regulation: since the shtibl needs repairs, a "tax" is imposed on the "hatanim" — whoever wishes to be a "hatan" must give 50 gulden [złoty]; if not, he is "no longer a hatan"...
The regulation threw a "fear" into all the candidates, and of all the "hatanim" up to now only two remained, who "signed up" to meet the new conditions; the rest made do with the "hakafot"...
— — —
In the Będzin synagogue the "tradition" is strictly upheld by the "heymishe" [the old regulars]; never mind them — the "heymishe" are great connoisseurs and do not let themselves be lured into the idolatry of "Ozer Dalim" [aid society for the poor]... This year too they "rejected" "Ozer Dalim's hakafot"...
— — —
The caretaker (house-warden) of the "Mizrachi" minyan in Old Sosnowiec has shown that he is not only a good caretaker but also a "qualified dentist": with one blow he knocked out several teeth of a poor Jew...
— — —
The "sensation" of the day was the pamphlet of the "Agudah", distributed against President[?] Mr. Yitzhak Aharon Landau, who dared not to obey what the "Agudah" wanted of him and voted for the united list for the kehilla administration.
The pamphlet, distributed on Friday before candle-lighting by heder boys, provoked bitterness among all strata of the population, who tolerate Mr. Landau's conduct. The aim of the "Agudah" was above all to incite that part of the Aleksander Hasidim who naively believe in the honesty of the "Agudah", but the result was the opposite: on the holiday Mr. Landau received the greatest honour in the Aleksander shtibl. On the other hand, in a number of minyanim protests were held against the attack of the "Agudah" on Mr. Landau.
Jews of Olkusz, You Have the Floor!

Not having the possibility of turning to you in person, I do so through the press, hoping that the result will be the desired one. For quite a long time the writer of these lines has been appealing to the local rabbi, may he live long, about appointing a teacher of religion in the public elementary school, where 40 percent of the pupils are Jewish children; the rabbi has always rejected my[?] important[?] proposals about the candidate for this post with unconvincing arguments. Some months ago Mr. K. of Miechów, who graduated with the highest distinction from the state[?] seminary for Jewish religion teachers in Warsaw, turned to me, asking me to exert myself so that he might obtain the post in the public school. I did so, and the school administration agreed.
The old "Agudah" members of the dozór [kehilla board], together with a couple of "Tseirim" youngsters, on learning of this, at once began a campaign against Mr. K. and applied to the school inspector to appoint[?] the "Beis Yaakov" teacher. The rabbi, may he live long, also helped in this, but the school inspector rejected the request regarding the "Beis Yaakov" teacher. Then the new "Agudah" dozór members took a very untactful path.
In the name of the kehilla a denunciation (mesirah) was submitted to the school inspector, full of various slanders against Mr. K. — that he is a heretic (apikoros), etc., etc. — and at the same time it was requested that the "Beis Yaakov" teacher be confirmed.
Neither the inquiry by the kehilla leaders helped, nor the written confirmation by the honoured rabbi and religious judge (moreh tsedek) of Miechów, may he live long; rather, they went on digging up[?] deceptions and inventing new slanders so that Mr. K. should not be confirmed as teacher. Let the Jewish children rather[?] have no Jewish teacher, let them not learn Jewish history — everything is worthwhile, so long as the unqualified "Beis Yaakov" teacher is confirmed...
The Zionist organisation in Olkusz, which ought to have reacted most sharply to all this, takes little interest in such matters — they have much more important affairs...
Jews of Olkusz! Will you allow your children not to receive the kind of education that the present time demands? You now have the floor! Fulfil, then, your duty towards your children!
M. Sh.

Festive Academy

[Będzin — youth movements.]
In honour of the unveiling of the "Gordonia" flag in Będzin.
Monday's festive academy at the "Capitol" in honour of the unveiling of the splendid flag of the Będzin pioneering youth organisation "Gordonia" turned out successful and impressive. A very large crowd came to the joyous[?] celebration, so that the hall and the two balconies of the theatre were overfilled.
The stage was tastefully decorated with the portraits of Dr. Herzl and Nordau, as well as with the portrait of the late spiritual leader of the Eretz-Israel workers, Aharon David Gordon, whose name the "Gordonia" movement bears. The stage was wrapped in much greenery and light. The presidium was taken by the members of the local leadership (hanhagah mekomit), the press and the representatives of a number of organisations who had come to greet the celebration.
The head of the branch (rosh ha-ken), Mr. Matek Hampel, opens the academy with a fine Hebrew speech. "In what hard times," the speaker begins, "for the Jewish people we come once again with the pioneering flag, which is to mobilise Jewish youth and to wave over the heads of the masses of the people. Our flag," Mr. Hampel continues, "is blue, symbolising the blue skies and waters of Eretz Israel; the flag is white, which denotes the purity of Jewish life, of the Jewish soul and of the Zionist idea of labour."
The speaker thanks those 37 organisations, parties, institutions and private persons who have immortalised themselves on the tokens (jetons) attached to the flag. On this occasion Mr. H[ampel] thanks the editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" for its warm attitude towards the pioneering youth organisation and for [covering] its life in the columns of the paper. As a token[?] of gratitude "Gordonia" has entered a silver jeton in the name of the editorial board.
Mr. Hampel greets the large audience present three times with the Gordonia greeting "Hagshem" ("Fulfil!"), to which all members of the federation (histadrut) respond loudly.
Then the representative of the central leadership (hanhagah rashit), Mr. Michał Rajzman (Łódź), cuts the ribbon of the flag. The flag is unveiled amid loud applause and cries of hurrah.
After the singing of "Hatikvah" come the greetings. On behalf of the Zionist Organisation, the chairman of the kehilla council, Mr. Wygodzki, extends greetings; on behalf of the Zionist faction in the kehilla — dozór (kehilla board) member Liwer; "Hitachdut" — Mr. Gertner; the district leadership of "Gordonia" in Sosnowiec — Mr. Zytman; "WIZO" — Mrs. Hutner; "Tarbut" — Mr. Bernsztajn; the "Yavneh" school — Mr. Zyder; the hachshara groups (Zagnańsk-Olkusz) — Mr. Kutner; the "A. N. Ber Borochov" hachshara kibbutz — Mr. Arbeter; Keren Kayemet — Mr. Kurc; He-Halutz — Mr. Kuperminc; "Youth-WIZO" — Miss Gutman; Ha-Shomer ha-Leumi — Mr. Horowicz; Herzliya — Mr. Gutman; Ha-Shahar — Mr. Berliner.
Many names are read out of "Gordonia" branches, "Hitachdut" (Sosnowiec), Keren Hayesod, the League for Labour Eretz Israel (Będzin), and hachshara groups which sent written greetings. A special impression is made by the cordial greeting which arrived from the Gordonia members in Eretz Israel. This warm blessing is applauded at length.
Then, to the sounds of the orchestra, a guard-of-honour parade (defilade) in honour of the flag takes place. 30 "Mitorerim" and "Magshimim" took part in the parade.
Mr. M. Rajzman later lectures on the tasks of youth, which is the vanguard of the Jewish people, for whom the pioneering youth movement is fighting for a better tomorrow in Eretz Israel.
The intervals are filled with fine concert numbers performed by the young music society "Lira".
Great success was achieved by the young Gordonia member Blima Wajsbort with her fine recitation "Di zun fun Hulda" ("The Sun [or: Son] of Huldah") by the Hebrew poet Yehuda Karni. Miss Wajsbort is received with great applause.
Also successful was the tableau vivant "Kadima Gordonaim" ("Forward, Gordonia members"), presenting pioneers marching on the road to Jerusalem with torches, pioneer flags and work tools.
The event is closed by the branch's own choir under the direction of Mr. Szymon Rus, which sings the newest Eretz-Israel pioneer songs.
With "Hatikvah" and hora dances the celebration closed at half past twelve at night; it left a very good impression on all those assembled.
