On Guard Against a Catastrophe

(II. Our "ornament" and the unbearable heavy burden. — The latest beggar affair and relief work.)
In the first chapter of our present article we dwelt on the grave problem of the world crisis, which sweeps away the Jew first of all and brings him down to the level of downfall and professional beggary — something to which we pay so little attention. We showed then that, thanks to our short-sightedness and negligence, we push fallen people into the position of permanent schnorrers, permanent beggars.
After every crisis that sets in, then, we must expect a fresh contingent of the fallen and the degraded, who within the shortest time are drawn into the camp of professional beggars. Well, these are such [?] unfortunate people whom the times cause to be thrown out of the ranks of the citizenry and pushed into the deep abyss of degradation [?].
But we also have an entirely different contingent of beggars, one that does not wait for a crisis or for bad times. On the contrary, it finds it easier to enter the stage of beggary precisely when times are good, when it makes no difference to the average strata of the population to take the alms out of their pocket.
Who are they, these individuals? We see them day in, day out; we meet them at every step. They are people of middle and even younger years; they are strong and healthy men and women, and they feel, God forbid, no shame at all in stretching out their hand for alms. On the contrary — they demand it of you with composure [?], just as if you owed them a debt. They hold that they are our "ornament," innocent poverty; but for heaven's sake, how much shame and humiliation does this "ornament" of ours bring upon the Jewish people, how much disgust and filth and dissoluteness and shamelessness has clung to these ranks? Can an average person even form an idea of how far the impudence of these irresponsible individuals goes? Do we even know how far their playing on the nerves of the people goes? We become an object of scorn and derision in the eyes of the nations of the world, when they watch what our "pride" looks like — how we care for it, how we concern ourselves with it, and what we finally do with it.
Among no nation or tongue, among no healthy and normal people, would it ever be heard of that one should remain so indifferent to this category of beggars, who bring us so much shame and humiliation in the eyes of others and drag our decent national honour down to the lowest level, to the most disgusting state.
We do not know whether it is better elsewhere; in any case we believe not by much. But here with us in Zagłębie it is something unheard of, incomprehensible, impermissible. Every Friday, on Rosh Chodesh and on other days of the week, regular beggar markets take place in Zagłębie. If you enter a shop on such a day, you see a whole crowd of Jewish men and women pouring in, deafening you with their "Good morning, six; good morning, ten" (that is: six or ten of us are here) — and you turn red with disgrace, when a Christian is present in the shop and you see what a dreadful impression this makes on him.
It goes without saying that among Christians this calls forth disgusting differences of opinion. One forms the opinion: what do I know — Jews are rich and not sensitive, so they can allow themselves such luxuries; to another it appears that, since the Jews are a gypsy people, it does not bother them that their brothers are also brought up [misprinted] in such a way.
And to tell the truth, we do not know by what yardstick we would measure these deeds if we saw [printed "were"] them among other peoples. Surely we would see more among them than among ourselves.
Where do they come from, these beggar families, and how do they come to us, since they need not wait for any crisis or bad times and have free access at every moment? In what way do they reach every Jewish room and house? With what certificate do they come to us that gives them the right to demand money from us and, in doing so, to desecrate the fair Jewish name so badly?
Unfortunately they need nothing whatsoever for it: a stick in the hand and a dose of impudence are enough. That is all one needs to go from door to door, collect alms in an impudent manner and become refined beggar-swindlers.
Where do they come from and what are they? They come, they come from our own ranks. Our own flesh and blood. What are they? What should they be? Idlers and loafers, cripples and craftsmen who never wanted to work. Swindling, schemes and shady dealings occupy the first item on their agenda. And this is what we support, this is what we patronise? And this is what we maintain on our heavy, weary shoulders, on our bent, worn-out backs?
And therefore — because we give right and left, because we give here, where it is needed and where it is not — therefore everything is so abnormal, clumsy, helpless and unbearable.
If we were to give ourselves an account of our deeds, we would come to the conviction that with such helplessness we do no one any good, and that it may not be tolerated any further like this, for what comes of such giving when everyone — the fallen and the beggars alike — is weighed with one and the same yardstick?
One ought, once and for all, to carry out a proper classification and draw a line between professional beggars, idlers, and beggar elders whom we must unconditionally maintain; then between fallen burghers, who can be raised up again if only we are willing to support them properly, and the "respectable poor," who must receive their maintenance in secret, quietly, so that no one should know.
Since nowadays there is so much refinement and scheming in "respectable" beggary that the ordinary Jew certainly cannot imagine it, one must know how to distinguish all this, and each category should be supported in a different way and regarded in a different manner.
It is high time to take the question seriously; let us not regard it as a beggar affair that is burdensome and superfluous to us. The question must be defined if only because poverty is growing and want is penetrating every corner of our everyday life.
We must not let perish those who can be saved, nor may we make professional beggars of them. Our professional trade institutions must do everything that is at all possible so that the oppressed burghers are pulled out of the critical swamp into which they fell in the blink of an eye. The people must provide the means to bring such burghers to the point where they can be set back on their feet, which have only just bent, and which we are able to straighten again. On the other hand, one must see to it that the loafers and idlers who do not want to work are compelled to accept work; otherwise they should not be supported; otherwise one should shun them and get rid of them.
In this way we would gain a great deal: first, we would get productive people capable of work out of the loafers and idlers; and second, thanks to the classification and to not giving alms right and left, we could support with a generous hand those who need support.
It is high time that we became more conscious, that we crystallised the various forms in our everyday life, into which so much pessimism penetrates, for which we need so much patience and endurance and boundless shrewdness and awareness.
Let us not regard this as a trifle; let us begin to rescue the building while it can still be caught.
L. Szpigelman.
We Are Still at Bereshit

[Będzin — satire; Agudat Israel and the kehilla.]
(A conversation of sorts.) Submitted for print by Ben Amotz.
Time does not stand still — the calendar plainly shows that we have already entered the year 5692, and yet
— and yet we are still only at Bereshit. After all the achievements in every field we have still not moved a single step forward. As my neighbour says: "So it was, so it is now, and so it will be as long as the 'Aguda' [Agudat Israel] busies itself with the laws of politics" and wants to hold sway over Israel's old nag.
Take us, the Jews of Będzin: we have many times been in great danger — not in the material sense, but the spiritual. Put simply, Jewishness, the main tenets of the Jewish faith, were more than once threatened with ruin, and only thanks to the few persons who stand on guard to protect the faith did the Sitra Achra [the "Other Side", the forces of evil] — which always appears disguised as Mizrachists — gain no dominion, and Jewishness, thank God, was saved... Who among us does not remember the danger Jewishness in Będzin was in at the rabbinical elections, and later at the first elections to the democratic kehilla. The whole rabbinical world was then pining [?] with fear lest, God forbid, the Jewish communities fall into the hands of the sinners, into the hands of those who want to abolish shochtim and supervisors, to sell off the Talmud Torahs to little Zionist tots and the like. Then a public proclamation was issued to the Jewish people, signed by no fewer than 450 rabbis and Torah giants of Israel, who warned the Jewish people to go in the straight path and vote only for the Aguda lists.
No smaller rescue campaign did the "Aguda" undertake at the last Sejm elections. And no wonder, for at the time the issue was that Jewish religious affairs in the Sejm should not, God forbid, be defended by the "Rabbiner" [state-style modern rabbi] Rabbi Rubig-stein [sic, = Rubinstein]..
And, thank God, it succeeded. The well-known Reb Leibele entered the Sejm under the banner of "Torah and Faith", and the honour of the whole of Polish Jewry was at once exalted. But today — where are the orderly [?] interventions of the "Aguda" regarding Jewish education, subsidies for Jewish societies? And the [?]... — cheap train tickets to Ger [Góra Kalwaria]...
We thought, after all, that no power in the world was any longer capable of humiliating, diminishing or doing any harm whatsoever to religious interests in general and those of the town of Będzin in particular; but it turns out that we are only at the beginning, at Bereshit... The situation has not changed at all; on the contrary, it has become even worse than before. Formerly, for example, when various elections were at stake, religious Jewry feared a collective force, organised groups, organisations — and today the state of Judaism has reached such a "sad level" that one creature of flesh and blood, no more than one man, has the audacity to presume "to shake to its foundations the Jewish communal life, which is based on the foundations of faith and Judaism"...
— Be astonished, O heavens! Open your eyes and see the terrible thing that was uncovered, for our many sins, during the past Chol HaMoed Sukkot by "the election committee of 'Agudat Israel' in Będzin", which put "on the pillory" the "honest swindler" Yitzchak Aharon Landa, who "committed a vile deed" and "sold out the Jewish public of Będzin"...
We read and read and did not believe what our eyes saw on that "pillory", but after a lengthier investigation it became clear to all of us that it is indeed so, that it accords with reality. "Yitzchak Aharon deserves the stick, and the verse besides"... For he thwarted and stood in the way of the Aguda's scales, on which hang all the secret agreements about a fourth moreh hora'ah [rabbinic decisor], about a sixth shochet, the pension for the secretary and other "concessions" which will, God willing, come into force when the kehilla is again ruled by our own people, by "anshei shlomenu". It is simply a delight when one of our own sits in the kehilla; Jews need a livelihood, and "sfot" [?] have little legs — over every little leg there will be its own special trustee; the first monies that come into the gmina [community] till would be shared out among our own, and it would have been a true idyll.
But no rest was destined: along comes a Jew like Yitzchak Aharon, who with the one word "No!" stopped the Aguda's carriage, already set to go on its way, in mid-course, and
— Stop!..
Now the "Aguda" in Będzin, which was already almost sure that Jewishness was beyond all danger, that all stumbling blocks which could cause one, God forbid, to stumble had been cleared from the path, must again take up the old, earliest means and tell the broad public about "the vile deed that was committed this Sukkot in our town of Będzin".
It is more than certain that "the Jewish public will not keep silent about it and will react against the traders in the mass of voters and their convictions, against those who undermine the standing of our kehilla",
— in the high windows [the upper echelons] too they will not keep silent about such a vile deed, and "we shall restore the crown to its former glory", but meanwhile "the foundations of the faith are undermined", especially at a time when the sausage [?] question [vursht-frage] is still not regulated in Będzin...
— — —
Yes, the upshot of our "conversation" today is that we have faint hopes that "the sky above our heads will ever clear up"; a feeling of despair seizes each of us as we see and hear what is going on before our eyes. It is a time when "God-fearing" Jews shed crocodile tears and rebuke others for the very deeds they themselves committed "before the new world was created"... They pretend to have forgotten that "what one sows, one reaps"... We mean to say that if one were to start putting up such "pillories", Poland would run short of trees... The largest number of "pillories" would be used for the "Torah-loyal" of the town of Będzin, of the town whose foundations "have been undermined" because a Mizrachist will take the role of an "Agudist"...
— — — — —
On the calendar the year 5692 — 1931 is marked in big letters, and yet
— we are still only at Bereshit...
Do the Economic Institutions Fulfil Their Tasks?

As every year, the citizens are now again receiving the payment orders (nakazy) for the income tax, which is one of the most just taxes. Every citizen understands that he must give a certain percentage of his earnings to the state as well. Unfortunately, this just law is completely crippled when it is carried out in practice. And here is why.
In assessing the income tax, what is taken as the basis is not the turnover of the enterprise, which has already been determined beforehand by the same office, but the so-called "materials" that the chairman of the assessment commission — that is, the head (naczelnik) of the office — possesses. Whether the above-mentioned materials concern [?] the turnover of the enterprise raised by 40 per cent (the chairman says that the turnover-tax assessment commission, poor thing, made a mistake...), or what kind of private life the taxpayer leads — does he spend his holiday at health resorts? If, let us say [?], he does not lead such a life of luxury, then another calculation is made for him: he lives in a three-room flat, supports a family of 4 persons, 2 children attend the gymnasium — all this amounts in figures to such-and-such a sum. Where did the taxpayer get it from, if not from the enterprise or from his trade? That sum is then already the final one, on which the income tax must be paid.
Had the assessment been made according to the turnover tax already fixed, with the office's own earnings table, the income tax would not have reached even a fifth of the above-mentioned sum. Yes — when we speak of the earnings table, we come up against an interesting phenomenon.
In the last few years the chambers of commerce have been working out quite a few tables of the various earnings in various branches. One would think that an institution such as the chamber of commerce deserved to be trusted and that the statistical material it supplies ought to be respected. The Ministry of Finance, however, takes account of these materials only where it pays, or, in business terms, where it profits more. The Ministry of Finance instead calculates, with the help of the tax chambers, by legendary earnings tables that had their place in the inflation years. Between the two kinds of tables, those of the chambers of commerce and those of the tax chambers, there is an enormous difference, simply astonishing — a full 40–50 per cent — and an even greater difference between both of them and the actual earnings of this or that enterprise.
Everyone knows, and government circles have confirmed it more than once, that earnings in 1930 fell to a minimum. Every enterprise lost enormous sums in 1930 and, at best, did not earn the sum it had earned in 1929. The enterprises that keep commercial books prove it clearly with figures.
In the present income-tax assessment almost everyone has received the same sums of income tax as in 1929, and some even more. Is that not absurd? In 1930 merchants lost through protested bills not only their own capital but also other people's, and yet they will have to pay income tax. And where [?] will they take it from? That is already a task for the bailiff. On paper, after all, the chairman of the assessment commission has reached the preliminary sum. The payers will come to the office with complaints: on what grounds were they assessed this legendary income from their business? The answer will be: the assessment commission — not, heaven forbid, the chairman of the commission.
At this very point one is left facing a hard problem. Are the members of the assessment commission, Jews and Christians alike, from another world? Are their own private businesses in better circumstances, where the earnings they assess still hold good?
After all, the economic organisations are steeped in the pain together with their tormented members. Do they not know about all this? Do the organisations have more important things to do than to stand on guard and not allow the taxpayers to be overwhelmed [?]? Year in, year out the same thing is drummed out, and from one year to the next the organisations and their delegated members on the assessment commissions lose more and more of their sense of responsibility for the tasks they must fulfil.
How can they allow an enterprise that lost large sums on the goods it sold in 1930, and whose turnover for 1930 was assessed by the same office at 35 per cent less than in 1929, to pay the same income tax for 1930 as for 1929?
Will all the cries of woe of the stricken [?] finally be heard in the appeals commission? Will the economic organisations bear more responsibility for the work of their delegated members on the assessment commissions? Will the elected members of the chamber of commerce at last say a word on this question!
Y. Dines.
Born with "Luck" (A Little Feuilleton)

When our kosher, modest Kehilla came to her time and had to give birth, her husband — the "kimpetor" (the new mother's husband) — immediately immersed himself in the holy mikveh, began saying Psalms ("ustaw" [statutes] in the vernacular) and praying that the woman in labour should get through the confinement quickly and in peace, without any mishap, God forbid. The Zionist midwives did not stand by with folded arms either: they bustled about[?], hovered around the woman in childbed, gave her advice, charms, and performed various "zabiegi" [procedures]. But nothing helped. She had a hard labour, such as is not meant for any Jewish daughter!
For long weeks she was in labour; twice she already lay on the birthing chair; the birth pangs were monstrous, her screams and cries for help went up to the heart of heaven, her pains and groans truly tore hearts apart, and every minute people thought that now, now God would have mercy, her womb would open and she would give birth to a young lad, a fine fellow with a head and sidelocks of pitch[?]-black hair and blue-white little eyes, who would be a jewel for the whole town...
But the woman in childbed is still not delivered; all the "zabiegi" and charms do not help; she still writhes in the strongest pains, her strength is already running out, and God alone knows whether, God forbid, mother and child together might not be lost!...
So the "kimpetor" and his family ran off to the starosta [district governor] to beg mercy of the specialist — the obstetrician — that he be so kind as to come and save the woman (printed: women) in labour and deliver the child, be it with forceps, be it even by Caesarean section. As long as it is a living child — for what is the whole of life and all the toil worth, so to speak[?], without the bit of joy one hopes to live to see from this very child?...
And the obstetrician did the favour: he came, and without delay at once began asking the woman in labour what kind of pains she had and how she felt; then he immediately told the "kimpetor" to recite aloud the few chapters of Psalms that are a great charm for the little soul to come into the world in peace. But the "kimpetor" is broken; he can barely bring out a word, and he answers that he can only do it in a whisper, when nobody hears...
Then the obstetrician calls in a Jew, a sort of member of the household, and asks him to say the few chapters of Psalms. The Jew says one chapter after another, and the woman in labour wants to scream, to cry out "gevalt", but the doctor is a harsh one: he tells her to scream only in Polish, and that was beyond her strength... He goes closer[?] to the woman in labour, busies himself there beside her for a while and — and —
Mazel tov!
Mazel tov to you, Sosnowiec and Będzin! The two[?] modest women in childbed, Mrs. Kehilla, has with luck given birth to a child, a living child, and his name was called — and they at once gave it a name: "Administration" (Ferwaltung, i.e. an appointed board).
You rejoice? So do we! Only — may we have better celebrations!...
M. M.
M. Chasid — Autumn Songs

M. Chasid.
Autumn Songs.
Mournful Days
Quietly the mournful days huddle together
toward the white, toward the pale, toward the distant road.
A shadow carries [—][?] its snail[?] away;
quietly the mournful days huddle together.

Black branches hang down like hands
to rake the wind from the naked fields,
to break the darkened walls of sadness;
black branches hang down like hands.

A night falls shut like a dead ghost
and lies in her way, which she knows, which you know.
The days lie somewhere on roads, athirst[?];
a night strangles them like a dead ghost.

The Night.
The night drips out lazily in the rain
and quietly flickers, tear-stained, like a candle.
An autumn crawls blindly over the roads,
wrapped thickly in shadows.
After it a little wind wanders sadly
and drags a lost cry,
like some bastard puppy,
like someone's overgrown woe.
When There's No Luck... (From the Homespun Tales)

[Feuilleton — a folk tale; matchmaking.]
The L. family are rich, distinguished people with big businesses[?]; they know nothing of any shortage of money, nothing of any headache. Yet God is a father who watches over His children. So perhaps He hung a little bundle of worries on the L. family too. For instance: for their eldest daughter it is hard to make a match. One would think that where there is money there is no obstacle. And still Miss G. is not yet a bride. Not because she does not want to, but simply — it just doesn't happen. The mother of the L. family complains to her own close relatives that she has "goods with money", but luck there is none. Every summer they take the daughter to a dacha and to spa resorts; perhaps it will happen after all, perhaps help will come from there. But all efforts are in vain. Last summer the L. family's prayer was heard. In Bystra luck was sent. Bystra had the merit of gladdening the L. family. Miss G. made the acquaintance of a young man, a very fine, intelligent "person" [printed "פענש", for "מענש"]. She liked him very much. She introduced him to her parents. The latter were utterly pleased that at last their daughter had chosen a groom. Mr. H. Z. of K. began to visit the L. family more often, and they received him with the greatest honour. Most of the time he spent with panna [Miss] G. They had a very good time together, went for walks together — and nothing more. The summer came to an end[?]. It cannot be summer forever; it has to get cold too. Although Miss L. [sic; read G.] did not feel like going home, she nevertheless had to fulfil her parents' wish and go home. On taking leave, she, Miss G., asked of Mr. H. Z. of K. a small thing: since on Chol HaMoed Sukkot she is writing tna'im [the engagement contract], she insists absolutely that Mr. H. Z. come to them. Mr. H. Z. promised her this with pleasure, but on condition that she write him a letter — then he would come at once.

At home Miss G. told her parents that she was becoming the bride of Mr. H. Z., that they had agreed that on Chol HaMoed Sukkot he would come for the tna'im. The parents received the long-awaited joy with gladness, and they began to prepare for the tna'im.

Mr. H. Z. arrived punctually. The joy at the L. family's was beyond description. They were so overwhelmed that they even forgot to ask why he had not brought any parents along, or just relatives. Night fell. The rooms decorated[?], the tables royally laid with every good thing. The bride dressed up "in vinegar and honey" [i.e. in full finery]. The guests sit around the richly laid tables. The shammes, pen in hand, sits impatiently and waits. What exactly they are waiting for, nobody knew. Everything, it seemed, was ready, even the tna'im lay ready — and still they wait. Everyone's heart is gripped, tense. It became quiet, very quiet. One can hear a fly buzzing. Mr. H. Z. [printed "T. Z."] was quite surprised why they had seated him at the head of the table like a groom... and everyone's eyes turn to him. So he was eager to get to know the groom. His thoughts were interrupted by the shammes, who, unable to withstand the temptation of the dishes, spoke up: "In-law, what are we waiting for? It seems everything is already in order — let us write the tna'im!"

The in-law (the bride's father) spoke up:
— Everything depends on the groom. On my side there is no obstacle at all. I do not spare money for my child. Let the groom say what he demands. —

After the in-law's just plea, the shammes rose, pen in hand, toward Mr. H. Z.: "Say, groom, what is your wish, for the floor — the shammes added — now belongs to the groom."

Mr. H. Z., hearing that — they were making him a groom in earnest, jumped up as if from a hot plate[?] [printed "היגער־פלעט"], drew himself up and cried:

— You are making me a groom? First you must ask my wife whether she wants another one beside her... for I have a wife and two children. —

There was a great uproar; all the guests began to look at one another. The bride fainted... The in-law remained sitting there utterly dumbfounded, and the mother-in-law burst out crying loudly[?] like a child. Mr. H. Z. understood what a mess panna G. had cooked up here; he was afraid of a verdict — so he grabbed his legs onto his shoulders and — "fled" [vayivrach], to where the pepper grows [i.e. far, far away]. All the guests began to creep out from under the tables. The rich, laid tables were left standing ashamed, orphaned, for who had the courage to put anything in his mouth. Even the shammes, with an aching heart, abandoned the rich dishes and fled as if from a plague.

It seems that Miss G. talked with Mr. D. Z. [sic; read H. Z.] about everything in the world, only one thing she forgot to ask: whether he, Mr. D. Z., is a bachelor, or whether he already has a wife with two children. I, the writer of these lines, warn all girls that such misunderstandings should no longer happen to them. Before one goes to write tna'im with a young man, one must come to an understanding that both sides will stand by it, and above all speak clear words and understand one another.

P. Polier.
Father Becomes a Bridegroom.

[Humorous story — in honour of Shabbat Bereshit.] By Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek?].
(Told in honour of Shabbat Bereshit.)

You are surprised that I have, as you say, suddenly gone grey and old? That I have become an old man before my time? Ah, if you only knew with what torments, with what heartache I go about. I am stronger than iron if I can endure the troubles; like a plague, like a calamity — I am right in the middle of them.

And from whom, do you think, do I have all these troubles and blows? You think perhaps from my bad business, from the "parateks" [?], or from the protests [of bills]? Heaven forbid! About my business I have nothing at all to complain of. For the more bills are exchanged, the better it is for me — I deal, as you know, in bill-of-exchange forms, so what do I care if bills get exchanged. As you say: "May they multiply"...

The trouble that makes me grey and old before my time is my daughters. Here I have one, the eldest so to speak, who by rights should already have celebrated her silver wedding, and she is still only before her "iron wedding". A girl, it would seem, with every virtue, a girl with golden hands and "silver" hair. She sings and dances, eats lemons and swallows slimming pills, writes love letters and keeps her "randkes" [dates] the way — to make a distinction — a pious Jew keeps the afternoon prayer. Every evening she "zaprasza" [invites] other "sympathies" to hear new "hits" which she buys (read: I buy), in order [?] to "bawić" [entertain] the "towarzystwo" [company]. Every night she strums on the gramophone, every evening she empties full bowls of apples with sweets, with chocolate, out of the sideboard. Now tea with pastries. Every evening she "przedstawia" [introduces] to me other "znajomi" [acquaintances], other "przyjaciele" [friends]. With all of them she is "na ty" [on first-name terms]. They keep up the same "tiken" [?] the whole time — "colleague" this [—], "colleague" so-called — and when it comes to anything "poważne" [serious], when I start talking about a purpose with one of those apple-and-chocolate "colleagues", as soon as I try to have a talk about "eighteen and thirteen", they, the gramophone cavaliers, dry up. If I have to go on preparing such stocks of apples and sweets every evening, I will yet have to take out a licence for a delicatessen shop.

If I had only that one daughter, it could still be endured. But the trouble is that after that daughter come two more, and after the two come another three, i.e. all in all I have in my possession a whole half-dozen — may they only be healthy and strong for me.

And as the saying goes: "With six daughters it's no laughing matter." Yes, I don't feel like laughing. When I remember that I have to prepare apples with sweets for six daughters, tea with hits for 6 daughters, everything goes dark before my eyes. A trifle [?], in present times: six bridegrooms, 6 gluttons on my neck, six flats to rent, six trousseaus, six weddings, six times to pay matchmaking fees. And later, God willing, six times to pay lying-in money, 6 "wózki" [prams]. To hear from six daughters stories about the "papkurakes" [?], about their husbands — you hear, when I remember that bundle of troubles, I turn grey and old before my time.

Eh, why am I telling you about my daughters precisely on Shabbat Bereshit? Why did I not tell you the story on Shabbat Nachamu, on Shabbat Chazon, why precisely Shabbat Bereshit? You will hear right away how, because of my daughter, I very nearly became a bridegroom, and how the matchmaker put [?] two heads into one sack, and I was blackened and darkened in the process.

It was a year ago today. On Simchat Torah I dug in my heels. Why should it be precisely Kopel Warszawer who gets to be Chatan Bereshit? Because, well — he has a "chazakah" [established right]. No matter, I argued, this time I will be the chatan.

Naturally Kopel Warszawer did not like that. There was a bit of a quarrel, and I got my way. I bought Chatan Bereshit.

Here begins my bundle of troubles.

A few days later, after Shabbat Bereshit, I am sitting at home, and as always among a whole gang [?] of my daughter's "przyjaciele". The table is set with bowls, with fruit plates, the gramophone trumpets one hit after another. The room is as smoky as a chimney. Right in the middle of it a Jew bursts in, with a yellow pointed little beard, his hat [?] pressed down over his ears, the tip of a red handkerchief peeping out of his pocket. He looks around on all sides, casts a glance at the table set with apples and chocolate, examines each item separately, and finally, when he has already looked into every corner, he asks: Who is the master of the house here?

What does a Jew want? I ask the unknown guest.

Are you the master of the house? He looks me straight in the eye.

Yes, I say, I am the master of the house. What does a Jew want?

What is the occasion at your place today? he asks in reply to my question — an engagement, a pidyon ha-ben, or just some celebration?

Eh, I say, just like that, the young people are having fun.

What do you want? I grow curious.

Do you have a good cigarette? he answers, still not to what I ask him.

I treat him to a cigar. He takes the cigar, and a second cigar he puts aside for himself for after supper.

Reb relative, I say to him for the third time, what have you come here about?

I have something to talk to you about, he says. About a very important matter. I would like to talk to you in another room.

Once we have gone into another room, he takes off his hat, remains sitting in just his skullcap, and clears his throat like a cantor before Musaf.

Are you, he says, Reb Menashe Zelig, son of Leizer?

Yes, I say, as if you had been standing right there.

I have, he says, a match for you. Everything you could call a match — pure schmaltz, "pimsen-holts" [?], as sure as I am a Jew.

On hearing "match", "schmaltz", "pimsen-holts", my soul rejoiced. At last someone had turned up who was an "amator" [admirer] of my goods. So I handed the Jew with the red handkerchief another cigar, and again he took [?] one more for after supper. I had tea served with a bite to eat. The Jew swallowed the "ciastka" [cakes] like pills. A fine glass of tea, he savoured it; perhaps one could get another glass of something warm, he asked.

I immediately had another glass of tea served and another bite to eat — why not? At last I'll be rid of the gang of apple-and-chocolate gobblers. It's high time I, too, lived to have some joy of my eldest daughter.

What, I ask him, does the other side want from me?

Nonsense [?], he answers, chewing the cakes all the while, with the Almighty's help we'll manage; the main thing, he says, is that it should be to your liking.

What, I say, does the "principal" himself look like? Is it respectable goods [?]?

Go on, go on, he tickled me in the side, only then will you know what life is, what the whole life of a person is — "mshteynsgezogt" [? — saving your presence]. It's no purpose.

He talks and talks, eats and talks, talks and eats. Only then shall I know what life is, what the life of a person is — just as if I did not know it myself. When I get rid of such a hump, only then shall I know what life is. But what can one do — that is the nature of a matchmaker, he has to talk.

To cut it short, what shall I tell you, it was arranged to meet the next day. A place was agreed upon, and may it be in a lucky hour.

At the appointed time I took my daughter, my wife, and the three of us set off for the appointed place.

We got there. The matchmaker with the red handkerchief was already there. The matchmaker, as a matchmaker does, led us up to a Jew and introduced us.

Very good, I say to the matchmaker, where do you have the bridegroom?

The matchmaker fixes a pair of calf's eyes on me: What do you mean? he says, where is the bridegroom? Meanwhile he leads me up to a young girl of about twenty, dyed and made up, in a little dress like a child's, with a short-cropped "polke" [a hairdo? ?].

Here, says the matchmaker to the girl, pointing at me — this is the bridegroom.

I looked at the matchmaker, the in-law looked at me, my daughter and the "bride" looked at each other like two hens. And my wife — my wife fainted. And what is so surprising about it? A man with a wife, a father of grown-up daughters, and in the midst of it all — a bridegroom! A bridegroom of a girl in a short little dress, with a chopped-off "polke". Is it any wonder she fainted?

How did this nasty misunderstanding come about? Quite simply:

On Simchat Torah, during the quarrel over Chatan Bereshit, when I kept shouting: "This time I want to be the chatan," just then a matchmaker came into the shtibl, and hearing me shout "I want to be a chatan [bridegroom]", he immediately asked a Jew what my name was and whether I was a man of means — and so he came to arrange a match for me.

Yes, yes, may you never get to taste what daughters are like. Why, you can't even be sure of uttering a word.
Mother and Wife (A Gripping Novel of Jewish Life) — Part 3

[Literature — serialized novel, instalment 3.] By S. Relkes.

For readers who have not read the beginning of this gripping novel, we give in brief the contents of the chapters so far.

A young man named David, one of those young fellows who catch in their nets innocent [?], naive girls who believe the sweet promises of their so-called lovers, took advantage of a poor girl, Sorele (Sarah), and then abandoned her to her fate. David's mother takes up the cause of the seduced girl and rebukes her son for bringing misfortune on young girls and breaking their lives forever. "With a human life," says the mother, "one does not play."

"David," the mother pleads, "have pity on me and do not cast her off; after all, I have done so much for you — have pity on me, my child."

During this conversation David turns to his mother with the question why, to this day, he does not know who his father was. "I feel," he says to his mother, "that you carried me off into the wilderness, left [?] me to grow up alone, without a whole person."

"Why are you silent, Mother, why do you hide this terrible secret from me?... If my father is no longer alive — then where is [?] Father's grave, where I could [?] go and look and read the tombstone? But Mother! Why have you never told me what Father's name was?"

The mother gave David no answer at all; she embraced him and pressed him to herself:

"Dovidl, good night!"

David wanted to leave the room, but he stayed, because he felt that everything had to become clear to him. If his mother went on carrying her secrets inside her, he would manage [?] to distance himself [?] from her; he would even [—] quarrel [?] with her.

David lay down on the bed. He half closed his eyes and tried to picture a home in which there are a father and a mother. Yes, both, a father and a mother. But the picture was so foreign to him that he could in no way see it clearly before him. The man whom he saw in his imagination as his father dissolved into a blur. What did he have to do with David? What connection did he have with him?

"My God, but who am I, after all?" he kept asking himself.

David did not sit [sic] like this for long, because the door opened and his mother looked into his room. She was paler than usual, her eyes tired, unrested, the skin of her face so thin and transparent.

"Up already, David? Good morning; it may still rain today."

"Good morning, Mama," David answered mechanically, and thought: what does she care whether it will rain or not? She has something else on her mind, after all.

Both were silent. A heavy silence hung in the room. His mother stood on the other side of the door, and it seemed to David that today she felt a stranger towards him. Suddenly the thought flashed through him: perhaps leave her altogether? If she goes on walking about so silent and carrying a secret around with her, the house will become a torment for him. He is young, every vein [printed "aber" — a misprint for "oder", vein] in him is full of life, and here it is becoming so hard. He feels as if a gigantic weight had been laid on his body and were pressing him with its whole burden. He must throw it off himself, so that he can breathe freely, move like a human being, look at the world with open eyes and take the measure [?] of the world with an open heart — otherwise he will go under.

David jumped down from the bed. He was trembling all over, his eyes were feverish, and unexpectedly even to himself he cried out:

"I can't go on, Mama. Why are you silent? Why don't you tell me the truth?"

His mother came into the room; she had turned paler still. But there was firmness and resolve in her bearing. She took him by the hand, looked deep into his eyes, as though she wanted to find out whether he was ready to hear the whole truth, and said quietly but firmly:

"Good, David, you want to hear the truth — I will tell you. But don't be so agitated," she added with a kind and bright smile. "Perhaps you'd like to have a bite first? It's already eleven o'clock; you overslept."

"No, Mama, I don't want anything, but I beg you: don't torment me."

"Less than anything in the world do I want to torment you, my little Dovidl. I know it is hard for you, and perhaps it really is time now for you to know the truth..."

Just then the bell rang and both of them started. Here, in the little room, they had been as if cut off from the whole world. They had quite forgotten that besides them there is still an outside world, and that there are still people who can ring and will come in. The ring brought them back to reality.

"Somebody is ringing; I'll go and open," said the mother with hidden vexation that their conversation had been disturbed, and that what she had been preparing for so long to tell her son, and still had not managed to, was once again put off.

The mother went out and David began to dress. For a few minutes silence reigned. David heard whispering on the other side. But who was there he did not know. Suddenly the door was flung open and Sorele came into the room. She was dressed lightly, in summer clothes. Her golden-blond hair looked like strips of sunlight. Her blue eyes were clouded with a cloud of sadness. Sorele was a girl of about eighteen — slender, light and playful.

"Good evening, David," she said with forced liveliness.

"Good morning, Sorele," David answered crossly, because she had come in in the middle and broken off the conversation he had waited for so long.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bereshit)

[Regular column — 'Oneg Shabbat': Torah remarks on parshat Bereshit and its haftarah.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Bereshit
The Portion
—o—
a) In the beginning God created (1:1)
The Midrash Rabbah relates:
When God, blessed be He, wished to create the world, He took counsel about it with the heavenly household. Kindness and Righteousness were for creating the world, since it would do charity and kindness. Truth and Peace, however, were against. Truth — because the world would be nothing but falsehood. Peace — because it would be nothing but strife. What does God do? He casts Truth down to the earth and creates the world.
The question arises: why was it precisely Truth that was cast away, and not the other opponent, Peace? —
There were two opinions for (— Kindness and Charity) and two against (Truth and Peace), and in order to have a majority for, one opponent had to be removed. Well, had Peace been cast away and Truth remained, then even with a majority of three against it, it would not have given in. Truth does not bow to a majority. Let everyone be against it — Truth will not retreat from its own[?]... Only when Truth lay in the earth did the majority win...
R' Aleksander Moshe Even Lapidot.
• • •
The 'Be'er Moshe', son of the Maggid of Kozienice, was an intimate friend of the Rebbe R' Bunem [of Przysucha], although ideologically they were the greatest opponents. Once the 'Be'er Moshe' sent a man to the Rebbe R' Bunem proposing that they become related by marriage. Rabbi Bunem was inclined to agree to the match. His close followers asked him: Rebbe, it is plainly a falsehood for two such opponents to become in-laws.
Rabbi Bunem answered:
— At the creation of the world God cast away Truth and not Peace, because without peace nothing at all can exist; whereas without truth — if one means it for the sake of peace, one arrives at the truth afterwards anyway...
• • •
'Truth springs out of the earth.'
Why must it be sown precisely in the earth for truth to sprout from it?
— If you bury falsehood and sow it deep in the ground, truth grows...
Nifla'ot Chadashot.
—o—
b) Let us make man in our image, after our likeness (1:26)
In the Midrash:
R' Simon says: When the Holy One, blessed be He, came to create man, the ministering angels split into factions: some said, yes, create him; some, no. While they were quarrelling, God meanwhile created man.
God came to take counsel with the angels whether He should create man. But He did not wait for their decision; in the midst of their arguing and quarrelling He quickly created man.
Because —
when God saw that the angels could not agree, how they disputed and quarrelled — one says, yes, create man; his fellow says, do not create — when God saw this confusion and squabbling, He said: 'Let us make man' — let Me quickly create man. This very scene is surely the best symbol of the future human being. From this scene of strife I shall surely have the best prototype for what man looks like...
Klil Tiferet ('farn'[?] the Dubno Maggid).
—o—
c) For on it He rested from all His work (2:3)
When the Malbim was rabbi in Bucharest, he was once walking in the street on a Friday night. He saw a poor Jewish transgressor go into a Christian restaurant and shake out his last few groszy for a glass of vodka.
The next morning, during the sermon, the Malbim saw that man standing among the congregation. In the middle of the sermon he told the following story:
Last night I dreamt that an angel came to me and invited me to the heavenly household to give a report on the religious state of my town. Up to the great scales, where the commandments are weighed against the sins, there crawls a defending angel with a full bag of money and pours it out onto the right-hand pan: this is the charity that Bucharest gives out. I think to myself that I have already been saved — when an angel of destruction crawls up and throws onto the left-hand pan a few groszy, which outweigh that bag of money. These are the few groszy of a poor Jewish transgressor who bought vodka from a gentile on the Sabbath.
I demand justice: how can it be that a few groszy outweigh a bag full of money?
They answer me: because those few groszy were that transgressor's last. His wife and children were starving at home, and he bought himself vodka on the Sabbath. In those few groszy there is more evil than there is good in the money-bag, for we know the worth of rich men's charity...
'I begged: what can be done? A good angel advised me: that I go and find a tzitzit thread[?] or a tefillin strap, tie the right-hand pan with it, and unnoticed[?] pull the pan down with my foot... I run quickly to look for a strap through the streets of Bucharest. A small matter: to save a congregation of Jews one may allow oneself even a swindle... I run looking for a strap or a tzitzit, but I ran all over Bucharest and did not find a single strap or tzitzit...
—o—
d) To till it and to keep it (2:15)
The homily says on this: 'To till it — this is a positive commandment. To keep it — a negative commandment.' This is simply understood to mean that Adam was then given the 'do's together with the 'do not's.
Characteristic, however, is the interpretation of the author of the 'Magen Avraham': to till it — this is a positive commandment: God commanded Adam to work the earth, and that is a positive commandment. To keep it — this is a negative commandment: Adam was forbidden, as a negative commandment, to neglect the earth and not work it.
A simple commandment: to work the earth... a commandment equal to all the commandments.
—o—
e) And He took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place (2:21; printed '2. sr.')
The letters of basar ('flesh') say: b'li rov sicha — 'without much talk' (woman was created not to talk too much...)
Nachal Kedumim.
—o—
f) I will make him a helpmate against him (2:18)
God could in fact have given Adam the power to create a woman for himself. After all, Adam was a partner in creation. But if he had been able to create her, he would have been able to kill her too. And then he would surely have said to her: 'Return[?] to your dust' [printed 'chov l'afrekh']...
Because 'against him' — because woman embitters man's life — therefore 'I will make': God had to create her, not man, who would surely have soon un-created[?] her.
Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
g) And the earth was without form and void (1:2)
'And the earth was without form — this means the deeds of the wicked. And God said, Let there be light — this means the deeds of the righteous. Which does God prefer? — The verse says: And God saw the light, that it was good; hence it follows that God chooses the deeds of the righteous.'
All the commentators raise a question on this Yalkut: is it even a question which God prefers, the deeds of the righteous or those of the wicked?
The author of 'Noda BiYehuda' answers in his book 'Ahavat Tziyon':
By the expression 'the deeds of the wicked' the Midrash means the commandments, the good deeds of the wicked. And here one might indeed have supposed that God prefers the commandments of the wicked to those of the righteous, because the wicked man, if he performs a commandment, does it with pomp, with great fanfare, with noise and tumult... But God forgoes the publicising of a commandment; He prefers the quiet, modest commandments of the righteous. 'The light, that it was good' — the modest, quietly burning candle.
—o—
h) The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me (3:12)
Thus Adam justified himself for eating from the Tree of Knowledge:
You, God, threatened me not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge, for 'in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die'; but You gave me a wife — 'the woman whom Thou gavest to be with me' — and had I not obeyed[?] her, it would have been worse for me than death... 'A bad wife is more bitter than death.'
Mator[?] Avraham [as printed].
• • •
'Who is a fool? One who loses what he is given.'
This refers to one who divorces his wife ('the woman whom Thou gavest to be with me' — 'what he is given') because of her wickedness. He is a fool for it, because the second one will surely be no better...
Shemu'ot Tovot.
—o—
i) 'Because thou hast done this... upon thy belly shalt thou go' (3:14)
According to the aggadah, the serpent, before the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, could speak and possessed a sharp tongue to make people giddy[?]. Later, however, it no longer needed this. Adam — the symbol of the human species — already carried its poison within himself. Now it can be 'upon thy belly shalt thou go'; it no longer needs a sharp tongue. Evil inclination, man already carries your poison within himself; you no longer need a fine appearance. Even if you crawl like a snake, man will 'open your heart' [as printed] before you...
Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
j) And thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee (3:16)
Because 'thy desire shall be to thy husband' — because the man feels your longing for him — he exploits your weakness and 'shall rule over thee'...
Kiflayim LeTushiya.
—o—
Haftarah
k) Hear, ye deaf; and look, ye blind, that ye may see! (Isaiah 42)
The prophet calls on the deaf to hear and on the blind to see?
It turns out, then, that it depends on the person himself not to be blind and not to be deaf...
Nifla'ot Chadashot (Rabbi Mendel of Kock).
—o—
l) Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? (ibid.)
Jacob is trampled[?], he is slain with the greatest cruelty, robbed and slaughtered, but 'Israel to the robbers' — the robbers are not they, the nations, but Israel itself.
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
What I Hear and See in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — travel impressions; Katowice — Zionism; a local character. Serialized article, part I.]
Yitzchak Margoshes.
I.
On my lecture tour I visited several larger cities of Congress Poland, Eastern and Western Galicia and Silesia; now, on my return journey, I am staying in Zagłębie, where I still have to give a few lectures.
It goes without saying that during my stay in various countries, as well as in various cities, I take the trouble to study the living conditions, the customs, the social and cultural activity of our brethren the Children of Israel wherever they may be.
I tried to follow this principle of mine in Zagłębie too, and collected materials on the specific conditions of Zagłębie; all of this I will publish in a special series of articles in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
This time, however, I will content myself with just a few characteristic sketches of Jewish reality in Katowice, Sosnowiec and Będzin.
— —
In Katowice I met with the representatives [?] of the Jewish public. We discussed various questions, mostly, however, of local importance. Everyone complains about the hard circumstances, which force them to give up on communal affairs and occupy themselves only with questions of a private character. It has gone so far that for these same reasons the local Zionist organization has almost ceased to exist. It comes to life from time to time, on the occasion of an important event, in order to be able to carry out an urgent action.
During my stay there the organization was called back to life, and there are plans to carry on the work normally from now on. But the organization is at present merely a closed society and not a popular movement. A sort of B'nai B'rith lodge, a society of Jewish intelligentsia, a place of refuge where one can meet, spend time together and also unburden one's heart a little.
If, however, one does not intend to content oneself with drowsiness [?], but rather that the organization's work should really bring positive results and serve to spread the Zionist ideal among the broad [an unclear word, "angefarene"] masses of the people, whom it is surely worthwhile and useful to draw into active Zionist work — then the organization must be reorganized anew, and on democratic foundations.
At the head of the local organization now stand energetic, hard-working and capable people such as Dr. Scheuer [?], Dr. Rappaport and Dr. Peter [?], and it is to be hoped that they will know what means to adopt to bring the organization back to its upswing.
— — —
The crisis in Zagłębie is not felt as much as in Poland in general, yet there are plenty of suffering and hungry people here too. Few here are the people who care for others; everyone has his own troubles. And yet — Israel is not widowed. A little man has turned up, a certain Mr. Itche Szajnberg, owner of a kosher restaurant at 19 Mariacka Street, a former tailor and, God forbid, not a man of education either, just an ordinary flesh-and-blood mortal — and he has persuaded himself that he has been called by God not only to help the suffering Jews in their hard struggle for existence (in the field of hospitality to wayfarers he wages a constant quarrel with the local kehilla providers), but actually to find a solution to all [?] the grave problems which have disorganized the world order, demoralized mankind and turned them into beasts (he is, mind you, no madman [printed "meshugemer"], but a normal and not a foolish man who suffers from delusions). And so he sends to the League of Nations, to the foreign ministries of the great powers, to Presidents Hoover and Hindenburg, to Messrs. Lord Rothschild, Marquess Reading and others, whole packs of memoranda with ready-made plans for how to liquidate the world crisis, how to fight communism and how to calm the prevailing hatred between the nations and bring true peace to the world. It happens that in reply to the memoranda he is invited to the local foreign consulates for a talk, or that representatives of the powers even come to him, in the hope of finding the world's salvation through his advice. But — as Mr. Szajnberg tells me — they, the present rulers of the world, are rather meagre sages, because — up to now — he has not yet seen even one plan of his put into practice, and that is precisely why our sufferings do not cease and indeed will not cease until... until people listen to the sage advice of the man called to this by God (so he also writes in all his memoranda) and through it bring the long-awaited salvation to the world.
Perhaps it would be worthwhile for our readers, too, to take an interest in all this and indeed to draw the world's attention to it.
Think it over and do not miss this extraordinary opportunity.

Theatre Notes

[Theatre — review.] „A Heart That Longs“ („A harts, vos benkt“), a life-picture in 3 acts by A. Lesh. From the guest performances of Maurice Lampe and Shoshana.
A man leaves his wife, child and old father-in-law in Russia and goes to America. From there he gives no sign of life for a long time; only after 6 years does he bring his wife and child over to America, leaving the father-in-law at home.
The wife does not know what her husband does for a living. To her questions he answers that he is employed by a „firm“, but it turns out that he is a common bandit, who is arrested during a robbery and sentenced.
The mother and child are left alone. Without means of living and having no other way out, she decides to give the child away temporarily, to be brought up by an acquaintance from Russia, now a rich childless woman.
Years pass; the boy has been raised in wealth, has finished a high school and signed the tnoim (engagement contract) with a rich girl of better society.
After various vicissitudes the son meets his mother and his grandfather. He faces the alternative: not to let himself be recognised by his real mother and remain in wealth with his bride, or to acknowledge her and lose everything. He chooses the second, and it all ends happily.
We have given [?] in broad strokes an overview of the play so that the reader may assess its „literary“ value, as well as the „problems“ and „tendencies“ that bubble out of it. It is a sensational trash (shund) play which might perhaps have suited an immigrant audience in America 50 years ago, but in no way a modern, cultured theatre-goer.
How does an actor like Maurice Lampe, who lays claim to greatness, dare to stoop so low and play in a play of such a genre? Had there at least been a role in it for a star (Samberg in „The Accursed One“), one could still have understood it (not forgiven it), but that is not the case either: it is a role that any one of the participants could have played with the same „artistry“. We could in no way find any greatness in Lampe's acting. The same applies to the actress Shoshana.
With such a play and ensemble Lampe and other „stars“ merely help to undermine the trust and prestige of the Jewish theatre, which stands on chicken legs as it is.
It is a crime, in the present hard times, to come and lure an audience into the theatre with the help of the „Shem ha-Meforash“ (the ineffable name) of a famous artist.
The largest contingent of theatre-goers is supplied by the workers and the workers' intelligentsia, for whom theatre is no luxury, no empty pastime, but an inner urge towards beauty, a need to switch off in an atmosphere of pure art. And if instead of art one serves them trash — that is an act of irresponsibility.
Sh. R.

A Jewish World Congress Must Be Convened

[Sosnowiec — Bialik; culture and Zionism.] Of [sic: „פוז“ for „פון“] all the spiritually creative forces in world Jewry. So says the poet H. N. Bialik.
On Wednesday evening Jewish Zagłębie — those who thirst to hear a spiritual Jewish word — gathered in the „Pałac“ cinema in Sosnowiec to hear the lecture of the great poet Chaim Nachman Bialik entitled „The great and the small reckoning in Zionism“.
Interest in the lecture was enormous among all strata of the Jewish population. But, as always, the organisation was clumsy, and this caused a terrible crush at the entrance; and later, when the police set about keeping order, many young people who had come to hear a Jewish word — received heavy blows...
On the stage sat the presidium and „Shomrim“ with 3 flags. The poet Bialik is received with stormy ovations. The evening is opened with a short greeting in Hebrew by Mr. G. Stawski, and the floor is given to the distinguished guest.
„Honoured audience — Bialik begins his lecture — I have come to bring you a greeting from Eretz Israel, from the land where colossal treasures are being created in the field of our culture, thanks to which the Jewish people was able to endure in exile for two thousand years.“
In a form rich in content the speaker develops the great role that Jewish culture played after the First and Second Destruction: the colossal works of the Written Torah, the Mishnah, the Oral Torah, the Masorah, the piyyutim — which were then created with a uniform character, not fragmented, but in one form, so that the giant works should not be interpreted according to the character of every land where the scattered and dispersed people would find itself, and [in] the lands of exile. „But what do we see in exile — Bialik cries out like a preacher to the people — nothing is being created, Jewish life has congealed, our possessions from the rich past are not guarded, the Jewish word, the Jewish book has been driven out of the Jewish home. It is not enough to talk about Zionism; one must accustom oneself to ‘practical commandments’. Ignorance in the Jewish street must be uprooted; without Jewish learning, without Jewish culture, one is no Jewish intellectual.“
Bialik turns especially to the youth: they should leave foot-culture and occupy themselves with head-culture. „New forces, energy must be poured into our old roots.
— Back to the cheder!“
The whole hall breaks into long-lasting applause, and cries are heard: Long live Bialik!
In the name of the presidium Mr. B. Tencer thanks the distinguished guest for his lecture, and „Techezakna“ and „Hatikvah“ are sung.
———
Later a banquet called „A Glass of Tea“ took place in the large hall of the Hotel Central. At the banquet the most painful question — that of Jewish education — was touched upon.
On this subject the speakers were: Stawski, Barensztajn, Jungster, Liwer, Feldman, Klarman, Mag. Goldsztajn (Warsaw), Wygodzki and Tencer.
The closing word was given to H. N. Bialik, who in witty thoughts developed the problem of education and how Jewish life in general ought to look.
His main conclusions are: a world congress of the spiritually creative Jewry must be convened in order to work out the constitution on which Jewish life is to be based; the holiday mood must cease and we must pass over to halakhah, to active deeds for the revival of Jewish culture, of the Jewish people.
———

An Appeal to Save the Będzin “Talmud Torah”

[Będzin — education and community.] Ten months ago, for the first time since the Będzin Talmud Torah (T.T.) has existed, a general meeting took place.
The meeting was called at the time in order to set the institution on firm foundations. Secular studies were finally to be introduced as well, on the model of a public elementary school (szkoła powszechna[?]).
At the head of the T.T. then stood Mr. Mordechaj Dafner, who made great efforts to bring order to the institution. The work was successful, the sympathy of the Jewish population for the T.T. grew, and there were prospects that the institution would take first place among all our societies.
But suddenly fear fell upon the “Torah-loyal” Jews; they took fright at the word “order”, and a “heavenly voice” went forth:
“Come, let us deal wisely” — let us all gird[?] our loins for battle, so that the T.T., God forbid, shall not be ruled by the “sinners”, by the Mizrachists and other similar “harmful” elements.
The “heavenly voice” roused the “Torah-loyal”, who indeed came to the meeting in great crowds, worked [“mshim” — doubtful reading], and… won a victory, drove out all the “fine spirits”, and the sanctity of the T.T., God forbid, was not diminished.
— —
That happened ten months ago. During all that time those who occupied the T.T. did nothing at all to improve the situation. The melamdim (teachers) are starving; they beg to be given at least 10 gulden a week, with which to buy dry bread for their families, but nobody hears their desperate pleas, and as the latest appeal of the Rabbinate says, things are reaching the point where the T.T. will have to be closed…
In this connection people again resorted to the old remedy — calling a “great assembly” at which the “most capable, most able” people, to whom the fate of the “Talmud Torah” is dear to the heart, would be elected.
Barely a minyan of people came to the great assembly, and the “ten righteous men” took the initiative to put together a list for a new board. But it turned out to be “the same Yente[?], only differently veiled[?]”: once again the well-known “fine Jews”, the former T.T. trustees, were honoured with being the “rescuers” and educators of the hundreds of poor Jewish children who study at the T.T…
Not wishing to bear responsibility for the further consequences, the hitherto active workers, Messrs. Mordechaj Mendel Janowski and Mordechaj Dafner, have resigned from further activity.

Professor Bałaban’s Lecture in Będzin

[Będzin — culture.] Last Monday Będzin had the opportunity of hearing a brilliant lecture by Prof. Majer Bałaban. Bałaban spoke about Jewish history throughout the whole world — how it was born among us in the most ancient times and with what eyes the later historians looked upon it, until he comes to Geiger, Graetz and Dubnow.
The audience had a truly intellectual pleasure, seeing in Bałaban the historian and researcher who lets nothing be lost that concerns Jewish history.
The lecture took place in the gymnastics hall of Fürstenberg’s gymnasium, so that many visitors, who had for the first time the opportunity of seeing the building, were delighted both with the beautiful hall and with the Jewish gymnasium.
The lecturer, too, said at the outset that this was the first time it had fallen to him, and he considered himself fortunate, to have the possibility of giving his lecture in such a splendid, modern, well-appointed Jewish building.
The lecture was arranged by the women’s association “WIZO”, which took advantage of the opportunity that Bałaban was in Katowice and invited the esteemed professor for an evening. The association deserves sincere thanks for this, and it would be desirable to enjoy similar instructive lectures like this one often.
Bałaban also visited the Będzin synagogue, which greatly pleased him, and he will also immortalise it in his historical researches.

An Interesting Trial at the Sosnowiec District Court

[Strzemieszyce–Sosnowiec — courts.] In the month of May 1930 a building, the property of Mr. Gershon Frenkel, burned down in Strzemieszyce.
The latter suspected that the arsonist was Mr. Mendel Szlezinger. On the strength of an old Christian woman, who gave “testimony” about the fire, Szlezinger’s son was brought to court.
The trial took place last week at the Sosnowiec District Court. The old Christian woman was also engaged for the trial as a witness. But before the judges’ bench the witness declared that “she does not recognise whether the gentleman [pan] is the guilty one”.
After the speech of the advocate Mr. Krzymuski[?], the court handed down an acquittal for Mr. Szlezinger.
The verdict aroused great satisfaction in Strzemieszyce, and the conduct of Mr. Frenkel is condemned — he himself being a Ger Hasid, he accused another Jew on a false charge.

This week Deputy Finance Minister Jastrzębski stayed in Katowice and held several conferences on how to preserve coal exports abroad after the fall of the English pound.
At the conferences it was decided to use all means to retain the English coal market.

Congress of employees and workers.
A congress of employees and workers took place in Kościuszko Park in Katowice. 100 delegates from 50 towns of Upper Silesia were represented. After the reports a series of resolutions was adopted, among them that the present workers' wage be guaranteed and that a 6-hour working day be introduced.
Saved from certain death.
On Monday the well-known aviator Captain Orliński flew from Katowice to Warsaw. Beyond Częstochowa an engine broke off and the aeroplane began to fall at great speed. Capt. Orliński, keeping his bearings in the situation and bringing himself down from a height, was saved.
Gathering of the "B'nai B'rith Lodge".
On Sunday and Monday a gathering of the members of the B'nai B'rith lodge in Poland took place in Katowice. Professor Bałaban, Professor Schorr and Dr. Brojda also took part in the gathering.
Shot his own wife and child.
In the month of August (sierpień) the unemployed Komar of Rybnik went with his wife and child for a walk in the Rybnik woods. There he shot both of them with a revolver.
This Tuesday the murderer stood before the district court in Katowice. The prosecutor demanded the death penalty, but the court sentenced him to 15 years of hard imprisonment.

A Letter to the Editors.
Esteemed Editors!
Allow me to publish the following open letter in your esteemed newspaper.
For nearly 2 years I was devoted heart and soul to the Będzin Talmud Torah, with the aim that this institution, so very important for the town, should stand at the proper level. During this time I met with great obstacles precisely from the side that ought to be vitally ("bloodily") interested in the Talmud Torah giving true education to the young Jewish generation of the poorest population. But my great will to work held me back from throwing up my activity; only in the last days have I finally realised that I am no longer able to accomplish anything, because my approach regarding the Talmud Torah is outvoted for the worse. I therefore consider it my duty to declare publicly that I resign as a further active worker in the Talmud Torah and no longer bear responsibility for anything in that respect.
Respectfully,
Mordechai Dafner.

On Guard Against a Catastrophe

[Editorial — the crisis and preparing for winter.] III. Winter is coming. — One must consider the situation.
We live in hard conditions today in general, and on top of that has come the merciless [misprinted] crisis, which has robbed us of everything. We cannot provide for ourselves, we are not able to improve our situation — let alone give a thought to doing something for the other, for the one who is unfortunate and lonely and helpless and cannot stir from his place.
It goes without saying that, because the Jewish masses are being impoverished, it is hard to say that they will help the other, that they will share his distress materially, that they will not let fall completely the one who must be helped, the one who must be lifted up.
It is still Sukkot; the short days and the long nights are beginning, and with them comes the heavy, so to speak loaded, winter, which is often quite hard to bear. From time immemorial we have been afraid of the dreadful winter with its long dark nights. In normal conditions one must prepare for it, and then one begins to receive it systematically, and yet it is not [printed "gisht"] easy to endure — let alone when it has to arrive [?] unexpectedly, when one day there is a warm summer climate and one simply wants to forget that it is still Sukkot, while the next day it is not excluded that the real frosts and colds will arrive quite unexpectedly; it is understood that then it is certainly not pleasant at heart.
Well then, when there is no crisis one does not count on any luck [?]: one saves a groszy for the winter, stocks up with coal, potatoes, with clothing and shoes. But now one thanks God that the climate is fooling us and it seems that the whole winter will be warm and fine — and when the guest arrives without one expecting him, that is certainly not one of the pleasant things.
For the middle classes, with whom things still turn over somehow, it will truly be hard to bring the wintry guest into the house all at once, but it will have to happen. Worse will it be with the one who is unemployed and wanders about without a stitch of work: where will he get the means to provide for the winter? How will he manage so as not to stumble and not have to be put to the test of stretching out his hand and coming to the shameful bread of begging? Does anyone among us take care that it should not come to this disgrace? Does one give an account of what it means when people who become victims of the times are abandoned? Surely one must stand on guard and take care that from these unfortunates no fresh national calamities should arise, that it should not come to suicides and that the camp of beggars should not grow.
If a people wants to preserve its prestige, if we do not want to be swallowed up and humiliated from all sides, we must take care to maintain the national honour at the proper height. For that purpose, first of all, attention must be paid to doing something about the unfortunate victims of the crisis, who have gone off the rails and cannot find a way out. First of all, one must not leave the unfortunates to God's mercy; one must care for their present — of those who have lost every hope of climbing back to their former position.
And this care must be taken precisely now, when winter is approaching, when it is hard to earn a livelihood and when from all sides voices are heard that there is no chance of the crisis easing; on the contrary, in Europe and in America people are very pessimistic about the near future. And therefore one must think what to do N O W, how to provide not for tomorrow but simply for today. And if one is to provide for today, one must do what lies before one's eyes: we must help to ease matters first of all with what is within our power, what lies within our competence.
Coal for the winter is an article of absolutely first necessity. We live above the coal, we tread on its seam, we dwell in its lap — and it is comical to relate that there are periods when we here overpay for this necessary article; there are moments when people from all over Poland sit in Zagłębie and wait for coal by the wagonload, and then we in Zagłębie are left without our "black diamonds", whose choking gases we breathe into our lungs the whole year round.
Of course the better-situated families do not know the taste of having nothing to put into the stove, not a piece of coal, in winter; they lay in their stocks in summer, so that for them the question does not exist. But what are those to do in winter who can barely [printed "kum"] get by from day to day? Why should it then be so hard for them to manage to buy that piece of coal? And when they do get it, why should they have to pay through the nose for nothing? Can such needless expenses not be avoided?
One ought therefore to give thought to it and to try to exert pressure on the coal-mine managements, so that they make it possible to supply the article to the local citizens at an especially low price, and that this price should apply the whole year round, summer as well as winter. Besides that, the charitable institutions should receive coal to distribute to the poor at very low prices. This at least the population of Zagłębie may surely have from the coal magnates.
True, coal is an article of first necessity, but with it alone one cannot get by, and there are other products that are needed. Precisely for that reason one must prepare for winter and see to it that the population receives the necessary articles at the lowest possible prices.
In the present crisis one must not prepare products only for the poor, for whom it is decided to distribute the articles free of charge. It is perhaps even more necessary than caring for the poor to make sure that the victims of the crisis do not fall altogether, that they have the possibility of buying with their groszy the important articles they need in order to live through the present day. This question must be considered seriously. We must see to rescuing those who can be rescued and who can still be given the possibility of standing on their feet. They must be rescued, they must be given a drink of brandy to last them as far as the tavern [idiom: kept going until they reach shelter]; if we do not let the unfortunates fall altogether, they will still have hope that it will not always be dark, that as soon as the bright horizon appears they will recover [? printed "oysregnen"], they will then straighten their bones and become people among people, as equals.
One does want to hope that the crisis will end sooner or later, that it is no more than a passing unhappy phenomenon, and then mankind will rise in a resurrection of the dead, and the unfortunate victims who have suffered will then also get a bone to lick [i.e. some benefit].
That is why we must care in the first place that those who have not yet lost their human dignity should not fall.
L. Szpigelman.
