Our Panorama

[Zagłębie — satire; synagogue life, Simchat Torah.] (Articles that do not lose their value. — A moratorium on gabbai-ships. — Young men who do not want[?] to make kiddush over wood shavings. — A desolate[?] look at "zekhiye kries neveyim"[?] (doubtful reading). — A craftsmen's campaign[?] over a Torah scroll.)
The "Englishman" [the pound] has fallen, the "American" [the dollar] is wobbling, the capitalist world is bankrupt — and nevertheless there are still articles which are still in force, still sit in full splendour, and no world upheaval whatsoever has had any adverse effect on them.
— Which articles, you ask?
— Gabbai-ships, hakafot, kehilla strongmen, and so on and so forth...
From "the four corners of the world", from "all the ends of the earth", from Łazy, Sosnowiec, Czeladź — and where then[?] is Będzin? After all, the town of traditions, the town where Jewishness grows constantly, where new religious societies sprout every day, where even on an ordinary Saturday night a new sect of Hasidim is created in the form of craftsmen... So we shall indeed begin with Będzin.
There has existed[?] in Będzin since ancient years, from old times, a minyan with the title "The Old Rebbe's Minyan". In this minyan there is a worshipper who in the year 5672 [1911/12] conceived a desire for the gabbai's cupboard[?] ("gabbai-shenkl").
And it came to pass, he lived to see the day when the article was put up for auction, and our man of desire did not hold back and "bought" the gabbai-ship for 150 gulden.
On handing over the gabbai's portfolio, the old retiring gabbai demanded the amount of the transaction, but here it turned out that the new gabbai wanted to take over the gabbai-ship according to the Łódź system — take a "packet" and set to work
— the 5 fingers...
Because of this two sides formed. The side of the old gabbai argues that there is an explicit "verse": "Rabbi Yaakov pays" — you want to be gabbai, then pay. Against this, the side of the new gabbai says the opposite: a gabbai-ship is no cheaper than manufactured textiles and other articles that one gets "on date" [on credit]...
After many quarrels a decision was taken that satisfies both sides, namely: it is recognised that for a gabbai-ship one must pay at once, but if the new gabbai wants to cover it with bills of exchange, the gabbai-ship shall take effect only when the bills have been paid...
Meanwhile the old gabbai stays[?] and the new gabbai will have to wait a whole year...
———
The youth of Łazy do not hold with that system — waiting; rather, when they owe someone, they pay him at once...
There is in Łazy a gabbai who is an adherent of the slogan: "Young men make kiddush over wood shavings" [?]. The upshot was that last Simchat Torah the gabbai of the beit midrash in Łazy issued a "prikaz" [order] that young men get no hakafot.
— Why?
— Because I want it so.
The young men — worldly even, nowadays — but how can one exist nowadays without a hakafa? They sent delegates, negotiated: let there at least be an "ozer dalim" hakafa, just so that it comes to an end...
And when the gabbai rejected the young men's proposal, the latter rolled up their sleeves and
— handed out the real "hakafot"...
As our "correspondent" assures us, the young men handed out the "hakafot" with a generous hand, sparing no one, so that those who received some of the "hakafot" will remember them perhaps[?] until Hanukkah...
———
Little was lacking for the hakafot in the Sosnowiec synagogue to have looked the same as in Łazy, but Sosnowiec, as is well known, is a modern town, civilisation is founded there like the peace agreement between the rabbis, and thanks to that the matter passed off in a diplomatic manner and very quietly:
As is the way of the world, the Simchat Torah hakafot "beigakhs"[?] (doubtful word) belong to the Chevra Kadisha. They are the ones with the say, and they honour whomever they please.
This time, too, the distribution in the Sosnowiec synagogue would have gone off in the best order, were it not for the notes...
By Satan's doing, the gabbai of the Chevra Kadisha suddenly sees that on the cantor's lectern lies a tuning fork and... music notes.
At first the gabbai did not believe what his eyes saw, but when he drew closer to the lectern he saw — O heavens! —
— notes...
The strange letters threw a great fright into the gabbai, and together with several other former[?] gabbaim he walked out of the synagogue.
In our opinion the gabbai's action was right, for how is it fitting that in a synagogue where pillars prop up the roof and the walls are black as in a poorhouse, the cantor should have the "audacity" to sing from notes — can such a thing be?!...
———
And last but not least. The report from the holy community of Czeladź really ought to arouse merriment in every single one[?] — a trifle, what happened in Czeladź last Simchat Torah?! Has a "Kiddush Hashem" not yet taken place? A struggle of life and death, and for what, do you think?
— For a Torah scroll!...
And this is how it happened. Into the Czeladź craftsmen's association there entered a "dybbuk"... The "dybbuk" "appealed" to the fellow craftsmen that they should go on the straight path, namely: leave the association and become Hasidim...
No sooner said than done: the "lecture" of the leader of the "anti-Hasidic movement" did not help — he gave his comrades to understand with parables that they must not listen to the "dybbuk", because "the Hasidim — he says — are, according to Darwin's theory, just like the monkeys"; but they made themselves a "shtibl" and took the Torah scroll of the craftsmen's minyan into the "shtibl".
The "anshei[?] Hasidim" (perhaps for "anti-Hasidim"), those who had "clearly" proved that "the new craftsman-Hasidim have been caught like monkeys", did not rest either, and they managed to get back their Torah scroll, which had been carried into the Craftsmen's Bank...
When the craftsman-Hasidim saw that they were left without a scroll for the hakafot, they went into the beit midrash and grabbed a scroll from there.
What will come of this grab-and-run story is still hard to say, but one thing is clear: the Jews of Czeladź this year on Simchat Torah sanctified the Name (printed "mekadesh hashem" with a misprint) and fought for "the honour of the Torah"...
Ben Amotz.
When Times Are Bad

[Essay — economy, religion and education; the crisis and suicides.] By Dr. A. Gottesdiener [? printed “Gotesdifer”] (Director of the “Mizrachi” school).

The economic situation of the Jews in Poland is a desperate one; poverty creeps, openly and secretly, into Jewish homes and lords it there ever more widely. It already strides over the Persian divans, already sleeps in Jewish mahogany beds, and throws the former householders out through the windows “na złamanie karku” [headlong, “to the breaking of the neck”]. Despair already goes so deep that even very pious Jews lose the “pintele” — the spark — of faith and trust in God and take their own lives. A sad phenomenon, which will not let itself be combated by the old means of “laying [them] under the fence” [burial of suicides at the cemetery's edge]; and the saddest thing about it is that the spiritual leaders, the so-called ones as well as the genuine ones, do not feel the great misfortune and seek no remedy for it.
In times of frequent suicides of a religious nature, in times of forced conversion and sharp religious persecution, various rabbis and great men of Israel also came out against it, and taught and admonished the public not to play the role of martyrs light-mindedly. Great and long is the history of our martyrology, but up to the present day we have not had to record such a black chapter of suicides for economic reasons. There were times when Jews were poor, very poor, and yet the bitterness of poverty did not dig itself deep into the Jewish soul; and even when it lasted for generations, it was generally regarded as a passing guest, as a “passing illness.” At times poverty was even made into a Jewish jewel, an adornment, and people preached “poverty befits Israel” [Aramaic, Hagigah 9b; printed “yat” for “ya'e”]. Poverty suits Jews only so that they should not be ashamed of it and should not let it bend them spiritually, morally, religiously and nationally. People sang to themselves the old “their idols are silver and gold” [? Ps. 115:4; printed garbled] and proudly carried their heads raised to the eternal God in heaven.
The Kozienice Maggid, of blessed memory, used to say: if you should hear that a Jew died of hunger, do not believe it. He died only of pride — for had he not been ashamed to say to Jews, “I am hungry!”, they would have given him something to eat. Today, however, people are so ashamed of poverty that one does not reveal the secret even to one's closest relatives; from above the public is taught to say “ki tov” [“it is good”]... “ki tov me'od” [“very good”]! And the bitter secret of present-day Jewish life is not allowed to be told openly; instead it is allowed to dig itself ever deeper inwards and to gnaw the Jewish soul away until its ruin.
When flaming words of comfort and trust ought to warm the numbed and despairing Jewish heart, tongues of fire, of hatred and enmity, go forth; when certain doors and certain gates, hearts and minds, ought to open under the pressure of the heavy squeeze of general Jewish want, they are blocked with personal, foolish, penny-worth little petitions, which are dressed in tallit and shtreimel and hung with the emerald [?] crown of Torah.
On the other hand, everything is again allowed to decay, to dry up and to freeze. What is demanded and required most of all is what we are least able to give — property. The soul is forgotten entirely; it is entirely forgotten that besides the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael [Jewish National Fund], into whose boxes one must throw [coins], there is another “Keren Kayemet LeIsrael”, which one must throw into the hearts, into the souls of the tormented Jews.
The political struggle for Jewish rights is one of the roads that lead to consolation, but that road can be walked only from time to time, and not every individual Jew can take part in it. On the other hand there are old, well-trodden roads on which we have always walked towards the light.
In plain Yiddish this is called “learning Torah”; others call it “the science of Judaism”; the very modern call it “cultural work”; but the rich content suffices for all the names, whereas the deeds do not suffice even for one of the names.
When there is no money, there is surely its equivalent — time; and idle time is, for poor people, the most wretched thing in the world. Therefore the time must be used to raise Jewish courage, to warm the Jew's heart, to revive his soul with spiritual nourishment, with “mazon ruhani”, which will give him strength and power to endure the material sufferings, the “sufferings of the body” of this bitter time. The long winter nights are coming, and not a single Jew should sit in an unheated room spinning his black, despairing thoughts. Let lessons be taught in these nights to the broad masses that they will be able to digest; let lectures be held on various topics of Jewish culture. Let clear and luminous thoughts drive away the worries and troubles of the Jewish heart, if only for an hour a day, if only for a few hours a week; and let Jewish brotherliness and warmth be created anew in that atmosphere, so that hungry Jews will not be ashamed to say “I am hungry”, and the sated will not pretend not to hear the sighs of their brothers.
The heat burns, and the little sheep must shade one another by the old tents of the shepherds. And the shepherds — let them take care of it.
Jews, You Are Going to Be Counted!

We have too many troubles in our lives right now, too many worries on our hearts, to be really able to pause even for a moment over the latest decree on a general population census. And that is truly a pity, even a great pity. A population census — that is, after all, truly a great event in the life of a state, a kind of "soul-searching" (cheshbon ha-nefesh) of a large, compact human mass on a firmly defined territory within the borders of a state organism.

On the day fixed by the government, census commissioners go out across cities and towns, villages and settlements, wherever in fact there is a human concentration, and they register and count the people, the citizens, men and women, small and great, with their whole households and their property, lock, stock and barrel. At first the citizen takes fright, especially in times like these. Is it possible that a state official should inquire about a citizen, his goods and chattels, and that this should not have even the slightest connection with the lamentable tax matters about which every Polish citizen has so much to sing and tell? Is it possible that all the information gathered at first hand will not be used by those interested in the true information — the organs of power?

So the citizen does take fright, the citizen battered by the days of crisis; he takes fright and does not want to give the true information.

The citizen must therefore be made to understand that he is, begging his pardon, mistaken, greatly mistaken. The information that the census commissioner needs has no connection whatsoever with tax matters, or with the actual state of his wealth. Nor can the information be exploited by the interested parties in their offices. Quite simply, the information is needed for the census itself, for its own sake; that is precisely why the decree of the Council of Ministers speaks of the urgent necessity of giving all correct, proper and true information.

We believe that the citizen will understand the important significance of the population census and will act in accordance with his conscience and good will. But let us also hope and believe that the Polish government, for the good of the matter itself, taking into account that Poland is a state of nationalities, will see to it that in those centres where compact masses of a given nationality live, census commissioners from that very nationality are appointed. That alone will create confidence in the census. A Jew will surely relate with more trust to an "own" census commissioner than to another. A Jew will also not make chance mistakes when stating his nationality or mother tongue and will, of course, not mix up these two concepts. The commissioner, incidentally, will see to that too. These are all questions that cannot be thrown "under the hand" [sic; i.e. brushed aside], but must be seriously considered. There must therefore be a proportional share of Jewish census commissioners and census officials, both paid and unpaid, in carrying out the coming population census.

The municipal council (Magistrat) must confirm the proper number of Jews for the forthcoming work (and also for the present preparatory work). Candidates, thank God, will not be lacking now, in the prevailing crisis...

Mother and Wife (A Gripping Novel of Jewish Life) — 4

[Serialized novel — from Jewish life; installment 4.]
Sh. Relkes.

But when he saw her bright face, he was grateful to her for coming. A strange girl, this Sarahle: she has no brains, she is poor, but she breathes so much joy that David feels good when she is near him. If she did not keep talking about getting married all the time, he would always be with her.

— Why are you so sulky, David? — Sarahle asked — slept badly?

— Sarahle, you, it seems, slept well; you always sleep...

— Don't be angry with your little girl...

David looked at her with astonished eyes: why is she pretending not to know? After all, he had told her clearly that between them everything was over. However many times she had asked him to take her somewhere, he had wriggled out of it. He has no time, or he is tired, or he has to study. And when she pressed close to him, he told her simply and openly: I'm fed up with you, Sarahle.

— Well, what are you waiting for? — Sarahle came up close to him — give me a kiss.

She smelled of freshness. Her body aroused him. Her full lips were as if wet with dew. David could not withstand the temptation. He put his arms around her, pressed her to himself and felt in his powerful arms how she trembled. Sarahle fastened herself onto his lips; his head spun...

— Do you love me, David? — she said quietly — say that you love me...

David answered nothing. He pressed her to himself still more tightly, as if he wanted to find comfort for himself in her. Whether he had the courage for it [?] — he himself did not know. Now he needed someone close. Now he needed Sarahle. She is as light as a summer bird. She is an alluring woman. When he holds her in his arms, he himself feels light, and the dark thoughts dissolve like smoke.

— David, say that you love me — Sarahle kept pleading with him.

— Silly girl, what are words? Women just love to prattle [?].

— I'm cross with you. Just one word, tell me: love. Dear Dovidl, just one word.

While David and Sarahle were in the room, the mother sat over a glass of coffee, and through her head ran all her years, one picture after another. As in a cinema, her own show passed before her. She saw everything as if alive, as though she had lived through it only yesterday.

Her decision was now made: to tell David, and Sarahle should be present too. If David, when he was alone, received her life story with resentment and perhaps with anger, then in Sarahle's presence he would be softer. The mother felt that precisely now David was attached to the girl whom he had earlier wanted to push away. Besides, she thought that if Sarahle were present it would influence David to change his attitude towards her, to become more humane and more compassionate.

— David, Sarahle — she called out from the dining room — come in and grab a bite; it's late anyway. You'll still have time to talk.

Sarahle was the first to jump in. She looked happy, she was all radiant, and with joyful tears she fell on the mother's neck, kissed her and said fluttering words that perhaps made no sense, but expressed the mood of a happy girl.

— Oh! It's so good... David is so dear... so kind.

Tears welled up in the mother's eyes too. She pressed the girl to herself, stroked her golden hair, kissed her forehead and in a trembling voice called her "my child", "my little girl".

Why this woman, David's mother, loved Sarahle so much, she herself did not know. After all, the girl is really not overly clever, not developed enough; she lacks the qualities that make a modern-day girl interesting. But she is so simple, so naive and open-hearted [?] that one can love her. Yet that alone would perhaps not have made David's mother so attached to her. The main thing is that the woman, who had herself lived through the bitterest tragedy of her life, was afraid that her son might bring almost the same tragedy upon an innocent girl. Should, God forbid, the misfortune happen, she saw Sarahle's life like an open book. She read it chapter after chapter, because she herself had lived through it.

Meanwhile David came in. He was flushed, his face was burning. Was he ashamed that he had only just cast off his sweetheart so, and now had fallen under her spell again? No, he did not think about that. He felt good. Instinctively he felt that Sarahle was destined for him and that today his fate had been sealed.

— Mama, I'm hungry as a wolf — he said jokingly, and watched with pleasure the scene of his mother holding Sarahle in her arms.

— Good, children, sit down at the table, and we'll have a royal feast.

My Song.

[Literature — poetry in translation.] H. N. Bialik. Translated [into Yiddish] by Roza Yakubovitsh [Róża Jakubowicz].

You ask where my song comes from?
Early on, my childish mind
listened to a blind cricket
that hid in the crack of the stove
in my mother's native home;
as a child I had a "krush" [?] in my throat,
and from pain I groaned hollowly to myself,
knowing that of the grown-ups, them,
no one grasps my dread of pain;
only when at times, tired of woe,
my mouth fell silent in my cradle,
the cricket would already chirp to me from the wall [?],
and it bores into my sick ear,
and it chirps and twitters on my skin,
teaching me already in my smallness
the song of suffering and want.
Sabbath — the wicks flicker
of the little candles in the sand
— the candlesticks are pawned too —
shadows creep along the walls,
we lack the kiddush wine,
but one must be merry after all!
Father strikes up the song:
"Come, Sabbath Queen"
to angels on high,
but Mother looks on, pale,
at how around the Sabbath table,
with the herring, salt and bread,
all the children sit ready,
how Father cuts and cuts,
divides with the blunt knife,
as if sinful and ashamed...
In the stomach the pain still rumbles,
when the "motzi" [the blessed bread] vanishes from us,
as if someone had robbed us...
"Kol mekadesh", everything praises
the day of the holy Sabbath today!
Father sings anew already,
and we little children beside him
help with the zemirot too,
and the cricket whistles its song...

The weekdays wind along,
like a little boat far from the shore
that cannot see any way.
What to do no one knows,
when there is no bread in the basket —
you might as well go away and die.
Father thinks, looks around
at the ugly, mute poverty [?],
seven children listen up,
the hunger too comes to an end [?],
and they hide in fear
facing the days of hunger —

You ask where my tear comes from?
In one night, when all at once
everything becomes desolate, empty and shattered.
Father is no more,
the piece of body of our body
goes to sleep in the earth,
the clock stands still, not a fly buzzes,
Mother's glances, orphaned,
wander: God in heaven, strengthen
me, that I may provide,
that I can [feed] my little worms alone!

She sets up a stall in the market,
she comes back from the street,
she is worn out, pale,
she sits until midnight,
sewing by the yellow lamp — for hours;
the tear must be mended!
She sits and sews, at every stitch [?]
an "oy" tears from her breast
and the little flame trembles grey:
so, so,
at last she lies down in bed,
the little bed groans; soon now
she will throw off the burden,
only the Shema — a murmur
carries in the darkness,
and the chirping between the walls
without a beginning, without an end.

And at dawn, the rooster crows,
I see her already dressed,
how she stands at the dough, kneading,
the kneading-trough rocks...
as she whispers her prayer
that knocks on the walls of the house:
"Sweet Father, hear me out,
I am, after all, just a widow!"
Whom is my life of use to?
And the tear fell into the dough.

In the morning Mother shares out
the bread from the stove-ledge [?],
I swallow my portion, hot,
and taste Mother's tear.
From the Past in Zagłębie.

[History — the Jews of Zagłębie; serial, part I.] (A leaf of Jewish history).
I.
Under the editorship of the well-known historian M. Kantor-Mirski, a series of monographs on Zagłębie has recently appeared. In these monographs we find, among other things, interesting figures and facts about the life of the Jews from the time they settled in Zagłębie up to the present day.
"The eternal wanderers," — Mr. Mirski begins — "having no fatherland of their own (?), the Jews arrived in Poland en masse in the year 1096. They settled in all the towns as well as in the villages. In Zagłębie the Jews appeared for the first time in March 1226. In the records of the Bytom [Beuthen] community it is written that the Jews at first occupied themselves with working the land, and together with all the burghers they were obliged to pay taxes (dziesięciny — tithes). A larger influx of Jews into Zagłębie became noticeable only in the XIIth century, when they were persecuted in almost all of Western Europe; at that time they found a place of refuge in Poland.
In the XIVth century they had already abandoned working the land and took up trade, opening various shops[?] (grajzleznie — grocery shops) and engaging in money-changing (wekslarstwo).
In the first half of the XVth century, after the expulsion from Spain, the Jews began to settle in almost all the larger towns of Poland, and of course in Będzin too, where they soon took over authority over all the Jews of the whole surrounding area. Already in the year 1450 we see the Jews well organised. In the XVIth century Będzin already had a kehilla, at whose head stood the rabbi.
The Jews in Poland were regarded as foreigners, because they were subject to the authority of the Polish kings. Responsible to the king for the Jews was the voivode, or in the smaller towns the burgrave (starosta), and for that reason the Jews were not subject to any [other] courts. If a dispute arose between Jews, it was judged in the first instance by a beth din consisting of the rabbi as chairman and assessors (ławnicy) delegated by the kehilla. On the other hand, if a dispute arose between a Jew and a Christian, it too had to pass through the "Jewish court", but in the presence of the voivode or the starosta. The sessions of this so-called court took place mostly in the synagogue. Next to the synagogue there was a jail, which was maintained by the Jews themselves. In the year 1591 regulations of the court in the Hebrew and Polish languages were hung up in the Będzin synagogue. To the voivode, for attending the sessions of the courts, the Jews of Będzin gave 100 gulden a year and 10 kilos of spices (saffron and cinnamon). Whether this was a fixed tax or a voluntary gift is not known.
At first the Jews of Będzin were severely restricted in their rights. They could settle only in certain parts of the town and had special days for trading. Only when they had grown somewhat stronger did they come forward, together with the Jews of Kraków, regarding privileges. The efforts were successful, and in the year 1453 the Polish king Kazimierz Jagiellończyk granted various privileges. Most probably on the basis of these privileges the synagogue and the cemetery were established, traces of which are still found[?] to this day in the streets Marzijowska[?] and Zawale. The privileges also permitted the Jews to conduct trade, but only wholesale, and even that only in such goods as were permitted to be bought abroad as well. For bringing goods from abroad the Jews had to pay a higher duty than the Christian merchants. From the beginning of the 16th century the policy towards the Jews changed for the better. In the year 1527 Zygmunt I, in a special ordinance, put the Jewish merchants on an equal footing with the Christian ones, so that the Jews now paid the same duty as the Christians, and they (the Jews) could begin to become competitive. A few years later we already see the Jews as lessees of taverns, owners of mills, as officials collecting the royal customs, etc.
King Stefan Batory permitted the Jews to live in the town proper and to trade at the market alongside the Christian merchants. In the year 1592 the Będzin magistrate received a rescript from King Zygmunt III, in which it is ordered that the Jews be defended against all wrongs[?] and attacks, and that the rights granted to the Jews be safeguarded.
The Jews were freest in the times of King Władysław IV, who was the first to recognise the Jews as full citizens of the country.
Always, when a new king ascended the Polish throne, the Jews of Będzin sent a delegation to him with a request to confirm the privileges already obtained. So it happened also when Jan Sobieski became king: a special delegation then travelled to him, but it came back with nothing, because the king answered that he was busy with more important matters. The Jewish kehilla, however, did not let the matter slip, and 11 years later it received from King Jan Sobieski a confirmation written on parchment. This document is today in the armoured safe of the Będzin magistrate, thanks to Dr. Maksymilian Reicher, in whose possession this document had been.

Sz. Szach.
Jewish Trades Are Going Under

For the attention of our ladies and young women.

The Jewish masses, the whole Jewish population, are now so preoccupied with their own worries that one does not see at all how, before our very eyes, ruins are taking place in which whole strata of the Jewish population are going under.

Entire trades in which Jewish workers still had a foothold are being torn out of their hands and are passing over to others. We do not wish to point here to trades such as shoemaking, baking and others, which are being torn out of Jewish hands for reasons of mechanisation and rationalisation. But it is worth pointing to trades which we ourselves are tearing out of Jewish hands, taking away the piece of bread from Jewish workers.

We wish to begin with the hairdressing trade (fryzjer), a trade which was eighty per cent in Jewish hands. The clientele was Jewish and the work was always good. New forces regularly entered the trade, and it was a source of livelihood for many Jewish workers.

When, several years ago, the season of ladies' work at the hairdressers began, when there could have been a prospect that unemployment among Jews in this trade would disappear and many dozens more workers would be able to join the trade, it turned out that the hopes were in vain.

Here one must already call the child by its name. The fault lies in the conduct of the Jewish women.

Ever since the fashion of short hair for women, of ondulation (waving) etc. etc., came up, these Jewish ladies and young women have developed a great demand solely for non-Jewish workers. It has become a fashion that one must, precisely, have one's hair cut by Jans, Bronisławs, Stanisławs and Romans. The non-Jewish shops began to be frequented by the Jewish women, and the existence of the Jewish hairdressing establishments was threatened. The masters, however, quickly grasped where the reason lay why their shops stood empty while [?] others were overcrowded. And they had to comply with the demands of the Jewish ladies' clientele and take on non-Jewish workers for ladies' work. And it seems that there are now almost no hairdressing establishments where non-Jewish workers are not employed in the ladies' salons; as for Jewish workers in non-Jewish shops — there can be no talk of that at all.

Thus, unnoticed [?] by all of us, because of the fault of the Jewish ladies and young women, Jewish workers are being pushed out of the trade in which they worked. It is not a matter of the masters here, but precisely of the workers; nor is there any influx of Jews into the trade, because the prospects of obtaining a post are minimal.

The Jewish trade unions are in a very difficult situation; from the trade-union point of view everything, it seems, is in order. But our ladies hinder and frustrate the struggle for the right to work. Jewish work is good; it is merely a matter of a whim and a fashion-thing, and because of it a Jewish trade is dying out.
The Catastrophic Situation of Polish Jewry

The picture of the catastrophic situation of Polish Jewry is already strikingly clear to everyone. The picture literally leaps to the eye in its cruel, tragic scale. One can no longer turn one's gaze and one's thoughts away from it.
Even the greatest pessimists among us could not have imagined that the process of pauperization of the broadest Jewish masses in Poland would grow and spread with such giant strides and take on such cruel forms.
As the situation presents itself today, it will be no exaggeration at all to assert that all of Polish Jewry — with the exception of only isolated individuals, who represent a mere negligible percentage of the whole Jewish population — has reached a complete and total ruin.
What the causes are that have led to this hopeless situation is more or less clear to everyone, and there is no need to say much about them.
On the one hand it was brought about by the economic policy pursued by all Polish governments and Sejms[?] without exception, whose leitmotif was to throw the whole burden of taxes onto the towns, and in the towns — onto the Jewish population. Then came the policy of étatism, which ruined many healthy and useful economic positions, bringing to nobody, literally nobody — for not even to the government itself — any benefit at all, and in many cases even double harm: on the one hand the étatist enterprises caused loss to the state treasury; on the other, the same treasury further lost the quite respectable taxes it used to collect from the owners of those economic enterprises which étatism had destroyed.
And as if all this were not enough, the state monopolies were added, from which the state treasury in the overwhelming majority of cases had more losses than profit (compared with the situation in the fields of trade before the monopolies were created). Not to speak of the state's loss in that thousands and tens of thousands of its citizens — good taxpayers, incidentally — became jobless and without a livelihood. In general the whole set-up and organization of economic life in the country bore a more or less (depending on which economic fields) marked antisemitic character, and that antisemitic character found its most marked expression in the attitude of the state banks towards the Jewish institutions, which knocked on their doors in vain and without success, asking for credit support in whatever measure, even in a smaller measure than that which the non-Jewish economic institutions enjoy.
All this led gradually and incessantly to today's catastrophic, almost hopeless situation on the one hand — on the other, it was brought about by the complete failure of the broadest Jewish popular strata in Poland to prepare themselves for today's economic conditions, which could have been foreseen some time ago. It is beyond any doubt for me that even if the catastrophe had not then passed us by, with proper preparation of the Jewish masses the situation would not have been as hopeless as it is today.
It is an unshakeable fact that today practically no trace whatever has remained of Jewish commerce in Poland, which in its time was so strong and durable[?]. At most there have remained, here and there, isolated signs of the ruins of the once so firmly grounded and powerful edifice of Jewish commerce. Having entirely lost their working capital, the Jewish merchants have been turned into the poorest middlemen, into that so tragic type of people who live on air, in the literal and cruel sense of the words.
No better at all is the situation of Jewish artisanry. Here too the picture is no less catastrophic and hopeless. Here too the crisis has taken on such a scale and such forms that until today it has had no equal, nor even anything similar. Good and skilled craftsmen, people with many years of practice and masters of their trade, must take up work that has nothing in common with their professional training. They become porters, street watchmen, etc., just to keep themselves alive. Of course these are already the good cases — when they can find even such menial work, they count themselves lucky. Mostly, however, they find no work at all and swell the already large enough and steadily growing army of the unemployed.
As for the Jewish worker, unemployment has been a plague in his ranks for several years already — and the plague grows with giant strides and takes the cruellest forms. And while the manual workers still find a little work, the Jewish intelligentsia, the brain-workers and people of the free professions have been left standing before a real abyss.
These[?] were the signs that some time ago already announced the coming of this situation. Nevertheless nothing, literally nothing, nothing substantial was done to prepare the broadest strata of the Jewish population for the unavoidable catastrophe and to create such conditions as would at least to a certain extent ease the resistance to the waves of ruin and give the staying power to get through hard, tragic times.
Our slogan about the regrouping (occupational restructuring) of the Jewish masses found no echo, in any case certainly not the proper echo, in the time of the good economic boom. The help of our brothers abroad too, and above all precisely of our American brothers, which[?] was so considerable and effective in quantity, was however not considerable and effective enough in quality: the tens of millions of dollars that reached us were squandered; in any case they were far, far from properly used. Because of the bad management of the funds they were quickly used up[?], bringing no lasting and successful benefit.
There were single, or perhaps dozens of, public workers who at the right time pointed to the great danger lurking for the Jewish population in Poland. But to our great regret they were not heeded, and their words of warning were decried as the words of sworn pessimists. It is therefore no wonder at all that today, when the Jewry of Poland is living through a catastrophe that has had no equal in the history of the Jews in Poland — all have remained powerless and helpless.
Deputy Dr. D.[?] Rozmaryn.
From the 10th Picture Exhibition (of the Zagłębie Artists in Sosnowiec)

Twenty-four painters with over 200 exhibits took part in the exhibition, not counting the pictures by Skoczylas, Juliusz and Wojciech Kossak, which happen to be there by chance.
Of all the exhibitors, worth considering are: Eugeniusz Gargen[?], who has a sense for colour, and in whose portraits and still lifes a painterly culture can be felt.
The same can be said of Władysław Araszkiewicz[?], who was especially successful with the still life „The Black Vase with Oranges“, which is kept in a warm, juicy tone and compels the viewer to linger over it longer.
Wacław Pilecki has a couple of good drawings of children's heads. On the other hand he is weak in colour. His „Będzin Castle“ is so pale, so poor in colour, that one really needed courage to exhibit it publicly.
The rest give the impression of run-of-the-mill („im kol ha-ne'arim“) exhibitors, over whom one can pass on to the order of the day with a clear[?] conscience.
Special attention is deserved by Ignacy Buchner, who is a specialist in ivory carving. He has a whole series of miniature portraits of great men such as: Marx, Einstein, Beethoven, Ibsen, etc., which are masterfully executed.
It is a very difficult task, both from the artistic and from the technical side, to bring out the smallest details of character traits in such miniature work.
Of the wood carvings, good ones are: „Yom Kippur“, after the painting by M. Gottlieb, and „Passover“ after Lilien.
Sh. R.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Noach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Noach
The Portion
—o—
a) "Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generations" (6:9).
"Some of our Rabbis interpret it to his credit... and some interpret it to his discredit"... Rashi.
The Torah bears witness that Noah was a blameless tzaddik — so why tell of him that some interpret it to his discredit?
The tzaddik of the generation, the true spiritual leader of the people, is only the one about whom there are those who interpret him unfavourably. Only the leader who flatters everyone has no opponents. It is praise for a leader when there are people who speak ill of him... Nechmad mi-Zahav (Rabbi Yechezkele of Kuzmir [Kazimierz Dolny]).
—o—
b) "And he sent forth the dove from him" (8:8).
Noah had to send a bird to the Land of Israel, where it did not rain during the Flood; only the subterranean deeps burst upward ("a land not rained upon in the day of wrath"). There trees had remained, and there one could tell whether "the waters had abated" —
He sent a dove because the Congregation of Israel is likened to a dove (Shabbat 49), and presumably [misprinted "mikhtama"] there is something alike in their root... And therefore, when the dove flew beyond the borders of the erased world, she was drawn to the Land of Israel, just as every Jewish heart is drawn instinctively to the Land of Israel. Be'er Mayim Chayim (Rabbi Chaim of Czernowitz).
• • •
A remarkable, strange thing is brought by Rabbi Jacob Emden in his book "Migdal Oz": that a dove does not pluck any leaf from an attached plant on the Sabbath...
This is written by Rabbi Jacob Emden, the great critic, who was far from superstitious...
• • •
An interesting folklore remark we found in the book "Likutei Maharil" by Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Zaklików — a disciple of the Seer [of Lublin]):
People say of someone who talks a lot: "He needs no leaf before his mouth." What does it mean?
It most probably comes from this portion. The dove could not speak, but hinted with the leaf in its mouth that the water [printed split, "what he"] had already subsided; and one who talks a lot does not use hints — he needs no leaf before his mouth...
—o—
c) "And lo, in her mouth an olive leaf plucked off" (8:11).
An aggadic homily:
"The dove said: I would rather eat something bitter as an olive from God's hand than sweet food like honey from the mouth of man." Eruvin 18.
In Grace after Meals we pray: "Do not make us dependent on the gift (singular) of flesh and blood nor on their loans" (— plural).
Why this inconsistent grammar? —
Because regarding a human gift, we pray that we should not need to come even to the gift of individuals. But a loan — every person must come to that; we pray only that from [printed "o"] the good friend to whom we go to ask a small interest-free loan we should get it at once, and not have to drag ourselves from one to another for a loan... "Nor on their loans" — not to need to come to many loans, going to borrow from one to the next... Sichat Chachamim.
—o—
d) "Flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat" (9:4).
This means not to drink another's blood: another's toil; not to rob and plunder... Nachal Kedumim.
—o—
e) "And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech" (11:1).
"One language" means, according to the homily, the Holy Tongue. But Hebrew was with them only "from the lips outward". They merely spoke Hebrew, but did not penetrate to the living root of the language; the tongue was not in the depths of their heart...
Mei ha-Shiloach (— Rabbi Mordechai Yosef of Izbica).
—o—
f) "And let us make us a name" (11:4).
The generation of the Dispersion strove for unity: "lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth." But unity can exist only among those who honestly mean one thing. Wickedness cannot bind in unity, because each has a different motive: one wants to make himself a name, another is after money, etc., etc. Only around truth can thousands of people be united and have one aspiration. But in falsehood each has his own particular falsehood.
Kli Yakar.
—o—
g) "Let us confound their language there" (11:7).
When God saw that unity was about to arise among the nations, He grew afraid for His Jews. For the Jews are well off only when the nations quarrel, tear at one another and forget the Jew. But as soon as there is peace, they begin devising decrees against the Jews... When the wolves bite one another, the little lamb can catch its breath...
Me'or va-Shemesh (— Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman).
• • •
"Pray for the welfare of the government."
When the kingdoms have peace among themselves, you, Jew, must pray well, for new decrees are presumably being prepared...
The Maggid of Kelm.
—o—
h) "So the Lord scattered them" (11:8).
See: Korah sinned against Moses — and he and his company sank alive into the earth; the generation of the Dispersion sinned against God — and their punishment was only to be scattered over the world. Because Korah conducted strife, while the generation of the Dispersion was united and preached unity.
Such is the power of unity, even among sinners!... Chen Tov.
—o—
Haftarah.
i) "And all thy children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of thy children" (Isaiah 54).
If there is peace for your builders ("read not 'your children' but 'your builders'"), if Torah scholars fare well in the world — then "all thy children shall be taught of the Lord", people will let their children study. But today they say that a Torah scholar must be a pauper, so nobody wishes to make his child a scholar... R' Zeev Margaliot.
—o—
j) "And all thy borders of precious stones" (ibid.).
"She is more precious than rubies" — the value of gold and pearls is only because there are few of them in the world. Were there much gold, it would lose its worth.
Torah and knowledge, however — the more of them there is, the more worth they have; they are "precious stones". Whereas where there is little Torah, even the few chosen Torah scholars enjoy no esteem... Kokhav mi-Yaakov.

A Second Artisans' Association Founded.

[Będzin — artisans/organisations.]
On Saturday night the founding meeting of the new Jewish artisans' association in Będzin took place in the premises of the Aguda [Agudat Yisrael].
In the presence of a large number of artisans Mr. Grosman opens the meeting and proposes Mr. Leibl Fuks as chairman, to which all agree. The chairman invites to the presidium R' Hirshl Dymant, Ch. R. Grosman, R' Avraham Leib Grünwald, R' Gavriel Feldman and Dovid Silbergold. Then Mr. Efraim Klajman speaks, who explains the reasons that led to a second association being created, and he calls on those assembled to register as members en masse. Messrs. Grünwald, Tuchsznajder and Grosman also speak. After the reading of the statute, which is adopted en bloc unanimously, the following administration is appointed: Chaim Dovid Grosman (president), Hirsh Dymant (vice), Leibl Fuks, Avraham Leib Grünwald (secretary), Avraham Springer (treasurer), Gavriel Feldman, Abba Zelinger, Bezalel Kupferwasser, Mendl Ropczyc, Dovid Silbergold, Shmuel Wolf Sochaczewski and Yosef Tuchsznajder.
Afterwards a melave malke was held in Hasidic fashion. The crowd is lively; the joining together of the Ger and Sochaczew Hasidim, the new rising “artisan stars”, with the modern artisans is very heartfelt. After the meal R' Leibl Fuks sings “Shir ha-Ma'alot”, R' Gavriel Feldman is the “bentsher” [leader of grace after meals], and at the end a “hora” is danced with the “Tse'irim” and the “Poalim” [Agudat Yisrael youth and workers]...
— May it be in a lucky hour!

Will the tax arrears be liquidated?

[Economy — taxes.] One of the latest decrees of the Ministry of Finance, which came into force on the 1st of September this year (Dz. Ust. No. 77, item 613), deals with a series of important questions concerning the organisation and competences of the fiscal authorities.
We shall dwell on that part of the decree which deals at length with the extended prerogatives of the Treasury Chambers and Treasury Offices in granting tax relief. As we shall see below, it is above all the old tax arrears that are taken into account; [otherwise?] the decree brings no particularly important novelties.
For a large part of the merchants it is nevertheless of interest to become acquainted with the new decree, because more than one has had to close his shop on account of tax arrears, not being able to pay them off.
Under § 27 of the new decree the Treasury Chamber (Izba Skarbowa) receives the right to cancel arrears of turnover tax (obrotowy) in cases where it recognises this as justified, up to 5,000 złoty for each taxpayer within a year, as well as outstanding fines for violating arts. 104, 97 [sic] of the turnover-tax law, for example for not holding a trade patent (licence) or for not holding the proper patent.
The "Izba" also has the right to cancel unpaid or underpaid income tax (dochodowy) up to 2000 złoty for each taxpayer for previous years. The provision also covers the old monetary fines provided for in arts. 91–94 [?] of the income-tax law, such as fines for not filing returns (zeznania) on time, for not giving explanations demanded by the authorities, etc.
The "Izba" may also spread into instalments arrears (except advance payments [zaliczki] of turnover tax and payments of income tax) for a sum of up to 20 thousand złoty for an unlimited time, and not, as until now, only for 6 months.
Tax debts of up to 50 thousand złoty the "Izba" may spread into instalments payable over 20 months, and sums of 100 thousand złoty — for a period of up to 12 months. It is worth noting that until now the "Izba" had no right at all to spread into instalments tax debts exceeding 20 thousand zł.
Besides this the "Izba" is given the right to defer payments of tax arrears for a period of 3 months, each sum not exceeding 100 thousand złoty, as well as payments of advance instalments for up to 2 months.
Arrears of real-estate tax (od nieruchomości) the "Izba" may cancel if the debt does not exceed the sum of 500 złoty.
In connection with the enlargement of the competence of the second instance there naturally also had to come proportional changes in the competences of the Treasury Offices (urzędy skarbowe) as the first instance.
Here too the prerogatives regarding tax relief have been considerably enlarged. The urząd skarbowy has the right (§ 54) to spread into instalments all direct tax arrears, if they do not exceed 20 thousand złoty. The urząd may also defer for a period of 2 months payments of tax arrears which were not remitted by the "Izba" [printed "Iofa"] and do not amount to more than 5000 złoty.
Especially important, however, is the clause dealing with the question of reducing the penalty for late payments (za zwłokę [?]). Point d. of § 84 of the decree stresses that on tax arrears which are spread into instalments or deferred, the fiscal authorities have the right at the same time to reduce the interest to as low as 1 per cent monthly.
In all the above-mentioned cases the taxpayer must, of course, submit a well-reasoned application, supported by evidence, which should convince the fiscal authorities that the [situation —] of the taxpayer is such that it deserves favourable treatment.
These, in brief, are the provisions of the new decree, which is already in force. As we see, the hopes that the tax arrears would be cancelled altogether have unfortunately not been fulfilled for the time being; it remains only to believe that perhaps the fiscal authorities, now receiving wider competences, will proceed to liquidate the old tax arrears, which in any case cannot be collected. This would put an end to the present state of uncertainty, and many former merchants would again set about seeking for themselves and their families some livelihood.

Chaim Nachman Bialik's Visit to Będzin / The President of the Będzin Merchants' Association, Mr. Rubinlicht, Intervenes About the Incorrect Assessment of Income Tax / Distributor of Counterfeit 5-Złoty Coins Arrested in Będzin / Prison for Anti-State Activity / Concert by Artur Rubinstein in Katowice / Strike at Fitzner's Factory Ended / The "HaTechiya" Organization in Sosnowiec / From the Zionist Organization in Sosnowiec / A List of Those Over-Assessed in the Income Tax / Theatre Repertoire

On Wednesday afternoon [21 October 1931] the poet H. N. Bialik came to Będzin; he had been invited as a guest of the family of H. Szejn. In the evening he was at the premises of the Zionist Org., where he touched on current Zionist matters.
On Thursday at 12 noon the distinguished guest was invited
to the Hebrew "Gan Yeladim" (kindergarten).
Present were the board of "WIZO" and several mothers, to whom Bialik spoke about Jewish education and Jewish life.
After the Hebrew greetings by Mrs. Ratner and the kindergarten teacher Miss Glinka, Bialik says a few warm Jewish words, especially to the Jewish mothers, that they should not spoil at home what their little children receive in the kindergarten.
A very fine impression is made by the greeting of 3 little children: they greet Bialik, present a bouquet of flowers, and create a homely atmosphere by dancing and singing Bialik's poem "El ha-Tzippor" ("To the Bird").
From the kindergarten Bialik went
to Firsztenberg's [Fürstenberg's] Gymnasium
In the large gymnastics hall all the pupils, from small to big, were assembled.
After the greetings by the pupil Skrowiński and the girl pupil Dafner, who presented Bialik with a bouquet of flowers, Bialik turns with a speech to the pupils. Here one hears Bialik the preacher of reproof: with pathos he speaks to the youth, that they should rebel against the fact that all other languages are taught to a sufficient extent, while to Hebrew only 6 hours a week are given.
"Study Torah," Bialik exclaims, "speak your own language, demand of your parents that the home, the surroundings, be Jewish..."
With the singing of "HaTikva" by all the pupils the visit comes to an end.

The Postal Minister's Visit to Zagłębie — The New Post Office Building in Będzin Opened

[Zagłębie — post and telecommunications.] On Saturday morning the Minister of Posts, Mr. Boerner, came to Sosnowiec. After the welcome at the railway station by the president of the Kraków Railway Directorate, the Minister went to the Sosnowiec post office. There he was welcomed by a number of representatives of municipal and economic organisations. Then the Minister visited all the departments of the post office, where 100 officials work in the worst hygienic conditions.
The Minister was disappointed by what his eyes saw — he could not, he says, believe that the Sosnowiec post office is housed in such premises.
On this question the Minister held a conference, and the plan arose that the P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank] should build a new post-office building, and the costs should be paid in instalments by the Postal Directorate.
It was also decided that, so that several rooms become free, the Sosnowiec central station for „zamiejskie“ [long-distance] telephone calls should be moved into the new Będzin post-office building.
The Minister visited the new telephone station on Małachowskiego Street in Sosnowiec. It [—?] next year [probably meant: will be handed over next year]. The station will be equipped with the newest automatic apparatus.
After the visit to the Dąbrowa post office the Minister came to Będzin to take part in the festive opening of the new post-office building on Narutowicza Street.

The „Activity“ of the Olkusz Kehilla (A Letter from Olkusz)

[Olkusz — kehilla.] As has already been reported, the Olkusz kehilla was dissolved by an order of the starosta on the basis of a complaint that „the elections were not in order“.
In connection with the new situation the kehilla administration gave a „surprise“ this Sunday: it called a meeting of all the shtiblekh and laid before the public a report on its activity. But the report was very lamentable and pale. Of any positive work there is absolutely nothing to record.
The aim of the meeting became clear only in the course of the debates: the intention is to create a „mood“ for the new elections.
The kehilla leaders did not at all understand that such meetings can also have a negative result — and so indeed it was. A flood of protests was heard against several of the leaders, especially against the „Agudah“: against their immoral conduct, against driving out the Jewish teacher of the public school by means of lies. To all these reproaches the Agudah president answered that „at holiday time he has no time for the kehilla“ [the printed word order is garbled].
When the writer of these lines remarked that kehilla leaders should be thanked only for achievements in work for the common good, and that if the shechita [ritual-slaughter revenue] has grown, perhaps the thanks are due to the Olkusz population and not to the kehilla, it burst like a bomb. The president dissolved the meeting and „fled“.
That is how the comedy ended which was played by the kehilla leaders up till now.
M. Sz.

A Heart-Rending Appeal — from an unfortunate to Jewish society

[Będzin — welfare; letter appealing for help.] Out of loneliness and want, with a pulse full of pain, I find myself obliged to turn for the first time with a letter to you, the Jewish population, and also to the communal workers in Będzin, as a son to his own father, to rescue me from the arms of death.
Know[?] that I am an orphan without a mother; my father is not of clear mind. Owing to the disunity of my family I was neglected, from which I became weakened, and for several years now I have been confined within four walls. I do not enjoy the air as every living person does. I am a young man, all of 20 years old — why should my young years rot prematurely in the earth? At a time when all my limbs are healthy and there is still a rescue for me. After all, I am still a young child, I have not yet enjoyed anything of the beautiful world — why must my young mind have to think that my fate, of hunger, want and loneliness, has been handed over to the arms of death, when my life can be saved by your sending me to a hospital, so that I may get back on my feet.
I am alone as a stone, I have nobody who would take an interest in me, and so I ask you, esteemed communal workers of the Jewish population in Będzin, to take an interest so that I may still be cured.
Respectfully,
J. Jakubowicz
Będzin, Podzamcze[?] 59.
Editorial note:
Having received the cry of woe of the unfortunate young man, we went to the address given, where we convinced ourselves that what is said in the letter is the minimum of the actual terrible situation. The man is drying up from day to day like a tree in autumn. All his senses are normal, he is quite conscious, but his legs will not carry him.
Merciful people! Take an interest in this man and remember the words "whoever saves one soul of Israel"...

Theatre Notes

[Sosnowiec — theatre; review.] "Roxy", a comedy in 3 acts by B. Conners, staged at the Municipal Theatre in Sosnowiec.
With the best impression, with contentment and satisfaction of artistic feeling one leaves the theatre after the excellent comedy "Roxy", which is now popular all over Poland as one of the best comedies in the Polish repertoire. For several months "Roxy" did not leave the Kraków stage at the Słowacki Theatre, and in Sosnowiec too "Roxy" has already been running for two weeks. The humour is very original. The sincere young girl "Roxy" has already learnt by heart, from a book containing one thousand four hundred and nineteen aphorisms[?], one hundred and twelve of them, and uses them on every occasion, declaiming in a poetic tone. Very often these are quite apt and clever opinions, yet they provoke laughter in the audience. The plot of the comedy creates a few pictures from the life of a present-day family. The hysterical mother, a coquette, helps her daughter in the chase after men, and both are ashamed of the father, who works hard as a commercial traveller (voyageur). He, poor man, does not want to buy a car, and for them it is surely not fitting to ride the tram. On the other side[?] stand the father and the youngest daughter, Roxy. We have already heard and seen all this; the whole plot is no news to us. Only the rich and original humour raises the value of the comedy. The actors play with great understanding, so that "Roxy" need not be ashamed even on the Warsaw stages.
Elge.
