On Watch Before a Catastrophe. (IV.) “Our Own People”, the Protection System, Politics, Intrigues and Ruins Get the Upper Hand Among Us

[Article — economy, the Jewish banks of Zagłębie.] “Our own people” — through them we become unfortunate. They are everywhere, and everywhere they tread themselves a path. They make a heap of ruins (tel-olam) of our communal interests, they bring everything to ruin, of everything they make ash and mud, and they overturn and twist everything with its feet in the air.
We created Jewish financial institutions; one bank was born after another, one credit institution after the other, and they began to develop. Gradually they cut themselves a path, step by step, slowly, systematically and consciously; out of a skeleton a body came into being, it was covered with flesh and skin, we saw before us the true human form, and people, strangers and our own, gained confidence in it. Christians began to hold Jewish financial institutions in esteem. Even Christians carried their money there. The sympathy and confidence in our credit institutions kept on growing, so that Christians as well as Jews, domestic as well as foreign firms, entrusted heavy fortunes to the Jewish banking businesses. With pride we could carry the banner of the Jewish cooperative financial institutions; in this field we broke the record, and therefore it hurt us when we saw that instead of popularising the cooperative idea in the financial field, people began to split up, turning the banks into little shops, little stalls. Instead of two fine big institutions in one town, six miniature little banks were created, which brought nothing but harm to the Jewish community as a whole; people began to crumble the grand edifice and gradually to tear whole pieces off it — every shtibl, every Hasid, every merchant and artisan and trade-branch man wanted to have his own little shop, and they achieved what they had aimed at, what they had been after. But that is not all: whoever says aleph must also say tav. Those who tore whole pieces limb by limb from the earlier institutions also had to go further; they evidently knew what they were aiming at and for what reason they must have their own little shops — they needed their own little banks, to be bosses themselves, and around this very “business” their own people began to circle, homely ones; and, as usual, at the very beginning they spent time “not for the sake of receiving a reward”, but already then they had a longer view and knew that it would not work “dry”, that something would stay stuck...
And, as usual, no account was taken of the fact that one must preserve the integrity of the bank — that however partisan it may be, it must still stand above that and remain above party. And when it came to elections, or when one needed to secure some representation or other, the management had already found a dispensation for how to take out money for the desired purpose.
But, of course, they did not stand still at that; they progressed, and those who received money assigned for the said purpose thought to themselves: since I receive money for my party, which is close to me, why indeed should I not take for myself too? After all, one cannot remain a stranger to oneself — and so they began to walk the slippery road, taking more and more, and the sums lent out began to reach tens of thousands of złoty. Besides, one must not forget: since Berl took, Shmerl raised a clamour[?] that he should be given too, otherwise he would “tell tales out of school” (literally: out of the heder). Well, it is understood that as soon as one starts to drown one wants to save oneself, and as there was no other way out, they began giving right and left; the bridle was torn, any system whatsoever ceased to exist, lawlessness (hefkerut) began to plunder[?] without any limit, and “our own people” always had access to their banks, and for them there was always money.
On the other hand, there was no money for the small and the middling people. When they came, whether in Będzin, in Sosnowiec or in Dąbrowa, to the “Bank Kupiecki” (Merchants' Bank) or the cooperative bank, there was not even the minimum sum for them. “This is a people's bank,” they were told, “and one must share it out to everyone; all must get some loan, a thousand or a few hundred złoty.” There was nothing for those whom one could have saved with such a sum — whereas tens of thousands of złoty were available at any time for every one of “our own people”. That is how far the management of the said institutions went; that is how they protected the people's interests, and how they accommodated the broad strata of the people with credit.
Who does not remember at what a high level the Spółdzielczy Bank (Cooperative Bank) once stood in Będzin, what confidence people had in it, what a great turnover it made and how large its own capital already was — and now, despite the attempts to save it by every possible means, it is being liquidated after all. Such is how easy it is to lose a good name, which one cannot buy for oneself, but which comes instinctively from the people. It is no different with the Będzin and Sosnowiec “Bank Kupiecki”: there too lawlessness began to get the upper hand. The protection system and “our own people” helped themselves in the meantime...
It is a disgrace and an anguish, and a deep pain seizes us when we begin to think in what way we ruin ourselves, how our guardians (apotropsim) care for their pockets and take no account of the fact that in this way they smash the most needed aid institutions, which were built up with so much toil and sweat. And actually, for when were these institutions built? And for whom were they built?
Why will people not take into account that the institutions are created by the people and entirely for the people? So by what right do these “own people” come and bury the institutions which are most useful in a time of distress, at a critical moment?!
There is a crisis now; a terrible time reigns over the whole world, capital starts to jump up and down, and one does not know in what world one finds oneself. It is understood that at such a time, in such a period, our own banks would have been useful to us, urgently necessary — banks that would serve the people, come to its aid, rescue it, help drag it out of the dangerous catastrophe that stands before its eyes.
When, if not today, has it been necessary that the credit institutions should rescue the people, so that it should not go off the rails, so that it should hold on and be able to stay in place?
It would seem that our credit institutions should above all have served to come to the aid of the people in such a time of distress as now — yet today we have ruins instead of healthy financial institutions.
This is what the splintering and fragmenting of large popular enterprises into small miniature banks has led to, where “politics” and intrigues played first fiddle, and thanks to which the elbowing-in[?] of “our own people” was made possible — they who have brought these useful institutions to their present sad state.
L. Szpigelman.
Gold parity and economic life

[Economy — essay; history of money.]
1.
It seems that the money-makers of old understood well the troubles that can arise from money which has no fixed and steady value. They therefore wanted to tie their currency of that time directly to marketable goods that played the greatest role in their economic life. The ancient Greeks wanted a fixed number of „drachmas" to represent an ox, and the Jews of old wanted a „shekel" to buy a fixed measure of olive oil (shemen zayit) — no more and no less. In this way they wanted to prevent the speculation and uncertainty bound up with the constantly fluctuating value of money.
This did not succeed. The history of antiquity is full of examples of how bad and debased money provoked an enormous rise in prices, wild speculation in products, the impoverishment of whole classes and the ruin of great nations.
This applies especially to the former Roman Empire.
The newest studies of Roman history prove that in the case of imperial Rome the blame lies not only with slavery — as [?] historians used to explain it until now; to an even greater degree the blame lay with the irresponsible monetary policy of its gold-thirsty emperors.
The silver coins, which were once the only currency of Rome, were in imperial times mixed more and more with baser metals (copper, iron, zinc). At the same time, however, they wanted to maintain a fixed exchange value of the bad silver money against the good gold money...
Naturally this was of no use. The result was that gold vanished from circulation. People hoarded it for coming generations, or sent it off to such distant lands as the rule of the Roman emperors did not reach. Much Roman gold accumulated in India, from where spices and other luxury articles used to be brought to Rome.
In Rome itself prices rose constantly because of the fallen value of the mixed and falsified silver money. The poor Roman citizens who were not slaves could not get by on their meagre income; the state budget, which was already based on money taxes, naturally could not be covered. The deficits and the extravagance of the Roman emperors forced them to mix ever more cheap metals into both the silver and the gold coins. By the year 270 of the Christian era Roman silver money already contained only two per cent silver.
Prof. Cunningham, one of the best economic historians of our generation, describes the resulting situation in the following words:
„The shortage of precious metals in Rome, together with their fluctuating value, made it ever harder to save money; it also took away the desire to engage in trade or industry. Trade was paralysed by the uncertainty of prices. There was even less desire to put money into agriculture; instead of investing money, people hoarded it. The consequence of this was a general disruption. Circulating capital is perhaps not necessary for primitive human life. But it is necessary to sustain such a civilised society as the Roman Empire was."
Do these lines not sound a little familiar? Could they not to a very great extent be said about the economic crisis we are living through today?
2.
Silver was used as money earlier than gold. Both in Greece and in Rome the first gold coins were struck some 200 years after the first silver coins had appeared.
As long as silver was the only coin — with the exception of copper, which was used for small everyday trade — all still went properly, especially when people were honest and did not mix the „noble metal" with various cheaper substances. But when gold came onto the scene and a fixed exchange value between gold and silver coins had to be set, economic life began to suffer.
The system of a two-metal currency („bimetallism") has proved a failure at all times. When new gold mines were discovered and the supply of gold grew, the silver coins were melted down and went out of circulation. When silver became cheaper, people began to hoard gold. When, on top of that, governments began to steal the real value of the coins by mixing all sorts of cheaper metals into them, it brought the greatest confusion into the economic life of the world and caused much suffering and discontent.
This is how the famous English historian Macaulay describes this situation:
„— It may well be doubted whether bad kings, bad ministers, bad parliaments and bad judges have brought the English people as much suffering as bad pounds and shillings. Events that are more conspicuous are not those that affect most the real life of the masses. The worst government from above did not disturb daily life. Under every regime the cattle-breeder drove his beasts to market; but when the money apparatus broke down, every trade, every industry was at once disrupted. The trouble was felt every day and every hour by every person — in the cowshed and on the threshing floor, at the anvil and the loom, on the waves of the ocean and in the depths of the mine. Worker and employer had to quarrel over wages every pay-day. The peasant was utterly ground down: for his products he had to accept bad money, but his debts and taxes he had to pay in full-weight metal."
Whoever lived through the famous „inflation" in Poland eighteen years ago will endorse every word of these excellent lines...
A. Rezavtski [?].
Free Opportunities to Work / For All Who Want to Work.

[Politics & economy — crafts; the Guild Law.]
The Jewish community activists are, it seems, worn out by the constant struggle over high politics and give no thought whatsoever to a problem such as Jewish craftsmanship, over which a net has been cast for years and which, if no attempt is made to free it, may one day be too late.
In the year 1927, on 15/6, the Guild Law (the craft-guild law) was published in Poland; it had been worked out by reactionary elements among the Polish artisans.
On the 15th of Grudzień [December] this year it will be 5 years since the Guild Law was published, and one can draw up a small balance of the law's fruits, and the sum total is — expenses and expenses. Not one single positive point in any field, neither in the material nor in the cultural. Poverty has not been eased by a hair, no export has been created, no new workshops to earn a living have been opened — on the contrary. For the Jewish population it has already in fact become impossible, on the basis of the law, to train the greater part of the apprentices. To this day almost none have been released [certified as journeymen], and consequently they can never be admitted as masters; that is to say, the possibility of building Jewish mass workshops has already been almost cut off, almost unnoticed?
How can Jewish public opinion pass over this question with indifference?
After all, it concerns the great majority of the Jewish population in Poland. How can one rest when in fact 60 percent of the Jewish workshops that provide a living are already threatened?
The Guild Law is a disguised "monopoly law". In the course of a few years several important branches of livelihood have been taken from the Jews, such as: the tobacco and spirits monopolies, the timber trade; the export of butter and eggs is being burdened. If the above-mentioned branches affected thousands of Jewish livelihoods, the law threatens tens of thousands of livelihoods!
It is no secret to anyone that the Chambers of Crafts and of Industry have to this day not a single positive achievement to show, either for the artisans or for the merchants; all that has been added is a network of new bureaucratic institutions. The Jewish community activists must categorically demand the complete annulment of the law. There must be free workshops, just as the broad Polish masses of land-workers, who to this day work mostly [?] in a primitive way, are free.
It does not occur to anyone at all to give the Polish peasant professional training. The agronomists rest and the tractors stand at the exhibitions [wystawy]. Nobody will ask the peasant whether he served so and so many years with a master, or force him to sit an extra "mistrzowski" [master's] examination (for 140 zł.) so that he may milk the cows with "gamkes" [?] etc. etc.
It does not occur to anyone to suddenly raise to such a high cultural level the greater part of the Polish population, which is in fact engaged in agrarian industry, cattle breeding, bee-keeping and fruit growing — far below the Western countries, not to speak of America or Australia.
For hundreds of years the Jews have worked and developed the crafts in Poland, have shod and clothed and even adorned both the common people and the rich classes.
From cheap goods [tandeta] to precise fine work, with primitive tools, up to the use of today's tools, the last word in technology.
Famous in the world are the Jewish tailors, the boot-upper makers. It does not occur to anyone to ask about an examination. Jewish craftsmen developed huge craft industries in America and England before the war — new branches of craft they are introducing in the last post-war years in the Western countries — such as: France, Germany and Belgium.
In the above-mentioned countries, where the population stands far higher in the cultural sense, no one thinks of holding qualification examinations for craftsmen. Craft, pure handicraft, has nothing to do with universities. For the craftsman the workshop is his university. The examination certificate of a boot-upper maker is his trained fingers, just like the eye of the watchmaker.
The years of work qualify him and already set the real stamp on his physiognomy. It is doubtful whether what is meant here is the high professional skill of the Jewish craftsman. For who can really examine, or even teach, a Będzin tailor, or a Sosnowiec shoemaker, a Dąbrowa or Zawiercie locksmith?
They want, in addition to the monopolised articles, to squeeze in a vice the Jewish mass production — the crafts.
The question of the Jewish butchers does not come off the agenda. Warsaw is the beginning of the end of a centuries-old Jewish source of livelihood. By formal resolutions they aimed for years to take the meat trade away from the Jews, and now it is becoming a fact. Thus one branch of livelihood after another is systematically taken away. But the greatest danger for the artisans lies in leaving the law of 15/6 1927 further in force. Therefore steps must already be taken in the competent spheres in order to annul the law.
The competent factors must be shown that pure handicraft has developed, and is developing, all over the world without the slightest interference from the organs of power — unless they fail to meet certain safety [printed "farvikhts"] and hygiene regulations.
One can in no way compare a craft workshop with a pharmacy. It is a clear fact that fitting a garment carries no danger to life, as does the slightest error of the pharmacist. Raising the culture of the craftsman and giving him diplomas will have no influence on his well-being. The world already suffers today from a surplus of intelligentsia. There is a bitter struggle over every post. And consequently the craft regulations cannot help, just as during the 5 years of the law's existence they have not helped to improve the situation of the craftsman in Poland.
The creators, the makers of the law, are permeated with unjustified hatred of the Jewish craftsman for reasons of competition, and therefore they want to protect themselves by the law — against which all democratic and even socialist circles of the population in Poland speak out. It is now being planned to introduce compulsory guilds, simply because the free guilds no longer satisfy those elements — guilds which, as a medieval institution, ought in general to be fought thoroughly.
Let the state give the artisans credits, and the artisans will find markets themselves. The tailors of Brzeziny [?] and the Białystok cloth factories found ways to export their products to England independently of the "guilds".
The slogan must be: free possibility of development for the crafts.
S. Straučinski [ש. סטראוטשינסקי].
A Dissatisfied World...

[Feuilleton — humour, everyday life.] (A little feuilleton.) By B. Kahner.
Nobody is satisfied today.
You borrow a few gulden [colloquial for złoty] from someone for a few days and you don't keep your word — so he is not satisfied, and you are not satisfied either, because he is not satisfied with your dissatisfaction.
You see that the other fellow has a fine house, a nice few thousand złotys, and you don't — so you are not satisfied; and the fellow who has all those things is not satisfied either: he would like to have a thousand times as much, and if he had a thousand times as much he still would not be satisfied, he would like to have a trillion times as much.
And who knows whether even then he would be satisfied...
Your friend has a good job and makes a fine living — you are not satisfied, because you have a bad job and make no living at all; and your friend is not satisfied either, because there are better jobs than his...
Your daughter married a doctor who charges 10 złotys a visit — she is not satisfied: after all, she could have married a professor who charges 50 and 75 zł. a visit.
Your wife buys a dress and pays 50 zł. a metre — she is not satisfied, she wanted a nicer dress at 100 zł. a metre; and had you bought her the hundred-złoty dress, she would not have been satisfied either, because there are still dearer fabrics.
Here I have bought my wife a fur coat for 500 zł. Nice money, you would think — and she is not satisfied: Mrs X has a coat for 1,000 zł.
You surely think that Mrs X is satisfied? It turns out she is not, because Mrs Y has a coat for 2,000 zł. You surely think that Mrs Y is satisfied? Not in the least, because Mrs Shmelkes's coat costs 3,000 zł. And so it goes, in due order.
Nobody is satisfied.
What more do you need: an acquaintance of mine was orphaned, and he received 50 thousand zł. from his father as an inheritance. Nice money, you would think — and he is not satisfied: another father died and left his son 100 thousand zł. And that one is not satisfied either.
Here I have written this feuilleton. Do you think I am satisfied? Not on your life [idiom „a nekhtiker tog“]! The feuilleton could have come out a lot better and wittier.
No, I am not satisfied.
B. Kahner.
From the Past in Zagłębie.

[History — the Jews of Będzin, the synagogue and the old cemetery; serial, parts 3–4.] (A page of Jewish history.) By Sh. Szach.
3.
As we have already mentioned, the Jews in Będzin were not permitted to live in the town proper, so the first group that arrived in Będzin settled in Zawale, Madziejowska [as printed; probably Modrzejowska]; later the Jews were allowed to live in the area of Zawale street, and finally in the area of today's Rybna and Targowa streets.
In the 15th century we see a wooden synagogue on Targowa street (today a brick synagogue stands on the same spot, under number 4). At the same time the town of Będzin gave the Jews a plot (from Rybna up to Zawala street) for a cemetery. In this cemetery, up to the middle of the 18th century, all the Jews who died were buried — not only from Będzin but from the whole surrounding area: from Mysłowice, Bytom (Beuthen), Chorzów [printed „Kharoshov“], Tychy and Sielce [?] they were brought here.
For the above-mentioned plot the Jewish kehilla paid the parish a special tax (dziesięcina — tithe) as well as a „danina“ [levy] for every grave.
Over the payment of the „dziesięcina“ and the „danina“ conflicts often arose between the Jewish kehilla and the parish. Thus the following characteristic case is told, which happened in the year 1687. The Jews, mainly those of Bytom, used to bury their dead in secret, at night, so as to avoid the payments for the grave. Since the Jews of Bytom and Mysłowice did not want to pay their share, the Jewish kehilla in Będzin also stopped paying the parish, defending itself by saying that the Jews of the surrounding area did not want to bear the burden of paying taxes for burying their dead, and it alone was not able to pay for the whole area. So it dragged on until in the year 1687 the Będzin priest Jan Katulecki sued the kehilla. The kehilla denied the charge that Jews from the surrounding area were being buried in the Będzin cemetery. The priest Katulecki, however, would not give way, and produced as a witness a Jewish woman who on 5 December 1687 swore an oath that Jews from Mysłowice and the surrounding area were indeed being buried in the Będzin cemetery. The matter dragged on for 8 years, until it reached the Bishop of Kraków, who in 1692 delegated to Będzin the Mysłowice priest Stanisław Zygmuntowicz, and in 1694 the priest of „Groyts“ [perhaps Grodziec] Mikołaj Jezierkiewicz. The latter heard as witnesses under oath, in the Mysłowice synagogue, the Jews: Jakob Meir Mordechai Majuszeszowicz [?], Jona Markowicz, Jakob Gada of Sielce, Moshe Jakubowicz of Tychy and a certain Mordechai of Kuszniczy [Kuźnica?]. The Jews of Bytom did not appear. Having acquainted himself with the whole matter, the priest Jezierkiewicz issued a verdict that the kehilla must pay the parish the whole „ferlegene“ [?; probably: outstanding] sum which it had remained owing.
4.
In the synagogue on Targowa street (z) [so printed] all Jewish affairs were settled. The Będzin rabbi of that time, who incidentally was a great rabbinic authority, led the kehilla with the help of four dayanim [rabbinic judges]; the dayanim watched over the kehilla institutions. There were so-called hevrot [confraternities], of which in the 16th century there were „ash“ [?] seven at the synagogue. Thus there were a Hevra Kadisha, a Hevra Talmud Torah, Bikur Holim, Hakhnasat Kalah, Malbish Arumim etc. At the head of each hevra stood a gabbai. The hevrot functioned excellently. Their great number is explained by the fact that to Będzin, as a border town, many homeless people used to come who had been persecuted in the neighbouring countries; naked and barefoot they came to the gates of the Będzin synagogue, where they received first aid. It also happened more than once that the hevrot — because of the great expenses they had in giving help to the homeless — had to go bankrupt. Then the confraternity attached to the parish of the Będzin church (Bractwo Różańcowe — the Rosary Confraternity) came to their aid. There is a document that the Będzin kehilla received a loan of 400 grzywnas to save the Jewish hevrot.
At the Będzin synagogue there was in the 16th century, besides the hadarim run by melamdim [teachers], a yeshiva. Of the yeshiva the most renowned was Rabbi Natan Meitels, who in the year 1587, when Będzin was threatened by an attack of the Austrian army, collected from the town's Jews a sum of 50 ducats and carried it to the burgrave at the castle, so that the town walls could be repaired with this money. Rabbi Meitels died at the age of 105 and was buried in the Będzin cemetery. In this cemetery are the graves of the eminent Będzin Jews Shlomo Markowicz and Jona Szmulewicz, who fought for and won the privileges signed in his own hand by King Jan III Sobieski. One might have thought that the cemetery in which found their eternal rest the leaders of the Będzin Jews — who in good times and in bad did not abandon their brethren, and who, almost always risking their lives, made long journeys in order to obtain privileges — would be a sacred place for the Jews of Będzin, for every gravestone, every word, is history. Is it actually sacred to the present-day Jews of Będzin? Unfortunately not! The Jews of Będzin have no interest — so it seems — in history. The old cemetery is covered with... rubbish, holed jugs, broken buckets and pots. In this way a piece of Jewish history is being lost. And the cemetery is surrounded by Jewish houses only! Will there really be nobody to be found who would bring the cemetery into some kind of order?
(To be continued)
Sh. Szach.
„Zangen“ (Ears of Grain) — Supplement for Culture and Art; Yitzchak Margoshes: To the Poet

Zangen [„Ears of Grain“] — Supplement for Culture and Art.

Yitzchak Margoshes [Icchak Margoszes].
To the Poet.

Oh, poor poet,
hide your dream — your image;
don't you know that your writings
are only an amusement?
* * *
Oh, you poet! Your writings
that you wrote with spirit,
and great drops of tears of pain
remained upon the page,
* * *
these very writings a little man
will calmly, calmly open,
and not look at the tears,
but merrily, heartily laugh at them.
* * *
And he will soil your pearls,
and he will laugh: be merry,
while you sit there at the little table
and write with weeping.
* * *
Poet! Why do you write,
why do you sacrifice your life?
Why should you give your pearls
away to every stranger?
* * *
Why do you open your soul,
your heart and your whole being,
why do you let a stranger
redeem [draw out] your secret?
* * *
Why do you write? Why do you write?
When others live in pleasure!
Why should you not live as well
and enjoy? —
— Say, why?
An Hour with Ch. N. Bialik

S. Lewkowicz.

By the room which the poet Ch. N. Bialik [Chaim Nachman Bialik] occupies at the „Central“ there is great commotion. Former friends, faithful pupils come to see the man whom people once treated with disdain and who has now risen to so high a rank, become so exalted. Among the visitors an old Jewish woman catches the eye. She too is waiting for „her turn“ to enter the room where Bialik is staying.
— Whom are you looking for, granny? — we ask her.
— I want to see him, Nachman I mean; when I — she says — sold pickled cucumbers at the Sosnowiec market, Nachman the teacher was my regular customer...
When the former pickle-seller reminds Bialik of this, he agrees with her words. It's true, I was a great lover — says Bialik — of pickled cucumbers, but today the doctors have forbidden me to eat that dish...
The „rebbe“ takes leave of his „Hasidim“. Happy, they go away, and we, i.e. the writer of these lines and Yosef Klarman, remain alone with Bialik in his room.
We begin our conversation around newspaper matters and the like, but here Bialik displays great „stubbornness“: he will not utter a single word until he is „convinced“ that we, who stand at the head of the editorial board, have a positive attitude towards Hebrew and towards the Jewish national revival...
In general Bialik's attitude to the present-day Jewish press is a negative one. Oh, the newspapers, oh, the newspapers! — he exclaims with irony...
— Is that possible? „The jealousy of scribes increases wisdom“!
— That was once; today, however, „the jealousy of scribes increases foolishness“...
* * *
Already two hours before the time of departure Bialik shows great nervousness. There is no time — he says — one must prepare for the further journey, one must not stay standing in one place, only lech lecha [„go forth“]...
Bialik packs his things and I prepare writing materials for him, although he repeats several times that „he will make no exception for the Sosnowiec people. When I leave Poland — he says — I shall take leave of the whole of Polish Jewry through the press.“
But „nothing stands in the way of the will“; already completely „ready for the journey“, he yielded to our request and, standing, writes these lines [in Hebrew in the original]:
„I remember Sosnowiec, the days of my youth. In her youth; now both of us have grown old. Her streets and alleys have changed their faces beyond recognition, her people have become strangers to me, my friends whom I left black-haired — I found white-haired. Her inhabitants have multiplied. My soul grieves for the days that have passed and are no more.
Chaim Nachman Bilik [sic].“
* * *
Only in the street does one see how popular Bialik is among all strata of the Jewish population. Look, that's Bialik! — exclamations are heard from passers-by. The photographers too have a „sense of smell“, and while we walk with Bialik the cameras are at work, and from all the pavements people hurry towards Bialik. We too want — they say — to be photographed with him...
Bialik hears and enjoys it...
The „commotion“ goes on like this all the way to the „Mizrachi“ school.
* * *
After the greeting by R' Avraham Shapira the pupils' choir sings „Techezakna“ and the young pupil Aryeh Friedman recites „El ha-Meshorer“ [„To the Poet“], a parody of „El ha-Tzippor“ [„To the Bird“]. Here Bialik becomes lively and with a beaming face speaks to the pupils in the tone in which a kind-hearted father speaks to his little children...
— I will tell you, children, a legend. The legend tells that in Egypt, when Pharaoh decreed that the newborn boys should be thrown into the water, the Jewish mothers went out to the field on the eve of their delivery and there gave birth to their children.
The mothers then went home, and God sent milk and honey to the children in the field; when the children grew bigger, they went to their mothers.
You too, dear children — says Bialik — are also in the fields of exile; you too receive the honey and milk, for the Torah is likened to milk and honey; but when you grow bigger, you should go home to your mother, to the Jewish home...
* * *
Walking back from the school, Bialik asks that we go with him not through the main streets, which are strange to him, but through the back alleys: the alleys remind me of the time when I lived here.
— And created here — the „rebbe“ Shapira remarks to him.
— True, created here; „El ha-Tzippor“, „Achen chatzir ha-am“, „Ha-Matmid“ are Sosnowiec „children“.
— How gladly I would — he says — visit my old comrades and good friends; it grieves me greatly. When we assure him that there is still a scant hour before the train must leave, he is very pleased and dashes into the flat of his friend Mr. Chaim Yosef Zajac [?], where the warm reunion lasts only a few counted minutes. In the course of the conversation[?] the talk turns to honour, and we hear from Bialik this sharp-witted saying:
— There is — he says — a saying that „whoever flees from honour, honour pursues him“: he who runs away from honour, honour chases after. The world asks a question: if someone runs away from honour, why does he deserve the punishment that honour should run after him?
But the answer is this: he who runs away from honour surely holds that honour is really a thing of some value; so the punishment rightly falls on him, that honour should chase him... But I — says Bialik — am already far from the opinion that honour has any value...
— Go then in good health — Chaim Yosef wishes him — may your words be fulfilled that you spoke at the „Palace“, that the „foot-culture should cease“.
— That will be — says Bialik on the spot — when „if thou turn away thy foot from the Sabbath“ [Isaiah 58:13], when the match-culture comes to an end...
— Keep well, Chaim Yosef! See to it that you come to the Land of Israel; you cannot have any idea of the feeling one has living in the Land of Israel, such freedom, such a Jewish life — come there, Chaim Yosef, and tell all the friends the same... Oh, how loathsome life in exile is. Let us hurry to the train.
— Keep well!
Golden Autumn.

N. Sternberg, Warsaw

Golden autumn everywhere, still it rests.
The grain is in the barn. The harvest is long past.
Bright, clear days stretch [?] along
like little silken clouds far off on the road...

Changes swirl [?], quiet tones and colours
of a dying summer that is already about to die,
and wrestles invisibly with forest and with field.
And covers everything with gold, gold that yellows.

The fields already empty. Potatoes and cabbage
one sees here, there. The peasant has cleared away
his bread — what earlier only "raben" [?] in plenty
covered the field like the sekhakh of the sukkahs.

So bright, clear days stretch along.
One lovelier than the next, far off on the road.
And the field is already silvered [?] with dew quite early.
Golden autumn everywhere, still it rests,
the grain is in the barn. The harvest is long past.
Bright, clear days stretch [?] along
like little silken clouds far off on the road...
A Man Alone.

Róża Jakubowicz.
Dedicated to Jakub Ber Zając.

In the little room the table is littered with unbound books, the bed strewn with papers and newspaper clippings, and in every corner on the floor books and papers are thrown about. One can barely make out the edge of the bed and the legs of the table.
Among the papers there are also scraps of "tavil" [?] (cardboard?) and little cigarette boxes, on which — having no free scrap of paper at hand — Elimelech sometimes notes down his moods and his various ideas for poems; such things, after all, must not be lost.
But how does one protect these sparks of thought, scattered here and there, from destruction? He decided to keep the whole little room, just as it is, locked against human eyes, and when someone comes, Elimelech the writer goes out to him in front of the door, and the visitor can only peer in from over the threshold.
And when one peers in like that from a distance, the little room seems to lose the form of a room and to be transformed into one great mountain of shemot [worn sacred pages], as in the old polish [vestibules] of the beit midrash.
When he singled me out, his former pupil, and allowed me to come in, that prerogative did not come easily to me. First I had to promise that I would not touch a single scrap of paper; then, with difficulty, I found a place to sit [?] here, from where there is no contact with his paper fortune.
— What shall I treat you to? — he asks, and leans against the wall, against a bundle of old clothes that hangs on it.
I contemplate his aged figure, his grey hair and the wrinkles on his forehead, and in my mind I see his silhouette of former days, of those times when he was my teacher. Tall and slender he looked then, his blond head radiant with faith and love of mankind. Today barely the outline of before remains, the mere trace.
— You ask what you should treat me to? With memories of your past, in which I was brought up.
— Do you still remember ["gdeynkst", so printed], Lena, my mother's little room?
— As if it were today. A large room that is never tidied. Between the two windows by the wall stands a low glass cabinet, out of which peep a Korban Minchah prayer book, a citron stuck into a little cup, and dried mushrooms. In the drawers of the chest of drawers lie [?] packed various objects that have no value at all for anyone and that only out of stubbornness your mother will not part with.
Above the low cabinet hangs a mirror in a mahogany frame, an heirloom, which reflects badly and hangs too high. Not far off stands a round, red-polished table with a knitted tablecloth, and around the table worn-out [?] old torn armchairs, on which your mother does not allow us children to sit down.
Elimelech feels a warmth flowing from the reminiscence into which his pupil Lena has already drawn him, and he himself begins to remember too.
— Yes, in the great inherited house that was never tidied I spent my childhood, together with my mother, who is always angry, and with my younger brother, who laughs at me as though he were the elder.
Do you remember my mother, the agunah, who always sits with bitten lips and hands folded on her apron, under which she hides the sugar? With me she is always cross; she sees, she says, from childhood on, that nothing will come of me.
He looks at me with a smile; he is sure that I too will laugh at how wrong his mother's prediction was.
My younger brother is her darling. He has a couple of kopecks — on Friday he buys himself a little fruit for Shabbat or a fresh collar.
— And you put everything into the shemot — by this she means the great mountain of books and newspapers next to the chest of drawers, over which you are always kneeling.
— And how long — asks my mother — is the measure that I should keep you? It is already time [printed "shoyn″ tsayt"] that you should work for me.
And when my mother grumbles [?] like this, I duck my head as if shielding myself from a blow. I do not know what I should do; should I get myself apprenticed to a shoemaker? I do not know where and what and when; mother is unhappy and angry and I cannot talk her round [?]. And if I myself do not know, it is surely my own fault. And all at once it seems to me that something heavy hangs upon me and will no longer leave me.
At that same time a little book of poems fell into my hands, in which an orphan laments his bitter lot, and it seemed to me that I myself was meant there, and I even added a few words to every line: that the world is so cruel, that for me, the thirteen-year-old, the world is so narrow, and if I did not pity mother I would commit suicide.
— Listen further, a wondrous thing I will tell you, Lena.
Once mother sent me to my uncle for a couple of gulden; passing the freshly ploughed field I felt as if perfumes had been poured out there, or all kinds of sweets scattered. A little stream was murmuring; I took off my shoes and waded across, and also tried to cool my head in the waves. Then I walked through the unfenced cemetery, sat down on a gravestone overgrown with green and looked at the sky, at the tumbled stone wall that had tried to separate the graves from the living street. Above, birds flew past in flocks, and the free air above the graves drew me to itself. It seemed to me that I was all alone in the whole world, as though it were now before the Creation. Every blade of grass that swayed and every stone that had gathered mould spoke to me in many languages.
And it was good for me there with the quiet, living nature, until I remembered that I had to go home, that mother would scold again.
(To be continued in the next issue).
Oneg Shabbat

[Oneg Shabbat — Torah thoughts on the weekly portion Lech Lecha.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion. Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Lech Lecha
The Portion
a) "Go forth... to the land that I will show thee" (12:1)
The root of the Jewish soul is in the Land of Israel. In exile the Jew is estranged from himself, from his own "I". Lech lecha — go back to yourself, to your root — "to the land", to the Land of Israel.   Kli Hemda.
— — —
Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav said:
There are those who talk themselves into believing that they love the Land of Israel and want to travel there, only they want to travel in comfort, not in hardship and sorrow. In truth, however, this is a false wish, for whoever truly wants to travel to the Land of Israel must go there even on foot, as God said to Abraham: "Lech lecha" — it means specifically to go, to go on foot.
— — —
And when his disciple, Rabbi Natan, asked him what he meant by saying that the Land of Israel is so great,
"he grew angry with me — writes Rabbi Natan — and said: I mean the Land of Israel in its plain sense, I mean really the rooms and the houses"...   Hayei Moharan.
b) "And I will bless thee" (ibid. 2)
"With thee they conclude, and not with them."   Rashi.
Jacob symbolized Torah in himself — "And Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents"; Isaac, in turn, embodied divine service — "God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son"; Abraham, the great host of guests, represented in himself the quality of loving-kindness (gemilut hasadim).
"With thee they conclude" — at the conclusion, in the time of the footsteps of the Messiah, the main thing will be Abraham's quality: loving-kindness; it will be worth more than Torah and divine service...
Nehmad mi-Zahav (Rabbi Yehezkele of Kuzmir).
c) "And make thy name great" (ibid.)
One will sooner say the blessing "Shield of Abraham" than God's blessing "Who revives the dead".   Bamidbar Rabbah.
Why is "Who revives the dead" more God's blessing than "Shield of Abraham"?
The Gemara (Sanhedrin 91) says that at the resurrection of the dead everyone will rise with his blemish, his defect, and [then] be healed. When they call: "Rise, so-and-so son of so-and-so!" — no one will recognize himself except by his blemishes, by his sufferings. The good that a person had in his life he does not remember; only in his troubles does he recognize himself...
Therefore "Who revives the dead" is God's blessing: to recognize one's own root — that is God's gift alone, to find oneself upon coming back to life...
Beit Yaakov (Rabbi Yaakov of Izhbitsa).
d) "And my soul shall live because of thee" (ibid. 13)
Ben Sira [printed "Ben Sura"] says: he who has a good wife lives double the years. "And my soul shall live because of thee" — thanks to your beauty and goodness I have indeed lived.   Olelot Efrayim.
"With a good wife one lives double the years."
Why double, of all things?
Because he who has a bad wife — says the Gemara — his life is no life. Well then, he who has a good wife gains also the years that a bad wife would have taken from him...   Milin de-Rabbanan.
e) "And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver and in gold" (13:2)
"And Abram was very heavy" — the gold and silver were very heavy on him; they were an unbearable burden to him...   Mei ha-Shiloah.
— — —
Further the verse says: "And he went on his journeys", and the midrash comments: on the way back Abraham paid his debts.
That is why the money was heavy on him, because it was not his own, because it was borrowed, and he had to give it back. Had it been his own money — it would not have been heavy on him...   Imrei Shefer.
— — —
For this reason Abraham gathered silver and gold: so that "he called upon the name of the Lord", so that he could proclaim God's truth. For people listen only to a rich man. "The poor man's wisdom is despised."
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
— — —
And therefore, when King Solomon asked God only for wisdom without wealth, God told him: if you want people to consider you a sage, you must be a rich man too... A poor sage is not recognized by the world...   Asam be-Shem[?].
f) "And he went on his journeys" (ibid. 3)
We have already mentioned the midrash that on the way back Abraham paid his debts.
What is the novelty?
A person goes to pay a debt himself only when he is going to take a fresh "bundle" [of goods]; if he is not about to get fresh credit, he is in no hurry to pay himself — let the other fellow come... At best he sends the debt along with someone who happens to be going. Abraham travelled himself to pay his debts, although he did not need fresh credit...   Divrei Shaul.
g) "And there was a strife... let there be no strife" (ibid. 7–8)
At first a little quarrel is in the category of "riv" (masculine form). But soon it becomes a "merivah" (feminine form). It becomes like a fertile woman in childbirth who gives birth to more and more little quarrels...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
h) "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars" (15:5 [printed 15:2])
The stars cannot be counted not because they are so many, but because they move with swift momentum, change and alter.
Those are the Jews...   Ohel Yaakov.
The Haftarah
"Thou worm Jacob" (Isaiah 40 [should be 41:14])
The Jews are compared to a worm. Every creature is created with various protective organs, such as nails, horns, etc.; the worm possesses only its mouth.
The Jews too have no other means of protection than the mouth...   Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
Who Is to Blame?

[Będzin — Talmud Torah; letter to the editor.] A letter to the editorial office.
In connection with the public appeal about the situation of the Będzin "Talmud Torah" ("Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 42), allow me, esteemed Mr. Editor, to give in your newspaper some explanations, which should demonstrate and shed light on the real causes that have brought the above-mentioned institution to such a catastrophic state.
About a year ago a general meeting of the local Talmud Torah was convened for the first time in Będzin, which was finally supposed to be put on the level due to this institution according to its nature and great tasks.
We, a group of Będzin residents, learning of the general meeting, held several consultations with the participation of the town notables, devoted to the restructuring of the "Talmud Torah", and decided to join in the work of so important an institution, under whose authority and education several hundred Jewish children had been entrusted.
When we came to the meeting and the "Agudah" saw us, it mobilized all its Hasidim with the Rabbi at their head, who wanted to continue the existing order in future too, raising an outcry that the Zionists and other not "faithful" Jews want, God save us, to turn the "Talmud Torah" into a modern pedagogical Jewish school. The Rabbi then solemnly proclaimed: "I see some new people. The Talmud Torah is mine and it will continue to be run according to the pattern of our forefathers' fathers."
All our words, which aimed only, with the purest intentions, at convincing [people] of the correctness of our view and of the hypocrisy of the Ger retinue, did not help, and the institution remained occupied by the "Agudah", in whose hands the devoted but simple-hearted Mr. Dafner served merely as a plaything.
We left the general meeting wishing [as it were] to see the "fruits" of the "Agudah's" work in the field of the Talmud Torah, which has been brought — thanks solely to the gentlemen of the "Agudah" — to such a grave situation, anarchy and the resignation of the Talmud Torah's activists to date.
Let the Jewish population know that the responsibility for the situation lies and falls only on the "Agudah", which is breaking up Jewish communal life and, through its deeds, supposedly in the name of religion and Torah, is bringing it to complete ruin.
Abraham Hampel.
Mother and Wife (5)

[Serialized novel — a novel of Jewish life; installment 5.]
Sh. Relkes.
(A gripping novel of Jewish life.)

They all sat down at the table. The mother served fruit, coffee, eggs, fresh butter and cheese. David ate with appetite, but he saw that his mother had prepared something for him. The worm of doubt began gnawing at him again. He was already annoyed that Sarahle had come in and interrupted the conversation. Perhaps he would already be a free man now? Perhaps the heavy stone that had been pressing on him for so many years would already have rolled off him? Then again, maybe it would be better if he did not know at all? After all, what difference does it make to him who his father was and what secrets his mother has hidden from him all these years? He is a man, he will finish [his studies as a] doctor, build himself a wide practice and live in the world.
David tried to persuade himself that it made no difference to him. But he felt that this was false, that it already made a great difference to him. A person has to come from somewhere; a person is not thrown into the world the way the wind carries off the pollen of flowers and sows [?] it wherever the soil is favourable.
David's mother, having made up her mind to reveal her secret, felt greatly relieved. The forty-year-old woman now looked much younger than her age. It seemed to her that she was now crossing the border into a new land, a new life, a bright life.
"Yes," she began, "what we were talking about when Sarahle arrived in the middle. I think, David, it would be better if I spoke to you both. Sarahle is as close to me as my own child, and I want her to know just as you do. What do you say, David?" she smiled at her son.
David said nothing. He only raised his eyes to his mother, saw how calm and radiant she was, and understood that now he must not disturb her. Sarahle did not understand at all what was going on here, but she felt that mother and son had been talking about something important.
"I will begin with an event of twenty-two years ago."
She thought for a while; her eyes carried her far into the past. She [printed "Vi"] seemed to see no one before her.
"It was the eve of Yom Kippur. The holiest day had arrived, and a dread had fallen upon the Jews. From midday on, elderly Jews had been gathering [?] in the synagogues and study houses. Before the sun had set, the final pre-fast meal had already been eaten, and young and old went to Kol Nidre to pray for a good year and to beat their breasts with 'we have sinned' for the sins of the past year. It goes without saying that the old cantor, Reb Chaim, was the first in the synagogue. He was a Jew of over seventy, bent and broken. The whole yoke of exile lay upon his shoulders. He had told the beadle to give him the lashes not in jest, but to really whip him. He had been to the bathhouse, immersed himself in the mikveh, and now he stood purified, with a pure heart, to lead the congregation in prayer. Reb Chaim stood by the Holy Ark and with quiet weeping recited chapters of Psalms. He did not turn round to see whether the synagogue was full, for he knew that when the sun set and the time came to say Kol Nidre, not a single Jew would be missing from the synagogue.
"The congregation of Jews assembled. Each one brought along big tallow candles and stuck them in the sand in the vestibule. The air grew thicker. On high, it seemed, hovered the wings of the Shekhinah. The beadle had already lit the bright lamps. Reb Chaim raised his sweet, broken voice: 'By the authority of the Omnipresent and by the authority of the congregation...'
"In the middle there was a commotion in the synagogue: gendarmes burst in, pushed the congregation aside and went straight to the cantor's lectern. Terror fell upon everyone. What are gendarmes doing in the synagogue at Kol Nidre? Whom are they looking for at the lectern? A calamity for the Jews, a blood libel against the community.
"The senior gendarme stood beside Reb Chaim, but the old cantor did not know what was happening behind his back; he went on saying the prayer. The congregation huddled together like a flock of sheep set upon by wolves. The cantor's voice tore at their hearts. They all felt that the calamity was coming upon him, upon old Reb Chaim. But nobody [said] a word, because they were afraid of the gendarmes. The senior one grabbed Reb Chaim by the shoulder and gave him an angry shake:
"'You are under arrest.'
"Reb Chaim broke off in the middle of the prayer, turned his face to the congregation and, seeing before him the burly gentile in uniform, let out a desperate cry. The tallis slipped off his head, and with trembling hands he tried to lift it.
"'Come, I have an order to take you to the police,' a gendarme called out loudly. 'You are accused of murder.'
"Reb Chaim did not understand what the gentile was saying to him. He only sighed and kept pulling the tallis over himself. Little by little the congregation came to its senses. The rabbi came out from beside the Holy Ark and tried to speak to the gendarme, to explain to him that there must be some mistake, but the man would not listen: he had a paper to detain Chaim Lazarov Bergman, who was accused of murder. He could do nothing about it; he had to carry out the order. Jews wept; Reb Chaim could barely stay on his feet — nothing helped: the gendarmes with their jingling spurs led Reb Chaim the cantor away from the lectern, took him and carried him off on the evening of Yom Kippur to prison.
"This scene took place in a small town twenty-two years ago. Kol Nidre was already said without the cantor. The rabbi himself stood at the lectern. The congregation wept bitterly, but nobody knew why the gendarmes had taken away Reb Chaim the cantor."
(To be continued.)
Będzin — Saturday night: election of a kehilla president.

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
Będzin
Saturday night — election of a kehilla president.
As is known, the kehilla president in office until now did not want to call the first meeting of the new kehilla board, which is to elect a president and a vice-president. This happened because of the bad "conjuncture" for the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel], which has no chance whatsoever of getting the "portfolio" of kehilla president. And since there was no luck to be expected, nobody hurried to convene the constituent meeting. But the "sulking game" [printed "bronze game", ?] is now coming to an end. This week the supervisory authority sent a notice to the present kehilla board that on Saturday night at 8 o'clock in the evening a board meeting is to take place, at which the president and a deputy are to be elected. If not — the notice says — the present president will pay a fine of 100 zł.
The stern warning has worked, and the meeting is being called for the above-mentioned date.
When things are bad, one becomes softer..

[Będzin — Municipality.]
Attendance at the municipal bath-house has fallen considerably. Therefore the magistrate [town board] has decided to lower the prices for bathtubs by 20 gr., i.e. from 1 Listopad [November] on a bathtub will cost 1 zł.
On Monday the establishment will not operate at all; the Tuesday price, 60 gr. per bathtub, remains unchanged.
Because of the crisis many shops in the market halls are being liquidated; and those who still keep their businesses complain that the takings are getting weaker all the time. Therefore a project has been worked out in the magistrate to reduce the rent of the hall shops.
The project must first be considered by the commissarial council.
It would be desirable for the councillors (ratmani) to submit a proposal that the relief of reduced rent should also apply to the "budkes" [stalls].
The monument on Third of May Square will winter in its present state.

[Będzin — Municipality.]
As is known, the monument on Third of May Square [plac 3 Maja] in Będzin was to be unveiled on 11 Listopad [November] this year. As we are informed, the committee dealing with the monument wanted to decide [?] that the unveiling should take place only in April 1932.
The public schools have received their proper names

[Będzin — Education.]
The school inspector has fixed names for the local public ("powszechne") schools.
School number 2 receives the name of Sienkiewicz, school no. 4 — Orzeszkowa, no. 8 — Konopnicka.
As we are informed, a children's feeding campaign has been undertaken. For a minimal price the children will receive pastries, milk etc. in the schools.
Cantor Badasz in the town synagogue.

[Będzin — Cantorial music.]
The Częstochowa cantor Mr. Badasz, who is well known to the local public, will lead the Kabbalat Shabbat this Sabbath and pray Shacharit and Musaf in the town synagogue.
Concert by Chief Cantor Koussevitzky.

[Będzin — Cantorial music.]
The local music lovers and admirers of nigun came on Tuesday evening to the "Świtowid" cinema to hear the concert given by the chief cantor of the Tłomackie synagogue in Warsaw, Mr. M. Koussevitzky.
And there was something to hear. Koussevitzky possesses a powerful tenor voice with which he reaches up to the highest level. Splendid and full of sweetness are his transitional passages; the tone is pure, without strain, heartfelt, and above all — Jewish.
In the religious works Koussevitzky feels at home; he is able to shake up the souls even of "Shehecheyanu" Jews [those who come to synagogue only on festivals] in the Tłomackie synagogue...
In the opera arias, on the other hand, Koussevitzky is no longer the same: the voice is strong, it rings, but this is not his genre [?]. The same goes for the folk songs. After "Akavya ben Mahalalel" and "Brikh Shmeh" the folk song "Menashe" does not fit...
The concert, with piano accompaniment by Mrs. Lichterman, left a strong impression on the audience. After every appearance the hall shook with stormy applause.
— — —
On Wednesday evening Koussevitzky led the Maariv prayer in the German synagogue. Those who were not "privileged" to be inside the synagogue "fulfilled their obligation" in the courtyard...

[Sosnowiec — relief.]
In connection with the fact that committees are being founded in all towns with the task of supporting the unemployed through the winter, the project arose to create a special committee to support Jewish unemployed only.
The committee holds regular meetings in the premises of the local “Dobroczynność” [charity society] on Kowalska Street. It was also decided to issue an appeal that the Jewish unemployed should register in order to receive assistance.

[Sosnowiec — theatre.]
A Jewish troupe has lately been touring Zagłębie, in which Dina Halpern and Tem [?] Broniecki, Marsław and others take part. The manager [representative] of the troupe applied to the deputy starost in Będzin for a permit for several performances in Sosnowiec. The deputy starost at first refused the request, giving as his reason that “he wants the Jews to attend the Sosnowiec Polish theatre”.
Finally a permit was obtained for 3 performances, i.e. today, Friday, 1 performance, and tomorrow, Saturday, 2 performances. “The Great Inheritance” and “Fifi, the Parisian Laundry Girl” will be played.

In Sosnowiec there is the only cooperative bank which is a model for all banks in Zagłębie. [Sosnowiec — border.]
On the Polish-German border in Upper Silesia the border guard wanted to detain a group of smugglers who had been smuggling various goods from Germany.

Dąbrowa — From the City Council

[Dąbrowa — city council.] At Monday's session of the local city council the B. B. club [BBWR, the pro-government bloc] brought in an urgent motion to exclude from their list councillor Bednarski (the well-known cashier); the motion was adopted...
During the reading of the statute of the water supply and sewerage a lively discussion developed around the question of how payment for water should be introduced. On this there are 2 conceptions: 1) that a bucket [wiadro] of water should cost 2 gr., and 2) that a lump-sum [ryczałt] payment should be levied according to the number of rooms each person uses. No decision has yet been adopted on this; the commission finds itself in a difficult position, because until now the Dąbrowa population has not paid for water.
At the session councillor B. Rechnic interpellated why the electricity works still charges 60 groszy per kilowatt of light, at a time when there is a city-council resolution not to pay more than 50 groszy.
President [mayor] Madejski declared that the matter is still in the hands of the ministry; in any case the question must be decided still in the year 1931.
— Meanwhile the population must pay.
Olkusz — The Cut Applies Only to the Sole Jewish Official

[Olkusz — municipality.] By a resolution of the city council the temporary commissioner of the city administration engaged Mr. B. Warszawski as collector. After a two-week trial Warszawski received a notice that, because of the order of the higher authority to reduce the budget, and also because during the trial period he had collected a small sum, he is dismissed from the post.
The cut, which was made only on the sole Jewish official, aroused great resentment among the whole Jewish population.
Because of this a sharp protest was submitted by several hundred citizens and separately by the kehilla administration.
The protests were handed to the commissioner by a delegation of the kehilla administration, the notables of the town, headed by the rabbi and Mr. A. Muszkatblat.

What Must One Already Know about the New Patents?

Although there are still two months left to buy patents [annual trading licences], it is nevertheless important to know already now many things that must be settled already now; otherwise one will suffer losses.
Before we enumerate here what must already be done regarding patents for the year 1932, we shall cite the new circular [okólnik] of the Ministry of Finance.
A few days ago the Ministry of Finance sent a circular to all tax offices, instructing them to make the appropriate preparations regarding patents for the new year 1932.
On 1 November posters will be put up throughout Poland announcing that the sale of patents and registration cards is beginning. To the official prices of the patents one must add a surcharge of 10 percent for the Treasury [skarb], 30 percent for the municipal institutions in the magistrat [town council], and a special surcharge for the chambers of commerce and industry and for schools. We draw attention to the fact that this year the levy for the chambers of commerce will be added to the patents throughout Poland.
The new circular of the Ministry of Finance provides for no reductions at all and no payment facilities whatsoever when buying the patents. By 1 January [styczeń] 1932 everyone must already hold patents. Whoever trades on 2 January without a patent will be fined 3 times the amount of the patent.
All merchants who hold third-category patents and keep in their shops a little merchandise for which, by law, a second-category patent is required, must apply in writing to the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office] and request permission to keep this merchandise in the shop.
For example, for silk goods, patent-leather shoes, woollen fabric, fur goods, clothing with silk lining, with fur collars, better garments, woollen jackets, woollen clothing, shawls, expensive cufflinks [spinki], silver articles etc. one must hold second-category patents. But the office has the right to permit keeping a little of such goods even on a third-category patent.
This permission is granted only to merchants whose estimated turnover in the last year was not greater than 30,000 zł. It is permitted to keep expensive articles up to 5 percent of the value of the remaining simple goods.
Whoever does not submit such a request between the first of November and 15 December [grudzień] at the latest will not be allowed to trade in these expensive articles on a third-category patent.
Merchants who wish, from the new year on, to change their trading patents to smaller ones, e.g. from the second category to the third, or whoever wishes to reduce from a third to a fourth category, must likewise apply about this to the Urząd Skarbowy by 15 December.
There are many merchants who until now held second-category patents for their half-wholesale, half-retail [hurt-detal] business, or for expensive goods. Now many of them want to reduce their businesses to the third category because they are giving up wholesale selling. Merchants who do not apply to the Urząd Skarbowy and report that they want to reduce their enterprises from the new year will be required to go on taking out the same patents as until now.

Hakoach — Zagłębie 2:5 (1:4)
After the Katowice Police Club, Zagłębie has again become the "scapegoat" [kapore] of the excellent forward quintet of Będzin's Hakoach. Scoring 3 goals within three minutes is something not seen for a long time. A Bloody Tragedy of a Young Couple in Szopienice

[Szopienice — tragedy.]
On Wednesday at 9 o'clock in the morning a policeman saw that in the hollows [?] around the „Ciesze“ [Giesche] coal mine in Szopienice there lay the dead body of a young man, and beside him, over him, lay a young girl with weak signs of life.
The investigation established that the young man is a Christian, a student of the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, and the girl is a Jewess, a certain Zonka Libler, both from Jordanów.
The couple had lately been living in the hotel „Central“ in Katowice.
On that same day, on leaving the hotel, they left a letter with the porter in which they wrote that one should search at the 7th tram stop [„pshistanek“, Polish przystanek].
The dead body of the student was taken to the prosectorium (mortuary) in Szopienice, and the Jewish girl was taken in a very serious condition to the Katowice hospital.
As it turns out, the student first shot at the girl and then himself.
The cause of the tragedy is that the girl's parents, Jewish people, naturally did not allow their daughter to marry the Christian student.
From the Dąbrowa City Council / How Much Will the Dąbrowa Population Pay for Water

[Dąbrowa — city council.]
On Tuesday a session of the Dąbrowa city council took place, which approved a series of statutes for the year 1932 according to the norm as hitherto.
While considering the petitions of local citizens who ask the magistrate to exempt them from the premises tax, Mr. Rechnic proposed also not to take any tax from the premises where the library of the Zionist Organisation is located. To this the chairman declared that this cannot be done, because all institutions, both Jewish and non-Jewish, pay tax on their premises. After this declaration Mr. Rechnic withdrew his proposal.
Because of a shortage of cash, the petition of the Jewish Scientific Institute [YIVO] in Wilno to give it a subsidy was also rejected.
—o—
How Much Will the Dąbrowa Population Pay for Water
[Dąbrowa — municipality.]
As we learn, the Dąbrowa magistrate is to levy a charge for water already from the 1st of November [listopad]. The water-supply commission has drawn up the following project concerning the water charge.
For every room one will pay 1 zł. a month. Exempt from paying for water are: 1) those who live in one room occupying up to 10 square metres, 2) the population living [—] 300 metres away from the water pumps, and 3) the unemployed.

[Dąbrowa — economy and banking.]

Against this proposal several members came out, who demanded that first of all the books be audited, in order to see who are the debtors that owe large sums, and when it turns out that the bank has no right to exist, then one should proceed to the liquidation.
For the „settlement“ [?] — as we are informed — the police were called, and they removed the „troublemakers“ from the meeting.

She Thought the Bailiff (Sequestrator) Was Knocking at the Door...

[Sosnowiec — a true story.] Often one reads sensational stories in the newspapers and somehow does not believe them — is it possible, how can such a thing happen at all?
But then life itself comes along and shows that it is richer than all fantasies. Here, listen to a story:
On Stara Street there sits an elderly woman, huddled[?] in her flat, and she does not stop worrying — what is to be done? Her husband earns nothing, in the house there is not a grosz to shop for the Sabbath, and any moment now the sequestrator (bailiff) is due to arrive — he wants to take away the last bits of belongings.
Suddenly she hears a knock at the door. She pretends not to hear, holds her breath and stays sitting motionless...
She does not know that outside, at her door, there is now a great commotion — all the neighbours have come running together and are waiting[?] impatiently for her to open.
What had happened?
In a droshky an elderly American couple had driven up, richly dressed, and begun asking after the above-mentioned woman, who, however, did not want to open. Until the neighbours assured her from behind the door that this was not the sequestrator...
And as soon as the door opened, the following dialogue took place between the old American and the poor Sosnowiec woman:
He: Mrs. K., do you have a brother in America?
She: Of course I have a brother. He has been there for forty-some years already. But all this time I have hardly heard from him. God knows whether he is even alive.
He: What a question, whether he is alive. I bring you greetings from him.
She: (surprised) From my brother? It cannot be.
He: Yes, yes, he is alive and...
The American did not finish — he threw himself on the poor woman's neck and both wept for a long time — no small thing. A sister and a brother who had not seen each other for forty-some years.
What happened next you can already imagine. In the poor little room it soon became bright in every corner. The American and his wife spent several days there. And now there is no longer any lack there for the Sabbath, nor is anything lacking on the days of the whole week...

Music Notes.

[Music — concert.]
On Saturday afternoon a concert took place in the "Nowości" cinema with the participation of Miss Bojarska, S. Gold, S. Weinberg and H. Barenblat.
The programme consisted of a series of works that are true pearls of classical music.
The concert was opened by the trio Gold, Weinberg and Barenblat with Bach's concerto "d moll" [in D minor], which they performed brilliantly. The good ensemble playing made it evident that we are dealing with people who have a strong musical sense.
It is no easy thing to play Bach, who is perhaps the deepest genius in musical literature; one must already be well advanced in music and have a fine, subtle ear in order to come out safely from the very difficult problems of Bach's works. The above-mentioned "trio" proved it, and it deserves a bravo.
Miss Bojarska played Liszt's "Concert Étude" very well. It was a fine piano rendition from which culture could be felt. Miss Bojarska commands the keyboard brilliantly. She possesses a good technique and with her playing gave the listeners aesthetic pleasure.
Miss Bojarska also sang. Her singing, however, stands at a lower level than her playing. She has quite a beautiful voice, but still too little cultivated. Her singing lacks expression; the coloratura range is not wide enough. Therefore her singing suffers from paleness. Further vocal study will remove the small defects.
S. Gold possesses a broad, warm and sure tone. He plays with expression and interprets very well the pieces he plays.
He was especially successful in Wieniawski's "Faust Fantasy" and Bloch's "Baal Shem". This was a technical and artistic high achievement that will long remain in the listeners' memory.
S. Weinberg, as second violinist in the "trio", did not lag behind. He has a warm-hearted tone and is on the rails that lead to an artistic career.
Henryk Barenblat accompanied brilliantly. We have more than once heard Barenblat accompany, and one must admit that he has a strong musical sense and is simply a master of accompaniment, and that means a great deal.
The initiative of the organisers in arranging such an afternoon concert is to be welcomed. In our conditions, where one so rarely gets to hear classical music, such concerts have great significance. It would therefore be very desirable that they take place more often.
S. R.
