The section is being opened because it happens very often that certain persons wish, on whatever occasion there is, to donate to the institution, which supports close to 100 orphans and widows in the present hard and bitter time.
The first donation, of 2[—] zł., we received from the Sewerin-Patak[?] family on the occasion of their little daughter's birthday.
Two new buildings — The railway station and the post-office building: for whom were they built and what use does the population get out of them?

(The railway station and the post-office building. — For whom were they built and what use does the population get out of them?)
Last week the Będzin post office moved into the newly built building, which was put up specially for this purpose, and the building looks very fine. The halls are comfortable, modern, aesthetically and hygienically arranged according to the last word in technology.
The building was put up outside the town, presumably so that the town should have the chance to expand; this may perhaps be understood, and it is even desirable. Let the town not be packed into narrow, compact masses where it is hard to breathe and the air is stifling; let free and wide streets be built, let hygienic and big [?] courtyards be laid out, where a little air and sun can get in.
What is annoying is that as soon as such a public institution, which serves the whole town, moves from a centre to a more distant district, one ought at the very least to have taken the interested parties into account and announced the change in town beforehand, either by notices in the press or by public announcements in the street. In whatever way it might be, one ought to have come to the citizens of the town and told them that from such-and-such a date the public should no longer come to the old building, but to the newly built one — and not that people should come and not know what is happening to them.
Such carelessness is unheard of. Why, one day earlier the population did not know that the post office was moving and that it would no longer be served at that place.
It is interesting: in summertime, before the opening of the new railway station, it was said that the building was not being opened because they wanted [?] to open the new station together with the post office. When it was said later that it had already been decided to open the new railway building, we enquired at the post-office administration whether it was true that the new post office would be opened at the same time as the station, which they then [?] confirmed to us, and which we passed on to our readers at the time. But in the end nothing came of it, and the post office did not even see itself obliged to apologise for the incorrect information. In exactly the same way the actual opening took place: no account was taken of the town and it was not thought necessary to give notice of the important change that concerns the town. It goes without saying that such frivolity is annoying. Such tactics are out of place.
We remember that during the occupation, as soon as the Germans had organised the postal service in Zagłębie, they announced every change, even through the press — and this was done both in a state of war and by temporary masters. All the more so must the population be treated differently when there is no state of war and the real masters are in charge.
And one more thing: we understand that newly built public buildings are created not only for the convenience of the officials, that is, of those who sit and work there, but also for the whole population. Everyone should enjoy the modernism, aesthetics and hygiene equally; unfortunately, though, here it is understood differently: that the population must not benefit from progress — on the contrary, the town must suffer from it. So it was with the railway, and so it is now with the post office.
When there was the old wooden station building („vokzal“), one could take out one's luggage quickly, and if one needed to complain one had the station master at hand at once. Now, however, it is quite different. Now, when there is a specially installed lift that hauls the goods up and down instantly, it takes a long time until one sees the goods brought from the platform into the storeroom. The same happened with the newspapers. Earlier one got them right after the train's departure, and now they wait with unloading the newspapers — which must be received instantly — until a later train arrives from another direction, so that all the goods can be taken into the storeroom together; and this involves a loss of time, which with newspapers plays a great role. Complaining to the station master is not one of the easy things, because firstly, under the new reformed arrangement he is not obliged to be present at the arrival and dispatch of every train, and secondly, if he is there after all, he sits in the innermost rooms and it is not so easy to see him.
Things are no better now, with the creation of the new post office. Earlier the entrance to the post-office boxes [was] open the whole twenty-four hours. After every mail train the letters were put into the post-office boxes, and at any time one could take out one's letters. One could also always buy stamps, postcards and the like. But now that we have a new post office, new rules must be made, and the rules are such that it should be worse for the population.
The post-office building is completely locked when the officials are not on duty, so that access to the boxes is impossible. After 6 o'clock, therefore, one can no longer take out one's mail, and [„hagoes“ — ?] no more than until 10 o'clock in the morning.
The question therefore arises whether the new buildings are really intended only for the benefit of the officials and to the detriment of the town. From whom does the actual revenue come in? We would understand that one must progress — that instead of delivering the mail in town twice, one should perhaps have done it three times — and not that a modus be adopted whereby one is to suffer from grandeur and aesthetics.
Besides that, another wrong has been done to the town: with the move into the new building it was absolutely necessary to leave a branch office (ekspozytura) in town, where one could also deal with the more important postal matters at another point in town. For one cannot demand that Czeladzka Street should have to walk such a distance. One could, we say, have left a branch office on Kołłątaja Street, which one part of the town could use. As soon as one aims to enlarge the town, one must adapt to the arrangements that the larger cities have.
First of all the post office should have left a branch in town and only afterwards moved — and not done exactly the opposite, so that afterwards it would be a lost cause, as the saying goes: done and finished.
Since we are already speaking of order and of the newly built buildings, let us take a look at what the square in front of the new railway station looks like. It is disgusting to look at this square as soon as one steps out of the station. As soon as one sets foot on Będzin soil, one falls straight into a swamp (bagno), and to the stranger's eye the old-time mud puddles of Będzin present themselves at once.
What face does this show to people, how does it look to the traveller? Must such a trifle really be left like this, to God's mercy? It is forbidden [?] whether this will fix itself overnight.
All this arises thanks to apathy and enormous carelessness, which must not be allowed. After all, we live in the very centre of Europe and find ourselves in the free, independent Polish Republic, where it is directly meant for the citizens to live in free and comfortable conditions.
R. Les.
Listen to Me, Mister Laksh!... A Letter from a Polish 'Magnate' to an American 'Pauper'.

By Y. Anerzhanek.
My beloved friend Mister Laksh in the holy community of New York!
As you know me, I am not one who takes revenge or bears a grudge; I don't hold with revenge. Even against my worst enemies I seek no revenge — after all, you have proof: my matchmaker is still alive...
Yes, true, I hate revenge, but in you, Mister Laksh, I have lived to see a great revenge; oh, little brother, do I have a revenge in you! When I hear how things are going with you butter-side down, when I hear of your downfall, I dance for joy.
Who was equal to you, Mister Laksh? Do you remember when you came to Poland in a pair of trousers like sacks, and the jacket [marynarka] swayed on your broad shoulders, and you wore red shoes with white toecaps, and on every finger three diamond rings — do you remember that?
And your language? "Yes" and "no" and "mister" and "lady", "chap"[?] and "business", "street" and "picture" and "papers" — may I know as much of you, Mister Laksh, as I understood what you[?] twanged under your nose.
Yes, Mister Laksh, as soon as you crossed the Polish border you promptly got a polyp in your nose and started to talk through your nose in English.
I argued with you: Shloyme Yoyne, how long is it since you stood in the Będzin fish market and shouted: "Ten a pound, she-fish!"? And now you already twang in English and go about in red shoes with white toecaps?
Do you remember, Mister Laksh, when our Polish marriageable girls stuck to you like flies to a plate of honey, and you promised all of them marriage? Do you remember how the Będzin "communal workers" and "askonim" bowed to your "golden calf". How they described you in the "gazettes" with your "picture", and in the end you escaped with one side[?] healthy? Do you still remember the times when for one American "laksh" you ate ten plates of Polish noodles [lokshn] with half a goose on top? Do you remember when relatives of the tenth generation turned up at your place and you became short-sighted — you recognised nobody? Do you remember all that, Mister Laksh?
Now sit down, good brother, and I will tell you prophecies of what will become of you.
America will set up a printing machine and will print dollars. First they will print thousand-dollar bills, ten thousands, hundred thousands, little millions, ten little millions, etc. To the watchman [stróż] you will give a million dollars for opening the gate, to the barber [fryzjer] you will give three million "na piwo" [a tip, "for beer"] for a shave. The zeros will swim before your eyes, you will talk of millions and billions and you will not have the means to keep the Sabbath...
Overnight new manufacturers and merchants will spring up. Doctors will trade in textiles, lawyers will manufacture trouser cloth, melamdim [cheder teachers] will produce thin soap. Bankers will make plum jam [powidła] with marmalade, butchers will buy a bundle of trousers and coats, and the "bundle" will rise[?] in value for them overnight. Whoever has a pen with a thick finger will write bills of exchange for millions, for billions of dollars, and will pay them off with one złoty...
In front of the stock exchange little Jews with walking sticks will mill about looking for the "rate". Everything will go by the "rate". The baker will sour[?] the leaven [rozczyn] according to the rate, the shoemaker will hammer in the hobnails [ćwieki] — according to the rate, the tailor will press the "przodek" [garment front] — according to the rate, the midwife [akuszerka] will deliver a child — according to the rate, the doctor will "zbadać" [examine] — according to the rate, the melamed will send the children home from cheder according to the rate, the butcher will chop the ribs for you — according to the rate; you will eat — rate, drink — rate, heaven and earth and rate!... You will go on "rating" until you are "rated out" altogether. The "billions" will grow and "Spekl" [the speculator?] will get consumption [suchoty]...
Then, good brother, we Zagłębie "magnates" will start a "rescue campaign" for our "impoverished" American brothers. A conference of "Beis Lechem" and "Malbish Arumim" will be convened, a "Joint" will be created with a basic capital of some three to four hundred złotys, "Polish parcels" and "Polish clothing" will be sent to America, in America a "Polish committee" of well-known American "askonim" will be formed, which will distribute the "Polish parcels" with the "Polish clothing"... to itself, and show the others a fig...
And then, oh then, Mister Laksh, I will have my Sabbath trousers pressed, with a wide freshly re-shaped hat [kapelusz]. I'll put a couple of "shiny glass stones" [błyszczące] on my fingers, I'll have letterheads printed with my firm, I'll have factories with chimneys and medals painted on them — and off to America!...
Well, there'll be some commotion in America! Rockefeller, Ford and other American "paupers" [dalfonim] will await me at the ship, delegations upon delegations from all the societies and institutions will pour in, I will smoke a genuine Polish "Perfar"[?] cigarette and will hear them all out. Then relatives, friends and landsleit will start pouring in, mothers will come with marriageable girls who are fit for the chuppah. The newspapers will print my "podobizna" [portrait] on the front page. I'll talk with "przepraszam" [excuse me] and "pszeszczeradla"[?], with "całuję rączki" [I kiss your hands] and "padam do nóg" [I fall at your feet], with "owszem" [indeed] and "psiakrew" [damn it], "i tak dalej" [and so on]. The Americans will choke on my Yiddish the way I choked on the Yiddish that Mister Laksh twanged in Będzin a few years ago; and when I'm about to travel back to "Yurop", I'll take out a chequebook of Era-Foyer's[?] People's Bank [Folks-Bank] in Będzin and hand out cheques "na prawo" and "na lewo" [right and left]...
Yes, Mister Laksh, in you I have lived to see a revenge!...
The Great Soul-Searching.

[Będzin — H. N. Bialik's visit; article.] Dr. A. Gottesdiener.
— And Będzin had the privilege of having with it, for not quite two whole days, the dear guest of all Polish Jewry, the greatest Jewish poet of our time, H. N. Bialik.
For the national-Zionist camp these were two festive days. People forgot all their worries, even those that have to do with politics, and rejoiced in Bialik.
They listened to him attentively, caught every word he spoke, and were truly refreshed by his words. For Bialik is very interesting in his conversations; some even say that here he is often more interesting than in his speeches. A quiet stream flows, casting onto its banks gold and pearls selected from the old Jewish treasury and set in a beautiful Bialikian art-form.
Bialik simply likes, like every Torah scholar, to talk words of Torah, only he brings the finest and best that we possess, and he interprets it according to his artistic taste. It is only a pity that no stenographer accompanies him at every step, to write everything, everything down.
Especially interesting were his speeches to the schoolchildren; one felt the scent of young flowers in his words, and his eyes sparkled with joy when the children asked him to speak only Hebrew.
But Bialik can, when he wants, conquer the urge of a gold-spinner, stop up the spring of gold and open the crater of a volcano spouting fire.
When he began to speak in Będzin at the banquet, people at first thought he would only tell memories of his time as a teacher in Sosnowiec and stories of his publishing ventures; but imperceptibly [?] Bialik passed from his business reports to the great soul-searching of Polish Jewry and of the Jewish people all over the world. His measured voice turned into the stifled roar of a lion, stifled with pain; a fire glowed in his eyes, his hands banged on the table, and from his mouth flew words like red-hot knives, which flew across the hall and struck the heart of every listener — each at a different spot.
He declared explicitly that he "wants to shame Jews", and he kept his word. The shame was great; of all those assembled almost nobody felt at ease. When Bialik asked the old question, "Has such a thing ever been?" — is it possible that a Polish intellectual should not know Polish, or a Russian Russian? When, with a strong sweep of his hand, he dismissed the Jewish intelligentsia which does not know the language of its people, a silent storm passed through the brains under the nicely combed hairdos — a silent storm which tore away the ironic smile [printed "iranish"] before it even had time to appear on some lips.
Bitter and sharp was his criticism of the neglected Jewish education, which makes Jewish studies into a kind of olive-sized morsel one puts on the table in order to say grace. A trifle which parents and educators could not care less about [literally: "which lies in their left, shaven-off side-lock"]. He grasped the problem of the education of the generation in all its sharpness — he spoke [?] of annihilation [?], God forbid; he lashed [?] them in the face with pulsa denura, with fiery strokes. It is only a pity that those Jews were not there whose faces most of all should have flamed with shame and fright at these words; it is only a pity that his words were not heard by all those who make a Purim play of Jewish education, who lead their children, like the Moloch-worshippers of old, straight into the fire of assimilation, and even drum along on little drums. —
There are phenomena which, had one not seen them with one's own eyes, one would absolutely not believe, so comic and at the same time so tragic are they. Bialik recognised the phenomena in Będzin, and more than that: as he recognised them, he felt them, and he called the child by its name; "decline" he called it: death of the soul, the passing of the Jewish spirit. A shudder went through the hall; people saw a generation standing on the edge of the abyss, and everyone was seized with fear. For a moment only — but one must not forget that moment. In that moment lies hidden the fate of Jewish youth: will it be ours, or alien to us, against us; will it be able to go on bearing the yoke of the nation's sufferings, or will it throw it off and make us bankrupt.
Deeply and earnestly must every Jew reflect on this and help Bialik in the great soul-searching.
A Little Feuilleton. Heaven and Earth and the Dollar.

[Feuilleton — satire; the dollar scare.]
After we had had a squeeze on the pound, we lately had further troubles with the "pud" [?] of the almighty "laks" [?], the American dollar, and it seemed as if the whole world was shaking.
A trifle, the dollar! What person does not have a few dollars — whether he gets them sent from America by a rich uncle, a relative, a brother, a sister, whether he just keeps them in his bosom, or under the pillow, dear as the afikoman, "against any trouble that may come". Zagłębie and America are, after all, firmly intertwined like one body and soul. Now imagine what we would look like if the dollar really slipped [?], God forbid? That would be, it seems, a greater blow for us than the war in China or the news that Edison has died and the electricity went out in him...
And what an impression it would have made on our sons and daughters, on the thousands of bridegrooms and brides — they would surely, it seems, have fainted under the four poles [of the wedding canopy], and more than one match would have been called off because of it. Rabbis, matchmakers and beadles would have been left without income [?], and the unemployment in the country would have grown still more — a trifle! The dollar is falling! And how would all the young householders, just out from under the needle, look with their fresh, quivering dowries, if not like beaten-off hoshanos?...
One can imagine the tumult in family life it would have caused. Man and wife [printed "men un khayev"] would not live in peace and would constantly keep tearing at each other and reproaching one another [?] that they had worried themselves sick; father and mother would go about having lost their heads, seeing [?] how the dowry for their daughters, stitched together with hardship and troubles, is trickling away and the green "sea [?] leaves" — the dollars — keep withering...
A ruin, a real ruin it would have wrought in the world; the black exchange would have become blacker still, and thousands of people would have flooded Modrzejowska Street, standing all the way up to the "haldes" [slag heaps] as if for tashlikh or for kapores...
Gabbais and their wives would run about distracted like mourners, worrying, supposedly, about their "dear" institutions, which are going under; the kehilla bowl would have run dry and they could no longer lick a fat little bone. Landlords would, poor things, have had to pay the tenants extra, just so as not to be left with the flats, because the dollars are worthless..
A whole upheaval would have taken place in our world order; everyone would go about like a muddled man, like an absent-minded one, loaded down with himself, with his wife, with the children, with America, with the whole world — not knowing what to do first, what to grab first.
It is a miracle that the remedy comes for the blow, that the American thief has still contrived to hold up the fallen dollar; oh, who knows what our sinful little world would have looked like — it would long ago have become a heap of ruins...
H. Matinka.
One Man

[Literature — serialized story.]
Róża Jakubowicz.
Dedicated to Yankev Ber Zayants.
(2)
And Mother did indeed receive me angrily: You great fool, where have you got to? Did you stand there gazing up into the sky, lost in thought about how the world turns?
At night I sat up over a book by Dickens and came upon a saying, that whoever is born on a Friday at daybreak lives badly and ends early.
I want to ask Mother when I was born. She groans in her sleep and suddenly opens her eyes, and seeing me sitting and reading she cries out: You great fool, what will become of you?
Mother, when was I born? I ask her all the same.
— It came out on a Friday, the eve of a holiday, when one gets up at daybreak to bake challahs, she answers and turns to the wall.
What are you saying, Lena — but Dickens knows what he is talking about. My life may be put to shame, but Dickens's words are true. He was pleased and came over to me to tap out his satisfaction on my bent shoulders.
Somewhere at a neighbour's a child was crying, and between Elimelech's shadowy walls it echoed mournfully.
— — — — — — —
You remember, there were the epidemics; our shtetl looked as if it had died out. There was not a house without a dead person. Everyone took fright and fled, wherever anyone could.
When my mother and my brother also left, it became quiet around me. A big piece of bread lay on the window sill. The yard was empty, the gutters whitewashed with lime and doused with carbolic, and only a cat exchanged glances with me.
First I gave myself a pinch [?] to see whether I was alive; then I took my stand in the deathly empty yard and began loudly declaiming Peretz's poems. And you know, I came to feel at home, as on the meadow in my childhood, and it seemed to me [?] that I heard a wonderful song somewhere in the distance.
I will write poetry, I told myself, poems like Peretz's, to give my mother joy. I know for certain that I will make everyone happy!
...Not always, I say. It used to be so quiet at your place. Why, you gathered at your home in those days Menke the idiot, Aryeh the cripple, and simply all the idlers of the town. And passing actors used to come to your house, little comedians whom nobody wanted to know; they had learned from Yosl the klezmer that at your place there were songbooks and sheet music, and they lodged with you. You got them tea and sugar and challah, and composed posters, and pleaded with your uncles to allow the performance to be held in the brewery, in the shed.
Only your brother Feivish, as if he were the elder, laughed at you and told your mother what the whole shtetl was saying about you: people said that once at night you set yourself on a bench in the middle of the river and counted the stars, and that you wanted to let your braids be undone [?] for the sake of all the old maids, poor orphan girls and cripples who had no hope of any match. Indeed you really did not want then to make any respectable, bourgeois match that your mother talked to you about.
— I, Lena, was in love then with the dayan's little daughter [or: your little daughter?], an orphan, and no beauty, so people said of her. I loved her in silence. When she came on Friday nights to my mother, I knew that it was me she meant. And, not wanting a shadow to fall on her good name, I made my heart like a stone, put on my coat and went down into the street, and there in the winter cold I stood so long, until she went home.
— — — — —
At last — he pauses a little, pensive — I threw over the unpaid Hebrew lessons I had been giving to the poor, packed up my notebooks, begged a few złotys from my mother, and with a letter in my pocket from Yosle the klezmer to his brother, the organ-grinder in Warsaw, I set off into the big city.
There, at the organ-grinder's, in a house of grimy children where I had left my bundle of things, as soon as I went out into the street for the first time the children fell upon my baggage and shared out my notebooks among themselves.
When, coming back from the street, I gave the children a thrashing, the klezmer's brother drove me out of the house and announced that my bones must not be found in Warsaw. Then I hung around where the trains run and spent the nights in the empty carriages. One fine day, when my pocket was already quite empty [lit. quite blue], I plucked up courage, went into the editorial office of "Tog" and presented my works, which were accepted.
Then my brother sent me the news that my mother had died. There are such days that stay stuck like a bone in the throat; such days one does not forget. Besides that, my brother sent me money for the sold house and things. I remained a Varsovian. I rented a place to live with a sock manufacturer, who, with my money, took me into the business as a partner.
I deliberately [?] handed my money over to the landlord, whom I trusted, so that I might be sure of my daily bread and be able to write in peace.
So, my dear child Lena, that is life, which was angry with me for so long, at times fell upon me like an avalanche [?], like a geyser, to smother me.
— — — — — — — —
I get up from my place, look at my little watch, then I ask: How did it come about that you married your partner's daughter?
...Some time passed, he begins to tell again, and my partner suddenly presented me with a reckoning: because of the general crisis, because of the many protested bills he had received, he had to stop all payments, and the business was stuck up to its ears in debts. So I took myself off from the business, spent whole days in libraries, ran about to get myself a cheap lunch. Coming in in the evening, I avoided meeting my former partner. I could not bear to see how ashamed he was before me for having swindled me. —
Once, however, he stopped me in the street and had a serious talk with me. He pities me, he says. What will I do now? He would propose that I marry his daughter, and he would set us up with a stocking shop.
I agreed to it, wanting to have something to live on, and a home in which to write. Plans for literary works were fermenting in me then in abundance.
And I became a man of comfortable living [?] beside my wife, the partner's daughter. At first it went somehow. Then my wife began to watch me, how I trade, how I speak to a merchant or a seller, and began to reproach me that everything I do is not businesslike, and that I am ruining the business. So it came about that when I had to talk with someone in her presence, I would deliberately [?] move off with the customer into a corner, so that she, my wife, should not hear how I talk. And as a result, however needed the man might not have been, he sensed my weakness in my speech and took control of my will.
(To be concluded).
One Must Not Keep Silent.

[Article — Będzin and Zagłębie; youth, card and domino playing.]
Card and domino playing, especially among the young, has become a plague.
Older and younger. Even near-children with naive little faces, merchants and workers, gymnasium pupils and clerks, and whomever else you like — but what's the truth, by now all of them are "has-beens" — absorbed, sweating and fuming with smoke, they sit buried in cards and clack the domino bones whole days and whole nights. Everywhere, in almost all societies and all associations, they gamble away their best time, their last hopes and also their last grosz — sometimes their own, sometimes a borrowed one, and perhaps also a "taken" one, because there is no other way left to go on "shporn" [?].
Perhaps it is not a problem for an article, someone will say; it is a deep tragedy. A social tragedy with all sorts of dramatic moments. And if you like, the card or domino player can even be a hero. He does not want to "shporn", but he MUST. The present time drives him to it: the living conditions, the economic situation, the lack of prospects and of hope. Nothing to take up, nothing to earn from, nowhere to work — so he "lives" [?] at the card table, at the domino bones, forgets himself, forgets the troubles and the worries, whiles away [?] the bitter time.
And it is not only so in Będzin. It is now a national plague. Indeed, travel to Sosnowiec and you will find the like, and also in Dąbrowa and in Zawiercie. True, not on such a scale, but the phenomenon as such exists — and that, after all, is what matters most.
I, however, consider this kind of thinking dangerous. It is the most dangerous determinism. It is the determinism that kills every will, every attempt to want to change the situation. It is the train of thought of the Angel of Death, of an angel who wants to kill the last bit of life, the last bit of courage, the last bit of Promethean aspiration [?].
No one denies the factor of the hard conditions, no one denies their great power either — but even a fervent Marxist will admit today that material conditions are not the one and only factors in life and that human will plays no role [sic; the sense intended is the opposite].
And therefore, if human will does play some role — be it the weakest role, be it the role of a regulator on the paths of necessity, of bitter MUST — one must not justify the terrible corruption of the young. One must not plead too much in its defence.
Otherwise it will come to this: the card and domino player will really see himself as a hero, a hero of his time — because of society's silence, because he is tolerated too much, because he is given a place in every association, because he is allowed to draw new companions to the card-and-domino intoxication — he already sees himself as somebody anyway and looks about him with pride. A trifle — a hero of his time!
And meanwhile the plague spreads like a pestilence; like leprosy it spreads everywhere, into every corner, over the whole body of the youth. To think nothing, want nothing, strive for nothing — it becomes an idea, a cult of card and domino playing — woe to us, that this is today the poetry of our life. There was a time when such a person would still now and then take a little book in hand, or, having no choice, even a holy book — and that was his poetry. Today he looks on all others as idlers; indeed, try talking with such a one: he is sure that his conduct is the most correct and that all others ought to behave the same way.
What should society do? First of all, stop accepting it as fate. Stop pleading in defence of this phenomenon. It is not a question of being opposed in principle to such amusements, and I am the last to preach asceticism. But once playing has taken the form of a plague, seizing a great part of the youth and killing their last hopes and will, one must take the path of the other EXTREME: to fight this card and domino playing by all means.
Wherever anyone has a say, let him wage war with the harshest means against this phenomenon. Diagnosing the disease will not help us. Nor will any palliatives; the disease must be torn out by the root, with its roots, without mercy.
Jewish society must not rest until this is achieved. In doing so, no one is to be shown favour. Nor may one take into account that this or that association sometimes draws income from this plague.
Otherwise Jewish society will have no new generation; there will grow up a wild, will-less generation of card drunkards, who later, when they grow older, will not be able to stand firmly on their tottering feet and will fall at the first wind.
L. G.
Where Is the Nationality?

[Satirical feuilleton — the Polish census.]
In our Jewish camp in Poland worlds are now being turned upside down — in the forthcoming population census they have "neglected" to include the heading "nationality".
So there is an uproar on all sides: where is the nationality?
But in truth we are not making a bad deal here at all.
On the contrary, let us just start doing the sums:
1) Not only Jews will be unable to declare their nationality, but also Poles, Germans, Ukrainians etc. So what then? Their nationality will have to be sought according to religion.
But what will happen with the freethinkers (apikorsim)?
We know very well that freethinkers are found among all peoples, but our "good friends" shout that these radicals are found only among Jews — and so, all freethinkers will be entered on our account, and we have not lost on the deal...
2) The assimilationists!
Had nationality been written down, they would all be Poles; but since it is only religion, they are, after all, all of the Mosaic faith — Jews!
So what shall we lose on the deal?
In short: on two sides we shall profit from the deal, and lose only on a third side — under the heading "language", because some Jews speak Polish.
But that is why we are merchants — who nowadays makes a deal that is all profit?..
Onkelos.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayera)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayera
The Portion
—o—
a) "And the Lord appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre as he sat in the tent door" (Gen. 18:1; printed "18:11")
A topsy-turvy world: "the Lord" — the good inclination — nowadays often lodges precisely "by the oaks of Mamre" (Mamre ~ mamrim, rebels): in the low places, among rebels and sinners. "And he" — the evil inclination — "sat in the tent door": he sits right in the tent of Torah... They have swapped places.
And something more:
"If this repulsive one [the evil inclination] meets you, drag him to the house of study" — and indeed the Torah scholars of old dragged the evil inclination into the house of study.. There, there is nothing to fear from him. But today, when there are no more people sitting in the house of study, he, the Adversary, strolls about free and easy in the streets. And here he is already more dangerous.. Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
b) "Do so, as you have said" (ibid. 5)
"The righteous say little and do much." The angels knew that Abraham was the opposite of all other hosts, and that however much he had listed here to serve them, he would serve them still more. And because they were in a hurry, they begged him: "Do so, as you have said" — give as much as you promised, and no more... Torat Moshe.
—o—
c) "Three measures of fine meal" (ibid. 6)
"He said 'meal' and she said 'fine flour' — from here [we learn] that a woman is stingy towards guests." Bava Metzia 87.
An old question: on the contrary — if Sarah ordered fine flour, better flour, to be brought, then she was more hospitable than Abraham.
They tell that once a rabbi came as a guest to R. Moshe Aharon of Kutno. He asks the rebbetzin to bring vodka to the meal in the guest's honour. R. Moshe Aharon gives [?] the bottle a shake: it doesn't foam — it is full of water. But the rebbetzin wriggles out of it: it is pure spirit, which doesn't foam either.. Says the Kutno rabbi: now I have the explanation of the Gemara in Bava Metzia: "She [sic, for: he] said 'meal' and she said 'fine flour'" — when Abraham said it was "meal", ordinary flour, Sarah actually wanted [?] to talk him into it [?] that it was the very finest of the fine. That [?] is the nature of women. So the Gemara rightly concludes from this that a woman is stingy towards guests.. Asifat Geonim.
—o—
d) "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is very great [printed 'rabbah'; the verse reads 'kaveda', grievous]" (ibid. 20)
"The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great" — the Sodomites cry out themselves. They tear at one another themselves. Therefore "their sin is very grievous" — it is hard to forgive them. "Forgiving iniquity and passing over transgression": if a Jew "passes over a transgression", commits a sin, God forgives the iniquity, bears the sin; but if the sinners sin against one another, kill one another and murder one another — it is too heavy for God to bear such sins anywhere... "Very grievous" — too heavy. Tiferet Shlomo.
—o—
e) "Perhaps there are fifty righteous [printed 'tzadikam'] within the city" (ibid. 24)
Thus Abraham argued with the Master of the Universe: if You want to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah, You must send down angels and open the heavens so that they spew fire and brimstone. What is all that for — if fifty righteous men live in the city, they will destroy it by themselves, without You, Master of the Universe.. and even twenty, and even only ten... From the mouth of the people.
— — —
"Righteous within the city" — such as are righteous not only in the house of study but even within the city: in the street, in trade, in dealing with people... Ahavat David.
—o—
f) "And the men of the city — the men of Sodom" (19:4)
The men of Sodom had beds on which they laid their guests. Whoever was too long had himself cut down, and whoever was too short was stretched out. Sanhedrin 109.
This is an allegorical hint at the extermination system of the men of Sodom of all generations and all countries. If the guest — the citizen of the minority — is too big, shows too much activity and develops trade [?] or production in the country, he is cut down. The short ones, on the other hand — the poor masses — they want to make rich: from them they want to squeeze taxes that will suffice for extravagant budgets. They are stretched out, they are considered rich, they must carry the whole burden of the state. Knesset Yisrael.
—o—
g) "And behold, behind him a ram caught in the thicket by his horns" (22:13)
"Behind" (ahar) — after all the generations, after all the deeds, Israel are caught in sins and entangled in troubles, and in the end they will be redeemed by the horns of the ram. Midrash.
"Thus shall the children of Israel eat their bread unclean among the nations." Our whole existence in exile is "caught in sins and entangled in troubles": we live only through sin. The bitter exile drives us to dishonest competition, to theft and robbery. Every people bases its existence on a different foundation; the foundation of our existence in exile is, alas, troubles and dishonesty.
Ohel Yaakov (the Dubno Maggid).
—o—
h) "And as the sand which is upon the seashore" (ibid. 17)
When the stormy sea waves dash against the sandy shores, they are broken. So it is with the Jews too: all the waves that rage against them and want to drown them are broken when they reach the Jewish sandy shore.
Olelot Efraim.
—o—
i) "And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" (ibid. 18; the verb apparently misprinted)
A Jew and a gentile converse:
The Christian: You know, surely, that all apostates are mostly rich, and all converts [to Judaism] are mostly poor people. Is that not a sign from God?
The Jew answers: The thing is very simple. When you change your faith you also change your luck, but not your head. Well then, an apostate exchanges his Jewish faith together with his Jewish luck, but his Jewish head stays with him.. A Christian, on the other hand, exchanges his Christian faith, his gentile luck, but his gentile head stays with him... Folk wit.
—o—
Haftarah.
j) "What have you in the house?" (2 Kings 4)
The blessing can rest only on what a person has earned himself ("what have you") with his own sweat — not robbed from strangers, nor [obtained] by various, formally [?] honest ways. Kokhav mi-Yaakov [?].
May a New Landlord Change an Agreement with an Old Tenant?

[Law — tenant protection.] The question mentioned concerns mainly tenants ("lokators") who live in, or are about to rent, flats in so-called new houses.
These tenants feel completely unprotected, exactly as though they were left to the sole mercy of their landlords. One must not forget, after all, that nobody moved into the new houses either — and even now nobody moves in — without paying beforehand, openly or covertly, considerable sums of key money, with which, incidentally, many a house was built or finished in the first place.
In an especially painful situation are precisely those tenants who had the misfortune to fall into the hands of such building speculators, who mostly proceed in such a way that soon afterwards they sell their houses, really or fictitiously, in order to be able to dictate fresh conditions to the tenants.
The tenants of these houses live in constant fear that the new landlord may demand such an increase as they will not be able to meet, and that they will therefore have to be thrown out onto the street. So this time we want to discuss the legal situation in this matter.
First of all we must dwell on the
Tenants of the old houses
Although these tenants are under the protection of the decree of 11 April 1924, before which all agreements not in accordance with the decree must yield, there nevertheless exist[?] two cases in which mutual agreements may be concluded, namely: when it is a matter of business premises or of a flat of more than 4 rooms — and that only insofar as it concerns the sum and the manner of payment, but in no case the obligation to move out after the agreed term. Even with regard to the permissible conditions, the agreement concluded is binding only for the period foreseen. After the agreed term the tenant has the choice not to renew[?] or extend the agreement, but to turn to the competent authorities (the court or the Urząd Rozjemczy — arbitration office) to have the basic rent fixed.
The circumstance that the house has passed to another landlord does not change the existing legal situation, not even with regard to the two exceptional agreements enumerated above.
Many new landlords apply to the Urz. Rozjemczy to have the basic rent re-assessed; this is not permissible.
The Urz. Rozjemczy is competent to fix the basic rent only in the case where the rent has not yet been fixed since the introduction of the złoty currency, where the composition of the rented flat has changed in the course of time, and where the basic rent cannot be established through the tenant who occupied the same premises in June 1924 or through any other indisputable proof (a contract).
Now concerning the
Tenants of new houses
If the legislator does not take this category of tenants under its protection, they must themselves endeavour, as far as at all possible, to protect their interests in various ways.
Some tenants hold contracts under which the house-owners renounce their exemption rights and place the rented premises temporarily under the operation of the decree on tenant protection. Such tenants are in every respect on an equal footing with the tenants of old houses.
Further, there are tenants who have contracts with fixed payment conditions for shorter or longer terms.
These contracts — if they were drawn up entirely by a notary (rejent), or the signatures were merely certified by a notary, or alternatively if they contain a confirmation of paid stamp duty — are binding on both parties for the agreed period, regardless of whether or not they have been entered in the mortgage register.
The same contracts bind the new landlords too, to their full extent, and therefore every attempt on the part of the new landlords not to recognise the current agreements and to demand increases, or otherwise to threaten evictions, is an explicit violation of the law, or a simple speculation on the tenants' fright.
On the other hand, the new landlords are not bound by any oral agreements, or agreements without precisely fixed dates.
D.
The Banquet — in Honour of Chaim Nachman Bialik

[Będzin — culture and Zionism.] As we reported in the previous issue of our paper, in honour of the visit of the great poet Ch. N. Bialik to Będzin a fine 'mesibah' (reception) was held last Thursday in the large hall of the Jewish school named after 'Sz. Fürstenbergowie' [S. Fürstenberg].
The 'glass of tea' with the participation of the guest from Eretz Israel aroused great interest among all sections of Będzin Jewry. There came the notables of the town, all the Zionist activists, public workers, the working intelligentsia, community elders and the pioneering (halutz) youth.
The hall where the banquet takes place is beautifully decorated. The tables are richly laid, and one sees that a tender Jewish woman's hand from WIZO took care of serving the tables. Above stand the banners of 'Gordonia', 'Sinai' and 'Betar'.
At 10 in the evening the great poet appears, and at the entrance he is received with shouts of welcome from the trumpeters[?] and the Gordonia members. The assembled public — numbering 200 people — receives the distinguished guest with resounding applause.
The chairman of the kehilla council, Mr. Wygorzki[?], opens the 'mesibah', and Dr. Weinzieher takes the chair. Before the greetings and speeches a letter is read from Mrs. Fürstenberg, who regrets her absence from the banquet. Mrs. F. sends the distinguished poet a beautiful bouquet of flowers.
The principal of the 'Yavneh' school, Dr. A. Gottesdiener, speaks in a vigorous Yiddish about Bialik's fruitful creative work. Mrs. Ratner delivers a very fine Hebrew speech about the 'People of the Book' and about Bialik as the greatest lyric poet in modern literature. Mrs. Ratner also recites an excerpt from Bialik's 'City of Slaughter' (Ir ha-Haregah).
Mr. Katzengold (in Hebrew) recalls the pleasant days he spent in Tel Aviv with the poet at the traditional 'Oneg Shabbat', where the poet appears before the people as 'Bialik by word of mouth'.
Mr. Abraham Liwer proclaims the campaign for the Hebrew book, which finds itself in a difficult situation.
Mr. Motek Hampel is the only young person to appear at the 'mesibah', with a successful greeting on behalf of the pioneering youth organisation 'Gordonia'. Mr. Hampel speaks about the spiritual decline of the people, about Jewish youth, about the essence of the 'Gordonia' movement, and about Bialik as the prince (nasi) of the newest Hebrew poetry.
During the interval pledges for the Hebrew book are taken. Those assembled contribute a sum of several hundred dollars. The members of 'Gordonia', who draw everyone's attention with their white shirts, cheer the public by singing pioneer songs and dancing an enthusiastic 'hora', thanks to which an Eretz-Israel mood spreads[?]. One forgets the daily, grey and heavy worries, spending a few elevated spiritual hours in the company of the greatest Jewish poet.
The interval is broken off, and the floor is given to Messrs. Dr. Weinzieher, Sider, Tencer, Präger (Sosnowiec) and Bialik's friend Mr. Twerski (Eretz Israel), who accompanies the poet on his propaganda tour for the Hebrew book.
Bialik takes the floor. Everyone concentrates in order to hear the spiritual Jewish father who has come from Eretz Israel to awaken the people from passivity and despair.
The poet describes his life: the days of the yeshiva in Volozhin, the 'Hibbat Zion' idea, which the poet joined, his move in 1897 to Sosnowiec, where he worked as a Hebrew teacher and where his first poems were published. After 3 years in Sosnowiec Bialik moves to Odessa, where he meets Ahad Ha'am and other Jewish men of spirit. In Odessa he founds the 'Moriah' publishing house and sets about his fruitful literary activity.
In 1921 he leaves Russia and moves to Berlin, where he continues his publishing work in 'Dvir'. In 1924 Bialik settles in Eretz Israel, making his home in Tel Aviv.
After describing his life story the poet passes on to the impressions he carries away from his visit to the lands of the Diaspora. Bialik speaks about the Jewish book, which is living through critical days, and calls on everyone to join the new society 'Friends of the Hebrew Book' (Yedidei ha-Sefer ha-Ivri).
Bialik's genial speech, which in some places turns into strong words of moral exhortation and rebuke, is received with great applause and cries of 'hurrah' in honour of the distinguished guest.
With the singing of 'Tehezaknah' the pleasant 'mesibah' ends at 3 o'clock in the morning.

S. Relkes — Mother and Woman (A Suspenseful Novel of Jewish Life), Part 6

S. Relkes.
Mother and Woman.
(A Suspenseful Novel of Jewish Life). 6

Only at the close of Yom Kippur did intercessors run to the pristav [the local police chief]. The finest Jews of the town moved heaven and earth: first of all one had to find out for what crime so kosher a Jew as Reb Chaim had been locked up. In short, the pristav showed a paper. As was written there, Reb Chaim had killed a child. An illegitimate child had been born to his granddaughter Rachel, and Reb Chaim had done away with it.
Reb Chaim had sent a living soul to the next world! The town was in an uproar. Everyone knew well that Reb Chaim had never in his life touched a fly. On the wall, that he had never raised a hand even against his own children. Whole days he sat over the holy book, and he lived only for the prayer-stand. Surely it was a blood libel against Reb Chaim. But nobody could understand where such enemies had come from, such bitter enemies of Reb Chaim's — and informers into the bargain! And what about his granddaughter Rachele! What had she to do [?] with the misfortune that had befallen her quiet, God-fearing grandfather? And on her account, too!
Rachele was a girl of eighteen. Her father had died when she was still a child, and Reb Chaim had taken her in: let her be a girl about the house, help the old grandmother with the housework, run errands, do the washing. So Rachele grew up in her grandfather's house, and nobody paid her any attention. Reb Chaim was busy with his books and the prayer-stand. The grandmother was a simple-minded Jewish woman, and she had no idea at all that there was such a thing in the world as sin. Yes, for her a transgression existed only in the tkhine [women's supplicatory prayer]. She repeated the words of Sarah bas Tovim [a famous author of tkhines] and begged the Master of the Universe to forgive her sins. But in her heart she knew that she had not sinned, that she had not transgressed the laws of the Torah. So it followed that sins are the sort of things the Almighty has to forgive, but that nobody commits. So thought the old grandmother, and she never felt it her duty to keep an eye on Rachele, her young granddaughter.
But Rachele grew; from a child she became a grown maiden, and the woman in her blossomed like a rosebush in ripe summer. Rachele secretly read storybooks about princes and princesses, about "holy love" and "wicked seducers". The girl read the little books through the nights by the meagre light of a small oil lamp, and her blood boiled. A girl of those years needs someone [?] before whom she can pour out her heart and share her experiences. But Rachele had no one; in her grandfather's house she was lonely and mute as a stone.
When Rachele turned seventeen, she began to go out for walks. Just beyond the shtetl stretched green meadows overgrown with colourful little flowers. A little further on the forest began, the deep old forest, with little paths and trails. The trees in the forest were broad, with dense crowns of branches. That is why, even in the middle of a bright day, it was half-dark there, as if it were an eternal dusk.
I describe the forest to you so precisely so that you may understand how young Rachele felt when she entered the half-darkness of the forest and around her floated the sounds of distant birdsong, and the scents of the wild plants struck her in the face like the smoke of a fire. So Rachele went for walks, mostly alone, for she wanted to dream out her little books, the novels of princes and princesses she had read her fill of.
When on a summer's day she came out of the forest, she was met by the colourful meadow, the quilt of red, yellow, green and blue little flowers. The sun danced towards her with burning, merry rays. And the shtetl with its low white houses looked at her with the homely gaze of a faithful mother.
It was in the middle of Tammuz. Rachele stole out of her grandfather's house, hid a little book under her arm and went into the forest. She was in the middle of the wonderful story, and her heart was full of the holy love of the two young people the storybook told of. She wanted to sit down at the edge of the forest so that the open meadow would still shine on her, and there go on reading the book. Forest and meadow and Rachele with her young heart full of love. Though she had no one.
(To be continued).

Repercussions of the Scandal at the Łódź Bank

[Sosnowiec — courts.]
In the month of March 2 Christians came into the local Trade and Industry Bank (known by the name of the Łódź Bank) and turned to the bank's deputy director, Mr. Goldman, saying they wanted to buy francs. Although Mr. Goldman explained to them several times that francs cannot be bought at the bank, the would-be buyers did not desist from their proposed transaction until it came to a sharp exchange of words between the deputy director and the Christians, which led to several bank employees detaining the Christians and calling the police.
One of the Christians, Mr. Łapuszański, brought the matter before the local municipal court, which issued a verdict by which Łapuszański is acquitted, whereas the employees, Messrs. Goldman, Klajnberg, Königsberg and Szapiro, are fined 50 zł. each.
Both parties were dissatisfied with this verdict and lodged an appeal with the district court.
Last week the trial took place at the district court, which annulled the first verdict; it found Messrs. Szapiro and Königsberg guilty and fined them 100 zł.

The Population Census.

(Sent by the Press Office of the Kielce[?] Voivodeship)
As is known, on 9 December of this year a general population census will take place throughout Poland. Judging by the publicity work, it appears that the idea of the census has met with deep understanding among the whole population. For the day of 9 December must bring full success to the executive apparatus, and at the same time moral satisfaction to the broad circles of the population, who, through the civic treatment by the census commissioners, will help establish all the necessary and exact information concerning the inhabitants of our country. The present census, which is the second of its kind, signifies — besides a manifestation of national and civic unity — also an exceptionally useful phenomenon for the normalisation of our economic life.
And with this thought, without any other tendentious intentions, the Main Statistical Office approaches the census operation. Society must therefore, in order to make the operation easier, show its cooperation, which consists first of all in trust in the census commissioner, that he will fulfil his task honestly and loyally.
Since the first census until now much has changed in Poland: the structure of the state has taken other forms; cultural life has been considerably revived, our prestige abroad has grown. In a word: we are steadily moving forward. And right now, when the country finds itself on the road to a better tomorrow, we have no idea: how many are we, with what national strength must we reckon? Of which parts does the great word consist: the Polish people?
To all these questions the day of 9 December must bring a clear answer.
Honest and detailed information on that day — this is a moral duty which every citizen in the country must fulfil. We too, the Jewish population, must energetically take part in the census and thus publicly and broadly document [our] right of existence in Poland. We must remember that economic policy in Poland must be changed so that it also satisfies the national minorities. The basis for this necessary change will surely be the result of the present census. The government will have to direct and orient itself in all questions according to this result. The number of the Jewish population in Poland must therefore not be diminished.
The day of 9 December must be a day of national and civic duty!
D. S—n.

The District Conference of the Gordonia Magshimim in Olkusz

Last week a "pegisha" (meeting) of "magshimim" of the Zagłębie pioneer youth organisation "Gordonia" took place in Olkusz. Up to 100 "bogrim" (graduates) came to this conference from the surrounding region, members of the local "Gordonia", pioneers from the Olkusz hachshara kibbutz and many Zionist guests.
The opening speech (in Hebrew) was given on behalf of the regional leadership (hanhagat ha-glilot) by Chalal[?] Menkarski[?] (Sosnowiec), who stressed the grave situation, the passivity and inertia in the Jewish and Zionist street, and touched on the question with which the meeting must concern itself.
Motek Hampel (Będzin) introduces a discussion: "The situation in Zionism, in Eretz Israel and in the Gordonia world". Discussing Zionism after the last Congress, which proved once again that the bearer of Zionist responsibility and realisation is Labour Zionism, the speaker talks about the strong development of the Gordonia movement, which today encompasses twenty thousand members in all the lands of the Diaspora and in Eretz Israel.
Israel Introligator (Sosnowiec): lectures on ideological problems, analysing the Zionist and socialist conception of "Gordonia" and the organic-synthetic kvutza, which is the way of the Gordonist in Eretz Israel.
Reuven Liwer (Będzin) lectures on "The paths of the magshim in the movement". He comes to the conclusion that the lack of aliyah and the prolongation of [stay at] the hachshara points must not drive the bogrim to despair: the magshim must strengthen his work in the movement, in "HeHalutz", "Tarbut", the League for Labour Eretz Israel, the KKL and KPAI; learn a productive trade, introduce work-shops in the organisations.
Israel Grojer (Kalisz) lectures on educational work.
Around all these papers an interesting discussion develops, in which take part: Stur[?], Wilf[?] (hachshara kibbutz Gadawarne[?]), Katek, Altman, Erner, Chana Poltorak, Glajtman (Sosnowiec), Magerkiewicz, Rachel Winryb (Dąbrowa), Miriam Frajtag, Jachimelfarb[?] (Będzin), Berman (Pilica), Etka Czeczora (Częstochowa), Sonia Uszyk (Wilga-Olkusz), Laufer (Chrzanów) and others.

For a Home for the Most Unfortunate!

Grown-up people manage in life in one way or another; children enjoy the care of their parents, but orphaned children have no assured[?] help from anywhere.
Do you know, citizens of Zagłębie, what the home of such an unfortunate, homeless orphan looks like?
Do you know in what conditions these unfortunates spend their lives?
We may perhaps not be contradicted if we say: no!
— Orphan children knock about in attic rooms in stifling air, or in damp, cold cellars, and often a dirty straw sack serves as a bed for a whole orphaned family. —
The Będzin Jewish Charitable Society therefore regards it as its most important task to protect these orphans, and, wishing to bring them up as capable, useful citizens, it has set about building the orphanage, which is to take in a hundred orphans.
Thanks to the donations of the local public, as well as the subsidies of the Magistrate [municipality] and the Jewish kehilla, we have succeeded in bringing the building up to the roof.
But to complete the house we still need a larger sum of money.
We therefore turn to you, fellow citizens, with this appeal, in the warm confidence that you will understand the importance and the great necessity of the matter.
By adding a brick to the above-mentioned building for the most unfortunate, you will fulfil not only a philanthropic but truly a civic duty.
The Board of the Jewish Charitable Society, Będzin.
Herszel Jedwab has died

[Łódź — culture; obituary.] From Łódź we have received the news that the well-known monologist and satirist Herszel Jedwab is no more.
The name Herszel Jedwab is no stranger in Zagłębie. More than once the Jewish theatre-goers in Będzin delighted in Jedwab's political monologues, among others also the well-known monologue "The Political Seder", for which he was arrested by the German occupiers and sat for several weeks in the Będzin prison.
Only a few months ago Jedwab was a guest in Będzin, but the audience left the theatre with the words:
— "No longer the same Jedwab as before."
This time his "Seder" was already without order... In general Jedwab was physically not the same either — broken, exhausted — until he breathed out his soul at the age of 61.
Honour to his memory!
—L.

[Zawiercie — court.] A trial that still has no remedy..
Two years ago Mr. Grinpoim[?] of Kromołów died in Zawiercie after an operation.
The operation had been carried out by Dr. Lewensztajn. In town, however, Dr. Zylbersztajn spread the news that Dr. Lewensztajn was guilty of the Jew's death.
Dr. Lewensztajn, hurt by the news that had been spread, sued Dr. Zylbersztajn for insult and for undermining his authority.
Over time the trial took place in several instances, also at the sessions of the Physicians' Association in Kraków, but Dr. Lewensztajn was not satisfied with any of these verdicts and kept appealing.
This week the trial again took place at the Sosnowiec district court, which sentenced Dr. Zylbersztajn to 2 weeks' arrest. The convicted man is again filing a cassation appeal.

At the police commissariat in Königshütte the 22-year-old Jan Plaw reported himself and declared that he had just killed his own father.

In the home of the Stańczyk family in Königshütte a tub of hot water had been placed on a bench in the kitchen. At that moment a child aged one and a half passed by and caught the tub. The result was gruesome: the child was scalded with the hot water and died in severe agony several hours later.

The Sick Fund, the Chamber of Crafts and the Chamber of Commerce (What are they doing for the citizens and what could they have done?) / A Car Makes a Ruin of a Little House

(What are they doing for the citizens and what could they have done?)
More than once have we discussed in this very place our social problems, the responsibility of the citizens towards the public institutions and also, conversely, of the institutions towards their members. We have said more than once, and also proved it with facts and figures, that we commit a crime against ourselves when we support our institutions which have no existence or which bring the community no benefit.
All this, however, was said about such institutions as we can decide upon: we can create them and liquidate them, we can maintain them on our own responsibility, and we can also bear the consequences on our own shoulders. But there are also genuine public institutions of a quite different type. These we have no possibility of creating at our own will, and we also cannot liquidate them when we might wish to. These are the official institutions, which are in the hands of the authorities, and we must maintain them under all circumstances, because they were created entirely for the people. To them belong the sick funds, the chambers of commerce and the chambers of crafts.
We have, for instance, more than once had occasion to touch upon the affairs of the sick fund, which stand far from a high level. It is no secret that because of the smallest error or oversight of an official the members suffer; besides, the sick do not receive the support which they ought to receive and which they badly need. The sick funds have at their disposal an enormously large budget, so that at the same time they also bear responsibility for the broad strata of the working masses. And indeed we quite often see no small disregard on the part of the officialdom, which arouses no small indignation. That is in general, but we Jews are disregarded there even more. No account is taken of us. Thus no communiqués at all are published here in Zagłębie in the Jewish press; the Jewish reader does not know when the general meetings take place and when new regulations come out. It goes without saying that the Jewish members occupy quite a respectable place there, so that one ought to reckon with us Jews.
Such institutions we cannot liquidate, and therefore nothing remains for us but to demand our rights there, in whatever way it may be. And by the way, we also have the right to demand that we be reckoned with and that our rights not be underrated.
Two new institutions have also arisen in the country for the benefit of the citizens. These are the chambers of commerce and the chambers of crafts. These institutions, too, take their budgets from the citizens. The chamber of commerce, for instance, draws its income from the merchants and industrialists, i.e. when a patent (trade licence) is taken out a surcharge for the chamber of commerce is at once added. So it turns out that the chambers of commerce are maintained mostly by merchants, because more commercial patents are issued than industrial patents; so it turns out that the greater part of the income flows in precisely from the merchant, from the average merchant element, which nowadays finds itself in very hard conditions.
It is a rare thing that [—?] [doubtful word "shtets"] turns out. Here, as everywhere, everything is borne by the middle class of the population. Every tax is aimed only at coming from the average citizen, and we know very well how hard it is now for the average citizen to get through life, how hard it is for him to fulfil his civic obligations for the benefit of the country and for the benefit of society.
For it is very well known that every holder of a patent must first of all set aside the greater part of his income for tax purposes, local expenses and the like, and only then, out of what remains of all the necessary expenses, can he set aside the rest for his own needs.
Well, when times were normal, when one could calculate what income and expenditure to set for the current month, and the situation was not so hard, one could restrict oneself and gain at least a little overview[?] of daily life; one knew what to economise on and what to allow oneself. But now, when the crisis has entered everyday life, because of which it becomes ever harder to breathe, the question arises: if the chamber of commerce is maintained by the merchant, if he must also maintain the newly created institution, then where does it give him anything, and what does he get from it? Surely the chambers of commerce ought to see to it that the merchant's situation improves, and if it is too weak for that, it must at least make an effort to reduce his expenses, which are bound up with so many payments that the merchant remains helpless and can afford himself nothing.
Why, for instance, should the chamber of commerce not see to it that the merchants' interests be eased: that a patent, for instance, could be bought twice a year, i.e. that a patent be issued for half a year; that the taxes could then be paid in the most far-reaching instalments; and also that the taxes in general be reduced to a minimum for the merchants, who have not yet died, but as for living, they have not lived for a long time. Why should the chambers of commerce not have the aim of helping the merchants to remain standing on their feet for as long as they toil and fulfil all their civic duties?
Surely the chambers of commerce must undertake an action to care for the merchants who are still on their feet and not let them fall into the abyss, because in that case they will be completely ruined, so that with the ruin of every merchant several citizens at the same time are brought down, and the state ceases to derive any benefit from him.
This is a serious question, on which the administrators of the chambers of commerce ought to dwell and which they ought to consider from every side.
R. Let[?].
