We Are Going Backwards... (In place of a homely letter).

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; kehilla, press, economy.] (In place of a homely letter). By Ben Amotz.
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
Your letter I have received, your letter has reached me. [I heard] of your grievance against me, that I have not written to you. What grief has befallen the chair of the kehilla president? — I laughed heartily; you are still — I thought to myself — naive, you do not know what is going on here and what our dithering looks like. Already close to 7 months have passed since the kehilla elections and
— it is all still as of old... The kehilla chair is like quicksilver: here, here, it seems the chair is in your hands, and suddenly it jumps back to the old one and shows everyone a fig... In general, the whole life of the place has become backward, not only our specific affairs; whatever you touch, you see torpor, backwardness, and to be frank one must admit that we are going backwards... Although technology performs wonders, trains run at enormous speeds, whole worlds are united by radio, and yet
— and yet we are going backwards.
And if you doubt it, we shall make it clear to you. Take, R' Shlomo, for example the story of Cain and Abel. It happened that two blood brothers quarrelled and one brother killed the other. That happened thousands of years ago, when culture and civilization stood at a very low level. Man in many qualities resembled the beasts of the field, four-footed creatures; nevertheless, He Himself, as it were, cursed the fratricide for the innocent blood that was shed.
And what do we see today? At a time when people fly in the heights like birds, when sitting in Zagłębie one hears what is being said in Rome? — nevertheless, when one brother puts his own brother to death, when public workers take from widows and orphans their last saved-up groszy, when thousands of people languish from hunger and want, when little children wither like leaves in autumn — it is hush, quiet; and if someone sighs, it is only for outward show, to fool the other into thinking he has a warm Jewish heart... It is a true generation of the Dispersion [of Babel], and with all that people open their mouths and call aloud:
— Culture! In the name of culture castles are built in the air; one shouts Hebrew! the second — Yiddish! the third — Yiddishize the Hebrew; and the masses? The true cause of culture is oppressed and strangled by "providers" of every kind, from the right and from the left; confusion of minds reigns in the Jewish street, the Jewish soul is torn to pieces, assimilation and boorishness have shaken hands, and the result?
— We are going backwards...
You remember, R' Shlomo, with what reverence one used to take a sheet of newspaper in hand. One first examined the paper from beginning to end, looked whether there was news of a new literary work, how many pages the paper contained and so on. But that was in the "dark" times, when the people was not cultured, was benighted, fanatical, still believed in and esteemed its authorities, snatched up every new word and naively envied whoever was learned...
Today, when the people already has "open eyes", when schoolchildren, under-age children, know by heart and can recite to you the names of all the film artists, whistle the newest revue[?] hits — there is no more patience for such foolishness as literature, good articles; on the contrary, the smaller the paper is, the more chances it has to exist. The press is making orderly progress: we are already, thank God, at 5 groszy a paper, and if "culture" continues to advance in the present manner, it is to be hoped that for 2 groszy one will get a paper, and instead of the yearly[?] novels so far there will be a short summary: how many "gypsy girls"[?], "dancing girls" and Chanele's fell into the hands of the pimps, how many young men betrayed their wives, and in addition there will be some illustrations of 13-year-old girls who are in maternity[?] homes...
* * *
We are going backwards in the economic field too. We do not mean that, for example, the number of liquidated businesses grows from day to day, that Kołłątaja Street will get back its first name "Before the Gate" — that we leave to Dr. Rotensztrajch[?], who keeps on shouting that "the shoemaking[?] is no good", and people heed him like last year's snow...
In the spheres of the organs of power, too, the idea has already ripened that we are not yet grown up for the present time, but one must begin to hold the public back a little
— one must go backwards...
Here I remember the time when you, R' Shlomo, still lived in our native shtetl; I remember it as though it had happened today: after breakfast you would sit down to write a little letter to the merchant of the nearby town with whom you traded. Then you would artfully close the little letter and go off to look for an opportunity [to send it]; mostly the little letters were taken along by Yechezkel the carter; a full bag of letters he had, and on coming into the town where the merchants lived he would plant himself in the middle of the market and distribute the letters according to the "gaddresses"...
We, the "civilized" of the twentieth century, are almost in the position of doing the same as our grandfathers. After all, there is no takings in the shops, so why spend 25 groszy on a postcard; better[?] that one writes little letters, seeks out Meir the carter, and the matter is settled.
Not only with letters shall we make "business", but with electricity too. We have just read that a tax (podatek) on electricity is going to be introduced. The news aroused great joy in me and in all my neighbours. Right after reading the sensation we went up to the attic, took down the old-time "Blitzer" [kerosene lamp], set it up in a place of honour, and we are waiting.
— For what, you ask?
For the new tax. No sooner will the tax come into force than we will throw out the modern chandelier (żyrandol) and go back to using
— the old Blitz lamp.
* * *
In Sosnowiec too "they are going backwards"; we thought that in the town they were already at the "tav", meanwhile it turns out that we are only at the "alef"...
"Once again the swords are clanging, the fronts are reinforced with fresh war material, in the general staffs a lively activity reigns, couriers run and bring fresh news about the enemy's camp, and people prepare feverishly
— for the winter campaign...
* * *
And in the middle stands Mephistopheles and laughs, rubs his hands for joy and sticks out a long tongue at everyone...
People! You take pride that you work wonders, that everything is in your hands, but where is your strength[?] — democracy, progress, civilization — bankrupt along the whole front. Reaction, the fist, falsehood, hypocrisy — those are the forms of existence of the time.
— We are going backwards.
Jewish Artisans' Guilds / in Old Poland.

Among Jewish historians there is a debate about how the guilds (cechs) came into being: were they created by the kehillot, or did they arise of themselves?
In my opinion those are right who hold that the guild was created on the initiative of the artisans themselves. The kahal of that time was expansively minded; it strove to seize as much power as possible, to have as much influence as possible over its "holy flock". By creating a guild and handing over to it the administration of the artisans' affairs, it would have narrowed its competences and limited its influence; therefore I am more inclined to accept the view that the Jewish guilds arose not with the consent of the kehillot but in struggle with the kehillot. More than that: it may well [?] be that the guilds arose in the first place not for external reasons but rather through internal ones — through the autocracy of the kahal, which in a scandalous manner treated the communal funds as its own property and in an unheard-of manner robbed and plundered the poor masses of the people, to whom first and foremost the artisans belonged.
The oldest information about a Jewish guild dates from the year 1613. In the 17th century the number of Jewish guilds began steadily to grow, and in almost every important kehilla we meet Jewish guilds. The statutes (takanot) of the guilds — group societies (chevrot) — are of various kinds, but they contain a whole series of main points that recur almost everywhere.
At the head of a guild stood a council of 4–5 elders and their two candidates, trustees (ne'emanim) and their candidates, and finally one member who was never changed, whereas the former used to change every month, just like the parnasim in the kahal.
In Płock it was a little different. There the "kehilla" [sic] administration consisted of 3 gabbaim, 3 trustees, 5 auditors and beadles. The elections of the administration were not democratic at all. It was not the general assembly of members that elected the guild elders; rather, this was done in an artful way whose aim was to secure the majority for the richer elements among the artisans. In Przemyśl the "elections" looked like this: the old administration would throw into an urn all those entitled to vote, cast lots and draw out 7 members, the so-called "Seven". The Seven would pick 5 electors, the so-called borerim, and only they would determine the administration of the society. In Płock the elections were a little more democratic: 3 kosher (worthy) men were drawn by lot, and they then elected the whole administration.
These "elections" strongly remind us of the elections in the democratic kehillot. Today's tricksters of all sorts of elections could well learn from the kehillot of that time how elections are made...
Besides the guild elders, every guild also had a special rabbi — a tailors' rabbi, etc. The office of guild rabbi was always held by one of the dayanim (rabbinic judges). The importance of the guild rabbi was very great: he kept the pinkas (minute book) of the society, he usually recorded the resolutions of the guild elders, and together with them he decided on the admission of new members, etc.
Just as among Christians the guilds were dependent on the magistrate (town council), so the Jewish artisans' societies were also more or less dependent on the kehillot; in different towns there were different degrees of dependence, and in some towns the societies were even entirely independent of the kehillot. In Przemyśl two representatives of the kahal took part in the meetings of the guild, who were supposed, so to speak, to supervise the activity of the guild. In the Lithuanian kehillot as much as half of the guild administration consisted of kahal representatives. In many communities the kahal even had the right to confirm the elections, to confirm newly adopted statutes and the like. Only in the so-called private towns, i.e. towns that belonged to private persons and not to the King, did the guilds — thanks to the fact that everything lay in the hands of the lord (poretz) — obtain complete freedom, complete independence from the kahal.
In general it can be established that in the 18th century, in the period of the death throes of Jewish autonomy, when the Council of Four Lands was losing its authority more and more, the rule of the kehilla over the guild also weakened. Thus, for example, it is interesting that the Płock pinkas of the tailors' society (chevra chayatim), which dates from those times, says nothing at all about this society standing in any kind of connection with the kehilla.
To become a master one had to be an apprentice for two years and a journeyman for one year — or, as they are called in Hebrew, na'ar (apprentice) and po'el. A young master — "ba'al habayit chadash" — had to be married; an unmarried man could not belong to the society. For three years after entering the guild the young master was called by the Polish word for "younger", młodszy. A "młodszy" did not have the same rights as an older master, the so-called "ba'al-habatishen"; in most towns a young master was not allowed to keep either journeymen or apprentices, nor did he have either the active or the passive right to vote for the guild administration. Only when he had become an older one was he allowed to keep them, but mostly only 2 journeymen and one or 2 apprentices.

A Clash between the Jews of Będzin and of Beuthen

(The Past of Zagłębie).
5.
Among the interesting moments in Jewish life we find the following interesting case. In the year 1724 the Jews of Będzin began a struggle with the Jews of Beuthen [Bytom] because a theft had been committed in a certain church by two Jews from Michałkowice near Beuthen, a certain Józefowicz and A. Jakubowicz. The court sentenced the said Jews to death and the sentence was carried out. The Beuthen Jews wanted to bury the bodies of the condemned in the Będzin cemetery, but when the cart reached the bridge over the Przemsza, the Będzin Jews closed the bridge and would not let the cart through. The elders of the Będzin Jews declared that they did not want any thieves in their cemetery. Things went so far that it came to a clash between the Beuthen and Będzin Jews. The Będzin Jews prevailed, however, and the Beuthen Jews were forced to take the bodies back and bury them in Beuthen. From then on, it is said, dates the beginning of a cemetery in Beuthen and of a Jewish community there.
The Jews of Mysłowice also separated from the Będzin kehilla, creating a kehilla of their own, but that happened because of the cholera which then raged in the Będzin district (1747).
Among the older generation, the following Jews were known in Będzin at the end of the eighteenth century: Herszel Aronowicz, Majer Szapiro, Herszel Salomonowicz, Ber Mojżeszowicz, Dawid Aronowicz, Jakub Lewkowicz, Szmul Tobiaszowicz, Lejb Aronowicz, Herszel Rubin, Jakub Erlich, Icchak Gitler, Szymon Landner, Lejb Zendlowicz, Wolf and Dawid Braner.
The situation of the Będzin Jews worsened greatly when the town passed to the German government (Rząd pruski [printed "pıuski"]). The Jews were deprived of their licences to keep taverns, they were not allowed to trade in salt, and the government also forbade the Jews to peddle in the surrounding villages. For not complying with the ordinance the Jews were punished with large sums of money.
After the taking of the Kingdom of Poland by Napoleon, the municipal authority in Będzin remembered the privileges granted to the Jews and wanted to ease their situation a little, but Napoleon's instructions said explicitly that no concessions were to be made with regard to Jews. Thus, when the Jews Abraham Gutman and Mendel Erlich applied to the authorities for a licence to open a tavern, they were answered that "it is not at all the will" of Prince Frederick Augustus of Warsaw that Jews be permitted to open taverns in the towns; on the contrary, in the same report (of 18 August 1808) it is said that the concession should rather be given to a Christian, even at a smaller profit for the town.
Starting from the year 1791 the number of Jews in Będzin begins to grow at a fast pace. Whereas in 1789 there were about 300 Jews out of 1200 inhabitants, in not even a full 50 years (1835) there were 1200 Jews out of a total of 2500. The Russian law of 13 April 1835 somewhat checked the arrival of foreign Jews in Będzin. Despite this, in 1852 there were 2231 Jews out of 3334 inhabitants. The statistics show that in 1883 there were 3800 Jews out of 5424 inhabitants.
———
With this M. Kantor-Mirski concludes his sketch on the Jews in Zagłębie, and although in some places the author was not overly accurately informed, he deserves thanks for his entirely objective treatment of the subject.
Sz. Szak.
If Only the Wagons Would Arrive...

[Satirical feuilleton — unemployment.] By „Fama“.
A commotion, a hubbub: people are caring for the unemployed. Alms are being collected, taxes levied, the postal tariff has been raised, etc. etc.
How many unemployed there are in the world, muses R' Yona the flour-packer. The number he does not know, but that they are thinking of him here too — of that there is no doubt at all.
He had worked as a flour-packer in a mill; beside him his wife worked too, patching sacks. He would tread the flour down in the big bin, and she would sit to one side and take delight in her white „Rusalek“ [a pet name for her husband], who peered out of the flour clouds [printed „mek-clouds“]. He used to call the bin „Ur Kasdim“, because the flour burns him all day long and he is not burned up. What is more, he even gets three złoty a day; our father Abraham did not have that currency either...
So they worked. She would sit beside him with a mountain of sacks, and he looked out of the bin like a snowman, with two black eyes like lumps of coal stuck in.
— Just[?] a broom in your hand, Yona, and you are like a snow-scarecrow[?] — she used to joke with him.
For months now they have been sitting without bread, unemployed. They live, with one child, on what thousands of Jewish families live on — on miracles.
While the mill was still an idyll, they lived in peace. Things turned bad. At home it became gloomy, overcast [chmurne]. He grumbled, and she either lamented her desolate spirits or sent her white „Rusalek“ to all the black years...
— Well, Yona, what will become of us? Winter is coming, with such cold, the stove smokes, one could choke, not a crumb of coal — she blows her nose and wipes her eyes with the front hem of her underskirt [spódnica].
— Coal, you say? A fine story! Don't you know that we have a whole wagon of coal, a whole wagon of bread? The papers write that whole wagons of coal will be given to us unemployed; after all, they are thinking of us unemployed. You mustn't take it so to heart! Thank God I am unemployed, for otherwise when would I, Yona the flour-packer, ever get a wagon of coal?...
Such are the conversations they always have, and he is busy only with the wagons that are on their way... he has become a regular merchant.
One day R' Yona comes running in, out of breath, neither dead nor alive. To his wife's question where he has been he answers in fragments, gasping for breath:
— I was, I was at the railway, what do you mean?...
— Maybe[?] you got work? — she asks, more cheerfully.
— There you go! I have something more important. I went to see whether m y wagon of coal is already here. My wagon! After all I am some sort of unemployed man, and if the newspapers write, surely they will not forget R' Yona the flour-packer. Yes, so I was at the railway too — it is already on its way...
Never mind, that is the main thing, my dear; very soon we will be making latkes, with babkas of the kind I like — you know my taste.
— What kind of holiday has come over you?
— What are you talking about? Wagons of potatoes are coming for u s unemployed. What else — they will give coal, wood and potatoes, everything: latkes, bubelekh, babkas as I like them.
Some time passed. At home it grew colder. Yona and his wife sit there downcast; it would seem — two people with one child, what do they need? And yet the „wagons“ did not fill them. They were truly going hungry.
— Listen — says R' Yona — I'll go to the railway. Maybe the wagons are already there; I read in the papers that they are due to arrive any day now... They write that wagons are coming for u s. Surely they are thinking kindly of us, and of R' Yona the flour-packer as well.
A little later he runs in breathless, flushed, as if after closing an important transaction.
— Already here!... — he shouts at the door.
— What, wood with potatoes? — asks the wife.
— Yes... no, there is a fresh newspaper with a report that they are already digging the potatoes.
— May you be buried, you and your luck! — shouts the wife [pun: graben „to dig“ / begraben „to bury“].
— Wait, wait, just look, one must prepare in advance. Hush, hush, I have real news: we shall have something more, you know — sugar. A whole wagon of sugar; you know, after all, that „cukier krzepi“ [„sugar strengthens“], the unemployed need to have the strength to wait... for work. Yes, just look how the head is downcast, well[?], and to order[?] a wagon. I won't ask you any more: when would you have heard of whole wagons if I, R' Yona, were not an unemployed man? So, first of all a new kapote for me... and you — whatever you like. Just imagine, a couple of wagons come crashing[?] in to me: first coal, then potatoes, then sugar... with... well, I tell you, today we shall already be stirring with the little spoon. Not so bad — the time has come at last...
Meanwhile the landlord comes in, angry, in a temper.
— What will happen? I can't wait any longer?
— I can't wait any longer either — says R' Yona, like a merchant.
— And what are you waiting for? — asks the landlord.
— What do you mean? For my wagons! Whole wagons are due to arrive for me. Today, tomorrow... everybody is thinking about me, Yona the unemployed. And you know, after all... just let the wagon of potatoes arrive for me, and a wagon of coal, sugar and clothes... What is there to say? Certainly I'll pay — today, tomorrow, if only the wagons arrive...
From an Inexhaustible Source

(On the 18th yahrzeit of the former Rabbi of Będzin, the great Rabbi R' Yisachar Berish, of blessed memory.)

1.
A shrug of the shoulders is no answer.
Once, during a debate in learning, one of the participants, having nothing to answer, shrugged his shoulders and said: "Eh." The rabbi remarked on this: the Gemara says "matters of the Oral Law you may not say in writing" (the laws that were transmitted orally must not be written down). That means they CAN be written down, only one MAY not write them down. Let me see then, on the contrary — show a trick and write down that shrug of the shoulders...

2.
In a small town it is harder to be a rabbi than in a big city.
To the request for advice from a small-town rabbi, whether he should take up a rabbinate in a larger city, the rabbi of blessed memory said: the rabbinate in a big city is in fact easier than in a small town. The Mishnah says: "Whoever has neither Scripture, nor Mishnah, nor good conduct (derekh eretz) is not part of the settlement (yishuv)." In a small town, if someone has difficulty with a passage of Chumash he asks the rabbi, so the rabbi must perforce know Chumash well; if another has difficulty with a passage of Mishnayot, he goes to the rabbi, so the rabbi must know Mishnayot too. A small-town rabbi usually lives in a cramped apartment, so that everyone sees his daily conduct. The rabbi is therefore forced to behave with derekh eretz. And so whoever does not know all this "is not of the yishuv" ("yishuv" here means a small town). In a big city, on the other hand, a rabbi is not obliged in all this...
Remark: related by the Rabbi of Strzemieszyce, the great Rabbi R' Shlomo David, of blessed memory.

2. [sic; should be 3]
On meetings.
Very often the rabbi used to call meetings on town affairs. But he used to be grieved that the participants "dismissed"[?] (wasted) the time with arguments. After one such meeting the rabbi said: the Midrash relates that when the Master of the Universe wished to create the first man, the angels split into factions and parties: Kindness said "Let him be created," for man does acts of kindness; Truth said "Let him not be created," for man is all falsehood; Righteousness said "Let him be created," for man gives charity; Peace said "Let him not be created," for man is quarrelsome — so the Almighty cast Truth down to the earth and created man. Now actually it is difficult: why does it not say that Kindness and Righteousness said "Let him be created," while Truth and Peace — "Let him not be created"? But the answer is: when Kindness says "Let him be created," Truth must say "Let him not be created" (he means nothing else, God forbid, but the truth...); when Truth in turn says "Let him not be created," Righteousness must then say "Let him be created"; at the end comes Peace and, "for the sake of peace," he says "Let him not be created."
The rabbi added:
Actually every angel had a just claim, and especially Truth. But the Master of the Universe cast him down to show that at a time when one wants [printed: "mouth"] to create something, talk and arguments are superfluous, even truthful ones...

4.
From the rabbi's sermons.
"The Torah of the Lord is perfect (temimah), restoring the soul." What does temimah — whole — mean? But[?] usually everyone remembers the commandments that suit him: the lender remembers that "repaying a creditor is a mitzvah," the borrower remembers that [?"mashpiyim"] "he shall not exact"; when the Torah of the Lord is whole, one will remember everything that is written in the Torah. Then it is "restoring the soul" ("nefesh" also means soul/neshamah).

5.
Better a good name than a precious stone.
On the verse "And the Lord spoke unto Moses ... that they take for me an offering" the Midrash says: "This is what is written: a good name is rather to be chosen than great riches — the name of Moses is preferable to the riches of Korah" (better the name of Moses our Teacher than Korah's wealth). How is this derived from "that they take for me an offering"?
But, as is the way of the world, when there are current matters touching religion, one convenes the Torah scholars and the Hasidim; for matters which need money, on the other hand, one invites the wealthy men of the town. Now for the Tabernacle one needed first of all gold and silver, so it should have said "And the Lord spoke unto Korah"; why did the Almighty speak again to Moses? It is proof that "the name of Moses is preferable to the riches of Korah."

6.
"For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you from all your sins." Now actually, once it already says "atonement shall be made," "to cleanse you from all your sins" is superfluous. But the plain meaning is: "for on this day He shall atone" — the Master of the Universe will grant atonement on this day, but "upon you" — it is incumbent upon you "to cleanse yourselves from all your sins"; Yom Kippur, as is known, atones only for those who repent.

7.
From the rabbi's last sermon.
On Shabbat Shuvah 5674, 6 weeks before his death, the rabbi of blessed memory felt very weak. Those close to him insisted that the rabbi should this time make an exception: not go to the synagogue and not deliver a sermon. The rabbi stipulated that he would go to the synagogue and promised not to preach. Being in the synagogue, however, and seeing a large crowd come for a sermon, he decided to speak after all. He did not begin the sermon, as always, with matters of the day, but thus: the Gemara, tractate Shabbat, relates that on the second day after the Jews came to Mount Sinai Moses said to them "And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation," i.e. you will be [printed: "see"] a people of priests and a holy people. Now why was the first thing said a praise of the Jews and not a commandment? The answer is: on the first day — according to the said Gemara — Moses told them nothing at all. The reason was the weariness of the journey. But since, when one loves someone, one speaks to him even when one is weak — so that the Jews should not suspect him of not loving them, he spoke praise to them on the second day.
"I say this in reference to the fact," the rabbi concluded, "that because of my weakness I did not want to deliver a sermon today, but since I love the congregation I do not reckon with my weakness."
The rabbi then spoke at length about all the current town affairs, such as: the cemetery, the synagogue, the mikveh, etc.

8.
From the eulogy for R' Avromele Hendels of blessed memory.
In the year 5670 the well-known scholar and Hasid R' Avromele Hendels of blessed memory died. The rabbi, in his eulogy, among other things also told the following parable: the Gemara says "What is the way of a creditor to take out? The least of the vessels" (usually the borrower brings out as a pledge for the lender the thing that is worth least). Once it happened that a borrower, an ignoramus, gave as a pledge an old set of the Talmud, believing that he was giving away a worthless thing. The lender happened to be a scholar and was [?] delighted with the "worthless" pledge.
The same applies to the deceased: according to the Midrash the righteous man is taken from the world as a pledge (a "zakładnik" [Polish: hostage]...). You may think that the deceased, being a pauper, is "the least of the vessels"; but in heaven R' Avromele Hendels is a very precious pledge...
The rabbi then interpreted the verse "Should Abner die as a fool dieth?" (II Samuel 3) as applying to the deceased of blessed memory.

9.
I do not bow to money-bags.
A householder once pointed out to the rabbi that he should flatter a certain wealthy man a little. God forbid — the rabbi recoiled — it is written "And Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence." Mordecai did not want to bow to idolatry.

10.
About a fool there is no question, about a clever man there is no answer.
How good it is to be a fool — the rabbi used to say — for every wrong deed an excuse is ready: "after all, he is a fool." And if once in a blue moon he does something clever, it is trumpeted in all the streets. About a clever man, on the other hand, there are always questions.
Roza Jakubowicz, Kalisz

To the memory of my father, Rabbi R' Yisachar Berish of blessed memory.
* * *
Who has spoken so of You, O God,
as his faithful eyes did?
Who, like him, by divine command
has bent the days of his life?
Who has sung so of Your greatness
as his clear voices did?
And who, like him, awaited Your wonder-miracle
which has no longer come...
One, a Human Being.

[Literature — serialized story, conclusion.] By Roza Jakubowicz.
Dedicated to Yankev Ber Zajonc [?].
(3)

I could not bear it any longer, and one evening, when, coming home from the street tired and worn out, my wife and my mother-in-law sat down on both sides of me and both together began to reckon up what I had to do today and what tomorrow, I quietly got up, stole out of the house and never came back. Since then I have lived right here in this little room, and I am well.
— What have you written? I ask, already getting up to leave.
— You will see one day everything I have written. All the problematic natures of our shtetl will live on the stage; just as in my heart, the world will be shaken!
— And why do you publish nothing? I ask once more, the last question.
— Why do I not publish? He stands up, as if he had been transformed into someone else. — Listen to this too, Lena, what I am going to tell you now.
Interest in film is so much more elevated than interest in the book that Charlie Chaplin, wanting to make his idea more acoustic and more beautiful, can, in his red villa in Hollywood, film every movement silently and record it loudly with microphones, until he sees his "City Lights". And I, quietly covering my whole life with paper [printed "tapirene", probably a misprint for "papirene"] sketches and novellas, must remain bankrupt, unable to make my way to the lights of the big city. Still, I consider myself similar to comrade Chaplin. You ask how?
His art does not lie in exposing the "eyno-margish" [the one who does not feel], who suffers and does not let it be seen on him; rather his art lies in unconsciously carrying such a one within himself. And I, with my "problematic natures of my shtetl", can beat my head against the wall, and, unable, like the master of the silent film, to make my way to the lights of the big city, I go about with the clown's [?] martyrdom within myself and for myself.
But do not hurry, as Heine says: the true work of art does not reckon with fleeting days and years!
I slowly rise from my place. After this life story has been unloaded here, it has grown darker in the little room; I leave the little room. He is still looking for something in it. I throw one more glance inside.
The afternoon rays of the autumn sun, which had barely managed to get in here through the closed little window, dimly gild his sunken, poor [?] shoulders, which are still rummaging among the papers. Out of the whole mountain of dark letters lying there, the rays lift up before my eyes [printed "agign"] and glide along with Dickens's saying, the prophecy about Elimelech's wasted youth, with the ideal of love of mankind that did not reach its goal, with the stifled longing for happiness, of which scraps of paper have remained.
At last he comes out, locks the little room once and once again, and tries again whether it is locked.
— I always told you, Lena — he looks at me with a look of triumph — that I would stay with literature!
(The End).
My Chance Catch of Fish in the Przemszanka.

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton.] (A Little Feuilleton).

The Przemszanka is a stream that cuts through, like a blood (or mud) artery, the heart, the very middle of the town of Będzin.
Like a thief [? "gapenik"] she scrapes past Serczarz's [?] "broiz" [?], cuts through beside the Great Synagogue, descends to the Linat ha-Cholim [hostel for the sick], bringing all her treasures down below the hill.
A modest stream it is; poets have not sung of it. I am the only one who has thought of it, I am the first who has gone down to the Linat ha-Cholim, to its banks, on a scientific mission.
First of all I noticed the remarkable property of her "clear" waters of reflecting with unusual accuracy the essence of certain things. Here, on the other side of the Przemszanka, a (let us say) secular-progressive communal activist has taken his stand. We take a look into the water and we immediately see something that stands on its head and is entirely black...
After this superficial observation I let my net down into the "depths" to see what is there.
The net was, indeed, full, but only of wild grass and wretched weeds; still, among them I spotted a strange creature in which I recognized the head of Beis Yaakov. He was so frightened by my sudden attack that he immediately began mumbling various Yiddish and Polish prayers and incantations...
The second time I pulled out my net with a luckier catch — a whole camp of elegant creatures. Frogs in tailcoats and white waistcoats, croaking in various languages, mostly in our state language. —
I immediately recognized our diploma-holding intelligentsia...
Full of self-importance, so shiny, so slippery.
At first they did not recognize me... They thought I was a mighty ruler, so they began to fawn on me and to insist loudly that they too are... Poles (adding quietly) of the faith of Moses our Teacher...
The third time I could barely drag my net out by force, so heavy was it. First of all I sensed a suspicious smell (a miracle that I have a cold). Looking closely, I saw that it was a whole lump, a hodgepodge of creatures, among which it is hard to make out individuals; still, I recognized among them many communal activists, town councillors, parnassim and other "cooking ladles" [busybodies].
You ask what sort of creatures these are? Certainly not fish — worms, rather...
• • •
I have no more desire to continue this rare catch of fish; enough...
The sun is shining — I propose to my cousin that we take a stroll.
Our youth strolls on the pavements, festive, so absorbed in lively conversation; how lovely it is — the sounds of our typical Jewish Polish reach my ears.
I think: if Eliza Orzeszkowa had heard how we defile her language and are ashamed of our own, she would have been a much smaller friend of the Jews...
One would like to stretch out a hand and drag these cavaliers with their panienki [young ladies] down to the Przemszanka and wash off them the make-up together with the "intelligentsia-ness".
— Let them become a bit like themselves...
* * *
Many feelings and thoughts you awaken, Przemszanka...
I sit by your bank, bewitched [?]
and drag out, so enchanted,
from your mud — groszy [?],
the well-known personages...
Y. A. [?]
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Chayei Sarah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Chayei Sarah
The Portion
—o—
a) "And the life of Sarah was" (Gen. 23:1)
"The Lord knows the days of the perfect... just as they are perfect, so their years are perfect." Midrash.
A person's life is like a little watch from a good firm... If one takes care of it, it runs regularly ["reyel"] and exactly according to the manufacturer's original setting. But the boy who tinkers with the watch and wants to know "where its legs grow from" — with such a watch-owner one cannot guarantee even the best watch...
Let life flow according to its preset regulation; do not try to tinker with it yourself, for you are no craftsman at it and you may yet break it...
Afikei Yehuda.
—o—
b) "A hundred years and twenty years" (ibid.)
"At a hundred she was as sinless[?] as a girl of twenty." Rashi.
Incomprehensible: of an old woman of a hundred, when one wants to say that she does not sin, one compares her to a girl of twenty? It would seem that at twenty one is more inclined to sin than at a hundred...
The meaning of Rashi's interpretation is a different one:
Sarah as an old woman was pious not because old age caused it, but because she was truly God-fearing — just like a girl of twenty: if she is pious, it is not because she has no desire for life, for in the blossoming years life does not yet interfere; it is only because she is sincerely pious. Such honest religiosity Sarah possessed also at a hundred. At that time — though a hundred years old — she still had plenty of desire for life and nevertheless did not sin. Karnei Re'em.
—o—
c) "And Abraham was old, well stricken in age, and the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things"
Only when Abraham reached old age could he be blessed with the blessing "in all things" — that he should have everything, that he should lack nothing... In youth, when life still seethes in a person, however much one may possess, something is always still missing; it is impossible to be blessed "in all things".
Tiferet Uziel (Rabbi Uziel Meisels).
—o—
The author of "Noda BiShe'arim" was a great timber merchant, exported goods to Danzig [Gdańsk], and at the same time was rabbi of Lublin. This rich rabbi used to argue constantly with a friend of his, a dayan (rabbinical judge) and a great pauper, that a person need lack nothing, and that however bad things may be for him, "a man must bless [God] for the bad as he blesses for the good". Thus the rich and fortunate gaon understood it: that one must not be broken by misfortune...
Once it happened that the rabbi sent off a whole transport of timber to Danzig. His entire fortune lay in that merchandise — and the ship went down.
Nobody dares to tell the rabbi the bad news. The mission falls to the dayan.
He goes in to him and conducts a conversation with him on their favourite theme: "a man must bless for the bad just as he blesses for the good".
"Do you feel within yourself," the dayan asks him, "that you would truly be capable of fulfilling this saying of the Sages and praising God with joy for a misfortune?"
"Certainly, surely, why of course, how else?..."
"If so, know that your ship has gone down."
The gaon turns deathly pale and cries out, bewildered:
"Ha?!.."
"Rebbe, the 'Ha?!' is also superfluous..."
From this story a folk saying arose in Lublin:
"The 'Ha?!' is also superfluous"...
—o—
d) "Perhaps the woman will not follow me" (ibid., 39)
Eliezer had a daughter and wanted to marry her into Isaac's family; so he wished that Rebecca would not want to come with him (not "ulay" [perhaps] but "elay" [to me] is written). Rashi.
But Eliezer had said the very same words to Abraham on his way there as well (see 24:5) — so the nuance "elay" should have been stressed there.
But on the way there Eliezer himself did not feel his own bias. When a person harbours some bad ulterior motive, he does not feel it himself. Only now, when Rebecca had already been destined to go to Isaac and nothing had come of his plan, did he realise for the first time that he had previously had an ulterior motive in the matter...
Nifla'ot Chadashot (on Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk [Kock]).
—o—
The fact that the coarse ignoramus wants to marry into a family of lineage is only so that he can boast of it before people. In truth "the cursed does not cleave to the blessed". The cursed one wants nothing [real]... he is after glory alone; that is why the nuance is stressed now, when Eliezer told it to Bethuel — for that was all he had in mind: to become related to Isaac so as to have something to tell about...
Divrei Shaul.
—o—
e) "And they sent away Rebecca... and they blessed Rebecca" (ibid., 59–60)
"And they sent away Rebecca" — "shiluchim" means sending off with a dowry (see Rashi, I Kings 9). And what kind of dowry did the Aramean family give Rebecca?
"And they blessed Rebecca" — blessings, blessings without measure..
Ktav Sofer.
—o—
f) "Our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of ten thousands" (ibid.)
Laban the deceiver knew that "all children take after their mother's brother", so[?] he wished his sister: have many children — then there will surely be many deceivers in the world... Peh Kadosh.
—o—
g) "And she alighted from the camel" (ibid., 64)
It is told (of the Rebbe R' Heshel) that when he became a bridegroom, while still almost a child, on coming to the engagement contract (tena'im), at which many dignitaries were present, his father asked him:
"Let me see whether you can recognise who the in-law is."
The boy had not yet seen the in-law, nevertheless he pointed at him: "That is he."
"How do you recognise him?"
"Because I already hate him..."
The moral:
Rebecca shuddered on seeing Isaac, and having fallen from the camel she understood that this was her future husband.
Sha'ar Bat Rabim (on R' Y. Ch. Sofer).
—o—
h) "And Abraham expired and died" (25:8)
"When our father Abraham died, all the great men of the generation stood in a row." Bava Batra.
While Abraham lived, his sun eclipsed all those "holchei nemishot[?]". All the "great ones" were overshadowed by the true great man of the generation. But when he died, all the "great ones" crawled out of their hiding places and each one shouted: "I am the great man of the generation!" All stood in a row — they all lined up in a row and wanted to snatch the crown of greatness...
Sichot Chulin HeChadash (on R' Shimshon Chmeides[?]).
—o—
In Lemberg [Lwów] an eminent scholar died. Rabbi Yosef Shaul Nathanson came to eulogise him together with a modern "rabbiner". The latter read his eulogy from a sheet of paper.
Says Rabbi Yosef Shaul: "A megah[?] that is not written — that is the death of the righteous", and with the rabbiner it is, after all, a written megah[?]...
—o—
Who can explain the "Baal HaTurim" in today's portion, chapter 24, verse 62?
On the cited verse the Baal HaTurim says: "And he dwelt in the land of the Negev. And next to it: 'And Isaac went out to meditate in the field' [printed: 'bisarah'] — a hint to what they said: he who wishes to become wise should go south." Where in fact is it inferred from the words "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field" that thanks to his living in the south-land he became wise?
I shall be grateful for a logical explanation.
Hirsh Niebielski, Kielce.
Edison Died Before His Time

In communal-worker circles people always used to say that Edison was busy inventing an electric gadget such that, when the communal worker comes to press the electric button (the doorbell) at rich men's houses, he will be able to see the master of the house already[?] from outside, and not let himself be misled by the maids, who always answer "pana nie ma" [Polish: "the master is not in"]...
And if he does get to the master of the house himself, he should be able, unnoticed, while shaking hands, to press an electric wire onto him that would soften his heart, so that he gives a handsome donation graciously ["bitshuot ḥen"].
And I always thought that for the communal workers themselves one needs an extra gadget, one that would push[?] and shove them and remind them to fulfil the duty they took upon themselves. Already before the war they were crowned with the title "paper communal workers", because they existed only on paper and in reality showed not a spark of life; and now, when we are going through such a severe crisis, we would badly need real, devoted communal workers who would care for the poor population.
We have become convinced that the true givers go on giving and do not stop because of the crisis; only the misers make use of the excuse: "it's a crisis".
Therefore we need as many collectors as possible, and perhaps for them Edison's gadgets would have been needed. It is truly a pity that he died before his time.
B. A. Gliksman.
Mother and Wife

S. Relkes. ("A gripping novel of Jewish life").
She came to the edge of the forest, sat down in the soft grass and became absorbed in the novel. Living people hovered before her eyes; every word that the beloved read in the little book resounded in her own ears, as if she were hearing it right here beside her. And suddenly she heard a man's voice:
— You are reading, Mademoiselle, a novel?
Rachele raised her eyes, and in the dream-mingled-with-reality it seemed to her that this was the hero of the book come to life and now standing before her. She saw before her a young man of about twenty: tall, strong, with burning eyes and thick coal-black hair.
She gave a start. She looked at him and could not believe that he was really a living person, or whether she was only seeing him in her imagination. But he was standing before her after all, and his voice — which at that moment sounded in her ears like wonderful music — did not come from another world, but from him, the man beside her.
— I am reading, — Rachele answered, and she did not recognize her own voice.
— A beautiful day today, — the young man began to speak, as if he had known her for a long time, — the forest is fresh, the sun shines mildly, the birds are singing...
He spoke as if out of a storybook. Who is he? Rachele did not know, and that in itself was very romantic for her. Her heart was pounding. She wanted to get up, but her legs felt as if they had been chopped off. The young man bowed politely before her and said, so big-city-like, so elegantly:
— Allow me to introduce myself to you. My name is Leo Ginzberg. With whom do I have the honour of speaking? — he asked her, looking her over with his eyes, as if he wanted to guess by himself with whom he had the honour of speaking.
Rachele wanted to behave as it is written in the books, and, of course, to be called simply Rachele is not romantic. So she thought how to change her name, but she did not find the suitable word, so she said:
— Rachel Berman, that is my name, Rachel Berman.
— Will you allow me to sit down beside you? We will talk a little.
— With the greatest pleasure, — Rachele answered, although in truth her heart trembled within her, and she wanted him to leave her here alone. But she had read in the books that this is how one usually answers at a first acquaintance with a young man. The whole experience was still not real to her, somehow as if it were happening not to her but to another girl, who was also called Rachel Berman.
The young man sat down beside her, took the book in his hand, looked through a few pages and said that he had already read it. He told her that he was a stranger here in town, that he had come for "lessons", and that he was seeking the acquaintance of educated people, such as she, Rachel Berman, is. Then they went for a walk in the forest, and when they came out, the meadow too was already dark. The sun had already set, and in the shtetl little lights were already burning, small and dear.
—
Here David's mother stopped. She looked at the two young people, how they sat there serious, intent, listening to her story with all their senses. She took a sip from the cup of coffee, as if to catch her breath, for at that moment she was living through again that first evening twenty-two years ago.
— When Rachele and Leo said goodbye, he asked her to come again tomorrow, because she was the only one here in the shtetl with whom he could talk. She understands him, she is educated and refined. Rachele's head was spinning, but her heart sang within her: I am playing at love, a real love. That night she slept badly. He kept standing before her eyes. She kissed him in her dream, told him in his ear that she loved him, that without him she could not live.
Rachele was, after all, a small-town girl, and she knew life only from storybooks. At first glance she fell in love with Leo and gave him her whole soul. True, she knew about bad men, about seducers, but a young heart does not want to believe in bad things, because it desires only good.
The summer went on its way. Rachele and Leo met in the forest almost every day. He grew bolder, she shyer. The closer he came to her, the more flustered[?] she became. He spoke refinedly, he promised her to marry her and that they would live in eternal love.
On one of those wonderful evenings they sat deep in the forest, and Leo embraced her, pressed her to him and kissed her. He whispered hot words to her:

Sosnowiec — Great Scandal in the Town Synagogue.

Sosnowiec
Great scandal in the town synagogue.
On Saturday morning the worshippers in the local synagogue witnessed a scene that vividly illustrates the newly flared-up struggle over the rabbinate question, and the results of the breaking of the peace agreement by those who support the candidacy of Rabbi Englard.
Accompanied by his close followers, Rabbi Englard came into the synagogue to deliver a sermon. But as soon as he went up onto the bimah, a storm of protests broke out, that he should not speak.
It was not long before a police sergeant (przodownik) with several policemen appeared in the synagogue, but they could not control and calm the heated tempers, and in the end Rabbi Englard did not get to speak.

Important Changes in Kehilla Affairs

[Poland — kehillas, new regulations; followed by five news items: Katowice — ice rink; Będzin — suicide; Sosnowiec–Mysłowice — fatal accident; Wolbrom — elections; Będzin — theft.]
A series of new regulations which the Będzin and Sosnowiec kehillas will have to reckon with.
A regulation of the Ministry of Religious Denominations concerning the kehillas has recently appeared. This regulation introduces certain changes into the kehilla system as it has existed until now.
Thus, for example, the approval of the kehillas' budgets depends on the voivodeship authority. The Ministry, however, has the right, in the case of some kehillas, to entrust the district (powiat) administrative authority, as the local supervisory authority, with approving these budgets.
Only such expenditures may be entered in the draft budgets as arise from the expenditures [sic; probably: tasks] that fall within the sphere of activity of the kehillas.
It is the duty of the kehilla board to send the supervisory authority the preliminary budgets for the following year by the first of October (since this regulation comes into force on 22 October, it is to be expected that, as regards this year, a supplementary regulation will be issued in which the deadline will be extended.
The supervisory authority has no right to approve a slaughter fee exceeding the following charges: for an ox or cow — 8 zł., calf or sheep — 3 zł., turkey — 1.40, goose 1 zł., duck 50 gr., hen — 40 gr., chicken (kurczak) 20 gr., pigeon 10.
In exceptional cases the chief supervisory authority may approve a fee exceeding this norm.
The charges for a burial plot (kever) in a town with a small gmina are from 10 to 500 zł., for a tombstone — 10 to 1000 zł. In large kehillas (Będzin belongs to the large kehillas) the charge for a plot is from 10 to 1000 zł. and for a tombstone from 10 to 10000 zł.
In the cemetery, both in the small kehillas and in the large ones, there must be a separate place for the poor population, where the charge for a plot and for a modest tombstone is at most 10 zł.
The kehilla tax („etat“) may be collected: from the head of the family, men as well as women, from unmarried women and childless widows, although women have no right to vote in the kehillas. Adult children may also be assessed for the kehilla tax, even though they live with their parents, provided the children earn independently. One may also assess for the tax a person who has a business in the given town, even though he lives in another town.
In the larger kehillas the determination of the amount of the tax belongs to the kehilla council; in the smaller kehillas, to the kehilla boards.
The amount of the tax for merchants and industrialists is determined according to the amount of the tax on real estate. For persons who run an independent workshop — according to the amount of income tax. The tax may not, however, exceed 10 per cent of the above-mentioned taxes. All other citizens who do not belong to these categories pay a minimum tax of 5 zł. and a maximum of 20 zł.
Exempt from the tax are citizens whose poverty has been officially established, those who live on charity, as well as rabbis and dayanim.
In order to establish the amount of the tax, the kehilla may apply to the tax authority for information.
In determining the amount of the tax the following factors must be taken into account: the income of the taxpayer, his family situation, and whether he is one who spends on public causes or merely a generous giver.
The kehilla board has the right to divide the annual tax into half-yearly and also quarterly instalments.
Slaughter may take place only on the basis of fixed fees. The kehillas are forbidden to collect higher charges than those approved. The shochtim are also forbidden to take a special payment for bedikah (inspection).
These are the most important paragraphs of the new regulation, on which it will be worthwhile to dwell and to explain them.

A New “Torah Shop” under the Cloak of the “Aguda”

The “secrets” are finally uncovered...
As our readers know, the Będzin Talmud Torah is in a disastrous state. A great share of the blame for this situation lies with the patented “Torah-loyal” [“patentirte toyre-traye”], who, seeing that thanks to the activity of Mr. Dafner and others order had been introduced in the Talmud Torah, that the public’s sympathy for the institution was getting better and better, and above all that the Talmud Torah might become a strong competitor of the “Yesodei ha-Torah” heder, began to “work deeds” [as printed] with the aim of breaking and disrupting everything that could bring the Talmud Torah any kind of benefit. Thus, for example, at the first general meeting almost all the Gerer Hasidim were mobilised; they came as one man and with their “attacks” drove back the people who had come with the conscious intention of helping the institution, where hundreds of poor children study, begin to function normally. But hardly had the victory over the “sinners” been achieved when the “Torah-loyal” already let their hands drop, and “a kapore the band with the horse” [idiom: to hell with everything] — let the Talmud Torah go under, let the melamdim with their families starve, whose business is it?...
Now, however, everything has become clear. The question has already been answered: is it possible? How can those who care for religion stay calm while before their very eyes the institution where 400 of the poorest children study is literally being destroyed?
But the question was answered these days. At the “Yesodei ha-Torah” heder a new society named “Ezrat Bnei Aniyim” [Help for Poor Children] has been founded, and it sets out across the town to collect monthly pledges for the “poor” children who study at the “Yesodei ha-Torah” heder.
It is also interesting to add that from the moment the “new Talmud Torah” was created at the “Aguda”, the hitherto Talmud Torah governors laid down their mandates. They throw back the “bundle” and are rid of the business...
As we are informed, the drive for the new “Talmud Torah society” has had no success. And that is quite understandable: if the gentlemen of the “Aguda” are out to support poor children, they ought, after all, to set to work so that the Talmud Torah can exist, and not create new little shops under the cloak of the Aguda!...

From the Revisionist Movement

Last Sabbath the Revisionist organisation in Będzin convened a large popular assembly devoted to the 14th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration.
Before a packed hall of various strata, Mr. Langfus opened the popular assembly.
After a short introduction the memory of Lord Balfour was honoured by rising. After the speeches of Messrs. Hofer, Klarman and others, it was resolved to send the English ambassador in Warsaw the following resolution:
“The popular assembly of the Jewish population of Będzin expresses its full recognition and esteem to the great Zionist friend, the late Lord Balfour, for his efforts in building the Jewish National Home in Eretz Israel.
The popular assembly states with regret that the English government has not fulfilled to this day the hopes of the Jewish people which were announced in the Balfour Declaration.
It states with regret that the Palestine administration, through its constant chicanery, has hindered Jewish construction in Eretz Israel.
It therefore calls on the British government to fulfil the obligations of the Mandate and to make possible, by fulfilling the Mandate entrusted to it, a Jewish National Home in Eretz Israel, and to open the gates to free Jewish immigration to Eretz Israel.

A chase after a car with smuggled goods
In Mikołów the border guard tried to stop a car full of goods smuggled from Germany.
A chase took place between the driver of the car and the border guard, but in the end the car fell into the hands of the border guard.

A loan of 5 million złoty.
The Friedenshütte (Huta Pokój) has received a loan from German banks in the amount of 5 million złoty.

Arthur Rubinstein's concert.
The concert of the piano master Arthur Rubinstein, which took place on Thursday in the Katowice Municipal Theatre, aroused extraordinary interest. The theatre hall was packed full; even the most expensive tickets (at 15 zł.) were completely sold out.
The programme: the pearls of the musical geniuses Bach, Beethoven, Wagner, Chopin, and of the Brazilian composer Villa-Lobos, who has now become famous in the musical world thanks to Rubinstein, who with his strong temperament and technique enchanted the auditorium.
After every number the ovations in honour of the great artist, who provides spiritual delight with his great artistry, went on for a long time. Rubinstein's concert will remain in the memory of the listeners.
Sosnowiec Commissioners' Council Opens Meat Stalls.

At the last session of the Commissioners' Council in Sosnowiec, a resolution of protest was adopted before the agenda against the American Senator Borah, who declared that the Polish borders must be revised.
After adopting the protest it was decided that the Magistrate should open meat stalls (jatki), so that [?] the poor population may get meat at cheap prices.
In connection with the approved investment tax, which is expected to bring in a revenue of 120 thousand zł., it was decided that out of this sum 50 thousand zł. be designated for building a school in Pogoń and 70 thousand for rebuilding Third of May Street.
Entertainment Evenings of the Będzin WIZO.

The board of the women's association 'WIZO' in Będzin has decided to hold 'entertainment evenings' every Tuesday. Besides a lecture, the visitors will receive tea with refreshments. Everything together will cost 75 gr.
The first entertainment evening takes place as early as next Tuesday, the 17th of this month, at 8 in the evening in the association's own premises, with the participation of Mrs. Dr. Moszkowska [?] (Kraków), who will lecture on the subject 'The spiritual development of the child according to the conception of individual psychology'.
As one can see, the board is making efforts to interest its members.
Zawiercie.

Unveiling of the banner of 'Bruria'.
On Sunday the local 'Bnos Mizrachi' celebrated the unveiling of their banner, on which the slogan 'Torah va-Avodah' is written.
Representatives of all Zionist groupings and of all Zionist and Jewish institutions came to the celebration and greeted it in warm words. Among others the Zionist veteran, the head of the kehilla of Zawiercie, Mr. Barnsztajn [?], also offered greetings.
Mr. Dr. Gottesdiener of Będzin appeared with a lecture on 'Torah va-Avodah'. Delegations came from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Olkusz.
After the official part a 'glass of tea' took place, at which people enjoyed themselves until late at night.
Sławków.

From Zionist life.
Last week a lecture by Mr. Papowski [?] (member of the Central Committee of the Keren Kayemet) on the tasks of the Keren Kayemet took place in the local synagogue.
After the lecture a meeting was held in the association's own premises, and the following board was elected: Y. Libermensz (president), Sh. Frajberger (vice), K. Herciger (secretary), L. Frajberger (treasurer).
The board is active in carrying out a broad campaign for the benefit of the Keren Kayemet.

Meeting of the Będzin 'Hechalutz'.
The annual general meeting of the Będzin 'Hechalutz' takes place tomorrow in the premises of the 'Hitachdut'.
On the agenda: reports on the activity so far, the situation in the 'Hechalutz' movement, and the election of a new committee.
Only those members who have discharged their obligations to the organisation will be admitted to the general meeting.
Chaim Hamburger, of blessed memory.

On Monday Jewish Sosnowiec accompanied to eternal rest one of its most respected householders, Reb Chaim Hamburger, of blessed memory.
The deceased was a type of that generation which conducted its business in good faith and was far removed from the hegemony that now rules the Jewish street.
In his will he left instructions to give 1000 zł. to the free-loan (gemilut chesed) fund, 1000 zł. to the Jewish hospital, 1000 zł. to the orphanage, 250 zł. to the Talmud Torah, and 2 beds to the 'Moshav Zkenim' (old-age home).
At the open grave Rabbi Hager spoke, urging the notables of the town to remember the hungry Jewish families in the present crisis.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
