The Completion Brick

L. Szpigelman.
(On the campaign that has begun for the orphans' home that has been built.)
Last week our paper printed a short but businesslike appeal from the Będzin charitable society, which turned to the Jewish population of Będzin asking us to support it and help complete the fine and useful building that the institution has undertaken to erect.
We believe that everyone in town knows which institution is meant. It is nothing more and nothing less than the realisation of a children's home for poor, forlorn little children, for Jewish orphans who have no home, who knock about in the most dreadful conditions. True, the Dobroczynność [charitable society] keeps under its protection the forlorn little children, who are guarded like the apple of one's eye and who are for the leaders of the institution perhaps the holiest ideal of their lives. But do they, with the best will, have the possibility of taking into their limited miniature premises all the children who need to be gathered like pearls and made into the people of the future, raised as good Jews and loyal citizens who will bring benefit both to the people and to the country in which they live? And even the few lucky ones, those who are today under the protection of the above-mentioned institution — do they have the possibility of being brought up as it ought to be? Do the prevailing conditions offer the possibility for it?
Of course it is very, very hard to urge people to give in the present critical time, when the situation everywhere is so strained, when misery and[?] want knock at so many doors among the most varied strata of the Jewish population; and yet one cannot keep a clean conscience if one stays indifferent to this campaign.
Our readers know very well that we are not quick to urge others to give just because this or that institution wants it, and we hear not a little because of that. We have pointed out more than once that precisely because of the hard situation one must not give money to an institution that brings no benefit to the population. Taking money from the public — we hold — is a great responsibility, and therefore much accountability is demanded of the institutions; and so we came to the conclusion that institutions that do not serve the community should be liquidated altogether, because they must not be a burden on the shoulders of the population. On the other hand we must support with every means the institutions that work for the people, that serve the purpose for which they were created.
Now it is a matter of completing a monumental work that will remain as a memorial for generations to come. Our "carp-heads"[?] have come to awareness and have taken upon themselves a hard and responsible task. Building a modern edifice specially for the orphans' home is without doubt a matter of the greatest importance, and however one looks at it[?], one must speak of such an undertaking with respect and reverence.
After all, one must not forget that this is not some party undertaking toward which this or that camp will have no sympathy. A children's home built by a local philanthropic institution is certainly non-partisan, so there can be no talk of this or that camp regarding it with antipathy — especially since no party possesses such a home to this day.
We must therefore come to the decision that the whole town without exception should gladly take part in building this edifice, which we see here in the picture. The building stands before us completed up to the roof. But with that the work is not yet fully finished. Inside, in the building itself, there is work, and the interior work must be carried out with the greatest responsibility. We must not forget that the building is being built in the 20th century and we must adapt ourselves to the times. The fitting-out must be modern, aesthetic, comfortable, hygienic, and the technology must follow the latest system.
True, much has been done so far; the splendid building, of course, did not build itself, and the building committee deserves a hearty yasher koach for the work accomplished; but one must go further, one must first of all[?] continue the interior work.
The work accomplished gives Jewish Będzin the best guarantee that the building committee stands at the proper height, and thereby it earns the sympathy of all strata of the Jewish population.
We, who have the opportunity to observe both from outside and from inside, know that Będzin gives constantly; on every occasion we do not lag behind. In every campaign Będzin takes a most honourable place, so that now too we are confident that the whole town will without doubt help realise this fine deed, which is no longer a fantasy. The building has been put up, the children's home has been built, and all that is needed is for each of us to lend a hand, and the doors will be able to open wide and freely for the benefit of our forlorn, poor little Moishes and Sarahs.
Well then, will you, sisters and brothers, not come to help materially, so that the gates can be opened for the little children, for whom we are obliged to care whether we want to or not? Will your hearts not tremble when you know that you are causing the little children to go on suffering and not to have the comfort that innocent souls ought to have? Will the well-to-do mothers who have not yet fulfilled their duty toward the poor child be able to rest easy? Will they be able with a quiet conscience to watch the smile of their little children, who rest at night in a clean, tidy bed, knowing that the poor little Moishe and Sarah do not have this?
We know that in the heart of every mother there are tender strings that have a magnetic power to feel along with the sufferings of helpless little children.
We are therefore sure that each of us will bring forward the necessary donation, so that we can say: we too helped build the splendid edifice, we did not stand by at a distance, we took part in the holy work.
But there is no time; one cannot wait until people come; therefore the campaign has already begun, and every house that has the means to contribute will be visited.
One gives quite differently when one is sure of the success of the donation; and so, had one come to collect a "brick" when there was only an empty plot, people would not have given with pleasure, because there would have been no certainty that all the bricks would be gathered. Now, however, since the great building no longer lacks a single brick, success is assured, and the public will gladly bring a "security brick", intended for nothing more and nothing less than the fitting-out, so that no one will want the completion to be held up on his account.
— And as the German folk saying goes: "All's well that ends well" — so let us help bring it to a good end.
What Was Heard, What Was Seen.

By Ben Amotz.

Sefirah season...
A brand-new trouble on the Jewish street — a counting season.
A count in autumn. An ordinary Jew ["a Jew of the whole year"] knows that from Passover to Shavuot he counts — the Sefirah [Counting of the Omer] time.
But Sefirah in the very middle of autumn? Worse still is something else. In spring the Jew counts, and in autumn they count him — the Jew, that is.
This time we do not mean the population census, which will only begin on the 9th of Grudzień [December]. That is a general matter. The 9th of December will be the "Day of Judgement" for all the "shefṭn"[?] in the state. The count we touch on here is a specifically Jewish one, a count of "scissors and iron" [the craftsman's tools]...
— It is bitter, terrible is the situation of the Jewish craftsman — an artisans' activist explains to us.
— What is it? — we ask.
— They are counting him...
Into the Jewish tailor's, the shoemaker's, the counters suddenly walk in — of course not Jewish ones — look around the workshop and count:
"Raz, dwa, trzy" [one, two, three]...
— Jaki patent jest? [What licence is there?]
The worn-out craftsman is struck dumb. A new affliction. For more than thirty years he has been working and never yet have they counted his apprentices. Now the guild law has come in, that very law to which the Jewish craftsman showed indifference, not believing what the newspaper wrote — and here he stands before a living fact and must answer the questions:
— Jaki patent? Ilu czeladników? Ile lat pan prowadzi pracownię[?]? [What licence? How many journeymen? How many years have you run the workshop, sir?]...
And the counters count, and protocols are written, and black clouds cover the horizon of the Jewish craftsmen, but
— yes, the "but"; here one must write a new lament over the destruction of Jewish craftsmanship in general, and of Zagłębie's in particular. Instead of doing something substantial, of thinking[?] about existence, about a better tomorrow — they smash the minimum that still exists, they wage wars among themselves, one wants to see the other's downfall, they warm themselves at the stove of the flickering fire, and...
— The inspectors go from workshop to workshop, visit every Jewish craftsman, and —
— they count... how many apprentices, what kind of licence one has — and they write it down...

"Oneg Shabbat in the Evening" [on Saturday night].
We are living through a very hard time today. Before our eyes we see the material decline of the Jewish people in Poland. Jewish fortunes and riches have become a heap of ruins, and Jewish society is like a broken shard.
And at such a twilight time it is necessary to bring a little cheerfulness, encouragement and freshness into the Jewish soul. A calm spiritual corner must be created, where a person can shake off his day-to-day worries and soak up hope and confidence in the future.
"Tze'irei Mizrachi" in Będzin deserves a yasher koach [well done] for the fact that the organisation has understood the command of the hour and arranges systematic lectures every Motzei Shabbat [Saturday night].
And one has to see how ordinary Jews, broken, throw off all their workaday cares, huddle up to one another in the uncomfortable hall and cling to the fine, interesting, instructive lectures given by the school director Dr. Abraham Gottesdiener [Gatesdiner].
And the audience, made up both of Torah scholars and of a Marxist "cheder", is carried away and swims in the sea of medieval Jewish philosophy; the great Jewish minds of that age float past.
The "Oneg Shabbat in the Evening" is a ray of light in the dark Jewish life. But it must be broadened and reformed on a large scale, so that everyone has the opportunity to get to know our ancient treasure.

Somebody has died...
The tumult on Modrzejowska Street ["Mandzhever gas"] in Sosnowiec stops for a while. Through the crush of people, slowly, step by step, drags
— the wagon...
Not the well-known "wagon" of the Skarb [the State Treasury, i.e. the tax office], which waits without fear for the "onlookers", but the wagon that leads there, from where one does not come back any more...
— Who is it that died? — one asks the other; even the question is only for form's sake, for nobody moves from the spot and nobody accompanies the wagon.
— Not even a single step...
The wagon is already in the "heart" of Modrzejowska Street, the crowd moves aside, again with the question?
— Who has died?... Even if it be a complete stranger, the mortal did after all live in a house where there are still Jewish residents — shall there not be even one single person to accompany him?
The little horse drags the wagon on and on, trudging with lowered head; it seems that the little horse is "ashamed" to look into the eyes of the people who will not pay the last honour to the dead it is pulling.
— If the horse had a "tongue", it would have rebuked them: how can it be? A lonely but honest Jewish woman dies, and in such a town there is not to be found a minyan of people to accompany her?...
Jewish Craftsmen's Guilds in Old Poland

[History — Polish Jewry.]
The clauses of the pinkasim (guild record-books) concerning journeymen and apprentices are permeated with the tendency to make access harder for strangers, for non-local elements. For a local apprentice the master in Płock pays 6 gulden; for a stranger — double.
The clauses impose harsh penalties for enticing away a journeyman or an apprentice. As long as the period stated in the agreement between the master and the journeyman or apprentice has not ended, another master may not take them on.
The guild statutes ostensibly [?] take the apprentices under their protection. In practice, however, they are delivered over to the arbitrary will of the masters, against whom the journeyman and apprentice are powerless. The statutes lay down that if a master treats his journeyman badly and the latter has proved this before the guild elders, then the agreement is void and the apprentice or journeyman may go and look for work with another master. But if the master proves that his journeyman did not behave properly, then the master has the right to dismiss the journeyman, and, as a punishment for him, no other master may take him on during the period stated in the agreement.
When we bear in mind that the final arbiters in these questions are the guild elders, who are confirmed by masters alone, and that the journeymen had no advocates of their own, it is not hard to guess who was always in the right.
So that the "chutzpah" of the journeymen and apprentices should not grow too great — as is well known, every demand by workers for a wage increase is "chutzpah" in the eyes of the masters — the craftsmen's guilds fix special wage tariffs which no master may exceed. In the Łuck pinkas of the tailors' guild there is even indignation "that much money is squandered on the hire of workers" (bidvar asher mevazbezim mamon harbe biskhirut hapoalim), and for that very reason the pinkas threatens all who transgress that "he shall surely be punished with a huge fine". This shows that the antagonisms between masters and journeymen were quite sharp in those times, if the author of the pinkas is so beside himself that a lot of money is squandered on "workers' wages". Who knows whether there did not exist in the Polish kehillot, just as among the other peoples, associations of journeymen, who by various means, and first of all by strikes, fought for and won better living conditions.
We have reason to believe that in the larger kehillot, where the antagonisms between rich and poor were quite sharp in the Jewish street too, [such things] also occurred, just as among other peoples, between the masters and the journeymen.
The most important task of the craftsmen's societies is to combat competition among the guild members. Most of the clauses in the various pinkasim deal with the question of how to avoid competition among the members. In some statutes it is laid down that every member has a chazakah (established right) to a certain number of clients; a guild member may not encroach on a fellow member's territory. He may not accept any work from another's client; in this connection the statute lays down that if a tailor, in an urgent case, accepts the work of a guild member, he is obliged to share half of it with him. The statutes go into the smallest details; they deal, for example, with the question of how one must act when the paritz (landowner), who is the chazakah of one tailor, goes with paritzim who are the chazakah of other tailors — what then is the law, etc., etc.
The societies of that time, however, did not concern themselves only with purely professional matters. Just like the Christian guilds, they also cared for the religious needs of their members.
How important this was held to be can be seen from the fact that the first clause of the Płock pinkas of the tailors' society (chevra chayatim) lays down: "Every tailor craftsman, when he is in his town, must rise promptly to the service of the Creator and come to the synagogue at least before Yishtabach and pray with the congregation. And if anyone transgresses this, he shall be fined one large one (groschen) p. for the tailors' society and two large ones p. for candles for the holy synagogue, God [protect it]." The trustee gabbaim and the auditors may not go about idle on the Sabbath; they must hear Torah from the sages of the town.
Larger guilds had their own synagogues or small prayer-houses, some of which still exist to this day (the tailors' synagogue and the like). Smaller guilds had their own Torah scrolls, books and the like.
In some towns the Jewish guilds, together with the Christian ones, fulfilled public, communal duties, namely: they defended the town against the enemy. As is well known, the Polish army then consisted of a small number of standing military regiments of hired soldiers and of the so-called "pospolite ruszenie" (general military service), to which every nobleman was obliged. The burghers (mieszczanie) and the Jews were exempt from military service. Only at a time when the enemy attacked the town did the burghers, sometimes also the Jews, especially the Jewish guilds, defend the town against the enemy. Of such a case we read in Reishe (Rzeszów). According to a privilege of the year 1686 the Jewish furriers' (kirzhner) guild there had to have its own military banner, its own guns, powder and bullets. Whether the case of Reishe is an exception or whether this was a general rule is hard to ascertain, because we still have, for the time being, too little information about the Jewish craftsmen.
This, approximately, is what the Jewish guilds in old Poland looked like. I am deeply convinced that, despite the changed conditions of the times, more than one custom of the Jewish artisans of former times has been preserved. The historical section of YIVO ought to collect all this through questionnaires and special investigations, so that the historian may be able to compare the customs of former times with those of today.

Katowice Pictures (From My Journey Through Upper Silesia)

Yoel Massboym [Joel Mastbaum].
Katowice Pictures.
(From my journey through Upper Silesia).
I love Katowice.
I love the small, symmetrical town with its railway station in the town centre, with its small, pleasant theatre and with its fine several hotels one next to another, and above all with its splendid main street.
For the hand that built the little town surely had in mind that a Berlin would be built here. No Berlin was built, but Katowice is a Berlin in miniature — so at least the inhabitants think[?].
Königshütte [Królewska Huta] is 25 minutes' journey from Katowice, but between the two towns lies a great distance in character. Königshütte strongly recalls the "Lagraner"[?] [perhaps: London] workers' quarters, where day and night one sees the "mass-man" going through the streets to work, or going for a stroll.
Katowice has little of this mass-man; it is a tasteful little town with a big-city intelligentsia.
I was in the theatre several times, and what pleased me, besides the stage and the pleasant theatre, is indeed the human being himself.
I sit the whole time and observe the audience. Jews, Poles and Germans — and yet some pleasant conversation swirls among them all.
One may say that among the three no grievances flare up, but the grievances stay "under the wall" of the theatre[?]. In the theatre itself it is still calm and quiet for the time being; here one has forgotten everything and everyone; one sits, one watches and one enjoys.
There sit a Polish lady and an elderly German woman and a Jewish gentleman, all with opera glasses, all intent on the stage, and all talking in one breath about this or that actress and actor.
Yes, this bit of culture still has the inner power to tear apart the hatred of national frictions; it still holds a legion of feelings, which awakens what is locked inside, from person to person — and this I felt precisely in this Katowice, so full of political contrasts.
Incidentally, a few words about the theatre and about our theatrical "imprezy" [shows], which are put on in Katowice by our Jewish or Polish-Jewish actors.
A few weeks ago the Qui Pro Quo, together with the Morskie Oko company, honoured Katowice with two performances. Mountains and hills were promised, and what was given were two "tshiptshe-driptshe"[?] [trifling] evenings, headed by Leo Fuks joke-pieces. But all the visiting troupes should be warned that they must know that Katowice is, of all places, exceptionally educated in theatre, and that if Warsaw really has first-rate actors, it should not be covered over with Leo Fuks bits. And those who run the theatre in Katowice are people with taste of no small level.
That is what I noticed in the course of the few short days I spent there.
———
This little town, which one can walk through in its length and breadth in 30 minutes, has something more: a wealth of faces of various kinds, strays — not only from Będzin and Sosnowiec, but children of distant Galicia and of the Kresy [Poland's eastern borderlands] and of Frankfurt am Main.
In the following chapters I will portray a series of figures I met in this miniature town, and the reader will imagine that he is standing not in Katowice but in a kind of New York, in a very large cauldron, which has swallowed up all sorts of human lives and human faces. But about that another time.
Greetings from Home.

(A packet of letters between Yosl Varshaver and Berl Zaglembyer.) Handed over for print by Y. B. Zayants.

Dear friend Berele[?], although I ought to be cross with you because till[?] now you have kept such a silence that it is simply a disgrace, upon my life — don't you know at all? After all, old friends; after all, we played "pilke" [ball] together on the hill, and after all in cheder we both had the same rebbe and the same strap...
What shall I tell you, Berele? We have been pondering all sorts of things about you here. The main thing for us was whether you are alive at all. One doesn't ask questions about a story in these times! Maybe[?] on an ordinary Wednesday you took a fancy, as is the fashion[?] nowadays, to become a "zeppelin". That is, to fly down from a "skyscraper" somewhere over there in Małobądz and forget to get up again...
Or maybe[?] a misfortune befell you; going[?] to "tashlikh" on the "Grobla" [the dyke], you fell into the river... and a dreadful "whale" from the "Przemsza" came and swallowed you... so now you live there like a lord in the "Leviathan's" belly, without a flat...
Or maybe you thought it over and simply did a "dying" the old-fashioned way, with a feather under your nose, and they buried you in the Czeladź cemetery, and you lie there like a count dressed "for the ball" — in white shrouds... and from time to time you peer over to the other side, towards "Mysłowice", to the former "Three Emperors' Corner", where Yekke [the German], Panie [the Pole] and Kire [the Russian] bordered each other so tightly that when a rooster crowed there once, three kings heard it...
Or maybe a madness got into you: you took a fancy to becoming a "dozór" [board] member of the Będzin Jewish community, and you worked there for the kahal so long that, poor thing, the purse in your breast pocket "swelled up", and you barely got out of there, poor thing, burdened with a few "teyerz"[?] — so, Berele, I don't envy you in the least... Now relatives from the whole world will come and simply pluck you apart... Now, Berele, you really are in a bad way, because the poor people of Zagłębie have a habit: not only do they themselves have nothing to eat, they don't let the next man eat either... Therefore, Berele, you must be clever: if somebody complains to you that he has no bread, tell him to eat cakes [ciastka]... If the other has no coal and is cold, tell him to go to Italy for the winter and he'll be warm...
A girl of the family comes to you to help her with a match? Talk her into converting instead and becoming a "Sister of Mercy" in a convent; then she will spare herself the wedding anyway... Someone comes to you leaning on a stick, with moist eyes and trembling hands, and complains to you that he's in a bad way, he's getting old? — he is advised to go to Professor Steinach, who will make him young...
Now, Berele my crown, write me whether it's true that the three well-known Będzin societies — "Dobroczynność" [Charity], Linas ha-Kholim and the Chevra Kadisha — have united and work splendidly: the "Dobroczynność" feeds the poor in such a way that the "Linas ha-Kholim" will have patients, and the Linas ha-Kholim in turn makes sure that the Chevra Kadisha won't stand idle...
Write me also, Berele, whether it's true that Gandhi, the naked prophet of India, doesn't want to come to Będzin for a lecture because he is afraid that the "Malbish Arumim" [Clothing the Naked] society will forcibly put a pair of trousers and a spencer jacket on him...
In particular, I can write you, Berele, that a good few weeks have already passed since the Będzin "Hakoach" was here in Warsaw, and it is still being talked about here at every table and on every bench... They say, for example, that your[?] "Hakoach" there has always been hated by the local sports clubs. A member of the Będzin "Hakoach" even threatened a Warsaw sportsman a while back that as soon as the Będzin "Hakoach" met here in the first "match" that came along, Warsaw would get such a "kicking with the feet" from Będzin that it would be remembered here for a long time... And truly it is hard to understand: the "Mannschaft" [team] of the "Hakoach" was excellent — no small thing! — it brought along the best "footballists" from the Będzin "Old-Age Home", and still they went home "bare" [goły], without a single goal...
Write me also, my Berele, whether it's true that the Sosnowiec fire-brigade organisation is being liquidated and it has been decided, in case of a fire, to make use of those two buckets [wiadra] with which big Ber used to water the horses in wartime... In the same breath people here also talk about the "town elders" of the holy community of Dąbrowa: with us it is already Hanukkah time, while with them there in the town council they have only reached "U-netaneh Tokef", and they ask there: "who by water?" — who should be harmed concerning the payment for water, the consumer or the waterworks' till? So they have been sitting for weeks pounding water... A lucky thing: Sosnowiec doesn't give a hoot for the "angel of fire", and Dąbrowa trembles before the angel of water...
Don't be lazy, Berele, and write me an answer straight away.
Your friend
Yosl Bitergemis ["Bitter-Vegetables"].
I forgot the main thing! I almost forgot to write you about the "bombshell" happening here: surely, Berele, you have read in the paper that Thomas Edison, the greatest inventor on the whole globe, died here not long ago. Now imagine: all of Warsaw is now seething with the news that Thomas Edison was actually a Jew, and indeed from our parts, and that he remembered us — the papers give as proof: in order to ease the "election system" in the various charitable institutions of Zagłębie, Edison, shortly before his death, specially invented a machine such that if you put the first pickpocket that comes along into one side, a famous benefactor comes out of the other side...
The above-mentioned.
Moon and Little Stars

[Feuilleton — prose poem ("impression").] By J. Fleischman. — Authorized translation by Yosef Perlberger. (Reprinting forbidden.)
(Impression.)
Days have their expression,
as varied as people,
nights too have their expression.
But a person's expression does not always correspond to his depths, and so too the expression of the day — it is not always the same.
Sometimes warmth brings — merriment...
Sometimes the rainstorm brings joy...
At times again the bright sun stings...
And always we await the night.
The night — it always has a true face, like a naive girl,
not yet spoiled by cultural progress...
like a child who looks at everything and everyone with a curious eye,
like a healthy and simple taste of violet blossoms.
The dark, black night is like a pit
into which one can fall into an abyss, where hundreds of many-headed snakes lie in wait — a terror...!
A grey night is like a resigned struggle over man's existence, dragging one foot after another, with the expression: "Everything is all the same to me".
A starry night is like a garden lit by cheerful sunbeams, where there reigns a twittering of hundreds of innocent little birds that strain toward the sky.
A moonlit night is like a king leading his beloved, to the song of harps, over marble stairs covered with Persian carpets, to the celebration of merriment and love...
• • •
And when the sky had been covered with thousands of little stars, and when the moon had swum out onto the firmament [printed "furmament"], the dance began.
Stars and little stars gathered together —
they made a ring...
for the dance...
The Great Bear ["the star-wagon"] shone out...
and mighty Mars sparkled like fire,
sweetly and coquettishly Venus cast a glance
and Jupiter awoke on his throne.
At his feet lay millions of most humble stars, and he sent messengers to the moon.
To the celebration...
He bedded the way with diamond stars...
waited for the guest.
And the guest floated solemnly,
across the sky he floated; at his side
he had millions of stars, by the oars millions of stars and in the little boat millions of stars.
He swam...
And meanwhile the stars held a "Sejm" [an assembly].
Moon... moon...
Oh [?], only to be nearer to him!
To warm themselves with his warmth,
to grow beautiful with his rays...
to sing him a song of greeting...!
The moon...?
• • •
The moon floated splendidly,
exalted [?] like a king,
bathed among the clouds,
vied [?] with the stars
and sometimes cast a glance at the earth,
at the black valley.
There in the valley, full of tears,
and here merriment and joy,
there in the valley fighters, fire, rivers of blood
and here in the sky one feels God's grace —
yet the valley interested him — — —
Although he tore his royal gaze away from the earth, still it drew him to itself
and he cast a glance once more...
and beheld...
how a brother kills a brother...
how a friend seduces his comrade's wife...
how an honest man robs widows and orphans...
how a mother weeps over a piece of bread for her children...
how here streams of wine flow —
and there — tears...
how drunken orgies reign there
and here — hunger, want...
And the old moon looked on...
forgot the celebration...
left Jupiter behind...
until the cock crowed...
and swam off home.
• • •
This is my little star
and that one, again, is Malkele's...
both are close to each other,
so sweetly they look at each other,
into each other's eyes they look
and into their souls...
for innocent are the little stars
like angels.
Angels with little white wings and with tearful little eyes.
Such a multitude they are...
like children...
like sand in the sea,
they run to the guest,
run, run without a stop...
They jostled against one another, tens, hundreds, thousands, millions...
white as milk their path became...
the milky way of the stars.
• • •
The child [printed "skind"; perhaps the little star] gave a pitiful sigh...
It has fallen!
She marked her way with fire..
lit up with a long streak...
and was extinguished...
It has fallen,
the little star!
Not mine! — — — not mine!
An eternal rest...
The little star has died...
vanished - - - —
and left behind in the heart a desolation,
what a pity about her, the little star!
In the quiet summer night..
A. Brezinski — A Karakul Coat and a Pair of Felt Boots with Galoshes

[Short story — feuilleton.]
With the coming of winter, two women went about the house wrapped in a fog of rosy dreams.
Mrs. Berman ("Bermantshikhe"), the broad, [?] ("yuste" — doubtful reading) mistress of the house, dreamed of a new karakul coat, and the old servant Sheyne-Dobe — of a pair of valenki (felt boots) with galoshes for her weak feet, shot through with rheumatism.
Is a pair of felt boots with galoshes such a big thing? But the fact is that Sheyne-Dobe is by now kept here more out of charity — after all, she served the household faithfully for so many years — but she gets no money. For besides her one still has to keep the real, healthy gentile maid to help with the heavy chores. Sheyne-Dobe has become an "invalid"!... She hasn't a penny to her soul and goes, poor thing, to meet the hard winter in her mistress's old, crooked shoes...
With the mistress, you see, it's something else: she is in no way short of money. Her husband, it's true, has lately been complaining that business has gone bad, but enough rent still comes in from the tenants — so what then? It is simply a disgrace for her to raise it with her husband, when a whole "stock" of coats hangs in the wardrobe, with last year's "źrebiak" (foal-skin coat) at the head!... Where does one find a bit of nerve, eh?...
But then — a lucky chance. One day her husband comes up from the courtyard in high spirits, smiling triumphantly, pleased:
— Well, what do you say, does one need to hurry or not?... The front flat stood empty all along, stood empty — and in the end it paid off after all! A young fellow and a girl, foolish enough, turn up, they're getting married, and they put down a crisp three hundred dollars for the flat. When it goes, it goes up in smoke... Ha-ha-ha!...
Noticing her husband in a "favourable hour", Mrs. Berman wrapped her white, pampered arms around his red neck, stroked him like a little child and... her prayer about the coat was granted.
And old Sheyne-Dobe, too, met with a strange piece of luck that same day.
Just then a letter reached her from a distant relative in "New York". She stood with her spectacles at the dusky window, toiling over the foreign American words. Suddenly a green gleam struck her eyes — a dollar! A little, darling dollar.
Tears began to drip from her eyes. They ran down her dried-up parchment cheeks as from little tin gutters, and very nearly soaked the dear, precious slip of paper.
But never mind!... In the shop they snatched the dollar from her and [gave her] in exchange [?] the felt boots with the galoshes, and the old woman actually groaned with delight, as if at that very moment the whole beauty of life had suddenly revealed itself to her...
* * *
But why does everything in the world go by such caprice?.. A few days later the following notice appeared in the newspaper:
"On the night from Tuesday to Wednesday thieves, having removed the putty from a windowpane, got into the flat of the house-owner Berman and began rummaging through the rooms. Fortunately the old servant just woke up; she raised the alarm and the thieves had to flee, taking with them only a pair of new felt boots with galoshes."
And old Sheyne-Dobe once again lost the meaning of life... and here comes such a hard, leap-year winter!
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Toldot)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Toldot
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Jacob was a simple [tam] man" (Gen. 25:27)
Jacob was clever enough: "Are you my brother in deceit?" — Laban said to him. But he used it only when necessary. Thus, in ordinary life, he was a simple, guileless man. But "ish tam" — he was master over his trait of simplicity. Sometimes, when he had to, he was no simpleton at all: he outdid Laban with his craft and cunning...
Imrei Tzaddikim (in the name of the Seer of Lublin).
—o—
"Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar in your tents."
Zebulun (the symbol of the merchant) laughs at Issachar (the Torah scholar) for being an idler, a good-for-nothing, while he, the merchant, is such a capable fellow and a man of the world.
But "rejoice, Zebulun", only as long as "Issachar is in your tents" — as long as Issachar sits over the Gemara; should Issachar just go out into the street, he will outdo you in resourcefulness... Alei Zayit.
—o—
b) "And Isaac entreated" (ibid. 21)
"Why were our matriarchs barren? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, longs for the prayer of the righteous." Midrash Rabbah.
The "Tiferet Shlomo" interprets the midrash jokingly: children make parents worried, one has no rest, one cannot pray and occupy oneself with spiritual matters. Worry over children enslaves a person.
And because "the Holy One, blessed be He, longs for the prayer of the righteous" — because He wants them to have a calm mind at their prayer and study — He wanted to make them childless...
—o—
c) "And the elder shall serve the younger" (ibid. 23)
"Once a man is appointed leader over the community below, he becomes wicked above."
The communal leader must be "below", under the yoke of the community. He must feel subservient to the community. But if he does not understand his role and wants to be "above", wants to ride the old nag [?] — "he becomes wicked": it makes him a villain.
"And the elder shall serve the younger" — the leader must serve society. "Do you think it is rulership I give you? — It is servitude I give you." Olelot Efraim.
—o—
d) "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau" (27:22)
There are those who, when it comes to praying and studying, are "the voice of Jacob" — they are very pious; but "the hands" — when it comes to opening the hand and counting out some charity — then it is "the hands of Esau": they have Esau-like, locked hands...
Ohel Yaakov (the Dubno Maggid).
— — — —
The Talmud says that Rabbi Judah the Prince was called "holy" because he never lowered his hands below his belt. Our rich men — said the Maggid of Rajcza [?] — are also such holy men, for they keep their money in their trouser pocket and never let their hands down there...
—o—
e) "And Rebecca said to Jacob" (27:6)
The Maggid of Kozienice used to say about this: "Where the wife rules, the husband goes astray" (in Polish: "Tam gdzie żona rządzi, mąż błądzi")... Imagine: had Rebecca not made the whole spectacle, and Esau really received the blessings, and Jacob — "and when you break loose you shall shake his yoke from your neck", then Jacob would surely have had all the blessings, since Esau would not have kept the Torah even for a moment. So the game is reversed: Jacob was blessed, and Esau has the blessings... A pity, really...
Milon Hadatin [?].
—o—
f) "And Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing" (27:41)
Why is it that when a Jew comes to ask a ritual question and the rabbi rules it treyf — even if it causes him the greatest loss, he will accept it with love and obey the rabbi; whereas even when a pious Jew robs and murders, and even when a rabbinical court rules that he must pay the robbed party, he does not begin to obey? Is robbery not as grave a sin as treyf?
Because with treyf he knows that no one will profit from his loss, whereas in money matters what hurts him is not so much his own loss as his fellow's gain. What bothers him is not what he must pay, but what the other will receive...
Ya'arot Dvash.
—o—
The Haftarah.
g) "My covenant was with him... and he feared Me" (Malachi 2:4)
Sometimes a strong-armed man snatches an important office; he is indeed respected on account of the office he holds, but in time, when he takes off the slippers, he becomes an ordinary flesh-and-blood man. But the leader who possesses virtues of his own is respected even when he leaves his "chair".
"My covenant was with him" — the priesthood was an eternal covenant for him, because "he feared Me", because he possessed fear of God and other virtues; therefore even when the priesthood was abolished he still bears its honoured name. Kokhav mi-Yaakov.
—o—
h) "And they shall seek Torah from his mouth, for he is a messenger of the Lord of Hosts" (ibid. 7)
The Gemara expounds on it: "If the rabbi is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, they shall seek Torah from his mouth."
People interpret it: "If the rabbi is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts" — if a rabbi comes and wants to take the rabbinical seat of the town because he is an "angel", a "grandson" [?] and a confidant of "him, may he live" [the Rebbe] — "they shall seek Torah from his mouth": just see whether he knows how to learn, just test him in learning, because these generally know little, very little learning, relying on the merit of their fathers...
The Antisemitic Incitement.

[Poland — antisemitism at the universities; article.] (On the anti-Jewish excesses in Warsaw).
Once again the "cultured" Endek [National Democrat] students have come out into the arena, demonstrating with fist and brutality their strangely contrived patriotism. As every year at this time, so this year too the "work" has begun which brings no honour to the Polish state. The anti-Jewish excesses have once again violated every measure of culture and humanity. Persecutions and harassment are, after all, nothing new for us; but in the twentieth century, at a time when the right to learning has already been recognised for all without any distinction of religion and nationality, when science is no longer the property of this or that nation but belongs to all mankind — these events appear a paradox, and only someone who has already come across the brutal and demagogic students of the Endek camp can believe in them: they bear no responsibility for the fate of the state, and in them a bridled[?] chauvinism has blinded any understanding of the interests of the state.
The outbreaks, which have a pogrom character because they spread from the universities into the streets, where Jewish children and women were beaten — must be condemned as harmful and punishable by all democratic and left-wing groupings. Special emphasis must be given to the speech of Deputy Miedziński of the Sanacja in the Sejm debate, who in sharp words laid the responsibility for the events on the Endecja, saying that the Polish people does not identify itself with such outbreaks.
Kraków was known as a very quiet city in the sphere of academic life. Only two years ago did excesses against the Jewish academics take place there for the first time. But things quickly calmed down, thanks to the highest university body, the Senate, which issued a verdict against the barbaric action as dishonourable and not in keeping with Catholic ethics. But could one describe otherwise such deeds as beating Jewish academics and — which must be particularly noted — women academics, who surely cannot stand up to brutality? Last year it was a near thing that excesses broke out; that was at the same time as the congress of the "International Intellectual Union" was opened by the late Count Skrzyński, to which a large number of foreign professors and scholars came; the Endek academics then threw themselves upon the Jews, but it did not come to very sharp outbreaks. This year's outbreaks, however, both in Kraków and in Warsaw, have surpassed all previous ones. The Endek demagogues have drawn into this struggle not only academics but also various people from the underworld and social filth.
And if in Kraków, thanks to the firm stand of Rector Michalski, things became quiet after a week, in Warsaw the situation is serious. Great guilt lies with the university authorities, which did not come out sharply against the excesses and take a wavering position. That the whole action did not break out spontaneously but was worked out according to a precise plan is best proved by the outrageous speech of the Endek deputy Stupiłowski[?] [probably Stypułkowski], who from the Sejm tribune justified the vandalism that took place in the streets of the Polish capital and within the walls of the temple of science. The heroic corporants [fraternity students], who declaim so much about honour and chivalrous combat, have, with the fight of thousands against hundreds, of armed against unarmed, of men against women, profaned the fundamental postulates of honour and chivalrous conduct.
Every year the sad events repeat themselves, and every year thousands of Jewish secondary-school graduates flock to all Polish and foreign universities in order to educate themselves. There is no power in the world that could frighten the Jews away and turn[?] them away from learning and education. There have been greater forces that wanted to stifle Jewish culture, greater persecutions against our book. We lived through the dark Middle Ages, when antisemitism, supported by religious fanaticism, turned against the Jewish book. We lived through times when entire states wanted to wipe us off the face of the earth. And when Endek students permit themselves to beat Jewish academics, we must cry out to them: you have no right to forbid us to enjoy the treasury of science, because ours is a larger share of the merits regarding the development of secular culture. There is no branch of science in which the Jews do not play the leading role. Your weapons are sticks; our weapon is the book and justice. You legitimise yourselves with beatings, and we legitimise ourselves with Einsteins, Warburgs, Freuds, with twelve Nobel Prizes. The wounded and the bloodied — those are your deeds; progress of science and righteousness — belong to us!
Jewish youth will not be frightened off and will not abandon the path on which it has walked until now. The savage argument of beatings, of clubs and brass knuckles will have the opposite effect: it will strengthen still more the will to endure!
Eliyahu Gertner.
Homey Little Tales.

[Sosnowiec — humour; local tale.] The Haftarah and the Little Barrel of Beer.
The story we want to tell you here is not made up; it did not happen somewhere with a yeshiva student or with a son-in-law boarding with his in-laws, but here at home in Sosnowiec, last week, with a simple young man who considers himself a "Jew" in small letters, if anything...
This young man made a bet with friends that on an ordinary Wednesday he would read through the Haftarah of the portion Chayei Sarah, with the true melody and the full cantillation, without a single mistake.
The bet was for 10 gulden [złoty]. The "Haftarah man" put down the said sum, and all the others also pooled the same amount among themselves; a little barrel of beer was brought, and it was agreed by all that whoever loses must pay for the little barrel of beer.
To this "examination" two knowledgeable experts were also invited — they were to "listen" and note down the mistakes during the reading, and a condition was set that up to two mistakes were allowed, but more than two mistakes — meant the bet was lost.
When the bridegroom-lad was handed a Chumash so that he could set about the "task"... he asked to be allowed to bring his own Chumash, which he was already used to... Well, they did him the favour; but seeing that he was taking too long, a couple of the fellows went over to his house, and they found him... going over the Haftarah with great diligence. Needless to say, they took him by the arms and led him with great pomp to the barrel...
After half an hour of hard "work" the examinee wiped the sweat from his forehead with a towel, and on learning that the experts had established four "gross" mistakes besides the "small change" ["drojb", from Polish drobne?]... and realising that they would probably soon be drinking his beer, he began to make a racket and a row, claiming that things had not been done honestly... so that he was ready to go through the little job once more before a different "examining commission"...
The "affair" took on a very serious character; two sides immediately formed, which, half in jest and half in earnest, "fought" among themselves. And in the tumult our said bridegroom made up his mind, grabbed the little barrel of beer on his shoulder and wanted to "flee". The fellows, however, tripped him up... and the little barrel of beer fell down with a mighty crash and burst.
What happened next you can already imagine. Some hurried to drink the remaining beer, some quarrelled and defended the Haftarah reader; but the party concerned himself vanished out of great shame, and with that the examination came to an end.
X.
Theatre Notes.

„Człowiek z teką“ ("The Man with the Briefcase")
(A drama in 7 scenes by Aleksei Faiko, staged by the actors of the Katowice City Theatre).
Dimitri Granatov, who held the post of professor at Leningrad University, is transferred from there to Moscow as professor at the "State Institute for Culture and Revolution".
In the railway carriage. During the journey to Moscow the professor meets a certain Likhamsky, with whom he once worked together in a counter-revolutionary organisation.
Likhamsky wants to exploit the professor's high position for his own selfish ends, and he threatens the professor with his past, which is very burdensome to him.
During a dialogue between the professor and Likhamsky, who are standing right at the carriage window, the professor throws him out of the window and he is killed.
This is noticed by Redutkin, a former servant of the professor's father, a Tsarist general. Redutkin and his wife, a very cunning woman, happen to be in the neighbouring compartment and have seen everything.
Egged on by his wife, Redutkin extorts sums of money from the professor as the price of his silence. Once, when Redutkin again comes for a considerable sum, Professor Granatov decides not to give any more. At a session of the professors' board, which has assembled to hear a lecture by Prof. Granatov, the latter tells about everything and in the end shoots himself.
This is the condensed content of the drama.
The author wanted to make of Prof. Granatov a type of Übermensch according to Nietzsche's conception, an idealist who strives to reach his goal and does not stop before any obstacles, even when he has to walk over human bodies.
Prof. Granatov has broken with the past and places himself entirely at the disposal of science.
But the past does not want to step aside; like a ghost it creeps through the cracks of life and shows itself on the surface like a thousand-headed hydra, and forces the professor to withdraw from his positions.
Not only the past hinders the professor from attaining his ideal; the present does the same. In his surroundings he is looked upon with suspicion. The mighty "G.P.U.", which has its "eyes" and "ears" everywhere, does not trust the idealistic professor, who truly wants to serve science and no longer occupies himself with politics. He wants to become "the man with the briefcase", who carries out the instructions of the higher authority, for whom the papers in the briefcase are a holy commandment to be carried out without comment.
In the professors' board, too, it is no better; there too sit the bespectacled men with fountain pens whose only aim is a career. Prof. Granatov mercilessly hurls the truth into their faces. He points at the chairman of the board, Prof. Andrasov, saying that he still lives in the spirit of "Petersburg" and not of "Leningrad", and as such he is therefore dangerous to the state.
Prof. Granatov does this out of pure idealism. Personally he is the best friend of Prof. Andrasov, who was his teacher and whom he esteems as a man and a scholar, but he still lives with the notions of "Petersburg" and his dreams of the future are also woven in that direction. Of this he was convinced by a brochure of Andrasov's that he had read.
But Prof. Granatov is not yet the ideal, Nietzschean type of Übermensch. He is not strong enough to destroy all obstacles; crushed by the past and the present, he is not strong enough to withstand the enormous pressure, and he puts an end to his life, sparing the "G.P.U." the work.
"He did it himself," says the secretary of the "Institute" when she is told to telephone for the agents of the "G.P.U."
The acting of the artists:
Roman Tański in the role of Prof. Granatov had strong moments; he was especially good in the monologue at the last meeting, where one strongly felt the tragic experiences of a pained human soul.
Excellent was Relski as Redutkin. He created a type of a vulgar[?] drunkard who is entirely under the influence of his cunning wife. It is very easy to fall into caricature in roles of this kind, but Relski came out of it safely and proved that he is an actor of artistic culture.
Very good, too, was Mrs Tańska in the role of Redutkin's wife.
She is a temperamental artiste with fine diction; her gesticulation is even a little too lively, but she is not at all shocking.
Józef Orchoń in the role of Likhamsky created a type of a cynical flatterer who seeks with sweet words to draw his victim into the net.
Orchoń is a talented actor with fine, expressive mimicry, and he works on the spectators artistically.
The sets, after the design of J. Kościeszy[?], are indeed modern, but a little too primitive; something is lacking in them for harmonious wholeness.
On the whole it is a very fine ensemble performance, in which the skilful hand of the director Tański is felt; it is therefore a theatre performance worth[?] seeing.
Sh. R.
When the President Does Not Want to Open, Everything Stays Closed...

[Będzin — kehilla.]
What Is Happening in Zagłębie?
Będzin
On Sunday a meeting of the old kehilla administration was to have taken place, in order to discuss the kehilla budget for the coming year.
Although there was a quorum, the president "went on strike" and would not open the meeting.
Because of this the dozór members (kehilla board members) L. Dymant, Mr Goldsztajn and A. Liwer lodged a protest against this way of acting and left the meeting.
The next day, when Mr President had got his "right" hand (a convenient majority), he called a meeting at which the budget was dealt with.
On the question of fixing the pensions a discussion developed which lasted several hours. Board member Liwer proposed reducing the pensions. Board members Diament and Buchwajc agreed with this proposal, but later they were "convinced" by board member Ryński, who declared that "the Będzin kehilla need not be the first to reduce the pensions", and everything remained as before.
At the meeting it was also decided to reduce this year the etat (salary scale), except for the existing maximum (2000 zł.), which is not to be changed.
For 100 zł. Everyone Can Be Immortalised in the Orphanage.

[Będzin — charity.]
On Monday evening a meeting was held in the premises of the charity society about launching a popular campaign for the purpose of completing the building of the orphanage.
The chairwoman of the finance committee, Mrs C. Szajn, gave a report on the activity so far; it turns out that the building has already cost 187,000 zł. The sum came from the magistrate (municipality) (81,000), the gmina (kehilla) (11,000), and the rest from a handful of donors, so that until now the majority of the local Jewish population has given almost nothing for this purpose.
It was decided to start a broad campaign to sell "bricks", i.e. whoever buys a brick for 100 zł. will have his name immortalised in golden letters on the special wall in the building. In addition a donation book will be introduced, in which everyone who gives 5 zł. will be inscribed for generations.
There is no doubt that the campaign will be warmly received by the Jewish population, and no one will hold back from lending a hand in order to finish the home for the orphans.
Subsidies for University Students Will Be Settled in Kielce.

[Będzin — municipality and students.]
As is known, every year a certain sum is preliminarily allocated in the municipal budget for the benefit of university students. Of this sum Jewish students receive 45 percent and non-Jews 55 percent.
So it has always been. This year the form of the distribution has been changed in the sense that the subsidies will be allotted not in Będzin but in Kielce...
— One would only like to ask whether the Jewish members of the commissars' council know about it, and what they have done so that the change should not happen?...
“Bank Kupiecki” Is Guaranteed by the Fortunes of Its Council and Board

[Będzin — economy and banks.]
Together with all the cooperative banks, the local "Bank Kupiecki" (Merchants' Bank) too was put in an unfavourable position because, at the time of the panic, the public withdrew deposits to the amount of a million zł. It goes without saying that such events give rise to various rumours which break the prestige of this or that financial institution.
In connection with this, some members of the council and of the board of "Bank Kupiecki", persons known as men of wealth, have decided to guarantee all the obligations of the bank with their own fortunes.
The official declaration with the appropriate signatures is in our possession at the editorial office.
All at Once No Longer a Merchant..

[Będzin — economic crisis and taxes.]
For a whole week now the closed, long-established haberdashery shop of Mr Rafał Liebermensch has been attracting attention. When we asked the owner for what reasons his shop has been closed, we received the answer: "The Skarb!" (the State Treasury). For 53 years already — he says — I have had the shop, and all at once I am no longer a merchant. It happened last Thursday: a bailiff came in and took away from me the most important articles of my shop, so that I have nothing to sell...
A Bandit Attack in Broad Daylight.

[Będzin — crime.]
On Monday at 2 in the daytime a bandit attack was carried out on the carter Sztyka; terrorising him with revolvers, the bandits robbed... 6 zł. One of the attackers was caught at once.
Stabbing Each Other with Knives over “Love” for a Woman.

[Będzin — crime.]
On Sunday evening, in Małobądzka Street, a quarrel broke out between two young Christian men over a woman. The quarrel turned into a fight, and one of them struck the other with a knife in the belly.

[Będzin — culture and education.] From the 15th of this month a people's university will be opened at the society "Evening Courses for Workers" in Będzin. Sosnowiec
The "P."-er [?] Kehilla Budget on the "Green Table".

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Under the chairmanship of Mr. Zendel, a meeting of the kehilla board took place on Sunday, which discussed the draft of the new kehilla budget.
The general tendency is that the budget should be drawn up within the framework of the last budget; only pensions [salaries] for the new trustees will be added.
Jewish Youth Must Fulfil Its Duty!

[Zagłębie — census.] In connection with the population census which is to take place soon, we have been asked by the official authorities in Sosnowiec and in Będzin to call the attention of the Jewish youth who are being invited to this work that they should not refuse to take part in carrying out the census.
One must bear in mind that here what matters is, firstly, the interest of the state, and secondly, that the census-takers should be able to communicate with the Jewish masses. The main thing, however, is that Jews should give Yiddish as their mother tongue.
90 percent of Zagłębie Jews speak Yiddish, and it would be a great national crime and historic oversight if, through the fault of unsuitable census-takers, a false picture of the Jewish population of Zagłębie were to emerge.
Let us hope that the Jewish youth will fulfil its duty.
Trial over a Sensational Bill-of-Exchange Affair.

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Last Monday a sensational bill-of-exchange trial began in the local district court. In the dock sit Manela Rozenberg, Hirsz Białka and J. Wilczyński, all of Sosnowiec, who are accused of having, with the help of forged bills of exchange, obtained various goods on credit, sold the goods at half price and let the bills be protested.
The chief culprit in the affair is Mr. Rozenberg, who everywhere presented himself as a big merchant and thanks to this obtained credit.
Several dozen witnesses were summoned to the trial; they were heard on Tuesday and Thursday.
An Embezzlement of 360 Thousand Złoty.

[Ogrodzieniec — crime.] This week an embezzlement was discovered at the "Wiek" cement works in Ogrodzieniec, carried out by the works' proxy (prokurent) Kołakowski with the help of Mr. Jungster, owner of the brickworks in Łazy.
The embezzlement amounts to 360 thousand złoty.
Went to Look for Bread, and Found Death.

[Dańdówka — accident.] Two mineworkers in Dańdówka started digging in order to find coal. Having already dug out an area 5 metres deep, they came upon an old, inactive shaft from which strong gases burst out.
The workers could no longer get out of the pit and were suffocated by the gases.
General Meeting of the "Bank Kupiecki"

[Sosnowiec — economy.] As is known, in connection with the events at the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank] a commission was elected with the task of putting current affairs in order and, if possible, rehabilitating the bank.
The commission, which has completed its mission, is convening next Sunday at 4 in the afternoon at the "Hotel Polski" an extraordinary meeting, at which the question of the bank's future fate will be discussed.
A representative of the Auditing Union in Warsaw will also be present at the meeting.
A Large Balfour Meeting in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.] In connection with the 14th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, the Revisionist organisation arranged a mass meeting chaired by Mr. Himmel. The meeting was opened by Lui [Levi?] Jungster, who described the plight of the Jewish people and the hope that Jewry had placed in the Balfour Declaration. Mr. Klarman, speaking about the Balfour Declaration, proved with documents that were issued as the basis of the Mandate that England had undertaken to make possible a Jewish majority [?] with Jewish self-government. Mr. Białobrow, discussing the situation in the Zionist Organisation, called on the youth to go on weaving Dr. Herzl's idea of the Jewish State.
A protest resolution was adopted against the English Mandatory power, which has not fulfilled its obligations. The resolution was sent to the English ambassador in Warsaw and to the English consulate in Katowice.
A resolution was also adopted against the hooligan attacks on the Jewish students.

Izrael Mosze Wajnryb, of blessed memory

[Sosnowiec — obituary; funeral.] Izrael Mosze Wajnryb has died!
Like a thunderbolt in broad daylight the terrible news struck everyone: the long-serving national activist is no longer alive.
The deceased was, so to speak, the veteran in the field of national and social activity in the town of Sosnowiec.
Everywhere, in all public[?] campaigns, he occupied the place of honour; over a number of years he held the office of president of the „Merchants' Association“ („Sokhrim Fareyn“), for a long time he was president of the kehilla, and in general he figured as the person regarded with the greatest respect.
All the national organisations, and also the Artisans' Association, issued notices calling all members to take part in the funeral.
In Targowa Street, where the deceased had lived, masses of people gather; delegations arrive from the neighbouring towns. At exactly 2 o'clock begins
The grandiose funeral procession.
Before the coffin walk delegations of Betar, Herzliya, Maccabi, the academics, Hashomer Hatzair, Gordonia, Hechalutz, Hashachar, the school youth of Mizrachi and the girls' gymnasium; after them [printed „under them“] the coffin, covered with a blue-and-white cloth. In the other streets the number of mourners grows enormously, so that thousands of people accompany the deceased to his eternal rest.
The Central Committee (C. K.) authorised Mr Icchak Wygodzki by telegram to represent it.
When the coffin is brought to the cemetery, the cantor recites the appropriate verses from Psalms and
Rabbi Hager eulogises the deceased.
The eulogy was a very moving one. Many times, when the rabbi described the great loss, the audience broke into bitter weeping. With many sayings of the Sages the rabbi showed that in the hardest time of the Jewish people its leaders are taken away. He appeals to the audience to remain loyal to the Jewish Torah, the Jewish people and the Jewish land.
With moving words Rabbi Hager takes leave of the deceased in the name of the entire Jewish kehilla of Sosnowiec.
In a very depressed mood the audience gradually leaves the place of eternal rest. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.

Będzin „Kraft“ goes up into Class „B“.
On Sunday a championship match for promotion into Class „B“ took place on the Hakoach ground between Sosnowiec „Gwiazda“ and Będzin „Kraft“. The game stood at a high level and was played at a very fast tempo and with great ambition on both sides. In the 20th minute Rapaport managed to score the first goal for Kraft. Kraft carries out several more fine attacks and the result remains unchanged until half-time; right after half-time Gwiazda's inside-left managed to score the equaliser. Kraft sets to work and attacks continuously, so that one had the impression of a training session at one goal. Yet Kraft's forwards did not manage to change the result. Best on the field — the Patak brothers. Referee Mr Mazur good.

The Endek Youth in Zagłębie Is Itching for a Fight... / Decisive Action by the Police.

[Zagłębie — anti-Jewish riots.] The little sons of the Endek homes[?] in Zagłębie have read so much about the "heroic" deeds of their colleagues in Warsaw, Wilno and elsewhere that their little eyes began to gleam too, the delicate aristocratic blood boiled over, and they started itching to use their fists.
They feel like doing something...
On Friday morning "the street" murmured that the Endek students were getting ready. This was confirmed only in the evening. On Główna Street a large number of students gathered with the intention of getting down to "work". But the police quickly frustrated their plans and dispersed them.
Part of the rampaging camp, on their way home the same evening after a "kateriga"[?], began smashing windows and doors of Jewish shops.
Windows were smashed in the beit midrash and in the apartments of Messrs. Grinbaum, Rodaler, Epsztajn, Erlich and others.
The same hooligan acts were carried out on Saturday night in Pogoń, where the gates of the beit midrash were smashed, as well as at Mr. Fridman's and Mr. Liberman's. The latter suffered heavy damage. The windows were smashed with stones and pieces of wood.
On Sunday morning the windows of the beit midrash in Old Sosnowiec were smashed.
On Sunday a memorial service was held in the church in honour of the Wilno "saint" Wacławski.
On leaving the church the Endek youth again tried to run riot in various parts of the town, but thanks to the intervention of the police the attempts came to nothing.
The excesses, although on a small scale, caused a mood of panic among the Jewish population. This was aggravated by the special circular of the School Council (Rada Szkolna) to all school directors that in the afternoon hours school youth should refrain from walking in the streets.
The younger pupils of the Endek "cheder" also took part in the holy work. Jewish pupils were abused by them and many times also beaten.
In Płacker's school in Sosnowiec, during a lesson, the inscription "Pogrom na Żydów w Sosnowcu" [Pogrom on the Jews in Sosnowiec] appeared on the blackboard...
A group of Endek students arrived at the state gymnasium in Sosnowiec. When the director, Mr. Mazur, learned of it, he grabbed a thick stick, ran into the classroom and drove the "guests" out.
———
In the Będzin Realschule leaflets with anti-Jewish slogans were pasted up in several places. The director, on receiving word of it, reacted properly and called on the pupils to refrain from excesses.
In the course of Sunday and also Monday there were cases of students attacking Jewish passers-by, but thanks to the energetic stance of the police order was not disturbed anywhere.
———
The Jewish population of Olkusz lived through no little fright. There too the Endek rabble raged like wild beasts. Around 7 in the evening the gang went through the little town and began beating Jews and smashing the windows of Jewish residents. The panic that broke out was indescribable; mortal terror gripped everyone. Only when the police intervened did the bacchanalia[?] stop.
———
The Endek organ "K. Z." justifies the excesses with the argument that Polish youth takes a far-sighted view of the future. They see that "all of Polish culture and art will end up in Jewish hands, and this — the author of the article concludes — is the cause of the outbreaks against the Jews...
We think that the editors of that newspaper should indeed reflect on the threatening danger from the Jews and refuse to accept advertisements from Jewish merchants...
———
The Legionnaires' Union in Sosnowiec held an urgent meeting at which Deputy Dr. Ganszewicz[?] reported on the economic and political situation in the country.
After the report a resolution was adopted stating that the anti-Jewish disturbances, into which school youth had been drawn, damage Poland's good name abroad.
Great Preparations for the Hibbat Zion and Bilu Jubilee / (Communiqué of the Keren Kayemet Head Office).

[Zionism — Jewish National Fund.] The main jubilee committee, recently formed at the meeting of the active Hovevei Zion in Warsaw, has already set about energetic work, conducted according to an imposing plan and aimed at carrying out the great jubilee celebrations throughout the country. Everywhere in the provinces local jubilee committees are being formed, which will be in close contact with the main jubilee committee and, in accordance with its instructions, will carry out, with the help of the Hovevei Zion and veteran Zionists, the individual collection campaign for the Keren Kayemet.
On the land to be redeemed by the KKL with the money collected, the village Hibbat Zion (Bilu) will be founded.
This lofty and concrete task — the building of the Hibbat Zion village — has awakened among Zionists of all parties and among all nationally sound Jews a deep interest in the jubilee campaign, and in dozens of places (Kutno, Kielce, Białystok, Kowel and others) jubilee bazaars, lotteries, evenings etc. are being organised.
In many towns the jubilee committees have decided to inscribe in the KKL Golden Book the deceased Hovevei Zion and meritorious Zionists who worked and were active in the various towns of the country.
The youth organisations are preparing to celebrate the double jubilee in a special way; they are already preparing various evenings, festive meetings etc.
At the same time the great jubilee mass campaign is being organised for the days of Hanukkah.
As can be seen, the preparations for the jubilee celebrations and the campaign are in full swing, and there is no doubt that they will bring corresponding substantial results for the founding of Kfar Hibbat Zion.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — news.] Echoes of the anti-Jewish excesses in Siemianowice.
At the Katowice district court last Monday the trial took place of 15 hooligans who in the month of July ran wild against the Jewish inhabitants of Siemianowice, beating them murderously.
After hearing the witnesses the court sentenced 10 hooligans to 3 months' prison. The sentence, however, is suspended for 2 years. The organizers of the anti-Jewish excesses, on the other hand — to 3 months of immediate prison.
Preparations for the kehilla elections.
As we have already written, kehilla elections will take place in Upper Silesia in December of this year.
In this connection a meeting took place last Sunday in Königshütte (Chorzów), at which, with the agreement of all groupings (except the society "Shomrei Shabbat"), it was decided to put up a united list of Agudah, Zionists, Mizrachi, small traders and artisans.
Celebration of a flag unveiling
In the premises of the Zionist Organization in Königshütte the flag unveiling of the youth organization took place.

Opening of an artificial ice rink.
In Katowice the festive opening took place of the artificial ice rink, which is, incidentally, the only one in all of Poland. At exactly 5 o'clock p.m. the rink is opened to the sounds of the police orchestra. Judge Kowalski holds a short speech, greets the representatives of the authorities as well as the representatives of the press. Dąbrowa Kehilla Leaders Hand Out Honours..

[Dąbrowa — kehilla.] At the last meeting of the Dąbrowa kehilla council, before the agenda was taken up, the late national activist R' Yisrael Moshe Wajgreb, of blessed memory, was honoured by rising, and a protest resolution was adopted against the Endek attacks on Jews.
The meeting was very "interesting". In Dąbrowa the regulations of the kehillas are "not recognized"; rather, whoever just has a mouth, even from the gallery, takes the floor and speaks...
At the meeting the proposal of the kehilla administration was considered that Mr. G. A. Gutman be granted the title of honorary member of the kehilla.
Some spoke out against the proposal, pointing out that the same honorary title should also be given to the young benefactor Mr. Yakov Rebbitz, who has just given 100 korzec of coal and 50 korzec of potatoes for the poor population.
The discussion led to the kehilla president Mr. Mittelman leaving the meeting, leaving the assembled a few "parliamentary" expressions... In the end the matter was settled in the sense that one should turn to "the wise and understanding" so that they indicate how the kehilla administration should distribute honours...
Theatre Notes.

[Theatre — review.] "The Pearl of Shanghai", staged by Jonas Turkow and Diana Blumenfeld.
The artist couple always uses on their tours such European plays as can be performed by a small ensemble. This time Turkow "took us out" to China and showed the cruel will of a rich Chinese mandarin against a white Englishman who carried on a love affair with the Chinese daughter, who is called "The Pearl of Shanghai".
Jonas Turkow as the mandarin and Diana (his daughter) tried hard to make an effect with their acting, but when the content is a pale one, or better said a banal one, nothing more remains than to listen to the monotonous sounds of the Chinese language.
We would like to see Jonas in a better repertoire.
"Śledztwo" ("The Investigation"), a drama in 5 acts, staged at the Katowice Municipal Theatre.
"Śledztwo" is a drama in which the authors have treated in a sensational manner the interesting problem of accusations of the innocent and of the errors that are made in the world of the courts. Much has already been discussed about this in juridical circles, but the means has not yet been found by which court judgements will always be in accord with reality and justice. People have perished from the world, and after long years they were officially[?] rehabilitated — but already as dead bodies. The inner tragedy of a person who knows that he is innocent and whom one suspects of a murder is depicted against a strong psychological background in the drama "Śledztwo". Karl Bernt finds himself under an indictment that he murdered a street-woman. Everything is against the unfortunate man, all traces lead to him, and yet he has a clear conscience. A chance saves him from the hangman's rope destined for him, and a chance uncovers the real murderer.
Mr. Horowitz in the role of the unfortunate student gave an excellent creation with a great understanding of the sad situation in which he finds himself. We did not at all believe that the artist whom we always see in the role of the lover would flawlessly convey every tremor of a tormented soul. Mr. Archan has again shown that he is irreplaceable in caricatural roles. The other artists complete the good acting, and the performance makes a gripping[?] impression on the audience.
Elge
