Consequences of the Times

[Article — education; pupils' riots and Jewish–Christian relations.]
L. Szpigelman.
(A few words in connection with the excesses of the school youth.)

The Ministry of Education has issued a decree that pupils may not be found in the street after 5 o'clock in the evening. The decree was sent out all over the country and the school directors have put it into force.
Everyone understands that the decree appeared in connection with the prevailing excesses of the young hooligans, who are unfortunately to be found among the „golden youth“. Without doubt we have seen in this that the government has the good will not to permit the planned excesses, so that the decree was indeed in place.
But the question arises: what has been done, both on our side and on the government's side, so that things should not have come to the present phenomenon in the first place? After all, pupils and students once knew that their whole world was the book and the school and the professor and the academy. They had no interest in looking out over the broad, great world; they did not know what was happening in it; they had no interest in it and no need of it; they did not know that apart from the teaching in the book there was anything else in the world that could interest them. Their whole self was steeped from head to foot in the book, in scholarship, in learning, in study. For them, as for their professors, no other problem existed. Apart from Torah for its own sake, apart from Torah in the true sense of the word, they knew of nothing, and this lasted until they had left the school benches and the temple of learning as finished people — and precisely because of this they were afterwards types of true yeshiva students, naive and honest. Decent and modest they went out into the world, where they had to prepare themselves for a calm tomorrow.
And the non-studying youth — those who were not academics, those who had no access there, and also those who could not afford such a luxury — they too gazed enviously at the golden youth and wanted to adapt themselves to the same needs; they strove to be bound to the book and to education. Of course, insofar as they could afford it. But they had aspirations to educate themselves, to be attached to the book and to the newspaper, which gave its readers a great deal. Of course, the newspaper of those years cannot be compared with the gutter sheets which, unfortunately, are still called „newspaper“ to this day. For one must not forget that formerly the writer of the daily paper — the belletrist as well as the publicist, the novelist as well as the reporter — approached the matter as something of a holy thing. The pen he held in his hand was to him a sacred tool; he knew how to bear on his shoulders the full responsibility for every stroke of the pen. With every sentence he wrote he aimed to achieve something, to create something, to help whomever it might be, to serve, to ease. Perhaps he did not help as much as he wanted to help, as much as he wanted to achieve, but the mere will, the strong desire, already counted for a great deal in those years, and because of that simplicity we could forgive him all his mistakes, for we knew that he meant well, that he aimed at the good.
Everything that[?] was intended for the better person, for the intelligent man, was honest and steeped in holiness; therefore a large percentage of average citizens wanted to raise themselves to the level of those people who were at the very top of the ladder[?].
And this was at a time when there were no compulsory schools in former Russian Poland, and when it was in general not easy for a Jew to get into a school. Today, by contrast, when everyone learns and when we have schools which everyone can enter, we have a youth of utter ignoramuses (amei ha-aretz), and demoralisation is gaining the upper hand not only among us Jews but also among all other peoples. Today a pupil in the lower classes is a politician and is brought up in the cinema, with the help of the worst trashy novels, which all sorts of penny boulevard sheets supply us with in such a large dose.
When we ride on the train or in the tram, we see how at every station pupils, boys and girls, get on, holding in their hands all kinds of cheap boulevard sheets, and at once they hurry to go on with the novel in which they are immersed, and they remember with the greatest precision the plot and the roles of the novel's heroes.
And the news items they read — are they not bound up with the revolver and with blood and with night-life in the most disgusting forms? Is it any wonder that with such a feeding of spiritual nourishment come the results we could have expected? Is it any wonder that there are so many suicides of minors, when the children fill themselves through reading with so much poison? Or when they go to the cinemas to the most exciting „chantage“ (blackmail) pictures[?]? And the juicy adults-only programmes, which are supposedly intended for older people — who goes to see them and who is sophisticated in them, if not the children's youth? It is, after all, a rule among cinema directors that first of all one must provide oneself with such pictures as will attract the school youth, and to attract that element one procures such things as are dangerous to the upbringing of children.
And the school directors, professors and all who are occupied with the upbringing of children — why does this not concern them? Why do they allow the children to be brought up in such a demoralising way? Why should their home be the street and the cinema, which act on them like a magnetic force? Must it really be permitted that instead of reading a good belletristic or scholarly work this should be exchanged for poison-literature and revolver-papers? And this happens today, when one is so much occupied with the psychology of the child and when one has, supposedly, the aspiration to bring up the future generation with so much piety!!
We know very well that the Christian pupils of the upper classes are incited to beat Jews, and that the inciters unconsciously make hooligans of their own children — which, incidentally, they will regret later; but could one have dreamt of anything similar if the youth had not been brought up in the prevailing demoralising conditions? Would the child have had the heart to raise a hand if it had not seen so much disgusting filth, and if the upbringing had not taken place in the street and in the night-clubs, to which such children have access — children whose childish little hearts are corrupted in their earliest years? And if nothing was done about it, if no account was taken of this modern child-rearing, in which self-rule and demoralisation of the first order take first place among the children — then one could not, after all, have hoped for anything better.
Perhaps these strained relations between Jews and Christians — who at least at school were comradely — will teach a certain lesson: that the youth must be brought up differently, that it must not be self-ruling from childhood on, that one must have an influence over it while they are still children and need to be brought up by professionals, by educators, by older, conscious people experienced in this field.
The Actor Abraham Morewski in Zagłębie — "Rabbi Dr. Silber" by Sholem Asch at the "Kapitol"

"Rabbi Dr. Silber" by Sholem Asch, with the title role performed by Abraham Morewski, here with us in Zagłębie.
"Rabbi Dr. Silber" is one of the pearls of Yiddish literature and one of the best dramas of the greatest Jewish writer, Sholem Asch, in which true, pure love of mankind is expressed. This drama only recently left the stages of America and Warsaw, where it was performed over a long period with the greatest success.
The great, famous dramatic actor Abraham Morewski performs the title role in the drama, "Rabbi Dr. Silber". This gifted actor is unique in the family of actors for his high intelligence and culture. (Mr. Abraham Morewski is also well known as a brilliant, profound writer.) With his masterly acting the esteemed actor embodies the role of "Rabbi Dr. Silber", which he plays with the full fire of his heart and soul. The spectator is truly carried away by the sufferings the hero lives through, and leaves the theatre purified and uplifted.
"Rabbi Dr. Silber" is one of Morewski's most splendid creations after the "Miropoler Tzaddik" in An-ski's "Dybbuk". "Rabbi Dr. Silber" is one of the latest and finest theatrical events on the Yiddish stage, and now we have the privilege of seeing one of the greatest Jewish actors in a play by the greatest Jewish writer.
For the first time Mr. Morewski is setting out with his well-assembled ensemble on a tour of the Polish provinces. The Jewish population of Zagłębie now has the pleasant opportunity to welcome the great actor and writer with the proper honour he deserves, and to come and admire his acting.
The performance takes place on Monday, the 30th of this month [30 November 1931], at the "Kapitol" cinema.
What I Heard, What I Saw — compiled by Ben Amotz

Compiled by Ben Amotz.
Troubles from the kilo...
The conversation takes place in a tram. A woman of middle years is sitting there; her appearance bears witness that if one held a matura [school-leaving exam] in eating, she would be among the first... She doesn't lack a tongue either; if I'm not mistaken, she took eight measures of talk for herself...
And she talks. About what not? But she pours out all her anger on the German, who during the occupation introduced the kilo weight. All the poverty — she says — grows only from the kilos...
You don't believe what she says? Well, you have a simple calculation, so try to deny[?] that it is not as she says.
I remember — she says — when I took two pounds of meat for dinner, it was a whole "yesh" [plenty]; it was simply impossible to finish such portions of meat. You know, after all — she calls as witness a neighbour of hers, who is also riding in the same car — you know, after all, that my husband gets a nice portion of meat, eh? And today? Lord of the universe — I take two kilos of meat, and when I begin to "divide" it, everything goes dark before my eyes: a plate of bones, you could choke...
— You are perfectly right, golden soul — a Jewish carter breaks in — golden words you have spoken here. I've been shouting[?] this for a long time, that from the kilo scale the horses suffer even more...
Once, before the war, I used to buy 35 pounds of oats on Friday and the horses had enough to eat until Sunday; not to mention if I mixed in a quarter of chaff — then they, the horses that is, had enough to eat until Wednesday. And today? When I buy 30 kilos of oats on Friday, the horses are dropping dead of hunger...
These fodder arguments interested me greatly, and I turned to "authoritative circles" to decide the kilo problem and pronounce their opinion on who is right: the Jewish woman with the meat, or the carter with his horses?
— Perhaps you know, dear beloved lady readers — the answer?...
The Jew with grievances.
Day in, day out I meet him[?] on Kołłątaja Street, and to tell the truth, I try to avoid meeting him — not because he is not likeable to me; on the contrary, quite a decent young man; but he has one "fault" — he pesters me and wants me to answer all his questions.
His biggest grievance against me, though, is why we don't write about the fact that our "intelligentki" [educated ladies] avoid Jewish shops and buy precisely there, where the children have a large share in the blessing of "and the hands are the hands of Esau"...
— — Here, take a look, you see that lady (pani)? She came to me to buy a shawl; I set out the shawl for her at a minimal profit, but the lady — a Hasidic daughter, by the way — only looked the shawl over in my shop and bought it from the non-Jew.
— Why should it be so — he seeks an excuse from me — times are bad, merchants are wasting away for a groschen of takings, and if a Jewish customer does turn up at last, he goes...
— Write about it! — he shouts after me, and
— We are writing...
Chełm wisdom...
Those who stand closer to community life and take an interest in the latest "strategy" introduced with regard to the old kehilla leaders often wonder that the newly elected parnassim and dozors [board members] are not admitted to power, but look like beaten-out hoshanas...
It is already several months after the elections and hush, quiet — no one takes them into account, no one asks them anything; instead the old dozors have been given back the whip and
— giddy-up!...
I myself, I confess and admit, also could not understand why the old dozors got back their rule. But hearing of the brilliant exploits of the old dozors, everything was explained to me. If we really have such sages, they deserve to be the leaders of our holy congregation...
But before we make public the latest stroke of genius, we must tell the Chełm story.
They tell [?]. And it came to pass, when[?] it was, that a new floor had to be made in the Chełm mikveh. The sages of Chełm gathered for a meeting.
At the meeting the question was discussed of how the floor should be made. If the boards are planed, the bathing public will slip; if the boards are nailed down as they are, people will prick their feet...
— So what does one do?
Luckily there was at the meeting a rich householder, and moreover the greatest "sage" of Chełm, who found a way to settle the matter in such a manner that everyone would be satisfied...
— Gentlemen! — he turned to the assembled — hear my plan.
— Let's hear! — voices were heard.
— The boards — cries the "sage" — shall indeed be planed; you are afraid the public will slip? Then lay the planed sides underneath...
Almost the same wisdom was uttered by the [anudhshe — garbled word; perhaps "our"?] dozors in Będzin.
At the budget meeting that took place, the dozors sighed over the difficult situation of the Będzin "Talmud Torah". While the meeting was taking place, the Talmud Torah was closed and hundreds of poor children had become idle strays.
And one of the dozors, who is the chief speaker at every meeting, banged on the table and cried out:
— Gentlemen! We must take care of the "Talmud Torah".
— Of course, of course, one really must do something substantial so that the institution may be rescued from its critical situation.
— If so — the chief speaker goes on — I have a brilliant plan.
— Let's hear, let's hear!...
— I hold that, so that the Talmud Torah should take the place of honour, the subsidy for the Talmud Torah should be the first of the other Jewish institutions...
And so thereafter the Talmud Torah was indeed "rescued"...
Well, do we still need to ask questions as to why the old dozors got back their rule?...
Our Language Is Yiddish.

From 7 to 13 December of this year, Poland will hold its second general population census, which is carried out in all countries of the world every 10 years on the basis of international agreements. The tasks of the census are purely statistical and serve to establish the number of inhabitants and peoples of each country separately, their number and growth over the past 10 years, as well as to establish the figures for everything we encounter as human beings in life.
In the present census in Poland — judging by the forms already sent to the census commissioners — special census tables have also been introduced for youth of school age, which will serve the Chief School Administration to establish the number of school-age youth who remain outside the schools, and their needs.
It is also worth mentioning that the Jewish population should know that there is no reason whatsoever to be afraid when answering questions such as "main source of livelihood" — on account of tax matters. For under Art. 4 of the law of 21 October 1919 (Dz. Ust. R.P. 85, item 464) the declarations given at the time of population censuses are statistical secrets and may not be used for any other purpose. On the other hand, failure to give correct declarations, or giving false declarations, carries a fine of 500 gulden or a month's arrest.
We wish, however, to dwell on a second question, which at the present moment concerns all the Jewish inhabitants of Poland and which the Jewish inhabitants of Zagłębie must also consider, namely: the question of the mother tongue that Jews are to state at the census.
In recent weeks irresponsible persons have raised an uproar that the Jewish inhabitants of Poland should state "Hebrew" under the heading "mother tongue" at the census. We do not wish to enter here into a discussion of the value of Hebrew, because the value of Hebrew, like that of other languages, does not come into consideration at the census. The census as a whole has a purely statistical character — to establish the number of people of each nation and which language they use in everyday life.
Therefore, when individuals have the nerve to order people to state Hebrew as their mother tongue at the census, it means knowingly helping to deny our own language, which is used by millions of Jews. Such a demonstration would later be exploited by hostile elements to prove that the Jews' demands to found schools for their children in their mother tongue, the language their parents speak, are unfounded, "because the Jews themselves have not come to agreement among themselves" — an argument which the opponents of rights for Jews use daily; and therefore the individuals who dare to agitate against Yiddish must be condemned.
We wish to stress in this connection that the census forms contain no question about Hebrew as a mother tongue, but explicitly Yiddish (Żydowski). And a characteristic detail: next to the heading "mother tongue" the forms have a heading "Can you read and write, and in which language?" If, for example, someone were demonstratively to state Hebrew as the language he supposedly uses in daily intercourse and at home, the question arises what that same person will answer to the second question: "In which language can you read and write?" And we know, after all, who can read and write Hebrew! The impression would therefore arise that the Jewish inhabitants of Poland are almost all illiterate — because, let us not be ashamed and tell the truth: 80 percent of the Jewish inhabitants know no other language in which to read and write than Yiddish.
Summing up, we stress that insofar as individuals are found who will simply go against the people's demands and will not want to state Yiddish as their mother tongue, they must remember that their demonstrations will only harm the Jewish community in its national-cultural rights in education, and will only give the opponents of Jewish rights yet another means of raising the old argument that the Jews themselves deny their own language. And therefore, together with all the organisations that have begun a broad campaign among the Jewish inhabitants of Poland to state Yiddish as the mother tongue of the Jewish population — such as the artisans' associations, the merchants' associations, the Folkspartei, the Yiddish Scientific Institute [YIVO], the Yiddish folk schools and many other organisations and parties — we too warn the Jewish inhabitants of Zagłębie not to let themselves be misled by unauthorised elements. We appeal to you, together with the entire community of the Jews of Poland: do not deny your language, in which you express your sorrows and joys, the language in which 4 million Jews in Poland and nearly 2 million [sic] in the whole world speak and live out their years! And all as one, state at the census as your mother tongue — Y-I-D-D-I-S-H.
Y. M. Vitsh.
The Passers-by and the Dogs.

(A fable after Krylov.)
Two good friends, once at dusk,
chatting together, went for a stroll;
suddenly from a gate
a yard-dog set upon them with barking;
after him another, and then two, three more,
and in a single moment, with enormous insolence,
half a hundred dogs had come running together.
One of the walkers already meant [?]
to pick up a stone. — "No [?], one mustn't, brother! —
the other told him: "You'll make the racket
of these curs still worse and greater;
we'll walk on: I know their nature better;"
and indeed, after a dozen steps, more quietly now
the doggish barking carried to them,
slowly it began to fall ever more silent,
until at last not a single bark could be heard.
—
This is said against the antisemites, be he even a professor:
It's true: he has a tongue like a knife;
but you — just ignore him, don't argue with him,
for you'll only further provoke that evil spirit.
He'll surely stop some day after all,
and then all his barking will be silenced!
Meraggel ["Spy"].
Excesses, Matchmaking and Other Troubles.

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton.] Y. Oberżanek [apparently a pen name]

Matchmakers have been sent "nakazy" [payment orders] to pay turnover tax
(From the press)

In all businesses it is dead as in a cemetery. The merchants doze, the employees yawn. The winter goods lie packed in naphthalene — so they shouldn't catch a "hangover" [i.e. moths]. In the shop windows they put out prices: "Before 5 — now 2 zł." Others hold "clearance sales", "liquidations", "white weeks", "cheap weeks" and "advertising weeks" — give an ox for a groschen, when the groschen is in... the "Izba Skarbowa" [the Treasury Chamber]!...
In all businesses it is dead. That is why lately the editorial office has a "season"...
In the very heat of work the door opens and in comes a Jew with an umbrella in his hand.
— May one come in? — he asks, when he is already sitting at the editor's desk.
— I meant — he begins — to have a talk with you.
— By all means — the editor replied, — let's hear, what news are you telling?
— I ask you, Panie [Mr.] Editor, where is justice? Is it really a free-for-all ["hefker petrushke"]? Is there no law and no judge?
The editor, understanding that the Jew means the Endek students' excesses, answers the Jew: Who tells you there is justice — it really is paskudne [vile].
— Paskudne, you say — the Jew moves closer to the editor's desk. — It's easy for you to say paskudne, when you are not among the victims.
— What do you mean — wonders [?] the editor. — All Jews are victims.
— What? All Jews — says the Jew — are victims? That's not true. The victims are only the sufferers, as you say? Whoever gets hit is the one who has the trouble.
— And you? — the editor asks him — are you then a sufferer?
— Who else? — maybe you? — the Jew got angry — of course I am a sufferer, they have made me miserable, and you, Panie Editor, care about it like last year's snow? That is why you are an editor, so that you take up the krzywda [wrong] of all Israel. Tell me, Panie Editor, why are you silent, why?
— Reb Jew — the editor answers — the newspaper does write about it, but in what way, explain to me, are you a sufferer? Have you suffered from the excesses?
— Eat or not eat [?] — the Jew gets angry — is the substance the main thing?...
— But who are you, — the editor does not understand. — Are you then a student?
— I don't even begin to understand — the Jew loses his temper — forget about students and forget about excesses! I am a matchmaker! I ask you, when was it ever heard that matchmakers should pay a "podatek szadchanowy" [matchmaking tax]? Have you ever heard of a matchmaking tax? You know [?] the "przekaz płatniczy" [payment order] I received from the "szwiżbe skarbowy" [sic; the tax office], that I, Hersh Makhl, the matchmaker, should take the trouble to "clang in" [pay up] for tax. And perhaps you think that only I myself received such a "przekaz" — all the matchmakers, men and women, of Zagłębie have been sent such "przekazy" for taxes.
Tell me, Panie Editor, do you know the matchmaking trade? Is it then a trade? In former times one could still make a living from matchmaking — support a wife and children, but that was all once, when young men were young men and girls were girls. Today, may I not sin with my words. The [?] young men polish their nails with powder-pomade, smooth their manes with wax. Grown-up lads who should already be going under the wedding-canopy poles still kick balls together with cheder boys, and the girls? The girls are — dolls: "shminge-dginge" [?], skin and bone. Green as grass, and they faint, may it not happen to you, into one's arms... Can you see much difference today between a young man and a girl? Bride-girls smoke cigarettes and blow the smoke out through the nose, like a man, to make the distinction...
Here, take it, read in my notebook ["mshekaves" — unclear word]. You see what's going on here? Widows, divorcees and girls. Young girls and overstrained "przechodzone" [past their prime]. Girls with dowries [?] and divorcees with ready "urządzenia" [furnishings], older widows with all the "wygody" [comforts] and young modern widows according to the latest "technique"...
As you see me, I am no upstart matchmaker. My father and my grandfather were already matchmakers, I am a matchmaker son of a matchmaker. The only difference is that my father had luck with matches. A year after the wedding the husband became a divorcé or the wife a widow, and he took a matchmaker's fee again, and with me? Do I bring off a match? Which matchmaker brings off a match today? For what on earth do they need a matchmaker today? It has become the fashion "z miłości" [for love] — may they go to the devil together with their "miłość"!... Do you really think anything comes of the "miłość"? — Nonsense [lit. "yesterday's day"]! Heartache they get, not "miłość". Tell me, Panie Editor, did you marry "z miłości" or through a matchmaker? Probably through a matchmaker! One can see at once that you married through a matchmaker. What else, like those little dancers with the shiny "prominades" [pomade?] on their heads, who kick balls and run to the "meczetn" (read: matches) and shoot at the "bramkarze" [goalkeepers]?
— Excuse me, uncle — the editor tried to interrupt the agitated [?] matchmaker — say what do you want of me?
— Listen to me — the Jew did not let the editor get a word in — leave your "secesses" [sic, for "excesses"] with the "wrazimet" [mangled "uniwersytet", university] and the students and take up instead my matchmaking tax. Give advice, what do I do with my matchmaking tax?
— You have one option — the editor answers him — write an appeal [rekurs].
— Ha... ha... ha... — the Jew burst out laughing, — that I've already done without you. Here you have a "copy". If you like, I'll read out to you right away what I wrote:
"My friend Reb Naczelnik [chief] of the honourable Szwiżbe Skarbowe in the holy community of Będzin.
Since you have sent me a przekaz płatniczy that jako [as] I, Hersh Mekhl, should pay a matchmaking tax, I must tell you, Panie Naczelnik, that the matchmaking trade lies nine ells deep in the ground. If you wish, I can send you sznurowane [officially bound] commercial books. I can send you my divorcees with the "wygody" and the widows of the latest technique and other "wartościowe" [valuable] goods which are worth nothing to anybody. If someone must pay the matchmaking tax, those who must pay it are: the dance halls, the "peypel" clubs [?], the cinemas. I beg you, Panie Naczelniku, be so kind and be done with me — 'skończyłem' [I have finished]."
— Well, what do you say, Panie Editor, to the "natelacja" [?, probably "petelacja" — petition]? It talks sense, eh?
— Excellent — the editor nodded his head.
— For that — asks the Jew — I came to you, so that you should give an expert opinion on my "petelacja"? You are, after all, an editor who takes up the krzywda of all suffering humanity.
— Well, what — the editor asks him — must I do?
— I demand of you — the Jew answered — one thing: throw away your "secesses" with the "warzimets" [universities] and describe in the newspaper my matchmaking tax.
We do as the Jew wishes. We keep silent about the "Mishpatim" portion [i.e. the trials] and about our Kraków and Warsaw "scholars", who are now learning with relish "khavl shokhtin" [? "the laws of slaughterers"] — we write instead... about the new "podatek szadchanowy"...
Oneg Shabbat

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion. Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayishlach
Parsha
a) "Im Lavan garti" — "I have sojourned with Laban" (32:5)
"With the wicked Laban I sojourned, and I kept the 613 commandments."
1.
Jacob said thus: Twenty years I was in Laban's house, lived together with him, worked for him, made him a fortune — and yet: "Im Lavan garti." With him I was only a ger, a stranger, because "I kept the 613 commandments," because I am a Jew... And a Jew may live eight hundred years in a country and have the greatest merits toward that country — he still remains the ger, the stranger, the homeless citizen...
Divrei Shaul.
2.
Jacob then went on to say: "And I have oxen and asses." When I, Jacob, was with Laban, I was poor "and kept the 613 commandments" — that is not yet such a great wonder. To be pious in poverty is no great feat. But when "I have oxen and asses," when I already had a fortune and still "kept the 613 commandments," and was still pious — that, it seems, is not so common.
Beit Shmuel Aharon.
b) "Vayehi li shor vahamor" — "And I have oxen and asses" (ibid. 6)
When Jacob sent a mission to his brother Esau, he was afraid that his rich brother would not want to hear the messengers at all, for he would think: if a brother wants something from a rich brother, it is probably a request for support... and the best remedy for that, as is well known, the rich have: not to want to hear anything, not to want to know anything about their poor relatives. So he ordered them first of all: "And I have oxen and asses" — I am a rich man myself. Now the brother will want to talk to him...
Kol Yehuda.
— — — —
A poor man walked behind Poznański's funeral, weeping and groaning. They ask him: why are you so upset about Poznański's death? Was he your relative?
— What a question[?]! That's exactly why I'm groaning so, because he was not my relative... Oh, if Poznański had been my relative and had died besides and left an inheritance...
Folk joke.
c) "Hatzileni na miyad ahi miyad Esav" — "Deliver me, I pray, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau" (ibid. 12)
In the Midrash[?] there is a parable:
Axes and saws were carried through a forest. The trees began to rustle and the forest trembled: now they will be cut down. A wise tree speaks up: if the axes are only iron, without handles made of wood, we have nothing to fear. Iron alone will not chop. It will be bad only when the irons have handles of wood, of our own kind, of our own brothers...
"From the hand of Esau" alone — of Esau we would not have been afraid. Bitter is only "from the hand of my brother" — the Jews, our brethren the children of Israel, who are mixed up in Esau's wicked plans... In all gentile decrees a Jewish hand is involved; they are the handles of the axes that chop off our heads.
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
d) "Vayivater Yaakov levado vaye'avek ish imo" — "And Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him" (ibid. 25)
1.
The Midrash compares the evil inclination to a fly, because a fly does not settle on a healthy spot of the body, only on a wound where there is pus. The evil inclination too clings only to the battered[?] and wounded...
"And Jacob was left alone." For the sake of small jars Jacob stayed behind overnight. This stinginess, this greed for money, the evil inclination noticed — and at once "a man wrestled with him." He is already there..
Kli Yakar.
2.
"And a man wrestled with him" — one says he appeared to him as a gentile, the other says he appeared to him as a Torah scholar (Tractate Hullin 91).
It is not only the gentile who wrestles with the Jew, but also the Torah scholar. Not the genuine scholar, but the one who "appears as a scholar," the one who makes a show of being a scholar... These are the misleaders[?] of the people.
Sefer HaBrit.
e) "Vegam holekh likratekha" — "And he also comes to meet you" (ibid. 7)
Jacob ordered flattering words to be said to Esau, because he was afraid of him; and Esau answered him in turn with sweet words. But "we came to your brother, to Esau": inwardly he bore an Esau-like hatred toward you and outwardly only spoke like a brother. "He comes to meet you" — the way you relate to him is the way he relates to you. "As in water face answers to face, so the heart of man to man."
Ohel Yaakov.
f) "And Esau said: I have much" (33:9)
Jacob said: "I have everything" — I have all, I lack nothing; and Esau, although he was much richer than Jacob, said: "I have much" — I have a lot, but not enough. Esau always lacks something, no matter how much he may have.
Shaar Bat Rabim.
g) "Na'aleh [sic, for Nis'a] venelekha lenegdekha" — "Let us journey and go, and I will go before you" (ibid. 12)
Esau asked Jacob: I want to go and live with you, you will make me better. But Jacob did not want it: "the children are tender" — he was afraid the children would learn from Esau before Esau would learn from Jacob...
Likkutei Hadashim.
h) "Kum aleh Beit El" — "Arise, go up to Bethel" (35:1)
In the affair of Shechem Jacob was, as always, in a dilemma: should he take revenge for his desecrated honour — but "I being few in number, they will gather against me and smite me, and I shall be destroyed." Should he keep silent again — but the sons argue: "a disgrace has been done in Israel," one may not live like a dog that has no sense of honour.
Where is the way out?
— "Arise, go up to Bethel."
Rise above all these scoundrels[?]; their shameful deed need not offend you — you are above them.
Drashot El Ami.
Haftarah.
i) "For the violence against your brother Jacob shame shall cover you" (Obadiah 1:10)
Esau complains more than once that the Jew robs him, beats him — and that is not a lie, but —
It recalls that father who had two children. One is a quiet one, wouldn't even anger a fly; the other — a rascal. Once the rascal comes to the father with a scratched face: "Look, Daddy, what your quiet son did to me!" The father doesn't think twice and gives him two slaps.
— It's not enough that my brother scratched me, you hit me too[?] — screams the rascal.
— Your brother is a quiet one — the father answers him — and if he scratched you, you probably caused him enough trouble, if you drove your quiet brother out of his patience...
If the Jew does something "from the violence of Jacob," if Jacob does once rob Esau — "shame shall cover you": you, Esau, may bury your face in shame, for you probably tormented him enough if he defended himself...
R. Yitzhak of Volozhin ("Woloszyner").

In Haynt of Friday, portion Vayetze, Mr. Yoshuahn[?] (in his column "From Our Old Treasury") raises a query about the words "dabraniyot hen" ("they are talkative") in the Da'at Zekenim on the verse (Genesis 28:20) "And Jacob vowed a vow" etc., which are quite incomprehensible.
In my opinion the words "dabraniyot hen" have no connection at all with the tithe of Jacob's children; rather they are the end of a longer piece of Midrash Rabbah which the Da'at Zekenim quoted in passing, probably at the verse "and behold, Rachel his daughter comes with the sheep," on which the Midrash Rabbah we have says: "this teaches that talk is common among women."
I must remark in this connection that in general the wording of our Midrash Rabbah differs a little from the wording the Da'at Zekenim quotes. Probably the Midrash Rabbah had various versions in those times. Naturally, when there was no printing press in the world yet and the Midrash Rabbah was a rarity, the Da'at Zekenim found it important to quote an important passage of the Midrash. Later, however, when the printing presses arose and the Midrash Rabbah had become widespread enough, the long quotation was no longer so necessary to reprint in the Da'at Zekenim, so the printers surely omitted it, giving only the beginning of the quotation "a heretic asked R. ..." [printed "שאל מין אחר את ריבל"[?]], which incidentally differs a little from our version, and the end of the quotation "dabraniyot hen," which is surely a variant of our version "that talk is common among women."
I believe this is the most correct explanation of these two words, which various scholars exploit for twisted, groundless interpretations.
Hirsz Giebelski[?], Kielce.
The "Honey-Bird" in Katowice.

In Katowice a certain person was caught who had passed himself off as a doctor of medicine by the name of Tadeusz Sawiński. This person drew the attention of the Katowice police by his suspicious behaviour. After he was arrested it turned out that one was dealing with a plain swindler. No documents were found on him, but after a long interrogation and inquiry it turned out that his real name is Włodzimierz Kapidłowski and that he comes from Widzew [?] near Łódź.
As the further investigation established, Kapidłowski, as [?] "Doctor Sawiński", sold in Katowice to the merchant Krakowski an empty suitcase, a military greatcoat, a small gold watch and ladies' rings and other things, without being able to show where he had taken the things from.
He merely declared that he had been summoned by telephone to Katowice by Dr. Wolmiński, in order to take part in an operation. When the police got in touch with Dr. Wolmiński, the latter declared that he knew nothing whatsoever about it.
Kapidłowski was transferred to the military prison, because while on military exercises he had robbed a soldier.
The would-be "Dr. Sadziński" has a whole series of sins on his conscience.

Synagogue Architecture.
By Moshe Poltrek.

(Conclusion)
Thus these synagogues, in contrast to the Spanish splendour, to ornaments, are cold and gloomy. Only the entrance doors and, here and there, the windows eventually bear some decoration. The style of the synagogues is mostly Romanesque or Gothic, depending on the time in which they were built. On the other hand, one finds no forms borrowed from the churches. One rather meets details from town halls, castles and vaulted dwelling-houses. The walls inside are smooth; only the almemar [bimah] and the Holy Ark possess splendid architectonic forms. On the other hand, the sacred vessels very often belong to the masterpieces of their kind. Among the famous ghetto synagogues in the world is the synagogue in Prague: a splendid two-nave building with an interesting cross-vault. When, after the year 1848, the walls of the ghetto begin to fall in Western Europe, and under the influence of Mendelssohn the divine service is reformed, the Jewish communities begin to build synagogues which have little in common with the medieval tradition. For one must add that with time a building tradition had been created which could eventually have led to a certain distinctive form. But people wanted to break with everything that had any connection with the ghetto. Therefore the synagogue architecture of the second half of the 19th century must [?] make on a person [?] the impression of a terrible jumble. And it is no wonder at all — it is a true Tower of Babel. Synagogues are built in every possible style, which very often do not correspond to the ritual needs of the synagogue. But no attention was paid to that. What mattered was that the building should present itself splendidly from the outside and be able to compete with its Christian neighbour. In the countries where the Jewish population lives in larger concentrations, and chiefly in Poland, Lithuania and Russia, where religious life does not stand still but pulsates constantly, synagogue architecture developed — in contrast to Western Europe — on the old traditions. Religious-ethical and even geographical factors had an enormous influence. Synagogue building among the Russian Jews divides according to the following sects: Misnagdim, Hasidim and Karaites (the Karaite synagogues were especially plain and monotonous; their cold walls were often covered with Hebrew verses from the Bible); finally there are also the synagogues of the Circassians.
In another part of the world, where within a short time a few million Jews settled — in the United States of North America — synagogue building had a truly American tempo of development. At first small Jewish communities built synagogues on the model of a number of Christian sects. This is an interesting classical style which was used with us in Europe at the end of the 18th century in building banks, parliaments, museums and theatres. This classical style made it possible to revive again [?] the Greek and Roman ornamental elements. Thanks to the development of the communities there, the American synagogues find a solution in a monumental and splendid architecture. The newer synagogues pass from the juicy domed tower built in the Moorish-Arab style to the rich modern architecture, subtle in its form and interesting in its construction. Also as regards the interior arrangements, the American Jews have gone other ways in synagogue architecture than the European ones. One can, for example, very often find seating built in amphitheatre fashion.
Everywhere that Jews live, synagogues are built which do not differ in their form and appearance from the churches and temples of other religions. The Jews have not managed to ward off the influences of foreign forms — and Jews, after all, live everywhere.
In China there are synagogues in pagoda form. In Algiers, Tunis and Morocco the synagogues have no windows and no ornaments whatever on the outside. They display [?], on the other hand, their whole splendour and richness of form in the courtyard; the same also in Syria and Persia [?]. The black Jews of India build their synagogues quite differently from the English Jews in Calcutta, for the former are built on the model of the Indo-Mohammedan mosques. Famous is the interior architecture of the synagogues in Lower India, where almost the whole walls are covered with polished coins [?]. Unforgettable, too, are the synagogues which the Moroccan Jews build underground in the desert lands of the Sahara. In Zionist Eretz Israel a new form of synagogue building is now developing — a form which has in it nothing of the sentimentalism of the ghetto or exile. In contrast to the Jerusalem synagogue architecture, which is only a reminiscence of the exile synagogues, synagogues are now being built which contain quite different elements: that is, oriental motifs which are used constructively and combined with the whole immensity of modern technology. This architecture does not correspond to the religious fragmentation and the faith of the exile Jews. But it is adapted to the secure national feeling, which is not built on religious piety but seeks to express the soul of the modern Jew and the secure and sober forms of the Eretz-Israel architecture.
Trade and Economic News: Is a New Business Owner Liable for the Debts of the Previous Owner?

Trade and Economic News
Is a new business owner liable for the debts of the previous owner?
The prevailing general crisis, with all its attendant phenomena, places masses of enterprises in so extraordinary a situation that they can in no way extricate themselves from the net of debts and must finally liquidate.
Certainly there is also no shortage of owners who give up their enterprises in a fictitious manner, thinking that by buying a patent [trade licence] and repainting the signboards in the name of a mother-in-law or an under-age daughter they are already free of all obligations.
We therefore consider it an important task to explain precisely when a new business owner is, or is not, liable for the debts of the previous proprietor.
Thus, if the business in question was taken over from the previous owner, one can claim from the new proprietor all its outstanding business debts. If, however, the new owner merely rented the business, he is not liable for the debts of the previous proprietor.
Now the legal difference between "renting" and "taking over" must be established.
"Taking over" means coming into contact, negotiating and acquiring from the former owner all or part of the remaining inventory (goods and fittings).
"Renting", on the other hand, means negotiating directly with the landlord and contracting for the business premises, without coming into any contact with the previous tenant at all, and consequently also taking over nothing from him.
It is understood that, be that as it may, a sequestration can nevertheless be laid on the business of the present owner on account of the debts left owing by the previous proprietor, especially when the character of the enterprise (the branch) is not changed and the creditor demands it, taking upon himself any possible consequences.
Regardless of whether it concerns a tax or a private debt, the affected owner can bring an action in court in accordance with the provisions of articles 1092,93 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
If he is able to prove that he rented the business premises in an empty state, and can also call witnesses from whom he bought or obtained the sequestered goods and fittings, the sequestration will be lifted, he will also be awarded court costs, and he will likewise be entitled to claim appropriate compensation.
It should be pointed out here that the relations in which the former owners stand with the present ones do not in any case change the legal position.
The last case must be understood in this sense: merely because the new enterprise is run in the name of a relative of the former proprietor, the change[?] cannot yet be qualified as fictitious.
Y. In.

When can one obtain an eviction?
The great shortage of cash has caused many disputes between landlords and tenants. A large proportion of tenants have fallen behind with the rent; they owe more than two instalments. The landlords demand eviction of such tenants, thinking it will be easy for them to put out the old tenant and get fresh key money from a new tenant.
But in reality it is not so easy. Landlords who think that owing 2 months' rent is already a sufficient reason to obtain an eviction are mistaken.
The Tenants' Law says that as an "important reason" for giving notice on the flat and obtaining an eviction — if one has not received [the rent], in such a case, when it comes to two instalments, one can obtain an eviction.
Now the question arises: in what manner must the act of demanding the rent be carried out?
Many landlords have therefore introduced the practice of sending the tenant, on every first of the month, a note via the caretaker with a bill stating that he must pay so-and-so much rent for the current month.
At first it was thought that these monthly slips from the landlord with the bill were sufficient proof that the "rent" had been "demanded". This was based on a ruling of the Supreme Court of 31 October 1927. Later, however, the Supreme Court issued another judgment, in which the requirement of the law is explained, and if one has issued bills for rent for two months without success, one still cannot obtain an eviction on that basis.
The great number of tenants pay the rent with bills of exchange, and so the question has arisen: if bills of exchange for rent go to protest, do these bills have the same privileges as [printed: "has"] a rent debt; that is, can one sue in court for an eviction over the unpaid bills?
There are many disputes in this connection. From the judgments already issued it is clear that if the rent was covered with bills of exchange, the rent counts as paid, and if something happens with the bills — they are not paid — they are regarded as ordinary bills of exchange and one cannot demand an eviction with them.
Tenants must, however, be warned against a certain carelessness and excessive trust when it is a matter of an eviction suit.
It often happens that before the eviction trial the tenant comes to a settlement with the landlord and manages to have the case cancelled. The tenant thinks that if the landlord does not go to court, the case lapses. That is a mistake.
If the landlord sues the tenant for eviction and neither party appears in court, the case is treated "zaocznie" [in absentia, by default] and the landlord is awarded an eviction. It is therefore necessary that the tenant present himself in court and inform the judge that he has already settled with the landlord; better still, obtain a receipt from the landlord stating that he withdraws the case.
Adv. G. Gr.
Homely Greetings.

[Feuilleton — satirical letter from Warsaw to Zagłębie; Warsaw — poverty, trade, kehilla; Będzin — kehilla.]
(A bundle of letters between Yosl the Varsovian and Berl the Zaglembian). Handed over for print by Y. B. Zayants.

Dear friend Berl! Your little letter truly revived us all — no small thing! My Yente Tsipe, may she live, already wanted to dash over to you in Będzin, to the graves of the ancestors... You should know that she, my Yente Tsipe, strength to her hands, is, no evil eye, as clever as the day... She, mine, may she live, says that the dead know everything... Well, recently thieves broke in on us and, God forbid, would have reduced us to poverty, but the dogs in the yard barked so loudly that the thieves had to clear out... In the morning our watchman [stróż] told us that thanks to his two „khinem“ [misprint for „dogs“] we got off with nothing but a fright... Hearing this, my Yente Tsipe, may she live, had a good laugh and whispered to me quietly: silly — she said — don't believe him. It was really the merit of our ancestors that protected us; the two dogs that barked like that — why, they were my father and mother from the other world...

You, Berele, want to know what is heard with us in Warsaw? Sad, very sad. Poverty whistles here in every corner... The poverty here is so great that whole shoes with goatskin trousers only a baron can afford with us... What a goose looks like, only a professor of zoology knows here... and the head of a herring is kept for Purim, to send as shalach-manos...

You ask me how trade looks here? It is, brother, „and Terah died in Haran“. If a man is a „kohen“ he will not walk past the Nalewki, because today there is a cemetery there... Quiet, you don't see a soul born of woman. Except for the bailiff [egzekutor], who comes from time to time to say an El male rachamim for a dead „taxpayer“ [płatnik]...

In short, death everywhere, except in the Jewish gmina on Grzybowska Street, where it is homely: the gang of dozors [kehilla board members] gives a concert there from time to time... They throw at each other's heads chairs, inkwells, spittoons, brooms and similar „musical instruments“. You surely read in the paper how not long ago here they made the president of the Warsaw kehilla, the Orthodox R' Eliyahu Mazur, into a modern dandy with a glass „monocle“ on one eye...

You write me, Berele, that your „yarmulkes“ [the Orthodox] there have grabbed the „Talmud Torah“ in Będzin and at once opened on the side a little shop „Yesodei-Torah“, and now even a brand-new little stall „Ezrat Yesodei Torah“. Rest easy, soon a branch [filia] will follow, „Ezra le-Ezrat Yesodei Torah“, later „Ezra le-Ezra me-Ezrat Yesodei Torah“ — that is how it goes with them; their „little Torah“ is not of parchment but of rubber — it stretches in all directions...

Write me, Berele, whether it is true that the artificial ice rink [?] in Katowice is closing because nobody visits it; to tell the truth, that ice rink is quite superfluous there by you, for let us not fool ourselves: of the total number of merchants in Zagłębie, the bigger half has long since „slipped out“ anyway...

And now, Berele, I come to bring you news: all Warsaw is in a stew over the president of the Jewish gmina in Będzin. No small thing: at a time when the Spanish king Alfonso the Thirteenth has also come down from his throne and crowns roll about in the gutters, the president of the Będzin Jewish gmina gets the idea of becoming a „self-ruler“ [autocrat] and introducing the new reformed calendar into the Będzin kehilla, with such a trick... What is it? On an ordinary Sunday, when a meeting of the kehilla administration is due to take place, the president says: with me today is „Yom Kippur“ and I am now at „Ne'ilah“ — the meeting is closed... „Zenen“ [?]. But there are such dozors there as Messrs Goldsztajn, Liwer and Dymant, who know the „Machzor“ by heart; they start to plead: „Open the gate for us at the time of the closing of the gate“! Sir, crown of our life, open the meeting! The president answers them: „Tomorrow shall this sign be“ — tomorrow, children, you'll have a surprise... Today, my little lambs [?], I don't have my rattle-gear here; tomorrow I'll have my „Yotzer meshartim“ [lit. „Creator of servants“ — his henchmen] here and it will be all right... Don't take it amiss, even a cantor like Sirota doesn't pray without choristers...

What Must One Know About Trade Patents for 1932?

[Commerce — taxes and licences.] A merchant who holds a patent [trade licence, świadectwo przemysłowe] of the second, third or fourth category may on market days trade in the same goods at various markets, and one does not need a special patent for each market separately. One must carry the trade patent on one's person. One may also travel on market days to the surrounding small towns, provided only that they belong to the same tax office [urząd skarbowy] to which the shopkeeper's place of residence belongs.
This is provided for in ministerial circular [okólnik] number 3 1566 of 30 September 1926.
According to circular number 3 3926 of 29 March 1927, if a merchant who has a shop also wants to trade at markets and fairs, he must have a special patent for that.
On the other hand, if a merchant who has a shop wants, on a market day held in his own town, to carry the goods out to the market and trade there, he does not need a special patent for it. He must, however, close his shop on the market day, and the patent must be kept at the market stall. This is permitted only in the same town where one has the shop. By contrast, to travel to markets in other towns one must have a special patent.
———
The critical times, which this year have pressed an even larger number of merchants, force many of them to reduce their businesses. Second-category merchants are reducing their shops and want to buy third-category [patents], and again, such merchants as hold the third category want to move down to the fourth.
In the latest circular of the Finance Ministry instructions are given to the offices [urzędy] that, if a merchant this year wishes to take out a smaller patent, a remark should be made on the reverse side that the smaller patent is issued according to the merchant's declaration, and if at an inspection it turns out that at that place of trade one must have a larger patent, he will be punished.
Merchants, again, who want to move from the third to the fourth category should know that on a fourth category one may not trade in premises that look like a normal shop or a room. On a fourth-category patent one may trade in a cellar dwelling, in a courtyard storehouse, in a small room that has no window. In the fourth category only the owner may be employed in the shop — one single person, without any assistance.
If, however, the trade takes place in a shop or in a room with a window, then the third category is unconditionally required, even if the smallest quantity of goods is present.

What everyone must know about the census on 9 December / A beggar abandons 4 children

The day of the census, the 9th of December, is approaching, and every Jew is obliged to know what he has to do on that day and what threatens him for negligence or for giving incorrect declarations.
The census is not meant to extract any secrets from the citizens. The census aims, with the help of figures on property[?], age, level of education, kind of occupation, housing conditions etc., to give a correct picture of the economic and social conditions in our country.
The figures of the census will not be used to impose any burdens on the citizens. The figures and data the citizen gives will remain secret with the census commissioners. On the other hand, whoever does not give correct figures will be punished with a fine of up to 500 zł.
How are the declarations given? Quite simply: on the 9th of December the census commissioner comes into everyone's home and asks in order: what one's name is, how old one is, etc.
It goes without saying that it is only fair to make the census commissioner's task easier and to have the passport, the marriage certificate etc. ready on the table, in which the commissioner checks whether the name is correct.
Then the census commissioner asks further questions in the order in which they are given in the questionnaire sheet, and all questions must be answered clearly.
So that not just anyone could come in and say: show me your documents, the authorities have ordered that when the commissioner enters a home he must immediately show his identification.
After he shows the identification, one shows him the documents and answers all the questions, which he writes down in the question sheet.
A child who is not at home has his name recorded with a note that he is absent. If a stranger is in the home, he too must be recorded.
Which nationality one belongs to is not recorded in the questionnaire; however, what language one speaks is recorded. Every Jew is therefore obliged to give his mother tongue as Yiddish.

Around the New Kehilla Elections in Olkusz

(From our correspondent.)
The present election fever has gripped almost all strata of the Jewish population, because everyone is interested in the fate of the Jewish kehilla and wants to see in the future kehilla the people who can represent the Jewish population of Olkusz both internally and externally.
The election fever grew even stronger when the Zionist list was submitted, of which the "Agudah" with its hangers-on became very frightened; they racked their brains over how to damage the list. Thus lists and little lists were created with the sole intention of breaking the Zionist front. Also a list meant to split the front of the artisans, because out of sheer habit the "Agudah" considers itself the guardian of the Jews of Olkusz, and it greatly vexes them, the impudence of the Zionists, who cannot put up with Agudist "integrity".
There is also much talk that the rabbi, may he live long, was badly frightened by the list and took an active part in creating a list with the well-known "Olkusz communal worker", who is supposed to teach the Zionists manners, and whom the learned (G.) rabbi hopes and strives to see also as president of the kehilla (printed "קה״ת"[?]).
Therefore let me be permitted to ask the learned rabbi: should a rabbi meddle at all in such matters, which concern the whole Jewish population, and use his influence as rabbi in favour of one side against another? Did you, learned rabbi, consult the local householders about your step? And if you really saw in list number 4 people dangerous to the kehilla and wish to remove that danger, could you find no other householders in the town but this one, whose deeds for the public good are not recognised by any decent person and have long brought no honour to the whole kehilla?...
But, learned rabbi, your trouble is in vain; the Jewish voters are already mature enough and they understand who ought to be their representative and who is worthy to bear the name of Jewish representative, and they will elect such people whose work in the kehilla will be for the public good, not for individuals.
M. Sh.
The Work Has Begun

Of the rescue committee for Jewish unemployed.
On Thursday, in the premises of the Sosnowiec Merchants' Association (Kowalska[?] 2), a larger meeting took place of the aid committee for supporting the Jewish unemployed in Sosnowiec.
The meeting is opened by the chairman, Mr. Kwiatek, who reports on the sad economic situation of the Jewish population and in particular on the Jewish unemployed. To alleviate the need of these people an aid committee was created, which has established contact with the general state aid committee as well as with the municipal committee, which will receive state support; in the coming days they will start distributing food, potatoes, coal.

The Jewish aid committee has to collect a one-time sum of 15,000 zł., which is urgently needed in order to broaden the action of supporting those persons who will be excluded from the state fund for supporting the unemployed. The committee is already proceeding in the coming days to open a Jewish free kitchen, which is to serve up to 250 lunches daily. The committee has also decided to clothe[?] Jewish schoolchildren.
In the coming days the general state aid committee will also carry out a collection among the merchants, who are to contribute according to categories of 25 — 5 zł. a month.

[Beuthen (German Upper Silesia) — crime; trafficking in women.]
On Sunday evening an unknown young man and a young girl who was accompanying him were arrested at the ticket office of the railway station in Beuthen [Bytom].
The unknown man was immediately taken for questioning, and it was established that his name is Greszyński [?], who is on record as a dangerous trafficker in women.
The arrested Greszyński, who comes from Częstochowa, has more than once “smuggled” various young girls across the Polish border, who had supposedly been engaged for positions abroad.
The arrested girl related that she had been engaged by the young man to travel to Antwerp for a position. The foreign passport the girl had on her turned out to be a forged one.
During the body search a notebook was found on Greszyński with the first names and surnames of girls whom he had already managed to take out of Poland.
Theatre Notes

[Theatre — play review; followed by “Letters to the Editor”: Będzin — the bus stop; Dąbrowa — kehilla.]
“Rabbi Dr. Silber”, a drama in 3 acts by Sholem Asch.
The Reverend Silber stands at the head of a congregation, and he preaches about family purity.
But while he preaches in the synagogue about morality, ethics and other lofty matters, his wife is carrying on a love affair with her music professor. This is noticed by the Reverend’s mother. She feels that it is not only the love of music. That binds the musician to the Reverend’s wife. But that there exist between them deep, personal love relations. The mother draws her son’s attention to the said relations and demands that he remove the woman from his house. The Reverend does not believe it and reproaches his mother that she accuses his wife groundlessly. Only when the mother throws the accusation directly in the woman’s face does she confess everything and leave the Reverend’s house together with her lover.
Time passes. The woman is abandoned by her lover, and it comes to the point that she becomes a streetwalker. When the Reverend learns that she has come back, he takes her back to himself and wants to go on leading a normal family life with her. This the mother and the congregation’s leaders do not permit. The woman commits suicide; the Reverend leaves his post and goes off to found a new synagogue.
That, in broad strokes, is the content of the drama.
Morewski is an actor with a very highly developed intellect. He is the true scholar [talmid khokhem] of the acting family. For him, playing theatre is a sacred service. But this time he unfortunately left us cold. There was no comparison to his master-creations of a “Dukus” or a “Miropoler Tsaddik”. The monologues were delivered quite nicely, but they had no effect. His voice did not yield the splendid modulations we have been used to hearing from him. But art is not a craft, and one cannot always create to order. When inspiration happens to be lacking, it’s all over. But we hope that this was only an accidental occurrence and that we will again see Morewski in his full splendour as high priest in the temple of Yiddish dramatic art.
Of the other participants the following distinguished themselves: the Reverend’s wife, who was outwardly effective, graceful, and played her role cleanly. The mother’s role, too, was good, finely stylised, and the actress brought out the effect the direction wanted: the creation of a kind of female “meshulekh” [emissary].
It is only a pity that the sets and the music stayed behind on the road. That disturbed the harmonious whole.
Sh. R.

Zagłębie — the Most Expensive Place in Poland. / (Living conditions must be eased in the present time of crisis.)

What the Statistical Office shows us we know ourselves; we have always known that the greatest dearness is not only in Sosnowiec but in all of Zagłębie. Constantly[?] food and all other products were the most expensive here in Zagłębie, but people paid little attention to the dearness, because Zagłębie was a place of livelihood, the złoty played no role, and therefore one let the other earn, graciously.
Zagłębie's inhabitants, from the poorest to the richest, used to think: I earn — let the one I buy from earn too. The motto "live and let live" could be seen most clearly in Zagłębie.
That is the reason why the inhabitants of Zagłębie have such a broad gesture. With us the złoty was never an idol; as long as one could pay one's way with money, all was well.
But all this was good while it was good, while things went as they should. Then came the catastrophic situation, the crisis began to spread its terrible wings over everything around us, and people began to reflect that here one overpays for everything. And that the grosz plays a role — there is no need even to say; one would gladly have taken from any side[?] just to keep alive, just to get through the day.
It is true that in Poland in general everything is cheap now, but what comes of it — an ox for a grosz, when the grosz isn't there. And this applies to Zagłębie's inhabitants too. Formerly the grosz played no role for any of us, and now, when it is gone, the coin is a "bastard"[?] — and what comes of it, when you never set eyes on the jingling coins: an ox for a grosz, when the grosz isn't there.
One must skimp and save, but what comes of it when there is nothing to do it with, when one goes about idle and empty, when the worker has no work — and as soon as the worker does not work, nobody can earn from him, and who here does not live off the worker? That is the first wheel: as soon as that wheel stops, not a single little wheel moves; all the power lies in the worker-wheel, and without this very wheel the whole construction is paralysed.
From the worker lived the merchant and the craftsman and the factory owner and everything that lives and moves under the sun.
And now, when there is no livelihood, when the worker goes about idle and empty, when at the craftsman's the tools are rusting and in the factories the machines are rusting, when nobody has the means to buy a warm shoe for the winter and a garment, and even for food there is quite often a shortfall — one must stop and ask: why is it dearer here than in all of Poland?
Well, when one was well situated, when, as the saying goes, business was going, money played no role and nobody stopped to ask why things were dearer here; one earned — and spent the earnings, and thought: what do I know, money is round — today it is here, tomorrow it goes away and the day after it will show up again.
But we have been waiting a long time now and the "guest" somehow does not come back. We thought he had left us for a while and would soon return, but somehow he is not to be seen. We look out for him impatiently, like a pious Jew awaiting the Messiah, and somehow he is taking too long, so that we are almost beginning to doubt whether those times will return — times we actually did not appreciate, and now we begin to long for the days when things were still good and when one could afford to live like other people.
Now a time has come when the grosz plays a decisive role and when Zagłębie is no better off than the whole of Poland, and the question arises: why should the population of Zagłębie overpay for articles of prime necessity? Why should food be dearer here than elsewhere? Why should the oppressed citizen, who can seldom[?] afford to buy his child an egg, pay more than it really ought to cost? And why should he overpay for a piece of meat and for potatoes and for butter and for all other basic foodstuffs?
The question ought to be regulated, since in the present critical time it has such great importance. Why should the local authority not make it possible for us to insist[?] that the said articles be sold at the same prices as in other large towns? It is a hard time, and in a hard and serious time every grosz counts, so it would be absolutely necessary to give this important question attention.
Well, saving is impossible in the present hard time — let us at least not be fleeced, let us not be exploited on articles that the poor, the unemployed and the middle-class citizen alike must buy for their daily sustenance. This question absolutely ought to be regulated. One must reckon with the seriousness of the situation.
One ought to go further still: one ought to see to it that Zagłębie's unemployed and needy can buy products at the lowest possible prices. To this end the most necessary products should be bought up, without making a profit, and then sold to the people at cost price.
The government and the municipal authority must together come to the aid of the citizens who need to buy the products as cheaply as possible.
In other countries the economy occupies a highly honoured place and citizens are protected by every possible means.
The government taxes the population; the citizens carry on their shoulders all the duties a citizen must fulfil. Therefore, in a time of trouble, the government must come to the rescue and protect all the inhabitants of the country.
Just as the government busies itself with tax matters — what must be collected from the citizens — so it must also take care not to let fall that same citizen from whom it has or had its revenues.
Nowadays, in the present hard situation, Zagłębie must not overpay. We here must not pay the highest prices in all of Poland.
Zagłębie always carries greater obligations toward the country than [the rest of] Poland; so one must also show it help in a time of trouble, when everything chokes and presses and a large part of the unemployed are starving together with their wives and children.
R. Let.
