Crisis and Learning

(Wherever the critical situation may penetrate — it must not be allowed to reach the walls of the schools.)
The crisis has already thrust its wings into every corner of human life. Everywhere we hear its tones. Everywhere it leaves behind signs of its mastery. The critical situation is thus the worst in the full sense of the word, and each of us must begin to reckon with the gravest danger, whether he wants to or not, whether it reaches X or Y, and whether it has done him direct or indirect harm.
Be that as it may, everyone who fights for his existence suffers from this dangerous disease, of which we not only cannot rid ourselves, but on the contrary — it keeps progressing, it spreads its cruel wings over countries and peoples, and therefore in the great world people are beginning to investigate and philosophise: what exactly is this crisis? Where did it come from, and how does one get rid of it? People study and interpret its character, its properties, and want[?] to get to the bottom of whether it is a passing phenomenon that sweeps through like a hurricane, after which it becomes beautiful again and the sun shines once more, or whether it tears along with it everything that lives and works, so that after it one can find no place for oneself, and those who remain find themselves as after a destruction, as in a wilderness, where one has to begin creating everything anew and seek means of getting rid of the damage done.
Undoubtedly this is a hard problem, a task which the greatest world geniuses cannot undertake to solve, and that is precisely the reason why it keeps developing and blossoms[?] rapidly[?] across all parts of the world.
The consequence of the spread of the disease are the suicides and the most terrible tragedies in our poor life, which has become such a frequent guest in our generation (printed "ד״ר"); we watch the most terrible tragedies and the most dreadful catastrophes with rare indifference, we have become dulled to the misfortunes that cry out to heaven, our delicate and sensitive nerves have become apathetic to everything that is terrible and that we could barely imagine in our thoughts we would be able to bear, that we would be strong enough to endure.
The newspapers feed us the most dreadful facts and we have grown used to reading them over breakfast, and it makes no impression on anyone. The events have become everyday affairs and we live with them just as with the most normal phenomena. We have begun to adapt to everything, and when we take a newspaper into our hands in which the tragic is absent, we already miss it, as if we had not found what we were looking for...
The prevailing crisis, however, has managed to draw to itself so many combinations that we would never have dared even to think of. Thus, for instance, we not infrequently meet, side by side with the most glaring suicides and tragedies, quiet, modest sufferings face to face — about which the newspapers do not write and make no noise, and no one knows what goes on in the hidden souls.
Nowadays there are in Zagłębie very many families who do not send their children to the cheders and schools only because they have nothing to pay the tuition fee with. The parents suffer enormously in a moral sense, and the children suffer spiritually, since[?] among them are mostly such who strive towards learning, such who thirst for education and knowledge.
The institutions mentioned do not want to know about anything; from there the child is sent straight home as soon as it does not bring with it the monthly obligation. It goes without saying that the schools must get what is theirs; they have, after all, their budgets which they must keep up, and if they are not paid on time they come to a standstill and cannot continue their systematic work, which has to be run regularly, like a clock.
But that is not yet to say that everything is fine and good as it is and that the question is thereby solved.
A catastrophic crisis reigns over the whole world; manufacturers, workers, artisans and merchants are reducing their goods and products. People now calculate differently, endeavour to earn less, and although the struggle for life is not any easier, people have nevertheless come to the realisation that if one cannot go over, one must go under, and these are the reasons why nowadays everything is cheaper. By how much have the schools and cheders come down? How much have they reduced their prices? Have they also given the possibility to those who cannot attend their institutions to get somehow inside the walls of education? Have they stopped to consider this serious question? Have they considered what situation the parents are now in, many of whom perhaps a year or two ago supported these institutions materially and now find themselves in such a state that they have no possibility of sending their children to learn? Has anyone stopped to consider all this? Has it been taken seriously into consideration? Has anyone at least tried to want to solve the question and find a way out? If so — why has the tuition fee not been reduced? If everything is cheaper, if everyone makes do with smaller earnings — why should this not be applied to the pedagogical institutions as well?
A school for our children is, after all, not some superfluous thing that one could do without; we are not dealing here with a matter of second or third rank, so that in this case one may not remain indifferent and say: "If you can pay — well and good; if not — keep your children at home, and good health to you[?]."
We by no means begrudge our educational institutions, which are poor enough and struggle hard for their existence, but to leave the question unsolved like this, with a large part of the children staying at home because of it, is certainly not proper, and one certainly cannot carry this on one's conscience with an easy conscience.
At a time when such a dreadful crisis reigns, sweeping away world magnates and rulers of money, one must after all reckon with it: the budgets of the institutions must be reduced as far as possible, provided only that it works out well for everyone; let one have compassion for the other, let him who stands on his feet help the one who is tottering and not let him fall.
One must not let the future generation, which needs to receive education and learning, be torn away from school; we must not abandon these suffering souls, who can grow up to be good citizens and useful Jews.
We must begin to consider the question and come to the realisation that the problem of education must not be a matter of chance with us, but that we should give all those who want to enter the possibility of making their way inside the walls of the schools.
R. Lesz.
Jewish Unemployed Must Organize.

Winter, with its cold and frost, is already at the threshold; the crisis, poverty and want rule the Jewish street ever more with their cruelty, and the ranks of the Jewish unemployed, the people without a livelihood and the plain destitute grow from day to day.
The impoverished Jewish street is unable by its own strength to relieve the want of its poverty — "a prisoner cannot free himself from prison" — one who is bound cannot untie himself, the old sages said... The Jewish street is so impoverished and powerless that every relief campaign is condemned to partial failure.
The general committees for the unemployed must also take care of the Jewish unemployed — this slogan must be heard from all Jewish public workers.
Fortunately, in Sosnowiec they are already well versed in the question of aid for the unemployed. Thus our news column tells us that at a meeting of the Committee for the Unemployed it was decided to set up a kitchen for the Jewish unemployed who will not want to make use of the general kitchen.
We understand that not every Jewish unemployed person will be ready to make use even of a Jewish kitchen, because among the Jewish element shame will work so strongly that some will even be ready to go hungry rather than make use of a public kitchen.
But one more factor must be taken into account here.
The non-Jewish unemployed have organized and form a body which comes forward jointly with its requests and demands.
The Jewish unemployed must therefore, first of all, register with the Committee for the Unemployed and then organize themselves into a body that will come before the public with its demands.
The want in the Jewish street is terrible; poverty and destitution have today become rooted citizens among the Jewish population; hundreds of Jewish unemployed and Jews without a livelihood stand at the edge of the abyss; now the hard winter is coming, and a remedy must be sought.
The Jewish unemployed must organize — that is the command of this hard hour.
P. Lazar.
I Become a Witness at the 'Brest' Trial...

By Graf Kali.
This week I read so much about the "Brest" trial that my nerves came unscrewed and jangled; whole nights the prosecutor gets tangled in my head together with the lawyers, peasants and politicians, toys [?] and dolls.
Last night, after reading my fill — like a drum — of a whole day of court proceedings, I dreamt that I was called as a witness at the trial of the "Brest" defendants. As far as I remember, the following dialogue took place between me and the presiding judge:
Presiding judge: What is your name?
I: Graf Kali.
Presiding judge: From which counts do you descend — the Radziwiłłs or the Zamoyskis?
I: The title of count I did not inherit from my parents; I received it for my own merits.
Presiding judge: But in Poland all titles have been abolished; you probably received the title from the Russian Tsar Nicholas II?
I: What? From that enemy of Israel, who has so much Jewish blood on his conscience, I would accept a title? I received the title from my first editor. Ah, what a generous man he was! What fine fees he paid! Oh, those good times! Does anyone pay anything for a poem today? You are, after all, a guardian of justice, so I ask you: is it fair that poets should go hungry?
Presiding judge: That does not belong to the trial... How old are you?
I: It depends... On Thursday night, when my wife asks for [money for] Shabbat and I don't have it, then "behold I am as a man of seventy years" — I look like a seventy-year-old elder... But when the dear summer comes, when my wife is at the dacha and there are a few jingling coins in my pocket, then — I feel young and fresh like a lad of twenty.
Presiding judge: What do you know about the trial?
I: What do you mean, what? Doesn't Your Honour know everything? We don't live behind the "Mountains of Darkness"! Everything that happens at home and abroad, the whole world knows the next day...
Presiding judge: What do you know about Witos?
I: With Witos I am not even a remote relation of a relation. What have I to do with him? He deals with pigs and I with poets... He lives in Wierzchosławice and I live in a garret room in Łódź. But we have a lot in common... He said: "Teraz źle, ale będzie gorzej" [Things are bad now, but they will get worse], and I say the same. He won't wear a necktie, and I can't afford any necktie...
Presiding judge: Does the witness know that Witos hates "Dziadek" [Grandpa — Piłsudski]?
I: Not only Dziadek — he hates a Jew too...
Presiding judge: What else can you tell me about Witos?
I: I know that he is a very idealistic man, that is: he hates pigs, and therefore, while he was Prime Minister, he had all the pigs transported abroad...
Adv. Szurlej: And where are the pigs today?
I: Plenty of them have still remained in the country; wherever you go and stand, you meet them...
Prosecutor: Do you think Witos is to blame for that?
I: A little Witos and a little the Polish soil, which is very fat and able to fatten [?] pigs...
Presiding judge: What do you know about Liberman?
I: Until now I knew him as a leader of the P.P.S.; now I know that he is a "meshlguber" [?]... a "Hershele"... but I ask him not to confuse him with my friend [przyjaciel] Hershele the artisans' activist...
Prosecutor: Does Liberman have any connection with the anonymous Jewish kingdom?
I: It seems so... because since he came out of... of... of that which one may not mention, he has a face like one of the "Elders of Zion"...
Prosecutor: I request that this be entered in the record.
Advocate Berenson: Did the witness take part in the Kraków Congress?
I: I take part in congresses with my wife and my little children; together we form the "Centrolew". When my wife reaches into the "centre" of my pocket, I defend myself like a "lewy" [leftist]...
Presiding judge: Do you know Ciołkosz?
I: Him I don't know, but his wife I know well. Although she is a Jewish daughter, she has never read my feuilletons.
Presiding judge: Have you heard Bagiński speak?
I: My mother-in-law can speak better than he. She gets out one hundred and thirty-six words a minute...
Presiding judge: Has the witness heard of Putek?
I: He could not take a watch from me, because I don't have one; but if he took my "watch-lady" [wife] from me, I would be very grateful to him for it...
Prosecutor: Where did the witness study?
I: With the rabbi in Brisk.
Presiding judge: Brisk must not be discussed here... And where else did you study?
I: Your Honour! Since I am a poet and it is very hard for me to speak in prose, I ask you to allow me to answer in rhyme. So, you ask where I studied?
Where did I study? Ah!
Two thousand years in order,
That I bear upon myself the heavy yoke
Of life... ruins... and still
To this day I go to cheder...
Teachers I have aplenty
In every land, at every step —
A gem... a Muse!
Sometimes there he's called Krushevan,
Sometimes Professor Cuza...
And Nowaczyński sometimes too;
They teach till the smoke rises,
It takes [?] my breath away...
Of all the Torah portions without measure
Two portions they study with me:
Oy, "Balak" and "Mishpatim"...
The presiding judge and the lawyers were getting ready to take me into cross-examination. A miracle that my little wife (she does come in useful once in a while) took it into her head to search my trouser pockets and look there for small change; from the noise I woke up [—]
Boycott, Exclude, Starve Out, Exterminate.

Yes, the earth does turn — but somehow lopsidedly: it stays stuck in its own mud, and the same thing happens to it as to the stork in the children's tale: in with the beak and out with the feet; out with the feet and in with the beak — and stayed stuck in the mud.
European civilisation bores through the earth, pushes into the very poles of the globe, tears up into the stratosphere — culture, they call it — strides across the world in seven-league boots; but in every little corner it sits and lies in wait [?] with its cat's eyes — the "yellow beast" — and lurks for its old victims, for the weak, for the defenceless.
Cultural progress has not ennobled the means; it has only made [?] them more refined — everything is done with taste and with an artistic sense.
The tasteless Middle Ages burned Jews at the stake; the fumes of the burnt flesh were carried across the whole world, and the wind blew the ashes of the victims into everyone's eyes. Truly tasteless!
— After all, one can do away with Jewish souls without pitch and without smoke, without knives and without blood — just quietly and calmly take their soul away from them — literally "with a kiss"!
— You cut off their roads to bread and water, you shut them out of work and education, and soon there will be nothing left of them but "Rabbi Tzadok's dried fig" [the Talmudic sage who fasted forty years — i.e., skin and bones]...
And why all this?
All this because they are strangers!
That is how the excuse goes — they are strangers, and that's that!
True, in every [printed "tsin"] state there are laws that regulate the question of foreigners and state precisely which people are citizens of the state and which are foreigners, guests, who can be shown the door whenever one likes. But there are people whom even the law cannot protect with its authority, people for whom even the very power of the state becomes powerless when they are attacked. Yes, even the highest power, religion — which, by the way, was born of a "in thy blood live" drop [Ezekiel 16:6] of the strangers — religion, which actually strives for God to be honoured and respected in every creature, in every being — it too, in its great, living heart that embraces and kisses the whole world, has no room for a little compassion for the "strangers".
And precisely those who shelter so piously and reverently under its white wings — precisely they spin the blackest plans.
That is why no one produces so many heretics and apikorsim, so many freethinkers and deniers of God, as His own guard of honour, which sings Him hymns over the altars of human sacrifices — and it makes no difference whether the human sacrifices are roasted in fire, boiled in water or dried out by hunger.
— But these are strangers, after all!
Strangers — how so?
Can hundreds [of years] of Jews living in this land, hundreds of years of duty and loyalty, and all, all the sacrifices of money and of blood, not inscribe the "strangers" in the register of citizens?
I do not mean the registers that lie in the town halls (magistrates) — only those that lie in the hearts, in the souls of the fellow citizens with whom one lives, works, struggles and lives together.
Are these human beings, or only beasts with licences on their muzzles; is this "Adam" — man, or is this "khalya" [?; probably "khivya", Aramaic for snake] — the serpent?
There were times when we were inwardly and outwardly closed off from our neighbours; then tales were told about us the way children tell tales about Gypsies. When in our cramped batei-midrash and yeshivas thousands of creative young men shone, who poured themselves out in various forms of ethics, morality, poetry and philosophy, jurisprudence and theology, Ma'aseh Bereshit and Ma'aseh Merkavah — outside they said and believed about us that we were man-eaters, blood-suckers, well-poisoners, Satans in human shape!
It would be worth asking a Spaniard of today of whom he is prouder: of Torquemada, or of R' Yehuda Halevi, or Don Isaac Abravanel?
But this the swastika-man in Vienna or Berlin does not remember; for him even the Düsseldorf [printed "Dipel-dorf"] murderer can be as well-born as Schnitzler, or even as the very Einstein himself.
When we did not know their languages and literatures, they hated us because we did not know them; when we began to know them, they hate us because we know too much. What then [?] are we to do?
Knowing would perhaps not have hurt — only living we must not.
The Endeks in Poland want to push us out of trade, which we have seized into our hands — very well, gentlemen democrats! Let us say that you really can, through your green [?; printed "easy"] ribbon-heroes, bring to ruin the "last of the Mohicans" of Jewish merchantry in Poland — where then are the hundreds of thousands of Jews to go to work? Into which factories? Into which government offices? Into which schools? On which railways? Into which enterprises?
So that means: [we] must [?] go — go from Germany, go from Hungary, go from Austria, go from Romania, go!
Go, as we once went — hungry, naked, pelted with mud, trampled by horses, bitten by dogs and hunted by people — that is what they mean by "go": the Awakening Magyars, the swastika-men, the Hitlerites and our own home-grown Endeks. And were the gates of our home and of the free foreign lands not closed, hundreds of thousands of Jews would surely have packed up and crossed overseas. But when the gates are closed, one must wait and stay. Yet in the souls of those who wait and stay the seed of suffering and despair is sown deep. At Wilno University the Endek students demand that their Jewish colleagues sit specifically on the left, and when they move away to the very [printed "sake"] left, only then does the old outcry rise: Jews sit on the left! So we must not sit — not on the left, not on the right; not trade, not work, not learn, not study, not live anywhere and not occupy any place, because — because we are weaker than others and because we are stronger than others.
Bernard Shaw made a great mistake when he asserted that the world has had its fill of us, only we have not had our fill of the world.
No, Bernard Shaw. Around the conditions of our life there still flutters constantly the black-and-red flag that was hung over our history in the darkest Middle Ages. We are still held responsible for everything that happens in the world: for the weakness of the weak and the insolence of the strong, for the big capitalists and for the unfortunate unemployed, for victories and for defeats. For all the fluctuations of life — the Jews are responsible.
Yes, the earth does turn after all, but always with the whip on our back and with the fist in our teeth — and it is bad for us, very bad, but no less bad for the world.
A. Gotesdiner.
How Does the Zagłębie Merchant and Shopkeeper Live?

How does the Jewish shopkeeper, merchant and artisan here in Będzin live and earn?
This very question surely interests everyone. Our editorial board has therefore decided to publish a series of articles about it, in the form of conversations with shopkeepers, merchants and artisans of the various branches and trades.
Our staff writer held the first conversation with a grocer.
— What is the situation of the grocers?
This branch is the worst and the poorest. In Będzin there are today more than hundreds [?] of grocery and colonial-goods shopkeepers; others possess their own [capital] of barely a couple of hundred złoty. There are also such whose shop's "merchandise" amounts to several dozen złoty.
— What are the earnings?
— In no branch is the profit reckoned so closely, down to the grosz, or even down to half a gr., as with foodstuffs. Take, for example, the main articles: sugar, flour and salt. A sack of sugar weighing 100 kilos costs 157 zł. at the warehouse. Nevertheless there are shopkeepers who, because of competition, sell it for 1.62 zł. and even 1.60 and a half a kilo. It goes without saying that there is also wastage on top of that.
The same is true of sugar [?] and salt. With the latter item there is another trouble: the state monopoly, which sells salt at 33 zł. per 100-kg sack, has drawn up a price list under which one must take 36 groszy a kilo at retail. That would have been tolerable, but the thing is that the sack is short in weight by 2 5 [?] kg. That is because the salt dries out. Those few missing kilos are the entire "profit".
— So why does it pay to sell at a loss?
You understand, of course, that if the housewife takes a little flour and salt, she also buys other items, on which one can after all earn something. That is exactly why every shopkeeper wants to sell flour, sugar and salt as cheaply as possible, in order to draw in the customer. But in the takings themselves there is also one great flaw. That is credit. While the shopkeeper has to buy 60–70 per cent of the goods for cash, he must lend almost [?] everything "on the book" or against long-term bills of exchange. In other towns it is not the custom, as it is with us, that foodstuffs are taken on credit or against bills. Everywhere people know that if the housewife or the maid goes into the shop to buy food, she must bring money; here, however, one brings a little book...
On top of this come the general matters. The shops must be closed 2 days a week [?], and in winter 2 and a half days. The heavy tax screw, and also the sanitary requirements, because of which the shopkeeper lives in constant fear of a protocol [a fine report]. All this falls like a heavy burden, and one cannot even earn a living "by the sweat of thy brow".
Next Friday: a conversation with a haberdashery shopkeeper.
Y. R—t.
Tna'im Are No Child's Play

Disputes often arise on the ground of tna'im [engagement contracts].
Usually one turns to rabbis with such disputes; but not everyone knows that the matters mentioned can also be settled by way of the courts; articles 239-243 of the Polish marriage law in fact regulate the relations in the field concerned [?].
In accordance with the provisions referred to, tna'im are regarded as an agreement under which a man and a woman undertake to marry.
As regards the form of such an agreement, the law recognises as valid not only written but even oral tna'im (a "yes-word"), insofar as they were concluded in the presence of witnesses.
Be that as it may, however, the legal force of tna'im does not go so far that anyone could be compelled on their basis to marry.
At most, the party which breaks the concluded tna'im without justified reasons is obliged to give the other party proper compensation for the expenses and the damages suffered.
Grave insult, a depraved or criminal way of life, deception, contempt for the in-laws — these enumerated circumstances can be recognised as sufficient reasons that justify breaking off tna'im without any compensation.
Finally it is worth pointing out the detail that if a bride has become pregnant by the groom and he wants to call off the match, he is obliged to pay maintenance for the child, and also for the mother, if she has no means of her own to live on.
Yiddish Is Spoken More Than Many Other Languages

Z. Haber
(Specially for our newspaper.)
There is a little story: when Columbus discovered America and was already greatly rejoicing at coming to a land where no human being had yet been, he caught sight from afar of a person who quickly ran up to him and greeted him with the Czech words: "Poyts'sa [?] pane Kolumbus, jsem taky tady" (Greetings, Mr. Columbus, I am here too). This was meant to say that the Czechs are so spread over all corners of the world that even there they had already been before Columbus...
Insofar as this little story is only a jest, so much is certain: there is not a single country in the world where there would be no Czechs and where one would not hear the Czech language.
The Czech nationalists make so much noise in their press that to an outside observer it gives the impression that after English, German, Russian and French, the world speaks mostly Czech.
The Leipzig Trade Fair Office [Messeamt] carries on propaganda all over the world and must make use there of all sorts of languages. In no fewer than [?] 34 languages, jargons and dialects correspondence is conducted there, and brochures, letters and appeals go out in languages of which we have not even an idea.
The tens of thousands of exhibitors from all over the world have the right to demand that the Fair Office conduct propaganda for them among the merchants of the whole world "in their own script and their own tongue".
It is therefore clear that the Leipzig Fair Office knows quite precisely which languages are spoken and in what numbers there are people who use each language.
And therefore it is worth looking at a statistic of the various languages. For instance in Europe, where the greatest jumble of languages exists — when one looks at this statistic, one arrives at results one could never even have expected.
First of all it is worth knowing that in all of Europe 120 languages are spoken — a kind of generation of the Dispersion... a Tower of Babel... Most of all, Europe uses the German language. No fewer than 81 million people speak German in Europe. Not only in Germany; in almost all countries large parts of the population speak German.
Of the 140 million people living in European Russia, only 70 million speak Russian. The other half speaks various languages: 34 million speak Ukrainian, and in the Caucasus 70 different languages are spoken; most of these languages are spoken by only quite a small group of people — thus there is in the Caucasus a dialect called Udi (it has nothing whatever to do with Yiddish), and this dialect is spoken only in two villages by about a hundred people.
In all, there are in Europe only 19 languages spoken by more than five million people, 37 languages are spoken [by] more than a million people, and 62 languages are spoken by more than a hundred thousand people.
After German and Russian, 47 million people in Europe speak English, 41 million Italian, 40 million French, 23 million Polish, 16 million Spanish, 11 million Dutch-Flemish, 10 million Hungarian, more than 9 million Serbo-Croatian and Portuguese, and about 9 million people in Europe speak Yiddish. Only after Yiddish come: Czech, Greek, Swedish, Bulgarian, Danish, Finnish, Norwegian, Turkish and other languages.
It is interesting to know that among the 19 largest European languages Yiddish too is counted, with its 9 million people in Europe itself.
Why Are Polish Jews Silent?

[Palestine — opinion; first article.] Shabtai Weiss (Tel Aviv).
I.
On the twentieth of November 1931 the term of office of the third High Commissioner in the Land of Israel, Sir John Chancellor, officially came to an end. On that very day the new, fourth High Commissioner, General Wauchope, arrived in the Land of Israel. It is therefore worth giving a survey of the period in which the fate of the Land of Israel lay in the hand of Sir Chancellor; it is worth considering the deeds and the events that took place during his period of rule — so that we may know the road we must go on.
II.
Chancellor took over his office after General Plumer. In the summer of 5688 [so printed; probably a misprint for 5685, i.e. 1925] General Plumer arrived in the Land of Israel, and he had barely managed to look around and get to know the conditions and the situation in the country when the Land of Israel, after the Fourth Aliyah, entered a severe economic crisis, which found its sharp expression in the number of 8—9 thousand unemployed halutzim [pioneers]. There came the hard years 5686—5687 [1926—1927]. The Land of Israel was then no synonym of heroic deeds, of stubborn tenacity, of self-sacrifice; on the contrary: dejection, shame and mockery, helplessness that reached as far as despair and cynicism — these were the feelings that sprouted then from the thousands of letters sent from the Land of Israel to the countries of the Diaspora. Similar [?] was the mood in Zionist circles too. At that time no one thought of protest meetings against limited or closed immigration; no, at that time people were busy with other plans: in part of the Zionist press the plan of Robert Weltsch to organise an emigration from the Land of Israel was then seriously discussed. And then, in that time of dejection and confusion, it was General Plumer who a c t i v e l y helped to liquidate the severe economic crisis: heavy thousands of pounds he took out of the government treasury, he ordered various public works with the exclusive purpose of employing our unemployed halutzim. In the time of Plumer's rule a law on protective tariffs for Jewish industry was issued for the first time. In Plumer's time the municipality of Tel Aviv received a loan from the government, which helped it overcome its financial difficulties. Plumer agreed to give from the government treasury a yearly, permanent subsidy for [?] the Hebrew educational work in the Land of Israel. He, the second High Commissioner of the Land of Israel, gave the order to hasten the surveying of the lands with the intention of handing over the vacant tracts of land for Jewish colonisation. In General Plumer's time the long-standing negotiations on organising the "Knesset Israel" came to a positive conclusion. And above all — in Plumer's time absolute security, order and quiet reigned in the Land of Israel. Who had heard then of the Mufti and of Subhi al-Khadra? The Arab press did not then fill its columns with inflammatory articles; the Arab Executive Committee existed then only on paper. And when at that time the flags of the Jewish Legions were brought over from America, and it was intended to receive them in Jerusalem with ceremonial festivity, and the representatives of the Arab Executive Committee turned to General Plumer that he should forbid this Jewish celebration, and if not — so they threatened him then — they would not be responsible for the consequences, Lord Plumer answered them briefly and sharply with the famous words: "You responsible? How do you come to be responsible for matters that occur in the country? For these things I am responsible!" And everything passed off in the greatest order.
III.
In the summer of 5688 [1928], when Chancellor began his term of office after Lord Plumer, the Land of Israel found itself in a state of flourishing and prosperity. Like a healthy body which, with the strong forces of inner resistance, overcomes a severe sudden illness, so our work of construction had then overcome the severe, bitter crisis of 5686—5687. There was then no trace of the great unemployment; the gates of the country were begging: open us for a broad aliyah. Within a few years the Jews managed to enlarge the [settled] area; Jewish industry, founded by the much-mocked Jews of Dzika Street and Nalewki [Jewish streets of Warsaw], took root in the country, developed and conquered the market in the Land of Israel and in the surrounding countries.
At that time Chancellor set up his high official Mills, who prepared his famous diagrams and calculations, according to which the Jews would within a few decades become the majority in the Land of Israel — if the development of the Jewish work of construction continued in this way at its pace so far. And then the English administration began to go other ways. Chancellor began to deal with the Arabs. And when he turned to them, he did not intend to draw up the creative energy hidden in the Arab people, to develop, organise and raise the enslaved and impoverished Arab people. That road was not to his taste. That road of creative and renewing constructive work might, after all, unite the peoples in the Land of Israel, might create prosperity and peace between them. He therefore chose another road. In Chancellor's period of rule there suddenly floated up onto the political arena all the Arab intriguers, all the "khabarniks" [bribe-takers], all kinds of agitators, the scum of the Arab people. And Chancellor's government gave them the right to appear in the name of the Arab people, to represent it; it listened attentively to all their demands and wishes, it spoke with them as if through a silk handkerchief, and so it, Chancellor's government, as it were added its own thin threads to the web of blood, wild fanaticism and darkness that was being woven before its eyes — until the bloody days of the month of Av 5689 [August 1929] came.
And then, after the terrible bloodbaths, after the sadly famous "trials" of the murderers, in which the hand of Chancellor's justice was too short to find the dozens of murderers of Motza, it released dozens of murderers of Hebron and Safed, and pardoned from the death penalty almost all the condemned murderers — the net of the great political intrigues against the Jewish work of construction began to be spun. Then came the Shaw Commission, which seeks [?] Arabs whom the Zionist leaders had thrown off their land, which speaks with foam on its lips of a horrible Zionism. Then all the dark forces of impurity were called out of every desolate hole, disguised in the garb of figures, painted up with so-called science, in order to besmirch what is purest and most idealistic in Zionism — and Chancellor took a chief part in all these deeds. Then Passfield issues the black-and-white book [the White Paper]. The gates of aliyah are hermetically closed. The greatest English coloniser, Simpson, is sent to the Land of Israel, and a report is "ordered" from him which is to "prove" that the Land of Israel has no more land for cultivation and can no longer absorb any aliyah. And Chancellor came up with the nonsense that it does not matter that the Jewish reality in the Land of Israel needs a large aliyah and has the possibility to absorb it and settle it, because... there are tens of thousands of unemployed Arabs, who must first of all be provided with work. And Chancellor's government suddenly creates a "statistic" of made-up figures [lit. "neither risen nor flown"] about unemployed Arabs, publishes them every month with the sole purpose of not opening any more the closed gates of Jewish aliyah. And he, the third High Commissioner of the Land of Israel, becomes the chief fighter for the prohibition of land purchase by Jews. He sends incessant telegrams to London that the rights of Jews in buying land should be restricted — and he obtains the consent of the central government and publishes a law according to which he, the High Commissioner, must confirm every land purchase. He is not satisfied with that, however; like Laban, he wants "to uproot everything"; he fights for a complete prohibition of land purchase by Jews, and the English Colonial Office confirms for him a very harsh law in this respect — meanwhile the Labour government in England falls, and the draconian land law remains lying in the High Commissioner's drawer, although it has not been annulled to this very day.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Miketz)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion and Hanukkah.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Miketz
The Portion
—o—
a) "And it came to pass at the end of two full years" (Gen. 41:1)
"'Happy is the man that maketh the Lord his trust' — this is Joseph. 'And turneth not unto the arrogant' — because he said to the chief butler 'remember me' and 'make mention of me', two years were added to him." Midrash Rabbah.
The Midrash is puzzling: first it describes Joseph as the one who trusts in God, and right after it tells that Joseph was punished with two extra years of prison for lack of trust.
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk answered: Joseph felt and saw his fault, and therefore, although he committed it, it counts as though he no longer possesses it. For seeing one's own shortcoming is already the cure...
Likutim Hadashim.
•
A Jew, a Torah scholar, came to the "Noda BiYehuda" [after?] a lawsuit before a rabbinical court which he had lost. Later the scholar asks the "Noda BiYehuda" to open the Choshen Mishpat and show him on what basis he lost the case. The Gaon takes out a book and opens it at the first blank page.
"Are you making fun of me?" the other wonders. "It's an empty page!"
"Just as you see nothing on the empty page, so you see nothing within yourself either, for nobody sees the bad in himself..."
—o—
b) "Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise" (ibid. 41:33)
"Three things — says the Gemara (Berakhot 54) — the Holy One, blessed be He, proclaims Himself: famine, plenty and a provider [parnas]" (because they are closely connected...). And if Joseph knew about the years of famine and plenty, you ought — Pharaoh told him — to be the provider as well...
Naftali Sova Ratzon.
—o—
c) "Forasmuch as God hath shewed thee" (ibid. 41:39)
You come to a merchant who has a big warehouse full of goods, and he says: I am a poor man, all this is on credit.
But had he been a poor man, nobody would have given him so much credit...
Joseph kept saying that he was no sage, that God gives him the wisdom. Pharaoh answered him: "If God gives you wisdom, you must surely be wise yourself, for God entrusts wealth only to the rich man and wisdom only to the wise..."
The Maggid of Dubno.
—o—
A.
In Lemberg [Lwów] there once lived a stingy rich man, Aharon Filim, whom everyone cursed for his piggish greed. Once he was asked: How did you become so rich, Reb Aharon?
"I became rich from curses... Every poor man who brings home at night a Rhenish [gulden] or half a day's earnings — his wife wishes him: 'May it be said of Aharon Filim!', 'May Aharon Filim earn it!' Well, from so many Rhenish wished upon me every night I have amassed such a fortune..."
B.
A friend comes to the said miser for an interest-free loan. He takes out a few hundred-złoty banknotes and... puts them back into his pocket.
The friend asks him: Why have you suddenly changed your mind?
"I haven't changed my mind. I only wanted to show you that I have money and don't want to lend it to you, so that you won't come to me a second time..."
—o—
d) "And one of them opened his sack" (Gen. 42:27)
Rashi says: "one" — meaning Levi. How is Rashi so sure? Perhaps another brother is meant.
Joseph's men had put the money — as follows from the verse — at the bottom of the sacks in which there was fodder for the donkeys. So they could discover it only on coming home and emptying the sacks. Levi, however, whose partner — Simeon — had been imprisoned, had to drive home two donkeys, Simeon's and his own, and he had only one sack of food, from which both donkeys ate; so he discovered it halfway...
Sihot Hakhamim.

Hanukkah.
—o—
e) "When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary"
First, in the days of King Ptolemy, the Torah was translated into Greek. "And that day was as hard as the day the Calf was made." Because this mixing with strangers, the wish to show them our beauty, caused that "the Greeks entered the Sanctuary" — that the Greeks, Greek culture, penetrated our Sanctuary too ("this Tanna calls carrying out 'bringing in'") and wrought devastation there. We must not take "holy things outside", because that causes bringing "profane things into the Temple court"... And the same process repeated itself in the time of the Mendelssohnian Haskalah with the translation of the Torah into German, which brought about that German took the upper hand even in the Sanctuary...
Drashot el Ami.
—o—
f) "Thou didst plead their cause"
On Purim we say in "Al HaNissim": "who pleaded our cause" — our quarrel. And on Hanukkah: "Thou didst plead their cause" — their quarrel.
Because Greeks who want to make Judaism gentile are few today; this particular struggle the gentile world has given up... Only the Hamans remain, who want to slaughter and butcher Jews. "Our cause" — because "the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation". This the Amalekites will never give up: slaughtering Jews...
Torat Moshe.
—o—
g) The Hanukkah light
"In earlier generations the lights were placed outside, and now — inside."
Today one need not set the light of the Torah outside. "If you see a generation that loves the Torah, spread it; and if you see a generation that does not love the Torah, gather it in." Better to concentrate inwardly, to kindle quietly for the household the light of Judaism, and not to thrust oneself before hostile eyes...
Olelot Efraim.
—o—
[A reader's remark — untitled]
In "Haynt" [the Warsaw Yiddish daily] of Friday, portion Vayishlach, Mr. Yashuahn[?] brings in his section "From Our Old Treasury" a query from Mr. Wolf Berent[?] on Midrash Rabbah Vayishlach (ch. 75), where it is stated that "Arise, O Lord" appears five times in Psalms, whereas in fact we find a sixth "Arise, O Lord" — in Psalm 132.
In my opinion the question is quite superfluous, because, considering the whole passage of the Midrash, its meaning is that five times King David called to God for help, but God answered him: even if you call Me several more times, I will not stir; only when you see that the poor are robbed and the needy, weary[?], are oppressed. In this sense the query from Psalm 132 falls away by itself, for there it was not a call for help for himself, but for God's own cause: "Arise, O Lord, into Thy resting place; Thou, and the ark of Thy strength."
Hirsch Nieszelski, Kielce.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved

Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov. (2)

— The Archimandrite Feofan wants to persuade the Tsaritsa that the fact that the Naslednik [the heir, Tsarevich Alexei] is so ill and suffers such terrible torments is a punishment from God, because there are Jews in the „holy" capital. Those who, according to his words, crucified Christ... Because there are Jews in the capital, therefore, he says, Satan has dominion over the heir to the throne. In order to drive Satan out of the imperial court and save the life of the heir to the throne, one must first drive all the Jews out of Petersburg... Otherwise God's wrath will not depart from the court... The Archimandrite Feofan is an obstinate Jesuit[?] and an embittered enemy of the Jews. He tries to work upon the Tsaritsa's motherly feelings. He knows how much she loves her only son, and he argues: see, your child suffers terrible pains, he writhes with agony — don't you want to help him? Don't you want, for the sake of doing the will of our God, to drive the Jews out of your capital?

— And what does the Tsaritsa say to that? — asked the Baron, and his face was clouded over.

The Tsaritsa answered nothing to it. As far as I know, the Archimandrite's words have so far had no effect. But — one cannot know what tomorrow will bring... The Tsaritsa is a very pious Christian. She is a strong believer; if the Naslednik does not get better, it is possible that she will begin to listen to the words of her priest, and then it will be very bad... Then a decree may come out that all Jews must leave Petersburg... That would be a terrible catastrophe for our whole community. We would have to abandon our fortunes to whoever takes them...

Mr. Dimentshtein rested for a while and looked with sad eyes at those assembled. All sat with gloomy faces and frightened eyes. All now grasped the seriousness of the situation. All now understood that if the Archimandrite succeeded in carrying it through and the Tsaritsa accepted his counsel, an order would then come out that all Jews must leave the capital within a short time, within twenty-four hours... For if the Tsaritsa really believed that driving the Jews out of Petersburg would help the Naslednik, the Jews would be given no time; they would not even be able to wind up their businesses, and that means all Jews would be completely ruined... would lose all their goods and possessions...

The banker went on:

— The Archimandrite Feofan is not alone in his evil agitation. He is supported by other representatives of the Pravoslav [Russian Orthodox] religion as well. I learned today that after an order was sent out yesterday to all the churches to hold services for the Naslednik's health, two telegrams arrived at court, one from Bishop Hermogen and the other from the most obstinate enemy of Israel, the black monk Iliodor. Both send their blessings to the sick boy and do not forget to mention that one should listen to the good counsel of the „holy father" Feofan. It seems all three are working hand in hand against the Jews... All this I learned this morning. And as I said: the Tsaritsa is very pious, and she loves the Naslednik more than her own life. One therefore cannot know what the coming day will bring... If the sick boy does not get better, a great danger hangs over us... I therefore decided to call you together here so that we may consult what we have to do... As you all now understand, the situation is very serious... My daughter is now at the salon of Countess Ignatova. I sent her there to find out how things stand with the sick boy and what the situation is, and to let us know. She will probably come home soon. Meanwhile we must look for ways to avert the terrible decree that may come.

The banker fell silent, breathed more deeply and soon added:

— And one more thing: as the Baron reports, it appears that at the service in the synagogue a court official will be present. That shows that the Jews are not believed to really pray for the health of the „Naslednik". From this one can see that Feofan's words have already had an effect... I propose to you, gentlemen, to consider the matter seriously... We must give the matter our full attention.

He fell silent. All sat without a word; on every face there was worry. What indeed could be done? What means could be found to avert the great danger that was approaching; with what power could one fight the black forces of the Archimandrite, the Bishop and the Jesuitical monk? All felt powerless. In their hearts there was despondency. Even the walls of the room, it seemed, were coated with heavy, dark worry.

— Why are you all silent? — asked the banker. — This is no time for silence; we must find some way out, for a great danger is approaching...

— On the contrary, what can be done? — asked one of those assembled, and his face expressed helplessness. — What counsel can we come up with?

Mr. Dimentshtein turned to the Baron:

— What do you say, Baron?

Everyone's eyes were now turned to the Baron. All knew him as a clever, practical man who always finds a clever, fitting, good piece of advice, and all now waited for his counsel.

The Baron sat deep in thought, in a heavy, depressed mood. His brow was furrowed, the brightness of his face was extinguished; he gazed before him with wide-open eyes and his lips were pressed together. So it lasted a long while. Then he began to speak calmly:

— Gentlemen, as I feel it, the situation is truly serious and grave. We are not able to wage war against the evil forces working against us... We will achieve nothing against them. So what then remains to be done?

He was not asking those assembled; he was asking himself. The city rabbi, who was also among those assembled and was beloved[?] by them all, spoke up with a pious face:

— Wage war against the enemies of the Jews we cannot. So we must be ready „for gifts and for prayer". We must hold a prayer service and truly pray for the sick Naslednik, that he may recover, and prepare gifts too...

The Baron said:

— The esteemed rabbi is right.

— Only one thing remains: to buy ourselves off. That has always been the only means among Jews. They bought themselves off. Now too I see no other way. We must try, as far as possible, to knock at the high windows... Where a gift is needed — let there be a gift. Whoever among us has influence in high-placed circles must use his influence... And above all, we must try to get to the Archimandrite himself; perhaps we can buy ourselves off with him? Perhaps our money can weaken his wickedness? Surely nobody would imagine that the priest really thinks that driving the Jews out of Petersburg will make the sick boy well. He knows perfectly well that it will not help and will not make anything better.. What do you think, Mr. Dimentshtein?

— I think you are right, Baron — answered the banker — I myself thought so too; we must approach the Archimandrite with a proper sum... That may perhaps help...

— I see no other way — the Baron said again — I believe this is the only way. I know Jewish money already has such power in it that it can avert various decrees from the Jews... I also know that the greatest enemies of the Jews already have such a nature that they are great lovers of Jewish money... Most likely this Archimandrite is no exception. Such is the Jewish fate — from decrees one must buy oneself free... Let us hope that in this case too it will help. Jewish money will cool the evil hatred of the priest Feofan.

The "Life Story" of a Tallit

[Story — the life story of a tallit, told in the first person.]
Told by A. D. Agoz [?].

If tallitot could speak, many of them would have interesting things to tell. Some would tell tragic tales, and some tragicomic ones.

Tallitot, like people, have their life stories. A tallit often goes through things that no other garment or object goes through. During its existence a tallit often has various times, better and worse. The fate of tallitot is not always one and the same. One tallit serves out [?] its years for the purpose for which it was made, while another has to pass through various transmigrations.

I know an interesting, though tragic, story of an old tallit that now lies about among the "shemot" [worn-out sacred texts awaiting burial] in the attic of a synagogue, and I will pass it on here. But I will do it in the form of the tallit itself speaking and telling, and imagine that it, the tallit, speaks in a weeping chant, in a tone that arouses pity.

So the tallit tells its story:

I come from the Lithuanian shtetl of Dubrowna, where tens of thousands of tallitot were made; there they spun the wool from which I was made. There I was woven and finished with a beautiful golden atarah [neckband] and with kosher tzitzit, as the law requires.

Honest, pious Jews were my makers. I was made in holiness and purity, for its own sake, for the sake of a tallit, for the sake of a holy garment that a Jew should put on every day to pray and, after a hundred years, take with him into the grave.

For a long time I lay on the shelf of a tallit dealer. There was no buyer for me. There were in fact many who wanted me. People [?] literally swallowed their saliva looking at me, because I was a "hadar" [a de-luxe tallit], one of the best and finest tallitot Dubrowna ever produced. But precisely because of that, because I was a "hadar", the merchant priced me too high, and not just anyone could afford to pay.

So the tallit dealer waited for the right buyer, and at last such a one was found.

The rich man of the shtetl had to marry off a daughter to a [?] ["vidnem", unclear word] young man, a scholar, an "illui" [prodigy], who was not far from the rabbinate. The in-law, the mother-in-law-to-be and the bride came to buy a tallit for the groom, and they chose me, the finest and best, and paid the asking price.

When the groom put me on for the first time, he felt happy beyond happy. He liked me very much, and he praised and thanked the Creator of the world for granting him such an in-law, or father-in-law, who had given him so fine a gift.

And the bride gave him a tallit bag of good velvet, sewn and embroidered with her own hands with a golden Star of David, a menorah and his name. So I had a beautiful home, a comfortable home, which other tallitot did not have.

And when the little master of the house, my owner, used to put me on in the beit midrash to pray, many envied him, because I truly adorned the beit midrash. People used to say that the tallit suited him like a crown on a king's head.

And father and mother and father-in-law and mother-in-law beamed with pride looking at the young man when he wore me on his shoulders. And he himself, the young man, beamed with pride.

And he guarded me like the apple of his eye, never let a speck of dust fall on me. After praying he would carefully fold me up and take care that I should not get creased.

And he always kissed me and my tzitzit with devotion and with true love, and I was well and content.

I lived to see my owner having to take a little boy of his to heder for the first time, and he, as was the custom then, brought the child to the melamed wrapped in me. And I enjoyed it. With me one trains a child in the commandments. That is very fine, very pleasant.

So years went by. My owner had joy from me and I from him.

But after the joy came sorrow. At first a little. Then more, and then a great deal.

Circumstances brought it about that my owner had to leave his home and emigrate abroad. He took me with him and all along the way gave me the same honour as at home. Not a day did he miss putting me on and kissing my atarah and the tzitzit, and perhaps with even more devotion, more fervour than before.

But already in Berlin his love for me cooled little by little. Being hard-pressed in the first period, he pawned me at "uncle's" [the pawnshop]. I lay there on a shelf with all sorts [?] of things. What he, my owner, did without me, I do not know. Perhaps he prayed in a borrowed tallit, perhaps he prayed without a tallit, or did not pray at all... But for Rosh Hashanah he redeemed me and prayed in me on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and afterwards pawned me again.

But it was no longer what it had once been. The love for me had cooled. He had become a businessman, my owner, and had no time to occupy himself with me. He would put me on, so to speak, for a few counted minutes, and sometimes not even that.

So it went on, at length and at breadth, until he gave me up entirely, and not only me — the tefillin too.

Apparently he had become rich. Wrapped up [?] [printed "gemen ferdreyms"] in business, he forgot all about me.

It went so far that my owner became so "civilized" that even on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur he did not air me out.

So I lay and grew mouldy among all sorts of old junk, until I was picked out to be a rag for washing the floors; and when they saw that I was no longer good even for that, I was sold together with weekday rags to a gentile yard-peddler.

As it happened a Jew caught sight of me and bought me from him, but since I was already worn through and torn, he laid me away here in the attic among the "shemot".

This is my sad story, and I console myself only with the thought that I am probably not the only one, and that there are other tallitot that share the same fate as I.

A trouble shared by many is half a consolation.
Będzin — Half a dozen kehilla councillors passed the new kehilla budget

3 for — 2 against — 1 abstention...
The "old" kehilla council rose from the dead ("tkhiyas ha-meysim") on Thursday evening. They were roused from their "years-long [?] sleep" to fulfil the "holy" mission of passing the budget for the year 1932.
But not all of them heard the call. Of the 20 councillors (parnasim) barely 6 (read: six) were present. And no more than three (read: three) raised their hands, and so the new kehilla budget, amounting to nearly four hundred thousand zł., was passed.
The meeting is chaired by the president, Mr. Yakiv (Jakub) Gutman. At the start of the meeting councillor K. Liwer proposes: since it is not worth debating the budget again, the budget should not even be read, but simply be passed en bloc.
And so it indeed was. With 3 votes of the Agudah councillors the budget was passed according to [?] Mr. Liwer's proposal. (Councillors Rechnic and Blumenfrucht voted against the proposal, councillor Szwajcer abstained.)
It is interesting to add that of the artisans' councillors (of both camps) none was present at the meeting. It turns out that the artisans' representatives already rely on the grace of the "Agudah" councillors, who subsidised a whole 500 zł. for artisans' courses...

The "bird" is out of the cage..
Some months ago there was a notice in our paper about a "young fellow", a certain Józef Frajman, who has a "weakness" for staging weddings... To that end he once visited the town of Sławków, where he began to spin his romantic plans. But the "trick" did not work for him, since [?] the Sławków girls are mature and in good time figured out what the "bird" with the sharpened tongue is, and sent him packing...
The young fellow took to wandering [?] through other towns, but nowhere did he find favour, until he came to Będzin, where he found luck and favour with Mrs. Bajla Frajzer [?] (Małachowska 14). Neighbours warned her that she would fall victim to the young fellow. But the woman, who — as she said — had nothing to lose, decided to marry him.
As soon as the "honeymoon" was over, domestic peace was disturbed for the couple. Yet they lived somehow. The husband sold shoes at fairs, and on these "earnings" the couple, together with her parents, made a living.
This Saturday the young fellow "revealed himself". He took from the house the bit of merchandise, clothes, money, also the ketubah (marriage contract), and vanished, abandoning his wife, who is pregnant, to her fate.
All Jewish newspapers are asked to reprint this notice. Whoever has any information about the "bird" should take pity on the unfortunate woman and immediately notify her father, Lejbisz Frajzer [?], Będzin, Małachowska 14.

A Bad Pre-Holiday Season

[Economy — trade.] It is now barely 2 weeks before the holidays [the Christian holidays — Christmas and New Year], and a dead silence reigns in trade. Last year at this time, when the crisis was in fact already being felt, the season was in full swing, but this year the takings are very small and amount to barely a quarter of last year's.
The want in town and country, the growing unemployment among employees and workers have led to this: whoever still has a few gulden [colloquial for złoty] to buy something with buys precisely the cheapest goods, and haggles with the merchants besides, to get the goods as cheaply as possible.
From the standstill in trade it is now chiefly the middling wholesalers and the small shopkeepers who suffer. The merchants groan. A mood of despair reigns in the market. People consoled themselves with the hope that the pre-holiday season would bring a bit of revival; it turns out it is still dead quiet, and so they are indeed disappointed.
Meanwhile the time has already come when the merchants must pay the income tax and an instalment of the turnover tax, and the patents [trade licences] must be bought. A large part of the merchants will certainly not be able to buy any patents, and they will have to close their businesses.
In such a situation, if the government does not make it possible for the merchants to buy their patents in instalments, many merchants will indeed have no other choice but to go [?] and shut their shops.
For this reason the merchants' associations turned with a request to the Ministry of Finance to allow the merchants to buy the patents in instalments. Since the Ministry of Finance has not granted the request, one can be sure that New Year's Eve 1931 will be, for many firms in Poland, the last day of their existence.
In many shop windows one sees advertising signs: „Clearance sale“, „Cheaper than anywhere“. These very advertisements give a vivid illustration of the conditions that reign today in large and small trade. Behind these signs and advertisements of cheap prices great tragedies are hidden.
The Będzin Kehilla Budget in Figures

[Będzin — kehilla.] Before us lies the new kehilla budget in Będzin, which amounts to no less than 291 [?] thousand 351 zł. and 48 gr.

This time we only intend to show our readers that from the budget for the year 1932 the population benefits no more (perhaps even less) than from the budgets in the year 1900... The difference is only this: that then we had 3 dozors [community board members] (would that there were no more today...) and today we have 32... Once the gmina [community] was housed in a small office, and today the gmina is modernly fitted out — large offices, beautiful lamps, washbasins [?] etc.

Salaries [„pensions“]: Rabbi Lewin 12 000 zł., Rabbi Telner 5 300 zł., Rabbi Friedberg 5000, Rabbi Lipszyc 4.800, Rabbi Lewental (Czeladź) 5.000, rabbinate shammes 2100, Rebbetzin Grojbart 4,500, Manela 3000, residence for the rabbi 665, for Grojbart 1,064, for travel and per-diems for board members and the rabbinate 500, lighting, heating, cleaning and water for the rabbinate 610 zł. Altogether a sum of 44,239 zł.
So this item costs the town nearly 45 thousand zł. But as soon as one of the community-tax payers needs the slightest thing that belongs to the functions of the above-mentioned officials, he must pay according to his means.
Account number 2 (synagogue).
Salaries for: cantor, choir, shammosim, lighting, heating, cleaning, wine for kiddush, repairs, etrogim, for minding the cloakroom etc. — in total 7.910 zł.

Our Russian Brethren Call to You! Have Pity on Our Brethren!

[Charity — the Novogrudok yeshivas; followed by the radio programme.] As is known, because of the terrible "persecutions" and oppression against the Jewish religion in Russia, several thousand young men from the Novogrudok yeshivas in Russia have fled to us in Poland. These young men went through a hard martyr's road until they managed to get across the Bolshevik borders. Many of them were arrested and thrown into the prisons, and many were also shot. All this, however, could not keep them from getting out of the hell there and coming to Poland in order to continue their study in the spirit of their master, Rabbi Israel Salanter, of blessed memory.
Now these young men suffer terrible want and hardship; they are starving, going about in rags and tatters, etc.
Unable to look on at the terrible misery of this youth, some communal workers have taken it upon themselves to visit several towns in Zagłębie with the aim of carrying out a relief campaign for the Novogrudok yeshiva in Siedlce.
We wish to believe that every Jew in whom even a Jewish spark still glimmers will come out to meet this delegation and receive them cordially, thereby showing our warmest sympathy for our suffering Russian brethren, who have always distinguished themselves by their warm hearts toward every Jewish cause.
