Must Poland, Too, Make Prices Cheaper?

[Economy — Poland and the price crisis; press review.] The "Gazeta Polska" dwells at length on our trade balance for the month of November, which, as is known, closed with a surplus. The paper concludes from this that we possess the ability to adapt to the conditions in which our industry and trade find themselves. It is only a question whether the results of the month of November will hold for a longer time, when we take into account the new fall of the English pound and the "emergency decrees" of the German government, which will strengthen the competitiveness of German trade and German industry.
Turning to the individual items of our exports and imports, the "Gazeta Polska" makes the following remarks:
"First of all we notice a fall in the import of textile products by over 5 and a half million zł., of which 3 million fall to wool and about two and a half million to cotton.
Among goods, the import of silk products fell to the greatest extent. This shows that the purchasing power of the textile industry has fallen further. This is explained by the reduced purchasing power of the population owing to the salary cuts of state and municipal officials.
"The rise in the export of our ready-made clothing is explained partly by the fact that people wanted to make use of the short time before protective duty was introduced in England, partly also by the enormously low wages in this branch of industry [and] by the great financial support on the part of the state in the form of refunding the customs duties[?]."
From the trade balance for the month of November the paper arrives at the following conclusion: "The causes that brought about the latest steps of the Brüning government are in fact also applicable to Polish conditions. One may modify Brüning's line, i.e. the line of a general reduction of prices, wages and production costs. One may, given the situation created on the international market, apply entirely different methods than in Germany, but the necessity of adapting to the general needs can no longer be denied by anyone."
The "Gazeta Warszawska", on the other hand, speaks out in the sharpest manner against applying the German methods in Poland. "One must not forget one thing — writes the said paper — the German recovery plan is adapted to German economic and social conditions; as its starting point is taken the circumstance that the Germans are not in a position to settle their foreign obligations. The Germans allow themselves such experiments counting on the fact that the foreign creditors, who have invested huge sums in Germany, will be forced to agree to a new settlement of the obligations. Poland is in an entirely different situation; different is her economic order and the international conditions.
"It is now already clear that every country must undertake a struggle against the crisis with its own methods; general remedies disappoint; the Germans manage in one way, France in another, or Great Britain. The crisis has further deepened the difference that exists between the individual countries. Our crisis is a different one, and therefore the methods of combating it must also be different."
The paper comes to the conclusion that the slogan of "holding over", "holding out", which is being thrown out by the authoritative circles, cannot satisfy. "One can wait only when one works positively on improving the foundations of economic life. When the vital forces of the national economy are being exhausted, then one can no longer wait."
But what does the remedy consist of? What are the own methods and means that Poland must apply to alleviate its own crisis? The Endek organ gives no answer to this; instead, the Sanacja Cracow "Ilustrowany Kuryer Codzienny" (printed "Tsaro.") tries to give an answer.
This paper first of all criticises the whole decree system of the Brüning government, which on the one hand is full of internal contradictions and on the other hand will not help at all, because with decrees one cannot cure anyone gravely ill. The decrees will reduce still further the confidence abroad in Germany. The decrees can only hasten the catastrophe in Germany.
Turning to Poland, the paper says that "Poland will not apply any emergency decrees. Although certain decrees would also have been right and suitable for us.
The paper then proposes that an action be carried out to reduce cartel and syndicate prices by 10 per cent.
The government must conduct negotiations with the cartels and syndicates, pointing out to them that their production will be considerably increased if they lower prices. The monopoly articles and the products of the state enterprises must also become cheaper.
The paper thus comes to the conclusion that with us too there must come a fall in prices. But this must happen not by way of a decree, but through a public action, similar to the public action to combat unemployment.
Such an action would help reduce imports and would improve the situation of our industry and agriculture.
The Struggle over the New Law on Marriages and Divorces in Poland

On the "Jewish street" [printed "יורישער"], where divorce comes relatively easily, people hardly knew of the chains that a wedding ceremony used to lay upon a Catholic husband and wife: and whoever had a lot of money could sooner or later still obtain a divorce, although it took years; but whoever did not had to seek other means, for instance changing religion, and with that the wedding ceremony already lost its force.
It is still very doubtful whether the new draft on civil marriages in Poland will really become law in the near future; meanwhile, however, a "cannonade" is going on in the Polish press between the supporters of the reform and pious folk of every kind.
As a defender of the draft law the Polish writer Helena Romer has come forward, pouring pitch and brimstone on the other side:
"Chaos, absurdities, bribery [chabar], false oaths and false medical certificates, hypocrisy and cynical changes of religion (in Warsaw there was a 'fashion' for Orthodoxy and in Wilno for Calvinism) — all this, one would think, ought to have aroused disgust and indignation in every decent person, and above all among the Catholic clergy.
For 11 years society and public opinion were thus allowed to grow accustomed to unheard-of dodges, to trafficking with several religions, to drawing the clergy, medicine and the legal profession into corruption, and to false oaths by many outside people; and this became so entrenched that no protests or demands to change the present state of affairs were ever raised against it.
After all, many people lived parasitically on it.
Today, when the very same circles that have a business interest in keeping the present state of affairs, those who take large sums for divorces, will now raise a protest and an outcry (always in the name of holiness and religion), it is therefore worth recalling what these things have looked like until now.
Everyone knew that rich people would, in 90 per cent [of cases], get their marriages annulled... On the other hand one could get no divorce in the case of a 20-year mental illness, of a contagious disease, etc. No pornography can compare with the advice given by specialists in these matters. People were advised to swear that the bridegroom had been drunk at the wedding; the virginity of women who had had children was measured in millimetres... and what advice was not given... And everyone would get his few groszy, and hush-hush.
And if the Catholic [misprinted] clergy could not, or would not, hinder what has gone on until now; if they took money for annulling marriages while knowing that in most cases falsehoods were being committed; if in the end they perform no wedding for free and have a material interest in the number of religious weddings (quite expensive ones, by the way) not decreasing — then let them not talk about marriage!?"
• • •
Although the draft reform of the marriage law has scant relevance to Jews, certain circles nevertheless seek to throw the blame on the Jews here too.
A certain priest, Dr. Trzeciak, has published an article under the title "The Talmud as the Source of the Marriage Laws in Soviet Russia and of the New Marriage Drafts in Poland".
In this article of his the priest proves "by signs and wonders" that both the authors of the Soviet marriage law and the authors of the Polish marriage draft are people under the influence of the rabbinical world-view, to whom the Christian world-view is entirely alien.
As his main proof, priest Trzeciak writes that the Polish marriage draft pays much attention to the material side, which is also the main characteristic of the Talmudic laws.
A second priest, Urban, holds that in the struggle against the new marriage drafts one must demand that the state should not permit divorces for other religions in Poland either.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

The shtreimel and the red flag...
Two forces:
— The shtreimel [the Hasidic fur hat — i.e. Agudas Yisroel] and the red flag have joined hands and „united“ to come out with common forces against the strong „enemy“.
— Against the bourgeois Jewish press.
With the first „force“[?] the enemy is attacked in a delicate way: „press“; whereas with the other side, the side on whose flag is written: Fight for rights! — the „enemy“ is called by a „democratic“ name: garbage-newspapers...
This fight is no news to us. Four times a year, after every „season“, when the circulation of the „holy and idealistic newspapers“ shrinks, they roll up their sleeves and the arsenal of ammunition starts to operate...
The difference is only this: with the force of the „Torah-loyal“ it is done in perfect holiness; that is already their nature — in every action that the „Aguda“ undertakes to carry out, they call the „little Torah“ to help; even when one has to get an Anshei Shlomeinu man [the Aguda list] into the city council — they also go out into the street with the slogan: „Judaism is in ‚danger‘ if[?] Itshe Meir does not become a council member[?]...“
And in the present holy campaign, too, the best forces have been mobilised, with which one wants to destroy the dangerous enemy:
— the non-Aguda press...
Let our readers not suspect us of setting out to defend the newspapers that are filled with such material as truly disgraces the honour of the Jewish press at the present moment. No, we do not want to bring anybody back to the right path; but when we look at the form in which this holy war is being waged, when we read the countless letters of our shepherds of Israel, who rouse the „holy flock“ not to read the „obscene newspapers“ — one really wants to ask: have the great sages of Israel already fulfilled their duty when Chaim Yekl [the ordinary Jew] reads only the Aguda sheet? Have the great sages of Israel given thought to the fact that tens of thousands of Jewish children, those who run [bplos mshtr?] to the „powszechniaki“ [Polish state elementary schools], grow up complete gentiles? Do our spiritual leaders not [see — printed „are“] how assimilation is settling[?] ever deeper and firmer into Jewish life, and whole limbs are being torn away from the Jewish people? Must the call of our geniuses be heard only when the Aguda sheet needs a few new subscribers?...
Where is your word of comfort at the moment when all of Polish Jewry is sinking — and being destroyed?
Of course it is the task of our great ones to warn and to draw attention to the matters that harm the young Jewish generation; but to sound the alarm about a trifle, about a matter that every religious Jew „keeps in his left sidelock“ [doesn't care about], and at the same time to be indifferent[?] to the matters that stand at the summit of the world, the fate of the Jewish generation — we take the full liberty to say:
Our teachers and rabbis, this is not the way...
That is not your task at the present moment. To approve[?] newspapers is only a matter for those who [?] the broad Jewish masses, the „harpashnikes“[?], that they should run away from „the hovels“[?] — from the bourgeois Jewish press; but should this be a matter for the shepherds of the people?
No, and a hundred times no...

All the same..
The situation is dreadful, Jewish livelihoods are going under, people groan, people sigh, and — new societies are founded.
To the list of the Będzin societies a fresh new society has been added:
— „Hachnoses Orchim“ [hostel for poor wayfarers].
An ordinary everyday Jew, far from politics, who hates honours with an utter hatred, wanted — so he says — to set himself a monument in his lifetime, so he donated 5 rooms of his little house for a „Hachnoses Orchim“... so that honourable guests should have somewhere to spend the night..
We enter the larger bedroom, which holds 12 beds. A big long table and a bench.
Who gave the beds, the whole furnishing?
Fiszinbarg[?] and Trafer gave 500 gulden [złoty] each.
— Well, and the rich „fine“ Jews, how did they respond to this mitzvah, which is among those „whose fruits a man eats in this world while the principal remains for him in the world to come“?...
They will probably give too — I get an answer. But meanwhile, as R' Mendel Rauszenzaft[?] says: meanwhile the „Daytshn“ [„Germans“ — the modernised Jews] give; when today's Hasidim become „Daytshn“ too, they will also give. And meanwhile? Meanwhile they give;
— All the same...

Taken over...
— I'm from Zawiercie, I am.
— Well, so what?
— So I've come to tell you, so you can „describe it in the paper“, what the takeover of power by the new kehilla administration in Zawiercie looked like.
And he tells how the chairman, instead of ringing a bell, knocked with a piece of wood on the table; instead of opening the meeting, he ordered the windows opened so that[?] a little fresh „powietrze“ [Polish: air] could „flow in“; then how the fresh „powietrze“ affected the chairman so strongly that he soon began... to doze etc. But the „finale“ came only when the secretary came in with the cash box. Here all the „dozores“ [kehilla board members] became livelier — no small thing: the cash box!
And when the chairman did not wake from his „lethargic sleep“ as quickly as everyone else, one of the dozores shouted:
— Henech! You're asleep! The cash box is on the table...
— No, no, I'm not asleep, let's see the money...
— Hush! — a voice is heard — let's hear what the secretary says.
In the cash box — says the secretary — there is, according to the books
— Books-shmooks — R' Meir interrupts him — in [Dzhorik?] there were never any books and people lived anyway. The main thing: how much cash is there?
— Cash — the secretary says slowly — there is no more than 27 groszy, only in the sum there is a protested bill of exchange for 28 zł., whose drawer has long been in paradise; the 8 zł. that are actually there are... counterfeit, and to take over there are only 27 groszy...
The 10 dozores put on their glasses and sign the minutes stating that they have taken over...
The Substance of Jewish Life in Upper Silesia

By Rabbi Kalman Chameides (Katowice).

The Soul.
Upper Silesia is a distinct entity within the Jewish world in Poland, a kind of tractate of its own. The youngest little branch of the old, patriarchal tree, that is to say: — Polish Jewry. Upper Silesia does not yet have a soul of its own. As soon as you hear the name Wilno, Kraków or, say, Lemberg (Lwów), memories awaken in you. The Jewish past comes alive in your imagination: you see before you the Vilna Gaon wrapped in tallit and tefillin, you recall the Rema, the Maharshal and the Taz, you hear the sighing and weeping of the Chmielnicki exile and the like, and the deeply mournful melody of study in an old beit midrash. The mere sound of the name Berdichev — so the Hasidim say — is a charm for the fear of Heaven. And I permit myself to add and to assert that, for instance, the mere word „Jerusalem“ has the power to uplift a person with genuine Jewish feeling, to rouse him, to fill him with fervour, with enthusiasm for holiness and beauty. Surely only one who has at least once in his life had the privilege of spending an hour of spiritual exaltation on one of the holy hills around Jerusalem, or the twilight of a Friday when the setting sun casts its last rays upon the coming Sabbath stillness, can understand this.
And — to distinguish between the holy and the profane — when you recall the name Katowice or Król. Huta (Królewska Huta, today Chorzów) and the like, there rises before you a smell of business, of café-house people, of advertising. There is even already a good deal of Jewishness, even so-called Hasidism; parties slowly spread their wings; people found things, hold elections, squabble; but when you go home and are within your own four cubits, you feel that a kind of emptiness reigns — only a body, without a soul. For the time being still without a soul.

Education.
The birth-pangs of the new Jewish world in Upper Silesia are felt especially by everyone who has anything to do with the education of the young. The Midrash says „until Abraham our father there was no old age“ — until the time of Abraham old age did not exist, that is, Abraham was a beginner. With him a new era began, a new chapter in the history of mankind. The old, the past, was missing. And we too must begin from the foundations, from the lowest rung. But it is a great principle of pedagogy that the school alone is not able to form and shape the child's character. The teacher only guides the child; he passes on to him a certain measure of knowledge, of ethics, of proper conduct. But education begins mainly at home, in the family. The Torah says „and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children“ — the father should study with the child, and by his own life be a model and an example for the child. Besides the school and the parental home there is also the street, life in public, an important factor in education. The images of the street penetrate deep into the child's mind and influence his development. We may therefore say that three partners play a great role in education: the school, the parental home and the street.
The face of the street in Upper Silesia is Western, big-city, without any particular expression, superficial, bearing more the stamp of civilisation than of genuine inner culture; noise, tumult, licentiousness, advertising — these are the most characteristic features of the street. Man lives among houses, factories, coal pits. In short, among masses of stone. The eye barely sees a scrap of sky, barely a flower, a blade of grass or a tree. Everywhere prose, workaday life, materialism. Hard, restless life. There is no room for concentration, for soul-searching, for quiet solitude — only distraction. Such surroundings are no favourable soil for the young person, and they are especially bad for the young Jewish person, who must struggle against the current in order to save the „pintele yid“, the surviving remnant.
And what can one expect from the parental home amid the great economic distress, when most livelihoods are tottering, when the Jew lives in a feverish, panicky mood and the worry of „what shall we eat“ weighs heavily on his mind? He lacks the patience[?] and the time, the composure and calm, to supervise the Jewishness in his home, to watch over kashrut, to guard and be strict that his household do not desecrate the Sabbath and festivals. One lives for the present, for the minute, one feels a wanderer, not rooted, not grown together with the soil, in a foreign land. Not seldom an abyss lies between the parental home, which is still run in the old manner, and the child, who is immersed head and body in another, foreign world. Often a rift arises, a split in the family, a wound that bleeds and does not heal so easily.
There remains, as the last anchor of rescue, as the last help and hope — the school, the Talmud Torah. In Katowice there has existed for years a Talmud Torah at the expense of the Jewish community. About 200 children study there today. There is also a school for girls on the „Beit Yaakov“ system. Unfortunately the running of a Talmud Torah here is not so simple; it consumes strength and brains. The children speak seventy languages: Polish, German, Yiddish-German and Yiddish-Polish etc. etc. — a jumble, a linguistic mixture. And over the curriculum too there are important differences of opinion. One father wants his child to be a Torah scholar, versed in Gemara, Rashi and Tosafot, a yeshiva student; another says the opposite is more reasonable — more important are modern Hebrew, Bible, grammar, history. One mother even demanded that the chapter on the Sabbath in the Torah not be studied with the children, for what difference does it make — they do not keep the Sabbath anyway. Who is able to satisfy all these demands together, on one foot? Not to forget that the children also attend the general schools for at least half a day, so that the mind is not capable of absorbing difficult studies.
Nevertheless one must say that the Talmud Torah here fulfils its task excellently, and the new generation will not bring us shame, God forbid. And the new generation is also our hope: it must be sound in body and soul, it must unite within itself the best of Western culture with the holiest and finest of the Torah, it must stand at a moral height and proudly carry the banner of Judaism in its hand, it must be imbued with idealism, but also not be an idler in real life; it must be pure, strong, whole, not broken, religious — not full of doubts, positive — not negative...
How Do the Zagłębie Shopkeeper, Merchant and Artisan Live?

What does a textile merchant say?
— What do you have to say about the textile (manufaktur) trade? I asked an elderly local textile shopkeeper.
— Będzin was once a great textile centre. There were a sizeable number of private and factory warehouses (sklady) of textiles here. People used to come here from the surrounding provinces to buy goods. Today, of course, everything has gone down. Even a merchant from Dąbrowa runs to Łódź to buy his stock.
The number of shopkeepers today is no smaller than before the war, but the quality has declined instead:
How is the turnover?
— Textiles were always an article sold on credit. Today, however, a situation has arisen in which the shopkeeper cannot sell on credit, because the manufacturer gives him no credit. If one still does give a package on credit, the manufacturer charges 18 20 [sic; probably 18–20] per cent more. Because the customer must pay cash, consumption has shrunk and the turnover gets worse from day to day.
Textile goods are, after all, bought mostly by women, who have this nature: if times are good and they have money, they can buy the best and most expensive things; but if times are not good and there is no money, they become great experts at economising...
That is precisely why the turnover has weakened enormously. A woman comes into the shop to buy extra pieces for her old clothes, which she restyles and turns over on every side.
In recent years the textile trade has also suffered because knitwear (tricot) products have pushed out a range of goods, such as underwear, blouses and the like.
— What kinds do people buy?
— When times are bad, people of course ask for the cheapest possible goods. Mainly artificial silk is used. Expensive silk is bought very[?] little. Foreign silks, for which there was once great demand, are hardly to be found. Because of the low prices of domestic silks it does not pay to bring them from abroad.
In a word, when the customer enters the shop, he asks for the cheapest possible goods. The women who can afford to have a very expensive dress made avoid Zagłębie altogether. They travel to Katowice to bring back the newest model from there...
How are the earnings?
Competition is tremendous. The textile shopkeepers are always harried: here a bill of exchange must be paid off, there a cash-on-delivery parcel (Nachnahme) redeemed, there taxes paid. That is why some sell at a loss. In general every kind of goods is fiercely competed for, so the earnings must be very small.
What could help the trade?
— Credit. If the shopkeeper had credit, he could sell to the customer on credit, and when one can get things on credit one allows oneself more than when one has to pay cash.
Secondly, the textile trade is squeezed by the heavy tax screw, as I already told you. — Goods have become 50 per cent cheaper, but this year the tax office assessed the turnover at the same level as last year. So it turns out that the trade pays 5 per cent turnover tax.

My Dear Health...

[Feuilleton — humour; a crisis-time monologue.]

Y. Weinsztejn.

(Monologue of a crisis-stricken Jew).

Ah, against that they've been chattering 'crisis' [?]...

Just imagine: I listen to it, this crisis, like the cat does... For what, really, do I have to fear from a crisis?

A wife I don't have — that is, I do have one, and what a wife: you'd have to search all the countries for such a one and then still not take her — I mean, not find her... But still, she's not really a wife, because she never demands money from me; I give her money — she takes it; I don't give her any — she doesn't talk... But that she should demand, the way other women do — not that? On the contrary, she even has a habit of blocking my way...

— If, she often tells me, you have no money, I'll manage without!

For what choice does she have? On the contrary, let her try not to manage...

As for rent money, I'd be doing not badly with that too...

I don't pay, and I'm rid of the business...

You think perhaps that, God forbid, I've quarrelled with the landlord? Heaven forbid! I'm not a nasty sort, and even if my life depended on it I wouldn't quarrel with him... I don't hold with quarrelling at all, because that kind of aggravation costs health — not so much the other fellow's as mine...

So what then? I 'take him' precisely with kindness...

First, I offer him a broad and handsome 'good morning', so that he may know what it means to keep a fine tenant... If he answers me 'a good year', fine; if not, I have him nine ells deep in the coal mines, and I'm rid of the business...

Of course he needn't know where I have him, because he isn't me, after all, and he might still get offended...

Second, I give him plainly to understand that from the crisis standpoint it doesn't pay him to take any rent from me now... Because a lot nobody can pay now anyway, and a little... what does one get from a little? So it's better for him (and indeed for me too, why should I deny it?) not to take anything at all, and at least let him have complaints against the world... And besides all that, today one doesn't know at all where the world stands... A question on a story... What if, God forbid, a little war, a revolution or some such calamity — what will apartments be worth then? This way, though, when one keeps tenants free of rent, one can at least console oneself a little: I had nothing from my apartment anyway, so the devil take it!

The other day I laid out to my landlord an entirely new kind of philanthropy.

— Imagine, I told him, that I've already paid you the rent, and explicitly for a whole half year — not monthly rent, as people pay now... And as soon as you got the money from me you came down, may it not happen to us, with abdominal typhus, and spent the groszy on doctors and pharmacies — so surely it's better not to take any rent and not to be ill...

Or — the other way round... What would the law be if, say, one fine morning I fell ill and spent your rent money on being sick — could you do anything to me? You wouldn't take my soul, after all; so imagine that I've already gone through my illness and haven't a grosz of rent for you...

That's exactly how I argue with my landlord... And I must tell you the truth: he's a fine little man, that is: when you don't give him, he doesn't take...

Interest-free loans I neither give nor take, so that nobody, thank God, owes me even a grosz...

Oh, and if I owe the world a few thousand, that bothers me very little, because, first, I'm still just as good a risk as today's world, and second, as long as I've lived I've never taken anything from anyone and never will... Sometimes I may not pay back at all. But to take from someone — that I don't hold with...

It's only bad with my children...

They, you see — no philosophy needed — don't stir a wheel...

Three sons and two daughters have settled on my head, and they don't lift a finger [lit. don't put a hand in cold water]...

One is unemployed, so he says... That is, to tell the truth, he has never in his life knocked a nail into a wall, but he heard that unemployment is the fashion, so he talked himself into being unemployed too...

So I ask him the other day why he doesn't become at least some kind of 'chairman' among the unemployed? Let there at least be honour, if not money — he answers that he doesn't ask me for opinions...

The second is a leftist...

He doesn't work, doesn't study, doesn't read, nothing at all... does nothing at all whole days. He has only one merit:

— He is left!

I want to get to the bottom of it with him: how much is the measure of being left, and what such leftness actually means, and whether one can get out of it at least enough for one meal at the market — he answers me short and sharp:

— It's not your 'business' [?], with the new orthography!

Can you have any complaints against him?

The third is a lover of singing... It doesn't matter what to sing, as long as the voice isn't blocked.

He plans, he told me the other day, to found a 'HaZamir' [choral society], and if he ever wants to marry, he will first become a cantor...

Meanwhile, though, he sits on my head...

And about my two daughters I needn't go on at length [?]...

It will be enough [?] if I tell you that both are already old, [each ?] more than what I owe in rent (taking a thousand for a single one); they are not particularly ugly, but not great beauties either. One is a feldsher [medical assistant], but she fell in love with a doctor who insists on a million in dowry — otherwise, he says, he'll die a bachelor...

The second is a teacher, but it's already a few years since she threw over that livelihood... because it really is no livelihood at all... going from house to house, dealing with capricious children, tearing out — may it befall my enemies — one's heart, and only afterwards falling in love with a teacher who (as it later turns out) already has somewhere a second wife with a child from the... third...

Well, I ask you, gentlemen: can a Jew like me be afraid of the crisis?

What can [?] this little crisis [do to] my dear health!
R' Yisrael Moshe Weinreb, of blessed memory

Shabtai Weiss (Tel Aviv).
(For the shloshim.)
I will not be comforted and will not let myself be comforted — there is no comfort after this great, terrible loss!
I will not speak [printed „rern“] of the tremendous merits and deeds of the great departed, who was among the very first in Poland in whom the national consciousness and conscience awoke with full force — in order to awaken them in thousands of others; who was in the great sense [?] of „I will awaken the dawn“ [Psalms 57:9] — at a time when all around it was pitch dark, when everyone was still sleeping a heavy, lethargic sleep, he, R' Yisrael Moshe, was one of the few, the counted ones, who by force tore down the morning star from the starless sky.
I will not speak of the giant scope of his achievements over 35 years, during which he stood at the battle-front as soldier and general, as leader and guide, as a true tribune of the people; over those 35 years, so full of storm and stress, so rich in transformations and trials: political Zionism, practical Zionism, Uganda, territorialism, Gegenwartsarbeit [work in the present], autonomism, Hebrew, Yiddish, the building of the kehillot — and all the shifting phases of our idea of revival did not for a single minute weaken the fire of his work, which had before it one single main goal: the revival of the Jewish people and of the Jewish land.
I will not dwell on the rare quality, on the excellence of his work: full of heart and soul, full of honesty, free of any ulterior motive, permeated with pure idealism. National and Zionist work was for R' Yisrael Moshe no pastime, no sport one takes up when in a good mood — but a holy service, performed with love and self-sacrifice, under all circumstances and in all conditions of life, according to the high degree of „In all thy ways acknowledge Him“ [Proverbs 3:6].
Of all this I do not want to speak; of all this one cannot speak in a few pain-choked lines in a newspaper article. All this must be told in a great book, dedicated to the holy memory of R' Yisrael Moshe Weinreb, of blessed memory. A great book must convey to all those who, in the last generation and in the present one, joined the national and Zionist cause, that R' Yisrael Moshe, of blessed memory, was one of the first chosen few who trod out the main roads and made possible the development of our movement.
But I want to devote a few words to the m a n, to the n o b l e m a n, to the splendid type R' Yisrael Moshe Weinreb. I want to mourn the loss of one of those luminous figures who are becoming ever rarer in our life. I want to mourn the loss of one of my best, most intimate friends, who was torn away b e f o r e his time.
In our present time, when the top place in social life is taken by coarse materialism with its partner, the upstart ignoramus who knows how to polish cleverly and cover up his hollow nothingness with the shiny lacquer of „donations“ and „charity“ — how exalted, how gigantic was the imposing noble figure of R' Yisrael Moshe Weinreb, with his truly aristocratic manners, his genuine style of a man of wealth, his innate intelligence, his aura of Torah, his radiance of the true Hasidism of old! How great, how irreplaceable is the loss!
Poor, orphaned Zagłębie — without the radiant figure of Rabbi Yisrael Moshe Weinreb!
One of Ours

(A little tale, cut, fitted and tailored for today's Zagłębie rich men.)
In a little town in the provinces there lived a great rich man named R' Avraham... a Jew blessed with a large fortune; he had [„also“?] his own big house, a real palace, with gardens and orchards where various precious fruits grew. He lent money at interest, and almost all the merchants and householders of the town ran their businesses with the rich man's money.
And it came to pass that this rich man was about to marry off a daughter; all the preparations had already been made for the grand wedding, which was to take place a short time later. Once the rich man went in person to the town rabbi to order from him the papers needed for his daughter's wedding, which was to take place on Tuesday of the following week.
The rabbi, hearing the rich man's request, changed countenance; he began to beg the rich man to postpone his daughter's wedding to another day, because he too had fixed the wedding of his own daughter for that same day, not knowing that the rich man was holding a wedding...
But the rich man gave the rabbi to understand that this was impossible, since everything was already prepared for the wedding, and having no choice they came to an agreement and made the following compromise between them: all the richer householders, the town's real men of wealth, would come to the rich man, and the middle and poorer classes would go to the rabbi's wedding...
On the wedding day, in the evening, the rabbi came with his beadles and some of the invited guests to the rich man's house; the bride was veiled and the rabbi performed the kiddushin; meanwhile the crowd dispersed, as is the custom in small towns, where people gather for the feast only at 10 o'clock at night.
Before 10 o'clock at night the rich man got ready at home to receive the guests who were to come to the feast [„kenas-mol“]. The in-laws from the groom's side had already arrived, but of the local guests no one was to be seen. The waiters, dressed in tailcoats with white aprons, run back and forth, looking out for the guests; they are ready and prepared to serve them and treat them to every good thing — but nobody is seen and nobody is heard. The in-law [father of the bride] grew agitated; a suspicion of the rabbi awoke in his heart: had he perhaps taken his guests too? He sends a messenger to the rabbi's house to take a look — what is going on there?... The messenger soon comes back and informs him that at the rabbi's house it is merry and lively, the crowd is enjoying itself, they eat, drink, sing, dance... as at a real Jewish wedding.
The rich man leaves the in-laws and runs, agitated and full of anger, to the rabbi, intending to quarrel with him over such meanness — taking away his guests and so shaming him before his in-laws...
As he entered the house the rabbi received him with great honour, with a broad „Barukh ha-ba“ [welcome]... and even before the rich man began to speak and to complain to the rabbi, the rabbi assured him that he had not taken from him even one single guest...
What do you mean — the rich man began to shout — and R' Moshe, R' Chaim, R' Yankel, R' David?... He listed a whole roll of names of the town's rich men...
„They are all paupers — the rabbi answered him — all of them, just as they sit here, trade and run their businesses with other people's money; in truth they do not own a single slice of bread!...“
„Oy gevalt, Rabbenu — he cried — if so, if it is as you say, then I am indeed ani-evyon [a destitute pauper]!...“
„True, true, exactly so, R' Avraham — the rabbi gave him to understand — it is just as it says in the prayers: „ve-kabtzenu yaḥad“ [„gather us together“ — punned here as „make us paupers together“]... so [?] don't delay, wash your hands and sit down at our table; you too belong among my guests — you are one of ours!“
Y. Ts. Hirshbeyn.
—o—
It is winter — watch the pavements.
It is a time of snow, cold, frost and slipperiness.
Będzin is a hilly town, and in slippery weather it is truly dangerous to walk the streets.
Although the police do warn — by means of fines [protocols], of course — that the house-owners should take care of the pavements, there are still frequent cases where the pavements are neglected and passers-by break arms and legs.
Sometimes people fall so unluckily that they feel it for several weeks.
If the pavements were looked after and strewn with sand on the broken and slippery spots, people would not suffer.
It is therefore necessary that during the winter months the house-owners take care of the pavements in front of their houses.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayechi)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayechi
The Portion
—o—
a) "Guiding his hands wittingly" (Gen. 48:14)
In the human body the strongest limbs are those on the right. The brain too is concentrated mainly on the right. The left limbs are weaker. But in return the left possesses — the heart. And this is also what the structure of our society looks like: the men of brains, the elders, the "settled" [?] ones belong to the right, while the young, the men of feeling, the sentimental ones belong to the left, where the heart is...
Jacob saw this and understood that it would be better if the elders had a little of the left, a little heart in them, and the young — a little brain and right... So he symbolically laid his left hand on the elder Ephraim and the right one — on the younger Manasseh... Derashot el Ami.
—o—
b) "And he blessed them that day" (ibid. 20)
He blessed them "on that day" — that they should be content [printed "begigenen", evidently for "begnugenen"] with today and not want to worry about tomorrow. That is the best blessing... Hasidic books.
——
A rich brother, to whom his pauper brother often comes for support, once says to him: you will receive from me year by year so-and-so many złoty, and don't come to me all the time.
The poor man does not agree to the yearly support. He does not want to be provided for years ahead.
— Why?
— Because I am afraid of a rich man's luck. If you undertake to pay me a fixed "sum year by year, your luck will play it [?] so that I won't last out the year... From the mouth of the people.
—o—
c) "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the end of days" (49:1)
The first exile — in Egypt — came about through hatred between brothers, through the brothers' intrigues against Joseph. Later the Temple too was destroyed because of groundless hatred. Therefore Jacob gave the blessing: "Gather yourselves" — assemble, do not tear yourselves apart, because that will decide [?] what is to happen to you in the end of days. Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
d) "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce" (ibid. 7)
Simeon and Levi were zealots, "those whom in the Jewish tongue one calls: frum". They were always ready, "every man his sword upon his thigh", to stab at once with the sword... True, their sharpness, their boldness comes from the Torah ("there is no strength but Torah"), but still: cursed be their anger, for it was fierce — cursed be that kind of piety... Maor va-Shemesh (for Rabbi Naftali of Ropczyce).
—o—
e) "I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel" (ibid.)
"You have no paupers, scribes and children's teachers except from Simeon" (Rashi).
I.
Jacob saw that Simeon and Levi were insolent. He feared that if on top of that they were also rich, there would be no bearing them... So he made them paupers, dependent on other people; then they would have to stifle their insolence and anger within themselves, for otherwise nobody would let them across the threshold.. Peli Hemda.
——
"Since he is so very insolent ('kulei hai'), learn from it"...
What does the expression "kulei hai" mean?
"The rich man answers insolently." A rich man may have a little insolence in him. It is his due. But only as much insolence as he is rich. But he who is "insolent kulei hai" — more of an upstart than a rich man — learn from it... Folk saying.
II.
The Men of the Great Assembly blessed the scribes of old that they should not become rich, so that they would not abandon their craft; and today one should pray for today's writers that they should not grow rich from their writing, so that they should not write too much... Asam [?] be-Shem.
—o—
f) "Assemble yourselves and hear" (49:2)
"He wished to reveal the End, but the Divine Presence departed from him and he began to say other things" (Bereshit Rabba).
In Yoma the Gemara says: "The former, whose sin was revealed — their end was revealed; the latter, whose sin was not revealed — their end was not revealed." So redemption can come only when the sins of the generation are public, when they are not hidden under a mask... Therefore Jacob first enumerated the sins of the tribes, and he wanted to reveal the End. Toldot Yaakov.
—o—
g) "He giveth goodly words" (ibid. 21)
The word "shefer" (goodly) equals "ashir" (rich) in gematria. For whatever the rich man says, whatever foolishness it may be, people take it for "goodly words", for wisdom... Nimukei Geonei Ashkenaz.
—o—
h) "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah" (ibid. 10)
"Shevet" also means: rod. "The rod shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come" — until the Messiah comes, the rod will not be lifted off the Jew's head... Be'er Mayim Hayyim.
—o—
Haftarah
—o—
i) "I go the way of all the earth" (1 Kings 2:2)
A Jew, a merchant, comes to Rabbi Gershon Henich of Radzyń and asks for a blessing. The rabbi blesses him:
— May God help you, and may you die an unusual death...
The Hasid is shaken by such a blessing. The clever rabbi smiles and explains his blessing to him:
— Usually a Jewish merchant dies in poverty, not leaving of his own even enough for shrouds — except bills of exchange and debts. So I wish you to die an unusual death, a death exceptional among all merchants, that is, in ease and wealth...
—o—
j) "And let not his hoar head go down to the grave (She'ol) in peace" (ibid. 6)
Wherever Jews speak of She'ol — "Gehenna" — "She'ol" is written defectively, without a vav. Because however bad a Jew may be, he still does not get the whole of Gehenna. The real Gehenna is only for gentiles. Rafui [?] Rokeah.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (4)

[Serialized historical novel — Russia, Rasputin; installment 4.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

Sonia drew a breath and answered:
— I had an unpleasantness at the countess's, in the salon.
— What happened? What? What sort of thing?
— I will tell you.
She knitted her brows and, with a little agitation in her voice, she told:
— Many highly placed persons were gathered in the salon today... All were waiting with great curiosity for the arrival of some new "saint", a "miracle-worker". Later the "saint" arrived, accompanied by Anna Vyrubova and the priest Ostrogov... When he appeared, everyone was left astonished. The "saint" is a muzhik [Russian peasant] from Siberia. He is dressed like a muzhik, in heavy boots, in a linen "rubashka" [peasant shirt], has a big beard, and on his head straight long hair, carelessly combed with a parting [?] in the middle...
She caught her breath, and Mr. Dimentshteyn asked impatiently:
— So what actually happened?
Sonia went on telling, and a kind of hidden fear could be felt in her.
— They introduced the new "saint" to those gathered, and everyone smiled slightly on hearing his name. He is called Rasputin (Rasputin in Russian means a "dissolute one"). The "saint" — whether he did not notice the smiling, or did notice it — was not at all embarrassed. He carried himself freely, behaved like a simple muzhik, spoke loudly, with a peasant pronunciation, and behaved towards everyone as if he were a close friend of every single one. He shook everyone's hands, and some young ladies he even embraced in a fatherly way... He was introduced to me. He came up very close to me, so that I felt his breath on my face. He took my hand into his broad peasant hand and looked deep into my face. His small blue eyes became sharp, passionate, commanding. Searching, and at the same time — very tender... I had the feeling that he was looking deep into me... His eyes began to burn with some hidden fire. I was uneasy... His eyes seemed to be searching for something in me, wanting to master me, and I felt fear in my heart... Suddenly he began to smile. Great tenderness appeared on his face, and in a soft, melodious voice he said:
— You have a beautiful, pure soul!
I felt that any moment now the muzhik would draw me to himself, would embrace me. The fear in me grew stronger. I made a great effort, tore my hand out of his and moved away from him. I was flustered; some people burst out laughing. Probably because the Christian "saint" had seen a beautiful soul in a Jewish daughter... I felt very unpleasant. The "saint" kept his eyes on me all the time... I did not stay there long... A while later I left...
The banker smiled;
— That is all? That is what one is upset about?
Sonia answered:
— Even now I feel the fear in my heart...
— Nonsense! What is there to be afraid of? Why should you be afraid? How does that come to you? Sonia?
— I do not know myself why, but in my heart I feel fear.
— Nonsense, daughter!
— You are right, father!
Sonia now smiled, her face brightened, her eyes became clearer and milder. But unrest remained in her, as if her heart were telling her that today's encounter would bring her great and grave unpleasantness in the future.
— — — — — — — — — —
After Sonia had calmed down somewhat, her father told her about everything that had been said here, and about the fact that she was the only person who could, with the help of Anna Vyrubova, reach the Archimandrite Feofan;
Sonia agreed to take the mission upon herself, and it was settled that tomorrow, at the time when a divine service for the health of the Russian heir to the throne would be held in the Great Synagogue, Sonia, the banker's daughter, should meet with Anna Vyrubova...

Chapter Two.
The "Holy Wanderer"
A week earlier, before the meeting took place in the house of the banker Mr. Dimentshteyn, the following happened:
In the monastery where the students and teachers of the Petersburg Theological Academy lived, there appeared a strange wanderer who had come there for a night's lodging.
He was a tall muzhik of about forty. He had broad, solidly built shoulders, was dressed in a peasant linen shirt over his wide trousers, and a leather belt ["poyasok"] was tightly girded about his loins. He wore heavy boots and was noisy in his movements. His big head was covered with uncombed brown hair, carelessly divided by a parting [?] in the middle of the head. The hair was straight and long and hung down over his nape. He had a high forehead, and on the forehead was the scar of a healed wound. His broad, blunt [?] nose stood out from his face, and his lips were thin and pale. His face, burnt by the sun, was heavily covered with wrinkles; his blue eyes were hidden under the brows, and he had a large light-brown beard that covered half his face.
This was the Siberian muzhik Grigory Yefimovich Rasputin.
It was already evening when he arrived at the monastery. He entered the large reception hall with heavy, noisy steps, sat down there, and it did not take long before he was surrounded by a group of young seminarians and some of their teachers.
At first, when he appeared, nobody paid him any special attention; people there were used to simple peasants coming for a night's lodging, and the young seminarians paid them no special attention. But it did not take long, and this wanderer drew their attention. Some seminarians stopped beside him and began asking him questions: Where does he come from? What is he doing here in the capital? How did he come all the way from distant Siberia?
They asked the questions and smiled a little at the peasant who looked so strange.
He answered their questions, and the more he answered, the more he won their attention. They began to listen more seriously to his words; he spoke in a soft, melodious voice, with the voice of a "saint", made a strong impression on them, and they became interested in him. The seminarians began to put various questions to him. More seminarians came up; some teachers who were passing by also stopped. The wanderer drew them all strongly to himself. He answered all questions with firm certainty. Now they asked him questions about God and about life, and he answered everything skilfully, nimbly and with assurance.
One of the seminarians, who was very skilled in theological discussions, who was a great expert at posing questions and embarrassing those with whom he debated, wanted to show off his expertise and embarrass the simple muzhik who talked like a "saint". The seminarian moved closer to the wanderer and said:
— I want to ask a few questions.
The wanderer smiled slightly, gave the seminarian a fatherly look, and with a calm that comes from his self-assurance he said:
— Ask, my son! I am ready to listen.
The seminarian breathed more deeply. His eyes became sharp and glittering, and he began putting questions to him concerning the Godhead and the "Trinity".

He Has, She Has.

[Humorous feuilleton — "Chats and Prattle of a Gossip"; part 1.]
Chats and prattle of a gossip. Related by A. D. Egoz.

Welcome. I, the gossip, am here.
But today I am not telling gossip. Today I am telling a true story with a moral.
The story consists of a lot of "has", and it is called: "He has, she has". So have patience and hear it out.
It isn't even anything new. Such a story has happened more than once; nevertheless it does no harm to tell it again as a warning to others.
So, we come to the text: He has, she has.
Who is the "he"? [?] The "he" is an elderly Jew, deep in his sixties, quite a serious person and, it seems, no fool — and yet he made an ugly fool of himself.
His name I will not give; he has already had enough "hot and cold" from those who know his story — why drum it out further?
And the "she" is actually not one, but one "she" and another "she". They are: his first wife, who packed up and moved over to the other world and already has a bright Paradise, and the wife he snatched up. And she has put him in the ground, here, in this world.
Let us first take up the first one.
He married her some forty-odd years ago, and has by her respectable children and grandchildren, of whom he has no need to be ashamed.
He had a good life with his wife. Almost the whole time they were married he loved her and she him too. He always "kutsenyu-mutsenyu'd" her [pet-talk, cuddled her] and she him. Neither did he ever say a crooked word to her, nor she to him.
So they lived nicely and finely, as God commanded. Domestic peace was kept in their home and people envied them.
But in the end the little wheel turned backwards — and hear what happened.
In her older years she began to ail a little, began to complain that she did not feel well. She lost her youthful strength and got — may it not happen to anyone — an ache in her legs and a muddle in her head. She began having to deal with doctors, and from time to time she lay down a little.
Nevertheless she did not stop being a good housewife; she looked after her "old man", saw to it that he had food in time and that everything was in order.
But he did not like it that his "old woman" was not in full health, and little by little she lost her charm in his eyes. His former love and loyalty to her he forgot, and began to look at her as at a superfluous thing.
It may be that he was waiting for her to close her eyes; but I do not want to suspect a Jew of that much. Maybe yes, and maybe not.
But be that as it may, God helped and the Jewish woman died. The old man even wept a little. I don't know whether in earnest or whether it was only a pretence, but his eyes did get a little moist. He gave her a fine funeral, buried her according to the custom of Israel and, as the law requires, sat shiva.
And already during shiva he began to think about "a purpose". "It is not good that man should be alone" — it buzzed [?] in his brain. But he was ashamed to bring it out of his mouth.
He barely got the seven days of shiva over with, and began to stand in front of the mirror, primping and dressing up, like a bridegroom.
He could not hold himself back. Afterwards, apparently, it pressed on him, and he began to take counsel with friends about getting married.
They told him it was still too early to think about it. The earth on his wife's fresh grave, they explained to him, had not yet dried; it is not fitting toward his children, nor toward God and people, to talk of matches.
They advised him that later, if he found it necessary, he would choose an older Jewish woman who suited him and stand under the canopy. But for now, they told him, he should get it out of his head.
But the old man had other ideas. Why, he decided to himself, wait until who knows when? And why — his reason dictated to him — take an old one? Why not a young one? Exchange a shoe for a patch?
So he asked no one any more; even with his own children he did not take counsel, and began courting, through a match, a poor young little widow who had lost her husband a year after the wedding, and with whom he had, as they write in novels, fallen in love head over heels.
"Let people laugh," he thought, "and I'll do well for myself." Rich he is, money he has, and a young wife he will have too; he heeds the whole world like the tomcat [i.e. not at all], and he will be well and happy.
And that she, the young widow, might hesitate — that the old man did not consider. Why should she? — the old man reckoned — on the contrary, she will consider herself lucky to fall into such a pit of fat.
But he made the reckoning without the host. When he came out with clear words and began persuading her about "abtaen" [?] and "draytsen" [?], as they say, she shook herself loose.
If she is to marry an old man after all — she gave him to understand — she wants a fat ketubah (marriage settlement); otherwise, she said, the deal isn't worth it to her.
He asked: what's the matter with you?! She answered that there is no limit to how much this is worth to him.
He offered to sign over ten thousand dollars in her name; she said that was too little.
He went further, promised several thousand in cash, and she let herself be begged.
He also offered his first wife's jewellery — she refused: jewellery of a dead woman she does not wear. "If you want me," she said openly, "you should buy me new jewellery."
In short, he apparently could not withstand the "veler" [?] and gave in to her in everything she wanted. He gave away to her almost his entire fortune, barely waited out the thirty days (shloshim), and held a quiet wedding with her.
By this he caused his children shame and disgrace. But he laughed at them and at the whole world. He thought he had caught a great bargain and patted himself on the belly for having the great privilege of having, in his old age, such a pretty, young wife.
But the old fool, as a German says, "pissed on himself" [i.e. did himself in], and now he has something to sing and tell about.
Here you have only half a story. The other half I will tell next Friday, and meanwhile — have a good and happy Sabbath.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: “It's Already Been Stitched Up”...

[Local section heading; Będzin — Jewish community.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 15 Tevet 5692 — piątek 25 grudnia 1931 [Friday, 25 December 1931].)
Będzin
“It's Already Been Stitched Up”...
On Tuesday the president of the kehilla called a meeting. The members of the dozór [the kehilla board] already know that if the president calls a meeting, it most likely has something to do with some matter in favour of the “Agudah” [Agudat Israel].
At this meeting too the matter under discussion was an allocation for the cheders of “Mizrachi” and of “Yesodei ha-Torah”. Before the meeting began, the president informed the secretary that “it's already been stitched up”, i.e. that between him and 2 more board members the allocation was already settled and it only needed to be entered in the minutes. Later board member Buchhajc [?] also arrived, and he protested against the allocation. In the course of this there were some painful moments between Mr. Buchhajc and the president.
The end was that the majority agreed with Mr. Buchhajc, and thanks to this the “Mizrachi” school was not wronged in the allocation.
Echoes of the Kehilla Elections

[Będzin — artisans; courts.]
Some time ago, when a split occurred in the local Artisans' Union, a group of artisans brought out a one-off publication in which Mr. A. Klajman was accused of a series of abuses during the time when he was the leader of the union.
Mr. K. took the matter to court, and last Monday the trial was supposed to take place in the Sosnowiec District Court.
Because Messrs. Mosze Kajzer and J. D. Lustiger did not appear, the trial was postponed to another date.

“Yenkel's Fur Doesn't Keep You Warm”, but It Can Cause Trouble...

[Będzin — everyday life; distraint.]
A resident of Modrzejowska [?] Street, fearing his creditors, carried a few valuables — among them also a fur coat — over to a neighbour who has a marriage-settlement deed (“akt intercyzy”, separation of property). But “when misfortune is fated, it comes right into the house”: the bailiff (komornik) comes to that same neighbour and wants to make a distraint (zajęcie) for 300 zł. that her husband owes. The woman is not frightened of the bailiff and shows him the marriage-settlement deed.
The bailiff acknowledges the deed. “But your husband's clothes,” he says, “surely do not come under the deed,” and without lingering long he went to the wardrobe and took the neighbour's fur coat...
25th Anniversary of “Linat ha-Cholim”

[Będzin — institutions and charity.]
In the first days of next month the society “Linat Cholim” will celebrate its 25th anniversary, and at the same time the celebration of the 2000th birth in the maternity ward at the institution.
In connection with this a jubilee committee has been formed, which includes, besides the present board, also all those who have rendered service to the society over the years.
On the occasion of the jubilee an “academy” (festive gathering) with a rich programme will take place at the “Nowości” [hall]. Among others, the musical society “Lira” will also take part, performing a series of musical numbers.
In honour of the celebration a sale of “galiepkes” [stickers? nalepki] is taking place, which — as we are told — is meeting with due success, as everyone, as far as he has the means, is discharging his duty towards the institution.
How Were 170 zł. Stolen from Mr. Sztybel? Beware of Swindlers!

[Będzin — crime.]
On Wednesday, in broad daylight, a young man came into the flat of Mr. Jona Sztybel on the Old Market and told Mrs. Sztybel to go quickly over to her house on Kościuszki Street, because an unknown tenant had broken open a flat and moved in there.
Mrs. Sztybel, hearing this, hurried off to her house in order to find out exactly who this tenant was who had seized a flat in her house. Together with her the bearer of the news also left, but soon afterwards he came back to the Sztybels' flat, where only the children were present, and told them that their father had sent him here to repair the wardrobe.
The children, having no suspicion whatsoever, did not disturb the “craftsman”, who on his own opened the wardrobe and took out of it 170 zł. in cash.
When Mrs. Sztybel came to her house and became convinced that the whole story was made up, she went to her husband at the market and told him her “miracles”. The husband found the matter suspicious and told his wife to go home quickly.
Coming home, she only then found out that she had been fooled by a cunning swindler, who in this way [?] had carried out the theft of 170 zł.
Hours for Collecting Mail from the Boxes Extended

[Będzin — post office.]
As is known, since the post office has been operating in the new building, access to the post-office boxes was permitted only during the official office hours. Following an intervention by the Merchants' Association it has been announced that the restriction is to be lifted and the post-office boxes can be used at any time.
Sugar for the Unemployed

[Będzin — relief; unemployment.]
This week the Citizens' Committee for the support of the unemployed received an allocation of 200 sacks of sugar, which were distributed to long-unemployed families.
—o—
Meeting at the “Merchants' Association”
[Będzin — societies.]
Next Sunday afternoon the annual general meeting of the members will take place in the premises of the “Merchants' Association”. The agenda is an important one, and the meeting ought to be well attended.
Lecture by Dr. Gottesdiener.

This coming Saturday night [motzei Shabbat, 26.12.1931] Dr. Abraham Gottesdiener will give a lecture from his new series, entitled „The Life and Work of Maimonides (the Rambam)“.
Dr. Gottesdiener's lectures are delivered in a very popular manner, and thanks to this the hall is always full of listeners.
Homeowners against the road tax (podatek drogowy).

The board of the Homeowners' Association has turned to the voivode with a memorandum asking that the road tax (podatek drogowy) be reduced.
This, however, does not hold back any homeowner, who can submit an appeal individually.
Excursion to Zakopane.

The ski club of the Society for Knowledge of the Land (Landkentenish) left on Wednesday [23.12.1931] for Zakopane, where they will stay for several days. The group, numbering 15 people, is led by A. Rudin and Miss Goldberg.
Experts at the municipal court.
At the request of the local municipal court, the Chamber of Commerce has nominated three locksmiths, who are to give their opinion in trials concerning this trade.
Sosnowiec — The Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is in a catastrophic situation.

Sosnowiec
The Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is in a catastrophic situation.
Jewish Zagłębie must come to its aid.
The Jewish hospital in our town, the only Jewish healing institution, finds itself in a terribly critical situation. And if Jewish Zagłębie continues to treat the hospital the way it has until now, there is a danger that the hospital will be closed, or that this important institution will suffer the fate of falling into other hands...
In connection with this, a meeting of the hospital committee took place, which decided to proclaim a collection campaign for the benefit of the Jewish hospital.
The campaign begins as early as this coming Sunday [27.12.1931], and it is to be hoped that every Jew will take part in it and contribute both money and produce for the benefit of the only Jewish healing institution in Zagłębie, where the suffering of our sick brothers and sisters is eased.
Grandchildren are „grateful“ to their grandmother...

Everyone knows her, the 80-year-old Ite Bursztyn. In her younger years, when she was still able to make a living by the labour of her hands, she supported her grandchildren with an open hand, truly sacrificing herself for them. But when her strength grew weaker, the grandmother was already superfluous, and the doors are shut to her.
Last Friday [18.12.1931] the old woman was brought to the kehilla office, from where she was driven in a droshky to her grandchildren, but the grandchildren did not let her in, and the old woman was brought back to the gmina [municipal office]. Then a further intervention with the magistrate [town council] succeeded in having the old woman admitted to the Christian almshouse (przytułek).
Daring bandit attack in the town centre.

On Tuesday [22.12.1931] at about 5 o'clock in the evening, Modrzejowska Street was stirred up by the daring bandit attack carried out in the flat of Mr. Jakub Fuks, Modrzejowska Street 19.
Two masked bandits entered the flat, tied the Christian maid to the tap of the water pipe, gagged her mouth, and wanted to get down to work.
At that moment Fuks arrived. One of the bandits threw himself at Fuks and, threatening him with a revolver, demanded money. Fuks, however, did not lose his head; he put up resistance and began shouting: „Bandits!“
The bandits were frightened by the shouts and left the flat. Fuks ran after them, and at the cries of „Catch the bandits!“ a policeman arrived, who caught one of the bandits on Małachowskiego Street. Later the second one was also caught in a „slinat“[?] on Perl Street.
Initiative of the Chamber of Commerce to grant credits to merchants. / Heavy punishment for deliberate bankruptcy.

At the meeting of the finance committee of the Chamber of Commerce the difficult situation of the merchants was discussed.
After a discussion it was resolved to intervene with the managements of Bank Polski and the Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (Economy Bank) that they should grant credits to merchants.
—o—
Heavy punishment for deliberate bankruptcy.
Great interest was aroused in local merchant circles by the trial at the local District Court against Mrs. Lea Lederman, owner of a shoe shop on Dekerta[?] Street, and her daughter Chaja.
The indictment states that Lea Lederman, with the aim of not paying her debts, handed over the entire stock of goods into the possession of her daughter Chaja.
For the trial[?] dozens of witnesses were summoned, among them a large number of creditors, who proved that the bankruptcy of the accused was a deliberate one.
The court handed down the following verdict: Lea Lederman is sentenced to 2 years, her daughter Chaja to 1 year of prison and to loss of (civic) rights.
At the prosecutor's demand the accused were immediately arrested until they post bail of 2,000 zł. for the mother and 1,000 zł. for the daughter.
Investigation into the last kehilla elections. / The post office on the holidays.

This week the authorities began an investigation into the last kehilla elections in our town. In connection with this, the rumour has already spread through the town that the elections have already been annulled and that new kehilla elections will take place.
—o—
The post office on the holidays.
Today, Friday, the post office will be closed. On Saturday the 26th of this month the post office will operate from 9 to 11 only to hand out the correspondence from the post-office boxes. On the 27th — from 9 to 11, as on all Sundays. On that day the mail will be delivered to homes.

General meeting of the "Gemilut Hasadim" fund.
This Saturday night the annual general meeting of the interest-free fund "Gemilut Hesed" of our town will take place in the "Agnielski[?] hall".
The fund is at present the only institution that plays an important role at the present moment, and it is a duty for the members to come to the meeting in order to strengthen the existence of the institution.
—o—
Studies at the Jewish private gymnasium are at a proper level.
This week the Jewish private gymnasium was inspected by Mrs. Dr. Lipska of Kraków, who attended individual lessons. The inspector expressed her recognition that the studies at the school are at the proper level and that the pupils[?] of the 8th class are already ready to sit for the matura.
—o—
A fire at "Janina".
On Tuesday afternoon a fire broke out in the workroom of the [?]-shop "Janina" on Warszawska Street. The firemen soon arrived and, after an energetic rescue effort, put out the fire. The damage is considerable.
—o—
Town lists at the Magistrate.
The kehilla administration resolved at its last meeting that in the first days of the month of January (styczeń) the town lists are to be sent to the Magistrate in order to collect [—] execution costs.
—o—
"Good tidings" for the New Year
Among the mine workers in Zagłębie the announcements that from the New Year on mass reductions (lay-offs) will take place in the mines have caused alarm.
—o—
Threw himself under the train.
On the railway line between Dąbrowa and Będzin a dead man with a severed head was found. The investigation established that the dead man was a resident of Dąbrowa and threw himself under a train with the aim of committing suicide.
